docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Authentication coercion is best understood as:

Attacker-Controlled Authentication Trigger

rather than:

Password Theft

The attacker exploits legitimate Windows behaviour:

Service
  |
  v
Access Remote Resource
  |
  v
Authenticate Automatically

The resulting authentication becomes dangerous when combined with another weakness.

The complete relationship is:

Coercion Primitive
        |
        v
Victim Identity
        |
        v
Authentication
        |
        v
Relay Opportunity
        |
        v
Target
        |
        v
Victim Privilege
        |
        v
Impact

This means that fixing only one named coercion technique does not necessarily remove the overall attack class.

For example:

PetitPotam Mitigated
        |
        X
All Authentication Coercion Eliminated

Other:

RPC Interfaces
Applications
Management Platforms
UNC Functions
WebDAV Workflows

may still cause outbound authentication.

Likewise:

Print Spooler Disabled
        |
        X
NTLM Relay Eliminated

because other authentication sources may remain.

The defensive objective is therefore broader:

Reduce Coercion
     |
     v
Restrict Outbound Authentication
     |
     v
Reduce NTLM
     |
     v
Enforce Relay Protections
     |
     v
Reduce Identity Privilege

For penetration testers, the preferred workflow is:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Understand the Primitive
   |
   v
Identify the Victim Identity
   |
   v
Determine the Protocol
   |
   v
Map Relay Targets
   |
   v
Map Privileges
   |
   v
Validate Minimally
   |
   v
Stop

rather than:

Run Every Coercion Tool
        |
        v
Against Every Server
        |
        v
Relay Every Authentication

The central assessment questions are:

Can this system be forced to authenticate?

Which identity authenticates?

Which protocol does it use?

Where can that authentication go?

What can that identity do there?

For defenders, the equivalent questions are:

Which systems expose coercion-capable interfaces?

Which systems can send SMB or WebDAV authentication
to untrusted destinations?

Where is NTLM still required?

Which services accept relayable authentication?

Which computer and service accounts have powerful
rights on other systems?

Which protocol protections are enforced?

The final model is:

Trigger
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Security Context
  |
  v
Authentication
  |
  v
Network Path
  |
  v
Relay Protection
  |
  v
Authorisation
  |
  v
Impact

Authentication coercion is therefore not merely an RPC problem.

It is a Windows authentication, network segmentation, service configuration, identity privilege, and protocol-hardening problem.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is an identity security and attack-path analysis platform used to model relationships between users, groups, computers, permissions, sessions, trusts, certificate services, and other identity objects.

During an authorised Active Directory assessment, BloodHound helps answer questions such as:

What can this user control?

Who can administer this computer?

Which principals can modify this group?

Who can reach Domain Admin?

Which systems contain privileged sessions?

Which ACLs create privilege escalation paths?

Which delegation relationships are dangerous?

Which certificate services relationships create attack paths?

Which paths become available after obtaining a new credential?

What should be investigated next?

BloodHound should not be treated simply as:

Run collector
    |
    v
Click "Shortest Path to Domain Admin"
    |
    v
Exploit everything

A better methodology is:

Collect
   |
   v
Build Identity Graph
   |
   v
Understand Relationships
   |
   v
Identify Interesting Paths
   |
   v
Verify Prerequisites
   |
   v
Validate Safely
   |
   v
Re-Collect / Re-Analyse
   |
   v
Evidence
   |
   v
Report

docs.title: Authorised Use
docs.text:
Use BloodHound and related collectors only for:

Authorised penetration testing
Internal security assessments
Red team exercises
Purple team exercises
Identity security assessments
Training environments
CTFs
Security research

Collection can generate:

LDAP queries
SMB connections
RPC activity
Session enumeration
Local group enumeration
Registry access
Kerberos activity
DNS queries
Authentication events
Endpoint telemetry

Always remain within the agreed scope and rules of engagement.

docs.title: BloodHound Ecosystem
docs.text:
BloodHound is better understood as an ecosystem rather than a single executable.

                    Active Directory
                           |
          +----------------+----------------+
          |                |                |
          v                v                v
      SharpHound      BloodHound.py      NetExec
          |                |                |
          |                |                |
          +----------------+----------------+
                           |
                           v
                    Collection Data
                           |
                 JSON / ZIP / Graph
                           |
             +-------------+-------------+
             |                           |
             v                           v
       BloodHound CE                 BloodBash
             |                           |
             v                           v
       Graph Analysis              Offline Analysis
             |
             v
       Attack Paths

Depending on the environment, collection may be performed using:

SharpHound CE
BloodHound.py CE
NetExec BloodHound ingestor
Other compatible collectors

Analysis may then be performed using:

BloodHound CE
BloodHound / Neo4j legacy environments
BloodBash
Custom graph analysis

docs.title: BloodHound Community Edition
docs.text:
BloodHound Community Edition (BloodHound CE) is the current community platform from SpecterOps.

It provides:

Graph-based identity analysis
Attack path visualisation
Active Directory analysis
AD CS relationships
Hybrid identity analysis
Cypher-based graph querying
Data ingestion
Attack path exploration

The basic architecture is:

Collector
   |
   v
JSON / ZIP
   |
   v
BloodHound CE
   |
   v
Graph Database
   |
   v
Web Interface
   |
   v
Attack Path Analysis

docs.title: BloodHound CE Installation
docs.text:
Current BloodHound CE deployments commonly use the BloodHound CLI and containerised services.

Follow the official BloodHound CE documentation for the current installation process.

After installation, the interface is commonly exposed locally through:

http://localhost:8080

Do not expose a local BloodHound instance to untrusted networks without appropriate authentication and network controls.

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text:
BloodHound is only as useful as the data supplied to it.

Incomplete Collection
        |
        v
Incomplete Graph
        |
        v
Missing Relationships
        |
        v
Potentially Missed Attack Paths

Collection strategy therefore matters.

docs.title: Collection Options
docs.text:
A practical AD assessment may use several collection methods.

Windows foothold
     |
     +--> SharpHound CE
     |
Linux foothold
     |
     +--> BloodHound.py CE
     |
     +--> NetExec
     |
Existing JSON / ZIP
     |
     +--> BloodHound CE
     |
     +--> BloodBash

The collector should be chosen based on:

Operating system
Network position
Credentials
Privileges
Endpoint controls
Available protocols
Assessment scope
Required data
Operational impact

docs.title: SharpHound CE
docs.text:
SharpHound CE is the official Active Directory collector for BloodHound CE.

It is written in C# and collects information through mechanisms including:

LDAP
Windows APIs
SMB
RPC
Registry access
Session enumeration
Local group enumeration

depending on the selected collection methods.

docs.title: Basic SharpHound Collection
docs.text:
From a domain-joined Windows system:

.\SharpHound.exe

Without additional collection flags, SharpHound uses its default collection method.

The resulting data is normally written into a ZIP archive containing BloodHound-compatible JSON.

docs.title: Specify a Domain
docs.text:
.\SharpHound.exe --Domain example.local

Short form:

.\SharpHound.exe -d example.local

DNS must be able to resolve the target domain correctly.

docs.title: SharpHound Collection Methods
docs.text:
Important collection methods include:

Default
All
DCOnly
ComputerOnly
Session
LoggedOn
Group
ACL
GPOLocalGroup
Trusts
Container
LocalGroup
LocalAdmin
RDP
DCOM
PSRemote
ObjectProps
UserRights
CARegistry
DCRegistry
CertServices

Always check the current SharpHound documentation because collection capabilities evolve.

docs.title: Default Collection
docs.text:
A default SharpHound CE collection gathers important information including:

Group memberships
Domain trusts
AD object permissions
AD CS object permissions
OU structure
Group Policy links
Object properties
Local group relationships
User sessions

depending on accessibility and permissions.

docs.title: DCOnly
docs.text:
For a lower-impact directory-focused collection:

.\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods DCOnly

Conceptually:

SharpHound
    |
    v
Domain Controller
    |
    +--> Groups
    +--> Trusts
    +--> ACLs
    +--> AD CS objects
    +--> OUs
    +--> GPO links
    +--> Object properties

DCOnly avoids directly querying every domain-joined workstation/server for computer-specific data.

This can be useful when:

Reducing endpoint connections
Performing initial collection
Working under restrictive ROE
Performing directory-only analysis

docs.title: Session Collection
docs.text:
Sessions are more dynamic than many directory relationships.

.\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session

Sessions can reveal relationships such as:

User
 |
 v
Logged onto
 |
 v
Computer

These relationships may change frequently.

docs.title: Session Loop
docs.text:
SharpHound can repeatedly collect session information:

.\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session --Loop

A custom loop duration can be supplied:

.\SharpHound.exe \
    --CollectionMethods Session \
    --Loop \
    --LoopDuration 03:00:00

Session looping can significantly increase network and endpoint activity.

Use it only when authorised.

docs.title: Stealth Collection
docs.text:
SharpHound provides:

--Stealth

for supported collection workflows.

Example:

.\SharpHound.exe \
    --CollectionMethods Session \
    --Stealth

"Stealth" should not be interpreted as:

Undetectable

It changes collection behaviour but still generates observable activity.

docs.title: Scope Collection
docs.text:
Limit collection where possible.

For example, collection can be constrained using:

Domain
Distinguished Name
Computer list
LDAP filter

This is useful for:

Large environments
Restricted assessment scope
Sensitive networks
Phased assessments
Testing specific OUs

docs.title: Track Computer Calls
docs.text:
SharpHound can track computer collection attempts.

This can help answer:

Which systems were contacted?

Which requests failed?

Which systems were unreachable?

This is useful for both troubleshooting and evidence.

docs.title: SharpHound Workflow
docs.text:
Windows Access
      |
      v
Confirm Domain
      |
      v
Confirm DNS
      |
      v
Choose Collection Method
      |
      v
Run SharpHound
      |
      v
Collect ZIP
      |
      v
Transfer Securely
      |
      v
BloodHound CE

docs.title: BloodHound.py
docs.text:
BloodHound.py is a Python-based BloodHound ingestor originally developed for performing BloodHound collection from Linux systems.

It is based heavily on Python Active Directory protocol implementations and is useful when:

No Windows foothold exists

You are testing from Kali Linux

LDAP and SMB are reachable

You possess domain credentials

SharpHound cannot be executed

A Linux-native collector is preferable

docs.title: BloodHound.py Legacy vs CE
docs.text:
This distinction is important.

The primary BloodHound.py branch targets legacy BloodHound versions.

For BloodHound Community Edition, use the CE-compatible version.

Conceptually:

BloodHound Legacy
       |
       +--> bloodhound-python

BloodHound CE
       |
       +--> bloodhound-ce-python

Do not assume data generated for one version is automatically correct for another.

docs.title: Install BloodHound.py for BloodHound CE
docs.text:
Using pipx:

pipx install bloodhound-ce

Check:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

docs.title: Install BloodHound.py Legacy
docs.text:
For legacy BloodHound:

pipx install bloodhound

Command:

bloodhound-python

Do not confuse this with the CE collector.

docs.title: BloodHound.py Authentication
docs.text:
BloodHound.py supports authentication using mechanisms including:

Username + password
NTLM hash
AES key
Kerberos TGT / ccache

The exact options depend on the installed version.

Always inspect:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

before running a collection.

docs.title: BloodHound.py Basic Context
docs.text:
Set useful variables:

export DOMAIN="example.local"
export DC="dc01.example.local"
export DC_IP="10.10.20.10"
export USER="alice"

Verify DNS:

dig "$DC"

Verify LDAP SRV:

dig SRV "_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.$DOMAIN"

Verify Kerberos:

dig SRV "_kerberos._tcp.$DOMAIN"

docs.title: BloodHound.py Collection
docs.text:
The exact command should always be based on the installed CE version.

General structure:

bloodhound-ce-python \
    -u <username> \
    -p '<password>' \
    -d <domain> \
    -ns <dns-server> \
    -c <collection-methods>

Check:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

for current options.

docs.title: Collection Methods
docs.text:
BloodHound.py supports many BloodHound collection categories.

Examples include:

Group
LocalAdmin
Session
Trusts
ACL
Container
RDP
DCOM
PSRemote
ObjectProps
All

Support may not be identical to SharpHound.

When complete coverage matters, understand the limitations of the collector being used.

docs.title: BloodHound.py Workflow
docs.text:
Kali
 |
 v
Domain Credential
 |
 v
DNS
 |
 v
LDAP / SMB
 |
 v
bloodhound-ce-python
 |
 v
JSON Collection
 |
 v
BloodHound CE

docs.title: Kerberos with BloodHound.py
docs.text:
Kerberos collection requires correct:

DNS
Time
Domain
KDC
FQDN
Credential cache

Check:

date

dig "$DC"

If using a ccache:

export KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/user.ccache

Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

docs.title: NetExec BloodHound Ingestor
docs.text:
NetExec can also perform BloodHound-oriented LDAP collection.

This is particularly useful when NetExec is already being used during an internal assessment.

Conceptually:

NetExec
   |
   v
LDAP Authentication
   |
   v
BloodHound Collection
   |
   v
JSON / ZIP
   |
   v
BloodHound

This can reduce tool switching during an assessment.

docs.title: NetExec LDAP Context
docs.text:
Start by validating LDAP access:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

Check the current BloodHound options:

nxc ldap --help

NetExec syntax changes over time, so use the installed version's help output rather than assuming older command syntax.

docs.title: NetExec BloodHound Collection
docs.text:
The NetExec LDAP protocol contains BloodHound collection functionality.

Before collection, confirm:

Domain
Domain Controller
DNS
Credentials
BloodHound edition
Collection scope

Then inspect:

nxc ldap --help

for the current BloodHound collection options.

docs.title: NetExec BloodHound Workflow
docs.text:
nxc smb
   |
   v
Discover Environment
   |
   v
Validate Credential
   |
   v
nxc ldap
   |
   v
Directory Access
   |
   v
BloodHound Collection
   |
   v
BloodHound CE

This integrates naturally with the broader NetExec methodology.

docs.title: Choosing a Collector
docs.text:
Where am I?
    |
    +--> Windows
    |      |
    |      +--> SharpHound CE
    |
    +--> Linux / Kali
           |
           +--> BloodHound.py CE
           |
           +--> NetExec

Then consider:

Need maximum official compatibility?
        |
        +--> SharpHound CE

Need Linux-native collection?
        |
        +--> BloodHound.py CE

Already using NetExec heavily?
        |
        +--> NetExec BloodHound ingestor

Only have collected JSON/ZIP?
        |
        +--> BloodHound CE
        |
        +--> BloodBash

docs.title: Collector Comparison
docs.text:
Collector Platform Best Use SharpHound CE Windows Official BloodHound CE AD collection BloodHound.py CE Linux / Kali Linux-native AD collection NetExec Linux / Kali Integrated LDAP/BloodHound collection during NetExec workflows

Collection capabilities are not necessarily identical.

docs.title: Importing Data into BloodHound CE
docs.text:
SharpHound and compatible collectors generate:

JSON
ZIP

BloodHound CE can ingest collection data through the web interface.

Typical workflow:

BloodHound CE
     |
     v
Administration
     |
     v
Data Collection
     |
     v
File Ingest
     |
     v
Upload JSON / ZIP

The exact interface may change between releases.

docs.title: BloodHound Graph Model
docs.text:
BloodHound represents identity relationships as a graph.

Node
 |
 +--> User
 +--> Group
 +--> Computer
 +--> Domain
 +--> OU
 +--> GPO
 +--> Certificate Authority
 +--> Certificate Template

Relationships are represented as edges.

User
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
Group

or:

User
 |
 | AdminTo
 v
Computer

docs.title: Nodes and Edges
docs.text:
A graph contains:

Nodes = objects

Edges = relationships

Example:

ALICE
  |
  | MemberOf
  v
HELPDESK
  |
  | GenericAll
  v
SERVER ADMINS
  |
  | AdminTo
  v
APP01

The value of BloodHound comes from chaining relationships.

docs.title: Attack Paths
docs.text:
An attack path is a sequence of relationships that may allow one identity to influence another security object.

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
Computer
 |
 v
Privileged Session
 |
 v
Tier-0 Identity

BloodHound helps identify these relationships.

It does not automatically prove that every path is exploitable.

docs.title: Edge Interpretation
docs.text:
For every interesting edge ask:

What does this edge mean?

What security control creates it?

What permissions are required?

Is the relationship current?

Can I independently verify it?

Does exploitation require state changes?

What is the impact?

Is validation authorised?

docs.title: Common Relationships
docs.text:
Important relationships may include:

MemberOf
AdminTo
HasSession
CanRDP
CanPSRemote
ExecuteDCOM
GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
ForceChangePassword
AddMember
Owns
DCSync-related rights
AllowedToDelegate
AllowedToAct
GPO relationships
AD CS relationships
Trust relationships

The exact BloodHound edge model evolves over time.

docs.title: MemberOf
docs.text:
Example:

ALICE
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
HELPDESK

Nested membership matters.

ALICE
 |
 v
HELPDESK
 |
 v
SERVER ADMINS
 |
 v
ADMINISTRATORS

Do not only examine direct memberships.

docs.title: AdminTo
docs.text:
User / Group
     |
     | AdminTo
     v
Computer

This indicates an administrative relationship.

It does not necessarily mean:

The user is currently logged on

The host is reachable

Remote administration is enabled

Execution is authorised

Those conditions should be verified separately.

docs.title: HasSession
docs.text:
User
 |
 | HasSession
 v
Computer

Session data is highly useful but dynamic.

A session discovered earlier may no longer exist.

Treat session information as:

Potentially Time Sensitive

docs.title: CanRDP
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | CanRDP
   v
Computer

This indicates an RDP-related relationship.

Still verify:

RDP reachable
Account permitted
Network path
Authentication restrictions
MFA / NLA controls

docs.title: CanPSRemote
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | CanPSRemote
   v
Computer

Verify:

WinRM reachable
Authentication works
Remote management rights
Network controls

docs.title: ExecuteDCOM
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | ExecuteDCOM
   v
Computer

This represents a DCOM-related relationship.

Actual usability depends on:

Permissions
Firewall
RPC
DCOM configuration
Endpoint controls

docs.title: ACL Relationships
docs.text:
BloodHound is particularly useful for finding dangerous ACL relationships.

Examples include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
ForceChangePassword
AddMember

These may form paths such as:

User
 |
 | GenericAll
 v
Group
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
Privileged Group

docs.title: GenericAll
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Principal
   |
   | GenericAll
   v
Object

This represents broad control over the target object.

The exact security impact depends on the object type.

For example:

User
Group
Computer
OU
GPO

can each produce different attack possibilities.

docs.title: GenericWrite
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | GenericWrite
   v
Object

This represents permission to modify certain properties.

Do not automatically equate:

GenericWrite

with:

Full Control

The exploitable effect depends on the target object's writable attributes.

docs.title: WriteDacl
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | WriteDacl
   v
Object

This can allow modification of the object's access control list.

This is often a high-impact relationship because new permissions may be introduced.

docs.title: WriteOwner
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | WriteOwner
   v
Object

Ownership changes can affect the ability to alter permissions.

Treat validation carefully because changing ownership modifies directory state.

docs.title: ForceChangePassword
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | ForceChangePassword
   v
User

This indicates a password reset relationship.

Do not validate against real users without explicit approval because it can disrupt access and business operations.

docs.title: DCSync Relationships
docs.text:
BloodHound can identify principals with directory replication rights.

Conceptually:

Principal
   |
   +--> GetChanges
   |
   +--> GetChangesAll
   |
   v
Domain

These relationships may indicate DCSync capability.

Treat them as high impact.

Validation should be explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify:

Unconstrained delegation
Constrained delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

Graph relationships should then be analysed together with:

SPNs
Accounts
Computers
Privileges
Protocol transition
S4U configuration

docs.title: RBCD
docs.text:
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation relationships may appear as paths involving control over:

Computer objects
msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity

BloodHound can help reveal who controls the objects involved.

Detailed analysis belongs in:

active-directory/rbcd.md

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text:
BloodHound models:

OU
 |
 v
GPO
 |
 v
Computers / Users

and potentially permissions over the GPO itself.

Interesting questions include:

Who can modify the GPO?

Where is the GPO linked?

Which computers receive it?

Which users receive it?

Can a low-privilege identity influence it?

docs.title: AD CS
docs.text:
Modern BloodHound collection includes Active Directory Certificate Services relationships.

This can help identify relationships involving:

Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
Enrollment permissions
Template permissions
Certificate services configuration

BloodHound should complement, not replace, dedicated AD CS analysis.

Use tools such as Certipy where detailed certificate-service enumeration is required.

docs.title: Trusts
docs.text:
BloodHound can model trust relationships between domains.

Domain A
   |
   | Trust
   v
Domain B

Analyse:

Direction
Transitivity
Trust type
SID filtering
Selective authentication
Cross-domain group membership
Cross-domain ACLs

docs.title: High-Value Targets
docs.text:
High-value objects commonly include:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Domain Controllers
Tier-0 systems
Certificate Authorities
Privileged service accounts
Identity management infrastructure

But environment-specific critical systems may be equally important.

Do not rely solely on BloodHound's default high-value marking.

docs.title: Owned Principals
docs.text:
When a credential or identity has been confirmed under the assessment scope, mark it appropriately in BloodHound.

Conceptually:

Known Controlled Identity
        |
        v
Mark as Owned
        |
        v
Analyse Outbound Paths

This helps answer:

What can I reach from here?

docs.title: Re-Analyse After New Access
docs.text:
New Credential
      |
      v
Mark Owned
      |
      v
Search Outbound Paths
      |
      v
New Relationships
      |
      v
Validate

docs.title: Shortest Paths
docs.text:
Shortest paths can be useful for triage.

Owned User
    |
    v
Shortest Path
    |
    v
High Value Target

However:

Shortest
   !=
Best

Shortest
   !=
Safest

Shortest
   !=
Most Reliable

A longer path may be more realistic or less disruptive.

docs.title: Path Prioritisation
docs.text:
Evaluate paths using:

Path length
Required privileges
Operational impact
Detection likelihood
Credential requirements
Network reachability
State changes
Business risk
Rules of engagement

A useful model:

Candidate Path
      |
      v
Technically Possible?
      |
      v
Reachable?
      |
      v
Credentials Available?
      |
      v
Safe?
      |
      v
Authorised?
      |
      v
Validate

docs.title: Neo4j
docs.text:
BloodHound historically used Neo4j directly as its graph database, and legacy BloodHound deployments are often encountered with Neo4j.

This remains relevant when:

Using legacy BloodHound

Reviewing older assessment environments

Working with existing Neo4j databases

Performing custom Cypher analysis

Conceptually:

BloodHound Data
      |
      v
Neo4j
      |
      v
Graph
      |
      v
Cypher

BloodHound CE architecture has evolved beyond the older "BloodHound desktop application + manually managed Neo4j" model.

Do not assume modern BloodHound CE installation instructions are identical to legacy BloodHound.

docs.title: Cypher
docs.text:
Cypher is a graph query language associated with Neo4j and graph-based BloodHound analysis.

Conceptually:

MATCH (n)
RETURN n
LIMIT 10

This returns graph nodes.

docs.title: Find Users
docs.text:
Example conceptual query:

MATCH (u:User)
RETURN u
LIMIT 25

docs.title: Find Computers
docs.text:
MATCH (c:Computer)
RETURN c
LIMIT 25

docs.title: Find Groups
docs.text:
MATCH (g:Group)
RETURN g
LIMIT 25

docs.title: Find Domain Admin Members
docs.text:
A conceptual relationship query may look like:

MATCH (u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)
WHERE g.name CONTAINS 'DOMAIN ADMINS'
RETURN u,g

Schema and query behaviour can vary between BloodHound versions.

Validate queries against the installed version.

docs.title: Find Administrative Relationships
docs.text:
Conceptually:

MATCH (u:User)-[:AdminTo]->(c:Computer)
RETURN u,c

docs.title: Find Sessions
docs.text:
Conceptually:

MATCH (u:User)-[:HasSession]->(c:Computer)
RETURN u,c

docs.title: Custom Queries
docs.text:
Custom graph queries are valuable when investigating:

Specific groups
Specific users
Specific servers
Delegation
ACL relationships
Cross-domain relationships
Privileged sessions
Certificate services

Do not rely only on pre-built queries.

docs.title: BloodBash
docs.text:
BloodBash is an open-source offline analyser for SharpHound and AzureHound data.

It is useful when you want to:

Analyse SharpHound data quickly

Avoid running a BloodHound server

Avoid maintaining Neo4j

Perform offline triage

Analyse collected JSON or ZIP files

Generate prioritised findings

Inspect attack paths from the terminal

Conceptually:

SharpHound
    |
    v
JSON / ZIP
    |
    v
BloodBash
    |
    v
Offline Graph
    |
    v
Prioritised Analysis

No BloodHound UI or Neo4j server is required.

docs.title: BloodBash Installation
docs.text:
Using pipx:

pipx install git+https://github.com/SquidSec/BloodBash

Check:

bloodbash --help

Advanced help:

bloodbash --help-advanced

docs.title: BloodBash Standalone Binary
docs.text:
BloodBash also provides standalone binaries.

After obtaining the appropriate binary from the official releases:

chmod +x bloodbash-linux-x64

Run:

./bloodbash-linux-x64 ./sharpout

docs.title: BloodBash Quick Analysis
docs.text:
Given a directory containing SharpHound output:

bloodbash ./sharpout

The default workflow performs quick-win analysis.

Equivalent:

bloodbash ./sharpout --quick-wins

docs.title: BloodBash ZIP Analysis
docs.text:
bloodbash ./collection.zip --quick-wins

This makes BloodBash particularly useful immediately after a collection.

docs.title: BloodBash Full Analysis
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --all

For larger graphs:

bloodbash ./sharpout --all --fast

docs.title: BloodBash Interactive Mode
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --wizard

This provides an interactive analysis workflow.

docs.title: BloodBash Owned User Analysis
docs.text:
If a user has been obtained during an authorised assessment:

bloodbash ./sharpout \
    --from-user alice \
    --from-user-export

Conceptually:

Owned User
    |
    v
BloodBash
    |
    v
Outbound Relationships
    |
    v
Potential Paths

docs.title: BloodBash Merge Collections
docs.text:
Multiple collections can be merged.

bloodbash ./lowpriv.zip \
    --merge ./additional.zip \
    --all \
    --fast

This is useful when:

New privileges produce better collection

Multiple domains are collected

Collection occurs at different stages

Different network segments are assessed

docs.title: BloodBash Domain Filtering
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout \
    --all \
    --domain EXAMPLE.LOCAL

Useful in multi-domain datasets.

docs.title: BloodBash Inspection
docs.text:
BloodBash supports focused node inspection.

Conceptually:

bloodbash ./sharpout \
    --inspect <NODE>

This can help understand:

Properties
Inbound edges
Outbound edges
Relationships

docs.title: BloodBash Path Analysis
docs.text:
BloodBash supports path-oriented analysis including:

Paths from owned principals
Paths to high-value targets
Arbitrary source-to-target paths
Indirect relationships

Use:

bloodbash --help

and:

bloodbash --help-advanced

docs.title: Collection Completeness
docs.text:
Before trusting the graph, ask:

Which domains were collected?

Which OUs were included?

Were ACLs collected?

Were sessions collected?

Were local groups collected?

Were trusts collected?

Was AD CS collected?

Were inaccessible hosts skipped?

Was collection performed with low privilege?

How old is the data?

Incomplete data can produce misleading conclusions.

docs.title: Collection Health
docs.text:
Keep a record of:

Collection date
Collector
Collector version
Collection methods
Identity used
Domain
DNS server
Failed hosts
Excluded hosts
Scope restrictions

This information makes graph interpretation more reliable.

docs.text:
Treat BloodHound data as:

Environment
     |
     v
Collection Time
     |
     v
Snapshot

not:

Permanent Truth

Especially:

Sessions
Group membership
ACLs
Computer availability
Trust configuration
Certificates
Delegation

docs.title: Re-Collection
docs.text:
Re-collect when:

New credentials are obtained

New privileges are obtained

A new subnet becomes reachable

A new domain is discovered

A trust is discovered

Previously inaccessible computers become reachable

Assessment conditions change

docs.text:
Do not report:

BloodHound found a path.

Report the underlying security condition.

For example:

A standard domain user possessed permission to modify
membership of a group that provides administrative access
to multiple application servers.

BloodHound is evidence supporting the finding.

It is not the finding itself.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
BloodHound itself is primarily an analysis platform.

Collection is what normally produces observable activity.

Potential telemetry includes:

LDAP queries
SMB connections
RPC connections
Session enumeration
Local group enumeration
Registry queries
DNS requests
Kerberos requests
Authentication events
Process execution
Endpoint security alerts

docs.title: Detecting SharpHound
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

SharpHound process execution
Large LDAP enumeration
Repeated host connections
Session enumeration
Local group enumeration
Known binary signatures
Command-line telemetry
EDR detections

However, defenders should avoid relying solely on binary names or hashes.

Behavioural detection is more resilient.

docs.title: Detecting Linux-Based Collection
docs.text:
BloodHound.py and NetExec may produce patterns such as:

LDAP enumeration from unusual systems
SMB enumeration
Kerberos authentication
Repeated connections across many hosts
Directory queries from non-standard management systems

Correlate:

Source host
Identity
Volume
Protocols
Targets
Time window

docs.text:

       |
       v
Usually Normal

Large Breadth
       +
Multiple Object Classes
       +
Host Enumeration
       +
Session Queries
       +
Unusual Source
       |
       v
Higher Signal

docs.title: Defensive Use
docs.text:
BloodHound is also valuable defensively.

Blue teams can use it to identify:

Privilege escalation paths
Excessive ACL permissions
Dangerous delegation
Tiering violations
Privileged sessions
Excessive local admin rights
Weak group design
AD CS attack paths
Cross-domain exposure

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Remediation should target the underlying relationship.

Examples:

Dangerous ACL
   |
   +--> Remove unnecessary ACE

Excessive Group Membership
   |
   +--> Reduce membership

Local Admin Sprawl
   |
   +--> Remove unnecessary local admin

Privileged Sessions
   |
   +--> Improve administrative tiering

Dangerous Delegation
   |
   +--> Reconfigure delegation

AD CS Path
   |
   +--> Correct template / CA permissions

Trust Exposure
   |
   +--> Harden trust configuration

Do not "remediate BloodHound."

Remediate the identity relationships BloodHound reveals.

docs.title: Treating Every Edge as Exploitable
docs.text:
Wrong:

Edge exists
   =
Finding

Correct:

Edge
 |
 v
Understand
 |
 v
Verify
 |
 v
Assess Impact

docs.title: Using Only Shortest Path
docs.text:
Shortest path is useful for discovery, but not sufficient for a complete assessment.

Also investigate:

ACL exposure
Delegation
Sessions
Local admin sprawl
GPO control
AD CS
Trusts
Kerberoastable privileged accounts
AS-REP candidates
RBCD
Tiering violations

docs.title: Ignoring Collection Failures
docs.text:
If half the environment was unreachable:

Graph
  !=
Complete Environment

Document collection limitations.

docs.title: Using Old Data
docs.text:
An old graph may contain:

Expired sessions
Removed users
Changed groups
Changed ACLs
Retired computers
Modified delegation

Always record collection time.

docs.text:

Relationship

not necessarily:

Successful exploitation

Network route

date

dig dc01.example.local

Domain
FQDN

Time
Ticket
SPN

docs.title: Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Kerberos Constrained Delegation (KCD) is an Active Directory feature that allows a service to impersonate users when accessing specifically configured backend services.

It was introduced to reduce the broad trust associated with unconstrained delegation.

The fundamental difference is:

Unconstrained Delegation
        |
        v
Broad Delegation
        |
        v
Many Kerberos Services

versus:

Constrained Delegation
        |
        v
Explicit Delegation
        |
        v
Configured Backend Services

A typical legitimate architecture is:

User
 |
 v
WEB01
 |
 | Kerberos delegation
 v
SQL01

Instead of allowing WEB01 to delegate authentication to arbitrary services, Active Directory can restrict delegation to specific Service Principal Names (SPNs), such as:

MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

The configured destinations are stored in the:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

attribute of the delegating account.

Constrained delegation significantly reduces the delegation scope compared with unconstrained delegation, but it remains security-sensitive. If an attacker compromises an account configured for constrained delegation, the attacker may be able to impersonate users to the services permitted by that delegation configuration.

Authorised testing only

Kerberos delegation testing can result in user impersonation and reusable service tickets. Only test delegation relationships, accounts, users, and services explicitly included in the engagement scope. Prefer enumeration and controlled test identities before attempting impersonation of privileged users.

docs.title: Delegation Overview
docs.text:
The main Active Directory Kerberos delegation models are:

Kerberos Delegation
       |
       +--> Unconstrained Delegation
       |
       +--> Constrained Delegation
       |
       +--> Resource-Based
            Constrained Delegation

At a high level:

Delegation Model Delegation Scope Configuration Location Unconstrained Broad Front-end account Constrained Specific services Front-end account RBCD Specific principals Back-end resource

docs.title: Why Constrained Delegation Exists
docs.text:
Consider a web application that accesses a database on behalf of its users.

Alice
 |
 v
WEB01
 |
 v
SQL01

The application needs:

Alice -> WEB01 -> SQL01

while preserving Alice's identity.

Without delegation:

Alice
 |
 v
WEB01
 |
 X
Cannot automatically authenticate
to SQL01 as Alice

Unconstrained delegation solves this by giving the front-end broad delegation capability.

WEB01
 |
 +--> SQL01
 +--> FILE01
 +--> APP02
 +--> Other Kerberos Services

Constrained delegation restricts this:

WEB01
 |
 +--> MSSQLSvc/SQL01
 |
 X
FILE01
 |
 X
APP02

The security boundary therefore becomes the configured service list.

docs.title: Core Architecture
docs.text:
The normal constrained delegation architecture is:

             User
              |
              v
        Front-End Service
              |
              v
       Delegating Account
              |
              v
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
              |
              v
      Approved SPN(s)
              |
              v
       Back-End Service

Example:

Alice
 |
 v
WEB01
 |
 v
svc_web
 |
 v
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
 |
 v
MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433
 |
 v
SQL01

docs.title: Delegating Account
docs.text:
Delegation is configured against the security principal running the front-end service.

This can be:

Computer Account

such as:

WEB01$

or:

User / Service Account

such as:

svc_web

Therefore, constrained delegation enumeration must inspect both:

Users

and:

Computers

docs.title: Service Principal Names
docs.text:
Kerberos identifies services using Service Principal Names.

Examples include:

cifs/fileserver01.corp.example
http/web01.corp.example
ldap/dc01.corp.example
host/server01.corp.example
MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

Constrained delegation permissions reference these SPNs.

For example:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo:
    cifs/fileserver01.corp.example
    MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

This means the delegating account has been configured to delegate to those services.

docs.title: msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
docs.text:
Traditional constrained delegation stores permitted destination services in:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

A conceptual object might look like:

Account:
svc_web

SPNs:
HTTP/web01.corp.example

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo:
MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

The trust relationship is:

svc_web
   |
   v
May delegate to
   |
   v
MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

docs.title: Constrained Delegation Modes
docs.text:
Traditional constrained delegation can operate in two important modes:

Kerberos Only

and:

Use Any Authentication Protocol

The distinction is important because the latter enables Kerberos protocol transition.

docs.title: Kerberos Only
docs.text:
The Active Directory GUI option is commonly presented as:

Trust this user/computer for delegation
to specified services only

Use Kerberos only

Conceptually:

User
 |
 | Kerberos
 v
Front-End
 |
 | Delegation
 v
Configured Back-End

The user's original authentication context is Kerberos-based.

docs.title: Protocol Transition
docs.text:
The second mode is commonly presented as:

Trust this user/computer for delegation
to specified services only

Use any authentication protocol

This enables protocol transition.

The relevant account-control flag is:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

Its userAccountControl value is:

0x01000000

or:

16777216

Protocol transition allows the service to obtain a Kerberos service ticket representing a user even when that user did not originally authenticate to the front-end using Kerberos.

docs.title: Why Protocol Transition Exists
docs.text:
Consider:

User
 |
 | Forms authentication
 | Certificate
 | NTLM
 | Other front-end authentication
 v
WEB01
 |
 | Needs Kerberos identity
 v
SQL01

The front-end may still need to access:

SQL01

using Kerberos as the user.

Protocol transition provides:

Non-Kerberos Front-End Authentication
               |
               v
            S4U2Self
               |
               v
Kerberos Service Ticket for User
               |
               v
            S4U2Proxy
               |
               v
Configured Back-End Service

docs.title: S4U
docs.text:
Kerberos Service-for-User extensions are central to constrained delegation.

The two important operations are:

S4U2Self
S4U2Proxy

A useful model is:

S4U
 |
 +--> S4U2Self
 |
 +--> S4U2Proxy

docs.title: S4U2Self
docs.text:
S4U2Self allows a service to request a service ticket to itself on behalf of a user.

Conceptually:

Front-End Service
       |
       | "Give me a ticket to myself
       | representing Alice"
       v
      KDC
       |
       v
Service Ticket
Alice -> Front-End

This allows the service to establish a Kerberos representation of the user.

docs.title: S4U2Proxy
docs.text:
S4U2Proxy allows the service to use an appropriate user service ticket to request another service ticket for a permitted backend service.

Conceptually:

Alice -> WEB01 Ticket
        |
        v
      WEB01
        |
        | S4U2Proxy
        v
       KDC
        |
        v
Alice -> SQL01 Ticket

The destination is restricted by the delegation configuration.

docs.title: Complete S4U Flow
docs.text:
A simplified protocol-transition flow is:

User
 |
 | Non-Kerberos Authentication
 v
WEB01
 |
 | S4U2Self
 v
KDC
 |
 v
Ticket:
Alice -> WEB01
 |
 | S4U2Proxy
 v
KDC
 |
 v
Ticket:
Alice -> SQL01
 |
 v
SQL01

The configured relationship is:

WEB01
 |
 v
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
 |
 v
MSSQLSvc/sql01

docs.title: Security Significance of S4U
docs.text:
S4U exists for legitimate impersonation.

The security problem appears when:

Delegating Account
        |
        v
Compromised
        |
        v
Attacker Controls Delegation Capability
        |
        v
User Impersonation
        |
        v
Configured Service

The attacker is still constrained by the services allowed by the delegation configuration.

However, those services may themselves be highly privileged.

docs.title: Constrained Does Not Mean Low Risk
docs.text:
Consider:

svc_app
 |
 v
AllowedToDelegateTo
 |
 v
cifs/dc01.corp.example

If the account can obtain an impersonated service ticket for a sufficiently privileged user to:

CIFS/DC01

the delegation scope is technically constrained, but the destination is extremely sensitive.

Therefore:

Constrained
    !=
Automatically Safe

docs.title: Service Class Matters
docs.text:
The SPN's service class is important.

Examples:

cifs/server01
ldap/dc01
http/web01
MSSQLSvc/sql01
host/server01

Different service classes provide different capabilities.

A delegation relationship to:

MSSQLSvc/sql01

is not equivalent to:

ldap/dc01

or:

cifs/dc01

Impact analysis must therefore include the actual SPN.

docs.title: Enumeration Strategy
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

Active Directory
       |
       v
Find msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
       |
       v
Identify Delegating Accounts
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
   v       v
Users   Computers
   |       |
   +---+---+
       |
       v
Enumerate Destination SPNs
       |
       v
Check Protocol Transition
       |
       v
Analyse Account Privilege
       |
       v
Analyse Destination Services
       |
       v
BloodHound Attack Paths

docs.title: Windows - Active Directory PowerShell
docs.text:
Enumerate users with traditional constrained delegation:

Get-ADUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' \
    -Properties ServicePrincipalName,msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,userAccountControl |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        ServicePrincipalName,
        msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,
        userAccountControl

docs.title: Enumerate Computers
docs.text:
Get-ADComputer \
    -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' \
    -Properties DNSHostName,ServicePrincipalName,msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,userAccountControl |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        DNSHostName,
        ServicePrincipalName,
        msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,
        userAccountControl

docs.title: Search All Relevant Objects
docs.text:
A broader LDAP approach is:

Get-ADObject \
    -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' \
    -Properties samAccountName,objectClass,msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,userAccountControl |
    Select-Object \
        samAccountName,
        objectClass,
        msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,
        userAccountControl

docs.title: Enumerate Protocol Transition
docs.text:
Search for:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

using the bit:

16777216

For users:

Get-ADUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216)' \
    -Properties ServicePrincipalName,msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,userAccountControl |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        ServicePrincipalName,
        msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,
        userAccountControl

For computers:

Get-ADComputer \
    -LDAPFilter '(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216)' \
    -Properties DNSHostName,msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,userAccountControl |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        DNSHostName,
        msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,
        userAccountControl

docs.title: Important Enumeration Nuance
docs.text:
Do not use only:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

to find constrained delegation.

Traditional constrained delegation may exist without protocol transition.

The broader indicator is:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

while:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

indicates the protocol-transition capability.

Therefore:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
        |
        v
Traditional Constrained Delegation


TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION
        |
        v
Protocol Transition Capability

docs.title: LDAP Matching Rule
docs.text:
The LDAP matching rule:

1.2.840.113556.1.4.803

allows bitwise comparison.

The protocol-transition filter is:

(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216)

docs.title: ldapsearch
docs.text:
From Linux, search for traditional constrained delegation using:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\alice' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' \
    sAMAccountName \
    objectClass \
    servicePrincipalName \
    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo \
    userAccountControl

This directly exposes the configured destination services.

docs.title: LDAP Protocol Transition Query
docs.text:
Search for the protocol-transition flag:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\alice' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216)' \
    sAMAccountName \
    servicePrincipalName \
    msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo \
    userAccountControl

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView can enumerate delegation relationships through LDAP-backed Active Directory queries.

A direct query is:

Get-DomainUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' \
    -Properties samaccountname,serviceprincipalname,msds-allowedtodelegateto,useraccountcontrol

For computers:

Get-DomainComputer \
    -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' \
    -Properties samaccountname,dnshostname,serviceprincipalname,msds-allowedtodelegateto,useraccountcontrol

For protocol transition:

Get-DomainObject \
    -LDAPFilter '(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216)' \
    -Properties samaccountname,msds-allowedtodelegateto,useraccountcontrol

PowerView forks and versions differ, so verify the installed implementation before relying on convenience switches.

docs.title: SPN Enumeration
docs.text:
After identifying a delegating account, inspect:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

Example:

svc_web
 |
 +--> cifs/fileserver01.corp.example
 |
 +--> MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

Each SPN should be analysed individually.

docs.title: Native setspn
docs.text:
Inspect the SPNs belonging to the delegating account:

setspn -L CORP\svc_web

For a computer:

setspn -L WEB01

Remember that:

ServicePrincipalName

and:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

serve different purposes.

The first describes services represented by the account.

The second describes services to which it may delegate.

docs.title: Linux - Impacket findDelegation
docs.text:
Impacket provides:

findDelegation.py

commonly installed as:

impacket-findDelegation

Check:

impacket-findDelegation -h

A typical enumeration pattern is:

impacket-findDelegation \
    'corp.example/alice:<PASSWORD>' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

The output can help distinguish:

Unconstrained
Constrained
RBCD

and the relevant delegation configuration.

docs.title: Analyse findDelegation Output
docs.text:
For every result, identify:

Account
Account Type
Delegation Type
Destination SPN
Protocol Transition

Do not stop at:

Delegation found

The meaningful question is:

Delegation to what?

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec LDAP can complement delegation enumeration.

Review:

nxc ldap --help

and:

nxc ldap -L

before relying on delegation-specific module names because available modules and syntax can change.

The general workflow is:

NetExec
   |
   v
LDAP Enumeration
   |
   v
Delegation Relationships
   |
   v
Privilege Analysis

For detailed NetExec usage:

NetExec

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is valuable because delegation should be analysed as an attack path rather than an isolated attribute.

The core questions are:

Who controls the delegating account?

and:

What service can it impersonate users to?

and:

What can that service access?

docs.title: BloodHound Attack Path
docs.text:
A conceptual path is:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Controls svc_web
        |
        v
Constrained Delegation
        |
        v
CIFS/SERVER01
        |
        v
Privileged Service Access

The delegation configuration becomes exploitable when the delegating principal itself can be compromised.

docs.title: Account Control Matters
docs.text:
Suppose:

svc_web

has constrained delegation.

Ask:

Who can reset svc_web's password?

Who can modify svc_web?

Who owns svc_web?

Who has GenericAll?

Who has GenericWrite?

Who has WriteDACL?

Who has WriteOwner?

Who controls the host where svc_web runs?

These relationships may transform a delegation configuration into a practical privilege-escalation path.

docs.title: BloodHound Questions
docs.text:
For every delegation account:

Which principal controls it?
        |
        v
Which SPNs are allowed?
        |
        v
Which systems host those SPNs?
        |
        v
Are those systems high-value?
        |
        v
Can privileged users be impersonated?
        |
        v
What access would the resulting
service ticket provide?

docs.title: Credential Requirement
docs.text:
To actively use traditional constrained delegation as the delegating account, an attacker normally needs usable authentication material for that account.

This might be:

Password
NT Hash / RC4 Key
AES Key
Kerberos Ticket

depending on the workflow.

Therefore:

Delegation Configuration
        |
        X
Immediate Exploitation

without control of the delegating identity.

The more complete path is:

Delegation Account
       |
       v
Credential / Account Compromise
       |
       v
Delegation Capability
       |
       v
User Impersonation
       |
       v
Configured Service

docs.title: Controlled S4U Validation
docs.text:
During an authorised assessment, a controlled validation may demonstrate:

Controlled Delegation Account
            |
            v
Request Ticket
            |
            v
S4U
            |
            v
Controlled Test User
            |
            v
Configured Backend Service
            |
            v
Authentication

Prefer a dedicated test identity rather than a privileged production user whenever this sufficiently proves the finding.

docs.title: Rubeus
docs.text:
Rubeus supports extensive Kerberos and S4U testing on Windows.

Its S4U functionality can be used in authorised environments to evaluate constrained delegation.

A conceptual workflow is:

Delegating Account Key
         |
         v
        TGT
         |
         v
       S4U2Self
         |
         v
User -> Delegating Service Ticket
         |
         v
       S4U2Proxy
         |
         v
User -> Allowed Backend Service

Because Rubeus evolves over time, review the current help and official repository before using exact command syntax.

docs.title: Impacket getST
docs.text:
Impacket provides:

getST.py

commonly installed as:

impacket-getST

It supports Kerberos service-ticket workflows including delegation scenarios.

Check the current options first:

impacket-getST -h

For an explicitly authorised constrained-delegation test, the general workflow is:

Delegating Account
       |
       v
Impacket getST
       |
       v
S4U Request
       |
       v
Impersonated User
       |
       v
Configured SPN
       |
       v
.ccache

docs.title: Controlled Impacket Pattern
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised and using a dedicated test account, the current Impacket getST utility can be used with an impersonated identity and target SPN.

A general pattern is:

impacket-getST \
    -spn '<SERVICE>/<TARGET_FQDN>' \
    -impersonate '<TEST_USER>' \
    'corp.example/<DELEGATING_ACCOUNT>:<PASSWORD>'

For example, in a controlled lab:

impacket-getST \
    -spn 'cifs/server01.corp.example' \
    -impersonate 'pt-test-user' \
    'corp.example/svc_test:<PASSWORD>'

Do not copy real credentials into documentation or shell history.

Use supported password-prompting or alternative credential mechanisms where practical.

docs.title: Resulting Ticket
docs.text:
A successful request may create a Kerberos credential cache such as:

pt-test-user@cifs_server01.corp.example@CORP.EXAMPLE.ccache

The exact filename depends on the tool version and requested service.

Treat it as a credential.

docs.title: Use KRB5CCNAME
docs.text:
Where a controlled test requires validating the resulting ticket:

export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/<TICKET>.ccache"

Inspect:

klist

Confirm:

Client Principal
Service Principal
Start Time
Expiration
Encryption Type

docs.title: Minimum-Impact Service Validation
docs.text:
If the ticket is for:

cifs/server01.corp.example

a low-impact validation may use:

impacket-smbclient \
    -k \
    -no-pass \
    'corp.example/<TEST_USER>@server01.corp.example'

The objective is:

Delegation
    |
    v
Impersonated Service Ticket
    |
    v
Authentication Proven

not:

Immediately execute commands

docs.title: Hostname and SPN
docs.text:
Use the hostname represented by the ticket.

Prefer:

server01.corp.example

rather than:

10.10.10.25

when Kerberos is intended.

The ticket might contain:

cifs/server01.corp.example

and therefore depends on the correct service identity.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Check:

getent hosts server01.corp.example

and:

getent hosts dc01.corp.example

Kerberos troubleshooting should always include:

DNS
Time
Realm
SPN
KDC
Ticket

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Check:

date

On Windows:

w32tm /query /status

Kerberos authentication is time-sensitive.

docs.title: SPN Target Analysis
docs.text:
A delegation relationship such as:

cifs/server01.corp.example

may allow authentication to SMB-related functionality on:

SERVER01

A relationship such as:

ldap/dc01.corp.example

targets LDAP on a domain controller.

A relationship such as:

MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

targets SQL Server.

Therefore:

Allowed SPN
     |
     v
Service Capability
     |
     v
Account Privilege
     |
     v
Impact

docs.title: Service Tickets Are Service-Specific
docs.text:
A ticket for:

MSSQLSvc/sql01

is not simply a generic administrator credential.

The normal Kerberos model is:

Service Ticket
      |
      v
Specific SPN

This distinction should remain clear in reporting.

docs.title: Service-Class Substitution
docs.text:
Delegation assessments sometimes encounter situations where service-class handling and host-account SPNs create broader practical impact than the originally displayed delegation entry might suggest.

This is highly environment-dependent.

Do not automatically report:

Allowed SPN
    =
Every service on host

Instead validate:

Account owning SPN
        |
        v
Registered SPNs
        |
        v
Kerberos service behaviour
        |
        v
Actual accepted ticket

Only report capabilities that were demonstrated or strongly supported by the configuration.

docs.title: Sensitive Users
docs.text:
Some identities should not be delegatable.

Active Directory provides:

Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated

which corresponds to:

NOT_DELEGATED

The userAccountControl bit is:

0x00100000

or:

1048576

docs.title: Enumerate Sensitive Users
docs.text:
Using PowerShell:

Get-ADUser \
    -Filter {AccountNotDelegated -eq $true} \
    -Properties AccountNotDelegated |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        AccountNotDelegated

Check a particular account:

Get-ADUser \
    -Identity '<USERNAME>' \
    -Properties AccountNotDelegated |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        AccountNotDelegated

docs.title: Protected Users
docs.text:
Membership in:

Protected Users

provides additional authentication protections for suitable sensitive accounts.

Protected Users should be considered during delegation analysis because some delegation scenarios that work for ordinary users may behave differently for protected identities.

Do not treat a failed impersonation of a protected user as proof that the entire delegation configuration is harmless.

docs.title: User Impersonation Scope
docs.text:
The security question is not merely:

Can I impersonate Administrator?

A better model is:

Which users can be represented?
        |
        v
Which are protected?
        |
        v
Which destination service is allowed?
        |
        v
What permissions does that user
have at the destination?

docs.title: Constrained Delegation vs Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
Unconstrained:

Compromised Service
       |
       v
Broad Delegation Capability

Constrained:

Compromised Service
       |
       v
Configured Backend SPNs

Comparison:

Property Unconstrained Constrained Backend scope Broad Explicit Primary configuration TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo S4U commonly relevant Not central Yes Protocol transition Not defining feature Optional Risk Broad credential exposure Targeted impersonation

For detailed coverage:

Unconstrained Delegation

docs.title: Constrained Delegation vs RBCD
docs.text:
Traditional constrained delegation defines:

Front-End
   |
   v
Where may I delegate?

using:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

RBCD defines:

Back-End
   |
   v
Who may delegate to me?

using:

msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity

The direction of trust is fundamentally different.

docs.title: Traditional KCD
docs.text:
WEB01
 |
 v
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
 |
 v
SQL01

The delegation setting is controlled on:

WEB01

docs.title: RBCD
docs.text:
SQL01
 |
 v
msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity
 |
 v
WEB01 may delegate

The delegation setting is controlled on:

SQL01

This distinction is central to understanding RBCD attack paths.

docs.title: Constrained Delegation vs Pass-the-Ticket
docs.text:
Constrained delegation:

Delegation Account
       |
       v
S4U
       |
       v
Obtain Service Ticket

Pass-the-Ticket:

Existing Ticket
       |
       v
Reuse Ticket

See:

Pass-the-Ticket

docs.title: Constrained Delegation vs Pass-the-Key
docs.text:
Pass-the-Key uses long-term Kerberos key material to obtain tickets.

Constrained delegation determines what impersonation capabilities an account has after it can authenticate.

Kerberos Key
     |
     v
Authenticate as
Delegation Account
     |
     v
Constrained Delegation
     |
     v
S4U

See:

Pass-the-Key

docs.title: Constrained Delegation vs Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Kerberoasting:

SPN
 |
 v
Request Service Ticket
 |
 v
Offline Password Guessing

Constrained delegation:

Delegating Principal
 |
 v
S4U
 |
 v
Impersonated Service Ticket

The two techniques use Kerberos for very different purposes.

See:

Kerberoasting

docs.title: Delegation and Account Compromise
docs.text:
The most important practical question is often:

Can the delegating account be compromised?

Potential paths include:

Weak service-account password
        |
        v
Kerberoasting

Excessive ACL
        |
        v
Password Reset / Key Control

Compromised Server
        |
        v
Service Credential Exposure

Credential Reuse
        |
        v
Delegating Account Compromise

Delegation should therefore be analysed together with broader Active Directory privilege relationships.

docs.title: Example Attack Chain
docs.text:
Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
Kerberoast svc_web
       |
       v
Service Password Recovered
       |
       v
svc_web Has Constrained Delegation
       |
       v
S4U User Impersonation
       |
       v
CIFS/SERVER01
       |
       v
Privileged Access

This demonstrates why a seemingly moderate service-account weakness can become a major privilege-escalation path.

docs.title: ACL-Based Attack Chain
docs.text:
Another example:

User Alice
   |
   v
GenericAll over svc_web
   |
   v
Control svc_web
   |
   v
Constrained Delegation
   |
   v
Impersonate User
   |
   v
Configured Backend Service

BloodHound is particularly useful for identifying these combinations.

docs.title: Machine Account Delegation
docs.text:
Computer accounts can also have constrained delegation.

Example:

WEB01$
 |
 v
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
 |
 v
cifs/FILE01

Compromise of:

WEB01

may therefore provide control over the machine account's delegation capability.

Do not enumerate only user service accounts.

docs.title: Protocol Transition Risk
docs.text:
Protocol transition is particularly important because:

User did not need to
authenticate with Kerberos
        |
        v
Front-End Service
        |
        v
S4U2Self
        |
        v
Kerberos Representation

Therefore, the service can potentially create a Kerberos representation of a user after authenticating that user through another mechanism.

This is expected functionality but expands the consequences of compromise of the front-end service.

docs.title: Authentication Protocol Is Not the Main Security Boundary
docs.text:
With protocol transition:

User Authentication Method
       |
       X
Must be Kerberos

The important trust boundary becomes:

Can the service legitimately
assert this user's identity?

This is why:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

deserves careful review.

docs.title: Delegation to Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Destination SPNs involving domain controllers deserve particular attention.

Examples:

ldap/dc01.corp.example
cifs/dc01.corp.example
host/dc01.corp.example

The exact risk depends on:

Service
Impersonated User
Permissions
Environment

Do not assign severity based solely on the hostname being a domain controller, but treat the relationship as high priority for analysis.

docs.title: Delegation to File Servers
docs.text:
Example:

cifs/fileserver01.corp.example

Potential impact depends on the impersonated user's access to:

Shares
Administrative shares
Sensitive files
Backup data
Deployment packages
Configuration files

docs.title: Delegation to SQL Server
docs.text:
Example:

MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.example:1433

Impact depends on:

SQL login mapping
Database roles
Server roles
Impersonated user's SQL privileges
Linked servers
Application permissions

docs.title: Delegation to HTTP
docs.text:
Example:

HTTP/app01.corp.example

Potential impact depends entirely on the application using Kerberos authentication.

Do not assume:

HTTP ticket
    =
Server administrator

docs.title: Delegation to LDAP
docs.text:
Example:

ldap/dc01.corp.example

This deserves careful privilege analysis because LDAP exposes Active Directory operations.

The ticket only represents the permissions of the impersonated identity.

Therefore:

LDAP Ticket
     +
Low-Privilege User
     =
Low-Privilege LDAP Access

whereas:

LDAP Ticket
     +
Highly Privileged User
     =
Potentially High-Impact AD Access

docs.title: Safe Testing Strategy
docs.text:
Use:

Enumeration
    |
    v
Identify Delegation
    |
    v
Analyse Account Control
    |
    v
Analyse Destination
    |
    v
Use Test User
    |
    v
Request Single Service Ticket
    |
    v
Validate Authentication
    |
    v
Stop

Avoid:

Immediately impersonating
Domain Admin

when a test identity proves the same security condition.

docs.title: When Active Exploitation Is Unnecessary
docs.text:
Suppose you establish:

svc_test
 |
 v
Constrained Delegation
 |
 v
cifs/server01

and:

Tester controls svc_test

The combination may already provide strong evidence of the attack path.

Depending on engagement requirements, a controlled service-ticket request using a dedicated user may be enough.

docs.title: Evidence of Configuration
docs.text:
Strong configuration evidence includes:

Delegating Account
Object Type
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION
SPNs
Destination Host
Destination Service

This is preferable to unnecessary destructive proof.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Detection should cover:

Delegation Configuration
       |
       +
Kerberos S4U Activity
       |
       +
Service Authentication
       |
       +
Endpoint Behaviour

docs.title: Event 4768
docs.text:
Event:

4768

records TGT requests.

It can help identify authentication by the delegating account.

Useful context includes:

Account
Client Address
Encryption Type
Pre-Authentication Type

docs.title: Event 4769
docs.text:
Event:

4769

records service-ticket requests.

This is particularly important for constrained delegation because S4U workflows ultimately involve service-ticket requests.

Analyse:

Account
Service Name
Client Address
Ticket Options
Ticket Encryption Type
Result

docs.title: Event 4624
docs.text:
The backend Windows service may generate:

4624

when the resulting Kerberos authentication is accepted.

Correlate:

4769 on DC
     |
     v
4624 on Backend

where possible.

docs.title: Event 4672
docs.text:
If the impersonated identity receives privileged rights on the backend:

4672

may provide useful context.

Do not treat it as a delegation-specific event.

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
Directory Service Changes auditing can generate:

5136

when Active Directory attributes are modified.

Monitor changes involving:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

and delegation-related:

userAccountControl

values.

docs.title: Configuration Monitoring
docs.text:
Maintain a baseline of:

Delegating Account
        |
        v
Allowed Destination SPNs
        |
        v
Protocol Transition?

Example:

Account     Destination                     Protocol Transition
-----------------------------------------------------------------
svc_web     MSSQLSvc/sql01:1433             No
WEB02$      cifs/fileserver01               Yes

Unexpected changes should be investigated.

docs.title: Monitor New Delegation Relationships
docs.text:
A useful defensive workflow is:

Scheduled AD Enumeration
        |
        v
Current Delegation
        |
        v
Compare to Baseline
        |
     +--+--+
     |     |
    Same  Changed
           |
           v
        Investigate

docs.title: Detect Protocol Transition Changes
docs.text:
Changes introducing:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

should be reviewed.

Ask:

Who changed it?

Why?

Which account?

Which destination SPNs?

Was a change request approved?

docs.title: Behavioural Detection
docs.text:
Because S4U is legitimate Kerberos functionality:

S4U Activity
     |
     X
Automatically Malicious

Detection should consider:

Delegating Account
       |
       v
Normal Source Host?
       |
       v
Expected User?
       |
       v
Expected Destination?
       |
       v
Expected Time?
       |

Expected Volume?

docs.text:
If the delegating account is compromised through an endpoint, telemetry may include:

Credential access
Service-account credential theft
Suspicious Kerberos tooling
Unexpected processes
Ticket manipulation
Remote administration

Correlate endpoint events with domain-controller Kerberos telemetry.

docs.text:
A controlled exercise can use:

Test Delegation Account

        v
Configured Test Service
        |
        v
Test User
        |
        v
S4U Ticket Request

        v
Backend Authentication
        |
        v

docs.text:
Defenders should determine:

Which account requested the tickets?

Which user was represented?

Which service was targeted?

Was protocol transition involved?

Was the delegation configuration expected?

Was the source host expected?

Was the resulting backend access expected?

Can the team identify how the
delegation account was compromised?

docs.text:
Useful metrics include:

Time to detect
Time to identify delegating account
Time to identify impersonated user
Time to identify target SPN
Time to identify source host
Time to reconstruct S4U flow
Time to identify configuration
Correct containment decision?
Correct remediation selected?

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
The primary defensive model is:

Delegation Required?
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
  No      Yes
   |       |
   v       v
Remove   Minimise Scope
           |
           v
      Protect Account
           |
           v
      Protect Users
           |
           v
       Monitor

docs.title: Remove Unnecessary Delegation
docs.text:
If the application no longer requires delegation:

Remove
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

and remove associated delegation flags where appropriate.

Do not make production changes during an assessment unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Minimise Delegation Scope
docs.text:
Avoid broad destination lists.

Bad:

svc_app
 |
 +--> cifs/server01
 +--> cifs/server02
 +--> cifs/server03
 +--> ldap/dc01
 +--> ldap/dc02
 +--> http/app01
 +--> MSSQLSvc/sql01

if the application only requires:

MSSQLSvc/sql01

Apply:

Minimum Required SPNs

docs.title: Avoid Sensitive Destination Services
docs.text:
Review delegation to:

Domain Controllers
Management Servers
Backup Infrastructure
Certificate Services
Deployment Systems
Identity Infrastructure

with particular care.

docs.title: Protect Delegating Accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts with delegation rights should be treated as sensitive identities.

Apply:

Strong unique credentials
Long random passwords
gMSA where appropriate
Restricted logon rights
Least privilege
Credential isolation
Monitoring

docs.title: gMSA
docs.text:
Where application compatibility allows, Group Managed Service Accounts can reduce risks associated with manually managed service-account passwords.

A gMSA provides automatically managed long, complex credentials.

Conceptually:

Traditional Service Account
        |
        v
Human-Managed Password
        |
        v
Reuse / Weakness / Age Risk

versus:

gMSA
 |
 v
Automatically Managed
Credential

Delegation permissions still require review even when a gMSA is used.

docs.title: Protect the Host
docs.text:
If a machine account has delegation rights, protecting the host itself is critical.

Apply:

Patching
EDR
Application control
Least privilege
Restricted administration
Network segmentation
Credential protection

docs.title: Protect Sensitive Users
docs.text:
For appropriate high-value accounts:

Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated

can reduce delegation exposure.

Example PowerShell configuration where explicitly authorised:

Set-ADAccountControl \
    -Identity '<USERNAME>' \
    -AccountNotDelegated $true

Operational compatibility should be assessed before deployment.

docs.title: Protected Users
docs.text:
Consider:

Protected Users

for suitable privileged human accounts.

Do not blindly place:

Service Accounts
Application Accounts
Legacy Identities

into Protected Users without compatibility analysis.

docs.title: Administrative Tiering
docs.text:
Prevent highly privileged identities from authenticating through lower-trust application tiers.

Bad:

Domain Admin
    |
    v
WEB01
    |
    v
Delegation

Better:

Domain Admin
    |
    v
PAW
    |
    v
Tier 0

docs.title: Privileged Access Workstations
docs.text:
Use dedicated administrative systems for Tier 0 administration.

This reduces:

Privileged Authentication
        |
        v
Application Servers

and therefore reduces delegation exposure.

docs.title: ACL Hardening
docs.text:
Protect the delegating account itself.

Review who has:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
Reset Password
WriteProperty

over:

Delegation Accounts

An attacker who can control the account may gain control of its delegation capability.

docs.title: Protect Delegation Attributes
docs.text:
Monitor and restrict write access to:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

and:

userAccountControl

Delegation configuration should be controlled through tightly managed administrative processes.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
A resulting service ticket should not automatically provide network access from arbitrary systems.

Example:

User Workstation Network
        |
        X
Management SMB
        |
        v
Sensitive Server

Network controls provide an additional barrier even when authentication material is compromised.

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
If a constrained-delegation account is compromised:

Delegation Account Compromised
          |
          v
Identify Account
          |
          v
Identify Allowed SPNs
          |
          v
Identify Protocol Transition
          |
          v
Identify Potentially Impersonated Users
          |
          v
Review 4768 / 4769
          |
          v
Review Backend Authentication
          |
          v
Contain Account / Host
          |
          v
Rotate Credential
          |
          v
Review Delegation Requirement
          |
          v
Investigate Lateral Movement

docs.title: Credential Rotation
docs.text:
If the delegating account's long-term credential is compromised:

Password / Key
      |
      v
Rotate
      |
      v
New Key Material

For machine accounts and managed service accounts, follow the appropriate Active Directory recovery procedures rather than manually changing credentials without understanding dependencies.

docs.title: Remove Attacker-Added Delegation
docs.text:
If incident response discovers unauthorised:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

changes:

Preserve Evidence
      |
      v
Identify Change Source
      |
      v
Identify Affected Account
      |
      v
Remove Malicious Configuration
      |
      v
Rotate Relevant Credentials
      |
      v
Hunt for Ticket Abuse

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Possible finding titles include:

Constrained Kerberos Delegation Enables Privileged User Impersonation

Excessive Kerberos Delegation Rights Assigned to Service Account

Compromised Service Account Can Impersonate Users to Sensitive Service

Kerberos Protocol Transition Enabled for High-Risk Service Account

docs.title: Avoid Overstatement
docs.text:
Do not report:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo exists
        =
Domain Compromise

Instead establish:

Delegating Account
       |
       v
Can Tester Control It?
       |
       v
Allowed Destination
       |
       v
Impersonatable User
       |
       v
User Privileges at Destination
       |
       v
Actual Impact

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Constrained Kerberos Delegation Enables User Impersonation to Sensitive Service

Affected Account:
CORP\svc_web

Delegation Destination:
cifs/server01.corp.example

Protocol Transition:
Enabled

Description:
The affected service account is configured for Kerberos constrained
delegation to the CIFS service on SERVER01.

The account is additionally configured for protocol transition,
allowing the service to obtain Kerberos authentication material
representing users even where the original front-end authentication
was not performed using Kerberos.

During the authorised assessment, control of the delegation account
was demonstrated using dedicated test credentials.

A service ticket representing a controlled test user was requested for
the configured CIFS service and used to authenticate successfully to
the designated test server.

No remote command execution was required to demonstrate the issue.

Impact:
An attacker who compromises the affected delegation account may be able
to impersonate users to the configured backend service.

The actual impact depends on the privileges held by the impersonated
identity on SERVER01.

Recommendation:
Confirm whether the delegation relationship remains operationally
required.

Remove unnecessary delegation, minimise the permitted destination SPNs,
protect the service account using strong managed credentials, restrict
who can modify the account and delegation attributes, protect sensitive
users from delegation where appropriate, and monitor changes to
delegation-related Active Directory attributes.

docs.text:
Record:

Delegating Account
Account Type
Distinguished Name
ServicePrincipalName
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
userAccountControl
TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION
Destination SPN
Destination Host
Destination Service

Command
