MITRE ATT&CK - Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

MITRE ATT&CK - Unsecured Credentials

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Credential Access should be treated as an identity-expansion problem.

The fundamental model is:

Controlled Identity
       |
       v
Credential Source
       |
       v
Additional Credential
       |
       v
Additional Identity
       |
       v
Additional Access

The most important question is not:

How many credentials can I dump?

It is:

Which credential can this identity access,
and what additional privilege does that provide?

A mature assessment therefore follows:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Identify Exposure
   |
   v
Confirm Permission
   |
   v
Understand Credential Type
   |
   v
Map Authentication Scope
   |
   v
Determine Resulting Privilege
   |
   v
Validate Minimally

Different credential types should remain clearly separated:

Password
   !=
NT Hash
   !=
NetNTLMv2 Response
   !=
Kerberos Key
   !=
Kerberos Ticket
   !=
Certificate
   !=
Private Key

Even though several of them may ultimately provide authentication capability.

The Active Directory credential-access landscape can be visualised as:

                   Active Directory
                          |
        +-----------------+-----------------+
        |                 |                 |
        v                 v                 v
     Directory          SYSVOL          Endpoints
        |                 |                 |
        v                 v                 v
      LAPS              GPP              LSASS
      gMSA              Scripts           SAM
    DCSync              Config            DPAPI
 Key Credentials                         Secrets
        |
        +-----------------+-----------------+
                          |
                          v
                  Credential Material
                          |
                          v
                     Authentication
                          |
                          v
                  Effective Privilege

For penetration testing:

Credential Source
       |
       v
Can I Access It?
       |
       +--> No
       |     |
       |     v
       |   Document Boundary
       |
       +--> Yes
             |
             v
      Can I Prove It Safely?
             |
             +--> Yes
             |     |
             |     v
             |   Minimum Evidence
             |
             +--> No
                   |
                   v
             Stop and Document

For defenders:

Where Are Credentials Stored?
        |
        v
Who Can Read Them?
        |
        v
Who Can Modify Authentication?
        |
        v
Where Are Privileged Users Logging On?
        |
        v
Can Credential Access Be Detected?
        |
        v
Can Compromised Credentials Be Rotated Quickly?

The strongest defensive strategy combines:

Least Privilege
      +
Managed Credentials
      +
Administrative Tiering
      +
Credential Guard
      +
LSA Protection
      +
Strong Kerberos Configuration
      +
Reduced NTLM
      +
Protected Backups
      +
Directory Auditing
      +
Endpoint Detection

Credential Access should ultimately be analysed as part of the complete Active Directory attack graph:

Identity
   |
   v
Credential
   |
   v
Identity
   |
   v
Privilege
   |
   v
Credential
   |
   v
Higher Privilege

Breaking any link in that chain can prevent a small credential exposure from becoming domain compromise.

docs.title: Active Directory DCOM - Remote Administration and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM) is Microsoft's technology for allowing Component Object Model (COM) objects to communicate across process and network boundaries.

DCOM is used by legitimate Windows components and management technologies for:

Remote Administration
Distributed Applications
Management Services
Enterprise Software
WMI
Microsoft Management Console
Application Automation
RPC-Based Communication

During an Active Directory security assessment, DCOM is important because an identity with sufficient remote permissions may be able to activate or interact with COM objects on another Windows system.

Some COM objects expose methods that can indirectly start processes or applications.

The resulting relationship can become:

Compromised Identity
        |
        v
Remote DCOM Access
        |
        v
Remote COM Object
        |
        v
Exposed Method
        |
        v
Process / Application
        |
        v
Target System

DCOM should therefore be understood as a legitimate Windows infrastructure technology that can become a lateral-movement mechanism when combined with excessive privileges and network reachability.

Authorised testing only

DCOM can invoke functionality on remote Windows systems and may create processes or applications. Begin with configuration and permission review. Only perform remote activation or execution testing against systems explicitly included in the assessment scope, and stop after sufficient evidence has been collected.

docs.title: DCOM at a Glance
docs.text:
The basic architecture is:

Client
  |
  v
COM Request
  |
  v
RPC
  |
  v
DCOM
  |
  v
Remote COM Object
  |
  v
Windows Component

From a lateral-movement perspective:

Identity
   |
   v
Network Reachability
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
DCOM Permissions
   |
   v
Remote Activation
   |
   v
COM Method
   |
   v
Remote Action

docs.title: COM
docs.text:
COM stands for:

Component Object Model

COM allows software components to expose:

Objects
Interfaces
Methods
Properties

to other applications.

Conceptually:

Application
    |
    v
COM Object
    |
    +--> Method A
    +--> Method B
    +--> Property A

docs.title: DCOM
docs.text:
DCOM extends COM across machine boundaries.

Conceptually:

COM
 |
 v
Local Component Interaction

becomes:

DCOM
 |
 v
Remote Component Interaction

docs.title: COM vs DCOM
docs.text:
A useful distinction is:

COM
=
Component interaction

while:

DCOM
=
Distributed COM interaction over RPC

A COM object may support local activation without being remotely usable through DCOM.

docs.title: DCOM and Active Directory
docs.text:
DCOM is not an Active Directory protocol itself.

However, in domain environments it frequently relies on:

Domain Identities
Kerberos
NTLM
Windows Groups
Local Administrators
Group Policy
RPC

This makes it relevant to Active Directory lateral movement.

docs.title: DCOM and RPC
docs.text:
DCOM uses:

RPC

for remote communication.

A simplified network flow is:

Client
  |
  v
TCP 135
  |
  v
RPC Endpoint Mapper
  |
  v
Dynamic RPC Port
  |
  v
DCOM Server

docs.title: TCP 135
docs.text:
The RPC Endpoint Mapper commonly listens on:

135/TCP

Test from Windows:

Test-NetConnection srv01.corp.example -Port 135

From Linux:

nmap -Pn -p135 srv01.corp.example

docs.title: TCP 135 Does Not Prove DCOM Access
docs.text:
An open:

135/TCP

only indicates that the RPC Endpoint Mapper is reachable.

Successful DCOM interaction still depends on:

Dynamic RPC Reachability
Authentication
Launch Permissions
Activation Permissions
Access Permissions
Object Availability
Object-Specific Security

docs.title: Dynamic RPC
docs.text:
After contacting the RPC Endpoint Mapper, the client may be directed to another TCP port.

Conceptually:

Client
  |
  v
135/TCP
  |
  v
Endpoint Mapper
  |
  v
Dynamic Port
  |
  v
Remote COM Server

This is why allowing only:

135/TCP

is generally insufficient for full DCOM functionality.

docs.title: DCOM Authentication
docs.text:
DCOM uses Windows authentication.

Depending on the environment, authentication may involve:

Kerberos
NTLM

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
In a properly functioning domain environment:

Domain Identity
      |
      v
Kerberos
      |
      v
RPC / DCOM
      |
      v
Remote Host

may be used.

Correct:

DNS
SPNs
Time Synchronisation
Domain Trust

remain important.

docs.title: NTLM
docs.text:
Where Kerberos cannot be used and NTLM remains available:

Identity
   |
   v
NTLM
   |
   v
RPC / DCOM

may occur.

This makes DCOM relevant to broader:

NTLM Reduction
Credential Reuse
Pass-the-Hash
Lateral Movement

analysis.

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Hostnames vs IP Addresses
docs.text:
When Kerberos is expected, prefer:

srv01.corp.example

instead of:

10.10.10.25

Using an IP address can alter authentication behaviour because Kerberos normally depends on service names rather than raw IP addresses.

docs.title: DCOM Security
docs.text:
DCOM access is controlled through several permission categories.

Important concepts include:

Access Permissions
Launch Permissions
Activation Permissions

docs.title: Remote Access
docs.text:
Remote Access determines whether a principal can access a running COM server remotely.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Remote Access Permission
 |
 v
Running COM Object

docs.title: Remote Launch
docs.text:
Remote Launch determines whether a principal can remotely start the COM server.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Remote Launch
 |
 v
COM Server Starts

docs.title: Remote Activation
docs.text:
Remote Activation determines whether a principal can remotely activate a COM object.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Remote Activation
 |
 v
COM Object Instance

docs.title: Permission Model
docs.text:
The effective DCOM path can therefore resemble:

Identity
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Remote Launch
   |
   v
Remote Activation
   |
   v
Remote Access
   |
   v
COM Object

Object-specific security can add further restrictions.

docs.title: Local Administrators
docs.text:
Members of:

Administrators

typically have broad remote management capabilities.

A compromised account with local administrator rights on another Windows host should therefore be evaluated for multiple lateral-movement mechanisms, including:

SMB
WinRM
WMI
DCOM
RDP

depending on network and system configuration.

docs.title: DCOM Is Not the Root Cause
docs.text:
If a domain group has:

Local Administrator

rights across hundreds of servers, the primary issue is usually:

Excessive Administrative Privilege

rather than:

DCOM Exists

DCOM is one mechanism through which that privilege may be exercised.

docs.title: DCOM Configuration
docs.text:
Windows provides:

Component Services

for viewing COM and DCOM configuration.

The graphical path is commonly:

Component Services
  |
  v
Computers
  |
  v
My Computer
  |
  v
DCOM Config

docs.title: DCOMCNFG
docs.text:
The Component Services interface can be opened with:

dcomcnfg.exe

During an assessment, use it for inspection rather than modifying permissions.

docs.title: Registry Locations
docs.text:
COM and DCOM registrations are represented in the Windows Registry.

Important areas include:

HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\CLSID
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Classes\CLSID
HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\AppID
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Classes\AppID

docs.title: CLSID
docs.text:
A:

CLSID

identifies a COM class.

Example format:

{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}

The actual value uniquely identifies a registered COM class.

docs.title: AppID
docs.text:
An:

AppID

can associate COM classes with configuration including DCOM security settings.

Conceptually:

CLSID
  |
  v
COM Class
  |
  v
AppID
  |
  v
DCOM Configuration

docs.title: Enumerate COM Registrations
docs.text:
PowerShell can inspect registered COM classes through the Registry.

Example:

Get-ChildItem 'Registry::HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\CLSID' |
    Select-Object -First 20

This is local enumeration.

Do not treat every registered COM class as remotely exploitable.

docs.title: Why COM Enumeration Is Difficult
docs.text:
Windows contains a very large number of COM registrations.

Most are:

Not Useful for Remote Execution
Not Remotely Activatable
Restricted
Application-Specific
Version-Specific

Therefore:

Enumerate Every CLSID

is usually less useful than:

Understand the Target
Review Permissions
Identify Known Administrative Components
Validate Only Relevant Objects

docs.title: DCOM Lateral Movement
docs.text:
DCOM lateral movement generally requires:

Valid Credential
      +
Network Reachability
      +
Remote DCOM Permissions
      +
Suitable COM Object

Conceptually:

Credential
   |
   v
Remote Authentication
   |
   v
DCOM
   |
   v
COM Object
   |
   v
Execution-Capable Method

docs.title: Commonly Discussed DCOM Objects
docs.text:
Security research has historically identified several COM objects that can expose methods useful for remote execution in certain Windows versions and configurations.

Examples include objects associated with:

MMC20.Application
ShellWindows
ShellBrowserWindow

Availability and behaviour can vary significantly between:

Windows Versions
Desktop vs Server
Installed Components
Session State
Security Configuration

Do not assume that an object documented in an old technique is present or remotely usable on a current target.

docs.title: MMC20.Application
docs.text:
One historically well-known DCOM lateral-movement technique uses:

MMC20.Application

The conceptual chain is:

Remote DCOM
    |
    v
MMC20.Application
    |
    v
Document.ActiveView
    |
    v
ExecuteShellCommand
    |
    v
Process

This technique should only be validated where remote execution testing is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: PowerShell DCOM Object Creation
docs.text:
PowerShell can request a COM object on another system using the .NET System.Activator class.

Conceptually:

Get COM Type
      |
      v
Remote Activator
      |
      v
COM Instance

A common pattern is:

$type = [type]::GetTypeFromProgID('MMC20.Application', 'srv01.corp.example')

Then:

$object = [Activator]::CreateInstance($type)

This attempts remote activation.

Do not invoke execution-capable methods unless required by the approved test plan.

docs.title: Safe DCOM Validation
docs.text:
A safe sequence is:

Confirm RPC Reachability
        |
        v
Confirm Identity
        |
        v
Attempt Remote Object Activation
        |
        v
Determine Whether Activation Succeeds
        |
        v
Stop if Evidence Is Sufficient

Remote object activation itself may already demonstrate excessive DCOM permissions.

docs.title: Execution Validation
docs.text:
If command execution must specifically be proven, use a harmless command.

For example, in an authorised lab:

cmd.exe /c echo authorised-dcom-test > C:\Windows\Temp\dcom-test.txt

Do not use:

Reverse Shell
Credential Dumper
Security-Control Disablement
Persistence Payload

when a harmless marker provides sufficient evidence.

docs.title: MMC ExecuteShellCommand
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised, the relevant MMC object exposes functionality conceptually similar to:

Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand

A lab-only PowerShell example is:

$type = [type]::GetTypeFromProgID('MMC20.Application', 'srv01.corp.example')
$object = [Activator]::CreateInstance($type)
$object.Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand(
    'cmd.exe',
    $null,
    '/c echo authorised-dcom-test > C:\Windows\Temp\dcom-test.txt',
    '7'
)

This changes the target by creating a process and marker file.

Use only when remote execution validation is explicitly required.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Where authorised administrative SMB access exists:

Remove-Item '\\srv01.corp.example\C$\Windows\Temp\dcom-test.txt'

Do not assume failure to access:

C$

means the DCOM execution failed.

SMB and DCOM have separate network and authorisation requirements.

docs.title: Why DCOM May Be Non-Interactive
docs.text:
DCOM execution generally does not provide:

Interactive Shell

by itself.

The model is closer to:

Remote Method
     |
     v
Remote Process

Tooling may add command-output handling around this mechanism.

docs.title: Impacket DCOMExec
docs.text:
Impacket provides:

dcomexec

for authorised DCOM-based remote execution testing.

Check current syntax:

impacket-dcomexec -h

Depending on installation, the script may also be available as:

dcomexec.py

docs.title: DCOMExec Password Authentication
docs.text:
For an approved test account:

impacket-dcomexec 'CORP/audit-admin:PASSWORD@srv01.corp.example'

Avoid placing production credentials directly in shell history where possible.

docs.title: DCOMExec Pass-the-Hash
docs.text:
Where pass-the-hash testing is explicitly authorised:

impacket-dcomexec -hashes ':NTHASH' 'CORP/audit-admin@srv01.corp.example'

See:

Pass-the-Hash

docs.title: DCOMExec Authentication Model
docs.text:
Credential
   |
   +--> Password
   |
   +--> NTLM Hash
   |
   +--> Kerberos where supported/configured
   |
   v
DCOM
   |
   v
Remote COM Object
   |
   v
Command Execution

Always verify options against:

impacket-dcomexec -h

because tool syntax can change.

docs.title: DCOMExec Object Selection
docs.text:
Impacket's DCOMExec implementation can support different DCOM object approaches depending on the installed version.

Do not assume an older object's availability.

Review:

impacket-dcomexec -h

before testing.

docs.title: Pass-the-Hash with DCOM
docs.text:
If NTLM is available and the account has sufficient remote rights:

NTLM Hash
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    v
DCOM
    |
    v
Remote Object
    |
    v
Remote Execution

may be possible.

The underlying security weakness may be:

Reusable Administrative Credential

rather than DCOM itself.

docs.title: Local Administrator Reuse
docs.text:
Example:

WS01
 |
 v
Local Administrator Hash
 |
 v
Same Credential on WS02
 |
 v
DCOM
 |
 v
Remote Execution

This is another reason to deploy:

Windows LAPS

See:

LAPS

docs.title: DCOM and Kerberos
docs.text:
Where Kerberos authentication is supported by the client and environment, ensure:

DNS
Time
Domain
SPNs
Credential Cache

are correct.

Linux:

klist

Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

docs.title: DCOM vs WMI
docs.text:
WMI commonly uses DCOM for traditional remote communication.

The relationship is:

WMI
 |
 v
DCOM
 |
 v
RPC

But DCOM can expose many COM objects unrelated to WMI.

Therefore:

WMI Lateral Movement

and:

DCOM Lateral Movement

are related but distinct.

See:

WMI

docs.title: DCOM vs SMB
docs.text:
SMB lateral movement commonly involves:

445/TCP
Administrative Shares
Named Pipes
Service Control Manager

DCOM commonly involves:

135/TCP
Dynamic RPC
Remote COM Activation

See:

SMB

docs.title: DCOM vs WinRM
docs.text:
WinRM:

5985 / 5986
      |
      v
WS-Management
      |
      v
PowerShell Remoting

DCOM:

135 + Dynamic RPC
      |
      v
RPC
      |
      v
Remote COM

See:

WinRM

docs.title: DCOM vs PsExec
docs.text:
PsExec-style execution:

SMB
 |
 v
ADMIN$
 |
 v
Service Control Manager
 |
 v
Temporary Service

DCOM execution:

RPC
 |
 v
DCOM
 |
 v
COM Object
 |
 v
Method
 |
 v
Process

docs.title: DCOM vs WMIExec
docs.text:
WMIExec:

RPC / DCOM
      |
      v
WMI
      |
      v
Win32_Process

DCOMExec:

RPC / DCOM
      |
      v
COM Application
      |
      v
Application-Specific Method

Both may ultimately create remote processes, but the execution path differs.

docs.title: DCOM vs RDP
docs.text:
DCOM:

Remote Object Invocation
Non-Interactive
RPC-Based

RDP:

Interactive Desktop
GUI Session
3389/TCP

For simple execution validation, creating an interactive desktop session is often unnecessary.

docs.title: DCOM and Microsoft Management Console
docs.text:
Microsoft Management Console:

MMC

is used by many Windows administrative tools.

Examples include:

Computer Management
Event Viewer
Services
Certificates
Group Policy

The existence of MMC-related COM components is therefore expected.

The security concern arises when:

Remote Activation
+
Execution-Capable Method
+
Excessive Privilege

are combined.

docs.title: DCOM and Office
docs.text:
COM automation is also heavily used by Microsoft Office and other desktop applications.

Do not treat:

Office COM Object Exists

as evidence of a lateral-movement path.

Remote usability depends on:

Object Registration
Remote Activation
Session Context
Permissions
Application Behaviour
Windows Version

docs.title: DCOM and Server Core
docs.text:
Some COM-based lateral-movement techniques depend on components that may not exist on:

Server Core

or may behave differently from full desktop installations.

Always validate the actual environment.

docs.title: Version Dependence
docs.text:
DCOM techniques can be highly:

Version Dependent

A method that works on:

Windows 10

may not behave identically on:

Windows 11
Windows Server 2022
Windows Server 2025

or later releases.

Do not build findings around assumptions from old offensive-security documentation.

docs.title: Object Availability
docs.text:
Before considering an object useful, establish:

Is It Registered?

Can It Be Remotely Activated?

Does the Identity Have Permission?

Does the Required Method Exist?

Does the Method Behave as Expected?

Is the Technique Necessary to Prove the Finding?

docs.title: DCOM Network Exposure
docs.text:
A weak network model may allow:

Any Workstation
      |
      v
RPC / DCOM
      |
      v
Every Server

A stronger design may restrict:

Privileged Admin Workstation
          |
          v
Management Network
          |
          v
RPC / DCOM
          |
          v
Managed Server

docs.title: Workstation-to-Workstation DCOM
docs.text:
Where not operationally required:

WS01
 |
 v
DCOM
 |
 v
WS02

should be restricted.

This can reduce lateral-movement opportunities after endpoint compromise.

docs.title: Windows Firewall
docs.text:
Windows Firewall should be used to restrict remote administration.

During an assessment, inspect existing firewall rules rather than enabling new ones.

Example:

Get-NetFirewallRule |
    Where-Object Enabled -EQ 'True' |
    Select-Object DisplayName,Direction,Action

Filter as needed for the specific RPC/DCOM service under review.

docs.title: Remote Address Restrictions
docs.text:
Firewall rules should ideally limit management traffic to approved source systems.

Review:

RemoteAddress

rather than checking only:

Enabled

docs.title: Do Not Enable DCOM for Testing
docs.text:
Do not modify DCOM settings merely to demonstrate a technique.

If DCOM is disabled or restricted:

The Control Is Working

and that should form part of the assessment evidence.

docs.title: DCOM Hardening
docs.text:
A practical DCOM hardening strategy includes:

Restrict RPC Network Exposure
Apply Least Privilege
Restrict Remote Launch
Restrict Remote Activation
Restrict Remote Access
Reduce Local Administrators
Deploy Windows LAPS
Separate Administrative Identities
Use Privileged Administrative Workstations
Reduce NTLM
Monitor RPC and DCOM
Use EDR
Use Application Control

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Review which principals genuinely require:

Remote Access
Remote Launch
Remote Activation

Remove unnecessary rights.

docs.title: Administrative Group Review
docs.text:
Review:

Local Administrators
Server Administrator Groups
Helpdesk Groups
Application Support Groups
Service Accounts

for unnecessary administrative rights across large numbers of systems.

docs.title: Windows LAPS
docs.text:
Unique local administrator credentials reduce the ability to reuse credentials for DCOM lateral movement.

See:

LAPS

docs.title: Reduce NTLM
docs.text:
Where possible:

Prefer Kerberos
Reduce NTLM

as part of a broader domain-hardening programme.

See:

NTLM

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Restrict RPC/DCOM traffic between security zones.

Examples:

User VLAN
   |
   X
   |
   v
Server Management RPC

while allowing:

Management VLAN
      |
      v
Server Management RPC

where required.

docs.title: Privileged Access Workstations
docs.text:
A mature administrative model can use:

Privileged Identity
       |
       v
Privileged Access Workstation
       |
       v
Management Network
       |
       v
DCOM
       |
       v
Managed System

docs.title: DCOM Hardening Changes
docs.text:
Microsoft has strengthened DCOM authentication requirements through modern Windows security updates.

Modern supported Windows systems enforce stronger DCOM authentication behaviour than older legacy environments.

This means historical DCOM techniques should not automatically be assumed to behave identically on current Windows versions.

Keep systems fully patched and validate legacy application compatibility before changing DCOM security configuration.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Application control technologies such as:

WDAC
AppLocker

can limit what processes may execute after a remote management mechanism is abused.

This provides another security boundary after remote access.

docs.title: EDR
docs.text:
Modern endpoint security products can observe:

RPC Connections
COM Activation
Parent-Child Process Relationships
Command Lines
Authentication
Network Connections

DCOM should not be considered an invisible lateral-movement technique.

docs.title: DCOM Detection
docs.text:
Detection should combine:

Authentication
RPC Network Activity
COM Activation
Process Creation
Source System
Account
Target

rather than relying on a single event.

docs.title: Authentication Events
docs.text:
Relevant Security events may include:

4624
4625
4648
4672

depending on the authentication workflow.

docs.title: Network Logon
docs.text:
Remote DCOM authentication commonly results in:

Logon Type 3

network authentication.

docs.title: Kerberos Events
docs.text:
Where Kerberos is used:

4768
4769
4771

can provide useful context.

docs.title: NTLM Events
docs.text:
Where NTLM is used:

4776

and NTLM Operational logging can provide additional visibility.

docs.title: Process Creation
docs.text:
If a DCOM object launches a process:

4688

may provide useful evidence where process creation auditing is enabled.

docs.title: Parent Process
docs.text:
The parent process depends on:

COM Object
COM Server
Activation Model
Windows Version

Do not create a detection rule that assumes all DCOM execution has the same parent process.

docs.title: MMC-Based DCOM Detection
docs.text:
For MMC-based techniques, investigate unusual relationships involving:

mmc.exe

followed by unexpected child processes.

Conceptually:

Remote DCOM
    |
    v
mmc.exe
    |
    v
cmd.exe / powershell.exe / other process

The exact behaviour should be validated against the organisation's Windows versions.

docs.title: Suspicious Child Processes
docs.text:
Examples requiring investigation can include administrative COM server processes launching:

cmd.exe
powershell.exe
wscript.exe
cscript.exe
rundll32.exe

when that behaviour is unusual for the environment.

These executables are legitimate Windows components and should not be treated as malicious solely by name.

docs.title: RPC Network Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

135/TCP

and dynamic RPC connections.

High-value questions include:

Which Source Initiated the Connection?

Is It an Approved Management System?

Which Account Authenticated?

What Process Followed the Connection?

docs.title: High Fan-Out DCOM
docs.text:
Example:

docs.title: Reporting DCOM Findings
docs.text:
Do not report:

DCOM Enabled

or:

TCP 135 Open

as vulnerabilities by themselves.

Report the actual weakness.

Examples:

Standard User Has Excessive Remote DCOM Rights

Shared Local Administrator Credentials Permit DCOM Lateral Movement

RPC/DCOM Management Interfaces Are Exposed to Standard Workstation Networks

Broad Administrative Group Membership Enables Remote DCOM Execution

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive DCOM Rights
docs.text:
Finding:
Domain Account Has Unnecessary Remote DCOM Execution Rights

Description:
The tested domain account was able to remotely activate a DCOM object
on SRV01 and invoke functionality capable of starting a process.

The account's documented role did not require remote administration of
the affected server.

A harmless command was used to validate the execution capability. No
credentials were collected and no persistence was created.

Impact:
Compromise of the affected account could allow an attacker to remotely
execute commands on SRV01 through legitimate Windows DCOM
functionality.

This provides a lateral-movement path and may expose additional systems
or credentials depending on the server's role.

Recommendation:
Review local administrative membership and DCOM access, launch and
activation permissions.

Remove unnecessary remote-management rights and restrict RPC/DCOM
network access to approved management systems.

docs.title: Example Finding - Broad RPC/DCOM Exposure
docs.text:
Finding:
RPC/DCOM Administrative Interfaces Reachable from Standard Workstations

Description:
Standard workstation networks were able to reach RPC/DCOM services on
multiple Windows servers.

Although authentication and authorisation are still required, the
network design exposes remote-management functionality directly to
lower-trust workstation systems.

Impact:
If a workstation and suitable administrative credential are
compromised, an attacker may have a direct network path for DCOM, WMI
or other RPC-based lateral-movement techniques.

Recommendation:
Restrict RPC/DCOM management traffic using network and host firewalls.

Permit remote administrative traffic only from approved jump hosts,
management servers and privileged administrative workstations where
operationally possible.

docs.title: Example Finding - Shared Administrator Credential
docs.text:
Finding:
Shared Local Administrator Credential Enables DCOM Lateral Movement

Description:
The same local administrator credential was valid on multiple Windows
systems.

The credential provided sufficient remote administrative rights to
activate DCOM functionality on more than one approved test system.

Impact:
Compromise of one affected endpoint may expose a reusable
administrative credential capable of providing lateral movement to
additional systems.

Recommendation:
Deploy Windows LAPS or an equivalent centrally managed solution to
provide unique local administrator passwords.

Restrict peer-to-peer RPC/DCOM administration and monitor remote
administrative activity.

docs.title: Example Finding - Broad Administrative Group
docs.text:
Finding:
Broad Domain Group Has Local Administrator Rights Across Servers

Description:
A domain group containing a large number of users was configured as a
local administrator across multiple Windows servers.

The resulting rights allowed members of the group to use remote
administration mechanisms including DCOM where network access was
available.

Impact:
Compromise of any group member could provide administrative access to
multiple servers and significantly increase the lateral-movement blast
radius.

Recommendation:
Remove broad groups from local Administrators and replace them with
role-specific administrative groups.

Apply administrative tiering and restrict privileged remote access to
dedicated management systems.

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
DCOM is a legitimate Windows technology.

Its existence is not a vulnerability.

The important questions are:

Who Can Reach RPC/DCOM?

Who Can Authenticate?

Who Has Remote Access?

Who Has Remote Launch?

Who Has Remote Activation?

Which COM Objects Are Available?

Can Those Objects Perform Security-Sensitive Actions?

Is That Administrative Relationship Required?

The preferred assessment sequence is:

Discover RPC
     |
     v
Determine Identity
     |
     v
Review Administrative Rights
     |
     v
Review DCOM Permissions
     |
     v
Identify Relevant Object
     |
     v
Minimal Activation
     |
     v
Minimal Execution if Required
     |
     v
Evidence
     |
     v
Cleanup

Do not move directly from:

135/TCP Open

to:

Remote Execution

An open RPC Endpoint Mapper is not proof of a DCOM vulnerability.

Likewise:

DCOM Enabled

does not mean:

DCOM Vulnerability

The actual weakness is more likely to be:

Excessive Administrative Rights

or:

Reusable Credentials

or:

Overly Broad DCOM Permissions

or:

Unnecessary RPC Network Exposure

When remote execution testing is necessary:

Use Minimum Impact

and stop when:

Security Impact Is Proven

A mature architecture should aim for:

Approved Administrative Identity
           |
           v
Hardened Administrative Workstation
           |
           v
Restricted Management Network
           |
           v
RPC / DCOM
           |
           v
Approved Managed System

rather than:

Any Compromised Workstation
          |
          v
RPC / DCOM
          |
          v
Every Windows Server

DCOM should therefore be viewed as:

Legitimate Remote Management
            +
Excessive Privilege
            +
Unrestricted Network Path
            =
Potential Lateral Movement

The next page moves from individual remote-management protocols to moving traffic through segmented networks:

Pivoting

docs.title: Active Directory Enumeration
docs.text:
Active Directory enumeration is the process of discovering and mapping the identities, computers, services, permissions, authentication mechanisms, trust relationships, and infrastructure that make up an Active Directory environment.

Enumeration should answer questions such as:

What domain am I connected to?

Where are the Domain Controllers?

Which users and groups exist?

Which accounts are privileged?

Which computers and servers exist?

Which accounts run services?

Which shares are accessible?

Which accounts have administrative access?

Which Kerberos configurations are security-relevant?

Which ACLs create control relationships?

Which GPOs exist?

Which trusts connect the domain to other domains?

Is AD CS deployed?

Which systems expose management protocols?

What relationships create attack paths?

Active Directory enumeration should not be treated as:

Run BloodHound
Run NetExec
Done

A better model is:

Network
   |
   v
Domain
   |
   v
Directory
   |
   +--> Users
   +--> Groups
   +--> Computers
   +--> OUs
   +--> GPOs
   +--> SPNs
   +--> Delegation
   +--> ACLs
   +--> Trusts
   +--> AD CS
   |
   v
Host Relationships
   |
   +--> Shares
   +--> Sessions
   +--> Local Administrators
   +--> Remote Management
   |
   v
Attack Graph

docs.title: Authorised Testing
docs.text:
These techniques are intended for:

Authorised penetration testing
Internal security assessments
Red team exercises
Purple team exercises
Training laboratories
CTFs
Security research

Enumeration can still create substantial security telemetry.

Activities such as:

Large LDAP queries
Large SMB sweeps
User enumeration
Kerberos ticket requests
Session enumeration
Remote registry queries
BloodHound collection
Password policy enumeration

may be detected.

Start with the least intrusive techniques and expand deliberately.

docs.title: Enumeration Philosophy
docs.text:
The objective is not to collect the largest possible amount of data.

The objective is to collect information that helps answer:

Where am I?

Who am I?

What exists?

What can I access?

What does my identity control?

What trusts my identity?

Where are privileged identities?

What security relationships connect these objects?

Use:

Discovery
   |
   v
Focused Enumeration
   |
   v
Relationship Analysis
   |
   v
Attack Path Identification
   |
   v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Keep an Enumeration Notebook
docs.text:
Record important environment information as it is discovered.

Example:

DOMAIN=example.local
NETBIOS=EXAMPLE

DC01=dc01.example.local
DC01_IP=10.10.20.10

DC02=dc02.example.local
DC02_IP=10.10.20.11

For shell usage:

export DOMAIN="example.local"
export DC="dc01.example.local"
export DCIP="10.10.20.10"
export USER="alice"

Avoid putting plaintext passwords directly into shell history where possible.

docs.title: Phase 3 - DNS Enumeration
docs.text:
DNS is one of the most important sources of AD infrastructure information.

Active Directory relies heavily on SRV records.

docs.title: Identify DNS Server
docs.text:
Linux:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Windows:

ipconfig /all

PowerShell:

Get-DnsClientServerAddress

docs.title: Query Domain
docs.text:
dig "$DOMAIN"

Nameservers:

dig NS "$DOMAIN"

docs.title: Locate Domain Controllers
docs.text: dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.$DOMAIN

docs.title: Locate Kerberos
docs.text: dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.$DOMAIN

docs.title: Global Catalog
docs.text: dig SRV _gc._tcp.$DOMAIN

docs.title: Kerberos Password Service
docs.text: dig SRV _kpasswd._tcp.$DOMAIN

docs.title: Windows DNS Queries
docs.text:
nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

Kerberos:

nslookup -type=SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

docs.title: PowerShell DNS
docs.text: Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

docs.title: Phase 4 - Domain Controller Identification
docs.text:
A Domain Controller commonly exposes:

53    DNS
88    Kerberos
135   RPC
389   LDAP
445   SMB
464   Kerberos password operations
636   LDAPS
3268  Global Catalog
3269  Global Catalog TLS

Do not identify a Domain Controller solely from one open port.

Combine:

DNS
LDAP
SMB metadata
Kerberos
RPC

docs.title: Nmap - Focused DC Discovery
docs.text:
Where network scanning is authorised:

nmap -Pn -p 53,88,135,389,445,464,636,3268,3269 10.10.20.10

For a subnet:

nmap -Pn -p 88,389,445 10.10.20.0/24

Keep scan volume appropriate for the environment.

docs.title: Phase 5 - SMB Enumeration
docs.text:
SMB can reveal substantial information about Windows hosts.

Questions include:

Which hosts expose SMB?

What hostname is associated with the host?

What domain does the host belong to?

Is SMB signing required?

Which shares exist?

Can the current identity authenticate?

Where does the identity have administrative access?

docs.title: NetExec - SMB Discovery
docs.text:
Single host:

nxc smb 10.10.20.10

Subnet:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24

Typical output may help identify:

Hostname
Domain
Operating system information
SMB signing configuration
SMB version-related information

depending on the target and NetExec version.

docs.title: Save SMB Discovery
docs.text: nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 | tee smb-discovery.txt

docs.title: smbclient - List Shares
docs.text:
Anonymous, where permitted:

smbclient -L //10.10.20.10 -N

Authenticated:

smbclient -L //FILE01.example.local -U 'EXAMPLE/alice'

docs.title: NetExec - Authenticated SMB
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -p 'Password'

Avoid unnecessarily testing credentials across very large ranges.

docs.title: NetExec - NTLM Hash Authentication
docs.text:
Where authorised:

nxc smb FILE01.example.local \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -H '<NT-HASH>'

The presence of valid NTLM credential material does not automatically imply administrative access.

docs.title: Authentication State
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Host reachable
      |
      v
Authentication accepted
      |
      v
Resource accessible
      |
      v
Administrative access

These are not equivalent states.

docs.title: Phase 6 - LDAP Enumeration
docs.text:
LDAP provides direct access to Active Directory directory information.

Typical targets:

Users
Groups
Computers
OUs
SPNs
Delegation
GPOs
Trusts
ACL-related attributes
Certificate infrastructure

docs.title: LDAP RootDSE
docs.text:
Start with RootDSE.

ldapsearch -x \
  -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
  -s base \
  -b "" \
  defaultNamingContext \
  rootDomainNamingContext \
  configurationNamingContext \
  schemaNamingContext \
  dnsHostName

This can help determine the correct LDAP base DN.

For:

example.local

the base DN is normally:

DC=example,DC=local

docs.title: Authenticated ldapsearch
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x \
  -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
  -D 'alice@example.local' \
  -W \
  -b 'DC=example,DC=local'

Using -W avoids putting the password directly on the command line.

docs.title: Search Specific Object Classes
docs.text:
Users:

ldapsearch -x \
  -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
  -D 'alice@example.local' \
  -W \
  -b 'DC=example,DC=local' \
  '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \
  sAMAccountName

docs.title: Computers
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x \
  -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
  -D 'alice@example.local' \
  -W \
  -b 'DC=example,DC=local' \
  '(objectClass=computer)' \
  sAMAccountName dNSHostName operatingSystem

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x \
  -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
  -D 'alice@example.local' \
  -W \
  -b 'DC=example,DC=local' \
  '(objectClass=group)' \
  cn member

docs.title: Service Principal Names
docs.text:
ldapsearch -x \
  -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
  -D 'alice@example.local' \
  -W \
  -b 'DC=example,DC=local' \
  '(servicePrincipalName=*)' \
  sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName

An SPN does not automatically mean an account is exploitable.

docs.title: Phase 7 - RPC Enumeration
docs.text: RPC can provide identity and domain information depending on target configuration.

docs.title: rpcclient
docs.text:
Authenticated:

rpcclient -U 'EXAMPLE/alice' dc01.example.local

It will prompt for the password.

Useful interactive commands can include:

srvinfo
enumdomains
querydominfo
enumdomusers
enumdomgroups

Availability depends on the target and account permissions.

docs.title: Query Domain Information
docs.text:
Inside rpcclient:

querydominfo

Users:

enumdomusers

Groups:

enumdomgroups

docs.title: SID Enumeration with Impacket
docs.text:
Impacket includes lookupsid.py for SID/RID-based enumeration over DCE/RPC.

Example authenticated use:

lookupsid.py 'example.local/alice@dc01.example.local'

The tool will prompt for the password when required.

Depending on installation, the command may instead be exposed with an impacket- prefix:

impacket-lookupsid 'example.local/alice@dc01.example.local'

Check:

which lookupsid.py
which impacket-lookupsid

docs.title: Phase 8 - Enumerating Users
docs.text:
Users are one of the central AD object types.

Collect:

sAMAccountName
Display name
Description
Enabled/disabled state
Group membership
Password last set
Last logon information
SPNs
UserAccountControl
Delegation configuration

docs.title: Windows Native
docs.text:
net user /domain

Specific user:

net user alice /domain

docs.title: PowerShell AD Module
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Filter *

Selected properties:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties DisplayName,Description,Enabled,LastLogonDate,PasswordLastSet |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,DisplayName,Description,Enabled,LastLogonDate,PasswordLastSet

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
If PowerView is available in an authorised environment:

Get-DomainUser

Specific user:

Get-DomainUser -Identity alice

Useful fields may include:

samaccountname
memberof
serviceprincipalname
useraccountcontrol
description
pwdlastset
lastlogon

docs.title: NetExec User Enumeration
docs.text:
NetExec can query domain users through appropriate protocols.

For example, using LDAP:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -p 'Password' \
  --users

NetExec options can change between versions.

Confirm current syntax with:

nxc ldap --help

docs.title: Impacket GetADUsers
docs.text:
Impacket provides GetADUsers.py.

Example:

GetADUsers.py \
  -all \
  'example.local/alice' \
  -dc-ip 10.10.20.10

The tool can return information such as:

Username
Email
Password last set
Last logon

depending on directory data and options.

If installed through a distribution package, check whether it is exposed as:

impacket-GetADUsers

docs.title: User Descriptions
docs.text:
User descriptions are worth reviewing because administrators sometimes place operational information in them.

PowerShell:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description |
    Where-Object {$_.Description} |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,Description

Do not assume that a description containing a password-like string is valid.

Validate carefully and only when authorised.

docs.title: Disabled Accounts
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Filter 'Enabled -eq $false'

Disabled accounts may still matter for:

Historical privileges
ACL ownership
Group membership
Service configuration
Stale attack paths

docs.title: Recently Created Users
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties whenCreated |
    Sort-Object whenCreated -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 20 SamAccountName,whenCreated

This can help identify:

New service accounts
Temporary accounts
Recently provisioned administrators

It is not inherently evidence of a vulnerability.

docs.title: Password Never Expires
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties PasswordNeverExpires |
    Where-Object {$_.PasswordNeverExpires -eq $true} |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,Enabled

This is a configuration observation that requires context.

docs.title: Phase 9 - Enumerating Groups
docs.text: Groups frequently define effective privilege.

docs.title: Windows Native
docs.text:
net group /domain

Domain Admins:

net group "Domain Admins" /domain

Enterprise Admins:

net group "Enterprise Admins" /domain

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Get-ADGroup -Filter *

Group members:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins"

Recursive membership:

Get-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Recursive

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
Get-DomainGroup

Specific group:

Get-DomainGroup -Identity "Domain Admins"

Members:

Get-DomainGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins"

docs.title: Custom Privileged Groups
docs.text:
Do not inspect only:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Administrators

Search for organisational groups such as:

Server Admins
SQL Admins
SCCM Admins
VMware Admins
Backup Admins
Citrix Admins
Helpdesk
Application Admins
Tier 0
Infrastructure Admins

Privilege often exists outside default AD groups.

docs.title: Group Nesting
docs.text:
Example:

alice
  |
  v
Helpdesk
  |
  v
Server Support
  |
  v
Production Admins

Always evaluate nested group membership.

docs.title: Phase 10 - Enumerating Computers
docs.text:
Computer objects reveal the structure of the environment.

Collect:

Hostname
Operating system
Operating system version
OU
DNS hostname
Service Principal Names
Delegation configuration
Last logon

docs.title: Windows AD Module
docs.text:
Get-ADComputer -Filter *

With properties:

Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties OperatingSystem,OperatingSystemVersion,IPv4Address |
    Select-Object Name,DNSHostName,OperatingSystem,OperatingSystemVersion,IPv4Address

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
Get-DomainComputer

Operating systems:

Get-DomainComputer |
    Select-Object Name,DNSHostName,OperatingSystem

docs.title: Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Get-ADDomainController -Filter *

PowerView:

Get-DomainController

docs.title: Identify Servers
docs.text:
Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties OperatingSystem |
    Where-Object {$_.OperatingSystem -like "*Server*"} |
    Select-Object Name,OperatingSystem

docs.title: Identify Potential Legacy Systems
docs.text:
Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties OperatingSystem |
    Select-Object Name,OperatingSystem

Do not classify a host as vulnerable based solely on the OS string stored in AD.

Confirm the actual system and patch state separately.

docs.title: Phase 11 - Password Policy
docs.text:
Before any authorised password testing, understand the password and lockout policy.

Questions:

What is the lockout threshold?

What is the lockout duration?

What is the observation window?

What is the minimum password length?

What is the password history?

Are fine-grained password policies used?

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: net accounts /domain

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy

Fine-grained password policies:

Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Filter *

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
Depending on the current NetExec version and protocol, password-policy enumeration may be available.

Always check:

nxc smb --help

and:

nxc ldap --help

before relying on remembered option names.

docs.title: Password Policy Before Spraying
docs.text:
Never perform a password spray simply because:

Valid usernames discovered

First establish:

Rules of engagement
Lockout threshold
Lockout duration
Observation window
Monitoring concerns
Number of candidate accounts
Number of attempts

docs.title: Phase 12 - SPN Enumeration
docs.text:
Service Principal Names associate services with AD principals.

They are important for:

Service discovery
Service account identification
Kerberos analysis
Delegation analysis
Kerberoasting assessment

docs.title: Windows setspn
docs.text:
Query all SPNs:

setspn -Q */*

This can produce substantial output in large domains.

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties ServicePrincipalName |
    Where-Object {$_.ServicePrincipalName} |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,ServicePrincipalName

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text: Get-DomainUser -SPN

docs.title: Impacket GetUserSPNs
docs.text:
Enumeration:

GetUserSPNs.py \
  'example.local/alice' \
  -dc-ip 10.10.20.10

Depending on installation:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
  'example.local/alice' \
  -dc-ip 10.10.20.10

This can identify user accounts associated with SPNs.

Requesting service tickets for offline analysis is a separate testing step and will be covered in the Kerberoasting note.

docs.title: Important Distinction
docs.text:
SPN exists
   !=
Kerberoasting finding

A useful assessment also considers:

Account privilege
Password strength
Password age
Service role
Encryption configuration
Business impact

docs.title: Phase 13 - AS-REP Candidates
docs.text: Accounts configured without Kerberos pre-authentication are relevant to AS-REP roasting analysis.

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
The DONT_REQ_PREAUTH flag can be identified through UserAccountControl.

For example:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth |
    Where-Object {$_.DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true} |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,Enabled

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text: Get-DomainUser -PreauthNotRequired

docs.title: Enumeration vs Ticket Request
docs.text:
Keep these separate:

Identify account configuration
          |
          v
Candidate

versus:

Request AS-REP material
          |
          v
Active validation

The latter is covered in the dedicated AS-REP Roasting note.

docs.title: Phase 14 - Delegation Enumeration
docs.text:
Kerberos delegation should always be reviewed.

Important types:

Unconstrained Delegation
Constrained Delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: PowerShell - Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties TrustedForDelegation |
    Where-Object {$_.TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} |
    Select-Object Name

docs.title: User Accounts Trusted for Delegation
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties TrustedForDelegation |
    Where-Object {$_.TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} |
    Select-Object SamAccountName

docs.title: Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo |
    Where-Object {$_.'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo'} |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo'

Computers:

Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo |
    Where-Object {$_.'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo'} |
    Select-Object Name,'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo'

docs.title: PowerView Delegation Enumeration
docs.text:
Depending on PowerView version:

Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained

Constrained delegation can also be identified by examining:

msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo

docs.title: Impacket findDelegation
docs.text:
Impacket provides findDelegation.py for identifying delegation relationships.

Example:

findDelegation.py \
  'example.local/alice' \
  -dc-ip 10.10.20.10

Depending on installation:

impacket-findDelegation \
  'example.local/alice' \
  -dc-ip 10.10.20.10

The dedicated delegation notes will cover interpretation and validation.

docs.title: Phase 15 - Organisational Units
docs.text: OUs help reveal administrative structure.

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter *

Selected properties:

Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * |
    Select-Object Name,DistinguishedName

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text: Get-DomainOU

docs.title: Why OUs Matter
docs.text:
OUs can reveal:

Administrative boundaries
Server groups
Workstation groups
Privileged systems
Delegated permissions
GPO application

Example:

example.local
│
├── Domain Controllers
├── Servers
│   ├── Production
│   └── Development
├── Workstations
└── Users
    ├── Administrators
    └── Employees

docs.title: Phase 16 - Group Policy Enumeration
docs.text:
Group Policy can control security-sensitive configuration across many systems.

Enumerate:

GPO names
GUIDs
Links
Affected OUs
Permissions
SYSVOL content
Scripts
Preferences

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Get-GPO -All

Requires the GroupPolicy module.

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text: Get-DomainGPO

docs.title: GPO Links
docs.text:
PowerView can assist with understanding where GPOs apply.

The important relationship is:

GPO
 |
 v
Site / Domain / OU
 |
 v
Users / Computers

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
SYSVOL commonly contains:

Group Policy files
Scripts
Configuration
Policy data

Typical UNC path:

\\example.local\SYSVOL

List using:

dir \\example.local\SYSVOL

or:

smbclient //dc01.example.local/SYSVOL -U 'EXAMPLE/alice'

docs.title: Group Policy Preferences
docs.text:
Legacy Group Policy Preferences credential exposure should still be considered when reviewing older environments or historical SYSVOL content.

Search for files such as:

Groups.xml
Services.xml
Scheduledtasks.xml
DataSources.xml
Printers.xml
Drives.xml

A dedicated GPP note will cover the issue.

docs.title: Phase 17 - ACL Enumeration
docs.text:
ACL analysis identifies which principals can control AD objects.

Important permissions include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
WriteProperty
ForceChangePassword
AddMember
CreateChild
DeleteChild
Extended Rights

docs.title: PowerView ACL Enumeration
docs.text:
Get-DomainObjectAcl

Resolve GUIDs:

Get-DomainObjectAcl -ResolveGUIDs

Specific object:

Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity alice -ResolveGUIDs

docs.title: ACL Analysis Model
docs.text:
For every interesting ACE:

Principal
    |
    v
Permission
    |
    v
Target
    |
    v
Affected Attribute / Operation
    |
    v
Resulting Capability

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Helpdesk
    |
    | GenericWrite
    v
svc_backup

Do not stop at:

GenericWrite found

Determine exactly what effective capability the permission provides.

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Object ownership matters because owners may have the ability to alter permissions under applicable security semantics.

Track:

Owner
ACL
Inheritance
Explicit ACEs
Inherited ACEs

docs.title: Phase 18 - Trust Enumeration
docs.text:
Trusts connect domains and forests.

Determine:

Trust partner
Direction
Type
Transitivity
Forest relationship
SID filtering
Selective authentication

docs.title: nltest
docs.text: nltest /domain_trusts

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text: Get-ADTrust -Filter *

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
Get-DomainTrust

Forest information:

Get-Forest

docs.title: Trust Direction
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Domain A
   |
   | Trust
   v
Domain B

Always determine:

Who trusts whom?

A trust existing does not automatically mean useful access exists across it.

docs.title: Phase 19 - SMB Share Enumeration
docs.text: Shares can expose sensitive operational information.

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
nxc smb FILE01.example.local \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -p 'Password' \
  --shares

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
smbclient -L //FILE01.example.local -U 'EXAMPLE/alice'

Connect:

smbclient //FILE01.example.local/Share -U 'EXAMPLE/alice'

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: net view \\FILE01

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
Get-SmbShare

Get-SmbShare enumerates shares on the local system unless remote management or another mechanism is used to query a remote host.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
Deployment scripts
Configuration
Backups
Password databases
Private keys
Certificates
Source code
Database backups
Administrative scripts
Unattended installation files
Remote desktop files
Documentation containing credentials

docs.title: Share Permissions
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Share exists

from:

Can list
Can read
Can write
Can modify

Writable shares may be particularly security-sensitive depending on how their contents are consumed.

docs.title: Phase 20 - Session Enumeration
docs.text:
Sessions help identify where users are currently or recently authenticated.

This matters because:

Privileged User
      |
      v
Session on Server
      |
      v
Server Compromise
      |
      v
Potential Credential / Token Exposure

Session data should be treated carefully because visibility varies by Windows version, permissions, EDR controls, and collection technique.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound collectors can gather certain session and local privilege relationships where permitted and technically available.

Treat session information as time-sensitive.

A session discovered ten minutes ago may no longer exist.

docs.title: Native Windows
docs.text:
Current local users:

query user

or:

quser

These commands describe sessions on the queried Windows system and require appropriate access for remote use.

docs.title: Phase 21 - Local Administrator Relationships
docs.text:
One of the most valuable questions is:

Where is my current identity an administrator?

This relationship can turn:

One Credential

into:

Many Hosts

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
Focused example:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -p 'Password'

Interpret the output carefully.

Authentication success and administrative access are different.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can model relationships such as:

AdminTo
CanRDP
CanPSRemote

depending on collected data.

Validate important relationships manually.

docs.title: Phase 22 - Remote Management Exposure
docs.text:
Enumerate management protocols such as:

SMB
WinRM
RDP
WMI
DCOM
SSH
MSSQL

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
Common ports:

5985
5986

Nmap:

nmap -Pn -p 5985,5986 10.10.20.0/24

docs.title: RDP
docs.text: nmap -Pn -p 3389 10.10.20.0/24

docs.title: MSSQL
docs.text: nmap -Pn -p 1433 10.10.20.0/24

docs.title: Management Protocol Matrix
docs.text:
Maintain:

Host SMB WinRM RDP MSSQL Notes DC01 Yes Yes Yes No Domain Controller FILE01 Yes Yes Yes No File server SQL01 Yes Yes Yes Yes Database server

This becomes useful later during lateral movement.

docs.title: Phase 23 - LAPS Enumeration
docs.text:
If LAPS is deployed, determine:

Which systems use LAPS?

Which implementation is deployed?

Who can read managed passwords?

Are permissions appropriately restricted?

The objective at enumeration stage is primarily to map the configuration and read permissions.

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
For Windows LAPS environments, the available cmdlets depend on installed management components and deployment model.

Do not assume the legacy Microsoft LAPS and Windows LAPS expose identical attributes or tooling.

Enumerate the actual environment before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
Modern BloodHound data may help identify LAPS-related read relationships depending on the collector and environment.

Validate the underlying directory permissions before reporting them.

docs.title: Phase 24 - gMSA Enumeration
docs.text:
Group Managed Service Accounts should be identified.

PowerShell:

Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter *

Questions:

Which gMSAs exist?

Which systems use them?

Who can retrieve their managed password?

What privilege does each account have?

The existence of a gMSA is not a vulnerability.

The important relationship is:

Principal
    |
    | Can retrieve managed password
    v
gMSA
    |
    v
Privileges / Services

docs.title: Phase 25 - Machine Account Quota
docs.text:
Determine the domain's machine account quota.

PowerShell:

Get-ADDomain |
    Select-Object DistinguishedName

The quota itself is stored in:

ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota

Using LDAP:

ldapsearch -x \
  -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
  -D 'alice@example.local' \
  -W \
  -b 'DC=example,DC=local' \
  '(objectClass=domain)' \
  ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota

docs.title: Important Distinction
docs.text:
MachineAccountQuota > 0
          !=
Vulnerability

It becomes relevant when combined with other relationships or misconfigurations.

docs.title: Phase 26 - AD CS Discovery
docs.text:
Determine whether Active Directory Certificate Services is deployed.

Look for:

Enterprise Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
Enrollment Services
Web Enrollment
Certificate-related directory objects

docs.title: Certipy
docs.text:
Where authorised and available, Certipy can assist with AD CS discovery.

The detailed syntax will be covered in the dedicated Certipy and AD CS notes.

At enumeration stage the workflow is:

Discover CA
    |
    v
Discover Templates
    |
    v
Map Permissions
    |
    v
Identify Candidate Misconfigurations

Do not automatically report every tool-identified ESC candidate without understanding its prerequisites.

docs.title: Phase 27 - BloodHound Collection
docs.text:
After manual baseline enumeration, collect graph data.

This ordering matters.

If BloodHound is run first without understanding the environment, it is easy to treat graph edges as magic rather than understanding the underlying AD relationship.

docs.title: Collection Model
docs.text:
Active Directory
       |
       v
Collector
       |
       v
BloodHound Data
       |
       v
Graph
       |
       v
Candidate Attack Paths
       |
       v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Windows Collection
docs.text:
SharpHound is commonly used for Windows-based collection.

Use collection options appropriate to the assessment and environment.

Do not automatically select the broadest collection mode without considering:

Scope
Network traffic
Session enumeration
Local group queries
EDR visibility
Assessment objectives

docs.title: Linux Collection
docs.text:
BloodHound-compatible collection from Linux is possible using supported collectors.

Check the collector documentation and BloodHound version because collection capabilities and compatibility can change.

docs.title: BloodHound Questions
docs.text:
Useful analysis questions include:

What can my current user reach?

Who controls privileged groups?

Who can modify privileged users?

Who can administer Domain Controllers?

Where are privileged sessions?

Which principals have dangerous ACL rights?

Which GPOs influence privileged systems?

Which delegation relationships exist?

Which AD CS relationships exist?

What paths lead from low privilege to Tier 0?

docs.title: Shortest Path Is Not Always Best Path
docs.text:
A path:

User
 |
 v
Host
 |
 v
Domain Admin

may look attractive but require a noisy or disruptive technique.

A longer path may be:

User
 |
 v
ACL
 |
 v
Service Account
 |
 v
Server
 |
 v
Privileged Session

and may be more realistic.

Evaluate:

Reliability
Intrusiveness
Detection
Prerequisites
Business impact

not merely graph length.

docs.title: Phase 28 - Name Resolution Enumeration
docs.text:
Internal Windows environments may use:

DNS
LLMNR
NBT-NS
mDNS

Determine which mechanisms are present before considering tools such as Responder.

docs.title: Passive First
docs.text:
Prefer understanding normal traffic before enabling active poisoning behaviour.

Questions:

Are clients generating LLMNR requests?

Are NBT-NS broadcasts visible?

Is mDNS present?

Are WPAD-related requests visible?

Which systems generate the traffic?

Responder will receive a dedicated note because capture, poisoning and relay require careful separation.

docs.title: Phase 29 - SMB Signing Enumeration
docs.text:
SMB signing is important for relay analysis.

NetExec SMB discovery can help identify signing configuration.

Conceptually record:

Host SMB Signing Role DC01 Yes Required DC FILE01 Yes Not required File server APP01 Yes Required Application

Do not conclude:

Signing not required
      =
Compromise

It represents one potential prerequisite in certain relay scenarios.

docs.title: Phase 30 - LDAP Security Controls
docs.text:
For Domain Controllers, review controls relevant to LDAP authentication and relay scenarios.

Consider:

LDAP signing
LDAPS availability
Channel binding
Extended Protection where applicable
Authentication methods

This will be covered in greater detail in the NTLM relay notes.

docs.title: Phase 31 - SYSVOL Enumeration
docs.text:
SYSVOL deserves explicit review.

Typical path:

\\example.local\SYSVOL

Linux:

smbclient //dc01.example.local/SYSVOL -U 'EXAMPLE/alice'

Windows:

dir \\example.local\SYSVOL

Look for:

Scripts
Policies
Configuration
Old files
Credential remnants
Deployment information

docs.title: Phase 32 - NETLOGON Enumeration
docs.text:
NETLOGON can contain logon scripts and other operational content.

Windows:

dir \\example.local\NETLOGON

Linux:

smbclient //dc01.example.local/NETLOGON -U 'EXAMPLE/alice'

Review scripts for:

Hard-coded credentials
Internal paths
Server names
Deployment commands
Administrative tooling

docs.title: Phase 33 - Service Account Discovery
docs.text:
Service accounts deserve special attention.

Indicators include:

SPNs
Naming conventions
Descriptions
PasswordNeverExpires
Delegation
Group membership
Service-related groups

Example naming conventions:

svc_sql
svc_backup
svc_web
svc_sccm
sa_app
app_service

Naming alone is not proof that an account is a service account.

docs.title: Phase 34 - Privileged Identity Discovery
docs.text:
Identify high-value identities beyond Domain Admins.

Examples:

Enterprise Admins
Administrators
Schema Admins
Backup Operators
Server Operators
Account Operators
DNSAdmins
Certificate administrators
SCCM administrators
Backup administrators
Virtualisation administrators
Tier-0 operators

Also identify users who can indirectly control these identities.

docs.title: Privilege Graph
docs.text:
Direct Privilege
      |
      +--> Group Membership
      |
      +--> Administrative Access

Indirect Privilege
      |
      +--> ACL
      +--> GPO
      +--> Credential Access
      +--> Session
      +--> Delegation
      +--> AD CS

Indirect privilege is often more interesting.

docs.title: Phase 35 - Recently Logged-On / Session Context
docs.text:
Where authorised and technically available, understand:

Where are administrators logging in?

Where are service accounts active?

Which systems are used as management hosts?

Where do privileged identities overlap with lower-tier systems?

This helps identify tiering weaknesses.

docs.title: Phase 36 - Domain Trusts and Foreign Principals
docs.text:
When trusts exist, look for:

ForeignSecurityPrincipals
Cross-domain group memberships
SIDHistory
Users from trusted domains
Groups containing foreign principals

These relationships may create unexpected privilege.

docs.title: Phase 37 - AD Sites and Subnets
docs.text:
Large environments often use AD Sites and Services.

Sites can reveal:

Geographical structure
Network segmentation
Domain Controller placement
Subnets
Remote locations

PowerShell:

Get-ADReplicationSite -Filter *

Subnets:

Get-ADReplicationSubnet -Filter *

This can help inform network and pivoting analysis.

docs.title: Phase 38 - Identify Additional Network Segments
docs.text:
Computer objects, DNS records, sites, routing information and compromised hosts can reveal networks not visible from the initial position.

Maintain:

10.10.20.0/24   - Initial network
172.16.10.0/24  - Server network
172.16.20.0/24  - Management network
10.50.30.0/24   - Remote site

These networks become inputs to the pivoting methodology.

Have SPNs

docs.title: Ignoring DNS
docs.text:

This is particularly important for Kerberos.

docs.title: Using IP Addresses Everywhere
docs.text:

Prefer understanding:

Hostname

docs.text:

Check Linux time:

w32tm /query /status

If Kerberos authentication fails unexpectedly, investigate time as well as credentials and DNS.
