docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Group Policy should be treated as a central administrative control plane.

The basic relationship is:

Administrator
      |
      v
GPO
      |
      v
OU
      |
      v
Users / Computers

This means a permission that initially appears limited to:

Can Edit GPO

may actually represent:

Can Influence Hundreds of Systems

depending on where the GPO applies.

The correct security model is therefore:

Principal
    +
GPO Permission
    +
GPO Link
    +
Effective Scope
    +
Target Privilege
    =
Security Impact

A complete assessment should analyse both halves of the GPO:

              GPO
               |
       +-------+-------+
       |               |
       v               v
Active Directory     SYSVOL

It should then determine:

Who Can Edit?
      |
      v
What Can They Edit?
      |
      v
Where Is It Linked?
      |
      v
Who Receives It?
      |
      v
What Privilege Results?

Do not stop at GPO enumeration.

Map:

GPO
 |
 v
OU
 |
 v
Computer / User
 |
 v
Security Role

Likewise, do not assume that a linked GPO necessarily applies.

Evaluate:

Link
 +
Inheritance
 +
Security Filtering
 +
WMI Filtering
 +
GPO Status
 =
Effective Application

The offensive attack-path model is:

Controlled Principal
        |
        v
GPO Control
        |
        v
Sensitive GPO
        |
        v
Sensitive OU
        |
        v
Privileged Systems

The defensive model is:

Inventory
   |
   v
Classify
   |
   v
Restrict Control
   |
   v
Protect Links
   |
   v
Protect SYSVOL
   |
   v
Monitor
   |
   v
Review

The strongest Group Policy assessment therefore combines:

Active Directory Enumeration
        +
ACL Analysis
        +
Group Analysis
        +
GPO Reports
        +
SYSVOL Review
        +
BloodHound
        +
Resultant Set of Policy

to answer the most important question:

Which identities can use Group Policy
to influence which systems?

For a penetration tester, this becomes:

What GPOs can the controlled identity influence?
        |
        v
Where do those GPOs apply?
        |
        v
What privilege exists on those targets?
        |
        v
Can the impact be proven without
modifying production policy?

For defenders:

Who can modify our security policy?
        |
        v
Who can modify where it applies?
        |
        v
Who can modify the files it trusts?
        |
        v
Would we detect those changes?

Those questions turn Group Policy enumeration into meaningful Active Directory security analysis.

docs.title: Active Directory Groups
docs.text:
Active Directory groups are one of the primary mechanisms used to assign permissions, administrative roles, application access, and resource access across a Windows domain.

From a security perspective, group analysis answers a fundamental question:

What privileges does this identity inherit?

A user may appear unprivileged when examined directly but inherit substantial access through one or more groups.

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
Nested Group
 |
 v
Privileged Group
 |
 v
Administrative Access

For example:

alice
 |
 v
Helpdesk
 |
 v
IT Operations
 |
 v
Server Administrators
 |
 v
Administrative Access to Servers

The security relationship is therefore rarely limited to:

User -> Direct Group

Instead, Active Directory commonly contains:

User
 |
 +--> Direct Group
 |
 +--> Nested Group
 |
 +--> Domain Local Group
 |
 +--> Global Group
 |
 +--> Universal Group
 |
 +--> Privileged Group
 |
 +--> Local Group on Computer
 |
 +--> Application Role

Group enumeration should therefore be part of every Active Directory security assessment.

Authorised testing only

Group membership changes can immediately grant administrative or application privileges and may affect production systems. Prefer read-only enumeration and attack-path analysis first. Only add or remove members when explicitly authorised, use dedicated test accounts where possible, record the original membership, and restore all changes after validation.

docs.title: Why Groups Matter
docs.text:
Groups simplify administration.

Instead of assigning permissions directly to every user:

Alice -> FILE01
Bob   -> FILE01
Carol -> FILE01
Dave  -> FILE01

administrators can create:

File Server Users

and assign:

Alice
Bob
Carol
Dave

to the group.

Then:

File Server Users
        |
        v
      FILE01

This is operationally efficient.

However, it also means group membership becomes part of the security boundary.

docs.title: Group Security Model
docs.text:
The basic model is:

Security Principal
       |
       v
Group Membership
       |
       v
Security Token
       |
       v
Permissions
       |
       v
Resource

When a user authenticates, Windows constructs an access token containing security identifiers associated with the user and applicable groups.

Conceptually:

Alice
 |
 v
Authentication
 |
 v
Access Token
 |
 +--> Alice SID
 |
 +--> Domain Users SID
 |
 +--> Helpdesk SID
 |
 +--> Server Admins SID
 |
 v
AccessCheck

Permissions granted to those group SIDs may therefore become available to Alice.

docs.title: Security Groups vs Distribution Groups
docs.text:
Active Directory supports:

Security Groups
Distribution Groups

The distinction is important.

docs.title: Security Groups
docs.text:
Security groups can be used to assign permissions.

Examples:

Domain Admins
Server Admins
File Server Users
SQL Administrators
Helpdesk
Backup Operators

Conceptually:

Security Group
      |
      v
ACL / Permission
      |
      v
Resource

docs.title: Distribution Groups
docs.text:
Distribution groups are primarily intended for email distribution.

Conceptually:

Distribution Group
       |
       v
Email Distribution

They are not normally used as security principals for assigning access permissions.

docs.title: Enumerate Group Category
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-ADGroup \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties GroupCategory |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        GroupCategory

Example output:

Name                 GroupCategory
----                 -------------
Domain Admins        Security
Helpdesk             Security
All Employees        Distribution

docs.title: Group Scope
docs.text:
Active Directory security groups have three principal scopes:

Domain Local
Global
Universal

Understanding group scope is important when analysing:

Membership
Trusts
Cross-Domain Access
Resource Permissions
Administrative Delegation

docs.title: Global Groups
docs.text:
Global groups are commonly used to collect users and computers from the same domain according to role.

Example:

CORP\Domain Helpdesk

Conceptually:

Users in CORP
     |
     v
Global Group

A global group can then be granted permissions to resources.

docs.title: Domain Local Groups
docs.text:
Domain local groups are commonly used to assign permissions to resources within the domain.

Conceptually:

Global Groups
     |
     v
Domain Local Group
     |
     v
Resource Permission

Example:

CORP\File Server Users
        |
        v
FILE01 Share

docs.title: Universal Groups
docs.text:
Universal groups can contain principals from multiple domains in the forest, subject to Active Directory membership rules.

They are useful in multi-domain environments.

Conceptually:

Domain A Users
       |
       +------+
              |
Domain B Users|
       |      |
       +------+
              |
              v
       Universal Group
              |
              v
          Resource

Universal groups are particularly important when assessing:

Multi-Domain Forests
Cross-Domain Privileges
Trust Relationships

docs.title: AGDLP
docs.text:
A common Microsoft group-design model is:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

This is commonly abbreviated:

AGDLP

or:

A -> G -> DL -> P

Example:

Alice
 |
 v
GG-Finance
 |
 v
DL-Finance-Share-RW
 |
 v
FILE01 Finance Share

docs.title: AGUDLP
docs.text:
In multi-domain environments, Universal groups may be added:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Universal Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

This is commonly described as:

AGUDLP

docs.title: Why Nested Groups Matter
docs.text:
Suppose Alice is only directly a member of:

Helpdesk

However:

Alice
 |
 v
Helpdesk
 |
 v
IT Operations
 |
 v
Server Admins

If:

Server Admins

has administrative access to servers, Alice may indirectly inherit that capability.

Therefore:

Direct Membership

is insufficient for complete privilege analysis.

docs.title: Direct vs Recursive Membership
docs.text:
Direct membership:

Alice
 |
 v
Helpdesk

Recursive membership:

Alice
 |
 v
Helpdesk
 |
 v
IT Operations
 |
 v
Server Admins

Always analyse both.

docs.title: Enumerate Groups with PowerShell
docs.text:
Using the Active Directory PowerShell module:

Get-ADGroup -Filter *

Useful properties:

Get-ADGroup \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties Description,GroupCategory,GroupScope,ManagedBy |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        SamAccountName,
        GroupCategory,
        GroupScope,
        ManagedBy,
        Description

docs.title: Enumerate One Group
docs.text:
Get-ADGroup \
    -Identity 'Domain Admins' \
    -Properties *

Useful fields include:

DistinguishedName
GroupCategory
GroupScope
ManagedBy
Member
ObjectGUID
ObjectSID
SamAccountName

docs.title: Enumerate Group Members
docs.text:
Get-ADGroupMember \
    -Identity 'Domain Admins'

Example:

distinguishedName : CN=Administrator,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=example
name              : Administrator
objectClass       : user
SamAccountName    : Administrator

docs.title: Recursive Group Membership
docs.text:
Use:

Get-ADGroupMember \
    -Identity 'Domain Admins' \
    -Recursive

This expands nested group membership.

Compare:

Direct Members
      |
      v
Nested Groups
      |
      v
Recursive Members

docs.title: Enumerate a User's Direct Groups
docs.text:
Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership \
    -Identity 'alice'

Readable output:

Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership \
    -Identity 'alice' |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        GroupScope,
        GroupCategory

docs.title: memberOf Attribute
docs.text:
The user's:

memberOf

attribute contains direct group memberships represented by distinguished names.

Example:

Get-ADUser \
    -Identity 'alice' \
    -Properties memberOf |
    Select-Object \
        -ExpandProperty memberOf

Example:

CN=Helpdesk,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example
CN=VPN Users,OU=Groups,DC=corp,DC=example

docs.title: memberOf Is Not the Complete Effective Membership
docs.text:
Do not treat:

memberOf

as a complete list of all effective groups.

Important reasons include:

Nested Groups
Primary Group
Cross-Domain Membership
Token Construction
SIDHistory

Use recursive and token-aware analysis where necessary.

docs.title: LDAP Matching Rule in Chain
docs.text:
Active Directory supports recursive group membership queries using the LDAP matching rule:

1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941

This is commonly known as:

LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_IN_CHAIN

Example:

Get-ADUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(memberOf:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:=CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=example)'

This can identify users recursively associated with the specified group.

docs.title: Recursive Membership with LDAP
docs.text:
Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Group A
 |
 v
Group B
 |
 v
Domain Admins

A normal:

memberOf=Domain Admins

filter would not necessarily identify the indirect relationship.

The matching-rule-in-chain query follows the nested membership chain.

docs.title: Enumerate with ldapsearch
docs.text:
Basic group enumeration:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\alice' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(objectClass=group)' \
    sAMAccountName \
    cn \
    groupType \
    member \
    managedBy

docs.title: Enumerate a Specific Group with ldapsearch
docs.text:
ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\alice' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(&(objectClass=group)(sAMAccountName=Domain Admins))' \
    distinguishedName \
    member \
    managedBy \
    groupType

docs.title: LDAP Group Attributes
docs.text:
Useful attributes include:

cn
sAMAccountName
distinguishedName
member
memberOf
managedBy
groupType
objectSid
adminCount
description
whenCreated
whenChanged

docs.title: groupType
docs.text:
The:

groupType

attribute stores group scope and security-group information as flags.

Most assessments do not require manually decoding every numeric value because tools such as PowerShell provide readable:

GroupScope
GroupCategory

fields.

However, raw LDAP output may expose the integer representation.

docs.title: Net Commands
docs.text:
Built-in Windows commands can provide quick enumeration.

Domain groups:

net group /domain

Members of Domain Admins:

net group "Domain Admins" /domain

Specific user:

net user alice /domain

These commands remain useful where the Active Directory PowerShell module is unavailable.

docs.title: whoami
docs.text:
For the current session:

whoami

Groups in the current token:

whoami /groups

This is particularly useful because it shows security groups associated with the current access token.

docs.title: Current Token vs Directory Membership
docs.text:
Remember:

Directory Membership Changed
        |
        X
Current Token Automatically Updated

A newly added group may not appear in an already existing logon token.

A new authentication session may be required.

This matters during both testing and troubleshooting.

docs.title: PowerView Group Enumeration
docs.text:
PowerView can enumerate domain groups.

Get-DomainGroup

Specific group:

Get-DomainGroup \
    -Identity 'Domain Admins'

docs.title: PowerView Group Members
docs.text:
Get-DomainGroupMember \
    -Identity 'Domain Admins'

Recursive behaviour and available parameters can vary by PowerView version.

Check:

Get-Help Get-DomainGroupMember -Full

docs.title: PowerView User Membership
docs.text:
Get-DomainGroup \
    -MemberIdentity 'alice'

Depending on the PowerView version, this can assist with identifying groups associated with a principal.

Always verify the loaded version's help before relying on exact parameters.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is extremely useful for analysing group membership because it represents membership as graph relationships.

Example:

alice
 |
 v
MemberOf
 |
 v
Helpdesk
 |
 v
MemberOf
 |
 v
Server Admins

The graph can then continue:

Server Admins
 |
 v
AdminTo
 |
 v
SERVER01

The complete attack path becomes:

alice
 |
 v
Helpdesk
 |
 v
Server Admins
 |
 v
SERVER01

docs.title: Group Membership in BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound commonly represents group relationships using:

MemberOf

This relationship may connect:

User -> Group
Computer -> Group
Group -> Group

depending on the directory configuration.

docs.title: BloodHound Group Questions
docs.text:
Useful questions include:

What groups is this user a member of?

What privileged groups are reachable recursively?

Who can modify this group?

Which users can reach Domain Admins?

Which groups provide local administrator rights?

Which groups control GPOs?

Which groups have DCSync rights?

Which groups control service accounts?

Which groups contain computers?

docs.title: Group Membership Is Only One Edge Type
docs.text:
Do not analyse:

MemberOf

in isolation.

A group may also participate in relationships such as:

AdminTo
GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
AddMember
Owns
GPO Control
DCSync
Delegation

The security impact comes from the complete graph.

docs.title: Privileged Groups
docs.text:
Some groups deserve immediate attention during Active Directory assessments.

Examples include:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Schema Admins
Administrators
Account Operators
Backup Operators
Server Operators
Print Operators
DnsAdmins
Group Policy Creator Owners
Protected Users

The exact security impact depends on the domain configuration, Windows version, assigned privileges, and resource ACLs.

docs.title: Domain Admins
docs.text:
Domain Admins is one of the most important privileged groups in a domain.

Conceptually:

Domain Admins
      |
      v
Broad Domain Administrative Control

Members commonly receive administrative control across domain systems through default and organisational configuration.

Any attack path reaching:

Domain Admins

should receive immediate attention.

docs.title: Enterprise Admins
docs.text:
Enterprise Admins exists in the forest root domain.

Conceptually:

Enterprise Admins
        |
        v
Forest-Wide Administrative Capability

This group is especially important in:

Multi-Domain Forests

A compromise may affect more than one domain.

docs.title: Schema Admins
docs.text:
Schema Admins controls Active Directory schema modifications.

Conceptually:

Schema Admins
      |
      v
AD Schema

Schema changes can have forest-wide consequences.

Membership should normally be tightly controlled and often temporary when legitimately required.

docs.title: Builtin Administrators
docs.text:
The domain's built-in:

Administrators

group is highly privileged.

Do not confuse:

BUILTIN\Administrators

with:

Domain Admins

although default memberships and resulting privileges can overlap significantly.

docs.title: Account Operators
docs.text:
Account Operators historically provides delegated account-management capabilities over many non-protected users and groups.

The exact effective rights should be validated rather than inferred solely from the group name.

Investigate:

Which accounts can they manage?

Which groups can they modify?

Are protected objects excluded?

Can managed accounts lead to higher privilege?

docs.title: Server Operators
docs.text:
Server Operators can have significant privileges on domain controllers under default configurations.

This group should be treated as highly sensitive.

Review actual assigned privileges and operational use.

docs.title: Backup Operators
docs.text:
Backup Operators is security-sensitive because backup-related privileges can bypass normal file ACL checks for legitimate backup and restore operations.

Conceptually:

Backup Privilege
      |
      v
Read Protected Files

or:

Restore Privilege
      |
      v
Write Protected Files

The practical impact depends on where the membership is effective.

docs.title: Print Operators
docs.text:
Print Operators has historically received significant privileges on domain controllers related to printer management.

Modern security configuration and service state can materially affect practical impact.

Do not assume exploitation solely from membership.

docs.title: DnsAdmins
docs.text:
DnsAdmins is an important group where Active Directory-integrated DNS is used.

Members can have substantial DNS administration capability.

Because DNS commonly runs on domain controllers, the group deserves careful review.

However:

DnsAdmins Membership

should not automatically be reported as:

Domain Admin

without demonstrating the relevant configuration and security impact.

docs.title: Group Policy Creator Owners
docs.text:
Group Policy Creator Owners can create Group Policy Objects.

This does not automatically mean the principal can:

Link any GPO anywhere

or:

Modify every existing GPO

Analyse:

GPO Creation
GPO ACL
OU ACL
GPLink Rights
Existing GPO Control

separately.

docs.title: Protected Users
docs.text:
Protected Users is primarily a defensive group.

Members receive additional authentication protections designed to reduce credential exposure and legacy authentication risks.

This group should not be treated as an administrative group merely because it is security-sensitive.

docs.title: Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Computer accounts for domain controllers are members of:

Domain Controllers

and other security contexts relevant to directory replication and domain operation.

Control of a domain-controller computer account is fundamentally different from control of an ordinary workstation account.

docs.title: Domain Computers
docs.text:
Computer accounts commonly belong to:

Domain Computers

This can matter where resources grant permissions broadly to:

Domain Computers

rather than individual systems.

docs.title: Domain Users
docs.text:
Most domain user accounts use:

Domain Users

as their primary group by default.

This means permissions granted to:

Domain Users

can have a very broad blast radius.

docs.title: Authenticated Users
docs.text:
Authenticated Users is broader than:

Domain Users

and should be analysed carefully when found in ACLs.

Conceptually:

Authenticated Identity
        |
        v
Authenticated Users
        |
        v
Permission

Broad permissions granted to this principal may expose resources to many authenticated security principals.

docs.title: Everyone
docs.text:
The:

Everyone

security principal can represent a very broad scope.

Its exact token and anonymous-access implications depend on Windows version and configuration.

Do not assume:

Everyone
 =
Unauthenticated Internet User

Instead determine the actual authentication and access context.

docs.title: Local Groups
docs.text:
Domain group analysis should also include local groups on member systems.

For example:

CORP\Server Admins
        |
        v
SERVER01\Administrators

This may provide:

Local Administrator on SERVER01

without providing domain-wide administrative privilege.

docs.title: Enumerate Local Administrators
docs.text:
On a Windows system:

Get-LocalGroupMember \
    -Group 'Administrators'

Older environments may use:

net localgroup Administrators

docs.title: Remote Local Group Enumeration
docs.text:
During authorised assessments, tools such as NetExec may help determine whether a supplied account has administrative access to remote systems.

For detailed NetExec usage:

NetExec

docs.title: Group Policy and Local Groups
docs.text:
Group Policy can manage local group membership using mechanisms such as:

Restricted Groups
Group Policy Preferences

This means:

Local Administrators

may be centrally controlled through Active Directory.

When unexpected local administrators are found, investigate the applicable GPOs.

docs.title: Group Membership and ACLs
docs.text:
Groups often receive rights through Active Directory ACLs.

Example:

Helpdesk
 |
 v
ForceChangePassword
 |
 v
Users OU

Every member of:

Helpdesk

may potentially inherit that delegated capability according to the effective ACL.

Therefore group analysis and ACL analysis should be performed together.

See:

Active Directory ACL and ACE Abuse

docs.title: Who Can Modify the Group?
docs.text:
For every privileged group, ask:

Who can change its membership?

Potential control paths include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
AddMember
Self
Ownership
Inherited ACE

A low-privilege user who can modify a privileged group may effectively possess a privilege-escalation path.

docs.title: Group Control Model
docs.text:
Alice
 |
 v
AddMember
 |
 v
Server Admins
 |
 v
Administrative Access

or:

Alice
 |
 v
WriteDACL
 |
 v
Server Admins
 |
 v
Grant AddMember
 |
 v
Add Controlled Account
 |
 v
Administrative Access

docs.title: Enumerate Group ACL
docs.text:
Native PowerShell:

$group = Get-ADGroup 'Server Admins'

(Get-Acl "AD:\$($group.DistinguishedName)").Access |
    Format-Table \
        IdentityReference,
        ActiveDirectoryRights,
        AccessControlType,
        ObjectType,
        InheritanceType,
        IsInherited \
        -AutoSize

docs.title: Group Owner
docs.text:
Check:

(Get-Acl "AD:\$($group.DistinguishedName)").Owner

Unexpected ownership of privileged groups should be investigated.

docs.title: managedBy
docs.text:
Groups may have a:

managedBy

attribute.

Enumerate:

Get-ADGroup \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties ManagedBy |
    Where-Object {
        $_.ManagedBy
    } |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        ManagedBy

However:

managedBy

does not by itself prove that the listed manager can modify membership.

The ACL remains authoritative.

docs.title: Manager Can Update Membership
docs.text:
Active Directory administration tools can configure a group so that the manager is permitted to update membership.

This is implemented through permissions rather than the managedBy attribute alone.

Therefore test:

managedBy
      |
      v
Check DACL
      |
      v
Membership Write Right?

docs.title: Group Membership Attack Path
docs.text:
A common path is:

Compromised User
      |
      v
Can Modify Group
      |
      v
Privileged Group
      |
      v
Administrative Capability

This is one of the simplest ACL-driven Active Directory privilege-escalation paths.

docs.title: Nested Group Attack Path
docs.text:
A less obvious path is:

Alice
 |
 v
Can Modify
 |
 v
Application Support
 |
 v
MemberOf
 |
 v
IT Operations
 |
 v
MemberOf
 |
 v
Server Admins

The first group may not appear privileged by name.

The nested relationship creates the actual impact.

docs.title: Group Names Can Be Misleading
docs.text:
Do not determine privilege from names alone.

For example:

Printer Support
Development
Application Team
Legacy Migration
Desktop Support

may possess substantial permissions.

Conversely:

Security Admins

may only provide access to a specific application.

Always determine:

What permissions does the group actually provide?

docs.title: Description Attribute
docs.text:
Group descriptions can provide useful context.

Enumerate:

Get-ADGroup \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties Description |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        Description

Descriptions may reveal:

Business Purpose
Managed Systems
Application Name
Administrative Role
Legacy Function

Treat descriptions as hints, not proof.

docs.title: Empty Groups
docs.text:
Empty groups may still matter.

An empty group can have:

Powerful ACL Rights
Local Administrator Rights
Application Permissions
GPO Permissions

If a low-privilege principal can modify the group, the empty state does not eliminate the attack path.

Example:

Alice
 |
 v
AddMember
 |
 v
Empty Privileged Group
 |
 v
AdminTo SERVER01

docs.title: Disabled Users in Groups
docs.text:
A privileged group may contain disabled users.

Enumerate membership and account status separately.

Example:

Get-ADGroupMember \
    -Identity 'Server Admins' \
    -Recursive |
    ForEach-Object {
        if ($_.objectClass -eq 'user') {
            Get-ADUser \
                -Identity $_.DistinguishedName \
                -Properties Enabled
        }
    } |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        Enabled

Disabled membership may represent:

Legacy Configuration
Dormant Privilege
Emergency Account
Poor Cleanup

docs.title: Stale Group Membership
docs.text:
Review privileged memberships for:

Former Employees
Role Changes
Temporary Projects
Old Service Accounts
Disabled Accounts
Migration Accounts
Vendor Accounts

Group membership frequently accumulates over time.

docs.title: Service Accounts in Groups
docs.text:
Service accounts may be members of privileged groups.

Example:

svc_backup
 |
 v
Backup Operators

or:

svc_deploy
 |
 v
Server Admins

This can increase the impact of:

Kerberoasting
Password Reuse
Credential Exposure
DCSync
Application Compromise

docs.title: Kerberoastable Privileged Group Members
docs.text:
A useful assessment question is:

Which privileged users have SPNs?

PowerShell:

Get-ADUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \
    -Properties ServicePrincipalName,MemberOf |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        ServicePrincipalName,
        MemberOf

Then analyse recursive privileged memberships.

For detailed Kerberoasting:

Kerberoasting

docs.title: Password-Not-Required Group Members
docs.text:
Look for unusual account settings among privileged identities.

Example:

Get-ADUser \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties PasswordNotRequired |
    Where-Object {
        $_.PasswordNotRequired
    } |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        Enabled,
        PasswordNotRequired

Configuration alone does not prove the account has a blank password.

It indicates that the directory does not require a password under that account flag.

docs.title: Password-Never-Expires Group Members
docs.text:
Get-ADUser \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties PasswordNeverExpires |
    Where-Object {
        $_.PasswordNeverExpires
    } |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        Enabled,
        PasswordNeverExpires

Prioritise privileged and service accounts for review.

docs.title: AS-REP Roastable Group Members
docs.text:
Identify accounts with:

Do not require Kerberos preauthentication

and determine whether they belong to privileged groups.

For detailed enumeration:

AS-REP Roasting

docs.title: Group Membership and Password Spraying
docs.text:
Group membership can help prioritise accounts during an authorised password-security assessment.

However, do not create an aggressive spray list consisting only of privileged users.

The testing methodology should still respect:

Lockout Policy
Scope
Rate Limits
Account Sensitivity
Operational Risk

See:

Password Spraying

docs.title: Primary Group
docs.text:
Active Directory users and computers have:

primaryGroupID

The primary group relationship is not represented in exactly the same way as ordinary memberOf relationships.

For most users, the default primary group is:

Domain Users

docs.title: Enumerate primaryGroupID
docs.text:
Get-ADUser \
    -Identity 'alice' \
    -Properties primaryGroupID |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        primaryGroupID

Do not rely only on:

memberOf

when performing precise token or membership analysis.

docs.title: SIDHistory and Groups
docs.text:
sIDHistory can cause a principal to receive access associated with historical SIDs.

Conceptually:

Current User SID
      |
      +
Historical SID
      |
      v
Access Token
      |
      v
Permissions

This becomes especially important in:

Domain Migrations
Forest Migrations
Trust Relationships
Legacy Environments

A dedicated SID History page should cover this in detail.

docs.title: Foreign Security Principals
docs.text:
Cross-domain and cross-forest group memberships may be represented through:

ForeignSecurityPrincipals

in Active Directory.

Example DN:

CN=S-1-5-21-...,CN=ForeignSecurityPrincipals,DC=corp,DC=example

These objects represent security principals originating outside the local domain.

docs.title: Foreign Group Membership
docs.text:
A trust-related path might be:

FOREST-A\Alice
      |
      v
FOREST-B\Domain Local Group
      |
      v
Resource in FOREST-B

This is why group analysis becomes essential when assessing Active Directory trusts.

docs.title: Cross-Domain Group Analysis
docs.text:
For multi-domain forests, investigate:

Universal Groups
Domain Local Groups
Foreign Security Principals
Enterprise Admins
Nested Groups
SIDHistory
Trust Direction
Trust Transitivity

Group analysis should eventually be combined with dedicated trust analysis.

docs.title: TokenGroups
docs.text:
Active Directory exposes constructed attributes such as:

tokenGroups

that can assist with determining security groups relevant to a principal's authorization context.

This can be useful where direct memberOf enumeration does not adequately represent effective group membership.

Specialised directory tooling usually handles this more conveniently than manually decoding raw LDAP values.

docs.title: AdminSDHolder and Groups
docs.text:
Certain privileged groups are protected by:

AdminSDHolder

and:

SDProp

This affects their ACL inheritance and protection model.

Conceptually:

AdminSDHolder
      |
      v
Security Descriptor
      |
      v
Protected Groups
      |
      v
Protected Members

See:

Active Directory ACL and ACE Abuse

docs.title: adminCount
docs.text:
Protected users and groups may have:

adminCount=1

Enumerate groups:

Get-ADGroup \
    -LDAPFilter '(adminCount=1)' \
    -Properties adminCount |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        GroupScope,
        adminCount

Remember:

adminCount=1

can remain after an account is removed from a protected group.

It is therefore useful context rather than definitive proof of current privilege.

docs.title: Group Membership Changes
docs.text:
Where authorised, PowerShell can modify group membership.

Add:

Add-ADGroupMember \
    -Identity '<GROUP>' \
    -Members '<TEST_USER>'

Verify:

Get-ADGroupMember \
    -Identity '<GROUP>'

Remove:

Remove-ADGroupMember \
    -Identity '<GROUP>' \
    -Members '<TEST_USER>' \
    -Confirm:$false

Only perform these operations against approved groups and accounts.

docs.title: Minimum-Impact Membership Validation
docs.text:
A safe workflow is:

Confirm Permission
       |
       v
Record Original Membership
       |
       v
Use Dedicated Test Account
       |
       v
Add Once
       |
       v
Verify Membership
       |
       v
Remove Immediately
       |
       v
Verify Original State

Do not leave temporary privileged membership in place.

docs.title: New Authentication Token
docs.text:
After membership changes:

Existing Session
      |
      X
Automatically Contains New Group

A fresh authentication context may be required.

For validation, distinguish:

Directory Membership Successfully Changed

from:

New Privilege Successfully Exercised

The first may already prove the ACL weakness.

docs.title: Do Not Over-Test
docs.text:
Suppose:

Alice
 |
 v
AddMember
 |
 v
Server Admins

and the group is already confirmed to provide administrator access to:

SERVER01

It may be unnecessary to:

Add Alice
   |
   v
Log into SERVER01
   |
   v
Execute Commands

when:

ACL Evidence
     +
Membership Evidence
     +
Existing Group Privilege Evidence

already proves the attack path.

docs.title: Group Membership and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Groups often define lateral movement opportunities.

Examples:

Server Admins
Desktop Admins
SQL Admins
Backup Admins
Remote Management Users
RDP Users

The model is:

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
Remote Access Right
 |
 v
System

docs.title: Remote Desktop Users
docs.text:
Membership in:

Remote Desktop Users

may provide RDP logon capability where other policy conditions permit it.

It does not automatically provide:

Local Administrator

docs.title: Remote Management Users
docs.text:
Membership in:

Remote Management Users

may be relevant to WinRM access.

Actual remote management access also depends on endpoint configuration and authorization.

docs.title: Local Administrators
docs.text:
A domain group placed into a remote computer's local:

Administrators

group may create an administrative lateral-movement path.

Example:

CORP\Server Admins
        |
        v
SERVER01\Administrators
        |
        v
Local Administrator

docs.title: NetExec and Group Context
docs.text:
NetExec can help evaluate remote administrative access using authorised credentials.

For example, an assessment may first identify:

Alice
 |
 v
Server Admins

then determine:

Which systems trust Server Admins?

For detailed commands and current syntax:

NetExec

docs.title: Groups and DCSync
docs.text:
Replication rights may be assigned to groups.

Example:

Identity Management
        |
        +--> GetChanges
        |
        +--> GetChangesAll
        |
        v
Domain

Any member of the group may inherit the directory replication capability.

Therefore, when DCSync rights are identified, resolve:

Direct Trustee
      |
      v
Group?
      |
      v
Recursive Members

docs.title: Groups and Delegation
docs.text:
Delegation-enabled accounts may be controlled indirectly through groups.

Example:

Alice
 |
 v
Helpdesk
 |
 v
GenericAll
 |
 v
svc_web
 |
 v
Constrained Delegation
 |
 v
SERVER01

The group is part of the attack path even though the final technique is Kerberos delegation.

docs.title: Groups and RBCD
docs.text:
Similarly:

Alice
 |
 v
Computer Management
 |
 v
GenericWrite
 |
 v
SERVER01$
 |
 v
RBCD
 |
 v
S4U

Group membership can therefore expose indirect delegation paths.

docs.title: Groups and GPOs
docs.text:
Groups may have rights to:

Create GPO
Modify GPO
Link GPO
Edit GPO Security

A group that appears unrelated to server administration may nevertheless control a GPO applied to privileged systems.

Always connect:

Group
 |
 v
GPO Permission
 |
 v
GPO
 |
 v
Linked OU
 |
 v
Affected Systems

docs.title: Groups and AD CS
docs.text:
Active Directory Certificate Services can use groups for:

Certificate Template Enrollment
Certificate Template ACLs
CA Administration
Enrollment Agent Restrictions

A seemingly ordinary group may therefore participate in an AD CS attack path.

Dedicated AD CS notes should analyse these relationships separately.

docs.title: Groups and Shares
docs.text:
File-share access frequently depends on domain groups.

Example:

Finance Users
      |
      v
Finance Share

Review both:

Share Permissions

and:

NTFS Permissions

Effective access depends on the combination.

docs.title: Groups and Applications
docs.text:
Applications commonly map Active Directory groups to application roles.

Example:

CORP\ERP-Admins
      |
      v
ERP Administrator

This privilege may not appear in native Active Directory administrative relationships.

Application-specific groups should therefore not be ignored.

docs.title: Groups and SQL Server
docs.text:
SQL Server environments may use Active Directory groups for:

SQL Login
Database Role
sysadmin
Application Access

Example:

CORP\SQL-Admins
      |
      v
SQL Server Login
      |
      v
sysadmin

The privilege exists outside normal AD group naming conventions.

docs.title: Groups and Azure / Hybrid Environments
docs.text:
Hybrid identity environments may synchronize groups between Active Directory and cloud identity systems.

This can create relationships involving:

On-Prem AD Group
      |
      v
Synchronization
      |
      v
Cloud Group / Role Assignment

Do not assume that changing an on-premises group has only on-premises impact.

Hybrid identity should be assessed separately according to scope.

docs.title: Group Membership Enumeration Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

Enumerate All Groups
       |
       v
Identify Privileged Groups
       |
       v
Enumerate Direct Members
       |
       v
Expand Nested Membership
       |
       v
Identify Group Controllers
       |
       v
Map Resource Permissions
       |
       v
Identify Attack Paths
       |
       v
Prioritise High-Impact Paths

docs.title: Prioritising Groups
docs.text:
Start with:

Tier 0 Groups
     |
     v
Server Administration Groups
     |
     v
Workstation Administration Groups
     |
     v
GPO Management Groups
     |
     v
Identity Management Groups
     |
     v
Backup Groups
     |
     v
Application Admin Groups
     |
     v
Remote Access Groups

Then expand into custom groups.

docs.title: Interesting Group Names
docs.text:
Names can help with initial triage.

Search for terms such as:

admin
administrator
server
backup
helpdesk
support
sql
database
exchange
dns
gpo
policy
deploy
deployment
remote
rdp
winrm
security
identity
certificate
pki
azure
cloud
service
operator

Example:

Get-ADGroup \
    -Filter * |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Name -match 'admin|server|backup|helpdesk|sql|gpo|deploy|remote|pki|identity'
    } |
    Select-Object Name

This is only triage.

Group names do not prove privilege.

docs.title: Find Large Groups
docs.text:
Large groups can create significant blast radius.

Get-ADGroup \
    -Filter * |
    ForEach-Object {
        $group = $_
        $count = @(
            Get-ADGroupMember \
                -Identity $group \
                -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        ).Count

        [PSCustomObject]@{
            Group = $group.Name
            Members = $count
        }
    } |
    Sort-Object Members -Descending

Large membership is not automatically a vulnerability.

It is useful for prioritising broad access relationships.

docs.title: Find Empty Groups
docs.text:
Get-ADGroup \
    -Filter * |
    ForEach-Object {
        $members = @(
            Get-ADGroupMember \
                -Identity $_ \
                -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        )

        if ($members.Count -eq 0) {
            $_
        }
    } |
    Select-Object Name

Then determine whether those groups still hold privileges.

docs.title: Find Groups with Managers
docs.text:
Get-ADGroup \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties ManagedBy |
    Where-Object {
        $_.ManagedBy
    } |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        ManagedBy

Again, verify the ACL before assuming the manager can alter membership.

docs.title: Find Groups with adminCount
docs.text:
Get-ADGroup \
    -LDAPFilter '(adminCount=1)' \
    -Properties adminCount |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        GroupScope,
        adminCount

This can help identify historically or currently protected groups.

docs.text:
A useful assessment table is:

docs.text:
Prioritise monitoring for changes involving:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Schema Admins
Administrators
Account Operators
Backup Operators
Server Operators
DnsAdmins

docs.title: Temporary Membership Detection
docs.text:
An important detection pattern is:

Member Added
    |
    v
Privileged Authentication
    |
    v
Administrative Activity
    |
    v
Member Removed

An attacker may intentionally keep membership short-lived.

Therefore:

Current Membership Review

alone may miss the activity.

Historical event monitoring is necessary.

docs.title: Correlate Authentication
docs.text:
After a privileged membership change, review:

4624
4672
4768
4769

and relevant remote-service events.

The question is:

Was the newly granted privilege actually used?

docs.title: Detect Unexpected Group Modifiers
docs.text:
Baseline:

Who normally manages each privileged group?

Then alert when:

Unexpected Principal
        |
        v
Changes Privileged Group

docs.title: Group ACL Monitoring
docs.text:
Membership events alone are insufficient.

An attacker may first modify:

Group DACL

and then change membership.

Detection chain:

ACL Change
   |
   v
New Membership Right
   |
   v
Member Added
   |
   v
Privilege Used

Monitor sensitive group ACLs as well as memberships.

docs.title: Purple Team Exercise
docs.text:
A controlled group exercise can use:

Dedicated Test User
       |
       v
Delegated Test Group
       |
       v
Temporary Membership
       |
       v
Detection
       |
       v
Removal
       |
       v
Verification

Avoid production Tier 0 groups unless specifically required and authorised.

docs.title: Purple Team Questions
docs.text:
Defenders should determine:

Which account changed the group?

Which group changed?

Which member was added?

Was the group privileged?

Who authorised the change?

Was the modifier expected?

Was the membership temporary?

Did a new logon follow?

Was administrative activity performed?

Was the group ACL changed first?

Was the change reverted?

Privileged and business-critical groups should have identifiable owners.

Who should belong

Complex nesting makes privilege difficult to understand.

Example:

User

Group B

Avoid:

administration.

Human administrators should use separate privileged identities where appropriate.

Conceptually:

Alice

Where organisational capabilities permit, prefer temporary privilege assignment rather than permanent privileged membership.

Administrator

Approved Task

Temporary Privilege

For privileged groups, review:

Owner
GenericAll

Bad:

or:

managedBy

docs.text:
An attacker may not add themselves directly to:

Domain Admins

Instead:

Attacker

Low-Visibility Group

Nested Group

or:

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Possible finding titles include:

Excessive Active Directory Group Membership Grants Administrative Access

Low-Privilege Account Can Modify Privileged Active Directory Group

Nested Group Membership Enables Privilege Escalation

Excessive Active Directory Group Permissions Enable Administrative Access

Service Account Holds Unnecessary Privileged Group Membership

Stale Privileged Group Membership Increases Domain Attack Surface

docs.title: Report the Complete Path
docs.text:
Avoid:

User Can Modify Group

Prefer:

CORP\alice
   |
   v
AddMember
   |
   v
CORP\Server Admins
   |
   v
Local Administrator
   |
   v
Production Servers

This explains the actual impact.

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Low-Privilege Account Can Modify Privileged Active Directory Group

Affected Principal:
CORP\helpdesk-user

Affected Group:
CORP\Server Admins

Permission:
AddMember

Description:
The CORP\helpdesk-user account has permission to modify membership of
the CORP\Server Admins group.

Members of CORP\Server Admins receive local administrative privileges
on production Windows servers.

A user controlling CORP\helpdesk-user could therefore add a controlled
account to the group and inherit the administrative access assigned to
the group.

During controlled validation, the effective group permission and
resulting attack path were confirmed. No unnecessary remote command
execution was performed.

Impact:
Successful abuse would allow a low-privilege domain user to obtain
administrative access to systems managed through the affected group.

Depending on the systems accessible to the group, this could enable
credential access, lateral movement, access to sensitive data, and
further privilege escalation.

Recommendation:
Remove the unnecessary membership-modification permission from
CORP\helpdesk-user.

Review the complete ACL of CORP\Server Admins, identify whether the
permission was explicitly assigned or inherited, restrict group
membership management to dedicated administrative identities, review
all current and nested members, and monitor privileged group membership
and ACL changes.

docs.text:
The basic model is:

User

The multi-domain model is:

Universal Groups

   |

Permissions

The ACL-driven group escalation model is:

The cross-domain model is:

        |

Domain A Group

A mature group assessment should answer:

Which groups exist?
       |

Group Name

    X

    +
Nesting

ACLs

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Active Directory groups should be analysed as privilege containers rather than simply lists of users.

The basic model is:

Identity
   |
   v
Group
   |
   v
Permission
   |
   v
Resource

However, real environments commonly contain:

Identity
   |
   v
Group
   |
   v
Nested Group
   |
   v
Another Group
   |
   v
Resource Permission

Therefore:

Direct Membership

is not sufficient.

Assess:

Recursive Membership
Group Scope
Group ACL
Group Owner
Membership Control
Resource Permissions
Cross-Domain Relationships

The most important offensive question is:

Which groups can my controlled
principal reach or modify?

The most important defensive question is:

Which principals can reach or
modify our privileged groups?

A complete attack path may look like:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Helpdesk
        |
        v
AddMember
        |
        v
Server Admins
        |
        v
Local Administrator
        |
        v
Production Servers

or:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
GenericWrite
        |
        v
Service Account
        |
        v
Privileged Group Membership
        |
        v
Administrative Access

Group names alone should never determine severity.

Instead:

Membership
    +
Nesting
    +
ACL Control
    +
Resource Access
    +
Resulting Privilege
    =
Security Impact

The assessment workflow should therefore be:

Enumerate Groups
      |
      v
Enumerate Members
      |
      v
Expand Nesting
      |
      v
Identify Privileged Groups
      |
      v
Identify Group Controllers
      |
      v
Map Resource Access
      |
      v
Build Attack Paths
      |
      v
Validate Safely
      |
      v
Collect Evidence

For defenders:

Inventory
   |
   v
Assign Ownership
   |
   v
Review Membership
   |
   v
Review Nesting
   |
   v
Review ACLs
   |
   v
Reduce Privilege
   |
   v
Monitor Changes
   |
   v
Repeat

The strongest Active Directory group assessments therefore combine:

PowerShell
   +
LDAP
   +
ACL Analysis
   +
BloodHound
   +
Host-Level Access Mapping
   +
Authentication Telemetry

to determine not simply:

Who belongs to which group?

but the much more important question:

What can each identity ultimately control?

docs.title: Impacket
docs.text:
Impacket is a collection of Python classes and command-line tools for working with network protocols commonly encountered during Windows and Active Directory security assessments.

It provides implementations and tooling for protocols including:

SMB1 / SMB2 / SMB3
MS-RPC
LDAP
Kerberos
NTLM
DCOM
WMI
TDS / MSSQL

For an Active Directory assessment, Impacket is especially useful because it provides focused tools for:

Directory enumeration
Kerberos enumeration
Kerberos ticket operations
SMB access
RPC enumeration
Delegation discovery
Credential access
Remote administration
NTLM relay testing
Ticket analysis

A useful way to think about Impacket is:

                    Impacket
                       |
       +---------------+---------------+
       |               |               |
       v               v               v
   Enumeration     Authentication     Protocols
       |               |               |
       v               v               v
      LDAP          Kerberos          SMB
      RPC             NTLM            RPC
      SMB            Password         WMI
                       Hash           DCOM
                       Ticket         MSSQL
                       Key

docs.title: Authorised Testing
docs.text:
The commands in this note are intended for:

Authorised penetration testing
Internal security assessments
Red team exercises
Purple team exercises
Training laboratories
CTFs
Security research

Some Impacket tools can:

Request Kerberos tickets
Validate credentials
Access remote shares
Dump credentials
Create services
Create scheduled tasks
Execute commands remotely
Relay authentication
Modify remote systems

Confirm that the specific activity is permitted by the rules of engagement before using intrusive functionality.

docs.title: Impacket in the AD Workflow
docs.text:
Impacket is most useful after basic network and domain context has been established.

Network Access
     |
     v
AD Discovery
     |
     v
Domain Controller
     |
     v
Credentials?
     |
 +---+---+
 |       |
No      Yes
 |       |
 v       v
Basic   Authenticated
Enum    Enumeration
         |
         +--> LDAP
         +--> SMB
         +--> RPC
         +--> Kerberos
         |
         v
   Relationships
         |
         v
   Focused Validation

NetExec is often useful for broad discovery and access mapping.

Impacket is often useful for focused protocol operations.

NetExec
   |
   v
Broad Discovery
   |
   v
Interesting Relationship
   |
   v
Impacket
   |
   v
Focused Investigation

docs.title: Current Version
docs.text:
Check your installed version rather than assuming commands from an older write-up still apply.

python3 -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('impacket'))"

The upstream repository should be checked when syntax differs from your installed package.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The upstream Impacket project recommends pipx for system-wide command-line installation.

Install pipx:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install pipx

Ensure the pipx path is configured:

pipx ensurepath

Install the current stable Impacket package:

python3 -m pipx install impacket

Open a new shell if necessary.

docs.title: Kali Linux
docs.text:
Kali also packages Impacket.

Search:

apt search impacket

Install:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3-impacket

Depending on the package and distribution, command names can differ from upstream pipx installations.

Always check:

which impacket-smbclient

and:

which smbclient.py

docs.title: Installed Commands
docs.text:
List Impacket-related commands:

compgen -c | grep '^impacket-' | sort -u

Or inspect the pipx environment:

pipx list

Common packaged command names may look like:

impacket-GetADUsers
impacket-GetNPUsers
impacket-GetUserSPNs
impacket-findDelegation
impacket-getTGT
impacket-getST
impacket-lookupsid
impacket-smbclient
impacket-secretsdump
impacket-psexec
impacket-wmiexec
impacket-smbexec
impacket-dcomexec
impacket-atexec
impacket-ntlmrelayx
impacket-ticketer
impacket-ticketConverter

When working directly from the source repository, the corresponding example files use names such as:

GetADUsers.py
GetNPUsers.py
GetUserSPNs.py
findDelegation.py
getTGT.py
getST.py
lookupsid.py
smbclient.py
secretsdump.py
psexec.py
wmiexec.py
smbexec.py
dcomexec.py
atexec.py
ntlmrelayx.py
ticketer.py
ticketConverter.py

This note uses the .py names conceptually.

Adapt them to the command names installed on your system.

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
Every Impacket tool has its own options.

Always check:

impacket-GetADUsers -h

or, from the source tree:

python3 examples/GetADUsers.py -h

This is particularly important because Impacket evolves and command-line options can change.

docs.title: Target Syntax
docs.text:
Many Impacket tools use a target format similar to:

domain/username:password@target

Example:

example.local/alice:Password@dc01.example.local

Other tools use:

domain/username

with the target or Domain Controller supplied separately.

Always check:

<tool> -h

docs.title: Authentication Models
docs.text:
Impacket supports several authentication models.

                   Authentication
                         |
       +-----------------+-----------------+
       |                 |                 |
       v                 v                 v
    Password            NTLM            Kerberos
                          |                 |
                          v                 |
                        Hash                |
                                            |
                             +--------------+-------------+
                             |              |             |
                             v              v             v
                          Password         TGT          AES Key
                                           |
                                           v
                                         ccache

docs.title: Password Authentication
docs.text:
Many tools accept:

domain/user:password@target

Example:

impacket-smbclient \
    example.local/alice:'Password'@file01.example.local

Be careful with:

Shell history
Process listings
Terminal logs
Screenshots
Evidence files

when supplying plaintext credentials.

docs.title: NTLM Hash Authentication
docs.text:
Many Impacket tools support:

-hashes LMHASH:NTHASH

A commonly used format when only the NT hash is known is:

-hashes :NTHASH

Example structure:

impacket-smbclient \
    example.local/alice@file01.example.local \
    -hashes :<NT-HASH>

This represents NTLM hash-based authentication.

The dedicated Pass-the-Hash note should cover the technique and its prerequisites in detail.

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
Many Impacket tools support:

-k

for Kerberos authentication.

Depending on the tool, Kerberos authentication may use:

Password
NTLM hashes
AES key
Kerberos credential cache

Kerberos workflows depend heavily on:

DNS
FQDNs
SPNs
Time synchronisation
Domain configuration
KDC reachability

docs.title: AES Keys
docs.text:
Where supported, Impacket tools commonly expose:

-aesKey

for Kerberos authentication using an AES key.

Always verify the tool's help:

<tool> -h

before using key-based authentication.

docs.title: Kerberos Credential Cache
docs.text:
Kerberos tickets are commonly stored in a credential cache:

.ccache

Set:

export KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/ticket.ccache

Verify:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

Then use a Kerberos-aware Impacket tool with its supported Kerberos options.

docs.title: Kerberos Ticket Inspection
docs.text:
If Kerberos utilities are installed:

klist

can be useful for reviewing the current credential cache.

The important relationship is:

Ticket
  |
  v
Identity
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Validity

docs.title: Kerberos Requirements
docs.text:
Before troubleshooting Impacket itself, verify:

DNS
Domain
FQDN
Domain Controller
KDC
Clock
SPN
Ticket

Check time:

date

Check the DC:

dig dc01.example.local

Check Kerberos:

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

Check LDAP:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

docs.title: Core Impacket Tool Map
docs.text:
A useful operational map is:

ENUMERATION

GetADUsers
GetNPUsers
GetUserSPNs
lookupsid
findDelegation
samrdump
rpcdump
net


KERBEROS

GetNPUsers
GetUserSPNs
