docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
MDT should be viewed as part of the Windows deployment trust chain.

The fundamental relationship is:

Deployment Infrastructure
        |
        v
Deployment Content
        |
        v
Windows Installation
        |
        v
Managed System

The important security questions are:

Who Can Read the Deployment Infrastructure?

Who Can Modify It?

What Credentials Does It Contain?

What Privileges Do Those Credentials Have?

Which Systems Trust the Deployment Content?

Legacy MDT environments deserve particular attention because reusable credentials may exist in:

Bootstrap.ini
CustomSettings.ini
Unattend.xml
Scripts
Boot Images
Old Media
Backups

The credential path is:

Deployment File
      |
      v
Credential
      |
      v
Account Privilege
      |
      v
Security Impact

The integrity path is:

Write Permission
      |
      v
Deployment Content
      |
      v
Task Sequence
      |
      v
Managed System

The strongest assessment does not modify production deployment content.

Instead, establish:

Permission
    +
Active Reference
    +
Execution Context
    +
Target Scope
    =
Demonstrated Risk

Because MDT is now retired, organisations still using it should also evaluate migration.

The objective should not simply be:

Replace MDT

but:

Remove Legacy Credential Exposure
        +
Preserve Least Privilege
        +
Protect Deployment Integrity
        +
Improve Administrative Separation
        +
Retire Old Infrastructure

The next infrastructure topic is:

System Center Operations Manager - SCOM

docs.title: Active Directory Penetration Testing Methodology
docs.text:
Active Directory penetration testing should be performed as a structured process rather than as a collection of unrelated tools and commands.

The objective is to understand how an attacker could move from the starting position provided by the engagement to progressively more valuable identities, systems, network segments, and ultimately business-critical infrastructure.

A useful model is:

Starting Position
       |
       v
Network Context
       |
       v
Domain Discovery
       |
       v
Enumeration
       |
       v
Attack Surface Mapping
       |
       v
Attack Path Analysis
       |
       v
Controlled Validation
       |
       v
New Access
       |
       v
Re-enumeration
       |
       v
Impact
       |
       v
Detection + Remediation

The methodology should remain applicable whether the assessment starts with:

No credentials
Domain credentials
VPN access
A workstation
A shell
Local administrator access
A compromised server
An assumed breach scenario

docs.title: Authorised Testing
docs.text:
The techniques described in these notes are intended for:

Authorised penetration testing
Internal security assessments
Red team exercises
Purple team exercises
Training laboratories
CTFs
Security research

Active Directory testing can affect authentication, endpoints, Domain Controllers, certificate services, and other critical infrastructure.

Before testing, confirm the rules of engagement for techniques such as:

Password spraying
Credential capture
NTLM relay
Authentication coercion
Credential dumping
Remote command execution
Service creation
Scheduled task creation
Account creation
Group membership modification
ACL modification
GPO modification
Certificate enrolment
Persistence
Domain Controller interaction
Trust exploitation

Use the least intrusive technique necessary to demonstrate the security issue.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Active Directory penetration testing is primarily:

Attack Path Analysis

rather than:

Run every AD tool

The central question is:

What can the current identity reach or control?

Then:

What new identity, system, permission,
credential, or network position does that provide?

The process repeats.

Enumerate
   |
   v
Analyse
   |
   v
Validate
   |
   v
Gain New Context
   |
   v
Enumerate Again

docs.title: Assessment Phases
docs.text:
A practical Active Directory assessment can be divided into:

 1. Scope and Rules of Engagement
 2. Starting Position
 3. Local Network Context
 4. Network Discovery
 5. Domain Discovery
 6. Unauthenticated Enumeration
 7. Authenticated Enumeration
 8. Identity Mapping
 9. Host and Service Mapping
10. Share and Data Discovery
11. BloodHound Collection
12. ACL and Permission Analysis
13. Authentication Analysis
14. Credential Exposure
15. Kerberos Analysis
16. NTLM and Relay Analysis
17. AD CS Analysis
18. Privilege Escalation
19. Lateral Movement
20. Pivoting
21. Re-enumeration
22. Trust Analysis
23. Enterprise Infrastructure
24. Domain / Forest Impact
25. Persistence Assessment
26. Detection Review
27. Evidence and Reporting
28. Retesting

Not every engagement will require every phase.

docs.title: Methodology Overview
docs.text:
AUTHORISED ACCESS
                           |
                           v
                   STARTING POSITION
                           |
             +-------------+-------------+
             |             |             |
             v             v             v
       No Credentials   Domain User   Host Access
             |             |             |
             +-------------+-------------+
                           |
                           v
                    NETWORK CONTEXT
                           |
                           v
                   DOMAIN DISCOVERY
                           |
                           v
                      ENUMERATION
                           |
        +------------------+------------------+
        |                  |                  |
        v                  v                  v
     Identities           Hosts          Infrastructure
        |                  |                  |
        +------------------+------------------+
                           |
                           v
                      BLOODHOUND
                           |
                           v
                    ATTACK PATHS
                           |
        +------------------+------------------+
        |                  |                  |
        v                  v                  v
     Kerberos             NTLM             ACL / GPO
        |                  |                  |
        +------------------+------------------+
                           |
                 +---------+---------+
                 |                   |
                 v                   v
            Credentials             AD CS
                 |                   |
                 +---------+---------+
                           |
                           v
                 PRIVILEGE ESCALATION
                           |
                           v
                  LATERAL MOVEMENT
                           |
                           v
                       PIVOTING
                           |
                           v
                 NEW NETWORK CONTEXT
                           |
                           v
                    RE-ENUMERATION
                           |
                           v
                        TRUSTS
                           |
                           v
                DOMAIN / FOREST IMPACT

docs.title: 1. Scope and Rules of Engagement
docs.text:
Before interacting with the environment, establish exactly what is permitted.

Record:

Target organisation
Target domains
Target forests
Allowed IP ranges
Excluded IP ranges
Provided credentials
Provided hosts
Testing window
Allowed tools
Restricted tools
Allowed protocols
Password spraying permission
Credential dumping permission
Relay permission
Coercion permission
Remote execution permission
Persistence permission
Social engineering permission
Data access restrictions
Production restrictions

Do not assume that because Active Directory is in scope, every system joined to the domain is also in scope.

docs.title: Define Intrusiveness
docs.text:
Classify planned activities.

Example:

Activity Typical Intrusiveness DNS enumeration Low LDAP enumeration Low SMB share enumeration Low BloodHound collection Low to Moderate Kerberoasting Low to Moderate Password spraying Moderate Credential capture Moderate Authentication coercion Moderate to High NTLM relay High Credential dumping High Remote execution High Account modification High GPO modification Very High Persistence Very High

The actual risk depends on the environment and implementation.

docs.title: 2. Determine the Starting Position
docs.text:
Document the exact starting position.

Examples:

Scenario A
---------
Internal network access
No credentials
Kali Linux

Scenario B
---------
Internal network access
Domain user credentials
Kali Linux

Scenario C
---------
Domain-joined Windows workstation
Standard domain user

Scenario D
---------
Windows server
Local administrator

Scenario E
---------
Compromised application server
Two network interfaces
Domain service account

The starting position determines the first enumeration strategy.

docs.title: Starting Position Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

What identity do I have?

What host am I on?

Is the host domain joined?

What network am I on?

What DNS server am I using?

What routes exist?

What credentials are available?

What privileges does the current user have?

Can I reach the Domain Controllers?

Can I resolve the domain?

Can I authenticate to LDAP or SMB?

docs.title: 3. Local Network Context
docs.text: Before scanning the network, understand the current host.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Identify interfaces:

ip addr

Routes:

ip route

DNS:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Hostname:

hostname

Current identity:

id

ARP/neighbour information:

ip neigh

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Identity:

whoami

Full token information:

whoami /all

Hostname:

hostname

Network configuration:

ipconfig /all

Routes:

route print

ARP cache:

arp -a

Domain:

echo %USERDOMAIN%

DNS domain:

echo %USERDNSDOMAIN%

Logon server:

echo %LOGONSERVER%

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:USERDNSDOMAIN
$env:LOGONSERVER

Network:

Get-NetIPConfiguration

Routes:

Get-NetRoute

Interfaces:

Get-NetAdapter

docs.title: Record the Network Position
docs.text:
Example:

Host: kali01
IP: 10.10.20.50
Subnet: 10.10.20.0/24
Gateway: 10.10.20.1
DNS: 10.10.20.10
Domain: corp.example.local

This becomes important when pivoting later.

docs.title: 4. Network Discovery
docs.text:
The objective is not immediately to scan every port on every host.

First determine:

What networks are reachable?

Where are the likely Domain Controllers?

Which hosts expose Windows services?

Where are management services?

Which infrastructure systems are visible?

docs.title: Useful AD Services
docs.text:
Look for services such as:

DNS
Kerberos
LDAP
LDAPS
SMB
RPC
Global Catalog
WinRM
RDP
MSSQL
HTTP/HTTPS

Common ports include:

Port Service 53 DNS 88 Kerberos 135 RPC 139 NetBIOS 389 LDAP 445 SMB 464 Kerberos password operations 636 LDAPS 3268 Global Catalog 3269 Global Catalog TLS 3389 RDP 5985 WinRM HTTP 5986 WinRM HTTPS

Port presence alone does not identify the security posture of the service.

docs.title: 5. Domain Discovery
docs.text:
Domain discovery should establish:

Domain name
Forest name
Domain Controllers
DNS namespace
AD sites
Trust relationships

docs.title: Windows Domain Discovery
docs.text:
echo %USERDOMAIN%
echo %USERDNSDOMAIN%

Find a Domain Controller:

nltest /dsgetdc:example.local

List Domain Controllers:

nltest /dclist:example.local

Trust information:

nltest /domain_trusts

docs.title: DNS Discovery
docs.text:
Domain Controllers are advertised through DNS SRV records.

LDAP:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

Kerberos:

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

Global Catalog:

dig SRV _gc._tcp.example.local

docs.title: RootDSE
docs.text:
LDAP RootDSE can reveal directory metadata.

ldapsearch -x \
  -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
  -s base \
  -b "" \
  defaultNamingContext \
  rootDomainNamingContext \
  configurationNamingContext \
  dnsHostName

Possible output may identify:

Domain naming context
Forest root
Configuration partition
Domain Controller hostname

docs.title: 6. Unauthenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
If no credentials are available, determine what information can be obtained without authentication.

Potential areas include:

DNS
SMB configuration
Anonymous SMB
LDAP RootDSE
RPC exposure
Kerberos username validation
Name-resolution behaviour
Web applications
Management interfaces
Certificate services

Do not immediately attempt password attacks.

Build the environment map first.

docs.title: SMB
docs.text:
Basic NetExec host identification:

nxc smb 10.10.20.10

Against a subnet:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24

This can help identify:

Hostname
Domain
SMB signing configuration
SMB dialect information

depending on the target and tool version.

docs.title: Anonymous SMB
docs.text:
Where authorised, test whether anonymous or guest access is exposed.

For example:

smbclient -L //10.10.20.10 -N

Do not interpret a failed anonymous query as evidence that SMB is securely configured overall.

docs.title: RPC
docs.text:
RPC may expose useful information depending on server configuration.

Example:

rpcclient -U "" -N 10.10.20.10

If a connection succeeds, determine what operations are actually permitted.

docs.title: 7. Authenticated Enumeration
docs.text:
A normal domain account often provides significant directory visibility.

Once valid credentials are available, systematically enumerate:

Domain
Users
Groups
Computers
Domain Controllers
SPNs
Delegation
Trusts
Password policy
Shares
Sessions
ACLs
GPOs
AD CS

docs.title: Credential Format
docs.text:
Keep authentication variables conceptually separate:

DOMAIN
USERNAME
PASSWORD
NTLM HASH
KERBEROS TICKET
AES KEY
TARGET
DOMAIN CONTROLLER

This prevents mistakes when switching tools.

Example lab values:

Domain: example.local
Username: alice
Target: dc01.example.local
DC IP: 10.10.20.10

docs.title: NetExec Workflow
docs.text:
NetExec is particularly useful for protocol-oriented enumeration.

Start with:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24

Then validate provided credentials:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -p 'Password'

LDAP:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -p 'Password'

The dedicated NetExec note will cover its functionality in detail.

docs.title: Avoid Unnecessary Authentication Volume
docs.text:
Do not repeatedly authenticate the same credentials against hundreds or thousands of hosts without considering:

Account lockout
SOC alerts
EDR telemetry
Authentication logs
Network load
Rules of engagement

Start narrow.

Expand deliberately.

docs.title: 8. Identity Mapping
docs.text:
Identify:

Users
Groups
Privileged groups
Service accounts
Computer accounts
Managed service accounts
Disabled accounts
Stale accounts
Administrative accounts

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Important questions:

Which users exist?

Which are privileged?

Which have SPNs?

Which do not require Kerberos pre-authentication?

Which accounts are service identities?

Which accounts appear stale?

Which accounts have unusual descriptions?

Which accounts can access sensitive systems?

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Do not inspect only default privileged groups.

Custom groups frequently matter more.

Examples:

SQL Administrators
Server Support
Backup Administrators
SCCM Administrators
VMware Administrators
Application Support
Certificate Managers
Helpdesk
Tier 0 Operators

docs.title: Nested Groups
docs.text:
Always investigate nested memberships.

Alice
 |
 v
Helpdesk
 |
 v
Server Support
 |
 v
Production Administrators

A user may possess privilege indirectly.

docs.title: 9. Host and Service Mapping
docs.text:
Map computers to:

Hostname
IP
Operating system
Role
Open services
Administrative relationships
Logged-on users
Network segments

docs.title: Host Categories
docs.text:
Useful categories include:

Domain Controllers
Workstations
Application servers
File servers
Database servers
Management servers
Certificate authorities
Backup servers
Virtualisation hosts
Jump servers
Developer systems
Security systems

docs.title: Why Host Role Matters
docs.text:
A server may be more valuable than its local privileges suggest.

For example:

SCCM Server
    |
    v
Endpoint Management
    |
    v
Hundreds of Computers

or:

Backup Server
    |
    v
Domain Controller Backups
    |
    v
Domain Credentials

docs.title: 10. Share and Data Discovery
docs.text:
Enumerate accessible SMB shares.

Questions:

Which shares exist?

Which shares can I read?

Which shares can I write?

What sensitive information exists?

Are scripts stored there?

Are credentials stored there?

Are deployment packages stored there?

Are backups exposed?

docs.title: NetExec Share Enumeration
docs.text:
Example:

nxc smb FILE01.example.local \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -p 'Password' \
  --shares

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
List shares:

smbclient -L //FILE01.example.local \
  -U 'EXAMPLE/alice'

Connect:

smbclient //FILE01.example.local/Share \
  -U 'EXAMPLE/alice'

docs.title: Sensitive Share Content
docs.text:
Look for:

*.xml
*.ini
*.config
*.conf
*.ps1
*.bat
*.cmd
*.vbs
*.kdbx
*.pfx
*.p12
*.pem
*.key
*.rdp
*.sql
*.bak
*.zip
*.7z

Also consider:

Passwords
API keys
Connection strings
Service credentials
Deployment credentials
Private keys
Certificates
Backup data

Do not collect unnecessary business data.

docs.title: 11. BloodHound Collection
docs.text:
BloodHound can convert AD relationships into a graph.

Conceptually:

Collection
    |
    v
Directory Objects
    |
    v
Relationships
    |
    v
Graph
    |
    v
Attack Paths

docs.title: BloodHound Is Not a Vulnerability Scanner
docs.text:
Treat BloodHound output as:

Attack Path Candidates

not:

Confirmed Vulnerabilities

Validate important edges manually.

docs.title: Important Relationships
docs.text:
Examples include:

MemberOf
AdminTo
HasSession
GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
ForceChangePassword
AddMember
Owns
CanRDP
CanPSRemote
Delegation relationships
Certificate relationships

docs.title: Attack Path Question
docs.text:
Instead of asking:

What can Alice do?

ask:

What can Alice reach after one relationship?

What can that new principal reach?

What happens after three relationships?

Example:

alice
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
Helpdesk
 |
 | GenericWrite
 v
svc_backup
 |
 | AdminTo
 v
BACKUP01
 |
 | Sensitive data
 v
Higher Privilege

docs.title: 12. ACL and Permission Analysis
docs.text:
Active Directory permissions are one of the most important attack surfaces.

Review:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
WriteProperty
ResetPassword
AddMember
CreateChild
DeleteChild
Extended Rights

The exact impact depends on the target object and effective permissions.

docs.title: ACL Methodology
docs.text:
Principal
    |
    v
Permission
    |
    v
Target Object
    |
    v
Security-Sensitive Attribute / Operation
    |
    v
Resulting Capability

Example:

Helpdesk
    |
    | Reset Password
    v
Service Account
    |
    v
New Authentication Context

docs.title: Do Not Stop at the Permission Name
docs.text:
For every interesting ACL:

Who has the permission?

Is it inherited?

What object does it apply to?

What property can be modified?

Can the principal actually exercise it?

What privilege would result?

docs.title: 13. Authentication Analysis
docs.text:
Analyse both:

Kerberos
NTLM

and their associated security controls.

docs.title: Kerberos Questions
docs.text:
Which accounts have SPNs?

Which accounts lack pre-authentication?

Which accounts use delegation?

Which services support Kerberos?

What ticket relationships exist?

Are service-account passwords appropriately managed?

docs.title: NTLM Questions
docs.text:
Where is NTLM still accepted?

Is SMB signing required?

Is LDAP signing enforced?

Is channel binding used where appropriate?

Are systems susceptible to name-resolution poisoning?

Can authentication be coerced?

Are relay destinations available?

docs.title: 14. Credential Exposure
docs.text:
Credential exposure should be assessed systematically.

Potential sources include:

Shares
Scripts
Configuration
Registry
Services
Scheduled tasks
Deployment systems
Backups
Managed accounts
User attributes
PowerShell history
Applications
Local credential stores

docs.title: Credential Access Model
docs.text:
Credential Source
      |
      v
Who Can Read It?
      |
      v
Credential Type
      |
      v
Where Is It Valid?
      |
      v
What Privilege Does It Provide?

docs.title: Credential Reuse
docs.text:
A credential becomes more significant when it works elsewhere.

Credential
   |
   +--> Host A
   |
   +--> Host B
   |
   +--> Host C

Avoid uncontrolled credential spraying.

Validate deliberately.

docs.title: 15. Kerberos Analysis
docs.text:
Important areas include:

AS-REP Roasting
Kerberoasting
Tickets
Delegation
S4U
RBCD
Service accounts

docs.title: Kerberoasting Workflow
docs.text:
Domain User
     |
     v
Enumerate SPNs
     |
     v
Identify Relevant Service Accounts
     |
     v
Request Service Ticket
     |
     v
Offline Analysis
     |
     v
Credential Validation

Do not assume every SPN represents a useful or weak credential.

docs.title: AS-REP Roasting Workflow
docs.text:
Enumerate Users
      |
      v
Identify Accounts Without Pre-Authentication
      |
      v
Request AS-REP
      |
      v
Offline Analysis

The root issue is account configuration combined with password strength.

docs.title: 16. NTLM and Relay Analysis
docs.text:
Separate:

Capture
Coercion
Relay

These are related but different.

docs.title: Capture
docs.text:
Victim
   |
   v
Authentication Attempt
   |
   v
Attacker-Controlled Listener
   |
   v
Captured Challenge/Response Material

docs.title: Coercion
docs.text:
Tester
   |
   v
Trigger
   |
   v
Target System
   |
   v
Outbound Authentication

docs.title: Relay
docs.text:
Victim
   |
   | Authentication
   v
Relay Host
   |
   v
Target Service

A successful relay path depends on the destination and its protections.

docs.title: Responder
docs.text:
Responder can help assess name-resolution and authentication behaviour involving:

LLMNR
NBT-NS
mDNS

Use carefully in production environments because poisoning can affect unrelated systems.

The dedicated Responder note will explain safe configuration and validation.

docs.title: Relay Protection Matrix
docs.text:
During an assessment, track protections.

Example:

Host SMB Signing LDAP Signing LDAPS Notes DC01 Required Enforced Yes DC FILE01 Not required N/A N/A Review relay exposure APP01 Required N/A N/A Application server

Do not report relay exposure without validating the relevant conditions.

docs.title: 17. AD CS Analysis
docs.text:
If Active Directory Certificate Services is deployed, treat it as a major identity system.

Workflow:

Discover AD CS
      |
      v
Enumerate CAs
      |
      v
Enumerate Templates
      |
      v
Analyse Permissions
      |
      v
Analyse Template Configuration
      |
      v
Identify ESC Conditions
      |
      v
Validate Safely
      |
      v
Determine Identity Impact

docs.title: Certipy
docs.text:
Certipy is commonly used for AD CS assessment.

Example discovery workflow conceptually:

Credentials
    |
    v
Certipy Enumeration
    |
    v
Certificate Authorities
    |
    v
Templates
    |
    v
Candidate Misconfigurations

Tool findings should be manually reviewed.

docs.title: 18. Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Privilege escalation in AD is usually relationship-driven.

Examples:

Weak ACL
Credential Exposure
Group Membership
Service Account
Delegation
GPO Control
AD CS
Local Administrator Access
Session Exposure
Trust Relationship

docs.title: Escalation Model
docs.text:
Current Principal
        |
        v
Security Relationship
        |
        v
New Capability
        |
        v
New Identity / Host
        |
        v
Higher Privilege

docs.title: Track Each Step
docs.text:
For each escalation:

Source principal
Target object
Permission
Prerequisite
Validation
Result
Evidence
Detection
Remediation

docs.title: 19. Lateral Movement
docs.text:
After obtaining additional credentials or privileges, determine where they are valid.

Potential management protocols include:

SMB
WinRM
WMI
DCOM
RDP
PowerShell Remoting

docs.title: Lateral Movement Decision
docs.text:
Credential
    |
    v
Target Host
    |
    v
Network Reachable?
    |
    +-- No --> Pivot / Route
    |
    +-- Yes
          |
          v
Authentication Valid?
          |
          +-- No --> Stop
          |
          +-- Yes
                |
                v
Required Privilege?
                |
                +-- No --> Enumerate
                |
                +-- Yes
                      |
                      v
              Authorised Validation

docs.title: Administrative Access Mapping
docs.text:
NetExec can assist with identifying systems where credentials have administrative access.

Do not treat authentication success as administrative access.

Keep these states separate:

Authentication Failed

Authentication Successful

Authentication Successful + User Access

Authentication Successful + Administrative Access

docs.title: 20. Pivoting
docs.text:
Pivoting is a core part of internal penetration testing.

After gaining access to a host, immediately inspect:

Interfaces
Routes
DNS
ARP / neighbours
Listening services
Reachable networks

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Kali
10.10.10.50
   |
   v
WEB01
10.10.10.20
172.16.20.10
   |
   v
172.16.20.0/24
   |
   +--> DC02
   +--> SQL01
   +--> FILE02

Kali cannot directly reach:

172.16.20.0/24

but WEB01 can.

WEB01 can therefore become a pivot.

docs.title: Pivoting Decision Tree
docs.text:
Need one remote service?
        |
        +--> Port Forwarding

Need several TCP services?
        |
        +--> SOCKS Proxy

Need tools to treat subnet as routed?
        |
        +--> TUN-Based Pivot

Need access through another pivot?
        |
        +--> Double Pivot

docs.title: Common Pivoting Technologies
docs.text:
Our dedicated pivoting notes will cover:

SSH
ProxyChains
Chisel
Ligolo-ng
socat
netsh portproxy

docs.title: Route Documentation
docs.text:
Always record pivot routes.

Example:

Network Reachable Through Method 10.10.10.0/24 Direct Local 172.16.20.0/24 WEB01 Ligolo-ng 10.50.30.0/24 APP02 via WEB01 Double pivot

Without this documentation, complex internal assessments quickly become confusing.

docs.title: DNS Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Routing packets does not automatically solve DNS.

Ask:

Which DNS server resolves the internal domain?

Can the tester reach it?

Does the pivot solution route DNS?

Should hostnames be added temporarily to /etc/hosts?

Does Kerberos require correct hostname resolution?

Kerberos frequently makes DNS and hostname accuracy particularly important.

docs.title: 21. Re-Enumeration
docs.text:
Every significant privilege or network change should trigger another enumeration cycle.

New Credential
      |
      v
Re-enumerate

New Host
      |
      v
Re-enumerate

New Network
      |
      v
Re-enumerate

New Group
      |
      v
Re-enumerate

New Domain
      |
      v
Re-enumerate

This is one of the most important habits in internal testing.

docs.title: Why Re-Enumeration Matters
docs.text:
A new identity may reveal:

Additional LDAP objects
Additional shares
Additional hosts
New BloodHound edges
New AD CS templates
New administrative access
New trust relationships

A new network position may reveal an entirely different environment.

docs.title: 22. Trust Analysis
docs.text:
Large AD environments may contain:

Child domains
Parent domains
Multiple forests
External trusts
Forest trusts

Enumerate:

Trust direction
Trust type
Transitivity
SID filtering
Selective authentication
Cross-domain groups
Cross-domain ACLs

docs.title: Trust Model
docs.text:
Domain A
   |
   | Trust
   v
Domain B

Do not interpret a trust as automatic compromise.

Determine what authentication and authorisation relationships actually cross the boundary.

docs.title: 23. Enterprise Infrastructure
docs.text:
AD assessments should not focus exclusively on Domain Controllers.

High-value infrastructure may include:

AD CS
SCCM
WSUS
MDT
SCOM
ADFS
DNS
PXE
Backup systems
Virtualisation
Password-management systems
Jump hosts

These systems may provide broad administrative capability.

docs.title: Infrastructure Impact
docs.text:
For example:

SCCM
  |
  v
Endpoint Management
  |
  v
Many Domain Computers

or:

AD CS
  |
  v
Certificate Authentication
  |
  v
Identity Infrastructure

docs.title: 24. Domain / Forest Impact
docs.text:
The objective is to determine realistic impact, not necessarily to perform every possible action.

Potential high-impact positions include:

Domain Admin
Enterprise Admin
Domain Controller control
Certificate Authority control
SCCM administrative control
Identity federation control
Backup infrastructure control
Tier-0 system control

docs.title: Minimum Necessary Proof
docs.text:
Prefer:

Prove capability

rather than:

Perform destructive action

For example, if an ACL clearly permits adding a principal to a privileged group, the rules of engagement may allow the attack path to be demonstrated without leaving the modification in place.

Always restore changes made during testing.

docs.title: 25. Persistence Assessment
docs.text:
Persistence should normally be considered only after impact has been established and only where explicitly authorised.

Review whether an attacker could persist through:

Account manipulation
Group membership
ACL changes
GPO changes
Certificate authentication
Kerberos-related mechanisms
Directory object modification
Trust manipulation

The assessment may only need to demonstrate that persistence is possible.

docs.title: 26. Detection Review
docs.text:
A mature assessment should identify detection opportunities.

Ask:

Would this activity be logged?

Would the SOC see it?

Would EDR detect it?

Would identity monitoring alert?

Would unusual LDAP enumeration be noticed?

Would account changes be detected?

Would certificate enrolment be monitored?

Would relay behaviour be visible?

docs.title: Important Telemetry
docs.text:
Potential sources include:

Windows Security logs
Domain Controller logs
Directory Service logs
PowerShell logs
Sysmon
EDR
Microsoft Defender for Identity
Network telemetry
SMB telemetry
Certificate Services logs
Authentication logs
Firewall logs
DNS logs

docs.title: Purple Team Integration
docs.text:
Where permitted, confirmed paths can be replayed collaboratively.

Red Team
   |
   v
Technique
   |
   v
Telemetry
   |
   v
Blue Team
   |
   v
Detection
   |
   v
Improvement

This can transform a penetration-test finding into a reusable detection capability.

docs.title: 27. Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Evidence collection should happen throughout the engagement.

Do not attempt to reconstruct the attack path at the end.

For every significant action record:

Timestamp
Source host
Source IP
Identity
Target
Tool
Command
Result
Security implication
Evidence file

docs.title: Example Evidence Record
docs.text:
Time:
2026-08-29 10:32

Source:
kali01 - 10.10.20.50

Identity:
EXAMPLE\alice

Target:
FILE01.example.local

Action:
SMB share enumeration

Result:
Authenticated successfully.
Readable share discovered.

Impact:
Share contains deployment configuration requiring review.

Evidence:
evidence/file01-shares.txt

docs.title: Save Tool Output
docs.text:
Example structure:

engagement/
│
├── evidence/
│   ├── dns/
│   ├── ldap/
│   ├── smb/
│   ├── bloodhound/
│   ├── kerberos/
│   ├── adcs/
│   └── screenshots/
│
├── credentials/
├── targets/
├── attack-paths/
└── notes/

Protect all assessment data appropriately.

docs.title: Command Logging
docs.text:
A shell history is not a sufficient engagement record.

Consider logging important commands and results explicitly.

For example:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 | tee evidence/smb/discovery.txt

Avoid storing plaintext passwords in shell history or evidence where possible.

docs.title: Credential Handling
docs.text:
Treat discovered credentials as sensitive client data.

Avoid unnecessary storage of:

Plaintext passwords
NTLM hashes
Kerberos tickets
Private keys
Certificates
Session tokens

Where evidence requires demonstrating credential exposure, redact appropriately.

docs.title: 28. Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation, verify the root cause.

Do not simply verify that the original command fails.

Example:

Original Finding
      |
      v
Excessive ACL
      |
      v
Remediation
      |
      v
Re-enumerate ACL
      |
      v
Verify Effective Permission Removed
      |
      v
Verify Attack Path Removed

This is stronger than:

Tool no longer works.

docs.title: Windows Workflow
docs.text:
A domain-joined Windows assessment may follow:

Current Identity
      |
      v
whoami /all
      |
      v
Network / Domain
      |
      v
Native Enumeration
      |
      v
PowerShell
      |
      v
PowerView
      |
      v
SharpHound
      |
      v
BloodHound
      |
      v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Windows Initial Commands
docs.text:
whoami
whoami /all
hostname
ipconfig /all
route print
arp -a
set

Domain:

echo %USERDOMAIN%
echo %USERDNSDOMAIN%
echo %LOGONSERVER%

docs.title: Native Domain Commands
docs.text:
net user /domain

Groups:

net group /domain

Domain Admins:

net group "Domain Admins" /domain

Current tickets:

klist

SPNs:

setspn -Q */*

Use large queries carefully in production environments.

docs.title: PowerShell Workflow
docs.text:
PowerShell can be used for:

Host enumeration
Domain enumeration
ACL analysis
Network analysis
File discovery
Configuration review

Prefer native cmdlets where practical.

docs.title: Linux / Kali Workflow
docs.text:
A Linux-based internal assessment commonly follows:

Network Context
      |
      v
DNS
      |
      v
SMB Discovery
      |
      v
LDAP
      |
      v
NetExec
      |
      v
Impacket
      |
      v
BloodHound
      |
      v
Certipy
      |
      v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Linux Tool Model
docs.text:
Discovery
  |
  +--> dig
  +--> nmap
  +--> NetExec
  |
Enumeration
  |
  +--> ldapsearch
  +--> NetExec
  +--> Impacket
  +--> bloodyAD
  |
Attack Path Analysis
  |
  +--> BloodHound
  |
AD CS
  |
  +--> Certipy
  |
Authentication Behaviour
  |
  +--> Responder
  +--> Impacket

docs.title: NetExec Methodology
docs.text:
Do not use NetExec merely as:

nxc <protocol> <entire-network> <everything>

Use it progressively.

Host Discovery
      |
      v
Protocol Identification
      |
      v
Credential Validation
      |
      v
Focused Enumeration
      |
      v
Privilege Identification

docs.title: NetExec Authentication Examples
docs.text:
Password:

nxc smb FILE01.example.local \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -p 'Password'

NTLM authentication may be possible where authorised and supported:

nxc smb FILE01.example.local \
  -d example.local \
  -u alice \
  -H '<NTLM-HASH>'

Use only credential material obtained or provided within the authorised assessment.

docs.title: NetExec Protocol Selection
docs.text:
Choose the protocol according to the question.

SMB
 |
 +--> Shares
 +--> Host information
 +--> Authentication
 +--> Administrative access

LDAP
 |
 +--> Domain information
 +--> Users
 +--> Groups
 +--> Directory relationships

WinRM
 |
 +--> Remote management access

MSSQL
 |
 +--> SQL Server authentication / access

RDP
 |
 +--> Remote desktop exposure / authentication context

The dedicated NetExec page will contain the detailed command reference.

docs.title: Impacket Methodology
docs.text:
Impacket tools should be selected according to protocol and objective.

Examples:

Kerberos
 |
 +--> GetNPUsers.py
 +--> GetUserSPNs.py
 +--> getTGT.py
 +--> getST.py
 +--> ticketer.py

SMB / Remote Management
 |
 +--> smbclient.py
 +--> psexec.py
 +--> smbexec.py
 +--> wmiexec.py

Credentials
 |
 +--> secretsdump.py

Relay
 |
 +--> ntlmrelayx.py

Do not treat Impacket as a single attack tool.

docs.title: Responder Methodology
docs.text:
Before using Responder, understand:

What protocols will it answer?

What interfaces will it listen on?

Will it poison name-resolution traffic?

Could unrelated users be affected?

Are captures permitted?

Is relay permitted?

A safer assessment workflow is:

Understand Environment
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Configure Only Required Protocols
      |
      v
Observe
      |
      v
Collect Minimum Evidence
      |
      v
Stop

docs.title: BloodHound Methodology
docs.text:
Use BloodHound as an analysis platform.

Collect
   |
   v
Import
   |
   v
Identify Candidate Path
   |
   v
Inspect Each Edge
   |
   v
Validate Permissions
   |
   v
Confirm Practical Path

Never report a multi-hop path without understanding the important edges.

docs.title: Tool Result != Finding
docs.text:
This rule applies throughout AD testing.

NetExec says authentication succeeded
        !=
Administrative compromise

BloodHound shows GenericWrite
        !=
Confirmed escalation

Certipy identifies a template
        !=
Confirmed certificate escalation

Responder captures authentication
        !=
Password recovered

Impacket requests a ticket
        !=
Account compromised

Port 445 open
        !=
SMB vulnerability

docs.title: Attack Path Tracking
docs.text:
Maintain a simple graph while testing.

Example:

alice
  |
  | MemberOf
  v
Helpdesk
  |
  | GenericWrite
  v
svc_backup
  |
  | AdminTo
  v
BACKUP01

Then annotate:

[1] alice -> Helpdesk
    Evidence: LDAP membership

[2] Helpdesk -> svc_backup
    Evidence: ACL

[3] svc_backup -> BACKUP01
    Evidence: administrative access

This makes reporting significantly easier.

docs.title: Attack Path Worksheet
docs.text:
For each path record:

Starting Identity:
Target:
Relationship:
Prerequisite:
Technique:
Validation:
Result:
New Access:
Detection:
Remediation:
Evidence:

docs.title: Re-Enumeration Trigger List
docs.text:
Re-enumerate after obtaining:

[ ] New domain credential
[ ] New local credential
[ ] New NTLM hash
[ ] New Kerberos ticket
[ ] New certificate
[ ] New group membership
[ ] New host access
[ ] Local administrator access
[ ] New network route
[ ] New domain access
[ ] New forest access

docs.title: OPSEC and Safety
docs.text:
Penetration testing and red teaming have different operational objectives, but both should consider the impact of testing.

Avoid unnecessary:

Large-scale authentication attempts
Aggressive LDAP queries
Massive SMB scans
Uncontrolled poisoning
Unnecessary credential dumping
Repeated remote execution
Persistent modifications
Service disruption
Account lockouts

docs.title: Prefer Read-Only Enumeration First
docs.text:
A good progression is:

Read
 |
 v
Understand
 |
 v
Analyse
 |
 v
Validate
 |
 v
Modify only if required

docs.title: Change Tracking
docs.text:
If an assessment requires modifying AD:

Record original value
        |
        v
Perform change
        |
        v
Validate
        |
        v
Restore original value
        |
        v
Verify restoration

Examples include:

Group membership
ACL
Attribute
Certificate mapping
Computer account
GPO

docs.title: Quick Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
When time is limited, use:

1. Identify current network and identity
2. Identify domain and Domain Controllers
3. Enumerate DNS, SMB, LDAP and Kerberos
4. Validate credentials
5. Enumerate users, groups and computers
6. Enumerate shares
7. Collect BloodHound data
8. Review privileged groups and ACLs
9. Review Kerberos attack surface
10. Review NTLM / relay protections
11. Review AD CS
12. Identify credential exposure
13. Identify administrative access
14. Validate the shortest meaningful attack paths
15. Re-enumerate after every access change
16. Check for additional network interfaces and routes
17. Pivot where necessary
18. Review trusts and management infrastructure
19. Determine realistic domain / forest impact
20. Document root causes, detection and remediation

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec, commonly invoked as nxc, is a network service assessment tool widely used during authorised internal penetration tests and Active Directory security assessments.

It is the community-maintained successor to CrackMapExec and provides a consistent interface for interacting with multiple network protocols.

NetExec is particularly useful for answering questions such as:

Which Windows systems are reachable?

Which hosts expose SMB?

What domain does each host belong to?

Is SMB signing required?

Do the supplied credentials authenticate?

Where does an account have administrative access?

Which SMB shares can the account access?

Which users and groups exist?

Which Domain Controllers exist?

What LDAP information can be queried?

Which systems expose WinRM?

Which SQL servers are reachable?

Which systems expose SSH or RDP?

What relationships should be investigated next?

NetExec should not be treated simply as:

Password
   |
   v
Spray entire network

A better model is:

Discover
   |
   v
Enumerate
   |
   v
Authenticate
   |
   v
Authorise
   |
   v
Map Access
   |
   v
Analyse
   |
   v
Validate

docs.title: Authorised Testing
docs.text:
The commands in this note are intended for:

Authorised penetration testing
Internal security assessments
Red team exercises
Purple team exercises
Training laboratories
CTFs
Security research

NetExec can generate significant authentication and network telemetry.

Before using functionality involving:

Credential testing
Password spraying
NTLM hashes
Remote execution
Credential extraction
SAM / LSA access
DPAPI
Modules
Large network ranges

confirm that the activity is permitted by the rules of engagement.

docs.title: NetExec in the AD Workflow
docs.text:
NetExec fits naturally into the Active Directory assessment workflow.

Initial Network Access
        |
        v
Network Discovery
        |
        v
NetExec SMB
        |
        +--> Hostnames
        +--> Domains
        +--> Operating Systems
        +--> SMB Signing
        |
        v
Credentials Available?
        |
    +---+---+
    |       |
   No      Yes
    |       |
    v       v
Continue   Validate
Discovery  Authentication
            |
            v
       Enumerate Access
            |
       +----+----+
       |         |
       v         v
     LDAP       SMB
       |         |
       v         v
 Directory     Shares
       |         |
       +----+----+
            |
            v
      Access Mapping
            |
            v
       BloodHound
            |
            v
      Attack Paths

docs.title: Kali Linux
docs.text:
NetExec is available through Kali's package repositories.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install netexec

Verify:

nxc --help

Check the installed binary:

which nxc

Version:

nxc --version

docs.title: Install Using pipx
docs.text:
The NetExec project recommends pipx for Unix-like systems when installing directly from the upstream repository.

Install dependencies:

sudo apt install pipx git

Ensure the pipx binary directory is available:

pipx ensurepath

Install NetExec:

pipx install git+https://github.com/Pennyw0rth/NetExec

Open a new terminal and verify:

nxc --help

docs.title: Updating a pipx Installation
docs.text:
Update:

pipx upgrade netexec

Force reinstall from the current upstream source:

pipx reinstall netexec

docs.title: Keep NetExec Updated
docs.text:
NetExec changes frequently.

This matters because:

Protocols change
Modules change
CLI options change
Dependencies change
Bugs are fixed
Security issues are fixed

Before relying on remembered syntax:

nxc --help

and:

nxc <protocol> --help

For example:

nxc smb --help

docs.title: NetExec Home Directory
docs.text:
By default NetExec stores its configuration and operational data under:

~/.nxc

Inspect:

ls -la ~/.nxc

Workspaces are normally stored under:

~/.nxc/workspaces

The location can be changed using the NXC_PATH environment variable.

Example:

export NXC_PATH="$HOME/.nxc"

docs.title: Tab Completion
docs.text:
NetExec supports shell completion through argcomplete.

Install:

sudo apt install python3-argcomplete

Bash:

register-python-argcomplete nxc >> ~/.bashrc

Zsh:

register-python-argcomplete nxc >> ~/.zshrc

Reload the shell.

Bash:

source ~/.bashrc

Zsh:

source ~/.zshrc

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
The general pattern is:

nxc <protocol> <target> [options]

Example:

nxc smb 10.10.20.10

A subnet:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24

A hostname:

nxc smb file01.example.local

A list of targets:

nxc smb targets.txt

docs.title: Protocol Discovery
docs.text:
Start with:

nxc --help

Protocol-specific help:

nxc smb --help

nxc ldap --help

nxc winrm --help

nxc mssql --help

nxc ssh --help

Do not assume that every protocol supports the same options.

docs.title: Common Protocols
docs.text:
Depending on the installed version, NetExec supports multiple protocols.

Common protocols relevant to internal assessments include:

SMB
LDAP
WinRM
WMI
MSSQL
SSH
RDP
FTP
NFS
VNC

Think of NetExec as:

                 NetExec
                    |
       +------------+------------+
       |            |            |
       v            v            v
      SMB          LDAP        WinRM
       |            |            |
       v            v            v
 Windows        Directory      Remote
 Systems          Data        Management
       |
       +------------+------------+
       |            |            |
       v            v            v
     MSSQL         SSH          RDP

docs.title: Target Formats
docs.text:
A single IP:

nxc smb 10.10.20.10

CIDR:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24

Hostname:

nxc smb file01.example.local

Multiple targets from a file:

nxc smb targets.txt

docs.title: Build a Target File
docs.text:
Example:

10.10.20.10
10.10.20.11
10.10.20.20
10.10.20.30

Save as:

targets.txt

Then:

nxc smb targets.txt

This is often preferable to repeatedly scanning an entire subnet.

docs.title: SMB Discovery
docs.text:
One of the most useful first NetExec commands is:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24

Depending on the environment and NetExec version, output may reveal information such as:

IP address
Hostname
Domain
Operating system information
SMB signing configuration
SMB-related metadata

docs.title: Save SMB Discovery
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 |
    tee smb-discovery.txt

For structured engagement evidence:

mkdir -p evidence/netexec

Then:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 |
    tee evidence/netexec/smb-discovery.txt

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
SMB discovery is particularly useful when reviewing SMB signing.

Record:

Host Role Signing DC01 Domain Controller Required FILE01 File Server Review APP01 Application Server Review

Do not interpret:

Signing not required

as:

Host compromised

The correct model is:

SMB Signing Configuration
          |
          v
Potential Relay Prerequisite
          |
          v
Additional Conditions Required
          |
          v
Controlled Validation

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
NetExec can validate credentials against supported services.

The important distinction is:

Authentication

versus:

Authorisation

A credential may successfully authenticate without having administrative access.

docs.title: Domain Password Authentication
docs.text:
Example:

nxc smb file01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

docs.title: Authentication Against a Subnet
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

Use network-wide credential validation deliberately.

A better workflow is often:

Identify Hosts
      |
      v
Reduce Target Set
      |
      v
Validate Credential
      |
      v
Map Access

rather than testing every available service indiscriminately.

docs.title: Avoid Passwords in Shell History
docs.text:
Commands such as:

nxc smb 10.10.20.10 \
    -u alice \
    -p 'ActualPassword'

may expose the credential through:

Shell history
Process listings
Terminal logging
Screenshots
Screen recordings
Evidence files

Use secure credential-handling practices appropriate to the engagement.

docs.title: NTLM Hash Authentication
docs.text:
Where authorised, NetExec supports NTLM hash authentication for applicable protocols.

Example:

nxc smb file01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -H '<NT-HASH>'

This is commonly described as:

Pass-the-Hash

The dedicated Pass-the-Hash note should cover the technique in detail.

docs.title: Local Accounts
docs.text:
Domain and local authentication must be distinguished.

Conceptually:

EXAMPLE\alice

is different from:

FILE01\alice

Do not assume an account with the same username on multiple machines represents the same security principal.

Check the current SMB help for local-authentication options:

nxc smb --help

docs.title: Authentication Interpretation
docs.text:
Think in stages:

Target Reachable
      |
      v
Service Available
      |
      v
Credential Accepted
      |
      v
Identity Established
      |
      v
Authorisation Evaluated
      |
      v
Accessible Resources

Never collapse all of these into:

Credential works = compromised

docs.title: Administrative Access
docs.text:
NetExec can help determine whether the supplied account has administrative privileges over a target.

The exact output formatting can vary between versions.

Treat an administrative indicator as:

Account
   |
   v
Administrative Access
   |
   v
Specific Host

not:

Account
   |
   v
Domain Admin

docs.title: Mapping Administrative Access
docs.text:
Example workflow:

nxc smb targets.txt \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

Record:

Host Authentication Administrative Access DC01 Yes No FILE01 Yes Yes APP01 Yes No WEB01 Yes Yes

This creates an access graph:

alice
 |
 +--> FILE01
 |
 +--> WEB01

docs.title: SMB Share Enumeration
docs.text:
Enumerate shares:

nxc smb file01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password' \
    --shares

docs.title: What to Record
docs.text:
For each share:

Share name
Read access
Write access
Purpose
Sensitive content
Business function

Example:

Share Read Write Notes Public Yes No General documents Deploy Yes Yes Deployment files Backups Yes No Backup data Software Yes Yes Software deployment

docs.title: Interesting Shares
docs.text:
Look for names such as:

Backup
Backups
Deploy
Deployment
Install
Installer
Software
Scripts
Admin
IT
Users
Profiles
Home
Finance
HR
Development
Dev
Projects
SYSVOL
NETLOGON

Names alone do not imply sensitive content.

docs.title: Share Analysis
docs.text:
The key relationship is:

Identity
   |
   v
Share Permission
   |
   v
File Permission
   |
   v
Content
   |
   v
How Content Is Used

A writable share becomes more interesting if privileged systems automatically execute or consume its contents.

docs.title: SMB Share Workflow
docs.text:
Discover SMB Hosts
        |
        v
Authenticate
        |
        v
Enumerate Shares
        |
        v
Identify Readable Shares
        |
        v
Identify Writable Shares
        |
        v
Review Relevant Content
        |
        v
Understand Consumption
        |
        v
Determine Security Impact

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
Domain users commonly have legitimate read access to SYSVOL.

Enumerate shares:

nxc smb dc01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password' \
    --shares

SYSVOL may contain:

Group Policy
Scripts
Configuration
Deployment information
Historical artefacts

docs.title: NETLOGON
docs.text:
NETLOGON may contain:

Logon scripts
Batch files
PowerShell scripts
Configuration
Internal server references
Deployment logic

Review it as part of the domain configuration rather than assuming sensitive information will necessarily exist.

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:
LDAP is one of the most important NetExec protocols during Active Directory assessments.

Basic connection:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

docs.title: LDAP Against the DC IP
docs.text:
nxc ldap 10.10.20.10 \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

For Kerberos-oriented workflows, correct DNS and hostname resolution are generally preferable to relying entirely on IP addresses.

docs.title: Enumerate Users
docs.text:
Current NetExec versions provide LDAP user enumeration options.

Check:

nxc ldap --help

A commonly available form is:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password' \
    --users

docs.title: Active Users
docs.text:
Some current NetExec versions also provide filtering for active users.

Always verify:

nxc ldap --help

before documenting results from a remembered option.

docs.title: Why LDAP Enumeration Matters
docs.text:
LDAP can help answer:

Who exists?

Which users are active?

Which groups exist?

Which computers exist?

Which accounts have SPNs?

Which delegation relationships exist?

Which privileged identities exist?

docs.title: Domain Controllers
docs.text:
LDAP and SMB discovery can help identify Domain Controllers.

Always corroborate with:

DNS SRV records
LDAP
SMB metadata
Kerberos

rather than relying on one tool result.

docs.title: Password Policy
docs.text:
Before performing any password-based testing, determine:

Lockout threshold
Lockout duration
Observation window
Password requirements
Fine-grained password policies

Check available protocol options:

nxc smb --help

nxc ldap --help

Do not perform password spraying based solely on a discovered user list.

docs.title: Password Spraying
docs.text:
NetExec can perform credential testing across multiple users and hosts.

Because this can:

Lock accounts
Trigger monitoring
Impact users
Generate large authentication volumes

it should only be performed when explicitly permitted.

The dedicated password-spraying.md note should contain the operational methodology.

Use this page primarily to remember:

ENUMERATE POLICY FIRST

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
NetExec supports Kerberos-aware workflows for appropriate protocols.

Before using Kerberos:

DNS must be correct
Hostname resolution must work
Domain must be correct
Clock skew must be acceptable
SPNs must match

Check protocol-specific options:

nxc smb --help

or:

nxc ldap --help

docs.title: Kerberos Troubleshooting
docs.text:
When Kerberos unexpectedly fails, check:

date

DNS:

dig dc01.example.local

Kerberos SRV records:

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

Then confirm:

Username
Domain
Hostname
DC
Time
DNS

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
WinRM is commonly exposed on:

5985/tcp
5986/tcp

Basic discovery:

nxc winrm 10.10.20.20

Credential validation:

nxc winrm 10.10.20.20 \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

docs.title: WinRM Workflow
docs.text:
Host
 |
 v
WinRM Reachable?
 |
 +-- No --> Continue
 |
 +-- Yes
       |
       v
Credential Valid?
       |
       v
Authorised for Remote Management?
       |
       v
Potential Lateral Movement Path

Remote execution should be treated as a separate, more intrusive validation step.

docs.title: MSSQL
docs.text:
NetExec can assess Microsoft SQL Server environments.

Basic discovery:

nxc mssql 10.10.20.30

Authentication:

nxc mssql sql01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

Check:

nxc mssql --help

for current authentication and enumeration options.

docs.title: Why MSSQL Matters in AD
docs.text:
SQL Server environments may involve:

Domain service accounts
Privileged service identities
Linked servers
Windows authentication
Delegation
Database-level privilege
Operating-system-level privilege

Therefore:

SQL Access
   |
   v
Database Context
   |
   v
Service Identity
   |
   v
AD Relationship

may create an attack path.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Where SSH is used internally:

nxc ssh 10.10.20.40

Credential validation:

nxc ssh 10.10.20.40 \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password'

SSH may be relevant for:

Linux servers
Network appliances
Administrative infrastructure
Mixed Windows/Linux environments

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
Check current RDP functionality:

nxc rdp --help

RDP-related assessment can help determine whether remote interactive access is available to an identity.

Remember:

3389 open
    !=
User allowed to RDP

docs.title: WMI
docs.text:
Current NetExec versions may expose WMI as its own protocol.

Check:

nxc wmi --help

WMI is particularly relevant for:

Remote administration
System information
Lateral movement
Administrative validation

Remote execution is more intrusive than simple enumeration and should be separated in the testing methodology.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
NetExec includes modules that extend protocol functionality.

List modules for a protocol:

nxc smb -L

LDAP:

nxc ldap -L

docs.title: Run a Module
docs.text:
General syntax:

nxc <protocol> <target> \
    -u <user> \
    -p <password> \
    -M <module>

docs.title: Module Help
docs.text:
Inspect module options:

nxc smb -M <module> --options

Example workflow:

Find Module
    |
    v
Read Description
    |
    v
Read Options
    |
    v
Understand Actions
    |
    v
Confirm Authorisation
    |
    v
Run

docs.title: Module Options
docs.text:
Module parameters use:

KEY=value

with the -o option.

General form:

nxc smb <target> \
    -u <user> \
    -p <password> \
    -M <module> \
    -o KEY=value

docs.title: Multiple Modules
docs.text:
Current NetExec supports specifying multiple modules using multiple -M options.

Conceptually:

nxc smb <target> \
    -u <user> \
    -p <password> \
    -M <module1> \
    -M <module2>

Do not run multiple modules simply because the feature exists.

Each module may create different:

Network traffic
Host artefacts
Authentication events
EDR telemetry
Operational impact

docs.title: Module Safety
docs.text:
Before running a module, ask:

What protocol does it use?

Does it require administrator access?

Does it execute code?

Does it write files?

Does it dump credentials?

Does it change configuration?

Does it start a service?

Does it create a scheduled task?

Does it touch LSASS?

What evidence will it leave?

docs.title: NetExec Database
docs.text:
NetExec automatically stores discovered information in its database.

This may include:

Hosts
Credentials
Shares
Groups
Protocol-specific information

depending on what was collected.

docs.title: nxcdb
docs.text:
Launch:

nxcdb

Typical prompt:

nxcdb (default) >

Help:

help

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
Workspaces allow separate engagements to be isolated.

Conceptually:

NetExec
   |
   +--> client-a
   |
   +--> client-b
   |
   +--> lab

This is important because assessment data can include sensitive:

Hostnames
Usernames
Credentials
Hashes
Share information

Never mix client data unnecessarily.

docs.title: Workspace Storage
docs.text:
By default:

~/.nxc/workspaces

Inspect:

find ~/.nxc/workspaces -maxdepth 2 -type f

Treat the directory as sensitive evidence.

docs.title: NetExec Database Security
docs.text:
The NetExec database may contain sensitive material.

Protect:

~/.nxc

using appropriate:

Filesystem permissions
Disk encryption
Evidence handling
Engagement separation
Secure deletion procedures

docs.title: BloodHound Integration
docs.text:
NetExec has BloodHound-related integration capabilities.

The current default configuration is oriented toward BloodHound Community Edition.

Configuration is stored in:

~/.nxc/nxc.conf

Inspect:

cat ~/.nxc/nxc.conf

Do not modify BloodHound-related settings without understanding whether the engagement uses:

BloodHound CE

or:

Legacy BloodHound

docs.title: NetExec and BloodHound
docs.text:
Use NetExec and BloodHound together rather than treating them as competing tools.

NetExec
   |
   +--> Host Discovery
   +--> Authentication
   +--> Shares
   +--> Protocol Access
   |
   v
Operational View

BloodHound
   |
   +--> Identity Relationships
   +--> ACL Relationships
   +--> Administrative Paths
   +--> Group Relationships
   |
   v
Graph View

Together:

Operational Access
        +
Identity Relationships
        |
        v
Better Attack Path Analysis

docs.title: Audit Mode
docs.text:
Current NetExec documentation includes an audit mode.

Before using it, review:

nxc --help

and the current official documentation.

Audit-oriented operation can be useful when the objective is:

Security assessment
Configuration review
Exposure mapping

rather than exploitation.

docs.title: Logging Output
docs.text:
Save relevant output:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 |
    tee evidence/netexec/smb.txt

LDAP:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password' |
    tee evidence/netexec/ldap.txt

Shares:

nxc smb file01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u alice \
    -p 'Password' \
    --shares |
    tee evidence/netexec/file01-shares.txt

docs.title: Suggested Evidence Structure
docs.text:
evidence/
└── netexec/
    ├── discovery/
    ├── smb/
    ├── ldap/
    ├── winrm/
    ├── mssql/
    ├── shares/
    ├── authentication/
    └── modules/

docs.title: Naming Output Files
docs.text:
Examples:

smb-discovery.txt
dc01-ldap.txt
file01-shares.txt
alice-access.txt
winrm-hosts.txt
mssql-hosts.txt
smb-signing.txt

docs.title: Credential Validation Workflow
docs.text:
A controlled credential-validation workflow is:

Credential Obtained
        |
        v
Identify Account Type
        |
        +--> Domain
        +--> Local
        +--> Service
        |
        v
Choose Relevant Protocol
        |
        v
Choose Small Target Set
        |
        v
Authenticate
        |
        v
Record Success
        |
        v
Determine Privilege
        |
        v
Expand Only If Needed

docs.title: New Credential Checklist
docs.text:
When a new credential is obtained:

[ ] Identify domain
[ ] Identify username
[ ] Determine account type
[ ] Determine group memberships
[ ] Validate against appropriate service
[ ] Check LDAP visibility
[ ] Check SMB access
[ ] Check shares
[ ] Check administrative relationships
[ ] Check WinRM where relevant
[ ] Check MSSQL where relevant
[ ] Update BloodHound analysis

docs.title: Host Discovery Workflow
docs.text:
Subnet
  |
  v
nxc smb
  |
  +--> Windows Hosts
  |
  +--> Hostnames
  |
  +--> Domains
  |
  +--> SMB Signing
  |
  v
Create Target Lists

Example:

nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 |
    tee smb-discovery.txt

Then build:

domain-controllers.txt
servers.txt
workstations.txt
interesting-hosts.txt

docs.title: Protocol Matrix
docs.text:
Maintain a simple matrix:

Host SMB LDAP WinRM MSSQL SSH RDP DC01 Yes Yes Yes No No Yes FILE01 Yes No Yes No No Yes SQL01 Yes No Yes Yes No Yes LINUX01 No No No No Yes No

This helps avoid repeatedly probing services that are already understood.

docs.title: Access Matrix
docs.text:
Track credentials separately:

Identity Host Protocol Auth Admin alice FILE01 SMB Yes No alice APP01 SMB Yes Yes svc_sql SQL01 MSSQL Yes Review

This becomes especially useful after multiple credentials are discovered.

docs.title: NetExec During Lateral Movement
docs.text:
NetExec can help answer:

Where can this identity authenticate?

Where is this identity privileged?

Which remote-management protocol is available?

What is the next useful host?

The workflow should be:

Credential
   |
   v
Access Mapping
   |
   v
Candidate Host
   |
   v
Business / Security Context
   |
   v
Controlled Validation
   |
   v
New Host

not:

Credential
   |
   v
Execute Everywhere

docs.title: Re-Enumerate After New Access
docs.text:
After obtaining access to a new host:

New Host
   |
   v
Local Identity
   |
   v
Interfaces
   |
   v
Routes
   |
   v
DNS
   |
   v
Connections
   |
   v
New Networks
   |
   v
NetExec Against New Segment

NetExec becomes particularly useful after pivoting because the same assessment workflow can be repeated against a newly reachable network.

docs.title: NetExec Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Kali
 |
 v
Pivot
 |
 v
Internal Segment
 |
 v
NetExec

The exact configuration depends on the pivot technology.

Examples include:

Ligolo-ng
SSH tunnels
SOCKS proxies
Chisel

Not every protocol or operation behaves identically through every type of proxy.

For broad internal assessment work, a routed/TUN-style pivot can often be easier than forcing all traffic through application-level SOCKS.

See:

active-directory/pivoting.md

docs.title: DNS Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Remember:

Network route works
        !=
DNS works

NetExec operations involving:

LDAP
Kerberos
Domain Controllers
Hostnames
SPNs

may depend on correct internal DNS resolution.

Always document:

Internal DNS server
Domain
Domain Controller FQDN
Reachability
Name resolution

docs.title: Kerberos Through a Pivot
docs.text:
Kerberos is particularly sensitive to:

DNS
Hostnames
SPNs
Time
Routing

A working TCP route to the Domain Controller does not guarantee that Kerberos-based tooling will work correctly.

docs.title: NetExec and Responder
docs.text:
NetExec and Responder have different roles.

Responder
    |
    v
Authentication / Name Resolution Analysis

NetExec
    |
    v
Service and Access Assessment

Potential workflow:

Authentication Material
        |
        v
Understand Identity
        |
        v
NetExec Validation
        |
        v
Map Authorised Access

Credential capture and relay require their own rules-of-engagement checks.

docs.title: NetExec and Impacket
docs.text:
NetExec and Impacket complement each other.

NetExec
   |
   +--> Broad Assessment
   +--> Multiple Hosts
   +--> Access Mapping
   +--> Protocol Enumeration

Impacket
   |
   +--> Focused Protocol Operations
   +--> Kerberos Workflows
   +--> SMB / RPC Operations
   +--> Specific AD Techniques

Example methodology:

NetExec
   |
   v
Find Interesting Relationship
   |
   v
Impacket
   |
   v
Focused Validation

docs.title: NetExec and PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView is useful from a Windows/domain context for directory-focused enumeration.

NetExec is useful from the assessment system for network/protocol-focused enumeration.

PowerView
   |
   v
Directory Relationships

NetExec
   |
   v
Network Relationships

Combine both perspectives.

docs.title: NetExec and Certipy
docs.text:
NetExec can identify domain infrastructure and authenticated LDAP access.

Certipy can then perform focused AD CS enumeration.

NetExec
   |
   v
Domain / DC / Credentials
   |
   v
Certipy
   |
   v
CA / Template Analysis

docs.title: Common Mistake - Scanning Everything
docs.text:
Avoid:

nxc smb 10.0.0.0/8 ...

without a clear reason.

Instead:

Understand Scope
      |
      v
Identify Subnets
      |
      v
Discover Services
      |
      v
Build Target Lists
      |
      v
Run Focused Checks

docs.title: Common Mistake - Credential Spray by Default
docs.text:
Do not treat NetExec as:

user.txt + password.txt + /16

Credential testing can have operational consequences.

Determine:

Lockout policy
Scope
Permitted accounts
Permitted attempts
Monitoring expectations
Timing

first.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Confusing Authentication and Administration
docs.text:
This is one of the most important NetExec interpretation mistakes.

[+] Authentication

does not necessarily mean:

Local Administrator

and local administrator does not mean:

Domain Administrator

docs.title: Common Mistake - Running Modules Blindly
docs.text:
Do not:

See interesting module
        |
        v
Run it

Instead:

Read Module
    |
    v
Understand Actions
    |
    v
Understand Privileges
    |
    v
Understand Artefacts
    |
    v
Confirm Scope
    |
    v
Run if Needed

docs.title: Common Mistake - Ignoring NetExec's Database
docs.text:
Repeated assessments can become confusing if you ignore stored state.

Know where NetExec stores:

Workspaces
Hosts
Credentials
Shares
Configuration

and keep client engagements separated.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Stale NetExec Installation
docs.text:
NetExec evolves quickly.

If a command from documentation does not work:

nxc --version

Then:

nxc <protocol> --help

Compare against the current official documentation.

Do not assume the syntax in an old CrackMapExec write-up applies unchanged.

docs.title: Common Mistake - Calling It CrackMapExec
docs.text:
Older material frequently uses:

crackmapexec
cme

Current NetExec uses:

NetExec
nxc

When translating older notes:

Old CME workflow
      |
      v
Check Current NetExec Documentation
      |
      v
Confirm Current Option

Do not mechanically replace crackmapexec with nxc and assume every option is identical.

docs.title: Command Not Found
docs.text:
Check:

which nxc

If installed with pipx:

pipx list

Then:

pipx ensurepath

Open a new terminal.

docs.title: Check Installation
docs.text:
nxc --version

nxc --help

docs.title: Check Protocol
docs.text: nxc smb --help

docs.title: DNS Problems
docs.text:
Check:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Then:

dig example.local

DC:

dig dc01.example.local

SRV:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

docs.title: Kerberos Problems
docs.text:
Check:

date

Then:

Domain
Username
DNS
FQDN
DC
Clock
SPN

docs.title: Authentication Problems
docs.text:
Verify whether the credential is:

DOMAIN\User

or

HOST\User

Then determine whether the target expects:

Domain authentication
Local authentication
Kerberos
NTLM
Certificate authentication

docs.title: Target Resolution
docs.text:
If:

nxc smb file01.example.local

fails but:

nxc smb 10.10.20.20

works, investigate DNS before continuing.

Do not permanently work around broken DNS with IP addresses if Kerberos testing is required later.

docs.title: Operational Noise
docs.text:
NetExec can generate:

SMB connections
LDAP queries
Authentication attempts
RPC activity
Remote-management traffic
Service interactions

Depending on the selected options and modules, telemetry can increase significantly.

Use the least intrusive command that answers the assessment question.

docs.title: Detection Perspective
docs.text:
Defenders may observe:

Authentication events
Failed logons
SMB connections
LDAP query patterns
Remote service access
WinRM activity
WMI activity
Network connections from unusual systems
Repeated connections across many hosts

This makes NetExec useful during purple team exercises as well.

docs.title: Purple Team Use
docs.text:
A useful purple team exercise can compare:

Action
   |
   v
Expected Telemetry
   |
   v
Observed Telemetry
   |
   v
Detection?
   |
   +--> Yes --> Validate Quality
   |
   +--> No --> Detection Gap

Example activities:

SMB discovery
LDAP enumeration
Share enumeration
Credential validation
WinRM access

docs.title: Evidence to Capture
docs.text:
For each meaningful NetExec finding record:

Date/time
Source system
Target
Protocol
Identity
Command category
Result
Privilege level
Security relevance

Avoid storing plaintext credentials in screenshots or report evidence.

docs.title: Reporting Authentication Results
docs.text:
Instead of:

NetExec showed [+].

write:

The supplied domain account successfully authenticated to the SMB
service on FILE01.

If administrative access was confirmed:

The account possessed local administrative privileges on FILE01.

This describes the security condition rather than the tool output.

docs.title: Reporting SMB Signing
docs.text:
Avoid:

NetExec says signing False.

Prefer:

SMB message signing was not required by the tested server.

Then explain the relevance and prerequisites for any relay-related risk separately.

docs.title: Reporting Share Access
docs.text:
Avoid:

--shares found Deploy.

Prefer:

The tested domain account had write access to the Deploy SMB share
on FILE01.

Then determine how that share is used before assigning impact.

docs.title: Reporting Access Relationships
docs.text:
Example:

The standard domain account alice possessed local administrative
access to APP01 through SMB-accessible administrative interfaces.

Then document:

Source identity
Target
Privilege
Validation
Potential impact

docs.title: Remediation Themes
docs.text:
NetExec findings frequently lead to remediation involving:

Least privilege
Local administrator management
Credential hygiene
SMB signing
Network segmentation
Remote management restrictions
Share permissions
Service account privilege
LDAP protections
Authentication hardening
Password policy
Tiering
Monitoring

The recommendation should address the underlying security condition rather than NetExec itself.

docs.text:
# SMB host discovery
nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24

# Save output
nxc smb 10.10.20.0/24 |

    -d example.local \
