docs.title: Active Directory Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials is an Active Directory attack technique that abuses write access to the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute of a user or computer object.

The attribute is used by legitimate certificate and key-based authentication mechanisms such as Windows Hello for Business.

If an attacker can modify this attribute on another security principal, they may be able to associate attacker-controlled key material with the victim account.

The simplified attack path is:

Attacker
   |
   v
Write msDS-KeyCredentialLink
   |
   v
Victim User / Computer
   |
   v
Attacker-Controlled Key Credential
   |
   v
Kerberos PKINIT
   |
   v
Authenticate as Victim

This is commonly referred to as:

Shadow Credentials

The technique is particularly important because it can turn seemingly indirect Active Directory object-control permissions into authentication as another principal.

Authorised testing only

Shadow Credentials modifies authentication-related data on an Active Directory object. During an authorised assessment, begin with ACL and attack-path analysis. Do not modify msDS-KeyCredentialLink on production identities unless active exploitation is explicitly authorised. Prefer a dedicated test account where possible, record the original attribute value before any modification, and restore the exact original state after validation.

docs.title: Core Concept
docs.text:
The attack relies on:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

This attribute can contain key credentials associated with an Active Directory object.

Conceptually:

User / Computer
      |
      v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Key Credential
      |
      v
Public Key
      |
      v
Authentication

An attacker who can write a new key credential may create:

Victim Account
      |
      +--> Legitimate Key
      |
      +--> Attacker Key

The victim's password does not need to be changed.

docs.title: Why It Is Called a Shadow Credential
docs.text:
The attacker adds another authentication credential behind the legitimate account.

Conceptually:

Victim
 |
 +--> Password
 |
 +--> Existing Authentication Material
 |
 +--> Shadow Credential
          |
          v
      Attacker Key

The attacker's credential exists alongside the legitimate credentials.

This can make the technique useful for:

Privilege Escalation
Lateral Movement
Alternative Authentication
Persistence

depending on the target and permissions.

docs.title: Important Distinction
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials does not normally mean:

Password Reset

The victim's existing password remains unchanged.

Instead:

Existing Account
      |
      v
Additional Key Credential

is created.

This is one reason the technique is important during Active Directory security assessments.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
A typical Shadow Credentials attack requires several conditions.

Conceptually:

Writable KeyCredentialLink
        +
Suitable Domain / PKINIT Environment
        +
Reachable KDC
        +
Usable Target Principal
        =
Potential Shadow Credentials Path

docs.title: Requirement 1 - Write Access
docs.text:
The attacker needs sufficient permission to modify:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

on the target object.

Potential paths may originate from rights such as:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteProperty
WriteDACL
WriteOwner

depending on the object's effective ACL and the exact ACEs involved.

See:

Active Directory ACL and ACE Abuse

docs.title: Requirement 2 - Target Object
docs.text:
The target is typically an Active Directory:

User

or:

Computer

object.

Example:

CORP\alice

or:

SERVER01$

docs.title: Requirement 3 - Kerberos PKINIT
docs.text:
The attack relies on Kerberos certificate/public-key authentication through:

PKINIT

Conceptually:

Certificate / Key
       |
       v
PKINIT
       |
       v
Kerberos AS-REQ
       |
       v
TGT

Therefore the domain must support the required certificate-based Kerberos authentication path.

docs.title: PKINIT
docs.text:
PKINIT stands for:

Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication in Kerberos

Instead of proving knowledge of a traditional password-derived Kerberos key, the client can authenticate using public-key cryptography.

Conceptually:

Traditional Kerberos

Password-Derived Key
        |
        v
AS-REQ
        |
        v
TGT

versus:

PKINIT

Private Key + Certificate
        |
        v
AS-REQ
        |
        v
TGT

docs.title: Domain Controller Certificate Requirement
docs.text:
In many Active Directory environments, PKINIT requires the domain controller to possess an appropriate certificate that can be used for Kerberos authentication.

This commonly exists where:

Active Directory Certificate Services

has been deployed and Domain Controllers have received appropriate certificates.

However:

AD CS Exists

and:

PKINIT Works

should not be treated as identical assumptions.

Validate the actual environment.

docs.title: Key Credential Link
docs.text:
The important attribute is:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

It contains one or more:

KeyCredential

values.

Conceptually:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink
        |
        +--> KeyCredential A
        |
        +--> KeyCredential B
        |
        +--> KeyCredential C

Each key credential can contain metadata describing the associated key.

docs.title: Key Credential Structure
docs.text:
The underlying KeyCredential data includes information associated with the authentication key.

Important concepts include:

Key Identifier
Key Material
Key Usage
Key Source
Device Identifier
Creation Information

The exact binary structure is defined by Microsoft protocol specifications.

During normal assessment work, specialised tools generally parse and construct these values.

docs.title: DeviceID
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials tooling frequently refers to:

DeviceID

or:

DeviceId

associated with a KeyCredential.

This can help identify individual entries when reviewing or cleaning up:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

values.

docs.title: Legitimate Uses
docs.text:
The presence of:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

does not automatically indicate malicious activity.

Legitimate technologies can use key credentials.

One important example is:

Windows Hello for Business

Therefore:

KeyCredentialLink Present
       |
       X
Confirmed Compromise

Instead analyse:

Who Added It?
When?
Which Account?
Which DeviceID?
Is It Expected?

docs.title: Windows Hello for Business
docs.text:
Windows Hello for Business can use key-based authentication associated with Active Directory identities.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Windows Hello for Business
 |
 v
Key-Based Credential
 |
 v
Active Directory

This legitimate use is important when detecting Shadow Credentials.

Defenders should avoid treating every KeyCredential as malicious.

docs.title: Attack Path
docs.text:
A common Shadow Credentials path is:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
GenericWrite
       |
       v
Privileged User
       |
       v
Write msDS-KeyCredentialLink
       |
       v
Attacker Certificate
       |
       v
PKINIT
       |
       v
TGT as Privileged User

docs.title: Computer Attack Path
docs.text:
The target can also be a computer account.

Attacker
   |
   v
Control Computer Object
   |
   v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink
   |
   v
Shadow Credential
   |
   v
Authenticate as COMPUTER$

This can become important when the computer account has:

Local Privilege
Delegated Rights
RBCD Relationships
Service Access
AD CS Permissions
Other Directory Rights

docs.title: User
docs.text:
Shadow User
    |
    v
Authenticate as User
    |
    v
User's Privileges

docs.title: Computer
docs.text:
Shadow Computer
      |
      v
Authenticate as COMPUTER$
      |
      v
Computer Account Privileges

Do not assume that a computer account has no useful privileges.

docs.title: Why Computer Accounts Matter
docs.text:
Computer accounts can participate in:

Kerberos
LDAP
SMB
RBCD
AD CS
Directory ACLs
Service Authentication

and may possess delegated rights.

Therefore:

Computer Account Compromise

can become an important Active Directory attack primitive.

docs.title: Common ACL Paths
docs.text:
Potential Shadow Credentials paths include:

GenericAll
    |
    v
Target

GenericWrite
     |
     v
Target

WriteProperty
     |
     v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink

WriteDACL
    |
    v
Grant Write Permission
    |
    v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink

WriteOwner
    |
    v
Take Ownership
    |
    v
Modify DACL
    |
    v
Write KeyCredential

The exact effective permission should always be validated.

docs.title: GenericWrite
docs.text:
Suppose:

alice
 |
 v
GenericWrite
 |
 v
bob

This may provide the ability to modify writable properties on Bob's object.

One possible abuse path may involve:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

depending on the effective permissions and object state.

docs.title: GenericAll
docs.text:
alice
 |
 v
GenericAll
 |
 v
bob

represents broad control over Bob's object.

Shadow Credentials may be one of several possible abuse paths.

Other paths could include:

Password Reset
SPN Modification
ACL Modification
Other Attribute Changes

depending on the target and environment.

Choose the least disruptive validation method.

docs.title: WriteProperty
docs.text:
An object-specific ACE may provide write access specifically to:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

This is a particularly direct Shadow Credentials relationship.

Conceptually:

Alice
 |
 v
WriteProperty
 |
 v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink
 |
 v
Bob

docs.title: WriteDACL
docs.text:
A principal with:

WriteDACL

may be able to modify the target object's discretionary ACL.

This can potentially create:

WriteProperty

access to:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

The attack chain becomes:

WriteDACL
    |
    v
Grant WriteProperty
    |
    v
Write KeyCredential
    |
    v
Authenticate as Target

docs.title: WriteOwner
docs.text:
A potential chain is:

WriteOwner
    |
    v
Take Ownership
    |
    v
Modify DACL
    |
    v
Write KeyCredential

This introduces more directory modifications and should not be used merely because it is possible.

See:

Active Directory ACL and ACE Abuse

docs.title: Enumeration Strategy
docs.text:
Use:

Enumerate Objects
      |
      v
Enumerate ACLs
      |
      v
Find KeyCredential Write Paths
      |
      v
Identify High-Value Targets
      |
      v
Validate Prerequisites
      |
      v
Decide Whether Active Validation Is Necessary

docs.title: PowerShell Enumeration
docs.text:
Retrieve the attribute for a user:

Get-ADUser `
    -Identity 'alice' `
    -Properties msDS-KeyCredentialLink |
    Select-Object `
        SamAccountName,
        DistinguishedName,
        msDS-KeyCredentialLink

For a computer:

Get-ADComputer `
    -Identity 'SERVER01' `
    -Properties msDS-KeyCredentialLink |
    Select-Object `
        SamAccountName,
        DistinguishedName,
        msDS-KeyCredentialLink

docs.title: Enumerate Users with Key Credentials
docs.text:
Get-ADUser `
    -LDAPFilter '(msDS-KeyCredentialLink=*)' `
    -Properties msDS-KeyCredentialLink |
    Select-Object `
        SamAccountName,
        DistinguishedName,
        msDS-KeyCredentialLink

docs.title: Enumerate Computers with Key Credentials
docs.text:
Get-ADComputer `
    -LDAPFilter '(msDS-KeyCredentialLink=*)' `
    -Properties msDS-KeyCredentialLink |
    Select-Object `
        SamAccountName,
        DistinguishedName,
        msDS-KeyCredentialLink

docs.title: Metadata First
docs.text:
The presence of values can be recorded without immediately modifying anything.

Use:

Read
 |
 v
Understand
 |
 v
Correlate
 |
 v
Validate

before:

Modify

docs.title: LDAP Enumeration
docs.text:
Using ldapsearch:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\alice' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(msDS-KeyCredentialLink=*)' \
    sAMAccountName \
    objectClass \
    distinguishedName \
    msDS-KeyCredentialLink

The raw attribute may not be human-friendly.

Specialised tools can parse KeyCredential structures more effectively.

docs.title: ACL Enumeration
docs.text:
PowerShell:

$target = Get-ADUser 'bob'

Get-Acl "AD:\$($target.DistinguishedName)"

Detailed:

(Get-Acl "AD:\$($target.DistinguishedName)").Access |
    Format-Table `
        IdentityReference,
        ActiveDirectoryRights,
        AccessControlType,
        ObjectType,
        IsInherited `
        -AutoSize

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView can help identify writable Active Directory objects.

Example:

Get-DomainObjectAcl `
    -Identity 'bob' `
    -ResolveGUIDs

Review for rights such as:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteProperty
WriteDacl
WriteOwner

Exact command behaviour depends on the PowerView version.

docs.title: Find Interesting ACLs
docs.text:
PowerView commonly provides:

Find-InterestingDomainAcl `
    -ResolveGUIDs

Use this as an attack-path discovery mechanism rather than treating every result as exploitable.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is particularly useful for discovering Shadow Credentials attack paths.

Depending on the BloodHound version and collected data, an attack relationship may be represented as:

AddKeyCredentialLink

Conceptually:

Alice
 |
 v
AddKeyCredentialLink
 |
 v
Bob

This means Alice may be able to add key-based authentication material to Bob's account.

docs.title: BloodHound Path
docs.text:
Example:

Owned User
    |
    v
MemberOf
    |
    v
Helpdesk
    |
    v
AddKeyCredentialLink
    |
    v
Server Admin
    |
    v
AdminTo
    |
    v
SERVER01

The important question is:

What privilege does the target identity provide?

docs.title: BloodHound Validation
docs.text:
Use:

BloodHound Edge
      |
      v
Identify Underlying ACE
      |
      v
Confirm Effective Permission
      |
      v
Check PKINIT Prerequisites
      |
      v
Determine Target Privilege

Do not assume graph presence guarantees successful exploitation.

docs.title: SharpHound
docs.text:
SharpHound can collect ACL and object information used to build these relationships.

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: Certipy
docs.text:
Certipy includes functionality useful for Shadow Credentials assessment in Active Directory certificate environments.

Before using:

certipy -h

and inspect the installed version's documentation.

Current syntax can change between major releases.

docs.title: Certipy Shadow Functionality
docs.text:
Modern Certipy versions provide a:

shadow

command family for working with Key Credentials.

Check:

certipy shadow -h

before use.

Operations may include functionality for:

Listing Key Credentials
Adding Key Credentials
Removing Key Credentials
Automatic Shadow Credential Workflows

depending on version.

docs.title: pyWhisker
docs.text:
pyWhisker is another tool specifically designed around Shadow Credentials and the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute.

It can support operations such as:

List
Add
Remove
Clear
Export
Import

depending on the installed version.

Check:

python3 pywhisker.py -h

before use.

docs.title: Whisker
docs.text:
The original Windows-oriented tooling associated with this technique includes:

Whisker

which can interact with KeyCredentialLink values.

Tool choice depends on:

Windows vs Linux
Authentication Material
Assessment Workflow
Environment

docs.title: Read-Only Tool Use
docs.text:
During initial enumeration, prefer operations equivalent to:

List

rather than:

Add
Remove
Clear

This prevents unnecessary modification of authentication data.

docs.title: Never Use Clear Casually
docs.text:
A command that:

Clears msDS-KeyCredentialLink

can remove legitimate key credentials.

This may disrupt:

Windows Hello for Business
Key-Based Authentication
Other Authentication Workflows

Therefore:

Clear

should not be used during routine penetration testing.

docs.title: Preserve Original State
docs.text:
Before active validation:

Read Existing Values
      |
      v
Record Exact Original State
      |
      v
Add Test Credential
      |
      v
Validate
      |
      v
Remove Only Test Credential
      |
      v
Verify Original State

Do not replace the complete attribute if an additive operation is available.

docs.title: Dangerous Cleanup Pattern
docs.text:
Avoid:

Attack
   |
   v
Clear Attribute

because legitimate credentials may have existed before testing.

The correct cleanup model is:

Identify Added DeviceID
       |
       v
Remove That Entry Only
       |
       v
Preserve Existing Entries

docs.title: Active Validation
docs.text:
If active exploitation is explicitly authorised, the workflow conceptually becomes:

Target
   |
   v
Add KeyCredential
   |
   v
Generate Certificate + Private Key
   |
   v
PKINIT
   |
   v
TGT
   |
   v
Authenticate as Target

The exact tooling may automate several of these steps.

docs.title: Certificate and Private Key
docs.text:
The attacker-controlled credential generally involves:

Private Key
+
Certificate / Public Key Material

The public-key information is associated with the target account through:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

while the attacker retains the corresponding private key.

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
Attacker Private Key
        |
        v
Certificate
        |
        v
PKINIT AS-REQ
        |
        v
Domain Controller
        |
        v
TGT for Victim

The password is not required.

docs.title: TGT
docs.text:
Successful PKINIT can result in:

Ticket Granting Ticket

for the target identity.

The attacker can then operate using normal Kerberos authentication according to the victim's privileges.

See:

Kerberos Tickets

docs.title: Pass-the-Ticket
docs.text:
Once a TGT exists:

Shadow Credential
      |
      v
PKINIT
      |
      v
TGT
      |
      v
Pass-the-Ticket

may become part of the workflow.

See:

Pass-the-Ticket

docs.title: Credential Extraction Implications
docs.text:
Some tooling can use PKINIT-derived Kerberos material to obtain information that can ultimately result in the target account's NT hash under suitable Active Directory conditions.

Conceptually:

Shadow Credential
      |
      v
PKINIT
      |
      v
Kerberos Session
      |
      v
Additional Kerberos Operations
      |
      v
Credential Material

This significantly increases the potential impact.

However, do not assume:

Shadow Credential
      =
Guaranteed NT Hash Recovery

in every environment.

Tooling, protocol support, account type, encryption configuration, and domain behaviour matter.

docs.title: UnPAC-the-Hash
docs.text:
The technique commonly associated with obtaining an NT hash after PKINIT authentication is often referred to as:

UnPAC-the-Hash

Conceptually:

PKINIT
   |
   v
TGT
   |
   v
PAC Credential Information
   |
   v
NT Hash

This is different from:

DCSync

and should not be described as directory replication.

docs.title: Why NT Hash Recovery Matters
docs.text:
If successful:

Shadow Credential
      |
      v
NT Hash

may enable additional authentication paths such as:

NTLM
Pass-the-Hash
Kerberos Key-Based Authentication

depending on target services and policy.

See:

Pass-the-Hash

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
Attacker
   |
   v
Reset Victim Password
   |
   v
Victim Password Changes

Potential consequences:

User Disruption
Helpdesk Alert
Authentication Failure
Immediate Visibility

docs.title: Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Attacker
   |
   v
Add Key Credential
   |
   v
Victim Password Unchanged

The second technique can be less disruptive to the victim.

docs.title: Shadow Credentials vs Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Kerberoasting:

SPN
 |
 v
Service Ticket
 |
 v
Offline Password Guessing

Shadow Credentials:

Write KeyCredential
      |
      v
PKINIT
      |
      v
Authenticate as Target

Shadow Credentials does not depend on cracking the target's password.

See:

Kerberoasting

docs.title: Shadow Credentials vs AS-REP Roasting
docs.text:
AS-REP Roasting depends on:

Kerberos Preauthentication Disabled

Shadow Credentials depends on:

Writable msDS-KeyCredentialLink

They are fundamentally different attack primitives.

See:

AS-REP Roasting

docs.title: Shadow Credentials vs RBCD
docs.text:
RBCD:

Write
msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity
        |
        v
Delegation
        |
        v
S4U

Shadow Credentials:

Write
msDS-KeyCredentialLink
        |
        v
PKINIT
        |
        v
Direct Authentication as Target

See:

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: Shadow Credentials vs gMSA
docs.text:
gMSA abuse:

Read
msDS-ManagedPassword
        |
        v
Service Account Credential

Shadow Credentials:

Write
msDS-KeyCredentialLink
        |
        v
Additional Authentication Credential

See:

Group Managed Service Accounts

docs.title: Shadow Credentials vs LAPS
docs.text:
LAPS:

Read LAPS Password
      |
      v
Local Administrator

Shadow Credentials:

Write KeyCredential
      |
      v
Domain Principal Authentication

See:

Active Directory LAPS

docs.title: Shadow Credentials vs AD CS
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials uses certificate/public-key authentication, but the technique is not identical to an AD CS certificate-template vulnerability.

AD CS abuse may involve:

Certificate Template
      |
      v
Certificate Authority
      |
      v
Certificate Issuance
      |
      v
Authentication

Shadow Credentials instead abuses:

Existing AD Object
      |
      v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink

A Certificate Authority does not necessarily need to issue the attacker-controlled certificate used by the technique.

However, PKINIT support in the environment remains important.

docs.title: AD CS Relationship
docs.text:
Because certificate-based Kerberos authentication is involved, Shadow Credentials should be considered alongside Active Directory Certificate Services during broader attack-path analysis.

Questions include:

Does PKINIT work?

Which DC certificates exist?

Is AD CS deployed?

Which certificate templates exist?

Are certificate-based attack paths also present?

A dedicated AD CS section should cover those topics separately.

docs.title: Machine Account Quota
docs.text:
Machine Account Quota is not a direct prerequisite for Shadow Credentials.

However, computer-account creation can interact with other Active Directory attack chains.

Do not conflate:

Create Computer

with:

Write KeyCredential

See:

Active Directory Machine Account Quota

docs.title: Protected Users
docs.text:
Membership in:

Protected Users

provides several authentication protections, but it should not be treated as a universal defence against every directory-object control path.

If an attacker can directly alter authentication-related attributes on a protected account, analyse the exact protocol behaviour rather than assuming group membership blocks the attack.

docs.title: AdminSDHolder
docs.text:
Privileged accounts protected by:

AdminSDHolder

may have special ACL behaviour.

This can influence:

Who Can Modify the Account?

See:

Active Directory ACL and ACE Abuse

Remember:

adminCount=1

alone is not definitive evidence that an account is currently protected.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials can potentially be used for persistence.

Conceptually:

Compromise Privileged Account
        |
        v
Add Shadow Credential
        |
        v
Lose Original Access
        |
        v
Shadow Credential Remains
        |
        v
Reauthenticate

This makes unexpected KeyCredential values particularly important during incident response.

docs.title: Persistence Risk
docs.text:
The victim may:

Change Password

while the attacker's key credential remains present.

Therefore:

Password Reset
      |
      X
Guaranteed Shadow Credential Removal

Incident responders should inspect authentication-related directory attributes separately.

docs.title: Password Rotation
docs.text:
Changing:

Victim Password

does not necessarily remove:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

entries.

This is a key incident-response consideration.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials detection should focus on:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink Changes
      +
Kerberos PKINIT Activity
      +
Unexpected Authentication
      +
ACL Changes

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
Active Directory object modifications can generate:

5136

when Directory Service Changes auditing is enabled.

This event is particularly relevant because Shadow Credentials requires modification of:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

docs.title: Monitor Attribute Changes
docs.text:
A useful detection target is:

Attribute:
msDS-KeyCredentialLink

Correlate:

Who Modified It?
Which Object?
When?
From Which System?
Was the Change Expected?

docs.title: 5136 Detection Model
docs.text:
Event 5136
    |
    v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink
    |
    v
User / Computer Object
    |
    v
Unexpected Modifier
    |
    v
Investigate

docs.title: Event 4662
docs.text:
With suitable object-access auditing and SACL configuration:

4662

may provide additional visibility into operations against directory objects.

Actual visibility depends on:

Audit Policy
SACL
Operation
Directory Configuration

docs.title: Kerberos Event 4768
docs.text:
A successful Kerberos TGT request can generate:

4768

on a Domain Controller.

Shadow Credentials authentication may therefore produce Kerberos authentication telemetry.

However:

4768

alone does not identify Shadow Credentials.

Correlation is required.

docs.title: PKINIT Detection
docs.text:
Potential detection opportunities include:

Certificate-Based TGT Request
        |
        +
Recent KeyCredential Modification
        |
        +
Unexpected Account / Host
        |
        v
Higher Confidence

docs.title: Detection Correlation
docs.text:
A strong sequence is:

5136
 |
 v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink Modified
 |
 v
4768
 |
 v
Certificate-Based Kerberos Authentication
 |
 v
Privileged Account Activity

This is much stronger than alerting on one event independently.

docs.title: Short-Lived Attribute Changes
docs.text:
Attack tooling may:

Add KeyCredential
      |
      v
Authenticate
      |
      v
Remove KeyCredential

quickly.

Therefore defenders should retain directory-change telemetry.

A short-lived modification may otherwise disappear before manual inspection.

docs.title: Add and Remove Pattern
docs.text:
10:01 Add KeyCredential
10:02 PKINIT
10:03 Remove KeyCredential

This sequence should be considered suspicious unless explained by legitimate identity-management activity.

docs.title: Baseline Legitimate Usage
docs.text:
Before alerting aggressively, understand whether the organisation uses:

Windows Hello for Business
Key Trust
Certificate Trust
Cloud Kerberos Trust
Other KeyCredential-Based Features

Detection should distinguish legitimate provisioning from suspicious manual or tool-driven modifications.

docs.title: Suspicious Indicators
docs.text:
Examples include:

KeyCredential Added to Domain Admin
KeyCredential Added by Helpdesk User
KeyCredential Added from Workstation
KeyCredential Added Then Removed Quickly
KeyCredential Added to Server Computer by Unrelated User
PKINIT Immediately After Attribute Change
Unexpected DeviceID
Unexpected KeyCredential Count Increase

docs.title: High-Value Targets
docs.text:
Prioritise monitoring for:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Privileged Service Accounts
Backup Accounts
Administrative Users
Domain Controllers
Certificate Authorities
Management Servers
Tier 0 Computers

docs.title: ACL Change Detection
docs.text:
Because an attacker might first gain:

WriteDACL

and then grant themselves KeyCredential write access, monitor:

ACL Modification
      |
      v
KeyCredential Modification

Relevant directory events may include:

5136
4662

depending on auditing configuration.

docs.title: BloodHound for Defensive Review
docs.text:
BloodHound can also help defenders identify:

AddKeyCredentialLink

paths before attackers exploit them.

Prioritise:

Low-Privilege Principal
      |
      v
AddKeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
High-Value Principal

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
The primary defence is:

Prevent Unauthorised Write Access

to:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

docs.title: ACL Hardening
docs.text:
Review:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteProperty
WriteDACL
WriteOwner

against sensitive users and computers.

Remove unnecessary delegation.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Helpdesk groups should receive only the permissions necessary for their operational responsibilities.

Avoid granting broad:

GenericWrite

or:

GenericAll

over large OUs merely for convenience.

docs.title: Protect Privileged Accounts
docs.text:
Apply additional scrutiny to ACLs on:

Privileged Users
Service Accounts
Domain Controllers
Management Servers
Certificate Infrastructure

docs.title: Review OU Delegation
docs.text:
Permissions may be inherited:

OU
 |
 v
User / Computer
 |
 v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink

Therefore inspecting only the target object's explicit ACL is insufficient.

Review:

Parent OU
Inheritance
Nested Delegation
Object-Specific ACEs

docs.title: Administrative Tiering
docs.text:
Avoid:

Tier 2 Helpdesk
      |
      v
Write Privileged User Objects

or:

Tier 1 Server Admin
      |
      v
Modify Tier 0 Computer Objects

Apply administrative boundaries consistently.

docs.title: Monitor KeyCredentialLink
docs.text:
Create monitoring around modifications to:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

especially for high-value accounts.

docs.title: Protect Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Because PKINIT and Kerberos authentication depend on domain infrastructure:

Domain Controllers

must remain strongly protected.

Apply:

Patching
Administrative Tiering
Restricted Logon
EDR
Certificate Lifecycle Management
Directory Auditing

docs.title: Protect AD CS
docs.text:
Where AD CS supports domain authentication infrastructure, secure:

Certification Authorities
Templates
Enrollment Permissions
CA Administrators
Private Keys
Web Enrollment
RPC Enrollment

Shadow Credentials should be considered within the wider certificate-based authentication threat model.

docs.title: Safe Validation Strategy
docs.text:
Use the following hierarchy:

Level 1
Identify ACL Path

Level 2
Confirm Write Permission

Level 3
Confirm PKINIT Prerequisites

Level 4
Use Dedicated Test Target

Level 5
Record Existing KeyCredentials

Level 6
Add One Test KeyCredential

Level 7
Request TGT

Level 8
Remove Test KeyCredential

Level 9
Verify Original State

Stop as soon as sufficient evidence exists.

docs.title: Preferred Validation
docs.text:
Where possible:

ACL Proof
+
BloodHound Path
+
PKINIT Capability

may already be sufficient to demonstrate risk.

Active modification is not always necessary.

docs.title: Controlled Test Account
docs.text:
Prefer:

TEST-SHADOW-USER

rather than:

Domain Administrator

for validating the mechanics.

The test account can be assigned a harmless privilege or controlled resource to demonstrate resulting authentication.

docs.title: Pre-Test Evidence
docs.text:
Before modification, record:

Target DN
Target SID
Original msDS-KeyCredentialLink Values
Current Time
Current Operator
Current ACL
Expected Cleanup

docs.title: Post-Test Evidence
docs.text:
After cleanup, confirm:

Test DeviceID Removed
Original Values Preserved
No Unexpected KeyCredentials
No ACL Changes
No Certificate Files Left Behind
No Kerberos Tickets Retained

docs.title: Credential Files
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials tools may create files such as:

PFX
PEM
CCACHE
KEY
CERT

Treat these as sensitive authentication material.

Store them only in approved assessment locations.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup should include:

Remove Added KeyCredential
Delete Private Key
Delete Certificate
Delete PFX
Delete Kerberos Cache
Verify Directory Attribute
Verify Original Values

docs.title: Kerberos Cache
docs.text:
On Linux, inspect:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

and:

klist

Remove temporary assessment credential caches when no longer required.

docs.title: Windows Kerberos Cache
docs.text:
Windows:

klist

can display Kerberos tickets.

Purging tickets:

klist purge

is disruptive to the current logon session and should not be performed casually on production systems.

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
If Shadow Credentials is suspected:

Identify Modified Account
       |
       v
Identify Modifier
       |
       v
Collect KeyCredential Values
       |
       v
Determine Legitimate vs Suspicious
       |
       v
Review 5136
       |
       v
Review Kerberos Authentication
       |
       v
Remove Malicious Credential
       |
       v
Investigate Initial ACL Compromise

docs.title: Do Not Immediately Clear Everything
docs.text:
During incident response:

Clear msDS-KeyCredentialLink

may disrupt legitimate Windows Hello for Business authentication.

Instead:

Identify Suspicious Entry
      |
      v
Preserve Evidence
      |
      v
Remove Malicious Entry

where possible.

docs.title: Determine Initial Access
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials usually requires a prior privilege:

GenericWrite
GenericAll
WriteProperty
WriteDACL
WriteOwner

Therefore removing the malicious KeyCredential alone is insufficient.

Investigate:

How Did the Attacker Obtain Write Access?

docs.title: Incident Response Chain
docs.text:
Initial Compromise
      |
      v
Directory Write Permission
      |
      v
Shadow Credential
      |
      v
Target Authentication
      |
      v
Privilege Use

Contain every stage.

docs.title: Password Reset Is Not Enough
docs.text:
Because Shadow Credentials are separate from the normal password:

Reset Password
      |
      X
Remove Shadow Credential

Incident response should explicitly inspect:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

docs.title: Review Target Sessions
docs.text:
If a privileged identity was shadowed, investigate activity performed using that identity.

Review:

Kerberos Tickets
Remote Logons
LDAP Activity
SMB
WinRM
RDP
WMI
Service Creation
Scheduled Tasks
Directory Changes
AD CS Activity

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Possible finding titles include:

Low-Privilege User Can Add Shadow Credentials to Privileged Account

Excessive Active Directory Permissions Allow KeyCredentialLink Modification

GenericWrite Permission Enables Shadow Credentials Attack

Computer Object Permissions Permit Shadow Credentials Authentication

Active Directory ACL Allows Alternative Authentication as Privileged User

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Low-Privilege User Can Add Shadow Credentials to Privileged Account

Source Principal:
CORP\alice

Target:
CORP\server-admin

Permission:
Write access affecting msDS-KeyCredentialLink

Description:
The CORP\alice account has effective Active Directory permissions that
allow modification of authentication-related attributes on the
server-admin user object.

The identified access permits modification of the
msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute, which can be used to associate
attacker-controlled public-key credential material with the target
identity.

Where Kerberos PKINIT is supported, this can enable authentication as
the target account without changing or knowing the target's password.

Impact:
Compromise of CORP\alice could provide an attacker with an alternative
authentication path as CORP\server-admin.

The resulting impact is determined by the privileges assigned to the
server-admin account and may include access to systems administered by
that identity.

Recommendation:
Remove the unnecessary write permission from CORP\alice.

Review inherited and explicit ACLs affecting the target account and its
parent OU.

Restrict modification of authentication-related attributes to approved
identity-management processes.

Monitor changes to msDS-KeyCredentialLink and correlate them with
Kerberos certificate-based authentication.

docs.title: Example Finding - Computer Account
docs.text:
Finding:
Delegated Permissions Allow Shadow Credentials Against Server Computer

Source:
CORP\helpdesk

Target:
APP01$

Description:
Members of CORP\helpdesk have effective write access to the APP01$
computer object that permits modification of msDS-KeyCredentialLink.

This permission can allow an attacker controlling a Helpdesk account to
associate attacker-controlled key material with APP01$ and potentially
authenticate as the computer account through Kerberos PKINIT.

Impact:
Compromise of a Helpdesk identity could lead to compromise of the
APP01$ computer identity.

The resulting access depends on privileges and trust relationships
associated with APP01$, including any delegated Active Directory
permissions or service relationships.

Recommendation:
Remove unnecessary write permissions over the APP01$ computer object.

Delegate only the specific properties required for Helpdesk operations
and review inherited permissions from the parent OU.

docs.title: Example Finding - Persistence
docs.text:
Finding:
Unexpected Key Credential Present on Privileged Active Directory User

Target:
CORP\admin-user

Description:
The admin-user object contains an msDS-KeyCredentialLink value that
could not be associated with an approved Windows Hello for Business or
other key-based authentication deployment.

Directory change logs indicate that the value was added by an
unexpected principal.

Impact:
The key credential may provide an alternative authentication mechanism
for the privileged account.

Changing the user's password alone may not invalidate this
authentication path.

Recommendation:
Preserve the suspicious KeyCredential value for investigation.

Determine whether the credential is legitimate before removing it.

Review directory-change and Kerberos authentication logs around the
creation time.

Investigate the principal responsible for the modification and review
the ACL path that allowed the change.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Source Principal
      +
Target Principal
      +
Write Permission
      +
PKINIT Availability
      +
Target Privilege
      +
Downstream Access
      =
Risk

Example:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
AddKeyCredentialLink
       |
       v
Low-Privilege Test User

may have limited impact.

Compare:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
AddKeyCredentialLink
       |
       v
Privileged Server Administrator
       |
       v
Administrative Infrastructure

which may represent a severe escalation path.

docs.title: Do Not Overstate Findings
docs.text:
Finding:

GenericWrite -> User

does not automatically prove:

Shadow Credentials Successfully Exploitable

Validate:

Can msDS-KeyCredentialLink Actually Be Modified?

Does PKINIT Work?

What Is the Target's Privilege?

Are Other Constraints Present?

Report the strongest claim supported by evidence.

docs.title: Evidence Checklist
docs.text:
Record:

Domain
Source Principal
Source SID
Target Principal
Target SID
Target Type
Target DN
Exact ACL
Explicit / Inherited
ObjectType GUID
msDS-KeyCredentialLink State
Existing DeviceIDs
PKINIT Availability
Domain Controller
Target Privileges
BloodHound Edge
Validation Level
Credential Added?
TGT Requested?
Credential Removed?
Relevant Events
Cleanup Verification

Do not include:

Private Key
PFX Password
Reusable Kerberos Ticket
NT Hash

in normal report evidence.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Confirm directory modification is authorised
  • Confirm certificate-based authentication testing is authorised
  • Confirm credential extraction restrictions
  • Confirm Tier 0 restrictions
  • Define cleanup procedure
  • Prepare secure credential storage

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• Enumerate users
  • Enumerate computers
  • Identify existing KeyCredentialLink values
  • Identify Windows Hello for Business usage
  • Identify PKINIT support
  • Identify AD CS deployment where relevant
  • Identify privileged targets

docs.title: ACL Analysis
docs.text:
• Review GenericAll
  • Review GenericWrite
  • Review WriteProperty
  • Review WriteDACL
  • Review WriteOwner
  • Review object-specific ACEs
  • Review inherited permissions
  • Review OU delegation
  • Resolve nested groups
  • Identify AddKeyCredentialLink paths

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
• Collect ACL information
  • Identify AddKeyCredentialLink
  • Identify paths from owned principals
  • Identify paths to high-value users
  • Identify paths to high-value computers
  • Validate graph edges against ACLs
  • Analyse downstream target privilege

docs.title: PKINIT
docs.text:
• Identify suitable Domain Controller
  • Confirm certificate-based Kerberos support
  • Confirm DNS resolution
  • Confirm time synchronisation
  • Confirm KDC reachability
  • Avoid assuming AD CS automatically means PKINIT works

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Prefer read-only evidence first
  • Prefer dedicated test target
  • Record original KeyCredential values
  • Add only one test credential
  • Record test DeviceID
  • Request only required authentication material
  • Avoid unnecessary remote execution
  • Remove only the test credential
  • Verify original state

docs.title: Credential Handling
docs.text:
• Protect PFX files
  • Protect PEM files
  • Protect private keys
  • Protect Kerberos caches
  • Protect recovered hashes
  • Do not commit credentials to Git
  • Do not place reusable credentials in reports
  • Delete temporary credentials after validation

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• Monitor event 5136
  • Monitor event 4662 where configured
  • Monitor msDS-KeyCredentialLink
  • Monitor privileged user objects
  • Monitor privileged computer objects
  • Monitor rapid add/remove sequences
  • Monitor event 4768
  • Correlate PKINIT with directory changes
  • Baseline legitimate Windows Hello provisioning
  • Investigate unexpected DeviceIDs

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
• Remove unnecessary GenericAll
  • Remove unnecessary GenericWrite
  • Restrict WriteProperty
  • Restrict WriteDACL
  • Restrict WriteOwner
  • Review OU inheritance
  • Apply administrative tiering
  • Protect privileged accounts
  • Protect Domain Controllers
  • Protect AD CS
  • Monitor KeyCredential modifications

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
• Identify affected account
  • Preserve suspicious KeyCredential
  • Identify modification time
  • Identify modifying principal
  • Review event 5136
  • Review Kerberos authentication
  • Identify suspicious PKINIT
  • Review downstream activity
  • Remove malicious KeyCredential
  • Review original ACL weakness
  • Contain source principal
  • Do not rely only on password reset

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• Remove test KeyCredential
  • Preserve legitimate KeyCredentials
  • Delete temporary certificate
  • Delete temporary private key
  • Delete PFX
  • Delete Kerberos cache
  • Remove temporary tickets
  • Verify original attribute state
  • Verify ACL unchanged
  • Record cleanup evidence

docs.title: Shadow Credentials Testing Model
docs.text:
The normal authentication model is:

User
 |
 +--> Password
 |
 +--> Kerberos Keys
 |
 +--> Approved Key Credentials

The Shadow Credentials model is:

User
 |
 +--> Legitimate Credentials
 |
 +--> Attacker-Controlled KeyCredential

The ACL model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
GenericWrite / WriteProperty
   |
   v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink
   |
   v
Victim

The authentication model is:

Private Key
    |
    v
PKINIT
    |
    v
Kerberos
    |
    v
TGT

The complete attack model is:

Compromised Principal
        |
        v
Directory Write Permission
        |
        v
Add KeyCredential
        |
        v
PKINIT
        |
        v
TGT as Victim
        |
        v
Victim Privileges

The computer-account model is:

Attacker
   |
   v
AddKeyCredentialLink
   |
   v
SERVER01$
   |
   v
Authenticate as SERVER01$
   |
   v
Computer Account Rights

The persistence model is:

Initial Compromise
      |
      v
Add Shadow Credential
      |
      v
Password Changes
      |
      X
Shadow Credential Removed
      |
      v
Alternative Access Remains

The detection model is:

5136
 |
 v
msDS-KeyCredentialLink Change
 |
 v
4768
 |
 v
PKINIT Authentication
 |
 v
Target Account Activity

The cleanup model is:

Record Original Values
      |
      v
Add Test DeviceID
      |
      v
Validate
      |
      v
Remove Test DeviceID Only
      |
      v
Verify Original Values

The unsafe cleanup model is:

Clear Attribute
      |
      v
Legitimate Credentials Removed
      |
      v
Authentication Disruption

The defensive model is:

Least Privilege
      |
      v
Restrict Object Write Access
      |
      v
Monitor KeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Monitor PKINIT
      |
      v
Protect Privileged Objects

The most important distinction is:

Password Unknown
      |
      X
Account Cannot Be Authenticated As

If an attacker can create an alternative authentication credential:

Password
   |
   X
Not Required

Another important distinction is:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink Present
        |
        X
Malicious

because legitimate technologies such as Windows Hello for Business may use the attribute.

The correct detection model is:

Attribute
   +
Modifier
   +
Time
   +
DeviceID
   +
Authentication
   +
Business Context
   =
Assessment

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Can I add a Shadow Credential?"

Ask:
"Which compromised principals can modify authentication
material for which identities, and what privilege would
those identities provide?"

For defenders:

Do Not Ask:
"Does msDS-KeyCredentialLink exist?"

Ask:
"Who can modify it, who actually modified it,
and was the resulting authentication expected?"

The final attack-path model is:

Source Principal
      |
      v
AddKeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Target Principal
      |
      v
PKINIT
      |
      v
Target Identity
      |
      v
Resulting Privilege

That relationship determines the actual security impact of a Shadow Credentials path.

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Shadow Credentials demonstrates an important Active Directory security principle:

Authentication Security
        |
        X
Only Password Security

An account may have:

Strong Password
MFA Elsewhere
Password Rotation

and still be compromised if an attacker can modify authentication-related directory attributes.

The core relationship is:

Principal
   |
   v
Write msDS-KeyCredentialLink
   |
   v
Target

That write permission can potentially become:

Directory Permission
      |
      v
Authentication Credential
      |
      v
Kerberos TGT
      |
      v
Target Identity

This is why Active Directory ACL analysis is critical.

A seemingly simple:

GenericWrite

relationship can represent much more than the ability to change harmless metadata.

For privileged identities:

GenericWrite
      |
      v
Authentication Attribute
      |
      v
Privilege Escalation

may represent a severe attack path.

The technique also highlights why password resets are not a complete incident-response strategy.

Password Reset
      |
      v
Password Credential Changed

does not necessarily affect:

KeyCredentialLink

Therefore incident response must review alternative authentication mechanisms.

For penetration testers, the preferred workflow is:

Enumerate ACL
      |
      v
Identify AddKeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Determine Target Privilege
      |
      v
Validate PKINIT
      |
      v
Use Controlled Test Object
      |
      v
Modify Only If Necessary
      |
      v
Restore Exact Original State

For defenders:

Restrict ACLs
      |
      v
Monitor msDS-KeyCredentialLink
      |
      v
Correlate Directory Changes
      |
      v
Monitor PKINIT
      |
      v
Investigate Unexpected Authentication

The central question is:

Who can add authentication material
to which Active Directory identity?

The second question is:

What can that identity access?

Together:

Write Permission
      +
Target Privilege
      =
Attack Path

Shadow Credentials should therefore be analysed as part of the broader Active Directory relationship:

ACL Control
   |
   v
Identity Control
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Privilege

rather than as an isolated certificate technique.

docs.title: Windows and Active Directory Shares
docs.text:
Windows file shares are one of the most important sources of information during an Active Directory security assessment.

Organisations commonly use SMB shares to store:

Documents
Scripts
Software
Configuration Files
Deployment Packages
Backups
Administrative Tools
User Profiles
Department Data
Application Files

From a security perspective, shares frequently reveal information that connects otherwise separate Active Directory attack paths.

A share may expose:

Credentials
Configuration Secrets
Deployment Scripts
Private Keys
Certificates
Connection Strings
Passwords
API Keys
Administrative Scripts
Sensitive Documents

The assessment model is:

Active Directory Identity
        |
        v
SMB
        |
        v
Share
        |
        v
Files and Directories
        |
        v
Permissions / Secrets / Information
        |
        v
Potential Security Impact

Authorised testing only

File-share enumeration can expose confidential business information and credentials. Access only systems and shares within scope. Prefer metadata and targeted searches over bulk downloading. Do not modify, delete or upload files unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Shares at a Glance
docs.text:
A Windows file share exposes a directory through SMB.

Example:

Server:

FILE01

Local directory:

D:\Departments\Finance

Share:

Finance

UNC path:

\\FILE01\Finance

Users access:

SMB
 |
 v
FILE01
 |
 v
Finance Share
 |
 v
NTFS Directory

docs.title: SMB
docs.text:
Modern Windows file sharing primarily uses:

SMB

Common port:

TCP 445

Older environments may also expose NetBIOS-related services such as:

TCP 139
UDP 137
UDP 138

See:

SMB

docs.title: Share Permissions vs NTFS Permissions
docs.text:
Windows file access commonly involves two permission layers:

Share Permissions
       +
NTFS Permissions
       |
       v
Effective Access

These should not be treated as the same control.

docs.title: Share Permissions
docs.text:
Share permissions apply when accessing a directory through SMB.

Common permissions include:

Read
Change
Full Control

docs.title: NTFS Permissions
docs.text:
NTFS permissions apply to the underlying file-system objects.

Common rights include:

Read
Read and Execute
Write
Modify
Full Control

docs.title: Effective Permissions
docs.text:
When a resource is accessed through a share, both permission sets matter.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Share ACL
 |
 v
NTFS ACL
 |
 v
Effective Permission

A permissive share ACL does not automatically mean that every user can modify the underlying files.

docs.title: Common Administrative Shares
docs.text:
Windows commonly creates administrative shares such as:

C$
ADMIN$
IPC$

Additional drives may appear as:

D$
E$

These normally require administrative privileges.

docs.title: C$
docs.text:
\\HOST\C$

maps to the system drive.

Example:

C:\

docs.title: ADMIN$
docs.text:
\\HOST\ADMIN$

normally maps to the Windows directory.

Typically:

C:\Windows

docs.title: IPC$
docs.text:
\\HOST\IPC$

is used for inter-process communication and SMB-related operations.

It is not a conventional file-storage share.

docs.title: Domain Controller Shares
docs.text:
Domain controllers normally expose important shares including:

SYSVOL
NETLOGON

These are expected and necessary for Active Directory.

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
SYSVOL contains domain-wide data used by:

Group Policy
Logon Scripts
Startup Scripts
Administrative Templates
Policy Distribution

Typical path:

\\corp.example\SYSVOL

or:

\\DC01\SYSVOL

docs.title: NETLOGON
docs.text:
NETLOGON commonly exposes logon-related scripts and files.

Typical path:

\\corp.example\NETLOGON

docs.title: SYSVOL Security Relevance
docs.text:
SYSVOL is intentionally readable by domain users in normal Active Directory environments.

The security question is therefore not:

Can Domain Users Read SYSVOL?

That is generally expected.

Instead ask:

What Sensitive Information Is Stored There?

docs.title: Common SYSVOL Findings
docs.text:
Potentially interesting content includes:

PowerShell Scripts
Batch Files
VBScript
Configuration Files
Legacy GPP Files
Deployment Scripts
Mapped Drive Scripts
Printer Scripts
Application Installers
Hard-Coded Credentials
Service Account Names
Internal URLs

docs.title: Group Policy Preferences
docs.text:
Historically, Group Policy Preferences could contain passwords encrypted using a publicly documented key.

The relevant value is commonly:

cpassword

Potential file names include:

Groups.xml
Services.xml
Scheduledtasks.xml
DataSources.xml
Printers.xml
Drives.xml

Modern Windows versions no longer allow administrators to create new GPP password configurations through the normal Group Policy interface, but legacy files may still remain.

If your dedicated page exists, see:

docs/active-directory/gpp-passwords.md

docs.title: Search SYSVOL for cpassword
docs.text:
Windows:

Get-ChildItem '\\corp.example\SYSVOL' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'cpassword'

This is a read-only search.

docs.title: Search for Password Keywords
docs.text:
A targeted search can identify suspicious configuration content.

Get-ChildItem '\\corp.example\SYSVOL' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','passwd','pwd','secret','credential'

Expect false positives.

Do not report keyword matches without examining context.

docs.title: Enumerating Shares from Windows
docs.text: Native Windows provides several methods for share enumeration.

docs.title: net view
docs.text:
Enumerate shares on a server:

net view \\FILE01

docs.title: PowerShell Get-SmbShare
docs.text:
When executed locally with appropriate permissions:

Get-SmbShare

This displays locally configured SMB shares.

docs.title: Get-SmbShareAccess
docs.text:
Inspect share-level permissions:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name 'Finance'

docs.title: UNC Access
docs.text:
Test an approved share:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance'

docs.title: Directory Listing
docs.text: dir \\FILE01\Finance

docs.title: Recursive PowerShell Enumeration
docs.text:
For a small approved directory:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Avoid recursive enumeration across very large production shares without considering performance and data volume.

docs.title: Search by Extension
docs.text:
Example:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.Extension -in '.xml','.ini','.config','.ps1','.bat','.cmd','.vbs' }

docs.title: Search Interesting File Names
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Name -match 'password|credential|secret|backup|config|connection'
    }

docs.title: Search File Contents
docs.text:
For approved text-based files:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','passwd','secret','apikey','connectionstring' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Use targeted extensions or directories where possible to reduce unnecessary access to business data.

docs.title: Enumerating Shares from Linux
docs.text:
Common tools include:

smbclient
NetExec
Impacket
rpcclient

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
List shares:

smbclient -L //10.20.30.40 -U 'CORP/audituser'

docs.title: Hostname
docs.text:
Prefer hostnames when Kerberos or domain context matters:

smbclient -L //files01.corp.example -U 'CORP/audituser'

docs.title: Connect to Share
docs.text:
smbclient //files01.corp.example/Finance -U 'CORP/audituser'

Inside the interactive client:

ls

docs.title: Browse Directory
docs.text:
cd Reports
ls

docs.title: Download a Specific Approved File
docs.text:
Inside smbclient:

get example.txt

Do not bulk-download a share simply because access is available.

docs.title: Kerberos with smbclient
docs.text:
Where Kerberos is configured, current smbclient versions provide Kerberos-related authentication options.

Because syntax can vary between Samba releases, verify the installed version:

smbclient --help

and use the supported Kerberos option for that version.

docs.title: NetExec Share Enumeration
docs.text:
NetExec is particularly useful for evaluating SMB access across authorised systems.

See:

NetExec

Check the installed syntax:

nxc smb --help

docs.title: Enumerate Shares with NetExec
docs.text:
nxc smb files01.corp.example -u audituser -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

This can show:

Share
Permissions
Description

depending on the server and permissions.

docs.title: Multiple Hosts
docs.text:
Against an explicitly authorised subnet:

nxc smb 10.20.30.0/24 -u audituser -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

Large-scale enumeration can generate substantial authentication and network telemetry.

Use scope-specific target lists where possible.

docs.title: Domain Credentials
docs.text: nxc smb files01.corp.example -d corp.example -u audituser -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

docs.title: Avoid Passwords in Shell History
docs.text:
Where possible, avoid placing production credentials directly in command-line arguments.

Prefer:

Dedicated Assessment Accounts
Environment-Specific Secure Credential Handling
Kerberos Tickets
Tool-Supported Prompts

according to the engagement environment.

docs.title: Null Session Testing
docs.text:
Some legacy or misconfigured SMB servers may expose information without authenticated credentials.

Example:

smbclient -L //files01.corp.example -N

Modern Windows environments normally restrict meaningful anonymous access.

docs.title: Guest Access
docs.text:
Anonymous and guest access are different concepts.

Possible states include:

Anonymous
Guest
Authenticated User
Domain User
Administrative User

Record which security context actually provided access.

docs.title: rpcclient
docs.text:
rpcclient can query certain SMB/RPC information.

Check options:

rpcclient --help

Anonymous connection attempt:

rpcclient -U '' -N files01.corp.example

Whether useful information is exposed depends on server configuration.

docs.title: Share Enumeration Through Active Directory
docs.text:
Active Directory itself may reveal systems likely to host shares.

Potential sources include:

Computer Objects
DFS Configuration
Group Policy
Logon Scripts
User Home Directories
Profile Paths
Application Configuration

docs.title: User Home Directory Attributes
docs.text:
Active Directory user objects may contain:

homeDirectory
homeDrive
profilePath
scriptPath

PowerShell:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties homeDirectory,homeDrive,profilePath,scriptPath |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,homeDirectory,homeDrive,profilePath,scriptPath

These values can reveal important file servers.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
User:
alice

homeDirectory:
\\FILE01\Users\alice

profilePath:
\\FILE02\Profiles\alice

This identifies:

FILE01
FILE02

as potential infrastructure of interest.

docs.title: Group Policy Drive Maps
docs.text:
Group Policy can map network shares to users.

Example:

Finance Users
      |
      v
GPO
      |
      v
\\FILE01\Finance

This provides useful information about:

Share Purpose
Target Users
File Servers
Department Boundaries

See:

Group Policy

docs.title: Logon Scripts
docs.text:
Logon scripts frequently contain:

net use

commands.

Example:

net use F: \\FILE01\Finance

or PowerShell equivalents.

Searching SYSVOL can reveal these mappings.

docs.title: Distributed File System
docs.text:
Organisations may use:

Distributed File System

or:

DFS

to provide a unified namespace.

Example:

\\corp.example\Shares

may redirect users to several backend servers.

docs.title: DFS Model
docs.text:
User
 |
 v
DFS Namespace
 |
 +--> FILE01
 +--> FILE02
 +--> FILE03

docs.title: Why DFS Matters
docs.text:
A single visible path may hide:

Multiple File Servers
Replication
Alternative Targets
Different Network Segments

Enumerating the namespace can therefore reveal additional infrastructure.

docs.title: Share Discovery Through SYSVOL
docs.text:
Search scripts for UNC paths.

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem '\\corp.example\SYSVOL' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern '\\\\[A-Za-z0-9._-]+\\[A-Za-z0-9$._-]+'

Review results manually.

docs.title: Share Discovery Through Local Configuration
docs.text:
Mapped drives:

net use

PowerShell:

Get-SmbMapping

These can reveal resources already used by the current user.

docs.title: PowerShell Drives
docs.text:
Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Mapped network drives may appear alongside local drives.

docs.title: File Share Access Model
docs.text:
For each discovered share:

Share
 |
 v
Can List?
 |
 v
Can Read?
 |
 v
Can Write?
 |
 v
Can Modify Existing Files?
 |
 v
Can Delete?

Do not treat all accessible shares as equivalent.

docs.title: Read Access
docs.text:
Read access can expose:

Confidential Information
Credentials
Configuration
Internal Architecture
Source Code
Backups

docs.title: Write Access
docs.text:
Write access may create additional risk if other users or systems consume content from the share.

The important question is:

What Uses This Directory?

docs.title: Writable Share Risk Model
docs.text:
User Can Write
      |
      v
Shared Directory
      |
      v
Another User / Service Reads File
      |
      v
Security-Relevant Behaviour

Write permission alone does not prove code execution.

docs.title: Write vs Modify
docs.text:
A user may be able to:

Create New Files

without being able to:

Modify Existing Files

or:

Delete Files

Always identify the actual effective permission.

docs.title: Safe Write Test
docs.text:
If write testing is authorised, use a uniquely named temporary text file.

PowerShell:

$path = '\\FILE01\TestShare\pentest-write-test.txt'
'Authorised write validation' | Set-Content -Path $path
Test-Path $path
Remove-Item $path

Use only an explicitly approved test location.

docs.title: Verify Cleanup
docs.text:
Test-Path '\\FILE01\TestShare\pentest-write-test.txt'

Expected:

False

docs.title: Linux Write Validation
docs.text:
Within an approved smbclient session, a harmless uniquely named local text file can be uploaded and immediately removed.

Do not perform write validation in:

Software Deployment
Logon Scripts
Startup Scripts
Application Executable Directories
Backup Locations

unless the specific impact test is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Sensitive File Types
docs.text:
During targeted review, pay attention to files such as:

*.ps1
*.bat
*.cmd
*.vbs
*.xml
*.config
*.ini
*.conf
*.yml
*.yaml
*.json
*.kdbx
*.rdp
*.ppk
*.pem
*.key
*.pfx
*.p12
*.cer
*.crt
*.sql
*.bak
*.zip
*.7z

A file extension alone does not make the file sensitive.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Potentially useful configuration files include:

web.config
appsettings.json
connectionStrings.config
database.ini
settings.xml
config.yml

Search carefully and avoid bulk collection.

docs.title: Connection Strings
docs.text:
Applications may store:

Database Server
Database Name
Username
Password
Integrated Security Settings

inside configuration files.

Example conceptual structure:

Server=SQL01
Database=AppDB
User ID=appsvc
Password=<secret>

If discovered, protect the evidence and avoid testing the credential outside scope.

docs.title: PowerShell Scripts
docs.text:
Administrative scripts may contain:

Credentials
Service Accounts
Server Lists
Remote Commands
Backup Paths
API Tokens

Search:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Scripts' -Recurse -Filter '*.ps1' -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','credential','secret','token','key'

docs.title: Batch Files
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Scripts' -Recurse -Include '*.bat','*.cmd' -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','pass=','pwd=','net use','runas'

docs.title: XML Files
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Config' -Recurse -Filter '*.xml' -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','cpassword','credential','connectionString'

docs.title: INI Files
docs.text:
Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Config' -Recurse -Filter '*.ini' -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','passwd','pwd','secret'

docs.title: Backup Files
docs.text:
Backups may expose older copies of:

Configuration
Credentials
Databases
Scripts
Certificates
Keys

Potential names include:

backup
old
archive
copy
previous
.bak

docs.title: Password Databases
docs.text:
Files such as:

*.kdbx

may contain password vaults.

Their existence is not automatically a vulnerability.

Assess:

Who Can Read It?
Why?
How Is It Protected?
Is It Intended to Be Shared?

docs.title: Private Keys
docs.text:
Files such as:

*.pem
*.key
*.ppk

may contain private cryptographic material.

If a private key is discovered:

Do Not Immediately Use It

First determine:

Owner
Purpose
Scope
Protection
Associated System

docs.title: PFX and P12 Files
docs.text:
Files such as:

*.pfx
*.p12

can contain:

Certificate
Private Key
Certificate Chain

They may be password protected.

Treat them as sensitive credential material.

docs.title: RDP Files
docs.text:
.rdp files may reveal:

Hostnames
Gateways
Usernames
Connection Settings

They do not normally contain a reusable plaintext password.

docs.title: Deployment Shares
docs.text:
Software deployment shares deserve particular attention.

Examples:

\\DEPLOY01\Software
\\SCCM01\Packages
\\MDT01\DeploymentShare$

These may contain:

Installers
Scripts
Configuration
Task Sequences
Drivers
Credentials

docs.title: Deployment Share Risk
docs.text:
The security model is:

Writable Deployment Share
          |
          v
Package / Script
          |
          v
Automated Deployment
          |
          v
Many Systems

This can produce substantial impact if inappropriate write permissions exist.

Do not modify deployment content during normal testing.

docs.title: SCCM
docs.text:
Microsoft Configuration Manager environments may expose:

Packages
Applications
Content Libraries
Scripts
Task Sequences

through network infrastructure.

See the planned page:

docs/active-directory/sccm.md

docs.title: MDT
docs.text:
Microsoft Deployment Toolkit commonly uses deployment shares.

A typical share might resemble:

\\MDT01\DeploymentShare$

See:

docs/active-directory/mdt.md

docs.title: WSUS
docs.text:
Windows Server Update Services can also introduce infrastructure and content-management relationships relevant to Active Directory assessments.

See:

docs/active-directory/wsus.md

docs.title: Backup Shares
docs.text:
Backup shares can be particularly sensitive.

Potential content:

System Backups
Database Backups
VM Images
Configuration Exports
Directory Backups
Private Keys

docs.title: Active Directory Backups
docs.text:
Backups containing:

NTDS.dit
SYSTEM Registry Hive
Domain Controller Images

should be treated as Tier 0 material.

See:

NTDS

docs.title: Database Backups
docs.text:
Files such as:

*.bak
*.sql
*.dump

may expose application data and credentials.

Do not restore or process production databases unless authorised.

docs.title: User Home Shares
docs.text:
User home directories may expose:

Documents
Scripts
SSH Keys
RDP Files
Configuration
Browser Exports
Developer Files

Privacy and proportionality are especially important.

Do not indiscriminately search user documents.

docs.title: Department Shares
docs.text:
Examples:

Finance
HR
Legal
Engineering
IT
Security

These can contain highly sensitive business information.

A penetration test should minimise access to unrelated content.

docs.title: Data Minimisation
docs.text:
A good assessment follows:

Find Permission
      |
      v
Identify Relevant File
      |
      v
Collect Minimum Evidence
      |
      v
Stop

rather than:

Download Everything

docs.title: File Metadata
docs.text:
Often sufficient evidence can be collected using:

File Name
Path
Owner
Size
Modification Date
ACL

without opening the file.

docs.title: PowerShell Metadata
docs.text:
Get-Item '\\FILE01\Finance\sensitive-config.xml' |
    Select-Object FullName,Length,CreationTime,LastWriteTime

docs.title: NTFS ACL
docs.text:
Get-Acl '\\FILE01\Finance\sensitive-config.xml' |
    Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: Directory ACL
docs.text:
Get-Acl '\\FILE01\Finance' |
    Format-List Owner,AccessToString

docs.title: icacls
docs.text:
Native Windows:

icacls "\\FILE01\Finance"

This can provide a compact view of NTFS permissions.

docs.title: Permission Inheritance
docs.text:
NTFS permissions may be inherited.

Conceptually:

Parent Directory
      |
      v
Inherited ACE
      |
      v
Child Directory
      |
      v
File

Identify whether an excessive permission originates from:

Direct ACE

or:

Inherited ACE

docs.title: Group-Based Permissions
docs.text:
A user may gain access through nested groups.

Example:

Alice
 |
 v
Finance Users
 |
 v
All Employees
 |
 v
Share ACL

See:

Groups

docs.title: Domain Local Groups
docs.text:
File-server permissions are commonly assigned through Domain Local groups.

Example:

User
 |
 v
Global Group
 |
 v
Domain Local Group
 |
 v
Resource ACL

This is a normal Active Directory design pattern.

docs.title: AGDLP
docs.text:
A common permissions model is:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

Often abbreviated:

AGDLP

docs.title: AGUDLP
docs.text:
Multi-domain environments may use:

Accounts
   |
   v
Global Groups
   |
   v
Universal Groups
   |
   v
Domain Local Groups
   |
   v
Permissions

Often abbreviated:

AGUDLP

docs.title: Why Group Resolution Matters
docs.text:
A share may appear restricted to:

FS-Finance-RW

but that group may contain:

Finance
Helpdesk
Legacy Migration Group
Foreign Security Principal

The full membership chain determines exposure.

docs.title: Foreign Principals
docs.text:
Trusted-domain users can potentially receive share access through:

Domain Local Groups
Foreign Security Principals
Direct ACL Entries

See:

Trust Relationships

docs.title: SID History
docs.text:
Legacy share permissions are a common reason organisations retain:

sIDHistory

See:

SID History

A migrated user may continue accessing a share because the ACL references the old SID.

docs.title: Share Permissions and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Writable or administratively accessible shares can contribute to lateral movement.

See:

Lateral Movement

However:

Share Access
!=
Remote Code Execution

Additional conditions are required.

docs.title: Administrative Shares and Remote Execution
docs.text:
Some Windows remote-management techniques use administrative shares as part of their workflow.

For example:

Administrative Access
      |
      v
ADMIN$ / C$
      |
      v
Remote Service Mechanism

The security weakness is usually:

Excessive Administrative Privilege

rather than the existence of ADMIN$.

docs.title: Impacket and SMB Shares
docs.text:
Impacket includes SMB-related tooling.

See:

Impacket

When testing remote administration, distinguish:

Share Enumeration

from:

Remote Execution

and use the least intrusive method needed.

docs.title: Share Access with Kerberos
docs.text:
SMB supports Kerberos authentication when:

DNS
SPN
Realm
Ticket

are correctly configured.

Prefer hostnames over raw IP addresses when intentionally validating Kerberos.

docs.title: Share Access Across Trusts
docs.text:
A trusted-domain identity may access a share when:

Trust Allows Authentication
        |
        v
User Authenticates
        |
        v
Group / ACL Authorises Access

The trust itself does not automatically grant access.

docs.title: Share Access and SID Filtering
docs.text:
For cross-domain access, SID filtering and SID History can influence the SIDs accepted across the trust.

See:

SID History

and:

Trust Tickets

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
SMB signing protects SMB message integrity and is particularly important when considering NTLM relay.

See:

NTLM Relay

Share enumeration and SMB-signing assessment should be considered together when evaluating SMB security.

docs.title: SMB Encryption
docs.text:
Modern SMB supports encryption.

This can protect SMB traffic from network interception.

Whether it is required depends on:

Server Configuration
Share Configuration
Data Sensitivity
Windows Version
Operational Requirements

docs.title: Share Discovery Workflow
docs.text:
A structured assessment can follow:

Active Directory
      |
      v
Identify File Servers
      |
      v
Enumerate Shares
      |
      v
Determine Access
      |
      v
Review Permissions
      |
      v
Identify Interesting Paths
      |
      v
Targeted Content Review
      |
      v
Validate Security Impact
      |
      v
Report

docs.title: Step 1 - Identify File Servers
docs.text:
Sources can include:

Active Directory Computer Objects
User Home Directories
Group Policy
Logon Scripts
DFS
DNS
Existing Drive Mappings
BloodHound

docs.title: Step 2 - Enumerate Shares
docs.text:
Windows:

net view \\FILE01

Linux:

smbclient -L //files01.corp.example -U 'CORP/audituser'

NetExec:

nxc smb files01.corp.example -d corp.example -u audituser -p 'PASSWORD' --shares

docs.title: Step 3 - Determine Access
docs.text:
Record whether the current identity has:

No Access
List
Read
Write
Modify
Full Control

Do not infer permission solely from a tool's abbreviated output if direct validation is required.

docs.title: Step 4 - Review ACLs
docs.text:
Where accessible:

Get-Acl '\\FILE01\Finance'

and:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name 'Finance'

if querying locally with appropriate permissions.

docs.title: Step 5 - Identify Interesting Files
docs.text:
Prefer metadata first.

Example:

Get-ChildItem '\\FILE01\Finance' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object {
        $_.Extension -in '.ps1','.bat','.cmd','.xml','.ini','.config','.json','.yml','.yaml','.kdbx','.pfx','.p12','.pem','.key','.bak'
    } |
    Select-Object FullName,Length,LastWriteTime

docs.title: Step 6 - Search Targeted Content
docs.text:
Only after identifying relevant files:

Select-String -Path '\\FILE01\Scripts\deploy.ps1' -Pattern 'password','credential','secret','token'

docs.title: Step 7 - Validate Impact
docs.text:
For a discovered credential:

Credential Found
      |
      v
Identify Owner
      |
      v
Identify Intended Use
      |
      v
Confirm Scope
      |
      v
Minimal Authentication Validation

Do not automatically test credentials against every reachable service.

docs.title: Step 8 - Preserve Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Share
Path
File
Permission
Relevant Content
Identity Used
Timestamp

Redact sensitive values where possible.

docs.title: Step 9 - Cleanup
docs.text:
If a write test was performed:

Verify Test File Removed

If no modification was required:

No Cleanup Necessary

docs.title: Searching Large Shares
docs.text:
Large recursive searches can create:

Network Load
File Server Load
EDR Telemetry
Large Result Sets
Privacy Exposure

Use targeted filtering.

docs.title: Better Search Strategy
docs.text:
Instead of:

Search Every File

prefer:

Identify Interesting Directory
        |
        v
Filter Extensions
        |
        v
Filter Names
        |
        v
Inspect Metadata
        |
        v
Read Relevant Files

docs.title: File Age
docs.text:
Old files can be highly relevant.

Examples:

Old Deployment Script
Old Backup
Old Password File
Old Configuration

But age alone does not prove that the content is still usable.

docs.title: Credential Validation
docs.text:
If a credential is found:

Found Credential
      |
      v
Is It In Scope?
      |
      v
Is Validation Permitted?
      |
      v
Identify Intended Service
      |
      v
Minimal Test

Avoid password spraying with discovered credentials unless explicitly part of the assessment.

docs.title: Secret Handling
docs.text:
Never place discovered production secrets into:

Public Notes
Screenshots Without Redaction
Git Repositories
Chat Logs
Unencrypted Reports

Use redaction.

Example:

Password:
P***********3

docs.title: Evidence Screenshot
docs.text:
A screenshot should show enough context to establish:

Share
Path
Permission
Relevant Finding

while hiding unnecessary confidential information.

docs.title: Writable Share Validation
docs.text:
A safe proof is:

Test Identity
     |
     v
Approved Directory
     |
     v
Create Harmless Text File
     |
     v
Verify
     |
     v
Delete
     |
     v
Verify Cleanup

docs.title: Avoid Executable Uploads
docs.text:
If the finding is simply:

User Can Write to Share

there is normally no need to upload:

EXE
DLL
Script Payload
Macro Document

A text file proves write access.

docs.title: Deployment Directory Validation
docs.text:
For a sensitive deployment directory:

Write Permission

may already be enough evidence.

Do not replace or modify deployment packages to demonstrate theoretical execution.

docs.title: Share Detection
docs.text:
Defenders should monitor:

Share Enumeration
Sensitive File Access
Unusual Recursive Reads
Administrative Share Access
File Creation
File Modification
File Deletion
Permission Changes

5140

A network share object was accessed

when the relevant auditing is enabled.

4624
4625

TCP 445 Connections
Source Host
Destination Host
Connection Volume
Authentication Identity

A workstation suddenly enumerating many file servers can be worth investigating.

docs.text:
High-value patterns include unusual access to:

C$
ADMIN$

Non-Administrative Accounts

docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

This can indicate:

Backup

docs.text:
Consider monitoring access to locations containing:

Deployment Scripts
Configuration Secrets
Private Keys
Backups
Password Vaults
