docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Active Directory trusts are:

Authentication Relationships

not automatic:

Administrative Relationships

The correct analysis is therefore not:

Trust Exists
   |
   v
Vulnerable

Instead:

Trust Exists
   |
   v
What Direction?
   |
   v
What Type?
   |
   v
What Transitivity?
   |
   v
What Authentication Scope?
   |
   v
What SID Controls?
   |
   v
Which Foreign Principals?
   |
   v
Which Groups and ACLs?
   |
   v
Which Resources?
   |
   v
What Security Impact?

A forest should generally be treated as the primary Active Directory security boundary.

When separate forests are connected, carefully evaluate:

Trust Direction
Selective Authentication
SID Filtering
Foreign Privileged Membership
Administrative Accounts
Network Connectivity
Tier 0 Dependencies

A trust can be technically configured correctly while still creating unnecessary risk through:

Broad Group Membership
Excessive ACLs
Shared Administrators
Unrestricted Network Paths
Legacy Migration Configuration

Likewise, discovering a trust to another organisation does not extend the penetration-testing scope.

The safe workflow remains:

Discover
   |
   v
Understand
   |
   v
Check Scope
   |
   v
Map Authentication
   |
   v
Map Authorisation
   |
   v
Validate Minimum Access
   |
   v
Report the Actual Weakness

For high-security forest relationships, the target architecture should move toward:

Minimum Required Trust
        |
        v
One-Way Where Possible
        |
        v
Selective Authentication
        |
        v
SID Filtering
        |
        v
Minimal Foreign Privilege
        |
        v
Restricted Network Access
        |
        v
Separate Privileged Administration

The next page drills further into how individual trust relationships are structured and interpreted:

Trust Relationships

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
Unconstrained Kerberos delegation is an Active Directory configuration that allows a trusted service to act on behalf of an authenticated user when accessing other Kerberos services.

It was designed to solve the Kerberos "double-hop" problem.

A simplified legitimate use case is:

User
 |
 v
Front-End Server
 |
 | Needs to access another resource
 | as the user
 v
Back-End Server

Without delegation:

User
 |
 v
Front-End Server
 |
 X
Cannot automatically reuse the
user's authentication context
for another Kerberos service

With delegation:

User
 |
 v
Delegation-Enabled Server
 |
 | Acts on behalf of user
 v
Back-End Service

Unconstrained delegation is the broadest and least restrictive form of Kerberos delegation.

Microsoft describes it as allowing the front-end service to access other services on the client's behalf without restricting the destination services, and recommends against using unconstrained delegation because of this broad trust model.

The security concern is therefore:

Unconstrained Delegation
        |
        v
Broad Delegation Capability
        |
        v
High-Value User Authenticates
        |
        v
Delegated Authentication Material
        |
        v
Compromise of Delegation Host
        |
        v
Potential Impersonation

Authorised testing only

Unconstrained delegation testing can expose reusable Kerberos authentication material belonging to other users. Only perform active validation against accounts and systems explicitly included in scope. Avoid coercing privileged production identities to authenticate unless this has been specifically approved. A configuration finding can often be demonstrated through enumeration and controlled test accounts without interacting with real administrator credentials.

docs.title: Delegation Types
docs.text:
Active Directory supports several Kerberos delegation models.

Kerberos Delegation
       |
       +--> Unconstrained Delegation
       |
       +--> Constrained Delegation
       |
       +--> Resource-Based
            Constrained Delegation

A useful comparison is:

Delegation Type Where Trust Is Defined Scope Unconstrained Delegation Front-end service account Broad Constrained Delegation Front-end service account Specific services RBCD Back-end resource Specific principals

Microsoft currently describes unconstrained delegation as the easiest model to implement but the least secure because the services to which the front-end can act on behalf of the user are not restricted.

docs.title: The Double-Hop Problem
docs.text:
The purpose of delegation is easiest to understand through the double-hop problem.

Consider:

User
 |
 | Hop 1
 v
Web Server
 |
 | Hop 2
 v
Database Server

The user authenticates to:

WEB01

The application on WEB01 then needs to access:

SQL01

as the user.

Without delegation:

User
 |
 v
WEB01
 |
 X
No suitable delegated user
authentication for SQL01

Delegation provides a mechanism for:

WEB01
 |
 v
Act on behalf of User
 |
 v
SQL01

docs.title: Why Unconstrained Delegation Exists
docs.text:
Legacy enterprise applications commonly required:

Client
 |
 v
Application Server
 |
 v
Database / File Server

while preserving the user's identity through the entire transaction.

Examples might include:

IIS
 |
 v
SQL Server

or:

Application Server
 |
 v
File Server

Unconstrained delegation provided a simple solution.

The problem is that its trust boundary is extremely broad.

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation Model
docs.text:
The core concept is:

User
 |
 | Kerberos Authentication
 v
Server Trusted for
Unconstrained Delegation
 |
 | Delegated user context
 v
Other Kerberos Services

Unlike constrained delegation:

Unconstrained
     |
     v
Any suitable Kerberos service

rather than:

Constrained
     |
     v
Explicitly configured services

docs.title: Security Impact
docs.text:
The main security risk appears when the delegation-enabled system itself is compromised.

Privileged User
      |
      v
Authenticates to
Delegation Server
      |
      v
Delegated Kerberos
Authentication Material
      |
      v
Attacker Controls Server
      |
      v
Authentication Material Exposed
      |
      v
Potential Impersonation

The problem is therefore not simply:

Delegation enabled

but:

Delegation enabled
       +
Sensitive identity authenticates
       +
Delegation host compromised

docs.title: Why It Is Dangerous
docs.text:
A server configured for unconstrained delegation becomes an important credential boundary.

Consider:

DC01
 |
 | Administrator authenticates
 v
APP01
 |
 | Unconstrained Delegation
 v
Reusable delegated context

If:

APP01

is compromised, the attacker may gain access to authentication material belonging to identities that authenticate to it.

The compromise can therefore expand from:

APP01

to:

Other resources accessible
by those identities

docs.title: Delegation Trust Flag
docs.text:
Unconstrained delegation is represented through the:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

flag.

The corresponding userAccountControl bit is:

0x00080000

or:

524288

Microsoft documents this as:

ADS_UF_TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

This flag indicates that the account is trusted for Kerberos delegation.

docs.title: Important Distinction
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

with:

TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION

They represent different delegation configurations.

A useful model is:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
        |
        v
Unconstrained Delegation


TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION
        |
        v
Protocol Transition
within Constrained Delegation

The second flag will be covered in the constrained delegation notes.

docs.title: User and Computer Accounts
docs.text:
Delegation configuration exists on the account under which the service operates.

This may be:

Computer Account

or:

User / Service Account

Examples:

WEB01$
APP01$
svc_web
svc_app

Therefore, enumeration should inspect both:

Computers

and:

Users

docs.title: Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Domain controllers are normally trusted for delegation because of their role in Active Directory.

Therefore:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

on a domain controller is not automatically a security finding.

When enumerating unconstrained delegation, separate:

Domain Controllers

from:

Non-DC Systems

The latter are generally the systems of greatest interest.

docs.title: Enumeration Strategy
docs.text:
A practical enumeration model is:

Active Directory
       |
       v
Find TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
       |
       v
Identify Accounts
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
   v       v
Users   Computers
   |       |
   +---+---+
       |
       v
Exclude / Identify DCs
       |
       v
Determine Services
       |
       v
Determine Privilege
       |
       v
Identify Authentication Paths

docs.title: Windows - Active Directory PowerShell
docs.text:
The Active Directory PowerShell module can identify computer accounts trusted for delegation.

Example:

Get-ADComputer \
    -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} \
    -Properties TrustedForDelegation,DNSHostName,OperatingSystem |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        DNSHostName,
        OperatingSystem,
        TrustedForDelegation

docs.title: Enumerate User Accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts configured for unconstrained delegation may also exist as user objects.

Get-ADUser \
    -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} \
    -Properties TrustedForDelegation,ServicePrincipalName |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        TrustedForDelegation,
        ServicePrincipalName

docs.title: Enumerate Using userAccountControl
docs.text:
The raw UAC bit can also be queried.

Get-ADComputer \
    -LDAPFilter '(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288)' \
    -Properties userAccountControl,DNSHostName |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        DNSHostName,
        userAccountControl

For users:

Get-ADUser \
    -LDAPFilter '(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288)' \
    -Properties userAccountControl,ServicePrincipalName |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        userAccountControl,
        ServicePrincipalName

docs.title: LDAP Matching Rule
docs.text:
The LDAP matching rule:

1.2.840.113556.1.4.803

performs a bitwise comparison.

The relevant filter is:

(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288)

Conceptually:

userAccountControl
       |
       v
Contains 0x80000?
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
  No      Yes
           |
           v
Trusted for Delegation

docs.title: ldapsearch
docs.text:
From Linux, LDAP can be used to search for delegation-enabled objects.

A general filter is:

(&(objectCategory=computer)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288))

Example:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\alice' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(&(objectCategory=computer)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288))' \
    sAMAccountName \
    dNSHostName \
    userAccountControl

For service accounts:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.corp.example \
    -D 'CORP\alice' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=corp,DC=example' \
    '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288))' \
    sAMAccountName \
    servicePrincipalName \
    userAccountControl

docs.title: PowerView
docs.text:
PowerView can be useful for Active Directory delegation enumeration.

A common conceptual workflow is:

PowerView
    |
    v
Enumerate Domain Computers
    |
    v
Inspect userAccountControl
    |
    v
Find TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

Depending on the PowerView version, delegation-specific switches or LDAP filters may be available.

When working with different PowerView forks or versions, verify:

Get-Help Get-DomainComputer -Full

before relying on copied syntax.

A direct LDAP-filter approach is generally less ambiguous:

Get-DomainComputer \
    -LDAPFilter '(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288)' \
    -Properties samaccountname,dnshostname,useraccountcontrol

docs.title: SPN Analysis
docs.text:
After identifying a delegation-enabled account, determine which services run under it.

For a user/service account:

Get-ADUser \
    -Identity '<SERVICE_ACCOUNT>' \
    -Properties ServicePrincipalName |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        ServicePrincipalName

For a computer:

Get-ADComputer \
    -Identity '<COMPUTER>' \
    -Properties ServicePrincipalName |
    Select-Object \
        Name,
        ServicePrincipalName

docs.title: setspn
docs.text:
Native Windows tooling can enumerate SPNs.

For a computer:

setspn -L APP01

For a service account:

setspn -L CORP\svc_app

This helps determine what Kerberos services are associated with the delegation-enabled identity.

docs.title: Linux - Impacket findDelegation
docs.text:
Impacket includes:

findDelegation.py

commonly installed as:

impacket-findDelegation

Check the installed syntax:

impacket-findDelegation -h

A typical domain enumeration pattern is:

impacket-findDelegation \
    'corp.example/alice:<PASSWORD>' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

The tool can help identify delegation relationships including:

Unconstrained
Constrained
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

depending on the environment and current Impacket version.

docs.title: Password Prompting
docs.text:
Where possible, avoid placing real passwords directly in shell history.

Prefer supported prompting mechanisms when available.

At minimum:

Do not place production credentials
in documentation or Git repositories.

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication with Impacket
docs.text:
Where a valid Kerberos context already exists, review the tool's current options:

impacket-findDelegation -h

Many Impacket tools support combinations of:

-k
-no-pass
-dc-ip

depending on the specific utility.

Always verify the installed version.

docs.title: NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec LDAP can assist with Active Directory enumeration.

Start by reviewing:

nxc ldap --help

and available modules:

nxc ldap -L

Delegation-related module names and options can change between releases, so avoid relying on old examples without checking the installed version.

The general workflow is:

NetExec LDAP
      |
      v
Delegation Enumeration
      |
      v
Identify Trusted Systems
      |
      v
Correlate with Privilege

For detailed NetExec coverage:

NetExec

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is particularly useful because delegation is not only a configuration issue.

The important question is:

Who can compromise the delegation host?

and:

Which high-value identities authenticate to it?

A BloodHound analysis model is:

Unconstrained Delegation Host
          |
          +--> Who administers it?
          |
          +--> Who can compromise it?
          |
          +--> Who has sessions?
          |
          +--> Is it on a path to Tier 0?
          |
          +--> Does a privileged identity use it?

For detailed BloodHound coverage:

BloodHound

docs.title: BloodHound Risk Analysis
docs.text:
A delegation-enabled host becomes much more interesting when:

Attacker-Controlled User
         |
         v
Can Compromise APP01
         |
         v
APP01 Has Unconstrained Delegation
         |
         v
Privileged User Authenticates to APP01
         |
         v
Potential Credential Exposure

The delegation configuration alone does not establish the complete attack path.

docs.title: Prioritising Delegation Hosts
docs.text:
Not every unconstrained delegation host presents equal risk.

Prioritise based on:

Delegation Host
      |
      +--> Non-DC?
      |
      +--> Internet-facing?
      |
      +--> User-accessible?
      |
      +--> Weakly administered?
      |
      +--> High-value sessions?
      |
      +--> Tier 0 connectivity?
      |
      +--> Legacy software?
      |
      +--> Broad inbound access?

docs.title: Domain Controller vs Member Server
docs.text:
A useful triage model is:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
          |
      +---+---+
      |       |
      v       v
     DC    Member Server
      |       |
      v       v
 Expected   Investigate
 by role    carefully

This does not mean domain-controller delegation should be ignored.

It means the configuration has a different security context.

docs.title: Ticket Behaviour
docs.text:
When a user authenticates using Kerberos to a service trusted for unconstrained delegation, the Kerberos delegation design can provide the service with delegated authentication capability that allows it to act as the client toward other services.

The security implication is:

User
 |
 v
Delegation Host
 |
 v
Delegated Authentication Context
 |
 v
Other Kerberos Services

This is why compromise of the delegation host is dangerous.

docs.title: Forwardable Tickets
docs.text:
Kerberos tickets can carry ticket flags such as:

forwardable
forwarded
renewable

Microsoft's Event 4769 documentation describes the Forwardable ticket option as allowing the ticket-granting service to issue a new TGT based on the presented TGT.

Ticket flags are therefore useful context when investigating delegation behaviour.

docs.title: Sensitive Accounts
docs.text:
Some accounts should not be delegated.

Active Directory provides the:

NOT_DELEGATED

account-control flag.

Its UAC bit is:

0x00100000

or:

1048576

Microsoft documents this as:

ADS_UF_NOT_DELEGATED

docs.title: Account Is Sensitive and Cannot Be Delegated
docs.text:
In Active Directory Users and Computers, the defensive setting is commonly displayed as:

Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated

Conceptually:

Sensitive User
      |
      v
NOT_DELEGATED
      |
      v
Delegation Restricted

This is useful for suitable privileged identities.

docs.title: PowerShell - AccountNotDelegated
docs.text:
The Active Directory PowerShell module exposes:

AccountNotDelegated

For example:

Get-ADUser \
    -Identity '<USERNAME>' \
    -Properties AccountNotDelegated |
    Select-Object \
        SamAccountName,
        AccountNotDelegated

Microsoft also provides:

Set-ADAccountControl \
    -Identity '<USERNAME>' \
    -AccountNotDelegated $true

for configuring this protection where appropriate.

Do not modify production accounts during an assessment unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Protected Users
docs.text:
Suitable privileged accounts can also be considered for membership in:

Protected Users

after compatibility testing.

Protected Users introduces additional authentication protections and can help reduce credential exposure associated with legacy authentication and delegation scenarios.

It is not appropriate for every service or application identity.

docs.title: Delegation and Privileged Accounts
docs.text:
A dangerous configuration is:

Privileged Admin
      |
      v
Authenticates to
Legacy Application Server
      |
      v
Unconstrained Delegation

A safer model is:

Privileged Admin
      |
      v
Dedicated Administrative Host
      |
      v
Tier 0 Resource

while avoiding authentication to delegation-enabled lower-tier systems.

docs.title: Credential Exposure vs Delegation
docs.text:
Keep the stages distinct.

Delegation Configuration
        |
        v
Authentication Material May
Become Available to Service
        |
        v
Host Compromise
        |
        v
Credential Exposure
        |
        v
Ticket Reuse

Unconstrained delegation itself does not mean:

Attacker automatically owns
every authenticating account

The attacker generally needs control over the trusted service or system.

docs.title: Relationship to Pass-the-Ticket
docs.text:
If reusable Kerberos ticket material becomes available:

Ticket
 |
 v
Pass-the-Ticket
 |
 v
Authentication

For detailed coverage:

Pass-the-Ticket

docs.title: Relationship to Kerberos Tickets
docs.text:
Understanding:

TGT
Service Ticket
Forwardable Ticket
Ticket Cache

is essential before analysing delegation.

See:

Kerberos Tickets

docs.title: Relationship to Pass-the-Key
docs.text:
Unconstrained delegation is primarily concerned with delegated ticket-based authentication.

Pass-the-Key instead begins with:

Kerberos Key

and obtains a new ticket.

See:

Pass-the-Key

docs.title: Relationship to Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Unconstrained delegation:

Front-End
   |
   v
Broad Delegation
   |
   v
Other Services

Constrained delegation:

Front-End
   |
   v
Explicit Allowed Services
   |
   +--> CIFS/server01
   |
   +--> HTTP/app01

Constrained delegation was introduced to reduce the broad trust inherent in unconstrained delegation.

docs.title: Relationship to RBCD
docs.text:
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation reverses where the delegation decision is configured.

Traditional constrained delegation:

Front-End
     |
     v
Defines backend services
it may delegate to

RBCD:

Back-End Resource
       |
       v
Defines which principals
may delegate to it

This difference becomes extremely important during ACL analysis.

docs.title: Relationship to S4U
docs.text:
Constrained delegation and RBCD frequently involve Kerberos Service-for-User extensions:

S4U2Self
S4U2Proxy

Unconstrained delegation operates differently and should not be conflated with S4U-based delegation paths.

docs.title: Active Validation Strategy
docs.text:
Prefer:

Enumeration
    |
    v
Configuration Confirmed
    |
    v
Privilege Analysis
    |
    v
Controlled Test Account
    |
    v
Authentication to Test Service
    |
    v
Observe Delegation Behaviour

over:

Immediately target privileged
production authentication

docs.title: Minimum-Impact Validation
docs.text:
If the objective is simply to prove:

APP01 is trusted for
unconstrained delegation

the following may already be sufficient:

LDAP evidence
      +
PowerShell evidence
      +
BloodHound evidence
      +
Configuration screenshot

Active credential exposure may not be necessary.

docs.title: Controlled Validation
docs.text:
Where the engagement requires behavioural proof, use:

Dedicated Test User
       |
       v
Controlled Authentication
       |
       v
Delegation-Enabled Test Host
       |
       v
Observe Kerberos Behaviour
       |
       v
Stop

Avoid using:

Domain Admin
Enterprise Admin
Production Service Admin

unless the test specifically requires it and has explicit approval.

docs.title: Coercion
docs.text:
In offensive-security research, unconstrained delegation is sometimes combined with authentication-coercion techniques.

Conceptually:

High-Value System
       |
       | Authentication induced
       v
Unconstrained Delegation Host
       |
       v
Delegated Authentication Material
       |
       v
Potential Impersonation

This creates a much higher-impact attack path.

Because coercion can affect production services and privileged systems, it should be treated as a separate active-testing phase requiring explicit scope approval.

The dedicated authentication-coercion notes should cover individual techniques.

docs.title: Do Not Assume Coercion Is Required
docs.text:
Unconstrained delegation risk can exist without coercion.

For example:

Administrator
      |
      v
Legitimately accesses APP01
      |
      v
Delegation Host

If the host is already compromised, normal authentication may create the relevant exposure.

Coercion merely attempts to deliberately trigger authentication.

docs.title: Privileged Authentication Paths
docs.text:
During an assessment, ask:

Who normally connects to this server?

Look for:

Administrators
Backup Operators
Deployment Accounts
Monitoring Accounts
Domain Admins
Server Admins
Service Accounts
Domain Controllers

The answer can substantially change the severity.

docs.title: Service Exposure
docs.text:
Determine why users authenticate to the delegation-enabled host.

Examples:

SMB
HTTP
MSSQL
WinRM
Custom Application

Map:

SPN
 |
 v
Service
 |
 v
Who uses it?
 |
 v
Which identities authenticate?

docs.title: Network Reachability
docs.text:
Delegation risk should also consider:

Who can reach the service?

A host reachable from:

Entire User Network

may present a different risk from one reachable only from:

Dedicated Management Network

docs.title: Host Privilege
docs.text:
Determine who can compromise or administer the delegation host.

Relevant relationships include:

Local Administrators
Server Operators
Application Administrators
Deployment Accounts
Service Control Permissions
Remote Management Rights
Software Deployment Systems

docs.title: Attack Path Model
docs.text:
A complete attack path might look like:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Weak Application
        |
        v
APP01 Compromised
        |
        v
APP01 Trusted for
Unconstrained Delegation
        |
        v
Privileged User Authenticates
        |
        v
Delegated Kerberos Material
        |
        v
Privileged Authentication
        |
        v
Additional Systems

The vulnerability chain should be reported as a chain rather than treating each stage as isolated.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Detection should cover both:

Delegation Configuration

and:

Delegation Abuse

A useful model is:

Configuration Monitoring
        |
        +--> Which accounts are trusted?
        |
        +--> Was delegation recently enabled?
        |
        v
Authentication Monitoring
        |
        +--> Who authenticates?
        |
        +--> Which source?
        |
        +--> Which services?
        |
        v
Endpoint Monitoring
        |
        +--> Ticket access?
        |
        +--> Credential access?
        |
        +--> Suspicious processes?

docs.title: Event 4768
docs.text:
Event:

4768

records Kerberos TGT requests.

This can help identify:

Account
Client Address
Ticket Encryption Type
Pre-Authentication Type

depending on the Windows version and audit configuration.

docs.title: Event 4769
docs.text:
Event:

4769

records Kerberos service-ticket requests on domain controllers.

Microsoft's newer event format can include useful information such as:

Target User
Service Name
Client Address
Ticket Options
Ticket Encryption Type
Supported Encryption Types

This can help reconstruct delegation-related Kerberos activity.

docs.title: Event 4770
docs.text:
Event:

4770

records Kerberos service-ticket renewal where the corresponding auditing is enabled.

It may provide additional context for long-running Kerberos sessions.

docs.title: Event 4624
docs.text:
Successful Windows logons may generate:

4624

Correlate:

Kerberos Ticket Activity
        |
        v
Target Authentication
        |
        v
4624

docs.title: Delegation Configuration Changes
docs.text:
Changes that enable delegation should be monitored as high-value Active Directory configuration changes.

Relevant attributes include:

userAccountControl
msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo
msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity

For unconstrained delegation specifically, focus on changes introducing:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
Where Directory Service Changes auditing is enabled, Active Directory object modifications can generate:

5136

This can be useful for detecting changes to delegation-related attributes.

A monitoring model is:

AD Object
   |
   v
userAccountControl Modified
   |
   v
5136
   |
   v
Did TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION change?

docs.title: Configuration Baseline
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory of all systems trusted for unconstrained delegation.

Example:

Hostname    Type        Delegation
----------------------------------------
DC01        DC          Expected by role
DC02        DC          Expected by role
APP01       Member      Investigate
WEB01       Member      Investigate

Changes to this baseline should generate review.

docs.title: Detect New Delegation Hosts
docs.text:
A useful defensive workflow is:

Daily / Scheduled AD Query
        |
        v
TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
        |
        v
Compare to Baseline
        |
    +---+---+
    |       |
 Same      New
            |
            v
         Investigate

docs.title: Monitor Privileged Authentication
docs.text:
High-value users should not routinely authenticate to unconstrained delegation hosts.

Monitor:

Privileged Account
       |
       v
Authentication
       |
       v
Delegation Host?
       |
    +--+--+
    |     |
   No    Yes
          |
          v
       Investigate

docs.title: Endpoint Detection
docs.text:
If a delegation-enabled server is compromised, defenders should monitor for:

Credential-access activity
LSASS access
Kerberos ticket enumeration
Ticket export
Suspicious security tooling
Unusual child processes
Remote administration

The exact telemetry depends on the endpoint security platform.

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Kerberos traffic itself is legitimate.

Therefore:

Kerberos Traffic
       |
       X
Proof of Delegation Abuse

Detection should combine:

Kerberos events
       +
Host telemetry
       +
Identity context
       +
Delegation configuration

docs.title: Purple Team Exercise
docs.text:
A controlled exercise can validate whether defenders recognise the risk.

Example:

Test User
    |
    v
APP-PT01
Unconstrained Delegation
    |
    v
Controlled Authentication
    |
    v
Kerberos Telemetry
    |
    v
Blue Team Investigation

docs.title: Purple Team Questions
docs.text:
The blue team should determine:

Which host has unconstrained delegation?

Is the host a DC or member server?

Which account controls the service?

Which SPNs are registered?

Which user authenticated?

Was the user privileged?

Which Kerberos tickets were requested?

Was delegation configuration recently changed?

Can the host access Tier 0 resources?

Who can administer the delegation host?

docs.title: Purple Team Metrics
docs.text:
Useful metrics include:

Time to identify delegation host
Time to identify user
Time to identify service
Time to identify privileged authentication
Time to identify configuration
Time to containment decision
Correct attack-path reconstruction?
Correct remediation selected?

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
The primary recommendation is:

Remove Unconstrained Delegation
where it is not strictly required

Microsoft recommends avoiding unconstrained delegation because it does not restrict which services can be accessed on behalf of the authenticated user.

docs.title: Migration Strategy
docs.text:
A safe migration model is:

Inventory
   |
   v
Identify Unconstrained Delegation
   |
   v
Identify Application Dependency
   |
   v
Determine Required Backend Services
   |
   v
Choose Safer Delegation Model
   |
   +--> Constrained Delegation
   |
   +--> RBCD
   |
   v
Test
   |
   v
Deploy
   |
   v
Remove Unconstrained Delegation

Do not simply disable delegation on production applications without understanding their authentication requirements.

docs.title: Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Where delegation is genuinely required, constrained delegation may reduce the trust scope.

Instead of:

APP01
 |
 v
Any Kerberos Service

configure:

APP01
 |
 +--> MSSQLSvc/SQL01

where operationally appropriate.

docs.title: Resource-Based Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Modern architectures may also use RBCD.

SQL01
 |
 v
Defines which front-end
principals may delegate to it

This can provide a clearer resource-side trust model.

RBCD still requires careful ACL management.

docs.title: Protect Sensitive Accounts
docs.text:
For suitable privileged accounts, consider:

Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated

Conceptually:

Privileged User
      |
      v
NOT_DELEGATED
      |
      v
Delegation Restricted

docs.title: Protected Users
docs.text:
Where compatible, Protected Users can provide additional safeguards for high-value identities.

Always evaluate:

Legacy Applications
Service Dependencies
Authentication Requirements

before broad deployment.

docs.title: Administrative Tiering
docs.text:
Do not allow Tier 0 credentials onto lower-tier delegation hosts.

Bad:

Domain Admin
     |
     v
Legacy APP01
     |
     v
Unconstrained Delegation

Better:

Domain Admin
     |
     v
PAW
     |
     v
Tier 0

docs.title: Privileged Access Workstations
docs.text:
Use dedicated administrative systems for privileged access.

This reduces:

Privileged Ticket
      |
      v
Exposure on Application Servers

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Reduce who can administer delegation-enabled servers.

Review:

Local Administrators
Remote Desktop Users
WinRM Rights
Service Control Rights
Deployment Rights
Application Administration

A delegation host should be treated as a sensitive credential boundary.

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Restrict access to delegation-enabled systems.

Example:

User Network
     |
     X
Administrative Services
     |
     v
Delegation Server

Allow only required application traffic.

docs.title: Service Hardening
docs.text:
Because compromise of the delegation host is central to exploitation, harden the server itself.

Priorities include:

Patch management
Application hardening
EDR
Least privilege
Service isolation
Restricted administration
Network segmentation
Secure configuration

docs.title: Monitor Delegation Changes
docs.text:
Alert on newly configured:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION

for non-domain-controller systems.

This is particularly important because unconstrained delegation should be uncommon in modern environments.

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
If an unconstrained delegation host is compromised:

Compromised Delegation Host
          |
          v
Isolate Host
          |
          v
Identify Authenticated Users
          |
          v
Identify Privileged Sessions
          |
          v
Review Kerberos Activity
          |
          v
Determine Ticket Exposure
          |
          v
Investigate Ticket Reuse
          |
          v
Reset / Rotate Credentials
where required
          |
          v
Remove Unsafe Delegation
          |
          v
Rebuild / Remediate Host

docs.title: Assume Credential Exposure Carefully
docs.text:
Do not automatically claim:

Every user who ever connected
is compromised

Instead determine:

Which identities authenticated?
When?
Which authentication protocol?
Was delegation applicable?
Was reusable material exposed?
Was it accessed?

Evidence should drive the conclusion.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Possible finding titles include:

Unconstrained Kerberos Delegation Enabled on Member Server

Unconstrained Delegation Exposes Privileged Kerberos Authentication Material

Legacy Kerberos Delegation Configuration Creates Credential Exposure Risk

Compromised Delegation Host Could Enable Privileged User Impersonation

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity should consider:

Delegation Host
      |
      +--> DC or Member Server?
      |
      +--> Compromisable?
      |
      +--> Internet-facing?
      |
      +--> High-value users connect?
      |
      +--> Tier 0 connectivity?
      |
      +--> Privileged service?
      |
      +--> Network exposure?

Example:

Unconstrained Delegation
on isolated legacy member server
with no privileged authentication

may present a different risk from:

Unconstrained Delegation
on widely accessible application server
regularly used by Domain Admins

docs.title: Do Not Report the Flag Alone
docs.text:
Avoid:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION found
therefore Critical

Instead report:

Configuration
      +
Host Exposure
      +
Privilege Relationships
      +
Authentication Paths
      +
Demonstrated Impact

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Unconstrained Kerberos Delegation Enabled on Member Server

Affected System:
APP01.corp.example

Affected Account:
APP01$

Description:
The affected member server is configured as trusted for unconstrained
Kerberos delegation.

This configuration allows the server to act on behalf of users that
authenticate to its Kerberos services without restricting delegation
to a predefined set of backend services.

Risk:
If the affected server is compromised, Kerberos authentication material
associated with users authenticating to the server may become exposed.

This is particularly significant if privileged users authenticate to
the affected system because their delegated authentication context may
provide access to additional systems within the domain.

Validation:
The TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION account-control flag was confirmed through
Active Directory enumeration.

BloodHound analysis identified the affected server as reachable by
administrative identities and demonstrated that compromise of the host
would create a credential-exposure path.

No production administrator authentication was deliberately induced
during testing.

Recommendation:
Determine whether Kerberos delegation is still operationally required.

Where delegation is necessary, migrate the application to constrained
delegation or resource-based constrained delegation where compatible.

Prevent privileged accounts from authenticating to the affected server,
apply the sensitive-and-cannot-be-delegated protection to appropriate
high-value accounts, restrict administrative access to the server, and
monitor changes to delegation-related Active Directory attributes.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Record:

Account
Object Type
Hostname
Distinguished Name
userAccountControl
TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
SPNs
Operating System
Domain Controller?
Service Purpose
Network Exposure
Administrators
Privileged Sessions
BloodHound Relationships
Authentication Paths
Relevant Event IDs
Enumeration Tool
Command
Timestamp

docs.title: Evidence Example
docs.text:
Account:
APP01$

Hostname:
APP01.corp.example

Object Type:
Computer

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION:
True

userAccountControl:
[VALUE]

Domain Controller:
No

SPNs:
HOST/APP01
HOST/APP01.corp.example
[REDACTED AS REQUIRED]

Privilege Analysis:
[SUMMARY]

Validation:
Configuration only

docs.title: Credential Evidence
docs.text:
If controlled validation results in ticket material:

TGT
.ccache
.kirbi

treat it as a credential.

Do not place it in:

Git
Public screenshots
Issue trackers
Shared chat
Unencrypted evidence folders

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
After controlled ticket testing:

unset KRB5CCNAME

Where appropriate:

kdestroy

Remove temporary ticket files according to evidence-retention requirements:

rm -f testuser.ccache

For dedicated Windows test sessions:

klist purge

may be appropriate, but remember that it can disrupt authentication in the current session.

docs.title: No Delegation Hosts Found
docs.text:
Possible explanations:

Environment does not use
unconstrained delegation

LDAP query incorrect

Insufficient directory access

Wrong search base

Wrong domain

Only DCs match

Validate using more than one enumeration method where practical.

docs.title: Only Domain Controllers Found
docs.text:
This may be normal.

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
        |
        v
Only DC accounts

means there may be no non-DC unconstrained delegation systems.

Document the result rather than forcing an attack path.

docs.title: PowerShell Filter Fails
docs.text:
Check whether the Active Directory module is available:

Get-Module -ListAvailable ActiveDirectory

Then:

Import-Module ActiveDirectory

If unavailable, use:

LDAP
PowerView
Impacket
BloodHound
NetExec

as appropriate.

docs.title: LDAP Authentication Fails
docs.text:
Check:

Username format
Password
Domain
LDAP vs LDAPS
Network access
DNS
Domain controller

docs.title: Impacket findDelegation Fails
docs.text:
Check:

impacket-findDelegation -h

Then validate:

Credential format
Domain name
DNS
DC address
Kerberos vs NTLM mode
Clock synchronisation

docs.title: Delegation Exists but No Ticket Exposure Observed
docs.text:
Possible explanations include:

No relevant user authenticated

Authentication used NTLM

Ticket not forwardable

Account protected from delegation

Protected Users restrictions

Application does not use expected
delegation path

Wrong logon/session context

Do not assume the configuration is broken without understanding the authentication flow.

docs.title: User Is Sensitive and Cannot Be Delegated
docs.text:
If:

AccountNotDelegated = True

the user's authentication context is protected against delegation even when the service is trusted for delegation.

This is a defensive control, not a testing failure.

docs.title: Authentication Uses NTLM
docs.text:
Kerberos delegation requires Kerberos.

If:

User
 |
 v
APP01
 |
 v
NTLM

the expected Kerberos delegation behaviour may not occur.

Verify the protocol rather than assuming.

docs.title: Kerberos Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Use:

DNS
Time
SPN
Realm
Ticket
KDC

as the troubleshooting sequence.

On Windows:

klist

On Linux:

klist

docs.title: Mistake 1 - Calling Every Delegation Setting Unconstrained
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Unconstrained
Constrained
RBCD

docs.title: Mistake 2 - Confusing Delegation Flags
docs.text:
TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
        =
Unconstrained


TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION
        =
Protocol transition capability
associated with constrained delegation

docs.title: Mistake 3 - Reporting Domain Controllers as Unexpected
docs.text:
Domain controllers have special Kerberos requirements.

Identify them separately.

docs.title: Mistake 4 - Assuming Delegation Means Immediate Compromise
docs.text:
The complete path normally requires:

Delegation Host
       +
Host Compromise
       +
Interesting Authentication

docs.title: Mistake 5 - Ignoring Service Accounts
docs.text:
Unconstrained delegation can be configured on:

Computer accounts

and:

User/service accounts

Enumerate both.

docs.title: Mistake 6 - Ignoring SPNs
docs.text: SPNs help identify what service the delegation-enabled account represents.

docs.title: Mistake 7 - Ignoring Privileged Authentication
docs.text:
The most important question is often:

Who authenticates here?

docs.title: Mistake 8 - Automatically Coercing a Domain Controller
docs.text:
Authentication coercion can create substantial operational and security impact.

Do not perform it without explicit approval.

docs.title: Mistake 9 - Confusing Ticket Theft with Delegation
docs.text:
Delegation creates the authentication relationship.

Ticket theft is a subsequent credential-access activity.

docs.title: Mistake 10 - Confusing Pass-the-Ticket with Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
Unconstrained Delegation
       |
       v
Potential Ticket Exposure


Pass-the-Ticket
       |
       v
Use of Ticket

docs.title: Mistake 11 - Assuming RC4 Is Required
docs.text:
Kerberos delegation is not fundamentally dependent on RC4.

Modern AES-based Kerberos environments can still have delegation risk.

docs.title: Mistake 12 - Ignoring NOT_DELEGATED
docs.text: Sensitive accounts may have delegation protections that alter the attack path.

docs.title: Mistake 13 - Ignoring Protected Users
docs.text: Protected identities can behave differently from ordinary accounts.

docs.title: Mistake 14 - Disabling Delegation Without Application Testing
docs.text:
Delegation may support legitimate multi-tier authentication.

Remediation must consider application dependencies.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Confirm delegation testing is authorised
  • Confirm permitted domains
  • Confirm permitted accounts
  • Confirm permitted systems
  • Confirm whether active ticket testing is allowed
  • Confirm whether authentication coercion is allowed
  • Identify domain controllers
  • Confirm DNS
  • Confirm Kerberos connectivity

docs.title: Enumeration
docs.text:
• Query TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
  • Enumerate computer accounts
  • Enumerate user/service accounts
  • Identify domain controllers
  • Identify non-DC delegation systems
  • Record userAccountControl
  • Enumerate SPNs
  • Identify operating systems
  • Identify service purpose

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
• Query TrustedForDelegation
  • Query UAC bit 524288
  • Enumerate service SPNs
  • Review sensitive accounts
  • Review AccountNotDelegated
  • Review Protected Users where authorised

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
• Query LDAP
  • Run impacket-findDelegation
  • Review NetExec LDAP capabilities
  • Compare results between tools
  • Validate DNS and time

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
• Identify unconstrained delegation systems
  • Identify who controls them
  • Identify local administrators
  • Identify active sessions where authorised
  • Identify paths to high-value assets
  • Identify Tier 0 relationships
  • Identify privileged users likely to authenticate

docs.title: Risk Analysis
docs.text:
• Is the system a domain controller?
  • Is the system externally exposed?
  • Is the system reachable by users?
  • Is the system easy to compromise?
  • Do privileged users authenticate?
  • Does it have Tier 0 connectivity?
  • Can lower-privileged users administer it?
  • Is delegation still operationally required?

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Prefer configuration evidence first
  • Use dedicated test identity
  • Use dedicated test target
  • Verify Kerberos is used
  • Avoid production privileged credentials
  • Avoid coercion unless explicitly approved
  • Stop once impact is demonstrated
  • Protect any resulting tickets

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• Review 4768
  • Review 4769
  • Review 4770 where relevant
  • Review 4624
  • Monitor delegation configuration changes
  • Review 5136 where available
  • Baseline delegation-enabled accounts
  • Monitor privileged authentication to delegation hosts
  • Correlate endpoint credential-access telemetry

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Determine whether delegation is required
  • Remove unnecessary unconstrained delegation
  • Migrate to constrained delegation where appropriate
  • Consider RBCD where appropriate
  • Protect sensitive accounts from delegation
  • Consider Protected Users
  • Implement administrative tiering
  • Use PAWs
  • Restrict administration of delegation hosts
  • Segment delegation-enabled services
  • Harden delegation hosts
  • Monitor future delegation changes

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• Remove temporary ticket caches
  • Remove .kirbi files
  • Remove .ccache files
  • Unset KRB5CCNAME
  • Purge dedicated test-session tickets where appropriate
  • Secure retained evidence
  • Remove temporary test configuration
  • Confirm no production configuration was changed

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation Testing Model
docs.text:
The normal delegation model is:

                           User
                            |
                            | Kerberos
                            v
                    Front-End Service
                            |
                            | Delegation
                            v
                     Back-End Service

The unconstrained model is:

                           User
                            |
                            v
                Unconstrained Delegation Host
                            |
             +--------------+--------------+
             |              |              |
             v              v              v
          Service A      Service B      Service C

The security problem is:

                     Privileged Identity
                            |
                            v
                 Delegation-Enabled Host
                            |
                            v
                Delegated Authentication
                         Material
                            |
                            v
                     Host Compromise
                            |
                            v
                  Credential Exposure
                            |
                            v
                  Ticket Authentication
                            |
                            v
                   Additional Systems

The configuration model is:

                     Active Directory Object
                              |
                              v
                       userAccountControl
                              |
                              v
                TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
                              |
                              v
                           0x80000
                              |
                              v
                  Unconstrained Delegation

The privilege model is:

              Unconstrained Delegation Host
                         |
          +--------------+--------------+
          |                             |
          v                             v
Who Can Compromise It?        Who Authenticates to It?
          |                             |
          v                             v
Low-Privilege Path?            Privileged Identity?
          |                             |
          +--------------+--------------+
                         |
                         v
                    Attack Path

The attack-chain model is:

Low-Privilege Access
        |
        v
Delegation Host Compromised
        |
        v
Wait for / Receive
Kerberos Authentication
        |
        v
Delegated Credential Material
        |
        v
Credential Reuse
        |
        v
Privilege Expansion

The safer delegation model is:

Unconstrained Delegation
          |
          v
       Migrate
          |
     +----+----+
     |         |
     v         v
Constrained   RBCD
Delegation
     |         |
     +----+----+
          |
          v
Explicit Delegation Scope

The defensive model is:

Unconstrained Delegation
          |
          +--> Remove where unnecessary
          |
          +--> Restrict delegation scope
          |
          +--> Protect privileged accounts
          |       |
          |       +--> NOT_DELEGATED
          |       +--> Protected Users
          |       +--> PAWs
          |
          +--> Protect delegation hosts
          |       |
          |       +--> Patching
          |       +--> EDR
          |       +--> Least Privilege
          |       +--> Segmentation
          |
          +--> Monitor
                  |
                  +--> Delegation Configuration
                  +--> 4768
                  +--> 4769
                  +--> 4624
                  +--> 5136
                  +--> Privileged Authentication

The assessment should answer:

Which accounts are trusted for
unconstrained delegation?
        |
        v
Which are domain controllers?
        |
        v
Which are non-DC systems?
        |
        v
What services run on them?
        |
        v
Who can compromise or administer them?
        |
        v
Which identities authenticate to them?
        |
        v
Do privileged identities authenticate?
        |
        v
Are those identities protected
from delegation?
        |
        v
Can the configuration be replaced
with a safer delegation model?
        |
        v
Can defenders identify both the
configuration and abuse path?

MITRE ATT&CK - Pass the Ticket

Fortra Impacket

Impacket findDelegation

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Unconstrained delegation is a legacy Kerberos delegation model that grants a service broad ability to act on behalf of authenticated users.

The fundamental architecture is:

User
 |
 v
Delegation-Enabled Service
 |
 v
Other Kerberos Services

The Active Directory configuration is associated with:

TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION
        |
        v
userAccountControl
        |
        v
0x00080000

The security risk becomes significant when:

Unconstrained Delegation
        +
Compromised Host
        +
Privileged Authentication
        |
        v
Potential Credential Exposure
        |
        v
User Impersonation

The most important distinction is:

Unconstrained Delegation
        =
Broad service delegation


Constrained Delegation
        =
Explicit destination services


RBCD
        =
Resource controls which
principals may delegate to it

Do not treat every system with the delegation flag as equally vulnerable.

A mature assessment should determine:

Which systems are trusted?
        |
        v
Which are non-DC systems?
        |
        v
Why is delegation required?
        |
        v
Which services use it?
        |
        v
Who can compromise the host?
        |
        v
Which users authenticate?
        |
        v
Are privileged users exposed?
        |
        v
Can a safer delegation model replace it?

From a defensive perspective, the preferred strategy is:

Remove Unconstrained Delegation
             |
             v
Use Explicit Delegation
Where Required
             |
             +
Protect Privileged Accounts
             |
             +
Protect Delegation Hosts
             |
             +
Monitor Delegation Changes
             |
             +
Monitor Privileged Authentication

Unconstrained delegation should therefore be assessed as part of a broader identity and attack-path model rather than as an isolated Active Directory flag. The meaningful risk comes from the combination of the delegation configuration, compromise potential of the trusted system, identities that authenticate to it, privileges associated with those identities, and the controls available to prevent or detect subsequent credential reuse.

docs.title: Active Directory WinRM - PowerShell Remoting and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is Microsoft's implementation of the WS-Management protocol and is commonly used for remote administration of Windows systems.

In Active Directory environments, WinRM is especially important because it provides a legitimate administrative channel that can also become a lateral-movement path when an attacker controls an identity with remote-management privileges.

Typical uses include:

PowerShell Remoting
Remote Administration
Configuration Management
Server Management
Automation
Command Execution
Administrative Scripting

From an offensive-security perspective, the fundamental relationship is:

Compromised Identity
        |
        v
WinRM Access
        |
        v
Remote PowerShell
        |
        v
Target System

WinRM access should therefore be analysed as an authorisation relationship, not simply as an open network port.

Authorised testing only

WinRM provides legitimate remote command execution. Only authenticate to systems included in the assessment scope and only use credentials you are authorised to test. Prefer harmless commands such as whoami and hostname when execution must be demonstrated.

docs.title: WinRM at a Glance
docs.text:
The basic architecture is:

Administrator
      |
      v
WinRM Client
      |
      v
WS-Management
      |
      v
WinRM Service
      |
      v
Windows Host

PowerShell Remoting commonly uses:

PowerShell
    |
    v
WinRM
    |
    v
Remote PowerShell Session

docs.title: Default WinRM Ports
docs.text:
The standard WinRM ports are:

5985/TCP - HTTP
5986/TCP - HTTPS

These are the first ports to check during WinRM discovery.

docs.title: WinRM HTTP
docs.text:
WinRM commonly listens on:

TCP 5985

The transport is HTTP.

This does not mean credentials are simply transmitted as plaintext.

Authentication mechanisms such as:

Kerberos
NTLM
Negotiate

provide authentication protection independently of the HTTP transport.

However, HTTPS provides additional transport protection and is preferable in environments where TLS is required.

docs.title: WinRM HTTPS
docs.text:
WinRM over HTTPS normally uses:

TCP 5986

and requires a suitable server certificate.

Conceptually:

Client
  |
  v
TLS
  |
  v
WinRM
  |
  v
Target

docs.title: Check WinRM Connectivity from Windows
docs.text:
Test HTTP:

Test-NetConnection srv01.corp.example -Port 5985

Test HTTPS:

Test-NetConnection srv01.corp.example -Port 5986

Example:

ComputerName     : srv01.corp.example
RemoteAddress    : 10.10.10.25
RemotePort       : 5985
TcpTestSucceeded : True

docs.title: Check WinRM from Linux
docs.text:
Using Nmap:

nmap -Pn -p5985,5986 srv01.corp.example

For an approved target range:

nmap -Pn -p5985,5986 10.10.10.0/24

docs.title: WinRM Endpoint
docs.text:
A typical HTTP endpoint is:

http://srv01.corp.example:5985/wsman

HTTPS:

https://srv01.corp.example:5986/wsman

The /wsman endpoint is expected for WinRM.

docs.title: Test-WSMan
docs.text:
PowerShell provides:

Test-WSMan

Example:

Test-WSMan srv01.corp.example

This can verify whether the target responds to WS-Management.

docs.title: Example Test-WSMan Output
docs.text:
Typical output may contain:

wsmid
ProtocolVersion
ProductVendor
ProductVersion

A successful response confirms:

WinRM Reachable

It does not prove that the current user has permission to establish a remote PowerShell session.

docs.title: WinRM Authentication
docs.text:
Common WinRM authentication mechanisms include:

Kerberos
Negotiate
NTLM
Certificate
CredSSP
Basic

Availability depends on:

Client Configuration
Server Configuration
Domain Membership
Transport
Policy
Authentication Method

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
In a normal Active Directory environment, Kerberos is generally the preferred authentication mechanism.

Conceptually:

Domain User
    |
    v
KDC
    |
    v
HTTP Service Ticket
    |
    v
WinRM

docs.title: WinRM SPN
docs.text:
Kerberos authentication for WinRM commonly involves HTTP-related SPNs.

Examples can include:

HTTP/srv01
HTTP/srv01.corp.example

The exact SPN behaviour depends on the environment and configuration.

docs.title: Why Hostnames Matter
docs.text:
Prefer:

srv01.corp.example

instead of:

10.10.10.25

when Kerberos authentication is expected.

Kerberos relies on:

DNS
SPNs
KDC
Time Synchronisation

Using an IP address can cause Kerberos authentication to fail or another authentication mechanism to be selected.

docs.title: NTLM
docs.text:
If Kerberos cannot be used and NTLM is permitted:

WinRM
  |
  v
NTLM

may be used.

This becomes relevant for:

Pass-the-Hash
NTLM Reduction
Authentication Monitoring
Relay Analysis

docs.title: Negotiate
docs.text:
PowerShell Remoting frequently uses:

Negotiate

which allows Windows to negotiate an appropriate authentication protocol.

In a healthy domain scenario this will often result in:

Kerberos

when Kerberos requirements are satisfied.

docs.title: Basic Authentication
docs.text:
Basic authentication should be treated carefully.

It relies on transport protection such as HTTPS to protect credentials in transit.

Review server configuration rather than assuming Basic authentication is enabled.

docs.title: CredSSP
docs.text:
Credential Security Support Provider can delegate credentials to a remote system.

Conceptually:

Client Credential
       |
       v
Remote Host
       |
       v
Second Resource

This can solve certain multi-hop authentication problems but increases credential exposure considerations.

Use CredSSP only when its delegation behaviour is understood and required.

docs.title: The Double-Hop Problem
docs.text:
PowerShell Remoting commonly encounters the:

Second Hop Problem

Example:

ADMIN-PC
    |
    v
SRV01
    |
    v
FILE01

The administrator authenticates to:

SRV01

but the remote session may not possess credentials that can automatically authenticate to:

FILE01

docs.title: Why the Second Hop Matters
docs.text:
Suppose:

Enter-PSSession -ComputerName srv01.corp.example

works.

Inside the remote session:

Get-ChildItem '\\files01.corp.example\Finance'

may fail because credentials were not delegated for the second network hop.

This behaviour should not automatically be interpreted as:

Access Denied to FILE01

The authentication context must be understood.

docs.title: PowerShell Remoting
docs.text:
The most common native WinRM interface is:

PowerShell Remoting

The two important patterns are:

Interactive Session

and:

Non-Interactive Remote Command

docs.title: Enter-PSSession
docs.text:
Interactive session:

Enter-PSSession -ComputerName srv01.corp.example

This attempts to create an interactive PowerShell session on the target.

docs.title: Exit-PSSession
docs.text:
Leave the remote session:

Exit-PSSession

docs.title: Explicit Credentials
docs.text:
Use:

$cred = Get-Credential

Then:

Enter-PSSession -ComputerName srv01.corp.example -Credential $cred

This avoids placing the password directly into command history.

docs.title: Invoke-Command
docs.text:
For a single remote command:

Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01.corp.example -ScriptBlock {
    whoami
}

This is often preferable during security testing because:

Connect
   |
   v
Execute Minimal Command
   |
   v
Return Result
   |
   v
Disconnect

docs.title: Multiple Harmless Commands
docs.text:
Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01.corp.example -ScriptBlock {
    hostname
    whoami
}

docs.title: Explicit Credential with Invoke-Command
docs.text:
$cred = Get-Credential

Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01.corp.example -Credential $cred -ScriptBlock {
    hostname
    whoami
}

docs.title: PSSession
docs.text:
Create a reusable session:

$session = New-PSSession -ComputerName srv01.corp.example

Inspect it:

Get-PSSession

Use it:

Invoke-Command -Session $session -ScriptBlock {
    hostname
}

Remove it:

Remove-PSSession $session

docs.title: PSSession Lifecycle
docs.text:
New-PSSession
     |
     v
Persistent Remote Session
     |
     +--> Invoke-Command
     |
     +--> Enter-PSSession
     |
     v
Remove-PSSession

Clean up test sessions when finished.

docs.title: WinRM Authorisation
docs.text:
A reachable WinRM service does not mean every domain user can use PowerShell Remoting.

The important question is:

Who Is Authorised?

docs.title: Common Authorised Groups
docs.text:
Depending on configuration, relevant groups can include:

Administrators
Remote Management Users

Group Policy and PowerShell session configuration can further restrict access.

docs.title: Remote Management Users
docs.text:
Check local membership:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Remote Management Users'

On systems where Get-LocalGroupMember is unavailable:

net localgroup "Remote Management Users"

docs.title: Local Administrators
docs.text:
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'

or:

net localgroup Administrators

docs.title: PowerShell Session Configurations
docs.text:
Inspect:

Get-PSSessionConfiguration

Common configurations may include:

Microsoft.PowerShell
Microsoft.PowerShell32

depending on the system.

docs.title: Session Configuration Permissions
docs.text:
PowerShell endpoints can have their own permissions.

Therefore:

WinRM Enabled

does not necessarily mean:

Every User Can Use Every PowerShell Endpoint

docs.title: Just Enough Administration
docs.text:
PowerShell supports:

JEA

or:

Just Enough Administration

JEA can expose constrained administrative capabilities without granting unrestricted administrative PowerShell access.

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
Restricted PowerShell Endpoint
 |
 +--> Approved Command
 +--> Approved Function
 |
 X
 |
 +--> Unrestricted Administration

docs.title: JEA Security Importance
docs.text:
If an organisation uses JEA, do not assume that obtaining a WinRM session means:

Full Shell

Review:

Available Commands
Language Restrictions
Run-As Context
Role Capabilities
Endpoint Permissions

docs.title: Check Current PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
Inside a session:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible values include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

Language mode is separate from WinRM authorisation.

docs.title: NetExec WinRM
docs.text:
NetExec supports WinRM assessment.

Check installed syntax:

nxc winrm -h

Basic authentication validation:

nxc winrm srv01.corp.example -u 'audit-user' -p 'PASSWORD'

docs.title: NetExec Target List
docs.text:
For an explicitly approved list:

nxc winrm targets.txt -u 'audit-user' -p 'PASSWORD'

Prefer a targeted list rather than unnecessarily authenticating against an entire enterprise range.

docs.title: Authentication Success vs Administrative Access
docs.text:
Always distinguish:

Valid Credential

from:

WinRM Authorised

and:

Local Administrator

These are different security properties.

docs.title: Evil-WinRM
docs.text:
Evil-WinRM is commonly used from Linux to interact with Windows systems through WinRM.

Check the installed version and options:

evil-winrm -h

Password authentication:

evil-winrm -i srv01.corp.example -u 'audit-user' -p 'PASSWORD'

docs.title: Avoid Passwords in Shell History
docs.text:
Where possible, avoid:

-p PASSWORD

with real production credentials.

Use secure prompting or approved temporary test credentials when available.

docs.title: Pass-the-Hash with WinRM
docs.text:
Depending on the authentication configuration and tool, an NTLM hash may be usable for WinRM authentication.

Evil-WinRM supports hash authentication.

Example:

evil-winrm -i srv01.corp.example -u 'audit-admin' -H 'NTHASH'

This is a:

Pass-the-Hash

scenario.

See:

Pass-the-Hash

docs.title: Pass-the-Hash Model
docs.text:
NTLM Hash
    |
    v
NTLM Authentication
    |
    v
WinRM
    |
    v
Remote Session

docs.title: WinRM and Kerberos from Linux
docs.text:
Linux tooling can also authenticate using Kerberos where supported.

Conceptually:

Kerberos Credential Cache
        |
        v
HTTP Service Ticket
        |
        v
WinRM

Exact configuration depends on the client tool.

docs.title: Kerberos Ticket Cache
docs.text:
Check:

klist

Environment:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

A credential cache may be configured using:

export KRB5CCNAME=./audit-user.ccache

docs.title: DNS Requirements
docs.text:
Kerberos-aware WinRM testing depends heavily on correct name resolution.

Check:

nslookup srv01.corp.example

or:

dig srv01.corp.example

Windows:

Resolve-DnsName srv01.corp.example

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Check Linux:

timedatectl

Windows:

w32tm /query /status

Kerberos authentication can fail when clock skew exceeds acceptable limits.

docs.title: WinRM TrustedHosts
docs.text:
In workgroup scenarios or situations where Kerberos cannot authenticate the remote system, Windows may use:

TrustedHosts

configuration.

Inspect:

Get-Item WSMan:\localhost\Client\TrustedHosts

docs.title: TrustedHosts Security
docs.text:
Avoid:

*

unless there is a justified and carefully controlled requirement.

A broad TrustedHosts configuration weakens server identity assurance when Kerberos is unavailable.

docs.title: Do Not Change TrustedHosts Just to Make Testing Easier
docs.text:
During an assessment, do not modify:

TrustedHosts

on production systems merely to bypass authentication configuration.

Instead document why the intended authentication method failed.

docs.title: Inspect WinRM Service
docs.text:
Get-Service WinRM

Example:

Status   Name   DisplayName
------   ----   -----------
Running  WinRM  Windows Remote Management

docs.title: WinRM Configuration
docs.text:
Display configuration:

winrm get winrm/config

docs.title: WinRM Service Configuration
docs.text: winrm get winrm/config/service

docs.title: WinRM Client Configuration
docs.text: winrm get winrm/config/client

docs.title: WinRM Listeners
docs.text:
winrm enumerate winrm/config/listener

PowerShell alternative:

Get-ChildItem WSMan:\localhost\Listener

docs.title: Listener Information
docs.text:
Review:

Transport
Address
Port
Hostname
Certificate Thumbprint

docs.title: HTTP Listener
docs.text:
Typical:

Transport = HTTP
Port = 5985

docs.title: HTTPS Listener
docs.text:
Typical:

Transport = HTTPS
Port = 5986

The listener should use an appropriate certificate.

docs.title: Review Authentication Configuration
docs.text:
winrm get winrm/config/service/auth

This can reveal whether methods such as:

Basic
Kerberos
Negotiate
Certificate
CredSSP

are enabled.

docs.title: PowerShell WSMan Provider
docs.text:
PowerShell exposes WinRM configuration under:

WSMan:

Example:

Get-ChildItem WSMan:\localhost\Service\Auth

docs.title: Do Not Use winrm quickconfig During Enumeration
docs.text:
The command:

winrm quickconfig

can modify the system by:

Starting WinRM
Creating a Listener
Changing Firewall Configuration

Therefore, do not run it merely to determine whether WinRM is enabled.

Use read-only commands instead.

docs.title: Enable-PSRemoting Is Also a Configuration Change
docs.text:
Similarly:

Enable-PSRemoting

changes the target system.

It may:

Start WinRM
Configure Startup
Create Listeners
Modify Firewall Rules
Enable Session Configurations

Do not run it during an assessment unless the change is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Remote Command Execution
docs.text:
Once WinRM access has been established:

Remote Command Execution

is already proven.

A harmless command is normally sufficient.

docs.title: Minimal Validation
docs.text:
Recommended:

Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01.corp.example -ScriptBlock {
    whoami
}

or:

Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01.corp.example -ScriptBlock {
    hostname
}

docs.title: Why Minimal Validation Matters
docs.text:
If the assessment objective is:

Can This User Execute Commands on SRV01?

and the output is:

corp\audit-user

then the objective has been proven.

There is usually no need to:

Create User
Disable Defender
Dump Credentials
Deploy Payload
Create Persistence

docs.title: WinRM and Local Administrator Rights
docs.text:
Local administrators frequently have remote-management capabilities, but configuration can affect actual access.

Do not assume:

Local Administrator
=
WinRM Access

until tested or confirmed from policy.

docs.title: UAC Remote Restrictions
docs.text:
Local accounts can be affected by:

UAC Remote Restrictions

which may filter administrative tokens during remote access.

This can produce different behaviour between:

Domain Administrator
Domain Account in Local Administrators
Built-In Local Administrator
Other Local Administrator

docs.title: Domain Accounts
docs.text:
A domain account placed in:

Local Administrators

on a member server may become a significant lateral-movement identity.

Example:

CORP\Helpdesk
      |
      v
Local Administrators on SRV01
      |
      v
WinRM
      |
      v
Remote Administration

docs.title: Excessive WinRM Rights
docs.text:
An account does not necessarily need full local administrator rights to be security relevant.

For example:

Remote Management Users

may provide remote PowerShell access.

The impact depends on what the account can do within that session.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can identify WinRM-related relationships.

See:

BloodHound

A relevant edge can include:

CanPSRemote

Conceptually:

User
 |
 v
CanPSRemote
 |
 v
Computer

docs.title: CanPSRemote
docs.text:
A CanPSRemote relationship indicates that the principal is expected to have PowerShell Remoting access to the computer based on collected configuration.

Treat it as:

Potential Remote Access

and validate only where required.

docs.title: Example BloodHound Path
docs.text:
Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
CanPSRemote
        |
        v
Application Server
        |
        v
Additional Privilege Path

docs.title: WinRM as a Lateral-Movement Path
docs.text:
A typical sequence:

Compromised User
       |
       v
Enumerate BloodHound
       |
       v
CanPSRemote SRV01
       |
       v
Authenticate through WinRM
       |
       v
Remote Session
       |
       v
Continue Assessment

docs.title: WinRM vs SMB
docs.text:
Both can provide remote administration, but they operate differently.

SMB
 |
 +--> Shares
 +--> Named Pipes
 +--> Service Management

WinRM:

WinRM
 |
 +--> WS-Management
 +--> PowerShell Remoting
 +--> Management Operations

docs.title: Prefer Existing Administrative Channels
docs.text:
If WinRM is already legitimately enabled and the account has remote-management rights, WinRM can be a cleaner validation mechanism than creating a temporary service through SMB.

For example:

WinRM
 |
 v
whoami

may generate less intrusive system modification than:

SMB
 |
 v
Upload Executable
 |
 v
Create Service

This does not mean WinRM is invisible.

It generates extensive telemetry.

docs.title: WinRM vs RDP
docs.text:
WinRM:

Command-Line / PowerShell
Non-Interactive or Interactive Shell
Automation Friendly

RDP:

Graphical Desktop
Interactive Session
Potential User Session Impact

For simple command-execution validation, WinRM is often preferable to creating an RDP session.

docs.title: WinRM vs WMI
docs.text:
WinRM:

WS-Management
PowerShell Remoting
5985 / 5986

WMI/DCOM:

RPC / DCOM
135 + Dynamic RPC

Modern PowerShell management frequently uses CIM over WS-Man.

docs.title: CIM over WinRM
docs.text:
PowerShell CIM can use WS-Management.

Example:

Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_OperatingSystem -ComputerName srv01.corp.example

This can provide remote management functionality without an interactive shell.

docs.title: CIM Session
docs.text:
$session = New-CimSession -ComputerName srv01.corp.example

Query:

Get-CimInstance -CimSession $session -ClassName Win32_OperatingSystem

Cleanup:

Remove-CimSession $session

docs.title: WinRM and PowerShell Versions
docs.text:
The remote PowerShell environment may differ from the client.

Inside the remote session:

$PSVersionTable

Review:

PSVersion
PSEdition
OS
WSManStackVersion

depending on version.

docs.title: Constrained Endpoints
docs.text:
A remote session may be intentionally constrained.

For example:

User
 |
 v
WinRM
 |
 v
Restricted Endpoint
 |
 +--> Get-Service
 +--> Restart Approved Service
 |
 X
 |
 +--> Arbitrary Command

This can be a valid security design.

docs.title: Do Not Report WinRM Enabled as a Vulnerability
docs.text:
The presence of:

5985

or:

5986

is not itself a vulnerability.

WinRM is a legitimate management technology.

Report weaknesses such as:

Excessive WinRM Access
Weak Authentication Configuration
Broad TrustedHosts
Unnecessary Network Exposure
Privileged Credential Exposure
Inadequate Segmentation
Insecure Basic Authentication Configuration

docs.title: WinRM Network Segmentation
docs.text:
A weak architecture:

Every Workstation
      |
      v
Every Server:5985

A stronger architecture:

Privileged Admin Workstation
          |
          v
Management Network
          |
          v
Server:5985/5986

docs.title: Restrict Source Systems
docs.text:
Firewall rules can limit WinRM to:

Administrative Jump Hosts
Privileged Access Workstations
Management Servers
Automation Platforms

rather than exposing it to every endpoint.

docs.title: Windows Firewall
docs.text:
Review WinRM-related firewall rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule |
    Where-Object DisplayName -Like '*Windows Remote Management*' |
    Select-Object DisplayName,Enabled,Direction,Action

docs.title: Firewall Address Restrictions
docs.text:
Inspect relevant rules in more detail:

Get-NetFirewallRule |
    Where-Object DisplayName -Like '*Windows Remote Management*' |
    Get-NetFirewallAddressFilter

Review whether remote addresses are:

Any

or limited to approved management networks.

docs.title: WinRM Hardening
docs.text:
A practical WinRM hardening strategy includes:

Restrict Network Exposure
Use Kerberos in Domain Environments
Use HTTPS Where Required
Disable Unnecessary Authentication Methods
Avoid Broad TrustedHosts
Apply Least Privilege
Use JEA Where Appropriate
Separate Administrative Accounts
Use Privileged Administration Workstations
Monitor Remote Sessions
Reduce NTLM

docs.title: Disable Unnecessary Basic Authentication
docs.text:
Review:

winrm get winrm/config/service/auth

If Basic authentication is unnecessary:

Basic = false

is generally preferable.

Any change should be tested for compatibility.

docs.title: Disable Unnecessary CredSSP
docs.text:
CredSSP should only be enabled where credential delegation is genuinely required.

Review:

winrm get winrm/config/service/auth

and:

winrm get winrm/config/client/auth

docs.title: Avoid Broad TrustedHosts
docs.text:
Review:

Get-Item WSMan:\localhost\Client\TrustedHosts

Prefer:

Specific Approved Hosts

over:

*

where TrustedHosts is required.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Review:

Administrators
Remote Management Users
PowerShell Endpoint ACLs
JEA Roles
Group Policy

Remove unnecessary remote-management access.

docs.title: Dedicated Administrative Identities
docs.text:
Avoid using normal daily accounts for privileged WinRM administration.

Prefer:

Standard User

for normal work and:

Dedicated Administrative Identity

for server administration.

docs.title: Privileged Access Workstations
docs.text:
Where appropriate:

Administrative Credential
        |
        v
Privileged Workstation
        |
        v
WinRM
        |
        v
Server

Avoid:

Administrative Credential
        |
        v
Normal Internet-Connected Workstation

docs.title: WinRM Detection
docs.text:
WinRM provides useful telemetry across several Windows logging sources.

Important sources include:

Security Log
WinRM Operational Log
PowerShell Operational Log
Process Creation
EDR Telemetry
Network Telemetry

docs.title: WinRM Operational Log
docs.text:
Review:

Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational

This log can provide information about WinRM activity and failures.

docs.title: PowerShell Operational Log
docs.text:
Review:

Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational

This is especially useful when PowerShell Remoting is used.

docs.title: Script Block Logging
docs.text:
Where enabled, PowerShell Script Block Logging can produce:

4104

events.

These can contain executed PowerShell content.

docs.title: PowerShell Module Logging
docs.text:
Module logging can provide additional visibility into PowerShell command execution.

The exact events depend on logging configuration.

docs.title: Process Creation
docs.text:
Remote PowerShell sessions commonly involve:

wsmprovhost.exe

on the target.

Conceptually:

WinRM
  |
  v
wsmprovhost.exe
  |
  v
Remote PowerShell Activity

docs.title: wsmprovhost.exe
docs.text:
The presence of:

wsmprovhost.exe

is not automatically malicious.

It is expected during legitimate PowerShell Remoting.

Detection should consider:

Source Host
User
Parent Process
Commands
Target

docs.text:
Relevant Security events can include:

4624 - Successful Logon

docs.text:

Logon Type 3

docs.title: Detect Unusual Source Systems
docs.text:

Normal:
PAW01 -> SRV01:5985

Suspicious:
