docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
ESC7 is fundamentally an administrative delegation problem.

The core relationship is:

Untrusted Principal
        |
        v
Trusted CA Administrative Permission

This is different from ordinary certificate enrollment.

A user who can request a certificate has:

Enrollment Capability

A user with ESC7 may have:

CA Administrative Capability

or:

Certificate Management Capability

Those capabilities can influence the certificate trust and issuance infrastructure itself.

The most important permissions to investigate are:

ManageCA
ManageCertificates

but the assessment should not stop at identifying their names.

Determine:

Who Has the Permission?
        |
        v
How Did They Receive It?
        |
        v
Can Their Group Membership Be Controlled?
        |
        v
What Administrative Actions Are Available?
        |
        v
Which Templates and Requests Are Affected?
        |
        v
Can a Certificate Privilege Path Be Reached?

Modern certificate mapping protections must still be considered when the final attack path involves certificate authentication.

However:

Strong Certificate Mapping

does not fix:

Excessive CA Administrative Permissions

The two controls operate at different layers.

ESC7 also demonstrates why AD CS findings should be analysed as chains rather than isolated configuration flags.

For example:

Group ACL Weakness
       |
       v
PKI Admin Group
       |
       v
ESC7
       |
       v
CA Administrative Control
       |
       v
Other AD CS Condition
       |
       v
Certificate Privilege Path

For defenders, the CA should be treated as part of the identity control plane.

For penetration testers, read-only evidence is often enough. There is rarely a need to alter a production CA merely to prove that an inappropriate principal possesses administrative control.

The strongest ESC7 finding documents:

Principal
    +
Effective Permission
    +
CA
    +
Administrative Capability
    +
Reachable Certificate Impact

rather than simply stating that an automated tool reported:

ESC7

docs.title: AD CS ESC8 - NTLM Relay to AD CS Web Enrollment
docs.text:
ESC8 is an Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) privilege escalation technique involving NTLM relay to an HTTP-based certificate enrollment endpoint.

Instead of stealing a password or NTLM hash, the attacker relays a victim's live NTLM authentication to an AD CS enrollment service.

If the enrollment endpoint accepts the relayed authentication and the victim can enroll in a certificate suitable for authentication, the attacker may obtain a certificate representing that victim.

A simplified ESC8 relationship is:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Attacker-Controlled Relay
  |
  v
AD CS HTTP Enrollment Endpoint
  |
  v
Certificate Request as Victim
  |
  v
Authentication Certificate
  |
  v
Certificate-Based Authentication

The classic target is:

/certsrv/

provided by the Certification Authority Web Enrollment role service.

Modern ESC8 assessments should also examine other IIS-hosted AD CS enrollment services, including Certificate Enrollment Web Service (CES), where NTLM is accepted without adequate relay protection.

The central ESC8 question is:

Can NTLM authentication from another domain
principal be relayed to an AD CS enrollment
endpoint and converted into a certificate
representing that principal?

Authorised testing only

NTLM relay can impersonate users and computers without obtaining their passwords. Begin with read-only endpoint, IIS, CA, and template enumeration. Do not coerce production domain controllers, relay production privileged identities, or request certificates for privileged systems merely to prove ESC8. Where active validation is explicitly authorised, use dedicated test identities and the minimum-impact authentication source available.

docs.title: ESC8 Concept
docs.text:
ESC8 combines two security mechanisms:

NTLM Authentication

and:

Certificate Enrollment

The attack converts:

Temporary Authentication

into:

Reusable Certificate Credential

Conceptually:

NTLM Authentication
       |
       v
Relay
       |
       v
Certificate Enrollment
       |
       v
Certificate

This conversion is what makes ESC8 particularly important.

docs.title: NTLM Relay
docs.text:
NTLM relay is different from:

NTLM Cracking

and:

Pass-the-Hash

In an NTLM relay attack, the attacker forwards authentication messages between:

Victim

and:

Target Service

without needing to recover the victim's password.

docs.title: Relay Model
docs.text:
The normal authentication model is:

Client
  |
  v
Server

The relay model is:

Client
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  v
Target Server

The attacker acts as an intermediary.

docs.title: ESC8 Relay Model
docs.text:
For ESC8:

Victim
  |
  v
Attacker
  |
  v
AD CS Web Enrollment
  |
  v
Certificate Authority

The target web service believes the relayed NTLM authentication belongs to the legitimate victim.

docs.title: Why Certificates Make ESC8 Powerful
docs.text:
A normal relayed NTLM session is temporary.

ESC8 can potentially transform that session into:

Certificate

which may remain valid for:

Hours
Days
Months
Years

depending on the template.

Conceptually:

One NTLM Authentication
       |
       v
Certificate Issuance
       |
       v
Longer-Lived Credential

docs.title: Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
If the resulting certificate supports Active Directory authentication, it may potentially be used for:

Kerberos PKINIT
Schannel Authentication
Client Certificate Authentication

depending on the certificate and environment.

docs.title: ESC8 Prerequisites
docs.text:
A successful ESC8 path generally requires:

AD CS Enrollment Endpoint
        +
Windows Integrated Authentication / NTLM
        +
Insufficient Relay Protection
        +
Relayable NTLM Authentication
        +
Victim Enrollment Rights
        +
Suitable Certificate Template
        +
Certificate Authentication Capability
        =
Potential ESC8

Every component should be validated.

docs.title: HTTP Enrollment Endpoints
docs.text:
AD CS can expose multiple web-based certificate services.

Important examples include:

Certification Authority Web Enrollment
Certificate Enrollment Web Service
Certificate Enrollment Policy Web Service

Their roles and protocols differ.

Do not assume they are interchangeable.

docs.title: Certification Authority Web Enrollment
docs.text:
The classic Web Enrollment interface is normally available at:

https://ca01.corp.example/certsrv/

or in older/insecure deployments:

http://ca01.corp.example/certsrv/

Microsoft documents the Web Enrollment pages at:

https://<servername>/certsrv

The role allows users with appropriate permissions to perform certificate enrollment operations through IIS.

docs.title: Common Web Enrollment Paths
docs.text:
During authorised enumeration, useful paths include:

/certsrv/
/certsrv/certfnsh.asp
/certsrv/certnew.cer
/certsrv/certcarc.asp

The presence of:

/certsrv/

is usually the primary indicator that classic CA Web Enrollment is installed.

docs.title: Certificate Enrollment Web Service
docs.text:
Certificate Enrollment Web Service is commonly abbreviated:

CES

It provides HTTPS-based certificate enrollment and supports scenarios such as:

Cross-Forest Enrollment
Extranet Enrollment
Automated Enrollment

CES can support Windows Integrated Authentication.

When NTLM is accepted without appropriate protection, relay exposure must be evaluated.

docs.title: Certificate Enrollment Policy Web Service
docs.text:
Certificate Enrollment Policy Web Service is commonly abbreviated:

CEP

CEP helps clients obtain certificate enrollment policy.

It should be inventoried during AD CS web-service assessment.

However, do not assume:

CEP

has the same certificate issuance behaviour as:

CA Web Enrollment

or:

CES

docs.title: Current Certipy Scope
docs.text:
Current Certipy ESC8 documentation is particularly important here.

Certipy's:

relay

function for ESC8 specifically targets the classic Web Enrollment service, including the:

/certsrv/certfnsh.asp

workflow.

Do not assume Certipy's ESC8 relay implementation automatically supports every CES or CEP deployment.

Always check:

certipy relay -h

for the installed release.

docs.title: ESC8 and HTTP
docs.text:
Plain HTTP provides no TLS channel to which authentication can be bound.

Conceptually:

HTTP
 |
 v
NTLM
 |
 v
No TLS Channel Binding
 |
 v
Relay Exposure

Therefore an AD CS enrollment endpoint that accepts NTLM over plain HTTP is a major ESC8 concern.

docs.title: ESC8 and HTTPS
docs.text:
HTTPS alone is not necessarily enough.

A deployment may have:

HTTPS

but still allow NTLM relay if:

Extended Protection for Authentication

is not appropriately enforced.

Conceptually:

HTTPS
  |
  v
NTLM
  |
  v
EPA Disabled
  |
  v
Potential Relay

docs.title: Extended Protection for Authentication
docs.text:
Extended Protection for Authentication is commonly abbreviated:

EPA

EPA provides additional protection against credential forwarding and relay attacks by binding authentication to properties of the protected connection.

Conceptually:

NTLM Authentication
        |
        v
TLS Connection
        |
        v
Channel Binding
        |
        v
Authentication Bound to Channel

docs.title: Channel Binding
docs.text:
Channel Binding Tokens can associate authentication with the underlying secure TLS channel.

This makes:

Authentication Captured on Connection A

less useful when forwarded to:

Connection B

Conceptually:

Victim TLS Channel
       |
       v
Authentication
       |
       X
Different Relay TLS Channel

docs.title: HTTP Cannot Provide TLS Channel Binding
docs.text:
Because plain HTTP has no TLS channel:

HTTP
 |
 v
No TLS
 |
 v
No TLS Channel Binding

This is one reason Microsoft recommends HTTPS together with EPA for AD CS IIS enrollment services.

docs.title: ESC8 Vulnerable Pattern
docs.text:
A typical vulnerable pattern is:

AD CS Web Enrollment
       |
       v
Windows Authentication
       |
       v
NTLM Accepted
       |
       v
HTTP

or:

AD CS Web Enrollment
       |
       v
Windows Authentication
       |
       v
NTLM Accepted
       |
       v
HTTPS
       |
       v
EPA Not Enforced

docs.title: Current Windows Server Context
docs.text:
ESC8 configuration defaults have evolved.

SpecterOps reported in 2025 that insecure NTLM-relay behaviour remained the default for older Windows Server generations such as Windows Server 2022 and earlier, while Windows Server 2025 changed the default posture for new deployments.

Therefore:

Windows Server Version

is useful context, but it is not proof of vulnerability.

Always inspect the actual IIS configuration.

docs.title: Microsoft Defender for Identity
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender for Identity currently includes a security posture assessment specifically for:

Insecure ADCS certificate enrollment IIS endpoints (ESC8)

Microsoft describes an endpoint as vulnerable when it allows NTLM authentication without appropriate protections such as HTTPS and EPA.

This reinforces that ESC8 remains a current configuration issue rather than only a historical technique.

docs.title: ESC8 vs ESC6
docs.text:
ESC6 concerns:

Requester-Supplied SAN

at the CA policy level.

ESC8 concerns:

NTLM Relay

to certificate enrollment.

They are different attack paths.

docs.title: ESC8 vs ESC7
docs.text:
ESC7 concerns:

CA Administrative Permissions

ESC8 does not require the attacker to administer the CA.

Instead:

Victim's Enrollment Rights

are used through relayed authentication.

docs.title: ESC8 vs ESC11
docs.text:
ESC8 and ESC11 are closely related but target different enrollment transports.

Conceptually:

ESC8
 |
 v
HTTP / HTTPS Enrollment

versus:

ESC11
 |
 v
RPC Certificate Enrollment

ESC11 becomes relevant where RPC enrollment does not enforce the required packet privacy protections.

docs.title: ESC8 vs NTLM Relay to LDAP
docs.text:
Traditional relay may target:

LDAP
LDAPS
SMB
HTTP
MSSQL

ESC8 specifically targets:

AD CS HTTP-Based Enrollment

The post-authentication action is:

Request Certificate

docs.title: ESC8 Attack Chain
docs.text:
A generic chain is:

Victim
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Relay Listener
  |
  v
AD CS Enrollment Endpoint
  |
  v
Victim Authenticated
  |
  v
Certificate Request
  |
  v
Certificate Issued

The certificate may then become an authentication credential.

docs.title: Authentication Source
docs.text:
ESC8 requires an NTLM authentication source.

This may occur naturally or through an explicitly authorised coercion test.

Potential sources include:

User Authentication
Computer Authentication
Application Authentication
Authentication Coercion

docs.title: Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
Authentication coercion causes a Windows system to authenticate to another host.

The relationship is:

Attacker
   |
   v
Coercion Trigger
   |
   v
Victim
   |
   v
Outbound NTLM Authentication

That authentication may then become relayable.

See:

Authentication Coercion

docs.title: Common Coercion Families
docs.text:
Historically relevant coercion techniques include:

MS-RPRN / PrinterBug
MS-EFSRPC / PetitPotam
MS-DFSNM / DFSCoerce
Other RPC-Based Coercion
WebDAV-Based Authentication Paths
Application-Specific Coercion

The available technique depends on:

Victim Services
Patching
Firewall
RPC Exposure
WebClient
Protocol Configuration

docs.title: Do Not Treat Coercion as ESC8
docs.text:
Coercion and ESC8 are separate stages.

Authentication Coercion
       |
       v
Produces Authentication

while:

ESC8
       |
       v
Relays Authentication to AD CS

A complete attack may combine both.

docs.title: High-Value Victims
docs.text:
Machine accounts can be particularly important.

For example:

Domain Controller$

may have enrollment rights for a machine or domain-controller authentication certificate.

Conceptually:

DC01$
  |
  v
NTLM Authentication
  |
  v
Relay to AD CS
  |
  v
Certificate for DC01$

This can have severe consequences.

docs.title: Do Not Coerce Domain Controllers by Default
docs.text:
A domain controller is a critical production system.

Do not perform:

DC Coercion

merely because a tool indicates that it may work.

Use:

Dedicated Test Computer

where possible.

docs.title: Machine Templates
docs.text:
Machine accounts commonly have access to templates such as:

Machine
Computer
Domain Controller
Domain Controller Authentication
Kerberos Authentication

depending on environment configuration.

The exact template must be enumerated.

docs.title: User Templates
docs.text:
Users may have access to:

User
Smartcard User
Custom Authentication Templates
VPN Certificates
Client Authentication Certificates

Again, the resulting certificate purpose matters.

docs.title: Template Requirement
docs.text:
The relayed victim must be authorised to enroll in the selected template.

Conceptually:

Relay Victim
      |
      v
Template ACL
      |
      v
Enroll?

If:

No

then the certificate request should fail.

docs.title: Authentication-Capable Certificate
docs.text:
A certificate useful for Active Directory authentication typically needs appropriate certificate purposes.

Relevant EKUs may include:

Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2

Smart Card Logon
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2

PKINIT Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.2.3.4

The complete certificate configuration should be evaluated.

docs.title: NTAuth Trust
docs.text:
For certificate-based domain authentication, the issuing CA must also participate appropriately in the domain's certificate trust model.

This can include:

NTAuthCertificates

where relevant.

A certificate issued by an unrelated CA does not automatically become a valid Active Directory authentication credential.

docs.title: Enumerating Web Enrollment
docs.text:
Start with normal HTTPS/HTTP service discovery.

For example:

curl -k -I https://ca01.corp.example/certsrv/

and, where HTTP is exposed:

curl -I http://ca01.corp.example/certsrv/

docs.title: Expected Responses
docs.text:
Possible responses include:

200 OK
401 Unauthorized
302 Redirect
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found

A:

401

can still be useful because authentication headers may reveal the supported mechanisms.

docs.title: Inspect Authentication Headers
docs.text:
Use:

curl -k -I https://ca01.corp.example/certsrv/

Review:

WWW-Authenticate

Potential values include:

Negotiate
NTLM

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Conceptually:

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate
WWW-Authenticate: NTLM

This indicates Windows Integrated Authentication mechanisms are being offered.

It does not by itself prove relayability.

docs.title: Discover with Nmap
docs.text:
For authorised service discovery:

nmap -Pn -p80,443 ca01.corp.example

Relevant services may include:

80/tcp
443/tcp

docs.title: HTTP Enumeration
docs.text:
Where approved:

nmap -Pn -p80,443 --script http-title ca01.corp.example

This may help identify IIS-hosted services.

docs.title: IIS Enumeration
docs.text:
From an authorised administrative session on the server:

Import-Module WebAdministration

Get-Website |
    Select-Object Name,State,PhysicalPath,Bindings

docs.title: Enumerate IIS Applications
docs.text:
Get-WebApplication |
    Select-Object Path,ApplicationPool,PhysicalPath

Look for AD CS-related applications.

docs.title: Windows Authentication
docs.text:
Inspect IIS Windows Authentication configuration.

For example:

Get-WebConfigurationProperty `
    -Filter '/system.webServer/security/authentication/windowsAuthentication' `
    -Name enabled `
    -PSPath 'IIS:\'

For production assessment, use IIS Manager or configuration-management tooling to verify the specific enrollment application's effective configuration.

docs.title: IIS Manager
docs.text:
The relevant configuration is typically under:

IIS Manager
   |
   v
Site / AD CS Enrollment Application
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Windows Authentication

Review:

Enabled / Disabled
Providers
Extended Protection

docs.title: Extended Protection
docs.text:
For the AD CS enrollment application, inspect:

Extended Protection

The secure target state should enforce the organisation's supported EPA configuration.

For ESC8 analysis, the important question is whether EPA is actually enforced on the relevant endpoint.

docs.title: Require SSL
docs.text:
Also inspect whether IIS requires:

SSL

for the enrollment application.

Conceptually:

Require SSL
    +
EPA
    =
Stronger Relay Protection

docs.title: Do Not Check Only Port 443
docs.text:
The presence of HTTPS does not mean HTTP has been disabled.

Test both:

80
443

where in scope.

A deployment may expose:

HTTPS Securely

while accidentally leaving:

HTTP

available.

docs.title: Redirect Is Not the Same as Protection
docs.text:
An HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect should not automatically be treated as equivalent to preventing NTLM authentication over HTTP.

Verify the actual authentication flow.

The secure objective is:

No Relayable Authentication over HTTP

not merely:

Browser Eventually Lands on HTTPS

docs.title: Certipy Discovery
docs.text:
Use:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

Review CA information for:

Web Enrollment
Enrollment Services
ESC8

depending on the installed Certipy release.

docs.title: Verify Certipy Version
docs.text:
certipy --version

Then:

certipy find -h

and:

certipy relay -h

This is especially important because relay behaviour and supported endpoint types can change between releases.

docs.title: Certipy Relay
docs.text:
Certipy provides:

relay

functionality for authorised ESC8 testing.

Before using it:

certipy relay -h

Review the exact syntax supported by the installed version.

Current Certipy documentation notes that its ESC8 relay implementation targets classic Web Enrollment rather than assuming support for every CES/CEP endpoint.

docs.title: Impacket ntlmrelayx
docs.text:
Impacket includes:

ntlmrelayx.py

which supports NTLM relay testing against multiple protocols and services.

Check the installed version:

ntlmrelayx.py -h

or:

impacket-ntlmrelayx -h

depending on packaging.

docs.title: Why Version Checking Matters
docs.text:
Relay tooling changes frequently.

Older guides may use options that:

No Longer Exist
Have Changed Names
Have Different Defaults
Support Different AD CS Endpoints

Always verify local help before active testing.

docs.title: Safe Relay Validation
docs.text:
The preferred validation model is:

Dedicated Test Computer
       |
       v
Approved NTLM Authentication
       |
       v
Relay Listener
       |
       v
Test AD CS Enrollment
       |
       v
Test Certificate

Do not begin with:

Domain Controller

or:

Privileged User

docs.title: Test Account Model
docs.text:
For example:

CORP\ESC8-TEST$

can represent a dedicated test computer.

The objective is to determine:

Can Its Authentication Be Relayed?

and:

Can Its Enrollment Rights Be Used?

without affecting a privileged production identity.

docs.title: Minimum Proof
docs.text:
A useful proof may establish:

NTLM Accepted
        +
EPA Not Enforced
        +
Test Authentication Relayed
        +
Test Certificate Issued

There is normally no need to escalate further once the vulnerability is proven.

docs.title: Stop After Certificate Issuance
docs.text:
If a certificate for the approved test account is successfully issued:

Certificate Obtained
       |
       v
ESC8 Proven

In many assessments this is sufficient.

Authentication with the certificate should only be performed when needed to establish impact.

docs.title: Certificate Inspection
docs.text:
Inspect the issued certificate.

Record:

Subject
SAN
Issuer
Serial Number
Thumbprint
Template
EKUs
Validity
SID Security Extension

docs.title: Windows Inspection
docs.text: certutil -dump esc8-test.cer

docs.title: OpenSSL Inspection
docs.text:
For DER:

openssl x509 -in esc8-test.cer -inform DER -text -noout

For PEM:

openssl x509 -in esc8-test.pem -text -noout

docs.title: Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
If authentication validation is explicitly required, review:

certipy auth -h

before testing.

Use only the approved test identity.

docs.title: ESC8 and Computer Accounts
docs.text:
Machine-account relay is important because computer certificates may enable:

PKINIT
Schannel
Machine Authentication

The resulting permissions depend on the computer account.

docs.title: Computer Account Does Not Mean Low Impact
docs.text:
A machine account may have access to:

Its Own Host
Network Services
Delegated Resources
Active Directory Objects
SCCM Infrastructure
Other Application Resources

Therefore evaluate the actual victim.

docs.title: Domain Controller Certificates
docs.text:
A certificate representing a domain controller is particularly sensitive.

Potential consequences can extend into:

Kerberos
Directory Services
Replication-Related Access
Domain Authentication

Do not actively demonstrate these effects unless explicitly required.

docs.title: ESC8 and S4U
docs.text:
A machine certificate may enable authentication as the machine account.

Depending on the environment and host relationship, subsequent Kerberos operations can potentially provide access to services on that machine.

This is a post-ESC8 impact path rather than part of the ESC8 configuration itself.

docs.title: ESC8 and SCCM
docs.text:
Modern enterprise environments may contain additional attack paths involving computer accounts with privileged access to systems such as:

Microsoft Configuration Manager

A relayed machine identity should therefore be evaluated based on its actual permissions rather than assuming all machine accounts have equal impact.

docs.title: ESC8 and Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
A common complete attack chain is:

Attacker
   |
   v
Coerce Victim
   |
   v
Victim NTLM
   |
   v
Relay
   |
   v
AD CS
   |
   v
Certificate

See:

Authentication Coercion

docs.title: ESC8 and PrinterBug
docs.text:
Historically:

MS-RPRN

could be used to trigger machine authentication from systems exposing the relevant print-spooler functionality.

Conceptually:

PrinterBug
    |
    v
Machine NTLM
    |
    v
ESC8 Relay

Availability depends on the target's configuration and hardening.

docs.title: ESC8 and PetitPotam
docs.text:
PetitPotam demonstrated authentication coercion through:

MS-EFSRPC

Conceptually:

EFSRPC
   |
   v
Victim Authentication
   |
   v
ESC8

Microsoft introduced mitigations and organisations may have additional controls.

Do not assume a specific coercion method is available.

docs.title: ESC8 and DFSCoerce
docs.text:
DFS-related RPC interfaces have also been used in authentication coercion research.

Again:

Coercion

is the authentication source.

ESC8

is the relay destination and certificate conversion.

docs.title: Coercer
docs.text:
Coercer can help identify authentication coercion opportunities in authorised environments.

Before using it:

coercer --help

Tool support and technique coverage evolve over time.

Use test systems before production infrastructure.

docs.title: Responder
docs.text:
Responder is frequently associated with NTLM capture and relay workflows.

However:

Capture

and:

Relay

are different objectives.

Conceptually:

NTLM Authentication
       |
       +--> Capture
       |
       +--> Relay

Do not unnecessarily collect or crack credentials when the assessment objective is relay validation.

docs.title: NTLM Relay Reflection Restrictions
docs.text:
NTLM contains protections that prevent several simple reflection scenarios.

The attacker generally relays authentication:

From One Security Context / Service

to:

Another Suitable Service

rather than simply reflecting authentication back to the exact same protected context.

docs.title: Signing and Relay Protection
docs.text:
Different protocols use different anti-relay controls.

Examples include:

SMB Signing
LDAP Signing
LDAP Channel Binding
HTTP EPA

For ESC8 the most important control is:

HTTP(S) Extended Protection

together with secure transport and authentication configuration.

docs.title: HTTPS Alone Is Insufficient
docs.text:
Remember:

HTTPS
   !=
Automatic NTLM Relay Protection

The stronger model is:

HTTPS
   +
EPA

where NTLM must remain enabled.

docs.title: Kerberos vs NTLM
docs.text:
Where possible, organisations should reduce reliance on:

NTLM

and prefer stronger authentication such as:

Kerberos

However, simply seeing:

Negotiate

does not prove that NTLM cannot be used.

The effective IIS provider and authentication configuration must be examined.

docs.title: NTLM Provider
docs.text:
IIS Windows Authentication may expose providers such as:

Negotiate
NTLM

If NTLM is unnecessary, removing or disabling its use can reduce relay exposure.

Test compatibility before changing production enrollment services.

docs.title: Endpoint Enumeration Workflow
docs.text:
A practical read-only workflow is:

Identify Enterprise CAs
       |
       v
Identify HTTP / HTTPS Services
       |
       v
Locate AD CS Enrollment Applications
       |
       v
Inspect Authentication
       |
       v
Is NTLM Accepted?
       |
       v
Is HTTP Available?
       |
       v
Is HTTPS Required?
       |
       v
Is EPA Enforced?
       |
       v
Enumerate Victim Enrollment Rights
       |
       v
Assess ESC8

docs.title: Template Enumeration Workflow
docs.text:
For each vulnerable enrollment endpoint:

Identify Target CA
       |
       v
Enumerate Published Templates
       |
       v
Who Can Enroll?
       |
       v
Authentication EKU?
       |
       v
Potential Relay Victims

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help represent AD CS relay relationships.

Modern BloodHound data can expose paths associated with:

CoerceAndRelayNTLMToADCS

and relationships between:

Principal
Certificate Template
Enterprise CA
Vulnerable Enrollment Endpoint

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: BloodHound Interpretation
docs.text:
A graph relationship may conceptually show:

Domain Computers
       |
       v
Enroll
       |
       v
Machine Template
       |
       v
Enterprise CA
       |
       v
Vulnerable ESC8 Endpoint

This does not mean every computer can automatically be compromised.

The attacker still requires:

Relayable Authentication

from the victim.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
ESC8 detection requires visibility across multiple stages.

A useful model is:

Coercion
   |
   v
NTLM Authentication
   |
   v
AD CS Enrollment
   |
   v
Certificate Issuance
   |
   v
Certificate Authentication

docs.title: Detect NTLM to AD CS
docs.text:
Monitor NTLM authentication to servers hosting AD CS enrollment endpoints.

Questions include:

Which Account?
Which Source?
Which CA Endpoint?
Was NTLM Expected?
Was the Source Unusual?

docs.title: Detect Unexpected Machine Enrollment
docs.text:
A suspicious pattern can be:

Machine Account
       |
       v
Web Enrollment

especially when machine certificate enrollment normally occurs through:

Autoenrollment
RPC

rather than interactive web enrollment.

docs.title: Event 4886
docs.text:
Where Certificate Services auditing is configured:

4886

can indicate that Certificate Services received a certificate request.

docs.title: Event 4887
docs.text:
4887

can indicate that Certificate Services approved a request and issued a certificate.

docs.title: Correlate Requester and Source
docs.text:
Where telemetry permits, correlate:

Requester
       |
       v
Certificate Request

with:

Network Source

An unusual source can indicate relay.

docs.title: Example Suspicious Pattern
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Requester:
DC01$

Enrollment:
Machine Certificate

HTTP Source:
Workstation Subnet

Time:
Immediately after RPC activity against DC01

This deserves investigation.

docs.title: IIS Logging
docs.text:
IIS logs can provide valuable ESC8 evidence.

Review:

Client IP
URI
Username
HTTP Method
Status Code
User Agent
Timestamp

for enrollment endpoints.

docs.title: Important URI
docs.text:
For classic Web Enrollment, monitor access to:

/certsrv/

and certificate-request processing pages.

docs.title: Correlate IIS and CA Logs
docs.text:
A strong detection correlation is:

IIS Authentication
       |
       v
/certsrv/ Request
       |
       v
CA Request
       |
       v
Certificate Issued

docs.title: Network Detection
docs.text:
Monitor unexpected NTLM authentication flows involving:

Workstation -> CA Web Server
Server -> CA Web Server
Domain Controller -> CA Web Server

based on expected architecture.

docs.title: Detect Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
Coercion detection may include:

Unexpected RPC Calls
Unusual SMB Connections
Outbound Authentication
Print Spooler Activity
EFSRPC Activity
DFS RPC Activity

Exact telemetry depends on the coercion method.

docs.title: Detect Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
If the issued certificate is subsequently used for Kerberos PKINIT, authentication telemetry may include:

4768

Correlate:

Certificate Issuance

with:

TGT Request

docs.title: Certificate Lifetime
docs.text:
A certificate can remain useful after the original NTLM relay session ends.

Therefore incident investigations should extend beyond:

Time of Relay

through:

Certificate Expiration

unless the certificate has been revoked and revocation is reliably enforced.

docs.title: Hardening ESC8
docs.text:
The primary defence is:

Remove or Protect HTTP-Based Enrollment

docs.title: Remove Web Enrollment If Unnecessary
docs.text:
If:

Certification Authority Web Enrollment

is not required, remove the role service.

This eliminates the classic:

/certsrv/

ESC8 target.

docs.title: Require HTTPS
docs.text:
Where web enrollment is required:

Require HTTPS

Do not permit authentication to the enrollment application over plain HTTP.

docs.title: Enable Extended Protection
docs.text:
Where Windows Authentication is required:

Enable Extended Protection for Authentication

and use the strongest setting supported by the environment.

Microsoft specifically recommends EPA as a mitigation for AD CS NTLM relay exposure.

docs.title: IIS Conceptual Hardening
docs.text:
The desired configuration is:

AD CS Enrollment
       |
       v
HTTPS Required
       |
       v
Windows Authentication
       |
       v
EPA Enforced

docs.title: IIS Manager
docs.text:
For CA Web Enrollment, the relevant controls are found around:

IIS Manager
   |
   v
AD CS Web Enrollment Site / Application
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Windows Authentication
   |
   v
Advanced Settings
   |
   v
Extended Protection

Test changes before production deployment.

docs.title: Certificate Enrollment Web Service
docs.text:
CES requires its own hardening review.

Do not assume that securing:

/certsrv/

also secures:

CES

Inventory every installed AD CS enrollment role service.

docs.title: Disable NTLM Where Possible
docs.text:
If business requirements permit:

Disable NTLM

for the enrollment endpoint.

This removes the authentication mechanism used by classic NTLM relay.

Compatibility testing is essential.

docs.title: Prefer Kerberos
docs.text:
Where supported:

Kerberos

provides a stronger authentication model than NTLM for integrated domain authentication.

However, provider configuration must ensure that clients cannot silently fall back to NTLM where that would recreate relay exposure.

docs.title: Restrict Enrollment Rights
docs.text:
Even with endpoint hardening, certificate templates should follow least privilege.

Review:

Domain Users
Domain Computers
Authenticated Users
Service Accounts
Custom Groups

for unnecessary enrollment rights.

docs.title: Harden Authentication Templates
docs.text:
Templates capable of:

Client Authentication
Smart Card Logon
PKINIT

deserve additional scrutiny.

docs.title: Disable Unnecessary Templates
docs.text:
If a template is not required:

Unpublish

or retire it according to organisational PKI procedures.

docs.title: Restrict Authentication Coercion
docs.text:
ESC8 becomes substantially harder if attackers cannot obtain relayable authentication.

Defensive controls include:

Disable Unnecessary Print Spooler
Restrict RPC Exposure
Harden EFSRPC Exposure
Restrict WebClient
Segment Networks
Restrict Outbound SMB
Restrict Inbound Services

according to business requirements.

docs.title: Restrict Outbound SMB
docs.text:
Where appropriate, block:

TCP/445

from internal systems to unnecessary destinations, particularly public networks.

This reduces several coercion and relay paths.

docs.title: Host Firewalling
docs.text:
Restrict unnecessary inbound access to:

RPC
SMB
HTTP
Other Coercion-Relevant Services

especially on sensitive systems.

docs.title: Domain Controllers
docs.text:
Domain controllers deserve particularly strict controls.

Consider:

Disable Print Spooler if not required
Restrict outbound authentication paths
Restrict unnecessary RPC exposure
Monitor certificate enrollment
Protect machine certificate templates

docs.title: EPA Validation
docs.text:
After remediation, do not assume the IIS setting is correct simply because:

HTTPS Works

Validate:

HTTP Rejected / Unavailable
NTLM Behaviour
EPA Enforcement
Normal Enrollment Functionality

docs.title: Microsoft Defender for Identity
docs.text:
Where available, Microsoft Defender for Identity's certificate security posture assessments can help identify:

Insecure AD CS Certificate Enrollment IIS Endpoints

This can provide continuous defensive visibility into ESC8 configuration.

docs.title: Baseline Enrollment Endpoints
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory of:

CA
Enrollment Server
Web Enrollment
CES
CEP
HTTP
HTTPS
Authentication Providers
EPA State
Templates

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
If ESC8 abuse is suspected:

Identify Enrollment Endpoint
       |
       v
Identify Relayed Identity
       |
       v
Identify Certificate Request
       |
       v
Identify Issued Certificate
       |
       v
Identify Authentication
       |
       v
Revoke Certificate
       |
       v
Remove Relay Condition

docs.title: Identify the Victim
docs.text:
Determine whether the relayed identity was:

User
Computer
Server
Domain Controller
Service Account

The potential impact differs significantly.

docs.title: Identify the Authentication Source
docs.text:
Determine how NTLM authentication was obtained.

Possible sources include:

Natural Authentication
Coercion
Poisoning
Application Behaviour
WebDAV
SMB
RPC

docs.title: Identify Certificate Requests
docs.text:
Review CA records for the affected account.

Record:

Request ID
Requester
Template
Subject
SAN
Issue Time
Disposition

docs.title: Identify Issued Certificate
docs.text:
Record:

Serial Number
Thumbprint
Issuer
Template
Subject
SAN
EKUs
Validity

docs.title: Review IIS Logs
docs.text:
Look for the corresponding web enrollment activity.

Correlate:

Timestamp
Username
Source IP
URI
HTTP Status

with the CA request.

docs.title: Identify Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
Review whether the certificate was subsequently used for:

Kerberos PKINIT
Schannel
Client TLS
VPN
Other Certificate Authentication

docs.title: Revoke the Certificate
docs.text:
If a malicious certificate was issued:

Revoke
   |
   v
Publish Updated CRL
   |
   v
Verify Revocation Distribution

docs.title: Password Reset Is Not Enough
docs.text:
ESC8 demonstrates why certificate compromise differs from password compromise.

Reset Password
     |
     X
Issued Certificate

A password reset does not inherently invalidate an already issued certificate.

docs.title: Disable the Relay Path
docs.text:
Remediation may include:

Remove Web Enrollment
Require HTTPS
Enable EPA
Disable NTLM
Restrict Coercion
Restrict Enrollment

depending on the architecture.

docs.title: Investigate Other Victims
docs.text:
Do not assume only one identity was relayed.

Review the exposure period for:

Other Users
Other Computers
Other Domain Controllers

that authenticated to the vulnerable endpoint.

docs.title: Review Other AD CS Endpoints
docs.text:
If one vulnerable IIS enrollment endpoint exists, inventory:

Other CAs
Other Web Enrollment Servers
CES
CEP
Legacy Enrollment Servers

for similar configuration.

docs.title: Reporting ESC8
docs.text:
Avoid finding titles such as:

ESC8 Found

Prefer:

AD CS Web Enrollment Is Vulnerable to NTLM Relay

or:

Missing Extended Protection Allows NTLM Relay to Certificate Enrollment

or:

Insecure AD CS HTTP Enrollment Permits Certificate-Based Identity Impersonation

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
AD CS Web Enrollment Is Vulnerable to NTLM Relay

Affected Host:
ca01.corp.example

Affected Endpoint:
https://ca01.corp.example/certsrv/

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Description:
The Active Directory Certificate Services Web Enrollment interface
accepts Windows Integrated Authentication and permits NTLM
authentication without enforcing Extended Protection for
Authentication.

This allows NTLM authentication from another domain principal to be
relayed to the certificate enrollment endpoint.

During controlled validation, authentication from a dedicated test
computer account was relayed to the Web Enrollment service.

The relayed identity was able to request a certificate from a
template for which the test computer possessed enrollment rights.

No privileged production identity was used during validation.

Impact:
An attacker able to obtain or coerce NTLM authentication from a user
or computer may be able to relay that authentication to AD CS and
request a certificate representing the victim.

Where the certificate supports Active Directory authentication, it
may provide reusable certificate credentials for the relayed
identity.

The severity depends on which identities can be coerced and what
permissions those identities possess.

A successfully relayed privileged computer or domain controller may
result in severe domain compromise.

Recommendation:
Remove the Certification Authority Web Enrollment role service if it
is not required.

Where web enrollment is required, enforce HTTPS and Extended
Protection for Authentication on the IIS enrollment application.

Disable NTLM for the enrollment endpoint where operationally
possible.

Review certificate-template enrollment permissions and restrict
authentication-capable templates according to least privilege.

Reduce authentication coercion opportunities and monitor NTLM
authentication, IIS enrollment activity, certificate issuance, and
subsequent certificate-based authentication.

docs.title: Severity Assessment
docs.text:
ESC8 severity depends on:

Vulnerable Endpoint
       +
Relayable NTLM
       +
Coercion / Authentication Source
       +
Victim Identity
       +
Enrollment Rights
       +
Certificate Purpose
       +
Victim Privileges
       =
Severity

docs.title: Critical Example
docs.text:
Domain Controller
      |
      v
Coerced NTLM
      |
      v
ESC8
      |
      v
Domain Controller Certificate
      |
      v
Certificate Authentication

This may represent a critical domain-level attack path.

docs.title: High-Risk Server Example
docs.text:
Privileged Server$
      |
      v
NTLM Relay
      |
      v
Machine Certificate
      |
      v
Machine Authentication
      |
      v
Privileged Resource Access

docs.title: Lower-Impact Example
docs.text:
Dedicated Test User
      |
      v
Relay
      |
      v
Certificate
      |
      v
No Privileged Access

This may prove the vulnerability without demonstrating high-impact compromise.

docs.title: Evidence Checklist
docs.text:
For an ESC8 finding record:

CA Name
CA Host
Enrollment Host
Enrollment Endpoint
HTTP / HTTPS
Windows Authentication
NTLM Accepted
EPA State
TLS Requirement
Victim Identity
Victim SID
Authentication Source
Coercion Method if Used
Certificate Template
Enrollment Rights
Authentication EKUs
Request ID
Certificate Serial Number
Certificate Thumbprint
Certificate Subject
Certificate SAN
Certificate Validity
SID Security Extension
Authentication Result
IIS Log Evidence
CA Log Evidence
Cleanup Result

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• Identify Enterprise CAs
  • Identify CA hosts
  • Identify enrollment servers
  • Identify /certsrv/
  • Identify CES
  • Identify CEP
  • Enumerate HTTP
  • Enumerate HTTPS
  • Identify IIS applications

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• Determine whether Windows Authentication is enabled
  • Determine whether NTLM is accepted
  • Inspect WWW-Authenticate
  • Determine whether Kerberos is available
  • Determine whether NTLM fallback is possible
  • Do not assume Negotiate means Kerberos only

docs.title: Relay Protection
docs.text:
• Determine whether HTTP is exposed
  • Determine whether HTTPS is required
  • Determine whether EPA is enabled
  • Determine whether EPA is enforced
  • Check each enrollment application separately
  • Do not treat redirects as equivalent to protection

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
• Enumerate templates published by target CA
  • Identify user enrollment rights
  • Identify computer enrollment rights
  • Identify Client Authentication
  • Identify Smart Card Logon
  • Identify PKINIT capability
  • Review certificate validity
  • Review SID security extension
  • Identify high-value eligible principals

docs.title: Authentication Sources
docs.text:
• Identify natural NTLM flows
  • Review authentication coercion exposure
  • Review Print Spooler exposure
  • Review EFSRPC exposure
  • Review DFS-related coercion
  • Review WebDAV where relevant
  • Review application-specific coercion
  • Do not coerce critical production systems unnecessarily

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
• Verify Certipy version

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Prefer read-only validation first
  • Obtain explicit approval for relay testing
  • Use dedicated test identity
  • Prefer dedicated test computer
  • Do not begin with domain controller
  • Relay only approved authentication
  • Request only approved test certificate
  • Stop after sufficient proof
  • Inspect certificate
  • Authenticate only if required
  • Revoke test certificate where appropriate
  • Delete private-key material

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• Monitor NTLM to enrollment servers
  • Monitor IIS /certsrv/ access
  • Monitor unusual machine enrollment
  • Monitor event 4886 where configured
  • Monitor event 4887 where configured
  • Correlate requester with network source
  • Correlate IIS and CA logs
  • Monitor coercion activity
  • Monitor certificate authentication
  • Correlate issuance with event 4768 where relevant
  • Monitor CA configuration changes

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
• Remove Web Enrollment if unnecessary
  • Require HTTPS
  • Enable EPA
  • Enforce EPA
  • Disable NTLM where possible
  • Prefer Kerberos
  • Review CES independently
  • Review CEP independently
  • Restrict enrollment rights
  • Harden authentication templates
  • Remove unnecessary templates
  • Reduce authentication coercion
  • Disable unnecessary Print Spooler
  • Restrict RPC exposure
  • Restrict outbound SMB
  • Apply host firewalling
  • Protect domain controllers
  • Baseline enrollment services
  • Use Defender for Identity posture assessments where available

docs.title: Incident Response
docs.text:
• Identify vulnerable endpoint
  • Identify relayed identity
  • Identify authentication source
  • Identify coercion technique
  • Identify certificate request
  • Identify request ID
  • Identify issued certificate
  • Record serial number
  • Record thumbprint
  • Review IIS logs
  • Review CA logs
  • Identify certificate authentication
  • Revoke malicious certificates
  • Publish revocation information
  • Remove relay condition
  • Review additional victims
  • Review other enrollment endpoints

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• Revoke approved test certificate where required
  • Remove test PFX
  • Remove private key
  • Remove temporary relay infrastructure
  • Remove temporary listener configuration
  • Verify no CA configuration changed
  • Verify no template configuration changed
  • Verify test account state
  • Record cleanup evidence

docs.text:
The normal enrollment model is:

The high-impact model is:

       |

Coercion

AD CS

Domain-Level Impact

The safe-testing model is:

Enumerate

Confirm Endpoint

IIS Enrollment

Certificate Request

Certificate Issuance

Certificate Authentication

The defensive model is:

Remove Unneeded Enrollment

HTTPS
          +
EPA
          +
Reduced NTLM
          +
Template Least Privilege
          +
Coercion Hardening
          +
Monitoring

Reduced ESC8 Risk

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Can I coerce the domain controller?"

First Ask:
"Is the enrollment endpoint relayable,
and can I prove that safely using a
dedicated test identity?"

For defenders:

Do Not Assume:
"We use HTTPS, so NTLM relay is fixed."

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
ESC8 is fundamentally an authentication relay problem combined with certificate enrollment.

The important transformation is:

NTLM Authentication
       |
       v
Certificate Credential

This distinguishes ESC8 from many ordinary NTLM relay attacks.

A successful relay session may last only briefly.

The certificate obtained through that session may remain valid significantly longer.

Therefore:

Relay Session Ends

does not necessarily mean:

Attacker Access Ends

ESC8 also demonstrates why AD CS cannot be assessed only by reviewing certificate templates.

A template may be securely configured while the enrollment transport remains vulnerable:

Secure Template
      |
      v
Insecure Enrollment Endpoint
      |
      v
NTLM Relay

Likewise, simply deploying HTTPS does not automatically remediate ESC8.

The modern defensive question is:

Is HTTPS Required?
        |
        v
Is NTLM Accepted?
        |
        v
Is EPA Enforced?

Microsoft's current Defender for Identity security posture guidance explicitly continues to assess insecure AD CS IIS enrollment endpoints as ESC8 when NTLM is accepted without the appropriate HTTPS/EPA protections.

Current relay research also shows that ESC8 remains operationally relevant in modern Active Directory environments.

The complete assessment should therefore examine:

Enrollment Endpoint
       +
Authentication Protocol
       +
Relay Protection
       +
Authentication Source
       +
Victim Enrollment Rights
       +
Certificate Purpose
       +
Victim Privileges

Do not assess ESC8 solely by asking:

Does /certsrv/ Exist?

and do not assess it solely by asking:

Does Certipy Print ESC8?

Instead determine the complete path:

Can Authentication Be Relayed?
        |
        v
Can the Relayed Identity Enroll?
        |
        v
What Certificate Can It Obtain?
        |
        v
What Can That Certificate Authenticate As?
        |
        v
What Privilege Does That Identity Have?

For penetration testers, a dedicated test machine account can often demonstrate the vulnerability without coercing a domain controller.

For defenders, the strongest approach is defence in depth:

Remove Unnecessary Enrollment Services
        +
Require HTTPS
        +
Enforce EPA
        +
Reduce NTLM
        +
Harden Certificate Templates
        +
Reduce Authentication Coercion
        +
Monitor Enrollment

rather than depending on only one control.

ESC8 should ultimately be understood as a trust conversion:

Relayable NTLM
      |
      v
Trusted Certificate

Preventing that conversion is the core objective.

docs.title: AD CS ESC9 - Certificate Template Omits the SID Security Extension
docs.text:
ESC9 is an Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) certificate-template misconfiguration where certificates issued from a template do not contain the Active Directory SID security extension.

The condition is associated with the certificate template enrollment flag:

CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

When this flag is enabled, the Certification Authority does not include the SID security extension in certificates issued from that template.

The simplified relationship is:

Certificate Template
        |
        v
CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
        |
        v
Certificate Issued
        |
        v
No SID Security Extension
        |
        v
Certificate Mapping Must Rely
on Other Identity Information

ESC9 became particularly important following Microsoft's certificate-based authentication hardening introduced through KB5014754.

The SID security extension provides a strong relationship between:

Certificate

and:

Active Directory Security Principal

Removing that extension can cause certificate authentication to depend on other mapping mechanisms.

However, modern fully patched domain controllers operate under Microsoft's Full Enforcement model. Therefore:

ESC9 Present

does not automatically mean:

Arbitrary User Impersonation

The actual certificate mapping path must be evaluated.

Authorised testing only

ESC9 validation can involve temporary changes to Active Directory identity attributes and certificate requests. Begin with read-only certificate-template enumeration. Do not modify the UPN or other mapping attributes of production users, administrators, service accounts, or domain controllers merely to demonstrate ESC9. Where active validation is required, use dedicated test identities and restore every changed attribute immediately after the approved test.

docs.title: ESC9 Concept
docs.text:
Modern AD CS certificates issued by an Enterprise CA can contain an extension linking the certificate to the SID of the Active Directory account that requested it.

Conceptually:

Certificate
    |
    +--> Subject
    |
    +--> SAN
    |
    +--> EKUs
    |
    +--> SID Security Extension
              |
              v
          Account SID

ESC9 removes the final component:

Certificate
    |
    +--> Subject
    |
    +--> SAN
    |
    +--> EKUs
    |
    X--> SID Security Extension

This weakens the certificate's built-in relationship to the requesting security principal.

docs.title: Why the SID Matters
docs.text:
Consider a user:

CORP\alice

with SID:

S-1-5-21-111111111-222222222-333333333-1105

A normally issued authentication certificate may conceptually contain:

UPN:
alice@corp.example

SID:
S-1-5-21-111111111-222222222-333333333-1105

The SID gives the domain controller a stronger way to associate the certificate with:

CORP\alice

rather than relying only on a name.

docs.title: ESC9 Certificate
docs.text:
With ESC9:

UPN:
alice@corp.example

SID Security Extension:
Not Present

The domain controller must therefore determine whether another acceptable certificate mapping exists.

That mapping behaviour is central to modern ESC9 analysis.

docs.title: The Important Flag
docs.text:
ESC9 is associated with:

CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

in:

msPKI-Enrollment-Flag

on the certificate template.

Conceptually:

Certificate Template
       |
       v
msPKI-Enrollment-Flag
       |
       v
CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

docs.title: Certificate Template Object
docs.text:
Certificate templates are stored in the Configuration naming context under:

CN=Certificate Templates,
CN=Public Key Services,
CN=Services,
CN=Configuration,...

The relevant attribute is:

msPKI-Enrollment-Flag

docs.title: ESC9 Is Template-Level
docs.text:
ESC9 applies to:

Certificate Template

rather than:

Entire Certification Authority

This distinguishes ESC9 from ESC16.

Conceptually:

ESC9
 |
 v
Template-Level

versus:

ESC16
 |
 v
CA-Level

docs.title: ESC9 vs ESC16
docs.text:
The distinction is important.

ESC9:

Template
 |
 v
NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
 |
 v
Certificates from This Template
Lack SID Security Extension

ESC16:

Certification Authority
 |
 v
CA-Wide Security Extension Suppression
 |
 v
Certificates Across Affected Templates
May Lack SID Security Extension

ESC16 will be covered separately.

docs.title: ESC9 vs ESC6
docs.text:
ESC6 concerns:

Requester-Supplied SAN

through CA configuration.

ESC9 concerns:

Missing SID Security Extension

through template configuration.

The two can interact.

Conceptually:

ESC6
 |
 +--> Requester-Controlled Identity
 |
ESC9
 |
 +--> No SID Security Extension
 |
 v
Certificate Mapping Risk

docs.title: ESC9 vs ESC10
docs.text:
ESC10 concerns weak certificate mapping configurations.

ESC9 removes one of the strong certificate identifiers.

ESC10 determines whether weaker certificate mapping can still succeed.

Conceptually:

ESC9
 |
 v
No SID Extension
 |
 v
ESC10
 |
 v
Weak Mapping Accepted
 |
 v
Potential Identity Impersonation

Therefore ESC9 and ESC10 should often be evaluated together.

docs.title: ESC9 vs ESC1
docs.text:
ESC1 normally involves:

Requester Controls Certificate Subject / SAN

ESC9 does not inherently require:

ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT

Instead, historical ESC9 exploitation can involve manipulating an Active Directory identity attribute that the CA automatically places into the certificate.

This distinction is important.

docs.title: ESC9 vs ESC4
docs.text:
ESC4 concerns control over a certificate-template object.

A principal with sufficient template modification rights may potentially create ESC9 by changing:

msPKI-Enrollment-Flag

Conceptually:

ESC4
 |
 v
Template Write Access
 |
 v
Enable NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
 |
 v
ESC9

Therefore template ACLs should also be reviewed.

docs.title: ESC9 vs ESC5
docs.text:
ESC5 concerns control over broader PKI objects or infrastructure.

ESC9 is specifically:

Certificate Template Configuration

The two may coexist but have different root causes.

docs.title: KB5014754
docs.text:
Microsoft introduced certificate-based authentication hardening through:

KB5014754

The changes were designed to address certificate spoofing and weak certificate mappings.

One important component was stronger binding between:

Certificate

and:

Active Directory Account

docs.title: SID Security Extension
docs.text:
Enterprise CAs can place the requester's object SID into the issued certificate.

Conceptually:

Requester
   |
   v
Active Directory SID
   |
   v
Certification Authority
   |
   v
Certificate SID Extension

This creates a strong identity relationship.

docs.title: Normal Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
A simplified normal model is:

alice
  |
  v
Request Certificate
  |
  v
Certificate
  |
  +--> alice@corp.example
  |
  +--> Alice SID
  |
  v
Domain Controller
  |
  v
Alice

docs.title: ESC9 Mapping Model
docs.text:
With ESC9:

alice
  |
  v
Request Certificate
  |
  v
Certificate
  |
  +--> alice@corp.example
  |
  X--> SID Extension
  |
  v
Domain Controller
  |
  v
Other Mapping Required

docs.title: Strong and Weak Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Microsoft distinguishes stronger mappings from weaker name-based mappings.

Strong mappings provide a stronger relationship between the certificate and the intended account.

Weak mappings can depend on identity information such as:

Subject
UPN
Email
Issuer / Subject combinations

depending on the mapping mechanism.

ESC9 matters because:

No SID Extension

can force the authentication process to consider other mapping mechanisms.

docs.title: Current 2026 Enforcement Context
docs.text:
Microsoft's KB5014754 rollout reached Full Enforcement beginning with the February 2025 security update.

Microsoft states that certificates that cannot be strongly mapped are denied authentication in Full Enforcement mode.

The temporary ability to return to Compatibility mode through:

StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement

remained available until the:

September 9, 2025

Windows security update.

After that update, Microsoft no longer supports that registry key as a compatibility fallback.

Therefore a normally patched Active Directory environment in 2026 should be assessed assuming:

Full Enforcement

unless evidence shows otherwise.

docs.title: Why This Changes ESC9 Testing
docs.text:
Historical ESC9 attack chains often relied on:

Certificate Without SID
        |
        v
Weak UPN Mapping
        |
        v
Target Account

That should not be assumed to work in a current environment.

The modern question is:

What Strong Mapping, If Any,
Can the Domain Controller Use?

docs.title: ESC9 Still Matters
docs.text:
Do not conclude:

Full Enforcement
    =
ESC9 Irrelevant

The missing SID extension remains a security-relevant certificate-template configuration.

The final impact depends on:

Certificate Mapping
Explicit Mapping
Template Configuration
Account Attributes
CA Configuration
Domain Controller State
Other ESC Conditions

docs.title: ESC9 Preconditions
docs.text:
A meaningful ESC9 path generally includes:

Enterprise CA
        +
Published Certificate Template
        +
Attacker Enrollment Rights
        +
Authentication-Capable Certificate
        +
NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
        +
No Manager Approval
        +
No Required Authorized Signature
        +
Usable Certificate Mapping Path

Not every ESC9 template results in privilege escalation.

docs.title: Enterprise CA
docs.text:
Identify Enterprise Certification Authorities.

Using Certipy:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

Review:

Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
Permissions
Vulnerabilities

docs.title: Certipy ESC9 Enumeration
docs.text:
Current Certipy releases can identify templates where the security extension is disabled.

Begin with:

certipy --version

Then:

certipy find -h

A typical enumeration command is:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

Look for:

ESC9

and verify the underlying template configuration manually.

docs.title: Do Not Trust the Label Alone
docs.text:
An automated result such as:

ESC9

should lead to:

Inspect Template
        |
        v
Confirm NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
        |
        v
Confirm Enrollment
        |
        v
Confirm Authentication EKU
        |
        v
Analyse Mapping

Do not report privilege escalation solely because the label appears.

docs.title: PowerShell Enumeration
docs.text:
Enumerate certificate templates:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKICertificateTemplate)' -Properties displayName,'msPKI-Enrollment-Flag' |
    Select-Object Name,displayName,'msPKI-Enrollment-Flag'

docs.title: Inspect One Template
docs.text:
$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$templateBase = "CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $templateBase -LDAPFilter '(cn=ESC9-Test)' -Properties * |
    Select-Object Name,displayName,'msPKI-Enrollment-Flag',pKIExtendedKeyUsage,'msPKI-Certificate-Application-Policy'

docs.title: Enrollment Flag Is a Bitmask
docs.text:
msPKI-Enrollment-Flag contains multiple flags.

Therefore:

Value != 0

does not automatically mean:

ESC9

The specific:

CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

bit must be present.

docs.title: PowerShell Bitmask Analysis
docs.text:
When performing detailed analysis, decode the template's enrollment flags rather than relying only on the raw decimal value.

Conceptually:

msPKI-Enrollment-Flag
        |
        v
Bitmask
        |
        +--> Flag A
        +--> Flag B
        +--> NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

docs.title: Certipy Output
docs.text:
Certipy may represent the condition using fields similar to:

No Security Extension

or:

ESC9

depending on release.

Verify the raw template attribute where important.

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound represents certificate-template properties including security-extension configuration.

See:

BloodHound

A template node may expose information related to:

No Security Extension
Enrollment Rights
Authentication EKUs
Template ACLs

docs.title: BloodHound Attack Paths
docs.text:
BloodHound can help connect:

User
 |
 v
Enroll
 |
 v
ESC9 Template

with other identity-control relationships.

However, the final certificate mapping behaviour still requires target-specific validation.

docs.title: Published Template Requirement
docs.text:
A vulnerable template must normally be published by a CA before it can be used for enrollment.

Enumerate Enterprise CAs and their published templates:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext
$enrollmentBase = "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $enrollmentBase -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' -Properties certificateTemplates,dNSHostName |
    Select-Object Name,dNSHostName,certificateTemplates

docs.title: Enrollment Rights
docs.text:
The requesting principal must normally have:

Enroll

rights over the template.

Common broad groups include:

Domain Users
Domain Computers
Authenticated Users

but broad enrollment is not automatically vulnerable.

It becomes significant when combined with the other ESC9 conditions.

docs.title: Manager Approval
docs.text:
Check whether:

Certificate Manager Approval

is required.

Conceptually:

Request
   |
   v
Pending
   |
   v
Manual Approval

This can interrupt straightforward exploitation.

docs.title: Authorized Signatures
docs.text:
Review:

msPKI-RA-Signature

A template requiring authorised signatures introduces an additional issuance requirement.

docs.title: Authentication EKUs
docs.text:
For certificate-based authentication, relevant EKUs can include:

Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2

PKINIT Client Authentication
1.3.6.1.5.2.3.4

Smart Card Logon
1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.2

Any Purpose
2.5.29.37.0

No-EKU templates require additional contextual analysis and should not be treated simplistically.

docs.title: Subject Alternative Name Source
docs.text:
An important ESC9 question is:

Where Does the Certificate Identity Come From?

For some templates, the CA builds certificate identity information from Active Directory attributes.

For example:

userPrincipalName

may become certificate identity information.

This is why historical ESC9 exploitation often involved temporary UPN manipulation.

docs.title: Historical ESC9 Chain
docs.text:
A classic historical chain can be represented as:

Attacker Controls Account
       |
       v
Can Modify Own UPN
       |
       v
UPN Temporarily Changed
       |
       v
Request ESC9 Certificate
       |
       v
Certificate Contains Target-Like UPN
       |
       v
No SID Security Extension
       |
       v
Restore Original UPN
       |
       v
Certificate Mapping
       |
       v
Target Identity

This should be understood as a mapping technique, not a guarantee of success in a fully patched 2026 environment.

docs.title: Why UPN Restoration Matters Historically
docs.text:
Suppose a test account is:

esc9-user@corp.example

and an approved second test account is:

esc9-target@corp.example

Historical validation might temporarily alter the requester's UPN so that the issued certificate contains the target-like identity.

After certificate issuance, the original UPN is restored.

The certificate then retains the identity information captured at issuance time.

docs.title: Do Not Use Administrator
docs.text:
Do not perform a routine test using:

Administrator

as the alternate identity.

Use:

ESC9-Requester
ESC9-Target

or equivalent dedicated assessment accounts.

docs.title: UPN Uniqueness
docs.text:
UPN manipulation can affect authentication and application behaviour.

Before any approved test:

Record Original UPN
Verify Target UPN
Confirm No Production Dependency
Define Rollback

docs.title: Read Original UPN
docs.text:
For an approved test account:

Get-ADUser -Identity 'ESC9-Requester' -Properties userPrincipalName |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,userPrincipalName

Record the result before making any change.

docs.title: Safe Active Validation
docs.text:
Prefer:

Read-Only Evidence

where sufficient.

If active proof is necessary:

Dedicated Test Requester
       |
       v
Dedicated Test Target
       |
       v
Approved Temporary Attribute Change
       |
       v
Certificate Request
       |
       v
Immediate Attribute Restoration
       |
       v
Certificate Inspection
       |
       v
Optional Mapping Test

docs.title: Change Only What Is Necessary
docs.text:
Do not combine ESC9 validation with unrelated changes such as:

Template Modification
CA Configuration Changes
CA Permission Changes
Production Account Changes

unless those are separately authorised assessment objectives.

docs.title: Request Certificate
docs.text:
Before using Certipy operationally:

certipy req -h

Verify the installed release's syntax.

For approved testing, request a certificate only from the identified test template and using the dedicated test account.

docs.title: Inspect Certificate Before Authentication
docs.text:
After issuance, inspect:

Subject
SAN
UPN
Issuer
Serial Number
Thumbprint
Template
EKUs
Validity
SID Security Extension

The critical ESC9 validation question is:

Is the SID Security Extension Absent?

docs.title: Windows Certificate Inspection
docs.text: certutil -dump esc9-test.cer

docs.title: OpenSSL Inspection
docs.text:
For DER:

openssl x509 -in esc9-test.cer -inform DER -text -noout

For PEM:

openssl x509 -in esc9-test.pem -text -noout

docs.title: Expected ESC9 Certificate
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Subject Alternative Name:
esc9-target@corp.example

Extended Key Usage:
Client Authentication

SID Security Extension:
Absent

This proves the template omitted the SID extension.

It does not by itself prove authentication as the target.

docs.title: Restore Identity Attributes Immediately
docs.text:
After the certificate request:

Restore Original UPN

before proceeding with any further approved validation.

Verify the restoration independently.

docs.title: Verify Restoration
docs.text:
Get-ADUser -Identity 'ESC9-Requester' -Properties userPrincipalName |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,userPrincipalName

Compare against the value recorded before testing.

docs.title: Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
If authentication testing is required:

certipy auth -h

Verify the syntax supported by the installed Certipy release.

Only use the approved test identity.

docs.title: Authentication Failure Is Useful Evidence
docs.text:
In a modern environment, authentication may fail because:

Certificate Cannot Be Strongly Mapped

That result is valuable.

Report:

ESC9 Template Misconfiguration Present

but:

Cross-Account Authentication Not Demonstrated
Under Current Strong Mapping Enforcement

if that is what testing establishes.

docs.title: Do Not Force Legacy Mapping
docs.text:
Do not weaken:

Strong Certificate Mapping

merely to demonstrate what ESC9 would have done historically.

That changes the security posture of the domain and is unnecessary for most assessments.

docs.title: ESC9 and Full Enforcement
docs.text:
In Full Enforcement:

Certificate
      |
      v
Strong Mapping Available?
      |
      +--> Yes -> Evaluate Mapping
      |
      +--> No -> Authentication Denied

This is the expected modern security model.

docs.title: ESC9 and Explicit Strong Mapping
docs.text:
A certificate without the SID extension may still have an explicit strong mapping configured.

Therefore:

No SID Extension

does not necessarily mean:

No Strong Mapping

Inspect the actual account and certificate mapping configuration.

docs.title: altSecurityIdentities
docs.text:
Explicit certificate mappings can be stored using:

altSecurityIdentities

This becomes especially important when analysing:

ESC10
ESC14

and other certificate mapping conditions.

docs.title: ESC9 and ESC14
docs.text:
ESC14 concerns weak explicit certificate mappings.

Conceptually:

ESC9
 |
 v
No SID Security Extension
 |
 v
Explicit Certificate Mapping
 |
 v
ESC14 Analysis

These conditions should not be conflated, but they can interact.

docs.title: ESC9 and ESC6
docs.text:
If the CA also accepts requester-controlled SAN attributes:

ESC6

the attack surface becomes more complex.

Conceptually:

ESC6
 |
 +--> Identity Manipulation
 |
ESC9
 |
 +--> No SID Extension
 |
 v
Certificate Mapping

docs.title: ESC9 and ESC16
docs.text:
ESC16 is the CA-wide analogue that should always be checked when ESC9-like certificates are observed.

If many unrelated templates unexpectedly omit the SID security extension:

Investigate ESC16

rather than assuming every template independently has ESC9.

docs.text:
A good workflow is:

Enumerate Enterprise CAs
        |
        v
Enumerate Published Templates
        |
        v
Check Enrollment Rights
        |
        v
Check Authentication EKUs
        |
        v
Check Manager Approval
        |
        v
Check Authorized Signatures
        |
        v
Check NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
        |
        v
Analyse Certificate Identity Source
        |
        v
Analyse Strong Mapping

docs.text:
ESC9 Template Identified
        |
        v
Is Read-Only Evidence Enough?
        |
        +--> Yes -> Report
        |
        +--> No
               |
               v
        Use Test Accounts
               |
               v
        Record Original Attributes
               |
               v
        Approved Identity Change
               |
               v
        Request Certificate
               |
               v
        Restore Attributes
               |
               v
        Inspect Certificate
               |
               v
        Test Mapping If Required

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
ESC9 detection should focus on:

Template Configuration
Identity Attribute Changes
Certificate Requests
Certificate Issuance
Certificate Authentication

docs.title: Detect Template Configuration
docs.text:
Monitor certificate templates for:

CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

and changes to:

msPKI-Enrollment-Flag

docs.title: Event 5136
docs.text:
Changes to certificate-template objects in Active Directory can generate:

5136

when Directory Service Changes auditing is appropriately configured.

Monitor changes under:

CN=Certificate Templates,
CN=Public Key Services,
CN=Services,
CN=Configuration,...

docs.title: Monitor Enrollment Flag Changes
docs.text:
A suspicious sequence is:

Template Modified
       |
       v
NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION Enabled
       |
       v
Certificate Requested
       |
       v
Template Restored

This may indicate an ESC4-to-ESC9 chain.

docs.title: Detect UPN Changes
docs.text:
Historical ESC9 abuse may involve changes to:

userPrincipalName

Monitor unexpected UPN modifications.

A particularly suspicious pattern is:

UPN Changed
    |
    v
Certificate Requested
    |
    v
UPN Restored

within a short period.

docs.title: Event 5136 and User Attributes
docs.text:
Where auditing is configured, changes to user objects may also be visible through Directory Service Changes telemetry.

Focus on changes to:

userPrincipalName
altSecurityIdentities

and other certificate mapping attributes.

docs.title: Event 4738
docs.text:
Changes to user accounts may generate:

4738

depending on the modified attributes and audit configuration.

Correlate account-change events with certificate enrollment.

docs.title: Certificate Request Events
docs.text:
Where Certificate Services auditing is enabled:

4886

can indicate receipt of a certificate request.

docs.title: Certificate Issuance
docs.text:
4887

can indicate that Certificate Services approved a request and issued a certificate.

docs.title: Correlate Events
docs.text:
A useful ESC9 detection chain is:

UPN Change
    |
    v
Certificate Request
    |
    v
Certificate Issued
    |
    v
UPN Restored
    |
    v
Certificate Authentication

docs.title: Detect Certificate Authentication
docs.text:
Kerberos certificate authentication may produce:

4768

for TGT requests.

Where certificate information is available, correlate authentication with recently issued ESC9 certificates.

docs.title: Monitor Template ACLs
docs.text:
Because ESC4 can be used to create ESC9, also monitor:

WriteDACL
WriteOwner
GenericWrite
GenericAll
WriteProperty

over certificate templates.

See:

AD CS ESC4

docs.title: BloodHound Monitoring
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify principals that can:

Enroll in ESC9 Template

or:

Modify ESC9 Template

Use graph analysis alongside direct configuration monitoring.

docs.title: Hardening ESC9
docs.text:
The primary remediation is:

Remove CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

from templates unless there is a documented and technically justified requirement.

docs.title: Restore SID Security Extension
docs.text:
Authentication-capable certificates should normally retain the SID security extension where supported.

Conceptually:

Certificate
   |
   +--> Identity
   |
   +--> SID

provides stronger binding than:

Certificate
   |
   +--> Name Only

docs.title: Review Authentication Templates
docs.text:
Prioritise templates containing:

Client Authentication
Smart Card Logon
PKINIT Client Authentication
Any Purpose

and other configurations that can participate in authentication.

docs.title: Review Enrollment Rights
docs.text:
Remove unnecessary:

Enroll

rights from broad groups.

Use least privilege.

docs.title: Review Manager Approval
docs.text:
For sensitive certificate workflows, determine whether:

Certificate Manager Approval

is appropriate.

This is defence in depth and does not replace correcting ESC9.

docs.title: Review Authorized Signatures
docs.text:
Sensitive templates may require:

Authorized Signatures

where operationally appropriate.

Again, correct the root cause rather than depending solely on additional issuance barriers.

docs.title: Maintain Full Enforcement
docs.text:
Keep domain controllers fully patched and maintain Microsoft's strong certificate mapping enforcement.

Do not weaken certificate mapping to support unnecessary legacy certificate workflows.

docs.title: Review Explicit Mappings
docs.text:
Audit:

altSecurityIdentities

for weak or unexpected certificate mappings.

This is particularly important when templates omit the SID security extension.

docs.title: Review ESC10
docs.text:
Whenever ESC9 is identified, evaluate:

ESC10

because weak mapping configuration may determine whether the missing SID extension becomes exploitable.

docs.title: Review ESC14
docs.text:
Also review:

ESC14

for weak explicit certificate mappings.

docs.title: Review ESC16
docs.text:
Determine whether the missing SID extension is caused by:

Template Configuration

or:

CA-Wide Configuration

If the latter:

ESC16

may be the more appropriate classification.

docs.title: Protect Template ACLs
docs.text:
Only authorised PKI administrators should be able to modify:

msPKI-Enrollment-Flag

or other security-sensitive template attributes.

docs.title: Baseline Templates
docs.text:
Maintain a baseline containing:

Template Name
Enrollment Flags
Name Flags
EKUs
Application Policies
Enrollment Rights
Manager Approval
Authorized Signatures
Template ACL
Published CAs

Compare regularly for drift.

docs.title: Change Control
docs.text:
Changes to:

NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

should require formal PKI change control.

Record:

Who
Why
Template
Previous Value
New Value
Approval
Rollback Plan

docs.text:
If ESC9 abuse is suspected:

      v
