docs.title: Determine Whether ESC9 Was Intentional
docs.text:
Establish whether:

NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

was:

Long-Standing Configuration

or:

Recently Enabled

A recent unexpected change may indicate abuse.

docs.title: Review Replication Metadata
docs.text:
For suspicious template changes, Active Directory replication metadata can help establish:

When

and:

Where

an attribute was changed.

On an authorised administrative system, tools such as:

repadmin

can assist with replication metadata analysis.

docs.title: Review Template Modification
docs.text:
Determine whether an attacker used an ESC4-like path to enable:

NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION

temporarily.

Compare against:

Known-Good Template Configuration

docs.title: Review User Attribute Changes
docs.text:
Search for temporary changes to:

userPrincipalName

around suspicious certificate requests.

Also inspect:

altSecurityIdentities

where relevant.

docs.title: Identify Certificate Requests
docs.text:
For suspicious requests record:

Request ID
Requester
Template
Subject
SAN
Submission Time
Disposition

docs.title: Identify Issued Certificates
docs.text:
Record:

Serial Number
Thumbprint
Issuer
Subject
SAN
Template
EKUs
Validity
SID Extension State

docs.title: Determine Whether Certificate Was Used
docs.text:
Review:

Kerberos PKINIT
Schannel Authentication
Client TLS Authentication
VPN Authentication
Application Authentication

depending on certificate purpose.

docs.title: Revoke Malicious Certificates
docs.text:
Where unauthorised certificates were issued:

Revoke Certificate
       |
       v
Publish Updated CRL
       |
       v
Verify Revocation Distribution

docs.title: Password Reset Is Not Enough
docs.text:
As with other AD CS abuse:

Password Reset
      |
      X
Issued Certificate

A certificate remains separate authentication material until it expires or is revoked and revocation is enforced.

docs.title: Restore Template Configuration
docs.text:
If ESC9 was introduced maliciously:

Restore Approved Enrollment Flags

and verify:

Template ACL
Enrollment Rights
Name Flags
EKUs
Issuance Requirements

for additional modifications.

docs.title: Investigate ESC4
docs.text:
If the attacker modified the template, identify how they obtained:

Template Write Access

See:

AD CS ESC4

docs.title: Reporting ESC9
docs.text:
Avoid reporting only:

ESC9

Prefer:

Authentication Certificate Template Omits SID Security Extension

or:

Certificate Template Disables Strong SID Binding

or:

Low-Privileged Users Can Enroll in Authentication Certificates Without SID Security Extension

docs.title: Example Finding - Configuration Present
docs.text:
Finding:
Authentication Certificate Template Omits SID Security Extension

Affected Template:
CorpLegacyAuthentication

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Description:
The CorpLegacyAuthentication certificate template is configured with
the NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION enrollment flag.

Certificates issued from this template therefore do not contain the
Active Directory SID security extension normally used to strongly
associate an Enterprise CA-issued certificate with the requesting
security principal.

Authenticated domain users can enroll in the affected template, and
the template issues certificates suitable for client
authentication.

Impact:
The absence of the SID security extension weakens the certificate's
built-in binding to the requesting Active Directory account.

Whether this results in cross-account impersonation depends on the
certificate mapping mechanisms available to domain controllers and
any explicit mappings configured in the environment.

The domain's current strong certificate mapping configuration should
therefore be evaluated before claiming privilege escalation.

Recommendation:
Remove CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION from the affected certificate
template unless there is a documented technical requirement.

Review all authentication-capable certificate templates for the same
configuration.

Maintain fully patched domain controllers and strong certificate
mapping enforcement.

Review weak and explicit certificate mappings, including relevant
altSecurityIdentities configurations.

docs.title: Example Finding - Controlled Mapping Demonstrated
docs.text:
Finding:
Certificate Template Configuration Permits Cross-Account Certificate
Mapping

Affected Template:
CorpLegacyAuthentication

Affected CA:
CORP-CA01

Description:
The CorpLegacyAuthentication template omits the SID security
extension from issued certificates.

During controlled validation, two dedicated assessment accounts were
used.

The requester account was able to enroll in the affected template,
and the resulting certificate did not contain the requester's SID
security extension.

The approved test demonstrated that the certificate could map to the
second test identity under the environment's certificate mapping
configuration.

No privileged production identity was used.

Impact:
A principal with enrollment rights may be able to obtain certificate
credentials that map to another Active Directory identity when the
required mapping conditions are satisfied.

The resulting impact depends on the privileges of the impersonated
identity.

Recommendation:
Remove the NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION flag from the affected template.

Review certificate mapping configuration and eliminate weak mappings
where possible.

Review enrollment permissions, explicit certificate mappings, and
other authentication-capable templates for similar conditions.

Revoke certificates issued through unauthorised identity mapping.

docs.title: Severity Assessment
docs.text:
ESC9 severity depends on:

NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
        +
Enrollment Rights
        +
Authentication Capability
        +
Identity Manipulation Path
        +
Certificate Mapping
        +
Reachable Identity
        =
Severity

docs.title: Do Not Rate ESC9 on Flag Alone
docs.text:
For example:

NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
        |
        v
Enabled

does not automatically mean:

Critical

The complete certificate mapping path matters.

docs.title: High-Risk Combination
docs.text:
A dangerous chain can look like:

Low-Privileged User
       |
       v
Enroll
       |
       v
ESC9 Template
       |
       v
Certificate Without SID
       |
       v
Usable Mapping Condition
       |
       v
Privileged Identity

docs.title: Reduced Exploitability
docs.text:
A modern result may instead be:

ESC9 Template
       |
       v
Certificate Without SID
       |
       v
No Valid Strong Mapping
       |
       v
Full Enforcement
       |
       v
Authentication Rejected

This is still a template-hardening issue, but the demonstrated impact is different.

docs.text:
The normal certificate model is:

Requester
   |
   v
Enterprise CA
   |
   v
Certificate
   |
   +--> Identity
   |
   +--> Requester SID

The ESC9 model is:

Requester
   |
   v
ESC9 Template
   |
   v
Certificate
   |
   +--> Identity
   |

The historical mapping model is:

Requester
   |
   v
Identity Attribute Change
   |
   v
ESC9 Certificate Request
   |
   v
Certificate Without SID
   |
   v
Restore Identity Attribute
   |
   v
Weak Certificate Mapping
   |
   v
Target Account

The modern Full Enforcement model is:

Certificate Without SID
        |
        v
Strong Mapping Available?
        |
        +--> Yes
        |      |
        |      v
        |   Evaluate Mapping
        |
        +--> No
               |
               v
        Authentication Denied

The ESC9 + ESC10 model is:

ESC9
 |
 +--> No SID Security Extension
 |
ESC10
 |
 +--> Weak Mapping Configuration
 |
 v
Potential Identity Mapping

The ESC9 + ESC6 model is:

ESC6
 |
 +--> Requester-Controlled SAN
 |
ESC9
 |
 +--> No SID Extension
 |
 v
Certificate Mapping Risk

The ESC4-to-ESC9 model is:

ESC4
 |
 v
Template Write Access
 |
 v
Modify Enrollment Flags
 |
 v
Enable NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION
 |
 v
ESC9

The ESC9 vs ESC16 model is:

Template-Level
     |
     v
ESC9

versus:

CA-Level
   |
   v
ESC16

The safe-validation model is:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Identify ESC9
   |
   v
Read-Only Evidence Enough?
   |
   +--> Yes -> Report
   |
   +--> No
           |
           v
       Test Requester
           |
           v
       Test Target
           |
           v
       Record Original Attributes
           |
           v
       Approved Temporary Change
           |
           v
       Request Certificate
           |
           v
       Restore Attributes
           |
           v
       Inspect Certificate
           |
           v
       Mapping Test If Required
           |
           v
       Revoke / Cleanup

The detection model is:

Identity Attribute Change
        |
        v
Certificate Request
        |
        v
Certificate Issuance
        |
        v
Identity Attribute Restored
        |
        v
Certificate Authentication

The defensive model is:

SID Security Extension
        +
Strong Mapping
        +
Restricted Enrollment
        +
Protected Template ACLs
        +
Current Patching
        +
Monitoring
        =
Reduced ESC9 Risk

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Does the template have ESC9?"

Ask:
"Does the template omit the SID security
extension, and does the target's current
certificate mapping configuration provide
a usable cross-account mapping path?"

For defenders:

Do Not Assume:
"Full Enforcement means the template
configuration no longer matters."

Ask:
"Why is the SID security extension disabled,
which identities can enroll, and what other
certificate mappings exist?"

Template Configuration
        |
        v
SID Extension State
        |
        v
Certificate Identity
        |
        v
Certificate Mapping
        |
        v
Active Directory Principal

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
ESC9 is fundamentally about removing one of the strongest identity-binding mechanisms available to Enterprise CA-issued certificates.

The normal model is:

Certificate
     |
     v
SID Security Extension
     |
     v
Active Directory SID
     |
     v
Security Principal

ESC9 changes that to:

Certificate
     |
     X
SID Security Extension
     |
     v
Other Mapping Required

This distinction became especially important after Microsoft's certificate-based authentication hardening.

Microsoft's current KB5014754 guidance confirms that domain controllers moved to Full Enforcement with the February 2025 security update and that the supported compatibility fallback ended with the September 9, 2025 security update.

Therefore, in a current environment:

No SID Security Extension

does not automatically imply:

Weak UPN Mapping Will Succeed

A modern assessment must determine the actual mapping path.

The correct analysis is:

ESC9 Template
      |
      v
Who Can Enroll?
      |
      v
What Certificate Is Issued?
      |
      v
Is SID Extension Missing?
      |
      v
What Mapping Is Available?
      |
      v
Does Full Enforcement Accept It?
      |
      v
Which Identity Is Reached?

This also explains why ESC9 should rarely be assessed in isolation.

It has important relationships with:

ESC4
ESC6
ESC10
ESC14
ESC16

For example:

ESC4
 |
 v
Template Modification
 |
 v
ESC9
 |
 v
No SID Extension
 |
 v
ESC10
 |
 v
Weak Mapping

can represent a much more meaningful attack chain than any one ESC condition alone.

For penetration testers, read-only evidence should be preferred. If active validation is required, two dedicated test accounts provide a much safer model than manipulating a production administrator's UPN.

For defenders, the preferred configuration is straightforward:

Authentication Certificate
        |
        v
SID Security Extension Present
        |
        v
Strong Certificate Mapping

rather than relying on weaker name-based identity information.

The central ESC9 question is therefore not merely:

Is NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION Enabled?

It is:

What prevents a certificate without its
requester's SID from mapping to a different
Active Directory security principal?

That is the distinction between identifying the ESC9 configuration and demonstrating its actual security impact.

docs.title: AD CS Golden Certificates - CA Private Key Compromise
docs.text:
A Golden Certificate is a forged certificate created using the private key of a trusted Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) Certification Authority.

Unlike many AD CS ESC techniques, Golden Certificates do not primarily depend on a vulnerable certificate template.

The core problem is:

Enterprise CA Private Key Compromised
                |
                v
Attacker Can Sign Certificates
                |
                v
Certificates Chain to Trusted CA
                |
                v
Forged Enterprise Identities

If an attacker obtains the private key belonging to an Enterprise CA trusted for Active Directory authentication, they may be able to create certificates representing users or computers without submitting normal certificate requests to the CA.

Conceptually:

CA Certificate
      +
CA Private Key
      |
      v
Attacker-Controlled Certificate Signing
      |
      v
Forged Certificate
      |
      v
Trusted by Domain

This is commonly called:

Golden Certificate

The concept is similar to a Golden Ticket in that compromise of a high-value trust key allows authentication material to be generated independently of the normal issuance workflow.

However:

Golden Ticket

and:

Golden Certificate

attack different trust systems.

Tier 0 compromise

Compromise of an Enterprise CA signing key should generally be treated as a Tier 0 security incident. An attacker capable of signing trusted authentication certificates may retain access independently of passwords, normal certificate-template controls and ordinary certificate enrollment monitoring.

Authorised testing only

Do not extract production CA private keys or generate certificates for privileged production identities merely to prove impact. During assessments, begin with CA architecture, key-protection, permissions, backup controls and configuration. If cryptographic validation is explicitly required, use a dedicated lab CA or an approved test CA and test identity.

docs.title: Golden Certificate at a Glance
docs.text:
Normal certificate issuance:

User
 |
 v
Certificate Request
 |
 v
Certificate Template
 |
 v
Enterprise CA
 |
 v
Policy Validation
 |
 v
Certificate Issued

Golden Certificate:

Attacker
 |
 v
CA Private Key
 |
 v
Offline Certificate Generation
 |
 v
No Normal Enrollment
 |
 v
No Template Approval
 |
 v
Trusted Certificate

The critical difference is:

Normal Certificate
=
CA Decides What to Sign

whereas:

Golden Certificate
=
Attacker Possessing CA Key
Decides What to Sign

docs.title: Why the CA Private Key Matters
docs.text:
Every CA certificate contains:

Public Key

The corresponding:

Private Key

is used by the CA to cryptographically sign certificates.

Conceptually:

CA Private Key
      |
      v
Signature
      |
      v
Issued Certificate
      |
      v
CA Public Key Verifies Signature

Clients trust certificates because they trust the issuing CA.

If the private key is stolen:

Trust in the CA

can potentially be abused by whoever possesses the key.

docs.title: PKI Trust Model
docs.text:
Consider:

Root CA
   |
   v
Enterprise Issuing CA
   |
   v
User Certificate

A domain controller does not normally contact the CA and ask:

"Did you really issue this certificate?"

for every authentication attempt.

Instead, it validates properties such as:

Certificate Signature
Certificate Chain
Validity
Revocation
EKUs
Identity Mapping

If an attacker can generate a cryptographically valid certificate using the CA private key, the certificate can appear legitimate from the perspective of signature validation.

docs.title: Golden Certificate Concept
docs.text:
The attack is:

Compromise CA Signing Key
        |
        v
Create Certificate
        |
        v
Sign with CA Private Key
        |
        v
Certificate Chains to Trusted CA
        |
        v
Use Certificate

The certificate may never have been:

Requested from CA
Approved by CA
Recorded in CA Database

That distinction has major detection implications.

docs.title: Golden Certificate vs Normal Certificate Abuse
docs.text:
Normal AD CS abuse:

Attacker
   |
   v
Vulnerable Template / CA
   |
   v
Certificate Request
   |
   v
CA Issues Certificate

Golden Certificate:

Attacker
   |
   v
CA Private Key
   |
   v
Attacker Signs Certificate

The second path bypasses the normal enrollment process entirely.

docs.title: Golden Certificate vs Golden Ticket
docs.text:
Golden Ticket:

KRBTGT Key
   |
   v
Forge TGT

Golden Certificate:

CA Private Key
   |
   v
Forge Certificate
   |
   v
Certificate Authentication
   |
   v
Obtain TGT

docs.title: Trust Root Comparison
docs.text:
Golden Ticket
     |
     v
Kerberos Trust
     |
     v
KRBTGT

Golden Certificate
     |
     v
PKI Trust
     |
     v
CA Signing Key

Both involve compromise of high-value cryptographic trust material.

docs.title: Why Golden Certificates Are Powerful
docs.text:
A Golden Certificate can potentially bypass controls around:

Password Changes
Password Rotation
Account Password Complexity
NTLM Restrictions
Certificate Enrollment Permissions
Certificate Template Permissions
Manager Approval
Authorised Signatures

because the attacker is no longer requesting a certificate through the normal CA workflow.

docs.title: Password Reset Does Not Fix the CA Key
docs.text:
Suppose an attacker forges a certificate for:

alice@corp.example

Then Alice's password is changed.

The attacker's certificate may still remain useful because:

Certificate Authentication

does not depend on Alice's password.

docs.title: Template Remediation Does Not Fix the CA Key
docs.text:
Suppose the organisation fixes:

ESC1

and removes:

Domain Users -> Enroll

from a vulnerable template.

If the CA private key has already been compromised:

Template Remediation

does not remove the attacker's ability to sign certificates.

docs.title: CA Key Compromise Is the Root Cause
docs.text:
The fundamental issue is:

Attacker Possesses
Trusted CA Signing Key

Therefore remediation must address:

The CA Trust Key

not merely the certificate template.

docs.title: Potential Sources of CA Private Key Compromise
docs.text:
A CA private key can become exposed through several paths.

Examples include:

CA Server Compromise
CA Backup Exposure
Private Key Export
Weak File Permissions
Weak Backup Permissions
Virtual Machine Snapshot
System-State Backup
CA Database Backup Workflow
HSM Misconfiguration
Cloud Backup Exposure
Administrator Credential Compromise
Malicious PKI Administrator

docs.title: CA Server Compromise
docs.text:
If the attacker obtains:

Local Administrator

or:

SYSTEM

on an Enterprise CA, the security impact is already extremely serious.

The attacker may potentially:

Modify CA Configuration
Issue Certificates
Access Backup Material
Interact with Key Storage
Modify Certificate Services
Manipulate Audit Configuration

Whether the private key itself can be exported depends on how it is protected.

docs.title: Exportable CA Keys
docs.text:
During CA setup or key generation, private-key properties determine whether the key can be exported.

A software-protected exportable CA key creates a substantially different risk profile from:

Non-Exportable HSM-Protected Key

However:

Non-Exportable

does not automatically mean:

Cannot Be Abused

An attacker controlling the CA may still be able to invoke signing operations.

docs.title: Software Key Storage
docs.text:
A CA key may be protected through Windows cryptographic providers such as:

CSP

or:

KSP

depending on the CA configuration and operating system.

The exact security properties depend on:

Provider
Key Storage
Export Policy
ACLs
Machine Protection
Credential Protection
Hardware Protection

docs.title: Hardware Security Modules
docs.text:
High-value CAs may store signing keys in:

HSM

or another hardware-backed key-protection system.

Conceptually:

certsrv.exe
     |
     v
Crypto Provider
     |
     v
HSM
     |
     v
CA Private Key

The intended security property is:

Private Key Never Leaves HSM

docs.title: HSM Does Not Eliminate All Risk
docs.text:
Even when the key cannot be extracted:

Attacker Controls CA

may still mean:

Attacker Can Request Signing Operations

depending on HSM policy and CA architecture.

Therefore distinguish:

Key Extraction

from:

Signing-Key Abuse

docs.title: ESC12 Relationship
docs.text:
ESC12 specifically concerns certain AD CS deployments using:

YubiHSM2

and weaknesses affecting CA private-key protection.

ESC12 can therefore become one path toward:

CA Signing Capability

or potentially:

CA Key Compromise

depending on the exact deployment.

See:

AD CS ESC12

docs.title: CA Backup Exposure
docs.text:
CA backup material is especially sensitive.

A CA backup can include:

CA Certificate
CA Private Key
CA Database
Configuration

depending on the backup method.

If a backup containing the CA private key is stolen:

CA Server Can Be Secure

while:

CA Trust Is Still Compromised

docs.title: Backup Security Model
docs.text:
Enterprise CA
     |
     v
CA Backup
     |
     v
Backup Server
     |
     v
Backup Repository

Every system in this chain can become part of the CA security boundary.

docs.title: Virtual Machine Snapshots
docs.text:
If the CA is virtualised:

VM Snapshot

or:

Hypervisor Backup

may contain sensitive CA state.

Therefore:

Virtualisation Administrators

and:

Backup Administrators

can become highly privileged in the PKI trust model.

docs.title: Offline Root CA vs Enterprise Issuing CA
docs.text:
Many enterprise PKI architectures use:

Offline Root CA
      |
      v
Enterprise Issuing CA

The offline root should normally remain:

Powered Off
Disconnected
Physically Protected

except when required for controlled PKI operations.

docs.title: Root CA Compromise
docs.text:
Compromise of the root CA private key can be even more severe than compromise of one issuing CA.

Conceptually:

Root CA Key
    |
    +--> Issuing CA 1
    |
    +--> Issuing CA 2
    |
    +--> Issuing CA 3

An attacker controlling the root trust key can potentially undermine the entire PKI hierarchy.

docs.title: Enterprise Issuing CA Compromise
docs.text:
Compromise of an Enterprise issuing CA typically affects:

Certificates Trusted
Through That CA

This can still represent domain-wide or forest-wide impact depending on the PKI architecture.

docs.title: Certificate Authentication Requirements
docs.text:
A forged certificate must still satisfy the authentication system's requirements.

These may include:

Trusted Chain
Valid Time
Suitable EKU
Identity Information
Certificate Mapping
Revocation Behaviour
Domain Controller Certificate
PKINIT Support

A CA private key is extraordinarily powerful, but certificate authentication still follows protocol validation rules.

docs.title: Authentication EKUs
docs.text:
Relevant EKUs can include:

Client Authentication
Smart Card Logon
PKINIT Client Authentication

docs.title: Modern Certificate Mapping
docs.text:
Golden Certificate analysis must account for modern strong certificate mapping.

Microsoft's certificate-based authentication hardening introduced stronger relationships between certificates and Active Directory identities.

Therefore a current assessment should not blindly reproduce historical:

UPN Only

certificate-forging techniques.

docs.title: SID Security Extension
docs.text:
The Microsoft NTDS CA security extension uses:

1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2

and can provide strong certificate-to-account binding.

docs.title: Forged Certificate Identity
docs.text:
An attacker controlling a CA private key can control certificate contents during offline certificate creation.

However, the exact identity information required for successful authentication depends on:

Domain Controller Version
Patch Level
Certificate Mapping
Strong Binding
Certificate Extensions
Authentication Protocol

docs.title: Current 2026 Assessment Principle
docs.text:
Do not assume:

Old Golden Certificate PoC
=
Works Unchanged Today

Instead determine:

Current DC Behaviour

and:

Current Certificate Mapping Requirements

before evaluating authentication impact.

docs.title: CA Certificate Enumeration
docs.text:
Before assessing Golden Certificate risk, identify the Enterprise CAs.

PowerShell:

Import-Module ActiveDirectory

Retrieve the Configuration naming context:

$configNC = (Get-ADRootDSE).configurationNamingContext

Enumerate Enterprise CAs:

$base = "CN=Enrollment Services,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,$configNC"

Get-ADObject -SearchBase $base -LDAPFilter '(objectClass=pKIEnrollmentService)' -Properties dNSHostName,cACertificate,certificateTemplates |
    Select-Object Name,dNSHostName,certificateTemplates

docs.title: Certipy Enumeration
docs.text:
Certipy provides useful AD CS discovery.

Check the installed version:

certipy --version

Then:

certipy find -u 'audit-user@corp.example' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 -stdout

Use:

certipy find -h

to confirm options for the installed release.

docs.title: Identify CA Host
docs.text:
Record:

CA Name
CA Hostname
CA Type
CA Certificate
Published Templates

Example:

CA Name:
CORP-CA

Hostname:
ca01.corp.example

docs.title: Native CA Configuration
docs.text:
On an authorised CA host:

certutil -getreg CA

This provides CA configuration information without changing the system.

docs.title: CA Certificate Store
docs.text:
On the CA:

certutil -store my

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My

Review certificates associated with:

Certificate Services

docs.title: Identify CA Certificate
docs.text:
Useful properties include:

Subject
Issuer
Serial Number
Thumbprint
Validity
Public Key Algorithm
Signature Algorithm

docs.title: Determine Private Key Presence
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\My |
    Select-Object Subject,Thumbprint,HasPrivateKey,NotAfter

For the CA certificate, expect:

HasPrivateKey = True

on the active CA host.

This confirms the host has access to the signing key.

It does not prove that the key is exportable.

docs.title: Identify Cryptographic Provider
docs.text:
Use CA configuration and certificate information to determine the provider protecting the key.

Useful questions include:

Software Provider?
Legacy CSP?
CNG KSP?
Hardware Provider?
HSM?

docs.title: certutil Key Information
docs.text:
Administrators can use:

certutil -store my

and relevant CA configuration commands to inspect key-provider information.

The objective during assessment is:

Determine Protection Model

not:

Extract the Key

docs.title: Private Key Exportability
docs.text:
Determine whether the CA key was configured as exportable.

This may be available through:

PKI Documentation
CA Build Records
Key Ceremony Records
Provider Configuration
HSM Configuration
Backup Procedures

Avoid attempting private-key export merely to answer this question in production.

docs.title: CA Backup Configuration
docs.text:
Review:

Backup Product
Backup Destination
Backup Encryption
Backup ACLs
Backup Operators
Retention
Offline Copies
Recovery Procedures

docs.title: Key Backup Procedures
docs.text:
Ask:

Is the CA private key backed up?

Where?

How is the backup encrypted?

Who knows the password?

Who can retrieve the backup?

Is access logged?

Is the backup offline?

Is the backup periodically tested?

docs.title: CA Private Key Protection Review
docs.text:
A strong assessment should evaluate:

Key Storage
      |
      +--> Software
      |
      +--> TPM / Hardware
      |
      +--> HSM

Then:

Exportability
Access Control
Administrative Access
Backup
Recovery
Auditing

docs.title: Tier 0 Classification
docs.text:
Enterprise CA systems should generally be treated as:

Tier 0

because compromise can affect:

Authentication
Identity
Trust
Code Signing
Server Identity
Client Identity

depending on the PKI.

docs.title: CA Administrator Review
docs.text:
Identify:

Local Administrators
Enterprise Admins
CA Administrators
Certificate Managers
Backup Operators
PKI Service Accounts
HSM Administrators
Hypervisor Administrators

where relevant.

docs.title: CA Network Exposure
docs.text:
Review whether the CA exposes unnecessary services.

Examples:

SMB
RDP
WinRM
RPC
Web Enrollment
Remote Registry
Third-Party Management Agents
Backup Agents

Every additional service increases the attack surface of a Tier 0 system.

docs.title: CA Application Control
docs.text:
Consider:

WDAC
AppLocker
EDR
Privileged Access Workstations
Restricted Administrative Logon

for Enterprise CA hosts.

docs.title: CA Interactive Logon
docs.text:
Administrative interactive logon to an Enterprise CA should be tightly restricted.

Review:

Who Can RDP?
Who Can WinRM?
Who Can Log On Locally?
Who Can Access Through Management Platforms?

docs.title: Safe Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
A production-safe Golden Certificate assessment can normally stop before private-key extraction.

Use:

Identify CA
    |
    v
Determine Trust Scope
    |
    v
Review CA Host Security
    |
    v
Review Key Protection
    |
    v
Review Exportability
    |
    v
Review Backup Security
    |
    v
Review Administrative Paths
    |
    v
Determine Potential Impact

docs.title: When Active Validation Is Necessary
docs.text:
If the engagement explicitly requires proof of cryptographic impact:

Use Dedicated Lab CA

or:

Approved Test CA

rather than extracting a production signing key.

docs.title: Lab Validation Model
docs.text:
Lab Enterprise CA
      |
      v
Export Test CA Key
      |
      v
Generate Test Certificate
      |
      v
Sign with Test CA
      |
      v
Authenticate Test Account

This demonstrates the Golden Certificate principle without compromising production trust.

docs.title: Certipy Golden Certificate Functionality
docs.text:
Certipy includes functionality for working with CA certificates and forging certificates.

Before any lab validation, inspect the current syntax:

certipy forge -h

A conceptual workflow is:

CA PFX
   |
   v
Certipy Forge
   |
   v
Forged PFX

Do not point this workflow at a production CA private key unless the engagement explicitly authorises CA-key compromise testing.

docs.title: Lab-Only Forge Example
docs.text:
In an isolated lab with a test CA key:

certipy forge \
    -ca-pfx lab-ca.pfx \
    -upn 'test-admin@lab.example' \
    -sid 'S-1-5-21-111111111-222222222-333333333-1105' \
    -out test-admin.pfx

Confirm current options first:

certipy forge -h

Tool syntax can change between releases.

docs.title: Why the SID Matters
docs.text:
Modern certificate mapping may require stronger identity information than:

UPN

alone.

The SID represents the specific Active Directory security principal.

Conceptually:

test-admin@lab.example
        |
        v
SID
        |
        v
S-1-5-21-...-1105

docs.title: Lab Authentication
docs.text:
After generating a test certificate in a controlled lab, Certipy can be used to test certificate authentication:

certipy auth -pfx test-admin.pfx -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

This should only target the approved test domain.

docs.title: Authentication Result
docs.text:
A successful certificate authentication may obtain:

TGT

and depending on the tooling and account conditions, additional authentication material may be recoverable.

The important Golden Certificate proof is:

Forged Certificate
       |
       v
Trusted by Domain
       |
       v
Authentication Accepted

docs.title: Golden Certificate Persistence
docs.text:
Suppose an attacker compromises:

CORP-CA

and obtains its signing key.

The organisation then:

Resets Administrator Password

The attacker's signing key remains valid.

They can potentially create another certificate.

docs.title: Persistence Model
docs.text:
CA Private Key
     |
     v
Forge Certificate A
     |
     v
Use Access
     |
     v
Certificate Revoked
     |
     v
Forge Certificate B

This continues until the underlying CA trust is remediated.

docs.title: Why Revoking One Certificate Is Insufficient
docs.text:
If the attacker controls the CA key:

Revoke Forged Certificate

does not solve:

Attacker Can Forge Another

The trust anchor itself is compromised.

docs.title: Forged Certificates May Not Be in the CA Database
docs.text:
A normal certificate:

Request
   |
   v
CA Database
   |
   v
Issued Certificate

A Golden Certificate:

Attacker
   |
   v
Offline Signing
   |
   v
Certificate

The forged certificate may therefore have:

No Corresponding CA Request

docs.title: Detection Challenge
docs.text:
This means:

Certificate Used

may exist without:

4886 Request Event

or:

4887 Issuance Event

for the certificate.

This mismatch can be a valuable detection signal.

docs.title: Detection Model
docs.text:
Certificate Authentication
        |
        v
Certificate Serial / Issuer
        |
        v
Search CA Database
        |
        +--> Found -> Normal Investigation
        |
        +--> Missing
                |
                v
         Possible Forgery

docs.title: Certificate Serial Numbers
docs.text:
Forged certificates may contain attacker-selected or tool-generated serial numbers.

Defenders should not rely solely on:

Serial Number Looks Strange

because legitimate CA serial-number behaviour varies.

Instead correlate:

Issuer
Serial
Certificate
CA Database
Authentication

docs.title: Certificate Validity
docs.text:
Attackers forging certificates can potentially select unusual validity periods.

Look for:

Unexpected NotBefore
Unexpected NotAfter
Excessive Lifetime

relative to the organisation's normal certificate policy.

docs.title: Certificate Template Information
docs.text:
Normal Enterprise CA-issued certificates may contain template-related information.

An offline forged certificate may differ from normal certificates in:

Extensions
Template Metadata
Issuance Policies
Serial Behaviour
Validity
CRL Distribution Points
Authority Information Access

depending on how it was generated.

docs.title: Avoid Single-Indicator Detection
docs.text:
Do not detect Golden Certificates only through:

Missing Template Extension

Attackers may attempt to mimic legitimate certificates.

Use multiple signals.

docs.title: Event 4768
docs.text:
Certificate-based Kerberos authentication can generate:

4768

TGT request events.

Modern Windows versions can expose certificate-related information useful for investigation.

docs.title: Correlate Authentication with CA Records
docs.text:
A high-value detection workflow is:

4768
  |
  v
Certificate Information
  |
  v
Issuer / Serial
  |
  v
CA Database Search

If the CA says:

Never Issued

the certificate deserves immediate investigation.

docs.title: CA Certificate Services Events
docs.text:
Useful CA auditing includes events such as:

4886
4887

for certificate requests and issuance.

Additional CA auditing should be enabled according to organisational requirements.

docs.title: CA Backup Events
docs.text:
Windows Certificate Services auditing can also provide visibility into CA backup and restore operations.

Events commonly associated with CA backup and restore include:

4876
4877

where relevant auditing is enabled.

Unexpected CA backup activity should be investigated.

docs.title: Private Key Access
docs.text:
Where supported by the provider and audit configuration, cryptographic activity can generate events such as:

5058
5059
5061

These can provide useful context around key-file or cryptographic operations.

Exact event availability depends on:

Provider
Audit Policy
Windows Version
Key Type
Operation

docs.title: File Access Auditing
docs.text:
If software key material or backup files are protected by filesystem ACLs, event:

4663

may provide access telemetry when appropriate object-access auditing and SACLs are configured.

docs.title: HSM Auditing
docs.text:
Hardware-protected CAs should use:

HSM Native Audit Logs

to monitor:

Authentication
Key Operations
Administrative Changes
Signing
Backup
Restore
Configuration

docs.title: CA EDR Monitoring
docs.text:
Enterprise CA hosts should receive strong endpoint monitoring.

High-signal behaviours include:

Unexpected PowerShell
Unexpected certutil
Private-Key Backup
PFX Creation
Registry Modification
New Administrative Tools
Credential Dumping
Security Tool Tampering
Unexpected Network Connections

docs.title: certutil Is Not Automatically Malicious
docs.text:
Administrators legitimately use:

certutil

for CA management.

Detection should therefore consider:

User
Command Line
Host
Time
Change Ticket
Parent Process
Related Activity

rather than alerting solely on process name.

docs.title: Monitor PFX Creation
docs.text:
Unexpected:

.pfx

or:

.p12

files on a CA are high-value signals.

Especially investigate files created in:

Temp
User Profiles
Public Directories
Network Shares
Backup Staging Areas

docs.title: Monitor CA Key Backup
docs.text:
A CA private-key backup should be:

Rare
Planned
Documented
Controlled
Audited

Unexpected key backup is a major incident indicator.

docs.title: Monitor CA Configuration Changes
docs.text:
Monitor:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CertSvc\Configuration

for unexpected changes.

docs.title: Monitor Certificate Services
docs.text:
Watch for unexpected:

CertSvc Stop
CertSvc Start
Configuration Changes
Backup Operations
Provider Changes

docs.title: Monitor Administrative Logons
docs.text:
Unexpected privileged logons to:

CA Server

should receive high priority.

Especially investigate:

Domain Admin
Enterprise Admin
Backup Administrator
Unusual Service Account
New Local Administrator

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify attack paths leading to:

Enterprise CA

or PKI administration.

Important relationships can include:

Administrative Rights
Remote Access
PKI Object Control
Template Control
CA Control

docs.title: GoldenCert Concept in BloodHound
docs.text:
Modern BloodHound AD CS modelling includes the concept of:

GoldenCert

representing control capable of enabling CA-certificate/private-key compromise or equivalent CA-level certificate forgery.

Use BloodHound as:

Attack Path Context

rather than proof that a private key has actually been extracted.

docs.title: GoldenCert Does Not Mean Key Already Stolen
docs.text:
A graph edge may indicate:

Principal Has Sufficient Control

to compromise the CA trust.

It does not necessarily mean:

CA Private Key Has Already Been Exported

Keep:

Potential

and:

Observed Compromise

separate.

docs.title: Protect the CA Host
docs.text:
The CA host should receive Tier 0 protections.

Recommended controls include:

Dedicated Administration
Privileged Access Workstations
Restricted RDP
Restricted WinRM
Host Firewall
EDR
Application Control
Credential Guard where appropriate
Secure Boot
Patch Management
Minimal Software
Network Segmentation

docs.title: Avoid General-Purpose Use
docs.text:
Do not use an Enterprise CA as:

File Server
Web Browsing Workstation
Administrative Jump Box
Software Development Host
General Management Server

Reduce the attack surface.

docs.title: Protect CA Administrators
docs.text:
CA administrators should use dedicated privileged identities.

Avoid:

Email
Web Browsing
Office Applications
General User Activity

from CA administrative accounts.

docs.title: Protect Backups
docs.text:
CA backups should use:

Strong Encryption
Restricted ACLs
Offline Protection
Separate Administrative Boundary
Access Logging
Secure Recovery Process

docs.title: Backup Passwords
docs.text:
If a CA private key is stored in a password-protected PFX:

The Password Becomes Tier 0 Material

Protect it accordingly.

Do not store the PFX and its password together.

docs.title: HSM Recommendations
docs.text:
For high-value enterprise CAs, consider hardware-backed key protection.

A strong design includes:

Non-Exportable CA Key
       |
       v
HSM
       |
       v
Restricted Authentication
       |
       v
Least Capabilities
       |
       v
Audited Signing

docs.title: HSM Administrative Separation
docs.text:
Where supported, separate:

CA Administrator

from:

HSM Administrator

and:

Backup / Recovery Administrator

to reduce single-person compromise.

docs.title: Root CA Protection
docs.text:
Offline roots should remain:

Offline
Physically Protected
Access Controlled
Audited
Used Only When Required

docs.title: Issuing CA Lifetime
docs.text:
Long-lived CA keys increase the potential persistence window following compromise.

CA lifetime and key-rotation strategy should be part of PKI governance.

docs.title: Incident Response - Suspected CA Key Theft
docs.text:
If CA private-key theft is suspected:

Treat as Major Identity Incident

The response may require:

CA Isolation
Forensic Preservation
Key Rotation
CA Certificate Replacement
Certificate Reissuance
Trust Store Updates
Revocation
CRL Publication
Application Validation

This is significantly more complex than resetting an account password.

docs.title: Do Not Immediately Destroy Evidence
docs.text:
Before rebuilding or rotating:

Preserve Evidence

where operationally possible.

Capture:

CA Configuration
Event Logs
EDR Telemetry
Registry
CA Database
CA Certificates
Backup Logs
HSM Logs
Administrative Logs
Network Telemetry

docs.title: Determine Compromise Type
docs.text:
Establish whether the attacker obtained:

CA Host Control

only,

Signing Capability

or:

Actual CA Private Key Material

These have different recovery implications.

docs.title: Key Extraction vs Signing Oracle
docs.text:
CA Host Compromised
       |
       v
Can Attacker Sign?
       |
       +--> Yes
       |
       v
Can Attacker Export Key?
       |
       +--> No -> Signing Abuse
       |
       +--> Yes -> Key Theft

Both are serious.

Key theft is especially dangerous because the attacker can continue signing:

Offline

after losing access to the CA host.

docs.title: Determine Key Exposure Window
docs.text:
Establish:

When Could the Key First Have Been Stolen?

Review:

Initial CA Compromise
Backup Exposure
Administrator Compromise
HSM Events
Key Backup Operations
PFX Creation
File Access

docs.text:
Do not search only the CA database.

docs.text:
Build an inventory:

Observed Certificate
       |
       +--> Issuer
       +--> Serial
       +--> Subject
       +--> SAN
       +--> EKU
       +--> Validity

Then compare against:

CA Database

docs.title: Revocation Challenges
docs.text:
If a forged certificate's serial number is known, it may potentially be revoked.

But:

Attacker Still Has CA Key

means another certificate can be created.

Therefore revocation alone is not sufficient.

docs.title: CA Key Rotation
docs.text:
If the CA private key is confirmed compromised, the organisation may need to:

Generate New CA Key

and potentially:

Renew CA Certificate

depending on the architecture and incident-response plan.

This should be performed by qualified PKI administrators.

docs.title: CA Replacement
docs.text:
In severe cases:

Rebuild / Replace CA

may be required.

The exact procedure depends on:

Root vs Issuing CA
PKI Hierarchy
Applications
Certificate Lifetimes
Revocation Infrastructure
Trust Distribution
HSM

docs.title: Reissue Certificates
docs.text:
Certificates issued under the compromised CA may need to be:

Reissued

under a new trust configuration.

This can include:

User Certificates
Computer Certificates
Domain Controller Certificates
Web Certificates
VPN Certificates
802.1X Certificates
Code-Signing Certificates
Service Certificates

depending on the CA's usage.

docs.title: Trust Store Updates
docs.text:
If the compromised CA certificate must be removed from trust:

Applications
Network Appliances
VPN Infrastructure
Linux Systems
Java Trust Stores
Browsers
Mobile Devices

may require updates.

docs.title: Domain Controller Certificates
docs.text:
Pay special attention to certificates used by:

Domain Controllers

because AD certificate authentication depends on PKI trust.

docs.title: CRL and Revocation Infrastructure
docs.text:
Review:

CRL Distribution Points
Authority Information Access
OCSP
CRL Publication
Replication
Availability

during recovery.

docs.title: CA Compromise Is an Enterprise Recovery Problem
docs.text:
A useful mental model is:

User Password Compromise
        |
        v
Reset User Password

versus:

CA Private Key Compromise
        |
        v
Repair Enterprise Trust

The second is substantially more complex.

docs.title: Reporting Golden Certificate Risk
docs.text:
Avoid a finding title such as:

Golden Certificate

without explaining the root cause.

Prefer:

Enterprise CA Private Key Can Be Compromised

or:

Insufficient Protection of Enterprise Certification Authority Signing Key

or:

Compromise of Enterprise CA Enables Trusted Certificate Forgery

docs.title: Example Finding - Exportable CA Key
docs.text:
Finding:
Enterprise Certification Authority Signing Key Is Insufficiently
Protected

Affected Host:
ca01.corp.example

Affected CA:
CORP-CA

Description:
The Enterprise Certification Authority signing key is protected by
software-based key storage and is configured in a manner that permits
private-key export by sufficiently privileged administrators.

The CA is trusted for Active Directory certificate authentication.

Compromise of the CA host or an account with sufficient administrative
rights could therefore expose the CA signing key.

Possession of this key would allow an attacker to generate certificates
that cryptographically chain to the organisation's trusted Enterprise
CA without submitting the certificates through the normal enrollment
workflow.

Impact:
An attacker obtaining the CA private key could potentially create
trusted authentication certificates for Active Directory principals.

Such certificates may remain useful independently of account password
changes and certificate-template remediation.

Because forged certificates can be generated offline, they may not
produce corresponding certificate request or issuance records in the
CA database.

Compromise of the signing key should therefore be treated as compromise
of a Tier 0 trust asset.

Recommendation:
Protect Enterprise CA signing keys using a hardware-backed,
non-exportable key where appropriate to the organisation's PKI
architecture.

Restrict administrative access to the CA, protect CA backups as Tier 0
assets, separate PKI administration roles and monitor private-key and
CA backup operations.

Develop and test a documented CA key-compromise recovery procedure.

docs.title: Example Finding - Exposed CA Backup
docs.text:
Finding:
Enterprise CA Private Key Exposed Through Insecure Backup Storage

Affected CA:
CORP-CA

Description:
A backup of the Enterprise Certification Authority containing private
key material was accessible to principals outside the intended PKI
administrative boundary.

The backup contains cryptographic material capable of representing the
trusted Enterprise CA.

Impact:
An attacker obtaining the backup and associated protection material may
be able to recover the CA signing key.

This could permit offline creation of certificates that chain to the
trusted CA, potentially enabling long-term certificate-based
impersonation.

The attacker would no longer require access to the CA server to
generate additional certificates.

Recommendation:
Immediately restrict access to the affected backup and investigate
whether it has been accessed.

Protect CA backup material using strong encryption and Tier 0 access
controls.

If compromise of the CA private key cannot be ruled out, initiate the
organisation's CA key-compromise recovery process and evaluate CA key
rotation or replacement.

docs.title: Example Finding - CA Host Compromise
docs.text:
Finding:
Administrative Control of Enterprise CA Enables PKI Trust Compromise

Affected Host:
ca01.corp.example

Affected CA:
CORP-CA

Description:
The tested security principal can obtain administrative control of the
Enterprise Certification Authority host.

The CA is trusted for Active Directory authentication and represents a
Tier 0 security asset.

Administrative control of the CA can permit modification of
Certificate Services configuration, unauthorised certificate issuance,
access to backup material and potentially abuse or extraction of the CA
signing key depending on the configured cryptographic provider.

Impact:
Successful compromise could allow an attacker to issue or forge trusted
certificates and impersonate Active Directory identities.

If the CA signing key can be extracted, the attacker may continue
creating certificates offline after access to the CA server has been
removed.

Recommendation:
Remove the identified administrative attack path and treat the
Enterprise CA as Tier 0 infrastructure.

Restrict administrative access, segment the CA, use dedicated privileged
administration, deploy application control and endpoint monitoring, and
review CA key protection and backup procedures.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Confirmed theft of an Enterprise CA private key used for Active Directory authentication should normally be treated as:

Critical

because the fundamental PKI trust boundary has been compromised.

docs.title: Potential vs Confirmed Compromise
docs.text:
Distinguish:

CA Key Could Be Exported

from:

CA Key Was Exported

and:

Attacker Possesses CA Key

These represent different evidence levels.

docs.title: Example Severity Model
docs.text:
Weak CA Hardening
       |
       v
Potential Key Exposure
       |
       v
High

versus:

CA Key Confirmed Stolen
       |
       v
Trusted Authentication Certificates
Can Be Forged
       |
       v
Critical

Severity should reflect the actual demonstrated conditions.

docs.text:
The normal PKI model is:

Certificate Request
       |
       v
Certificate Template
       |
       v
CA Policy
       |
       v
CA Private Key
       |
       v
Certificate

The Golden Certificate model is:

       |
       v
Attacker
       |
       v
Offline Certificate
       |
       v
Trusted Signature

The authentication model is:

       |
       v

       |
       v
Trusted Enterprise CA
       |
       v
Identity Mapping
       |
       v
Certificate Authentication
       |
       v
Kerberos TGT

The persistence model is:

Compromise CA Key
       |
       v
Forge Certificate
       |
       v
Password Reset
       |
       v
Forge Another Certificate
       |
       v
Continued Access

The detection model is:

Certificate Authentication
       |
       v
Issuer + Serial
       |
       v
CA Database
       |
       +--> Matching Issuance
       |
       +--> No Matching Issuance
                |
                v
        Investigate Forgery

The compromise model is:

CA Host Access
      |
      v
Signing Capability?
      |
      +--> No
      |
      +--> Yes
             |
             v
       Key Exportable?
             |
             +--> No
             |     |
             |     v
             | Signing-Key Abuse
             |
             +--> Yes
                   |
                   v
              Offline Key Theft

The recovery model is:

CA Key Compromise
       |
       v
Preserve Evidence
       |
       v
Determine Exposure
       |
       v
Replace / Rotate Key
       |
       v
Reissue Certificates
       |
       v
Update Trust
       |
       v
Monitor for Old Certificates

The backup attack model is:

Secure CA
   |
   v
Insecure Backup
   |
   v
CA Private Key
   |
   v
Attacker
   |
   v
Golden Certificate

The HSM model is:

CA
 |
 v
HSM
 |
 +--> Key Cannot Be Exported
 |
 +--> Signing Operations Restricted
 |
 +--> Authentication Protected
 |
 +--> Audit Logs

The Tier 0 model is:

Domain Controllers
       +
KRBTGT
       +
Enterprise PKI
       +
Identity Infrastructure
       =
Tier 0

For penetration testers:

Do Not Ask:
"Can I dump the production CA key
and forge Domain Admin certificates?"

Ask:
"Can I establish whether an attacker
with the identified access could
compromise the CA signing capability
without unnecessarily extracting
Tier 0 cryptographic material?"

For defenders:

Do Not Assume:
"Our certificate templates are secure,
therefore our PKI is secure."

"Who can access, use, export, back up
or recover the private key that signs
every certificate we trust?"

Enterprise CA

      v
CA Private Key

      v
Key Compromise

      v

      |

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
Golden Certificates represent a fundamentally different class of AD CS risk from ordinary certificate-template vulnerabilities.

With a template vulnerability:

Attacker
   |
   v
Abuses CA Policy

With a Golden Certificate:

Attacker
   |
   v
Becomes the CA

from the perspective of certificate signing.

The critical trust relationship is:

CA Private Key
      |
      v
Trusted Certificate Signature

Once the private key is compromised, normal enrollment controls such as:

Template Permissions
Manager Approval
Authorised Signatures
Enrollment Restrictions

cannot prevent the attacker from creating certificates offline.

This is why:

Enterprise CA Private Key

must be treated as one of the most sensitive cryptographic assets in an Active Directory environment.

The most important assessment distinction is:

CA Administrative Access

versus:

CA Signing Capability

versus:

CA Private Key Extraction

These are related but not identical.

A hardware-protected key may prevent straightforward extraction while still allowing an attacker controlling the CA to misuse signing operations.

Conversely, compromise of an old CA backup may expose the private key without requiring any access to the current CA server.

Therefore assess the entire trust chain:

CA Host
   +
CA Administrators
   +
Cryptographic Provider
   +
HSM
   +
Backups
   +
Virtualisation
   +
Recovery Material
   =
CA Key Security

From a detection perspective, remember the defining property of Golden Certificates:

Forged Offline

A certificate may therefore authenticate successfully even though:

The CA Has No Record
of Issuing It

Correlating certificate-authentication telemetry with CA issuance records can provide valuable evidence of certificate forgery.

From an incident-response perspective:

Resetting Passwords

is not enough.

Revoking One Certificate

is not enough.

Fixing Certificate Templates

is not enough.

If the CA signing key has been stolen:

The Trust Key Itself
Must Be Recovered

through an appropriate PKI key-compromise recovery process.

For penetration testers, production validation should therefore stop well before unnecessary key extraction whenever the risk can already be demonstrated through:

CA Control
       |
       v
Key Protection Analysis
       |
       v
Export / Signing Capability
       |
       v
Trusted Authentication Scope

For defenders, the central question is simple:

If someone compromises this CA,
can we still trust certificates
signed by it?

If the CA private key has been compromised, the answer is:

No.

That is why Golden Certificate capability represents one of the highest-impact compromise scenarios in an Active Directory PKI.

docs.title: Active Directory Tool Selection
docs.text:
A useful mental model:

Need broad Windows / AD enumeration?
    -> NetExec

Need protocol-level tooling?
    -> Impacket

Need relationship / path analysis?
    -> BloodHound

Need AD CS analysis?
    -> Certipy

Need Windows host enumeration?
    -> PowerShell / Seatbelt / winPEAS

Need Linux-side AD queries?
    -> ldapsearch / Kerberos tools / Samba tools

No single tool provides a complete AD assessment.

docs.text:
Do not confuse:

Authentication Success

Administrative Access

Service Accessible
User Authorised

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
Use the BloodHound Cheatsheet to understand Active Directory relationships and privilege paths.

BloodHound is not simply a visualisation tool.

It helps answer:

Who can control what?

Which relationships create privilege?

Where are privileged sessions?

Which computers are strategically important?

Which ACLs create attack paths?

Which delegation relationships matter?

Which certificate relationships matter?

What is the shortest path to a sensitive object?

What should defenders remediate first?

More collection is not automatically better.

Coverage

Network Traffic

docs.title: BloodHound Analysis
docs.text:
High-value questions include:

What can the current user control?

What can the current user's groups control?

Where does the user have local administrator rights?

Where are privileged users logged on?

Which principals can modify privileged groups?

Which computers have paths to domain control?

Which ACL relationships are exploitable?

Which delegation paths exist?

Which certificate paths exist?

Which trust relationships expand the attack surface?

docs.title: BloodHound Edge Interpretation
docs.text:
Never report an edge solely because it exists.

For each relationship determine:

Source
Target
Edge Type
Required Privilege
Prerequisites
Reachability
Operational Constraints
Security Impact

Then validate the relationship independently where appropriate.

docs.title: Re-Enumeration
docs.text:
Re-enumeration is essential.

After obtaining:

New Credentials
New Group Membership
New Host Access
New Network Segment
New Certificate
New Kerberos Ticket
New API Role
New Application Role

repeat relevant enumeration.

Initial Access
     |
     v
Enumerate
     |
     v
New Access
     |
     v
Re-Enumerate
     |
     v
New Attack Surface

Do not assume the original attack surface remains complete after privilege changes.

docs.title: Context Before Commands
docs.text:
A command without context is easy to misuse.

Before using a command ask:

What question am I answering?

What permissions do I currently have?

What protocol does this use?

What traffic will it generate?

Could it modify state?

Could it expose credentials?

Could it affect another user?

Could it trigger account lockout?

Could it cause service disruption?

What evidence do I need?

docs.title: Safe Validation
docs.text:
Prefer the least intrusive test that proves the issue.

Observation
    |
    v
Hypothesis
    |
    v
Low-Impact Test
    |
    v
Confirmed?
    |
    +--> No -> Reassess
    |
    +--> Yes
           |
           v
      Minimum Evidence

Do not automatically escalate from:

Can enumerate

to:

Can exploit

if enumeration already proves the relevant security weakness.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Good evidence should answer:

What was tested?

When was it tested?

From where?

As which user?

Against which target?

What command or request was used?

What was the relevant output?

What changed?

What security boundary was crossed?

docs.title: Evidence Quality
docs.text:
Prefer:

Relevant Command
Relevant Output
Target
Identity
Timestamp
Short Explanation

Avoid:

Huge terminal dumps
Unrelated secrets
Full credential databases
Unnecessary personal data
Screenshots without context
Scanner output without validation

docs.title: Reporting Model
docs.text:
A defensible finding should connect:

Observation
     +
Prerequisites
     +
Security Boundary
     +
Reproducibility
     +
Impact
     =
Finding

docs.title: Do Not Overreport
docs.text:
Examples of observations that require context:

Port 445 is open
PowerShell is installed
PowerShell uses FullLanguage
rundll32.exe exists
A directory is writable
A domain user can query LDAP
SMB signing is disabled
A certificate template exists
A BloodHound edge exists
A technology version is visible
A security header is missing
A tool authenticates successfully

The question is:

What security boundary can be crossed because of this condition?

docs.title: Remediation Thinking
docs.text:
Do not stop at:

Disable Feature

Consider:

Why does the feature exist?

Who requires it?

What security boundary failed?

Can permissions be reduced?

Can access be segmented?

Can stronger authentication be applied?

Can monitoring detect abuse?

Can the dangerous relationship be removed?

Can the architecture eliminate the path?

docs.title: Purple Team Perspective
docs.text:
The same cheatsheets can support purple teaming.

For each technique:

Red Team

    v

    |

Blue Team

    v

    +--> Yes -> Evaluate Quality
    |
    +--> No  -> Identify Gap

                    v

                    |
                    v
                  Re-Test

Useful questions:

Was the activity logged?

Which host produced telemetry?

Which identity was visible?

Which process was visible?

Which protocol was visible?

Did the SIEM receive the event?

Was an alert generated?

Was the alert actionable?

Could the analyst reconstruct the activity?

docs.title: Active Directory Pentesting Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Quick-reference methodology, commands, enumeration paths and security-control checks for authorised Active Directory penetration testing and red-team assessments.

This cheatsheet is designed around an important principle:

Do not assume credentials.
Do not assume domain membership.
Do not assume local access.
Do not assume administrative privileges.

Instead, determine where the assessment begins:

                    START
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |                       |
       External                 Internal
          |                       |
    No AD Access          +-------+-------+
                          |               |
                    Unauthenticated   Authenticated
                          |               |
                          |          Domain User
                          |               |
                          +-------+-------+
                                  |
                           AD Enumeration
                                  |
                           Attack Paths
                                  |
                         Host Assessment
                                  |
                      Privilege Escalation
                                  |
                         Lateral Movement
                                  |
                             AD CS
                                  |
                             Trusts
                                  |
                        Controlled Impact

Authorised testing only

Use these techniques only against Active Directory environments you own or are explicitly authorised to assess. Authentication testing, password spraying, coercion, relay, certificate abuse, credential access, privilege escalation and lateral movement can affect production systems. Follow the agreed scope, rate limits and rules of engagement.

For deeper explanations use:

Active Directory Notes

docs.title: Assessment Starting Positions
docs.text:
Before running tools, identify your starting position.

Position Credentials Network Access Typical Objective External None Internet only Discover exposed AD-related services Internal unauthenticated None Internal network Discover domain infrastructure Internal authenticated Domain user Internal network Enumerate AD and attack paths Local Windows user Local/domain account Endpoint Host + AD enumeration Local administrator Administrative Endpoint Security-control and credential-path assessment Privileged domain user Elevated AD rights Internal network Validate privilege boundaries

The available attack surface changes dramatically between these positions.

docs.text:

Internet

Do not immediately assume Active Directory is unreachable.

Look for externally exposed identity infrastructure.

docs.title: External DNS
docs.text:
dig example.com

Name servers:

dig NS example.com

Mail:

dig MX example.com

TXT:

dig TXT example.com

SRV records where publicly exposed:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.example.com

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.com

docs.title: External Identity Infrastructure
docs.text:
Look for:

VPN
RD Gateway
OWA
Exchange
AD FS
Microsoft Entra ID
SSO
Remote Desktop Gateway
Citrix
VMware Horizon
Password Reset Portals
Webmail
Hybrid Authentication
Autodiscover

The objective is reconnaissance.

Do not attempt credential attacks unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: External Port Discovery
docs.text:
Where external infrastructure is in scope:

nmap -Pn -sV <target>

Potential AD-related exposure:

53    DNS
88    Kerberos
135   RPC
389   LDAP
445   SMB
464   Kerberos Password Change
636   LDAPS
3268  Global Catalog
3269  Global Catalog TLS
3389  RDP
5985  WinRM
5986  WinRM TLS

Direct exposure of these services to the Internet deserves investigation but is not automatically a vulnerability.

cat /etc/resolv.conf

docs.text:
ipconfig /all

route print

arp -a

docs.text:
Linux:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Windows:

ipconfig /all

docs.text: dig -x 10.10.10.10

docs.text:
Once the suspected domain is known:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

Global Catalog:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.gc._msdcs.example.local

nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

or:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

Hostnames

Domains
SMB Signing
SMB Availability

docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 --gen-relay-list relay.txt

nmap -p 445 --script smb2-security-mode 10.10.10.10

Important:

SMB Signing Not Required
          !=
Immediate Compromise

Relay still requires a usable authentication source and suitable target conditions.

docs.text:
nmap -p 445 --script smb-protocols 10.10.10.10

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 389

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 636

docs.text:
Where explicitly permitted:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://10.10.10.10 \
    -s base \
    namingContexts

If anonymous queries return useful directory information, determine exactly what is exposed before reporting.

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
nc -vz 10.10.10.10 88

Kerberos may support limited username validation depending on configuration and tooling.

Avoid high-volume enumeration.

docs.title: RPC
docs.text:
rpcclient -U '' -N 10.10.10.10

If anonymous/null-session access is permitted, begin with low-impact enumeration.

For example:

Domain Information
Users
Groups
Shares

Do not assume null sessions are enabled.

docs.title: Phase 3 - Authenticated Domain User
docs.text:
A normal domain account is extremely valuable for enumeration.

Starting point:

DOMAIN\user
      |
      v
Authenticated AD Access
      |
      v
Users
Groups
Computers
ACLs
GPOs
Kerberos
Delegation
AD CS
Trusts
Attack Paths

A standard domain account is not a low-value position.

Many AD privilege escalation paths begin with ordinary authenticated access.

whoami /priv

net accounts /domain

docs.text: Get-ADGroup -Filter *

docs.text:

docs.title: LDAP Enumeration
docs.text:
RootDSE:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
    -s base \
    namingContexts

Authenticated:

ldapsearch \
    -x \
    -H ldap://dc01.example.local \
    -D 'user@example.local' \
    -W \
    -b 'DC=example,DC=local'

Avoid putting passwords directly into command history.

docs.title: NetExec LDAP
docs.text:
nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

Users:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --users

Groups:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
