docs.title: NetExec SMB
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

Look for hosts where the authenticated user has administrative rights.

Do not immediately execute commands.

docs.title: Shares
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --shares

docs.title: Interesting Shares
docs.text:
Look for:

SYSVOL
NETLOGON
IT Shares
Deployment Shares
Software Distribution
Backups
User Shares
Scripts
Configuration Repositories
Administrative Shares

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
Windows:

dir \\example.local\SYSVOL

Linux:

smbclient //dc01.example.local/SYSVOL -U username

Review:

Logon Scripts
GPO Files
Configuration
Legacy Credentials
Deployment Scripts
References to Internal Systems

docs.title: NETLOGON
docs.text:
dir \\example.local\NETLOGON

Look for operational scripts and configuration.

docs.title: GPP Passwords
docs.text:
Legacy Group Policy Preferences may contain credential material.

Search SYSVOL for:

Groups.xml
Services.xml
Scheduledtasks.xml
DataSources.xml
Printers.xml
Drives.xml

Presence alone does not mean credentials are exposed.

docs.title: Kerberos
docs.text:
Tickets:

klist

Linux:

klist

docs.title: SPNs
docs.text:
Native:

setspn -Q */*

PowerShell:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties ServicePrincipalName |
    Where-Object ServicePrincipalName |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,ServicePrincipalName

docs.title: Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Identify accounts with SPNs:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
    example.local/username \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

Request service tickets where permitted:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
    example.local/username \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
    -request

The underlying issue is normally:

Service Account
      +
Kerberos SPN
      +
Weak Password

not simply the existence of an SPN.

docs.title: AS-REP Roastable Accounts
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-ADUser \
    -Filter 'DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true' \
    -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth

Impacket:

impacket-GetNPUsers \
    example.local/username \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
    -request

docs.title: Password Spraying
docs.text:
Never spray before checking lockout policy.

Password Policy
      |
      v
Fine-Grained Policies
      |
      v
Approved Accounts
      |
      v
Small Attempt Set
      |
      v
Observation Window
      |
      v
Controlled Testing

docs.title: BloodHound
docs.text:
BloodHound is valuable because Active Directory privilege escalation often depends on relationships rather than isolated misconfigurations.

Think:

User
 |
 v
Group
 |
 v
ACL
 |
 v
Computer
 |
 v
Session
 |
 v
Admin

See:

BloodHound Cheatsheet

docs.title: BloodHound Collection
docs.text:
Using SharpHound in an authorised Windows assessment:

SharpHound.exe -c All

Use collection options appropriate to the assessment.

Some collection methods can generate substantial network traffic.

docs.title: BloodHound Analysis
docs.text:
Useful starting queries:

Shortest Paths to Domain Admins
Shortest Paths to High Value Targets
Kerberoastable Users
AS-REP Roastable Users
Unconstrained Delegation
Principals with DCSync Rights
Users with Foreign Domain Group Membership
Computers with Unsupported Operating Systems

Do not treat every BloodHound edge as directly exploitable.

Validate:

Permission
Context
Reachability
Authentication
Security Controls

docs.title: ACLs
docs.text:
High-value rights can include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
ForceChangePassword
AddMember
AllExtendedRights
DCSync Rights
Validated-SPN
WriteProperty

docs.title: ACL Assessment Model
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   v
Permission
   |
   v
Target
   |
   v
Security Effect

Ask:

Who has the right?
What object does it affect?
Can the right change authentication or privilege?
Is inheritance involved?
Is the path actually reachable?

docs.title: Group Membership
docs.text:
Review:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Administrators
Account Operators
Backup Operators
Server Operators
DNSAdmins
Group Policy Creator Owners
Protected Users
Remote Desktop Users
Remote Management Users

Membership is context dependent.

Not every privileged-sounding group produces domain compromise.

docs.title: MachineAccountQuota
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-ADDomain |
    Select-Object DistinguishedName

Query directly where AD module access permits:

Get-ADObject \
    -Identity (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName \
    -Properties ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota |
    Select-Object ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota

A non-zero MachineAccountQuota is not automatically a vulnerability.

It becomes relevant when combined with another attack path.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
Identify:

Unconstrained Delegation
Constrained Delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation
S4U

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-ADComputer \
    -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} \
    -Properties TrustedForDelegation

docs.title: Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Get-ADUser \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo |
    Where-Object { $_.'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo' }

Computers:

Get-ADComputer \
    -Filter * \
    -Properties msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo |
    Where-Object { $_.'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo' }

docs.title: RBCD
docs.text:
Important attribute:

msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity

Assess:

Who can modify the target computer?
Who controls a usable security principal?
What SPNs exist?
What Kerberos path is possible?

docs.title: gMSA
docs.text:
Look for:

Group Managed Service Accounts
Principals Allowed to Retrieve Password
Service Usage
Group Membership
ACL Exposure

PowerShell:

Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter *

Do not retrieve password material unless required and authorised.

docs.title: LAPS
docs.text:
Determine whether the environment uses:

Legacy Microsoft LAPS
Windows LAPS

Then assess:

Who can read passwords?
Which computers are covered?
Are passwords rotating?
Are ACLs appropriately restricted?

docs.title: Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Relevant attribute:

msDS-KeyCredentialLink

The key question is:

Who can modify this attribute?

rather than simply whether the attribute exists.

docs.title: AD CS
docs.text:
Active Directory Certificate Services should be treated as a major AD attack surface.

Discovery:

Certificate Authorities
Certificate Templates
Enrollment Services
Web Enrollment
Certificate Permissions
Template Permissions
Enrollment Agent Configuration
Authentication EKUs

docs.title: Certipy Enumeration
docs.text:
Where authorised:

certipy find \
    -u user@example.local \
    -p 'Password' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
    -stdout

Focus potentially vulnerable configurations:

certipy find \
    -u user@example.local \
    -p 'Password' \
    -dc-ip 10.10.10.10 \
    -vulnerable \
    -stdout

Treat automated ESC classifications as leads requiring validation.

docs.title: AD CS ESC Overview
docs.text:
Keep the major categories in mind:

ESC1
ESC2
ESC3
ESC4
ESC5
ESC6
ESC7
ESC8
ESC9
ESC10
ESC11
ESC12
ESC13
ESC14
ESC15
ESC16
ESC17

See the dedicated:

AD CS Notes

docs.title: AD CS Questions
docs.text:
For every template ask:

Who can enroll?
What EKUs exist?
Can the subject be supplied?
Can SAN be supplied?
Is manager approval required?
Are signatures required?
Who controls the template?
Who controls the CA?
Can authentication certificates be issued?
Can another identity be represented?

docs.title: AD CS Web Enrollment
docs.text:
Look for:

/certsrv/

Where present, assess authentication and relay exposure according to scope.

Do not perform coercion or relay automatically.

docs.title: Trusts
docs.text:
Discover:

nltest /domain_trusts

PowerShell:

Get-ADTrust -Filter *

Forest:

Get-ADForest

docs.title: Trust Questions
docs.text:
Determine:

Direction
Transitivity
Forest vs Domain Trust
SID Filtering
Selective Authentication
Foreign Group Membership
Authentication Scope

docs.title: SID History
docs.text:
Review SID history where authorised:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties SIDHistory |
    Where-Object SIDHistory |
    Select-Object SamAccountName,SIDHistory

SIDHistory is legitimate functionality.

The security question is whether unexpected privileged historical SIDs exist.

docs.title: Host Assessment
docs.text:
Once local access to a Windows system exists, AD enumeration alone is insufficient.

Assess the endpoint.

Identity
   |
   v
Privileges
   |
   v
PowerShell
   |
   v
Application Control
   |
   v
Writable Locations
   |
   v
Services
   |
   v
Scheduled Tasks
   |
   v
Credentials / Configuration
   |
   v
Network Access

docs.title: Host Identity
docs.text:
whoami /all

hostname

systeminfo

docs.title: Local Users
docs.text: net user

docs.title: Local Groups
docs.text:
net localgroup

Administrators:

net localgroup administrators

docs.title: Current Privileges
docs.text:
whoami /priv

Pay attention to privileges such as:

SeImpersonatePrivilege
SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege
SeBackupPrivilege
SeRestorePrivilege
SeDebugPrivilege
SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege
SeLoadDriverPrivilege

Presence alone is not a vulnerability.

Determine:

Is it enabled?
What security context exists?
What resource can it affect?
Can privilege actually cross a security boundary?

docs.title: PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible results:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

Interpret carefully.

FullLanguage
     !=
Vulnerability

FullLanguage is the normal PowerShell language mode when application control is not enforcing restrictions.

For hardened workstations, kiosks, jump hosts and other high-security endpoints, FullLanguage may indicate that PowerShell is not being constrained by application-control policy.

docs.title: PowerShell Version
docs.text: $PSVersionTable

docs.title: Execution Policy
docs.text:
Get-ExecutionPolicy -List

Important:

Execution Policy
       !=
Security Boundary

Do not report a permissive execution policy as an independent privilege escalation vulnerability.

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
Effective policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Summary:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType,EnforcementMode

Look for:

Exe
Script
MSI
DLL
Appx

docs.title: AppLocker Rule Collections
docs.text:
(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Format-List

Important:

Rule Exists
    !=
Secure Policy

Binary Allowed
    !=
Vulnerability

Binary Blocked
    !=
All Execution Prevented

Evaluate the complete execution-control model.

docs.title: Test-AppLockerPolicy
docs.text:
For a known file:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy \
        -Path 'C:\Path\To\File.exe' \
        -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

PowerShell does not use Bash-style backslash continuation.

Prefer a one-liner:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective | Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path 'C:\Path\To\File.exe' -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

docs.title: AppLocker Default Path Risk
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to broad path rules such as:

%WINDIR%\*
%PROGRAMFILES%\*

These rules are safe only when standard users cannot write attacker-controlled files into allowed locations.

Therefore:

Allowed Path
    +
User Writable
    =
Execution-Control Concern

docs.title: App Control / WDAC
docs.text:
App Control for Business is Microsoft's preferred application-control technology.

Look for deployed policy information using supported administrative tooling available on the endpoint.

Do not conclude WDAC is absent merely because one particular query method fails.

Windows versions and management configurations differ.

docs.title: PowerShell + Application Control
docs.text:
Important relationship:

Application Control
        |
        v
PowerShell System Lockdown
        |
        v
Constrained Language

Therefore check both:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

and:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

where available.

docs.title: PowerShell Logging
docs.text:
Where access permits, assess:

Script Block Logging
Module Logging
Transcription
PowerShell Operational Logs

Event log:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational' -MaxEvents 20

Do not disable logging during an assessment.

docs.title: AMSI
docs.text:
AMSI is another defence layer.

Assess whether security products and PowerShell integrate correctly with AMSI.

Do not treat AMSI as a substitute for:

Application Control
Least Privilege
EDR
Logging
Attack Surface Reduction

docs.title: Defender
docs.text:
Where available:

Get-MpComputerStatus

Useful fields include:

AntivirusEnabled
RealTimeProtectionEnabled
BehaviorMonitorEnabled
AntispywareEnabled
AMServiceEnabled

docs.title: Defender Preferences
docs.text:
Where permissions allow:

Get-MpPreference

Review:

Exclusions
ASR Configuration
Cloud Protection
Controlled Folder Access
Network Protection

Do not modify these settings during enumeration.

docs.title: ASR Rules
docs.text:
Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids,AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

Interpret rule IDs against current Microsoft documentation.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
netsh advfirewall show allprofiles

Rules:

netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name=all

docs.title: Writable Directory Assessment
docs.text:
This is particularly important when application-control policies trust directories.

Common locations to assess include:

C:\Temp
C:\Windows\Temp
C:\ProgramData
C:\Users\Public
%TEMP%
%TMP%
%LOCALAPPDATA%
%APPDATA%
Custom Application Directories
Deployment Directories
Service Directories
Script Directories

Do not assume these are writable.

Test permissions.

docs.title: Current Temporary Directory
docs.text:
CMD:

echo %TEMP%

echo %TMP%

PowerShell:

$env:TEMP
$env:TMP

docs.title: ACL Inspection
docs.text:
icacls C:\Temp

icacls C:\Windows\Temp

icacls C:\ProgramData

docs.title: Common ACL Indicators
docs.text:
Look for:

F   Full Control
M   Modify
W   Write
RX  Read and Execute
R   Read

Principals of interest:

Everyone
BUILTIN\Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Users
Current User

docs.title: Writable Directory Validation
docs.text:
Permission listings can be complex.

When authorised, a harmless create/delete test is often clearer.

PowerShell:

$p='C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder'; $f=Join-Path $p "write-test-$PID.tmp"; try { New-Item -ItemType File -Path $f -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null; Write-Host '[+] Writable'; Remove-Item $f -Force } catch { Write-Host '[-] Not writable' }

This verifies actual write capability without executing code.

docs.title: Search Common Writable Locations
docs.text:
PowerShell:

$paths = @(
    $env:TEMP,
    'C:\Temp',
    'C:\Windows\Temp',
    'C:\ProgramData',
    'C:\Users\Public'
)

foreach ($path in $paths) {
    if (Test-Path $path) {
        Write-Host "`n=== $path ==="
        icacls $path
    }
}

docs.title: Writable PATH Directories
docs.text:
Display PATH:

echo %PATH%

PowerShell:

$env:PATH -split ';'

Review whether standard users can modify directories referenced in PATH.

Do not report a writable PATH directory without identifying a privileged process that relies on unsafe path resolution.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
List:

sc query

Detailed:

sc qc ServiceName

PowerShell:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

docs.title: Service Assessment
docs.text:
For each interesting service determine:

Service Account
Executable Path
Arguments
Directory Permissions
Binary Permissions
Service ACL
Start Mode
Current State

Potential risk:

Privileged Service
      +
User Writable Binary / Directory
      =
Privilege Escalation Candidate

docs.title: Search Services for Candidate Directory
docs.text:
$needle = [regex]::Escape('C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder')

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object PathName -Match $needle |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

docs.title: Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object {
        $_.PathName -match ' ' -and
        $_.PathName -notmatch '^"'
    } |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,PathName

Important:

Unquoted Path
     !=
Exploitable

You must also identify a location in the resolution chain that the current user can write to.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

Review:

Principal
Run Level
Action
Executable
Arguments
Trigger
Writable Script
Writable Binary
Writable Directory

docs.title: Scheduled Task Assessment
docs.text:
Potential path:

Privileged Task
      +
User Writable Action
      =
Privilege Escalation Candidate

Do not modify production tasks merely to prove the issue.

docs.title: Startup Locations
docs.text:
Review:

Startup Folder
Run Keys
RunOnce Keys
Services
Scheduled Tasks
Winlogon
Application Startup Configuration

Current user Run key:

reg query HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

Machine:

reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

docs.title: AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
Check both locations:

reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated

reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated

Both configuration conditions matter.

Do not generate or execute an MSI merely to confirm the registry configuration unless explicitly required.

docs.title: Installed Software
docs.text:
Registry:

reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall

64-bit and 32-bit environments may use additional registry locations.

PowerShell:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher

Avoid Win32_Product for routine enumeration because it can trigger MSI consistency checks.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
driverquery /v

Review old or unusual third-party drivers as potential security-relevant components.

Version presence alone does not prove vulnerability.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
tasklist /v

Services:

tasklist /svc

PowerShell:

Get-Process

docs.title: Listening Ports
docs.text:
netstat -ano

Map PID:

tasklist /fi "PID eq 1234"

docs.title: Network Connections
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-NetTCPConnection

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
Check service:

sc query TermService

Port:

netstat -ano | findstr :3389

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
sc query WinRM

Ports:

netstat -ano | findstr :5985

netstat -ano | findstr :5986

docs.title: Credential Manager
docs.text:
Safe inventory:

cmdkey /list

This reveals stored credential targets.

Do not automatically attempt credential extraction.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Look for security-relevant configuration in:

Web Applications
Deployment Scripts
Backup Scripts
Database Clients
Scheduled Jobs
Automation
Build Systems
Service Configuration

Search narrowly rather than recursively reading every user file.

docs.title: Common File Names
docs.text:
Potentially interesting:

web.config
appsettings.json
application.properties
settings.xml
unattend.xml
unattended.xml
sysprep.xml
*.config
*.ini
*.kdbx
*.rdp

Presence does not imply exposed credentials.

docs.title: PowerShell History
docs.text:
Location:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Inspect only where authorised.

History may contain sensitive information.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
CMD:

set

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Look for configuration rather than assuming every variable is secret.

docs.title: Security Products
docs.text:

docs.title: Lateral Movement Assessment
docs.text:
After obtaining authorised access to another identity or host, determine:

Where can this identity authenticate?
Where is it administrator?
Which protocols are available?
Which security controls apply?

Possible protocols:

SMB
WinRM
WMI
DCOM
RDP
SSH
MSSQL

Do not automatically execute remote commands simply because authentication succeeds.

docs.title: NetExec Administrative Access
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

Interpret administrative markers carefully.

Validate the account's intended permissions before treating access as excessive.

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
Check:

nxc winrm 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

Successful authentication does not necessarily mean the account has unrestricted administrative rights.

docs.title: DCSync Exposure
docs.text:
DCSync-relevant directory replication rights include combinations of replication extended rights.

BloodHound can identify principals with replication privileges.

Treat these rights as highly sensitive.

Do not perform actual credential replication unless explicitly required and authorised.

docs.title: Example - Writable Directory
docs.text:
Weak conclusion:

C:\ProgramData\Example is writable.

Better analysis:

C:\ProgramData\Example
       |
       v
Writable by standard users
       |
       v
Contains executable used by service
       |
       v
Service runs as LocalSystem
       |
       v
Service consumes user-controlled file

Now a security boundary may exist.

docs.text:

        v

        |
        v
Is that content permitted?
        |
        v
Does this cross the intended application-control boundary?

        v

        |
        v
Untrusted Code Capability
        |
        v
Does this violate intended execution restrictions?

Services
   ->

The most important question is not:

What tool can I run?

It is:

What security context do I currently have?

What can that identity control?

What security boundary exists?

What other principal or system consumes that control?

Can the relationship be converted into meaningful security impact?

That model turns Active Directory enumeration into an actual security assessment rather than a collection of tool output.

docs.title: Authorised Use
docs.text:
Use BloodHound and related collectors only for authorised:

Penetration testing
Internal security assessments
Red team exercises
Purple team exercises
Identity security reviews
Active Directory reviews
Training environments
CTFs
Security research

BloodHound collection can generate:

LDAP queries
DNS queries
Kerberos activity
SMB connections
RPC connections
Session enumeration
Local group enumeration
Registry queries
Authentication events
Endpoint telemetry

Always remain within the agreed scope and rules of engagement.

docs.title: What BloodHound Does
docs.text:
BloodHound models identity relationships as a graph.

Instead of asking only:

Who is Domain Admin?

BloodHound helps answer:

Who can influence Domain Admin?

Who controls privileged groups?

Who controls computers used by privileged users?

Which identities have dangerous ACL rights?

Which identities can modify GPOs?

Where do privileged sessions exist?

Which delegation relationships create risk?

Which certificate relationships create privilege paths?

Which trusts create cross-domain paths?

Which permissions connect low privilege to high privilege?

pipx install bloodhound-ce

Check:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

docs.title: Legacy BloodHound.py
docs.text:
Legacy environments may use:

pipx install bloodhound

Command:

bloodhound-python

Use the collector matching the BloodHound generation being analysed.

docs.title: BloodHound.py CE Help
docs.text:
bloodhound-ce-python --help

Treat the installed command's help as the version-specific reference.

docs.title: BloodHound.py Authentication
docs.text:
Depending on collector version, authentication can involve:

Username + Password
NTLM
Kerberos
Kerberos Credential Cache

Confirm exact options:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

docs.title: Basic BloodHound.py CE Pattern
docs.text:
bloodhound-ce-python -u alice -p 'Password' -d example.local -ns 10.10.20.10 -c All

Warning

Supplying passwords on the command line can expose them through shell history, screenshots and process inspection.

docs.title: ZIP Output
docs.text:
Where supported:

bloodhound-ce-python -u alice -p 'Password' -d example.local -ns 10.10.20.10 -c All --zip

docs.title: Specify Domain Controller
docs.text:
Typical pattern:

bloodhound-ce-python -u alice -p 'Password' -d example.local -dc dc01.example.local -ns 10.10.20.10 -c All --zip

Verify current syntax:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

docs.title: Focused BloodHound.py Collection
docs.text:
Instead of immediately using:

-c All

consider focused methods such as:

bloodhound-ce-python -u alice -p 'Password' -d example.local -ns 10.10.20.10 -c Group,ACL,Trusts

Exact collection methods depend on collector version.

docs.title: Kerberos Collection
docs.text:
If using a credential cache:

export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/alice.ccache"

Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

klist

Then inspect supported Kerberos options:

bloodhound-ce-python --help

docs.title: Kerberos Collection Model
docs.text:
ccache
   |
   v
Correct Principal?
   |
   v
Correct Realm?
   |
   v
DNS Working?
   |
   v
DC FQDN?
   |
   v
Time Correct?
   |
   v
Collection

docs.title: BloodHound.py Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If collection fails:

1. Verify CE vs legacy collector
2. Verify DNS
3. Verify domain
4. Verify DC FQDN
5. Verify credentials
6. Verify LDAP
7. Verify SMB if required
8. Verify Kerberos
9. Verify collection methods
10. Verify collector version

docs.title: Collector Differences
docs.text:
Do not assume:

BloodHound.py All
       =
SharpHound All

Different collectors may have different capabilities or implementation details.

Therefore:

Relationship Missing
       |
       v
Configuration Absent?
       |
       OR
       |
Collector Did Not Collect It?

docs.title: BloodHound CE
docs.text:
BloodHound CE provides interactive graph analysis.

Typical workflow:

Collection
    |
    v
BloodHound CE
    |
    v
Ingest
    |
    v
Graph
    |
    v
Relationships
    |
    v
Paths

Follow the official CE installation documentation for the current deployment method.

Do not expose assessment infrastructure to untrusted networks.

docs.title: First Analysis Steps
docs.text:
After ingestion:

1. Confirm domain
2. Confirm collection timestamp
3. Review collection health
4. Confirm collector and methods
5. Mark controlled principals
6. Identify high-value assets
7. Review group relationships
8. Review administrative relationships
9. Review ACLs
10. Review sessions
11. Review delegation
12. Review GPO control
13. Review AD CS
14. Review trusts
15. Review replication rights
16. Investigate candidate paths

docs.title: Mark Owned Principals
docs.text:
When an identity is confirmed under the assessment:

Known Credential
      |
      v
Confirmed Identity
      |
      v
Mark Owned
      |
      v
Analyse Outbound Paths

Only mark identities as owned when control has actually been established.

docs.title: Mark High-Value Assets
docs.text:
Default high-value objects are useful, but also consider organisation-specific assets.

Examples:

Domain Controllers
Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Certificate Authorities
Identity Servers
Backup Infrastructure
Virtualisation Platforms
SCCM
AD FS
Privileged Access Workstations
Tier-0 Systems
Critical Application Servers

docs.title: Graph Basics
docs.text:
Node
   =
Object

Edge
   =
Relationship

Example:

ALICE
  |
  | MemberOf
  v
HELPDESK
  |
  | AdminTo
  v
APP01

docs.title: Common Node Types
docs.text:
Examples include:

User
Group
Computer
Domain
OU
GPO
Certificate Authority
Certificate Template
Root CA
Enterprise CA

The BloodHound schema evolves over time.

docs.title: Relationship Families
docs.text:
Think about edges in categories.

Identity Relationships
    |
    +--> MemberOf
    +--> SIDHistory

Host Relationships
    |
    +--> AdminTo
    +--> HasSession
    +--> CanRDP
    +--> CanPSRemote
    +--> ExecuteDCOM

ACL Relationships
    |
    +--> GenericAll
    +--> GenericWrite
    +--> WriteDacl
    +--> WriteOwner
    +--> AddMember
    +--> ForceChangePassword

Kerberos Relationships
    |
    +--> Delegation
    +--> RBCD

Policy Relationships
    |
    +--> GPO Control
    +--> OU / Container Relationships

PKI Relationships
    |
    +--> Enrollment
    +--> Template Control
    +--> CA Control

Domain Relationships
    |
    +--> Trusts
    +--> Replication Rights

docs.title: Edge Interpretation Rule
docs.text:
Never use:

Edge Exists
    =
Exploit Confirmed

Use:

Edge
 |
 v
Read Edge Meaning
 |
 v
Identify Required Permission
 |
 v
Identify Target Object
 |
 v
Check Preconditions
 |
 v
Check Reachability
 |
 v
Check Controls
 |
 v
Determine Impact
 |
 v
Validate Only If Necessary

docs.title: MemberOf
docs.text:
User
 |
 | MemberOf
 v
Group

Always account for nested membership:

User
 |
 v
Group A
 |
 v
Group B
 |
 v
Privileged Group

docs.title: AdminTo
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | AdminTo
   v
Computer

This indicates an administrative relationship.

It does not automatically prove:

Host reachable
SMB reachable
WinRM reachable
Remote execution possible
Endpoint controls permit execution
Testing is authorised

docs.title: HasSession
docs.text:
User
 |
 | HasSession
 v
Computer

Treat session data as:

Dynamic
Time-Sensitive
Collector-Dependent

A session observed yesterday may not exist today.

docs.title: CanRDP
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | CanRDP
   v
Computer

Validate separately:

3389 reachable
RDP enabled
Network path exists
Identity accepted
NLA requirements
MFA requirements
Host restrictions

docs.title: CanPSRemote
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | CanPSRemote
   v
Computer

Check:

WinRM reachable
5985 / 5986
Authentication
Remote management permissions
Network controls
PowerShell policy
Endpoint configuration

docs.title: ExecuteDCOM
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | ExecuteDCOM
   v
Computer

Usability can depend on:

RPC
DCOM
Firewall
Permissions
Endpoint controls

docs.title: ACL Relationships
docs.text:
High-value ACL relationships can include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDacl
WriteOwner
ForceChangePassword
AddMember
Owns
Property-Specific Rights
Extended Rights

docs.title: GenericAll
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | GenericAll
   v
Object

Impact depends on object type.

User
Group
Computer
OU
GPO
Certificate Template
Other AD Object

Do not describe all GenericAll relationships as equivalent.

docs.title: GenericWrite
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | GenericWrite
   v
Object

Remember:

GenericWrite
    !=
GenericAll

Determine which attributes are relevant to the target object.

docs.title: WriteDacl
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | WriteDacl
   v
Object

Potentially high impact because ACLs define who can perform actions on the object.

Validation that changes a DACL modifies directory state.

Prefer ACL inspection as evidence where possible.

docs.title: WriteOwner
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | WriteOwner
   v
Object

Changing ownership is a state-changing operation.

Ask:

Who currently owns it?

Who can change ownership?

What can the new owner subsequently modify?

Is ownership change necessary to prove impact?

docs.title: ForceChangePassword
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | ForceChangePassword
   v
User

Do not reset a production user's password merely to prove the edge.

The ACL may already provide sufficient evidence.

docs.title: AddMember
docs.text:
Concept:

Principal
   |
   | AddMember
   v
Group

Then ask:

What does the group control?

Is membership nested?

Is the group privileged?

Would adding a member change production state?

Can the impact be demonstrated without modifying membership?

docs.title: Owns
docs.text:
Principal
   |
   | Owns
   v
Object

Ownership can influence the ability to modify the object's security descriptor.

Investigate the actual ACL and owner semantics before determining impact.

docs.title: ACL Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
Interesting ACL
      |
      v
Which Principal?
      |
      v
Which Object?
      |
      v
Which Right?
      |
      v
Inherited or Explicit?
      |
      v
What Can Actually Be Changed?
      |
      v
What Security Boundary Changes?
      |
      v
Evidence Sufficient?

docs.title: DCSync
docs.text:
BloodHound can identify principals with directory replication relationships.

Concept:

Principal
   |
   +--> GetChanges
   |
   +--> GetChangesAll
   |
   v
Domain

Depending on configuration, additional replication-related rights can also matter.

Treat unexpected replication rights as high impact.

Do not replicate production credential material unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: DCSync Analysis
docs.text:
Ask:

Which identity has the rights?

Are the rights direct or inherited?

Were they intentionally delegated?

Is the identity Tier-0?

Can the rights access domain credential material?

Can the condition be demonstrated without dumping the domain?

docs.title: Kerberoastable Accounts
docs.text:
BloodHound can help identify service accounts and their relationships.

Do not report:

Kerberoastable

as a vulnerability by itself.

Assess:

SPN
 |
 v
Account
 |
 v
Password Age
 |
 v
Password Strength
 |
 v
Privileges
 |
 v
Reachable Assets
 |
 v
Security Impact

docs.title: AS-REP Roastable Accounts
docs.text:
Likewise:

Preauthentication Disabled
        |
        v
Account Context
        |
        v
Password Security
        |
        v
Privileges
        |
        v
Impact

The configuration matters more when combined with weak credential hygiene or excessive privilege.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
Review:

Unconstrained Delegation
Constrained Delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation
S4U Relationships

BloodHound provides relationship context.

Use:

Active Directory Cheatsheet

and the detailed delegation notes for prerequisite analysis.

docs.title: Unconstrained Delegation
docs.text:
Investigate:

Which computer/account?

Domain Controller or non-DC?

Which users can authenticate there?

Are privileged identities protected?

Is the configuration still required?

docs.title: Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Investigate:

Delegating Principal
Target SPN
Protocol Transition
Who Controls Delegating Principal
Target Service
Security Boundary

docs.title: RBCD
docs.text:
Relevant relationships may involve:

Computer Control
AllowedToAct
Object ACLs
Machine Accounts

Concept:

Controlled Principal
       |
       v
RBCD Relationship
       |
       v
Target Computer
       |
       v
Kerberos S4U
       |
       v
Target Service

See:

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: Machine Account Relationships
docs.text:
When a path involves computer creation or control, also consider:

MachineAccountQuota
Existing Computer Objects
Computer ACLs
RBCD
Who Can Create Computer Objects
Which OU Receives Them

docs.title: Group Policy
docs.text:
Investigate:

Who can modify the GPO?

Who owns the GPO?

Where is it linked?

Which OUs receive it?

Which computers receive it?

Which users receive it?

Can a low-privileged identity influence it?

Is the GPO Tier-0 relevant?

Concept:

Principal
   |
   v
GPO
   |
   v
OU
   |
   v
Computers / Users

docs.title: GPO Path Analysis
docs.text:
Write Right
    |
    v
GPO
    |
    v
Linked OU
    |
    v
Affected Objects
    |
    v
Privilege Context

Do not stop analysis at:

Can modify GPO

Determine what the GPO actually influences.

docs.title: AD CS
docs.text:
Modern BloodHound can model certificate-related relationships.

Review:

Certificate Authorities
Enterprise CAs
Certificate Templates
Enrollment Rights
Template Permissions
CA Permissions
Certificate Mappings
Authentication Relationships

Use Certipy and the dedicated AD CS notes for deeper validation.

docs.title: AD CS Analysis Model
docs.text:
Principal
    |
    v
Enrollment / Control Right
    |
    v
Certificate Template
    |
    v
Certificate Authority
    |
    v
Authentication Capability
    |
    v
Privilege Boundary

Do not rely only on an ESC label.

Understand the underlying configuration.

docs.title: AD CS Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Who can enroll?

Who controls the template?

Who controls the CA?

What EKUs are configured?

Can the subject be supplied?

Is manager approval required?

Are authorised signatures required?

How are certificates mapped?

Which identities could be represented?

Is the CA trusted for authentication?

docs.title: Trusts
docs.text:
Review:

Trust Direction
Trust Type
Transitivity
SID Filtering
Selective Authentication
Cross-Domain Groups
Cross-Domain ACLs
Cross-Domain Sessions
Cross-Domain Administrative Rights

docs.title: Trust Mental Model
docs.text:
Domain A
   |
   | Trust
   v
Domain B
   |
   v
Authentication Boundary
   |
   v
Authorisation Relationships

A trust does not automatically mean:

Domain A owns Domain B

docs.title: SIDHistory
docs.text:
SID history can create cross-object or cross-domain privilege relationships.

Investigate:

Which object has SIDHistory?

Which SID is present?

Does the SID still map to a privileged object?

Is SID filtering relevant?

Is the value expected?

docs.title: High-Value Targets
docs.text:
Common examples:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Domain Controllers
Tier-0 Systems
Certificate Authorities
Identity Infrastructure
Privileged Service Accounts
Backup Infrastructure
SCCM
AD FS
Virtualisation Management
Privileged Access Workstations

Also define organisation-specific high-value systems.

docs.title: Tier-0 Analysis
docs.text:
Do not limit Tier-0 to:

Domain Controllers

Consider systems or identities capable of controlling:

Active Directory
Domain Controllers
PKI
Identity Federation
Privileged Management
Virtualisation Hosting DCs
Backup / Restore of DCs
Security Management of Tier-0

docs.title: Sessions on Privileged Systems
docs.text:
Review:

Privileged User
      |
      v
HasSession
      |
      v
Lower-Trust Computer

This may indicate a tiering issue even without constructing an offensive path.

docs.title: Local Administrator Sprawl
docs.text:
BloodHound is useful defensively for identifying:

One User
   |
   +--> AdminTo Host A
   +--> AdminTo Host B
   +--> AdminTo Host C
   +--> AdminTo Host D

Questions:

Is this expected?

Is a shared admin account used?

Are workstation and server tiers separated?

Could compromise of one credential affect many systems?

docs.title: Shortest Paths
docs.text:
Shortest paths are useful for triage.

Owned Principal
      |
      v
Shortest Path
      |
      v
High-Value Target

But:

Shortest
   !=
Safest

Shortest
   !=
Most Reliable

Shortest
   !=
Least Detectable

Shortest
   !=
Most Important

docs.title: Path Prioritisation
docs.text:
Consider:

Path Length
Privileges Required
Credential Availability
Network Reachability
State Changes
Operational Impact
Detection Surface
Business Impact
Rules of Engagement
Reliability
Currentness of Data

docs.title: Path Validation
docs.text:
Candidate Path
      |
      v
Relationship Current?
      |
      v
Correct Identity?
      |
      v
Reachable?
      |
      v
Prerequisites Present?
      |
      v
Security Controls?
      |
      v
Safe?
      |
      v
Authorised?
      |
      v
Minimal Validation

docs.title: Attack Path vs Finding
docs.text:
A path can contain multiple security conditions.

Example:

Low-Privilege User
       |
       v
WriteDacl
       |
       v
Helpdesk Group
       |
       v
AdminTo
       |
       v
Application Server

Possible findings might concern:

Excessive AD ACL
Excessive Group Privilege
Administrative Tiering

Do not automatically report the entire graph path as one vague finding.

docs.title: Choke Points
docs.text:
Some relationships appear in many paths.

Concept:

Path A ---+
          |
Path B ---+--> Shared Relationship --> High Value
          |
Path C ---+

These are particularly useful for defensive remediation.

Removing one unnecessary relationship may eliminate many attack paths.

docs.title: Path Remediation Model
docs.text:
Attack Paths
      |
      v
Common Relationship
      |
      v
Why Does It Exist?
      |
      v
Business Requirement?
      |
   +--+--+
   |     |
  Yes    No
   |     |
   v     v
Harden Remove
   |     |
   +--+--+
      |
      v
Re-Collect
      |
      v
Verify Paths Removed

docs.title: BloodBash
docs.text:
BloodBash provides offline analysis of SharpHound and AzureHound collection data without requiring a BloodHound server.

It is useful for:

Fast day-zero triage
Offline analysis
Terminal workflows
Attack-path analysis
Owned-user analysis
Collection comparison
AD / Entra analysis
Remediation analysis
Report generation
Large dataset triage

docs.title: BloodBash Installation
docs.text:
Using pipx:

pipx install git+https://github.com/DotNetRussell/BloodBash

Check:

bloodbash --help

Advanced help:

bloodbash --help-advanced

docs.title: BloodBash Standalone Binary
docs.text:
The project also publishes standalone binaries.

After obtaining the approved release:

chmod +x bloodbash-linux-x64

Run:

./bloodbash-linux-x64 ./sharpout --all

Verify release provenance before using downloaded security tooling.

docs.title: BloodBash Quick Analysis
docs.text:
Directory:

bloodbash ./sharpout

The default performs quick-win analysis.

Explicit:

bloodbash ./sharpout --quick-wins

ZIP:

bloodbash ./collection.zip --quick-wins

docs.title: BloodBash Quick-Wins Model
docs.text:
Current quick-win analysis can surface high-signal areas such as:

Unexpected DCSync
AD CS
Dangerous ACLs
Interesting non-high-value ACLs
RBCD
Can-configure RBCD
Unconstrained Delegation
Constrained Delegation
Shadow Credentials
LAPS Readers
Trusts
Kerberoastable Accounts
AS-REP Accounts
Privileged Roastable Accounts
Password-in-Description
PasswordNotRequired
Sessions
Local Admin Relationships
Collection Health
Shortest Paths
Busiest Paths
Path Breaks

Treat these as analysis leads, not automatically confirmed vulnerabilities.

docs.title: BloodBash Full Analysis
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --all

Large graph:

bloodbash ./sharpout --all --fast

docs.title: BloodBash Wizard
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --wizard

Useful when exploring an unfamiliar collection.

docs.title: List Domains
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --list-domains

docs.title: Domain Filter
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --all --domain EXAMPLE.LOCAL

docs.title: Owned User Workflow
docs.text:
If alice is a confirmed controlled identity:

bloodbash ./sharpout --from-user alice --from-user-export

Concept:

Owned User
    |
    v
Nested Groups
    |
    v
Administrative Rights
    |
    v
ACL Rights
    |
    v
Paths to High Value

docs.title: Inspect Owned User
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --from-user alice --inspect alice

docs.title: Explicit Path
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --path-from alice --path-to 'domain admins@corp.local'

Multiple sources:

bloodbash ./sharpout --path-from alice,bob --path-to 'domain admins,enterprise admins'

docs.title: Shortest Paths
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --shortest-paths

Include indirect relationships:

bloodbash ./sharpout --shortest-paths --indirect --fast

docs.title: Busiest Paths
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --busiest-paths short --busiest-paths-top 10

This can help identify principals or relationships appearing repeatedly across paths.

docs.title: Path Break Analysis
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --path-break --path-break-top 20

This is especially useful defensively.

Many Paths
    |
    v
Shared Edge
    |
    v
Path Break Candidate
    |
    v
Business Review
    |
    v
Remediation

docs.title: Deep Analysis
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --deep-analysis

Useful for slower graph operations such as group nesting and cycle analysis.

docs.title: Inspect Node
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --inspect 'DOMAIN ADMINS@CORP.LOCAL'

docs.title: Merge Collections
docs.text:
bloodbash ./lowpriv.zip --merge ./additional.zip --all --fast

Multiple collections:

bloodbash ./forest-root --merge ./child-a.zip ./child-b.zip --quick-wins

docs.title: Why Merge Collections?
docs.text:
Useful when:

Initial low-privilege collection exists

New privilege produced additional data

Another subnet became reachable

A child domain was discovered

Collection occurred at different stages

Multiple collectors produced complementary data

docs.title: Collection Comparison Model
docs.text:
Collection A
    |
    +----+
         |
         v
      Merge
         ^
         |
    +----+
    |
Collection B

Be careful with time-sensitive relationships such as sessions when merging collections from different times.

docs.title: BloodBash Inventory
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --inventory

docs.title: Password Age
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --password-age

docs.title: Stale Accounts
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --stale-accounts

docs.title: Privilege Inventory
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --privilege-inventory

docs.title: Combined Inventory
docs.text: bloodbash ./sharpout --stale-accounts --password-age --privilege-inventory

docs.title: Owned Inventory
docs.text:
bloodbash ./sharpout --owned alice --owned-inventory

Note the distinction:

--from-user
    =
Outbound analysis from controlled principal

--owned
    =
Owned-principal-oriented path/inventory analysis

Use current help for exact semantics.

docs.title: BloodBash Profiles
docs.text:
Quick:

bloodbash ./sharpout --profile quick

Quick wins:

bloodbash ./sharpout --profile quick-wins

AD CS:

bloodbash ./sharpout --profile adcs-heavy

Hygiene:

bloodbash ./sharpout --profile hygiene

Custom:

bloodbash ./sharpout --profile ./my-engagement.yaml

docs.title: Trust Analysis
docs.text:

docs.title: Cypher Basics
docs.text:
Legacy/general graph example:

MATCH (n)
RETURN n
LIMIT 10

docs.text:
MATCH (u:User)
RETURN u
LIMIT 25

docs.title: List Groups

RETURN g
LIMIT 25

docs.text:
MATCH (c:Computer)
RETURN c
LIMIT 25

docs.title: MemberOf Relationships
docs.text:
MATCH (u:User)-[:MemberOf]->(g:Group)
RETURN u,g
LIMIT 50

docs.text:
MATCH p=(u:User)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)
RETURN p
LIMIT 50

docs.title: Administrative Relationships
docs.text:

RETURN u,c
LIMIT 50

docs.text:

LIMIT 50

docs.title: Domain Admin Membership
docs.text:
Conceptual legacy query:

MATCH p=(u)-[:MemberOf*1..]->(g:Group)
WHERE g.name CONTAINS 'DOMAIN ADMINS'
RETURN p

Graph schemas differ between BloodHound generations.

Always validate queries against the environment being used.

docs.title: Better Analysis Questions
docs.text:
Do not ask only:

How do I reach Domain Admin?

Also ask:

Which users have excessive ACL rights?

Which groups control many systems?

Which identities have broad local admin rights?

Where are privileged sessions appearing?

Who can modify GPOs?

Which principals have replication rights?

Which delegation relationships cross tiers?

Which AD CS relationships create identity risk?

Which trusts create cross-domain exposure?

Which identities can modify Tier-0 objects?

Which service accounts have excessive privilege?

Which computers create privilege concentration?

Which edges appear on many paths?

Which single remediation removes the most paths?

docs.title: Blast Radius Analysis
docs.text:
Ask:

If this identity is compromised, what can it influence?

Concept:

Identity
   |
   +--> Groups
   |
   +--> Computers
   |
   +--> ACLs
   |
   +--> GPOs
   |
   +--> PKI
   |
   +--> Domains

This is often more useful to management than a single attack path.

docs.title: Privilege Concentration
docs.text:
Look for identities that control many objects.

One Principal
     |
     +--> Many Computers
     +--> Many Groups
     +--> Many ACLs
     +--> Critical GPOs

A compromise of such an identity can create disproportionate impact.

docs.title: Reporting Principle
docs.text:
Do not report:

BloodHound found an attack path.

Prefer:

The tested user possesses permissions over a group that
provides administrative access to multiple application servers.

BloodHound is evidence.

The underlying security condition is the finding.

docs.title: Reporting an Attack Path
docs.text:
Document:

Starting Identity
Relationship
Intermediate Object
Relationship
Target
Prerequisites
Validation
Impact
Remediation

docs.title: Reporting ACLs
docs.text:
Avoid:

BloodHound shows GenericAll.

Prefer:

The tested domain user possesses GenericAll permissions
over the target Active Directory group, providing broad
control over that directory object.

docs.title: Reporting Sessions
docs.text:
Avoid:

BloodHound found Domain Admin on APP01.

Prefer:

Collection data indicated that a privileged domain account
had an active session associated with APP01 at the time of
collection.

Always preserve the collection timestamp.

docs.title: Reporting Local Admin Sprawl
docs.text:
Instead of:

BloodHound found lots of AdminTo edges.

Prefer:

The tested administrative identity has local administrator
rights across a broad set of workstations and servers,
increasing the potential blast radius of credential compromise.

docs.title: Reporting Path Remediation
docs.text:
A useful defensive format:

Observed path:
User -> Group -> Server -> Privileged Session

Root condition:
Excessive local administrator assignment

Recommended change:
Restrict administrative membership to systems required
for the user's operational role

Verification:
Re-collect and confirm the administrative relationship
and dependent attack paths are removed

docs.title: Relationship Interpretation Cheatsheet
docs.text:
MemberOf
    -> Group membership relationship

AdminTo
    -> Administrative relationship to computer

HasSession
    -> Session relationship observed around collection time

CanRDP
    -> Potential RDP access relationship

CanPSRemote
    -> Potential PowerShell remoting relationship

ExecuteDCOM
    -> Potential DCOM access relationship

GenericAll
    -> Broad control over target object

GenericWrite
    -> Ability to modify supported target properties

WriteDacl
    -> Ability to modify target security descriptor permissions

WriteOwner
    -> Ability to change object ownership

ForceChangePassword
    -> Ability to reset target user's password

AddMember
    -> Ability to influence group membership

Owns
    -> Ownership relationship

AllowedToDelegate
    -> Kerberos delegation relationship

AllowedToAct
    -> RBCD-related relationship

DCSync
    -> Directory replication capability relationship

Always consult current BloodHound edge documentation for precise semantics.

NetExec can integrate collection into an existing AD workflow.

BloodBash provides offline CLI analysis.

Legacy Neo4j knowledge remains useful for older deployments.

An edge is evidence of a relationship, not automatic proof of exploitation.

A path is a hypothesis until its prerequisites are understood.

Collection is a point-in-time snapshot.

Session data is especially time-sensitive.

Incomplete collection means an incomplete graph.

Different collectors can produce different coverage.

Shortest path does not mean best path.

BloodHound is useful for offensive and defensive analysis.

Path-break analysis can identify high-value remediation opportunities.

Re-collect when security context changes.

Report the underlying security condition, not the tool output.

docs.title: Impacket Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Quick-reference commands and workflows for using Impacket during authorised Windows and Active Directory security assessments.

Impacket is a collection of Python classes and example tools for interacting with Microsoft network protocols.

It is particularly useful for:

Active Directory Enumeration
SMB
MSRPC
Kerberos
NTLM
LDAP
WMI
DCOM
MSSQL / TDS
Remote Registry
Service Control
Task Scheduler
Credential Assessment
Delegation
ACL Analysis
NTLM Relay

Authorised testing only

Some Impacket tools can access credentials, modify Active Directory objects, perform remote administration, create services or scheduled tasks, manipulate delegation, or interact with domain replication functionality. Use these capabilities only when explicitly permitted by the assessment scope and rules of engagement.

For detailed explanations of the underlying techniques see:

Impacket

Active Directory Cheatsheet

NetExec Cheatsheet

BloodHound Cheatsheet

docs.title: Quick Tool Map
docs.text: Goal Impacket Tool Enumerate AD users GetADUsers Enumerate AD computers GetADComputers Find AS-REP candidates GetNPUsers Enumerate SPNs GetUserSPNs Enumerate SIDs / RIDs lookupsid Enumerate delegation findDelegation Read LAPS passwords where authorised GetLAPSPassword Review legacy GPP passwords Get-GPPPassword Enumerate RPC endpoints rpcdump Map RPC interfaces rpcmap Enumerate SAMR information samrdump Query WMI wmiquery Access SMB shares smbclient Host an SMB share smbserver Enumerate MSSQL instances mssqlinstance Access MSSQL mssqlclient Validate RDP authentication rdp_check Request a TGT getTGT Request a service ticket getST Inspect delegation findDelegation Convert Kerberos tickets ticketConverter Describe Kerberos tickets describeTicket Create Kerberos tickets ticketer Inspect PAC information getPac Access Windows secrets secretsdump Service-based remote administration psexec WMI remote administration wmiexec SMB/service remote administration smbexec DCOM remote administration dcomexec Task Scheduler remote administration atexec Change an authorised password changepasswd Read/edit AD ACLs dacledit Read/edit AD object ownership owneredit Review/manage RBCD rbcd NTLM relay testing ntlmrelayx

docs.title: Current Version
docs.text:
Check the installed version:

python3 -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('impacket'))"

At the time this cheatsheet was updated:

Stable:      Impacket 0.13.1
Development: Impacket 0.14.0-dev

Do not assume commands from master are available in the stable release.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The upstream project recommends pipx for system-wide installations.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install pipx

pipx ensurepath

Install:

python3 -m pipx install impacket

Check:

pipx list

docs.title: Kali Linux
docs.text:
Kali may provide Impacket through its repositories:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3-impacket

Check:

apt policy python3-impacket

Find a command:

which impacket-GetADUsers

The Kali package version may differ from upstream.

docs.title: Command Naming
docs.text:
Packaged commands commonly use:

impacket-GetADUsers
impacket-GetADComputers
impacket-GetNPUsers
impacket-GetUserSPNs
impacket-lookupsid
impacket-findDelegation
impacket-smbclient
impacket-getTGT
impacket-getST
impacket-secretsdump

Source installations may instead use:

GetADUsers.py
GetADComputers.py
GetNPUsers.py
GetUserSPNs.py
lookupsid.py
findDelegation.py
smbclient.py
getTGT.py
getST.py
secretsdump.py

List installed packaged tools:

compgen -c | grep '^impacket-' | sort -u

docs.title: Help First
docs.text:
Always check the installed version:

impacket-GetADUsers -h

impacket-GetADComputers -h

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

impacket-getTGT -h

impacket-getST -h

impacket-secretsdump -h

This is especially important for development-version features.

docs.title: Assessment Variables
docs.text:
A convenient shell setup:

export DOMAIN="example.local"
export DC="dc01.example.local"
export DC_IP="10.10.20.10"
export USER="alice"

Check:

printf 'DOMAIN=%s\nDC=%s\nDC_IP=%s\nUSER=%s\n' "$DOMAIN" "$DC" "$DC_IP" "$USER"

docs.title: Before Impacket - DNS
docs.text:
Resolve the Domain Controller:

dig "$DC"

LDAP:

dig SRV "_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.$DOMAIN"

Kerberos:

dig SRV "_kerberos._tcp.$DOMAIN"

Resolver:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Kerberos and LDAP operations frequently fail because of DNS rather than credentials.

docs.title: Before Impacket - Time
docs.text:
date

timedatectl

Kerberos is time-sensitive.

Think:

Kerberos Failure
      |
      +--> DNS?
      |
      +--> Time?
      |
      +--> Realm?
      |
      +--> FQDN?
      |
      +--> SPN?
      |
      +--> KDC?
      |
      +--> Ticket?
      |
      +--> Credential?

docs.title: Authentication Quick Reference
docs.text:
Impacket commonly supports:

Password
NTLM Hash
Kerberos Ticket
AES Key
Kerberos Credential Cache

The exact authentication options vary by tool.

docs.title: Password Authentication
docs.text:
Common target form:

domain/user:password@target

Example:

impacket-smbclient 'example.local/alice:Password@file01.example.local'

Prefer interactive prompting where supported:

impacket-smbclient 'example.local/alice@file01.example.local'

Warning

Passwords supplied directly on the command line can appear in shell history, process listings, screenshots and terminal logs.

docs.title: NTLM Hash Authentication
docs.text:
Common option:

-hashes LMHASH:NTHASH

When only the NT hash is available:

-hashes :NTHASH

Example structure:

impacket-smbclient \
    'example.local/alice@file01.example.local' \
    -hashes ':<NT-HASH>'

Treat hashes as credentials.

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
Many Impacket examples support:

-k
-no-pass
-aesKey
-dc-ip
-target-ip

Exact support depends on the tool.

Check:

<tool> -h

docs.title: Kerberos Credential Cache
docs.text:
Set:

export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/alice.ccache"

Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

Inspect:

klist

Protect .ccache files like passwords.

docs.title: Kerberos Checklist
docs.text:
[ ] Correct domain
[ ] Correct username
[ ] Correct DC
[ ] FQDN resolves
[ ] Internal DNS works
[ ] KDC reachable
[ ] Time synchronised
[ ] Correct ticket loaded
[ ] Correct SPN used
[ ] Correct realm used

docs.title: AES Authentication
docs.text:
Where supported:

-aesKey <AES_KEY>

Check:

impacket-getTGT -h

AES keys are authentication material and should receive the same protection as passwords and hashes.

docs.title: GetADUsers
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-GetADUsers -h

Enumerate users:

impacket-GetADUsers \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER" \
    -dc-ip "$DC_IP" \
    -all

Enter the password interactively when prompted.

Useful fields may include:

Username
Email
Password Last Set
Last Logon
Description

docs.title: Specific AD User
docs.text:
Current versions support querying specific user information.

Check:

impacket-GetADUsers -h

Use targeted enumeration where possible rather than collecting unnecessary directory information.

docs.title: GetADComputers
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-GetADComputers -h

Enumerate computer objects:

impacket-GetADComputers \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER" \
    -dc-ip "$DC_IP"

Resolve discovered computer addresses where supported:

impacket-GetADComputers \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER" \
    -dc-ip "$DC_IP" \
    -resolveIP

Useful information can include:

Computer Account
DNS Hostname
Operating System
Operating System Version
Last Logon
IP Address

docs.title: Computer Enumeration Workflow
docs.text:
GetADComputers
       |
       v
Computer Objects
       |
       +--> Workstations
       +--> Servers
       +--> Domain Controllers
       +--> Legacy Systems
       +--> Stale Objects
       |
       v
Network Validation

Remember:

AD computer object
        !=
currently reachable host

docs.title: GetNPUsers
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-GetNPUsers -h

This tool is relevant to accounts configured without Kerberos pre-authentication.

Think:

Domain User
    |
    v
Preauthentication Required?
    |
 +--+--+
 |     |
Yes    No
 |     |
 v     v
Normal Candidate

Do not assume an account is exploitable merely because pre-authentication is disabled.

Consider:

Password Strength
Account Privilege
Account Purpose
Monitoring
Compensating Controls

See:

active-directory/asrep-roasting.md

docs.title: GetUserSPNs
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

Enumerate SPN accounts:

impacket-GetUserSPNs \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER" \
    -dc-ip "$DC_IP"

Useful output can include:

ServicePrincipalName
Account
Group Membership
Password Last Set
Last Logon
Delegation

docs.title: SPN Analysis
docs.text:
Do not report:

SPN exists

as a vulnerability.

Use:

SPN
 |
 v
Account
 |
 v
Service Account?
 |
 v
Password Age
 |
 v
Password Strength
 |
 v
Privileges
 |
 v
Security Impact

docs.title: Cross-Domain SPN Enumeration
docs.text:
Current versions may support:

-target-domain

Check:

impacket-GetUserSPNs -h

This is useful where trusted domains are explicitly in scope.

docs.title: lookupsid
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-lookupsid -h

Example:

impacket-lookupsid \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER@$DC"

docs.title: findDelegation
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-findDelegation -h

Enumerate:

impacket-findDelegation \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER" \
    -dc-ip "$DC_IP"

Review:

Unconstrained Delegation
Constrained Delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

docs.title: Delegation Analysis
docs.text:
Principal
    |
    v
Delegation Type
    |
    v
Target Service
    |
    v
Who Controls Principal?
    |
    v
Prerequisites
    |
    v
Security Boundary
    |
    v
Potential Path

Do not equate:

Delegation configured

with:

Exploitable privilege escalation

docs.title: GetLAPSPassword
docs.text:
Modern Impacket includes LAPS-related functionality.

Check:

impacket-GetLAPSPassword -h

Use only with an identity that is explicitly authorised for the assessment.

The important security question is:

Who can read the managed local administrator password?

not merely:

Does LAPS exist?

docs.title: LAPS Assessment Model
docs.text:
Computer
   |
   v
LAPS Enabled?
   |
   v
Password Attribute
   |
   v
Who Can Read?
   |
   v
Expected?
   |
   v
Privilege Boundary

See:

active-directory/laps.md

docs.title: Get-GPPPassword
docs.text:
Check:

impacket-Get-GPPPassword -h

This tool is relevant to legacy Group Policy Preferences credentials stored in SYSVOL.

The assessment question is:

Does SYSVOL contain legacy GPP credential material?

rather than indiscriminately searching every domain file.

See:

active-directory/gpp-passwords.md

docs.title: rpcdump
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-rpcdump -h

Typical form:

impacket-rpcdump \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER@$DC"

Useful for identifying:

RPC Interfaces
Endpoints
Protocol Sequences
Exposed Windows Services

docs.title: rpcmap
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-rpcmap -h

Use it when a specific RPC interface or transport needs investigation.

RPC exposure itself is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: samrdump
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-samrdump -h

Typical structure:

impacket-samrdump \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER@$DC"

Depending on permissions, SAMR may expose:

Users
Groups
Account Information
Domain Information

docs.title: smbclient
docs.text:
Connect:

impacket-smbclient \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER@file01.$DOMAIN"

Use:

help

inside the interactive client.

docs.title: SMB Workflow
docs.text:
NetExec --shares
       |
       v
Interesting Share
       |
       v
impacket-smbclient
       |
       v
Focused Inspection
       |
       v
Evidence

Avoid recursively downloading entire corporate file shares.

docs.title: Interesting Share Content
docs.text:
Depending on scope, review:

Configuration Files
Deployment Scripts
PowerShell Scripts
Batch Files
Backup Files
Connection Strings
Certificates
Keys
Administrative Documentation
Software Deployment Content

Validate whether discovered information is actually sensitive before reporting.

docs.title: smbserver
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-smbserver -h

Create a controlled share directory:

mkdir -p /tmp/assessment-share

Start:

impacket-smbserver ASSESSMENT /tmp/assessment-share

Bind/expose the server only as required by the engagement.

docs.title: SMB Server Checklist
docs.text:
[ ] Correct interface
[ ] Firewall understood
[ ] Share contents reviewed
[ ] Authentication considered
[ ] No customer secrets exposed
[ ] Server stopped after testing

docs.title: SMB Information
docs.text:
Impacket also contains tools useful for obtaining SMB/NTLM information.

List your installation:

compgen -c | grep '^impacket-' | grep -Ei 'smb|ntlm'

Use tool-specific help before testing.

docs.title: wmiquery
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-wmiquery -h

Connect:

impacket-wmiquery \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER@server01.$DOMAIN"

This provides a WQL-oriented shell.

Safe inventory-style examples include:

select Caption,Version from Win32_OperatingSystem

select Name,State,StartMode from Win32_Service

select Name,ProcessId from Win32_Process

Use:

describe Win32_Process

to inspect a class.

docs.title: WMI Security Model
docs.text:
WMI access depends on more than successful SMB authentication.

Think:

Identity
   |
   v
DCOM Connectivity
   |
   v
WMI Namespace
   |
   v
Namespace Permissions
   |
   v
RPC Authentication Level
   |
   v
Query / Management Access

docs.title: mssqlinstance
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-mssqlinstance -h

This can assist with identifying Microsoft SQL Server instances where the relevant discovery service is reachable.

Confirm results with normal network/service enumeration.

docs.title: mssqlclient
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-mssqlclient -h

Connect using an authorised account:

impacket-mssqlclient \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER@sql01.$DOMAIN"

Authentication may involve:

SQL Authentication
Windows Authentication
NTLM
Kerberos

depending on configuration and command options.

docs.title: MSSQL Assessment Questions
docs.text:
Determine:

Authentication Method
Database User
Database Roles
Server Roles
Accessible Databases
Linked Servers
Service Account
Domain Context
Impersonation Rights
Network Reachability

Do not enable command-execution functionality merely because the account can connect.

docs.title: rdp_check
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-rdp_check -h

Use it for targeted authentication validation where RDP is in scope.

Successful authentication means:

Credential accepted by RDP

It does not automatically mean:

Local administrator

or:

Unrestricted interactive access

docs.title: getTGT
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-getTGT -h

Concept:

Credential
    |
    v
getTGT
    |
    v
KDC
    |
    v
TGT
    |
    v
ccache

Typical password-based structure:

impacket-getTGT \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER"

Enter the password when prompted.

After obtaining a ticket:

export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/$USER.ccache"

Check:

klist

docs.title: TGT with NTLM Hash
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised:

impacket-getTGT \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER" \
    -hashes ':<NT-HASH>'

Check your installed version's syntax first:

impacket-getTGT -h

docs.title: TGT with AES Key
docs.text:
Where authorised:

impacket-getTGT \
    "$DOMAIN/$USER" \
    -aesKey '<AES-KEY>'

Protect the resulting ticket and key material.

docs.title: getST
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-getST -h

getST is relevant to:

Service-Specific Kerberos Access
Constrained Delegation
S4U2Self
S4U2Proxy
RBCD
Impersonation Workflows

The exact command depends heavily on the delegation relationship.

Use the dedicated notes:

active-directory/constrained-delegation.md
active-directory/rbcd.md
active-directory/s4u.md

docs.title: S4U Model
docs.text:
Controlled Principal
       |
       v
Delegation Configuration
       |
       v
S4U2Self
       |
       v
S4U2Proxy
       |
       v
Service Ticket
       |
       v
Target Service

Do not run an impersonation workflow simply because findDelegation returned an entry.

Validate the relationship first.

docs.title: ticketConverter
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-ticketConverter -h

Concept:

kirbi
  |
  v
ticketConverter
  |
  v
ccache

or:

ccache
  |
  v
ticketConverter
  |
  v
kirbi

Conversion changes the storage format.

It does not change:

Identity
Privileges
Lifetime
Service
Cryptographic Validity

docs.title: describeTicket
docs.text:
Where present in your installed version:

impacket-describeTicket -h

Use ticket inspection to understand:

Client Principal
Service Principal
Realm
Flags
Validity
Encryption Type
PAC-related Information

without immediately attempting to use the ticket.

docs.title: getPac
docs.text:
Check:

impacket-getPac -h

PAC-related tooling is useful when investigating Kerberos authorisation information and advanced Kerberos behaviour.

Use it only when relevant to the assessment objective.

docs.title: ticketer
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-ticketer -h

This is advanced Kerberos functionality associated with:

Golden Tickets
Silver Tickets
Trust Tickets
Kerberos Persistence

Danger

Ticket creation can materially alter the security context of an assessment and should only be used where explicitly authorised.

Use the dedicated Kerberos and persistence notes rather than treating ticketer as a routine enumeration tool.

docs.title: changepasswd
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-changepasswd -h

Password modification is a state-changing operation.

Use it only where:

The account is approved
The password change is approved
Impact is understood
Rollback is defined

For most assessments, password-change capability can be documented without actually changing a production user's password.

docs.title: dacledit
docs.text:
Check:

impacket-dacledit -h

This tool can inspect or modify Active Directory DACL information.

Prefer read-only inspection first.

Think:

Principal
   |
   v
ACE
   |
   v
Object
   |
   v
Right
   |
   v
Security Impact

Examples of rights worth understanding include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
Extended Rights
Property-Specific Rights

Do not modify ACLs merely to prove that an ACE exists.

docs.title: owneredit
docs.text:
Check:

impacket-owneredit -h

Ownership can influence an identity's ability to modify an object's DACL.

Assess:

Current Owner
Who Can Change Owner?
What Object?
What Security Boundary?
What Additional Rights Become Possible?

Prefer read-only validation unless modification is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: rbcd
docs.text:
Check:

impacket-rbcd -h

Current Impacket supports operations around:

msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity

Read-only assessment should come first.

Concept:

Controlled Principal
        |
        v
RBCD Attribute
        |
        v
Target Computer
        |
        v
S4U
        |
        v
Target Service

See:

active-directory/rbcd.md

docs.title: Machine Accounts
docs.text:
Some Impacket tooling can interact with computer accounts.

Before any state-changing machine-account operation, understand:

MachineAccountQuota
Existing Computer Objects
Delegated Create/Delete Rights
Target OU
RBCD Relationship
Cleanup Requirements

See:

active-directory/machine-account-quota.md

docs.title: secretsdump
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-secretsdump -h

Potential credential sources include:

SAM
LSA Secrets
Cached Domain Credentials
NTDS
Domain Replication

Danger

Credential dumping is highly sensitive. Only perform it when credential-access testing is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: secretsdump Security Model
docs.text:
Do not think:

Admin Credential
      =
Dump Everything

Use:

Assessment Objective
       |
       v
Credential Access Required?
       |
    +--+--+
    |     |
   No    Yes
    |     |
    v     v
   Stop  Minimum
         Required
         Collection

docs.title: Local Secrets vs Domain Replication
docs.text:
These are different security boundaries.

Remote Windows Host
       |
       +--> SAM
       +--> LSA Secrets
       +--> Cached Credentials

versus:

Domain Controller
       |
       v
Directory Replication
       |
       v
Domain Credential Material

Domain replication access has substantially greater impact.

docs.title: DRSUAPI
docs.text:
secretsdump can use directory replication mechanisms when the identity has the necessary rights.

This should be treated as a high-impact capability.

The important finding may be:

Unexpected Identity
       |
       v
Directory Replication Rights
       |
       v
Domain Credential Exposure

rather than the volume of credentials that can be collected.

docs.title: Targeted Replication Validation
docs.text:
Current secretsdump versions provide options for narrowing domain-controller collection.

Check:

impacket-secretsdump -h

Prefer targeted validation over full-domain extraction whenever the assessment objective can be proven with less sensitive data.

docs.title: Offline Secrets Assessment
docs.text:
secretsdump can also work with authorised offline registry/database material.

This can be preferable in a controlled lab or forensic assessment because it avoids interacting with a live production host.

Check:

impacket-secretsdump -h

for the exact offline-input options supported by the installed version.

docs.title: Credential Evidence Handling
docs.text:
Credential-related evidence may contain:

NTLM Hashes
AES Keys
Passwords
Cached Credentials
Service Secrets
Machine Secrets
Kerberos Keys

Store it separately from normal screenshots and notes where possible.

Apply the engagement's data-retention requirements.

docs.title: Remote Administration
docs.text:
Common tools:

psexec
smbexec
wmiexec
dcomexec
atexec

They use different Windows mechanisms.

docs.title: Remote Administration Comparison
docs.text:
Tool Primary Mechanism Typical Dependencies Operational Consideration psexec SMB + SCM SMB, Service Control Manager Creates/uses a service smbexec SMB + SCM SMB, Service Control Manager Service-based activity wmiexec WMI/DCOM RPC, DCOM, WMI WMI/DCOM telemetry dcomexec DCOM RPC/DCOM DCOM-specific activity atexec Task Scheduler RPC/Task Scheduler Scheduled-task activity

The exact telemetry depends on Windows version, configuration, security products and tool version.

docs.text:

docs.title: psexec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-psexec -h

This uses SMB and service-management functionality.

Consider it intrusive because service creation or service-control activity may occur.

docs.title: smbexec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-smbexec -h

Also relies on SMB/service-management mechanisms.

Do not treat it as "stealthy" simply because it behaves differently from psexec.

docs.title: wmiexec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-wmiexec -h

RPC Endpoint Mapper
DCOM
WMI
Dynamic RPC Ports
Appropriate Permissions

docs.title: dcomexec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-dcomexec -h

Use only when DCOM remote administration is explicitly within scope.

docs.title: atexec
docs.text:
Help:

impacket-atexec -h

Uses Task Scheduler interfaces.

Scheduled-task creation is state-changing and can generate security telemetry.

docs.title: Authentication Before Execution
docs.text:
Prefer:

Credential
    |

    |

    |

Before testing:

[ ] Protocol approved

[ ] State-changing action understood

docs.text:

Examples:

smbexec

docs.text:

docs.text:

Correct Hostnames

docs.text:
Usually:

Do not assume every SQL Server listens on 1433.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE
docs.text:
Usually investigate:

Username
Password
Domain
Local vs Domain Account
Authentication Method
Account State

Do not repeatedly retry a credential without understanding lockout policy.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED
docs.text:
This often means:

Authentication succeeded
        |
        v
Requested operation not authorised

Distinguish:

Authentication

from:

Authorisation

docs.text:

Credential
AES Key
NT Hash
Account
Realm
Encryption Type

Do not assume the KDC itself is unavailable.

docs.text:
Investigate:

SPN
Hostname
FQDN
Service Name
DNS
Realm

Kerberos is service-principal oriented.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW
docs.text:
Check:

date

Compare against the domain environment.

This error commonly indicates clock skew.

docs.title: Troubleshooting - Kerberos Uses IP
docs.text:
Prefer:

server01.example.local

over:

10.10.20.25

for Kerberos-oriented operations where possible.

SPNs are normally hostname/service based.

docs.text:
Think:

SMB Authentication
        |
        v
Credential Valid

but WMI additionally needs:

RPC
DCOM
WMI Namespace Access
Firewall
Dynamic RPC
Appropriate Permissions

Therefore:

SMB success != WMI success

docs.text:

Administrative Rights
Service Control Manager Access
ADMIN$ Access
SMB Configuration
UAC Remote Restrictions
Endpoint Security

docs.text:
dig "$DC"

dig SRV "_kerberos._tcp.$DOMAIN"

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

Renewal

docs.text:
Always distinguish:

EXAMPLE\alice

from:

FILE01\alice

Same username does not mean same security principal.

docs.text:

[ ] Scheduled tasks removed
[ ] Temporary accounts removed
[ ] ACL changes restored
[ ] Ownership restored
[ ] RBCD changes restored
[ ] Temporary files removed
[ ] SMB server stopped
[ ] Sensitive ticket files protected/deleted

[ ] Evidence retained securely

docs.title: Do Not Overreport
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

SMB Is Open
RPC Is Open
LDAP Is Open
An SPN Exists
Delegation Exists
A User Can Authenticate
A Computer Object Exists
LAPS Is Enabled
MSSQL Is Reachable
RDP Authentication Works
A Kerberos Ticket Can Be Requested
Impacket Can Connect

Instead determine:

Configuration
     +
Identity
     +
Permission
     +
Reachability
     +
Security Boundary
     +
Impact
     =
Finding

docs.title: SPN
docs.text:
Weak:

Kerberoasting possible because an SPN exists.

Better:

A service account has an SPN. Assess the account's password
strength, age and privileges before determining whether the
configuration creates meaningful offline password-guessing risk.

docs.title: Delegation
docs.text:
Weak:

Constrained delegation found.

Better:

The account is configured for constrained delegation to the
identified service. Determine who controls the account and whether
the relationship permits an unintended privilege boundary to be crossed.

docs.title: SMB Authentication
docs.text:
Weak:

User can access SMB.

Better:

The domain user successfully authenticated to SMB. Review accessible
shares and permissions to determine whether the access exceeds the
user's intended role.

docs.title: LAPS
docs.text:
Weak:

LAPS password accessible.

Better:

The tested identity can read the managed local administrator
credential for the specified computer. Determine whether this
permission is expected for the identity and whether it creates an
unintended administrative path.

docs.title: Replication Rights
docs.text:
Weak:

DCSync possible.

Better:

The identity possesses directory replication rights capable of
accessing domain credential material. This represents a domain-level
security boundary and should be validated using the minimum evidence
necessary.

docs.title: Rules to Remember
docs.text:
Tool output != vulnerability

SPN != weak password

Delegation != exploitable path

SMB signing not required != successful relay

Authentication != administration

Local administrator != Domain Admin

Ticket != access to every service

Credential found != permission to dump more credentials

Administrative access != permission to execute remotely

Write permission != permission to modify production

BloodHound edge != automatically exploitable path

Successful Impacket command != security finding

docs.title: Final Impacket Model
docs.text:
Do not use Impacket as:

Credential
    |
    v
Run Every Tool
    |
    v
Dump Everything
    |
    v
Execute Everywhere

Use:

Understand Scope
      |
      v
Understand Network
      |
      v
Understand Identity
      |
      v
Identify Protocol
      |
      v
Choose Specific Tool
      |
      v
Read-Only Enumeration
      |
      v
Understand Relationship
      |
      v
Manual Validation
      |
      v
Need State Change?
      |
   +--+--+
   |     |
  No    Yes
   |     |
   v     v
Evidence Approval
          |
          v
       Minimal
       Change
          |
          v
       Cleanup
          |
          v
       Evidence

The goal is not:

How many Impacket commands can I run?

The goal is:

Which protocol, identity, permission or Active Directory
relationship explains the observed security boundary?

Impacket is most valuable when it turns:

Potential Relationship

into:

Protocol-Level Understanding
        +
Permission Validation
        +
Minimal Evidence
        =
Defensible Security Finding

docs.title: Linux Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Quick-reference commands for Linux enumeration, networking, files, permissions, services, credentials, containers and privilege-escalation analysis during authorised security assessments.

This cheatsheet is designed for:

Initial Access

Privilege Analysis

Configuration Review

Minimal Validation
     |
