Authorised testing only

Use these commands only on systems you own or are explicitly authorised to assess. Prefer read-only enumeration and the lowest-impact validation method. Do not modify privileged files, create SUID binaries, change sudoers, alter scheduled tasks, extract unnecessary credentials or establish persistence unless explicitly authorised.

Current User
     |

     |

Allowed Binary
     |
     v
Binary Capability
     |
     +--> Command Execution?
     +--> Shell Escape?
     +--> File Read?
     +--> File Write?
     +--> Library Load?

When a binary appears in sudo -l, check whether its permitted functionality can cross the intended privilege boundary.

GTFOBins is useful for this analysis.

docs.title: GTFOBins
docs.text:
GTFOBins is a curated reference for legitimate Unix-like executables whose normal functionality can become security-relevant when exposed through unsafe configurations.

Useful contexts include:

Unprivileged
Sudo
SUID
Capabilities

Useful function categories include:

Shell
Command
File Read
File Write
Upload
Download
Library Load
Privilege Escalation

Do not assume:

Binary Listed in GTFOBins
=
Vulnerable System

The relevant model is:

Binary
   +
Privileged Context
   +
Useful Functionality
   =
Potential Security Boundary Bypass

Example assessment workflow:

sudo -l
   |
   v
Identify Binary
   |
   v
Check GTFOBins
   |
   v
Understand Required Conditions
   |
   v
Validate Configuration
   |
   v
Report

Reference:

GTFOBins

docs.title: GTFOBins Workflow
docs.text:
When you discover:

sudo
SUID
Capability

use:

GTFOBins

Search the binary.

Then determine:

Does the Required Context Match?
Does the Binary Have the Required Permission?
Does the Technique Modify State?
Can Impact Be Proven Read-Only?

GTFOBins itself notes that listed programs are not necessarily vulnerable; the issue is how legitimate functionality can interact with unsafe security configuration.

A strong finding should demonstrate:

Low-Privilege Principal

Misconfiguration
        |

Privileged Resource

Example:

User

sudo Permission

Binary with Unsafe Functionality

The finding is the unsafe privilege relationship, not simply that a binary exists.

Instead determine:

docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
For Linux assessments, start simple:

Who Am I?
   |
   v
What System Is This?
   |
   v
What Can I Run?
   |
   v
What Runs as Root?
   |
   v
What Can I Modify?

The highest-value initial commands are often:

id
sudo -l
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
ps aux
ss -tulpn
find / -type f -perm -4000 2>/dev/null
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
systemctl list-timers --all

When you discover an unusual privileged binary:

Binary
   |
   v
Check Permission Context
   |
   v
GTFOBins
   |
   v
Exploit Notes
   |
   v
Vendor Documentation
   |
   v
Validate Preconditions

The important distinction is:

Interesting Configuration
        !=
Confirmed Privilege Escalation

For example:

SUID Binary

alone is not the finding.

The relevant question is:

Can the Current User Use
That Binary's Functionality
to Cross a Security Boundary?

Similarly:

Old Kernel

does not automatically mean:

Kernel Privilege Escalation

and:

Docker Installed

does not automatically mean:

Root Access

Always validate the complete path:

Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Specific Misconfiguration
        |
        v
Reachable Privileged Capability
        |
        v
Security Boundary Crossed

For authorised penetration testing, prefer:

Enumeration
    |
    v
Analysis
    |
    v
Minimal Validation
    |
    v
Evidence
    |
    v
Cleanup

over unnecessary system modification.

The Linux cheatsheet should therefore function as:

Command Reference
      +
Privilege Checklist
      +
Research Map

with GTFOBins and Exploit Notes used as supporting references when a potentially dangerous Unix executable or privilege-escalation condition is discovered.

docs.title: NetExec Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Quick-reference guide for using NetExec during authorised internal penetration tests, Active Directory assessments and red-team engagements.

NetExec, commonly invoked as nxc, is a network service enumeration and assessment framework descended from CrackMapExec.

It supports multiple protocols and can be used for:

Host Discovery
Service Enumeration
Authentication Validation
SMB Assessment
LDAP Enumeration
WinRM Assessment
MSSQL Enumeration
SSH Assessment
RDP Assessment
NFS Assessment
FTP Assessment
WMI Assessment
VNC Assessment
Security Configuration Review
Share Enumeration
Active Directory Enumeration
BloodHound Collection
Module-Based Enumeration

Authorised testing only

NetExec can authenticate to many systems quickly and can perform actions that generate significant authentication traffic or modify remote systems. Use it only against systems you own or are explicitly authorised to assess. Understand account lockout policy and the rules of engagement before authentication testing.

For deeper Active Directory methodology see:

Active Directory Cheatsheet

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
A useful NetExec workflow:

Targets
   |
   v
Protocol Discovery
   |
   v
Unauthenticated Enumeration
   |
   v
Security Configuration
   |
   v
Authorised Credentials
   |
   v
Authentication Validation
   |
   v
Users / Groups / Shares
   |
   v
LDAP / AD Enumeration
   |
   v
Administrative Access Mapping
   |
   v
Modules
   |
   v
Manual Validation

Typical starting commands:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

nxc ldap dc01.example.local

nxc winrm 10.10.10.0/24

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
Global help:

nxc --help

Protocol help:

nxc smb --help

nxc ldap --help

nxc winrm --help

Always check the installed version's help before relying on an option copied from an older cheatsheet.

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
nxc --version

NetExec changes regularly.

Commands and modules may differ between releases.

docs.title: Installed Protocols
docs.text:
Run:

nxc --help

The available protocols depend on the installed NetExec version.

Common protocols include:

SMB
LDAP
WINRM
WMI
MSSQL
SSH
FTP
RDP
NFS
VNC

docs.title: Target Formats
docs.text:
NetExec accepts several target forms.

Single IP:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10

Hostname:

nxc smb server01.example.local

CIDR:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

Range:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10-20

Target file:

nxc smb targets.txt

docs.title: Target File
docs.text:
Example:

10.10.10.10
10.10.10.11
server01.example.local
server02.example.local

Run:

nxc smb targets.txt

Target files are useful for separating discovery from later authenticated testing.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Active Directory testing depends heavily on DNS.

Before troubleshooting Kerberos or LDAP, confirm:

dig dc01.example.local

nslookup dc01.example.local

Check your resolver:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

A large percentage of Kerberos problems are actually:

DNS
Time
Hostname
Realm
SPN

problems.

docs.title: Starting Position - No Credentials
docs.text:
A common internal assessment begins with:

Internal Network
      |
      v
No Credentials
      |
      v
NetExec SMB Discovery

Start with:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

This can provide useful host and SMB information without assuming domain credentials.

docs.title: SMB Host Discovery
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

Useful output may include:

IP
Hostname
Domain
Operating System
SMB Signing
SMB Version Information

This is one of the most useful initial NetExec commands during an internal Windows assessment.

docs.title: Save Discovery Output
docs.text:
Standard shell redirection:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 | tee smb-discovery.txt

Preserve raw evidence before filtering.

docs.title: Extract Hosts
docs.text:
Example shell processing:

grep 'SMB' smb-discovery.txt

For complex engagements, prefer NetExec's database and workspaces rather than relying entirely on text parsing.

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
SMB signing is particularly important when assessing NTLM relay exposure.

Generate a relay candidate list:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 --gen-relay-list relay.txt

Review:

cat relay.txt

Important:

SMB Signing Not Required
          !=
NTLM Relay Vulnerability

A complete relay path still depends on:

Authentication Source
Target Protocol
Target Authentication
Signing / Binding
Privileges
Network Reachability
Protocol Configuration

Treat the relay list as a candidate list.

docs.title: SMBv1
docs.text:
Check protocol help first:

nxc smb --help

For dedicated SMB protocol-version validation, Nmap is also useful:

nmap -p 445 --script smb-protocols 10.10.10.10

Do not infer SMBv1 status from unrelated SMB output.

docs.title: SMB Shares - Authenticated
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --shares

Subnet:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --shares

Look for:

Readable Shares
Writable Shares
Administrative Shares
Deployment Shares
Backup Shares
User Shares
Software Shares
SYSVOL
NETLOGON

docs.title: Avoid Passwords in Shell History
docs.text:
This:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 -u username -p 'Password'

is convenient for examples but may expose credentials through:

Shell History
Process Listings
Terminal Logging
Assessment Notes
Screenshots

Use credential-handling methods appropriate to the engagement.

docs.title: Domain Authentication
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -d example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

The domain can also often be represented through other accepted username formats.

Check:

nxc smb --help

for the installed version.

docs.title: Multiple Targets
docs.text:
nxc smb targets.txt \
    -d example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

NetExec is designed for parallel network assessment.

This is powerful but can create substantial authentication traffic.

docs.title: Authentication Safety
docs.text:
Before testing credentials determine:

Domain Password Policy
Fine-Grained Password Policies
Account Lockout Threshold
Lockout Observation Window
Lockout Duration
Approved Accounts
Approved Passwords
Allowed Rate

Do not use NetExec as a blind password-spraying engine.

docs.title: Single Credential Validation
docs.text:
Prefer validating one approved credential against one target first:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -d example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

Then expand only where necessary.

docs.title: Username File
docs.text:
Where explicitly authorised:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u users.txt \
    -p 'ApprovedPassword'

This may generate many authentication attempts.

Understand lockout behaviour first.

docs.title: Password File
docs.text:
Similarly:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p passwords.txt

Do not use uncontrolled password lists against production accounts.

docs.title: Username + Password Lists
docs.text:
NetExec can work with lists, but this can quickly become a high-volume authentication test.

Before doing so:

STOP
 |
 v
Check Lockout Policy
 |
 v
Check Scope
 |
 v
Check Attempt Count
 |
 v
Check Rate
 |
 v
Proceed Only If Approved

docs.title: Local Authentication
docs.text:
When assessing a local account rather than a domain account, check the protocol help for the current local-authentication option:

nxc smb --help

Keep local and domain credentials clearly separated in notes.

A reused local administrator credential can have a very different impact from a domain credential.

docs.title: Pass-the-Hash Validation
docs.text:
Where NTLM hash authentication is explicitly authorised, NetExec supports NTLM-based authentication workflows.

Check the installed syntax:

nxc smb --help

Example form:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -H '<NTLM_HASH>'

Do not collect or use password hashes outside the approved credential-access scope.

The existence of NTLM authentication does not itself constitute a vulnerability.

docs.title: Kerberos Authentication
docs.text:
Kerberos should be preferred where the assessment requires testing Kerberos-specific behaviour.

Check:

nxc smb --help

and:

nxc ldap --help

for current Kerberos options.

Before troubleshooting Kerberos verify:

date

dig dc01.example.local

klist

docs.title: Kerberos Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Think:

Kerberos Failure
      |
      +--> DNS?
      |
      +--> Time?
      |
      +--> Realm?
      |
      +--> Hostname?
      |
      +--> SPN?
      |
      +--> Ticket?
      |
      +--> Credential?

Do not immediately assume the account password is wrong.

docs.title: SMB Users
docs.text:
Authenticated enumeration:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --users

Availability and behaviour can depend on target configuration and NetExec version.

docs.title: SMB Groups
docs.text:
nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --groups

docs.title: Logged-On Users
docs.text:
Where supported and authorised:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --loggedon-users

This can reveal sensitive session information.

Use only where required by scope.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Session enumeration can be security sensitive because it helps map credential and lateral-movement paths.

Check current options:

nxc smb --help

Collect only what is required for the assessment.

docs.title: Local Administrators
docs.text:
When authenticated with appropriate rights, identify local administrative relationships rather than immediately performing remote execution.

A useful assessment question is:

Where is this identity an administrator?

rather than:

Where can I execute commands?

docs.title: Administrative Access
docs.text:
NetExec output may identify elevated access.

Interpret this as:

Credential
   |
   v
Target
   |
   v
Administrative Relationship

Then determine whether that relationship is intended.

Do not automatically perform command execution.

docs.title: SYSVOL
docs.text:
Enumerate shares:

nxc smb dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --shares

Then use a dedicated SMB client for careful file inspection:

smbclient //dc01.example.local/SYSVOL -U username

Look for:

Logon Scripts
Group Policy Files
Deployment Scripts
Configuration
Legacy Credentials
Internal Hostnames

docs.title: NETLOGON
docs.text:
Similarly:

smbclient //dc01.example.local/NETLOGON -U username

Review scripts carefully.

Do not modify domain logon scripts during enumeration.

docs.title: Spidering Shares
docs.text:
NetExec includes modules and capabilities that can search accessible SMB content.

Before using broad spidering:

How large is the share?
Is sensitive user data present?
Will the operation generate excessive traffic?
Is downloading allowed?

Prefer targeted searches over indiscriminate collection.

docs.title: Important spider_plus Security Note
docs.text:
Keep NetExec updated.

Older NetExec versions had a security issue affecting the spider_plus module that was fixed in the 1.5.1 release.

Check:

nxc --version

and update according to the official project documentation before using the tool in an engagement.

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text:
LDAP is one of the most useful NetExec protocols for authenticated Active Directory enumeration.

Basic:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local

Authenticated:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

docs.title: LDAP Domain
docs.text:
Specify domain where required:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -d example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

docs.title: LDAP Users
docs.text:
nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --users

docs.title: LDAP Active Users
docs.text:
Current NetExec versions may provide filtering for active users.

Check:

nxc ldap --help

Where supported:

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --active-users

This is useful for reducing noise from disabled accounts.

docs.title: LDAP Groups
docs.text:
nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    --groups

docs.title: LDAP Computers
docs.text:
Check current LDAP options:

nxc ldap --help

NetExec capabilities evolve, so use built-in help rather than relying on old CrackMapExec syntax.

docs.title: LDAP Password Policy
docs.text:
Password-policy enumeration is particularly useful before authentication testing.

Check:

nxc ldap --help

and use the current password-policy option supported by the installed version.

Cross-check important lockout values with native AD tooling where possible.

docs.title: LDAP AS-REP Candidates
docs.text:
NetExec can assist with identifying Active Directory account configurations relevant to Kerberos assessment.

Check:

nxc ldap --help

Validate candidate accounts manually before reporting.

The relevant condition is:

Kerberos Preauthentication Disabled

not merely whether a tool labels an account interesting.

docs.title: LDAP Kerberoasting Candidates
docs.text:
Service Principal Names can be enumerated through LDAP.

Think:

User
 |
 v
SPN
 |
 v
Service Account
 |
 v
Password Strength
 |
 v
Privileges

An SPN is normal Active Directory functionality.

The security risk depends on account password strength and privileges.

docs.title: LDAP Delegation
docs.text:
Review current LDAP options and modules for delegation-related enumeration:

nxc ldap --help

Look for:

Unconstrained Delegation
Constrained Delegation
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

Validate relationships against AD attributes and BloodHound.

docs.title: LDAP Trusts
docs.text:
Trust enumeration should determine:

Trusted Domain
Direction
Transitivity
Trust Type
Forest Relationship

Check current LDAP capabilities:

nxc ldap --help

Cross-check with:

nltest /domain_trusts

or:

Get-ADTrust -Filter *

where available.

docs.title: LDAP AD CS Discovery
docs.text:
NetExec includes LDAP modules and functionality that can assist with Active Directory Certificate Services assessment.

List LDAP modules:

nxc ldap -L

Search for relevant certificate and AD CS modules in the installed version.

For comprehensive AD CS enumeration also use:

Certipy
Certify
Native Certificate Tools
LDAP

See:

Active Directory Cheatsheet

docs.title: LDAP Security Controls
docs.text:
When assessing LDAP, think beyond directory objects.

Review:

LDAP Signing
LDAP Channel Binding
LDAPS
NTLM Authentication
Certificate Configuration
Relay Exposure

Do not infer LDAP security solely from port 636 being open.

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
Discovery:

nxc winrm 10.10.10.0/24

Authenticated validation:

nxc winrm 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

docs.title: WinRM Interpretation
docs.text:
Successful WinRM authentication indicates remote management access.

Determine:

Which user?
Which target?
Which group grants access?
Is access expected?
Is the account administrative?

Do not automatically treat WinRM access as a vulnerability.

docs.title: Remote Management Users
docs.text:
On Windows:

net localgroup "Remote Management Users"

Membership may explain intended WinRM access.

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
Check current protocol support:

nxc rdp --help

Basic discovery:

nxc rdp 10.10.10.0/24

Authentication testing should follow the same lockout precautions as SMB and WinRM.

docs.title: MSSQL
docs.text:
Discovery:

nxc mssql 10.10.10.0/24

Authenticated assessment:

nxc mssql 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

SQL Server authentication and Windows authentication may behave differently.

Check:

nxc mssql --help

docs.title: MSSQL Assessment Questions
docs.text:
Determine:

Authentication Method
Database Role
Server Role
Linked Servers
Service Account
Domain Context
Impersonation Rights
Network Reachability

Do not immediately enable or invoke command-execution features.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Discovery:

nxc ssh 10.10.10.0/24

Authenticated:

nxc ssh 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password'

Use only approved credentials.

docs.title: FTP
docs.text:
Discovery:

nxc ftp 10.10.10.0/24

Check:

nxc ftp --help

Assess:

Anonymous Access
Authentication
Readable Files
Writable Locations
Sensitive Files

Do not upload test files unless permitted.

docs.title: NFS
docs.text:
Where supported:

nxc nfs 10.10.10.0/24

Check:

nxc nfs --help

Review:

Exports
Permissions
Root Squashing
Writable Exports
Sensitive Data

docs.title: WMI
docs.text:
Check:

nxc wmi --help

WMI can provide remote-management functionality.

Successful authentication or management access should first be treated as an access-control relationship.

Do not automatically perform command execution.

docs.title: VNC
docs.text:
Check:

nxc vnc --help

Use VNC protocol assessment only where the service is in scope.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
NetExec modules extend protocol functionality.

List SMB modules:

nxc smb -L

LDAP:

nxc ldap -L

MSSQL:

nxc mssql -L

The available module set depends on the installed NetExec version.

docs.title: Module Help
docs.text:
Module options:

nxc smb -M <module> --options

Example structure:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    -M <module>

docs.title: Module Options
docs.text:
Options generally use:

-o KEY=value

Example structure:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    -M <module> \
    -o OPTION=value

Always inspect:

nxc smb -M <module> --options

before running a module.

docs.title: Multiple Modules
docs.text:
Current NetExec versions support specifying multiple modules.

General form:

nxc smb 10.10.10.10 \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' \
    -M module1 \
    -M module2

However, running many modules simultaneously can generate unnecessary traffic and complicate evidence collection.

Prefer targeted execution.

docs.title: Module Categories
docs.text:
Modules may perform different classes of operations.

Examples include:

Enumeration
Privilege Escalation
Credential Access
Remote Interaction
Configuration Assessment

Read the module description before execution.

Do not assume a module is read-only.

docs.title: Safe Module Workflow
docs.text:
Use:

List Modules
    |
    v
Read Description
    |
    v
Check Options
    |
    v
Understand Privileges
    |
    v
Understand Side Effects
    |
    v
Run Against One Target
    |
    v
Review Output
    |
    v
Expand If Necessary

docs.title: Audit Mode
docs.text:
Recent NetExec documentation includes an audit mode.

Check the installed version:

nxc --help

and the protocol-specific help.

Audit-oriented operation is useful when the engagement prioritises enumeration and configuration assessment over invasive actions.

docs.title: BloodHound Integration
docs.text:
NetExec supports integration with BloodHound-oriented workflows.

Check current LDAP options:

nxc ldap --help

and the official NetExec documentation.

BloodHound should be used to analyse relationships rather than as proof that every discovered edge is exploitable.

See:

BloodHound Cheatsheet

docs.title: BloodHound Workflow
docs.text:
NetExec / LDAP
      |
      v
AD Information
      |
      v
BloodHound Collection
      |
      v
Graph
      |
      v
Candidate Path
      |
      v
Manual Validation

docs.title: NetExec Database
docs.text:
NetExec stores assessment information in its own database.

Launch:

nxcdb

This is particularly useful during larger engagements.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
Workspaces separate engagement data.

Launch:

nxcdb

Then:

workspace list

Create:

workspace create assessment

Switch:

workspace assessment

Use separate workspaces for separate engagements.

docs.title: Database Location
docs.text:
NetExec workspaces are normally stored under:

~/.nxc/workspaces/

Protect this directory.

It may contain sensitive assessment data and credentials.

docs.title: Protocol Database
docs.text:
Inside nxcdb:

proto smb

Return:

back

Another protocol:

proto ldap

docs.title: Database Help
docs.text:
Inside:

help

Protocol-specific database commands differ.

Always inspect help before exporting or deleting data.

docs.title: Database Credentials
docs.text:
NetExec can store credentials discovered or used during an assessment.

Treat:

~/.nxc/

as sensitive engagement material.

Protect:

Permissions
Backups
Screenshots
Exports
Terminal Logs

docs.title: Database Export
docs.text:
NetExec supports exporting information from its database.

Inside the SMB database:

help export

Example structure:

export shares detailed shares.csv

Export only the data required for reporting or analysis.

docs.title: Workspace Hygiene
docs.text:
Recommended:

One Engagement
      =
One Workspace

Avoid mixing:

Customer A
Customer B
Lab Data
CTF Data
Personal Testing

in the same workspace.

docs.title: Authentication Mapping
docs.text:
A useful NetExec workflow is to build an access matrix.

Example:

Identity Host SMB WinRM Admin user1 WS01 Yes No No user1 SRV01 Yes Yes No admin1 SRV01 Yes Yes Yes

This is more useful than immediately executing commands.

docs.title: Access Mapping Model
docs.text:
Credential
    |
    v
Targets
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    v
Access Level
    |
    v
Expected?

docs.title: Local Administrator Reuse
docs.text:
If an approved local administrative credential is available, assess whether it is reused across multiple hosts.

The security issue is:

Same Local Administrative Secret
              |
              v
Multiple Hosts
              |
              v
Lateral Movement Risk

Do not perform uncontrolled authentication attempts.

docs.title: Domain Administrator Exposure
docs.text:
Do not routinely test highly privileged credentials across every workstation.

This creates unnecessary authentication exposure and may generate credentials on systems where they should never appear.

Prefer:

Least Privileged Test Account
      |
      v
Targeted Validation

docs.title: Authentication Failure Analysis
docs.text:
Common errors can indicate:

Bad Password
Disabled Account
Expired Password
Locked Account
Logon Restriction
Protocol Restriction
Signing Requirement
Authentication Policy
Network Failure
DNS Failure

Do not retry repeatedly without understanding the error.

docs.title: Password Spraying with NetExec
docs.text:
NetExec can perform high-volume authentication testing.

That does not mean it should be used blindly.

Before spraying:

Get Password Policy
        |
        v
Get Fine-Grained Policies
        |
        v
Determine Lockout Threshold
        |
        v
Determine Observation Window
        |
        v
Define Approved Accounts
        |
        v
Define Attempt Count
        |
        v
Obtain Approval

Prefer dedicated controlled spray procedures where the assessment specifically includes password auditing.

docs.title: Credential Types
docs.text:
Keep credential types distinct:

Domain Password
Local Password
NTLM Hash
Kerberos Ticket
Certificate
SSH Key
Database Credential

They have different security implications.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
Modern NetExec versions include certificate-related authentication functionality for supported protocols.

Check:

nxc <protocol> --help

Use certificate authentication only where the certificate and associated identity are within scope.

docs.title: Kerberos Tickets
docs.text:
If using an existing authorised Kerberos credential cache:

klist

Check:

echo "$KRB5CCNAME"

Then consult:

nxc <protocol> --help

for current Kerberos options.

docs.title: Relay Candidate Discovery
docs.text:
A safe early relay workflow is:

Discover Hosts
      |
      v
Check SMB Signing
      |
      v
Identify Candidates
      |
      v
Review LDAP Protections
      |
      v
Review HTTP Endpoints
      |
      v
Determine Authentication Source
      |
      v
Obtain Approval
      |
      v
Controlled Validation

NetExec can help with the discovery stages.

Do not jump directly from:

Signing Not Required

to:

Perform Relay

docs.title: LDAP Relay Considerations
docs.text:
Assess:

LDAP Signing
LDAP Channel Binding
LDAPS
EPA
Authentication Method
Target Privileges

Relay viability depends on the complete chain.

docs.title: Coercion Considerations
docs.text:
Authentication coercion can affect production services.

Before testing:

Is coercion in scope?
Which protocol is triggered?
Which account authenticates?
Where will authentication go?
Could the service become unstable?
Is relay also authorised?

Discovery and exploitation are separate phases.

docs.title: AD CS Relay Considerations
docs.text:
When AD CS is present, investigate:

Certificate Authority
Web Enrollment
Enrollment Services
HTTP vs HTTPS
Extended Protection
Authentication
Templates
Enrollment Rights

Use dedicated AD CS tooling for comprehensive analysis.

See:

Active Directory Cheatsheet

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
For evidence:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 | tee smb.txt

nxc ldap dc01.example.local \
    -u username \
    -p 'Password' |
    tee ldap.txt

Be aware that logs may contain:

Usernames
Domains
Hostnames
Credentials
Hashes
Share Names
Sensitive Paths

Protect them appropriately.

docs.title: Timestamp Evidence
docs.text:
Before important tests:

date -Is

Record:

Timestamp
Source
Target
Identity
Command
Result

This helps correlate testing with:

SIEM
EDR
Windows Event Logs
Firewall Logs
SOC Alerts

docs.title: Evidence Model
docs.text:
For each important NetExec result record:

Source Host
Source IP
Target Host
Target IP
Protocol
Identity
Authentication Type
Observed Access
Security Control
Impact

docs.title: Example - SMB Signing
docs.text:
Weak evidence:

Signing: False

Better:

Host: WS01
IP: 10.10.10.25
Protocol: SMB
SMB signing required: No
Authentication source available: Not yet established
Relay path: Not validated

Conclusion:

Potential relay target requiring additional validation.

docs.title: Example - Administrative Access
docs.text:
Weak:

Pwn3d!

Better:

Identity:
EXAMPLE\user1

Target:
SRV01

Protocol:
SMB

Observed:
Administrative access

Expected:
User should not administer server

Impact:
Potential excessive privilege and lateral movement path

docs.title: Example - Writable Share
docs.text:
Weak:

Share is writable.

Better:

Identity
   |
   v
Writable Share
   |
   v
What consumes files?
   |
   v
Privileged deployment process?
   |
   v
Security boundary?

A writable share is not automatically privilege escalation.

docs.title: Example - WinRM
docs.text:
Weak:

WinRM login successful.

Better:

Domain User
     |
     v
WinRM Authentication
     |
     v
Remote Management Group?
     |
     v
Administrative Rights?
     |
     v
Expected Access?

docs.title: Example - Kerberoast Candidate
docs.text:
Weak:

SPN found.

Better:

Account
   |

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid:

Running password lists without checking lockout policy
Testing Domain Admin credentials everywhere
Assuming Pwn3d means a vulnerability
Assuming SMB signing disabled means relay is guaranteed
Running every module
Dumping credentials by default
Spidering every share recursively
Mixing customer data in the same workspace
Using old CrackMapExec syntax without checking help
Ignoring DNS during Kerberos troubleshooting
Treating tool output as final evidence

docs.title: NetExec vs CrackMapExec
docs.text:
NetExec is the actively maintained continuation/fork of the CrackMapExec project lineage.

Modern documentation and commands use:

nxc

rather than relying on old:

crackmapexec
cme

examples.

When an old write-up says:

crackmapexec smb ...

look for the equivalent current NetExec syntax:

nxc smb ...

and verify options using:

nxc smb --help

docs.title: Internal Unauthenticated Workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify network
2. Identify DNS
3. Discover SMB hosts
4. Identify domains
5. Identify DCs
6. Check SMB signing
7. Identify LDAP
8. Identify Kerberos
9. Identify WinRM
10. Build target lists

Example:

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24

nxc smb 10.10.10.0/24 --gen-relay-list relay.txt

nxc ldap dc01.example.local

2. Enumerate SMB
3. Enumerate shares
4. Enumerate LDAP

7. Identify Kerberos candidates
8. Identify delegation
9. Identify AD CS

11. Map administrative access
12. Validate candidate paths

docs.title: Local Administrator Workflow
docs.text:
When an authorised local administrator credential is provided:

1. Test one target
2. Determine local vs domain context
3. Map where credential works
4. Identify credential reuse
5. Determine whether reuse is intended
6. Avoid unnecessary command execution
7. Document lateral movement exposure

docs.title: Assessment Checklist
docs.text:
• Check NetExec version
  • Confirm engagement workspace
  • Confirm target scope
  • Confirm credential scope
  • Check password lockout policy
  • Identify DNS
  • Identify domain
  • Identify DCs
  • Enumerate SMB hosts
  • Check SMB signing
  • Identify SMB shares
  • Identify LDAP
  • Enumerate domain users
  • Enumerate active users
  • Enumerate groups
  • Identify Kerberos candidates
  • Review delegation
  • Review AD CS
  • Identify WinRM
  • Identify MSSQL
  • Map administrative relationships
  • Review NetExec modules before use
  • Avoid unnecessary credential collection
  • Avoid unnecessary remote execution
  • Preserve evidence

docs.title: Reporting Checklist
docs.text:
For each result ask:

What did NetExec observe?

What identity was used?

What target was tested?

Was authentication required?

What permissions were present?

Is the access expected?

What security boundary exists?

Can the result be reproduced manually?

What is the actual security impact?

docs.title: Do Not Overreport
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

SMB Is Open
LDAP Is Open
WinRM Is Open
A Domain User Can Authenticate
A Share Exists
An SPN Exists
A User Appears in LDAP
SMB Signing Is Not Required
WinRM Authentication Works
NetExec Shows Administrative Access
A Module Produces Red Output

Instead determine:

Configuration
     +
Identity
     +
Permission
     +
Reachability
     +
Security Boundary

Security Impact

docs.title: Final NetExec Model
docs.text:
Do not use NetExec as:

Get Credentials
      |
      v
Spray Entire Network
      |
      v
Run Every Module
      |
      v
Dump Everything

Use:

Understand Scope
      |
      v
Identify Network
      |
      v
Discover Services
      |
      v
Identify Security Controls
      |
      v
Validate One Credential
      |
      v
Enumerate Relevant Data
      |
      v
Map Access
      |
      v
Identify Candidate Paths
      |
      v
Manual Validation
      |
      v
Minimal Proof
      |
      v
Report Impact

NetExec is most valuable when it answers questions such as:

Which Windows hosts exist?

Which domain do they belong to?

Where is SMB signing not required?

Which shares can this identity access?

Which systems accept this approved credential?

Where does this identity have elevated access?

Which domain objects should be investigated further?

Which protocols expose additional attack paths?

The goal is not:

Run as many NetExec commands as possible.

The goal is:

Turn network-scale Windows and Active Directory information
into a validated map of identities, systems, permissions,
security controls and attack paths.

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 445

Nmap:

nmap -p 445 --script smb2-security-mode,smb2-time 10.10.10.10

SMB protocol information:

nmap -p 445 --script smb-protocols 10.10.10.10

Use the dedicated SMB, NetExec and Active Directory notes for deeper assessment.

docs.title: LDAP Connectivity
docs.text:
LDAP:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 389

LDAPS:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 636

Global Catalog:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 3268

TLS Global Catalog:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 3269

docs.title: Kerberos Connectivity
docs.text:
TCP:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 88

UDP availability depends on the Netcat implementation and network behaviour.

docs.title: RDP
docs.text:
nc -vz 10.10.10.10 3389

Nmap:

nmap -p 3389 -sV 10.10.10.10

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
HTTP:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 5985

HTTPS:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 5986

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Banner:

nc 10.10.10.10 22

Client verbose:

ssh -v user@10.10.10.10

More verbose:

ssh -vvv user@10.10.10.10

Use verbose output carefully because it may contain usernames, key paths and environment information.

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text:
Connectivity:

nc -vz mail.example.com 25

TLS:

openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect mail.example.com:25

docs.title: IMAP
docs.text:
TLS:

openssl s_client -connect mail.example.com:993

STARTTLS:

openssl s_client -starttls imap -connect mail.example.com:143

docs.title: POP3
docs.text:
TLS:

openssl s_client -connect mail.example.com:995

docs.title: FTP
docs.text:
ftp 10.10.10.10

Nmap:

nmap -p 21 -sV 10.10.10.10

FTP sends credentials in cleartext unless protected by an appropriate TLS configuration.

docs.title: SNMP
docs.text:
Common port:

UDP 161

Basic version detection:

sudo nmap -sU -p 161 -sV 10.10.10.10

SNMP enumeration can disclose significant infrastructure information.

Use only where authorised.

docs.title: NFS
docs.text:
Common port:

TCP/UDP 2049

List exports:

showmount -e 10.10.10.10

Nmap:

nmap -p 111,2049 10.10.10.10

docs.title: RPC
docs.text:
Linux RPC:

rpcinfo -p 10.10.10.10

Windows RPC Endpoint Mapper commonly uses:

TCP 135

RPC services may then use dynamic ports.

docs.title: MSSQL
docs.text:
Default:

TCP 1433

Test:

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 1433

docs.title: MySQL
docs.text:
Default:

TCP 3306

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 3306

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Default:

TCP 5432

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 5432

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
Default:

TCP 6379

nc -vz 10.10.10.10 6379

Do not assume a database is unauthenticated based only on port exposure.

docs.title: Proxy Discovery
docs.text:
Linux:

env | grep -i proxy

Windows:

netsh winhttp show proxy

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Env: |
    Where-Object Name -match 'proxy'

docs.title: Public IP
docs.text:
When Internet access is authorised:

curl https://ifconfig.me

IPv4:

curl -4 https://ifconfig.me

IPv6:

curl -6 https://ifconfig.me

Do not use external IP-check services from sensitive networks unless permitted.

docs.title: Linux Firewall
docs.text:
nftables:

sudo nft list ruleset

iptables:

sudo iptables -L -n -v

UFW:

sudo ufw status verbose

docs.title: Windows Firewall
docs.text:
netsh advfirewall show allprofiles

PowerShell:

Get-NetFirewallProfile

Rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule

docs.title: Packet Capture - tcpdump
docs.text:
Interfaces:

tcpdump -D

Capture:

sudo tcpdump -i eth0

No name resolution:

sudo tcpdump -n -i eth0

Verbose:

sudo tcpdump -nn -i eth0

docs.title: tcpdump - Host Filter
docs.text:
sudo tcpdump -nn host 10.10.10.10

Source:

sudo tcpdump -nn src host 10.10.10.10

Destination:

sudo tcpdump -nn dst host 10.10.10.10

docs.title: tcpdump - Port Filter
docs.text:
sudo tcpdump -nn port 443

Source port:

sudo tcpdump -nn src port 443

Destination:

sudo tcpdump -nn dst port 443

docs.title: tcpdump - Protocol
docs.text:
TCP:

sudo tcpdump -nn tcp

UDP:

sudo tcpdump -nn udp

ICMP:

sudo tcpdump -nn icmp

docs.title: tcpdump - Multiple Conditions
docs.text:
HTTP or HTTPS:

sudo tcpdump -nn 'port 80 or port 443'

Host and port:

sudo tcpdump -nn 'host 10.10.10.10 and port 443'

docs.title: Save PCAP
docs.text:
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap

Read:

tcpdump -nn -r capture.pcap

PCAP files may contain:

Credentials
Session Tokens
Internal Addresses
DNS Queries
Application Data
Personal Information

Treat them as sensitive evidence.

docs.title: tshark
docs.text:
Interfaces:

tshark -D

Capture:

sudo tshark -i eth0

Read PCAP:

tshark -r capture.pcap

Display filter:

tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'http'

DNS:

tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'dns'

docs.title: Wireshark Display Filters
docs.text:
IP:

ip.addr == 10.10.10.10

Source:

ip.src == 10.10.10.10

Destination:

ip.dst == 10.10.10.10

TCP port:

tcp.port == 443

HTTP:

http

DNS:

dns

SMB:

smb2

Kerberos:

kerberos

LDAP:

ldap

TLS:

tls

docs.title: Capture vs Display Filters
docs.text:
Important distinction:

Capture Filter
     |
     +--> Determines what enters the PCAP

Display Filter
     |
     +--> Determines what Wireshark shows

Example capture filter:

host 10.10.10.10 and port 443

Example Wireshark display filter:

ip.addr == 10.10.10.10 && tcp.port == 443

docs.title: Network Discovery
docs.text:
A practical workflow:

Interface
   |
   v
Local Address
   |
   v
Subnet
   |
   v
Gateway
   |
   v
Routes
   |
   v
Neighbours
   |
   v
Reachable Hosts
   |
   v
Open Ports
   |
   v
Services

docs.title: Passive Before Active
docs.text:
Where practical:

Local Configuration
        |
        v
Routes
        |
        v
ARP / Neighbours
        |
        v
DNS
        |
        v
Existing Connections
        |
        v
Active Scanning

This can reduce unnecessary network traffic.

docs.title: Host Discovery
docs.text:
Authorised subnet:

nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24

Remember:

No Response
    !=
Host Offline

Host discovery can be affected by:

Firewalls
ICMP Filtering
Network ACLs
Routing
Endpoint Security

docs.title: ARP Discovery
docs.text:
On the local Ethernet segment, ARP-based discovery can be useful.

If installed:

sudo arp-scan --localnet

Specific subnet:

sudo arp-scan 192.168.1.0/24

Only scan authorised networks.

docs.title: Service Enumeration Workflow
docs.text:
Host
 |
 v
Open Port
 |
 v
Protocol
 |
 v
Service
 |
 v
Version
 |
 v
Configuration
 |
 v
Authentication
 |
 v
Security Controls

Do not jump directly from:

Port 443 Open

to:

HTTPS Application Vulnerable

docs.title: Network Segmentation
docs.text:
Test expected paths rather than indiscriminately scanning everything.

Example:

Workstation
    |
    X
    |
Server Management Network

A useful segmentation test asks:

Can Source A Reach Destination B
on Protocol C?

PowerShell:

Test-NetConnection 10.20.30.40 -Port 445

Linux:

nc -vz 10.20.30.40 445

Record:

Source
Destination
Protocol
Port
Expected Result
Actual Result

docs.title: Network Segmentation Matrix
docs.text:
Example:

Source Destination Port Expected Actual User VLAN DC 445 Allowed Allowed User VLAN SQL Admin 1433 Blocked Blocked Guest VLAN Internal Server 443 Blocked Allowed Server VLAN Management 5985 Restricted Allowed

The matrix provides stronger evidence than an isolated connectivity test.

docs.title: Pivoting
docs.text:
Pivoting allows traffic to reach networks not directly accessible from the assessment host.

Concept:

Attacker / Tester
       |
       v
Compromised or Authorised Pivot
       |
       v
Internal Network
       |
       v
Target

Use pivoting only where explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Routing vs Proxying
docs.text:
Routing
   |
   +--> Network-layer path

Proxying
   |
   +--> Application/session forwarding

Port Forwarding
   |
   +--> Specific listener -> destination

SOCKS
   |
   +--> Dynamic application proxy

docs.title: SSH Local Port Forward
docs.text:
Authorised example:

ssh -L 8443:10.10.20.10:443 user@pivot.example.com

Flow:

localhost:8443
      |
      v
SSH Tunnel
      |
      v
10.10.20.10:443

Then:

curl https://127.0.0.1:8443/

Certificate hostname mismatches may occur because the connection uses localhost.

docs.title: SSH Remote Port Forward
docs.text:
General form:

ssh -R REMOTE_PORT:DESTINATION:DESTINATION_PORT user@ssh-server

Example for a controlled lab service:

ssh -R 8080:127.0.0.1:8000 user@jump.example.com

Review SSH server forwarding policy before use.

docs.title: SSH Dynamic SOCKS Proxy
docs.text:
ssh -D 1080 user@pivot.example.com

This creates a local SOCKS proxy.

Concept:

Application
    |
    v
127.0.0.1:1080
    |
    v
SSH
    |
    v
Pivot
    |
    v
Internal Destination

docs.title: ProxyChains
docs.text:
Configuration commonly resides at:

/etc/proxychains4.conf

Example SOCKS entry:

socks5 127.0.0.1 1080

Then, for tools that work correctly through the proxy:

proxychains4 curl http://10.10.20.10/

Not every protocol or scanning mode works reliably through SOCKS.

docs.title: Nmap Through Proxy
docs.text:
Full SYN scanning does not operate through a normal SOCKS proxy in the same way as direct raw-packet scanning.

For limited TCP connect testing:

proxychains4 nmap -sT -Pn -n -p 80,443 10.10.20.10

Expect limitations and slower performance.

docs.title: Chisel
docs.text:
Project:

Chisel

Chisel can transport connections over HTTP using an SSH-secured tunnel.

Typical assessment use cases include:

Port Forwarding
SOCKS Proxying
Traversing Restricted Network Paths

Use the current project documentation for exact client/server syntax because options can change between versions.

docs.title: Ligolo-ng
docs.text:
Project:

Ligolo-ng

Ligolo-ng provides network tunnelling using a TUN-based approach.

Conceptually:

Tester
  |
  v
Ligolo Proxy
  |
  v
Agent
  |
  v
Internal Network

A TUN approach can make many tools behave more naturally than application-level SOCKS proxying.

Use the project's current documentation for exact deployment and route configuration.

docs.title: socat
docs.text:
TCP listener forwarding to a controlled service:

socat TCP-LISTEN:8080,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:8000

Concept:

:8080
  |
  v
socat
  |
  v
127.0.0.1:8000

Be careful about listener binding.

A listener exposed on all interfaces can unintentionally expose an internal service to other networks.

docs.title: SSH Tunnels - Security Considerations
docs.text:
Before creating a tunnel determine:

Who Can Connect to the Listener?
Where Does It Forward?
Does It Cross a Segmentation Boundary?
Does It Expose an Internal Service?
Will It Persist?
How Will It Be Removed?

Prefer loopback listeners where remote access is unnecessary.

docs.title: Linux IP Forwarding
docs.text:
Check:

sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

or:

cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward

Do not enable forwarding on production systems merely for testing without explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Windows IP Forwarding
docs.text:
Inspect routing-related configuration rather than enabling forwarding by default.

Routing behaviour may also be provided by:

RRAS
VPN Software
Hyper-V
Containers
Security Products
Third-Party Networking Software

docs.title: Network Namespaces - Linux
docs.text:
List:

ip netns list

Interfaces can also exist in:

Containers
Network Namespaces
Virtual Machines
VPNs

so the default namespace may not show every relevant network path.

docs.title: VPN Interfaces
docs.text:
Linux:

ip addr

Look for interfaces such as:

tun0
tap0
wg0
ppp0

Windows:

Get-NetAdapter

docs.title: WireGuard
docs.text:
Linux:

wg show

Routes still matter:

ip route

docs.title: Docker Networking
docs.text:
Networks:

docker network ls

Inspect:

docker network inspect bridge

Container interfaces and routes can expose additional network paths.

Only query Docker where authorised and accessible.

docs.title: Kubernetes Networking
docs.text:
Basic context:

kubectl cluster-info

Services:

kubectl get services -A

Pods:

kubectl get pods -A -o wide

Network assessment of Kubernetes should use dedicated container/Kubernetes methodology rather than relying solely on host networking commands.

docs.title: Cloud Metadata Addresses
docs.text:
A commonly used link-local address is:

169.254.169.254

Cloud providers use metadata services differently and modern deployments often require additional authentication or request controls.

Do not query metadata endpoints outside explicit scope.

docs.title: Loopback Services
docs.text:
Linux:

ss -ltnp

Look for:

127.0.0.1
::1

Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen |
    Where-Object {
        $_.LocalAddress -eq '127.0.0.1' -or
        $_.LocalAddress -eq '::1'
    }

A loopback-only service may still matter after obtaining authorised local access or through an approved tunnel.

docs.title: Binding Addresses
docs.text:
Important distinction:

127.0.0.1:8080

means IPv4 loopback only.

0.0.0.0:8080

generally means all IPv4 interfaces.

[::]:8080

generally means all IPv6 interfaces and can have platform-specific dual-stack behaviour.

docs.title: Network Exposure Model
docs.text:
Process
   |
   v
Socket
   |
   v
Bind Address
   |
   v
Firewall
   |
   v
Routing
   |
   v
Network ACL
   |
   v
Remote Client

An open local socket does not automatically mean it is remotely reachable.

docs.title: Proxy Awareness
docs.text:
When testing HTTP connectivity consider:

Application Proxy
System Proxy
Environment Proxy
Transparent Proxy
Security Gateway
Direct Route

The path observed by curl may differ from the path used by another application.

docs.title: HTTP Proxy with curl
docs.text:
curl -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 https://example.com/

SOCKS5:

curl --socks5 127.0.0.1:1080 https://example.com/

SOCKS with proxy-side DNS resolution:

curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 https://example.com/

The DNS distinction is important during pivoting.

docs.title: DNS Through a Proxy
docs.text:
A common mistake is:

Application traffic -> Proxy
DNS lookup -> Local machine

This can:

Fail to resolve internal names
Leak DNS queries
Produce misleading results

Use proxy-aware DNS resolution where supported.

docs.title: HTTPX
docs.text:
Project:

httpx

Probe hosts:

httpx -l hosts.txt

Useful information:

httpx -l hosts.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect

Save:

httpx -l hosts.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect -o alive.txt

Use only against authorised targets.

docs.title: Subdomain to Alive Host Workflow
docs.text:
Subdomain Enumeration
        |
        v
DNS Resolution
        |
        v
HTTP Probe
        |
        v
Alive Web Services

Example:

subfinder -d example.com -silent > subdomains.txt

Then:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -o alive.txt

This confirms responsive HTTP/HTTPS services, not whether the host itself is "alive" for every protocol.

docs.title: Nmap vs httpx
docs.text:
Nmap
 |
 +--> Network ports
 +--> Service detection
 +--> TCP / UDP

httpx
 |
 +--> HTTP / HTTPS
 +--> Status
 +--> Titles
 +--> Web technologies

They complement rather than replace one another.

docs.title: Curl vs Test-NetConnection
docs.text:
Test-NetConnection
       |
       +--> Can TCP connection be established?

curl / Invoke-WebRequest
       |
       +--> Does the application protocol work?

For example:

Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443

may succeed while:

Invoke-WebRequest https://example.com/

fails because of:

TLS
Proxy
HTTP Authentication
Application Behaviour
Certificate Validation

docs.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Use layers:

Interface
   |
   v
Address
   |
   v
Route
   |
   v
DNS
   |
   v
TCP
   |
   v
TLS
   |
   v
Application

Example:

ip addr
ip route
dig example.com
nc -vz example.com 443
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com
curl -v https://example.com/

docs.title: Windows Connectivity Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute
Resolve-DnsName example.com
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443
Invoke-WebRequest https://example.com/

docs.title: Linux Connectivity Troubleshooting
docs.text:
ip addr
ip route
ip neigh
cat /etc/resolv.conf
dig example.com
ping -c 4 example.com
traceroute example.com
nc -vz example.com 443
curl -v https://example.com/

docs.title: Network Segmentation Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Identify Source Zone
        |
        v
Identify Destination Zone
        |
        v
Define Expected Policy
        |
        v
Test Required Ports
        |
        v
Compare Expected vs Actual
        |
        v
Record Evidence

Avoid unnecessary full-port scans where the assessment objective can be answered with specific connectivity tests.

docs.title: Internal Network Enumeration
docs.text:
After obtaining authorised access to an internal host, start with local information:

Linux:

ip addr
ip route
ip neigh
ss -tulpn
cat /etc/resolv.conf

Windows:

Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute
Get-NetNeighbor
Get-NetTCPConnection
Get-DnsClientServerAddress

This often reveals:

Internal Subnets
Gateways
DNS Servers
Domain Controllers
Management Networks
VPN Networks
Local Services
Existing Connections

without immediately scanning the network.

docs.title: Existing Connections
docs.text:
Linux:

ss -tanp

Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established

Existing connections can reveal important infrastructure without generating new scan traffic.

docs.title: Network Shares
docs.text:
Windows:

net use

PowerShell:

Get-SmbMapping

Linux mounts:

mount

NFS:

mount -t nfs

Existing mounts can reveal trusted infrastructure.

docs.title: Hosts File
docs.text:
Linux:

cat /etc/hosts

Windows:

Get-Content "$env:WINDIR\System32\drivers\etc\hosts"

Hosts-file entries may reveal:

Internal Names
Development Systems
Legacy Infrastructure
Overrides

docs.title: Linux Network Configuration Files
docs.text:
Depending on distribution:

/etc/network/interfaces
/etc/netplan/
/etc/NetworkManager/
/etc/systemd/network/
/etc/resolv.conf

Do not modify network configuration during enumeration.

docs.title: Windows Network Configuration
docs.text:
Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetAdapter
Get-NetIPAddress
Get-NetRoute
Get-DnsClientServerAddress

docs.title: Active Directory Networking
docs.text:
Important protocols commonly include:

Port Protocol 53 DNS 88 Kerberos 135 RPC Endpoint Mapper 389 LDAP 445 SMB 464 Kerberos password change 636 LDAPS 3268 Global Catalog 3269 Global Catalog TLS 5985 WinRM HTTP 5986 WinRM HTTPS

RPC also uses dynamic ports.

Do not assume AD communication is limited to this table.

docs.title: Domain Controller Discovery
docs.text:
Windows:

nltest /dsgetdc:example.local

List:

nltest /dclist:example.local

DNS:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.example.local

Kerberos:

dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.local

docs.title: SMB Signing
docs.text:
Nmap:

nmap -p 445 --script smb2-security-mode 10.10.10.10

Signing configuration is especially important when assessing NTLM relay exposure.

See the dedicated Active Directory and SMB notes for deeper analysis.

docs.title: LDAP TLS
docs.text:
Test LDAPS:

openssl s_client -connect dc01.example.local:636 -servername dc01.example.local

LDAP StartTLS can be assessed using appropriate LDAP tooling.

Certificate presence alone does not prove that all LDAP clients are protected.

docs.title: Proxy Protocol Limitations
docs.text:
Not all protocols work through all proxies.

SOCKS
 |
 +--> TCP applications generally work well
 |
 +--> UDP support depends on tool/proxy
 |
 +--> Raw packets generally do not work
 |
 +--> SYN scanning does not behave like direct scanning

Choose tooling based on the actual transport path.

docs.title: Network Performance
docs.text:
Linux interface statistics:

ip -s link

Socket summary:

ss -s

Windows adapter statistics:

Get-NetAdapterStatistics

docs.title: Listening Service Review
docs.text:
Linux:

ss -ltnp

Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

For every unexpected listener determine:

Process
   |
   v
Service
   |
   v
Bind Address
   |
   v
Firewall Exposure
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Business Requirement

docs.title: External Exposure vs Internal Exposure
docs.text:
Listening on 0.0.0.0
        |
        v
Host Firewall
        |
        v
Network Firewall
        |
        v
NAT / Load Balancer
        |
        v
Internet

A service bound to all interfaces is not necessarily Internet exposed.

Validate the complete path.

docs.title: NAT
docs.text:
Concept:

Private Host
    |
    v
NAT Gateway
    |
    v
Public Address

Common forms:

SNAT
DNAT
PAT

NAT is not itself a security control equivalent to a firewall.

docs.title: Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Concept:

Listener A
    |
    v
Forwarder
    |
    v
Destination B

Port forwarding can be legitimate:

Load Balancing
Reverse Proxy
SSH Administration
Containers
Development

or security-sensitive when it crosses intended network boundaries.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy
docs.text:
Concept:

Client
   |
   v
Reverse Proxy
   |
   +--> Application 1
   +--> Application 2
   +--> Application 3

Common technologies include:

Nginx
Apache
HAProxy
Traefik
IIS ARR
Cloud Load Balancers

When testing a reverse proxy, distinguish proxy behaviour from backend behaviour.

docs.title: Forward Proxy
docs.text:
Client
   |
   v
Forward Proxy
   |
   v
Internet / Destination

Forward proxies can enforce:

Authentication
URL Filtering
TLS Inspection
Logging
Network Egress Policy

docs.title: Egress Testing
docs.text:
Define exactly what should be allowed.

Example:

Endpoint
   |
   v
TCP 443
   |
   v
Approved Proxy
   |
   v
Internet

Testing should answer questions such as:

Can the host connect directly?
Must it use the proxy?
Which ports are allowed?
Which destinations are allowed?
Is DNS restricted?

Avoid unnecessary external callbacks when a simple controlled connectivity test answers the question.

docs.title: HTTP Connectivity Test
docs.text:
Linux:

curl -I https://example.com/

Windows:

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://example.com/' -Method Head

TCP-only:

Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443

These test different layers.

docs.title: Network Evidence
docs.text:
For every network finding record:

Source Host
Source IP
Destination Host
Destination IP
Protocol
Port
Timestamp
Command
Result
Expected Policy
Actual Policy

docs.title: Example Segmentation Finding
docs.text:
Weak:

Port 445 is open.

Better:

A standard-user workstation in the User VLAN was able to
establish an SMB connection to TCP/445 on a server in the
restricted management network, despite the documented
segmentation policy requiring SMB traffic between these
zones to be blocked.

docs.title: Example Listener Finding
docs.text:
Weak:

Port 8080 is listening.

Better:

The administrative web service listens on 0.0.0.0:8080
and is reachable from the standard user network without
an intermediate access-control boundary.

Then validate authentication and business requirements before assigning severity.

docs.title: Example DNS Finding
docs.text:
Weak:

DNS zone transfer works.

Better:

The authoritative DNS server permitted an unauthenticated
AXFR request for the assessed zone from the testing network,
disclosing the zone's host and service records.

docs.title: Example Firewall Finding
docs.text:
Weak:

Firewall allows traffic.

Better:

The assessed endpoint was able to establish direct outbound
TCP/443 connections to Internet destinations despite the
documented requirement that Internet traffic traverse the
organisation's authenticated web proxy.

docs.title: Local Host
docs.text:
• Identify hostname
  • Identify interfaces
  • Identify IPv4 addresses
  • Identify IPv6 addresses
  • Identify MAC addresses
  • Identify gateways
  • Identify DNS servers
  • Review routing table
  • Review ARP / neighbours
  • Review hosts file

docs.title: Local Services
docs.text:
• Enumerate TCP listeners
  • Enumerate UDP listeners
  • Map ports to processes
  • Identify bind addresses
  • Review host firewall
  • Identify loopback-only services
  • Identify unexpected exposed services

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• Determine authorised ranges
  • Perform passive discovery first
  • Perform host discovery where required

docs.title: Quick Troubleshooting Checklist
docs.text:
When a service cannot be reached:

1. Is the local interface up?
2. Does the host have the expected IP?
3. Is there a route?
4. Does DNS resolve correctly?
5. Is the destination reachable?
6. Is the TCP/UDP port reachable?
7. Is TLS working?
8. Is the application responding?
9. Is a proxy required?
10. Is a firewall or ACL blocking the path?

Linux:

ip addr
ip route
dig example.com
ping -c 4 example.com
nc -vz example.com 443
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com
curl -v https://example.com/

Windows:

Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute
Resolve-DnsName example.com
Test-Connection example.com
Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443
Invoke-WebRequest https://example.com/

For internal assessments, begin with information already available from the host before generating additional network traffic.

The goal is not simply to discover as many open ports as possible.

Should it communicate?

    -OutFile 'C:\Temp\file.txt'

$response

docs.title: Base64
docs.text:
Encode UTF-8:

$text = 'test'

$bytes = [Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($text)

[Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes)

Decode:

$encoded = 'dGVzdA=='

$bytes = [Convert]::FromBase64String($encoded)

[Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString($bytes)

docs.title: PowerShell EncodedCommand
docs.text:
PowerShell's -EncodedCommand expects Base64 representing UTF-16LE command text.

Create an encoded command:

$command = 'Get-Date'

$bytes = [Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)

$encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes)

$encoded

Decode for analysis:

$bytes = [Convert]::FromBase64String($encoded)

[Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString($bytes)

Encoded commands are not encryption.

They are frequently used for legitimate automation as well as malicious activity.

InternalAllTheThings also highlights the UTF-16LE requirement for PowerShell encoded commands.

docs.title: Execution Policy
docs.text:

All scopes:

Get-ExecutionPolicy -List

Common values:

Restricted
AllSigned
RemoteSigned
Unrestricted
Bypass
Undefined

Important:

Execution Policy
       !=
Security Boundary

Execution Policy is intended primarily as a safety feature controlling script execution behaviour.

Do not treat it as equivalent to AppLocker or WDAC.

docs.title: Language Mode
docs.text:
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible values include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

docs.title: FullLanguage
docs.text:
FullLanguage provides the normal PowerShell language capabilities.

It is common on ordinary Windows systems.

Do not automatically report:

LanguageMode = FullLanguage

as a vulnerability.

Instead determine whether the endpoint's intended security architecture requires application control and PowerShell restrictions for untrusted users.

docs.title: Constrained Language Mode
docs.text:
Constrained Language Mode restricts access to certain PowerShell language features and .NET capabilities.

Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

A result such as:

ConstrainedLanguage

should be evaluated together with:

AppLocker
WDAC / App Control
PowerShell Version
Security Product
Policy Scope

Do not attempt to bypass Constrained Language Mode merely to test whether it can be bypassed unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: InternalAllTheThings and Constrained Mode
docs.text:
InternalAllTheThings includes historical PowerShell constrained-mode techniques.

Treat historical techniques carefully.

For modern Windows environments, validate:

Windows Version
PowerShell Version
WDAC/AppLocker
Patch State
Current Microsoft Behaviour

before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:

docs.title: Test AppLocker Policy
docs.text:
Executable:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy `
        -Path 'C:\Path\candidate.exe' `
        -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Script:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy `
        -Path 'C:\Path\candidate.ps1' `
        -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

This is preferable to executing a candidate merely to discover whether policy allows it.

docs.text:

    Where-Object DisplayName |
    Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher |

docs.title: SecureString Security Note
docs.text:
SecureString should not be treated as a universal encrypted-secret storage solution.

Its behaviour and security properties depend on the platform and how it is persisted.

Do not convert protected secrets to plaintext merely for convenience during an assessment.

InternalAllTheThings includes SecureString-to-plaintext handling, but credential disclosure should only be performed where explicitly required and authorised.

Invoke-Command `

    -ScriptBlock {
        hostname

Avoid embedding plaintext passwords directly in scripts.

docs.text:
A useful object:

[PSCustomObject]@{
    Timestamp = Get-Date
    Computer  = $env:COMPUTERNAME

}

$evidence = [PSCustomObject]@{

docs.title: Redact Secrets
docs.text:
Avoid including:

Passwords
Private Keys
Access Tokens
Session Tokens
API Keys
Credential Hashes
Recovery Keys

in screenshots or reports unless strictly necessary.

Prefer:

Secret Present
Value Redacted
Current User Has Read Access

docs.title: PowerShell Security Assessment Flow
docs.text:
PowerShell Version
       |
       v
Execution Policy
       |
       v
Language Mode
       |
       v
Logging
       |
       v
AMSI / Defender Context
       |
       v
AppLocker / WDAC
       |
       v
Effective Restrictions

No single item provides the full security picture.

docs.title: Execution Policy vs Application Control
docs.text:
Execution Policy
       |
       +--> Script Safety / User Intent

AppLocker / WDAC
       |
       +--> Application Control

Language Mode
       |
       +--> PowerShell Language Restrictions

Defender / AMSI
       |
       +--> Content Inspection / Detection

Do not treat these as interchangeable controls.

docs.title: Encoded Commands
docs.text:
InternalAllTheThings highlights PowerShell encoded-command handling.

For assessment and incident response, decoding an observed command is often more useful than executing it.

Decode:

$encoded = 'RwBlAHQALQBEAGEAdABlAA=='

[Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString(
    [Convert]::FromBase64String($encoded)
)

Use:

Decode
  |
  v
Inspect
  |
  v
Understand

rather than executing unknown encoded content.

docs.title: Script Loading
docs.text:
Import a trusted local script:

. C:\Path\script.ps1

This is dot-sourcing and places functions/variables from the script into the current scope.

Module:

Import-Module C:\Path\module.psm1

Before loading third-party scripts:

Get-FileHash C:\Path\script.ps1
Get-AuthenticodeSignature C:\Path\script.ps1

Only execute assessment tooling where explicitly permitted.

docs.title: Reflection and .NET
docs.text:
PowerShell can access .NET directly.

Example:

[Environment]::MachineName

Loaded assemblies:

[AppDomain]::CurrentDomain.GetAssemblies() |
    Select-Object FullName,Location

This capability is legitimate and widely used by administration and development tooling.

It is also one reason application-control and PowerShell security architecture should be assessed as a whole.

This cheatsheet intentionally does not include shellcode runners or memory-execution examples.

docs.title: CIM vs WMI
docs.text:
Prefer modern CIM cmdlets where practical:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem

rather than older:

Get-WmiObject

Get-WmiObject belongs to Windows PowerShell and is not available in the same way in modern cross-platform PowerShell.

docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

FullLanguage Mode
ExecutionPolicy Bypass at Process Scope

Was Supposed to Exist?

        v
Can This User Cross It?

docs.title: Safe Validation Model
docs.text:

Read Configuration
       |
       v
Read ACL
       |
       v
Read Effective Policy
       |
       v
Test Policy Decision
       |
       v
Document Result

Change Policy
Execute Untrusted Binary
Disable Defender
Modify AppLocker
Modify Registry
Change Service
Create Persistence

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Product

for routine software inventory when registry-based inventory is sufficient.

Avoid broad recursive searches such as:

Search every file on C: for "password"

without a clear reason.

Avoid assuming:

FullLanguage = Vulnerable

or:

ExecutionPolicy Restricted = Secure

or:

EncodedCommand = Malicious

or:

AppLocker Rule Allows Binary = Exploitable

Context matters.

Get-Content
Get-FileHash
Get-AuthenticodeSignature

# ACL
Get-Acl C:\Path

# Registry
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion'

# HTTP
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://example.com/'
Invoke-RestMethod -Uri 'https://example.com/api'

# Defender
Get-MpComputerStatus
Get-MpPreference

# AppLocker
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

# Events
Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 50

# AD
Get-ADDomain
Get-ADForest
Get-ADDomainController -Filter *

docs.title: Testing Model
docs.text:
PowerShell should be assessed as part of the wider Windows security model:

User
 |
 v
PowerShell
 |
 +--> Language Mode
 |
 +--> Execution Policy
 |
 +--> Modules / .NET
 |
 +--> Logging
 |
 +--> AMSI
 |
 +--> Defender
 |
 +--> AppLocker / WDAC
 |
 v
Effective Security Boundary

The key distinction is:

PowerShell Capability
        !=
Vulnerability

For example:

Invoke-WebRequest Available

does not itself mean:

Security Control Bypass

and:

FullLanguage

does not itself mean:

Privilege Escalation

A finding should demonstrate:

Principal
   |
   v
PowerShell Capability
   |
   v
Expected Restriction
   |
   v
Restriction Ineffective
   |
   v
Security Impact

docs.title: InternalAllTheThings
docs.text:
InternalAllTheThings - PowerShell Cheatsheet

Useful coverage reference for:

Execution Policy
Language Mode
Encoded Commands
Downloads
PowerShell Script Loading
.NET / Reflection
SecureString Handling

Some material is offensive-security focused or historical. Validate techniques against the Windows version, PowerShell version and current security controls before using them.

docs.text: Microsoft Learn - PowerShell Documentation

docs.text: Microsoft Learn - about_Execution_Policies

docs.text: Microsoft Learn - about_Language_Modes

docs.text: Microsoft Learn - powershell.exe
