docs.title: Final Notes
docs.text:
For everyday PowerShell use:

Get
 |
 v
Filter
 |
 v
Select
 |
 v
Export

For security assessment:

Identity
   |
   v
Environment
   |
   v
System
   |
   v
Processes / Services
   |
   v
Network
   |
   v
Files / Registry
   |
   v
Security Controls

The most useful initial commands are often:

whoami /all
$PSVersionTable
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode
Get-ExecutionPolicy -List
Get-ComputerInfo
Get-Process
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service
Get-ScheduledTask
Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen
Get-MpComputerStatus
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

When analysing PowerShell security, do not focus on a single setting.

Use:

Execution Policy
      +
Language Mode
      +
Logging
      +
AMSI
      +
Defender
      +
Application Control
      =
Effective PowerShell Security Posture

When encountering encoded or unfamiliar PowerShell:

Capture
   |
   v
Decode
   |
   v
Read
   |
   v
Understand
   |
   v
Decide Whether Execution Is Necessary

Do not execute unknown content merely to understand what it does.

For authorised assessments, the preferred workflow remains:

Enumerate
   |
   v
Analyse
   |
   v
Validate Safely
   |
   v
Collect Evidence
   |
   v
Report

docs.title: Web Application Security Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Quick-reference workflows, commands, testing ideas, tools, and validation checklists for authorised web application and API security assessments.

This cheatsheet is designed for the question:

What should I check next during a web assessment?

For detailed explanations, prerequisites, impact, remediation, and vulnerability-specific methodology, use the main Web Application Security notes.

docs.title: Authorised Use
docs.text:
Use these techniques only for:

Authorised penetration testing
Web application security assessments
API security assessments
Red team exercises
Purple team exercises
Bug bounty programmes within scope
Training environments
CTFs
Security research

Always follow:

Scope
Rules of Engagement
Rate Limits
Test Account Restrictions
Data Handling Requirements
Third-Party Restrictions
Production Safety Requirements

Some techniques can:

Create accounts
Send email
Trigger SMS
Lock users out
Modify application state
Upload files
Generate large numbers of requests
Cause backend requests
Interact with internal services
Create database records
Affect caches
Consume application resources
Trigger monitoring

Use the least intrusive test that answers the security question.

docs.title: Core Assessment Model
docs.text:
Scope
  |
  v
Reconnaissance
  |
  v
Technology Identification
  |
  v
Attack Surface Mapping
  |
  v
Content Discovery
  |
  v
Parameter Discovery
  |
  v
Authentication
  |
  v
Authorisation
  |
  v
Session Management
  |
  v
Input Handling
  |
  v
Business Logic
  |
  v
API / Client-Side Features
  |
  v
Infrastructure Behaviour
  |
  v
Manual Validation
  |
  v
Evidence
  |
  v
Reporting

The important principle is:

Discover
   |
   v
Understand
   |
   v
Hypothesise
   |
   v
Test
   |
   v
Validate
   |
   v
Assess Impact

rather than:

Run Scanner
    |
    v
Report Everything

docs.title: Starting Position
docs.text:
Web testing changes significantly depending on the access provided.

Internet / Unauthenticated
        |
        v
External Attack Surface

Authenticated Low-Privilege User
        |
        v
Authorisation + Business Logic

Multiple User Roles
        |
        v
Horizontal + Vertical Access Control

Administrator Account
        |
        v
Administrative Trust Boundaries

API Token
        |
        v
API Object + Function Authorisation

Source Code Available
        |
        v
White-Box Testing

Internal Application
        |
        v
Internal Trust + Identity + Infrastructure

docs.title: Assessment Perspectives
docs.text:
Always consider at least these perspectives:

Unauthenticated User
Authenticated User A
Authenticated User B
Higher-Privilege User
Administrator
API Client
Mobile Client
Internal Service
Third-Party Integration

A vulnerability may only become visible when comparing two contexts.

docs.title: Initial Target Setup
docs.text:
Useful shell variables:

export TARGET="https://app.example.com"
export HOST="app.example.com"
export DOMAIN="example.com"

Check:

printf 'TARGET=%s\nHOST=%s\nDOMAIN=%s\n' "$TARGET" "$HOST" "$DOMAIN"

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
dig "$HOST"

dig A "$HOST"

dig AAAA "$HOST"

dig CNAME "$HOST"

Nameservers:

dig NS "$DOMAIN"

Mail:

dig MX "$DOMAIN"

TXT:

dig TXT "$DOMAIN"

docs.title: Quick HTTP Inspection
docs.text:
Headers:

curl -I "$TARGET"

Verbose:

curl -v "$TARGET"

Follow redirects:

curl -L "$TARGET"

Headers and body:

curl -i "$TARGET"

Save response:

curl -sS "$TARGET" -o response.html

docs.title: HTTP Methods
docs.text:
OPTIONS:

curl -i -X OPTIONS "$TARGET"

HEAD:

curl -I "$TARGET"

Do not report unusual methods solely because they are advertised.

Determine whether they create meaningful unintended behaviour.

docs.title: Technology Identification
docs.text:
Technology fingerprinting helps guide testing.

Look for:

Web Server
Framework
Programming Language
CMS
JavaScript Framework
Reverse Proxy
CDN
WAF
Authentication Platform
API Framework
Cloud Platform
Version Information
Third-Party Components

docs.title: WhatWeb
docs.text:
Basic:

whatweb "$TARGET"

Verbose:

whatweb -v "$TARGET"

Higher aggression:

whatweb -a 3 "$TARGET"

Input file:

whatweb -i urls.txt

JSON logging:

whatweb --log-json=whatweb.json "$TARGET"

Treat fingerprinting as evidence, not proof.

WhatWeb Result
      |
      v
Verify Manually
      |
      v
Search Known Behaviour
      |
      v
Version Relevant?
      |
      v
Test Configuration

docs.title: Wappalyzer
docs.text:
Wappalyzer can identify technologies using public application signals such as:

HTML
JavaScript
Headers
Cookies
Meta Tags
Script Paths
Framework Patterns

Useful for identifying:

CMS
Framework
Analytics
CDN
Web Server
JavaScript Libraries
E-Commerce Platforms
Authentication Technology

Verify results independently.

docs.title: Technology Fingerprinting Sources
docs.text:
Combine:

WhatWeb
Wappalyzer
HTTP Headers
HTML Source
Cookies
JavaScript
Favicon
Error Pages
Default Pages
TLS Certificates
URL Structure
Static Asset Paths

docs.title: Default 404 Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Request a random path:

curl -i "$TARGET/this-page-should-not-exist-928374"

Inspect:

Status Code
Server Header
Framework Error Page
Page Title
HTML Structure
Response Length
Cookies
Debug Information

Default error pages can reveal:

Framework
CMS
Reverse Proxy
Application Server
Hosting Platform

The 0xdf Default 404 Pages reference is useful for visual fingerprinting.

docs.title: Favicon Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Download:

curl -sS "$TARGET/favicon.ico" -o favicon.ico

Hash:

md5sum favicon.ico

sha256sum favicon.ico

Favicon hashes can support technology identification but should not be treated as definitive proof.

docs.title: Subdomain Enumeration
docs.text:
Common sources:

Certificate Transparency
DNS
Search Engines
Passive DNS
Subfinder
Amass
Assetfinder
crt.sh

Subfinder:

subfinder -d "$DOMAIN" -silent

Save:

subfinder -d "$DOMAIN" -silent -o subdomains.txt

docs.title: Probe Discovered Hosts
docs.text:
httpx -l subdomains.txt

Useful metadata:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect

Add IP:

httpx -l subdomains.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect -ip

docs.title: Attack Surface Inventory
docs.text:
Record:

Hostname
IP
Port
Protocol
Status
Title
Technology
Authentication Required?
Application Purpose
Environment
Interesting Paths
Notes

Example:

app.example.com
api.example.com
admin.example.com
dev.example.com
staging.example.com
files.example.com
auth.example.com
sso.example.com

docs.title: Virtual Host Enumeration
docs.text:
A single IP may host multiple applications.

Check:

Host Header
TLS Certificate
DNS
Reverse DNS
Application Redirects
Error Responses

Fuzzing example:

ffuf -w subdomains.txt -u https://10.10.10.10/ -H 'Host: FUZZ.example.com'

Use response filtering to remove the default virtual-host response.

docs.title: robots.txt
docs.text:
curl -sS "$TARGET/robots.txt"

Look for:

Disallowed Paths
Administrative Paths
Old Endpoints
Uploads
Backups
Internal Features

Remember:

Disallow
   !=
Access Control

docs.title: sitemap.xml
docs.text:
curl -sS "$TARGET/sitemap.xml"

Useful for discovering:

Routes
Products
Profiles
Legacy URLs
Localized Paths
Application Sections

docs.title: security.txt
docs.text:
curl -sS "$TARGET/.well-known/security.txt"

Useful for understanding:

Security Contact
Disclosure Policy
Acknowledgements
Scope Information

docs.title: Common Interesting Files
docs.text:
Check where appropriate:

/robots.txt
/sitemap.xml
/.well-known/security.txt
/favicon.ico
/manifest.json
/asset-manifest.json
/openapi.json
/swagger.json
/swagger-ui/
/api-docs
/graphql
/graphiql
/.git/
/.env
/server-status
/phpinfo.php

Do not assume these paths exist.

docs.title: Content Discovery
docs.text:
Useful tools:

ffuf
feroxbuster
gobuster
dirsearch
Burp Content Discovery

docs.title: ffuf
docs.text:
Basic:

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-words.txt -u "$TARGET/FUZZ"

Extensions:

ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-words.txt -u "$TARGET/FUZZ" -e .php,.asp,.aspx,.jsp,.json,.txt,.xml,.bak

docs.title: feroxbuster
docs.text:
feroxbuster -u "$TARGET"

With wordlist:

feroxbuster -u "$TARGET" -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt

docs.title: gobuster
docs.text: gobuster dir -u "$TARGET" -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt

docs.title: Soft 404s
docs.text:
Do not rely only on status codes.

Compare:

Status
Length
Words
Lines
Title
Body Similarity
Redirect Location

Example:

/random-1234 -> 200, 4812 bytes
/admin       -> 200, 4812 bytes

This may indicate a soft 404.

docs.title: Discovery Workflow
docs.text:
Known URL
   |
   v
Random 404 Baseline
   |
   v
Wordlist
   |
   v
Filter Baseline
   |
   v
Interesting Responses
   |
   v
Manual Inspection

docs.title: Backup Files
docs.text:
Look for accidental copies such as:

.bak
.old
.orig
.save
.tmp
~
.zip
.tar
.tar.gz
.7z

Focus on known filenames rather than generating excessive requests.

docs.title: Git Repository Exposure
docs.text:
Check:

curl -I "$TARGET/.git/HEAD"

Potential exposure can reveal:

Source Code
Commit History
Deleted Secrets
Configuration
Internal URLs
Credentials
API Keys

Do not download an entire repository unless authorised and necessary.

docs.title: JavaScript Discovery
docs.text:
JavaScript frequently reveals hidden application functionality.

Look for:

API Endpoints
Routes
Parameters
Feature Flags
Internal Hosts
WebSocket URLs
GraphQL Endpoints
Authentication Logic
Source Maps
Secrets
Debug Features
Third-Party Integrations

docs.title: Find JavaScript References
docs.text:
From downloaded HTML:

grep -Eo 'src="[^"]+\.js[^"]*"' response.html

docs.title: Search Downloaded JavaScript
docs.text:
grep -RniE 'api|token|secret|password|graphql|websocket|admin|internal|debug' js/

Use findings as leads.

Do not automatically report every string containing token or secret.

docs.title: Source Maps
docs.text:
Look for:

.js.map
sourceMappingURL

Example:

grep -Rni 'sourceMappingURL' js/

Source maps may reveal:

Original Source
Component Names
Internal Routes
API Calls
Developer Comments

docs.title: Crawling
docs.text:
Useful tools:

Katana
Burp Suite
gau
waybackurls
hakrawler

docs.title: Katana
docs.text:
katana -u "$TARGET"

Save:

katana -u "$TARGET" -o katana.txt

JavaScript crawling:

katana -u "$TARGET" -jc

docs.title: Historical URLs
docs.text:
gau:

gau "$DOMAIN"

waybackurls:

echo "$DOMAIN" | waybackurls

Historical URLs may reveal:

Old Endpoints
Old Parameters
Deprecated APIs
Legacy File Names
Removed Features

Historical availability does not prove the endpoint still exists.

docs.title: Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Parameters can appear in:

Query Strings
POST Forms
JSON
XML
Headers
Cookies
Path Segments
GraphQL Variables
Multipart Requests
WebSocket Messages

docs.title: Arjun
docs.text: arjun -u "$TARGET"

docs.title: ParamSpider
docs.text:
Typical workflow:

python3 paramspider.py -d example.com

Review discovered URLs before sending additional probes.

docs.title: Parameter Inventory
docs.text:
Record:

Endpoint
Method
Parameter
Location
Type
Authentication Required
Observed Behaviour
Potential Sink

docs.title: Input Location Model
docs.text:
User Input
   |
   +--> Query
   +--> Body
   +--> JSON
   +--> XML
   +--> Header
   +--> Cookie
   +--> Path
   +--> File
   +--> WebSocket
   |
   v
Application

Do not test only URL parameters.

docs.title: Burp Suite Core Workflow
docs.text:
Proxy
  |
  v
HTTP History
  |
  v
Target Map
  |
  v
Repeater
  |
  v
Compare Behaviour
  |
  v
Intruder / Extensions
  |
  v
Manual Validation

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Use Repeater for:

Parameter Modification
Role Comparison
Header Testing
Cookie Testing
Method Changes
Content-Type Changes
API Testing
Authentication Testing
Business Logic
Race Condition Preparation
Cache Testing

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Useful for comparing:

User A vs User B
Authenticated vs Unauthenticated
Valid vs Invalid ID
GET vs POST
Different Content Types
Different Host Headers
Cache Hit vs Miss

docs.title: Useful Burp Extensions
docs.text:
Depending on the test:

Autorize
AuthMatrix
Logger++
Param Miner
HTTP Request Smuggler
Turbo Intruder
JWT Editor
JSON Web Tokens
Backslash Powered Scanner
Collaborator Everywhere
Upload Scanner
Java Deserialization Scanner
Software Vulnerability Scanner
GraphQL Raider
JS Link Finder
Content Type Converter

Install only trusted extensions and review what traffic they generate.

docs.title: Burp Param Miner
docs.text:
Useful for discovering:

Hidden Headers
Unkeyed Headers
Hidden Parameters
Cache Inputs
Host Header Behaviour

Especially useful during:

Cache Poisoning
Host Header Testing
Parameter Discovery

docs.title: Collaborator / Out-of-Band Testing
docs.text:
Useful for validating blind interactions such as:

SSRF
XXE
Blind XSS
Blind Command Injection
External Service Interaction

Use only an approved callback service.

Avoid exposing sensitive application data to third-party infrastructure.

docs.title: Authentication Testing
docs.text:
Map:

Registration
Login
Logout
Password Reset
Password Change
MFA
Remember Me
Account Recovery
Email Verification
SSO
OAuth
SAML
API Authentication
Session Creation

docs.title: Login Checklist
docs.text:
Check:

[ ] Username enumeration
[ ] Email enumeration
[ ] Error-message differences
[ ] Response-length differences
[ ] Timing differences
[ ] Rate limiting
[ ] Lockout behaviour
[ ] MFA
[ ] CAPTCHA
[ ] Session rotation
[ ] Password policy
[ ] Remember-me behaviour
[ ] SSO fallback paths

docs.title: Username Enumeration
docs.text:
Compare:

Known User
Unknown User
Wrong Password
Locked User
Disabled User

Look for differences in:

Message
Status
Length
Timing
Headers
Redirects
Cookies

Avoid high-volume enumeration unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Password Policy
docs.text:
Assess:

Minimum Length
Maximum Length
Character Requirements
Common Password Blocking
Breached Password Detection
Password Reuse
Password History
Password Change Controls

Do not equate complexity requirements with strong password security.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Test carefully.

Questions:

Is limiting per IP?

Per account?

Per session?

Per device?

Per endpoint?

Global?

Does it apply across equivalent endpoints?

Does it reset unexpectedly?

Can concurrent requests bypass the intended control?

Avoid intentionally locking accounts unless authorised.

docs.title: Anti-Automation
docs.text:
Review:

CAPTCHA
Rate Limiting
Progressive Delay
Account Lockout
Device Signals
Risk-Based Authentication
MFA
Transaction Limits

A CAPTCHA alone is not a complete anti-automation control.

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
Map:

Request Reset
    |
    v
Token Creation
    |
    v
Token Delivery
    |
    v
Token Validation
    |
    v
Password Change
    |
    v
Session Handling

Check:

User Enumeration
Token Entropy
Token Lifetime
Single Use
Account Binding
Host Header Dependence
Email Change Interaction
Session Invalidation
MFA Interaction
Rate Limiting

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
Check:

Duplicate Accounts
Email Verification
Username Normalisation
Case Sensitivity
Reserved Names
Role Assignment
Invite Codes
Tenant Assignment
Referral Logic
Registration Limits
Domain Restrictions

docs.title: Account Recovery
docs.text:
Ask:

Can recovery bypass MFA?

Can recovery change account identity?

Can recovery tokens be reused?

Does recovery invalidate sessions?

Are old email addresses trusted?

Are security questions predictable?

docs.title: MFA
docs.text:
Check:

Enrollment
Activation
Challenge
Recovery
Backup Codes
Device Trust
Remember Device
MFA Reset
Alternative Login Paths
SSO Paths
API Paths

The key question is:

Can authentication reach the same privilege without satisfying MFA?

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
Inspect:

Session Cookie
Session Token
Refresh Token
CSRF Token
Remember-Me Token
Device Token

docs.title: Cookie Attributes
docs.text:
Look for:

Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
Path
Domain
Expires
Max-Age

Example:

curl -I "$TARGET"

Missing attributes should be interpreted in application context.

docs.title: Session Rotation
docs.text:
Check whether the session identifier changes after:

Login
Privilege Change
Password Change
MFA
Account Recovery
Role Change

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text:
Concept:

Pre-Authentication Session
          |
          v
Victim Authenticates
          |
          v
Same Session Identifier?

Secure behaviour normally involves appropriate session regeneration at authentication boundaries.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:
Check:

Server-Side Session Invalidated?
Cookie Removed?
Refresh Token Revoked?
Back Button Behaviour?
Multiple Sessions?
API Token Still Valid?

docs.title: Concurrent Sessions
docs.text:
Determine:

Are multiple sessions allowed?

Can users view sessions?

Can sessions be revoked?

Does password change revoke old sessions?

Does MFA reset revoke old sessions?

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Always test authorisation independently from authentication.

Authentication
      !=
Authorisation

Use at least:

Unauthenticated
User A
User B
Administrator

where permitted.

docs.title: Horizontal Authorisation
docs.text:
Example concept:

User A -> /account/1001
User B -> /account/1002

Test whether User A can access User B's object.

docs.title: Vertical Authorisation
docs.text:
Example:

Normal User
    |
    v
Administrative Function

Check whether server-side authorisation prevents access.

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
Look for identifiers in:

URL Paths
Query Parameters
JSON
GraphQL Variables
Headers
Cookies
File Names
UUIDs
Numeric IDs
Encoded Values

Use two controlled accounts where possible.

docs.title: IDOR Testing Model
docs.text:
User A
   |
   v
Object A
   |
   v
Capture Request
   |
   v
Change Identifier
   |
   v
Object B
   |
   v
Server-Side Authorisation?

Do not access unrelated real-user data unnecessarily.

docs.title: Function-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Check:

GET vs POST
UI-hidden endpoints
Admin APIs
Bulk actions
Export functions
Import functions
Delete operations
Role-management endpoints

Removing a button from the UI is not authorisation.

docs.title: Method-Based Access Control
docs.text:
Compare:

GET
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

Do not assume an endpoint applies identical authorisation to every method.

docs.title: Content-Type Differences
docs.text:
Compare where appropriate:

application/json
application/x-www-form-urlencoded
multipart/form-data
application/xml
text/plain

Different parsers may reach different validation or authorisation paths.

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities often require understanding what the application is supposed to do.

Map:

Workflow
State
Role
Limit
Price
Quantity
Ownership
Approval
Sequence
Trust Boundary

docs.title: Business Logic Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Can steps be skipped?

Can steps be repeated?

Can steps occur out of order?

Can values become negative?

Can limits be exceeded?

Can the same benefit be claimed twice?

Can another user's state be referenced?

Can client-controlled values override server values?

Can approval be bypassed?

Can stale state be reused?

docs.title: Workflow Testing
docs.text:
Step 1
  |
  v
Step 2
  |
  v
Step 3

Try:

1 -> 3
2 -> 1
3 directly
2 twice
3 twice
Old Step 2 after Step 3

Only where safe and authorised.

docs.title: Client-Side Validation
docs.text:
If validation exists only in:

JavaScript
HTML Attributes
Mobile Client
Frontend Framework

verify whether the server independently enforces it.

docs.title: Server-Side Validation
docs.text:
Test:

Boundary Values
Unexpected Types
Missing Fields
Duplicate Fields
Null Values
Empty Values
Negative Values
Large Values
Alternative Encodings

Avoid resource-exhaustion testing unless explicitly permitted.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Race conditions occur when concurrent requests interact with shared state incorrectly.

Common areas:

Coupon Redemption
Gift Cards
Balance Transfers
Inventory
Invitations
Password Reset
Email Verification
MFA
Account Registration
Voting
Promo Codes
Single-Use Tokens
File Processing

docs.title: Race Condition Model
docs.text:
Check State
    |
    v
Action Allowed?
    |
    v
Update State

If multiple requests reach the vulnerable window:

Request A ----\
               > Check Before Update
Request B ----/

both may be accepted.

docs.title: Race Condition Testing
docs.text:
Prefer controlled test data.

Use Burp Repeater's parallel request functionality or Turbo Intruder where appropriate.

Start with a very small number of requests.

Do not perform uncontrolled concurrency against production systems.

docs.title: Rate-Limit Race Conditions
docs.text:
A limit may be correctly enforced sequentially but fail under concurrency.

Check carefully:

Sequential Requests
        |
        v
Limit Works

Parallel Requests
        |
        v
Same Limit?

docs.title: HTTP Basics
docs.text:
Understand:

Request Line
Headers
Body

Example:

POST /api/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: session=...

{"displayName":"test"}

docs.title: Response Analysis
docs.text:
Inspect:

Status
Headers
Cookies
Redirect
Content-Type
Content-Length
Body
Timing
Cache Headers
Security Headers

docs.title: Security Headers
docs.text:
Common headers:

Content-Security-Policy
Strict-Transport-Security
X-Content-Type-Options
Referrer-Policy
Permissions-Policy
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy

Legacy:

X-Frame-Options

Do not report missing headers without understanding application context and actual risk.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Basic inspection:

openssl s_client -connect "$HOST:443" -servername "$HOST"

Certificate:

echo | openssl s_client -connect "$HOST:443" -servername "$HOST" 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

Nmap:

nmap -p443 --script ssl-cert,ssl-enum-ciphers "$HOST"

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Inspect:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Access-Control-Allow-Methods
Access-Control-Allow-Headers
Vary

Test with a controlled Origin:

curl -i "$TARGET" -H 'Origin: https://example.invalid'

docs.title: CORS Model
docs.text:
Attacker-Controlled Origin
        |
        v
Browser Sends Request
        |
        v
Server CORS Policy
        |
        v
Browser Permits Response Reading?

A permissive-looking header is not automatically exploitable.

Consider:

Credentials
Sensitive Response
Origin Reflection
Browser Behaviour
Preflight

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
Ask:

Does request change state?

Does browser automatically attach authentication?

Is there an unpredictable CSRF token?

Is token bound appropriately?

Are SameSite cookies relevant?

Does Origin/Referer validation exist?

Can content type be changed?

docs.title: CSRF Testing Model
docs.text:
State-Changing Request
       |
       v
Authentication via Browser?
       |
       v
Anti-CSRF Control?
       |
       v
Can Cross-Site Request Be Sent?
       |
       v
Impact

docs.title: Clickjacking
docs.text:
Inspect:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors
X-Frame-Options

Check whether sensitive UI can be framed.

Do not report frameability alone without considering what user actions could be induced.

docs.title: Open Redirect
docs.text:
Look for parameters such as:

url
uri
redirect
redirect_uri
return
returnUrl
next
continue
dest
destination
callback

Assess impact in context:

Phishing
OAuth
SSO
Trusted-Domain Bypass
Security-Control Bypass

docs.title: XSS
docs.text:
Types:

Reflected
Stored
DOM-Based

Identify:

Source
Context
Sink
Encoding
Sanitisation
CSP
Execution
Impact

docs.title: XSS Contexts
docs.text:
HTML
HTML Attribute
JavaScript
URL
CSS
DOM
Template

Payloads are context-dependent.

Do not blindly paste large payload lists.

docs.title: Safe XSS Validation
docs.text:
Start with harmless markers:

XSS_TEST_12345

Determine:

Reflected?
Encoded?
Stored?
Context?

Then use the minimum harmless proof needed to demonstrate script execution in the authorised test environment.

docs.title: DOM-Based Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Review sources such as:

location
location.hash
location.search
document.URL
document.referrer
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage

Potential sinks include:

innerHTML
outerHTML
document.write
eval
setTimeout with string
setInterval with string
location assignment

Context determines whether the flow is dangerous.

docs.title: DOM Clobbering
docs.text:
DOM clobbering abuses HTML elements and named properties to influence JavaScript assumptions about global variables or object properties.

Look for code patterns that trust:

window.someName
document.someName
element.id
element.name

without verifying the expected object type.

Testing model:

Attacker-Controlled HTML
        |
        v
Named DOM Element
        |
        v
JavaScript Property Resolution
        |
        v
Unexpected Object / Value
        |
        v
Security-Relevant Sink?

Do not report clobbering unless it affects meaningful application behaviour.

docs.title: HTML Injection
docs.text:
Test whether attacker-controlled HTML is rendered as markup.

Differentiate:

HTML Injection
      !=
JavaScript Execution

Assess impact such as:

UI Manipulation
Content Spoofing
Phishing
Form Injection
Security Messaging Manipulation

docs.title: Blind XSS
docs.text:
Potential sinks include:

Admin Panels
Support Tickets
Log Viewers
CRM Systems
Moderation Interfaces
Analytics Dashboards
Back-Office Applications

Use only approved callback infrastructure.

Do not send sensitive data to third-party collectors.

docs.title: XS-Leaks
docs.text:
Cross-site leaks can use browser side channels to infer information about another origin.

Areas include:

Framing
Window References
Resource Loading
Cache State
Timing
Navigation
Browser APIs

Assess browser protections and whether sensitive cross-origin state can actually be inferred.

docs.title: Third-Party JavaScript
docs.text:
Review:

Analytics
Chat Widgets
Tag Managers
Payment Scripts
CDN Libraries
Advertising
Support Widgets

Questions:

Who controls the script?

Does it execute in the application's origin?

Is integrity checking used where appropriate?

What data can it access?

What happens if the supplier is compromised?

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
Look for database-backed input in:

Query Parameters
Search
Filters
Sorting
Login
IDs
JSON
Headers
Cookies
API Parameters

Start with controlled behavioural testing.

docs.title: SQLi Signals
docs.text:
Compare:

Normal Input
Special Character
Boolean Condition
Type Mismatch
Unexpected Value

Observe:

Error
Status
Length
Timing
Returned Rows
Application Behaviour

docs.title: sqlmap
docs.text:
Use only after manual evidence suggests SQL injection.

Basic:

sqlmap -u 'https://app.example.com/item?id=1'

Request file:

sqlmap -r request.txt

Avoid aggressive options by default.

Do not dump production databases simply because a tool can.

docs.title: SQLi Validation Model
docs.text:
Input
  |
  v
Database Query?
  |
  v
Behaviour Difference
  |
  v
Repeatable?
  |
  v
Injection Confirmed?
  |
  v
Minimum Evidence

docs.title: NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
Potential technologies:

MongoDB
CouchDB
Elasticsearch
Other document/query stores

Look for:

JSON Objects
Filter Parameters
Search
Authentication
Nested Objects
Operator Handling
Type Confusion

docs.title: NoSQL Testing Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Can scalar input become an object?

Are query operators accepted from user input?

Are types enforced?

Are filters constructed directly from JSON?

Does authentication compare user-controlled query objects?

Use harmless differential testing before attempting broader extraction.

docs.title: LDAP Injection
docs.text:
LDAP-backed functionality may include:

Authentication
Directory Search
Employee Lookup
Group Search
Address Books
Internal Portals

Look for unsafely constructed LDAP filters.

Test with controlled syntax changes and observe whether directory query behaviour changes.

docs.title: OS Command Injection
docs.text:
Potential sinks:

Ping
Traceroute
DNS Lookup
File Conversion
Backup
Archive
Image Processing
Git Operations
System Utilities
Administrative Features

Start with non-destructive behavioural tests.

docs.title: Command Injection Model
docs.text:
Input
  |
  v
Application
  |
  v
Shell / Process?
  |
  v
User Input Reaches Command?
  |
  v
Observable Behaviour?

Avoid destructive commands.

docs.title: Commix
docs.text:
Where command injection is already suspected:

commix --url='https://app.example.com/example?parameter=value'

Review tool behaviour before using automated exploitation options.

docs.title: SSTI
docs.text:
Potential template engines include:

Jinja2
Twig
Freemarker
Velocity
Smarty
Handlebars
ERB

Start with simple arithmetic/template-expression detection appropriate to the suspected engine.

Determine:

Template Engine
Evaluation Context
Sandbox
Available Objects
Impact

Do not immediately attempt command execution.

docs.title: XXE
docs.text:
Potential XML entry points:

SOAP
XML APIs
SAML
SVG
Document Upload
RSS
XML Configuration

Check:

DOCTYPE handling
External entity resolution
XInclude
Parser configuration
Out-of-band interaction

Use controlled resources.

docs.title: Blind XXE
docs.text:
When output is not reflected:

XML Input
   |
   v
External Reference
   |
   v
Approved Callback
   |
   v
Interaction?

Do not request sensitive local files merely to prove external entity processing if a harmless callback is sufficient.

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
Potential URL-taking functionality:

URL Preview
Webhook
Import
Image Fetch
PDF Generator
Proxy
Callback
Avatar
Feed Import
Cloud Integration
Document Conversion

docs.title: SSRF Testing
docs.text:
Start with an approved controlled URL.

Application
    |
    v
Fetch URL
    |
    v
Controlled Server
    |
    v
Observe Request

Then determine:

Protocol Restrictions
Redirect Handling
DNS Resolution
Allowlist
Blocklist
Internal Reachability
Response Visibility

Avoid probing sensitive internal services unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Blind SSRF
docs.text:
Use approved out-of-band infrastructure.

Evidence can be as simple as:

Timestamp
Source IP
Hostname
Requested Path
Headers

Do not escalate to internal metadata access unless required and permitted.

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Potential parameters:

file
path
page
template
download
document
folder
filename

Start with known harmless application files where possible.

Assess:

Canonicalisation
Encoding
Path Normalisation
Allowlist
Base Directory Enforcement

docs.title: File Inclusion
docs.text:
Differentiate:

Path Traversal
Local File Inclusion
Remote File Inclusion
Template Inclusion

Determine what the application actually does with the supplied path.

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
Map the complete pipeline:

Upload
  |
  v
Validation
  |
  v
Storage
  |
  v
Processing
  |
  v
Retrieval
  |
  v
Rendering / Execution

docs.title: File Upload Checklist
docs.text:
Check:

Extension
MIME Type
Magic Bytes
Filename
Path Handling
Storage Location
Randomisation
Overwrite
Access Control
Direct Access
Content-Disposition
Image Processing
Archive Extraction
Antivirus
Execution
Public Exposure
Metadata

docs.title: Safe Upload Validation
docs.text:
Prefer harmless files.

For antivirus validation, the EICAR test file may be appropriate where explicitly approved.

Do not upload executable malware to production systems merely to prove that file validation is incomplete.

docs.title: Image Processing
docs.text:
Upload pipelines may invoke:

ImageMagick
GraphicsMagick
ExifTool
Ghostscript
PDF Libraries
Office Converters
Thumbnail Generators

Fingerprint processing behaviour carefully.

A component version alone does not prove vulnerability.

docs.title: Dynamic PDF / Document Generation
docs.text:
Features such as:

Print to PDF
Invoice Generation
Report Export
HTML to PDF
Document Preview
Screenshot Generation

may introduce additional server-side processing.

Assess:

External Resource Loading
Internal URL Fetching
HTML Interpretation
Template Injection
File Access
JavaScript Handling
Metadata Exposure

Use harmless controlled resources for validation.

docs.title: Insecure Deserialization
docs.text:
Potential formats:

Java Serialization
.NET Serialization
PHP Serialization
Python Pickle
Ruby Marshal
Custom Binary Formats
Signed Application Objects

Look for:

Opaque Encoded Blobs
Serialized Cookies
State Parameters
Base64 Objects
Binary Request Bodies
Framework-Specific Markers

Do not send gadget chains to production systems without explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Relevant primarily to JavaScript ecosystems.

Distinguish:

Client-Side Prototype Pollution
Server-Side Prototype Pollution

Look for unsafe recursive merging or property assignment involving attacker-controlled keys.

Interesting keys conceptually include:

__proto__
constructor
prototype

Start with non-destructive property behaviour.

docs.title: HTTP Host Header
docs.text:
Test whether application behaviour trusts:

Host
X-Forwarded-Host
Forwarded
X-Host
X-Original-Host

Potentially affected functionality:

Password Reset
Absolute URL Generation
Routing
Cache Keys
Virtual Hosting
Security Links

docs.title: Host Header Testing
docs.text:
Controlled example:

curl -i "$TARGET" -H 'Host: example.invalid'

Proxy environments may behave differently.

Do not report Host reflection unless it leads to meaningful security impact.

docs.title: HTTP Header Injection / CRLF
docs.text:
Potential sinks include:

Redirect Locations
Download Filenames
Custom Headers
Logging
Proxy Headers
Email Headers

Look for unsafe inclusion of user-controlled data in response headers.

Assess whether newline characters can alter:

Response Headers
Cookies
Redirects
Body Interpretation

Use harmless custom-header proofs.

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggling
docs.text:
Request smuggling involves disagreement between HTTP components about request boundaries.

Concept:

Client
  |
  v
Front End
  |
  v
Back End

If they parse boundaries differently:

Request Desynchronisation

can occur.

docs.title: Request Smuggling Safety
docs.text:
This testing can affect other users.

Prefer:

Burp HTTP Request Smuggler
Dedicated Test Environment
Single-User Test Host
Non-Destructive Detection

Do not perform aggressive desynchronisation testing against production unless explicitly approved.

docs.title: Web Cache Poisoning
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker Input
      |
      v
Application Response
      |
      v
Cache
      |
      v
Other Users

Look for:

Unkeyed Headers
Unkeyed Parameters
Host Variations
Forwarded Headers
Path Normalisation
Cache-Key Differences

docs.title: Cache Poisoning Workflow
docs.text:
Identify Cache
     |
     v
Find Unkeyed Input
     |
     v
Observe Response Influence
     |
     v
Determine Cacheability
     |
     v
Controlled Cache Test

Avoid poisoning shared production responses.

docs.title: Web Cache Deception
docs.text:
Cache deception differs from cache poisoning.

Cache Poisoning
    =
Attacker influences cached content

Cache Deception
    =
Cache stores sensitive victim-specific content

Test whether URL/path transformations cause private responses to become publicly cacheable.

Use only controlled accounts and your own sensitive test data.

docs.title: Cache Indicators
docs.text:
Inspect:

Age
Cache-Control
Vary
ETag
X-Cache
CF-Cache-Status
Via
Server-Timing
CDN-Specific Headers

Headers vary by platform.

docs.title: Broken Link Hijacking
docs.text:
Broken-link hijacking occurs when an application references an external resource whose destination can potentially be re-registered or reclaimed.

Look for:

Dead Social Links
Expired Domains
Deleted GitHub Repositories
Removed Package Names
Unused Cloud Resources
External JavaScript
External CSS
Documentation Links

Assessment model:

Application Reference
       |
       v
External Resource Missing
       |
       v
Can Resource Be Reclaimed?
       |
       v
What Trust Does Application Place In It?
       |
       v
Impact

Do not register third-party domains or resources unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: HTML Smuggling
docs.text:
HTML smuggling uses browser-side functionality to construct files locally rather than transferring the final file directly from the server.

During defensive web assessments, review whether:

JavaScript constructs Blob objects
Data is embedded or encoded client-side
Downloads are generated dynamically
Security controls depend only on network-layer file inspection

Do not generate malicious payloads.

The relevant question is whether security architecture assumes that every downloaded file crosses the network in its final form.

docs.title: WebDAV
docs.text:
Check whether WebDAV is exposed:

curl -i -X OPTIONS "$TARGET"

Look for methods such as:

PROPFIND
MKCOL
COPY
MOVE
LOCK
UNLOCK
PUT
DELETE

Exposure alone is not a vulnerability.

Assess:

Authentication
Authorisation
Writable Locations
File Types
Execution Context
Information Disclosure

docs.title: Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Look for:

Stack Traces
Debug Pages
Internal IPs
Internal Hostnames
Source Paths
Database Errors
Framework Versions
Secrets
API Keys
Tokens
Credentials
Environment Variables
Cloud Metadata
Source Code
Backups
Comments

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Compare malformed requests.

Look for:

Framework Error
Stack Trace
SQL Error
Filesystem Path
Internal Host
Source File
Line Number
Debug Mode

Avoid causing repeated server errors.

docs.title: Debug Interfaces
docs.text:
Potential examples:

/debug
/console
/actuator
/server-status
/phpinfo.php
/swagger
/graphiql

Do not assume a debug-looking endpoint is vulnerable.

Assess actual information or functionality exposed.

docs.title: API Security
docs.text:
First inventory:

Base URL
Version
Authentication
Endpoints
Methods
Objects
Identifiers
Roles
Scopes
Rate Limits
Documentation

docs.title: API Discovery
docs.text:
Look for:

/api/
/api/v1/
/api/v2/
/rest/
/graphql
/swagger.json
/openapi.json
/api-docs

Also inspect:

JavaScript
Mobile Applications
Network Traffic
Documentation
Historical URLs

docs.title: OpenAPI / Swagger
docs.text:
If documentation is exposed, review:

Endpoints
Methods
Parameters
Schemas
Authentication
Deprecated Endpoints
Administrative Operations
Hidden Functionality

Documentation exposure alone is not necessarily a vulnerability.

docs.title: API Authorisation
docs.text:
Test:

Object-Level Authorisation
Function-Level Authorisation
Property-Level Authorisation
Tenant Isolation
Role Enforcement

docs.title: BOLA
docs.text:
User A
   |
   v
/api/orders/1001
   |
   v
Change Object ID
   |
   v
/api/orders/1002
   |
   v
Server Checks Ownership?

Use controlled accounts and controlled objects.

docs.title: BFLA
docs.text:
Broken Function Level Authorisation:

Normal User
    |
    v
Administrative API Function
    |
    v
Server-Side Role Check?

docs.title: Property-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Look for sensitive fields such as:

role
isAdmin
owner
tenantId
accountId
status
verified
permissions
credit
price

Determine whether clients can read or modify fields beyond their intended privilege.

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Mass assignment occurs when application frameworks automatically bind user-controlled object properties.

Testing model:

Expected Fields
      |
      v
Add Non-UI Field
      |
      v
Server Accepts?
      |
      v
Security-Relevant Property Changed?

Use harmless account/profile properties first.

docs.title: API Versioning
docs.text:
Check:

/v1/
/v2/
/v3/

Older API versions may have:

Weaker Authorisation
Missing Rate Limits
Deprecated Authentication
Additional Fields
Legacy Endpoints

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
Common endpoints:

/graphql
/api/graphql
/graphql/v1

Check:

Introspection
Schema
Queries
Mutations
Subscriptions
Authorisation
Object Access
Field Access
Aliases
Batching
Depth
Complexity

docs.title: GraphQL Introspection
docs.text:
Where permitted, determine whether introspection is available.

Introspection exposure itself is not necessarily a vulnerability.

The schema is useful for mapping:

Objects
Fields
Queries
Mutations
Arguments
Types

docs.title: GraphQL Authorisation
docs.text:
Do not assume resolver-level authorisation is consistent.

Test:

Same Object via Different Query
Nested Object
Direct Object Query
Mutation
Alternative Field
Different Role

docs.title: GraphQL DoS Safety
docs.text:
Avoid aggressive:

Deeply Nested Queries
Huge Alias Sets
Large Batches
Recursive Queries

unless availability testing is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
Identify:

HTTP/2
gRPC Content-Type
Protocol Buffers
Reflection
Service Definitions

Security testing should consider:

Authentication
Authorisation
Method Exposure
Message Validation
Metadata
Streaming
Rate Limiting
Reflection

Do not assume traditional REST controls automatically apply.

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
Identify upgrade:

Connection: Upgrade
Upgrade: websocket

Test:

Authentication
Authorisation
Origin Validation
Message-Level Access Control
Input Validation
Session Expiry
Reconnect Behaviour

docs.title: WebSocket Model
docs.text:
HTTP Handshake
      |
      v
WebSocket Connection
      |
      v
Messages
      |
      v
Application Actions

Authorisation must often be enforced at the message/action level, not only during the handshake.

docs.title: JWT
docs.text:
JWT structure:

HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

Decode for inspection:

python3 - <<'PY'
import base64
import json

token = "HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE"

for part in token.split(".")[:2]:
    part += "=" * (-len(part) % 4)
    print(json.dumps(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(part)), indent=2))
PY

docs.title: JWT Checklist
docs.text:
Review:

alg
kid
typ
iss
aud
sub
exp
nbf
iat
jti
roles
scope
permissions

Check:

Signature Verification
Algorithm Enforcement
Key Selection
Issuer
Audience
Expiry
Role Trust
Revocation
Key Rotation

Do not treat base64 decoding as token compromise.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect
docs.text:
Map:

Client
Authorisation Server
Resource Server
Redirect URI
State
Nonce
PKCE
Scopes
Tokens
UserInfo
Logout

docs.title: OAuth Testing
docs.text:
Review:

Redirect URI Validation
state
nonce
PKCE
Scope Enforcement
Client Binding
Token Audience
Token Leakage
Account Linking
SSO Session
Open Redirect Interaction

docs.title: OAuth Mental Model
docs.text:
User
 |
 v
Client
 |
 v
Authorisation Server
 |
 v
Code / Token
 |
 v
Client
 |
 v
Resource Server

Understand which party trusts which value.

docs.title: SAML
docs.text:
Review:

Service Provider
Identity Provider
Assertion
Signature
Audience
Recipient
Destination
InResponseTo
NameID
Attributes
Session

Prefer dedicated SAML tooling and controlled test identities.

docs.title: Web LLM Applications
docs.text:
Modern applications may expose LLM-backed functionality through:

Chatbots
Support Assistants
Search
Document Analysis
Agentic Workflows
Tool Calling
RAG
Automated Actions
AI-Powered Scanners

docs.title: LLM Security Model
docs.text:
User Prompt
    |
    v
Model
    |
    +--> System Instructions
    +--> Retrieved Data
    +--> Tools
    +--> APIs
    +--> Internal Services
    |
    v
Application Action

The primary security question is not:

Can I make the model say something strange?

It is:

Can untrusted input cross a security boundary?

docs.title: LLM Testing Areas
docs.text:
Review:

Direct Prompt Injection
Indirect Prompt Injection
Tool Authorisation
Data Leakage
RAG Poisoning
Cross-User Data Isolation
Sensitive System Prompts
Excessive Agency
Unsafe Output Handling
SSRF Through Tools
Privilege Boundaries
External Content Trust

Use harmless instructions and controlled documents.

docs.title: LLM Tool Calling
docs.text:
For agentic applications ask:

Which tools can the model invoke?

Which arguments can it control?

Does the server independently authorise each action?

Can retrieved content instruct the model?

Can one user influence another user's context?

Can tools access internal services?

Are dangerous actions confirmed?

Never assume model instructions are an authorisation boundary.

docs.title: Secrets Exposure
docs.text:
Search:

JavaScript
Source Maps
Git History
Configuration
Backups
Environment Files
CI/CD Files
Documentation
Error Messages
API Responses

Useful local search:

grep -RniE 'api[_-]?key|secret|token|password|passwd|authorization|bearer' .

Validate whether a discovered value is:

Real
Current
Sensitive
In Scope
Privileged
Revoked
Test Data

Do not use third-party credentials outside scope.

docs.title: Dependency Security
docs.text:
Identify:

Framework
Library
Plugin
CMS
Package
Version

Then determine:

Is version accurate?

Is component actually reachable?

Is vulnerable feature enabled?

Does configuration mitigate it?

Is authentication required?

Is the known vulnerability applicable?

docs.title: Known Vulnerability Research
docs.text:
Useful sources:

Vendor Advisories
NVD
GitHub Security Advisories
CISA KEV
Exploit-DB
Packet Storm
Project Repositories
Security Research Blogs

Prioritise vendor and primary research sources.

docs.title: searchsploit
docs.text:
searchsploit nginx

Specific product:

searchsploit 'Apache Tomcat'

Do not execute public exploit code without reviewing it.

docs.title: Nuclei
docs.text:
Basic:

nuclei -u "$TARGET"

List:

nuclei -l urls.txt

Use focused templates where possible.

Treat scanner results as leads requiring validation.

docs.title: Nikto
docs.text:
nikto -h "$TARGET"

Useful for broad web-server checks, but findings require manual validation.

docs.title: WAF Detection
docs.text:
Possible tools include:

wafw00f
Nmap
HTTP Response Analysis

Example:

wafw00f "$TARGET"

A WAF fingerprint should guide testing, not become a finding by itself.

docs.title: CDN / Reverse Proxy
docs.text:
Look for:

Cloudflare
Akamai
Fastly
CloudFront
Azure Front Door
Application Gateway
NGINX
HAProxy
Traefik
Varnish

Understand:

Client
  |
  v
CDN / WAF
  |
  v
Reverse Proxy
  |
  v
Application

Many advanced HTTP vulnerabilities involve disagreement between layers.

docs.title: Origin Exposure
docs.text:
Assess whether an application behind a CDN/WAF has a directly reachable origin.

Sources can include:

Historical DNS
Certificates
Old Records
Email Headers
Other Subdomains
Infrastructure Reuse

Do not attempt to bypass protection unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Server Misconfiguration
docs.text:
Review:

Directory Listing
Default Files
Debug Mode
Verbose Errors
Dangerous Methods
Backup Files
Default Credentials
Exposed Admin Interfaces
Weak TLS
Unnecessary Services
Sensitive Headers
Source Code Exposure

docs.title: Product-Specific Testing
docs.text:
If fingerprinting identifies a product such as:

Apache Tomcat
ActiveMQ
Jenkins
WordPress
Drupal
Next.js
Grafana
GitLab
Confluence
Exchange
WebLogic
JBoss

use this workflow:

Fingerprint
    |
    v
Confirm Product
    |
    v
Confirm Version if Possible
    |
    v
Review Vendor Documentation
    |
    v
Review Security Advisories
    |
    v
Check Exposed Features
    |
    v
Determine Applicability
    |
    v
Safe Validation

Do not build a finding solely from a banner.

docs.title: Web Server Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Nmap:

nmap -sV -p80,443 "$HOST"

HTTP scripts:

nmap -p80,443 --script http-title,http-headers "$HOST"

docs.text:

docs.title: Broken Access Control vs Business Logic
docs.text:
Use:

Access Control
    =
Can this identity perform this action?

Business Logic
    =
Should this action be possible in this state?

Both should be tested independently.

docs.title: Input Validation vs Output Encoding
docs.text:
Input Validation
    =
Is supplied data acceptable?

Output Encoding
    =
Is data safely represented in its destination context?

Do not treat them as interchangeable.

docs.title: Client vs Server Trust
docs.text:
Browser
   |
   | Untrusted
   v
Server

Values controlled by the client can include:

Price
Role
User ID
Tenant ID
Feature Flags
Hidden Fields
Disabled Fields
JavaScript Variables
Headers
Cookies

The server must enforce security-sensitive decisions.

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Applications
docs.text:
Always test tenant isolation where authorised.

Tenant A
   |
   v
Object A

Tenant B
   |
   v
Object B

Check isolation across:

Objects
Users
Files
Exports
Search
APIs
Reports
Invitations
Administration
Billing
Logs

docs.title: File Download Functions
docs.text:
Check:

Authorisation
Path Handling
Filename
Content-Type
Content-Disposition
Caching
Range Requests
Signed URLs
Expiry
Tenant Isolation

docs.title: Export Functions
docs.text:
Exports can reveal more data than the UI.

Check:

CSV
PDF
Excel
JSON
ZIP
Reports
Bulk Exports

Compare exported fields with what the user is authorised to view.

docs.title: Import Functions
docs.text:
Imports may introduce:

File Upload
Parser Vulnerabilities
Formula Injection
Mass Assignment
Business Logic Abuse
Duplicate Processing
External Resource Loading

Use harmless test data.

docs.title: CSV Injection
docs.text:
If user-controlled values are exported to spreadsheets, assess whether spreadsheet formula interpretation creates risk.

Use harmless formula-like test markers.

Do not trigger external commands.

docs.title: Email Functionality
docs.text:
Review:

Recipient Control
Template Injection
Header Handling
HTML Rendering
Links
Password Reset
Invitations
Verification
Rate Limiting

Avoid sending unsolicited messages to real users.

docs.text:

URL Validation

Authentication
Signature Verification
Replay Protection
Secret Rotation
Event Authorisation

Retry Behaviour

docs.text:

docs.text:

page

Maximum Limit

Very Large Values

Avoid resource-exhaustion testing.

docs.title: Sorting and Filtering
docs.text:
Parameters such as:

sort
order
filter
fields
include
expand
search
q

may influence backend queries or expose additional fields.

docs.title: Hidden Fields
docs.text:
Do not trust:

<input type="hidden">

Security decisions must be enforced server-side.

docs.title: Duplicate Parameters
docs.text:
Applications and proxies may interpret duplicate parameters differently.

Concept:

?id=1&id=2

Assess parser behaviour carefully.

This can matter for:

Validation
WAF Behaviour
Caching
Authorisation
Backend Routing

docs.title: Parameter Pollution
docs.text:
Different layers may interpret parameters differently.

Proxy
   |
   v
Framework
   |
   v
Application

Check only where there is evidence that parser disagreement may matter.

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
Common encodings:

URL Encoding
Double URL Encoding
HTML Entities
Unicode
Base64
JSON Escaping
XML Entities

Encoding is not encryption.

Use encoding variations to understand parser and validation behaviour, not merely to bypass controls.

docs.title: Normalisation
docs.text:
Check whether components disagree about:

Case
Slashes
Backslashes
Dots
Percent Encoding
Unicode
Duplicate Separators
Trailing Characters
Path Segments

Relevant to:

Routing
Access Control
Caching
Path Traversal
Proxy Behaviour

docs.title: HTTP Parameter Locations
docs.text:
Always inspect:

GET Query
POST Form
JSON
XML
Multipart
Headers
Cookies
Path
Fragment - client-side only

docs.title: Response Difference Analysis
docs.text:
When testing a hypothesis compare:

Status Code
Response Length
Word Count
Line Count
Headers
Cookies
Redirect
Body
Timing
Cache Behaviour

Do not rely on one signal.

docs.title: Baseline First
docs.text:
Before fuzzing:

Normal Request
      |
      v
Record Baseline
      |
      v
Change One Variable
      |
      v
Compare

Changing one variable at a time makes results easier to interpret.

docs.title: Safe Proof Principle
docs.text:
Prefer:

Can I prove the issue without:
    accessing unrelated data?
    executing OS commands?
    dumping a database?
    changing another user's password?
    poisoning a shared cache?
    causing downtime?

If yes, use the lower-impact proof.

docs.title: Scanner Result Model
docs.text:
Scanner Finding
      |
      v
Understand Detection
      |
      v
Reproduce Manually
      |
      v
Check Context
      |
      v
Assess Exploitability
      |
      v
Determine Impact
      |
      v
Report

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Common causes:

Generic Error Pages
WAF Responses
Soft 404s
Reflected but Encoded Input
Version Fingerprinting
Rate-Limit Responses
Authentication Redirects
CDN Behaviour
Scanner Heuristics

docs.title: Evidence Directory
docs.text:
mkdir -p evidence/web/{recon,http,auth,access-control,input,api,business-logic,files,screenshots,requests,responses}

Suggested:

evidence/
└── web/
    ├── recon/
    ├── http/
    ├── auth/
    ├── access-control/
    ├── input/
    ├── api/
    ├── business-logic/
    ├── files/
    ├── screenshots/
    ├── requests/
    └── responses/

docs.title: Save HTTP Evidence
docs.text:
Request:

POST /api/example HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
...

Response:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
...

Remove:

Passwords
Session Tokens
API Keys
Personal Data
Unrelated Sensitive Data

where they are not required for evidence.

docs.title: Evidence Record
docs.text:
For each confirmed issue record:

Timestamp:
Target:
Endpoint:
Method:
User / Role:
Preconditions:
Request:
Response:
Observed Behaviour:
Expected Behaviour:
Security Impact:
State Changed:
Cleanup:

docs.title: Screenshot Naming
docs.text:
Useful naming:

01-login-page.png
02-user-a-object.png
03-user-b-object-access.png
04-server-response.png

Keep screenshots focused.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
A good web finding explains:

What is wrong?

Where is it?

Who can reach it?

What prerequisites exist?

What can an attacker actually do?

What evidence proves it?

What should be changed?

docs.title: Do Not Overreport
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

Server Header Present
Technology Detected
Old-Looking Version
Missing Security Header
robots.txt Entry
Swagger Documentation
GraphQL Introspection
WebDAV OPTIONS Response
CORS Header
Open Port
Debug-Looking Path
SPF/DMARC Issue During Web Scope
Cookie Without Attribute
WAF Detected
Directory Exists

Determine actual security impact.

docs.title: Better Finding Model
docs.text:
Observation
    +
Reachability
    +
Prerequisites
    +
Security Boundary
    +
Impact
    =
Finding

docs.title: Example - IDOR
docs.text:
Weak:

The ID parameter can be changed.

Better:

An authenticated standard user can modify the object identifier
in the order-details API request and retrieve another test user's
order information because the server does not enforce object-level
authorisation.

docs.title: Example - Technology
docs.text:
Weak:

The application uses Apache.

Better:

No finding unless the identified Apache configuration or version
creates a demonstrable security condition relevant to the application.

docs.title: Example - CORS
docs.text:
Weak:

The Origin header is reflected.

Better:

Determine whether an attacker-controlled origin can read a
credentialed response containing sensitive information.

docs.title: Example - File Upload
docs.text:
Weak:

PDF files can be uploaded.

Better:

Determine whether the upload pipeline permits a file to cross a
security boundary, become publicly accessible, execute, trigger unsafe
server-side processing, or expose other users to active content.

docs.title: Example - Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Weak:

No rate limiting header exists.

Better:

Demonstrate whether the security-sensitive operation can be repeated
at a rate that creates a realistic authentication, recovery, abuse,
or resource-consumption risk.

docs.text:
Subdomains

Alive HTTP
    -> httpx

Technology

Content

Crawling

Historical URLs

WAF

docs.text:

    -> Burp Repeater / sqlmap

Command Injection
    -> Burp Repeater / Commix

docs.title: One-Minute Reference
docs.text:
DNS
    dig app.example.com

Headers
    curl -I https://app.example.com

Verbose HTTP
    curl -v https://app.example.com

Technology
    whatweb https://app.example.com

Subdomains
    subfinder -d example.com -silent

Alive
    httpx -l subdomains.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect

Content
    ffuf -w WORDLIST -u https://app.example.com/FUZZ

Crawl
    katana -u https://app.example.com

Historical
    gau example.com

404 fingerprint
    curl -i https://app.example.com/random-928374

TLS
    openssl s_client -connect app.example.com:443 -servername app.example.com

WAF
    wafw00f https://app.example.com

OPTIONS
    curl -i -X OPTIONS https://app.example.com

CORS
    curl -i https://app.example.com -H 'Origin: https://example.invalid'

Nuclei
    nuclei -u https://app.example.com

Nikto
    nikto -h https://app.example.com

                                |
             +------------------+------------------+
             |                  |                  |
             v                  v                  v
            API             Client Side       HTTP Layers
             |                  |                  |
             +------------------+------------------+
                                |
                                v
                          HYPOTHESIS
                                |
                                v
                         MANUAL TEST
                                |
                                v
                         REPRODUCIBLE?
                                |
                          +-----+-----+
                          |           |
                         No          Yes
                          |           |
                          v           v
                       Discard     IMPACT
                                      |
                                      v
                              MINIMUM SAFE PROOF
                                      |
                                      v
                                  EVIDENCE
                                      |
                                      v
                                   REPORT

The goal is not:

How many payloads can I send?

The goal is:

How does this application establish trust,
and can an untrusted user cross one of those
security boundaries?

A strong web assessment therefore combines:

Reconnaissance
      +
Protocol Understanding
      +
Application Understanding
      +
Role Comparison
      +
Business Logic
      +
Manual Validation
      +
Minimal Evidence
      =
Defensible Security Finding

docs.title: Windows Cheatsheet
docs.text:
Quick-reference commands for Windows enumeration, local privilege analysis, services, processes, networking, permissions, credentials, security controls and common administrative tasks during authorised security assessments.

This cheatsheet focuses primarily on:

Windows Host
    |
    v
Identity
    |
    v
System
    |
    v
Users / Groups
    |
    v
Privileges
    |
    v
Processes / Services
    |
    v
Network
    |
    v
Files / Registry
    |
    v
Scheduled Execution
    |
    v
Credentials
    |
    v
Security Controls
    |
    v
Privilege Analysis

Authorised testing only

Use these commands only on systems you own or are explicitly authorised to assess. Prefer read-only enumeration and minimal validation. Do not change services, registry values, scheduled tasks, security policies, ACLs, Defender settings or application-control policies merely to prove a finding unless the rules of engagement explicitly permit it.

docs.title: Token Privileges

A privilege being listed does not automatically mean it is enabled or practically exploitable.

Record:

Privilege
State
Process Context
OS Version
Security Boundary

docs.title: Privilege Analysis
docs.text:
Conceptually:

User Token
   |
   v
Privilege
   |
   v
Windows Security Capability
   |
   v
Can It Cross a Boundary?

Do not report:

SeImpersonatePrivilege Present

alone.

Determine whether the privilege is expected for the account and whether it creates an unintended escalation path in the actual environment.

docs.title: Service Security Review
docs.text:
For each privileged service:

Service
   |
   v
Service Account
   |
   v
Executable
   |
   v
Directory
   |
   v
Configuration
   |
   v
Permissions

Questions:

Can the current user modify the service?
Can the current user modify its executable?
Can the current user modify its directory?
Can the current user modify loaded configuration?
Does the service run with higher privilege?

docs.title: Service ACL
docs.text:
Built-in representation:

sc sdshow SERVICE_NAME

This returns SDDL.

Do not modify the service ACL merely to validate a finding.

docs.title: Service Executable Permissions
docs.text:
Get path:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,PathName

Then inspect the relevant file:

Get-Acl 'C:\Path\service.exe' |
    Format-List

Directory:

Get-Acl 'C:\Path' |
    Format-List

docs.title: Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
Enumerate service paths:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object {
        $_.PathName -match ' ' -and
        $_.PathName -notmatch '^"'
    } |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

This produces candidates, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

A meaningful finding requires conditions such as:

Unquoted Path
    +
Space in Path
    +
Current User Can Write a Candidate Location
    +
Service Runs More Privileged

docs.title: Service Path Analysis
docs.text:
Example path:

C:\Program Files\Example Service\service.exe

Do not assume this is exploitable merely because it contains spaces.

Validate permissions on relevant path components.

docs.text:

Get-ScheduledTask |
    ForEach-Object {
        [PSCustomObject]@{
            TaskPath = $_.TaskPath
            TaskName = $_.TaskName
            Actions  = ($_.Actions.Execute -join '; ')
        }
    }

Task
 |
 v
Execution Identity

docs.text:
Current user:

dir "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"

dir "C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem "$env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"

docs.title: Autorun Registry Locations
docs.text:
Current user:

reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"

Machine:

reg query "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"

RunOnce:

reg query "HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce"
reg query "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce"

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
Query key:

reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion"

Recursive:

reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Vendor" /s

PowerShell:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion'

docs.title: Registry Permissions
docs.text:
Get-Acl 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Vendor\Product' |
    Format-List

docs.title: Search Registry
docs.text:
Use targeted searches.

Example:

reg query HKCU /f "password" /t REG_SZ /s

Machine scope can be very noisy:

reg query HKLM /f "password" /t REG_SZ /s

Prefer known application paths rather than blindly searching the entire registry.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
List:

dir

Hidden:

dir /a

Recursive:

dir /s

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem

Hidden:

Get-ChildItem -Force

Recursive:

Get-ChildItem -Recurse

docs.title: File Permissions
docs.text:
CMD:

icacls "C:\Path\file.exe"

Directory:

icacls "C:\Path"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl 'C:\Path\file.exe' |
    Format-List

docs.title: icacls Permission Reference
docs.text:
Common rights include:

F   Full control
M   Modify
RX  Read and execute
R   Read
W   Write

Inheritance indicators can include:

OI  Object inherit
CI  Container inherit
IO  Inherit only
I   Inherited

docs.title: Writable Location Test
docs.text:
First inspect:

Get-Acl 'C:\Path' |
    Format-List

If an actual write test is necessary and authorised, use a temporary uniquely named file and remove it immediately.

Do not leave test artifacts behind.

docs.title: Common Writable Locations
docs.text:
Examples often writable by standard users include:

%TEMP%
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp
C:\Users\<user>\

Other writable locations depend on ACL configuration.

A writable directory is not itself a privilege-escalation finding.

The important question is:

Does a More-Privileged Process Trust It?

docs.title: Search Files by Name
docs.text:
CMD:

dir C:\ /s /b *config* 2>nul

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem C:\ -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object Name -like '*config*'

Targeted searches are strongly preferred.

docs.title: Search File Contents
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem 'C:\Path' -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern 'password','secret','token'

Avoid broad searches across large production volumes unless necessary.

docs.title: Interesting Configuration Files
docs.text:
Common examples:

web.config
appsettings.json
*.config
*.xml
*.ini
*.yml
*.yaml
*.json
unattend.xml
unattended.xml
sysprep.inf
sysprep.xml

The presence of a file does not mean it contains credentials.

docs.title: Unattended Installation Files
docs.text:
Potential historical locations include:

C:\Windows\Panther\
C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend\
C:\Windows\System32\Sysprep\

Search:

Get-ChildItem C:\Windows -Recurse -Include unattend.xml,unattended.xml,sysprep.xml -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Handle discovered credentials as sensitive evidence.

docs.title: IIS Configuration
docs.text:
Common location:

C:\inetpub\

Application configuration commonly uses:

web.config

Search targeted IIS directories:

Get-ChildItem C:\inetpub -Recurse -Filter web.config -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: PowerShell History
docs.text:
Current user:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Read:

Get-Content (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Common default path:

%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt

History may contain sensitive commands but is not a complete audit trail.

docs.title: PowerShell Transcription
docs.text:
Potential policy settings:

reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription"

PowerShell:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Transcripts may contain sensitive command output and credentials.

docs.title: PowerShell Logging
docs.text:
Script block logging:

reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging"

Module logging:

reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging"

docs.title: PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible values include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

FullLanguage is normal on many Windows systems and is not automatically a vulnerability.

Interpret it in the context of the organisation's application-control and endpoint-hardening requirements.

docs.title: PowerShell Version
docs.text: $PSVersionTable

docs.title: Credential Manager
docs.text:
List stored credential metadata:

cmdkey /list

Do not attempt to extract stored credential secrets merely because entries exist.

docs.title: Windows Vault / Stored Credentials
docs.text:
Credential metadata can also be inspected through normal Windows interfaces and authorised management tooling.

The security question is:

Can the Current Security Context
Access Reusable Authentication Material?

docs.title: Wi-Fi Profiles
docs.text:
List profiles:

netsh wlan show profiles

Do not extract stored wireless keys unless the assessment scope specifically includes credential recovery.

docs.title: DPAPI
docs.text:
Windows uses DPAPI to protect many user and machine secrets.

Common DPAPI-backed data includes:

Browser Credentials
Credential Manager
Certificates
Application Secrets
Wireless Credentials

The existence of DPAPI-protected data is normal.

Report only unintended access to protected secrets.

docs.title: SAM and SYSTEM
docs.text:
Registry hives include:

SAM
SYSTEM
SECURITY

These contain security-sensitive system data.

Do not save, copy or dump these hives during routine enumeration unless credential extraction is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: LSA Protection
docs.text:
Check RunAsPPL configuration:

reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v RunAsPPL

Interpret alongside the actual Windows version and security configuration.

docs.title: Credential Guard
docs.text:
Useful system information:

Get-ComputerInfo |
    Select-Object DeviceGuard*

On supported environments, additional Device Guard/Credential Guard state can be obtained through appropriate Windows management interfaces.

Do not assume absence from one query means the control is disabled.

docs.title: Windows Defender
docs.text:
Status:

Get-MpComputerStatus

Selected fields:

Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,BehaviorMonitorEnabled,IoavProtectionEnabled,AntispywareEnabled

docs.title: Defender Preferences
docs.text:
Get-MpPreference

Review relevant configuration such as:

Exclusions
Cloud Protection
Network Protection
ASR
Controlled Folder Access

Do not change Defender configuration during routine testing.

docs.title: Defender Exclusions
docs.text:
Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object ExclusionPath,ExclusionProcess,ExclusionExtension

Access may be restricted.

An exclusion is not automatically a vulnerability; assess whether it creates an exploitable trust boundary.

docs.title: Attack Surface Reduction
docs.text:
Rules:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids,AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
Get-NetFirewallProfile

Enabled rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule |
    Where-Object Enabled -eq 'True'

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
Effective policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

XML:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml

Collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType,EnforcementMode

docs.title: Test AppLocker Policy
docs.text:
For a specific file:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path 'C:\Path\test.exe' -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

For a script:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path 'C:\Path\test.ps1' -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

This tests policy evaluation without executing the target.

docs.title: AppLocker Collections
docs.text:
Common collections include:

Exe
Msi
Script
Dll
Appx

Important distinction:

Collection Not Configured

does not necessarily mean:

No Application Control Exists

WDAC or another security product may also enforce policy.

docs.title: WDAC / Application Control
docs.text:
Windows Defender Application Control is now commonly documented under App Control for Business.

Useful checks depend on the Windows version and available management interfaces.

Potential indicators include:

Code Integrity Policies
Device Guard Configuration
Code Integrity Event Logs

Do not rely on one command alone to declare WDAC enabled or disabled.

docs.title: Code Integrity Logs
docs.text:
Useful logs include:

Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational

Query recent events:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational' -MaxEvents 50

docs.title: AppLocker Logs
docs.text:
Examples:

Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script

Query:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL' -MaxEvents 50

docs.title: Security Products
docs.text:
Installed security products should be identified carefully.

Processes:

Get-Process

Services:

Get-Service

Defender:

Get-MpComputerStatus

Do not terminate or disable endpoint security controls during routine enumeration.

docs.title: Installed Software
docs.text:
Registry:

$paths = @(
    'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*',
    'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*'
)

Get-ItemProperty $paths -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object DisplayName |
    Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher |
    Sort-Object DisplayName

Current user applications may also appear under HKCU.

docs.title: MSI - AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
Check machine policy:

reg query "HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" /v AlwaysInstallElevated

Check user policy:

reg query "HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" /v AlwaysInstallElevated

PowerShell:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer' -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer' -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

The classic unsafe condition requires the relevant policy configuration in both machine and user contexts.

Do not install a test MSI merely to prove the risk unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: WSL
docs.text:
Check:

wsl --status

Distributions:

wsl --list --verbose

WSL presence is not itself a vulnerability.

Review its relevance to:

Credential Boundaries
Filesystem Access
Development Tooling
Network Exposure

docs.title: Named Pipes
docs.text:
List:

Get-ChildItem \\.\pipe\

Named pipes are normal Windows IPC mechanisms.

Investigate only where:

Pipe Security
   +
Privileged Service
   +
Unsafe Client/Server Trust

creates an actual boundary issue.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
List:

driverquery

Verbose:

driverquery /v

PowerShell:

Get-CimInstance Win32_SystemDriver |
    Select-Object Name,State,StartMode,PathName

docs.title: Driver Security
docs.text:

docs.title: Privilege Escalation - Core Model
docs.text:
Most local Windows privilege escalation can be reduced to:

Low-Privilege User

        |

Common categories:

Services
Scheduled Tasks
File ACLs
Registry ACLs
Credentials
Token Privileges
Installers
Drivers
Applications

docs.title: Impersonation Privileges
docs.text:
Review:

whoami /priv

Particularly:

SeImpersonatePrivilege
SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege

These privileges are common for some service identities.

Their presence should trigger context analysis rather than automatic exploitation.

docs.title: Backup Operators
docs.text:
Check groups:

whoami /groups

Backup-related privileges:

SeBackupPrivilege
SeRestorePrivilege

These can provide broad access that bypasses ordinary file permissions when used through appropriate backup semantics.

Do not use them to extract credential stores unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Take Ownership
docs.text:
Relevant privilege:

SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege

Check:

whoami /priv

Do not change ownership merely to prove the privilege exists.

docs.title: Debug Privilege
docs.text:
SeDebugPrivilege

Check:

whoami /priv

This privilege can grant powerful process access.

Do not access sensitive processes unnecessarily.

docs.title: Driver Loading
docs.text:
Relevant privilege:

SeLoadDriverPrivilege

Review:

whoami /priv

Do not load a driver as part of routine validation.

docs.text:
Useful authorised host-enumeration tools include:

docs.title: Software Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Installed software:

$paths = @(
    'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*',
    'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*'
)

Get-ItemProperty $paths -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object DisplayName |
    Select-Object DisplayName,DisplayVersion,Publisher

Then verify versions against vendor advisories.

docs.title: LOLBins
docs.text:
Windows contains many legitimate binaries and scripts that can perform security-sensitive operations.

The presence of such a binary is not a vulnerability.

The security question is:

Is a Legitimate Administrative Capability
Exposed in a Way That Violates
the Intended Security Boundary?

Application-control testing should focus on effective policy rather than merely listing installed binaries.

docs.title: Application Control Test Model
docs.text:
Candidate Binary / Script
          |
          v
Effective AppLocker / WDAC Policy
          |
          v
Test Policy Decision
          |
          v
Execution Needed?
          |
          +--> No --> Record Read-Only Result
          |
          +--> Yes --> Only If Authorised

docs.title: AppLocker Example
docs.text:
Check executable policy without execution:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\wscript.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Interpret:

Allowed
Denied
DeniedByDefault

alongside the matching rule and other application-control layers.

docs.title: PowerShell Execution Policy
docs.text:
Get-ExecutionPolicy -List

Execution Policy is not a security boundary.

Do not equate:

Restricted

with comprehensive PowerShell application control.

docs.title: AMSI
docs.text:
AMSI is an antimalware scanning interface used by supported applications and scripting engines.

Do not attempt to patch or disable AMSI during routine enumeration.

Assess endpoint protection through supported status, configuration and test mechanisms.
