 +--> Credentials
 |
 +--> Groups
 |
 +--> Containers
 |
 +--> Unix Sockets
 |
 +--> NFS
 |
 +--> Custom Applications
 |
 +--> Kernel
 |
 +--> Security Controls

The Linux explorer groups techniques into categories such as:

Category Examples sudo NOPASSWD, SETENV, wildcards, interpreters, editors SUID / SGID SUID binaries, custom SUID applications, SGID binaries Capabilities CAP_SETUID, CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE systemd Writable units, service scripts, binaries, environment files, timers Cron Writable scripts, unsafe PATH usage, privileged scheduled jobs Filesystem Writable files, directories, ACLs, parent-directory replacement Credentials Shell history, environment variables, SSH keys, application secrets Groups docker, disk, shadow, LXD, libvirt and administrative groups Containers Docker socket, privileged containers, sensitive host mounts NFS Export configuration and no_root_squash candidates Libraries Writable libraries, linker configuration and Python imports Applications Writable configuration, plugins and privileged management agents Kernel Kernel LPE candidates and exploitability controls

Open the Linux PrivEsc Explorer.

docs.title: Technique Cards
docs.text:
Explorer results are presented as technique cards.

A card can contain:

Technique
 |
 +--> Platform
 |
 +--> Category
 |
 +--> Severity
 |
 +--> Confidence
 |
 +--> Summary
 |
 +--> What You Found
 |
 +--> Preconditions
 |
 +--> Enumeration Commands
 |
 +--> Validation
 |
 +--> Detection
 |
 +--> Remediation
 |
 +--> MITRE ATT&CK
 |
 +--> Tags
 |
 +--> Related Notes

The goal is to provide enough context to move from an enumeration result to a defensible security conclusion.

docs.title: Candidate Does Not Mean Vulnerable
docs.text:
One of the most important principles of the explorer is:

A candidate is not automatically a vulnerability.

For example, finding:

SeImpersonatePrivilege

does not by itself prove privilege escalation.

Likewise:

SUID binary

does not automatically mean the binary can be abused.

And:

docker group membership

must still be interpreted in the context of the Docker daemon, rootless operation, authorisation controls, and the intended administrative model.

The explorer therefore separates discovery from validation.

docs.title: Confidence Levels
docs.text: Explorer entries use confidence levels to help communicate how strongly the discovered condition supports a privilege escalation conclusion.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
A potentially relevant condition has been discovered, but additional context is required.

Interesting Condition
        |
        v
Candidate

Examples:

SUID binary discovered
CAP_SYS_PTRACE discovered
custom privileged service discovered
writable configuration discovered

These require further investigation.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
The important privilege relationship appears to exist, but practical impact may still depend on additional context.

Condition
    +
Privilege Relationship
    |
    v
Likely

Examples might include:

CAP_SETUID on a flexible executable
docker group access to a rootful daemon
writable privileged library

Further validation should still be performed.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
The privilege boundary itself has been established with sufficient evidence.

Lower-Privileged User
        |
        v
Controls Resource
        |
        v
Privileged Consumer
        |
        v
Confirmed Boundary

For example:

Root Service
    |
    v
Executes Script
    |
    v
Script Writable by Normal User

The relationship can often be confirmed without modifying the script or triggering privileged execution.

docs.title: Severity Is Contextual
docs.text:
Severity is provided as an assessment aid rather than an automatic final rating.

A technique may appear as:

Critical
High
Medium
Low
Informational

but the final severity should consider:

Required Access
      +
Exploit Preconditions
      +
Privilege Obtained
      +
Reliability
      +
Business Context
      +
Security Controls
      =
Final Risk

For example, a root-owned writable service executable is generally much more significant than an ordinary writable temporary file with no privileged consumer.

docs.title: Safe Validation
docs.text:
Privilege escalation testing can affect operating-system stability, services, scheduled jobs, authentication, and security controls.

Prefer the least invasive evidence that establishes the privilege relationship.

docs.title: Preferred
docs.text:
Inspect permissions
Inspect ownership
Inspect ACLs
Inspect service configuration
Inspect sudo rules
Inspect capabilities
Inspect execution identity
Inspect PATH
Inspect task definitions
Inspect mount configuration
Inspect application configuration

docs.title: Avoid When Not Required
docs.text:
Replacing production binaries
Modifying privileged scripts
Restarting critical services
Changing scheduled tasks
Loading kernel modules
Exploiting kernel vulnerabilities
Creating persistent privileged users
Disabling security controls
Modifying production configuration

A strong assessment demonstrates the security boundary with the minimum necessary system modification.

docs.title: Evidence Model
docs.text:
Useful evidence usually contains four elements:

1. Identity
2. Controlled Resource
3. Privileged Consumer
4. Security Impact

For example:

Identity
--------
CORP\user

Controlled Resource
-------------------
C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe

Privileged Consumer
-------------------
ExampleService

Execution Identity
------------------
LocalSystem

or:

Identity
--------
www-data

Controlled Resource
-------------------
/opt/example/backup.sh

Privileged Consumer
-------------------
root cron job

Execution Identity
------------------
root

This is considerably stronger than reporting only:

File is writable

because the evidence establishes the complete privilege relationship.

docs.title: Validation Questions
docs.text:
When a candidate is discovered, ask:

Who owns the resource?

Who can modify it?

Who consumes it?

What identity does the consumer run as?

When is it consumed?

Can the current user influence execution?

Are there additional security controls?

Is the behaviour intentional?

What privilege would actually be obtained?

Only then determine whether the condition represents a security finding.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
Privilege escalation paths frequently produce observable behaviour.

Useful defensive telemetry may include:

Process creation
Service changes
Scheduled-task changes
sudo execution
File permission changes
ACL changes
SUID changes
Capability changes
systemd unit changes
Cron changes
Registry changes
DLL loading
Driver loading
Container creation
Docker API activity
Authentication events
Sensitive file access

Explorer cards include detection guidance where relevant so the same technique can support both offensive testing and defensive validation.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Most privilege escalation findings ultimately involve one or more trust-boundary problems.

Common remediation themes include:

Least privilege
        |
        +--> Remove unnecessary administrative rights
        |
        +--> Restrict sudo delegation
        |
        +--> Remove unnecessary SUID / SGID
        |
        +--> Remove unnecessary capabilities
        |
        +--> Restrict privileged groups

Trusted resources
        |
        +--> Protect executables
        |
        +--> Protect scripts
        |
        +--> Protect configuration
        |
        +--> Protect libraries
        |
        +--> Protect registry keys
        |
        +--> Protect service definitions

Execution controls
        |
        +--> Use absolute paths
        |
        +--> Control PATH
        |
        +--> Harden application control
        |
        +--> Restrict privileged interpreters
        |
        +--> Harden service identities

Credential protection
        |
        +--> Remove plaintext secrets
        |
        +--> Rotate exposed credentials
        |
        +--> Protect private keys
        |
        +--> Use secret-management systems

The objective is not simply to block one command. It is to remove the underlying unsafe privilege relationship.

docs.title: Structured Data
docs.text:
The explorer interface is backed by structured JSON rather than hard-coded technique cards.

The current data files are:

docs/data/privesc/windows.json
docs/data/privesc/linux.json

Each technique can contain fields such as:

{
  "id": "example-technique",
  "name": "Example Technique",
  "platform": "windows",
  "category": "Services",
  "severity": "high",
  "confidence": "candidate",
  "summary": "Short description of the condition.",
  "found": [
    "What the tester discovered."
  ],
  "requires": [
    "Conditions required for practical impact."
  ],
  "commands": [
    "enumeration command"
  ],
  "validation": [
    "Safe validation guidance."
  ],
  "detection": [
    "Defensive detection guidance."
  ],
  "remediation": [
    "Recommended remediation."
  ],
  "mitre": [],
  "tags": [
    "example"
  ],
  "related": []
}

Keeping the data separate from the interface makes it easier to expand and maintain the explorer.

docs.title: Search Architecture
docs.text:
The explorer uses the following model:

User Query
    |
    v
Tokenise Search
    |
    v
Search Technique Data
    |
    +--> Name
    +--> ID
    +--> Platform
    +--> Category
    +--> Severity
    +--> Confidence
    +--> Summary
    +--> Findings
    +--> Preconditions
    +--> Commands
    +--> Validation
    +--> Detection
    +--> Remediation
    +--> MITRE ATT&CK
    +--> Tags
    |
    v
Apply Filters
    |
    v
Sort Results
    |
    v
Render Technique Cards

This allows searches such as:

writable service

or:

docker root

or:

SeBackup

without requiring the tester to know the internal technique ID.

docs.title: Recommended Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
Use the explorer as part of a broader privilege escalation methodology.

1. Establish current identity
          |
          v
2. Enumerate privileges and groups
          |
          v
3. Enumerate privileged execution
          |
          v
4. Identify writable resources
          |
          v
5. Search PrivEsc Explorer
          |
          v
6. Review candidate prerequisites
          |
          v
7. Validate safely
          |
          v
8. Determine actual privilege impact
          |
          v
9. Collect evidence
          |
          v
10. Review detection opportunities
          |
          v
11. Recommend remediation

Do not rely exclusively on automated enumeration.

Automated tools are useful for finding candidates, but the tester still needs to understand the privilege relationship.

docs.title: Useful Enumeration Tools
docs.text:
PrivEsc Explorer is designed to complement manual enumeration and established assessment tools.

Examples include:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
WinPEAS
PowerUp
Seatbelt
AccessChk
Process Monitor
Process Explorer
PowerShell
sc.exe
schtasks.exe
whoami.exe
icacls.exe
Get-Acl
Get-AppLockerPolicy

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
LinPEAS
LinEnum
pspy
sudo
find
getcap
getfacl
namei
systemctl
journalctl
ss
findmnt
capsh

Tool output should be treated as a starting point for investigation rather than automatic proof of a vulnerability.

docs.title: GTFOBins and Related References
docs.text:
For Linux, GTFOBins is an important reference for understanding security-sensitive functionality exposed by Unix binaries.

For Windows, LOLBAS documents Windows binaries, scripts, and libraries that can provide security-relevant functionality.

For Active Directory, LOlAD provides a useful reference for Active Directory attack techniques and commands.

PrivEsc Explorer does not attempt to duplicate these projects.

Instead, it focuses on the question:

What privilege escalation condition did I discover,
what must be true for it to matter,
and how should I validate and report it?

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK
docs.text:
Where applicable, explorer techniques include mappings to MITRE ATT&CK.

Common privilege escalation and execution-related areas include:

T1548 - Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
T1548.001 - Setuid and Setgid
T1548.003 - Sudo and Sudo Caching
T1068 - Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
T1574 - Hijack Execution Flow
T1543 - Create or Modify System Process
T1053 - Scheduled Task/Job
T1552 - Unsecured Credentials

ATT&CK mappings provide useful context, but the presence of an ATT&CK technique does not determine exploitability or severity by itself.

docs.title: Explorer Principles
docs.text: PrivEsc Explorer follows several core principles.

docs.title: Evidence Before Exploitation
docs.text: Prefer configuration and permission evidence before modifying privileged resources.

docs.title: Context Before Severity
docs.text: A dangerous-looking permission is only meaningful when connected to a privileged consumer.

docs.title: Candidates Before Conclusions
docs.text: Enumeration produces candidates. Validation produces findings.

docs.title: Minimal Impact
docs.text: Use the least invasive technique necessary to establish the security boundary.

docs.title: Offensive and Defensive Context
docs.text: Where practical, each technique includes both testing and defensive guidance.

docs.title: Structured Knowledge
docs.text: Technique data is maintained separately from presentation logic so the explorer can grow without turning into an unmaintainable collection of hard-coded pages.

docs.title: Future Expansion
docs.text:
The explorer architecture can be expanded without changing the overall workflow.

Possible future areas include:

Active Directory Explorer
        |
        +--> Kerberos
        +--> Delegation
        +--> ACL / ACE
        +--> AD CS
        +--> NTLM Relay
        +--> Trusts

Command Explorer
        |
        +--> Windows
        +--> Linux
        +--> PowerShell
        +--> Active Directory
        +--> Networking

Detection Explorer
        |
        +--> ATT&CK Technique
        +--> Data Source
        +--> Event ID
        +--> Sigma
        +--> Detection Logic

Web Testing Explorer
        |
        +--> Observation
        +--> Vulnerability Class
        +--> Validation
        +--> Burp Workflow
        +--> Remediation

The same structured-data approach can therefore support other operational areas of the knowledge base.

Perform active validation only where explicitly authorised and use the least invasive method necessary to demonstrate the security impact.

docs.title: Linux PrivEsc Explorer
docs.text:
Linux PrivEsc Explorer

Search Linux privilege escalation techniques based on sudo permissions, SUID and SGID binaries, capabilities, services, scheduled jobs, filesystem permissions, credentials, containers, groups, sockets, and system configuration discovered during an authorised assessment.

Linux PrivEsc Interactive

docs.title: Search Examples
docs.text:
Try searching for:

sudo
NOPASSWD
SETENV
SUID
SGID
cap_setuid
cap_dac_override
cap_sys_admin
systemd
cron

PATH
Docker
docker.sock
LXD
NFS
no_root_squash
socket
credential
SSH
kernel

The explorer searches across technique names, categories, descriptions, prerequisites, commands, validation guidance, MITRE ATT&CK information, and tags.

docs.title: Linux Privilege Escalation Model
docs.text:
Linux privilege escalation commonly involves a lower-privileged user being able to influence a resource or execution path associated with a more privileged identity.

Current User
    |
    v
Enumeration
    |
    +--> sudo
    +--> SUID / SGID
    +--> Capabilities
    +--> Services
    +--> systemd
    +--> Cron
    +--> Filesystem
    +--> PATH
    +--> Libraries
    +--> Credentials
    +--> Groups
    +--> Containers
    +--> Unix Sockets
    +--> NFS
    +--> Applications
    +--> Kernel
    |
    v
Candidate
    |
    v
Validate Privilege Relationship
    |
    v
Determine Impact

The presence of an interesting configuration does not automatically prove privilege escalation.

docs.title: Establish the Current Security Context
docs.text:
Start with:

id

whoami

groups

Additional context:

uname -a

cat /etc/os-release

hostname

Understanding the current identity and system context prevents incorrect assumptions later in the assessment.

docs.title: sudo
docs.text:
Inspect delegated sudo privileges:

sudo -l

Look for:

NOPASSWD
SETENV
Wildcards
Interpreters
Editors
File utilities
Package managers
Service-management commands
Shell-capable applications
User-controlled arguments
User-controlled environment variables

A sudo entry is not automatically vulnerable.

The delegated command and its argument restrictions must be understood.

docs.title: sudo NOPASSWD
docs.text:
Example:

(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/example

Questions include:

What can the executable do?
Can it execute commands?
Can it write files?
Can it load plugins?
Can it invoke an editor?
Can it invoke a pager?
Can it execute child processes?
Can arguments influence files or commands?

Use GTFOBins as a reference where applicable, but verify the exact local binary and sudo rule.

docs.title: sudo SETENV
docs.text:
SETENV can allow environment variables to be preserved or supplied to delegated commands.

Potentially security-sensitive variables depend on the command and execution context.

The presence of SETENV should be treated as a candidate requiring contextual analysis rather than automatic privilege escalation.

docs.title: sudo Wildcards
docs.text:
Wildcard rules may become dangerous when a privileged program interprets attacker-controlled filenames as command-line options or arguments.

The relevant relationship is:

Privileged Command
      |
      v
Wildcard Expansion
      |
      v
User-Controlled Filename
      |
      v
Argument Interpretation

Validate the exact command behaviour before reporting the condition.

docs.title: SUID
docs.text:
Find SUID files:

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

SUID causes an executable to run with the effective UID of its owner.

A SUID binary is not automatically vulnerable.

Review:

Owner
Binary purpose
Arguments
Environment handling
File operations
External commands
Library loading
Configuration
Version
Custom code

docs.title: SGID
docs.text:
Find SGID files:

find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null

SGID can provide access to security-sensitive groups or resources.

The impact depends on the owning group and the functionality exposed by the executable.

docs.title: Custom SUID Applications
docs.text:
Custom SUID applications deserve additional attention.

Useful review areas include:

system()
popen()
exec*()
Relative executable paths
Temporary files
Environment variables
Writable configuration
Writable libraries
Unsafe file handling
User-controlled input

Prefer static analysis and permission inspection before executing invasive tests.

docs.title: Linux Capabilities
docs.text:
Enumerate file capabilities:

getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

Common security-sensitive capabilities include:

CAP_SETUID
CAP_SETGID
CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE
CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH
CAP_SYS_ADMIN
CAP_SYS_PTRACE
CAP_SYS_MODULE
CAP_NET_ADMIN
CAP_NET_RAW

Capabilities should always be interpreted in the context of the executable receiving them.

docs.title: CAP_SETUID
docs.text:
CAP_SETUID allows applicable processes to manipulate user IDs.

When assigned to a flexible interpreter or executable capable of arbitrary code execution, this can represent a strong privilege escalation candidate.

Verify:

getcap /path/to/binary

Do not assume every executable with CAP_SETUID provides arbitrary code execution.

docs.title: CAP_SETGID
docs.text:
CAP_SETGID can allow manipulation of group IDs.

Impact depends on which groups can be assumed and what those groups can access.

docs.title: CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE
docs.text:
This capability can bypass discretionary access-control checks for applicable file operations.

Potential impact includes access to otherwise protected files.

The exact executable functionality determines practical exploitability.

docs.title: CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH
docs.text:
This capability can bypass certain file read and directory search restrictions.

It can be security sensitive where the executable exposes flexible file-reading functionality.

docs.title: CAP_SYS_ADMIN
docs.text:
CAP_SYS_ADMIN is extremely broad.

Depending on the context, it can expose security-sensitive operations involving:

Mounts
Namespaces
Filesystem operations
Kernel interfaces
System administration

The presence of this capability warrants careful investigation.

docs.title: CAP_SYS_PTRACE
docs.text:
This capability can permit tracing or inspection of processes outside normal restrictions.

Impact depends on:

Target process
Credential material
Process protections
Namespace boundaries
Kernel restrictions

docs.title: CAP_SYS_MODULE
docs.text:
This capability can permit kernel-module operations in applicable contexts.

Kernel module testing is potentially destabilising and should not be performed on production systems unless specifically authorised.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Enumerate services:

systemctl list-units --type=service --all

Installed service definitions:

systemctl list-unit-files --type=service

Inspect a service:

systemctl cat <service>

Useful fields include:

User=
Group=
ExecStart=
ExecStartPre=
ExecStartPost=
Environment=
EnvironmentFile=
WorkingDirectory=

docs.title: systemd
docs.text:
A useful systemd assessment model is:

systemd Unit
    |
    v
Privileged Identity
    |
    v
ExecStart
    |
    +--> Binary
    +--> Script
    +--> EnvironmentFile
    +--> Configuration
    |
    v
Can Current User Modify It?

Inspect ownership and permissions before changing anything.

docs.title: Writable systemd Executable
docs.text:
Example relationship:

root service
    |
    v
ExecStart=/opt/example/service.sh
    |
    v
service.sh writable by normal user

Validate:

ls -l /opt/example/service.sh

namei -l /opt/example/service.sh

getfacl /opt/example/service.sh

The permission relationship itself may provide sufficient evidence without modifying the script.

docs.title: systemd Environment Files
docs.text:
A privileged service may consume an environment file:

EnvironmentFile=/etc/example/example.env

Inspect:

ls -l /etc/example/example.env

getfacl /etc/example/example.env

Whether this creates privilege escalation depends on how the service uses those variables.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Enumerate system cron configuration:

cat /etc/crontab

ls -la /etc/cron.d/

ls -la /etc/cron.daily/

ls -la /etc/cron.hourly/

User cron:

crontab -l

Look for privileged jobs executing writable resources.

docs.title: Writable Cron Script
docs.text:
A strong candidate relationship is:

root cron job
    |
    v
Executes Script
    |
    v
Script Writable by Normal User

Inspect:

ls -l /path/to/script

getfacl /path/to/script

Prefer demonstrating permissions and execution identity without modifying the script.

docs.title: Cron PATH
docs.text:
Review PATH definitions inside:

/etc/crontab
/etc/cron.d/*

A candidate may exist when:

Privileged cron job
        +
Relative executable name
        +
Writable earlier PATH directory

All three conditions matter.

docs.title: Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Useful commands:

ls -la

stat /path/to/file

namei -l /path/to/file

getfacl /path/to/file

Interesting conditions include:

Root-owned file writable by current user
Root-owned directory writable by current user
Privileged script writable by current user
Privileged configuration writable by current user
Writable parent directory
Unexpected ACL

docs.title: Writable Directories
docs.text:
Find writable directories carefully:

find / -type d -writable 2>/dev/null

The result set may be large.

Writable directories such as /tmp are expected and are not automatically vulnerabilities.

Determine whether a privileged process consumes attacker-controlled resources from the directory.

docs.title: PATH
docs.text:
Inspect:

echo "$PATH"

Readable format:

printf '%s\n' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'

A PATH candidate usually requires:

Privileged Process
       +
Relative Command
       +
Writable PATH Directory
       +
Writable Directory Appears Earlier

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Potential locations include:

Shell history
Environment variables
Configuration files
Backup files
SSH keys
Application credentials
Database configuration
Deployment files
Cloud credentials
Service configuration

Search only within authorised scope.

docs.title: Shell History
docs.text:
Examples:

cat ~/.bash_history

cat ~/.zsh_history

History may contain:

Passwords
Tokens
SSH commands
Database commands
Administrative commands
Internal hosts
API keys

Treat discovered credentials as sensitive assessment evidence.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Inspect:

env

or:

printenv

Look for secrets only where authorised.

docs.title: SSH Keys
docs.text:
Common location:

~/.ssh/

Inspect permissions:

ls -la ~/.ssh/

Private keys should not be copied unnecessarily.

Establish relevance and scope before using discovered authentication material.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Enumerate:

id

groups

Security-sensitive group memberships can include:

sudo
wheel
docker
lxd
disk
shadow
libvirt
adm

The impact depends on system configuration.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Check:

id

docker info

Docker access can be highly privileged when the client can communicate with a rootful Docker daemon.

Relevant factors include:

docker group membership
Docker socket permissions
Rootful vs rootless daemon
Remote API exposure
Authorisation plugins
Host mounts
Container privileges

docs.title: Docker Socket
docs.text:
Inspect:

ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

The key question is:

Can the current user control a rootful Docker daemon?

If yes, the access may effectively represent host-level administrative authority.

docs.title: LXD
docs.text:
Check:

id

lxc list

Membership in an LXD administrative group can be security sensitive depending on configuration and available host integration.

Do not assume all LXD environments are configured identically.

docs.title: NFS
docs.text:
Inspect mounted filesystems:

mount

findmnt

Client-visible NFS configuration can provide useful context.

Server-side export configuration should be reviewed where authorised.

A security-sensitive configuration can include:

no_root_squash

but practical impact depends on export permissions, write access, mount access, and server configuration.

docs.title: Unix Sockets
docs.text:
Enumerate listening Unix sockets:

ss -lx

Inspect:

find / -type s 2>/dev/null

Privileged local APIs can be exposed through Unix sockets.

Review:

Socket ownership
Socket permissions
Server identity
Protocol
Authentication
Authorisation
Available operations

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
Privilege escalation candidates can involve privileged applications loading resources from writable locations.

Investigate:

Shared libraries
Plugin directories
Python modules
Application extensions
Configuration-controlled paths
Dynamic linker configuration

Do not report generic writable library directories without establishing a privileged consumer.

docs.title: Python Import Paths
docs.text:
For privileged Python applications, inspect:

Imports
Working directory
sys.path
Custom modules
Writable module directories
Environment

The important question is whether a privileged Python process imports a module that a lower-privileged user can control.

docs.title: Custom Applications
docs.text:
Custom privileged applications should be reviewed for:

Relative commands
Writable configuration
Writable plugins
Writable libraries
Temporary files
Environment variables
Unsafe file permissions
Local sockets
Credential storage
Service integration
Scheduled execution

docs.title: Kernel
docs.text:
Kernel privilege escalation should generally be considered after configuration-based paths have been investigated.

Collect:

uname -a

cat /etc/os-release

Relevant factors include:

Exact kernel version
Distribution patches
Architecture
Exploit prerequisites
Namespaces
Capabilities
Security modules
Exploit mitigations
System stability

Do not infer vulnerability from a version string alone.

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text:
Understand controls such as:

SELinux
AppArmor
seccomp
Namespaces
Capabilities
sudo policy
Filesystem mount options
Container isolation
Kernel hardening

Examples:

getenforce 2>/dev/null

aa-status 2>/dev/null

findmnt

Security controls may materially affect exploitability.

docs.title: Candidate Validation
docs.text:
Use:

Finding
   |
   v
Who Controls It?
   |

Who Consumes It?
   |

What UID/GID Is Used?
   |

   |

   |

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Strong evidence should establish:

Current identity
Controlled resource
Permission
Privileged consumer
Execution identity
Impact

Example:

Current identity:
www-data

Resource:
/opt/example/backup.sh

Permissions:
-rwxrwxr-x root www-data

Privileged consumer:
root cron job

Execution identity:
root

This is stronger than simply stating that a file is writable.

docs.title: Windows Privilege Escalation Model
docs.text:
Windows privilege escalation usually involves a lower-privileged user being able to influence something that is later consumed by a more privileged security context.

Current User
    |
    v
Enumeration
    |
    +--> Services
    +--> Scheduled Tasks
    +--> Privileges
    +--> Access Tokens
    +--> Filesystem ACLs
    +--> Registry ACLs
    +--> PATH
    +--> DLL Loading
    +--> Credentials
    +--> Application Control
    +--> UAC
    +--> Installed Software
    +--> Drivers
    +--> Named Pipes
    +--> Autoruns
    |
    v
Candidate
    |
    v
Validate Privilege Relationship
    |
    v
Determine Impact

The presence of an interesting condition does not automatically prove privilege escalation.

docs.title: Establish the Current Security Context
docs.text:
Start by understanding the current identity.

whoami

whoami /user

whoami /groups

whoami /priv

whoami /all

Useful PowerShell context:

[System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Name

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

The current user, group memberships, privileges, integrity level, and execution restrictions determine which privilege escalation paths are relevant.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Windows services are an important privilege escalation surface because many services execute as privileged identities such as:

LocalSystem
LocalService
NetworkService
Domain service accounts
Custom privileged accounts

Enumerate services:

Get-Service

sc query

Inspect service configuration:

sc qc <SERVICE_NAME>

PowerShell:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

Useful fields include:

Name
StartName
State
PathName
StartMode

The central question is:

Can the current user influence something executed by a privileged service?

docs.title: Writable Service Executable
docs.text:
A service executable may represent a privilege escalation candidate when:

Service
    |
    v
Runs as Privileged Identity
    |
    v
Executes Binary
    |
    v
Binary Writable by Lower-Privileged User

Inspect permissions:

icacls "C:\Path\service.exe"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Path\service.exe" | Format-List

Do not replace the executable merely to prove the condition.

The combination of privileged execution identity and writable executable permissions may already provide sufficient evidence.

docs.title: Writable Service Directory
docs.text:
Even if the service executable itself is protected, inspect its parent directory.

icacls "C:\Path"

A writable parent directory can be security relevant because it may permit:

File replacement
Dependency placement
Configuration modification
Application resource modification

Always determine whether the privileged service actually consumes the controlled resource.

docs.title: Weak Service Object Permissions
docs.text:
Service Control Manager permissions can allow users to modify service configuration independently of filesystem permissions.

Inspect service configuration:

sc qc <SERVICE_NAME>

Where authorised tooling is available, inspect the service security descriptor.

The important permissions may include the ability to:

Change service configuration
Change binary path
Change service account
Start service
Stop service
Modify service security

A writable service object running as LocalSystem can represent a significant privilege boundary.

docs.title: Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
An unquoted service path may be interesting when:

Service path contains spaces
        +
Path is not quoted
        +
Earlier interpreted location is writable
        +
Service runs privileged

Example:

C:\Program Files\Example Service\service.exe

The issue is not simply that the path is unquoted.

You must also establish whether a lower-privileged user can control a path Windows could resolve before the intended executable.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Enumerate scheduled tasks:

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

Inspect task actions:

Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object TaskName,TaskPath,State

Useful questions include:

What executes?
Who executes it?
When does it execute?
Is the executable writable?
Is the script writable?
Is the working directory writable?
Can the task definition be modified?

docs.title: Writable Scheduled Task Action
docs.text:
A common relationship is:

Scheduled Task
      |
      v
Privileged Identity
      |
      v
Executes Script or Binary
      |
      v
Resource Writable by Current User

Inspect the target resource:

icacls "C:\Path\task-script.ps1"

or:

Get-Acl "C:\Path\task-script.ps1" | Format-List

Prefer demonstrating the permission relationship without modifying or triggering production tasks.

docs.title: Windows Privileges
docs.text:
Enumerate privileges:

whoami /priv

Security-sensitive privileges include:

SeImpersonatePrivilege
SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege
SeBackupPrivilege
SeRestorePrivilege
SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege
SeDebugPrivilege
SeLoadDriverPrivilege

A privilege being present does not automatically mean practical privilege escalation is possible.

docs.title: SeImpersonatePrivilege
docs.text:
SeImpersonatePrivilege allows a process to impersonate certain security tokens.

It is commonly associated with service identities and application pools.

Relevant contexts can include:

IIS application pools
SQL Server services
Service accounts
LocalService
NetworkService
Other service processes

Validation should focus on:

Current process identity
Privilege state
Available token context
Operating-system protections
Security boundaries involved

docs.title: SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege
docs.text:
This privilege can permit assignment of primary tokens under specific circumstances.

Enumerate with:

whoami /priv

The privilege should be treated as a candidate requiring contextual validation rather than automatic proof of escalation.

docs.title: SeBackupPrivilege
docs.text:
SeBackupPrivilege can permit security-sensitive read operations that bypass normal filesystem access checks in applicable contexts.

Potentially sensitive targets include:

Registry hives
Configuration files
Credential material
Protected system data

The security significance depends on whether access can expose material that enables further privilege escalation.

docs.title: SeRestorePrivilege
docs.text:
SeRestorePrivilege can permit security-sensitive write operations that bypass normal filesystem restrictions in applicable contexts.

The impact depends on which privileged resources can actually be modified.

docs.title: SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege
docs.text:
This privilege may allow ownership of securable objects to be changed.

The important chain is:

Take Ownership
      |
      v
Change Permissions
      |
      v
Control Privileged Resource

Do not change ownership of production resources unless explicitly required and authorised.

docs.title: SeDebugPrivilege
docs.text:
SeDebugPrivilege provides powerful access to processes and can cross important process-security boundaries.

Determine:

Is the privilege enabled?
What processes are accessible?
What protection mechanisms are present?
Does the current context already have administrative authority?

docs.title: SeLoadDriverPrivilege
docs.text:
This privilege may permit driver loading in applicable contexts.

Driver-based privilege escalation is high impact and potentially destabilising.

Prefer configuration-based validation rather than loading arbitrary drivers on production systems.

docs.title: Access Tokens
docs.text:
Windows access tokens define the security context associated with processes and threads.

Useful concepts include:

User SID
Group SIDs
Privileges
Integrity level
Restricted SIDs
Token type
Impersonation level

Enumerate:

whoami /all

Understanding token context is especially important when investigating service accounts and impersonation-related privilege escalation.

docs.title: Integrity Levels
docs.text:
Windows integrity levels commonly include:

Low
Medium
High
System

An administrator running a medium-integrity process is different from a standard user with no administrative membership.

Do not report UAC-related observations without establishing the actual token and administrative context.

docs.title: Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Inspect permissions with:

icacls "C:\Path"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Path" | Format-List

Interesting permissions may include:

FullControl
Modify
Write
WriteData
CreateFiles
CreateDirectories
Delete
ChangePermissions
TakeOwnership

Interesting principals may include:

Everyone
Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Users
Current user
Current user's groups

docs.title: Program Files and ProgramData
docs.text:
Useful locations include:

C:\Program Files
C:\Program Files (x86)
C:\ProgramData

Do not assume a writable directory under ProgramData is automatically vulnerable.

Determine whether a privileged application, service, task, or other security-sensitive process consumes the writable content.

docs.title: PATH Configuration
docs.text:
Inspect PATH:

echo %PATH%

PowerShell:

$env:PATH -split ';'

For each directory, consider:

Who can write there?
Does a privileged process use PATH resolution?
Does the privileged process execute a relative command?
Is the intended executable found later in PATH?

A writable PATH directory without a privileged consumer is not automatically a privilege escalation vulnerability.

docs.title: DLL Loading
docs.text:
DLL-related candidates can involve:

Missing DLLs
Writable application directories
Writable dependency directories
Unsafe DLL search order
User-controlled working directories
Custom privileged applications

Useful investigation tools include:

Process Monitor
Process Explorer
AccessChk
Filesystem ACL inspection
Application configuration review

Avoid placing arbitrary DLLs into production application directories unless active exploitation is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Registry Permissions
docs.text:
Inspect a registry key:

Get-Acl "Registry::HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Example" | Format-List

Service registry configuration can be inspected under:

HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services

Potentially sensitive writable values include those controlling:

Service executable paths
Application configuration
Autoruns
Security configuration
Environment values
Privileged application settings

docs.title: AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
Check:

reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated

reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated

Both policy locations and the actual operating context should be considered before reaching a conclusion.

docs.title: Credential Exposure
docs.text:
Potential credential locations include:

Credential Manager
PowerShell history
Environment variables
Configuration files
Unattended installation files
Application configuration
Deployment scripts
Saved administrative credentials
RDP configuration
Backup files

Credential discovery should remain within the agreed assessment scope.

docs.title: Credential Manager
docs.text:
Enumerate stored credential targets:

cmdkey /list

The existence of a target does not necessarily mean credential material can be extracted or reused.

Determine the actual security impact.

docs.title: PowerShell History
docs.text:
Common history path:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Review only where authorised.

History may contain:

Credentials
Tokens
Administrative commands
Internal hosts
API keys
Deployment commands

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Enumerate:

set

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Look for secrets only within authorised scope.

docs.title: Unattended Files
docs.text:
Potential locations can include:

C:\Windows\Panther
C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend
C:\Windows\System32\Sysprep

Search carefully and avoid indiscriminate collection of unrelated sensitive information.

docs.title: UAC Context
docs.text:
Useful questions include:

Is the user a local administrator?
What integrity level is the current process?
Is UAC enabled?
What is the configured elevation behaviour?
Is the scenario a real privilege escalation or an elevation boundary?

UAC observations should be reported with accurate context.

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
Where available:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Inspect rule collections:

Executable
Windows Installer
Script
Packaged app
DLL

An application-control gap can be security relevant, but the ability to execute a particular signed binary does not automatically prove a privilege escalation vulnerability.

docs.title: PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible values include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

FullLanguage is normal on many Windows systems.

It becomes more interesting where the endpoint is intended to enforce restrictive application-control boundaries for lower-privileged users.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
Enumerate installed drivers using appropriate system tooling.

Driver assessment should consider:

Driver version
Signature
Vendor
Known vulnerability
Loaded state
Accessible device objects
Required privileges
Exploitability mitigations

Do not assume an old driver version is exploitable without confirming the exact affected version and conditions.

docs.title: Named Pipes
docs.text:
Named pipes may expose privileged local interfaces.

Assess:

Pipe ACL
Server identity
Client authentication
Impersonation behaviour
Protocol
Authorisation

A named pipe being present is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: Autoruns and Startup Resources
docs.text:
Potential persistence and privilege escalation surfaces can include:

Run keys
Startup folders
Services
Scheduled tasks
Application-specific startup mechanisms

The important relationship remains:

Lower-Privileged Write Access
        +
Privileged Execution
        =
Candidate

docs.title: Custom Applications
docs.text:
Custom privileged software deserves particular attention because application-specific trust relationships may not be covered by generic operating-system hardening.

Investigate:

Installation directory
Configuration
Plugins
Libraries
Update mechanisms
Service integration
Named pipes
Local sockets
Temporary files
Log directories
PATH usage
Credential storage

docs.title: Security Products
docs.text:
Understand the defensive context before interpreting findings.

Relevant controls can include:

Microsoft Defender Antivirus
Attack Surface Reduction
AppLocker
Windows Defender Application Control
Credential Guard
LSA protection
EDR
Privilege-management products

The objective is not to disable these controls.

Their presence may materially affect whether a candidate is exploitable.

docs.title: Candidate Validation
docs.text:
A useful validation model is:

Finding
   |
   v
Who Controls It?
   |
   v
Who Consumes It?
   |
   v
What Identity Is Used?
   |
   v
Can the Resource Be Influenced?
   |
   v
Are Security Controls Present?
   |
   v
What Privilege Would Be Obtained?

Example:

Writable service.exe
        |
        v
Writable by normal user?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
Service runs as SYSTEM?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
Service executes that exact binary?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
Strong PrivEsc Candidate

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Strong evidence should identify:

Current user
Affected object
Relevant permissions
Privileged consumer
Execution identity
Security impact

For example:

Current user:
CORP\user

Affected resource:
C:\Program Files\Example\Service.exe

Permission:
BUILTIN\Users:(M)

Privileged consumer:
ExampleService

Execution identity:
LocalSystem

This demonstrates the security relationship without replacing the executable.

docs.title: What Not to Report Automatically
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

Writable temporary directory
Old software version
FullLanguage PowerShell
Allowed Windows binary
Unquoted service path
SUID-like application behaviour
Interesting privilege
Writable ProgramData directory
Stored credential target
Named pipe
Driver

Each requires context.

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Useful telemetry may include:

Process creation
Service configuration changes
Service creation
Scheduled-task changes
Registry changes
File permission changes
Sensitive file writes
DLL loading
Driver loading
PowerShell activity
Credential access
Application-control events

Where available, correlate activity with:

Process
Parent process
Integrity level
Target resource
Timestamp
Host

docs.text:
Privilege escalation remediation commonly involves:

docs.title: Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teaming is a structured, collaborative security approach in which offensive and defensive security teams work together to improve an organisation's ability to prevent, detect, investigate and respond to cyber attacks.

Rather than treating red and blue teams as isolated functions, purple teaming creates a feedback loop between them.

                PURPLE TEAMING

       Offensive              Defensive
       Perspective            Perspective
            |                      |
            v                      v
        Red Team               Blue Team
            |                      |
            +----------+-----------+
                       |
                       v
                  Collaboration
                       |
                       v
                Security Testing
                       |
                       v
                   Telemetry
                       |
                       v
                   Detection
                       |
                       v
                   Response
                       |
                       v
                    Improve
                       |
                       v
                    Retest

The goal is not simply to determine whether an attack succeeds.

The goal is to understand:

What happened?

Why did it happen?

What did the attacker observe?

What did the defender observe?

Was the behaviour prevented?

Was telemetry generated?

Was the telemetry collected?

Was the behaviour detected?

Was an alert generated?

Did the security team respond?

What can be improved?

Did the improvement work when retested?

Purple is a function, not necessarily a separate team

Purple teaming does not require a permanent organisational team called the Purple Team. The purple function can be created through structured collaboration between red teams, blue teams, SOC analysts, detection engineers, incident responders, security engineers and other relevant stakeholders.

docs.title: Core Objective
docs.text:
A useful purple team model is:

Attack
   |
   v
Observe
   |
   v
Understand
   |
   v
Detect
   |
   v
Improve
   |
   v
Retest
   |
   v
Learn

The cycle should produce measurable security improvement rather than only a list of vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Red Team
docs.text:
The red team provides the offensive perspective.

Typical responsibilities include:

Threat modelling

Attack-path analysis

Technique selection

Adversary emulation

Execution

Privilege escalation

Credential access

Lateral movement

Persistence

Command and control

Objective execution

docs.title: Blue Team
docs.text:
The blue team provides the defensive perspective.

Typical responsibilities include:

Security monitoring

Endpoint protection

Network monitoring

Identity monitoring

SIEM

Detection engineering

Threat hunting

Incident investigation

Containment

Response

Recovery

docs.title: Purple Team
docs.text:
Purple teaming connects both perspectives.

Red Team
   |
   | "This is what I did."
   |
   v
Purple Collaboration
   ^
   |
   | "This is what we observed."
   |
Blue Team

The resulting conversation should answer:

Did the technique work?

What telemetry was generated?

Which security controls observed it?

Was the activity detected?

Could analysts understand what happened?

What should be changed?

Can the improvement be validated?

docs.title: Purple Teaming Is Not
docs.text:
Purple teaming should not simply become:

Red Team
   |
   v
Runs Attack
   |
   v
Blue Team
   |
   v
Watches

It should instead become:

Red
 |
 v
Execute
 |
 v
Blue
 |
 v
Observe
 |
 v
Discuss
 |
 v
Understand
 |
 v
Improve
 |
 v
Retest
 |
 v
Shared Learning

docs.title: Purple Teaming vs Penetration Testing
docs.text:
Penetration testing typically focuses on identifying and validating vulnerabilities.

Question:

What vulnerabilities can be exploited?

Purple teaming focuses more heavily on collaborative defensive improvement.

Question:

Can the organisation prevent, detect and respond to realistic
attacker behaviour, and can those capabilities be improved?

docs.title: Purple Teaming vs Red Teaming
docs.text:
Red teaming commonly evaluates whether an attacker can achieve an objective.

Initial Access
      |
      v
Execution
      |
      v
Privilege Escalation
      |
      v
Credential Access
      |
      v
Lateral Movement
      |
      v
Objective

Purple teaming focuses on what happens defensively at each stage.

Attack Step
    |
    v
Security Control
    |
    v
Telemetry
    |
    v
Detection
    |
    v
Response
    |
    v
Improvement

docs.title: Purple Teaming vs Vulnerability Assessment
docs.text:
A vulnerability assessment may identify:

Missing patch

Weak configuration

Exposed service

Excessive permission

Purple teaming may ask:

If this weakness were used during an attack, what would the
organisation observe and how would defenders respond?

docs.title: Purple Teaming vs Adversary Emulation
docs.text:
Adversary emulation attempts to reproduce behaviours associated with realistic threats.

Purple teaming can use adversary emulation as the testing mechanism.

Threat Intelligence
       |
       v
Adversary Behaviour
       |
       v
ATT&CK Technique
       |
       v
Purple Team Exercise
       |
       v
Detection Validation

docs.title: Why Purple Teaming Matters
docs.text:
Security controls are often deployed independently.

For example:

EDR

SIEM

Firewall

IDS / IPS

Email Security

Identity Protection

Application Control

Cloud Monitoring

DLP

Having these technologies does not automatically mean the organisation can detect realistic attacks.

Purple teaming validates whether they work together.

docs.title: Security Control Reality
docs.text:
A control may be:

Installed

Enabled

Configured

Generating telemetry

Sending telemetry

Parsed correctly

Monitored

Detected

Investigated

Responded to

These are different levels of capability.

docs.title: Prevention, Detection and Response
docs.text: Purple team exercises should distinguish between three outcomes.

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text: Was the activity blocked?

docs.title: Detection
docs.text: Was the activity identified?

docs.title: Response
docs.text: Did defenders take appropriate action?

docs.title: Possible Outcomes
docs.text:
A test may result in:

Prevented and Detected

Prevented but Not Detected

Allowed and Detected

Allowed and Logged

Allowed without Useful Visibility

Each outcome provides different information.

docs.title: Purple Team Lifecycle
docs.text:
A practical purple team lifecycle is:

                 PLAN
                   |
                   v
             DEFINE OBJECTIVES
                   |
                   v
             SELECT TECHNIQUES
                   |
                   v
             DEFINE EXPECTATIONS
                   |
                   v
                EXECUTE
                   |
                   v
                OBSERVE
                   |
                   v
                ANALYSE
                   |
                   v
                 IMPROVE
                   |
                   v
                 RETEST
                   |
                   v
                 MEASURE
                   |
                   v
                 REPORT
                   |
                   v
                  LEARN
                   |
                   +--------+
                            |
                            v
                       NEXT CYCLE

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
Before testing, define:

Business objective

Security objective

Learning objective

Scope

Systems

Identities

Techniques

Expected telemetry

Expected detections

Participants

Communication

Stop conditions

Evidence requirements

docs.title: Business Objectives
docs.text:
Purple teaming should support meaningful organisational goals.

Examples:

Improve ransomware detection.

Validate Active Directory monitoring.

Test lateral movement visibility.

Evaluate endpoint detection coverage.

Improve cloud identity monitoring.

Validate SOC response to credential misuse.

Improve detection of attacker discovery activity.

docs.title: Security Objectives
docs.text:
A business objective should be converted into technical security objectives.

Example:

Business Objective:

Improve resilience against ransomware.

Security Objectives:

Detect credential access.

Detect privilege escalation.

Detect lateral movement.

Detect unusual remote administration.

Detect mass file modification.

Validate containment procedures.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
Purple team exercises should also define what participants are expected to learn.

Examples:

Understand attacker decision making.

Understand endpoint telemetry.

Understand authentication telemetry.

Understand how SIEM detections are constructed.

Understand which events are required for investigation.

Understand how red and blue teams interpret the same activity.

docs.title: Objective Hierarchy
docs.text:
Business Objective
        |
        v
Security Objective
        |
        v
Technical Objective
        |
        v
Learning Objective
        |
        v
Exercise Activity

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Purple teaming can involve more than red and blue teams.

Potential participants include:

Red Team

Blue Team

SOC Analysts

Detection Engineers

Threat Hunters

Incident Responders

Security Engineers

Identity Engineers

Network Engineers

Cloud Security

Application Security

Threat Intelligence

Security Architects

docs.title: Red Team Role
docs.text:
The red team should explain:

What technique is being executed?

Why would an attacker use it?

What prerequisites exist?

What is the expected result?

What alternative techniques exist?

What indicators may be generated?

docs.title: Blue Team Role
docs.text:
The blue team should determine:

What telemetry exists?

Where is it collected?

What fields are useful?

Does a detection exist?

Does an alert exist?

Can the activity be investigated?

Can related activity be correlated?

docs.title: SOC Role
docs.text:
SOC analysts validate operational effectiveness.

Questions include:

Did the alert reach the SOC?

Was it prioritised correctly?

Was the alert understandable?

Could the analyst identify the affected host?

Could the analyst identify the account?

Could the analyst reconstruct the attack?

Was escalation appropriate?

Was containment appropriate?

docs.title: Detection Engineering Role
docs.text:
Detection engineers help translate attacker behaviour into detection logic.

Technique
    |
    v
Behaviour
    |
    v
Telemetry
    |
    v
Detection Hypothesis
    |
    v
Detection Rule
    |
    v
Test
    |
    v
Tune
    |
    v
Retest

docs.title: Threat Intelligence Role
docs.text:
Threat intelligence can help determine:

Which adversaries matter?

Which behaviours are relevant?

Which ATT&CK techniques should be prioritised?

Which attack paths are realistic?

docs.title: Security Engineering Role
docs.text:
Security engineers may improve:

Logging

EDR policy

Firewall rules

Identity controls

Application control

Network segmentation

Cloud monitoring

Hardening

docs.title: Exercise Types
docs.text:
Purple team exercises can take several forms.

Technique Validation

Detection Validation

Attack-Path Exercise

Threat-Informed Exercise

Adversary Emulation

Tabletop Exercise

Detection Engineering Workshop

Continuous Security Validation

docs.title: Technique Validation
docs.text:
A single technique is tested.

Technique
    |
    v
Execute
    |
    v
Observe
    |
    v
Detect

Useful for focused detection engineering.

docs.title: Attack-Path Exercise
docs.text:
Multiple techniques are chained.

Initial Access
      |
      v
Execution
      |
      v
Discovery
      |
      v
Credential Access
      |
      v
Lateral Movement
      |
      v
Objective

This tests whether defenders can correlate activity across the complete attack path.

docs.title: Threat-Informed Exercise
docs.text:
Threat intelligence determines which techniques are selected.

Threat Intelligence
       |
       v
Relevant Adversary
       |
       v
Observed Behaviours
       |
       v
ATT&CK Mapping
       |
       v
Exercise

docs.title: Collaborative Exercise
docs.text:
Red and blue teams communicate throughout the exercise.

Execute
   |
   v
Observe
   |
   v
Discuss
   |
   v
Tune
   |
   v
Retest

This is particularly effective for rapid learning.

docs.title: Blind Phase
docs.text:
A purple team exercise can include a blind phase.

Red Team Executes
       |
       v
Blue Team Responds Normally
       |
       v
Results Recorded

This provides a baseline.

docs.title: Collaborative Phase
docs.text:
After the baseline:

Red Explains
     |
     v
Blue Reviews
     |
     v
Detection Tuned
     |
     v
Technique Repeated

This allows direct improvement.

docs.title: Two-Phase Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

PHASE 1
Baseline

Red executes.
Blue operates normally.
Interaction is limited.

        |
        v

PHASE 2
Collaboration

Red explains.
Blue investigates.
Detection is improved.
Technique is repeated.

docs.title: Exercise Scenario
docs.text:
An exercise should have a scenario.

Example:

Scenario:

An attacker has obtained access to a standard employee
workstation.

Objective:

Determine whether the organisation can detect the attacker's
progression toward a sensitive internal application.

docs.title: Starting Position
docs.text:
Possible starting points include:

External attacker

Compromised employee account

Assumed-breach workstation

Compromised server

Cloud test identity

Insider scenario

Document the starting position clearly.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Define:

Hosts

Networks

Domains

Applications

Cloud environments

Accounts

Techniques

Testing windows

docs.title: Out of Scope
docs.text:
Explicitly define:

Production disruption

Destructive testing

Unapproved social engineering

Unapproved credential access

Third-party systems

Sensitive production data

Unavailable systems

docs.title: Rules of Engagement
docs.text:
Rules of engagement should define:

Authorised techniques

Prohibited techniques

Testing hours

Communication

Escalation

Stop conditions

Emergency contacts

Data handling

Cleanup

docs.title: Stop Conditions
docs.text:
Examples:

Unexpected service disruption

Real security incident discovered

Unintended production data access

Testing reaches an out-of-scope system

Customer requests immediate stop

Unexpected security-control instability

docs.title: Technique Selection
docs.text:
Select techniques based on:

Threat relevance

Business risk

Detection uncertainty

Attack-path importance

Previous incidents

Control maturity

Exercise objectives

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK provides a common language for purple team exercises.

Tactic
  |
  v
Technique
  |
  v
Sub-Technique
  |
  v
Procedure

For example:

Discovery
   |
   v
Account Discovery
   |
   v
Controlled Procedure

docs.title: ATT&CK Exercise Matrix
docs.text:
Example:

Phase Technique Objective Expected Detection Execution Command Interpreter Validate process telemetry Endpoint alert Discovery Account Discovery Validate discovery visibility Behaviour detection Credential Access Credential behaviour Validate endpoint visibility Credential alert Lateral Movement Remote Services Validate authentication monitoring Lateral movement alert

docs.title: ATT&CK Is Not the Objective
docs.text:
Avoid:

We tested 50 ATT&CK techniques.

without context.

Prefer:

We tested the techniques required to evaluate the selected
attack path and defensive capabilities.

docs.title: Procedure Design
docs.text:
Each procedure should define:

Technique

Purpose

Preconditions

Target

Identity

Procedure

Expected system result

Expected telemetry

Expected detection

Expected response

Cleanup

docs.title: Procedure Record
docs.text:
Example:

Test ID:
PT-001

Technique:
Account Discovery

Host:
WS01

Identity:
CORP\purple-test

Objective:
Validate visibility of account enumeration.

Expected Telemetry:
Process creation
Directory-service telemetry

Expected Detection:
Discovery activity visible to analysts

Cleanup:
None

docs.title: Test IDs
docs.text:
Use unique identifiers.

Example:

PT-001

PT-002

PT-003

or:

PT-T1087-001

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Use consistent timestamps.

Prefer:

UTC

Record:

Start time

End time

Operator

Host

Identity

Technique

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
During execution, the red team performs the approved procedure.

The goal should be:

Minimum activity required to produce meaningful evidence.

Avoid unnecessary actions once the test objective has been proven.

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
The blue team observes:

Endpoint telemetry

Windows Event Logs

Linux logs

Authentication logs

Network traffic

DNS

Firewall events

Proxy events

Cloud audit logs

SIEM events

EDR alerts

docs.title: Expected Telemetry
docs.text:
Before executing a technique, define what should be visible.

Example:

Technique:
Remote Services

Expected:

Authentication event

Source IP

Destination host

Account

Remote-service process activity

Network connection

docs.title: Telemetry Pipeline
docs.text:
Activity
   |
   v
Event Generated
   |
   v
Collected
   |
   v
Forwarded
   |
   v
Parsed
   |
   v
Stored
   |
   v
Detection
   |
   v
Alert

docs.title: Telemetry Gap
docs.text:
A missing alert does not automatically mean the detection rule failed.

The event may never have reached the SIEM.

No Alert
   |
   v
Telemetry Exists?
 /          \
No           Yes
|             |
v             v
Telemetry    Detection
Problem      Review

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
For each technique ask:

Was telemetry generated?

Was it collected?

Was it parsed correctly?

Was it searchable?

Was a detection rule triggered?

Was an alert created?

Did an analyst investigate?

Was the activity correctly understood?

docs.title: Detection Result Categories
docs.text:
Use consistent categories.

Prevented

Detected

Telemetry Only

Partially Detected

Not Detected

Not Tested

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text:
Example:

The security control prevented the approved procedure from
executing.

docs.title: Detected
docs.text:
Example:

The procedure completed and generated the expected high-fidelity
alert.

docs.title: Telemetry Only
docs.text:
Example:

The activity was visible in endpoint telemetry but no dedicated
alert was generated.

docs.title: Partial Detection
docs.text:
Example:

An alert was generated, but it did not identify the relevant
user or destination system.

docs.title: Not Detected
docs.text:
Example:

The procedure completed without generating useful telemetry or
an actionable detection.

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis
docs.text:
Before testing, define a hypothesis.

Example:

Account discovery performed by a standard employee workstation
should generate endpoint telemetry that can be correlated with
other discovery behaviour.

docs.title: Detection Engineering Cycle
docs.text:
Hypothesis
    |
    v
Technique
    |
    v
Telemetry
    |
    v
Detection Rule
    |
    v
Execute
    |
    v
Evaluate
    |
    v
Tune
    |
    v
Retest

docs.title: Detection Tuning
docs.text:
Tuning may involve:

New fields

Additional data sources

Threshold changes

Context enrichment

Asset criticality

Identity context

Parent-child relationships

Sequence correlation

docs.title: Avoid Over-Tuning
docs.text:
Do not create a detection that only identifies the exact test command.

For example:

Detect:

whoami.exe

may be less useful than understanding:

Why is identity discovery occurring?

Which user executed it?

Which parent process launched it?

What happened immediately before and after?

docs.title: Behaviour-Based Detection
docs.text:
A stronger model is:

Behaviour
   |
   v
Context
   |
   v
Sequence
   |
   v
Correlation
   |
   v
Detection

docs.title: Attack-Chain Correlation
docs.text:
Individual events may appear legitimate.

Account Discovery
      +
Network Discovery
      +
Remote Authentication
      +
Credential Access
      |
      v
Suspicious Attack Path

Purple teaming can help defenders identify these relationships.

docs.title: SOC Validation
docs.text:
Detection is not complete when an alert exists.

The SOC must be able to use it.

Validate:

Alert received

Alert prioritised

Host identified

User identified

Technique understood

Related events found

Attack path reconstructed

Escalation performed

Response initiated

docs.title: Response Validation
docs.text:
Potential response actions include:

Investigate host

Investigate identity

Block account

Isolate endpoint

Block network communication

Revoke token

Reset credential

Escalate incident

Exercise response actions should be coordinated to avoid unintended production impact.

docs.title: Detection Maturity
docs.text:
A useful maturity progression is:

No Visibility
     |
     v
Raw Telemetry
     |
     v
Searchable Telemetry
     |
     v
Detection
     |
     v
Alert
     |
     v
Investigation
     |
     v
Response
     |
     v
Automated Response

docs.title: Knowledge Transfer
docs.text:
Purple teaming should transfer knowledge between participants.

Red team knowledge may include:

Attacker objectives

Technique prerequisites

Attack-path reasoning

Alternative techniques

Privilege relationships

Credential opportunities

Blue team knowledge may include:

Telemetry sources

SIEM architecture

Detection logic

Environmental baselines

Alert triage

Incident response

The goal is shared understanding.

docs.title: Knowledge Transfer Cycle
docs.text:
Red Knowledge
      |
      v
Exercise
      |
      v
Blue Observation
      |
      v
Discussion
      |
      v
Shared Understanding
      |
      v
Improvement
      |
      v
Retest

docs.title: Explain the Why
docs.text:
A useful purple team discussion should not stop at:

Run this command.

Instead explain:

Why would an attacker perform this action?

What information does it provide?

What does the defender see?

Which data source records it?

Why is the behaviour suspicious?

How could legitimate activity look similar?

docs.title: Shared Mental Model
docs.text:
The objective is to move from separate perspectives:

Red:

Technique -> Objective

and:

Blue:

Event -> Alert

toward:

Technique
   |
   v
Attacker Objective
   |
   v
System Behaviour
   |
   v
Telemetry
   |
   v
Detection
   |
   v
Response

docs.title: Learning During Exercises
docs.text:
Learning can occur through:

Observation

Discussion

Demonstration

Hands-on practice

Detection tuning

Retesting

Reflection

docs.title: Pre-Exercise Measurement
docs.text:
Before an exercise, measure baseline knowledge where useful.

Possible topics:

ATT&CK

Offensive techniques

Endpoint telemetry

Network telemetry

Identity monitoring

Detection engineering

Incident response

docs.title: Post-Exercise Measurement
docs.text:
After the exercise, repeat comparable questions.

Compare:

Pre-Exercise
     |
     v
Exercise
     |
     v
Post-Exercise

docs.title: Knowledge Improvement
docs.text:
A simple model is:

Knowledge Improvement =
Post-Exercise Result - Pre-Exercise Result

This should be interpreted carefully and combined with other evidence.

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
Observers can record:

Participant interaction

Questions asked

Information exchanged

Detection improvements

Decision making

Communication

Areas of confusion

Successful collaboration

docs.title: Qualitative Evidence
docs.text:
Useful qualitative evidence may include:

Participant comments

Observer notes

After-action discussion

Detection-engineering decisions

Lessons learned

Examples of changed understanding

docs.title: Quantitative Evidence
docs.text:
Possible quantitative measures include:

Detection rate

Telemetry coverage

Time to detect

Time to triage

Time to respond

Number of techniques validated

Number of detection gaps identified

Number of detections improved

Pre/post knowledge scores

docs.title: Detection Rate
docs.text:
A simple metric is:

Detected Tested Techniques
--------------------------  * 100
Tested Techniques

This should not be treated as a complete measure of defensive capability.

docs.title: Telemetry Coverage
docs.text:
Techniques With Useful Telemetry
--------------------------------  * 100
Techniques Tested

docs.title: Time to Detect
docs.text: TTD = Detection Time - Technique Start Time

docs.title: Time to Triage
docs.text: TTT = Analyst Triage Time - Detection Time

docs.title: Time to Respond
docs.text: TTR = Response Time - Detection Time

docs.title: Baseline vs Retest
docs.text:
One of the strongest purple team measurements is:

Baseline
   |
   v
Gap Identified
   |
   v
Improvement
   |
   v
Retest
   |
   v
Result

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Before:

Technique:
Account Discovery

Telemetry:
Available

Detection:
None

After tuning:

Technique:
Account Discovery

Telemetry:
Available

Detection:
Behaviour correlated with additional discovery activity

Alert:
Generated

SOC:
Successfully investigated

docs.title: Improvement Categories
docs.text:
Purple team findings may lead to improvements in:

Prevention

Logging

Telemetry collection

Parsing

Detection

Alerting

Triage

Response

Architecture

Process

Training

docs.title: Gap Classification
docs.text:
Classify gaps precisely.

Control Gap

Telemetry Gap

Collection Gap

Parsing Gap

Detection Gap

Alerting Gap

Triage Gap

Response Gap

Knowledge Gap

Process Gap

docs.title: Control Gap
docs.text:
A preventive security control did not stop the behaviour as
expected.

docs.title: Telemetry Gap
docs.text: The required security event was not generated.

docs.title: Collection Gap
docs.text: The event existed locally but was not collected centrally.

docs.title: Parsing Gap
docs.text:
The event reached the security platform but important fields
were not parsed correctly.

docs.title: Detection Gap
docs.text:
Useful telemetry existed but no detection logic identified the
behaviour.

docs.title: Alerting Gap
docs.text: Detection logic matched but did not create an actionable alert.

docs.title: Triage Gap
docs.text:
An alert existed but analysts could not efficiently determine
what happened.

docs.title: Response Gap
docs.text:
The activity was detected but the operational response was
insufficient or delayed.

docs.title: Knowledge Gap
docs.text:
Participants lacked the knowledge required to understand or
investigate the behaviour.

docs.title: Process Gap
docs.text:
Technology worked, but organisational procedures prevented an
effective response.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
For every test record:

Test ID

Technique

Host

Identity

Timestamp

Procedure

Expected result

Actual result

Expected telemetry

Observed telemetry

Expected detection

Observed detection

SOC response

Improvement

Retest result

docs.text:
Maintain a timeline.

Example:

09:00 - Exercise begins

09:10 - Execution technique tested

09:13 - Endpoint telemetry confirmed

09:20 - Discovery technique tested

09:25 - Detection gap identified

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
Purple teaming depends heavily on communication.

Useful communication channels include:

Dedicated Teams channel

Exercise room

docs.title: Exercise Controller
docs.text:
For larger exercises, designate an exercise controller.

Responsibilities may include:

Track exercise progress

Record timestamps

Coordinate red and blue teams

Manage stop conditions

Resolve deconfliction

Track evidence

docs.title: Observer
docs.text:
An observer can record:

Participant interaction

Knowledge exchange

Decision making

Communication quality

Confusion

Detection changes

Learning outcomes

The observer should avoid unnecessarily influencing the exercise.

docs.title: Facilitator
docs.text:
A facilitator can help maintain productive collaboration.

Red
 |
 +--------+
          |
      Facilitator
          |
 +--------+
 |
Blue

The facilitator may help translate offensive and defensive terminology.

docs.title: Exercise Cadence
docs.text:
A collaborative exercise may use short cycles.

For example:

Technique
   |
   v
Execute
   |
   v
Observe
   |
   v
Discuss
   |
   v
Improve
   |
   v
Retest

Then move to the next technique.

docs.title: Technique Cards
docs.text:
A useful exercise artefact is a technique card.

Example:

Technique:
Account Discovery

ATT&CK:
T1087

Preconditions:
Standard employee workstation.

Expected Telemetry:

Directory-service activity

Expected Detection:

Red Team:

Blue Team:

Learning Objective:

Cleanup:
None.

docs.title: Coverage Colours
docs.text:
If using an ATT&CK heatmap, define the meaning.

Example:

Green:
Tested and expected detection confirmed.

Yellow:
Telemetry available but detection incomplete.

Red:
Tested without useful detection.

Grey:
Not tested.

docs.title: Avoid Vanity Metrics
docs.text:
Metrics such as:

500 ATT&CK techniques mapped

may look impressive but provide little evidence of operational effectiveness.

Prefer:

12 high-priority techniques tested.

10 produced useful telemetry.

8 generated actionable detections.

6 resulted in successful SOC investigation.

4 detection gaps were remediated and successfully retested.

docs.text:

docs.title: Positive Findings
docs.text:
Document successful controls.

Examples:

EDR prevented execution.

Application control blocked the procedure.

Network segmentation prevented lateral movement.

Authentication telemetry identified the source account.

SOC correctly correlated multiple attack stages.

Containment occurred before the objective was reached.

docs.title: Finding Example
docs.text:
Title:
Account Discovery Activity Is Logged but Not Detected

Technique:
T1087 - Account Discovery

Observation:
The approved account-discovery procedure generated process
creation telemetry on the test workstation.

The events were successfully forwarded to the SIEM.

No detection rule generated an alert during the baseline phase.

Improvement:
Detection logic was introduced to correlate unusual account
discovery with additional host discovery activity.

Retest:
The same approved procedure generated the expected alert.

Result:
Detection improved from Telemetry Only to Detected.

docs.title: Knowledge Transfer Finding
docs.text:
Example:

Observation:

During the baseline phase, analysts initially identified the
individual process events but did not associate them with an
attacker discovery sequence.

During the collaborative phase, the red team explained the
purpose and sequence of the discovery actions.

Following discussion and detection tuning, the blue team
successfully identified the repeated activity as a related
discovery sequence during retesting.

Which detections improved?

Which gaps remain?

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Purple teaming can be reduced to:

Define the business objective.

Define what participants should learn.

Select relevant attacker behaviour.

Map behaviour to ATT&CK where useful.

Establish a baseline.

Execute the minimum required test.

Observe the defender's view.

Validate telemetry before judging detection.

Separate prevention from detection.

Separate detection from response.

Explain attacker decision making.

Explain defensive telemetry.

Encourage direct red-blue collaboration.

Identify the actual gap.

Improve the control.

Repeat the same test.

Measure whether capability improved.

Capture knowledge.

Convert useful tests into repeatable validation.

Repeat the cycle.
