Retesting is what turns testing into improvement

Identifying a detection gap is useful, but repeating the same controlled procedure after the control has been improved provides evidence that the change actually works.

Share reasoning, not only commands

One of the most valuable parts of purple teaming is explaining why an attacker performs an action and why a defender interprets the resulting telemetry in a particular way. This helps transfer knowledge that cannot be captured by tool output alone.

Do not measure purple teaming only by ATT&CK coverage

A large number of mapped techniques does not prove defensive capability. Prioritise meaningful threat scenarios and distinguish techniques that are mapped, executed, observed, detected, responded to and successfully retested.

docs.title: Red Teaming
docs.text:
Red teaming is a goal-driven security assessment discipline that evaluates how well an organisation can prevent, detect, investigate, and respond to realistic adversary activity.

Unlike a vulnerability assessment that primarily identifies individual weaknesses, a red team assessment evaluates how multiple weaknesses, trust relationships, identities, systems, and security controls interact across an attack path.

Reconnaissance
      |
      v
Attack Surface
      |
      v
Initial Access
      |
      v
Execution
      |
      v
Command and Control
      |
      v
Credential Access
      |
      v
Privilege Escalation
      |
      v
Lateral Movement
      |
      v
Objective
      |
      v
Detection and Response Evaluation

Red teaming should always be performed under explicit authorisation, an agreed scope, defined rules of engagement, and appropriate operational controls.

docs.title: Red Teaming Notes
docs.text:
• Infrastructure

    Design and operate redirectors, domains, servers, payload delivery infrastructure, logging, segmentation, and supporting services.

    Infrastructure

  • Initial Access

    Understand externally reachable attack surfaces and the paths through which an authorised assessment may establish an initial foothold.

    Initial Access

  • Command and Control

    Understand C2 architecture, communication channels, redirectors, operational security, traffic considerations, and defensive visibility.

    Command and Control

  • Credential Access

    Assess how credentials, authentication material, tokens, secrets, and privileged identities can affect an attack path.

    Credential Access

  • Lateral Movement

    Evaluate how access can propagate between systems through credentials, remote administration protocols, trust relationships, and management infrastructure.

    Lateral Movement

  • Persistence

    Understand persistence mechanisms and evaluate whether security controls can identify unauthorised mechanisms designed to retain access.

    Persistence

  • Defence Evasion

    Study the security controls, telemetry gaps, execution restrictions, and defensive assumptions that affect detection and prevention.

    Defence Evasion

docs.title: Red Teaming vs Penetration Testing
docs.text:
Penetration testing and red teaming overlap technically, but their objectives are different.

Area Penetration Testing Red Teaming Primary goal Identify and validate vulnerabilities Evaluate security against realistic attack paths Scope Often broad technical coverage Usually objective-driven Visibility Usually known to security stakeholders Often limited to selected stakeholders Testing style Vulnerability-oriented Adversary-oriented Detection testing Useful but not always central Usually a major objective Attack chaining Common Fundamental Operational security Moderate High Social engineering Scope dependent Scope dependent Physical security Less common Scope dependent Success measurement Vulnerabilities and impact Objectives, detection, response, and resilience

A red team assessment should not simply attempt to generate the largest possible number of findings.

The objective is to understand whether realistic attack paths can reach agreed objectives and how effectively the organisation responds.

docs.title: Red Teaming vs Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Red teaming focuses on adversary simulation and objective achievement.

Purple teaming introduces deliberate collaboration between offensive and defensive teams to improve detection, prevention, response, and knowledge transfer.

Red Teaming

Red
 |
 v
Adversary Activity
 |
 v
Blue Team Detection and Response


Purple Teaming

Red <------> Blue
 |             |
 +---- Share --+
       |
       v
Detection Improvement
       |
       v
Validation
       |
       v
Repeat

The two approaches are complementary.

A red team assessment can identify defensive gaps, while a later purple team exercise can reproduce selected behaviours collaboratively and improve the corresponding controls.

docs.title: 1. Planning
docs.text:
Planning establishes why the assessment is being performed.

Questions include:

What security capability is being evaluated?
What business risk is being tested?
What systems are relevant?
What attacker profile is appropriate?
What constitutes success?
What activities are prohibited?
Who must know about the assessment?

The engagement should have measurable objectives rather than an unrestricted instruction to "hack the organisation."

docs.title: 2. Scope
docs.text:
The scope defines where testing is permitted.

Examples include:

Domains
IP ranges
Cloud tenants
Applications
Endpoints
Active Directory
Identity providers
Email infrastructure
VPN infrastructure
Wireless networks
Physical locations
Third-party systems

Scope should also identify exclusions.

Production-critical systems
Safety systems
Medical systems
Payment systems
Specific accounts
Specific subsidiaries
Third-party infrastructure
Destructive actions

Never infer authorisation from technical reachability.

docs.title: 3. Rules of Engagement
docs.text:
The Rules of Engagement define how the assessment may operate.

Typical subjects include:

Authorised dates and times
Permitted targets
Prohibited targets
Testing source addresses
Social engineering permissions
Credential handling
Persistence restrictions
Payload restrictions
Data access restrictions
Data exfiltration restrictions
Cloud restrictions
Availability restrictions
Escalation contacts
Emergency stop procedure
Cleanup requirements
Evidence handling
Reporting requirements

The Rules of Engagement should be available to the assessment team throughout the engagement.

docs.title: 4. Objectives
docs.text:
Red team objectives should represent meaningful security outcomes.

Examples:

Obtain access to a defined application
Reach a designated server
Demonstrate access to a protected dataset
Obtain a specified privilege level
Access a representative administrative interface
Reach a simulated crown-jewel system
Evaluate detection of a defined attack chain

Where possible, use synthetic objectives rather than accessing real sensitive data.

docs.title: 5. Threat Modelling
docs.text:
Threat modelling helps determine which behaviours are relevant to the organisation.

Potential inputs include:

Industry
Geography
Technology stack
Threat intelligence
Known threat actors
Previous incidents
Existing security controls
Business processes
Critical assets
Identity architecture
Cloud architecture

MITRE ATT&CK can provide a useful common language for describing adversary behaviours.

docs.title: Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Reconnaissance attempts to understand the externally visible attack surface before interacting deeply with individual systems.

Useful information can include:

Domains
Subdomains

Autonomous systems
Cloud infrastructure
VPN gateways
Remote-access services
Email infrastructure
Technology stacks
Public applications
Public repositories
Metadata

Public documents

Third-party relationships

Reconnaissance should remain within the authorised scope and applicable engagement rules.

docs.title: Passive Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Passive reconnaissance attempts to collect information without directly interacting with the target infrastructure where practical.

Sources can include:

DNS records
Certificate transparency
Search engines
Public code repositories
Public documentation
Internet scanning datasets
WHOIS / RDAP
Public cloud references
Job advertisements
Technology documentation

docs.title: Active Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Active reconnaissance interacts directly with target systems.

Examples include:

DNS resolution
Port scanning
Service identification
HTTP probing
Content discovery
Technology fingerprinting
Authentication-surface discovery

The amount and rate of active reconnaissance should reflect the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Attack Surface Mapping
docs.text:
Raw reconnaissance should be converted into an understandable attack surface.

Organisation
     |
     +--> Domains
     |
     +--> Applications
     |
     +--> Remote Access
     |
     +--> Identity
     |
     +--> Cloud
     |
     +--> Email
     |
     +--> Third Parties

Each exposed service should be considered in terms of:

Ownership
Technology
Authentication
Internet exposure
Privilege relationship
Business importance
Potential attack path

docs.title: Initial Access
docs.text:
Initial access is the point at which the assessment establishes an authorised foothold.

Potential categories can include:

External application weakness
Exposed remote service
Credential-based access
Cloud identity weakness
Misconfiguration
Approved social engineering
Approved physical access
Supply-chain scenario

The exact techniques permitted depend on the Rules of Engagement.

See:

Initial Access

docs.title: Foothold
docs.text:
A foothold is not necessarily the final objective.

After obtaining access, first establish context.

Who am I?
Where am I?
What system is this?
What privileges do I have?
What network can I reach?
What security controls are present?
What data is accessible?
What should I avoid touching?

On Windows:

whoami /all

On Linux:

id

Avoid immediately performing broad automated activity before understanding the host and its role.

docs.title: Situational Awareness
docs.text:
After obtaining a foothold, gather enough information to understand the environment.

Potential areas include:

Operating system
Hostname
Network configuration
Domain membership
Current identity
Privileges
Processes
Services
Security software
Local users
Logged-on users
Network connections
Mounted resources
Installed applications
Environment variables

docs.title: Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Privilege escalation attempts to move from the current security context to a more privileged one where required by the engagement objective.

Windows areas include:

Services
Scheduled tasks
Privileges
Filesystem permissions
Registry permissions
DLL loading
PATH configuration
Credentials
Drivers
Custom applications

Linux areas include:

sudo
SUID
SGID
Capabilities
systemd
cron
Filesystem permissions
PATH
Credentials
Containers
Sockets
Kernel

Use the interactive privilege escalation references:

  • Windows PrivEsc Explorer
  • Linux PrivEsc Explorer

docs.title: Credential Access
docs.text:
Credentials and authentication material frequently connect otherwise separate systems.

Relevant material can include:

Passwords
Password hashes
Kerberos tickets
Access tokens
API keys
SSH keys
Cloud credentials
Application secrets
Service-account credentials
Browser credentials
Configuration secrets

Credential handling requires particular care because real credentials can provide access beyond the intended assessment scope.

See:

Credential Access

docs.title: Internal Discovery
docs.text:
Internal discovery establishes what the compromised identity or system can access.

Potential questions include:

What networks are reachable?
What hosts exist?
What services are exposed?
What domain is the host joined to?
What trusts exist?
What shares are accessible?
What management infrastructure exists?
What cloud services are reachable?
Which identities are privileged?

Discovery should be deliberate rather than unnecessarily noisy.

docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Where Active Directory is in scope, relevant areas can include:

Domain structure
Users
Groups
Computers
ACLs
Kerberos
NTLM
Delegation
Certificate Services
Trusts
Group Policy
Management infrastructure
Credential exposure

Use the dedicated documentation:

Active Directory

docs.title: Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Lateral movement attempts to move from one authorised system or identity to another as part of an attack path.

Potential mechanisms include:

Remote administration
Shared credentials
Administrative protocols
SSH
SMB
WinRM
WMI
RDP
Cloud management interfaces
Application administration
Management infrastructure

The existence of valid credentials does not automatically authorise access to every system where those credentials work.

Scope remains authoritative.

See:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Command and Control
docs.text:
Command and control provides communication between assessment infrastructure and authorised test systems.

A simplified architecture may look like:

Operator
   |
   v
Team Server
   |
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Internet
   |
   v
Authorised Test Host

Operational considerations include:

Infrastructure isolation
Domain management
TLS
Logging
Redirectors
Access control
Firewall rules
Payload control
Traffic profiles
Cleanup
Defensive visibility

See:

Command and Control

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Red team infrastructure should be treated as production security infrastructure for the duration of an engagement.

Important controls include:

Strong authentication
Restricted administration
SSH key authentication
Firewall restrictions
Logging
Patch management
Encrypted communications
Separate engagement infrastructure
Minimal exposed services
Backups of required configuration
Credential protection

See:

Infrastructure

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Persistence mechanisms attempt to maintain access across changes such as:

Process termination
User logoff
System restart
Credential rotation
Service restart

Persistence can create substantial operational risk.

For many engagements, demonstrating that persistence is possible is preferable to deploying a persistent mechanism.

See:

Persistence

docs.title: Defence Evasion
docs.text:
Defence evasion testing evaluates how security controls respond to authorised adversary behaviours.

Relevant defensive layers can include:

Antivirus
EDR
Application control
PowerShell controls
AMSI
Attack Surface Reduction
Firewalling
Proxy controls
Email security
Identity protection
SIEM
Network detection
Cloud security controls

The goal should be to evaluate security controls, not disable protections unnecessarily.

See:

Defence Evasion

docs.title: Objective Execution
docs.text:
The engagement should define what constitutes successful objective completion.

A useful model is:

Objective
   |
   v
Can It Be Reached?
   |
   +--> No --> Document Blocking Control
   |
   +--> Yes
          |
          v
   Minimum Evidence Required
          |
          v
   Stop

Do not collect additional sensitive information simply because access is technically possible.

docs.title: Proof of Access
docs.text:
Where an objective involves sensitive systems or data, use the minimum evidence necessary.

Prefer:

Synthetic marker
Filename
Directory listing
Metadata
Hash of approved test file
Screenshot of authorised test object
Controlled test account

Avoid unnecessary copying of:

Personal information
Production databases
Customer records
Medical information
Financial information
Authentication databases
Large datasets

docs.title: Data Exfiltration Simulation
docs.text:
Where exfiltration testing is required, synthetic data is preferable.

Synthetic Dataset
      |
      v
Approved Channel
      |
      v
Controlled Destination
      |
      v
Detection Measurement

The purpose is usually to evaluate whether exfiltration behaviour is detected, not to remove real organisational data.

docs.title: Operational Security
docs.text:
Red team operational security helps prevent the assessment itself from creating unnecessary risk.

Consider:

Infrastructure attribution
Credential storage
Payload storage
Logging
Operator access
Source addresses
DNS records
Certificates
Cloud metadata
Repository exposure
Screenshots
Reports
Temporary files
Engagement data

docs.title: Engagement Data
docs.text:
Treat engagement data as sensitive.

Potentially sensitive material includes:

Credentials
Hashes
Tokens
Hostnames
Internal IP addresses
Architecture information
Vulnerability evidence
Screenshots
Customer data
Source code
Configuration files

Store only what is required.

docs.title: Detection Engineering Perspective
docs.text:
Red team activity should produce useful defensive learning.

For each meaningful action, consider:

What happened?
What telemetry should exist?
Was it logged?
Was it detected?
Was an alert generated?
Was the alert investigated?
Was the activity prevented?
How quickly did the organisation respond?

This converts technical execution into measurable defensive outcomes.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
Useful telemetry can include:

Endpoint process creation
Authentication events
PowerShell logs
Service changes
Scheduled-task changes
Network connections
DNS queries
Proxy logs
Firewall logs
EDR telemetry
Cloud audit logs
Identity-provider logs
Email security logs
Application logs

Telemetry requirements should ideally be considered during engagement planning rather than only after testing.

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK provides a useful framework for mapping observed behaviours.

A red team attack path may span several tactics:

Reconnaissance
      |
Resource Development
      |
Initial Access
      |
Execution
      |
Persistence
      |
Privilege Escalation
      |
Defence Evasion
      |
Credential Access
      |
Discovery
      |
Lateral Movement
      |
Collection
      |
Command and Control
      |
Exfiltration
      |
Impact

Not every engagement needs to exercise every tactic.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Evidence should be collected throughout the assessment.

Useful evidence includes:

Timestamp
Source host
Target host
Current identity
Technique
Command or action
Result
Privilege level
Relevant screenshot
Relevant log
Objective relationship
Detection result

A simple evidence model:

Action
  |
  v
Technical Result
  |
  v
Security Impact
  |
  v
Detection Result
  |
  v
Evidence

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
Maintain a reliable operational timeline.

Example:

Time Source Target Action Result 09:12 Operator Web application Authentication test Access obtained 09:37 Foothold Endpoint Host enumeration User context identified 10:04 Endpoint Internal service Connection test Service reachable 10:31 Endpoint Target system Objective validation Objective reached

Use UTC or an explicitly documented timezone consistently.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup is part of the engagement, not an optional final step.

Track changes such as:

Created files
Created accounts
Modified files
Modified permissions
Created services
Created scheduled tasks
Registry changes
SSH keys
Persistence mechanisms
Cloud resources
Firewall rules
DNS records
Temporary infrastructure

A useful workflow is:

Change Made
    |
    v
Record Change
    |
    v
Assessment Ends
    |
    v
Reverse Change
    |
    v
Verify

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
A red team report should explain the attack path rather than presenting only isolated findings.

Initial Condition
      |
      v
Weakness 1
      |
      v
Access
      |
      v
Weakness 2
      |
      v
Privilege
      |
      v
Weakness 3
      |
      v
Lateral Movement
      |
      v
Objective

This helps stakeholders understand how individual weaknesses combine into business risk.

docs.title: Finding Structure
docs.text:
A useful finding structure is:

Title
Severity
Affected Systems
Description
Attack Path
Evidence
Impact
Detection Observations
Remediation
References

docs.title: Attack Path Narrative
docs.text:
The report should explain:

Where the attack started
What weakness enabled access
What privileges were obtained
What credentials or trust relationships were used
How lateral movement occurred
Which objective was reached
Which controls detected the activity
Which controls failed to detect the activity

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity should reflect the actual demonstrated impact.

Consider:

Starting access
Required privileges
Exploit complexity
User interaction
Attack reliability
Affected systems
Privilege obtained
Data exposure
Business impact
Detection capability
Attack chaining

Avoid assigning critical severity simply because a technique sounds powerful.

docs.title: Red Team Success Metrics
docs.text:
Useful metrics can include:

Objective reached
Time to initial access
Time to detection
Time to investigation
Time to containment
Number of attack stages detected
Number of attack stages prevented
Number of meaningful attack paths
Telemetry coverage
Alert quality
Response effectiveness

The number of vulnerabilities discovered is usually not the best measure of red team effectiveness.

docs.title: Stop Conditions
docs.text:
Operators should know when testing must stop.

Potential stop conditions include:

Unexpected production impact
System instability
Access to excluded systems
Unexpected sensitive data
Third-party infrastructure reached
Safety concern
Incident-response escalation
Customer instruction
Loss of infrastructure control
Uncertain scope

When scope becomes uncertain, do not assume permission.

docs.title: Emergency Communication
docs.text:
The engagement should have an escalation path.

Operator
   |
   v
Red Team Lead
   |
   v
Authorised Customer Contact
   |
   v
Security / Incident Response

Emergency contact details should be available before testing begins.

docs.title: Before the Engagement
docs.text:
• Written authorisation confirmed
  • Scope confirmed
  • Rules of Engagement approved
  • Objectives defined
  • Exclusions documented
  • Testing window confirmed
  • Emergency contacts confirmed
  • Stop conditions understood
  • Infrastructure prepared
  • Operator access restricted
  • Logging enabled
  • Evidence handling agreed
  • Cleanup process defined

docs.title: Reconnaissance
docs.text:
• Domains identified
  • Subdomains investigated
  • IP ranges understood
  • External services identified
  • Applications mapped
  • Identity surfaces identified
  • Remote-access services reviewed
  • Cloud exposure considered
  • Third-party boundaries respected

docs.title: Initial Access
docs.text:
• Permitted techniques confirmed
  • Initial access documented
  • Source and target recorded
  • Security context established
  • Scope revalidated after access

docs.title: Post-Compromise
docs.text:
• Current identity established
  • Host role understood
  • Security controls identified
  • Privilege escalation assessed
  • Credentials handled securely
  • Internal discovery controlled
  • Lateral movement remained in scope

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
• Objective reached or blocking control identified
  • Minimum required evidence collected
  • Sensitive data collection minimised
  • Detection status recorded

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• Files removed
  • Accounts removed
  • Persistence removed
  • Configuration restored
  • Cloud resources removed
  • Infrastructure decommissioned
  • Cleanup verified

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
• Timeline complete
  • Attack path documented
  • Findings evidenced
  • Detection observations included
  • Remediation included
  • MITRE ATT&CK mappings reviewed
  • Executive impact explained

docs.text:
A mature red team workflow can be summarised as:

docs.text:

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework
  • NIST SP 800-115 - Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
  • OWASP Web Security Testing Guide
  • Atomic Red Team
  • MITRE Caldera

Authorised testing only

Red teaming can involve actions that affect production systems, identities, credentials, applications, cloud environments, security controls, and sensitive information. Perform testing only with explicit written authorisation and within the approved scope and Rules of Engagement. Stop when scope, safety, or authorisation becomes uncertain.

docs.title: Red Team Adversary Emulation
docs.text:
Adversary emulation is a threat-informed security assessment approach in which authorised testers reproduce selected behaviours associated with realistic threat actors or intrusion scenarios.

The objective is not to copy every technique ever attributed to an adversary.

The objective is to answer:

If an attacker relevant to this organisation used these
behaviours, would our controls prevent, detect and respond?

A useful adversary emulation model is:

Threat Intelligence
        |
        v
Relevant Adversary
        |
        v
ATT&CK Techniques
        |
        v
Emulation Plan
        |
        v
Controlled Procedures
        |
        v
Security Telemetry
        |
        v
Detection
        |
        v
Response
        |
        v
Lessons Learned

Authorised testing only

Adversary emulation can include behaviours that resemble real intrusions. Scope, systems, identities, techniques, infrastructure, payloads, test windows, prohibited actions, stop conditions and cleanup requirements should be explicitly defined before execution.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
Adversary emulation can help answer:

Can the organisation detect relevant attacker behaviour?

Which attack paths are realistic?

Which controls prevent progression?

Where are telemetry gaps?

Where are detection gaps?

Can the SOC correlate activity across multiple systems?

Can responders reconstruct the attack chain?

How quickly can the organisation respond?

Which ATT&CK techniques have actually been validated?

docs.title: Adversary Emulation vs Penetration Testing
docs.text:
Penetration testing often asks:

What vulnerabilities exist?

Adversary emulation asks:

How would a realistic attacker combine behaviours to pursue
an objective?

The two approaches overlap but have different emphasis.

docs.title: Adversary Emulation vs Red Teaming
docs.text:
Adversary emulation is often part of a broader red team engagement.

Red Teaming
    |
    +--> Objective-based operations
    |
    +--> Attack-path testing
    |
    +--> Social engineering
    |
    +--> Physical testing
    |
    +--> Adversary emulation

A red team may use an adversary profile to guide the engagement without attempting to reproduce every historical behaviour of that actor.

docs.title: Adversary Emulation vs Purple Teaming
docs.text:
A useful distinction is:

Red Team Emulation
        |
        v
Behaviour Executed
        |
        v
Blue Team Detects / Responds

Purple teaming adds direct collaboration:

Red Team
   |
   v
Technique
   |
   v
Blue Team
   |
   v
Detection Review
   |
   v
Tune Control
   |
   v
Retest

Both approaches can use the same ATT&CK techniques.

docs.title: Threat-Informed Testing
docs.text:
Adversary emulation should begin with threat relevance.

Sources may include:

Threat intelligence reports

Industry reporting

Internal incidents

SOC observations

Sector threats

MITRE ATT&CK

CISA advisories

Vendor research

ISAC information

The goal is to select behaviours relevant to:

Organisation

Industry

Technology stack

Geography

Business model

Known threat landscape

docs.title: Threat Model
docs.text:
A simple model is:

Threat Actor
     |
     v
Motivation
     |
     v
Target
     |
     v
Capabilities
     |
     v
Likely Techniques
     |
     v
Relevant Attack Paths

docs.title: Threat Relevance
docs.text:
Before selecting an adversary, ask:

Does this actor target our sector?

Does the actor operate in our geography?

Does the actor target our technology?

Are the actor's objectives relevant?

Are the attributed techniques sufficiently documented?

Can the important behaviours be safely tested?

docs.title: Avoid Actor Name Chasing
docs.text:
Do not choose an adversary merely because the name is well known.

For example:

Famous Threat Actor
        |
        v
Poor Relevance
        |
        v
Low-Value Exercise

A less famous intrusion set may provide a more realistic scenario.

docs.title: Behaviour Matters More Than Branding
docs.text:
Threat attribution can change.

Therefore, prioritise:

Observed behaviours

ATT&CK techniques

Attack paths

Security-control implications

rather than treating an adversary label as absolute truth.

docs.title: ATT&CK
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK provides a common language for describing adversary behaviour.

Enterprise tactics include areas such as:

Reconnaissance

Resource Development

Initial Access

Execution

Persistence

Privilege Escalation

Defence Evasion

Credential Access

Discovery

Lateral Movement

Collection

Command and Control

Exfiltration

Impact

docs.title: ATT&CK Hierarchy
docs.text:
Tactic
  |
  v
Technique
  |
  v
Sub-technique
  |
  v
Procedure

Example concept:

Credential Access
      |
      v
OS Credential Dumping
      |
      v
Specific Procedure

docs.title: Tactic
docs.text:
A tactic represents the adversary's objective.

Examples:

Initial Access

Discovery

Credential Access

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Technique
docs.text:
A technique describes how an adversary may achieve that objective.

For example:

Valid Accounts

Remote Services

Scheduled Task/Job

docs.title: Sub-Technique
docs.text:
A sub-technique provides more specific behaviour.

This allows detection coverage to be mapped more precisely.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
A procedure is the concrete implementation of a technique.

Different adversaries may implement the same ATT&CK technique differently.

Same Technique
     |
     +--> Native OS command
     |
     +--> PowerShell
     |
     +--> Custom tool
     |
     +--> Administrative utility

docs.title: ATT&CK Is Not a Checklist
docs.text:
Do not treat ATT&CK as:

Execute every technique.

Instead:

Threat Intelligence
       |
       v
Relevant Behaviours
       |
       v
Relevant ATT&CK Techniques
       |
       v
Safe Procedures

docs.title: Selecting an Adversary
docs.text:
Create an adversary profile containing:

Name or scenario

Motivation

Typical targets

Initial access patterns

Credential behaviour

Discovery behaviour

Lateral movement

Persistence

Command and control

Collection

Exfiltration

Relevant ATT&CK techniques

docs.title: Generic Scenario Profiles
docs.text:
A named threat actor is not always required.

Useful profiles may include:

Ransomware affiliate

Credential-focused intruder

Cloud identity attacker

Business email compromise actor

External espionage actor

Malicious insider

Compromised administrator

This can reduce dependence on uncertain attribution.

docs.title: Scenario Example
docs.text:
Scenario:
Credential-Focused External Intruder

Objective:
Reach a sensitive internal application using compromised
employee access.

Initial Access:
Synthetic test account

Primary Behaviours:
Account discovery
Host discovery
Credential access
Remote services
Lateral movement
Collection

Final Objective:
Access customer-provided synthetic objective file

docs.title: Define the Objective
docs.text:
Every emulation should have a business-relevant objective.

Examples:

Reach a sensitive application

Access a synthetic crown-jewel file

Reach a privileged identity

Access a controlled database record

Demonstrate movement between security tiers

Validate ransomware precursor detections

docs.title: Crown Jewels
docs.text:
Identify:

Critical applications

Identity infrastructure

Sensitive databases

Administrative systems

Cloud control planes

Business-critical services

Use synthetic proof where possible.

docs.title: Emulation Plan
docs.text:
The emulation plan converts threat intelligence into a controlled test.

Example structure:

1. Scenario

2. Threat rationale

3. Objective

4. Scope

5. Assumptions

6. ATT&CK techniques

7. Procedures

8. Expected telemetry

9. Expected detections

10. Stop conditions

11. Cleanup

docs.title: Technique Matrix
docs.text:
Example:

Phase Technique Test Objective Status Initial Access Valid Accounts Test authentication controls Planned Discovery System Information Discovery Validate endpoint visibility Planned Credential Access Credential-related behaviour Validate detection Planned Lateral Movement Remote Services Validate segmentation Planned Collection Data from Local System Validate access controls Planned

docs.title: Procedure Matrix
docs.text:
A more useful matrix adds implementation context.

Technique Procedure Host Expected Telemetry Expected Detection System Discovery Native system command WS01 Process creation Discovery alert Account Discovery Native identity query WS01 Process/identity telemetry Behaviour correlation Remote Services Approved remote administration SRV01 Authentication/network logs Lateral movement alert

docs.title: Preconditions
docs.text:
Every procedure should document prerequisites.

Example:

Technique:
Remote Services

Preconditions:
Valid synthetic account
Network reachability
Approved destination
Required service enabled

This prevents failed tests from being misclassified as successful defensive controls.

docs.title: Expected Outcome
docs.text:
Document:

What should happen?

Which control should prevent it?

Which telemetry should appear?

Which alert should trigger?

What should the SOC do?

docs.title: Procedure Safety
docs.text:
Procedures should be:

Minimal

Reversible

Observable

Scoped

Repeatable

Non-destructive where possible

docs.title: Safe Validation Ladder
docs.text:
1. Confirm scope

2. Confirm preconditions

3. Run minimal procedure

4. Verify expected system effect

5. Check telemetry

6. Check detection

7. Check response

8. Stop if objective is proven

9. Cleanup

docs.title: Atomic Testing
docs.text:
An atomic test validates one behaviour at a time.

Technique
    |
    v
Small Procedure
    |
    v
Telemetry
    |
    v
Detection

Atomic testing is particularly useful during purple team exercises.

docs.title: Atomic vs Chained Emulation
docs.text:
Atomic:

Technique A
   |
   v
Validate Detection

Chained:

Technique A
   |
   v
Technique B
   |
   v
Technique C
   |
   v
Objective

Atomic testing helps identify individual control gaps.

Chained testing evaluates whether defenders can understand the overall attack path.

docs.title: Atomic Red Team
docs.text:
Atomic Red Team provides small tests mapped to ATT&CK techniques.

Before using an atomic test:

Review the test

Review dependencies

Review cleanup

Confirm scope

Understand expected system changes

Confirm telemetry

Use only the required test

Do not bulk-execute an entire library against production systems.

docs.title: Atomic Red Team Repository
docs.text:
A typical local review workflow is:

git clone https://github.com/redcanaryco/atomic-red-team.git

Then review the relevant technique directory before running anything.

The repository contains tests that can alter systems, create files, modify configuration or execute tools.

Treat every test as code requiring review.

docs.title: Atomic Test Record
docs.text:
Test ID:
EMU-T1059-001

Technique:
T1059

Host:
WS01

Procedure:
Approved benign command interpreter validation

Expected Telemetry:
Process creation
Command-line telemetry

Expected Detection:
Command interpreter activity available in EDR

Cleanup:
None required

docs.title: CALDERA
docs.text:
MITRE CALDERA is an automated adversary emulation platform.

It can model:

Adversaries

Abilities

Operations

Agents

Objectives

Use automation carefully.

docs.title: CALDERA Model
docs.text:
Adversary Profile
       |
       v
Abilities
       |
       v
Operation
       |
       v
Agent
       |
       v
Endpoint
       |
       v
Telemetry

docs.title: Automation Safety
docs.text:
Automated emulation introduces risks such as:

Unexpected technique execution

Large numbers of commands

Scope expansion

Repeated actions

System changes

Cleanup complexity

Use:

Small test groups

Reviewed abilities

Explicit hosts

Controlled operations

Defined stop conditions

docs.title: Manual vs Automated Emulation
docs.text:
Manual execution provides:

Fine control

Immediate judgement

Easy stop decisions

Automation provides:

Repeatability

Scale

Regression testing

Consistent procedure execution

A mature programme can use both.

docs.title: Emulation Execution Modes
docs.text:
Possible modes include:

Blind

Semi-blind

Collaborative

Purple team

Detection engineering

docs.title: Blind Exercise
docs.text:
The defensive team is not informed of exact timing or procedures.

Useful for:

Operational detection

SOC response

Escalation

Incident handling

It provides less opportunity for immediate tuning.

docs.title: Purple Team Mode
docs.text:
Red and blue teams collaborate during execution.

Execute
   |
   v
Observe
   |
   v
Explain
   |
   v
Tune
   |
   v
Retest

Useful for rapidly improving detection coverage.

docs.title: Hybrid Model
docs.text:
A practical model is:

Phase 1
Blind Validation

Phase 2
Collaborative Review

Phase 3
Detection Tuning

Phase 4
Retest

docs.title: Deconfliction

Because adversary emulation resembles real attacker behaviour, establish a deconfliction process.

Suspicious Activity

       v
Security Team

Authorised Contact
       |
       v
Exercise or Real Attack?
       |
       +--> Exercise
       |

Never assume suspicious activity belongs to the exercise.

For production testing, translate this into safe security-control validation.

For example:

docs.text:
Every emulated technique should ideally have a detection hypothesis.

Example:

Technique:
Account Discovery

Hypothesis:

process or directory-service telemetry visible to the SOC.

Expected Sources:
Endpoint telemetry
Process creation
Directory-service telemetry

Expected Result:
Relevant activity is searchable and can be correlated with
other discovery behaviour.

docs.text: Technique Endpoint Identity Network SIEM Alert Account Discovery Yes Yes - Yes Partial Remote Services Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Collection Yes - - Yes No Exfiltration Yes - Yes Yes Yes

docs.text:
Keep results separate.

Prevented

means the action could not complete.

Detected

Possible outcomes include:

Prevented but Not Detected

Allowed and Detected

Allowed and Logged

Parsing Gap

docs.title: Telemetry Gap
docs.text: Required event was not generated.

docs.title: Collection Gap
docs.text: Event existed locally but was not forwarded.

docs.title: Parsing Gap
docs.text: Event reached the platform but important fields were not parsed.

docs.title: Detection Gap
docs.text:
Useful telemetry existed but no detection logic identified the
behaviour.

docs.title: Alerting Gap
docs.text: Detection logic matched but did not create an actionable alert.

docs.title: Response Gap
docs.text: An alert existed but the operational response was insufficient.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
Individual techniques may appear benign.

For example:

System Discovery

Network Discovery

Together:

User Discovery
      +
System Discovery
      +
Network Discovery
      +
Remote Connection

      v

docs.title: Sigma
docs.text:
Sigma provides a generic format for describing log-based detections.

A high-level example:

title: Example Discovery Behaviour
status: experimental

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows

detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\whoami.exe'
      - '\hostname.exe'
  condition: selection

This is only an illustrative detection example.

Production rules require environment-specific tuning.

docs.text:
A useful adversary emulation finding includes:

Title

Scenario

Threat relevance

Observation

docs.title: Example Finding - Discovery Visibility Gap
docs.text:
Title:
Internal Discovery Activity Is Logged but Not Correlated

Scenario:
Assumed-breach credential-focused intruder

ATT&CK:
Account Discovery
System Information Discovery
System Network Configuration Discovery

Observation:
The emulation executed several approved discovery procedures
from the synthetic compromised workstation.

Endpoint telemetry for the individual processes was available in
the SIEM.

No detection correlated the sequence of discovery activity, and
no SOC investigation was observed during the agreed validation
window.

Impact:
An attacker operating from a compromised workstation may be
able to perform internal situational awareness without
generating an actionable alert.

Recommendation:
Develop behavioural correlation for unusual sequences of
account, host and network discovery, particularly when observed
from non-administrative endpoints. Validate the detection using
the same controlled procedures.

docs.title: Example Finding - Segmentation Success
docs.text:
Title:
Network Segmentation Prevents Tested Lateral Movement Path

Scenario:
Assumed-breach employee workstation

ATT&CK:
Remote Services

Observation:
The assessment attempted the approved remote-service validation
from the compromised test workstation to the protected server
segment.

Network controls prevented the connection.

Firewall telemetry identified the source and destination and was
successfully ingested by the SIEM.

Conclusion:
The tested segmentation control successfully prevented the
emulated lateral movement path and provided useful defensive
telemetry.

docs.title: Example Finding - Detection Without Response
docs.text:
Title:
High-Fidelity Lateral Movement Alert Does Not Result in Timely Investigation

Observation:
The approved remote-service procedure generated the expected
high-severity SIEM alert.

The alert correctly identified the source host, user and target
server.

No analyst investigation was observed during the 45-minute
validation window.

Impact:
Effective detection logic may not reduce attacker dwell time if
alerts are not triaged and escalated promptly.

Recommendation:
Review alert routing, ownership, severity and SOC procedures.
Retest the attack path after operational changes.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text: The environment may lack detection for account discovery.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
The relevant endpoint telemetry is available but no corresponding
detection rule was identified.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
The approved account-discovery procedure was executed and
recorded in endpoint telemetry, but no alert was generated during
the agreed validation window.

docs.title: Accurate Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

The organisation cannot detect this threat actor.

A limited emulation cannot prove that.

Prefer:

The assessment tested six behaviours associated with the
selected threat scenario. Four generated the expected alerts,
one generated telemetry without an alert and one lacked useful
visibility.

docs.title: Attack Path Narrative
docs.text:
Example:

The exercise began from an assumed-breach workstation using a
customer-provided standard user account.

The emulation performed host and domain discovery before
validating access to an approved credential source.

The resulting synthetic credential permitted authentication to
a server in the application segment.

Network authentication telemetry was generated, and the SOC
detected the remote access before the final collection objective
was attempted.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Adversary emulation can be reduced to:

Start with threat relevance.

Define a business objective.

Prioritise behaviour over actor branding.

Map relevant behaviour to ATT&CK.

Do not treat ATT&CK as a checklist.

Document preconditions.

Choose the safest procedure that validates the behaviour.

Use synthetic identities and data where possible.

Execute only authorised techniques.

Measure prevention separately from detection.

Validate telemetry before blaming detection logic.

Measure SOC response.

Correlate the complete attack path.

Document positive security outcomes.

Stop when the objective is proven.

Clean up every system change.

Retest failed controls.

Convert valuable procedures into repeatable regression tests.

Emulate behaviour, not malware

A useful emulation does not require reproducing an adversary's exact malware. If a safe native or synthetic procedure generates the relevant behaviour and telemetry, it may provide a better and more repeatable detection test.

ATT&CK coverage is not automatically security coverage

Mapping a control or detection to an ATT&CK technique does not prove that the organisation can detect that behaviour. Distinguish techniques that are mapped, tested, observed, detected and successfully responded to.

docs.title: Red Team Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup is the controlled removal, reversal or handover of artifacts created during an authorised red team engagement.

A red team operation should not be considered complete when the final objective is reached.

It is complete when:

Testing Stops
     |
     v
Artifacts Identified
     |
     v
Changes Reversed
     |
     v
Access Removed
     |
     v
Infrastructure Decommissioned
     |
     v
Credentials Revoked
     |
     v
Cleanup Verified
     |
     v
Exceptions Documented
     |
     v
Customer Handover

Cleanup should be planned before testing begins rather than reconstructed from memory at the end of the engagement.

Do not remove evidence of a real incident

If activity discovered during cleanup may belong to an actual attacker rather than the authorised assessment, stop and follow the engagement's deconfliction and incident-response procedures. Do not delete unknown artifacts merely because they resemble red team activity.

docs.title: Cleanup Objectives
docs.text:
Cleanup should ensure that:

Temporary files are removed

Test accounts are removed or disabled

Temporary privileges are revoked

Persistence is removed

Credentials are revoked or rotated

Sessions and tokens are invalidated

Temporary routes and tunnels are removed

C2 infrastructure is disabled

Cloud resources are removed

Phishing infrastructure is retired

Test data is removed

Customer configuration is restored

Residual access is eliminated

Exceptions are documented

Cleanup is independently verified

docs.title: Cleanup Is Part of the Engagement
docs.text:
The operational lifecycle should be:

Plan
  |
  v
Deploy
  |
  v
Test
  |
  v
Track Changes
  |
  v
Achieve Objective
  |
  v
Cleanup
  |
  v
Verify
  |
  v
Report

Not:

Test
  |
  v
Finish
  |
  v
Try to Remember What Changed

docs.title: Plan Cleanup Before Execution
docs.text:
Before creating an artifact, know:

What will be created?

Where will it exist?

Who owns it?

How will it be removed?

How will removal be verified?

A useful rule is:

No deployment without a cleanup plan.

docs.text:

Example:

docs.title: Cleanup Order
docs.text:
A practical cleanup order is:

1. Stop active testing

2. Stop active sessions

3. Remove persistence

4. Remove temporary privileges

5. Remove temporary accounts

6. Remove host artifacts

7. Remove tunnels and routes

8. Revoke credentials and tokens

9. Disable C2

10. Remove cloud resources

11. Retire phishing infrastructure

12. Remove synthetic test data

13. Verify systems

14. Document exceptions

15. Decommission operator infrastructure

docs.title: Stop Active Operations
docs.text:
Before cleanup begins:

Stop new tasking

Stop new payload deployment

Stop new phishing messages

Stop automated emulation

Stop scheduled testing

Stop active scanning

Otherwise new artifacts may appear while cleanup is being performed.

docs.text:
At cleanup start:

Active Inventory

docs.text:
Host cleanup may involve:

docs.title: Windows Artifact Review
docs.text:
Review engagement-created artifacts such as:

Files

Directories

Services

Scheduled tasks

Registry values

Startup entries

PowerShell profiles

Temporary users

Group memberships

Certificates

Firewall rules

Environment variables

Test scripts

docs.title: Windows Files
docs.text:
Maintain the exact paths of files deployed during testing.

Example inventory:

C:\Windows\Temp\rt-test.txt

C:\ProgramData\RedTeam\marker.txt

C:\Temp\test.dll

Remove only files confirmed to belong to the engagement.

docs.title: Verify Before Deleting
docs.text:
Before removing a file:

Get-Item -LiteralPath 'C:\Windows\Temp\rt-test.txt' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If the file is part of the engagement and cleanup is authorised:

Remove-Item -LiteralPath 'C:\Windows\Temp\rt-test.txt' -Force

Verify:

Test-Path -LiteralPath 'C:\Windows\Temp\rt-test.txt'

Expected:

False

docs.title: Hash Before Cleanup
docs.text:
For important artifacts, retain a hash in the evidence inventory before deletion.

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath 'C:\Windows\Temp\rt-test.txt'

This allows the report to identify the artifact without retaining it on the customer system.

docs.title: Windows Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Review only tasks associated with the engagement.

Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object TaskName,TaskPath,State

For a known test task:

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'RT-Test-01' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Remove the known test task:

Unregister-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'RT-Test-01' -Confirm:$false

Verify:

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'RT-Test-01' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Windows Services
docs.text:
Review known engagement-created services.

Get-Service | Sort-Object Name

For a known test service:

Get-Service -Name 'RTTestService' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If the engagement created the service, remove it using the documented cleanup procedure and verify that it no longer exists.

Do not delete an unfamiliar service simply because its name looks suspicious.

docs.title: Windows Registry
docs.text:
Record exact keys and values changed during testing.

Example inspection:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'

Cleanup should restore the original state rather than blindly deleting entire keys.

docs.title: Registry Cleanup Model
docs.text:
Original:
Value absent

Test:
Value created

Cleanup:
Remove test value

or:

Original:
Value = A

Test:
Value = B

Cleanup:
Restore A

The distinction matters.

docs.title: Windows Accounts
docs.text:
Review accounts created specifically for testing.

Get-LocalUser

For domain environments, use approved administrative tooling to identify the exact test identity.

Do not remove accounts based only on naming assumptions.

docs.title: Group Membership
docs.text:
If temporary membership was added:

Original:
Test user not member

Test:
Test user added to group

Cleanup:
Remove test user

Verify:
Membership matches original state

docs.title: Windows Firewall
docs.text:
If temporary firewall rules were created, record their exact names.

Inspect:

Get-NetFirewallRule | Select-Object DisplayName,Enabled,Direction,Action

Remove only engagement-created rules using their recorded identifiers.

docs.text:

Authentication certificates

Thumbprint

Store

before deployment.

Temporary output

Downloaded tools

docs.text:
Cleanup does not mean destroying telemetry.

These may be required for detection validation, incident response or evidence.

docs.text:

ls -la /tmp/rt-test.txt

rm -- /tmp/rt-test.txt

test ! -e /tmp/rt-test.txt && echo "removed"

docs.text:
If testing changed sudo configuration, validate syntax before and after restoration.

Do not remove unrelated entries.

docs.text:
Review only keys added during the engagement.

Common location:

Before editing:

cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Do not replace the entire file.

docs.title: SSH Key Fingerprints
docs.text:
Record the fingerprint of a test public key.

ssh-keygen -lf redteam_test.pub

This helps distinguish the engagement key from legitimate keys.

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Review:

crontab -l

and, where authorised:

ls -la /etc/cron.d/
ls -la /etc/cron.daily/
ls -la /etc/cron.hourly/

Remove only engagement-created jobs.

docs.text:

systemctl list-unit-files --type=service

If a temporary unit was created, restore the system according to the documented cleanup procedure.

Verify that:

Reload completed

Associated files removed

docs.text:
Review engagement changes to:

/etc/profile

Restore only the exact modifications made during testing.

docs.title: Linux Firewall
docs.text:
Depending on the system, review:

sudo nft list ruleset

or:

sudo ufw status numbered

docs.text:

If temporary permissions were created, verify:

Role

ClusterRole

RoleBinding

ClusterRoleBinding

ServiceAccount

and restore the original RBAC state.

docs.title: Phishing Cleanup
docs.text:
Phishing campaigns may leave:

Domains

Mailboxes

Mail server configuration

DNS

Landing pages

Campaign databases

Target lists

Tracking identifiers

Test accounts

OAuth applications

TLS certificates

docs.title: Stop Campaign Delivery
docs.text:
Before cleanup:

Stop scheduled messages

Stop campaign automation

Disable landing-page submissions

Stop tracking where appropriate

docs.title: Landing Pages
docs.text:
Disable test forms before deleting campaign data.

A temporary page may display:

Campaign Closed

until infrastructure is fully retired.

docs.title: Phishing Credentials
docs.text:
If synthetic credentials were used:

Disable or remove test account

Rotate retained test account password

Revoke sessions

Remove stored test values

docs.title: Unexpected Real Credentials
docs.text:
If real credentials were unexpectedly submitted:

Stop collection

Notify authorised customer contact

Rotate affected credential

Revoke relevant sessions

Remove retained sensitive value

Document the event

docs.title: OAuth Applications
docs.text:
For test OAuth applications:

Revoke consent

Revoke tokens

Remove secrets

Remove certificates

Delete application where appropriate

Verify audit trail

docs.title: Target Lists
docs.text:
Target lists may contain personal information.

Apply the agreed:

Retention period

Access control

Encryption

Deletion procedure

docs.title: Social Engineering Cleanup
docs.text:
Review:

Synthetic identities

Test phone numbers

Test mailboxes

Visitor badges

USB devices

QR codes

Printed materials

Test documents

docs.title: Physical Artifacts
docs.text:
Recover:

USB devices

Badges

Printed pretexts

Test access cards

Temporary equipment

where applicable.

docs.title: Collection Cleanup
docs.text:
Collection testing should normally use synthetic data.

Review:

Staging directories

Archives

Temporary copies

Screenshots

Exports

Database extracts

docs.title: Synthetic Data
docs.text: Delete temporary synthetic datasets from customer systems when they are no longer required.

docs.title: Production Data
docs.text:
If production data was accessed during the engagement, do not automatically delete the source data.

Only remove:

Red team copies

Temporary exports

Temporary archives

created by the engagement.

docs.title: Exfiltration Cleanup
docs.text:
Review:

Destination storage

Transferred synthetic files

Temporary archives

Cloud buckets

Upload endpoints

Transfer logs

docs.title: Exfiltration Destination
docs.text:
After evidence requirements are satisfied:

Disable upload endpoint

Remove synthetic data

Remove temporary credentials

Remove temporary storage

Retain only approved evidence

docs.title: Persistence Cleanup
docs.text:
Persistence deserves a dedicated review because forgotten persistence can create continuing access.

Review:

Scheduled tasks

Services

Registry autoruns

Startup folders

PowerShell profiles

WMI subscriptions

Cron

systemd

SSH keys

Accounts

Group memberships

AD ACLs

Certificates

Cloud identities

OAuth applications

See:

Persistence

docs.title: Persistence Verification
docs.text:
Do not rely solely on:

I removed the one mechanism I remember.

Compare against the persistence inventory maintained during testing.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Cleanup
docs.text:
Review changes involving:

Group membership

sudo configuration

File permissions

Service configuration

ACLs

Tokens

Temporary privileges

Cloud roles

AD rights

See:

Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Temporary Administrative Access
docs.text:
If a test identity received administrative access:

Remove privilege

Verify membership

Revoke sessions where necessary

Retest access

docs.title: Credential Access Cleanup
docs.text:
Credential-access testing may produce sensitive artifacts.

Review:

Credential files

Hashes

Tickets

Tokens

Certificates

SSH keys

API keys

Tool output

Screenshots

See:

Credential Access

docs.title: Sensitive Tool Output
docs.text:
Tools may produce output files containing:

Credentials

Hashes

Hostnames

Usernames

Tokens

Directory data

Protect and remove them according to the engagement's evidence-retention policy.

docs.title: Kerberos Artifacts
docs.text:
If test tickets or credential caches were created on operator systems, remove them when no longer required.

If account secrets were exposed, follow the agreed credential rotation procedure.

docs.title: Browser Sessions
docs.text:
If testing used dedicated browser profiles:

Sign out

Revoke test sessions

Remove test profile

Remove cookies

Remove downloaded artifacts

Do not retain customer sessions for convenience after the engagement.

docs.title: VPN Access
docs.text:
Review engagement VPN access.

Test account

Certificate

VPN profile

MFA registration

Device registration

Remove or hand over according to the agreed lifecycle.

docs.title: Remote Access
docs.text:
Review:

RDP access

WinRM access

SSH access

VPN access

Jump-host access

Cloud console access

Temporary access should not remain simply because it may be useful for future retesting.

docs.title: Tool Cleanup
docs.text:
Tools copied to customer systems should be inventoried.

Examples:

Enumeration tools

Network utilities

Test scripts

Framework agents

Portable binaries

Configuration files

Remove engagement copies unless the customer requests otherwise.

docs.title: Tool Hashes
docs.text:
Maintain SHA-256 hashes for deployed tooling.

This assists:

Cleanup

SOC deconfliction

Threat hunting

Reporting

docs.title: Temporary Web Servers
docs.text:
If temporary web servers were used:

Stop server

Verify port closed

Remove hosted files

Remove firewall rule

Remove service if created

docs.title: Listener Verification
docs.text:
Linux:

ss -lntup

Windows:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

Compare against the engagement listener inventory.

docs.title: Network Cleanup
docs.text:
Review:

Routes

Firewall rules

Port forwards

Proxy settings

DNS changes

VPN configuration

Temporary listeners

docs.title: Proxy Settings
docs.text:
If system proxy settings were changed, restore the original values.

Do not assume that "no proxy" was the original configuration.

docs.title: DNS Changes
docs.text:
If local DNS configuration was modified:

Hosts file

Resolver configuration

DNS server

Search suffix

restore the recorded original state.

docs.title: Hosts Files
docs.text:
Common locations:

Windows:

C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts

Linux:

/etc/hosts

Remove only engagement-created entries.

docs.title: Evidence Is Not the Same as an Artifact
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Customer-System Artifact

from:

Red-Team Evidence

For example:

C:\Temp\rt-test.txt

may need removal.

A screenshot proving it existed may need retention.

docs.title: Evidence Retention
docs.text:
Retain only what is required by:

Statement of Work

Rules of Engagement

Customer policy

Legal requirements

Reporting requirements

docs.title: Evidence Classification
docs.text:
Classify evidence such as:

Public

Internal

Confidential

Restricted

according to the engagement's data-handling requirements.

docs.title: Evidence Storage
docs.text:
Protect evidence using:

Encryption

Access control

Dedicated storage

Backup policy

Retention schedule

docs.title: Evidence Minimisation
docs.text:
Avoid retaining unnecessary:

Passwords

Tokens

Private keys

Personal data

Large production datasets

Complete mailbox contents

docs.title: Evidence Sanitisation
docs.text:
Reports may use:

Redacted screenshots

Partial usernames

Masked tokens

Synthetic data

Hashes

instead of raw sensitive material.

docs.title: Retention Schedule
docs.text:
Example:

Data Retention Action Final report Contract defined Retain Screenshots Contract defined Retain/delete Raw tool output Short term Delete Production credentials None Rotate/delete Synthetic data Engagement only Delete

docs.title: Do Not Delete Defensive Telemetry
docs.text:
Red team cleanup should preserve evidence useful to defenders.

Do not delete:

SIEM events

EDR events

Firewall logs

Authentication logs

Cloud audit logs

Email security events

SOC tickets

unless the customer explicitly owns a separate retention decision.

docs.title: Detection Validation During Cleanup
docs.text:
Cleanup itself may generate useful telemetry.

Examples:

Account deletion

Privilege removal

Task deletion

Service removal

Token revocation

Cloud resource deletion

Defenders may use this to validate administrative monitoring.

docs.title: Cleanup Verification
docs.text:
Cleanup should be verified rather than assumed.

Cleanup Action
      |
      v
Artifact Query
      |
      v
Still Present?
   /        \
 Yes         No
 |            |
 v            v
Retry      Mark Verified

docs.title: Independent Verification
docs.text:
For high-risk artifacts, consider:

Operator A removes artifact

Operator B verifies removal

This reduces errors.

docs.title: Verification Methods
docs.text:
Use:

File existence check

Account query

Group membership query

Service query

Task query

Port scan

Route table review

Cloud inventory

DNS query

Authentication test

Token validation

docs.title: Authentication Verification
docs.text:
For a revoked test credential:

Credential Revoked
      |
      v
Controlled Authentication Test
      |
      v
Authentication Fails
      |
      v
Verified

Avoid repeated authentication attempts that could trigger lockouts.

docs.title: Network Verification
docs.text:
Confirm temporary services are no longer exposed.

Examples:

ss -lntup

and, from an authorised validation host:

nmap -sT -Pn -p 443,8000,8080 <approved-test-host>

Use only against approved engagement infrastructure or in-scope hosts.

docs.title: DNS Verification
docs.text:
Use:

dig example.test

or:

nslookup example.test

to confirm retired records behave as expected.

docs.title: Cloud Verification
docs.text:
After cleanup, review the engagement tag or naming convention.

The desired result is:

No unexpected temporary resources remain.

docs.title: Residual Artifact Hunt
docs.text:
Perform a final search using known engagement identifiers.

Examples:

Campaign ID

Test username

Payload filename

Tool hash

Domain

Service name

Task name

Directory name

This is more reliable than relying on memory.

docs.title: Engagement Naming Convention
docs.text:
Consistent names make cleanup easier.

Example:

RT-2026-04

RT-Test-User

RT-Test-Task

rt-2026-04-vm

Do not use predictable red team naming when it would invalidate an explicitly authorised detection objective, but still maintain an internal artifact inventory.

docs.title: Threat Hunting After Cleanup
docs.text:
Provide defenders with relevant engagement indicators where agreed.

Examples:

Domains

IPs

File hashes

Account names

Process names

Tool hashes

Certificate fingerprints

This allows the blue team to verify whether residual activity remains.

docs.title: Indicator Handover
docs.text:
Example:

Type Value Purpose Domain test.example C2 SHA-256 <hash> Test binary Account RT-Test-01 Synthetic identity IP 192.0.2.10 Test infrastructure

docs.title: False Attribution Risk
docs.text:
After the engagement, defenders may later encounter a historical artifact.

Without documentation, they may interpret it as a real compromise.

Maintain sufficient records to answer:

Was this ours?

When was it deployed?

Where?

Why?

Was it removed?

docs.title: Unexpected Artifacts
docs.text:
During cleanup, you may find an artifact that was not created by the red team.

Examples:

Unknown account

Unknown scheduled task

Unknown SSH key

Unknown service

Unknown web shell

Unknown cloud identity

Do not remove it automatically.

docs.title: Unexpected Artifact Decision Model
docs.text:
Unknown Artifact
      |
      v
Created by Red Team?
   /          \
 Yes           Unknown / No
 |                |
 v                v
Cleanup       Preserve Evidence
                  |
                  v
              Notify Contact
                  |
                  v
             Incident Process

docs.title: Real Compromise
docs.text:
If cleanup reveals indicators of a real compromise:

Stop normal cleanup where necessary

Preserve evidence

Notify authorised contacts

Separate red team activity from unknown activity

Support deconfliction

Follow incident-response procedures

docs.title: Do Not Contaminate Evidence
docs.text:
Avoid modifying unknown artifacts merely to investigate them.

The incident-response team may need:

Timestamps

Metadata

Logs

File hashes

Memory state

Cloud audit history

docs.title: Customer-Owned Artifacts
docs.text:
Some artifacts may intentionally remain.

Examples:

Detection rules

Synthetic test accounts

Dedicated lab systems

Test certificates

Automation

Purple team infrastructure

Mark these:

Customer Owned

rather than "not cleaned."

docs.title: Handover
docs.text:
If an artifact remains, document:

Artifact

Location

Owner

Reason retained

Credentials

Security considerations

Expiration

Required future action

docs.title: Cleanup Exceptions
docs.text:
Not every artifact can always be removed immediately.

Examples:

Customer requests retention

System unavailable

Change freeze

Production risk

Third-party dependency

Evidence preservation requirement

docs.title: Exception Record
docs.text:
Example:

Artifact:
RT-Test-Account

Location:
Active Directory

Status:
Retained by Agreement

Reason:
Customer detection engineering team requires account for
retesting.

Owner:
Security Engineering

Expiration:
2026-10-01

Required Action:
Disable and remove after validation programme.

docs.title: Cleanup Failure
docs.text:
If cleanup fails:

Do not silently mark complete.

Record:

What remains

Why it remains

Risk

Owner

Required action

Deadline

docs.title: High-Risk Residuals
docs.text:
Prioritise residual artifacts that provide continuing access.

Examples:

Privileged accounts

SSH keys

API keys

Cloud roles

OAuth applications

Certificates

C2 agents

Persistence

Open firewall rules

Exposed listeners

docs.title: Residual Risk
docs.text:
A cleanup exception should have a risk assessment.

Example:

Residual:
Temporary cloud API key remains active.

Risk:
Key retains read access to test subscription.

Immediate Action:
Customer cloud administrator to revoke key.

Compensating Control:
Associated identity disabled.

Status:
Open.

docs.title: Operator Infrastructure
docs.text:
After customer cleanup, decommission engagement infrastructure.

Review:

VPS instances

Team servers

Redirectors

Domains

DNS

Object storage

VPN servers

Mail servers

Landing pages

Databases

Backups

docs.title: VPS Decommissioning
docs.text:
Before deleting a VPS:

Export required logs

Remove customer data

Remove credentials

Remove private keys

Remove payloads

Verify no dependency remains

Destroy instance

docs.title: Cloud Provider Review
docs.text:
After deleting the instance, check for:

Detached disks

Snapshots

Public IPs

Security groups

Backups

Images

Load balancers

DNS records

Deleting a VM alone may not remove all resources.

docs.title: Operator Workstations
docs.text:
Review:

Downloads

Payload builds

Target lists

Credentials

Screenshots

Browser profiles

SSH keys

VPN profiles

Terminal logs

Clipboard managers

Temporary directories

docs.title: Engagement Workspace
docs.text:
A typical workspace might contain:

engagement/
├── evidence/
├── infrastructure/
├── logs/
├── payloads/
├── reports/
├── screenshots/
└── targets/

Apply retention requirements separately to each category.

docs.title: Build Artifacts
docs.text:
Payload development may leave:

Source

Compiled binaries

Debug builds

Symbols

Temporary files

Configuration

Secrets

Remove unnecessary build artifacts after evidence requirements are satisfied.

docs.title: Git Repositories
docs.text:
Review:

git status
git diff

Ensure customer secrets were not accidentally committed.

docs.title: Secret Scanning
docs.text:
Where appropriate, review engagement repositories for:

Passwords

Tokens

API keys

Private keys

Certificates

Connection strings

If a secret was committed, deleting the current file may not remove it from Git history.

Rotate exposed secrets.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Check whether sensitive engagement data exists in:

Cloud backups

VM snapshots

Filesystem backups

Sync folders

External drives

Deletion from the primary workspace may not remove backups.

docs.title: Browser Cleanup
docs.text:
Dedicated engagement browser profiles should be reviewed for:

Cookies

Sessions

Downloads

Saved passwords

Client certificates

Cached documents

Revoke server-side sessions before deleting local browser data.

docs.title: Password Managers
docs.text:
Temporary credentials stored in an engagement vault should be:

Removed

Archived only if required

Rotated where necessary

Do not retain production credentials merely for future convenience.

docs.title: Communication Platforms
docs.text:
Review sensitive material in:

Email

Teams

Slack

Ticketing systems

Shared documents

Follow the agreed retention policy rather than deleting organisational records without approval.

docs.title: Cleanup Evidence
docs.text:
Cleanup itself should produce evidence.

Examples:

Before state

Cleanup action

After state

Verification result

Timestamp

Operator

docs.title: Cleanup Evidence Example
docs.text:
Artifact:
RT-Test-Task

Host:
WS01

Before:
Scheduled task present

Action:
Task removed

After:
Task query returned no matching task

Verified:
Yes

Operator:
A

Time:
2026-09-05 16:22 UTC

docs.title: Screenshot Strategy
docs.text:
Screenshots can show:

Artifact before removal

Cleanup command

Verification result

But avoid generating excessive screenshots for low-risk artifacts.

docs.title: Cleanup Report
docs.text:
A cleanup appendix may include:

Artifact Type Created Removed Verified Exceptions Files 14 14 14 0 Accounts 3 2 2 1 Tasks 2 2 2 0 Cloud Resources 5 5 5 0 C2 Agents 4 4 4 0

docs.title: Cleanup Statement
docs.text:
Example:

All red team artifacts recorded in the engagement inventory were
reviewed during cleanup.

Temporary payloads, scheduled tasks, routes, C2 sessions and
cloud resources were removed and their removal was verified.

One synthetic Active Directory account was retained at the
customer's request for subsequent detection-engineering
validation. Ownership and expiration are documented in the
cleanup exceptions register.

docs.title: Avoid Absolute Claims
docs.text:
Avoid:

There are absolutely no red team artifacts anywhere.

Prefer:

All artifacts recorded in the engagement inventory were
reviewed and either removed, verified or documented as approved
exceptions.

This is more defensible.

docs.title: Cleanup Metrics
docs.text:
Useful metrics include:

Artifacts created

Artifacts removed

Artifacts verified

Exceptions

High-risk residuals

Time to cleanup

Cleanup failures

docs.title: Cleanup Completion Rate
docs.text:
Verified Removed Artifacts
--------------------------  * 100
Artifacts Requiring Removal

docs.title: Exception Rate
docs.text:
Approved Exceptions
-------------------  * 100
Tracked Artifacts

docs.title: High-Risk Residual Count
docs.text:
Track separately:

Privileged accounts

Credentials

Persistence

Cloud access

C2 access

Network exposure

The desired final value is normally:

0

unless explicitly retained by agreement.

docs.title: Cleanup Retest
docs.text:
After cleanup, test whether engagement access still works.

Examples:

Test account authentication fails

SSH key authentication fails

API key rejected

C2 callback absent

Temporary port closed

Route removed

Landing page disabled

Use minimal verification.

docs.title: Do Not Recreate the Artifact During Verification
docs.text:
For example:

Remove persistence
      |
      v
Verify persistence absent

not:

Remove persistence
      |
      v
Recreate persistence to test cleanup

docs.title: Cleanup and Detection Validation
docs.text:
Cleanup can also test whether defenders observe:

Account deletion

Privilege removal

Service deletion

Task removal

Cloud resource deletion

However, cleanup quality takes priority over creating additional detection scenarios.

docs.title: Cleanup and OPSEC
docs.text:
Cleanup reduces exposure of:

Customer data

Red team infrastructure

Credentials

Payloads

Evidence

Target information

See:

Red Team OPSEC

docs.title: Cleanup and Reporting
docs.text:
The final report should state:

Cleanup completed

Cleanup date

Scope of cleanup

Verification performed

Exceptions

Residual risk

Customer-owned artifacts

See:

Red Team Reporting

docs.title: Cleanup and Persistence
docs.text:
Persistence should receive dedicated cleanup verification.

See:

Persistence

docs.title: Cleanup and C2
docs.text:
C2 cleanup should include both:

Customer endpoint artifacts

Operator infrastructure

See:

Command and Control

docs.title: Cleanup and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Review:

Routes

Tunnels

Temporary remote access

Pivot agents

Proxy configuration

See:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Cleanup and Phishing
docs.text:
Review:

Mail infrastructure

Landing pages

Target lists

Synthetic accounts

OAuth applications

Campaign databases

See:

Phishing

docs.title: Cleanup and Adversary Emulation
docs.text:
Automated emulation platforms may leave artifacts across multiple hosts.

Use the operation log as an additional cleanup source.

See:

Adversary Emulation

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Red team cleanup can be reduced to:

Plan cleanup before deployment.

Track every meaningful change.

Record the original state.

Assign every artifact an owner.

Stop active operations before cleanup.

Remove only confirmed engagement artifacts.

Restore configuration instead of blindly deleting it.

Remove persistence.

Remove temporary privileges.

Remove temporary accounts.

Revoke credentials and tokens.

Terminate sessions.

Remove tunnels and routes.

Remove payloads and tools.

Decommission C2 infrastructure.

Review cloud residuals.

Retire phishing infrastructure.

Remove unnecessary customer data.

Preserve defensive telemetry.

Do not clear logs.

Do not delete unknown artifacts.

Escalate possible real compromise.

Verify every high-risk cleanup action.

Document customer-owned artifacts.

Document every exception.

Retain only required evidence.

Verify residual access is gone.

Close the engagement only after cleanup is verified.
