docs.title: Scheduled Task Persistence Assessment
docs.text:
A persistence path can be represented as:

Trigger
   |
   v
Scheduled Task
   |
   v
Configured Action
   |
   v
Assessment Component

Important questions include:

Who can create the task?
Who can modify it?
Which identity executes it?
Does it survive reboot?
Is task creation monitored?
Is the action protected from modification?

docs.title: Safe Scheduled Task Validation
docs.text:
Where task creation is explicitly authorised, prefer a harmless proof such as writing a marker file rather than launching a remote-access component.

Example PowerShell:

$action = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'cmd.exe' -Argument '/c echo PersistenceTest > C:\Windows\Temp\persistence-test.txt'
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Once -At (Get-Date).AddMinutes(2)
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Assessment-Persistence-Test' -Action $action -Trigger $trigger -Description 'Authorised security assessment persistence validation'

Verify:

Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Assessment-Persistence-Test'

After the test:

Unregister-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Assessment-Persistence-Test' -Confirm:$false

Remove the marker:

Remove-Item 'C:\Windows\Temp\persistence-test.txt' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: Windows Services
docs.text:
Services can provide persistence because they can start:

Automatically at boot
On demand
Through service dependencies
Through administrative action

Enumerate:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, State, StartMode, PathName

Services should be assessed together with:

Service permissions
Executable permissions
Directory permissions
Service identity
Startup mode
Configuration protection

docs.title: Service Persistence Model
docs.text:
System Boot
    |
    v
Service Control Manager
    |
    v
Service
    |
    v
Configured Executable

A service running as LocalSystem represents a particularly sensitive persistence location.

docs.title: Service Creation
docs.text:
Service creation is a significant system modification.

Where explicitly authorised, a benign test service can validate whether the current security context can create a persistent service without deploying an operational payload.

Example:

sc.exe create AssessmentPersistenceTest binPath= "C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /c exit 0" start= demand

Inspect:

sc.exe qc AssessmentPersistenceTest

Remove:

sc.exe delete AssessmentPersistenceTest

Use unique assessment names to make cleanup and detection correlation easier.

docs.title: Registry Run Keys
docs.text:
Windows supports programs that run when users log on.

Common locations include:

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

Enumerate:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'

System-wide:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'

The current-user location generally affects that user, while machine-level locations can have broader impact depending on configuration.

docs.title: Run Key Validation
docs.text:
Where modification is authorised, a harmless marker command can demonstrate persistence.

Example current-user test:

New-ItemProperty -Path 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' -Name 'AssessmentPersistenceTest' -Value 'cmd.exe /c echo PersistenceTest > %TEMP%\persistence-test.txt' -PropertyType String

Verify:

Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'

Cleanup:

Remove-ItemProperty -Path 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' -Name 'AssessmentPersistenceTest'

docs.title: Startup Folder
docs.text:
Windows also supports startup folders.

Current-user startup folder:

[Environment]::GetFolderPath('Startup')

Common startup folder:

[Environment]::GetFolderPath('CommonStartup')

Assess:

Who can write to the directory?
Which users are affected?
What files already exist?
Are changes monitored?

docs.title: Startup Folder Model
docs.text:
User Logon
    |
    v
Startup Folder
    |
    v
Configured File
    |
    v
Execution

Writable startup locations can become persistence opportunities when an attacker has sufficient access.

docs.title: User Accounts
docs.text:
Account creation can provide persistent access.

Review local users:

Get-LocalUser

Review local groups:

Get-LocalGroup

Administrators:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'

Account creation should only be tested when explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Test Accounts
docs.text:
If a temporary assessment account is approved:

Use a recognisable name
Use a unique strong password
Record creation time
Record group membership
Do not reuse the password
Remove the account after testing
Verify removal

Prefer customer-provided test identities where possible.

docs.title: Local Group Persistence
docs.text:
An existing account may gain persistent administrative access through group membership.

Conceptually:

User
  |
  v
Local Administrators
  |
  v
Persistent Administrative Access

Monitor changes to sensitive groups such as:

Administrators
Remote Desktop Users
Remote Management Users
Backup Operators

docs.title: PowerShell Profiles
docs.text:
PowerShell profiles can execute PowerShell content when certain PowerShell hosts start.

List profile paths:

$PROFILE | Format-List *

Current profile:

$PROFILE

Check whether it exists:

Test-Path $PROFILE

PowerShell profiles are legitimate customisation mechanisms but can also become persistence locations if writable by an inappropriate user.

docs.title: PowerShell Profile Assessment
docs.text:
Review:

Profile path
Owner
ACL
Affected user
Affected PowerShell host
Existing content
Application-control policy
PowerShell language mode

Do not overwrite an existing profile during testing.

docs.title: WMI Event Subscription
docs.text:
WMI supports permanent event subscriptions that can react to system events.

The conceptual structure is:

Event Filter
     |
     v
Consumer
     |
     v
Binding

Permanent WMI subscriptions are sensitive because they can survive reboots.

Assessment should normally focus on whether such persistence is detectable and whether inappropriate identities can create it.

docs.title: WMI Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Useful defensive areas include:

WMI-Activity logs
WMI repository changes
Process creation
PowerShell telemetry
EDR telemetry
Unusual permanent event consumers

docs.title: Logon Scripts
docs.text:
Windows and Active Directory can execute scripts during user logon.

Potential locations include:

Local policy
Group Policy
Domain logon scripts
SYSVOL
Application-specific login processes

Changes to domain-managed logon scripts can affect many users and should not be performed unless specifically approved.

docs.title: Application Persistence
docs.text:
Applications may provide their own startup or extension mechanisms.

Examples include:

Plugins
Modules
Startup scripts
Scheduled jobs
Hooks
Extensions
Application services
Administrative automation

An application-specific persistence path should be assessed against the application's intended security model.

docs.title: Linux Persistence
docs.text:
Common Linux persistence mechanisms include:

Cron
systemd
Shell startup files
SSH authorized_keys
User accounts
Sudo configuration
Application startup
Init scripts
Timers
Container configuration

docs.title: Linux Persistence Model
docs.text:
Linux Persistence
      |
      +--> Cron
      |
      +--> systemd
      |
      +--> SSH
      |
      +--> Shell Startup
      |
      +--> Accounts
      |
      +--> Sudo
      |
      +--> Applications
      |
      +--> Containers

docs.title: Cron
docs.text:
Cron executes commands on schedules.

Review system crontab:

cat /etc/crontab

List cron directories:

ls -la /etc/cron.d/

ls -la /etc/cron.daily/

Current user:

crontab -l

Cron persistence depends on:

Who owns the cron entry?
Which identity executes it?
Which command is executed?
Can the command or script be modified?

docs.title: Cron Persistence Model
docs.text:
Cron Scheduler
      |
      v
Cron Entry
      |
      v
Script / Command
      |
      v
Execution

A privileged cron entry that references a writable script is also a privilege escalation concern.

docs.title: Safe Cron Validation
docs.text:
For a dedicated authorised test account, a harmless marker can validate persistence.

Example user crontab entry:

*/5 * * * * /usr/bin/touch /tmp/assessment-persistence-test

After validation, remove the entry and marker.

Do not modify production cron jobs merely to prove persistence.

docs.title: systemd
docs.text:
systemd manages services on many Linux distributions.

List services:

systemctl list-unit-files --type=service

Inspect a specific unit:

systemctl cat SERVICE

Review:

Unit path
ExecStart
User
Group
EnvironmentFile
Restart policy
Enablement
File permissions

docs.title: systemd Persistence Model
docs.text:
Boot
 |
 v
systemd
 |
 v
Unit
 |
 v
ExecStart
 |
 v
Application

A service enabled at boot can provide persistent execution.

docs.title: systemd Timers
docs.text:
systemd timers provide scheduled execution similar to cron.

List:

systemctl list-timers --all

Conceptually:

Timer
  |
  v
Service Unit
  |
  v
Command

Review timers together with the service units they trigger.

docs.title: Shell Startup Files
docs.text:
Shells can execute user configuration during login or interactive startup.

Examples include:

~/.bashrc
~/.bash_profile
~/.profile
~/.zshrc

These are normally user-level persistence locations.

Review:

ls -la ~

Inspect only files relevant to the authorised identity.

docs.title: Shell Startup Persistence Model
docs.text:
User Starts Shell
      |
      v
Startup File
      |
      v
Configured Command

The exact startup files depend on the shell and invocation mode.

docs.title: SSH authorized_keys
docs.text:
SSH public-key authentication commonly uses:

~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Review:

ls -la ~/.ssh/

Where authorised:

cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Adding a public key can provide persistent SSH access to that identity.

This is a significant account modification and should only be performed where explicitly permitted.

docs.title: SSH Key Persistence Model
docs.text:
Operator Public Key
       |
       v
authorized_keys
       |
       v
SSH Authentication
       |
       v
User Account

The private key remains with the operator.

Only the public key should be added to the authorised account.

docs.title: SSH authorized_keys Options
docs.text:
Entries can include restrictions such as:

from=
command=
no-agent-forwarding
no-port-forwarding
no-pty

Restricting keys can reduce the impact of specialised automation or service keys.

docs.title: SSH Persistence Cleanup
docs.text:
If an assessment key is added:

Record exact public key
Record file before modification
Add only one unique line
Validate access
Remove exact line
Verify file
Verify permissions

Do not replace the complete authorized_keys file.

docs.title: Linux User Accounts
docs.text:
Review:

cat /etc/passwd

Current identity:

id

Privileged group membership:

getent group sudo

or on some distributions:

getent group wheel

Account creation or privilege modification should only occur when specifically authorised.

docs.title: Sudo Persistence
docs.text:
Changes to sudo configuration can create long-lived privileged access.

Relevant locations include:

/etc/sudoers
/etc/sudoers.d/

Review safely:

sudo -l

Do not modify production sudo policy merely to demonstrate that a privileged user could modify it.

docs.title: Sudoers Safety
docs.text:
When legitimate sudo configuration must be changed, administrators should use:

visudo

For assessment purposes, prefer configuration review and permission validation rather than changing security-critical policy.

docs.title: Application Persistence on Linux
docs.text:
Applications may provide:

Plugins
Modules
Startup hooks
Worker services
Scheduled jobs
Configuration callbacks
Custom scripts

Assess whether lower-privilege users can modify components executed by more privileged application identities.

docs.title: Container Persistence
docs.text:
Containers introduce additional persistence considerations.

Examples include:

Restart policies
Mounted host directories
Container images
Orchestrator configuration
Startup commands
Volumes
Secrets
Kubernetes workloads

Persistence at the container layer may disappear when the container is replaced.

Persistence at the orchestration layer may survive replacement.

docs.title: Docker Restart Policies
docs.text:
Docker containers can use restart policies.

Inspect:

docker inspect CONTAINER

A container configured to restart automatically may survive host or daemon restarts depending on configuration.

Do not create persistent containers on production infrastructure unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Kubernetes Persistence
docs.text:
Kubernetes persistence may involve objects such as:

Deployment
DaemonSet
StatefulSet
CronJob
ServiceAccount
RoleBinding
ClusterRoleBinding
Admission configuration

These objects can affect many systems.

Kubernetes persistence testing should be restricted to the authorised cluster and namespaces.

docs.title: Active Directory Persistence
docs.text:
Active Directory persistence can have a significantly larger blast radius than local host persistence.

Potential categories include:

Privileged group membership
Directory ACLs
Kerberos keys
Delegation
Certificates
Authentication configuration
Group Policy
SIDHistory
Service accounts
Machine accounts
Trust relationships

docs.title: Active Directory Persistence Model
docs.text:
Domain Identity
      |
      v
Directory Modification
      |
      v
Persistent Trust / Permission
      |
      v
Future Authentication

Directory persistence should only be tested where specifically included in the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Privileged Group Membership
docs.text:
Sensitive groups can include:

Domain Admins
Enterprise Admins
Administrators
Account Operators
Backup Operators
Server Operators
DNSAdmins

Membership changes can create straightforward persistent privilege.

Review:

Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins'

where the Active Directory PowerShell module is available and the query is authorised.

docs.title: Nested Group Persistence
docs.text:
Privilege may also be inherited through nested groups.

User
 |
 v
Group A
 |
 v
Group B
 |
 v
Privileged Group

Reviewing only direct membership can therefore miss persistence paths.

BloodHound can help visualise these relationships.

See:

BloodHound

docs.title: ACL-Based Persistence
docs.text:
Active Directory objects have access control lists.

Persistent control can result from rights over objects such as:

Users
Groups
Computers
Organisational Units
Group Policy Objects
Certificate infrastructure
Domain objects

Examples of sensitive permissions include:

GenericAll
GenericWrite
WriteDACL
WriteOwner
Specific attribute write permissions

Use:

ACL and ACE

docs.title: Group Policy Persistence
docs.text:
Group Policy can affect large numbers of systems and users.

GPO
 |
 +--> Workstations
 |
 +--> Servers
 |
 +--> Users

Changes to GPOs can therefore create broad persistence.

During normal assessments, avoid modifying production GPOs unless the scenario explicitly requires it.

docs.title: SIDHistory
docs.text:
SIDHistory can influence access because Windows authorization can consider historical SIDs associated with an account.

Unexpected privileged SIDHistory values can represent a serious security concern.

Use:

SIDHistory

docs.title: Kerberos Persistence
docs.text:
Kerberos persistence can involve long-term domain authentication material.

High-impact examples can involve compromise of:

KRBTGT key material
Service account keys
Machine account keys
Trust keys

Such testing can have domain-wide implications.

docs.title: Golden Ticket Concept
docs.text:
A Golden Ticket scenario relates to compromise of the Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket account key material.

Conceptually:

KRBTGT Key Material
       |
       v
Forged TGT Capability
       |
       v
Domain Authentication Impact

This represents extremely sensitive domain-level access.

Do not perform Golden Ticket persistence testing unless explicitly required and approved.

docs.title: Trust Tickets
docs.text:
Inter-domain trust relationships introduce additional Kerberos trust material.

Use:

Trust Tickets

and:

Trust Relationships

docs.title: Shadow Credentials
docs.text:
Active Directory authentication can involve key-based credential attributes.

Improper control of these attributes can provide persistent authentication to an account.

Use:

Shadow Credentials

docs.title: Resource-Based Constrained Delegation
docs.text:
Resource-Based Constrained Delegation can alter which identities may act to services associated with a computer object.

Misconfigured object permissions can sometimes create durable attack paths.

Use:

RBCD

docs.title: Machine Accounts
docs.text:
Computer objects are security principals.

Machine account manipulation can sometimes become part of a persistence chain.

Use:

Machine Account Quota

docs.title: AD CS Persistence
docs.text:
Active Directory Certificate Services can create powerful authentication paths.

A certificate and corresponding private key may continue to authenticate independently of the account password.

Certificate
     +
Private Key
     |
     v
Authentication

This makes certificate lifecycle management important during incident response.

docs.title: Certificate Persistence
docs.text:
A simplified model is:

Privileged Certificate
       |
       v
Password Rotated
       |
       v
Certificate Still Valid?
       |
      Yes
       |
       v
Authentication May Remain Possible

This is one reason password rotation alone may be insufficient after certificate-based compromise.

docs.title: Golden Certificate
docs.text:
Compromise of a certificate authority's signing key can have severe consequences.

Use:

Golden Certificate

Testing CA key compromise should be considered exceptionally sensitive and is rarely necessary in production assessments.

docs.title: AD CS
docs.text:
Use the dedicated AD CS section for certificate-service attack paths:

Active Directory Certificate Services

docs.title: Cloud Persistence
docs.text:
Cloud persistence can involve:

User accounts
API keys
Application registrations
Service principals
Certificates
Role assignments
Federated identities
Automation accounts
Access policies
CI/CD credentials
OAuth applications
Long-lived tokens

docs.title: Cloud Persistence Model
docs.text:
Cloud Identity
      |
      v
Persistent Credential
      |
      v
Role / Permission
      |
      v
Cloud Resource Access

Cloud modifications can affect multiple subscriptions, projects, accounts, or tenants.

docs.title: Cloud Access Keys
docs.text:
Long-lived access keys can provide persistent programmatic authentication.

Assess:

Owner
Creation date
Last use
Permissions
Expiry
Rotation
Source restrictions

Prefer short-lived or managed credentials where possible.

docs.title: Service Principals
docs.text:
Application identities can provide persistent cloud access.

Potential credential types include:

Client secrets
Certificates
Federated credentials
Managed identities

Service principals should have narrowly scoped permissions and controlled credential lifecycle.

docs.title: OAuth Applications
docs.text:
OAuth applications may receive delegated or application permissions.

Persistence risk depends on:

Consent
Scopes
Application permissions
Refresh tokens
Administrative consent
Publisher trust
Credential lifetime

Unexpected high-privilege applications should be investigated.

docs.title: Cloud Role Assignments
docs.text:
Persistent privilege can also result from assigning an identity a role.

Conceptually:

Identity
   |
   v
Role Assignment
   |
   v
Resource Access

Monitor creation and modification of privileged role assignments.

docs.title: CI/CD Persistence
docs.text:
CI/CD environments can provide durable access through:

Pipeline modifications
Deployment credentials
Repository hooks
Runner configuration
Build agents
Service connections
Automation identities

Changes can propagate into production environments.

Treat CI/CD persistence as high impact.

docs.title: Web Application Persistence
docs.text:
Applications may contain mechanisms such as:

Administrative accounts
API tokens
OAuth clients
Plugins
Scheduled jobs
Webhooks
Extensions
Service integrations

If an attacker gains application administration, these legitimate features may provide persistent access.

The root cause should be reported accurately.

docs.title: Database Persistence
docs.text:
Database environments can contain:

Database users
Roles
Scheduled jobs
Stored procedures
External integrations
Credentials

Do not create persistent database objects merely to demonstrate administrative access unless the engagement specifically requires it.

docs.title: Persistence Through Credentials
docs.text:
Sometimes no startup mechanism is required.

A long-lived credential can itself provide persistence.

Initial Access
      |
      v
Create / Obtain Credential
      |
      v
Original Foothold Removed
      |
      v
Credential Still Valid
      |
      v
Access Restored

Examples include:

SSH key
API key
Cloud access key
Certificate
Service-account password
Refresh token

docs.title: Persistence Through Remote Access
docs.text:
Remote access configuration can also provide continued access.

Examples include:

SSH authorization
VPN account
RDP permission
WinRM permission
Remote-management group membership
Cloud administrative role

The persistence mechanism is the retained trust or permission rather than the remote protocol itself.

docs.title: Persistence and Credential Rotation
docs.text:
Credential rotation can remove some persistence mechanisms but not others.

Password Changed
      |
      +--> Old Password Invalid
      |
      +--> Existing Certificate May Still Work
      |
      +--> SSH Key May Still Work
      |
      +--> OAuth Grant May Still Work
      |
      +--> API Key May Still Work

Incident response should consider all authentication mechanisms associated with the compromised identity.

docs.title: Persistence and Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Persistence may be established on a system reached through lateral movement.

Initial Host
     |
     v
Lateral Movement
     |
     v
Server
     |
     v
Persistence

Use:

Lateral Movement

docs.title: Persistence and Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
A common attack chain is:

Initial Access
      |
      v
Low Privilege
      |
      v
Privilege Escalation
      |
      v
Administrator / root
      |
      v
Privileged Persistence

Use:

  • Windows PrivEsc Explorer
  • Linux PrivEsc Explorer

docs.title: Persistence and C2
docs.text:
A persistence mechanism may restart an authorised C2 component after a reboot or user logon.

System Boot
     |
     v
Persistence Mechanism
     |
     v
Assessment Component
     |
     v
C2

Use:

Command and Control

docs.title: Persistence and Defence Evasion
docs.text:
Persistence can overlap with defence evasion, but they have different objectives.

Persistence:
Maintain access

Defence Evasion:
Avoid or reduce defensive interference

A persistence mechanism should not automatically be made stealthier merely because stealth is technically possible.

Use:

Defence Evasion

docs.title: Detection Opportunities
docs.text:
Persistence can produce telemetry across:

Endpoint
   |
   +--> Process
   |
   +--> File
   |
   +--> Registry
   |
   +--> Services
   |
   +--> Scheduled Tasks
   |
   +--> Accounts
   |
   v
Identity
   |
   v
Cloud
   |
   v
SIEM

docs.title: Windows Scheduled Task Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

New task creation
Task modification
Unexpected execution identity
Unusual action path
Execution from writable directories
Task started shortly after creation
EDR alerts

Useful Windows security telemetry can include event ID:

4698 - Scheduled task created
4699 - Scheduled task deleted
4702 - Scheduled task updated

Availability depends on auditing configuration.

docs.title: Windows Service Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

New service
Changed service executable
Changed service account
Changed startup type
Unexpected service binary
Service creation followed by execution

A commonly investigated System event is:

7045 - A service was installed in the system

docs.title: Registry Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Monitor security-sensitive autostart locations.

Examples include:

Run keys
RunOnce keys
Winlogon-related configuration
Service registry configuration

Useful telemetry can come from:

EDR
Sysmon
Registry auditing
Configuration monitoring

docs.title: Account Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

Account creation
Account enablement
Password reset
Group membership changes
Privilege assignment
Remote-access group changes

Sensitive group changes should receive additional scrutiny.

docs.title: PowerShell Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Potential telemetry includes:

PowerShell process execution
Script block logging
Module logging
Profile modifications
File monitoring
EDR alerts

Monitor unusual modifications to PowerShell profile locations.

docs.title: WMI Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

Permanent event filters
Event consumers
Filter-to-consumer bindings
WMI repository activity
WMI operational logs
Unexpected child processes

docs.title: Linux Cron Detection
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

Crontab modification
New files under /etc/cron.d/
Unexpected root cron entries
Unexpected scripts
File integrity changes
Audit events

docs.title: Linux systemd Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

New unit files
Changed unit files
daemon-reload activity
New enabled services
Unexpected ExecStart
Unexpected service users
New timers

docs.title: Linux SSH Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

authorized_keys modifications
New SSH keys
SSH login from unusual source
Unexpected key fingerprint
File permission changes
Account changes

docs.title: Linux Account Detection
docs.text:
Monitor:

/etc/passwd changes
/etc/shadow changes
Group membership changes
sudoers changes
New home directories
SSH key creation

docs.title: Active Directory Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Potential high-value events include:

Privileged group membership changes
Directory ACL changes
GPO changes
Certificate changes
Delegation changes
Account modifications
SIDHistory changes
New machine accounts
Authentication policy changes

docs.title: Cloud Persistence Detection
docs.text:
Cloud monitoring should include:

New user
New access key
New service principal credential
New application
New OAuth consent
New role assignment
New federation configuration
New certificate
New API token
Policy modification

docs.title: Persistence Baselines
docs.text:
Defenders should know what normal persistence looks like.

Examples:

Approved scheduled tasks
Approved services
Approved startup applications
Approved systemd units
Approved cron jobs
Approved SSH keys
Approved privileged groups
Approved cloud applications
Approved service principals

Baselines make unexpected changes easier to identify.

docs.title: Persistence Detection Model
docs.text:
Configuration Change
       |
       v
Telemetry
       |
       v
Baseline Comparison
       |
       v
Expected?
   /       \
 Yes        No
  |          |
  v          v
Allow     Investigate
             |
             v
         Persistence?

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
Track whether the persistence action is visible.

Example:

Activity Logged Alerted Prevented Investigated Test scheduled task Yes Yes No Yes Test service creation Yes Yes Yes Yes SSH key modification Yes No No No Cloud role change Yes Yes No Yes

This is often more valuable than attempting multiple persistence mechanisms.

docs.title: Persistence Evidence
docs.text:
Record:

Timestamp
System or identity
Persistence mechanism
Original state
Modified state
Required privilege
Validation result
Detection result
Cleanup action
Cleanup verification

docs.title: Example Evidence
docs.text:
Timestamp:
2026-09-05 14:20 UTC

Host:
TEST-WKS01

Identity:
CORP\test-admin

Mechanism:
Scheduled task

Task:
Assessment-Persistence-Test

Purpose:
Validate detection of scheduled-task persistence

Result:
Marker file created successfully

Detection:
EDR alert generated

Cleanup:
Task and marker file removed

Verification:
Task no longer present

docs.title: Evidence Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots should demonstrate:

Persistence location
Assessment-specific identifier
Security context
Validation result
Detection result
Cleanup

Avoid capturing unrelated sensitive information.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
A location could potentially provide persistence.

Examples:

Writable startup directory
Writable service configuration
Writable systemd unit
Writable authorized_keys
Directory ACL permission
Cloud role-management permission

No persistent modification has been demonstrated.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text: The tester has sufficient permission and the mechanism appears capable of surviving the relevant lifecycle event.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text: A controlled authorised test demonstrates the persistence mechanism operates as expected.

docs.title: Persistence Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on:

Privilege
Affected identity
Affected systems
Duration
Authentication strength
Scope
Ease of creation
Ease of detection
Ability to survive credential rotation
Blast radius
Attack chaining

A user-level startup entry is not automatically equivalent to domain-level certificate persistence.

docs.title: Persistence Hierarchy
docs.text:
A simplified impact model is:

User-Level Host Persistence
           |
           v
Administrative Host Persistence
           |
           v
Server Persistence
           |
           v
Identity Persistence

docs.title: What Not to Report Automatically
docs.text:
Do not automatically report:

Task Scheduler exists
systemd exists
Cron exists
SSH supports authorized_keys
Windows has Run keys
Administrators can create services
Domain Admins can modify the directory
Cloud administrators can create identities

These are expected platform capabilities.

A security finding requires an inappropriate permission, trust relationship, control failure, or demonstrated attack path.

docs.title: Reporting Persistence
docs.text:
Weak:

Scheduled tasks can be used for persistence.

Better:

The compromised standard-user account had write access to the
action script executed by a scheduled task running as a privileged
service identity.

A non-destructive marker-file test confirmed that modifying the
script caused code to execute in the privileged task context.

docs.title: Reporting Directory Persistence
docs.text:
Weak:

Active Directory allows persistence.

Better:

The delegated support group had WriteDACL permission over a
privileged administrative group.

This permission could allow members of the support group to grant
themselves durable control over the privileged group without
requiring membership at the time of modification.

docs.text:

docs.title: Cleanup Verification
docs.text:
Do not assume a deletion command succeeded.

Verify:

Service no longer exists
Registry value removed
Startup file removed
SSH key removed
Cron entry removed
systemd unit removed
Account removed
Group membership restored
Cloud role removed
Certificate revoked where required

docs.title: Reboot Validation
docs.text:
Persistence is often defined by surviving reboot, but rebooting production systems can cause disruption.

Only perform reboot validation when explicitly permitted.

Otherwise, document:

Mechanism configured for startup
Configuration verified
Reboot not performed due to availability constraints

Do not create operational risk merely to prove an already established configuration property.

Authorised testing only

Persistence testing creates deliberate changes that may survive logoff, restart, credential changes, or other lifecycle events. Only create accounts, scheduled tasks, services, startup entries, SSH keys, directory permissions, certificates, cloud identities, role assignments, or other persistent changes when explicitly permitted by the Rules of Engagement. Record every modification before deployment, use recognisable assessment identifiers, minimise the blast radius, avoid modifying production-wide controls unless specifically required, and verify complete cleanup at the end of testing.

docs.title: Red Team Phishing
docs.text:
Phishing is a social engineering technique that uses electronic communication to influence a target into performing an action.

Typical attacker objectives include:

Open a link

Open an attachment

Submit credentials

Approve authentication

Execute content

Provide information

Initiate a business process

In an authorised red team assessment, phishing should instead be treated as a controlled test of:

Email Security

User Awareness

Identity Controls

Endpoint Controls

Reporting

SOC Detection

Incident Response

A safe phishing model is:

Authorised Objective
        |
        v
Approved Target Group
        |
        v
Controlled Message
        |
        v
Safe Landing Page / Test Artifact
        |
        v
User Action
        |
        v
Security Controls
        |
        v
Detection / Reporting
        |
        v
Evidence
        |
        v
Debrief / Cleanup

Explicit authorisation required

Phishing directly targets people and may interact with production email, identity and endpoint controls. Campaign scope, recipients, sending infrastructure, domains, landing pages, credential handling, attachments, QR codes, MFA interactions, data retention and stop conditions should be explicitly approved before testing.

docs.title: Phishing Objectives
docs.text:
Typical objectives include:

Validate secure email gateway controls

Validate anti-phishing controls

Validate domain authentication

Validate malicious-link protection

Validate attachment controls

Validate browser protections

Validate endpoint protections

Validate identity controls

Validate user reporting

Validate SOC visibility

Measure incident-response performance

docs.title: Phishing Is More Than Click Rate
docs.text:

A better model is:

Message Delivery
      |
      v

      |
      v
User Decision
      |
      v
Identity / Endpoint Control
      |
      v
User Reporting
      |
      v
SOC Detection
      |
      v
Response

A user clicking a test link does not automatically mean the organisation has suffered a serious control failure.

For example:

User Clicks
    |
    v
Browser Blocks
    |
    v
Security Alert
    |
    v
SOC Responds

may demonstrate successful defence in depth.

A phishing assessment can also evaluate whether the organisation's own domains are protected against spoofing.

docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.title: Phishing-Resistant MFA
docs.text:
Examples of stronger authentication approaches include:

These can significantly reduce traditional credential-phishing risk.

docs.title: MFA Push Fatigue
docs.text:
Repeatedly generating MFA prompts can disrupt users and may cause account or security incidents.

Do not conduct MFA fatigue testing unless explicitly approved.

A tabletop or synthetic-account exercise is usually safer.

docs.text:
When antivirus validation is specifically part of the exercise, the EICAR test file can provide a standard non-malicious antivirus test.

Canonical EICAR string:

X5O!P%@AP[4\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*

Coordinate EICAR testing

EICAR is intentionally detected by security products. Sending it through production email can trigger gateways, antivirus, EDR and SOC workflows. Use it only when the defensive team has approved that test.

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis - Link
docs.text:
Hypothesis:
A user visiting the approved phishing simulation domain should
generate email, proxy, DNS and endpoint telemetry sufficient for
the security team to identify the event.

Test:
Send the approved link-based scenario to the pilot group.

Expected:
The email platform records delivery, web controls record the
click and the SIEM receives relevant telemetry.

Result:
Record prevention, telemetry, alerting and user reporting.

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis - Attachment
docs.text:
Hypothesis:
Opening the approved test attachment should generate endpoint
telemetry and allow the SOC to correlate the activity with the
original phishing message.

Test:
Deliver the benign attachment scenario to approved test users.

Expected:
Email and endpoint telemetry are available for investigation.

Result:
Record visibility and response.

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis - Identity
docs.text:
Hypothesis:
A credential-submission event involving the synthetic test
identity should be visible through identity monitoring.

Test:
Use only the dedicated synthetic account and approved landing
page.

Expected:
Relevant identity telemetry is generated without exposing
production credentials.

Result:
Record detection and response.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
The organisation may permit messages from lookalike external
domains.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
The test message reached the secure email gateway without being
rejected.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
The approved phishing simulation message was delivered to 41 of
50 targeted mailboxes.

docs.title: Accurate Reporting
docs.text:
Avoid:

Eight employees were compromised.

when:

Eight users clicked a safe test link.

Prefer:

Eight of 41 recipients who received the simulation visited the
approved landing page. No production credentials were collected,
and subsequent identity controls were not bypassed.

docs.title: Example Finding - Email Impersonation
docs.text:
Title:
External Email Impersonation Controls Do Not Reliably Identify Synthetic Executive Display Names

Observation:
The authorised campaign used a customer-approved external test
domain and a synthetic executive-style display name.

The test messages were delivered without a prominent
impersonation warning to the tested recipients.

No production executive mailbox or domain was spoofed.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to create messages that appear familiar
to recipients and increase the likelihood of successful social
engineering.

Recommendation:
Review anti-phishing and impersonation-protection policies,
particularly for high-risk identities. Combine technical
controls with clear external-sender indicators and user
reporting mechanisms.

docs.title: Example Finding - Weak User Reporting
docs.text:
Title:
Phishing Reporting Mechanism Is Not Consistently Used

Observation:
The campaign delivered 41 authorised simulation messages.

Eight recipients visited the controlled landing page, while only
three messages were reported through the organisation's
designated phishing-report mechanism during the agreed
observation period.

Impact:
Low reporting rates may delay security-team awareness of
phishing campaigns and reduce the organisation's ability to
protect other recipients.

Recommendation:
Reinforce the phishing-reporting process, ensure the reporting
mechanism is easily accessible and provide periodic scenario-
based awareness exercises.

docs.title: Example Finding - Missing SOC Correlation
docs.text:
Title:
Phishing Link Interaction Is Logged but Does Not Generate Actionable SOC Detection

Observation:
The approved campaign generated email delivery, DNS and proxy
telemetry when users visited the controlled phishing simulation
domain.

The events were successfully ingested by the SIEM, but no
correlated alert was generated.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to interact with users through phishing
infrastructure without producing an actionable alert despite
relevant telemetry being available.

Recommendation:
Develop correlation logic combining email delivery, web
navigation, domain reputation and endpoint or identity events.
Validate the resulting detection using repeatable phishing
simulation scenarios.

docs.title: Example Positive Security Result
docs.text:
Control:
Secure Email Gateway

Scenario:
Approved link-based phishing simulation

Result:
The gateway quarantined the message before delivery.

Telemetry:
The event was forwarded to the SIEM.

SOC:
An analyst reviewed the event and correctly identified the
campaign domain.

Conclusion:
The tested phishing message was successfully prevented and
detected.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Phishing testing can be reduced to:

Define the objective.

Obtain explicit authorisation.

Target only the approved population.

Use controlled infrastructure.

Use safe scenarios.

Avoid harmful pretexts.

Prefer synthetic identities.

Prefer synthetic credentials.

Do not store production passwords.

Do not capture live sessions unless explicitly approved.

Use harmless attachments where possible.

Treat user reporting as success.

Measure the entire defensive chain.

Validate email security.

Validate browser and endpoint controls.

Validate identity controls.

Validate SIEM visibility.

Measure SOC response.

Report aggregate control behaviour.

Do not shame employees.

Debrief appropriately.

Remove campaign infrastructure and sensitive data.

Retest after improvements.

Measure the defensive chain, not just the employee

A useful phishing exercise evaluates message delivery, gateway controls, user reporting, browser protection, identity controls, endpoint visibility, SIEM correlation and SOC response. Click rate is only one small part of that picture.

Never make real credentials the objective

If the campaign can prove that a user attempted to submit credentials, that is normally sufficient. Production passwords, session tokens and live authentication sessions introduce unnecessary risk and should not be collected unless an exceptional scenario has been explicitly authorised and controlled.

docs.title: Red Team Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Privilege escalation is the process of moving from the current security context to one with additional permissions or authority.

In a red team assessment, privilege escalation is not limited to:

User -> Administrator

or:

User -> root

Privilege boundaries can exist across:

Operating systems

Applications

Active Directory

Cloud platforms

Containers

Databases

Service accounts

Administrative tiers

Security tooling

A useful model is:

Current Context
      |
      v
Enumerate Privilege Boundaries
      |
      v
Identify Candidate Paths
      |
      v
Validate Preconditions
      |
      v
Minimal Safe Validation
      |
      v
Higher Privilege
      |
      v
Reassess Attack Path

The objective is to determine whether an attacker who already has an authorised foothold can cross a security boundary that should prevent access to more privileged resources.

Authorised testing only

Privilege escalation can affect highly sensitive operating-system and identity controls. Validate only the minimum conditions required to demonstrate the security boundary. Avoid destructive changes, production disruption, unnecessary credential access, or persistent privileged modifications.

docs.title: Privilege Escalation Objectives
docs.text:
Common objectives include:

Determine current privilege

Identify local privilege boundaries

Identify misconfigured services

Identify scheduled execution paths

Identify writable privileged resources

Identify excessive user rights

Identify credential-based escalation paths

Identify identity and group escalation paths

Identify Active Directory privilege paths

Identify cloud privilege paths

Validate application-control assumptions

Determine defensive visibility

Reach an engagement objective

docs.title: Privilege Is Contextual
docs.text:
Privilege should not be treated as one universal level.

Examples:

Local standard user

Local administrator

Domain user

Server operator

Database administrator

Cloud contributor

Cloud owner

Application administrator

Service account

Domain administrator

An identity may be privileged in one system while unprivileged in another.

Domain User -> Domain Administrator

docs.title: Candidate vs Confirmed
docs.text:

Candidate

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
A potentially interesting configuration exists.

Example:

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Required preconditions appear to exist.

Example:

The service executes as SYSTEM and a referenced directory appears
writable by the assessment user.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
Minimal authorised validation demonstrates the boundary.

Example:

The assessment confirmed that the standard user could modify the
privileged service resource and that the service executes the
resource under a higher-privileged context.

docs.title: Safe Write Validation
docs.text:
When write access is uncertain:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID-$(Get-Random).tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Output "Write succeeded: $file"
}
catch {
    Write-Output "Write failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}
finally {
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

This validates write access without replacing privileged files.

            [PSCustomObject]@{
                TaskName  = $task.TaskName
                TaskPath  = $task.TaskPath
                Execute   = $action.Execute
                Arguments = $action.Arguments

The goal is proof, not maximum exploitation complexity.

docs.title: Finding Titles
docs.text:
Good:

Standard Users Can Modify Resource Executed by SYSTEM Service

Privileged Scheduled Task References User-Writable Script

Excessive Sudo Permission Enables Root-Level Operations

Docker Daemon Access Grants Host-Level Administrative Control

Active Directory ACL Grants Unintended Control Over Privileged Group

Avoid:

WinPEAS Finding

GTFOBins Exploit

PowerShell PrivEsc

BloodHound Vulnerability

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Explain the actual boundary crossed.

Example:

A standard user who gains execution on the affected server can
modify a resource subsequently executed by a service running as
LocalSystem.

Successful exploitation provides operating-system-level
administrative control of the affected server.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Common root causes include:

Excessive file permissions

Excessive directory permissions

docs.title: Severity Example

A local escalation from:

Standard User -> SYSTEM

But if the affected system is:

Domain Controller

and the path materially enables domain compromise, the overall attack-path impact may be Critical.

Severity should reflect context.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Privilege escalation testing can be reduced to:

Understand the current identity.

Understand the current privilege.

Enumerate before exploiting.

Identify the exact security boundary.

Validate every prerequisite.

Separate candidates from confirmed findings.

Prefer the lowest-risk path.

Use harmless validation where possible.

Do not access sensitive data unnecessarily.

Confirm the resulting privilege.

Determine what defenders observed.

Preserve sufficient evidence.

Remove introduced artifacts.

Explain the root cause.

Connect the escalation to the wider attack path.

Privilege escalation is a relationship

A writable file, SUID binary, Windows privilege, sudo rule, Active Directory ACL, or cloud role is not automatically a vulnerability. The important question is whether the current identity can use that condition to cross a security boundary and obtain authority it should not possess.

Stop when the boundary is proven

Obtaining SYSTEM, root, a privileged domain identity, or an equivalent cloud or application privilege is usually sufficient evidence that the escalation path exists. Do not perform additional destructive actions or access unrelated sensitive information simply because the elevated context makes it possible.

docs.title: Red Team Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Reconnaissance is the process of collecting and analysing information about a target before and during an authorised red team assessment.

The objective is not simply to collect as much information as possible.

The objective is to transform external and internal observations into an accurate attack-surface model that supports the engagement objectives.

Authorised Scope
      |
      v
Passive Reconnaissance
      |
      v
Asset Discovery
      |
      v
Active Validation
      |
      v
Technology Mapping
      |
      v
Identity Mapping
      |
      v
Attack Surface
      |
      v
Candidate Entry Points
      |
      v
Initial Access

Reconnaissance should answer:

What does the organisation expose?

Which assets actually belong to the organisation?

Which systems are alive?

Which technologies are present?

Where are authentication boundaries?

Which identities are externally visible?

Which cloud and SaaS services are used?

Which assets are likely to be security-relevant?

Which observations justify further testing?

Authorised testing only

Passive discovery may reveal systems belonging to subsidiaries, suppliers, cloud providers, CDNs, SaaS platforms, or unrelated third parties. Discovery does not establish authorisation. Validate ownership and scope before performing active testing.

docs.title: Reconnaissance Objectives
docs.text:
Typical objectives include:

Identify Internet-facing assets

Discover domains and subdomains

Identify IP ranges and network ownership

Map DNS infrastructure

Identify web applications

Identify remote-access services

Identify authentication portals

Identify externally exposed technologies

Identify cloud infrastructure

Identify public code repositories

Identify exposed documents and metadata

Identify publicly exposed identities

Identify email infrastructure

Identify candidate initial-access paths

Validate scope boundaries

docs.text:
ORGANISATION

          +--------------+--------------+
          |              |              |
          v              v              v
       Domains          IPs          Identities
          |              |              |
          v              v              v
      Subdomains      Services       Accounts
          |              |              |
          +--------------+--------------+

                         |
                         v
                    Applications
                         |
                         v
                Authentication Surface
                         |
                         v
                   Attack Surface

docs.title: Passive vs Active Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Reconnaissance can broadly be divided into:

Passive Reconnaissance

Active Reconnaissance

docs.title: Passive Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Passive reconnaissance uses information available without directly interacting with the target application or system where practical.

Examples:

Search engines

Certificate Transparency

Public DNS information

WHOIS/RDAP

Public code repositories

Public documents

Job advertisements

Company websites

Public cloud references

Internet archives

Public vulnerability information

Search-engine indexes

docs.title: Active Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Active reconnaissance directly interacts with target infrastructure.

Examples:

DNS queries

HTTP requests

Port scanning

Service identification

TLS inspection

Content discovery

Technology fingerprinting

Application mapping

Active reconnaissance should only be performed against authorised targets.

docs.text:
A practical workflow:

    v

docs.title: Create an Engagement Workspace
docs.text:
Keep reconnaissance data separated by engagement.

Example:

mkdir -p recon/{domains,dns,subdomains,hosts,http,ports,cloud,identities,repositories,evidence}

Example structure:

recon/
├── domains/
├── dns/
├── subdomains/
├── hosts/
├── http/
├── ports/
├── cloud/
├── identities/
├── repositories/
└── evidence/

docs.title: Seed Information
docs.text:
Reconnaissance usually begins with known information.

Possible seeds:

Primary domain

Known applications

Known IP addresses

Company name

Known subsidiaries

Cloud tenant

Known email domain

Known authentication portal

Example:

example.com

docs.title: Maintain Scope Separately
docs.text:
Keep discovered assets separate from authorised assets.

Example:

scope/
├── domains.txt
├── ips.txt
└── excluded.txt

recon/
└── discovered-assets.txt

Do not automatically copy every discovered asset into scope.

docs.title: Domain Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Start with the primary authorised domain.

Questions:

Who controls the domain?

Which nameservers are authoritative?

Which mail providers are used?

Which TXT records exist?

Which subdomains are visible?

Which certificates reference the domain?

Which external services depend on the domain?

docs.text:
A records:

dig AAAA example.com

Mail:

dig MX example.com

docs.title: DNS TXT Records
docs.text:
TXT records can reveal information about:

SPF

Domain verification

SaaS providers

Cloud services

Email security

Ownership verification

Query:

dig TXT example.com

Treat these as infrastructure clues rather than vulnerabilities by themselves.

docs.title: SPF
docs.text:
An SPF record may identify authorised mail infrastructure.

Example structure:

v=spf1 include:... -all

Reviewing SPF can help identify:

Mail providers

Third-party mailing services

SaaS dependencies

docs.title: DMARC
docs.text:
Query:

dig TXT _dmarc.example.com

DMARC information can help understand the organisation's email-security architecture.

docs.title: DKIM
docs.text:
DKIM selectors are provider-specific and should not be guessed aggressively without a reason.

If a selector is known from authorised email samples or documentation, query:

dig TXT selector._domainkey.example.com

docs.title: WHOIS and RDAP
docs.text:
Domain registration information may provide:

Registrar

Registration dates

Nameservers

Registration status

Traditional query:

whois example.com

Modern registration data is increasingly provided through RDAP.

Registration data may be privacy protected.

docs.title: Certificate Transparency
docs.text:
Certificate Transparency logs are valuable for discovering hostnames associated with certificates.

Useful sources include:

crt.sh

Search concept:

%.example.com

Certificate data may reveal:

vpn.example.com

mail.example.com

portal.example.com

api.example.com

legacy.example.com

docs.title: Certificate Discovery Limitations
docs.text:
A certificate hostname does not guarantee:

The host still exists

The host is reachable

The organisation still owns it

The system is in scope

Treat certificate results as candidates.

docs.title: Subdomain Enumeration
docs.text:
Subdomain enumeration combines multiple data sources.

Useful tools include:

Subfinder

Amass

Certificate Transparency

DNS data

Search engines

Historical sources

docs.title: Subfinder
docs.text:
Subfinder performs passive subdomain discovery.

Basic usage:

subfinder -d example.com

Save results:

subfinder -d example.com -silent -o subfinder.txt

docs.title: Amass
docs.text:
OWASP Amass can be used for attack-surface discovery.

Passive enumeration:

amass enum -passive -d example.com

Save:

amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt

docs.title: Combine Enumeration Results
docs.text:
Example:

cat subfinder.txt amass.txt | sort -u > subdomains.txt

Count:

wc -l subdomains.txt

docs.title: Normalise Results
docs.text:
Remove empty lines:

sed '/^[[:space:]]*$/d' subdomains.txt | sort -u > subdomains-clean.txt

This produces a clean candidate list.

docs.title: Candidate vs Resolved vs Alive
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

Discovered Subdomain
        |
        v
DNS Resolved
        |
        v
Network Reachable
        |
        v
HTTP Reachable

These represent different states.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Use dnsx to validate DNS candidates.

Example:

dnsx -l subdomains-clean.txt -silent

Save resolved names:

dnsx -l subdomains-clean.txt -silent -o resolved.txt

docs.title: Resolve with IP Information
docs.text:
dnsx -l subdomains-clean.txt -silent -a -resp

This can help map hostnames to addresses.

docs.title: HTTP Validation
docs.text:
Use httpx to identify HTTP/HTTPS services.

Basic:

httpx -l resolved.txt -silent

Save:

httpx -l resolved.txt -silent -o alive-http.txt

docs.title: HTTP Metadata
docs.text:
A useful reconnaissance probe:

httpx -l resolved.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -ip

This may provide:

URL

Status code

Page title

Technology

IP address

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
https://portal.example.com [200] [Customer Portal] [nginx] [203.0.113.10]
https://vpn.example.com [302] [Login] [203.0.113.20]
https://old.example.com [404] [Not Found] [203.0.113.30]

A 404 host can still be relevant because the web service itself is alive.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
Redirects can reveal:

Canonical hostnames

Authentication systems

SSO providers

Application paths

External SaaS dependencies

Inspect:

curl -I https://example.com/

docs.title: HTTP Headers
docs.text:
Headers may reveal:

Server software

Reverse proxies

CDNs

Authentication products

Frameworks

Security controls

Internal naming

Inspect:

curl -I https://example.com/

Do not assume a disclosed Server header is perfectly accurate.

docs.text:
Technology identification helps determine which testing methodology is relevant.

Useful tools:

WhatWeb

Wappalyzer

Nuclei technology templates

Manual inspection

docs.title: WhatWeb
docs.text:
WhatWeb:

docs.title: Technology Mapping
docs.text:
Record technologies by asset.

Example:

Asset Technology Confidence www.example.com nginx High portal.example.com ASP.NET High api.example.com Unknown API Medium auth.example.com SSO portal High

docs.title: Technology Confidence
docs.text:
Useful levels:

Low

Medium

High

Confirmed

Do not report technology fingerprinting as confirmed merely because one scanner guessed it.

docs.title: HTTP Screenshots
docs.text:
Screenshots can make large HTTP attack surfaces easier to review.

Useful tools include:

EyeWitness

gowitness

Screenshots help identify:

Login pages

Administrative interfaces

Default pages

Legacy applications

Error pages

Development environments

Duplicate applications

docs.text:
gowitness can capture web screenshots.

Review the project's current command syntax before using it because CLI options can change between releases.

docs.text:

VPN

API

Development

Testing

Staging

docs.text:
Authentication endpoints deserve specific attention.

Look for:

/login

/signin

/auth

/oauth

/saml

/oidc

/admin

/vpn

/remote

/password-reset

Do not assume these exact paths exist; identify them through normal application discovery.

docs.title: Authentication Inventory
docs.text:
Example:

Asset Authentication MFA Identity Provider VPN Username/password Yes Entra ID Portal SSO Yes Entra ID Legacy App Local account Unknown Local API Token N/A Application

docs.text:
Common identity systems include:

Active Directory Federation Services

Okta

Ping Identity

Auth0

Google Workspace

Custom SAML/OIDC

Identity architecture often determines the most important attack surface.

docs.title: Microsoft Tenant Information
docs.text:
Public authentication behaviour may reveal whether an organisation uses Microsoft cloud identity.

Do not treat the existence of a Microsoft tenant as a vulnerability.

Record it as architecture information.

docs.title: Remote Access Surface
docs.text:
Look for externally exposed services such as:

VPN

Remote Desktop gateways

VDI

Citrix

SSH

File transfer

Remote support

Web administration

These may represent important initial-access boundaries.

docs.title: Port Discovery
docs.text:
Port scanning is active reconnaissance and should only target authorised addresses.

A basic Nmap scan:

nmap -sT -Pn -T3 192.0.2.10

A targeted service scan:

nmap -sT -Pn -sV -p 22,80,443,445,3389 192.0.2.10

Use conservative timing appropriate to the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Why TCP Connect Scanning?
docs.text:
-sT

uses the operating system's TCP connect mechanism.

It is useful when:

Raw socket privileges are unavailable

Traffic is being routed through certain proxy mechanisms

A simple validation scan is sufficient

docs.title: Nmap Output
docs.text:
Save normal output:

nmap -sT -Pn -sV 192.0.2.10 -oN nmap.txt

XML:

nmap -sT -Pn -sV 192.0.2.10 -oX nmap.xml

docs.title: Port State Interpretation
docs.text:
Common states:

open

closed

filtered

filtered does not necessarily mean the host is offline.

A firewall may be preventing a definitive response.

docs.title: Service Identification
docs.text:
Common Internet-facing services:

Port Typical Service 22 SSH 25 SMTP 53 DNS 80 HTTP 443 HTTPS 445 SMB 587 SMTP Submission 993 IMAPS 3389 RDP

Ports are indicators, not proof of the application protocol.

docs.title: IP Address Reconnaissance
docs.text:

Network ownership

docs.title: ASN
docs.text:
An Autonomous System Number identifies a network participating in Internet routing.

ASN information may help determine whether an organisation operates its own address space.

Do not assume all addresses announced by an organisation's ASN are automatically authorised for testing.

docs.text:
Organisation

    ASN

docs.title: IP Ownership
docs.text:
Differentiate:

Organisation-owned IP

Cloud-hosted IP

CDN IP

SaaS IP

Third-party IP

This distinction is important for scope.

docs.title: CDN and Reverse Proxy
docs.text:
An application's DNS may point to:

Cloudflare

Akamai

Fastly

CloudFront

Other reverse proxies

The visible edge address may not be the origin server.

Do not attempt to bypass a third-party edge service unless explicitly authorised.

docs.text:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com

Useful certificate fields include:

docs.title: TLS Certificate Information
docs.text:
A simpler certificate extraction:

echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

docs.title: Subject Alternative Names
docs.text:
SANs may reveal additional names associated with the certificate.

Example:

DNS:example.com
DNS:www.example.com
DNS:portal.example.com

Again, these are candidates rather than automatically authorised targets.

docs.title: Cloud Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Modern attack surfaces frequently extend into cloud environments.

Look for evidence of:

AWS

Microsoft Azure

Google Cloud

Cloud storage

Cloud-hosted applications

Serverless services

Container registries

Cloud identity

CI/CD platforms

docs.text:
Cloud Asset

docs.title: Cloud Storage
docs.text:
Public references may identify storage services.

Examples:

Amazon S3

Azure Blob Storage

Google Cloud Storage

Discovery does not justify accessing data outside the authorised scope.

docs.title: Cloud Metadata in Applications
docs.text:
Application code may reference:

Storage names

API endpoints

Tenant IDs

Region names

Cloud resource names

CDN hostnames

These are useful for architecture mapping.

docs.title: Public Code Repositories
docs.text:
Search authorised public sources for repositories associated with the organisation.

Potential sources:

GitHub

GitLab

Bitbucket

Public package registries

docs.title: Repository Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Look for:

Domain references

API endpoints

Infrastructure configuration

Documentation

Cloud resource names

Email formats

Technology information

Accidentally committed secrets

Do not use discovered credentials against systems unless credential validation is explicitly authorised.

docs.title: GitHub Search
docs.text:
Useful search concepts include:

"example.com"

org:example

"@example.com"

Search should focus on publicly available information.

docs.title: Repository Secret Exposure
docs.text:
Potential secret types include:

API keys

Cloud credentials

Passwords

Private keys

Tokens

Database connection strings

If discovered during an authorised engagement:

Preserve minimal evidence

Do not unnecessarily expose the secret

Do not commit it into notes

Follow the Rules of Engagement

Coordinate rotation where required

docs.title: Git History
docs.text:
A secret removed from the current branch may remain in repository history.

The security issue is therefore:

Secret exposed in repository history

rather than merely:

Secret in current file

docs.title: Public Documents
docs.text:
Publicly available documents can reveal useful architecture information.

Examples:

PDF

DOCX

XLSX

PPTX

Potential information:

Author names

Usernames

Software versions

Internal hostnames

File paths

Organisation names

Document templates

docs.title: Metadata Extraction
docs.text:
ExifTool can inspect metadata.

Example:

exiftool document.pdf

For multiple files:

exiftool documents/

docs.title: Metadata Interpretation
docs.text:
Metadata should be treated carefully.

A username in a document may be:

Current employee

Former employee

External contractor

Template author

Generic build account

Validate before drawing conclusions.

docs.title: Identity Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Public information may reveal:

Employee names

Job titles

Departments

Email formats

Technology teams

Administrators

Developers

Security personnel

Identity information can be sensitive even when publicly available.

docs.title: Identity Sources
docs.text:
Possible sources:

Company website

Public professional profiles

Conference presentations

Public repositories

Public documents

Press releases

Job advertisements

docs.title: Email Format
docs.text:
Public addresses may reveal a naming convention.

Examples:

firstname.lastname@example.com

firstinitiallastname@example.com

firstname@example.com

Do not automatically generate or test large account lists merely because a pattern is known.

docs.title: Username Validation
docs.text:
Username enumeration against authentication systems can trigger:

Account lockouts

Security alerts

Rate limits

Privacy concerns

Only perform active account validation when explicitly permitted.

This information helps build hypotheses but does not confirm deployment.

docs.text:
Search engines can reveal indexed content such as:

Subdomains

Documents

Login pages

Old applications

Public directories

Error messages

Use normal public search functionality within the engagement rules.

docs.title: Search Examples
docs.text:
Examples of search syntax:

site:example.com

site:example.com filetype:pdf

site:example.com filetype:xlsx

site:example.com login

These queries search publicly indexed content.

docs.title: Internet Archive
docs.text:
Historical web data can reveal:

Old endpoints

Previous applications

Historical paths

Retired technologies

Old documentation

Historical existence does not mean the system still exists.

docs.title: robots.txt
docs.text:
Review:

curl https://example.com/robots.txt

It may identify:

Crawler exclusions

Application paths

Administrative paths

Legacy content

robots.txt is not an access-control mechanism.

docs.title: sitemap.xml
docs.text:
Review:

curl https://example.com/sitemap.xml

Sitemaps may reveal application structure.

docs.title: security.txt
docs.text:
Check:

curl https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt

This may provide:

Security contact

Disclosure policy

Acknowledgement information

docs.title: Content Discovery
docs.text:
Once a web application is confirmed in scope, content discovery may identify:

Directories

Files

APIs

Administrative interfaces

Backup files

Documentation

Hidden application paths

See:

Content Discovery

docs.title: Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Parameters may reveal additional application functionality.

Sources include:

HTML forms

JavaScript

Historical URLs

Application links

API documentation

See:

Parameter Discovery

docs.title: JavaScript Reconnaissance
docs.text:
JavaScript files can reveal:

API routes

Internal application paths

Feature flags

Service names

Cloud endpoints

Authentication logic

Client-side configuration

See:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: API Discovery
docs.text:
Look for:

/api/

/v1/

/v2/

/graphql

/swagger

/openapi

These are common conventions, not guaranteed paths.

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
An exposed OpenAPI specification can provide:

Endpoints

Methods

Parameters

Authentication schemes

Schemas

The existence of API documentation is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL endpoints may provide a distinct application attack surface.

Common architecture:

Client
  |
  v
GraphQL Endpoint
  |
  v
Resolvers
  |

docs.title: Virtual Hosts
docs.text:
Multiple applications may share one address.

Concept:

203.0.113.10
     |
     +--> www.example.com
     |
     +--> portal.example.com
     |
     +--> api.example.com

Hostname-based discovery can therefore reveal more than IP-only scanning.

docs.title: Development and Staging Systems
docs.text:
Look for naming patterns such as:

dev

test

qa

uat

stage

staging

preprod

demo

old

legacy

Do not assume such systems have weaker security.

Validate configuration independently.

docs.title: Environment Classification
docs.text:
Example:

Host Environment Confidence www.example.com Production High dev.example.com Development Medium uat.example.com UAT High old.example.com Unknown/legacy Medium

docs.title: Forgotten Assets
docs.text:
Potential forgotten assets include:

Old portals

Temporary applications

Legacy VPNs

Development systems

Deprecated APIs

Old DNS records

Unused cloud resources

These can be valuable reconnaissance findings because asset management is itself a security control.

docs.title: Dangling DNS
docs.text:
A DNS record may reference a resource that no longer exists.

Concept:

sub.example.com
       |
       v
External Service
       |
       v
Resource Removed

This may represent a subdomain takeover candidate depending on the provider and exact configuration.

Do not claim takeover until safely confirmed according to scope.

docs.title: DNS Wildcards
docs.text:
Wildcard DNS can make every tested hostname appear to resolve.

Test random names:

dig +short random-name-that-should-not-exist.example.com

If arbitrary names resolve, account for wildcard behaviour when processing subdomain results.

docs.title: HTTP Wildcards
docs.text:
Applications may also respond identically to unknown hostnames or paths.

Compare:

Status

Content length

Title

Response body

Redirect destination

before treating every response as a unique asset.

docs.title: Catch-All Authentication
docs.text:
Some identity providers deliberately return similar responses for valid and invalid accounts.

Do not infer account existence solely from one response difference.

docs.title: Vulnerability Intelligence
docs.text:
Once technologies are identified, research relevant vulnerabilities.

Sources include:

NIST National Vulnerability Database

CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog

GitHub Security Advisories

docs.title: Version Matching
docs.text:
A version banner is not sufficient to confirm vulnerability.

Use:

Observed Version
      |
      v
Affected Version?
      |
      v
Required Configuration?
      |
      v
Reachable Attack Surface?
      |
      v
Safe Validation

docs.title: Do Not Report CVEs from Version Strings Alone
docs.text:
Weak:

nginx version X is vulnerable to CVE-XXXX-XXXX.

Better:

The service disclosed a version potentially associated with
CVE-XXXX-XXXX. Exploitability was not confirmed during the
assessment.

docs.title: Automated Template Scanning
docs.text:
Tools such as Nuclei can assist with authorised attack-surface validation.

Example against one authorised target:

nuclei -u https://example.com

For a target list:

nuclei -l alive-http.txt

Use appropriate rate limits and template selection for the environment.

docs.title: Nuclei Results

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Reconnaissance tools can generate substantial traffic.

Consider:

Application capacity

WAF thresholds

IDS/IPS

Rate limits

Customer monitoring

Testing window

Rules of Engagement

Start conservatively.

docs.title: OPSEC
docs.text:
Reconnaissance itself generates observable activity.

Defenders may observe:

DNS queries

Sequential connections

HTTP requests

TLS handshakes

Port scans

Directory discovery

Repeated user agents

Do not attempt to conceal activity outside the engagement requirements.

Maintain enough logging for deconfliction.

docs.title: Source Infrastructure
docs.text:
Track which infrastructure performs active reconnaissance.

Example:

Source Purpose RT01 HTTP reconnaissance RT02 Approved scanning Operator VPN Manual validation

docs.title: Deconfliction
docs.text:
Provide assessment indicators when required:

Source IP addresses

Domains

Testing windows

Operator identifiers

Known payload hashes

This helps distinguish authorised reconnaissance from unrelated malicious activity.

docs.title: Example Pipeline
docs.text:
For an authorised domain:

subfinder -d example.com -silent -o subfinder.txt

amass enum -passive -d example.com -o amass.txt

Combine:

cat subfinder.txt amass.txt | sort -u > subdomains.txt

Resolve:

dnsx -l subdomains.txt -silent -o resolved.txt

Probe HTTP:

httpx -l resolved.txt -silent -status-code -title -tech-detect -ip -o http.txt

This produces a useful first-pass HTTP attack-surface inventory.

docs.title: Reporting Reconnaissance Findings
docs.text:
Potential reportable issues include:

Unknown Internet-facing assets

Legacy systems

Exposed administrative interfaces

Sensitive metadata

Public credential exposure

Dangling DNS

Unexpected cloud resources

Excessive technology disclosure

Not every reconnaissance observation is a vulnerability.

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Title:
Unmanaged Internet-Facing Application Identified

Observation:
An externally reachable application was discovered through
Certificate Transparency and confirmed through DNS and HTTPS.

The asset was not present in the customer-provided Internet asset
inventory.

Impact:
Unknown or unmanaged Internet-facing systems may fall outside
normal vulnerability management, monitoring, and patching
processes.

Recommendation:
Validate ownership, assign an asset owner, include the system in
the central asset inventory, and ensure vulnerability management
and monitoring controls apply.

Confirmed Finding

docs.title: Assuming Every Subdomain Is Alive
docs.text:
Discovery does not equal reachability.

Validate DNS and service state.

docs.title: Assuming Every IP Is Owned by the Customer
docs.text: Cloud and CDN addresses may be shared or third-party controlled.

docs.title: Treating Technology Detection as Proof
docs.text: Fingerprinting tools can be wrong.

docs.title: Treating Version Detection as Vulnerability Confirmation
docs.text: Version matching is only one prerequisite.

docs.title: Ignoring Redirects
docs.text: A redirect may reveal the real authentication or application endpoint.

docs.title: Ignoring Non-200 Responses
docs.text:
Interesting systems may return:

301

302

401

403

404

500

A non-200 response does not mean the service is irrelevant.

docs.title: Ignoring DNS
docs.text: DNS frequently provides some of the most valuable attack-surface context.

docs.title: Ignoring Authentication
docs.text: Authentication surfaces often matter more than static corporate websites.

docs.title: Ignoring Third Parties
docs.text: Testing a discovered third-party asset without authorisation creates unnecessary risk.

docs.title: Collecting Without Analysing
docs.text:
Thousands of subdomains are not useful unless they are:

Resolved

Classified

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Reconnaissance can be reduced to:

Start with known authorised assets.

Collect passive information.

Discover candidate assets.

Resolve and validate them.

Identify live services.

Map technologies.

Map authentication.

Understand identity and cloud dependencies.

Separate customer assets from third parties.

Record confidence.

Prioritise security-relevant systems.

Preserve evidence.

Turn observations into attack hypotheses.

Revalidate scope before active testing.
