Reconnaissance should produce decisions

A list containing thousands of hostnames is not yet useful reconnaissance. The value comes from resolving, validating, classifying, scoping, enriching, and prioritising those assets until they form an understandable attack surface that can guide the next phase of the assessment.

Discovery does not equal permission

Certificate Transparency, DNS, search engines, repositories, ASN information, and cloud metadata can reveal infrastructure beyond the authorised target. Treat newly discovered assets as candidates until ownership and scope have been confirmed. Do not actively test third-party or uncertain infrastructure merely because it appears related to the organisation.

docs.title: Red Team Reporting
docs.text:
Red team reporting converts assessment activity into information that an organisation can use to reduce risk.

A useful red team report should explain:

What happened?

How did access begin?

Which security boundaries were crossed?

Which systems and identities were affected?

What attack paths were demonstrated?

Which controls prevented activity?

Which controls detected activity?

Which activity remained undetected?

How did the SOC respond?

What was the realistic impact?

What should be fixed first?

How can the organisation verify the improvements?

The objective is not to produce the largest possible collection of screenshots or commands.

The objective is to communicate the security story clearly.

Authorised assessments only

Reports should contain only information obtained during the authorised assessment. Protect credentials, customer data, internal architecture, screenshots, payload information, and other sensitive evidence according to the Rules of Engagement and applicable data-handling requirements.

docs.title: Reporting Model
docs.text:
A red team report normally serves several audiences.

                    RED TEAM REPORT
                           |
          +----------------+----------------+
          |                |                |
          v                v                v
      MANAGEMENT       SECURITY TEAM     TECHNICAL TEAM
          |                |                |
          v                v                v
     Business Risk     Attack Paths       Evidence
     Key Outcomes      Detection Gaps     Technical Detail
     Priorities        SOC Response       Remediation

Each audience needs different information.

docs.title: Core Reporting Principle
docs.text:
Do not make the reader reconstruct the engagement from raw evidence.

Instead:

Evidence
   |
   v
Observation
   |
   v
Attack Path
   |
   v
Security Impact
   |
   v
Root Cause
   |
   v
Recommendation

docs.title: Suggested Report Structure
docs.text:
A practical structure is:

1. Executive Summary

2. Engagement Overview

3. Scope

4. Objectives

5. Rules of Engagement

6. Assessment Methodology

7. Attack Narrative

8. Attack Path Summary

9. Key Findings

10. Detection and Response Assessment

11. MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

12. Recommendations

13. Strategic Improvement Roadmap

14. Retest Results

15. Cleanup Confirmation

16. Technical Findings

17. Evidence Appendix

18. Technical Appendix

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The executive summary should be understandable without requiring deep technical knowledge.

Focus on:

Overall security outcome
Business impact
Attack path
Critical weaknesses
Detection effectiveness
Response effectiveness
Priority improvements

Avoid filling the executive summary with:

Tool names
Long commands
Payload details
Raw logs
Excessive ATT&CK identifiers
Low-level technical terminology

docs.title: Executive Summary Example
docs.text:
The assessment demonstrated that an attacker with access to a
standard user account could progress through multiple security
boundaries and obtain access to systems containing elevated
administrative privileges.

The attack path was primarily enabled by excessive credential
reuse, insufficient network segmentation, and weaknesses in
administrative access controls.

Endpoint security controls detected several stages of the
assessment, including suspicious process execution and remote
administration activity. However, some authentication and lateral
movement activity did not generate actionable alerts.

The highest-priority improvements are to reduce privileged
credential exposure, strengthen administrative tiering, restrict
east-west administrative protocols, and improve correlation of
authentication and endpoint telemetry.

docs.title: Management Summary
docs.text:
A shorter management summary can follow:

Initial Access
     |
     v
Standard User
     |
     v
Credential Exposure
     |
     v
Internal Movement
     |
     v
Privileged System
     |
     v
Business Impact

Management should understand the security boundaries that failed, not every command used to cross them.

docs.title: Engagement Overview
docs.text:
Document:

Customer
Engagement type
Assessment dates
Testing team
Primary contact
Assessment model
Scope
Objectives
Assumptions
Limitations

docs.title: Engagement Type
docs.text:
Clearly identify whether the work was:

Red Team Assessment
Purple Team Assessment
Assumed Breach
Internal Red Team
External Red Team
Adversary Simulation
Detection Validation
Penetration Test

Do not use these terms interchangeably.

docs.title: Assessment Dates
docs.text:
Record:

Testing start
Testing end
Reporting period
Retest date

Use a consistent timezone.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
Examples:

Determine whether an external attacker could obtain internal access.

Determine whether a compromised standard user could reach
privileged systems.

Evaluate whether security controls detect credential access and
lateral movement.

Evaluate whether the SOC can reconstruct the attack path.

Identify opportunities to improve prevention, detection, and
response.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Document the authorised scope.

Examples:

Domains
IP ranges
Applications
Cloud tenants
User accounts
Workstations
Servers
Active Directory
Email
Physical locations
Wireless networks

docs.title: Exclusions
docs.text:
Also document exclusions.

Example:

Production denial-of-service testing

Third-party infrastructure

Destructive testing

Unapproved social engineering

Unapproved credential collection

Data modification

Persistence beyond the agreed period

docs.title: Rules of Engagement
docs.text:
Summarise relevant operational restrictions.

Examples:

Testing window
Permitted techniques
Prohibited techniques
Authentication limits
Social-engineering rules
Data-access limits
Persistence limits
Stop conditions
Emergency contacts

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Be explicit about limitations.

Examples:

Certain production systems were excluded.

Testing was limited to standard-user privileges.

Password spraying was not performed.

Social engineering was excluded.

No destructive actions were performed.

Some detection validation was performed collaboratively with the
SOC and therefore should not be interpreted as blind-response
testing.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
Examples:

Customer-provided credentials were assumed to represent a
compromised standard user.

Assessment infrastructure was assumed to be external to the
customer network.

Customer-provided asset lists were assumed to be accurate.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
Explain the assessment process.

Example:

Planning
   |
   v
Reconnaissance
   |
   v
Initial Access
   |
   v
Foothold
   |
   v
Discovery
   |
   v
Privilege Escalation
   |
   v
Credential Access
   |
   v
Lateral Movement
   |
   v
Objective
   |
   v
Detection Validation
   |
   v
Cleanup

docs.title: Methodology Should Match the Engagement
docs.text:
Do not claim:

Full red team simulation

if the engagement actually consisted of:

Known credentials
Limited internal testing
Predefined systems
Collaborative detection validation

Describe what was actually tested.

docs.title: Attack Narrative
docs.text:
The attack narrative is one of the most important parts of a red team report.

It explains the assessment as a connected sequence.

Example:

External Exposure
       |
       v
Initial Access
       |
       v
Standard User
       |
       v
Credential Discovery
       |
       v
Internal Server
       |
       v
Administrative Context
       |
       v
Sensitive Resource

docs.title: Narrative vs Findings
docs.text:
Individual findings may look like:

F01 - Credential Exposure

F02 - Weak Network Segmentation

F03 - Excessive Administrative Rights

F04 - Missing Lateral Movement Detection

But the attack narrative explains:

F01
 |
 v
enabled
 |
 v
F02
 |
 v
enabled
 |
 v
F03
 |
 v
resulting in
 |
 v
Objective

This relationship is critical.

docs.title: Attack Path Summary
docs.text:
A concise attack-path table is useful.

Stage Source Target Security Boundary Result Initial Access External WS01 Perimeter Access obtained Credential Access WS01 Local secrets Credential boundary Credential identified Lateral Movement WS01 SRV01 Network boundary Remote access obtained Privilege Escalation SRV01 Admin context Privilege boundary Elevated access Objective SRV01 Sensitive service Business boundary Access demonstrated

docs.title: Attack Path Diagram
docs.text:
Example:

                      INTERNET
                          |
                          v
                    Initial Access
                          |
                          v
                    +-----------+
                    |   WS01    |
                    | User: A   |
                    +-----------+
                          |
                    Credential
                      Exposure
                          |
                          v
                    +-----------+
                    |   SRV01   |
                    | Service   |
                    +-----------+
                          |
                   Privilege Path
                          |
                          v
                    +-----------+
                    |   ADM01   |
                    | Elevated  |
                    +-----------+
                          |
                          v
                     OBJECTIVE

docs.title: Security Boundary Model
docs.text:
A useful report should identify the boundaries crossed.

Examples:

Internet -> Internal Network

Standard User -> Local Administrator

Workstation -> Server

User Network -> Management Network

Application User -> Database

On-Premises -> Cloud

Standard Account -> Privileged Account

docs.title: Why Security Boundaries Matter
docs.text:
A remote service being reachable is not necessarily a vulnerability.

The meaningful question is:

Did the attacker cross a security boundary that should have
prevented or restricted the attack path?

docs.title: Attack Path Evidence
docs.text:
For each major transition record:

Source
Target
Identity
Privilege
Technique
Timestamp
Evidence
Security control
Result

docs.title: Attack Path Record
docs.text:
Example:

Transition:
WS01 -> SRV01

Identity:
CORP\test-user

Technique:
Approved remote administration

Expected Control:
Network segmentation and access control

Observed:
TCP/445 reachable and authentication accepted.

Result:
Security boundary crossed.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Each finding should describe a specific weakness or control gap.

Recommended structure:

Title

Severity

Description

Observation

Evidence

Attack Path

Impact

Likelihood

Root Cause

MITRE ATT&CK

Detection

Recommendation

Validation

References

docs.title: Finding Title
docs.text:
A title should describe the weakness.

Good:

Privileged Credentials Accessible to Standard Users

Better than:

Mimikatz

Good:

Workstation-to-Server Administrative Traffic Is Insufficiently Restricted

Better than:

SMB Lateral Movement

docs.title: Avoid Tool-Based Finding Titles
docs.text:
Avoid titles such as:

BloodHound Finding

NetExec Vulnerability

PowerShell Issue

Impacket Exploit

The tool is not the vulnerability.

docs.title: Finding Description
docs.text:
Explain the security condition.

Example:

Standard-user systems were able to initiate administrative
protocol connections directly to server systems.

This increases the ability of an attacker who compromises a
workstation to attempt credential reuse and lateral movement
against internal servers.

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
Describe what happened during the assessment.

Example:

From workstation WS01, the assessment team confirmed TCP
connectivity to the SMB service on SRV01.

The customer-provided assessment identity was accepted by the
remote system and provided access beyond the original workstation.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Evidence should demonstrate the observation.

Possible evidence:

Command output
Screenshot
Event log
SIEM event
EDR process tree
Authentication record
HTTP request/response
Configuration
Network capture
Cloud audit event

docs.title: Evidence Should Be Minimal
docs.text:
Do not include ten screenshots when one demonstrates the issue.

Prefer:

Evidence
   |
   v
Clear Proof

instead of:

Evidence
   |
   v
Large Raw Data Dump

docs.title: Evidence Identifier
docs.text:
Use identifiers:

EVID-001
EVID-002
EVID-003

Example:

EVID-014 - Successful authentication from WS01 to SRV01

docs.title: Evidence Metadata
docs.text:
Record:

Evidence ID
Finding ID
Timestamp
Host
User
Operator
Source
Target
Description
File
Hash where required

docs.title: Evidence Naming
docs.text:
Example:

20260905-1042-F03-WS01-SRV01-authentication.png

docs.title: Screenshot Caption
docs.text:
Example:

Figure 4 - Successful authorised authentication from WS01 to SRV01
using the assessment identity.

Captions should explain what the reader should notice.

docs.title: Sensitive Evidence
docs.text:
Do not expose reusable secrets in the report.

Redact:

Passwords
API tokens
Session cookies
Private keys
Reusable hashes
Authentication tokens
Personal data

Retain original evidence securely if required.

docs.title: Command Evidence
docs.text:
Commands can be useful when they explain reproducibility.

Example:

Test-NetConnection SRV01 -Port 445

Do not turn the main report into a command transcript.

docs.title: Output Evidence
docs.text:
Show only relevant output.

Example:

ComputerName     : SRV01
RemotePort       : 445
TcpTestSucceeded : True

This demonstrates reachability without unnecessary output.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Explain what the weakness enables.

Weak:

An attacker could use this.

Better:

An attacker who compromises a standard workstation may be able to
reuse valid credentials against internal server systems, increasing
the likelihood that a single endpoint compromise progresses into a
broader internal compromise.

docs.title: Impact Categories
docs.text:
Consider:

Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Privilege
Identity
Network reach
Business process
Detection capability
Recovery capability

docs.title: Do Not Overstate Impact
docs.text:
If testing demonstrated:

Remote service reachable

do not automatically report:

Full domain compromise possible.

Use evidence-based language.

docs.title: Evidence Strength
docs.text:
Useful classifications:

Candidate

Likely

Confirmed

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text:
Example:

A potentially exploitable configuration was identified but was not
validated.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
Example:

The prerequisite conditions appear to be present, but exploitation
was not performed because of engagement restrictions.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
Example:

The assessment team successfully crossed the security boundary
using the authorised validation procedure.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Root cause describes why the weakness exists.

Examples:

Credential reuse

Excessive privilege

Missing segmentation

Weak application control

Inadequate secret management

Insufficient authentication policy

Legacy protocol dependency

Missing logging

Missing detection logic

Configuration drift

Inadequate administrative tiering

docs.title: Root Cause vs Symptom
docs.text:
Example symptom:

Remote administration succeeded.

Potential root cause:

Administrative access from user workstations is not restricted.

Fixing the root cause is more valuable.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity should represent demonstrated risk.

Consider:

Impact

Likelihood

Privilege obtained

Asset criticality

Attack complexity

Prerequisites

User interaction

Security boundary crossed

Detection capability

Compensating controls

docs.title: Example Severity Model
docs.text:
Critical
Direct path to highly privileged or business-critical compromise
with limited prerequisites.

High
Significant security boundary can be crossed and meaningful
privilege or sensitive access obtained.

Medium
Useful attacker capability exists but meaningful prerequisites,
limitations, or compensating controls apply.

Low
Limited security impact or significant constraints.

Informational
Observation or improvement opportunity without demonstrated
security impact.

docs.title: Severity Is Not Technique Severity
docs.text:
Do not assign severity because:

Pass-the-Hash = High

or:

PowerShell = Medium

Severity depends on the actual environment and impact.

docs.title: Attack Path Severity
docs.text:
An individual weakness may be moderate alone but important in a chain.

Example:

Weakness A - Medium
       |
       v
Weakness B - Medium
       |
       v
Weakness C - Medium
       |
       v
Domain-Level Impact

The report should highlight this chain.

docs.title: Likelihood
docs.text:
Consider:

Required access
Required privilege
Required credentials
Network reachability
User interaction
Exploit reliability
Existing security controls
Attacker knowledge
Repeatability

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Recommendations should address the root cause.

Weak:

Block PowerShell.

Better:

Restrict unnecessary PowerShell capabilities for standard users,
enforce application-control policy, enable appropriate PowerShell
logging, and ensure endpoint detections cover suspicious
interpreter behaviour.

docs.title: Recommendation Layers
docs.text:
Useful structure:

Immediate
   |
   v
Tactical
   |
   v
Strategic

docs.title: Immediate Recommendation
docs.text:
Example:

Rotate the exposed credential and terminate active sessions.

docs.title: Tactical Recommendation
docs.text:
Example:

Remove the credential from the affected configuration and migrate
the application to an approved secret-management mechanism.

docs.title: Strategic Recommendation
docs.text:
Example:

Implement centralised secret management and automated secret
scanning across repositories and deployment pipelines.

docs.title: Recommendation Ownership
docs.text:
Where practical, associate recommendations with responsible teams.

Example:

Recommendation Owner Restrict SMB between workstation and server networks Network Security Deploy LAPS Endpoint Engineering Improve 4624/4648 correlation Detection Engineering Rotate service account Identity Team

docs.title: Recommendation Priority
docs.text:
Example:

P0 - Emergency

P1 - Immediate

P2 - Near Term

P3 - Planned Improvement

docs.title: Remediation Roadmap
docs.text:
Example:

Priority Improvement Target P1 Rotate exposed credentials Immediate P1 Restrict workstation-to-server admin protocols 30 days P2 Deploy LAPS broadly 60 days P2 Improve lateral movement detections 60 days P3 Implement privileged access workstations Strategic

docs.title: Prevention, Detection, Response
docs.text:
For each important attack path, consider all three.

                     Attack Technique
                           |
          +----------------+----------------+
          |                |                |
          v                v                v
      Prevention       Detection         Response

docs.title: Prevention Reporting
docs.text:
Document:

Control expected
Control observed
Whether activity was prevented
Control weakness
Recommendation

docs.title: Detection Reporting
docs.text:
Document:

Telemetry expected
Telemetry observed
EDR event
SIEM event
Detection rule
Alert
Severity
Time to detect

docs.title: Response Reporting
docs.text:
Document:

Alert received
Analyst acknowledgement
Investigation
Escalation
Containment
Recovery

docs.title: Detection Result Table
docs.text: Technique Prevented Telemetry Alert SOC Response Result Controlled PowerShell No Yes Yes Yes Effective Scheduled Task No Yes No No Detection gap Lateral Movement No Yes Yes Yes Effective HTTPS C2 Simulation No Partial No No Visibility gap

docs.title: Positive Security Results
docs.text:
A red team report should also document controls that worked.

Examples:

Microsoft Defender blocked the EICAR test artifact.

AppLocker prevented execution from the tested user-writable path.

The SOC detected remote authentication within two minutes.

Network segmentation prevented direct RDP access.

MFA prevented authentication using the compromised password.

This gives a balanced assessment.

docs.title: Detection Gap Categories
docs.text:
Useful categories:

Telemetry Gap

Collection Gap

Parsing Gap

Detection Gap

Correlation Gap

Alerting Gap

Triage Gap

Response Gap

docs.title: Detection Gap Example
docs.text:
The endpoint generated the expected process telemetry and the event
was successfully forwarded to the SIEM.

No detection rule generated an alert.

This represents a detection-logic gap rather than a telemetry gap.

docs.title: Telemetry Gap Example
docs.text:
The controlled activity was successfully executed, but the
required endpoint telemetry was not available locally or in the
central security platform.

docs.title: Collection Gap Example
docs.text:
The expected event was present on the endpoint but was not present
in the SIEM during the assessment window.

docs.title: SOC Response
docs.text:
Record:

Detection time
Acknowledgement time
Triage time
Investigation time
Containment time
Escalation path
Correctness of conclusion

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
Maintain a timeline of important events.

Example:

Time Stage Source Target Result 09:05 Initial Access External WS01 Access 09:32 Discovery WS01 AD Successful 10:04 Credential Access WS01 Local Credential identified 10:42 Lateral Movement WS01 SRV01 Successful 10:44 Detection EDR SOC Alert 10:47 SOC Analyst Alert Investigating 11:02 Objective SRV01 Resource Demonstrated

docs.title: Attack Timeline Diagram
docs.text:
09:05              10:04              10:42              11:02
  |                   |                  |                  |
  v                   v                  v                  v
Initial            Credential          Lateral          Objective
Access              Access             Movement
  |                   |                  |
  +-------------------+------------------+
                      |
                      v
                 SOC Detection
                    10:44

docs.title: Time to Detect
docs.text: TTD = Detection Time - Activity Time

docs.title: Time to Respond
docs.text:
Define the response point clearly.

Example:

TTR = Containment Time - Detection Time

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Useful metrics may include:

Objectives achieved
Security boundaries crossed
Critical attack paths
Findings by severity
Techniques tested
Techniques prevented
Techniques detected
Techniques not detected
SOC investigations
Mean time to detect
Mean time to respond
Retests passed

docs.title: Example Metrics
docs.text:
Assessment objectives:        5

Objectives achieved:          4

Security boundaries crossed:  3

Techniques validated:         18

Prevented:                    5

Detected:                    11

Logged but not alerted:       4

No useful visibility:         3

SOC investigations:           9

docs.title: Metrics Need Context
docs.text:
Avoid:

EDR detected 75 percent of attacks.

unless the methodology supports that conclusion.

Prefer:

Nine of the twelve selected techniques for which an EDR alert was
expected generated the anticipated alert during the assessment.

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK Mapping
docs.text:
Map observed behaviour to ATT&CK where useful.

Example:

Stage ATT&CK Tactic Technique Execution Execution PowerShell Credential Access Credential Access Unsecured Credentials Lateral Movement Lateral Movement Remote Services Persistence Persistence Scheduled Task/Job C2 Command and Control Application Layer Protocol

docs.title: ATT&CK Mapping Purpose
docs.text:
ATT&CK can help:

Standardise terminology

Map attack paths

Map detections

Identify coverage gaps

Compare exercises

Plan retesting

ATT&CK should support the report, not dominate it.

docs.title: Do Not Over-Map
docs.text:
One command may theoretically map to several techniques.

Only include mappings that meaningfully describe the tested behaviour.

docs.title: ATT&CK Coverage
docs.text:
A useful model:

Technique Tested
      |
      v
Telemetry?
 /        \
No         Yes
|           |
Gap         v
        Detection?
         /      \
       No        Yes
       |          |
      Gap         v
              Response?
               /     \
             No       Yes
             |         |
            Gap      Validated

docs.title: ATT&CK Coverage Table
docs.text: Technique Tested Telemetry Detection Response T1059.001 Yes Yes Yes Yes T1021.002 Yes Yes No No T1053 Yes Yes Yes No

docs.title: ATT&CK Heatmaps
docs.text:
If an ATT&CK heatmap is included, explain what the colours represent.

Example:

Green  = Tested and detected

Yellow = Tested with partial visibility

Red    = Tested without expected detection

Grey   = Not tested

Do not present untested techniques as validated coverage.

docs.title: Technical Findings
docs.text:
Technical findings should contain enough detail for remediation and retesting.

Recommended format:

Finding ID

Title

Severity

Affected Systems

Description

Prerequisites

Observation

Evidence

Impact

Attack Path

Detection

Root Cause

Recommendation

Validation Procedure

References

docs.title: Finding ID
docs.text:
Use consistent identifiers.

Example:

RT-01
RT-02
RT-03

or:

FIND-001
FIND-002

docs.title: Affected Systems
docs.text:
List:

Hostname
IP
Application
Domain
Cloud resource
Identity

Do not write:

All systems

unless that was actually established.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Document what an attacker needs.

Examples:

Internal network access

Standard domain account

Local workstation access

Compromised service account

Access to specific subnet

docs.title: Reproduction
docs.text:
For findings where reproduction is useful, document a minimal validation procedure.

Prefer:

1. Authenticate using an authorised test identity.

2. Confirm the target service is reachable.

3. Perform the minimum action required to demonstrate the boundary.

4. Record the result.

5. Stop.

6. Cleanup.

Avoid unnecessary destructive or intrusive reproduction steps.

docs.title: Validation Procedure
docs.text:
The recommendation should be testable.

Example:

After implementing network restrictions, repeat the TCP
connectivity test from a standard workstation.

Administrative SMB and WinRM access to server networks should no
longer be available unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
A retest should answer:

Was the original weakness fixed?

Can the original attack path still be completed?

Did the remediation introduce another path?

Does detection now work?

Is the control consistently enforced?

docs.title: Retest Status
docs.text:
Use:

Resolved

Partially Resolved

Not Resolved

Not Retested

Risk Accepted

docs.title: Retest Table
docs.text: Finding Original Retest Status RT-01 High Blocked Resolved RT-02 High Partial restriction Partially Resolved RT-03 Medium Alert generated Resolved

docs.title: Retest Evidence
docs.text:
Preserve:

Original evidence

Remediation description

Retest date

Retest action

Retest evidence

Final result

docs.title: Attack Path Retesting
docs.text:
Do not only retest individual findings.

Retest the complete path where appropriate.

Original:

A -> B -> C -> D


After remediation:

A -> B -> X

This demonstrates whether the attack chain was actually broken.

docs.title: Strategic Recommendations
docs.text:
Individual findings often share root causes.

Group them into themes.

Examples:

Identity Security

Privileged Access

Network Segmentation

Endpoint Hardening

Application Control

Credential Management

Detection Engineering

Security Monitoring

SOC Response

Cloud Security

docs.title: Strategic Roadmap
docs.text:
Example:

0-30 Days
    |
    +--> Rotate exposed credentials
    +--> Restrict high-risk remote administration
    +--> Fix critical detection gaps

30-90 Days
    |
    +--> Deploy LAPS
    +--> Improve segmentation
    +--> Improve central logging
    +--> Expand identity detections

90+ Days
    |
    +--> Administrative tiering
    +--> Privileged access workstations
    +--> Continuous ATT&CK validation
    +--> Purple team programme

docs.title: Prioritise Attack-Path Breakers
docs.text:
A useful question is:

Which remediation breaks the largest number of demonstrated
attack paths?

Example:

                 Credential Reuse
                       |
          +------------+------------+
          |            |            |
          v            v            v
        SRV01        SRV02        SRV03

Eliminating credential reuse may remove multiple paths at once.

docs.title: Compensating Controls
docs.text:
If immediate remediation is difficult, document compensating controls.

Examples:

Network restriction
Additional monitoring
MFA
Temporary account restrictions
Increased alerting
Manual review
EDR policy
Firewall rule

docs.title: Risk Acceptance
docs.text:
If a risk is accepted, record:

Finding
Risk owner
Reason
Compensating controls
Review date
Approval

docs.title: Cleanup Reporting
docs.text:
The report should confirm introduced artifacts were addressed.

Possible artifacts:

Payloads
Scripts
Accounts
Services
Scheduled tasks
Registry modifications
SSH keys
Certificates
Routes
Tunnels
C2 sessions
Cloud resources
DNS records
Firewall rules
Temporary files

docs.title: Cleanup Statement
docs.text:
Example:

All known assessment artifacts introduced by the red team were
removed at the conclusion of testing.

Temporary infrastructure and assessment credentials were revoked
or decommissioned according to the engagement cleanup inventory.

docs.title: Cleanup Exceptions
docs.text:
If something remains:

Artifact:
RT monitoring account

Reason:
Customer requested retention for retesting.

Owner:
Customer Security Team

Action:
Customer assumes ownership.

docs.title: Evidence Appendix
docs.text:
A technical evidence appendix can contain:

Evidence ID

Finding

Timestamp

Host

User

Description

docs.title: Report Language
docs.text:
Use evidence-based language.

Prefer:

docs.title: Avoid Absolute Claims
docs.text:

docs.title: Accurate Control Language
docs.text:
Distinguish:

Allowed

Blocked

Logged

Detected

Alerted

Investigated

Contained

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Do not write:

when the evidence shows:

alert that was visible in the security platform.

That is a detection success, not a complete failure.

docs.title: Another Example
docs.text:
Do not write:

when:

The tested binary was allowed because the applicable AppLocker
collection did not contain an enforced rule restricting that path.

Report the actual policy condition.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
A red team report can be reduced to:

Do not report only what commands worked.

Explain the attack path.

Explain which security boundaries were crossed.

Explain why those boundaries could be crossed.

Show enough evidence to prove the result.

Separate prevention from detection.

Explain what defenders saw.

Explain what defenders missed.

Describe the realistic business impact.

Recommend controls that break the attack path.

Provide a way to validate those controls.

Retest the complete path where appropriate.

Report attack paths, not just vulnerabilities

The most useful red team report explains how multiple weaknesses interacted. A credential exposure issue, permissive network path, excessive privilege, and missing detection may each appear manageable in isolation but together form a path to a critical objective. Prioritising controls that break these paths usually provides more value than treating every observation as an independent vulnerability.

Protect the report

A red team report may provide a detailed map of an organisation's security weaknesses, identities, internal architecture, detection gaps, and attack paths. Treat the report and its evidence as sensitive security information, distribute it only through approved channels, remove reusable credentials from distributed copies, and apply the agreed retention and deletion requirements.

docs.title: Red Team Social Engineering
docs.text:
Social engineering tests whether an attacker can influence people or abuse organisational processes to gain access, obtain information or advance an attack path.

Technical security controls may be strong while human and procedural controls remain vulnerable.

Examples include:

Help desk verification

Telephone requests

Impersonation scenarios

Physical access requests

Information elicitation

Account recovery

Password reset processes

MFA recovery

Visitor procedures

Third-party verification

Business process manipulation

Social engineering should be treated as a controlled security exercise rather than an unrestricted attempt to deceive employees.

Authorised Scenario
       |
       v
Defined Target Group
       |
       v
Approved Pretext
       |
       v
Controlled Interaction
       |
       v
Security Decision
       |
       v
Detection / Escalation
       |
       v
Evidence
       |
       v
Debrief / Cleanup

Explicit authorisation required

Social engineering directly involves people and may expose personal information, cause distress or disrupt business processes. The exact techniques, target groups, communication channels, prohibited actions, escalation procedures and stop conditions should be explicitly defined in the Rules of Engagement.

docs.title: Social Engineering Objectives
docs.text:
Typical objectives include:

Validate employee security awareness

Validate help desk identity verification

Validate password reset procedures

Validate MFA recovery procedures

Validate visitor management

Validate physical security processes

Validate sensitive-information handling

Validate escalation procedures

Validate reporting mechanisms

Measure SOC or security-team visibility

docs.title: Social Engineering Is a Process Test
docs.text:
A successful social engineering interaction does not necessarily mean:

Employee failed.

The underlying problem may instead involve:

Weak verification procedures

Ambiguous policy

Insufficient training

Poor escalation paths

Excessive help desk authority

Weak visitor controls

Missing technical enforcement

Unsafe recovery procedures

Focus reporting on the security process rather than blaming individuals.

docs.title: Human Layer of Security
docs.text:
Security controls can be represented as:

Technology
    |
    v
Process
    |
    v
People

An attacker may target whichever layer provides the easiest path.

For example:

Strong MFA
   |
   v
Account Recovery
   |
   v
Help Desk
   |
   v
Weak Verification
   |
   v
Account Access

The technical control may be strong while the recovery process undermines it.

docs.text:
Weak verification may rely on information such as:

Employee name

Job title

Department

Manager name

Office location

Email address

Much of this information may be publicly available.

These attributes should generally not be treated as strong authentication factors.

docs.text:

docs.text:
If password reset testing is authorised, prefer a dedicated test account.

Example:

Objective:

verification process before initiating password recovery.

Do not reset a real employee's password merely to prove the process weakness.

docs.title: MFA Recovery
docs.text:
MFA recovery may include:

Authenticator replacement

Phone-number change

Temporary access pass

Hardware-token replacement

MFA reset

New-device enrolment

These are high-impact actions and should be specifically addressed in the ROE.

docs.title: Information Elicitation
docs.text:
Information elicitation tests whether personnel disclose information that should be protected.

Potential categories include:

Internal processes

System names

Employee information

Technology details

Support procedures

Vendor information

Office procedures

Avoid requesting real credentials or unnecessary personal information.

docs.title: Information Classification
docs.text:
Before testing, define which information is:

Public

Internal

Confidential

Restricted

A useful finding requires demonstrating disclosure of information that actually should have been protected.

docs.title: Public Information Is Not a Finding
docs.text:
For example:

Employee reveals company headquarters address.

If the address is public, this is not meaningful information disclosure.

Instead test whether restricted information can be obtained.

docs.title: Minimal Information Collection
docs.text:
If an employee begins disclosing more information than required:

Objective Proven
      |
      v
Stop Collection
      |
      v
Record Minimum Evidence

Do not continue gathering sensitive information unnecessarily.

docs.text:

Escort requirements

Visitor logging

Physical testing requires particularly clear authorisation.

docs.title: Physical Scope
docs.text:
Define:

Buildings

Floors

Rooms

Restricted areas

Working hours

Allowed entrances

Prohibited areas

Safety-critical areas

docs.title: Areas Commonly Excluded
docs.text:
Possible exclusions include:

Data centres

Medical areas

Industrial control areas

Safety-critical facilities

Executive residences

Childcare areas

Emergency facilities

The actual exclusions depend on the engagement.

docs.title: Visitor Management
docs.text:
A mature visitor process may require:

Identity verification

Host confirmation

Visitor registration

Temporary badge

Escort

Badge return

Entry/exit logging

docs.title: Visitor Test Model
docs.text:
Arrival
   |
   v
Reception
   |
   v
Identity Checked?
   |
   v
Host Confirmed?
   |
   v
Badge Issued?
   |
   v
Escort Required?
   |
   v
Access Decision

docs.title: Tailgating
docs.text:
Tailgating occurs when an unauthorised person follows an authorised person through a controlled entry point.

In testing, define:

Which doors may be tested?

Can employees be approached?

Can testers follow employees?

What happens if challenged?

When must the test stop?

Do not force doors or physically pressure employees.

docs.title: Piggybacking
docs.text:
Piggybacking generally involves an authorised person knowingly allowing another person to enter.

The assessment should record whether:

Badge verification occurred

Visitor status was checked

Escort policy was followed

Security was contacted

docs.title: Restricted Area Validation
docs.text:
Once access to a controlled area is achieved:

Stop when the objective is proven.

Do not continue deeper into the building merely because additional access appears possible.

docs.title: Physical Proof
docs.text:
Possible proof includes:

Timestamp

Approved photograph

Location identifier

Access log

Tester notes

Customer-provided marker

Avoid photographing employees or sensitive material unnecessarily.

docs.title: Clean Desk Testing
docs.text:
If explicitly authorised, physical testing may evaluate whether sensitive material is exposed.

Potential examples:

Printed confidential documents

Unlocked workstations

Visible credentials

Sensitive whiteboards

Unattended access cards

Do not collect or remove real employee property.

docs.title: USB Drop Exercises
docs.text:
USB-drop exercises may test whether employees connect unknown removable media.

A safe exercise should use:

Customer-approved devices

Clearly inventoried media

Non-malicious content

Unique identifiers

Controlled telemetry

Avoid deploying executable payloads unless separately authorised and necessary.

docs.title: Safe USB Marker
docs.text:
A test device could contain:

README.txt

with an engagement identifier.

The goal might be to measure:

Device insertion

Security alert

Employee reporting

SOC response

rather than executing code.

docs.title: QR Code Exercises
docs.text:
QR codes can be used in awareness exercises.

A controlled QR code should lead only to:

Customer-controlled test page

Red-team-controlled approved test page

Do not collect real credentials.

docs.title: QR Test Metrics
docs.text:
Possible metrics include:

Scans

Unique test sessions

Reporting

Time to report

Security-team response

docs.title: Third-Party Impersonation
docs.text:
Vendor or supplier impersonation can create legal and reputational risks.

Only use an actual third-party identity if explicitly approved.

Prefer:

Synthetic vendor

Customer-created test supplier

Generic support scenario

docs.title: Executive Impersonation
docs.text:
Executive impersonation may be particularly persuasive.

It may also create:

Reputational risk

Employee stress

Financial risk

Escalation risk

Use only when explicitly authorised and necessary.

docs.title: Finance Scenarios
docs.text:
Finance-related social engineering may test:

Payment-change procedures

Supplier verification

Invoice handling

Bank-detail changes

Approval workflows

Do not request or cause real financial transfers.

docs.title: Safe Finance Test
docs.text:
Use:

Synthetic supplier

Test invoice

Dummy account information

Non-production workflow

The objective should be to test the process without creating financial impact.

docs.title: Business Email Compromise Simulation
docs.text:
BEC-style exercises may test whether:

Payment requests are independently verified

Supplier changes require secondary approval

Executive requests bypass normal process

Employees report suspicious messages

No real payment should occur.

docs.title: HR Scenarios
docs.text:
HR processes may expose:

Employee information

Account onboarding

Account termination

Identity information

Payroll processes

Avoid collecting real HR data unless explicitly necessary.

docs.title: Onboarding
docs.text:
Potential test questions include:

Can an unverified person obtain account details?

Can equipment be collected without sufficient identity verification?

Can access be provisioned before approval?

docs.title: Offboarding
docs.text:
Potential security questions include:

Are accounts disabled promptly?

Are badges revoked?

Are sessions terminated?

Are devices recovered?

Are tokens revoked?

These are usually better tested with synthetic or controlled accounts.

docs.title: Remote Work
docs.text:
Remote working introduces additional verification challenges.

Examples:

Employees cannot physically verify colleagues

Help desk interactions occur remotely

Personal phone numbers may be used

Courier delivery may be involved

Video meetings may substitute in-person contact

docs.title: Video Conferencing
docs.text:
Video calls should not automatically be considered strong identity proof.

Consider:

Known corporate account

Meeting invitation origin

Existing authenticated identity

Secondary verification

Do not design exercises around deceptive synthetic media unless explicitly authorised.

docs.title: Deepfake and Synthetic Media
docs.text:
AI-generated voice or video introduces new social engineering risks.

Testing with synthetic media requires explicit approval because it can create significant:

Reputational risk

Privacy risk

Psychological impact

Legal concerns

A safer initial exercise is tabletop validation:

Would the help desk accept a video call as identity proof?

Would finance accept voice approval?

What secondary controls exist?

docs.title: Reporting Mechanisms
docs.text:
Employees need a clear way to report suspicious activity.

Possible channels include:

Phishing-report button

Security mailbox

Help desk

SOC hotline

Teams/Slack security channel

Incident portal

docs.title: Reporting Validation
docs.text:
Measure whether employees:

Recognise suspicious behaviour

Know where to report it

Report quickly

Provide useful context

docs.title: Positive Security Behaviour
docs.text:
Examples include:

Employee refuses the request

Employee follows verification procedure

Employee contacts manager

Employee reports the interaction

Reception challenges the visitor

Help desk escalates the request

These should be reported as positive security outcomes.

docs.title: Do Not Punish Employees for Reporting
docs.text:
If an employee becomes suspicious and reports the exercise:

That is success.

The red team should not continue manipulating the person merely to achieve a technical objective.

docs.title: Security Awareness
docs.text:
Awareness should focus on behaviours such as:

Verify unusual requests

Use approved communication channels

Do not share authentication factors

Challenge unknown visitors

Report suspicious interactions

Follow payment verification procedures

Escalate uncertainty

docs.title: Detection Validation
docs.text:
Social engineering can also test organisational detection and response.

Potential telemetry includes:

Help desk tickets

Password reset logs

MFA reset logs

Identity audit logs

Visitor management logs

Physical access logs

Email telemetry

Endpoint telemetry

Security reports

docs.title: Identity Telemetry
docs.text:
Account recovery may generate:

Password reset events

MFA changes

Authentication events

New-device registration

Temporary access credentials

Administrative actions

Validate whether these events reach the SIEM where appropriate.

docs.title: Help Desk Audit
docs.text:
Help desk platforms may record:

Ticket creation

Requester identity

Agent identity

Actions taken

Approval

Notes

Timestamps

These records can provide valuable evidence.

docs.title: Physical Access Telemetry
docs.text:
Possible sources include:

Badge access

Visitor-management platform

Reception logs

CCTV

Door alarms

Security reports

Use CCTV only according to organisational policy and engagement authorisation.

docs.title: Detection Hypothesis
docs.text:
Example:

Hypothesis:
An unusual MFA recovery request for the synthetic red team
account should require enhanced verification and generate
identity audit telemetry.

Test:
Request MFA recovery through the authorised help desk scenario.

Expected:
The help desk performs the documented verification process and
the recovery request is logged.

Result:
Record verification, approval, telemetry and escalation.

docs.title: Physical Detection Hypothesis
docs.text:
Hypothesis:
An unknown visitor attempting to enter a restricted office area
without an escort should be challenged and reported.

Test:
Use the approved visitor scenario at the agreed location.

Expected:
Reception or staff challenge the tester and follow the visitor
management procedure.

Result:
Record whether the procedure was followed.

docs.title: Detection Outcomes
docs.text:
Classify outcomes as:

Prevented and Reported

Prevented but Not Reported

Allowed and Detected

Allowed and Logged

Allowed without Detection

docs.title: Human Outcome Classification
docs.text:
For social engineering, another useful classification is:

Request Refused

Verification Performed

Request Escalated

Information Disclosed

Sensitive Action Initiated

Sensitive Action Completed

docs.title: Example Outcome
docs.text:
Scenario:
SE-006

Objective:
Help desk account recovery

Account:
Synthetic test user

Result:
Agent requested employee ID and manager name.

Both values were part of the approved pretext and were publicly
available within the test scenario.

No secondary verification was performed.

Password recovery was initiated.

Classification:
Sensitive Action Initiated

Security Team Alert:
None

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text: The help desk appears to rely on knowledge-based verification.

docs.title: Likely
docs.text:
The requested verification information can be obtained from
public or organisational sources.

docs.title: Confirmed
docs.text:
The help desk initiated account recovery for the synthetic test
account using only the approved knowledge-based information.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Social engineering evidence may include:

Scenario ID

Date and time

Channel

Target function

Tester identity

Approved pretext

Request

Verification performed

Information disclosed

Action performed

Escalation

Security report

Detection result

Outcome

docs.title: Personal Data in Evidence
docs.text:
Avoid recording unnecessary:

Employee names

Personal phone numbers

Private conversations

Personal email addresses

Photographs

Voice recordings

Use role-based descriptions where possible.

For example:

Service Desk Agent 1

instead of a full employee name.

docs.title: Recording Calls
docs.text:
Do not record telephone or video interactions unless explicitly approved and legally reviewed.

Tester notes may provide sufficient evidence.

docs.title: Evidence Example
docs.text:
Scenario ID:
SE-003

Channel:
Telephone

Target:
Service Desk

Objective:
Validate identity verification for test account recovery

Identity:
Synthetic employee

Request:
Password recovery

Verification:
Employee ID and manager name requested

Result:
Recovery initiated

Additional Verification:
None

Security Report:
None observed

Production Credentials Collected:
No

Impact:
The tested recovery process relied on information available to
the approved test scenario.

docs.title: Evidence Strength
docs.text:
Use:

Observed

Likely

Confirmed

Do not convert assumptions into confirmed findings.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
A social engineering finding should explain:

Which process was tested?

What was requested?

Which verification occurred?

Which security decision was made?

What technical or procedural control was missing?

What was the potential impact?

How should the process improve?

docs.title: Avoid Employee-Blaming Language
docs.text:
Avoid:

The employee was careless and gave the attacker access.

Prefer:

The tested visitor process allowed access without requiring the
documented host verification step.

Focus on systemic improvement.

docs.title: Example Finding - Help Desk Verification
docs.text:
Title:
Help Desk Account Recovery Relies on Publicly Obtainable Information

Observation:
During an authorised telephone social engineering scenario, the
assessment requested account recovery for a customer-provided
synthetic user.

The service desk requested the employee identifier, department
and manager name before initiating the recovery process.

No existing authenticator, trusted device or independent
approval was required.

The information used during the test was part of the approved
scenario and did not include production credentials.

Impact:
An attacker who obtains basic employee information may be able
to abuse the tested recovery process to weaken or bypass normal
authentication controls.

Recommendation:
Strengthen account-recovery verification using independent
factors such as existing authenticators, managed devices,
verified manager approval or dedicated identity-verification
workflows. Do not rely solely on publicly obtainable employee
attributes.

docs.title: Example Finding - Visitor Management
docs.text:
Title:
Visitors Can Enter Restricted Office Area Without Host Verification

Observation:
During the approved physical security scenario, the tester
requested access to the office using the agreed synthetic vendor
pretext.

A visitor badge was issued without contacting the stated host.

The tester stopped after entering the authorised test area.

No restricted rooms or employee systems were accessed.

Impact:
An unauthorised individual may be able to gain physical access
to office areas without confirmation from an employee sponsor.

Recommendation:
Require host verification before issuing visitor credentials,
enforce escort requirements and periodically review visitor
management procedures with reception and security personnel.

docs.title: Example Finding - Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Title:
Internal Support Information Disclosed Without Requester Verification

Observation:
During the authorised telephone scenario, the tester requested
internal support information while using the approved synthetic
employee identity.

The requested information was provided without verifying the
requester's identity.

Impact:
Disclosure of internal operational information may assist an
attacker in developing more convincing social engineering
scenarios or identifying additional attack paths.

Recommendation:
Define which support information requires requester verification
and provide staff with clear escalation procedures for unusual
requests.

docs.title: Example Positive Security Result
docs.text:
Control:
Service Desk Identity Verification

Scenario:
The tester requested MFA recovery for a synthetic employee.

Result:
The service desk refused to perform the recovery because the
tester could not complete verification using the existing
registered authenticator.

The agent also created a security ticket and escalated the
interaction.

Conclusion:
The tested recovery process successfully resisted the social
engineering scenario.

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text:
Common root causes include:

Weak identity verification

Knowledge-based authentication

Unclear procedures

Inconsistent processes

Insufficient staff training

Missing escalation paths

Excessive help desk authority

Weak visitor management

Lack of secondary approval

Insufficient audit logging

Weak recovery controls

docs.title: Remediation - Help Desk
docs.text:
Consider:

Documented verification workflows

Existing-authenticator verification

Managed-device verification

Independent manager approval

Risk-based recovery

High-risk action escalation

User notifications

Audit logging

Regular process testing

docs.title: Remediation - Identity Recovery
docs.text:
Consider:

Recovery controls equivalent to primary authentication strength

Multiple independent verification signals

Temporary recovery credentials

Short validity periods

Immediate user notification

Administrative audit

SIEM integration

docs.title: Remediation - Physical Security
docs.text:
Consider:

Visitor registration

Identity checks

Host confirmation

Visitor badges

Escort requirements

Badge expiration

Badge return

Restricted-area controls

Security awareness

docs.title: Remediation - Employees
docs.text:
Provide practical guidance:

Verify unusual requests

Use official directories

Do not trust caller ID alone

Do not disclose authentication factors

Do not bypass procedures because a request appears urgent

Report suspicious interactions

Challenge unknown visitors according to policy

docs.title: Remediation - Finance
docs.text:
Consider:

Independent payment verification

Known contact details

Dual approval

Supplier-change verification

Out-of-band confirmation

Transaction limits

Fraud monitoring

docs.title: Debriefing
docs.text:
Social engineering exercises should include a controlled debrief.

Possible objectives:

Explain the exercise

Reduce employee uncertainty

Reinforce positive behaviour

Explain observed weaknesses

Provide practical guidance

Collect participant feedback

docs.title: Individual vs Group Debrief
docs.text:
Depending on the exercise:

Immediate individual debrief

Delayed individual debrief

Team debrief

Organisation-wide awareness session

may be appropriate.

The engagement plan should define the approach.

docs.title: Protect Participants
docs.text:
Reports should normally avoid creating a public list of:

Employees who clicked

Employees who answered calls

Employees who disclosed information

Aggregate metrics and process-level findings are often more useful.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Useful metrics may include:

Interactions attempted

Interactions completed

Requests refused

Verification performed

Requests escalated

Security reports submitted

Sensitive actions initiated

Sensitive actions completed

Time to report

Time to security response

docs.title: Example Metrics
docs.text:
Telephone scenarios:
10

Requests refused:
6

Requests escalated:
3

Sensitive action initiated:
1

Sensitive action completed:
0

Security reports:
4

Median time to report:
7 minutes

docs.title: Success Rate
docs.text:
A simple scenario success rate can be calculated as:

Successful Scenarios / Completed Scenarios * 100

But do not use this metric without context.

For example:

2 of 10 interactions resulted in information disclosure

does not explain:

What information?

How sensitive?

Which process?

What verification was expected?

docs.title: Better Metrics
docs.text:
Prefer metrics linked to control behaviour:

Percentage performing required verification

Percentage escalating unusual requests

Percentage reporting suspicious interactions

Percentage of high-risk actions requiring secondary approval

docs.title: Time to Report
docs.text:
TTR = Security Report Time - Interaction Time

This can measure awareness and reporting effectiveness.

docs.title: Scenario Inventory
docs.text:
Maintain:

ID Channel Target Function Objective Status SE-001 Phone Help Desk Password recovery Complete SE-002 Physical Reception Visitor control Complete SE-003 Phone Finance Process verification Stopped SE-004 QR General Staff Reporting Planned

docs.title: Stop Conditions
docs.text:
Stop immediately if:

Employee becomes distressed

Emergency services are contacted

Real financial action begins

Unexpected sensitive data is disclosed

A production account may be disrupted

A third party becomes involved unexpectedly

Physical safety is affected

Tester enters an excluded area

The scenario leaves the approved scope

docs.title: Emergency Contact
docs.text:
The red team should have:

Primary engagement contact

Backup contact

Security contact

Physical security contact

Emergency stop phrase

available during testing.

docs.title: Deconfliction
docs.text:
Security teams may encounter activity that appears malicious.

A deconfliction process should allow authorised personnel to determine:

Is this part of the exercise?

Is this a real attack?

Should the exercise continue?

Should the test be stopped?

without unnecessarily revealing the exercise to all participants.

docs.title: Social Engineering and OPSEC
docs.text:
Protect:

Target lists

Employee information

Pretexts

Synthetic identities

Scenario documents

Call notes

Physical access information

Evidence

See:

Red Team OPSEC

docs.title: Social Engineering and Detection Validation
docs.text:
The exercise should evaluate:

Human detection

Technical telemetry

Reporting

Escalation

SOC correlation

Response

See:

Detection Validation

docs.title: Social Engineering and Reporting
docs.text:
Report:

Process weaknesses

Control strengths

Observed verification

Observed escalation

Detection

Response

Business impact

Remediation

Avoid unnecessary personal attribution.

See:

Red Team Reporting

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
After remediation:

Original Scenario
       |
       v
Same Process
       |
       v
Equivalent Synthetic Identity
       |
       v
Repeat Test
       |
       v
Compare Verification

Do not necessarily retest the same employee.

The control is usually the process.

docs.title: Retest Status
docs.text:
Use:

Resolved

Partially Resolved

Not Resolved

Not Retested

Risk Accepted

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
Social engineering testing can be reduced to:

Test the process, not the person.

Obtain explicit authorisation.

Define target groups.

Use approved pretexts.

Prefer synthetic identities.

Avoid unnecessary personal data.

Never request real payments.

Avoid psychologically harmful scenarios.

Use dedicated test accounts for recovery testing.

Stop when the objective is proven.

Recognise employees who challenge or report the scenario.

Validate help desk and identity telemetry.

Validate physical security procedures.

Measure reporting and escalation.

Protect participant information.

Report systemic weaknesses rather than blaming individuals.

Debrief appropriately.

Retest the process after remediation.
