A refusal is a successful control

When an employee refuses an unusual request, performs the required verification or reports the interaction, record it as a positive security result. The purpose of the assessment is to identify where organisational controls succeed and where they need improvement.

Do not turn the exercise into a contest

The goal is not to manipulate an employee until they eventually make a mistake. Once the tested control has succeeded or failed and sufficient evidence exists, end the interaction and follow the agreed debrief procedure.

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text:
Source code review is the process of analysing application source code to identify security weaknesses, understand application behaviour, trace attacker-controlled data, and determine whether security-sensitive operations can be reached in an unsafe way.

Unlike black-box web application testing, source code review provides visibility into the application's internal implementation.

A reviewer can examine:

Routes
Controllers
Endpoints
Middleware
Authentication
Authorisation
Input handling
Validation
Business logic
Database access
File operations
HTTP requests
Template rendering
Deserialisation
Cryptography
Secrets
Configuration
Dependencies
Security controls
Dangerous sinks

The primary objective is not simply to search for dangerous functions.

The objective is to understand:

SOURCE
   |
   v
ATTACKER-CONTROLLED DATA
   |
   v
TRANSFORMATIONS
   |
   +--> Parsing
   +--> Decoding
   +--> Validation
   +--> Sanitisation
   +--> Normalisation
   +--> Business Logic
   +--> Authorisation
   |
   v
SINK
   |
   v
SECURITY-SENSITIVE OPERATION

A dangerous function found in source code is therefore only a review candidate.

Dangerous function found
          !=
Vulnerability confirmed

The complete data flow and security controls must be analysed.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform source code review only against applications, repositories, source packages, or systems for which you have explicit authorisation. Source code may contain credentials, personal data, internal infrastructure information, cryptographic material, API keys, proprietary business logic, and other sensitive information. Handle reviewed material according to the engagement rules and applicable data-handling requirements.

docs.title: Source Code Review vs Black-Box Testing
docs.text:
Black-box testing primarily observes the application externally.

Tester
  |
  v
HTTP Request
  |
  v
Application
  |
  v
HTTP Response

The tester attempts to infer what happens internally.

Source code review provides another perspective:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Route
     |
     v
Middleware
     |
     v
Controller
     |
     v
Validation
     |
     v
Authorisation
     |
     v
Business Logic
     |
     v
Sensitive Operation

This can reveal attack paths that are difficult to identify through black-box testing alone.

docs.title: Black-Box
docs.text:
The tester has no source code.

External Behaviour
        |
        v
Infer Internal Behaviour

Examples:

Burp Suite
HTTP testing
Content discovery
Parameter discovery
Fuzzing
Application interaction

docs.title: Grey-Box
docs.text:
The tester has partial knowledge.

Examples:

API documentation
Limited source code
Architecture diagrams
Test credentials
Configuration files
Selected repositories

docs.title: White-Box
docs.text:
The tester has extensive internal visibility.

Examples:

Full source code
Configuration
Dependency manifests
Infrastructure information
Database schemas
Build files
Deployment configuration
Architecture documentation

Source code review is primarily associated with white-box and grey-box testing.

docs.title: Why Source Code Review Matters
docs.text:
Many security weaknesses are easier to identify when implementation details are visible.

Examples include:

Missing authorisation checks
Unsafe SQL construction
Command execution
Dangerous deserialisation
Weak cryptography
Hard-coded credentials
Hidden API endpoints
Debug functionality
Unused legacy routes
Internal administrative endpoints
Unsafe file handling
SSRF sinks
Mass assignment
Business logic flaws
Race conditions
Inconsistent validation
Framework misconfiguration

Source review also helps answer:

Where does user input enter?

Where does it go?

What security controls are applied?

Can those controls be bypassed?

Where are sensitive operations performed?

Which endpoints expose those operations?

docs.title: The Core Source Code Review Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

ATTACK SURFACE
      |
      v
ENTRY POINT
      |
      v
SOURCE
      |
      v
DATA FLOW
      |
      v
SECURITY CONTROLS
      |
      v
SINK
      |
      v
IMPACT

Each stage should be understood.

docs.title: Attack Surface
docs.text:
Before searching for vulnerabilities, understand the application's attack surface.

Identify:

Web routes
API routes
GraphQL endpoints
gRPC services
WebSocket handlers
Authentication endpoints
Administrative functionality
File upload endpoints
Import/export functionality
Webhooks
Callbacks
Background jobs
Scheduled tasks
Message consumers
Third-party integrations
Internal APIs
Debug endpoints
Health endpoints
Management interfaces

Source review should complement:

Attack Surface Analysis

docs.title: Entry Points
docs.text:
An entry point is somewhere external data enters application logic.

Examples:

HTTP request
API request
WebSocket message
gRPC message
GraphQL query
File upload
Webhook
Message queue
Database record
Configuration
Environment variable
Command-line argument
Scheduled job
Third-party API

Not every entry point is directly attacker-controlled.

The trust boundary must be determined.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
A source is a location where potentially untrusted data enters the application's data flow.

Examples:

Query parameters
Path parameters
Form fields
JSON properties
XML elements
HTTP headers
Cookies
Uploaded files
Filename metadata
WebSocket messages
GraphQL arguments
gRPC fields
Webhook payloads

Language-specific examples differ.

For example:

PHP

$_GET
$_POST
$_REQUEST
$_COOKIE
$_FILES

Python Flask:

request.args
request.form
request.json
request.files
request.headers
request.cookies

Django:

request.GET
request.POST
request.FILES
request.COOKIES
request.headers

Express:

req.query
req.params
req.body
req.headers
req.cookies

ASP.NET:

Request.Query
Request.Form
Request.Headers
Request.Cookies
RouteData

Java/Spring:

@RequestParam
@PathVariable
@RequestBody
@RequestHeader
@CookieValue

These are starting points for tracing.

docs.title: Sinks
docs.text:
A sink is a security-sensitive operation where attacker-controlled data may become dangerous.

Examples include:

SQL execution
Operating-system command execution
Template evaluation
LDAP queries
File access
URL fetching
Deserialisation
HTML generation
Redirects
Dynamic code execution
XML parsing
Header construction
Logging
Email generation
Expression evaluation

Conceptually:

Source
   |
   v
User Input
   |
   v
Sink

is interesting.

But:

Source
   |
   v
Validation
   |
   v
Safe API
   |
   v
Sink

may be secure.

Therefore sinks identify review locations, not automatically vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Sources and Sinks
docs.text:
The central question during source review is:

Can attacker-controlled input reach a dangerous sink?

Then:

What happens between the source and the sink?

Example:

request parameter
       |
       v
controller
       |
       v
validation
       |
       v
service
       |
       v
database query

The reviewer must inspect the complete chain.

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Consider:

SOURCE
  |
  v
request.getParameter("id")
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATION
  |
  v
Integer.parseInt()
  |
  v
DATABASE QUERY

If the application converts the value to an integer before safely binding it to a parameterised query, SQL injection may not be possible.

Compare:

SOURCE
  |
  v
request.getParameter("name")
  |
  v
String concatenation
  |
  v
SQL query

This requires closer inspection.

docs.title: Taint Analysis
docs.text:
Taint analysis tracks potentially untrusted data through an application.

Conceptually:

TAINTED SOURCE
      |
      v
Variable A
      |
      v
Function B
      |
      v
Object C
      |
      v
Function D
      |
      v
SENSITIVE SINK

Example:

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
username
      |
      v
buildQuery(username)
      |
      v
executeQuery()

The objective is to determine whether the data remains attacker-controlled when it reaches the sink.

docs.title: Taint Propagation
docs.text:
Input may move through multiple variables.

Example:

request.body.url
      |
      v
target
      |
      v
validatedTarget
      |
      v
fetchUrl()

Do not stop at variable names.

Inspect what actually happens.

For example:

validatedTarget

does not prove that validation exists.

Read the implementation.

docs.title: Interprocedural Data Flow
docs.text:
Data often crosses multiple functions.

Example:

Controller
   |
   v
Service
   |
   v
Utility
   |
   v
Repository
   |
   v
Database

The vulnerable operation may be several functions away from the original request.

docs.title: Reverse Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Sometimes it is faster to start at dangerous sinks.

Example:

exec()

Then work backwards:

exec()
  ^
  |
command
  ^
  |
buildCommand()
  ^
  |
request parameter

This is particularly useful when reviewing large applications.

docs.title: Forward Analysis
docs.text:
Forward analysis starts at attacker-controlled input.

HTTP Input
    |
    v
Where does it go?

This is useful when reviewing security-sensitive endpoints.

docs.title: Backward Analysis
docs.text:
Backward analysis starts at a dangerous operation.

Dangerous Sink
      |
      v
Where did its arguments originate?

Both techniques should be used.

docs.title: Sources Are Not Always HTTP Inputs
docs.text:
An important source-review principle is:

Untrusted data
    !=
Only HTTP parameters

Potentially untrusted sources may include:

Database values
Message queues
Uploaded documents
CSV imports
Email
Third-party APIs
Webhooks
Cache values
Environment-specific integrations
User-generated content stored earlier

This matters for second-order vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Second-Order Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
A value may be stored safely initially but become dangerous later.

Example:

User Input
    |
    v
Database
    |
    v
Later Retrieved
    |
    v
Dangerous Sink

Examples include:

Stored XSS
Second-order SQL injection
Stored command injection
Stored template injection
Stored path manipulation

Do not assume database data is trusted merely because it came from the database.

docs.title: Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Identify where data crosses trust boundaries.

Example:

Internet
   |
   | Trust Boundary
   v
Web Application

But modern applications often have many more:

Browser
   |
   v
API Gateway
   |
   v
Application
   |
   v
Internal API
   |
   v
Database

or:

External SaaS
     |
     v
Webhook
     |
     v
Application

Trust must be based on architecture, not assumptions.

docs.title: Start With Application Structure
docs.text:
Before looking for individual vulnerabilities, understand the repository.

Useful questions:

What language is used?

Which framework?

Where are routes defined?

Where are controllers?

Where is authentication implemented?

Where is authorisation implemented?

Where is configuration stored?

Where are templates?

Where are database queries?

Where are API clients?

Where are file operations?

Where are dependencies defined?

Where are tests?

Where are deployment files?

docs.title: Initial Repository Enumeration
docs.text:
Start with:

pwd

Then:

find . -maxdepth 2 -type f | sort

For larger repositories:

find . -maxdepth 3 -type f | sort | less

Directories:

find . -maxdepth 3 -type d | sort

docs.title: Tree
docs.text:
If available:

tree

Limit depth:

tree -L 3

Ignore common noise:

tree -L 3 -I 'node_modules|vendor|venv|.venv|dist|build|target|bin|obj'

This provides a quick architecture overview.

docs.title: Identify Languages
docs.text:
Useful command:

find . -type f | sed 's/.*\.//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr

This provides a rough extension count.

For example:

450 java
220 js
90 html
50 xml
20 properties

This can immediately indicate the application's technology stack.

docs.title: Identify Frameworks
docs.text:
Look for dependency and build files.

Common examples:

.NET

*.csproj
*.sln
Directory.Build.props
packages.lock.json

Java:

pom.xml
build.gradle
build.gradle.kts
settings.gradle

PHP:

composer.json
composer.lock

Python:

requirements.txt
pyproject.toml
Pipfile
Pipfile.lock
poetry.lock
setup.py

JavaScript:

package.json
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml

docs.title: Dependency Files
docs.text:
Dependency manifests reveal:

Framework
Libraries
Database drivers
Template engines
Authentication libraries
Cloud SDKs
Serialization libraries
HTTP clients
Security libraries

They are also important for dependency security.

Refer to:

Dependency Security

docs.title: Identify Configuration
docs.text:
Search for:

.env
.env.example
application.properties
application.yml
appsettings.json
web.config
settings.py
config.py
config.php
php.ini
package.json
docker-compose.yml
Dockerfile

Also inspect:

CI/CD files
Kubernetes manifests
Terraform
Helm charts
Cloud configuration

Configuration often reveals security-relevant behaviour.

docs.title: Secrets Exposure
docs.text:
Search repositories for potential:

Passwords
API keys
Tokens
Private keys
Database credentials
Cloud credentials
Signing secrets
JWT secrets
OAuth secrets
Encryption keys

Refer to:

Secrets Exposure

Do not assume every high-entropy string is a valid credential.

Validate carefully and safely.

docs.title: Route Discovery
docs.text:
One of the first major source-review tasks is finding all routes.

The objective is to build:

HTTP Method
    |
    v
Route
    |
    v
Handler
    |
    v
Authentication
    |
    v
Authorisation

Example inventory:

Method Route Handler Authentication Authorisation GET /profile profile() Required Current user POST /admin/user createUser() Required Admin GET /api/orders/{id} getOrder() Required Object check POST /upload upload() Required User

docs.title: Why Route Mapping Matters
docs.text:
Route mapping reveals:

Hidden endpoints
Legacy endpoints
Administrative functionality
Debug endpoints
Internal APIs
Alternate versions
Unauthenticated functionality
Different HTTP methods

It also provides the foundation for systematic review.

docs.title: Authentication Mapping
docs.text:
Find:

Login handlers
Session creation
Token generation
JWT validation
OAuth callbacks
SAML handlers
Password reset
MFA
Remember-me functionality
API key validation

Then determine:

Which endpoints require authentication?

Which do not?

How is authentication enforced?

Is it middleware-based?

Annotation-based?

Decorator-based?

Manually implemented?

Refer to:

Authentication Testing

docs.title: Authorisation Mapping
docs.text:
Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Authorisation answers:

Are you allowed to perform this action?

Search for:

Role checks
Permission checks
Ownership checks
Tenant checks
Policy checks
Authorisation middleware
Security annotations
Decorators
Access-control helpers

The key question is:

Can a user reach a sensitive operation without the required authorisation check?

Refer to:

Authorisation Testing

IDOR and BOLA

docs.title: Object-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
For endpoints such as:

GET /api/orders/123

trace:

123
 |
 v
Object Lookup
 |
 v
Ownership / Permission Check
 |
 v
Return Object

A secure lookup may conceptually be:

Find order
WHERE
order.id = requested_id
AND
order.user_id = current_user

rather than:

Find order
WHERE
order.id = requested_id

followed by no ownership check.

docs.title: Input Validation Mapping
docs.text:
Find where the application validates:

Types
Length
Range
Format
Enumerations
Business rules
Schemas
Files
URLs
Identifiers

Then determine whether validation occurs:

Client-side only
Server-side
Controller
Schema
Service
Domain layer
Database

Refer to:

Input Validation

docs.title: Security Control Mapping
docs.text:
During review, build an inventory of reusable security controls.

Examples:

Authentication middleware
Authorisation middleware
CSRF middleware
Input validators
Output encoders
HTML sanitisers
URL validators
File validators
SQL abstraction layers
Logging helpers
Cryptographic utilities
Rate limiters

Then determine:

Where are they used?

Where are they missing?

Can they be bypassed?

Are there alternate implementations?

docs.title: Identify Security Control Inconsistency
docs.text:
One of the most productive review techniques is comparing similar endpoints.

Example:

/api/v1/users/{id}
        |
        +--> authorisation check

/api/v2/users/{id}
        |
        +--> no authorisation check

or:

POST /profile
    |
    +--> validation

PATCH /profile
    |
    +--> no validation

Security inconsistencies frequently reveal vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Dangerous Sink Categories
docs.text:
A useful source-review strategy is to classify sinks.

Database Sinks
Command Sinks
File Sinks
Network Sinks
Template Sinks
Deserialisation Sinks
HTML / DOM Sinks
Redirect Sinks
XML Sinks
Dynamic Code Sinks
Cryptographic Sinks
Logging Sinks

docs.title: Database Sinks
docs.text:
Potential security issues:

SQL Injection
NoSQL Injection
LDAP Injection
Mass Assignment
Data exposure

Review:

Raw queries
String concatenation
Dynamic query fragments
Native queries
ORM escape hatches
User-controlled filters
Sort expressions
Column names
Table names

docs.title: Command Sinks
docs.text:
Look for APIs capable of launching:

Commands
Processes
Shells
Scripts
External programs

Then trace:

Can attacker-controlled data influence:

Executable?
Arguments?
Environment?
Working directory?
Shell syntax?

Refer to:

OS Command Injection

docs.title: File Sinks
docs.text:
Review:

File reads
File writes
File deletion
Directory creation
Archive extraction
Upload storage
File downloads
Template loading
Configuration loading

Trace attacker-controlled:

Filename
Path
Extension
Directory
Archive entry

Refer to:

Path Traversal

File Inclusion

File Upload Security

docs.title: Network Sinks
docs.text:
Look for:

HTTP clients
URL fetchers
Webhook clients
Image downloaders
Document importers
Cloud SDKs
FTP clients
Socket connections

Trace:

URL
Hostname
Port
Scheme
Redirect destination

Refer to:

Server Side Request Forgery

docs.title: Template Sinks
docs.text:
Review:

Dynamic template creation
Template strings
Template compilation
Template evaluation

The key distinction is:

User input as data

versus:

User input as template source

Refer to:

Server-Side Template Injection

docs.title: Deserialisation Sinks
docs.text:
Look for APIs that convert serialized data into objects.

Formats may include:

Native object serialization
JSON
XML
YAML
Pickle
Binary formats
Custom serialization

Not all deserialisation is unsafe.

Review:

Data source
Type restrictions
Allowed classes
Parser configuration
Integrity protection

Refer to:

Insecure Deserialization

docs.title: XML Sinks
docs.text:
Identify XML parsers.

Review:

External entity support
DTD handling
Schema handling
Network access
Parser configuration

Refer to:

XML External Entity Injection

docs.title: HTML and DOM Sinks
docs.text:
Review places where attacker-controlled data reaches:

HTML
JavaScript
DOM APIs
Attributes
URLs
CSS

Context matters.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

DOM-Based Vulnerabilities

HTML Injection

docs.title: Redirect Sinks
docs.text:
Look for:

Redirect functions
Location headers
Callback URLs
Return URLs
Next parameters
Continue parameters

Trace whether the destination is attacker-controlled.

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: Dynamic Code Execution
docs.text:
High-value review candidates include APIs capable of:

Evaluating code
Executing expressions
Compiling code
Loading dynamic modules
Interpreting scripts

Examples differ by language.

These require careful source tracing.

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
Many important vulnerabilities do not have an obvious dangerous function.

Examples:

Negative quantities
Invalid state transitions
Discount manipulation
Workflow bypass
Approval bypass
Double spending
Tenant confusion
Race conditions
Privilege transitions

These require understanding the application.

Source code review should therefore not be reduced to sink searching.

Refer to:

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

Race Conditions

docs.title: Security-Relevant Variables
docs.text:
Search for names such as:

admin
role
permission
privilege
owner
user_id
account_id
tenant_id
price
amount
quantity
discount
balance
status
state
approved
verified
mfa
password
token
secret
key
redirect
callback
url
filename
path
command
query

These searches can identify important logic quickly.

But:

Interesting variable name
        !=
Vulnerability

docs.title: Search Tools
docs.text:
Useful tools include:

grep
ripgrep
find
git
Semgrep
CodeQL
Language-specific static analysers
IDE references
Call hierarchy

docs.title: ripgrep
docs.text:
ripgrep, commonly invoked as rg, is extremely useful for source review.

Basic search:

rg 'pattern' .

Case-insensitive:

rg -i 'password|secret|token' .

Line numbers are displayed by default.

Restrict by file type:

rg -t py 'subprocess|os\.system' .

List matching files:

rg -l 'pattern' .

docs.title: Search Multiple Security Concepts
docs.text:
Example:

rg -n -i \
'password|passwd|secret|token|api[_-]?key|private[_-]?key' \
.

Treat results as candidates requiring manual validation.

docs.title: Exclude Dependencies
docs.text:
Large repositories may contain third-party code.

Example:

rg \
-g '!node_modules/**' \
-g '!vendor/**' \
-g '!venv/**' \
-g '!.venv/**' \
-g '!dist/**' \
-g '!build/**' \
'pattern' \
.

This can significantly reduce noise.

docs.title: Search Configuration Files
docs.text:
find . \
-type f \
\( \
-name '*.env' \
-o -name '*.yml' \
-o -name '*.yaml' \
-o -name '*.json' \
-o -name '*.xml' \
-o -name '*.properties' \
-o -name '*.config' \
\) \
-print

Review relevant results manually.

docs.title: Search TODO and Debug Code
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'todo|fixme|hack|debug|temporary|bypass|disable|disabled' \
.

These comments may reveal unfinished security controls or development functionality.

Do not assume comments accurately describe current behaviour.

docs.title: Search Authentication Terms
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'login|logout|authenticate|authentication|authorize|authorization|permission|role|admin|session|jwt|oauth|saml|mfa' \
.

docs.title: Search Potential Secrets
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'password|passwd|secret|token|api[_-]?key|client[_-]?secret|private[_-]?key|access[_-]?key' \
.

Then determine:

Example value?
Test credential?
Production credential?
Placeholder?
Environment variable reference?
Actually usable secret?

docs.title: Git History
docs.text:
Current source code is only one point in time.

Security-relevant data may exist in Git history.

Useful commands:

git log --oneline --all

Search commit changes:

git log -p --all

Search for a string:

git log -S 'password' --all -p

Search commits whose patches match a regex:

git log -G 'secret|token|api[_-]?key' --all -p

Handle historical secrets carefully.

A removed credential may still be active.

docs.title: Review Security Fixes
docs.text:
Git history can reveal previous vulnerabilities.

Search commit messages:

git log --all --oneline --grep='security'

git log --all --oneline --grep='auth'

git log --all --oneline --grep='sanitize'

git log --all --oneline --grep='validation'

A previous fix can reveal similar unfixed code elsewhere.

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Variant analysis means:

Find one security weakness
        |
        v
Understand its root cause
        |
        v
Search for the same pattern elsewhere

Example:

Missing ownership check
        |
        v
Search all object lookup endpoints

or:

Unsafe raw SQL construction
        |
        v
Search all raw query usage

This is one of the most effective source-review techniques.

docs.title: Code Duplication
docs.text:
Similar vulnerable logic may have been copied.

Search:

Same helper
Same query pattern
Same validation function
Same controller logic
Same authorisation pattern

Do not stop after finding the first instance.

docs.title: IDE-Assisted Review
docs.text:
An IDE can significantly improve manual analysis.

Useful features include:

Go to definition
Find references
Call hierarchy
Type hierarchy
Search symbols
Find implementations
Rename preview
Data-flow features

For example:

Dangerous Sink
      |
      v
Find References
      |
      v
Identify Callers
      |
      v
Trace Back to Routes

docs.title: Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
Useful source-review functionality includes:

Global search
Go to Definition
Peek Definition
Find All References
Call Hierarchy
Symbol Search
Git integration

Extensions should be reviewed before installation in sensitive environments.

docs.title: Semgrep
docs.text:
Semgrep can identify source patterns using static-analysis rules.

Typical workflow:

Repository
    |
    v
Semgrep
    |
    v
Candidate Findings
    |
    v
Manual Review

Semgrep results should not automatically be treated as confirmed vulnerabilities.

Official project:

https://semgrep.dev/

docs.title: CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL supports semantic code analysis and can model data flow.

Conceptually:

Source
   |
   v
Data Flow
   |
   v
Sink

This makes it particularly useful for vulnerability classes such as:

Injection
Path traversal
XSS
Unsafe deserialisation

depending on the supported language and query.

Official documentation:

https://codeql.github.com/docs/

docs.title: Static Analysis vs Manual Review
docs.text:
Static analysis is useful for:

Pattern detection
Data flow
Known dangerous APIs
Large codebases
Variant analysis

Manual review remains important for:

Business logic
Authorisation
Workflow
Context
Architecture
False-positive elimination
Exploitability

The strongest approach combines both.

Static Analysis
       +
Manual Review
       +
Dynamic Testing

docs.title: SAST Findings Are Leads
docs.text:
A scanner may report:

Potential SQL Injection

This means:

Investigate

not automatically:

Confirmed SQL Injection

Verify:

Source controllability
Data flow
Sanitisation
Parameterisation
Reachability
Authentication
Authorisation
Impact

docs.title: Reachability
docs.text:
A dangerous function may not be reachable.

Example:

Legacy function
    |
    v
No callers

or:

Debug endpoint
    |
    v
Only compiled in development

Determine whether the code is actually reachable in the target deployment.

docs.title: Deployment Context
docs.text:
Source code alone may not reveal which functionality is enabled.

Consider:

Environment variables
Build flags
Feature flags
Configuration
Reverse proxy
API gateway
Cloud environment
Container configuration
Runtime version

docs.title: Source Code Review Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

1. Understand the Repository

2. Identify Languages and Frameworks

3. Identify Build and Dependency Files

4. Identify Configuration

5. Map Routes and Entry Points

6. Map Authentication

8. Map User-Controlled Sources

12. Review Business Logic

14. Review Dependencies

15. Review Git History

16. Run Static Analysis

17. Perform Variant Analysis

18. Validate Findings Dynamically Where Permitted

19. Determine Security Impact

20. Document Evidence

docs.title: Finding Classification
docs.text:
A useful classification is:

Candidate
   |
   v
Reachable?
   |
   +-- No --> Informational / discard
   |
   v
Attacker Controlled?
   |
   +-- No --> Review context
   |
   v
Security Control?
   |
   +-- Effective --> Not vulnerable
   |
   v
Exploitable?
   |
   +-- No --> Defence-in-depth / discard
   |
   v
Security Impact?
   |
   +-- No --> Low significance
   |
   v
Confirmed Finding

docs.title: Avoid Scanner-Driven Reporting
docs.text:
Do not report:

Semgrep found exec()

Report:

Attacker-controlled filename reaches a shell command without safe argument handling, allowing command injection.

The finding should describe:

Cause
Reachability
Exploitability
Impact

docs.title: Finding Template
docs.text:
Title:
[Specific vulnerability]

Affected Component:
[Route / class / function]

Source:
[Attacker-controlled input]

Sink:
[Security-sensitive operation]

Data Flow:
[Source -> transformations -> sink]

Security Control:
[Missing / ineffective / bypassable control]

Impact:
[What an attacker can achieve]

Evidence:
[Relevant source locations and controlled runtime evidence]

Recommendation:
[Root-cause remediation]

docs.title: Example Source Review Finding
docs.text:
Title:
Server-Side Request Forgery Through User-Controlled Report URL

Affected Component:
Report generation functionality

Source:
POST /api/report
JSON property: url

Data Flow:

request.body.url
      |
      v
ReportController
      |
      v
ReportService
      |
      v
HTTP client
      |
      v
Remote request

Observed Control:
Only the URL scheme is checked.

Impact:
An authenticated attacker can cause the application server to make requests to attacker-controlled destinations.

Recommendation:
Restrict server-side requests to explicitly permitted destinations where possible. Validate the resolved destination, account for redirects and DNS behaviour, and apply network-level egress restrictions appropriate to the application's requirements.

docs.title: Quick Review Questions
docs.text:
For every endpoint ask:

Where is the route defined?

What HTTP methods are allowed?

Is authentication required?

How is authentication enforced?

What role is required?

How is authorisation enforced?

Which objects can the user reference?

Are ownership checks performed?

Which parameters are attacker-controlled?

How are they validated?

Where do they flow?

Do they reach SQL?

Do they reach a shell?

Do they reach LDAP?

Do they reach a template?

Do they reach the filesystem?

Do they reach an HTTP client?

Do they reach HTML?

Do they reach a redirect?

Do they reach a deserialiser?

Can the user control object properties?

Can the user influence state transitions?

Are operations rate-limited?

Are secrets involved?

Are sensitive values logged?

Can requests race?

Does another route implement the same operation differently?

docs.title: Vulnerability Review Matrix
docs.text: Vulnerability Primary Source Review Question SQL Injection Can untrusted data alter SQL syntax? NoSQL Injection Can untrusted data alter NoSQL query semantics? LDAP Injection Can untrusted data alter LDAP filters? Command Injection Can untrusted data influence shell/command execution? SSTI Can untrusted data become template source? XSS Can untrusted data reach an unsafe output context? SSRF Can untrusted data control a server-side destination? Path Traversal Can untrusted data influence filesystem paths? File Upload Can attacker-controlled files be stored or processed unsafely? XXE Can attacker-controlled XML reach an unsafe parser? Deserialisation Can attacker-controlled serialized data reach dangerous object construction? IDOR / BOLA Is object access restricted to authorised users? Mass Assignment Can users bind security-sensitive object properties? Open Redirect Can users control redirect destinations? CSRF Can authenticated state-changing actions be triggered cross-site? CORS Can untrusted origins read sensitive responses? Authentication Can identity verification be bypassed or abused? Authorisation Can users perform unauthorised actions? Session Management Can sessions be stolen, fixed, reused or remain valid incorrectly? JWT Are tokens generated and validated securely? OAuth/OIDC Are authorization flows and tokens validated correctly? SAML Are assertions and protocol fields validated correctly? Business Logic Can valid functions be combined or manipulated unexpectedly? Race Conditions Can concurrent operations violate security assumptions? Rate Limiting Can sensitive operations be automated excessively? Secrets Exposure Are usable secrets exposed in code/config/history? Dependency Security Are vulnerable or unsupported components reachable?

docs.title: Final Source Code Review Model
docs.text:
The complete methodology can be reduced to five questions:

1. WHERE CAN AN ATTACKER ENTER DATA?

                  SOURCE

                     |
                     v

2. WHERE DOES THAT DATA GO?

                 DATA FLOW

                     |
                     v

3. WHAT SECURITY CONTROLS DOES IT CROSS?

        VALIDATION
        SANITISATION
        ENCODING
        AUTHENTICATION
        AUTHORISATION

                     |
                     v

4. WHAT SECURITY-SENSITIVE OPERATION DOES IT REACH?

                   SINK

                     |
                     v

5. WHAT CAN AN ATTACKER ACTUALLY ACHIEVE?

                  IMPACT

Or:

SOURCE
   |
   v
DATA FLOW
   |
   v
SECURITY CONTROLS
   |
   v
SINK
   |
   v
EXPLOITABILITY
   |
   v
IMPACT

The most important rule is:

Search results identify code.

Data-flow analysis identifies candidates.

Security-control analysis determines whether the path is protected.

Dynamic validation demonstrates behaviour.

Impact determines whether there is a vulnerability worth reporting.
