docs.title: Flask Source Code Review
docs.text:
Flask is a lightweight Python web framework commonly used for web applications, REST APIs, internal services, microservices and administrative interfaces.

Unlike frameworks that provide a large integrated security model, Flask intentionally provides a relatively small core. Security controls are therefore often implemented through:

  • Flask itself
  • Werkzeug
  • Jinja
  • Flask extensions
  • Application-specific middleware and decorators
  • Reverse proxies
  • API gateways
  • External identity providers

This makes source-code review especially important.

A Flask application may appear simple:

@app.route("/profile")
def profile():
    ...

but the actual security model may involve:

Browser
   |
   v
Reverse Proxy
   |
   v
Flask
   |
   +-- Authentication Extension
   |
   +-- CSRF Extension
   |
   +-- ORM
   |
   +-- Jinja
   |
   +-- Background Worker
   |
   +-- External APIs
   |
   v
Application Logic

The objective of Flask source-code review is to identify:

Routes
User-controlled input
Authentication boundaries
Authorisation boundaries
Validation
Trust boundaries
Dangerous sinks
Security-sensitive configuration

and then trace attacker-controlled data through the application.

The core methodology is:

SOURCE
  |
  v
USER-CONTROLLED INPUT
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  +-- parsing
  +-- validation
  +-- decoding
  +-- sanitisation
  +-- business logic
  |
  v
SECURITY CONTROLS
  |
  +-- authentication
  +-- authorisation
  +-- CSRF
  +-- tenant isolation
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
SECURITY-SENSITIVE OPERATION

Remember:

Dangerous function found
        !=
Confirmed vulnerability

Instead:

Candidate
   |
   v
Reachability
   |
   v
Attacker Control
   |
   v
Security Controls
   |
   v
Exploitability
   |
   v
Impact

Authorised Security Testing

Perform source-code review and dynamic validation only against applications, repositories and environments for which you have explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Review Strategy
docs.text:
A practical Flask review can follow:

1. Identify Flask and Python versions

2. Identify application entry points

3. Identify application factory

4. Identify configuration

5. Identify installed extensions

6. Map Blueprints

7. Map routes

8. Identify input sources

9. Map authentication

10. Map authorisation

11. Review object-level access

12. Review input validation

13. Review database access

14. Review template rendering

15. Review redirects

16. Review CSRF

17. Review CORS

18. Review file uploads

19. Review filesystem operations

20. Review outbound HTTP requests

21. Review command execution

22. Review serialization

23. Review session security

24. Review proxy trust

25. Review business logic

26. Review background workers

27. Search secrets

28. Review dependencies

29. Run static analysis

30. Perform variant analysis

31. Validate findings dynamically where authorised

docs.title: Identify Flask
docs.text:
Search dependency files:

rg -n -i \
'flask|werkzeug|jinja|flask-' \
requirements*.txt pyproject.toml Pipfile* poetry.lock uv.lock setup.py setup.cfg 2>/dev/null

Typical dependencies may include:

Flask
Flask-SQLAlchemy
Flask-Login
Flask-WTF
Flask-CORS
Flask-Limiter
Flask-JWT-Extended
Flask-RESTful
Flask-SocketIO

Do not assume an extension is active merely because it appears in a dependency file.

Trace where it is configured and initialised.

docs.title: Determine Versions
docs.text:
If the environment is available:

python3 -c "import flask; print(flask.__version__)"

Depending on the installed Flask version, package metadata may be the more appropriate way to inspect the installed version:

python3 -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('flask'))"

List relevant packages:

python3 -m pip list | grep -Ei \
'flask|werkzeug|jinja|sqlalchemy|wtf|cors|jwt|limiter|socketio'

Dependency files:

rg -n -i \
'flask|werkzeug|jinja|sqlalchemy' \
requirements*.txt pyproject.toml Pipfile* poetry.lock uv.lock 2>/dev/null

Version identification matters because security behaviour and supported APIs change.

docs.title: Application Structure
docs.text:
Common Flask layouts include:

project/
├── app.py
├── config.py
├── requirements.txt
├── templates/
├── static/
└── models.py

Larger applications may resemble:

project/
├── run.py
├── config.py
├── requirements.txt
├── app/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── models.py
│   ├── extensions.py
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── routes.py
│   │   └── forms.py
│   ├── api/
│   │   ├── routes.py
│   │   └── schemas.py
│   ├── admin/
│   │   └── routes.py
│   ├── services/
│   ├── templates/
│   └── static/
└── migrations/

High-value files include:

app.py
__init__.py
config.py
routes.py
views.py
models.py
forms.py
schemas.py
services.py
auth.py
permissions.py
decorators.py
extensions.py
tasks.py

docs.title: Find Flask Application Entry Points
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Flask\(__name__\)|Flask\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Typical:

app = Flask(__name__)

docs.title: Application Factory
docs.text:
Larger Flask projects frequently use:

def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    ...
    return app

Search:

rg -n \
'def create_app\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Follow everything initialised inside the factory:

create_app()
   |
   +-- Configuration
   |
   +-- Database
   |
   +-- LoginManager
   |
   +-- CSRFProtect
   |
   +-- CORS
   |
   +-- Limiter
   |
   +-- Blueprints

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'app\.config|from_object|from_envvar|Config|SECRET_KEY|SESSION_|DEBUG|TESTING|SERVER_NAME|TRUSTED_HOSTS|MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH|PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Potential sources include:

app.config.from_object(...)

app.config.from_pyfile(...)

app.config.from_envvar(...)

app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = ...

Trace which configuration is actually loaded in production.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Find:

find . -type f \( \
-name 'config.py' \
-o -name 'settings.py' \
-o -name '.env' \
-o -name '.flaskenv' \
-o -name '*.cfg' \
\) -print

Be careful when handling real secret files.

docs.title: DEBUG
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'DEBUG\s*=|app\.debug|debug\s*=\s*True|FLASK_DEBUG' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

app.run(debug=True)

Development debug functionality must not be assumed safe for hostile production exposure.

However:

debug=True in local development code
    !=
Confirmed production vulnerability

Confirm deployment reachability and configuration.

docs.title: Development Server
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'app\.run\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review whether the development server is accidentally used in production.

Production deployments commonly use a dedicated WSGI server or another supported deployment architecture.

docs.title: SECRET_KEY
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'SECRET_KEY|secret_key' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = "development-secret"

Determine whether it is:

Example value
Test value
Development value
Production value

Flask uses the secret key for security-sensitive signing functionality such as its default session mechanism.

A compromised production key may therefore have serious consequences depending on application design.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'os\.environ|os\.getenv|dotenv|load_dotenv' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = os.environ["SECRET_KEY"]

Environment-variable use is not automatically secure.

Review:

Secret lifecycle
Access permissions
Logging
Container configuration
Deployment manifests
Fallback values

docs.title: Flask Extensions
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'LoginManager|SQLAlchemy|CSRFProtect|CORS\(|Limiter\(|JWTManager|SocketIO|Migrate|Marshmallow' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Create an extension inventory:

Extension Purpose Security Relevance Flask-Login Authentication/session helpers High Flask-WTF Forms/CSRF High Flask-SQLAlchemy Database High Flask-CORS CORS High Flask-Limiter Rate limiting High Flask-JWT-Extended JWT High Flask-SocketIO WebSockets High

docs.title: Route Discovery
docs.text:
Flask routes commonly use:

@app.route()

or:

@blueprint.route()

Search:

rg -n \
'@\w+\.route\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Broader:

rg -n \
'\.route\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Route Example
docs.text:
@app.route(
    "/users/<int:user_id>",
    methods=["GET"],
)
def user_detail(user_id):
    ...

Map:

GET /users/<user_id>
          |
          v
user_detail(user_id)

docs.title: Route Methods
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'methods\s*=\s*\[' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Routes without an explicit methods argument normally need to be interpreted according to Flask's route behaviour rather than assumed to accept every method.

docs.title: Method-Specific Decorators
docs.text:
Modern Flask also supports shortcuts such as:

@app.get("/users")
def users():
    ...

@app.post("/users")
def create_user():
    ...

Search:

rg -n \
'@\w+\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: add_url_rule
docs.text:
Routes may also be registered programmatically.

Search:

rg -n \
'add_url_rule\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

app.add_url_rule(
    "/health",
    view_func=health,
)

Do not rely only on decorator searches.

docs.title: Blueprints
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Blueprint\(|register_blueprint\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

auth = Blueprint(
    "auth",
    __name__,
    url_prefix="/auth",
)

and:

app.register_blueprint(auth)

Route construction:

Blueprint prefix
      +
Route path
      =
Final endpoint

docs.title: Route Inventory
docs.text:
Create a table:

Method Route Function Authentication Authorisation GET /profile profile() Login Self GET /users/<id> user() Login ? POST /upload upload() Login User POST /admin/user/<id> update_user() Login Admin?

This exposes inconsistent controls quickly.

docs.title: Runtime Route Enumeration
docs.text:
If authorised source execution is available:

flask routes

This can help identify routes that are difficult to locate through static searches.

Do not assume every route is externally reachable.

docs.title: Input Sources
docs.text:
Common Flask input sources include:

request.args
request.form
request.values
request.json
request.get_json()
request.files
request.headers
request.cookies
request.data
request.get_data()
request.view_args

Route parameters are also attacker-controlled.

docs.title: Input Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'request\.(args|form|values|json|files|headers|cookies|data|view_args)|request\.get_json\(|request\.get_data\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
search = request.args.get("q")

Search:

rg -n \
'request\.args' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Form Data
docs.text:
rg -n \
'request\.form' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: request.values
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.values' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

request.values can combine multiple input locations, which may make trust and parameter-precedence reasoning less obvious.

Review carefully where duplicate parameter names matter.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.json|request\.get_json\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

data = request.get_json()

Trace fields from data individually.

docs.title: Raw Body
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.data|request\.get_data\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Raw request bodies deserve particular attention when passed to:

XML parsers
Deserializers
Template engines
Signature verification
Custom protocol parsers

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.headers' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

token = request.headers.get(
    "Authorization"
)

Potentially attacker-controlled headers include:

Host
Origin
Referer
User-Agent
X-Forwarded-For
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Forwarded-Proto
Custom application headers

Whether forwarded headers are trustworthy depends on proxy configuration.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.cookies' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Do not treat a cookie as trusted merely because it came from a browser.

docs.title: Uploaded Files
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.files' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

file = request.files["file"]

Trace:

Filename
Content
MIME type
Storage location
Processing
Serving

docs.title: Route Parameters
docs.text:
Example:

@app.get("/documents/<int:document_id>")
def document(document_id):
    ...

document_id is attacker-controlled.

Map route variables into downstream queries.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Flask itself does not prescribe one single authentication system.

Applications may use:

Flask-Login
JWT
OAuth/OIDC
SAML
API keys
Custom sessions
Reverse-proxy authentication

Start with:

rg -n -i \
'login|logout|authenticate|authentication|current_user|login_required|jwt_required|Authorization|api.?key' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Flask-Login
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'flask_login|LoginManager|login_user|logout_user|current_user|login_required|user_loader' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: login_required
docs.text:
Example:

@app.get("/profile")
@login_required
def profile():
    ...

This establishes an authentication requirement.

It does not automatically establish:

Object ownership
Role authorisation
Tenant isolation
Action-level permission

docs.title: Authentication Coverage
docs.text:
Compare:

@app.get("/account")
@login_required
def account():
    ...

with:

@app.post("/account/delete")
def delete_account():
    ...

A missing decorator on a sensitive route deserves investigation.

docs.title: user_loader
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@.*user_loader|user_loader\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

@login_manager.user_loader
def load_user(user_id):
    return User.query.get(int(user_id))

Review:

Identifier handling
Account state
Disabled users
Deleted users
Tenant assumptions

docs.title: Custom Authentication Decorators
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'def .*required|def .*permission|def .*auth|wraps\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

def admin_required(func):
    ...

Read the implementation rather than trusting the decorator name.

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'role|permission|authorize|authorise|admin|owner|current_user|tenant|organization|organisation|workspace' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Object-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Candidate:

@app.get("/documents/<int:document_id>")
@login_required
def document(document_id):
    document = Document.query.get(
        document_id
    )

    return render_template(
        "document.html",
        document=document,
    )

Data flow:

document_id
     |
     v
Document.query.get()
     |
     v
Document
     |
     v
Response

Question:

Where is the ownership or tenant check?

docs.title: Scoped Object Lookup
docs.text:
A stronger pattern may resemble:

document = Document.query.filter_by(
    id=document_id,
    owner_id=current_user.id,
).first_or_404()

For a tenant-based application:

document = Document.query.filter_by(
    id=document_id,
    tenant_id=current_user.tenant_id,
).first_or_404()

The correct rule depends on application policy.

docs.title: Query Object Access
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\.query\.(get|filter|filter_by|all|first|one|one_or_none)|session\.(get|execute|query)' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Prioritise attacker-controlled identifiers.

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA Search Strategy
docs.text:
Search likely object identifiers:

rg -n -i \
'user_id|account_id|document_id|invoice_id|order_id|tenant_id|organization_id|organisation_id|workspace_id' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Then compare each lookup against:

current_user
tenant
role
permission
ownership

Refer to:

IDOR and BOLA

Authorisation Testing

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Applications
docs.text:
Map:

User
 |
 v
Membership
 |
 v
Tenant
 |
 v
Tenant-Scoped Query
 |
 v
Object

A dangerous pattern may be:

Invoice.query.get(invoice_id)

where the application requires:

Invoice.query.filter_by(
    id=invoice_id,
    tenant_id=current_user.tenant_id,
).first()

Do not assume every global lookup is vulnerable.

Determine intended visibility.

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
Flask applications may use:

WTForms
Marshmallow
Pydantic
Custom validation
JSON Schema
Application-specific validators

Search:

rg -n -i \
'wtforms|marshmallow|pydantic|validate|validator|schema|Form\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Flask-WTF
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'FlaskForm|validate_on_submit|DataRequired|Length|Regexp|Email|FileAllowed' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

class ProfileForm(FlaskForm):
    username = StringField(
        "Username",
        validators=[
            DataRequired(),
            Length(max=64),
        ],
    )

Validation helps establish input constraints.

It does not automatically provide:

Authorisation
Safe SQL construction
Safe command construction
Safe HTML output

docs.title: Marshmallow
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Schema|fields\.|@validates|@validates_schema|load\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Trace which fields can be supplied by clients.

Pay special attention to:

role
admin
is_admin
owner_id
tenant_id
status
approved
verified
balance
permissions

docs.title: Pydantic
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'BaseModel|field_validator|model_validator|model_validate' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Again:

Schema validation
    !=
Authorisation

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
Flask applications frequently use:

SQLAlchemy
Flask-SQLAlchemy
Raw database drivers

Normal ORM query construction reduces SQL injection risk when values are bound correctly.

The highest-value review targets are raw SQL and dynamic query construction.

docs.title: SQLAlchemy Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'SQLAlchemy|db\.session|session\.execute|text\(|execute\(|from_statement|\.query\.' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Raw SQL
docs.text:
Candidate:

username = request.args.get("username")

query = (
    "SELECT * FROM users "
    "WHERE username = '"
    + username
    + "'"
)

result = db.session.execute(
    query
)

Trace user input into SQL syntax.

docs.title: f-string SQL
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'f["'\''].*(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE)|format\(.*(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE)' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Manual review is required because grep cannot determine whether the interpolated values are attacker-controlled.

docs.title: SQLAlchemy text()
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\btext\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

query = text(
    f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
)

Safer parameter binding resembles:

query = text(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = :name"
)

result = db.session.execute(
    query,
    {"name": name},
)

docs.title: Database Driver Calls
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'cursor\.execute\(|cursor\.executemany\(|execute\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review parameter handling for:

sqlite3
psycopg
PyMySQL
mysqlclient
other DB-API drivers

docs.title: Dynamic Identifiers
docs.text:
Even parameterised value handling does not automatically make attacker-controlled SQL structure safe.

Example:

sort = request.args.get("sort")

If sort influences:

Column names
Table names
ORDER BY expressions
Operators

use server-controlled mappings or allowlists.

Refer to:

SQL Injection

docs.title: NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
Flask applications may use MongoDB or other NoSQL databases.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'pymongo|mongoengine|mongodb|find_one|find\(|aggregate\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

query = request.get_json()

user = users.find_one(query)

Potential issue:

Attacker controls query structure
rather than only expected values

Review whether operators can be injected.

Refer to:

NoSQL Injection

docs.title: LDAP Injection
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'ldap|ldap3|search_filter|filterstr|search\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

username = request.form["username"]

search_filter = (
    "(uid="
    + username
    + ")"
)

Trace attacker-controlled values into LDAP filter syntax.

LDAP escaping must be appropriate for the specific LDAP context.

Refer to:

LDAP Injection

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'os\.(system|popen)\(|subprocess\.(run|Popen|call|check_call|check_output)\(|shell\s*=\s*True' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

host = request.form["host"]

subprocess.run(
    f"ping -c 1 {host}",
    shell=True,
)

Trace:

request.form["host"]
        |
        v
Command String
        |
        v
Shell

docs.title: Safer Process Invocation
docs.text:
Prefer avoiding shell interpretation where possible.

Example:

subprocess.run(
    [
        "ping",
        "-c",
        "1",
        host,
    ],
    check=True,
)

However:

Argument list
    !=
Automatically safe

The called executable may interpret attacker-controlled arguments in security-sensitive ways.

Validation and allowlisting may still be required.

Refer to:

OS Command Injection

docs.title: Dynamic Python Execution
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\beval\(|\bexec\(|\bcompile\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

expression = request.form["expression"]

result = eval(expression)

Attacker-controlled input reaching dynamic Python execution is a high-priority review target.

docs.title: Server-Side Template Injection
docs.text:
Flask uses Jinja templates.

Normal usage:

return render_template(
    "profile.html",
    username=username,
)

normally uses a server-controlled template file.

The highest-value SSTI target is runtime template source.

docs.title: render_template_string
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'render_template_string\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

template = request.args.get("template")

return render_template_string(
    template
)

Data flow:

request.args
     |
     v
Template Source
     |
     v
Jinja Parser
     |
     v
Template Execution

This deserves immediate investigation.

docs.title: Jinja Environment
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Environment\(|from_string\(|Template\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

template = env.from_string(
    user_input
)

Again, determine whether attacker-controlled data becomes template source.

Refer to:

Server-Side Template Injection

docs.title: XSS
docs.text:
Jinja normally autoescapes HTML templates rendered through Flask's standard template integration.

Example:

<p>{{ username }}</p>

High-value review targets intentionally bypass escaping.

docs.title: safe Filter
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\|\s*safe\b' \
--glob '*.html' \
--glob '*.jinja' \
--glob '*.jinja2' \
.

Candidate:

{{ biography|safe }}

Trace where biography originates.

docs.title: Markup
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\bMarkup\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

return Markup(
    request.args.get("html")
)

Treat attacker-controlled values marked as safe as high-priority review candidates.

docs.title: autoescape false
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'autoescape\s+(false|False)|autoescape=False' \
--glob '*.html' \
--glob '*.jinja' \
--glob '*.jinja2' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: HTML Response Construction
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Response\(|make_response\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

name = request.args.get("name")

return Response(
    f"<h1>Hello {name}</h1>",
    mimetype="text/html",
)

Trace attacker-controlled content into HTML responses.

docs.title: JavaScript Context
docs.text:
Candidate:

<script>
    const username = "{{ username }}";
</script>

HTML escaping and JavaScript-string safety are different contexts.

Review data inserted into:

JavaScript
HTML attributes
CSS
URLs
Inline event handlers

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

HTML Injection

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
Flask core does not automatically add CSRF protection to arbitrary application routes.

Many applications use Flask-WTF:

CSRFProtect(app)

Search:

rg -n \
'CSRFProtect|csrf\.init_app|csrf\.exempt|@csrf\.exempt|WTF_CSRF' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: CSRF Exemptions
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'csrf\.exempt|@.*csrf.*exempt' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Do not report every exemption.

Determine:

Does the endpoint change state?
Does it use cookie-based authentication?
Is another anti-CSRF mechanism present?
Is it a machine-to-machine API?

docs.title: Form CSRF
docs.text:
Flask-WTF forms commonly include CSRF integration.

Search:

rg -n \
'FlaskForm|hidden_tag\(|csrf_token' \
--glob '*.py' \
--glob '*.html' \
.

Refer to:

docs/web/csrf.md

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Flask applications often use Flask-CORS.

Search:

rg -n \
'flask_cors|CORS\(|cross_origin\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

CORS(
    app,
    origins="*",
)

Do not report broad CORS solely from this line.

Determine:

Credentials
Sensitive responses
Authentication mechanism
Origin restrictions
Endpoint-specific configuration

docs.title: credentials
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'supports_credentials|origins\s*=|allow_headers|expose_headers' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Refer to:

docs/web/cors.md

docs.title: Open Redirect
docs.text:
Flask commonly redirects using:

redirect()

Search:

rg -n \
'\bredirect\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

next_url = request.args.get("next")

return redirect(next_url)

Trace whether external URLs are permitted.

docs.title: Login next Parameter
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.(args|values).*next|next_url|redirect_url|return_url|return_to' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

A common flow:

/login?next=/dashboard

Review destination validation.

docs.title: URL Parsing
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'urlparse\(|urlsplit\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Validation should correctly account for:

Scheme
Host
Port
Protocol-relative URLs
Encoded values
Parser behaviour

Refer to:

Open Redirect

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'requests\.(get|post|put|patch|delete|request)\(|httpx\.|urllib\.request|urlopen\(|aiohttp\.ClientSession' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

url = request.form["url"]

response = requests.get(
    url
)

Trace:

User URL
   |
   v
Validation
   |
   v
HTTP Client
   |
   v
Destination

Review:

Scheme
Hostname
Port
DNS resolution
Redirects
IPv4
IPv6
Loopback
Private ranges
Link-local addresses
Cloud metadata
Egress restrictions

docs.title: Stored SSRF
docs.text:
Example:

POST /webhooks
      |
      v
Webhook URL
      |
      v
Database
      |
      v
Celery Task
      |
      v
requests.post()

This is why interprocedural and second-order tracing matters.

Refer to:

Server Side Request Forgery

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\bopen\(|Path\(|os\.path\.join\(|send_file\(|send_from_directory\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

filename = request.args.get("file")

path = os.path.join(
    "/srv/files",
    filename,
)

return send_file(path)

Do not assume os.path.join() enforces containment.

Trace the final resolved path.

docs.title: send_file
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'send_file\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review whether the path is:

Server-controlled
Mapped from an object ID
Directly attacker-controlled
Canonicalised
Restricted to an expected directory

docs.title: send_from_directory
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'send_from_directory\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

send_from_directory() is intended for serving files from a specified directory and uses Werkzeug's safe path handling, but application-level authorisation and correct directory selection still matter.

Do not automatically flag it as path traversal.

Refer to:

docs/web/path-traversal.md

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.files|save\(|secure_filename\(|send_file\(|send_from_directory\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

file = request.files["file"]

file.save(
    os.path.join(
        upload_dir,
        file.filename,
    )
)

Review whether the original filename is trusted.

docs.title: secure_filename
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'secure_filename\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

filename = secure_filename(
    file.filename
)

This is useful filename normalisation, but:

secure_filename()
    !=
Complete upload security

Still review:

File content
Extension
MIME type
Storage
Permissions
Overwrite behaviour
Serving
Downstream processing
Authorisation

docs.title: Upload Size
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

app.config[
    "MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"
] = 16 * 1024 * 1024

Request-size restrictions can help reduce resource abuse.

Infrastructure limits may also exist.

docs.title: Archive Extraction
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'zipfile|ZipFile|tarfile|TarFile|extractall\(|unpack_archive\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review uploaded archive extraction for:

Traversal
Overwrite
Symlinks
Resource exhaustion
Unexpected file types

Refer to:

File Upload Security

docs.title: Insecure Deserialization
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'pickle\.(load|loads)\(|dill\.(load|loads)\(|cloudpickle|joblib\.load|yaml\.(load|unsafe_load)\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

data = pickle.loads(
    request.data
)

Untrusted pickle data must not be deserialized.

docs.title: YAML
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'yaml\.(load|unsafe_load|safe_load)\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review which loader is used and whether the input is trusted.

Do not flag safe_load() merely because YAML is involved.

Refer to:

docs/web/deserialization.md

docs.title: XML / XXE
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'xml\.etree|ElementTree|lxml|etree|xml\.dom|minidom|sax|XMLParser' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Determine:

Parser implementation
Parser configuration
DTD handling
Entity resolution
Network access
Input trust

Do not report XML parsing itself as XXE.

Refer to:

XML External Entity Injection

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
Flask's default session mechanism stores session data in a signed cookie.

This means an important distinction is:

Signed
    !=
Secret

Do not place sensitive plaintext data in client-visible session contents merely because integrity protection is present.

docs.title: Session Usage
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\bsession\[|session\.get\(|session\.pop\(|session\.clear\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

session["user_id"] = user.id

Review:

What is stored?
What security decisions rely on it?
How is it invalidated?
What happens after password changes?
What happens after privilege changes?

docs.title: Session Cookie Configuration
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'SESSION_COOKIE_(SECURE|HTTPONLY|SAMESITE|DOMAIN|PATH|NAME)|PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

High-value settings include:

SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE
SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY
SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE
SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN
PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME

Confirm effective deployment configuration.

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text:
Review login flows.

Search:

rg -n \
'login_user\(|session\.clear\(|session\[' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Determine whether session state is appropriately replaced or cleared across authentication transitions.

docs.title: Remember-Me Functionality
docs.text:
Flask-Login can support persistent login functionality.

Search:

rg -n \
'remember\s*=|REMEMBER_COOKIE_|login_user\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

Lifetime
Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
Revocation expectations

docs.title: Host Header Security
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.host|request\.host_url|request\.url_root|request\.url|SERVER_NAME|TRUSTED_HOSTS' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

High-value contexts include:

Password reset
Email verification
Account activation
OAuth callbacks
Absolute URL generation
Security-sensitive redirects

docs.title: url_for with _external
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'url_for\(.*_external\s*=\s*True' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

reset_url = url_for(
    "auth.reset",
    token=token,
    _external=True,
)

Determine which host and scheme influence the generated URL.

Refer to:

HTTP Host Header Attacks

docs.title: ProxyFix
docs.text:
Flask deployments behind reverse proxies may use Werkzeug's ProxyFix.

Search:

rg -n \
'ProxyFix|x_for|x_proto|x_host|x_port|x_prefix' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

app.wsgi_app = ProxyFix(
    app.wsgi_app,
    x_for=1,
    x_proto=1,
    x_host=1,
)

The security of this configuration depends on the real proxy topology.

The application must only trust the number of proxy hops that are actually controlled.

Incorrect proxy trust can cause attacker-supplied forwarded headers to be interpreted as trusted request metadata.

docs.title: Forwarded Header Usage
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'X-Forwarded-For|X-Forwarded-Host|X-Forwarded-Proto|Forwarded' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Map:

Internet
   |
   v
Trusted Proxy
   |
   v
Forwarded Header
   |
   v
ProxyFix
   |
   v
Flask Request Metadata

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'forgot.?password|password.?reset|reset.?password|reset_token|generate.*token|verify.*token' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

Token generation
Entropy
Expiration
Single use
User binding
Enumeration
Rate limiting
Host generation
Session invalidation

docs.title: Token Generation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'itsdangerous|URLSafeTimedSerializer|Serializer\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Flask applications commonly use ItsDangerous for signed tokens.

Review:

Secret key
Salt/purpose separation
Expiration
What claims are signed
How verified data is used

A correctly signed token does not automatically prove that the resulting action is authorised.

Refer to:

Password Reset Security

docs.title: Password Hashing
docs.text:
Werkzeug provides password hashing helpers.

Search:

rg -n \
'generate_password_hash|check_password_hash|password_hash|bcrypt|argon2' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate safe-style flow:

password_hash = generate_password_hash(
    password
)

Review custom cryptographic implementations carefully.

docs.title: Dangerous Password Storage
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'password\s*=|user\.password|password_hash' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Determine whether plaintext or reversible password storage occurs.

Do not infer this from a variable named password.

docs.title: MFA
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'totp|hotp|otp|mfa|2fa|two.?factor|recovery.?code|backup.?code|pyotp' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

Enrollment
Secret generation
Verification
Replay prevention
Rate limiting
Recovery
Reset
Remember-device
Bypass paths

Refer to:

Multi-Factor Authentication Security

docs.title: JWT
docs.text:
Common Flask JWT packages include:

Flask-JWT-Extended
PyJWT
Authlib
python-jose

Search:

rg -n -i \
'jwt|JWTManager|jwt_required|create_access_token|decode_token|encode\(|decode\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Flask-JWT-Extended
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'JWTManager|@jwt_required|create_access_token|get_jwt|get_jwt_identity|JWT_' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

Token location
Signing algorithm
Secret/key management
Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Revocation
Refresh tokens
CSRF when cookies are used
Privilege claims

docs.title: JWT Claims and Authorisation
docs.text:
Candidate:

claims = get_jwt()

if claims["role"] == "admin":
    ...

Review:

Where was role assigned?
Can stale tokens retain privileges?
Is server-side authorisation also performed?
How are tokens revoked?

Refer to:

JSON Web Token Security

docs.title: OAuth / OIDC
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'oauth|openid|oidc|authlib|client_id|client_secret|redirect_uri|state|nonce|code_verifier|token_endpoint' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

State
Nonce
PKCE
Issuer
Audience
Redirect URI
Token validation
Account linking
Email trust
Session creation

Refer to:

OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect Security

docs.title: SAML
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'saml|python3-saml|xmlsec|onelogin|pysaml' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

Signature validation
Issuer
Audience
Destination
Recipient
Replay protection
Attribute mapping
Account linking

Refer to:

SAML Security

docs.title: API Keys
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'api.?key|x-api-key|authorization|bearer' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

Storage
Comparison
Rotation
Logging
Scope
Rate limiting
Revocation

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Flask applications may use Flask-Limiter or infrastructure-level controls.

Search:

rg -n \
'Limiter\(|@.*limit\(|RATELIMIT|rate.?limit' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Sensitive Rate-Limit Targets
docs.text:
Prioritise:

Login
Password reset
MFA verification
Registration
Email verification
OTP
API authentication
Expensive searches
Exports

Do not conclude that rate limiting is absent merely because no Flask code implements it.

It may exist at:

Nginx
Cloud proxy
WAF
API gateway
Load balancer

Refer to:

Rate Limiting and Anti-Automation

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'price|amount|balance|discount|coupon|refund|credit|quantity|inventory|approved|verified|status|role|permission' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

Payments
Refunds
Credits
Coupons
Inventory
Approval workflows
State transitions
Verification
Role changes
Tenant changes

docs.title: Trust Client-Supplied Prices
docs.text:
Candidate:

price = request.form["price"]

order = Order(
    product_id=product_id,
    price=price,
)

Question:

Should the server derive the price from trusted product data?

This is business-logic analysis rather than generic input validation.

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Flask applications frequently convert request dictionaries directly into model constructors or updates.

Search:

rg -n \
'\*\*request\.(json|form)|\*\*data|setattr\(|\.update\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Candidate:

data = request.get_json()

user = User(
    **data
)

Review whether the client can control:

is_admin
role
permissions
owner_id
tenant_id
verified
status
balance

docs.title: Generic setattr
docs.text:
Candidate:

for key, value in data.items():
    setattr(
        user,
        key,
        value,
    )

This deserves careful field-level analysis.

Refer to:

docs/web/mass-assignment.md

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'with_for_update|begin\(|commit\(|rollback\(|transaction|redis.*lock|Lock\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

High-value workflows:

Balances
Credits
Coupons
Inventory
One-time tokens
Approvals
Password resets
Invitations

docs.title: Race Example
docs.text:
Request A              Request B

Read balance=100       Read balance=100
      |                      |
Check >= 80            Check >= 80
      |                      |
Subtract 80            Subtract 80
      |                      |
Commit                 Commit

Review database transaction isolation and application-level locking.

Refer to:

Race Conditions

docs.title: Background Workers
docs.text:
Flask applications commonly use:

Celery
RQ
Dramatiq
Custom queues

Search:

rg -n -i \
'celery|shared_task|@.*task|\.delay\(|apply_async\(|rq\.|enqueue\(|dramatiq' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Second-Order Flow
docs.text:
HTTP Request
     |
     v
Database
     |
     v
Background Job
     |
     v
Dangerous Sink

Example:

POST /integrations
       |
       v
Webhook URL
       |
       v
Database
       |
       v
Celery
       |
       v
requests.post()

docs.title: Signals / Hooks
docs.text:
Flask extensions and SQLAlchemy may introduce event-driven behaviour.

Search:

rg -n \
'@event\.listens_for|event\.listen|before_request|after_request|teardown_request|before_app_request' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: before_request
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@.*before_request|before_request\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Security controls may be applied globally here.

Do not assume a route lacks authentication merely because no decorator is visible.

docs.title: after_request
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@.*after_request|after_request\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Security headers may be added here.

docs.title: Error Handlers
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@.*errorhandler|register_error_handler' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review whether exceptions expose:

Stack traces
Internal paths
Database errors
Secrets
Tokens
User data

docs.title: Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'traceback|print_exc|logger\.exception|debug\s*=\s*True|DEBUG\s*=|str\(.*exception|repr\(.*exception' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'logger\.(debug|info|warning|error|critical|exception)\(|logging\.(debug|info|warning|error|critical|exception)\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review for:

Passwords
Authorization headers
JWTs
Session cookies
API keys
Reset tokens
MFA codes
Sensitive request bodies

docs.title: HTTP Security Headers
docs.text:
Flask applications may configure headers using:

after_request
Flask-Talisman
Reverse proxy
CDN
WAF

Search:

rg -n -i \
'Content-Security-Policy|X-Frame-Options|Strict-Transport-Security|X-Content-Type-Options|Referrer-Policy|Permissions-Policy|Talisman' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Do not infer missing deployed headers from application source alone.

Validate actual responses.

Refer to:

docs/web/http-security-headers.md

docs.title: Clickjacking
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'X-Frame-Options|frame-ancestors|Content-Security-Policy' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Again, reverse proxies may supply these headers.

Refer to:

docs/web/clickjacking.md

docs.title: Cache Security
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'cache|Cache\(|cached\(|memoize\(|Cache-Control|Vary' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Flask applications may use Flask-Caching.

Review cache separation for:

User
Role
Tenant
Cookies
Authorization headers
Host
Query parameters
Language

docs.title: Cache Key Construction
docs.text:
Candidate:

@cache.cached(
    timeout=300
)
@login_required
def account():
    ...

Determine whether the cache varies appropriately for authenticated users.

Refer to:

docs/web/web-cache-poisoning.md
docs/web/web-cache-deception.md

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
Common Python GraphQL frameworks include:

Graphene
Ariadne
Strawberry

Search:

rg -n -i \
'graphene|ariadne|strawberry|graphql|resolver|mutation' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Review:

Resolvers
Mutations
Authentication
Object-level authorisation
Field-level access
Depth
Complexity
Batching
Introspection

Refer to:

GraphQL API Security

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
Flask applications may use Flask-SocketIO.

Search:

rg -n \
'SocketIO|socketio\.on|@.*\.on\(' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Example:

@socketio.on("join")
def join(data):
    ...

Review:

Connection authentication
Event authorisation
Room access
Object access
Origin handling
State-changing events

Refer to:

WebSocket Security

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
A Flask application may act as a gRPC client or coexist with gRPC services.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'grpc|Stub\(|Servicer' \
--glob '*.py' \
.

Map trust boundaries:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Flask
     |
     v
gRPC Client
     |

Internal Service

gRPC Security

docs.title: Secrets Exposure
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'secret|password|passwd|api[_-]?key|client[_-]?secret|access[_-]?key|private[_-]?key|token|database_url|redis_url' \
.

docs.title: Common Flask Secret Locations
docs.text:
Review:

.env
.flaskenv
config.py
settings.py
docker-compose.yml
Dockerfile
Kubernetes manifests
CI/CD configuration
Shell scripts
Deployment files

docs.title: Git History
docs.text:
Current source may no longer contain a secret while repository history does.

Useful commands:

git log --all --oneline

Search history:

git log -S 'SECRET_KEY' --all

Inspect a commit:

git show <commit>

Use secret-scanning tools where authorised.

Refer to:

docs/web/secrets-exposure.md

docs.title: Dependency Security
docs.text:
Find dependency files:

find . -maxdepth 3 -type f \( \
-name 'requirements*.txt' \
-o -name 'pyproject.toml' \
-o -name 'Pipfile*' \
-o -name 'poetry.lock' \
-o -name 'uv.lock' \

Review:

Jinja
SQLAlchemy
Authentication packages
JWT packages

XML libraries
Image libraries
Serialization libraries
Cloud SDKs

docs.title: pip-audit
docs.text:
pip-audit

Against requirements:

pip-audit \
-r requirements.txt

docs.title: OSV-Scanner
docs.text:
osv-scanner scan source -r .

A dependency match means:

Potentially vulnerable version

not automatically:

Exploitable application

Affected version
Affected functionality

Deployment

Dependency Security

docs.title: Static Analysis
docs.text:
Useful tools include:

Semgrep

TruffleHog

docs.title: Semgrep
docs.text:
Run:

semgrep scan \
--config auto \
.

Command execution
Raw SQL
Unsafe deserialization
SSTI candidates
XSS candidates
Hard-coded secrets
Unsafe HTTP requests

docs.title: Bandit
docs.text:
Run:

bandit -r .

Exclude tests where appropriate:

bandit \
-r . \
-x ./tests

Bandit is useful for Python security patterns but cannot reliably determine:

Object authorisation
Tenant isolation
Business logic
Workflow vulnerabilities

docs.title: CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL can assist with:

Data flow
Taint tracking
Interprocedural analysis
Variant analysis

Conceptually:

request.args
      |
      v
Controller
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Helper
      |
      v
requests.get()

docs.title: Broad Flask Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'@\w+\.route\(|@\w+\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)\(|add_url_rule\(|request\.(args|form|values|json|files|headers|cookies|data|view_args)|request\.get_json\(|login_required|current_user|jwt_required|\.query\.(get|filter|filter_by)|session\.execute\(|cursor\.execute\(|render_template_string\(|\|\s*safe\b|Markup\(|csrf\.exempt|redirect\(|requests\.(get|post|put|patch|delete|request)\(|httpx\.|urlopen\(|send_file\(|send_from_directory\(|pickle\.(load|loads)\(|yaml\.(load|unsafe_load)\(|os\.(system|popen)\(|subprocess\.|shell\s*=\s*True|\beval\(|\bexec\(' \

.

.

docs.title: File Search

docs.title: Compare Similar Routes
docs.text:
Suppose:

GET /documents/<id>
    -> login_required
    -> ownership check

POST /documents/<id>/edit
    -> login_required
    -> ownership check

POST /documents/<id>/delete
    -> login_required
    -> no ownership check

The inconsistent route is immediately interesting.

docs.title: Compare Interfaces
docs.text:
The same functionality may exist through:

HTML route
REST API
GraphQL
WebSocket
Admin route
Background task

Map them together:

User Account
    |
    +-- /account
    |
    +-- /api/account
    |
    +-- GraphQL
    |
    +-- SocketIO

Security controls should be compared across all interfaces.

docs.title: Example Finding - IDOR
docs.text:
Title:
Missing Object-Level Authorisation on Invoice Endpoint

Route:
GET /invoices/<invoice_id>

Source:
invoice_id route parameter

Data Flow:

invoice_id
    |
    v
Invoice.query.get(invoice_id)
    |
    v
Invoice
    |
    v
render_template()

Authentication:
@login_required

Authorisation:
No ownership or tenant restriction was identified.

Impact:
An authenticated user may be able to access invoices belonging to another account by changing the invoice identifier.

Recommendation:
Scope the database lookup to objects the authenticated user is authorised to access or perform an equivalent object-level permission check.

docs.title: Example Finding - SSTI
docs.text:
Title:
Server-Side Template Injection in Template Preview

Route:
POST /template/preview

Source:
request.form["template"]

Data Flow:

request.form["template"]
        |
        v
render_template_string()
        |
        v
Jinja Template Evaluation

Security Control:
No restriction prevents user-controlled input from becoming template source.

Impact:
The impact depends on the Jinja environment and application context and must be validated safely in the authorised environment.

Recommendation:
Do not interpret attacker-controlled input as template source. Keep template source server-controlled and pass untrusted values as template data.

docs.title: Example Finding - SSRF
docs.text:
Title:
Server-Side Request Forgery in URL Preview Endpoint

Route:
POST /preview

Source:
request.form["url"]

Data Flow:

request.form["url"]
        |
        v
requests.get(url)

Security Control:
No effective destination restriction was identified.

Impact:
The server may perform outbound requests to destinations selected by the user, potentially including internal services depending on network access.

Recommendation:
Prefer server-controlled destinations. Where user-selected URLs are required, implement strict destination validation and network-level egress restrictions.

docs.title: Example Finding - SQL Injection
docs.text:
Title:
SQL Injection Through Dynamically Constructed SQL Query

Route:
GET /search

Source:
request.args["q"]

Data Flow:

request.args["q"]
       |
       v
f-string SQL
       |
       v
db.session.execute()

Security Control:
No parameter binding was identified.

Recommendation:
Use ORM query construction or bind attacker-controlled values as parameters rather than concatenating them into SQL syntax.

docs.title: Example Finding - Stored XSS
docs.text:
Title:
Stored Cross-Site Scripting Through Jinja Safe Filter

Source:
Profile biography

Data Flow:

POST /profile
      |
      v
Biography
      |
      v
Database
      |
      v
{{ biography|safe }}
      |
      v
Browser

Security Control:
Jinja's normal output escaping is explicitly bypassed.

Recommendation:
Do not mark attacker-controlled values as safe. If rich HTML is required, use an appropriate allowlist-based sanitisation strategy.

docs.title: Flask Means No Security Controls
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Security controls may be implemented through:

Extensions
Decorators
before_request hooks
Reverse proxies
API gateways
External identity providers

Map the actual architecture.

docs.title: login_required Means Authorisation Exists
docs.text:
Incorrect.

login_required
      |
      v
Authenticated

does not automatically prove:

Object ownership
Role permission
Tenant membership
Action permission

docs.title: SQLAlchemy Means SQL Injection Is Impossible
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Raw SQL and dynamic SQL construction can still occur.

Search:

text()
execute()
cursor.execute()

docs.title: Every execute() Is SQL Injection
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Determine whether:

SQL syntax is dynamic
Values are bound
Input is attacker-controlled

docs.title: Every render_template_string Is SSTI
docs.text:
Incorrect.

A static developer-controlled string may be safe.

The critical question is:

Can attacker-controlled data become template source?

docs.title: Every safe Filter Is XSS
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Trace the value.

Trusted static HTML
    !=
Attacker-controlled HTML

docs.title: Every requests.get Is SSRF
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Trace who controls the destination.

docs.title: Every redirect Is Open Redirect
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Determine whether attacker-controlled external destinations are accepted.

docs.title: Every send_file Is Path Traversal
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Determine who controls the final path.

docs.title: secure_filename Solves File Upload Security
docs.text:
Incorrect.

It addresses filename safety concerns, not the entire upload threat model.

docs.title: Every ProxyFix Is Vulnerable
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Its security depends on correct deployment topology and trusted proxy counts.

docs.title: Missing Flask-Limiter Means No Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Rate limiting may be enforced outside the application.

docs.title: SECRET_KEY Found Means Secret Exposure
docs.text:
Incorrect.

Determine whether the value is:

Real
Production
Sensitive
Committed
Reachable

docs.title: Final Flask Review Model
docs.text:
FLASK APPLICATION
                                 |
                                 v
                               ROUTE
                                 |
          +----------------------+----------------------+
          |                      |                      |
          v                      v                      v
     request.args          request.form          request.json
          |                      |                      |
          +----------------------+----------------------+
                                 |
                                 v
                           VALIDATION
                                 |
                                 v
                         AUTHENTICATION
                                 |
                                 v
                          AUTHORISATION
                                 |
                                 v
                         BUSINESS LOGIC
                                 |
       +-------------------------+-------------------------+
       |                         |                         |
       v                         v                         v
    DATABASE                  TEMPLATE                  FILE
       |                         |                         |
       v                         v                         v
 SQL / NoSQL                   Jinja                  Filesystem

       +-------------------------+-------------------------+
       |                         |                         |
       v                         v                         v
   HTTP CLIENT               PROCESS                  QUEUE
       |                         |                         |
       v                         v                         v
      SSRF                Command Injection        Second-Order
                                                     Flows

The central question is:

Can attacker-controlled data reach a security-sensitive operation
without an effective validation, authentication, authorisation or
framework security boundary?

Evaluate:

Source
+
Route
+
Transformations
+
Validation
+
Authentication
+
Authorisation
+
Framework/extension protections
+
Sink
+
Reachability
+
Exploitability
+
Impact

Only then classify the candidate as a confirmed vulnerability.

docs.title: Java / Spring Source Code Review
docs.text:
Java source code review involves identifying attacker-controlled input, tracing it through the application, identifying security controls, and determining whether that data can reach security-sensitive operations in an unsafe way.

This note focuses primarily on:

Java
Spring Boot
Spring MVC
Spring WebFlux
Spring Security
Spring Data
JPA
Hibernate
JDBC
Jakarta Servlet
Jakarta REST / JAX-RS
Jackson
Thymeleaf
JSP
FreeMarker
XML processing
Java serialization

The primary review model is:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Route / Controller
     |
     v
Request Binding
     |
     v
Validation
     |
     v
Authentication
     |
     v
Authorisation
     |
     v
Service Layer
     |
     v
Repository / Business Logic
     |
     v
SECURITY-SENSITIVE SINK

The objective is not:

grep Runtime.exec()
        =
Command Injection

Instead:

SOURCE
   |
   v
DATA FLOW
   |
   v
TRANSFORMATIONS
   |
   v
SECURITY CONTROLS
   |
   v
SINK
   |
   v
EXPLOITABILITY
   |
   v
IMPACT

Authorised Security Testing

Perform source code review and dynamic validation only against applications and source code for which you have explicit authorisation. Repositories can contain credentials, API keys, personal information, cryptographic material, internal infrastructure details and other sensitive information.

docs.title: Review Strategy
docs.text:
A practical Java review can be approached as:

1. Identify projects and modules

2. Identify Java version

3. Identify frameworks

4. Identify application entry points

5. Enumerate routes

6. Map filters and interceptors

7. Map authentication

8. Map authorisation

9. Identify attacker-controlled sources

10. Identify validation

11. Identify dangerous sinks

12. Trace source-to-sink paths

13. Review business logic

14. Review configuration and secrets

15. Review dependencies

16. Run static analysis

17. Perform variant analysis

18. Validate findings dynamically where authorised

docs.title: Identify the Application
docs.text:
Start by locating build and project files.

find . -type f \( \
-name 'pom.xml' \
-o -name 'build.gradle' \
-o -name 'build.gradle.kts' \
-o -name 'settings.gradle' \
-o -name 'settings.gradle.kts' \
-o -name 'gradle.properties' \
-o -name 'mvnw' \
-o -name 'gradlew' \
\) -print

Common Java build systems include:

Maven
Gradle

docs.text:

cat pom.xml

hibernate
jackson
thymeleaf
freemarker

rg -n -i \
