docs.title: Node.js and Express Source Code Review
docs.text:
Node.js is widely used for REST APIs, web applications, GraphQL services, WebSocket applications, microservices, background workers and server-side rendering.

Express is one of the most common Node.js web frameworks, but the same review methodology applies to many JavaScript and TypeScript server applications.

Node.js applications are particularly interesting during source-code review because JavaScript applications commonly combine:

  • Dynamic typing
  • Object merging
  • JSON processing
  • Asynchronous execution
  • Large dependency trees
  • Middleware-based security controls
  • Multiple data stores
  • Server-side template engines
  • Client-side and server-side JavaScript
  • Background jobs
  • WebSockets
  • GraphQL
  • External APIs

The objective of source-code review is not simply to search for dangerous functions.

The objective is to identify:

Routes
Input sources
Authentication
Authorisation
Validation
Trust boundaries
Data transformations
Dangerous sinks
Security configuration

and determine whether attacker-controlled data can reach security-sensitive operations.

The core methodology is:

SOURCE
  |
  v
User-Controlled Input
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  +-- parsing
  +-- decoding
  +-- validation
  +-- sanitisation
  +-- object merging
  +-- business logic
  |
  v
SECURITY CONTROLS
  |
  +-- authentication
  +-- authorisation
  +-- tenant isolation
  +-- CSRF
  +-- rate limiting
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
Security-Sensitive Operation

Remember:

grep match
    !=
vulnerability

and:

Dangerous sink found
        !=
Confirmed vulnerability

A finding normally requires:

Attacker-controlled source
        +
Reachable code path
        +
Dangerous operation
        +
Missing or ineffective control
        +
Security impact

Authorised Security Testing

Perform source-code review and dynamic validation only against applications, repositories and environments for which you have explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Review Strategy
docs.text:
A practical Node.js review can follow:

1. Identify Node.js version

2. Identify package manager

3. Identify dependencies

4. Identify application entry points

5. Identify framework

6. Map middleware

7. Map routers

8. Map routes

9. Identify input sources

10. Map authentication

11. Map authorisation

12. Review object-level access

13. Review validation

14. Review database access

15. Review command execution

16. Review filesystem access

17. Review outbound HTTP requests

18. Review template engines

19. Review redirects

20. Review sessions and cookies

21. Review JWT handling

22. Review CORS

23. Review CSRF

24. Review proxy trust

25. Review file uploads

26. Review object merging and prototype pollution

27. Review GraphQL

28. Review WebSockets

29. Review business logic

30. Review asynchronous workflows

31. Review background jobs

32. Search secrets

33. Review dependencies

34. Run static analysis

35. Perform variant analysis

36. Validate candidates dynamically where authorised

docs.title: Identify the Project
docs.text:
Start with:

find . -maxdepth 3 -type f \( \
-name 'package.json' \
-o -name 'package-lock.json' \
-o -name 'yarn.lock' \
-o -name 'pnpm-lock.yaml' \
-o -name 'bun.lock' \
-o -name 'bun.lockb' \
-o -name 'tsconfig.json' \
-o -name '.npmrc' \
-o -name '.yarnrc*' \
\) -print

High-value files include:

package.json
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml
tsconfig.json

app.js
server.js
index.js
main.js

app.ts
server.ts
index.ts
main.ts

routes/
controllers/
middleware/
services/
models/
repositories/
graphql/
websocket/
workers/
jobs/
config/

docs.title: package.json
docs.text:
Inspect:

cat package.json

Important sections:

{
  "scripts": {},
  "dependencies": {},
  "devDependencies": {},
  "engines": {}
}

Look for:

express
fastify
koa
hapi
nestjs
mongoose
mongodb
sequelize
typeorm
prisma
knex
pg
mysql
mysql2
sqlite
jsonwebtoken
jose
passport
express-session
cookie-session
helmet
cors
csurf
express-rate-limit
multer
axios
got
node-fetch
undici
ejs
pug
handlebars
mustache
socket.io
ws
graphql
apollo

Dependencies reveal much of the attack surface.

docs.title: Node.js Version
docs.text:
Check:

node --version

Project requirements may appear in:

{
  "engines": {
    "node": ">=..."
  }
}

Search:

rg -n \
'"node"\s*:|node-version|NODE_VERSION' \
package.json .nvmrc .node-version Dockerfile* .github 2>/dev/null

Also inspect:

Docker images
CI workflows
Deployment manifests
Runtime configuration

Do not assume the developer's local Node.js version equals the production version.

docs.title: JavaScript vs TypeScript
docs.text:
Find:

find . -type f \( \
-name '*.js' \
-o -name '*.mjs' \
-o -name '*.cjs' \
-o -name '*.ts' \
-o -name '*.tsx' \
\) | head -100

TypeScript configuration:

cat tsconfig.json

TypeScript improves type safety but does not automatically prevent security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Common Application Structure
docs.text:
A typical Express project may resemble:

src/
├── app.ts
├── server.ts
├── routes/
│   ├── auth.ts
│   ├── users.ts
│   └── admin.ts
├── controllers/
│   ├── authController.ts
│   └── userController.ts
├── middleware/
│   ├── auth.ts
│   └── permissions.ts
├── services/
│   ├── userService.ts
│   └── webhookService.ts
├── models/
│   └── User.ts
├── repositories/
├── jobs/
├── config/
└── views/

Trace:

Route
  |
  v
Middleware
  |
  v
Controller
  |
  v
Service
  |
  v
Repository
  |
  v
Database / External System

docs.title: Identify Express
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'require\(["'\'']express["'\'']\)|from ["'\'']express["'\'']|express\(\)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Typical:

const express = require("express");
const app = express();

or:

import express from "express";

const app = express();

docs.title: Application Entry Points
docs.text:
Inspect package scripts:

rg -n \
'"(start|dev|serve)"\s*:' \
package.json

Example:

{
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node dist/server.js",
    "dev": "tsx src/server.ts"
  }
}

Trace the actual startup file.

docs.title: Middleware Order
docs.text:
Express security often depends heavily on middleware ordering.

Example:

app.use(express.json());

app.use(authenticate);

app.use("/api", apiRouter);

app.use(errorHandler);

Middleware order matters.

A route registered before authentication middleware may not receive the expected protection.

Search:

rg -n \
'app\.use\(|router\.use\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Map middleware sequentially.

docs.title: Route Discovery
docs.text:
Common Express routes:

app.get()
app.post()
app.put()
app.patch()
app.delete()

router.get()
router.post()
router.put()
router.patch()
router.delete()

Search:

rg -n \
'\b(app|router)\.(get|post|put|patch|delete|options|head|all)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Route Example
docs.text:
router.get(
    "/users/:id",
    authenticate,
    getUser
);

Map:

GET /users/:id
      |
      v
authenticate
      |
      v
getUser

docs.title: Router Mounting
docs.text:
Routes may be split across files.

Example:

app.use(
    "/api/users",
    userRouter
);

and:

router.get(
    "/:id",
    getUser
);

Final route:

GET /api/users/:id

Search:

rg -n \
'app\.use\(|router\.use\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Always combine:

Mount path
    +
Router path
    =
Final endpoint

docs.title: Express Router
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'express\.Router\(\)|Router\(\)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Typical:

const router = express.Router();

docs.title: Dynamic Routes
docs.text:
Route parameters:

router.get(
    "/users/:userId",
    handler
);

Attacker-controlled source:

req.params.userId

docs.title: Route Inventory
docs.text:
Build:

Method Route Handler Authentication Authorisation GET /users/:id getUser JWT ? POST /users createUser JWT Admin? PATCH /users/:id updateUser JWT Owner? DELETE /users/:id deleteUser JWT Admin?

This makes inconsistent security controls easier to identify.

docs.title: User-Controlled Input Sources
docs.text:
The primary Express sources are:

req.query
req.params
req.body
req.headers
req.cookies
req.signedCookies
req.file
req.files

Other sources include:

req.get()
req.header()
req.hostname
req.ip
req.ips
req.protocol
req.originalUrl
req.url

docs.title: Input Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'req\.(query|params|body|headers|cookies|signedCookies|file|files|hostname|ip|ips|protocol|originalUrl|url)|req\.(get|header)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Query Parameters
docs.text:
Example:

const search = req.query.q;

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.query' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Route Parameters
docs.text:
const id = req.params.id;

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.params' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Request Body
docs.text:
const data = req.body;

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.body' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Treat nested fields individually.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
const token =
    req.headers.authorization;

Search:

rg -n \
'req\.headers|req\.get\(|req\.header\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Potentially attacker-controlled headers include:

Host
Origin
Referer
User-Agent
Authorization
X-Forwarded-For
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Forwarded-Proto
Custom headers

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'req\.cookies|req\.signedCookies' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Signed cookies provide integrity when implemented correctly.

They are not automatically secret.

docs.title: Body Parsers
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'express\.json\(|express\.urlencoded\(|bodyParser\.' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review:

Body size
Accepted content types
Nested object behaviour
Raw body requirements
Signature verification

docs.title: Raw Bodies
docs.text:
Webhooks may require raw request bodies.

Search:

rg -n \
'express\.raw\(|express\.text\(|req\.rawBody' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

This is particularly important for:

Webhook signatures
Payment providers
Custom protocols

docs.title: Input Validation
docs.text:
Common validation libraries include:

Joi
Zod
Ajv
express-validator
Yup
class-validator
Valibot

Search:

rg -n -i \
'joi|zod|ajv|express-validator|class-validator|yup|valibot|validate|schema' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Validation Example
docs.text:
const schema = z.object({
    email: z.string().email(),
    name: z.string().max(100)
});

const input =
    schema.parse(req.body);

Validation establishes constraints.

It does not automatically provide:

Authorisation
Safe SQL construction
Safe command construction
Safe HTML output
Object ownership

docs.title: Unknown Fields
docs.text:
Review whether schemas:

Reject unknown fields
Strip unknown fields
Preserve unknown fields

This matters for mass assignment.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Search broadly:

rg -n -i \
'authenticate|authentication|authorize|authorization|passport|jwt|bearer|session|login|logout|api.?key|currentUser|req\.user' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Authentication Middleware
docs.text:
Typical:

function authenticate(
    req,
    res,
    next
) {
    ...
}

Routes:

router.get(
    "/profile",
    authenticate,
    profile
);

Search:

rg -n \
'authenticate|authMiddleware|requireAuth|isAuthenticated|req\.user' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Read middleware implementations.

Do not trust names alone.

docs.title: Middleware Coverage
docs.text:
Compare:

router.get(
    "/account",
    authenticate,
    account
);

with:

router.post(
    "/account/delete",
    deleteAccount
);

The second route deserves investigation.

docs.title: Router-Level Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication may be applied globally:

router.use(authenticate);

Therefore:

No route-level middleware
    !=
Unauthenticated

Trace parent routers and application middleware.

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'role|permission|authorize|authorise|admin|owner|tenant|organization|organisation|workspace|req\.user' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Role Middleware
docs.text:
Example:

function requireAdmin(
    req,
    res,
    next
) {
    if (!req.user.isAdmin) {
        return res.sendStatus(403);
    }

    next();
}

Determine where req.user originates.

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
Candidate:

router.get(
    "/documents/:id",
    authenticate,
    async (req, res) => {
        const document =
            await Document.findById(
                req.params.id
            );

        res.json(document);
    }
);

Data flow:

req.params.id
      |
      v
Document.findById()
      |
      v
Document
      |
      v
Response

Question:

Where is ownership or tenant authorisation?

docs.title: Scoped Lookup
docs.text:
A stronger pattern may resemble:

const document =
    await Document.findOne({
        _id: req.params.id,
        ownerId: req.user.id
    });

For multi-tenant applications:

const document =
    await Document.findOne({
        _id: req.params.id,
        tenantId: req.user.tenantId
    });

The correct scope depends on application policy.

docs.title: Object Lookup Search
docs.text:
MongoDB/Mongoose:

rg -n \
'\.(findById|findOne|find|findOneAndUpdate|findByIdAndUpdate|findOneAndDelete|findByIdAndDelete)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

SQL ORMs:

rg -n \
'(findOne|findUnique|findFirst|findByPk|findAll|select|where)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Prioritise attacker-controlled identifiers.

Refer to:

IDOR and BOLA

Authorisation Testing

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Security
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'tenantId|tenant_id|organizationId|organisationId|workspaceId|accountId|ownerId' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Map:

Authenticated User
       |
       v
Tenant Membership
       |
       v
Tenant Identifier
       |
       v
Database Query
       |
       v
Object

Look for queries that omit tenant scope.

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
Node.js applications may use:

pg
mysql
mysql2
sqlite
Knex
Sequelize
TypeORM
Prisma
Raw SQL

Search:

rg -n \
'\.(query|execute|raw|queryRaw|executeRaw)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Raw SQL
docs.text:
Candidate:

const username =
    req.query.username;

const sql =
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" +
    username +
    "'";

db.query(sql);

Trace:

req.query.username
        |
        v
SQL String
        |
        v
db.query()

docs.title: Template Literal SQL
docs.text:
Candidate:

const sql =
    `SELECT * FROM users
     WHERE username = '${username}'`;

Search candidates:

rg -n \
'`[^`]*(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE)[^`]*\$\{' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: PostgreSQL Parameterisation
docs.text:
Safer style:

await pool.query(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1",
    [userId]
);

Review dynamic structural elements separately:

Column names
Table names
ORDER BY
Operators
Directions

These usually require server-controlled mappings or allowlists.

docs.title: MySQL Parameterisation
docs.text:
Example:

connection.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?",
    [userId]
);

Review the actual driver and API semantics.

docs.title: Sequelize
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'sequelize\.query|Sequelize\.literal|literal\(|replacements|bind' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Raw query functionality deserves particular attention.

docs.title: Knex
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'knex\.raw|\.whereRaw|\.orderByRaw|\.havingRaw|\.joinRaw' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Prisma
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\$queryRaw|\$executeRaw|\$queryRawUnsafe|\$executeRawUnsafe' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Raw and explicitly unsafe query APIs deserve investigation.

Do not report normal ORM queries as SQL injection merely because attacker-controlled values are used as query values.

Refer to:

SQL Injection

docs.title: NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
NoSQL injection is especially relevant to Node.js applications using MongoDB.

Sources such as:

req.body
req.query

may contain nested objects rather than only strings.

Candidate:

const user =
    await User.findOne({
        username: req.body.username,
        password: req.body.password
    });

The security significance depends on:

Parser behaviour
ODM behaviour
Input validation
Object sanitisation
MongoDB operator handling
Library versions

Do not assume every object passed to Mongoose is injectable.

docs.title: Raw Query Object
docs.text:
Higher-risk pattern:

const query =
    req.body;

const user =
    await User.findOne(query);

Data flow:

req.body
   |
   v
Mongo Query Object
   |
   v
findOne()

docs.title: MongoDB Search
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\.(find|findOne|findById|aggregate|updateOne|updateMany|deleteOne|deleteMany|findOneAndUpdate)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: MongoDB Operators
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\$(where|regex|expr|ne|gt|gte|lt|lte|in|nin|or|and|lookup|function)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Operator use is not automatically vulnerable.

Trace whether attackers control:

Operator names
Query structure
Expressions
Regular expressions
Aggregation stages

Refer to:

NoSQL Injection

docs.title: LDAP Injection
docs.text:
Node.js applications may use:

ldapjs
ldapts
Active Directory libraries
Custom LDAP clients

Search:

rg -n -i \
'ldap|ldapjs|ldapts|searchFilter|filter:' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

const filter =
    `(uid=${req.body.username})`;

Trace attacker-controlled values into LDAP filter syntax.

Refer to:

LDAP Injection

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
Node.js exposes process execution through:

child_process.exec()
child_process.execSync()
child_process.spawn()
child_process.spawnSync()
execFile()
execFileSync()

Search:

rg -n \
'child_process|execSync\(|execFileSync\(|execFile\(|spawnSync\(|spawn\(|\bexec\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: exec()
docs.text:
High-risk candidate:

const host =
    req.body.host;

exec(
    `ping -c 1 ${host}`,
    callback
);

Flow:

req.body.host
      |
      v
Shell Command
      |
      v
exec()
      |
      v
Shell

Node.js documentation explicitly warns against passing unsanitised user input to shell-backed child-process execution.

docs.title: execSync()
docs.text:
Candidate:

const output =
    execSync(
        `nslookup ${domain}`
    );

Search:

rg -n \
'execSync\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: spawn()
docs.text:
Prefer argument arrays where possible:

spawn(
    "ping",
    [
        "-c",
        "1",
        host
    ]
);

This avoids shell parsing by default.

However:

spawn() with argument array
        !=
Automatically secure

Review:

Executable control
Argument semantics
Option injection
Working directory
Environment

docs.title: shell: true
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'shell\s*:\s*true|shell\s*=\s*true' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Example:

spawn(
    command,
    {
        shell: true
    }
);

Treat attacker-controlled input reaching shell-enabled execution as high priority.

Refer to:

OS Command Injection

docs.title: Dynamic JavaScript Execution
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\beval\(|new Function\(|Function\(|vm\.runIn(New|This)Context|vm\.runInContext|vm\.runInThisContext' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

const expression =
    req.body.expression;

const result =
    eval(expression);

Trace attacker control carefully.

docs.title: vm Module
docs.text:
The Node.js vm module is not a general security boundary for executing hostile code.

Search:

rg -n \
'node:vm|require\(["'\'']vm["'\'']\)|from ["'\'']node:vm["'\'']|runInNewContext|runInContext' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review any attempt to use it as an untrusted-code sandbox.

docs.title: Server-Side Template Injection
docs.text:
Common Node.js template engines include:

EJS
Pug
Handlebars
Mustache
Nunjucks
Liquid

Search dependencies:

rg -n -i \
'ejs|pug|handlebars|mustache|nunjucks|liquid' \
package.json package-lock.json yarn.lock pnpm-lock.yaml 2>/dev/null

docs.title: res.render()
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.render\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Normal:

res.render(
    "profile",
    {
        username
    }
);

Passing attacker-controlled values as template data is not the same as allowing the attacker to control template source.

docs.title: Dynamic Template Names
docs.text:
Candidate:

res.render(
    req.query.template,
    data
);

Review whether users can select unintended templates or influence template resolution.

docs.title: EJS
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'ejs\.render|ejs\.renderFile|<%-' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts,ejs}' \
.

In EJS:

<%= value %>

and:

<%- value %>

have different escaping behaviour.

Review unescaped output carefully.

docs.title: Handlebars
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Handlebars\.compile|handlebars\.compile|{{{' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts,hbs,handlebars}' \
.

Triple braces can produce unescaped output.

docs.title: Pug
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'!=|!{' \
--glob '*.pug' \
.

Review unescaped output contexts.

docs.title: Template Source
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\.compile\(|\.render\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Determine whether attacker-controlled data becomes:

Template data

or:

Template source

This distinction is essential.

Refer to:

Server-Side Template Injection

docs.title: XSS
docs.text:
Server-side Node.js applications can introduce XSS through:

Unescaped templates
HTML string construction
Unsafe redirects into script contexts
Stored data rendered without encoding
Client-side JavaScript

docs.title: res.send()
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.send\(|res\.end\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

const name =
    req.query.name;

res.send(
    `<h1>Hello ${name}</h1>`
);

Trace:

req.query.name
      |
      v
HTML String
      |
      v
res.send()
      |
      v
Browser

docs.title: HTML Construction
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.send\(`|res\.send\(".*<|res\.send\('\''.*<' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Manual review is required.

docs.title: JSON Is Not Automatically XSS
docs.text:
Example:

res.json({
    username
});

This is not automatically XSS simply because username contains HTML characters.

The downstream browser context matters.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

HTML Injection

docs.title: Open Redirect
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.redirect\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

res.redirect(
    req.query.next
);

Trace whether attacker-controlled external destinations are accepted.

docs.title: Common Redirect Parameters
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'next|redirect|returnUrl|return_url|returnTo|continue|callbackUrl' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Validate destinations using an explicit policy.

Refer to:

docs/web/open-redirect.md

docs.title: SSRF
docs.text:
Common HTTP clients include:

fetch
axios
got
undici
node-fetch
http
https
superagent

Search:

rg -n \
'\bfetch\(|axios\.|got\(|got\.|request\(|http\.request\(|https\.request\(|undici|superagent\.' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: SSRF Candidate
docs.text:
const url =
    req.body.url;

const response =
    await fetch(url);

Flow:

req.body.url
      |
      v
fetch()
      |
      v
Network

Review:

Scheme
Hostname
Port
DNS resolution
IPv4
IPv6
Redirects
Private ranges
Loopback
Link-local
Cloud metadata
Egress controls

docs.title: Axios
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'axios\.(get|post|put|patch|delete|request)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Stored SSRF
docs.text:
Example:

POST /webhooks
       |
       v
req.body.url
       |
       v
Database
       |
       v
Background Worker
       |
       v
fetch()

Search beyond direct request-to-fetch flows.

Refer to:

Server Side Request Forgery

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Common filesystem APIs:

fs.readFile()
fs.readFileSync()
fs.writeFile()
fs.writeFileSync()
fs.createReadStream()
fs.createWriteStream()
fs.stat()
fs.unlink()

Search:

rg -n \
'fs\.(readFile|readFileSync|writeFile|writeFileSync|createReadStream|createWriteStream|stat|unlink|rm|readdir)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Path Construction
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'path\.(join|resolve|normalize)\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

const file =
    req.query.file;

const fullPath =
    path.join(
        "/srv/files",
        file
    );

res.sendFile(fullPath);

Do not assume:

path.join()

or:

path.resolve()

alone establishes containment.

Review the final canonical path and base-directory boundary.

docs.title: res.sendFile()
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.sendFile\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Determine who controls:

Filename
Path
Root
Extension

docs.title: res.download()
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'res\.download\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Trace attacker-controlled paths.

Refer to:

docs/web/path-traversal.md

docs.title: File Upload

Node.js applications commonly use:

Multer

express-fileupload

rg -n -i \

.

docs.title: Multer

.

Destination

Original filename
Extension

Size
Number of files
Memory storage

Processing

docs.title: originalname
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'originalname|mimetype|req\.file\.path|req\.file\.filename' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

filename:
    (
        req,

docs.title: Archive Extraction
docs.text:

docs.title: Deserialization
docs.text:
JSON parsing itself is not equivalent to unsafe native-code deserialization.

However, applications may use dangerous serialization packages or convert untrusted objects into executable structures.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'serialize|deserialize|node-serialize|unserialize|yaml\.load|js-yaml|JSON\.parse' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Do not flag every:

JSON.parse()

as insecure deserialization.

Review:

Library
Object type
Revivers
Prototype handling
Dynamic execution
Trust boundary

Refer to:

Insecure Deserialization

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Prototype pollution is especially important in JavaScript source review.

Potential sources:

req.body
req.query
JSON.parse()

Potential dangerous operations include:

Object.assign()
deep merge libraries
recursive setters
dynamic property assignment
lodash merge functions

Search:

rg -n \
'Object\.assign\(|merge\(|mergeWith\(|defaultsDeep\(|set\(|setWith\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Dynamic Property Assignment
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\[[A-Za-z0-9_.$]+\]\s*=' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Candidate:

object[
    req.body.key
] = req.body.value;

Review whether keys such as:

__proto__
constructor
prototype

can affect object prototypes.

docs.title: Recursive Merge
docs.text:
Candidate:

function merge(
    target,
    source
) {
    for (
        const key in source
    ) {
        ...
    }
}

Custom recursive merge implementations deserve careful review.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Impact
docs.text:
Pollution alone may not establish meaningful impact.

Trace polluted properties into:

Authorisation
Command execution
Template engines
Configuration
HTTP options
Filesystem operations
Privilege checks

Refer to:

Prototype Pollution

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Candidate:

const user =
    await User.create(
        req.body
    );

Potential attacker-controlled fields:

role
isAdmin
permissions
verified
status
tenantId
ownerId
balance
credits

Search:

rg -n \
'(create|update|findOneAndUpdate|findByIdAndUpdate)\(\s*req\.body|Object\.assign\(.*req\.body|\.\.\.req\.body' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Object Spread
docs.text:
Candidate:

const user = {
    ...req.body
};

Search:

rg -n \
'\.\.\.req\.(body|query|params)' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: Safer Field Selection
docs.text:
Example:

const {
    name,
    email
} = req.body;

await User.updateOne(
    {
        _id: req.user.id
    },
    {
        name,
        email
    }
);

Explicit field selection makes the writable model clearer.

Refer to:

Mass Assignment

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
CSRF relevance depends heavily on the authentication mechanism.

Cookie-authenticated state-changing routes deserve particular attention.

Bearer tokens supplied explicitly in an Authorization header have a different CSRF threat model.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'csrf|csurf|csrfToken|sameSite' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.title: State-Changing Routes
docs.text:
Map:

POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

against:

Authentication mechanism
Cookie behaviour
SameSite
CSRF controls
Origin validation

Do not report missing CSRF middleware without understanding authentication.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Express applications commonly use the cors package.

Search:

rg -n \
'require\(["'\'']cors["'\'']\)|from ["'\'']cors["'\'']|cors\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs.text:

app.use(
    cors()
);

Sensitive responses
Credentials
Authentication mechanism

Endpoint exposure

docs.title: Dynamic Origin
docs.text:
Candidate:

cors({
    origin:
        (
            origin,
            callback
        ) => {
            ...
        }
});

Review origin validation.

Dangerous patterns may include:

Substring matching
Suffix matching without boundary checks
Regex mistakes
Reflection of arbitrary Origin

Refer to:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

docs.text:

app.use(
    session({
        secret:
            process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
        resave: false,
        saveUninitialized: false,

            httpOnly: true,

Secret

Store

docs.text:

Do not infer production behaviour solely from local development configuration.

.

Anonymous
   |
   v
Login
   |
   v
Authenticated Session

Determine whether session identifiers and state are appropriately handled.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text:

rg -n \

.

docs/web/session-management.md

docs.title: jwt.verify
docs.text:
Typical:

const payload =
    jwt.verify(
        token,
        publicKey,
        options
    );

Signature verification
Allowed algorithms

Audience

Not-before

docs.title: jwt.decode
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'jwt\.decode\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Decoding a JWT is not equivalent to verifying it.

A high-value pattern is:

const claims =
    jwt.decode(token);

if (
    claims.role === "admin"
) {
    ...
}

when security decisions occur before cryptographic verification.

docs.title: JWT Authorisation
docs.text:
Review:

Who issues role claims?
Can roles become stale?
Are revoked accounts still accepted?
Are tenant claims trusted?
Are refresh tokens protected?

JSON Web Token Security

docs.text:

const resetUrl =
    `${req.protocol}://${req.get("host")}/reset/${token}`;

Host Header

docs.title: trust proxy
docs.text:
Express provides the trust proxy setting for deployments behind reverse proxies.

Search:

rg -n \
'trust proxy|trustProxy|app\.set\(["'\'']trust proxy' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Example:

app.set(
    "trust proxy",
    1
);

Review this against the actual proxy topology.

Incorrect proxy trust may affect:

req.ip
req.ips
req.hostname
req.protocol
Secure-cookie behaviour
IP-based access controls
Rate limiting
Logging
Absolute URL generation

Do not automatically report trust proxy.

Determine whether the configured trust boundary matches deployment.

docs.title: Forwarded Headers

rg -n -i \
'x-forwarded-for|x-forwarded-host|x-forwarded-proto|forwarded' \

.

Map:

Internet
   |
   v
Trusted Reverse Proxy
   |
   v
Forwarded Headers
   |
   v
Express

docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'req\.ip|req\.ips|socket\.remoteAddress|connection\.remoteAddress' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

If IP addresses control:

Admin access
Rate limits
Allowlisting
Internal-only endpoints

docs.text:
Common packages include:

express-rate-limit
rate-limiter-flexible
Bottleneck
Redis-backed custom limits

rg -n -i \
'express-rate-limit|rate-limiter|rateLimit|limiter|too many requests|429' \

.

Prioritise:

Login
Password reset
MFA
Registration
OTP
Email verification
Expensive APIs
Exports

Do not conclude rate limiting is absent solely from application source.

It may be enforced by:

Nginx
CDN
WAF
API gateway
Load balancer

Refer to:

Rate Limiting and Anti-Automation

docs.text:
Express applications frequently use Helmet.

Search:

rg -n \
'helmet\(|Content-Security-Policy|X-Frame-Options|Strict-Transport-Security|X-Content-Type-Options|Referrer-Policy|Permissions-Policy' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

docs/web/http-security-headers.md

docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'frameguard|X-Frame-Options|frame-ancestors|helmet' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Refer to:

docs/web/clickjacking.md

docs.title: Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'console\.(log|error|debug)|res\.send\(.*err|res\.json\(.*err|err\.stack|error\.stack|stack' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review whether clients receive:

Stack traces
Filesystem paths
Database errors
Tokens
Secrets
Internal hostnames
Dependency details

docs.title: Error Middleware
docs.text:
Express error handlers commonly resemble:

app.use(
    (
        err,
        req,
        res,
        next
    ) => {
        ...
    }
);

Search:

rg -n \
'err\.stack|error\.stack|NODE_ENV|app\.use\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Check production behaviour.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Common libraries:

Winston
Pino
Morgan
Bunyan
Console

Search:

rg -n \
'console\.(log|error|debug|warn)|logger\.(info|debug|warn|error|fatal)|pino\(|winston|morgan\(' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review for:

Authorization headers
JWTs
Session cookies
Passwords
API keys
Reset tokens
MFA codes
Personal data
Request bodies

docs.title: Log Injection
docs.text:
Candidate:

logger.info(
    `Login failed for ${req.body.username}`
);

Determine:

Log format
Structured logging
Escaping
Downstream consumers

Do not automatically classify user-controlled log content as exploitable log injection.

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'price|amount|balance|credit|discount|coupon|refund|quantity|inventory|approved|verified|status|role|permission' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Prioritise:

Payments
Refunds
Credits
Coupons
Inventory
Subscriptions
Approval workflows
Verification
Role changes
Tenant changes

docs.title: Client-Controlled Price
docs.text:
Candidate:

const {
    productId,
    price
} = req.body;

await Order.create({
    productId,
    price
});

Question:

Should price come from trusted server-side product data?

Refer to:

Business Logic Vulnerabilities

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Node.js being event-driven does not eliminate race conditions.

Example:

const account =
    await Account.findById(id);

if (
    account.balance >= amount
) {
    account.balance -= amount;

    await account.save();
}

Concurrent requests may interact with the same logical state.

docs.title: Race Review
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'transaction|startSession|withTransaction|lock|mutex|version|optimistic|increment|decrement|\$inc' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Review:

Read-check-write sequences
One-time tokens
Credits
Coupons
Inventory
Balances
Approvals

docs.title: Database Atomic Operations
docs.text:
Look for atomic operations such as:

$inc
findOneAndUpdate
transactions
conditional UPDATE
optimistic locking

Their presence does not automatically prove the workflow is race-safe.

Refer to:

Race Conditions

docs.title: Promise and Async Control Flow
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'async |await |Promise\.all|Promise\.race|forEach\(async|map\(async' \
--glob '*.{js,mjs,cjs,ts}' \
.

Security bugs can occur through incorrect asynchronous assumptions.

docs.title: forEach(async)
docs.text:
Candidate:

items.forEach(
    async item => {
        await authorise(item);
    }
);

performAction();

The surrounding code may continue before asynchronous callbacks finish.

Review security-sensitive async flows carefully.

docs.title: Missing await
docs.text:
Source review should inspect security functions that return promises.

Candidate:

if (
    checkPermission(user)
) {
    performSensitiveAction();
}

If checkPermission() returns a Promise, this logic may not behave as intended.

TypeScript and linting can help identify these mistakes.

docs.text:

Bull

HTTP Request

Queue

Worker

Dangerous Sink

Reverse Proxy

Load Balancer
  |

HTTP Request Smuggling

docs.text:
Inspect:

.env

config/

Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
Kubernetes manifests
Terraform
CI/CD files
Shell scripts
PM2 configuration

Find:

docs.text:
CodeQL supports JavaScript and TypeScript and provides data-flow and taint-tracking analysis.

Service

HTTP Client

Helper

docs.text:
For large repositories, starting at dangerous sinks is often efficient.

Example:

Controller
        ^

High-value sinks include:

Function()

raw SQL

Mongo raw query structures

fetch()
axios()
got()

fs.readFile()
fs.writeFile()
res.sendFile()

res.send()
unescaped templates

res.redirect()

Object.assign()
deep merge functions

Before reporting:

     |
     v

docs.title: Example Finding - IDOR
docs.text:
Title:
Missing Object-Level Authorisation on Document Endpoint

Route:
GET /api/documents/:id

Source:
req.params.id

Data Flow:

req.params.id
      |
      v
Document.findById()
      |
      v
Document
      |
      v
res.json()

Authentication:
Authentication middleware is present.

Authorisation:
No ownership or tenant restriction was identified before returning the document.

Impact:
An authenticated user may be able to access another user's document by supplying its identifier.

Recommendation:
Scope the lookup to objects the authenticated user is authorised to access or perform an equivalent object-level permission check.

docs.title: Example Finding - Command Injection
docs.text:
Title:
OS Command Injection in Diagnostics Endpoint

Route:
POST /api/diagnostics

Source:
req.body.host

Data Flow:

req.body.host
      |
      v
Template Literal
      |
      v
child_process.exec()
      |
      v
Shell

Security Control:
No effective validation prevents attacker-controlled input from altering shell syntax.

Recommendation:
Avoid shell command construction. Invoke the required executable directly with controlled arguments and validate attacker-controlled values according to the expected input format.

docs.title: Example Finding - SSRF
docs.text:
Title:
Server-Side Request Forgery in URL Preview Endpoint

Route:
POST /api/preview

Source:
req.body.url

Data Flow:

req.body.url
      |
      v
fetch()
      |
      v
Network

Security Control:
No effective destination restriction was identified.

Impact:
The application may make server-side requests to destinations selected by the user, potentially including internal services depending on network access.

Recommendation:
Prefer server-controlled destinations. Where arbitrary external URLs are required, implement strict destination validation and network-level egress restrictions.

docs.title: Example Finding - NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
Title:
User-Controlled MongoDB Query Structure

Route:
POST /api/users/search

Source:
req.body

Data Flow:

req.body
      |
      v
User.find(req.body)
      |
      v
MongoDB

Security Concern:
The complete query object is supplied by the client rather than being constructed from server-controlled query structure.

Recommendation:
Define the permitted query structure server-side and copy only explicitly supported fields and operators from validated client input.

docs.title: Example Finding - Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Title:
Mass Assignment in User Profile Update

Route:
PATCH /api/users/me

Source:
req.body

Data Flow:

req.body
      |
      v
User.findByIdAndUpdate(
    req.user.id,
    req.body
)
      |
      v
User Model

Security Concern:
The client may be able to modify fields that were not intended to be user-controlled.

Recommendation:
Define an explicit allowlist of writable profile fields and construct the update object from those validated fields.

docs.title: Example Finding - Stored XSS
docs.text:
Title:
Stored Cross-Site Scripting Through Unescaped EJS Output

Source:
req.body.biography

Data Flow:

POST /profile
      |
      v
req.body.biography
      |
      v
Database
      |
      v
<%- biography %>
      |
      v
Browser

Security Control:
Template output escaping is explicitly bypassed for the stored value.

Recommendation:
Use escaped template output for attacker-controlled values. If rich HTML is required, use an appropriate allowlist-based HTML sanitisation strategy.

Load balancer

Validate deployed responses.

docs.text:
Incorrect.

Its correctness depends on the real network topology.

docs.text:
Incorrect.

Validate:

Version
Reachability
Affected functionality
Attacker control
Deployment

docs.title: Final Node.js Review Model
docs.text:
NODE.JS / EXPRESS
                              |
                              v
                            ROUTE
                              |
        +---------------------+---------------------+
        |                     |                     |
        v                     v                     v
    req.query             req.params             req.body
        |                     |                     |
        +---------------------+---------------------+
                              |
                              v
                          MIDDLEWARE
                              |
              +---------------+---------------+
              |                               |
              v                               v
       AUTHENTICATION                   VALIDATION
              |                               |
              +---------------+---------------+
                              |
                              v
                        AUTHORISATION
                              |
                              v
                       BUSINESS LOGIC
                              |
    +-------------+-----------+-----------+-------------+
    |             |           |           |             |
    v             v           v           v             v
 DATABASE      TEMPLATE      FILE       HTTP          PROCESS
    |             |           |           |             |
    v             v           v           v             v
SQL/NoSQL      XSS/SSTI    Traversal     SSRF       Command
                                                   Injection

                    +----------------------+
                    |
                    v
              OBJECT OPERATIONS
                    |
          +---------+---------+
          |                   |
          v                   v
   Mass Assignment      Prototype Pollution

                    +----------------------+
                    |
                    v
              ASYNC / BACKGROUND
                    |
          +---------+---------+
          |                   |
          v                   v
       Queue              Worker
          |                   |
          +---------+---------+
                    |
                    v
              Second-Order Sink

The central question is:

Can attacker-controlled data reach a security-sensitive operation
without an effective validation, authentication, authorisation or
other security boundary?

Evaluate:

Source
+
Route
+
Middleware
+
Transformations
+
Validation
+
Authentication
+
Authorisation
+
Framework protections
+
Sink
+
Reachability
+
Exploitability
+
Impact

Only then classify a candidate as a confirmed vulnerability.
