docs.title: Routes and Entry Points
docs.text:
Finding every application entry point is one of the first and most important tasks during source code review.

Before analysing vulnerabilities, the reviewer needs to understand how attacker-controlled data can enter the application.

An entry point is any location where data, events, requests, or messages originating outside the current trust boundary cause application code to execute.

The obvious examples are HTTP routes:

GET /api/users
POST /login
PUT /api/profile
DELETE /api/documents/{id}

However, modern applications frequently expose many other entry points:

REST endpoints
GraphQL queries
GraphQL mutations
GraphQL subscriptions
gRPC methods
WebSocket messages
Webhooks
File uploads
File imports
Message queues
Background workers
Scheduled jobs
Serverless functions
CLI interfaces
Authentication callbacks
OAuth callbacks
SAML endpoints
Administrative interfaces
Internal APIs
Health and management endpoints

The objective is to create an attack-surface map that answers:

What can cause this application to execute code?

What data can enter through that path?

Who can reach it?

What security controls protect it?

Where does the data go?

docs.title: Authorised Testing
docs.text:
Use these techniques only against source code, applications, systems, and environments that you are authorised to assess.

Source code may expose sensitive information including:

Internal routes
Administrative functionality
Credentials
API keys
Infrastructure
Authentication logic
Authorisation logic
Debug functionality
Internal services
Undocumented APIs

Handle this information according to the rules of engagement.

docs.title: Why Route Discovery Matters
docs.text:
Dynamic testing only reveals functionality that can be discovered from the running application.

Source code review can reveal functionality that is:

Undocumented
Hidden from navigation
Accessible only through APIs
Role-restricted
Feature-flagged
Environment-specific
Internal
Legacy
Partially deprecated
Called asynchronously
Triggered through another service

A source-assisted review therefore begins with:

Repository
    |
    v
Application Structure
    |
    v
Entry Points
    |
    v
Routes
    |
    v
Inputs
    |
    v
Security Controls
    |
    v
Sensitive Operations

docs.title: Route Discovery Is Attack-Surface Discovery
docs.text:
Do not think of route discovery as merely finding URL strings.

The actual goal is:

ENTRY POINT
     |
     +--> METHOD / PROTOCOL
     |
     +--> PATH / MESSAGE TYPE
     |
     +--> HANDLER
     |
     +--> INPUT
     |
     +--> AUTHENTICATION
     |
     +--> AUTHORISATION
     |
     +--> VALIDATION
     |
     +--> SENSITIVE OPERATION

For every discovered entry point, determine as much of this model as possible.

docs.title: Entry Point Categories
docs.text:
A useful classification is:

Application Entry Points
|
+-- HTTP
|   |
|   +-- REST
|   +-- MVC
|   +-- Form handlers
|   +-- File upload
|   +-- Authentication
|   +-- Administrative
|
+-- API Protocols
|   |
|   +-- GraphQL
|   +-- gRPC
|   +-- WebSockets
|   +-- Server-Sent Events
|
+-- External Integrations
|   |
|   +-- Webhooks
|   +-- OAuth callbacks
|   +-- SAML endpoints
|   +-- Payment callbacks
|
+-- Asynchronous
|   |
|   +-- Message queues
|   +-- Event consumers
|   +-- Background workers
|   +-- Scheduled jobs
|
+-- Data Processing
|   |
|   +-- File uploads
|   +-- File imports
|   +-- Archive processing
|   +-- Document processing
|
+-- Operational
    |
    +-- Health endpoints
    +-- Metrics
    +-- Debug
    +-- Management
    +-- Internal APIs

docs.title: The Route Inventory
docs.text:
Create an inventory while reviewing.

Example:

Method Route Handler Authentication Authorisation Inputs Notes GET /api/users/{id} getUser() Required Ownership? id Review IDOR POST /login login() No N/A username/password Authentication POST /api/import importFile() Required Admin? file Upload/import GET /preview preview() Required Unknown url SSRF candidate POST /webhook/payment paymentWebhook() Signature N/A JSON Verify signature

The inventory should evolve during the review.

docs.title: Entry Point Confidence
docs.text:
It can be useful to classify discovered routes:

Confirmed
Potential
Disabled
Environment-specific
Unknown

For example:

/admin/debug

may exist in source but only be enabled when:

DEBUG=true

Do not automatically treat every route found in source as externally reachable.

docs.title: Route Reachability
docs.text:
For each route ask:

Is it registered?

Is the controller instantiated?

Is the router mounted?

Is the feature enabled?

Is the module included?

Is it behind a reverse proxy?

Is it restricted by environment?

Is it restricted by network location?

Is authentication required?

Is authorisation required?

docs.title: Start With Repository Structure
docs.text:
Before searching individual routes, inspect the repository.

ls

and:

find . -maxdepth 2 -type d | sort

Look for directories such as:

controllers
routes
api
handlers
views
services
resolvers
graphql
grpc
proto
websocket
webhooks
workers
jobs
tasks
consumers
middleware
security
auth
admin
internal

docs.title: Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
Open the repository:

code .

Use Visual Studio Code as the primary manual review environment.

Useful features:

Explorer
Global Search
Regex Search
Go to Definition
Find All References
Call Hierarchy
Workspace Symbols
Integrated Terminal
Git Integration
Debugger

docs.title: Global Search
docs.text:
Use:

Ctrl + Shift + F

to search across the repository.

Search for framework-specific route declarations and generic terms:

route
router
controller
endpoint
handler
mapping
resolver
webhook
socket
consumer
listener
job
task

docs.title: ripgrep
docs.text:
ripgrep is extremely useful for initial route discovery.

General syntax:

rg -n 'pattern' .

Case-insensitive:

rg -n -i 'pattern' .

Search selected source files:

rg -n 'pattern' \
-g '*.java' \
-g '*.cs' \
-g '*.py' \
-g '*.php' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: ASP.NET Core
docs.text:
ASP.NET Core applications commonly expose endpoints through:

Controllers
Minimal APIs
Razor Pages
SignalR hubs
gRPC services
Middleware

docs.title: ASP.NET Controller Discovery
docs.text:
Typical controller:

[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class UsersController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("{id}")]
    public IActionResult GetUser(int id)
    {
        ...
    }
}

Result:

GET /api/users/{id}

Search:

rg -n \
'\[(Route|HttpGet|HttpPost|HttpPut|HttpDelete|HttpPatch|HttpHead|HttpOptions)' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: ASP.NET Route Attributes
docs.text:
Look for:

[Route(...)]
[HttpGet(...)]
[HttpPost(...)]
[HttpPut(...)]
[HttpDelete(...)]
[HttpPatch(...)]

Example:

[Route("api/admin")]
public class AdminController
{
    [HttpPost("users/{id}/disable")]
    ...
}

Combine controller and method routes:

/api/admin
+
users/{id}/disable
=
POST /api/admin/users/{id}/disable

docs.title: ASP.NET Minimal APIs
docs.text:
Modern ASP.NET Core applications may use Minimal APIs.

Example:

app.MapGet(
    "/api/users/{id}",
    GetUser
);

app.MapPost(
    "/api/users",
    CreateUser
);

Search:

rg -n \
'Map(Get|Post|Put|Delete|Patch|Methods|Group|Fallback)\(' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

Also search:

rg -n \
'MapControllers|MapRazorPages|MapHub|MapGrpcService' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: ASP.NET Route Groups
docs.text:
Example:

var api =
    app.MapGroup("/api");

var users =
    api.MapGroup("/users");

users.MapGet(
    "/{id}",
    GetUser
);

The final route is:

GET /api/users/{id}

Do not inspect individual MapGet() calls without considering parent route groups.

docs.title: ASP.NET Authentication and Authorisation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Authorize|AllowAnonymous|RequireAuthorization|AddAuthorization|AddAuthentication' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

Look for:

[Authorize]
[AllowAnonymous]
RequireAuthorization()
Policies
Roles
Claims

Example:

[Authorize]
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public IActionResult GetUser(int id)

Authentication is visible.

Object-level authorisation still needs separate review.

docs.title: ASP.NET Inputs
docs.text:
Sources include:

Route values
Query strings
Headers
Cookies
Form values
JSON bodies
Uploaded files

Search:

rg -n \
'Request\.(Query|Form|Headers|Cookies)|IFormFile|FromBody|FromQuery|FromRoute|FromHeader|FromForm' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: ASP.NET SignalR
docs.text:
SignalR exposes message-style entry points.

Search:

rg -n \
'Hub\b|MapHub|HubConnection|Clients\.' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

A public Hub method may effectively be an externally callable operation.

Review:

Hub authentication
Method authorisation
Connection identity
Object-level authorisation
Input validation

docs.title: ASP.NET gRPC
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'MapGrpcService|BindableService|ServerCallContext|override.*Task' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

Also inspect:

.proto

files.

rg -n \
'^\s*(service|rpc)\s+' \
-g '*.proto' \
.

docs.title: Java / Spring
docs.text:
Spring applications commonly expose endpoints through:

@RestController
@Controller
@RequestMapping
@GetMapping
@PostMapping
@PutMapping
@DeleteMapping
@PatchMapping

docs.title: Spring Controller Discovery
docs.text:
Example:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public User getUser(
        @PathVariable Long id
    ) {
        ...
    }
}

Final route:

GET /api/users/{id}

Search:

rg -n \
'@(RestController|Controller|RequestMapping|GetMapping|PostMapping|PutMapping|DeleteMapping|PatchMapping)' \
-g '*.java' \
-g '*.kt' \
.

docs.title: Spring Parent Mappings
docs.text:
Always combine:

Class-level @RequestMapping

with:

Method-level mapping

Example:

@RequestMapping("/admin")

plus:

@PostMapping("/users/{id}")

becomes:

POST /admin/users/{id}

docs.title: Spring Request Inputs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@(RequestParam|PathVariable|RequestBody|RequestHeader|CookieValue|RequestPart|ModelAttribute)' \
-g '*.java' \
.

Potential sources include:

@RequestParam
@PathVariable
@RequestBody
@RequestHeader
@CookieValue
@RequestPart
@ModelAttribute
MultipartFile
HttpServletRequest

docs.title: Spring Security
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@(PreAuthorize|PostAuthorize|Secured|RolesAllowed)|authorizeHttpRequests|requestMatchers|permitAll|authenticated|hasRole|hasAuthority' \
-g '*.java' \
.

Review:

Global route rules
Method security
Role checks
Permission checks
Object-level checks

docs.title: Spring Functional Routing
docs.text:
Not all Spring applications use controllers.

Spring WebFlux can use functional routes.

Search:

rg -n \
'RouterFunctions|route\(|GET\(|POST\(|PUT\(|DELETE\(' \
-g '*.java' \
-g '*.kt' \
.

docs.title: Spring Actuator
docs.text:
Search configuration for:

management.endpoints
management.endpoint
management.server

Example:

rg -n \
'management\.(endpoints|endpoint|server)' \
.

Review exposure of management functionality.

Do not treat the presence of Actuator dependencies or configuration alone as proof that sensitive endpoints are externally accessible.

docs.title: Java Servlets
docs.text:
Legacy Java applications may use servlets.

Search:

rg -n \
'@WebServlet|extends HttpServlet|doGet\(|doPost\(|doPut\(|doDelete\(' \
-g '*.java' \
.

Also inspect:

web.xml

for servlet mappings.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
PHP applications may use:

Framework routers
Controller annotations
Route configuration files
Direct script endpoints

Direct .php files themselves may be entry points.

docs.title: PHP File Discovery
docs.text:
find . -type f -name '*.php' | sort

Look especially for:

index.php
api.php
upload.php
login.php
admin.php
callback.php
webhook.php
download.php

Do not assume filenames alone determine exposure.

docs.title: Laravel
docs.text:
Laravel routes commonly appear in:

routes/web.php
routes/api.php
routes/console.php
routes/channels.php

Search:

rg -n \
'Route::(get|post|put|patch|delete|options|any|match|resource|apiResource|group|prefix)' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Example:

Route::get(
    '/users/{id}',
    [UserController::class, 'show']
);

docs.title: Laravel Route Groups
docs.text:
Example:

Route::prefix('admin')
    ->middleware('auth')
    ->group(function () {

        Route::get(
            '/users',
            [AdminController::class, 'users']
        );
    });

Final route:

GET /admin/users

with:

auth middleware

Route groups must be included when mapping effective security controls.

docs.title: Laravel Middleware
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'->middleware\(|middleware\(|Route::middleware|auth:|can:|Gate::|authorize\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Review:

Authentication middleware
Authorisation middleware
Policies
Gates
Controller checks
Model ownership

docs.title: Symfony
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'#\[Route|@Route|Routing\\Annotation\\Route' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Example:

#[Route(
    '/users/{id}',
    methods: ['GET']
)]

Also inspect routing configuration files such as:

config/routes.yaml
config/routes/

docs.title: Generic PHP Inputs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'\$_(GET|POST|REQUEST|FILES|COOKIE|SERVER)' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Sources include:

$_GET
$_POST
$_REQUEST
$_FILES
$_COOKIE
$_SERVER

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Python applications may expose routes through:

Django
Flask
FastAPI
Starlette
aiohttp
Custom frameworks

docs.title: Django
docs.text:
Django commonly defines routes in:

urls.py

Search:

rg -n \
'path\(|re_path\(|url\(|include\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

Example:

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "users/<int:id>/",
        views.user_detail
    )
]

docs.title: Django Nested URL Configuration
docs.text:
Example:

path(
    "api/",
    include("users.urls")
)

and inside:

path(
    "users/<int:id>/",
    user_detail
)

Final route:

/api/users/<id>/

Always follow include() chains.

docs.title: Django Views
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'def (get|post|put|delete|patch)\(|class .*View|APIView|ViewSet|ModelViewSet|GenericAPIView' \
-g '*.py' \
.

Django REST Framework requires additional attention.

docs.title: Django REST Framework
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'APIView|ViewSet|ModelViewSet|GenericViewSet|router\.register|DefaultRouter|SimpleRouter|@api_view|@action' \
-g '*.py' \
.

A router may automatically generate multiple routes.

Example:

router.register(
    r"users",
    UserViewSet
)

may expose actions for:

list
retrieve
create
update
partial_update
destroy

depending on the ViewSet.

docs.title: Django Authentication and Permissions
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'permission_classes|authentication_classes|IsAuthenticated|AllowAny|IsAdminUser|has_permission|has_object_permission|login_required|permission_required' \
-g '*.py' \
.

Pay particular attention to:

has_object_permission()

when reviewing IDOR/BOLA.

docs.title: Django Inputs
docs.text:
Typical sources:

request.GET
request.POST
request.body
request.data
request.FILES
request.COOKIES
request.headers

Search:

rg -n \
'request\.(GET|POST|body|data|FILES|COOKIES|headers)' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Flask
docs.text:
Flask routes commonly use:

@app.route(...)

or:

@blueprint.route(...)

Search:

rg -n \
'@(app|bp|blueprint|[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\.(route|get|post|put|delete|patch)\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Flask Example
docs.text:
@app.route(
    "/users/<int:id>",
    methods=["GET"]
)
def get_user(id):
    ...

Final route:

GET /users/<id>

docs.title: Flask Blueprints
docs.text:
Example:

api =
    Blueprint(
        "api",
        __name__,
        url_prefix="/api"
    )

Then:

@api.route("/users")
def users():
    ...

Final route:

/api/users

Review:

Blueprint prefix
Application registration
Nested prefixes

docs.title: Flask Inputs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'request\.(args|form|json|files|cookies|headers|values|get_json)' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Flask Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication may be implemented through:

Decorators
before_request
Middleware
Flask-Login
JWT libraries
Custom wrappers

Search:

rg -n \
'login_required|current_user|before_request|jwt_required|roles_required|permission' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: FastAPI
docs.text:
FastAPI routes commonly use:

@app.get(...)
@app.post(...)
@router.get(...)
@router.post(...)

Search:

rg -n \
'@(app|router)\.(get|post|put|delete|patch|options|head)\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: FastAPI Routers
docs.text:
Example:

router =
    APIRouter(
        prefix="/users"
    )

and:

@router.get("/{id}")

mounted with:

app.include_router(
    router,
    prefix="/api"
)

Final route:

GET /api/users/{id}

Multiple prefixes may need to be combined.

docs.title: Node.js / Express
docs.text:
Express applications commonly define routes through:

app.get()
app.post()
router.get()
router.post()

Search:

rg -n \
'\.(get|post|put|delete|patch|options|head|all|use)\(' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

This is intentionally broad and requires manual triage.

docs.title: Express Example
docs.text:
router.get(
    "/users/:id",
    auth,
    getUser
);

Route:

GET /users/:id

Middleware:

auth

Handler:

getUser

docs.title: Express Router Mounting
docs.text:
Example:

app.use(
    "/api",
    userRouter
);

Inside:

router.get(
    "/users/:id",
    getUser
);

Final route:

GET /api/users/:id

Always follow router mounting.

docs.title: Express Inputs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'req\.(query|params|body|headers|cookies|file|files)' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Express Middleware
docs.text:
Routes may be protected through middleware.

Example:

router.delete(
    "/users/:id",
    authenticate,
    requireAdmin,
    deleteUser
);

Map:

DELETE /users/:id
        |
        +--> authenticate
        |
        +--> requireAdmin
        |
        +--> deleteUser

Do not only record the handler.

Record the middleware chain.

docs.title: NestJS
docs.text:
NestJS uses decorators similar to Spring.

Search:

rg -n \
'@(Controller|Get|Post|Put|Delete|Patch|Options|Head|UseGuards|UseInterceptors)' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Example:

@Controller("users")
export class UserController {

    @Get(":id")
    getUser() {
        ...
    }
}

Final route:

GET /users/:id

docs.title: Next.js
docs.text:
Modern Next.js applications can expose server-side endpoints.

Review both:

Pages Router
App Router

docs.title: Next.js Pages Router
docs.text:
Look under:

pages/api/

Example:

pages/api/users/[id].js

may map to:

/api/users/{id}

Search:

find . \
-path '*/pages/api/*' \
-type f \
| sort

docs.title: Next.js App Router
docs.text:
Look for:

app/**/route.js
app/**/route.ts

Search:

find . \
\( -name 'route.js' -o -name 'route.ts' \) \
-type f \
| sort

Inside route handlers:

export async function GET(request) {
    ...
}

export async function POST(request) {
    ...
}

Search:

rg -n \
'export\s+(async\s+)?function\s+(GET|POST|PUT|DELETE|PATCH|OPTIONS|HEAD)' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Next.js Server Actions
docs.text:
Server Actions may also expose security-sensitive functionality indirectly from client interactions.

Search:

rg -n \
'["'\'']use server["'\'']' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.jsx' \
-g '*.ts' \
-g '*.tsx' \
.

Review:

Authentication
Authorisation
Input validation
Object ownership
Sensitive operations

Do not assume a Server Action is safe merely because it is not a conventional REST endpoint.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL attack surfaces are different from traditional REST.

The primary entry point may simply be:

POST /graphql

but the real attack surface is:

Queries
Mutations
Subscriptions
Resolvers
Fields
Arguments

docs.title: GraphQL Schema Discovery
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'type Query|type Mutation|type Subscription|extend type Query|extend type Mutation' \
.

Also search:

find . \
\( -name '*.graphql' -o -name '*.gql' \) \
-type f \
| sort

docs.title: GraphQL Resolver Discovery
docs.text:
JavaScript/TypeScript:

rg -n \
'Query\s*:|Mutation\s*:|Subscription\s*:|Resolver|resolve\s*\(' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Python:

rg -n \
'resolve_|mutation|graphene|strawberry|ariadne' \
-g '*.py' \
.

Java:

rg -n \
'@QueryMapping|@MutationMapping|@SubscriptionMapping|@SchemaMapping|DataFetcher' \
-g '*.java' \
.

.NET:

rg -n \
'QueryType|MutationType|ObjectType|Resolver|GraphQL' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: GraphQL Route Inventory
docs.text:
Do not record only:

POST /graphql

Record operations:

Type Operation Resolver Authentication Authorisation Query user(id) userResolver Required Ownership? Query documents documentResolver Required Tenant filter? Mutation deleteUser(id) deleteUserResolver Required Admin? Mutation updateRole(...) roleResolver Required Admin?

docs.title: GraphQL Object-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
Trace:

GraphQL Argument
      |
      v
Resolver
      |
      v
Object Lookup
      |
      v
Authorisation?
      |
      v
Return / Mutation

GraphQL frequently exposes BOLA-style issues when object-level checks are missing.

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
gRPC exposes services and RPC methods rather than conventional URL routes.

Start with .proto files.

find . -type f -name '*.proto' | sort

Search:

rg -n \
'^\s*(service|rpc)\s+' \
-g '*.proto' \
.

docs.title: gRPC Example
docs.text:
service UserService {

    rpc GetUser(
        GetUserRequest
    ) returns (
        UserResponse
    );

    rpc DeleteUser(
        DeleteUserRequest
    ) returns (
        DeleteUserResponse
    );
}

Inventory:

UserService.GetUser
UserService.DeleteUser

docs.title: gRPC Security Review
docs.text:
For every RPC method determine:

Request fields
Metadata
Authentication
Interceptors
Authorisation
Object-level checks
Input validation
Sensitive sinks

docs.title: gRPC Interceptors
docs.text:
Security may be implemented centrally.

Search for:

Interceptor
ServerInterceptor
UnaryServerInterceptor
StreamServerInterceptor

Do not assume an interceptor provides object-level authorisation.

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
WebSocket applications often expose only one connection endpoint:

/ws
/socket
/socket.io

but many message handlers.

The actual attack surface is:

Connection
    |
    +--> message type A
    +--> message type B
    +--> message type C

docs.title: WebSocket Search
docs.text:
JavaScript:

rg -n \
'WebSocket|socket\.on|io\.on|on\(["'\'']connection|on\(["'\'']message' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Python:

rg -n \
'websocket|WebSocket|receive_text|receive_json|send_text|send_json' \
-g '*.py' \
.

Java:

rg -n \
'@ServerEndpoint|WebSocketHandler|TextWebSocketHandler|WebSocketConfigurer' \
-g '*.java' \
.

.NET:

rg -n \
'WebSocket|MapHub|Hub\b' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: WebSocket Message Inventory
docs.text:
Example:

socket.on(
    "delete-document",
    async (id) => {
        ...
    }
);

Inventory:

Protocol:
WebSocket

Event:
delete-document

Input:
id

Authentication:
Connection-level?

Authorisation:
Object ownership?

docs.title: WebSocket Authentication
docs.text:
Do not assume:

Authenticated WebSocket

means:

Every message is authorised

Review:

Connection authentication
Session expiry
Token refresh
Per-message authorisation
Object-level authorisation
Tenant isolation

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
Webhooks are externally triggered entry points.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'webhook|callback|hook|notification|event' \
.

Potential examples:

/payment/webhook
/github/webhook
/stripe/webhook
/callback
/events

docs.title: Webhook Security Model
docs.text:
External Service
      |
      v
Webhook Endpoint
      |
      v
Authenticity Verification
      |
      v
Payload Validation
      |
      v
Business Operation

Review:

Signature verification
Shared secret
Timestamp validation
Replay protection
Content validation
Event type validation
Idempotency

docs.title: Webhook Verification Ordering
docs.text:
Important:

Webhook Request
      |
      v
Signature Verification
      |
      v
Processing

Potentially dangerous:

Webhook Request
      |
      v
Sensitive Processing
      |
      v
Signature Verification

docs.title: OAuth Callbacks
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'oauth|oidc|callback|redirect_uri|authorization_code|code_verifier|state|nonce' \
.

Identify routes such as:

/oauth/callback
/auth/callback
/login/oauth2/code/*

Review:

state
nonce
PKCE
redirect handling
token validation
identity mapping
session creation

docs.title: SAML Endpoints
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'saml|acs|assertionconsumer|metadata|singlelogout|sso' \
.

Potential entry points:

ACS endpoint
SSO endpoint
SLO endpoint
Metadata endpoint

docs.title: File Upload Entry Points
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'upload|multipart|IFormFile|MultipartFile|request\.files|req\.files|multer|UploadedFile' \
.

Record:

Route
Accepted file type
Filename handling
Storage destination
Parser
Post-processing
Authentication
Authorisation

docs.title: File Import Entry Points
docs.text:
Uploads and imports should be distinguished.

An import may trigger:

CSV parsing
XML parsing
Spreadsheet parsing
Archive extraction
PDF processing
Image processing
Object deserialisation

Search:

rg -n -i \
'import|parse|csv|xlsx|xml|zip|archive|pdf' \
.

Manual triage is required because these terms are broad.

docs.title: Message Queues
docs.text:
Applications may receive attacker-influenced data asynchronously.

Technologies include:

RabbitMQ
Kafka
AWS SQS
Azure Service Bus
Google Pub/Sub
Redis queues
Celery
BullMQ
MassTransit
Spring Kafka

docs.title: Queue Consumer Discovery
docs.text:
Search broadly:

rg -n -i \
'consumer|listener|subscriber|subscribe|queue|kafka|rabbit|sqs|servicebus|pubsub|celery|bullmq|masstransit' \
.

docs.title: Spring Queue Consumers
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@(KafkaListener|RabbitListener|JmsListener|SqsListener)' \
-g '*.java' \
.

Example:

@KafkaListener(
    topics = "documents"
)
public void process(
    String message
) {
    ...
}

The queue message is an entry point.

docs.title: Celery
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'@.*task|@shared_task|Celery\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

Example:

@shared_task
def process_document(path):
    ...

Then determine who can cause the task to be queued and whether task arguments can contain attacker-controlled data.

docs.title: Bull / BullMQ
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'new Worker|new Queue|process\(|bullmq|bull' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
Background jobs may process previously stored attacker-controlled data.

Example:

HTTP Request
     |
     v
Database
     |
     v
Background Worker
     |
     v
Dangerous Sink

This is an important second-order path.

docs.title: Scheduled Jobs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'cron|schedule|scheduled|scheduler|timer|periodic' \
.

Framework-specific examples follow.

docs.title: Spring Scheduled Jobs
docs.text:
rg -n \
'@Scheduled' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET Background Services
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'BackgroundService|IHostedService|ExecuteAsync|AddHostedService' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: Python Scheduled Jobs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'celerybeat|apscheduler|schedule\.|crontab|periodic_task' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Node Scheduled Jobs
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'node-cron|cron\.schedule|setInterval|agenda|bullmq' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Serverless Functions
docs.text:
Applications may expose:

AWS Lambda
Azure Functions
Google Cloud Functions
Cloudflare Workers
Vercel Functions

Search for platform configuration.

docs.title: AWS Lambda
docs.text:
Look for:

serverless.yml
serverless.yaml
template.yaml
samconfig.toml

Search:

rg -n -i \
'handler:|events:|httpApi:|http:|schedule:|sqs:|sns:|s3:' \
-g '*.yml' \
-g '*.yaml' \
.

docs.title: Azure Functions
docs.text:
Search:

find . -name 'function.json' -o -name 'host.json'

Also search:

rg -n \
'HttpTrigger|QueueTrigger|TimerTrigger|BlobTrigger|ServiceBusTrigger' \
.

docs.title: Serverless Trigger Types
docs.text:
A function may be triggered by:

HTTP
Queue
Object upload
Database event
Timer
Message topic
Authentication event

All relevant triggers belong in the entry-point map.

docs.title: CLI Entry Points
docs.text:
Some web application repositories include administrative CLI tools.

Search:

rg -n \
'argparse|click\.command|commander|yargs|CommandLineRunner|ICommand|Main\(' \
.

CLI interfaces may be relevant when:

User-controlled data is passed into them indirectly
Web functionality invokes them
Background jobs invoke them
Operators process untrusted files

docs.title: Internal APIs
docs.text:
Routes named:

/internal
/private
/service
/admin
/management
/debug

should receive additional attention.

But naming does not prove exposure.

Determine:

Network restriction
Authentication
Authorisation
Reverse proxy routing
Environment configuration

docs.title: Administrative Routes
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'admin|administrator|management|manage|internal|debug' \
.

Review actions such as:

Create user
Delete user
Change role
Impersonate user
Reset MFA
Generate token
Change configuration
Run diagnostics
Import data
Export data

docs.title: Debug Endpoints
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'debug|diagnostic|trace|testendpoint|devonly|development' \
.

Also inspect conditional configuration:

DEBUG
ENVIRONMENT
NODE_ENV
ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
FLASK_ENV
DJANGO_DEBUG

docs.title: Health and Metrics
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'health|metrics|prometheus|actuator|status|ready|readiness|live|liveness' \
.

These endpoints are not automatically vulnerabilities.

Review whether they expose sensitive operational information or privileged functionality.

docs.title: Feature Flags
docs.text:
Feature flags may expose hidden routes.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'feature.?flag|featureflag|isEnabled|enabledFeatures|toggle' \
.

Map:

Route
   |
   v
Feature Flag
   |
   v
Handler

Determine whether the feature is active in the target environment.

docs.title: Environment-Specific Routes
docs.text:
Example:

if (
    process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production"
) {
    app.use(
        "/debug",
        debugRouter
    );
}

Record:

/debug

as:

Environment-specific

rather than automatically exposed.

docs.title: Middleware Mapping
docs.text:
Route discovery without middleware mapping is incomplete.

Example:

POST /admin/users
        |
        +--> authenticate
        |
        +--> csrfProtection
        |
        +--> requireAdmin
        |
        +--> validateBody
        |
        +--> createUser

This is much more useful than:

POST /admin/users -> createUser

docs.title: Global Middleware
docs.text:
Security controls may apply before routes.

Examples:

Authentication
CSRF
CORS
Rate limiting
Security headers
Tenant resolution
Request validation
Logging

Identify global middleware.

docs.title: Express Global Middleware
docs.text:
Example:

app.use(authenticate);
app.use(apiRouter);

Every route mounted after the authentication middleware may inherit it.

Ordering matters.

docs.title: ASP.NET Middleware Ordering
docs.text:
Review:

UseRouting
UseAuthentication
UseAuthorization
MapControllers

Security middleware ordering can affect behaviour.

Do not infer a vulnerability solely from unusual ordering without confirming framework semantics and runtime behaviour.

docs.title: Spring Security Filter Chain
docs.text:
Look for:

SecurityFilterChain
HttpSecurity
requestMatchers
authorizeHttpRequests

Map route rules such as:

/admin/** -> ADMIN
/api/**   -> authenticated
/public/** -> permitAll

Then compare those rules against discovered routes.

docs.title: Route-Level vs Object-Level Authorisation
docs.text:
A route may correctly require:

Authenticated user

but still fail object-level authorisation.

Example:

GET /api/documents/{id}
       |
       v
Authenticated
       |
       v
DocumentRepository.findById(id)
       |
       v
Return Document

Missing:

Does this document belong to the user?

docs.title: Route Parameters
docs.text:
Examples:

/users/{id}
/documents/:id
/accounts/<account_id>
/tenant/{tenantId}/users/{userId}

These should immediately trigger review for:

IDOR
BOLA
Tenant isolation
Authorisation

docs.title: Sensitive Parameter Names
docs.text:
Search route and request definitions for:

id
userId
accountId
documentId
tenantId
organisationId
role
permission
admin
owner
url
path
file
filename
redirect
callback
command
query
template

These names are only review indicators.

They are not findings.

docs.title: Route-to-Sink Mapping
docs.text:
After discovering a route:

ROUTE
  |
  v
HANDLER
  |
  v
SERVICE
  |
  v
REPOSITORY / HELPER
  |
  v
SINK

Example:

GET /preview
     |
     v
PreviewController
     |
     v
PreviewService
     |
     v
HttpClient.get()

Potential review category:

SSRF

docs.title: Route-to-Sink Example
docs.text:
@app.get("/preview")
def preview():

    url =
        request.args.get("url")

    return preview_service.fetch(url)

Service:

def fetch(url):
    return requests.get(url).text

Map:

GET /preview
      |
      v
request.args["url"]
      |
      v
preview_service.fetch()
      |
      v
requests.get()

docs.title: Route-to-Authorisation Mapping
docs.text:
Example:

DELETE /api/users/{id}
        |
        v
authenticate()
        |
        v
deleteUser(id)
        |
        v
UserRepository.delete(id)

Ask:

Where is administrative permission checked?

Where is object-level authorisation checked?

docs.title: Route-to-Validation Mapping
docs.text:
Example:

POST /api/import
      |
      v
Multipart Upload
      |
      v
validateFile()
      |
      v
parseDocument()

Record both:

Source
Security control
Sink

docs.title: Build an Attack Surface Table
docs.text:
A useful working table:

Entry Point Type Input AuthN AuthZ Sensitive Sink Review /login HTTP credentials No N/A Session creation Auth /users/{id} REST id Yes Unknown DB read IDOR /preview REST url Yes N/A HTTP client SSRF deleteUser GraphQL mutation id Yes Unknown DB delete BOLA DeleteUser gRPC request ID Yes Unknown DB delete AuthZ delete-document WebSocket ID Yes Unknown DB delete AuthZ /payment/webhook Webhook JSON Signature N/A Payment update Webhook

docs.title: Hidden Entry Points
docs.text:
Pay additional attention to:

Legacy controllers
Unused-looking routes
Test endpoints
Debug handlers
Administrative endpoints
Internal APIs
Alternative API versions
Old GraphQL mutations
Deprecated RPC methods
Unused WebSocket events
Migration endpoints
Import/export functions

docs.title: API Versioning
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'/v[0-9]+/|api/v[0-9]+|version' \
.

Applications may simultaneously expose:

/api/v1/
/api/v2/
/api/v3/

Older versions may have weaker security controls.

Do not assume deprecated routes remain externally accessible.

Verify reachability.

docs.title: Duplicate Functionality
docs.text:
Look for the same operation through multiple entry points.

Example:

REST:
DELETE /api/users/{id}

GraphQL:
deleteUser(id)

gRPC:
UserService.DeleteUser()

Admin:
POST /admin/delete-user

Security controls should be consistent across all paths.

docs.title: Alternate Entry Point Analysis
docs.text:
This is extremely important.

A secure operation may exist through one path:

REST
 |
 v
Authentication
 |
 v
Authorisation
 |
 v
Sensitive Operation

while another path may expose:

GraphQL
 |
 v
Authentication
 |
 v
Sensitive Operation

with missing authorisation.

docs.title: Security Control Consistency
docs.text:
For every sensitive operation ask:

How many ways can this operation be reached?

Then compare:

Authentication
Authorisation
Validation
Rate limiting
Audit logging
CSRF
Business rules

docs.title: Authentication Endpoint Inventory
docs.text:
Search for:

login
signin
authenticate
token
session
logout
refresh
password
reset
forgot
mfa
2fa
otp
verify

Example:

rg -n -i \
'login|signin|authenticate|logout|refresh|forgot.?password|reset.?password|mfa|2fa|otp' \
.

Map all identity-related entry points separately.

docs.title: Account Creation
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'register|signup|sign.?up|create.?account|invite' \
.

Review:

Role assignment
Email verification
Tenant assignment
Invitation handling
Duplicate accounts
Mass assignment

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'forgot.?password|reset.?password|password.?reset|reset.?token' \
.

Map:

Request reset
Generate token
Deliver token
Validate token
Change password
Invalidate token

docs.title: MFA
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'mfa|2fa|totp|otp|authenticator|recovery.?code|backup.?code' \
.

Entry points may include:

Enable MFA
Disable MFA
Verify MFA
Generate recovery codes
Use recovery code
Reset MFA

docs.title: OAuth / OIDC
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'oauth|openid|oidc|callback|redirect_uri|state|nonce|pkce|code_verifier' \
.

Map:

Login initiation
Callback
Token exchange
Account linking
Logout
Refresh

docs.title: SAML
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'saml|assertion|acs|single.?sign.?on|single.?logout|metadata' \
.

docs.title: API Key Entry Points
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'api.?key|x-api-key|apikey' \
.

Determine which routes support:

Session authentication
JWT
API keys
mTLS
Internal service tokens

Different authentication mechanisms may produce different authorisation paths.

docs.title: Host and Proxy-Dependent Routes
docs.text:
Review routing logic that depends on:

Host
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Forwarded-Proto
X-Forwarded-Prefix
Tenant hostname
Subdomain

Search:

rg -n -i \
'host|hostname|x-forwarded-host|x-forwarded-proto|subdomain|tenant' \
.

Manual triage is essential because these terms are broad.

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Routing
docs.text:
Applications may derive tenant context from:

Hostname
Route
Header
JWT claim
Session
Database lookup

Example:

/{tenantId}/documents/{id}

Map:

Attacker tenant identifier
        |
        v
Tenant resolution
        |
        v
Object lookup
        |
        v
Tenant authorisation

docs.title: Route Discovery Through Tests
docs.text:
Tests often reveal hidden routes.

Search:

find . \
\( -path '*test*' -o -path '*spec*' \) \
-type f \
| sort

Look for:

GET
POST
PUT
DELETE
PATCH
/graphql
/api/
admin
login

Tests may document expected security behaviour.

docs.title: Route Discovery Through OpenAPI
docs.text:
Search:

find . \
\( \
-name 'openapi*.json' -o \
-name 'openapi*.yaml' -o \
-name 'openapi*.yml' -o \
-name 'swagger*.json' -o \
-name 'swagger*.yaml' -o \
-name 'swagger*.yml' \
\) \
-type f

OpenAPI specifications can reveal:

Routes
Methods
Parameters
Schemas
Authentication schemes
Deprecated endpoints

docs.title: Swagger Configuration
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'swagger|openapi|springdoc|swashbuckle' \
.

Do not assume Swagger UI is externally exposed simply because the dependency exists.

docs.title: GraphQL Schema Files
docs.text:
find . \
\( -name '*.graphql' -o -name '*.gql' \) \
-type f \
| sort

These can provide an extremely accurate map of the GraphQL attack surface.

docs.title: Proto Files
docs.text:
find . \
-name '*.proto' \
-type f \
| sort

These provide the primary gRPC service map.

docs.title: Infrastructure Configuration
docs.text:
Routes may also appear in:

nginx.conf
Apache configuration
Ingress resources
API gateways
Terraform
Kubernetes manifests
Reverse proxy configuration
Cloud routing configuration

Search:

rg -n -i \
'location |proxy_pass|ingress|path:|route|gateway|rewrite|upstream' \
.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Paths
docs.text:
Example:

External:
/service/users

Reverse Proxy:
rewrite -> /users

Application:
/users

The source-code route may differ from the externally visible route.

Record both where known.

docs.title: Kubernetes Ingress
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'kind:\s*Ingress|path:|pathType:|backend:' \
-g '*.yaml' \
-g '*.yml' \
.

This can reveal externally routed application paths.

docs.title: API Gateways
docs.text:
Search for configuration relating to:

AWS API Gateway
Kong
Traefik
NGINX
Azure API Management
Apigee
Envoy

These may provide:

Authentication
Rate limiting
Path rewriting
Header modification
Network restrictions

Do not assume application-level exposure without considering these controls.

docs.title: Frontend Route Discovery
docs.text:
Client-side code can reveal server endpoints.

Search:

rg -n \
'fetch\(|axios\.|XMLHttpRequest|\.ajax\(|/api/' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.jsx' \
-g '*.ts' \
-g '*.tsx' \
.

This is useful for identifying:

Undocumented APIs
Parameter names
HTTP methods
GraphQL operations
WebSocket endpoints

docs.title: JavaScript API Calls
docs.text:
Example:

axios.delete(
    `/api/users/${userId}`
);

This reveals:

DELETE /api/users/{userId}

even before the server implementation is found.

docs.title: Source Maps
docs.text:
Where source maps are available during an authorised assessment, they may help map frontend functionality to original source.

Review:

API clients
Route definitions
Feature flags
Administrative functionality
GraphQL queries
WebSocket events

Source map availability alone is not automatically a vulnerability.

docs.title: Dynamic Route Validation
docs.text:
After building the source map, compare it with the running application.

Use Burp Suite:

Proxy
HTTP history
Site map
Repeater
Logger

Compare:

Source Routes
     |
     v
Runtime Routes

docs.title: Source vs Runtime
docs.text:
Classify:

Source + Runtime
    = Confirmed exposed route

Source only
    = Investigate reachability

Runtime only
    = Find implementation / proxy mapping

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
For each interesting route:

1. Find route in source.

2. Determine expected HTTP method.

3. Determine parameters.

4. Determine expected authentication.

5. Capture a legitimate request where possible.

6. Send to Repeater.

7. Compare runtime behaviour with source.

8. Test security controls within scope.

9. Map the route to relevant source-to-sink flows.

docs.title: Do Not Blindly Request Every Route
docs.text:
Source review may reveal:

Destructive administrative actions
Account deletion
Payment actions
Production integrations
Bulk operations

Understand the route before testing it dynamically.

Use safe testing procedures appropriate to the engagement.

docs.title: Semgrep / OpenGrep
docs.text:
Static analysis can automate framework-specific route discovery.

Conceptual example:

rules:
  - id: flask-route
    languages:
      - python
    message: Flask route
    severity: INFO
    pattern: |
      @$APP.route($PATH, ...)
      def $FUNC(...):
        ...

This can produce an initial route candidate list.

docs.title: Route Rules as Reconnaissance Rules
docs.text:
Static-analysis rules can identify:

Controllers
Route decorators
Anonymous routes
Admin routes
Upload handlers
Webhooks
GraphQL resolvers
Dangerous route/sink combinations

Example conceptual target:

HTTP Route
   +
Command Execution

docs.title: CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL becomes useful when route-to-sink analysis requires deeper semantic tracing.

Conceptually:

HTTP Source
     |
     v
Controller
     |
     v
Service
     |
     v
Repository / Helper
     |
     v
Sensitive Sink

Queries can model:

Request sources
Framework routes
Data flow
Taint tracking
Sensitive sinks

docs.title: Route Discovery Is Not Vulnerability Discovery
docs.text:
Remember:

Interesting Route
      !=
Vulnerability

Likewise:

/admin route
      !=
Broken Access Control

and:

/debug route
      !=
Information Disclosure

and:

/upload route
      !=
File Upload Vulnerability

The route identifies where deeper analysis should occur.

docs.title: Prioritising Routes
docs.text:
After mapping routes, prioritise security-sensitive functionality.

A useful review order is:

1. Authentication

2. Password reset

3. MFA

4. Administrative functionality

5. Role / permission changes

6. User and tenant management

7. File upload / import

8. URL fetching / previews

9. Command / diagnostics functionality

10. Financial / transactional actions

11. Object access by identifier

12. GraphQL mutations

13. gRPC write operations

14. WebSocket state-changing messages

15. Webhooks

16. Internal / debug endpoints

This is a review-priority model, not a severity ranking.

docs.title: High-Value Route Names
docs.text:
Search for terms such as:

admin
internal
debug
diagnostic
execute
command
shell
upload
import
export
download

Route AuthN AuthZ Validation Rate Limit CSRF Audit /login N/A N/A Yes ? N/A ? /password/reset N/A N/A Yes ? N/A ? /api/users/{id} Yes ? Yes ? N/A ? /admin/users Yes Admin Yes ? ? Yes /upload Yes Yes ? ? ? ?

docs.text:
Use a repeatable format.

RT-001

Protocol:

External Path:

Required

Unknown

Integer conversion

Unknown

N/A

Potential Review:

Confirmed

Notes:

Unknown

docs.title: Combining With Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Route mapping answers:

Where does execution begin?

Source-to-sink analysis answers:

Where can attacker-controlled data go?

Together:

ENTRY POINT
     |
     v
ROUTE
     |
     v
SOURCE
     |
     v
TRANSFORMATION
     |
     v
SECURITY CONTROL
     |
     v
SINK
     |
     v
IMPACT

This should become the central model for source-assisted application security testing.

docs.title: Combining With Static Analysis
docs.text:
Use the tools together:

ripgrep
   |
   v
Find route declarations quickly
   |
   v
Semgrep / OpenGrep
   |
   v
Find structural route patterns
   |
   v
CodeQL
   |
   v
Trace complex route-to-sink flows
   |
   v
VS Code
   |
   v
Manual analysis
   |
   v
Burp Suite
   |
   v
Runtime validation

docs.title: Only Searching Controllers
docs.text:
Modern applications may expose:

Minimal APIs
GraphQL
gRPC
WebSockets
Webhooks
Queues
Serverless functions

Controllers alone are insufficient.

docs.title: Ignoring Parent Routes
docs.text:
Example:

/api
  +
/users
  +
/{id}

must be reconstructed as:

/api/users/{id}

docs.title: Ignoring Middleware
docs.text: A route definition without its middleware does not show the complete security model.

docs.title: Treating Authentication as Authorisation
docs.text:
Authenticated
    !=
Authorised for every object

docs.title: Ignoring Alternate Protocols
docs.text:
The same sensitive operation may be exposed through:

REST
GraphQL
gRPC
WebSocket
Admin API

docs.title: Assuming Internal Means Trusted
docs.text:
/internal

is only a name.

Verify actual network and authentication controls.

docs.title: Assuming Source Means Reachable
docs.text:
A route found in source may be:

Disabled
Unregistered
Feature-flagged
Development-only
Legacy
Dead code

docs.title: Assuming Missing Annotation Means Missing Security
docs.text:
Security may be implemented:

Globally
Through middleware
Through filters
Through interceptors
Through base classes
Through infrastructure

Trace the complete execution path.

docs.title: Treating Route Discovery as a Finding
docs.text:
A route is attack-surface information.

A vulnerability requires additional evidence.

docs.title: What Proves a Vulnerability?
docs.text:
Route discovery itself proves only that code defines or references an entry point.

For a security finding, establish:

Entry point
    +
Reachability
    +
Attacker-controlled input or action
    +
Missing / ineffective security property
    +
Security impact

For example:

DELETE /api/users/{id}

does not prove broken access control.

A stronger finding would establish:

Authenticated low-privileged user
        |
        v
DELETE /api/users/{id}
        |
        v
Attacker chooses another user's ID
        |
        v
No object/role authorisation
        |
        v
Another user's account is deleted

docs.title: Final Testing Model
docs.text:
The final route and entry-point model is:

                        REPOSITORY
                            |
                            v
                     APPLICATIONS
                            |
                            v
                       ENTRY POINTS
                            |
       +----------+---------+---------+----------+
       |          |         |         |          |
       v          v         v         v          v
      HTTP     GraphQL     gRPC   WebSockets   Async
       |          |         |         |          |
       +----------+---------+---------+----------+
                            |
                            v
                         HANDLER
                            |
                            v
                         INPUT
                            |
                            v
                    ATTACKER CONTROL?
                            |
                       +----+----+
                       |         |
                      No        Yes
                       |         |
                       v         v
                  Review Logic  AUTHENTICATION
                                      |
                                      v
                                AUTHORISATION
                                      |
                                      v
                                  VALIDATION
                                      |
                                      v
                               SOURCE-TO-SINK
                                      |
                                      v
                              SENSITIVE ACTION
                                      |
                                      v
                              RUNTIME EXPOSURE
                                      |
                                      v
                                  SECURITY
                                   IMPACT

The key principle is:

Do not begin by asking:

"What vulnerabilities are in this repository?"

Begin by asking:

"What can cause this application to execute code,
what can an attacker control through those entry points,
what security controls apply,
and where does that data or action ultimately go?"

Once the complete entry-point map exists, vulnerability discovery becomes significantly more systematic.
