'\.execute\(|\.executemany\(|\.raw\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: PHP SQL Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'->query\(|mysqli_query|PDO|DB::raw|whereRaw|selectRaw' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Node.js SQL Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\.query\(|\.execute\(|sequelize\.query|\$queryRaw|\$executeRaw' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Then determine whether attacker-controlled input reaches dynamically constructed queries.

docs.title: Command Injection Variants
docs.text:
Confirmed model:

User Input
   |
   v
Command Construction
   |
   v
Process Execution

Search execution APIs.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Process\.Start|ProcessStartInfo' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rg -n \
'os\.system|os\.popen|subprocess\.(run|Popen|call|check_output|check_call)' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\b(system|exec|shell_exec|passthru|popen|proc_open)\s*\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text:
rg -n \
'child_process|exec\(|execSync\(|spawn\(|spawnSync\(' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: SSRF Variants
docs.text:
Confirmed model:

Attacker URL
    |
    v
HTTP Client
    |
    v
Server-Side Request

Search HTTP clients.

docs.title: Python SSRF Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'requests\.(get|post|put|delete|request)|httpx\.|urllib\.request|aiohttp' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Java SSRF Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'HttpClient|RestTemplate|WebClient|URLConnection|openConnection' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET SSRF Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'HttpClient|WebClient|HttpWebRequest|WebRequest' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: Node.js SSRF Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'axios\.|fetch\(|got\(|request\(|http\.request|https\.request' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: PHP SSRF Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'curl_exec|curl_init|file_get_contents|fopen|Guzzle' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Then determine which URLs can be attacker-controlled.

docs.title: Path Traversal Variants
docs.text:
Model:

User-Controlled Path
       |
       v
Path Construction
       |
       v
Filesystem Operation

Search:

read
write
delete
move
copy
download
extract

docs.title: Python File Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'open\(|Path\(|send_file|send_from_directory|os\.remove|shutil\.' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Java File Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Files\.(read|write|copy|move|delete)|FileInputStream|FileOutputStream|new File\(' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET File Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'File\.(Read|Write|Open|Delete|Copy|Move)|FileStream|Path\.Combine' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: Node.js File Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'fs\.(readFile|writeFile|createReadStream|createWriteStream|unlink|rename)|path\.join|path\.resolve' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: PHP File Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'file_get_contents|file_put_contents|fopen|readfile|unlink|move_uploaded_file' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: File Upload Variants
docs.text:
If one vulnerable upload exists, search for every upload implementation.

rg -n -i \
'upload|multipart|IFormFile|MultipartFile|request\.files|req\.files|multer|move_uploaded_file' \
.

Compare:

Filename validation
Extension validation
MIME handling
Storage location
Randomised naming
Parser behaviour
Archive extraction
Authorisation

Different upload routes may use different controls.

docs.title: Deserialization Variants
docs.text:
Search deserialization APIs and wrappers.

Java:

rg -n \
'ObjectInputStream|readObject\(' \
-g '*.java' \
.

.NET:

rg -n \
'BinaryFormatter|LosFormatter|NetDataContractSerializer|ObjectStateFormatter' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

Python:

rg -n \
'pickle\.loads?|yaml\.load|marshal\.loads?' \
-g '*.py' \
.

PHP:

rg -n \
'unserialize\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Node.js:

rg -n -i \
'deserialize|node-serialize|serialize-javascript' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

A deserialization API match is not automatically exploitable.

Trace attacker control and configuration.

docs.title: SSTI Variants
docs.text:
Search dynamic template creation and rendering.

Python:

rg -n \
'render_template_string|Template\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

Java:

rg -n -i \
'freemarker|velocity|thymeleaf|template\.process|evaluate' \
-g '*.java' \
.

PHP:

rg -n -i \
'twig|blade|render\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Node.js:

rg -n \
'res\.render|ejs\.render|Handlebars\.compile|pug\.render' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Determine whether attacker input controls template source rather than ordinary template data.

docs.title: XSS Variants
docs.text:
Confirmed model:

Attacker Input
     |
     v
HTML / DOM Sink
     |
     v
Browser Interpretation

Search both server-side output and browser sinks.

docs.title: Browser JavaScript Sinks
docs.text:
rg -n \
'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|document\.writeln|srcdoc|createContextualFragment' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.jsx' \
-g '*.ts' \
-g '*.tsx' \
.

docs.title: Dynamic Execution
docs.text:
rg -n \
'eval\(|new Function|setTimeout\([^,]*["'\'']|setInterval\([^,]*["'\'']' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Manual review is required.

docs.title: React
docs.text:
rg -n \
'dangerouslySetInnerHTML' \
-g '*.jsx' \
-g '*.tsx' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Angular
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'bypassSecurityTrustHtml|bypassSecurityTrustScript|bypassSecurityTrustUrl|bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Vue
docs.text:
rg -n \
'v-html' \
-g '*.vue' \
.

docs.title: Open Redirect Variants
docs.text:
Model:

User-Controlled URL
       |
       v
Redirect / Navigation Sink

Search server-side redirects.

rg -n \
'redirect\(|Redirect\(|RedirectToAction|sendRedirect|header\(["'\'']Location' \
.

Client-side:

rg -n \
'location\.(href|assign|replace)|window\.open' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Then determine whether destinations are appropriately constrained.

docs.title: XXE Variants
docs.text:
Search XML parsers.

Java:

rg -n \
'DocumentBuilderFactory|SAXParserFactory|XMLInputFactory|TransformerFactory|SchemaFactory' \
-g '*.java' \
.

.NET:

rg -n \
'XmlDocument|XmlReader|XmlTextReader|XDocument' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

Python:

rg -n \
'xml\.etree|lxml|ElementTree|minidom|sax' \
-g '*.py' \
.

PHP:

rg -n \
'DOMDocument|SimpleXML|simplexml_load|XMLReader' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Review parser configuration rather than reporting parser presence alone.

docs.title: LDAP Injection Variants
docs.text:
Search LDAP operations.

Java:

rg -n \
'LdapTemplate|DirContext|InitialDirContext|search\(' \
-g '*.java' \
.

.NET:

rg -n \
'DirectorySearcher|DirectoryEntry|SearchRequest' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

Python:

rg -n -i \
'ldap|ldap3' \
-g '*.py' \
.

PHP:

rg -n \
'ldap_search|ldap_bind|ldap_list|ldap_read' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Trace whether LDAP filters are dynamically constructed from attacker input.

docs.title: NoSQL Injection Variants
docs.text:
Search database operations involving:

MongoDB
Mongoose
DynamoDB
CouchDB
Elasticsearch

Node.js:

rg -n \
'findOne\(|find\(|findById\(|updateOne\(|deleteOne\(|\$where|\$regex' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Python:

rg -n \
'find_one\(|find\(|update_one\(|delete_one\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

The database method itself is not a vulnerability.

Review attacker-controlled query structure.

docs.title: Mass Assignment Variants
docs.text:
Search for patterns where entire request objects are passed to models.

Node.js:

rg -n \
'create\(req\.body|update\(req\.body|Object\.assign\([^,]+,\s*req\.body' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Python:

rg -n \
'\*\*request\.(json|data)|\*\*serializer\.validated_data' \
-g '*.py' \
.

PHP:

rg -n \
'->create\(\$request->all|->update\(\$request->all|fill\(\$request->all' \
-g '*.php' \
.

Review allowlists, DTOs, serializers, model fillable fields, and framework protections.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Variants
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'Object\.assign|lodash\.merge|_.merge|_.set|deepmerge|merge\(' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Then trace:

Attacker-Controlled Key
        |
        v
Recursive Merge / Property Assignment
        |
        v
Prototype Modification
        |
        v
Security-Relevant Impact

Prototype pollution requires meaningful impact.

docs.title: Authentication Variants
docs.text:
If one authentication bypass is discovered, search all paths capable of creating authentication state.

Password Login
OAuth
OIDC
SAML
Magic Link
Password Reset
MFA Recovery
Remember Device
API Login
Mobile Login
Legacy Login

Search:

rg -n -i \
'login|signin|authenticate|session|token|oauth|oidc|saml|magic.?link|password.?reset|mfa|2fa' \
.

docs.title: MFA Variant Analysis
docs.text:
If MFA is bypassed through one flow, map every path to:

Full Session

Example:

Password
    |
    v
MFA
    |
    v
Session


OAuth
    |
    v
Session

The second path deserves investigation if policy requires MFA.

docs.title: Authorisation Variants
docs.text:
Confirmed issue:

REST endpoint missing ownership check

Search:

Same object
Same service
Same repository
Same controller
GraphQL resolver
gRPC method
WebSocket handler
Admin API

docs.title: Business Logic Variants
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities often require conceptual rather than textual searches.

Known flaw:

Discount can be applied repeatedly

Search for all:

Coupon application
Discount calculation
Promotion processing
Order recalculation
Refund calculation

The implementation may use entirely different function names.

docs.title: Race Condition Variants
docs.text:
If a race exists around:

Balance check
      |
      v
Update balance

search similar:

Check then update
Check then insert
Check then delete
Inventory check then purchase
Token check then consume
Coupon check then redeem

docs.title: Security Header Variants
docs.text:
If one response path lacks expected security headers, determine whether:

Headers are global
Headers are middleware-based
Specific routes override them
Static content bypasses middleware
Error responses differ

Do not simply search for header strings.

Understand where headers are applied.

docs.title: Secret Exposure Variants
docs.text:
A discovered credential should trigger broader secret analysis.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'password|passwd|secret|api.?key|access.?key|private.?key|token|client.?secret' \
.

Use dedicated secret-scanning tools as well.

Do not assume every match is an active secret.

docs.title: Error Handling Variants
docs.text:
If one endpoint leaks stack traces:

Exception
   |
   v
Detailed Error Response

search:

Global exception handlers
Debug middleware
Error serializers
Development settings
Custom exception responses

docs.title: Logging Variants
docs.text:
If one sensitive token is logged:

Token
 |
 v
Logger

search similar logging.

rg -n -i \
'log.*token|logger.*token|log.*password|logger.*password|log.*secret|console\.log' \
.

docs.title: Dependency Variants
docs.text:
If one vulnerable dependency is identified, check:

Other manifests
Other lockfiles
Monorepo packages
Containers
Build files
Frontend dependencies
Backend dependencies
Development tooling

Repositories may contain multiple dependency trees.

docs.title: API Variants
docs.text:
One vulnerable REST operation may have equivalent:

GraphQL
gRPC
WebSocket
Mobile API
Legacy API
Internal API

Search by business operation rather than protocol.

docs.title: Route Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose:

POST /api/users/{id}/role

is vulnerable.

Search:

rg -n -i \
'role|changeRole|updateRole|assignRole|grantRole|permission' \
.

Then identify every entry point.

docs.title: Alternate API Versions
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n \
'/v[0-9]+/|api/v[0-9]+' \
.

Compare:

v1
v2
v3

A vulnerability fixed in a newer API may remain in an older route.

Verify runtime exposure.

docs.title: Legacy Code
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'legacy|deprecated|old|v1|compat|backward' \
.

These are indicators only.

Legacy code may still be secure or may not be reachable.

docs.title: Copy-Paste Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Git history can help identify copied vulnerable code.

Search the vulnerable line:

git grep \
'vulnerableFunction'

Then:

git log -S 'vulnerableFunction' --all

This may reveal when the pattern was introduced and where it was copied.

docs.title: Git Blame
docs.text:
Use:

git blame path/to/file

This can identify the commit introducing a security-sensitive pattern.

Then inspect:

git show <commit>

Look for related changes elsewhere in the same commit.

docs.title: Git Diff Variant Analysis
docs.text:
If a vulnerability has been patched:

git diff <old> <new>

Study the fix.

The patch often reveals the precise missing security control.

Example:

 document =
     repository.findById(id);

+authorizeDocument(
+    currentUser,
+    document
+);

Now search for other calls to:

repository.findById()

without:

authorizeDocument()

docs.title: Patch-Diff Analysis
docs.text:
A patch provides:

Vulnerable Pattern
        +
Security Fix

This is excellent input for variant analysis.

Model:

Before
   |
   v
Vulnerability

After
   |
   v
Security Control

Search for other code resembling the "before" state.

docs.title: Semgrep Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Once a vulnerable structure is understood, encode it as a Semgrep rule.

Example vulnerable code:

@app.get("/documents/<id>")
def document(id):

    document =
        Document.query.get(id)

    return jsonify(
        document.to_dict()
    )

Conceptual rule:

rules:
  - id: document-lookup-review
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review document lookup for object-level authorisation
    severity: WARNING
    patterns:
      - pattern: |
          $OBJ = Document.query.get($ID)

This identifies candidates.

It does not prove missing authorisation.

docs.title: Improve the Rule
docs.text:
Add contextual structure where appropriate.

rules:
  - id: flask-document-lookup
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review Flask document lookup for object-level authorisation
    severity: WARNING
    patterns:
      - pattern-inside: |
          def $FUNC(...):
            ...
      - pattern: |
          $OBJ = Document.query.get($ID)

Project-specific rules can become increasingly precise.

docs.title: Negative Patterns
docs.text:
If secure code always uses:

authorize_document(...)

a rule can attempt to exclude functions containing that control.

Conceptually:

patterns:
  - pattern: |
      $OBJ = Document.query.get($ID)

  - pattern-not-inside: |
      def $FUNC(...):
        ...
        authorize_document(...)
        ...

Negative-pattern logic must be used carefully.

The presence of a helper somewhere in a function does not necessarily prove it protects the relevant object or path.

docs.title: OpenGrep Variant Analysis
docs.text:
OpenGrep can be used similarly for structural rules.

Workflow:

Confirmed Finding
       |
       v
Extract Pattern
       |
       v
Create OpenGrep Rule
       |
       v
Scan Repository
       |
       v
Review Matches
       |
       v
Improve Rule

docs.title: Taint-Based Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Some vulnerability classes are better represented as:

SOURCE
   |
   v
SINK

than simple structural patterns.

Example:

request.args
    |
    v
subprocess.run

Taint analysis can search for multiple data-flow variants.

docs.title: Conceptual Taint Rule
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: flask-command-execution-review
    languages:
      - python
    message: User-controlled input may reach command execution
    severity: WARNING
    mode: taint

    pattern-sources:
      - pattern: request.args.get(...)

    pattern-sinks:
      - pattern: subprocess.run(...)

Add sanitizers only when they genuinely prevent the relevant vulnerability.

docs.title: Sanitizer Modelling
docs.text:
Be careful with:

Validation
Escaping
Encoding
Normalisation

A sanitizer that prevents:

SQL injection

does not necessarily prevent:

Command injection

Sanitizer modelling must be vulnerability-specific.

docs.title: CodeQL Variant Analysis
docs.text:
CodeQL is particularly useful for deeper semantic variants.

A CodeQL query can model:

Source
Sink
Data flow
Taint flow
Additional flow steps
Framework behaviour

This is useful when:

Controller
   |
   v
Service A
   |
   v
Helper
   |
   v
Service B
   |
   v
Sink

cannot be represented reliably through simple textual patterns.

docs.title: CodeQL Data-Flow Model
docs.text:
Conceptually:

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
Controller
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Helper
      |
      v
Dangerous API

A CodeQL query can search all paths matching the relevant source and sink definitions.

docs.title: CodeQL Path Queries
docs.text:
Path queries are especially useful during variant analysis because they show:

Source
  |
  v
Intermediate Steps
  |
  v
Sink

This makes manual validation significantly easier.

docs.title: CodeQL Variant Workflow
docs.text:
Confirmed Finding
       |
       v
Identify Source
       |
       v
Identify Sink
       |
       v
Write / Adapt Query
       |
       v
Run Against Database
       |
       v
Inspect Paths
       |
       v
Classify Candidates
       |
       v
Improve Models
       |
       v
Run Again

docs.title: Framework Models
docs.text:
Variant analysis becomes more accurate when framework-specific sources and sinks are modelled.

Examples:

ASP.NET request parameters
Spring request annotations
Django request objects
Flask request objects
Express req objects
GraphQL arguments
gRPC request fields

docs.title: Custom Wrappers
docs.text:
Real applications frequently wrap dangerous APIs.

Example:

def fetch_url(url):
    return requests.get(url)

If searching only:

requests.get

you may find the wrapper but miss every caller.

Treat:

fetch_url()

as an application-specific SSRF sink during variant analysis.

docs.title: Wrapper Expansion
docs.text:
Model:

Known Sink
   |
   v
Wrapper
   |
   v
Find All References
   |
   v
Application Callers

This is extremely useful.

docs.title: Security Wrapper Analysis
docs.text:
The same applies to security controls.

Example:

authorize()
    |
    v
canAccess()
    |
    v
PolicyEngine

Understand wrappers before deciding whether a route lacks authorisation.

docs.title: Helper Functions
docs.text:
If one vulnerable helper exists:

buildQuery()
fetchUrl()
runCommand()
renderTemplate()
openFile()
deserialize()

search every caller.

A single unsafe helper can create many vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Shared Utility Analysis
docs.text:
Prioritise directories such as:

utils
helpers
common
shared
core
services
lib
libraries

A security-sensitive bug in shared code may have wide impact.

docs.title: Base Classes
docs.text:
Security logic may exist in:

BaseController
BaseService
BaseRepository
AbstractHandler
Middleware superclass

A variant may occur where a class bypasses or overrides the secure base behaviour.

docs.title: Overrides
docs.text:
Search:

override
extends
implements
super

depending on language.

Review security-sensitive overrides.

docs.title: Inheritance Variants
docs.text:
Example:

SecureBaseController
        |
        +--> UserController
        |
        +--> AdminController
        |
        +--> LegacyController

If:

LegacyController

overrides authentication behaviour, it deserves attention.

docs.title: Configuration Variants
docs.text:
A vulnerability may result from configuration rather than code.

Examples:

CORS
Authentication
Security headers
Debug mode
JWT validation
XML parser settings
Proxy trust

Search every environment configuration:

application.yml
application-prod.yml
appsettings.json
appsettings.Production.json
.env
settings.py
config.js
config.production.js

docs.title: Environment Variants
docs.text:
Compare:

Development
Testing
Staging
Production

A secure default may be overridden in one environment.

docs.title: Infrastructure Variants
docs.text:
Security may differ across:

NGINX
API gateway
Kubernetes ingress
Cloud load balancer
Reverse proxy
Service mesh

A source-level fix may not address alternate infrastructure routes.

docs.title: Microservice Variant Analysis
docs.text:
In microservices:

Service A
Service B
Service C

may implement the same business operation independently.

Example:

User lookup
Tenant validation
Role checking
Document access

Search across the entire repository or organisation-controlled codebase where authorised.

docs.title: Monorepos
docs.text:
Do not restrict searches to the first application directory.

Use:

rg -n \
'pattern' \
.

from the repository root where appropriate.

Identify:

apps/
services/
packages/
libs/
frontend/
backend/
workers/

docs.title: Cross-Language Variants
docs.text:
A monorepo may contain:

Java backend
Node.js gateway
Python worker
JavaScript frontend

The same vulnerability concept may appear in several languages.

Search conceptually, not only syntactically.

docs.title: Cross-Protocol Variants
docs.text:
Always consider:

REST
GraphQL
gRPC
WebSocket
Webhooks
Queues
CLI

The same business operation may be reachable through several protocols.

docs.title: Second-Order Variants
docs.text:
Some vulnerabilities occur when attacker input is stored first.

Attacker Input
     |
     v
Database
     |
     v
Background Worker
     |
     v
Dangerous Sink

If one second-order issue is found, search:

Who writes this field?

Who reads this field?

Where else is it consumed?

docs.title: Stored Data Is Still a Source
docs.text:
During variant analysis:

Database Value
    !=
Trusted Value

if the value originally came from an attacker-controlled source.

docs.title: Background Worker Variants
docs.text:
Search:

rg -n -i \
'worker|job|queue|consumer|listener|task|scheduled' \
.

Then trace whether stored attacker data reaches:

Commands
Templates
File paths
URLs
Parsers
Logs

docs.title: Webhook Variants
docs.text:
If one webhook lacks correct verification, search all webhook handlers.

rg -n -i \
'webhook|callback|event.?handler|notification' \
.

Compare:

Signature verification
Timestamp validation
Replay protection
Event validation

docs.title: Validation Variants
docs.text:
Suppose one endpoint lacks:

validateFilename()

Search every file operation.

Then determine:

Which routes use the validator?

Which routes implement their own validation?

Which routes perform no equivalent validation?

docs.title: Validation Helper Search
docs.text:
rg -n -i \
'validate|sanitize|sanitise|escape|normalize|normalise|allowlist|whitelist' \
.

A validation-looking function must be inspected to determine what it actually guarantees.

docs.title: Partial Validation
docs.text:
One common variant is inconsistent validation.

Route A
 |
 v
validateUrl()
 |
 v
fetch()


Route B
 |
 v
fetch()

The second path deserves investigation.

docs.title: Validation Context
docs.text:
A validator safe for one context may not be safe for another.

Examples:

HTML escaping
SQL parameterisation
Shell argument handling
URL validation
Filesystem path validation

Do not treat generic sanitize() functions as universally protective.

docs.title: Variant Candidate Classification
docs.text:
Classify results:

Confirmed Variant
Likely Variant
Needs Runtime Validation
Protected
False Positive
Not Reachable
Dead Code
Unknown

This prevents a large scan result set from becoming unmanageable.

docs.title: Candidate Tracking Table
docs.text: ID Location Pattern Entry Point Control Status VA-001 DocumentController.java IDOR REST Missing Confirmed VA-002 DocumentResolver.java IDOR GraphQL Unknown Review VA-003 DocumentGrpc.java IDOR gRPC Present Protected VA-004 LegacyDocument.java IDOR REST Missing Reachability?

docs.title: Variant Families
docs.text:
Group related findings.

Example:

VA-DOCUMENT-IDOR
    |
    +-- REST read
    +-- REST delete
    +-- GraphQL read
    +-- GraphQL delete

This helps explain the systemic root cause.

docs.title: Root Cause vs Individual Findings
docs.text:
Sometimes variants should be reported separately.

Sometimes they are better represented as one systemic finding.

Consider:

Different affected endpoints
Different privileges
Different data
Different impact
Different remediation

Avoid artificially splitting or merging findings.

docs.title: Variant Severity
docs.text:
Do not automatically assign the same severity to every variant.

Example:

IDOR read public profile

may have different impact from:

IDOR download confidential document

Severity should reflect actual impact and exploitability.

docs.title: Runtime Validation
docs.text:
Static variant discovery produces candidates.

Where appropriate and authorised:

Candidate
   |
   v
Understand Route
   |
   v
Understand Expected Control
   |
   v
Safe Runtime Test
   |
   v
Confirmed / Rejected

docs.title: Burp Suite
docs.text:
Burp Suite is useful for validating web-accessible variants.

Use:

Proxy
HTTP history
Site map
Repeater
Comparer
Logger

docs.title: Access-Control Variant Validation
docs.text:
For IDOR:

User A -> Object A -> Allowed

User A -> Object B -> Should be denied

Compare source behaviour with runtime behaviour.

docs.title: Injection Variant Validation
docs.text:
For an injection candidate:

Source
  |
  v
Candidate Flow
  |
  v
Sink

first understand:

Validation
Encoding
Parameterisation
Framework behaviour

before dynamic testing.

docs.title: Do Not Blindly Validate Every Candidate
docs.text:
Variant analysis can produce many candidates.

Prioritise:

Externally reachable
Unauthenticated
Low privilege
Sensitive operation
High-value data
Dangerous sink
Missing common control

docs.title: Prioritisation Model
docs.text:
Candidate
   |
   v
Reachable?
   |
   v
Attacker-Controlled?
   |
   v
Sensitive Sink?
   |
   v
Security Control?
   |

docs.title: High-Value Variant Targets
docs.text:
Prioritise variants involving:

Authentication
Authorisation
Role changes
Password reset
MFA
Administrative operations
Command execution
SQL
SSRF
File access
File uploads
Deserialization
Template rendering
Sensitive exports
Secrets
Tenant boundaries

docs.title: False Positive Reduction
docs.text:
For every candidate ask:

Is the code reachable?

Is the source attacker-controlled?

Is the sink security-sensitive?

Is there validation?

Is there sanitisation?

Is there authorisation?

Is there framework protection?

Is there infrastructure protection?

Is the data transformed?

Does the vulnerable path actually execute?

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Variant searches can miss issues because of:

Custom wrappers
Reflection
Dynamic dispatch
Dependency injection
Generated code
Runtime configuration
Framework magic
Metaprogramming
Dynamic routes
ORM abstractions

Combine tools.

docs.text:

                        |
                        v

docs.title: Practical Mental Model
docs.text:
When a vulnerability is found, do not ask only:

Where else is this exact code?

Ask:

Where else can the same attacker-controlled data enter?

Where else is the same sink used?

Where else is this security control missing?

Where else is the same object accessed?

Where else is the same business operation exposed?

Where else is the same helper called?

Where else does another protocol expose this operation?

Where else was this vulnerable pattern copied?

Where else does an equivalent semantic data flow exist?

That is variant analysis.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Variant analysis transforms an individual vulnerability into a systematic search strategy.

The workflow is:

Confirmed Vulnerability
        |
        v
Understand Root Cause
        |
        v
Identify Source
        |
        v
Identify Sink
        |
        v
Identify Missing Control
        |
        v
Search Exact Pattern
        |
        v
Search Structural Pattern
        |
        v
Search Semantic Pattern
        |
        v
Review Alternate Entry Points
        |
        v
Manual Source-to-Sink Analysis
        |
        v
Runtime Validation
        |
        v
Confirmed Variants
        |
        v
Systemic Remediation
        |
        v
Regression Detection

The most important principle is:

Do not stop when you find a vulnerability.

Use the vulnerability to teach you
how the application fails securely,
then search the entire attack surface
for every other place where it fails
in the same way.

A strong source code review therefore follows:

Find
  |
  v
Understand
  |
  v
Generalise
  |
  v
Search
  |
  v
Validate
  |
  v
Repeat

That is the foundation of effective variant analysis.

docs.title: Static Analysis for Source Code Review
docs.text:
Static analysis is the examination of source code without relying solely on executing the application.

During a security-focused source code review, static analysis helps identify:

Application entry points
User-controlled input
Authentication controls
Authorisation controls
Dangerous functions
Security-sensitive APIs
Potential source-to-sink flows
Hard-coded secrets
Unsafe configuration
Vulnerable dependencies
Repeated vulnerable patterns

Static analysis should not be treated as:

Scanner Result
     =
Confirmed Vulnerability

Instead:

Static Analysis
      |
      v
Candidate Finding
      |
      v
Manual Source Review
      |
      v
Source-to-Sink Analysis
      |
      v
Security Control Analysis
      |
      v
Exploitability Assessment
      |
      v
Dynamic Validation
      |
      v
Confirmed Finding

This section focuses on four tools that complement each other:

ripgrep
Semgrep
OpenGrep
CodeQL

They solve different problems.

docs.title: Tool Overview
docs.text:
A practical way to think about the tools is:

ripgrep
   |
   +--> Fast text and regex searching
   |
   +--> Manual source/sink discovery
   |
   +--> Excellent for initial reconnaissance

Semgrep
   |
   +--> Syntax-aware static analysis
   |
   +--> Security rules
   |
   +--> Custom pattern matching
   |
   +--> Data-flow and taint-oriented analysis

OpenGrep
   |
   +--> Open-source static analysis
   |
   +--> Semgrep-style rules and workflows
   |
   +--> Custom security rule development
   |
   +--> Useful for local and CI scanning

CodeQL
   |
   +--> Semantic code analysis
   |
   +--> Data-flow analysis
   |
   +--> Taint tracking
   |
   +--> Cross-function investigation
   |
   +--> Advanced variant analysis

The tools should not necessarily compete with each other.

A strong review can use all four.

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
SOURCE REPOSITORY
                            |
                            v
                    Understand Project
                            |
                            v
                    Identify Technology
                            |
                            v
                  Map Application Structure
                            |
             +--------------+--------------+
             |              |              |
             v              v              v
         ripgrep        Semgrep        OpenGrep
             |              |              |
             |              |              |
             +--------------+--------------+
                            |
                            v
                    Candidate Findings
                            |
                            v
                    Manual VS Code Review
                            |
                            v
                    Source-to-Sink Trace
                            |
                            v
                    Security Controls
                            |
                            v
                       Exploitability
                            |
                            v
                    Dynamic Validation
                            |
                            v
                    Confirmed Finding
                            |
                            v
                     Variant Analysis
                            |
                            v
                          CodeQL

This is not a mandatory sequence.

For some applications, CodeQL may be used much earlier.

For others, a few well-designed ripgrep searches may reveal the most important attack surface quickly.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
The most important rule in this section is:

Tool finding
    !=
Vulnerability

Similarly:

Dangerous API
    !=
Exploitable vulnerability

For example:

ProcessBuilder

does not automatically mean:

Command Injection

Likewise:

HttpClient

does not automatically mean:

SSRF

and:

createNativeQuery()

does not automatically mean:

SQL Injection

The reviewer must establish the complete data flow.

docs.title: What Proves a Vulnerability?
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Attacker-Controlled Source
           |
           v
      Reachable Flow
           |
           v
     Transformations
           |
           v
   Security Controls
           |
           v
Security-Sensitive Sink
           |
           v
        Impact

A candidate becomes much stronger when all of the following can be established:

[+] Attacker controls the input

[+] The relevant code is reachable

[+] The input reaches the sink

[+] The input remains attacker-controlled

[+] Security controls are absent or ineffective

[+] The sink operates in a dangerous context

[+] Exploitation produces meaningful security impact

docs.title: Static Analysis and Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
Static-analysis tools become significantly more useful when combined with an IDE.

Visual Studio Code can be used to:

Open scanner findings
Navigate definitions
Find references
Inspect callers
Inspect callees
Search the repository
Trace variables
Compare security controls
Review Git changes
Run tools from the terminal

A practical workflow is:

Static Analysis Result
        |
        v
Open File in VS Code
        |
        v
Inspect Function
        |
        v
Go to Definition
        |
        v
Find References
        |
        v
Show Call Hierarchy
        |
        v
Trace Input
        |
        v
Inspect Security Controls
        |
        v
Determine Exploitability

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text: Static analysis becomes much easier when code is viewed in terms of sources and sinks.

docs.title: Source
docs.text:
A source is a location where potentially attacker-controlled data enters the application.

Examples:

HTTP query parameter
HTTP request body
HTTP header
Cookie
Path parameter
Uploaded file
GraphQL argument
WebSocket message
gRPC message
Webhook
Message queue
Database value originating from a user

docs.title: Sink
docs.text:
A sink is a security-sensitive operation.

Examples:

SQL query
Operating system command
File read
File write
HTTP request
HTML output
Template rendering
Deserialisation
XML parsing
Dynamic code execution
Redirect
LDAP query

The basic model is:

SOURCE
  |
  v
User-Controlled Data
  |
  v
TRANSFORMATIONS
  |
  +-- validation
  +-- parsing
  +-- normalisation
  +-- sanitisation
  +-- encoding
  +-- authorisation
  +-- business logic
  |
  v
SINK

docs.title: Forward Analysis
docs.text:
Forward analysis starts at a source.

Example:

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
Controller
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Repository
      |
      v
SQL Query

Questions:

Where does this input go?

Is it validated?

Is it normalised?

Is it encoded?

Is it parameterised?

Is authorisation performed?

Does it reach a dangerous sink?

docs.title: Reverse Sink Analysis
docs.text:
Reverse analysis starts with dangerous functionality.

Example:

ProcessBuilder
      ^
      |
CommandService
      ^
      |
ReportService
      ^
      |
ReportController
      ^
      |
HTTP Parameter

This approach can be extremely efficient.

Large applications may have:

Thousands of input parameters

but only:

A few command execution sinks

A few deserialisation sinks

A few outbound HTTP clients

A few raw SQL construction locations

Therefore:

Find Sink
   |
   v
Trace Backwards
   |
   v
Find Source

is often a useful review strategy.

docs.title: Use Both Directions
docs.text:
The strongest approach combines:

SOURCE -> SINK

with:

SINK -> SOURCE

For example:

Route Mapping
     |
     v
Input Sources
     |
     v
Forward Analysis

        +

Dangerous API Search
     |
     v
Sink Discovery
     |
     v
Reverse Analysis

docs.title: Static Analysis Layers
docs.text:
A useful static-analysis model has several layers.

Layer 1 - Text Search
        |
        v
Layer 2 - Syntax-Aware Matching
        |
        v
Layer 3 - Data Flow
        |
        v
Layer 4 - Taint Tracking
        |
        v
Layer 5 - Semantic / Program Analysis
        |
        v
Layer 6 - Manual Context Analysis

The four tools in this section fit approximately into these layers.

docs.title: Layer 1 - ripgrep
docs.text:
ripgrep performs extremely fast repository-wide text and regular-expression searching.

Example:

rg -n 'ProcessBuilder' .

Search multiple sinks:

rg -n \
'ProcessBuilder|Runtime\.getRuntime|Process\.Start|os\.system|child_process\.exec' \
.

This is excellent for:

Reconnaissance
Route discovery
Source discovery
Sink discovery
Authentication discovery
Authorisation discovery
Configuration discovery
Secret hunting
Variant hunting

But ripgrep generally does not understand program semantics.

It sees text.

docs.title: Layer 2 - Semgrep
docs.text:
Semgrep understands source code structure.

Instead of simply searching for text such as:

exec(

a rule can describe code patterns.

Conceptually:

patterns:
  - pattern: dangerous_function(...)

Semgrep can therefore reduce some of the noise associated with raw regular expressions.

It is useful for:

Dangerous API detection
Security anti-patterns
Framework-specific rules
Custom vulnerability patterns
Rule-based source review
Taint-oriented analysis
CI scanning

docs.title: Layer 3 - OpenGrep
docs.text:
OpenGrep provides an open-source static-analysis workflow with Semgrep-style rule concepts and is particularly useful when you want to maintain local security rules and scanning workflows.

A practical use case is:

Manual Review
     |
     v
Discover Vulnerable Pattern
     |
     v
Create OpenGrep Rule
     |
     v
Scan Entire Repository
     |
     v
Discover Variants

For example, suppose manual review discovers a dangerous internal helper:

executeSystemCommand()

Instead of manually searching every call site, a rule can be created to identify usage across the codebase.

OpenGrep is therefore particularly useful for:

Custom rules
Security pattern libraries
Local SAST
CI scanning
Variant analysis
Organisation-specific dangerous APIs

Because OpenGrep is actively developed, verify the installed version's current CLI and supported rule features before building automation around a particular command or rule feature.

docs.title: Layer 4 - CodeQL
docs.text:
CodeQL models code semantically.

Instead of asking only:

Does this function exist?

CodeQL can help answer questions such as:

Can data from this source reach this sink?

Conceptually:

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
Controller
      |
      v
Helper
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Repository
      |
      v
SQL Sink

This makes CodeQL particularly useful for:

Data-flow analysis
Taint tracking
Cross-function analysis
Variant analysis
Complex applications
Custom security research

docs.title: Tool Comparison
docs.text:
Capability ripgrep Semgrep OpenGrep CodeQL Fast text search Excellent Not primary purpose Not primary purpose No Regex search Excellent Limited role Limited role No Syntax-aware analysis No Yes Yes Yes Custom rules Regex-based Yes Yes Yes Data-flow analysis Manual Yes, depending on rule/engine Depends on supported engine/features Strong Taint analysis Manual Supported workflows Depends on supported engine/features Strong Cross-function analysis Manual Engine/rule dependent Engine/rule dependent Strong Variant analysis Good manually Good Good Excellent Initial reconnaissance Excellent Good Good Usually heavier CI integration Scriptable Yes Yes Yes Learning curve Low Medium Medium High Manual review companion Excellent Excellent Excellent Excellent

The exact capabilities of Semgrep and OpenGrep can evolve between versions.

Always verify tool-specific functionality against the installed release.

docs.title: Why ripgrep Still Matters
docs.text:
Advanced SAST does not replace simple searching.

A reviewer may want to answer:

Where are all controllers?

Where is authentication configured?

Where is HttpClient used?

Where is ProcessBuilder used?

Where are files written?

Where is JWT parsed?

Where are redirects created?

Where are secrets referenced?

For these questions, ripgrep is often faster than creating a static-analysis query.

docs.title: Why Semgrep Matters
docs.text:
Semgrep becomes useful when:

Text search creates too much noise

You need syntax-aware matching

You want reusable security rules

You want framework-specific detection

You want automated scanning

You want to turn manual findings into rules

Example:

Manual Finding
      |
      v
Understand Code Pattern
      |
      v
Write Semgrep Rule
      |
      v
Scan Repository
      |
      v
Find Variants

docs.title: Why OpenGrep Matters
docs.text:
OpenGrep is useful when you want an open-source static-analysis workflow that can be incorporated into:

Local pentesting environments
Source code review workstations
CI pipelines
Custom security tooling
Internal rule repositories
Security research

A useful model is:

Security Researcher
       |
       v
Find Interesting Pattern
       |
       v
Write Rule
       |
       v
Run OpenGrep
       |
       v
Review Matches
       |
       v
Improve Rule
       |
       v
Build Rule Library

Over time this creates a personal security knowledge base encoded as executable rules.

docs.title: Why CodeQL Matters
docs.text:
CodeQL becomes particularly useful when:

The repository is large

Data passes through many functions

Simple pattern matching is insufficient

You need semantic analysis

You are performing variant analysis

You are researching vulnerability classes

You need custom taint tracking

Example:

Source
 |
 v
Controller
 |
 v
DTO
 |
 v
Service
 |
 v
Utility
 |
 v
Repository
 |
 v
Sink

Manually tracing this is possible.

CodeQL can help automate portions of the analysis.

docs.title: Static Analysis Is Not Just Vulnerability Scanning
docs.text:
Static analysis should also be used for architecture discovery.

Examples:

Routes
Controllers
Services
Repositories
Authentication
Authorisation
Middleware
Filters
Interceptors
Database clients
HTTP clients
File APIs
Template engines
Message queues
Background jobs
WebSockets
GraphQL
gRPC

This information helps build the application security model before individual vulnerabilities are investigated.

docs.title: Phase 1 - Repository Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Start by identifying the project.

ls -la

Useful discovery:

find . -maxdepth 2 -type f | sort

Look for:

pom.xml
build.gradle
build.gradle.kts
*.sln
*.csproj
composer.json
requirements.txt
pyproject.toml
package.json
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
application.yml
application.properties
appsettings.json
.env

docs.title: Phase 2 - Identify Languages
docs.text:
Useful:

find . -type f | sed 's/.*\.//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr

This can provide a rough view of file extensions.

Do not rely on extensions alone to determine the application architecture.

docs.title: Phase 3 - Exclude Noise
docs.text:
Common generated or dependency directories include:

node_modules
vendor
target
build
dist
bin
obj
coverage
.git

For ripgrep, exclusions can be added with:

rg \
-g '!node_modules/**' \
-g '!vendor/**' \
-g '!target/**' \
-g '!build/**' \
-g '!dist/**' \
PATTERN \
.

Static-analysis tools should similarly be configured to avoid spending excessive time analysing irrelevant generated or vendored code unless those files are intentionally part of the review.

docs.title: Phase 4 - Route Discovery
docs.text: Before searching for vulnerabilities, map the attack surface.

docs.title: Java / Spring
docs.text:
rg -n \
'@RequestMapping|@GetMapping|@PostMapping|@PutMapping|@PatchMapping|@DeleteMapping|@RestController|@Controller' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\[Route|\[HttpGet|\[HttpPost|\[HttpPut|\[HttpPatch|\[HttpDelete|MapGet\(|MapPost\(|MapPut\(|MapDelete\(' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: Flask
docs.text:
rg -n \
'@.*\.route\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Django
docs.text:
rg -n \
'path\(|re_path\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Express
docs.text:
rg -n \
'app\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)|router\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Phase 5 - Authentication Discovery
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni \
'authenticate|authentication|login|logout|password|jwt|oauth|oidc|saml|mfa|totp|session' \
.

The objective is to map:

Login
  |
  v
Credential Validation
  |
  v
Identity
  |
  v
Session / Token
  |
  v
Authenticated Request

docs.title: Phase 6 - Authorisation Discovery
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni \
'authorize|authorise|permission|role|policy|access.?control|isAdmin|hasRole|hasAuthority|PreAuthorize' \
.

Then determine:

Where is authorisation performed?

Route?

Middleware?

Service?

Repository?

Database query?

docs.title: Phase 7 - Source Discovery
docs.text:
Language-specific source patterns can identify potentially attacker-controlled input.

Examples:

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rg -n \
'getParameter|getHeader|getCookies|getInputStream|getReader|@RequestParam|@PathVariable|@RequestBody|@RequestHeader|@CookieValue' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Request\.Query|Request\.Form|Request\.Headers|Request\.Cookies|RouteData|FromQuery|FromRoute|FromBody|FromHeader' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\$_GET|\$_POST|\$_REQUEST|\$_COOKIE|\$_FILES|\$_SERVER' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rg -n \
'request\.args|request\.form|request\.json|request\.files|request\.headers|request\.cookies|request\.GET|request\.POST|request\.FILES' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text:
rg -n \
'req\.query|req\.params|req\.body|req\.headers|req\.cookies' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Phase 8 - Sink Discovery
docs.text: Once the attack surface and sources are understood, search for dangerous operations.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rg -n \
'executeQuery|executeUpdate|createNativeQuery|createQuery|JdbcTemplate|PreparedStatement|Statement' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'SqlCommand|FromSqlRaw|ExecuteSqlRaw|SqlQueryRaw|QueryAsync|ExecuteAsync' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rg -n \
'mysqli_query|->query\(|->exec\(|->prepare\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rg -n \
'cursor\.execute|cursor\.executemany|\.raw\(|RawSQL|text\(' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text:
rg -n \
'\.query\(|\.execute\(|\$queryRaw|\$executeRaw' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

These are candidate locations.

Parameterized query APIs may be entirely safe.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Runtime\.getRuntime\(\)\.exec|ProcessBuilder|/bin/sh|bash -c|cmd\.exe|powershell' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Process\.Start|ProcessStartInfo|cmd\.exe|powershell|/bin/sh|bash' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rg -n \
'system\(|exec\(|shell_exec\(|passthru\(|popen\(|proc_open\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rg -n \
'os\.system|subprocess\.(run|Popen|call|check_output|check_call)|shell\s*=\s*True' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text:
rg -n \
'child_process|exec\(|execSync\(|spawn\(|spawnSync\(' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rg -n \
'HttpClient|RestTemplate|RestClient|WebClient|URLConnection|openConnection|new URL|URI\.create' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'HttpClient|WebClient|WebRequest|HttpWebRequest' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rg -n \
'requests\.(get|post|put|delete|request)|urllib|urlopen|httpx\.' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rg -n \
'curl_exec|curl_init|file_get_contents|fopen\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text:
rg -n \
'axios|fetch\(|http\.request|https\.request|got\(' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Files\.(read|write)|FileInputStream|FileOutputStream|new File|Paths\.get|Path\.of|\.resolve\(' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'File\.(Open|Read|Write|Delete|Move|Copy)|Path\.Combine|Directory\.' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rg -n \
'file_get_contents|file_put_contents|fopen|readfile|include\(|require\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rg -n \
'open\(|pathlib|send_file|send_from_directory' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text:
rg -n \
'fs\.(readFile|writeFile|createReadStream|createWriteStream|unlink|rename)' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rg -n \
'ObjectInputStream|readObject\(|readUnshared\(|XMLDecoder|XStream|activateDefaultTyping|enableDefaultTyping|Yaml\(' \
-g '*.java' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'BinaryFormatter|LosFormatter|ObjectStateFormatter|NetDataContractSerializer|Deserialize\(' \
-g '*.cs' \
.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rg -n \
'unserialize\(' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rg -n \
'pickle\.loads|pickle\.load|yaml\.load|marshal\.loads' \
-g '*.py' \
.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text: Search application-specific serialisation libraries and unsafe dynamic object reconstruction rather than assuming ordinary JSON.parse() is equivalent to native object deserialisation.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rg -n \
'th:utext|response\.getWriter|PrintWriter|\.write\(|\.print\(' \
-g '*.java' \
-g '*.html' \
-g '*.jsp' \
.

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rg -n \
'Html\.Raw|WriteLiteral|Response\.Write' \
-g '*.cs' \
-g '*.cshtml' \
.

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rg -n \
'echo|print|printf' \
-g '*.php' \
.

docs.title: Browser JavaScript
docs.text:
rg -n \
'innerHTML|outerHTML|insertAdjacentHTML|document\.write|eval\(|new Function' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

These searches can produce substantial false positives.

Context is essential.

docs.title: Open Redirect Candidates
docs.text:
rg -n \
'redirect\(|RedirectView|sendRedirect|Response\.Redirect|res\.redirect|location\.href|window\.location' \
.

Then trace the destination source.

docs.title: LDAP Injection Candidates
docs.text:
rg -n \
'LdapTemplate|DirContext|SearchControls|ldap_search|DirectorySearcher|DirectoryEntry' \
.

Then inspect how LDAP filters are constructed.

docs.title: Template Injection Candidates
docs.text:
Search template engines and dynamic expression evaluation.

rg -ni \
'render_template_string|Template\(|FreeMarker|Velocity|Thymeleaf|SpelExpressionParser|parseExpression|RazorEngine|eval\(' \
.

Do not confuse:

Untrusted template data

with:

Untrusted template source

docs.title: XXE Candidates
docs.text:
rg -n \
'DocumentBuilderFactory|SAXParserFactory|XMLInputFactory|TransformerFactory|SchemaFactory|XmlDocument|XmlReader|lxml|etree' \
.

Parser security depends on:

Parser
Version
Configuration
Runtime
Input trust

Do not report XXE from parser presence alone.

docs.title: Mass Assignment Candidates
docs.text:
Search for direct request-to-domain-object binding.

Examples:

Request body -> Entity
Request body -> Model
Request body -> ORM object

Potential keywords:

rg -ni \
'BeanUtils\.copyProperties|ModelMapper|@ModelAttribute|UpdateModel|TryUpdateModel|Object\.assign|\.update\(req\.body|\.create\(req\.body' \
.

Manual analysis is particularly important here.

docs.title: Secrets Candidates
docs.text:
rg -ni \
'password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|access[_-]?token|refresh[_-]?token|private[_-]?key|client[_-]?secret' \
.

Also search likely credential formats where appropriate.

Do not automatically report placeholders, test values or documentation examples.

docs.title: Security Configuration Discovery
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni \
'cors|csrf|csp|content-security-policy|frame-options|sameSite|secureCookie|httponly|allowedOrigins|permitAll|allowAnonymous' \
.

This helps identify:

CORS
CSRF
Security headers
Cookie configuration
Authentication exceptions
Authorisation exceptions

docs.title: Dependency Discovery
docs.text:
Search manifests:

find . -type f \( \
-name 'pom.xml' -o \
-name 'build.gradle' -o \
-name 'build.gradle.kts' -o \
-name '*.csproj' -o \
-name 'composer.json' -o \
-name 'composer.lock' -o \
-name 'requirements.txt' -o \
-name 'pyproject.toml' -o \
-name 'package.json' -o \
-name 'package-lock.json' -o \
-name 'yarn.lock' -o \
-name 'pnpm-lock.yaml' \
\)

Dependency analysis is a separate problem from code pattern analysis.

Combine SAST with software composition analysis where appropriate.

docs.title: Static Analysis by Vulnerability Class
docs.text:
A useful workflow is to perform dedicated passes.

Pass 1
Attack Surface

Pass 2
Authentication

Pass 3
Authorisation

Pass 4
IDOR / BOLA

Pass 5
Input Validation

Pass 6
SQL / NoSQL / LDAP Injection

Pass 7
Command Injection

Pass 8
SSRF

Pass 9
Path Traversal / Files

Pass 10
File Upload

Pass 11
XXE

Pass 12
Deserialisation

Pass 13
SSTI

Pass 14
XSS / HTML Injection

Pass 15
CSRF / CORS

Pass 16
Redirects / Host Handling

Pass 17
Mass Assignment

Pass 18
Business Logic

Pass 19
Race Conditions

Pass 20
Secrets

Pass 21
Dependencies

Pass 22
Cryptography

Pass 23
Logging / Information Disclosure

Pass 24
API Security

This is often more systematic than running a scanner once and reviewing whatever it returns.

docs.title: Static Analysis by Technology
docs.text:
The exact source and sink patterns depend on the application stack.

The language-specific source code review notes contain deeper patterns for:

.NET / ASP.NET Core
Java / Spring
PHP
Python
Django
Flask
Node.js / Express
Client-Side JavaScript

Static-analysis rules should be adapted to framework behaviour.

docs.title: Framework Awareness
docs.text:
Consider:

Framework autoescaping

ORM parameterisation

Authentication middleware

Authorisation annotations

CSRF middleware

CORS middleware

Model binding

Request validation

Session handling

Proxy configuration

A generic rule may misunderstand framework protections.

docs.title: Example - SQL Injection Candidate
docs.text:
Suppose a scanner finds:

String sql =
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '"
    + name
    + "'";

entityManager.createNativeQuery(sql);

The scanner should lead to:

Where does name originate?

Trace:

@RequestParam
    |
    v
Controller
    |
    v
Service
    |
    v
name
    |
    v
String Concatenation
    |
    v
createNativeQuery()

This creates a strong SQL injection candidate.

docs.title: Example - False Positive
docs.text:
Suppose the scanner finds:

PreparedStatement stmt =
    connection.prepareStatement(
        "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"
    );

stmt.setLong(1, id);

A raw text search may flag:

SELECT

and:

prepareStatement

Manual review identifies parameter binding.

Result:

Protected

docs.title: Example - SSRF Candidate
docs.text:
url = request.args.get("url")

response = requests.get(url)

Flow:

HTTP Parameter
     |
     v
url
     |
     v
requests.get()

Now inspect:

URL validation
Host allowlisting
Scheme validation
Redirect behaviour
DNS resolution
Network egress

The sink alone does not prove SSRF.

docs.title: Example - IDOR
docs.text:
Static scanners may struggle with logic such as:

@GetMapping("/documents/{id}")
public Document getDocument(
    @PathVariable Long id
) {
    return repository
        .findById(id)
        .orElseThrow();
}

The security question is not primarily:

Is findById dangerous?

It is:

Where is ownership or permission checked?

This demonstrates why manual review remains essential.

docs.title: Example - Business Logic
docs.text:
Consider:

POST /coupon/apply

coupon.used = false
      |
      v
Apply Discount
      |
      v
coupon.used = true

The code may appear individually safe.

But concurrent requests could potentially interact with the workflow.

This requires reasoning about:

Transactions
Concurrency
Atomicity
Database constraints

rather than searching for one dangerous API.

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
One of the highest-value uses of static analysis is finding variants after discovering one real vulnerability.

Workflow:

Confirmed Vulnerability
        |
        v
Identify Root Pattern
        |
        v
Identify Source
        |
        v
Identify Sink
        |
        v
Identify Missing Control
        |
        v
Search Repository
        |
        v
Find Similar Flows

docs.title: Example Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose a vulnerable helper is discovered:

public void executeReport(
    String command
) {
    Runtime.getRuntime().exec(command);
}

Search:

rg -n \
'executeReport\(' \
.

Then:

Find All References

in VS Code.

Potential result:

ReportController
AdminController
ExportController
ScheduledReportJob

Every caller becomes a candidate.

docs.title: Turn Findings Into Rules
docs.text:
A powerful long-term workflow is:

Manual Finding
      |
      v
Understand Pattern
      |
      v
Create Search Pattern
      |
      +--> ripgrep
      |
      +--> Semgrep
      |
      +--> OpenGrep
      |
      +--> CodeQL
      |
      v
Scan for Variants

This transforms one vulnerability into reusable security knowledge.

docs.title: Personal Rule Library
docs.text:
A security reviewer can maintain a repository such as:

security-rules/
│
├── java/
│   ├── command-execution.yml
│   ├── unsafe-sql.yml
│   └── ssrf.yml
│
├── dotnet/
│   ├── process-start.yml
│   ├── raw-sql.yml
│   └── unsafe-file-access.yml
│
├── python/
│   ├── shell-true.yml
│   ├── pickle.yml
│   └── unsafe-yaml.yml
│
├── php/
│   ├── command-execution.yml
│   └── unserialize.yml
│
└── javascript/
    ├── child-process.yml
    ├── dom-xss.yml
    └── unsafe-eval.yml

The exact rule syntax depends on the analysis engine.

docs.title: Finding Triage
docs.text:
Static-analysis output should be triaged.

Useful classifications:

Confirmed
Likely
Needs Review
Protected
Not Reachable
False Positive
Informational

docs.title: Triage Priority
docs.text:
A simple prioritisation model:

                 Attacker Control
                      High
                       |
                       v
High Impact Sink -> Highest Priority
                       |
                       v
Missing Control

High-priority sinks often include:

Command execution
Raw SQL
Deserialisation
Dynamic code execution
File write
Sensitive file read
Outbound HTTP requests
Authentication decisions
Authorisation decisions

docs.title: Confidence Model
docs.text:
For each result consider:

Source Confidence
Sink Confidence
Flow Confidence
Control Confidence
Impact Confidence

Example:

Source Confidence: High
Sink Confidence: High
Flow Confidence: High
Control Confidence: Medium
Impact Confidence: High

The remaining work is obvious:

Investigate security control.

docs.title: Dynamic Validation
docs.text:
Where authorised and appropriate:

Static Candidate
      |
      v
Identify Endpoint
      |
      v
Run Application
      |
      v
Burp Suite
      |
      v
Controlled Test
      |
      v
Observe Behaviour

Dynamic validation can help confirm assumptions made during static analysis.

docs.title: Static Analysis + Burp Suite
docs.text:
Example:

Semgrep / OpenGrep / CodeQL
          |
          v
Potential SSRF
          |
          v
VS Code
          |
          v
Find Controller
          |
          v
/api/import?url=
          |
          v
Burp Repeater
          |
          v
Controlled Validation

This creates a strong white-box testing workflow.

docs.title: Static Analysis + Debugger
docs.text:
When source and a test environment are available:

Request
  |
  v
Breakpoint
  |
  v
Inspect Variable
  |
  v
Continue
  |
  v
Breakpoint at Sink

This can directly confirm the runtime data flow.

docs.title: Static Analysis + Git
docs.text:
Git is useful for understanding:

When code was introduced

What changed

Whether security controls were removed

Whether a vulnerability has variants

Whether secrets existed historically

Useful commands:

git log --oneline --all

git diff

git blame path/to/file

git log -S 'dangerousFunction' -p

docs.title: Diff-Based Static Analysis
docs.text:
When reviewing a pull request or release:

Changed Code
    |
    v
New Sources?
    |
    v
New Sinks?
    |
    v
Changed Security Controls?
    |
    v
Changed Dependencies?

Start with:

git diff --name-only main..feature

Then:

git diff main..feature

Prioritise:

Authentication
Authorisation
Input handling
Database queries
Command execution
File handling
Network requests
Dependencies
Configuration

docs.title: Baseline vs Diff Review
docs.text:
Baseline Review
      |
      +--> Entire application

Diff Review
      |
      +--> Changed code

Hybrid Review
      |
      +--> Understand baseline
      |
      +--> Deep review changes

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
Static analysis can also run automatically.

Conceptually:

Developer Commit
      |
      v
Pull Request
      |
      v
CI Pipeline
      |
      +--> Semgrep
      |
      +--> OpenGrep
      |
      +--> CodeQL
      |
      +--> Dependency Scan
      |
      +--> Secret Scan
      |
      v
Security Results

Do not configure CI to blindly block every scanner match.

Poorly tuned rules can create:

False positives
Alert fatigue
Developer bypass behaviour
Ignored security results

Rule quality matters.

docs.title: SARIF
docs.text:
Static Analysis Results Interchange Format, or SARIF, is commonly used to represent static-analysis findings.

Where a tool and workflow support SARIF, it can help integrate findings with:

CI systems
Code scanning interfaces
Security dashboards
IDE workflows

Verify the exact output support and CLI options for the installed version of each tool.

docs.title: Scanner Output Preservation
docs.text:
During an assessment, preserve:

Tool name
Tool version
Command
Rule set
Repository commit
Branch
Timestamp
Output

Example:

Tool:
OpenGrep

Version:
<record installed version>

Repository:
example-app

Commit:
abc123...

Rules:
custom/java-security/

Command:
<record exact command>

Result:
scanner-output.json

This makes results reproducible.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
A static-analysis result should ideally be reproducible against:

Same repository commit
Same rules
Same tool version
Same configuration

Record:

git rev-parse HEAD

Also record tool versions.

docs.title: Do Not Scan the Wrong Revision
docs.text:
Before beginning:

git status

git branch --show-current

git rev-parse HEAD

The reviewed source must correspond to the intended assessment target.

docs.title: Generated Code
docs.text:
Generated code can create noise.

Examples:

Generated API clients
ORM models
Bundled JavaScript
Build output
Protocol buffers
Vendor libraries
Minified files

Determine whether generated code should be:

Excluded

Reviewed selectively

Reviewed through its source generator/configuration

Do not blindly exclude code merely because it is generated if it forms part of a meaningful security boundary.

docs.title: Vendored Dependencies
docs.text:
Vendored code may be relevant when:

Application modifies the dependency

Dependency is directly deployed

Security behaviour depends on it

No package manager metadata exists

Otherwise dependency scanning may be more efficient than running every application rule against third-party code.

docs.title: Test Code
docs.text:
Do not automatically exclude tests.

Tests may reveal:

Hidden endpoints
Test credentials
Authentication assumptions
Authorisation expectations
Security feature flags
Business logic
Example payloads
Internal API usage

But findings affecting only non-production test code should be classified appropriately.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Static review must include configuration.

Examples:

application.yml
application.properties
appsettings.json
settings.py
.env
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
nginx.conf
Kubernetes manifests
Terraform
CI/CD workflows

Security behaviour can change dramatically based on configuration.

docs.title: Deployment Context
docs.text:
Static analysis alone may not reveal:

Reverse proxy protections
API gateway policies
WAF controls
Cloud IAM
Network egress controls
Rate limiting
TLS termination
Secret injection
Runtime environment

Therefore avoid conclusions such as:

No application rate-limit code exists,
therefore the endpoint has no rate limiting.

The control may exist elsewhere.

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggling
docs.text:
Application source can reveal:

Custom HTTP parsing
Header handling
Proxy assumptions
Content-Length logic
Transfer-Encoding handling
Framework/server versions

But HTTP request smuggling frequently depends on the complete chain:

Client
  |
  v
CDN
  |
  v
Reverse Proxy
  |
  v
Load Balancer
  |
  v
Application Server

Do not report request smuggling based solely on an application code pattern without understanding the HTTP processing chain.

docs.title: Cache Security
docs.text:
Static analysis can identify:

Cache key construction
@Cacheable
Redis usage
Memory caches
HTTP cache headers

Ask:

Does the cache key include user identity?

Does it include tenant?

Does it include authorisation context?

Can private responses become shared?

docs.title: Security Headers
docs.text:
Static analysis can identify header configuration.

Search:

rg -ni \
'Content-Security-Policy|X-Frame-Options|Strict-Transport-Security|Referrer-Policy|Permissions-Policy|X-Content-Type-Options' \
.

Missing configuration in source code does not prove headers are absent in production.

Headers may be applied by:

Reverse proxy
CDN
API gateway
Web server
Platform

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Search:

rg -ni \
'cors|allowedOrigins|allowedOriginPatterns|Access-Control-Allow-Origin|credentials' \
.

Then analyse:

Allowed origins
Credentials
Methods
Headers
Dynamic origin reflection
Deployment context

Do not report CORS simply because:

*

appears somewhere in source.

Determine the actual response behaviour and credential model.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
Static analysis should identify:

CSRF middleware
CSRF exclusions
Disabled CSRF
Ignored routes
Cookie authentication
Bearer-token authentication

CSRF risk depends heavily on how credentials are automatically attached to requests.

For example, a stateless API using an Authorization: Bearer token supplied explicitly by client-side code has a different CSRF threat model from a browser application authenticated by cookies.

docs.title: Authentication and Authorisation Rules
docs.text:
Custom rules are particularly useful for detecting:

Anonymous endpoints
permitAll()
AllowAnonymous
Missing security decorators
Administrative handlers
Object lookup without obvious ownership checks

However, access control is highly contextual.

Automated rules should be treated as prioritisation mechanisms.

docs.title: Security-Sensitive Internal APIs
docs.text:
One of the best uses of custom rules is detecting application-specific dangerous functions.

Example:

Internal helper:

CommandRunner.execute()

or:

ReportService.renderUnsafeTemplate()

or:

HttpHelper.fetchRemoteResource()

Once discovered:

Create Rule
    |
    v
Find Every Caller
    |
    v
Review Input

This can outperform generic vulnerability rules during targeted source review.

docs.title: Custom Rule Development Workflow
docs.text:
1. Find interesting security pattern manually

2. Identify the minimum vulnerable code pattern

3. Identify safe variants

4. Create test cases

5. Write rule

6. Run rule against test cases

7. Run against repository

8. Triage matches

9. Reduce false positives

10. Add rule to rule library

docs.title: Rule Test Cases
docs.text:
For every custom rule, ideally maintain:

rule-name/
│
├── rule.yml
│
├── vulnerable-example.*
└── safe-example.*

This makes rule behaviour easier to maintain.

docs.title: Rule Quality
docs.text:
A useful rule should balance:

Recall

and:

Precision

High recall:

Find as many real candidates as possible.

High precision:

Avoid irrelevant matches.

During manual penetration testing, somewhat lower precision may be acceptable because a human is triaging the results.

In large CI environments, excessive false positives become much more expensive.

docs.title: Scanner Chaining
docs.text:
The tools can be used together.

Example:

ripgrep
   |
   v
Find custom dangerous function
   |
   v
OpenGrep / Semgrep
   |
   v
Find structural variants
   |
   v
CodeQL
   |
   v
Investigate deeper data flows

Another workflow:

CodeQL Finding
     |
     v
Understand Vulnerable Pattern
     |
     v
Create Lightweight OpenGrep Rule
     |
     v
Use During Future Assessments

docs.title: Tool Selection
docs.text:
A simple decision model:

Need to find text quickly?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
     ripgrep

Need syntax-aware pattern matching?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
Semgrep / OpenGrep

Need custom reusable security rules?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
Semgrep / OpenGrep

Need deeper semantic data flow?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
      CodeQL

Need business logic understanding?
        |
       Yes
        |
        v
   Manual Review

docs.title: Practical Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
For an unfamiliar repository:

1. Open repository in VS Code

2. Identify languages

3. Identify frameworks

4. Identify configuration

5. Map routes

6. Map authentication

7. Map authorisation

8. Search user-controlled sources

9. Search dangerous sinks with ripgrep

10. Run Semgrep and/or OpenGrep

11. Triage scanner findings

12. Trace candidates manually

13. Run CodeQL where deeper data-flow analysis is valuable

14. Perform variant analysis

15. Dynamically validate high-confidence candidates

16. Document confirmed findings

docs.title: Suggested Review Directory
docs.text:
Assessment artefacts can be organised as:

review/
│
├── notes/
│
│   ├── architecture.md
│   ├── routes.md
│   ├── authentication.md
│   ├── authorisation.md
│   └── candidates.md
│
├── ripgrep/
│   ├── routes.txt
│   ├── sql-sinks.txt
│   ├── command-sinks.txt
│   ├── ssrf-sinks.txt
│   └── secrets.txt
│
├── semgrep/
│   └── results/
│
├── opengrep/
│   └── results/
│
├── codeql/
│   └── results/
│
└── findings/

Avoid storing sensitive assessment data insecurely.

docs.title: Candidate Record
docs.text:
Example:

ID:
CAND-001

Type:
Potential SSRF

Source:
GET /api/fetch?url=

Source File:
FetchController.java

Source Variable:
url

Sink:
HttpClient.send()

Flow:
FetchController
    ->
FetchService
    ->
HttpClient.send()

Security Controls:
URLValidator.isAllowed()

Status:
Investigate URLValidator implementation.

docs.title: Scanner Finding Record
docs.text:
Example:

Tool:
OpenGrep

Rule:
custom.java.ssrf-http-client

File:
src/main/java/example/FetchService.java

Line:
84

Candidate:
User-controlled URL may reach outbound HTTP client.

Manual Review:
Required.

Status:
Investigating.

docs.title: Confirmed Finding Record
docs.text:
ID:
FIND-001

Type:
Server-Side Request Forgery

Route:
GET /api/fetch

Source:
url query parameter

Sink:
HttpClient.send()

Data Flow:

HTTP Parameter
      |
      v
FetchController
      |
      v
FetchService
      |
      v
URI.create()
      |
      v
HttpClient.send()

Security Control:
Scheme restricted to HTTP/HTTPS.

Weakness:
No destination host or resolved-address restriction.

Dynamic Validation:
Confirmed in authorised test environment.

Impact:
Application server can be induced to make requests to unintended destinations.

docs.title: Treating Scanner Output as Findings
docs.text:
Wrong:

Semgrep reported SQL injection.

Therefore SQL injection exists.

Better:

Semgrep identified a potential SQL injection data flow.

Manual review is required to determine whether attacker-controlled input reaches the query without effective parameterisation.

docs.title: Running Only One Tool
docs.text:
No single tool provides complete coverage.

ripgrep

may find patterns that a rule set does not contain.

Semgrep / OpenGrep

may identify structural patterns missed by regex.

CodeQL

may identify deeper flows.

Manual review

may identify business logic that none of them understand.

docs.title: Running Every Rule Available
docs.text:
More rules do not automatically mean better testing.

Large generic rule sets can produce:

Noise
Irrelevant findings
Duplicate findings
Low-value warnings

Use broad scanning initially if useful, then move toward targeted rules based on:

Technology
Framework
Attack surface
Assessment objectives
Observed patterns

docs.title: Ignoring Safe Variants
docs.text:
When creating custom rules, study both:

Vulnerable code

and:

Safe code

Otherwise the rule may match every usage of a security-sensitive API.

docs.title: Ignoring Framework Behaviour
docs.text:
Example:

Output operation detected

may be safe because the framework performs context-aware encoding.

Conversely:

Framework has autoescaping

does not mean every output path is safe.

Look for bypass mechanisms and alternate output APIs.

docs.title: Ignoring Custom Security Functions
docs.text:
Applications often contain helpers such as:

validateUrl()
sanitizeInput()
checkPermission()
safeQuery()
verifyToken()

These functions are extremely important.

Open them.

Do not infer their behaviour from their names.

docs.title: Ignoring Second-Order Flows
docs.text:
Example:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
Database
    |
    v
Scheduled Job
    |
    v
ProcessBuilder

A request-to-sink scanner may not always identify the complete lifecycle.

Manual review remains important.

docs.title: Ignoring Business Logic
docs.text:
Static analysis is weakest when the vulnerability depends on understanding:

Money
Roles
Workflow
Ownership
State
Timing
Relationships
Organisation rules

These require human reasoning.

docs.title: Final Static Analysis Model
docs.text:
SOURCE REPOSITORY
                                |
                                v
                         IDENTIFY STACK
                                |
                                v
                         MAP ARCHITECTURE
                                |
                                v
                       MAP ATTACK SURFACE
                                |
              +-----------------+-----------------+
              |                 |                 |
              v                 v                 v
          ripgrep           Semgrep           OpenGrep
              |                 |                 |
              +-----------------+-----------------+
                                |
                                v
                         CANDIDATE CODE
                                |
                                v
                        MANUAL VS CODE
                             REVIEW
                                |
                     +----------+----------+
                     |                     |
                     v                     v
               SOURCE -> SINK        SINK -> SOURCE
                     |                     |
                     +----------+----------+
                                |
                                v
                       SECURITY CONTROLS
                                |
                                v
                          EXPLOITABILITY
                                |
                       +--------+--------+
                       |                 |
                       v                 v
                   Protected         Candidate
                                         |
                                         v
                                DYNAMIC VALIDATION
                                         |
                                         v
                                CONFIRMED FINDING
                                         |
                                         v
                                 ROOT PATTERN
                                         |
                                         v
                                  VARIANT ANALYSIS
                                         |
                       +-----------------+----------------+
                       |                 |                |
                       v                 v                v
                    ripgrep        Semgrep/OpenGrep    CodeQL
                       |                 |                |
                       +-----------------+----------------+
                                         |
                                         v
                                  OTHER VARIANTS

The objective is therefore not:

Run scanners.

It is:

Understand the application.

Use tools to locate security-relevant code.

Trace attacker-controlled data.

Understand security controls.

Determine whether a dangerous operation is reachable.

Validate exploitability.

Find variants.

Report the root cause.
