docs.title: CodeQL for Security Source Code Review
docs.text:
CodeQL is a semantic static analysis engine that allows source code to be queried as data.

Instead of searching only for text or syntax patterns, CodeQL creates a database representing the source code and allows security researchers to query:

Functions
Methods
Classes
Calls
Expressions
Types
Inheritance
Control flow
Data flow
Taint flow
Sources
Sinks
Security controls
Relationships between program elements

For security source code review, CodeQL is particularly useful when:

Simple grep searches are no longer sufficient
Source-to-sink flows cross functions
Framework abstractions hide important behaviour
You need semantic rather than textual matching
You need global data-flow analysis
You want path explanations
You want repository-wide variant analysis
You want reusable custom security queries

A practical workflow is:

Repository
    |
    v
ripgrep
    |
    v
Fast Reconnaissance
    |
    v
OpenGrep / Semgrep
    |
    v
Pattern and Taint Analysis
    |
    v
CodeQL
    |
    +--> Semantic Analysis
    +--> Data Flow
    +--> Taint Tracking
    +--> Path Queries
    +--> Variant Analysis
    |
    v
Visual Studio Code
    |
    v
Manual Source-to-Sink Review
    |
    v
Dynamic Validation
    |
    v
Confirmed Finding

Authorised Security Testing

Use CodeQL only against source code and repositories that you are authorised to assess. A CodeQL result is a security-review candidate. It does not automatically prove that a vulnerability is reachable or exploitable.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
The most important rule is:

CodeQL result
      !=
Confirmed vulnerability

CodeQL can identify:

Interesting code structures
Potentially dangerous APIs
Security-sensitive calls
Possible data flows
Possible taint flows
Missing expected patterns
Source-to-sink paths
Variants of known vulnerable patterns

The security reviewer still needs to determine:

Is the code reachable?

Can an attacker influence the source?

Can the source reach the sink?

What transformations occur?

Is validation present?

Is sanitisation appropriate?

Does authentication apply?

Does authorisation apply?

Does the framework provide protection?

Does infrastructure provide protection?

Is the path feasible at runtime?

What security impact exists?

Use:

CodeQL Result
      |
      v
Candidate
      |
      v
Manual Data-Flow Review
      |
      v
Security-Control Review
      |
      v
Runtime Validation
      |
      v
Confirmed / Rejected

docs.title: Why CodeQL Is Different
docs.text:
Consider:

String host =
    request.getParameter("host");

String command =
    buildCommand(host);

executeDiagnostic(command);

The dangerous operation may exist somewhere else:

void executeDiagnostic(
    String command
) throws IOException {

    Runtime
        .getRuntime()
        .exec(command);
}

A text search can find:

Runtime.getRuntime().exec

but does not inherently understand:

request.getParameter()
        |
        v
host
        |
        v
buildCommand()
        |
        v
command
        |
        v
executeDiagnostic()
        |
        v
Runtime.exec()

CodeQL is designed to reason about relationships in the program.

docs.title: CodeQL Mental Model
docs.text:
CodeQL transforms source code into a queryable database.

SOURCE CODE
     |
     v
CodeQL Extractor
     |
     v
CodeQL Database
     |
     +--> AST
     +--> Types
     +--> Calls
     +--> Control Flow
     +--> Data Flow
     +--> Program Relationships
     |
     v
QL Queries
     |
     v
Results

You query the database using the QL query language.

docs.title: CodeQL vs ripgrep vs OpenGrep vs Semgrep
docs.text:
These tools should complement each other.

Tool Best Use ripgrep Extremely fast text and regex reconnaissance OpenGrep Structural matching, custom rules and taint analysis Semgrep Structural matching, custom rules and taint analysis CodeQL Semantic queries, global data flow and deeper variant analysis VS Code Manual reasoning and navigation Burp Suite Runtime validation

A practical model:

Repository
    |
    +--------------------+
    |                    |
    v                    v
ripgrep             OpenGrep/Semgrep
    |                    |
    +---------+----------+
              |
              v
       Candidate Areas
              |
              v
            CodeQL
              |
              v
      Semantic Analysis
              |
              v
         VS Code
              |
              v
       Manual Review
              |
              v
       Burp Validation

Do not think:

CodeQL replaces ripgrep

or:

CodeQL replaces manual review

Instead:

ripgrep
    =
fast discovery

OpenGrep / Semgrep
    =
syntax-aware rules

CodeQL
    =
semantic and data-flow reasoning

VS Code
    =
human understanding

Burp
    =
runtime validation

docs.title: Supported Languages
docs.text:
Current CodeQL language identifiers include:

Language CodeQL Identifier C / C++ c-cpp C# csharp Go go Java / Kotlin java-kotlin JavaScript / TypeScript javascript-typescript Python python Ruby ruby Rust rust Swift swift

Alternative identifiers may also be accepted for some languages.

Examples:

c
cpp
java
kotlin
javascript
typescript

docs.title: Important PHP Limitation
docs.text:
PHP is not currently one of the CodeQL languages listed by GitHub for database creation.

Therefore, for PHP source code review use tools such as:

ripgrep
OpenGrep
Semgrep
PHP-specific static analysis
Manual review

Do not write:

codeql database create php-db \
  --language=php

and expect official PHP CodeQL support.

For this notes repository:

.NET
    -> CodeQL supported

Java
    -> CodeQL supported

Python
    -> CodeQL supported

Django
    -> Python CodeQL

Flask
    -> Python CodeQL

Node.js
    -> JavaScript/TypeScript CodeQL

Client JavaScript
    -> JavaScript/TypeScript CodeQL

PHP
    -> use ripgrep/OpenGrep/Semgrep instead

docs.title: CodeQL Components
docs.text:
A practical CodeQL environment consists of:

CodeQL CLI
    |
    +--> Database creation
    +--> Database analysis
    +--> Query execution
    +--> Pack management
    +--> SARIF output

CodeQL Queries
    |
    +--> Built-in queries
    +--> Custom queries
    +--> Query suites

CodeQL for VS Code
    |
    +--> Query development
    +--> Database selection
    +--> Query execution
    +--> Result inspection
    +--> Path visualization
    +--> Model editing
    +--> Variant analysis

docs.title: CodeQL CLI
docs.text:
The CodeQL CLI is used to:

Create databases
Analyze databases
Run queries
Compile queries
Manage query packs
Generate SARIF
Inspect available languages

Verify installation:

codeql version

Display help:

codeql --help

docs.title: Check Available Languages
docs.text:
Use:

codeql resolve languages

This shows the language extractors available to your CodeQL installation.

This is useful because the exact available extractors depend on the installed CodeQL bundle.

docs.title: Check Available Packs
docs.text:
Use:

codeql resolve packs

This helps verify that CodeQL can locate:

Language libraries
Query packs
Standard queries
Custom packs

docs.title: CodeQL Database
docs.text:
CodeQL does not normally run directly against arbitrary source files.

First create a database.

Repository
    |
    v
Extractor
    |
    v
CodeQL Database
    |
    v
Queries

A database contains a representation of one programming language.

docs.title: Create a Python Database
docs.text:
From the repository root:

codeql database create codeql-db-python \
  --language=python

docs.title: Create a JavaScript / TypeScript Database
docs.text:
codeql database create codeql-db-js \
  --language=javascript-typescript

This covers both JavaScript and TypeScript.

docs.title: Create a C# Database
docs.text:
A basic example:

codeql database create codeql-db-csharp \
  --language=csharp

For compiled languages, database creation may involve:

No-build extraction
Autobuild
Manual build

depending on the language and chosen build mode.

docs.title: Create a Java Database
docs.text:
codeql database create codeql-db-java \
  --language=java-kotlin

For Java-only projects, no-build analysis may be available.

For Kotlin, build requirements differ.

docs.title: Build Modes
docs.text:
CodeQL supports different database build approaches depending on language.

Conceptually:

none
    |
    +--> analyze without normal application build

autobuild
    |
    +--> CodeQL attempts to determine build process

manual
    |
    +--> you provide the build command

docs.title: No-Build Mode
docs.text:
For supported languages:

codeql database create codeql-db \
  --language=csharp \
  --build-mode=none

No-build mode can simplify analysis where CodeQL supports it.

However, database quality can depend on:

Dependencies
Generated source
Framework information
Build configuration
Language
Project structure

Do not automatically assume:

No-build database
      =
identical semantic information to successful real build

docs.title: Autobuild
docs.text:
Example:

codeql database create codeql-db \
  --language=csharp \
  --build-mode=autobuild

CodeQL attempts to determine the appropriate build process.

This works well for many conventional projects.

docs.title: Manual Build
docs.text:
For a custom build:

codeql database create codeql-db \
  --language=csharp \
  --command="dotnet build"

For Java Maven:

codeql database create codeql-db \
  --language=java-kotlin \
  --command="mvn clean package -DskipTests"

For Gradle:

codeql database create codeql-db \
  --language=java-kotlin \
  --command="./gradlew build -x test"

Use the application's real build process where practical.

docs.title: Interpreted Languages
docs.text:
Python and JavaScript/TypeScript do not normally require you to supply an application build command to CodeQL database creation.

For Python:

codeql database create codeql-db \
  --language=python

For JavaScript/TypeScript:

codeql database create codeql-db \
  --language=javascript-typescript

Do not add a build command merely because the project itself has one unless CodeQL's extraction workflow specifically requires it.

docs.title: Multi-Language Repositories
docs.text:
A repository may contain:

C#
JavaScript
Python

CodeQL databases are language-specific.

You can create a database cluster:

codeql database create codeql-dbs \
  --db-cluster \
  --language=csharp,javascript-typescript,python

Conceptually:

Repository
    |
    +--> C# Database
    |
    +--> JavaScript Database
    |
    +--> Python Database

docs.title: Source Root
docs.text:
If running outside the repository root:

codeql database create codeql-db \
  --language=python \
  --source-root=/path/to/project

docs.title: Verify Database
docs.text:
Once created:

codeql database info codeql-db

Use this to inspect database information.

docs.title: Database Creation Problems
docs.text:
Common causes include:

Dependencies unavailable
Build failure
Wrong language
Wrong source root
Unsupported language
Generated code missing
Private dependency feeds unavailable
Wrong JDK
Wrong .NET SDK
Wrong Node.js version
Custom build tooling
Monorepo layout

A badly extracted database can produce misleadingly low coverage.

docs.title: Query Suites
docs.text:
CodeQL ships with built-in query suites.

The two main current suites are:

default
security-extended

docs.title: Default Suite
docs.text:
The default suite prioritises high-precision results.

Conceptually:

default
    |
    +--> higher precision
    +--> fewer findings
    +--> lower expected false-positive rate

This is a good initial scan.

docs.title: Security-Extended Suite
docs.text:
The security-extended suite includes:

default queries
        +
additional security queries

Conceptually:

security-extended
        |
        +--> broader security coverage
        +--> more findings
        +--> potentially more false positives

For manual penetration-testing source review, this broader coverage can be useful because the reviewer will manually triage candidates.

docs.title: Important Suite Note
docs.text:
Older examples may mention other suite names.

Always verify current suite availability.

For current GitHub CodeQL code scanning, the primary built-in suites documented by GitHub are:

default
security-extended

docs.title: Analyze a Database
docs.text:
General form:

codeql database analyze \
  <database> \
  <queries-or-suite> \
  --format=sarif-latest \
  --output=results.sarif

docs.title: Example - JavaScript
docs.text:
codeql database analyze \
  codeql-db-js \
  codeql/javascript-queries \
  --format=sarif-latest \
  --output=javascript-results.sarif

docs.title: Example - Python
docs.text:
codeql database analyze \
  codeql-db-python \
  codeql/python-queries \
  --format=sarif-latest \
  --output=python-results.sarif

docs.title: Example - Java
docs.text:
codeql database analyze \
  codeql-db-java \
  codeql/java-queries \
  --format=sarif-latest \
  --output=java-results.sarif

docs.title: Example - C
docs.text:
codeql database analyze \
  codeql-db-csharp \
  codeql/csharp-queries \
  --format=sarif-latest \
  --output=csharp-results.sarif

docs.title: SARIF
docs.text:
SARIF is a standard format for static-analysis results.

CodeQL
   |
   v
SARIF
   |
   +--> CI
   +--> GitHub Code Scanning
   +--> Analysis tooling
   +--> Result processing

Example:

--format=sarif-latest

and:

--output=results.sarif

docs.title: Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
Visual Studio Code is particularly useful for CodeQL development.

Install the official:

CodeQL

extension.

The extension supports:

Writing QL queries
Running queries
Selecting databases
Viewing query results
Viewing path explanations
Managing query packs
Testing queries
Working with model packs
Variant analysis

docs.title: VS Code Workflow
docs.text:
1. Open repository

2. Add CodeQL database

3. Open custom query

4. Run query

5. Inspect result

6. Open source location

7. View data-flow path

8. Use Go to Definition

9. Use Find All References

10. Use Call Hierarchy

11. Trace security controls

12. Validate candidate dynamically

docs.title: CodeQL Query Language
docs.text:
CodeQL queries use QL.

A simple query generally has:

import
from
where
select

Conceptually:

import <language>

from <variables>
where <conditions>
select <results>

docs.title: Simple JavaScript Query
docs.text:
Example:

import javascript

from CallExpr call
where
  call.getCalleeName() = "eval"
select call, "Review dynamic JavaScript execution."

This demonstrates the general idea:

Find call expressions
        |
        v
Filter to eval()
        |
        v
Return matching locations

A real security query may need additional semantic checks.

docs.title: Simple Python Query
docs.text:
import python

from Call call
where
  call.getFunc().toString() = "eval"
select call, "Review dynamic Python evaluation."

Treat simple examples as learning queries.

Production security queries normally require stronger modelling.

docs.title: QL Classes
docs.text:
CodeQL exposes classes representing program elements.

Examples conceptually include:

Function
Method
Class
Call
Expression
Parameter
Variable
Type
Statement
File

The exact classes depend on the language library.

docs.title: Predicates
docs.text:
Predicates express relationships.

Conceptually:

predicate isInteresting(Call call) {
    ...
}

Then:

from Call call
where isInteresting(call)
select call

Predicates allow complex analysis to be decomposed into reusable logic.

docs.title: AST Analysis
docs.text:
CodeQL can query the abstract syntax representation.

This is useful for questions such as:

Where is this function called?

What argument is passed?

What type is this expression?

What method does this invocation resolve to?

What class contains this method?

What annotation is attached?

docs.title: Control Flow
docs.text:
Control-flow analysis reasons about execution paths.

Example:

Input
  |
  v
if authenticated
  |
  +--> true --> sensitive operation
  |
  +--> false --> reject

Security review may use control flow to understand whether:

Validation executes before sink
Authorisation executes before action
Error path bypasses checks
Dangerous code is reachable

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
Data-flow analysis determines how values propagate.

Example:

String value =
    request.getParameter("name");

String copy =
    value;

process(copy);

Data flow:

request parameter
      |
      v
value
      |
      v
copy
      |
      v
process()

docs.title: Data-Flow Graph
docs.text:
CodeQL data flow is based on a data-flow graph.

Conceptually:

AST
    =
program syntax

Data-Flow Graph
    =
how values move through the program

Not every AST element is a data-flow node.

docs.title: Local Data Flow
docs.text:
Local data flow operates within a single function or callable.

Example:

def example(request):
    value = request.args.get("cmd")
    copy = value
    os.system(copy)

Flow:

request.args
     |
     v
value
     |
     v
copy
     |
     v
os.system

Local data flow is generally:

Faster
More precise
Less computationally expensive

than global data flow.

docs.title: Global Data Flow
docs.text:
Global data flow can track relationships across functions and broader program structure.

Example:

def get_input(request):
    return request.args.get("cmd")

def execute(value):
    os.system(value)

def handler(request):
    value = get_input(request)
    execute(value)

Conceptually:

request.args
     |
     v
get_input()
     |
     v
handler()
     |
     v
execute()
     |
     v
os.system()

docs.title: Important Global Data-Flow Limitation
docs.text:
Global analysis is more powerful than local analysis.

However:

More powerful
     !=
Perfect

Global data flow is generally:

More computationally expensive
Less precise
Potentially capable of producing spurious flows
Dependent on library/framework models

Therefore:

CodeQL global flow
       !=
guaranteed runtime flow

Manual validation remains necessary.

docs.title: Data Flow vs Taint Tracking
docs.text:
CodeQL distinguishes normal data flow from taint tracking.

Normal data flow focuses on value-preserving flow.

Taint tracking also models transformations where the exact value changes but attacker influence remains.

Example:

let input =
    req.query.name;

let value =
    "hello-" + input;

sink(value);

The value changed.

But:

input
   |
   v
String Concatenation
   |
   v
value

is still attacker-influenced.

That is where taint tracking is useful.

docs.title: Security Source-to-Sink Model
docs.text:
Most security data-flow queries can be understood as:

SOURCE
   |
   v
PROPAGATION
   |
   v
TRANSFORMATION
   |
   v
SINK

Examples:

HTTP parameter
      |
      v
String operations
      |
      v
Runtime.exec()

or:

HTTP parameter
      |
      v
URL builder
      |
      v
HTTP client

or:

HTTP parameter
      |
      v
Path construction
      |
      v
File read

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Typical sources include:

HTTP query parameters
Route parameters
Request body
Headers
Cookies
Uploaded files
WebSocket messages
GraphQL arguments
gRPC request fields
Queue messages
Environment-dependent external input
Stored attacker-controlled database values

docs.title: Sinks
docs.text:
Typical sinks include:

SQL execution
OS command execution
HTTP requests
Filesystem operations
Template evaluation
HTML rendering
Dynamic code execution
LDAP queries
XML parsing
Deserialisation
Redirects
Sensitive logging

docs.title: Sanitizers
docs.text:
A sanitizer prevents a dangerous flow for a particular context.

Examples:

SQL parameterisation
Path containment
URL allowlisting
HTML encoding
Shell-safe argument construction
Strict type validation

But:

sanitizer
    !=
universal security

For example:

HTML encoding
    !=
SQL injection protection

and:

SQL parameterisation
    !=
command injection protection

docs.title: Path Queries
docs.text:
Path queries are especially useful for security research.

Instead of returning only:

Potential sink here

they can return:

Source
  |
  v
Step
  |
  v
Step
  |
  v
Step
  |
  v
Sink

This makes source-to-sink analysis significantly easier.

docs.title: Path Query Metadata
docs.text:
A path query uses:

@kind path-problem

Conceptually:

/**
 * @kind path-problem
 */

The query then defines:

Source
Sink
Flow configuration
Path graph

docs.title: Modern Data-Flow API
docs.text:
Current CodeQL uses the modular data-flow API.

A conceptual path-query structure is:

/**
 * @kind path-problem
 */

import <language>

module MyConfig implements DataFlow::ConfigSig {
  predicate isSource(DataFlow::Node source) {
    ...
  }

  predicate isSink(DataFlow::Node sink) {
    ...
  }
}

module MyFlow =
  TaintTracking::Global<MyConfig>;

import MyFlow::PathGraph

from
  MyFlow::PathNode source,
  MyFlow::PathNode sink

where
  MyFlow::flowPath(source, sink)

select
  sink.getNode(),
  source,
  sink,
  "Potential attacker-controlled flow."

The exact imports and classes differ between language libraries.

Always use the current language-specific documentation when building real queries.

docs.title: DataFlow::Global
docs.text:
For value-preserving global data flow:

DataFlow::Global<...>

is used.

Conceptually:

module MyFlow =
    DataFlow::Global<MyConfig>;

docs.title: TaintTracking::Global
docs.text:
For taint propagation:

TaintTracking::Global<...>

can be used.

Conceptually:

module MyFlow =
    TaintTracking::Global<MyConfig>;

This includes additional propagation steps appropriate for taint analysis.

docs.title: isSource
docs.text:
A data-flow configuration defines where interesting flow begins.

Conceptually:

predicate isSource(
    DataFlow::Node source
) {
    ...
}

Examples:

HTTP request parameter
Request body
Header
Cookie
GraphQL argument

docs.title: isSink
docs.text:
The configuration also defines security-sensitive destinations.

Conceptually:

predicate isSink(
    DataFlow::Node sink
) {
    ...
}

Examples:

Runtime.exec()
Process.Start()
os.system()
child_process.exec()
requests.get()
File.ReadAllText()

docs.title: Additional Flow Steps
docs.text:
Applications often use wrappers.

Example:

Input
  |
  v
Custom Sanitizer
  |
  v
DTO
  |
  v
Helper
  |
  v
Sink

If CodeQL does not understand a project-specific propagation step, a custom model or additional flow step may be required.

Conceptually:

predicate isAdditionalFlowStep(
    DataFlow::Node pred,
    DataFlow::Node succ
) {
    ...
}

Use additional flow steps carefully.

Overly broad modelling can create many false positives.

docs.title: Framework Models
docs.text:
CodeQL libraries include modelling for many common frameworks and libraries.

This is important because source code for framework internals may not exist in the repository.

Examples include modelling of:

HTTP frameworks
Standard libraries
String transformations
Filesystem APIs
HTTP clients
Promises
Collections
Framework request objects

However:

Framework model exists
      !=
Every application abstraction is modeled

Custom frameworks and wrappers may need additional modelling.

docs.title: Model Packs
docs.text:
CodeQL model packs can extend analysis without directly modifying standard query libraries.

They can help model:

Custom sources
Custom sinks
Custom sanitizers
Custom summaries
Application frameworks
Third-party libraries

This is useful for large applications with internal security abstractions.

docs.title: Model Editor
docs.text:
The CodeQL VS Code extension provides tooling for model packs.

A useful workflow:

Unknown Application API
        |
        v
Understand Behaviour
        |
        v
Model API
        |
        v
Re-run Data Flow
        |
        v
Find Additional Paths

docs.title: Command Injection Analysis
docs.text:
Consider:

@GetMapping("/ping")
public String ping(
    @RequestParam String host
) throws Exception {

    Runtime
        .getRuntime()
        .exec(
            "ping " + host
        );

    return "done";
}

Desired analysis:

@RequestParam
      |
      v
host
      |
      v
String concatenation
      |
      v
Runtime.exec()

A CodeQL query can model:

HTTP input
      =
source

Runtime.exec argument
      =
sink

Then use taint tracking to search for flows.

docs.title: Command Injection Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose one vulnerability is found:

Request
   |
   v
executeDiagnostic()
   |
   v
Runtime.exec()

Instead of searching only for Runtime.exec, identify the application's wrapper:

executeDiagnostic()

Then query:

Where is executeDiagnostic called?

What reaches its argument?

Which calls originate from HTTP input?

This can reveal variants missed by generic rules.

docs.title: SQL Injection Analysis
docs.text:
A useful SQL injection model is:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
Query Construction
    |
    v
Raw SQL Execution

The key distinction is between:

SQL code

and:

SQL parameters

A sink alone is not enough.

Example:

PreparedStatement statement =
    connection.prepareStatement(
        "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"
    );

statement.setString(
    1,
    userId
);

This is fundamentally different from:

Statement statement =
    connection.createStatement();

statement.executeQuery(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '" +
    userId +
    "'"
);

CodeQL data-flow analysis can help distinguish where attacker-influenced values reach SQL query construction.

docs.title: NoSQL Injection
docs.text:
For Node.js applications, model:

req.query
req.params
req.body
      |
      v
Mongo Query Object
      |
      v
find()
findOne()
aggregate()

The dangerous behaviour may involve:

Operator injection
Object injection
$where
Regex abuse
Query structure manipulation

CodeQL queries can be useful where the database library is semantically modeled.

docs.title: LDAP Injection
docs.text:
Model:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
LDAP Filter Construction
    |
    v
LDAP Search

Potential sinks include framework-specific LDAP query APIs.

Custom enterprise LDAP wrappers may require project-specific modelling.

docs.title: SSRF Analysis
docs.text:
SSRF is a strong CodeQL use case.

Model:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
URL Construction
    |
    v
HTTP Client

Potential sinks include:

Java HttpClient
RestTemplate
WebClient
.NET HttpClient
Python requests
Python httpx
Node fetch
axios

Then manually review:

Scheme restrictions
Host allowlisting
Port restrictions
Redirect handling
DNS resolution
Private network blocking
Loopback blocking
Link-local blocking
Cloud metadata protection

docs.title: Path Traversal Analysis
docs.text:
Model:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
Path Construction
    |
    v
Filesystem Sink

Potential sinks include:

File reads
File writes
File deletion
Directory access
Archive extraction
File streaming

Review transformations such as:

Path.Combine
Paths.get
Path.resolve
resolve()
normalize()
realpath()
canonical paths

A normalisation function does not automatically guarantee containment.

docs.title: File Upload Analysis
docs.text:
Trace:

Uploaded File
     |
     +--> Filename
     +--> MIME Type
     +--> Extension
     +--> Content
     |
     v
Validation
     |
     v
Storage Path
     |
     v
Later Processing

CodeQL can help find flows from uploaded filenames or content into:

Filesystem paths
Archive extraction
Image processors
Document processors
Template engines
Command execution

docs.title: Deserialisation
docs.text:
Model:

Untrusted Data
     |
     v
Deserializer

Potential APIs depend on language.

Examples:

Java ObjectInputStream
Python pickle
.NET serializers
YAML loaders

A deserializer call is not automatically vulnerable.

Determine whether attacker-controlled serialized content can reach it.

docs.title: XXE
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker XML
     |
     v
XML Parser
     |
     v
External Entity Resolution?

The important questions are:

Which parser?
Which configuration?
DTD enabled?
External entities enabled?
External resources accessible?

Static analysis is particularly useful for finding parser configuration.

docs.title: SSTI
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker Input
     |
     v
Template Source
     |
     v
Template Evaluation

Do not confuse:

attacker-controlled template data

with:

attacker-controlled template source

The latter is normally the more dangerous condition.

docs.title: XSS
docs.text:
Server-side XSS:

HTTP Input
     |
     v
Application
     |
     v
HTML Output

Client-side DOM XSS:

location.search
     |
     v
JavaScript
     |
     v
innerHTML

CodeQL includes security queries for JavaScript and TypeScript and can model many client-side flows.

docs.title: DOM XSS
docs.text:
Potential sources:

location.href
location.search
location.hash
document.URL
document.referrer
window.name
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage

Potential sinks:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
eval
Function
script.src
iframe.srcdoc

The important question is:

Can attacker-controlled browser data reach the sink without effective context-specific protection?

docs.title: Open Redirect
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker URL
     |
     v
Navigation Sink

Potential sinks:

redirect()
location.href
location.assign()
location.replace()
window.open()

Review validation carefully.

Substring checks are often insufficient.

docs.title: Authentication Review
docs.text:
CodeQL can help locate:

Login endpoints
Authentication middleware
Authentication annotations
Password verification
Session creation
JWT verification
OAuth callbacks
SAML processing
MFA logic

But authentication correctness often requires architecture-level reasoning.

docs.title: Authorisation Review
docs.text:
Authorisation is especially important because it is often application-specific.

Model:

Request
   |
   v
Authentication
   |
   v
Object Identifier
   |
   v
Object Lookup
   |
   v
Authorisation
   |
   v
Sensitive Action

CodeQL can help answer:

Where is this object retrieved?

Which functions call this repository method?

Which callers perform permission checks?

Which sensitive operations lack the expected security wrapper?

docs.title: IDOR / BOLA
docs.text:
Model:

Attacker-Controlled ID
        |
        v
Object Retrieval
        |
        v
Ownership / Permission Check?
        |
        v
Sensitive Object

A powerful strategy is to identify the application's standard authorisation helper.

Example:

checkOwnership()

Then query sensitive object access paths and compare whether the helper is used consistently.

docs.title: Variant Analysis for Authorisation
docs.text:
Suppose:

UserController.delete()

correctly calls:

authorizationService.canDeleteUser()

but another endpoint:

AdminApi.deleteUser()

does not.

Variant analysis can search for:

All calls to userRepository.delete()

and inspect whether each path contains the expected authorisation control.

docs.title: Mass Assignment
docs.text:
Model:

Request Body
     |
     v
Object Binder
     |
     v
Sensitive Domain Object

Review fields such as:

role
isAdmin
permissions
ownerId
tenantId
status
balance
verified

CodeQL can help locate direct request-to-model flows where the framework is modeled.

docs.title: JWT
docs.text:
Review:

JWT decode
JWT verify
Algorithm handling
Key selection
Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Not-before
Claims
Authorisation

Important:

Valid JWT
    !=
Authorised operation

Authentication and authorisation must be reviewed separately.

docs.title: OAuth / OIDC
docs.text:
Trace:

Authorization Request
       |
       v
Callback
       |
       v
State Validation
       |
       v
Code Exchange
       |
       v
Token Validation
       |
       v
Identity Mapping
       |
       v
Session

Review:

state
nonce
PKCE
redirect URI
issuer
audience
token validation
identity mapping
account linking

docs.title: SAML
docs.text:
Trace:

SAMLResponse
      |
      v
XML Parsing
      |
      v
Signature Validation
      |
      v
Assertion Validation
      |
      v
Identity Mapping
      |
      v
Session

Review:

Signature
Audience
Recipient
Destination
InResponseTo
Replay
Identity mapping
Authorisation

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
Search for:

reset token creation
reset token validation
password update
email generation
absolute URL generation
session invalidation

CodeQL can be especially useful when tracing:

Host Header
     |
     v
Reset URL Generation
     |
     v
Email

docs.title: MFA
docs.text:
Review:

OTP verification
TOTP verification
Recovery codes
MFA state
Session state
Step-up authentication

Trace whether sensitive endpoints require the correct authentication state.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
CodeQL can help identify:

CORS configuration
Origin reflection
Wildcard configuration
Credentials configuration
Framework middleware

But runtime behaviour must be validated.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
Look for:

CSRF middleware
CSRF exemptions
State-changing routes
Cookie authentication
SameSite configuration

A missing source-code control does not prove missing infrastructure or framework protection.

docs.title: Host Header Attacks
docs.text:
Trace:

Host
X-Forwarded-Host
Forwarded
      |
      v
URL Generation
      |
      v
Security-Sensitive Output

Examples:

Password reset links
OAuth redirect URLs
Invitation links
Email links
Canonical URLs

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
For JavaScript/TypeScript review, inspect flows involving:

Object.assign
Deep merge functions
Recursive setters
Dynamic property writes
__proto__
constructor
prototype

CodeQL can be useful because dangerous behaviour often involves relationships rather than one exact text pattern.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
Model:

GraphQL Argument
      |
      v
Resolver
      |
      v
Authorisation
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
Database

Review:

Object-level authorisation
Field-level authorisation
Mutations
Batching
Subscriptions
Input validation
Resource limits

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
Model:

gRPC Request
     |
     v
RPC Handler
     |
     v
Interceptor
     |
     v
Authorisation
     |
     v
Service
     |
     v
Sensitive Sink

Review:

Authentication interceptors
Authorisation interceptors
Message fields
Object IDs
Service methods
Streaming RPCs

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
Model:

Handshake
   |
   v
Connection
   |
   v
Message
   |
   v
Message Handler
   |
   v
Authorisation
   |
   v
Sensitive Action

Handshake authentication does not automatically authorise every WebSocket message.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
Do not restrict analysis to HTTP routes.

Look for:

Schedulers
Workers
Queue consumers
Message listeners
Cron jobs
Background services
Event handlers

Potential flow:

HTTP Input
    |
    v
Database
    |
    v
Queue
    |
    v
Worker
    |
    v
Command Execution

docs.title: Second-Order Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Second-order flows may cross persistence boundaries.

Attacker Input
      |
      v
Database
      |
      v
Later Query
      |
      v
Background Worker
      |
      v
Dangerous Sink

Not every persistence boundary will be automatically represented as a complete CodeQL flow.

Manual architecture understanding remains essential.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
CodeQL can detect some security-sensitive patterns involving secrets.

But use dedicated tools too:

TruffleHog
Git history review
Secret scanners
Repository search

A hardcoded-looking string is not automatically a valid secret.

docs.title: Cryptography
docs.text:
Use CodeQL to identify:

Weak algorithms
Insecure random generation
Hardcoded cryptographic keys
TLS verification problems
Certificate validation problems
Weak password hashing
Unsafe cipher modes

Context matters.

For example:

MD5 for non-security cache deduplication

is not equivalent to:

MD5 for password storage

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Review flows from sensitive information to logging sinks.

Examples:

Passwords
Tokens
Session IDs
API keys
Personal data
Authentication headers
Reset tokens

Model:

Sensitive Source
      |
      v
Logger

docs.title: Information Disclosure
docs.text:
CodeQL can help identify:

Stack traces
Debug responses
Verbose exceptions
Secrets in responses
Sensitive logging
Debug endpoints
Development configuration

But actual exposure often requires runtime validation.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Static analysis can identify candidate patterns involving:

Check-then-act
Read-modify-write
Missing transaction
Missing locking
Shared mutable state

But exploitability generally depends on runtime concurrency and persistence behaviour.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Source review can locate:

Throttle middleware
Rate-limit decorators
Attempt counters
Quota checks

But:

No application rate limiter
      !=
No production rate limiting

Controls may exist at:

CDN
WAF
API gateway
Reverse proxy
Service mesh

docs.title: Query Metadata
docs.text:
Security queries should include metadata.

Example:

/**
 * @name Potential command injection
 * @description Finds potentially untrusted input reaching command execution.
 * @kind path-problem
 * @problem.severity error
 * @security-severity 8.8
 * @precision high
 * @id custom/java/command-injection
 * @tags security
 *       external/cwe/cwe-078
 */

Metadata controls how results are interpreted and presented.

docs.title: Alert Queries
docs.text:
An alert query identifies a suspicious location.

Conceptually:

Dangerous API Call
       |
       v
Alert

Example use:

Find all Runtime.exec calls

docs.title: Path Queries
docs.text:
A path query identifies:

Source
   |
   v
Flow
   |
   v
Sink

For security research, path queries are often much more informative.

docs.title: Query Development Strategy
docs.text:
Do not begin by writing an extremely complicated global taint query.

Use:

Step 1
Find the sink

Step 2
Understand its AST representation

Step 3
Find the source

Step 4
Understand its AST representation

Step 5
Test local data flow

Step 6
Add global flow

Step 7
Add taint tracking

Step 8
Add path visualization

Step 9
Add framework models

Step 10
Reduce false positives

docs.title: Start with Sink Discovery
docs.text:
Suppose you want command injection.

First query:

Where are command execution APIs?

Then manually inspect them.

Only after understanding the application should you build:

HTTP Input
      |
      v
Command Execution

This makes query development easier.

docs.title: Source-First Analysis
docs.text:
Sometimes start from the source.

HTTP Request
      |
      v
Where does this data go?

Useful for:

File upload
Password reset
GraphQL resolver
Webhook
WebSocket message
gRPC request

docs.title: Sink-First Analysis
docs.text:
Often more efficient:

Dangerous Sink
      |
      v
Who calls it?
      |
      v
What reaches it?
      |
      v
Can attacker input reach it?

Useful for:

Command execution
SQL
Filesystem
HTTP client
Deserialisation
Template evaluation
Dynamic execution

docs.title: Partial Flow
docs.text:
When a data-flow query unexpectedly produces no results, do not immediately conclude:

No vulnerability exists

The model may be incomplete.

Use partial-flow debugging techniques to determine:

How far did taint propagate?

Where did the model stop?

Is a library model missing?

Is a wrapper missing?

Is an additional flow step needed?

docs.title: Missing Models
docs.text:
Example:

Request
   |
   v
Custom Framework Wrapper
   |
   X
   |
   v
Sink

CodeQL may not know that:

Custom Framework Wrapper

propagates attacker-controlled data.

You may need to model it.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Reflection can complicate static analysis.

Examples:

Java reflection
.NET reflection
Dynamic JavaScript property access
Python getattr()
Dependency injection
Runtime plugin loading

Do not assume static analysis sees every dynamically resolved relationship.

docs.title: Dynamic Dispatch
docs.text:
Object-oriented applications may call:

Interface
   |
   v
Implementation A
Implementation B
Implementation C

Static analysis must determine possible call targets.

This can increase:

Complexity
Analysis time
False-positive possibilities

docs.title: Generated Code
docs.text:
Generated code may:

Increase noise
Contain important security behaviour
Represent framework bindings
Contain protocol code

Do not blindly exclude it.

Understand what it represents first.

docs.title: Framework Magic
docs.text:
Frameworks often use:

Annotations
Decorators
Dependency injection
Reflection
Convention
Generated proxies
Configuration

This can make source-to-sink reasoning more difficult.

CodeQL's framework models help, but manual review remains necessary.

docs.title: Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Variant analysis is one of the strongest CodeQL use cases.

Confirmed Vulnerability
        |
        v
Understand Root Cause
        |
        v
Create Query
        |
        v
Run Against Repository
        |
        v
Find Similar Patterns
        |
        v
Triage Variants

docs.title: Example Variant Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose you confirm:

String command =
    request.getParameter("cmd");

commandService.execute(command);

and:

void execute(
    String command
) {

    Runtime
        .getRuntime()
        .exec(command);
}

Instead of searching only:

Runtime.exec

build a query around:

commandService.execute()

Then ask:

Which HTTP sources can reach this helper?

This may reveal additional vulnerable routes.

docs.title: Variant Analysis Across Repositories
docs.text:
The CodeQL VS Code extension includes variant-analysis functionality for running suitable queries at scale against repositories available through the supported GitHub workflow.

This can be useful when:

The same vulnerable library is used across repositories
The same internal framework is reused
The same dangerous helper is copied
The same coding pattern appears across projects

Always ensure assessment authorisation covers every repository being analyzed.

docs.title: Project-Specific Queries
docs.text:
Generic query:

Find Runtime.exec()

Project-specific query:

Find attacker-controlled values reaching DiagnosticService.execute()

Generic query:

Find HttpClient.SendAsync()

Project-specific query:

Find user-controlled URLs reaching ExternalPreviewService.fetch()

Generic query:

Find SQL execution

Project-specific query:

Find HTTP values reaching ReportingRepository.runRawQuery()

Project-specific queries can dramatically improve signal.

docs.title: Query Packs
docs.text:
CodeQL queries can be organised into packs.

A useful structure:

codeql/
├── qlpack.yml
├── java/
│   ├── command-injection.ql
│   ├── ssrf.ql
│   └── authorization.ql
├── csharp/
├── javascript/
└── python/

However, CodeQL packs are language/library-aware, so in practice you may maintain separate packs where dependencies differ.

docs.title: Example Pack Purpose
docs.text:
security-review-java
security-review-csharp
security-review-javascript
security-review-python

Then:

Confirmed Finding
       |
       v
Custom Query
       |
       v
Security Review Pack
       |
       v
Future Assessments

docs.title: Query Tests
docs.text:
Custom security queries should be tested.

Test cases should contain:

Expected positive examples
Expected negative examples
Edge cases
Wrapper functions
Sanitised flows
Unsafe flows
Framework variants

The purpose is to prevent:

Query regression
False-positive growth
False-negative regressions

docs.title: Query Precision
docs.text:
A security query may have precision metadata such as:

very-high
high
medium
low

Do not confuse query precision with vulnerability severity.

A query can be:

High precision

while identifying:

Medium severity vulnerability

or vice versa.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Common causes include:

Spurious global flows
Trusted sources
Unreachable code
Effective validation
Effective sanitisation
Framework protections
Security checks not modeled
Test code
Generated code
Impossible call target
Infrastructure controls

docs.title: False Negatives
docs.text:
Common causes include:

Missing framework model
Custom wrapper
Reflection
Dynamic dispatch
Generated behaviour
Cross-service flow
Database persistence
Message queue
Background job
Unsupported library
Custom sanitizer
Dynamic language behaviour

Therefore:

No CodeQL result
      !=
No vulnerability

docs.title: Triage Workflow
docs.text:
For each result:

CodeQL Result
      |
      v
Open File in VS Code
      |
      v
Review Source
      |
      v
Review Path
      |
      v
Review Sink
      |
      v
Review Validation
      |
      v
Review Sanitisation
      |
      v
Review Authentication
      |
      v
Review Authorisation
      |
      v
Review Runtime Feasibility
      |
      v
Validate Dynamically

docs.title: Triage Template
docs.text:
ID:
CQL-001

Query:
custom/java/request-to-command

File:
src/main/java/controllers/ToolsController.java

Source:
@RequestParam("host")

Sink:
Runtime.exec()

Path:
ToolsController
    -> DiagnosticService
    -> CommandBuilder
    -> Runtime.exec

Reachable:
Yes / No / Unknown

Attacker Controlled:
Yes / No / Unknown

Validation:
None / Present / Unknown

Sanitisation:
None / Present / Unknown

Authentication:
...

Authorisation:
...

Framework Controls:
...

Runtime Validation:
...

Impact:
...

Status:
Investigating / Confirmed / Rejected

docs.title: Dynamic Validation
docs.text:
Static analysis should guide dynamic testing.

Example:

CodeQL

@RequestParam
      |
      v
DiagnosticService
      |
      v
Runtime.exec

Map it to:

POST /api/tools/ping

Then use Burp:

Proxy
   |
   v
Repeater
   |
   v
Controlled Input
   |
   v
Observe Behaviour

Do not dynamically test systems outside the authorised scope.

docs.title: Burp + CodeQL Workflow
docs.text:
CodeQL
   |
   v
Potential Source-to-Sink Path
   |
   v
Find Controller / Route
   |
   v
Burp HTTP History
   |
   v
Identify Request
   |
   v
Repeater
   |
   v
Controlled Validation
   |
   v
Confirmed / Rejected

This combination is especially effective for:

SQL Injection
Command Injection
SSRF
Path Traversal
XSS
Open Redirect
IDOR
Mass Assignment
Authentication flaws
Authorisation flaws

docs.title: Baseline Review
docs.text:
For an initial assessment:

Full Repository
      |
      v
CodeQL Database
      |
      v
Built-In Security Queries
      |
      v
Custom Queries
      |
      v
Manual Triage

This establishes a security baseline.

docs.title: Diff-Based Review
docs.text:
For later reviews:

Previous Version
      |
      v
New Commit / Pull Request
      |
      v
Changed Code
      |
      v
Security-Sensitive Changes
      |
      v
Targeted CodeQL Queries

Focus on changes involving:

Routes
Authentication
Authorisation
SQL
Command execution
HTTP clients
Filesystem
Uploads
Deserialisation
Templates
Security configuration
Dependencies

But remember that a small code change can alter a flow through unchanged code.

docs.title: Security Review Strategy
docs.text:
A strong workflow is:

PASS 1
Architecture

PASS 2
Routes

PASS 3
Authentication

PASS 4
Authorisation

PASS 5
Sources

PASS 6
Sinks

PASS 7
Built-in CodeQL security queries

PASS 8
Source-to-sink queries

PASS 9
Custom project models

PASS 10
Variant analysis

PASS 11
Dynamic validation

docs.title: Recommended Vulnerability Passes
docs.text:
Pass 01 - Authentication

Pass 02 - Authorisation

Pass 03 - IDOR / BOLA

Pass 04 - SQL Injection

Pass 05 - NoSQL Injection

Pass 06 - LDAP Injection

Pass 07 - Command Injection

Pass 08 - SSRF

Pass 09 - Path Traversal

Pass 10 - File Upload

Pass 11 - Deserialisation

Pass 12 - XML / XXE

Pass 13 - SSTI

Pass 14 - XSS

Pass 15 - DOM XSS

Pass 16 - Open Redirect

Pass 17 - Prototype Pollution

Pass 18 - Mass Assignment

Pass 19 - JWT

Pass 20 - OAuth / OIDC

Pass 21 - SAML

Pass 22 - Password Reset

Pass 23 - MFA

Pass 24 - GraphQL

Pass 25 - gRPC

Pass 26 - WebSockets

Pass 27 - Secrets

Pass 28 - Cryptography

Pass 29 - Logging

Pass 30 - Background Jobs

Pass 31 - Business Logic Variants

Pass 32 - Confirmed Vulnerability Variants

docs.title: Java / Spring Strategy
docs.text:
Start with:

Controllers
@RequestMapping
@GetMapping
@PostMapping
@PutMapping
@PatchMapping
@DeleteMapping

Then:

@RequestParam
@PathVariable
@RequestBody
@RequestHeader
@CookieValue

Then security:

SecurityFilterChain
@PreAuthorize
@PostAuthorize
@Secured
hasRole
hasAuthority
permitAll

Then sinks:

Runtime.exec
ProcessBuilder
SQL
HTTP clients
Filesystem
XML
Deserialisation
Templates
Redirects

Then CodeQL data flow.

docs.title: .NET Strategy
docs.text:
Start with:

Controllers
Minimal APIs
MapGet
MapPost
MapPut
MapDelete

Sources:

Request.Query
Request.Form
Request.Headers
Request.Cookies
Route values
Model binding

Security:

[Authorize]
[AllowAnonymous]
Policies
Roles
Claims

Sinks:

Process.Start
Raw SQL
HttpClient
Filesystem
XML
Deserialisation
Razor
Redirects

Then CodeQL data flow.

docs.title: Python Strategy
docs.text:
Sources:

Flask request
Django request
FastAPI parameters
Headers
Cookies
Uploads

Sinks:

os.system
subprocess
eval
exec
SQL
requests
httpx
open
pickle
YAML
XML
Templates
Redirects

Then:

Local data flow
      |
      v
Global data flow
      |
      v
Taint tracking

docs.title: Django Strategy
docs.text:
Review:

urls.py
Views
ViewSets
Serializers
Authentication classes
Permission classes
get_queryset
get_object
Raw SQL
CSRF exemptions
Uploads
Redirects
Templates
Settings
Celery tasks

Use CodeQL Python analysis for deeper source-to-sink relationships.

docs.title: Flask Strategy
docs.text:
Review:

@app.route
Blueprints
request.args
request.form
request.values
request.json
request.files
session

Then:

SQL
os.system
subprocess
requests
httpx
open
pickle
render_template_string
redirect

docs.title: Node.js Strategy
docs.text:
Sources:

req.query
req.params
req.body
req.headers
req.cookies
WebSocket messages
GraphQL arguments

Sinks:

child_process
SQL
MongoDB
fetch
axios
fs
eval
Function
templates
redirects

Then review:

Authentication middleware
Authorisation middleware
Middleware order
Prototype pollution
Mass assignment
JWT
GraphQL
WebSockets

docs.title: Client-Side JavaScript Strategy
docs.text:
Sources:

location
document.URL
document.referrer
window.name
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage
API responses

Sinks:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
eval
Function
location
window.open
script.src
iframe.srcdoc

CodeQL JavaScript analysis can be particularly useful for DOM source-to-sink analysis.

docs.title: PHP Strategy
docs.text:
CodeQL currently does not provide official PHP database support.

Use:

ripgrep
     |
     v
OpenGrep / Semgrep
     |
     v
Manual Source-to-Sink Review
     |
     v
Burp Validation

Do not omit PHP from source review simply because CodeQL does not support it.

docs.title: Query Performance
docs.text:
Global data-flow queries can be expensive.

Avoid:

Every expression
      ->
Every expression

Instead define specific:

Sources
Sinks
Frameworks
Types
APIs

Conceptually:

Broad Global Flow
       |
       v
Huge Search Space

versus:

HTTP Sources
      |
      v
Command Sinks
      |
      v
Focused Search

docs.title: Performance Strategy
docs.text:
1. Start with AST query

2. Narrow sink

3. Narrow source

4. Test local flow

5. Add global flow

6. Add taint

7. Add framework constraints

8. Add path output

9. Profile slow query if necessary

docs.title: Do Not Overmodel
docs.text:
Suppose you add:

Every function return
      ->
Every caller

as an additional taint step.

You may generate huge numbers of impossible flows.

Models should reflect actual program semantics.

docs.title: Security Controls Must Be Modeled Carefully
docs.text:
Do not automatically treat a function named:

sanitize()
validate()
clean()
secure()
check()

as a sanitizer.

Inspect what it actually does.

Example:

def sanitize(value):
    return value.replace("<", "")

This may not provide meaningful protection for:

SQL
Shell
URL
Filesystem
HTML attributes
JavaScript contexts

docs.title: CodeQL Does Not Understand Business Intent Automatically
docs.text:
Suppose:

Manager
    can
approve invoice

and:

Employee
    cannot
approve invoice

CodeQL can help identify:

approveInvoice()
callers
role checks
permission checks

But it does not inherently know the organisation's intended business policy.

Manual review remains essential.

docs.title: Variant Analysis Model
docs.text:
One Confirmed Finding
        |
        v
Identify Primitive
        |
        +--> Source
        +--> Sink
        +--> Wrapper
        +--> Missing Control
        |
        v
Write CodeQL Query
        |
        v
Run Against Database
        |
        v
Find Variants
        |
        v
Manual Triage

docs.title: Example Missing Authorisation Variant
docs.text:
Known safe pattern:

Controller
    |
    v
checkPermission()
    |
    v
deleteDocument()

Potential variant:

Controller
    |
    v
deleteDocument()

A custom query can search:

All callers of deleteDocument()

Then investigate whether each path has the expected security control.

Do not assume absence of one exact helper proves missing authorisation.

docs.title: Mistake 1
docs.text:
CodeQL found it
    =
vulnerability confirmed

Incorrect.

docs.title: Mistake 2
docs.text:
No CodeQL finding
    =
secure

Incorrect.

docs.title: Mistake 3
docs.text:
Only running built-in queries.

Built-in queries are valuable, but application-specific vulnerabilities may require custom queries.

docs.title: Mistake 4
docs.text:
Only searching sinks.

A sink is not automatically vulnerable.

docs.title: Mistake 5
docs.text:
Ignoring authorisation.

Many serious application vulnerabilities are caused by business and access-control logic rather than classic injection sinks.

docs.title: Mistake 6
docs.text:
Using global data flow for everything.

Start with narrower queries.

docs.title: Mistake 7
docs.text:
Ignoring framework models.

Incorrect modelling can produce both false positives and false negatives.

docs.title: Mistake 8
docs.text:
Treating every apparent sanitizer as effective.

Review the implementation.

docs.title: Mistake 9
docs.text:
Ignoring second-order flows.

Data may pass through:

Database
Queue
Cache
File
Background worker

before reaching a sink.

docs.title: Mistake 10
docs.text:
Forcing CodeQL onto unsupported languages.

For PHP, use other static-analysis tools.

docs.title: Complete CodeQL Workflow
docs.text:
1. Obtain authorised repository

2. Record commit

3. Open repository in VS Code

4. Identify languages

5. Identify frameworks

6. Map application architecture

7. Map trust boundaries

8. Map routes

9. Map authentication

10. Map authorisation

11. Identify sources

12. Identify sinks

13. Install / verify CodeQL CLI

14. Verify language extractor

15. Create CodeQL database

16. Verify database

17. Run built-in queries

18. Review default-suite findings

19. Run broader security queries where appropriate

20. Triage findings

21. Identify interesting sinks

22. Identify interesting sources

23. Write custom AST queries

24. Test local data flow

25. Add global data flow

26. Add taint tracking

27. Convert useful queries to path queries

28. Review path explanations

29. Add project-specific models

30. Perform variant analysis

31. Validate candidates dynamically

32. Confirm vulnerabilities

33. Search for related variants

34. Save queries and evidence

35. Document remediation

36. Retest

docs.title: Final CodeQL Testing Model
docs.text:
SOURCE
  |
  v
Can an attacker control it?
  |
  v
DATA FLOW
  |
  +--> local flow
  +--> function calls
  +--> method calls
  +--> object properties
  +--> framework models
  +--> additional flow steps
  |
  v
TAINT PROPAGATION
  |
  +--> concatenation
  +--> transformations
  +--> collections
  +--> wrappers
  |
  v
SECURITY CONTROLS
  |
  +--> validation
  +--> sanitisation
  +--> authentication
  +--> authorisation
  |
  v
SINK
  |
  v
Is the sink security-sensitive?
  |
  v
PATH QUERY
  |
  v
Manual Path Review
  |
  v
Runtime Validation
  |
  v
Impact

A meaningful vulnerability requires:

Reachable source
       +
Attacker control
       +
Feasible propagation
       +
Security-sensitive sink
       +
Absent / ineffective controls
       +
Security impact

Not merely:

CodeQL produced a result

docs.title: OpenGrep for Security Source Code Review
docs.text:
OpenGrep is an open-source static analysis engine designed for syntax-aware code searching, security analysis, custom rules and taint tracking.

It is a fork of Semgrep and maintains compatibility with Semgrep-style rules while continuing to develop additional open-source static analysis capabilities.

For security source code review, OpenGrep is particularly useful for:

Finding dangerous APIs
Finding security-sensitive coding patterns
Searching for vulnerability variants
Building custom security rules
Source-to-sink taint analysis
Cross-function taint analysis within files
Reviewing framework-specific security patterns
Automating repeatable source code review
Producing JSON and SARIF results
Reusing many Semgrep-compatible rules

A practical source review workflow is:

Repository
    |
    v
Visual Studio Code
    |
    +--> Understand application
    |
    +--> Map routes
    |
    +--> Map authentication
    |
    +--> Map authorisation
    |
    v
ripgrep
    |
    v
Fast Reconnaissance
    |
    v
OpenGrep
    |
    +--> Structural Search
    +--> Security Rules
    +--> Taint Analysis
    +--> Variant Analysis
    |
    v
Candidate Vulnerabilities
    |
    v
Manual Source-to-Sink Review
    |
    v
Dynamic Validation
    |
    v
Confirmed Finding

Authorised Security Testing

Use OpenGrep only against source code and applications that you are authorised to assess. An OpenGrep result is a security-review candidate, not automatic proof that a vulnerability is exploitable.

docs.title: Core Principle
docs.text:
The most important rule is:

OpenGrep finding
      !=
Confirmed vulnerability

OpenGrep can tell you that code:

Matches a security pattern
Calls a dangerous API
Contains a potential source
Contains a potential sink
Contains a possible taint flow
Uses suspicious configuration

It cannot automatically establish the complete security context.

The reviewer must determine:

Is the code reachable?

Can an attacker influence the source?

Does the source actually reach the sink?

What transformations occur?

Is validation performed?

Is sanitisation appropriate for the sink?

Does the framework provide protection?

Does authorisation exist elsewhere?

Does infrastructure enforce the control?

Can the behaviour be triggered?

What impact is possible?

Use:

OpenGrep Result
      |
      v
Candidate
      |
      v
Manual Data-Flow Analysis
      |
      v
Security-Control Review
      |
      v
Exploitability Analysis
      |
      v
Dynamic Validation
      |
      v
Confirmed / Rejected

docs.title: OpenGrep, Semgrep, ripgrep and CodeQL
docs.text:
These tools overlap, but they are not identical.

A useful mental model is:

Tool Main Role ripgrep Extremely fast text and regex search OpenGrep Open-source syntax-aware rules and taint analysis Semgrep Syntax-aware static analysis and security rules CodeQL Semantic queries and deeper program/data-flow analysis VS Code Manual code navigation and reasoning Burp Suite Dynamic web application validation

Do not choose only one.

Use them together.

ripgrep
   |
   v
Find Interesting Code
   |
   v
OpenGrep
   |
   v
Structural / Taint Analysis
   |
   v
VS Code
   |
   v
Manual Review
   |
   +--> Simple enough?
   |       |
   |       v
   |     Validate
   |
   +--> Complex flow?
           |
           v
         CodeQL
           |
           v
       Validate

docs.title: Why OpenGrep?
docs.text:
OpenGrep is useful when you want an open-source static analysis engine that supports Semgrep-style rules.

Important capabilities include:

Semgrep-compatible rules
Custom pattern rules
Taint-mode rules
Intrafile cross-function taint analysis
Higher-order-function taint tracking
JSON output
SARIF output
Multiple languages
Self-contained binaries
Open-source development

OpenGrep was forked from Semgrep 1.100.0.

Since the fork, the projects have developed independently.

Therefore:

Semgrep rule compatibility
        !=
Permanent feature parity

Always test important rules against the engine you intend to use.

docs.title: Language Support
docs.text:
OpenGrep supports many programming and configuration languages.

Security-relevant examples include:

C
C++
C#
Java
Kotlin
JavaScript
TypeScript
JSX
TSX
PHP
Python
Go
Ruby
Rust
Scala
Bash
HTML
XML
YAML
JSON
Dockerfile
Terraform
Solidity
Visual Basic
Apex
Elixir

Language support continues to evolve.

Always check current OpenGrep documentation when relying on specific parser or taint-analysis capabilities.

docs.title: Linux and macOS
docs.text:
The current OpenGrep project provides an installation script.

curl -fsSL \
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/opengrep/opengrep/main/install.sh \
| bash

Verify:

opengrep --version

Help:

opengrep --help

Scan help:

opengrep scan --help

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
The project also provides a PowerShell installation method.

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/opengrep/opengrep/main/install.ps1 | iex

Verify:

opengrep --version

docs.title: Manual Installation
docs.text:
Prebuilt binaries are available from the OpenGrep GitHub releases.

After installation:

which opengrep

Then:

opengrep --version

docs.title: Basic Structural Search
docs.text:
OpenGrep can perform quick syntax-aware searches without creating a YAML rule.

Example:

opengrep scan \
  -e 'os.system(...)' \
  -l python \
  .

Search Python execution calls:

opengrep scan \
  -e 'subprocess.run(...)' \
  -l python \
  .

Search function definitions:

opengrep scan \
  -e 'def $FUNC(...): ...' \
  -l python \
  .

Search method calls:

opengrep scan \
  -e '$OBJ.execute(...)' \
  -l python \
  .

This is useful during reconnaissance.

docs.title: Structural Search vs ripgrep
docs.text:
Suppose the code contains:

subprocess.run(
    command,
    shell=True
)

A text search:

rg 'subprocess\.run'

finds text.

OpenGrep:

opengrep scan \
  -e 'subprocess.run(...)' \
  -l python \
  .

parses source syntax and searches structurally.

Conceptually:

ripgrep

Source File
    |
    v
Characters
    |
    v
Regex
    |
    v
Text Match

OpenGrep:

Source File
    |
    v
Parser
    |
    v
Syntax Tree
    |
    v
Structural Pattern
    |
    v
Code Match

Use ripgrep when speed and broad recall matter.

Use OpenGrep when code structure matters.

docs.title: First Security Scan
docs.text:
From the repository root, a ruleset can be run using:

opengrep scan \
  --config p/security-audit \
  .

Depending on the rule source and environment, other compatible rule configurations may also be available.

Do not assume a generic ruleset provides complete application coverage.

The purpose of the first scan is:

Reconnaissance
    |
    v
Interesting Areas
    |
    v
Manual Review
    |
    v
Custom Rules

docs.title: Scan a Local Rule
docs.text:
Suppose:

rules/command-injection.yml

contains a custom rule.

Run:

opengrep scan \
  -f rules/command-injection.yml \
  .

Or:

opengrep scan \
  --config rules/command-injection.yml \
  .

docs.text:
A useful structure is:

rules/
├── java/
├── dotnet/
├── php/
├── python/
├── django/
├── flask/
├── nodejs/
└── javascript/

Run the desired rules against the target project.

docs.text:
For repeatable assessments:

docs.text:
Open the repository:

code .

Then:

VS Code
   |
   +--> Explorer

   |

Recommended workflow:

1. Understand project structure

2. Identify languages

3. Identify frameworks

4. Map routes

5. Map authentication

6. Map authorisation

7. Find user-input sources

8. Find dangerous sinks

9. Run OpenGrep

10. Open results in VS Code

11. Trace data manually

12. Validate findings dynamically

docs.title: Anatomy of an OpenGrep Rule
docs.text:
A basic rule:

rules:
  - id: python-os-system
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review operating system command execution
    severity: WARNING
    pattern: os.system(...)

Important components:

id
languages
message
severity
pattern

docs.title: Pattern Matching
docs.text:
Example:

pattern: os.system(...)

Matches calls structurally resembling:

os.system(command)

or:

os.system(
    build_command()
)

docs.title: Metavariables
docs.text:
Metavariables capture parts of code.

Example:

pattern: os.system($COMMAND)

Given:

os.system(user_input)

then:

$COMMAND

represents:

user_input

Given:

os.system(build_command(host))

it represents the expression:

build_command(host)

docs.title: Ellipsis
docs.text:
The ellipsis:

...

matches arbitrary syntax in many contexts.

Example:

pattern: subprocess.run(...)

This allows argument differences.

docs.title: pattern-either
docs.text:
Use pattern-either when multiple APIs represent the same security concept.

Example:

rules:
  - id: python-command-execution
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review command execution
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: os.system(...)
      - pattern: os.popen(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.run(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.Popen(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.call(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.check_output(...)

This is useful for sink discovery.

It does not prove command injection.

docs.title: patterns
docs.text:
Multiple conditions can be combined.

Conceptually:

patterns:
  - pattern: ...
  - pattern-inside: |
      def $FUNCTION(...):
          ...

This allows a rule to require context.

docs.title: Negative Patterns
docs.text:
OpenGrep-compatible rule syntax can use negative patterns to exclude known cases.

Conceptually:

patterns:
  - pattern: dangerous(...)
  - pattern-not: known_safe(...)

Be careful.

An overly broad exclusion can create false negatives.

docs.title: Rule Severity
docs.text:
Common severities include:

INFO
WARNING
ERROR

Use severity for triage.

Do not interpret:

ERROR

as:

Confirmed critical vulnerability

Rule severity and vulnerability severity are different concepts.

docs.title: Sink-First Analysis
docs.text:
A strong source review technique is to start from dangerous sinks.

Dangerous Sink
      |
      v
Find Callers
      |
      v
Trace Arguments Backwards
      |
      v
Find Source
      |
      v
Review Validation
      |
      v
Determine Exploitability

OpenGrep is excellent for sink discovery.

docs.title: Python Command Execution
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: python-command-execution
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review operating system command execution
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: os.system(...)
      - pattern: os.popen(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.run(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.Popen(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.call(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.check_call(...)
      - pattern: subprocess.check_output(...)

docs.title: Python shell=True
docs.text:
A higher-interest pattern:

rules:
  - id: python-shell-true
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review subprocess execution using shell=True
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: subprocess.run(..., shell=True, ...)
      - pattern: subprocess.Popen(..., shell=True, ...)
      - pattern: subprocess.call(..., shell=True, ...)
      - pattern: subprocess.check_output(..., shell=True, ...)

Review:

Can the attacker control the command?

Can the attacker control part of the command?

Is concatenation used?

Is shell expansion possible?

Are fixed arguments used?

docs.title: Java Command Execution
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: java-command-execution
    languages:
      - java
    message: Review operating system command execution
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...)
      - pattern: new ProcessBuilder(...)

Trace:

@RequestParam
      |
      v
Controller
      |
      v
Service
      |
      v
ProcessBuilder

docs.title: .NET Command Execution
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: dotnet-process-execution
    languages:
      - csharp
    message: Review process execution
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: Process.Start(...)
      - pattern: new ProcessStartInfo(...)

Manual review is required because safe fixed command execution is common.

docs.title: PHP Command Execution
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: php-command-execution
    languages:
      - php
    message: Review command execution
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: system(...)
      - pattern: exec(...)
      - pattern: shell_exec(...)
      - pattern: passthru(...)
      - pattern: popen(...)
      - pattern: proc_open(...)

docs.title: Node.js Command Execution
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: node-command-execution
    languages:
      - javascript
      - typescript
    message: Review child process execution
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: child_process.exec(...)
      - pattern: child_process.execSync(...)
      - pattern: child_process.spawn(...)
      - pattern: child_process.spawnSync(...)
      - pattern: child_process.execFile(...)
      - pattern: child_process.execFileSync(...)

Import aliases and destructuring must also be considered.

Example:

const {
    exec
} = require("child_process");

exec(command);

A rule matching only:

child_process.exec(...)

may miss this variant.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: python-dynamic-code
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review dynamic code execution
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: eval(...)
      - pattern: exec(...)

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: javascript-dynamic-code
    languages:
      - javascript
      - typescript
    message: Review dynamic JavaScript execution
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: eval(...)
      - pattern: new Function(...)

docs.title: SQL Injection Review
docs.text:
Do not simply search for:

execute()

and report SQL injection.

The security question is:

How was the query constructed?

Review:

Parameterisation
Prepared statements
Raw SQL
String concatenation
Template literals
ORM escape hatches
Dynamic identifiers
Stored procedures

docs.title: Python SQL Sink Discovery
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: python-sql-execution
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review SQL construction and parameterisation
    severity: INFO

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: $CURSOR.execute(...)
      - pattern: $CURSOR.executemany(...)

This intentionally finds safe and unsafe calls.

docs.title: Django Raw SQL
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: django-raw-sql
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review raw SQL usage
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: $MODEL.objects.raw(...)
      - pattern: RawSQL(...)
      - pattern: $CURSOR.execute(...)
      - pattern: $QUERYSET.extra(...)

docs.title: Java SQL Review
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: java-sql-review
    languages:
      - java
    message: Review SQL construction
    severity: INFO

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: $CONNECTION.createStatement(...)
      - pattern: $STATEMENT.executeQuery(...)
      - pattern: $STATEMENT.executeUpdate(...)
      - pattern: $ENTITY.createNativeQuery(...)
      - pattern: $ENTITY.createQuery(...)

docs.title: .NET SQL Review
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: dotnet-sql-review
    languages:
      - csharp
    message: Review SQL construction and parameterisation
    severity: INFO

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: $DB.Database.ExecuteSqlRaw(...)
      - pattern: $DB.Database.FromSqlRaw(...)
      - pattern: new SqlCommand(...)

docs.title: PHP SQL Review
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: php-sql-review
    languages:
      - php
    message: Review SQL construction and parameterisation
    severity: INFO

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: mysqli_query(...)
      - pattern: $DB->query(...)
      - pattern: $DB->exec(...)
      - pattern: $DB->prepare(...)

prepare() may indicate safer parameterisation.

Do not report it as SQL injection merely because it matched.

docs.title: NoSQL Injection Review
docs.text:
Useful Node.js areas include:

find()
findOne()
findById()
updateOne()
updateMany()
deleteOne()
aggregate()
$where
$regex

The important question is whether attacker-controlled objects or operators can alter query semantics.

Conceptually:

req.body
   |
   v
Mongo Query
   |
   v
Database

Search:

rg -n \
'findOne|findById|updateOne|aggregate|\$where|\$regex' \
-g '*.js' \
-g '*.ts' \
.

Use OpenGrep to model application-specific unsafe query construction after identifying the database library.

docs.title: LDAP Injection Review
docs.text:
Search Java:

DirContext
InitialDirContext
search()
SearchControls

Search .NET:

DirectorySearcher
DirectoryEntry

Search PHP:

ldap_search
ldap_bind
ldap_list

The important flow is:

Attacker Input
      |
      v
LDAP Filter Construction
      |
      v
LDAP Search

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: python-http-client
    languages:
      - python
    message: Review outbound HTTP destination
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: requests.get(...)
      - pattern: requests.post(...)
      - pattern: requests.request(...)
      - pattern: httpx.get(...)
      - pattern: httpx.post(...)
      - pattern: httpx.request(...)
      - pattern: urllib.request.urlopen(...)

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: java-http-client
    languages:
      - java
    message: Review outbound request destination
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: new URL(...)
      - pattern: URI.create(...)
      - pattern: $REST.getForObject(...)
      - pattern: $REST.getForEntity(...)
      - pattern: $CLIENT.send(...)

docs.title: .NET
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: dotnet-http-client
    languages:
      - csharp
    message: Review outbound HTTP request destination
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: $CLIENT.GetAsync(...)
      - pattern: $CLIENT.GetStringAsync(...)
      - pattern: $CLIENT.SendAsync(...)

docs.title: PHP
docs.text:
rules:
  - id: php-outbound-request
    languages:
      - php
    message: Review outbound request destination
    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: curl_init(...)
      - pattern: file_get_contents(...)
      - pattern: fopen(...)

Some APIs also perform filesystem operations.

Context matters.

docs.title: Node.js
docs.text:
rules:

    languages:
      - javascript
      - typescript

    severity: WARNING

    pattern-either:
      - pattern: fetch(...)
      - pattern: axios.get(...)
      - pattern: axios.post(...)
      - pattern: axios.request(...)

docs.title: SSRF Validation Model
docs.text:
Finding:

requests.get(url)

is only the beginning.

Trace:

HTTP Parameter
     |
     v
URL Parser
     |
     v
Validation
     |
     v
DNS Resolution

docs.title: Authorisation Review
docs.text:
Authorisation is one of the most important areas for manual review.

Route
  |
  v
Authentication

  v
Object Identifier
  |
  v
Object Retrieval

Authorisation Check

  v
Sensitive Operation

Object lookups
Permission functions
Authorisation annotations
Role checks
Tenant checks
Ownership checks

But the reviewer must understand the intended policy.

docs.title: Spring Security
docs.text:

SecurityFilterChain
authorizeHttpRequests

permitAll

rules:

    severity: INFO

Do not report permitAll() itself as a vulnerability.
