docs.title: Business Logic Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities occur when an application correctly processes a request from a technical perspective but allows the application's intended rules, workflows or assumptions to be violated.

Unlike vulnerabilities such as SQL injection or Cross-Site Scripting, business logic vulnerabilities often do not involve malformed input.

The request may be completely valid.

The problem is that the application allows something that should not be possible according to the business rules.

For example:

Product price: €100
        ↓
Customer changes quantity
        ↓
Application calculates total
        ↓
Checkout

A technical security test may ask:

Can the quantity parameter contain SQL syntax?

A business logic assessment asks:

Can quantity be negative?

Can the price be changed?

Can the discount be applied repeatedly?

Can checkout occur without payment?

Can the same voucher be reused?

Can a cheaper product be replaced after payment?

Can the workflow be completed out of order?

This requires understanding the business process before testing it.

Authorised Security Testing

Business logic testing should be based on functionality included in the authorised assessment scope. Avoid actions that cause financial loss, create real orders, consume limited resources or affect other users unless specifically agreed with the system owner.

docs.title: Business Logic Testing Mindset
docs.text:
Business logic testing should begin with:

What does this functionality do?

followed by:

What rules are supposed to govern it?

and then:

What happens if those rules are violated?

A useful methodology is:

Understand Business Function
          ↓
Identify Business Rules
          ↓
Identify Actors
          ↓
Identify Assets
          ↓
Identify State Transitions
          ↓
Identify Trust Assumptions
          ↓
Create Logic Threat Model
          ↓
Derive Test Cases
          ↓
Test Rules and Transitions
          ↓
Validate Business Impact

This makes business logic testing highly dependent on scope.

docs.title: Scope First
docs.text:
Do not begin business logic testing by searching for generic payloads.

First identify the business functions contained in the application.

For example, an application may contain:

Pricing
Payments
Shopping basket
Discounts
Subscriptions
Account registration
Account recovery
Approvals
Document workflows
Booking
Reservations
Loyalty points
Credits
Refunds
Returns
Invitations
User roles
Resource allocation

Each business function creates a different threat model.

For example:

Scope: Pricing
    ↓
Threat Model: Price Manipulation

Scope: Account Recovery
    ↓
Threat Model: Account Takeover

Scope: Approval Workflow
    ↓
Threat Model: Approval Bypass

Scope: Booking
    ↓
Threat Model: Reservation Manipulation

Scope: Subscription
    ↓
Threat Model: Entitlement Manipulation

This is more useful than applying the same generic checklist to every application.

docs.title: Logic Threat Modelling
docs.text:
For each important business function, create a small threat model.

A practical structure is:

BUSINESS FUNCTION

What is being protected?

Who can perform the action?

What rules should apply?

What states exist?

Which transitions are allowed?

Which transitions must never occur?

Which values influence the outcome?

Which values are controlled by the client?

What does the server trust?

What happens if steps are skipped?

What happens if steps are repeated?

What happens if requests arrive in an unexpected order?

The answers become your test cases.

docs.title: Business Logic Threat Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Business Function
       ↓
Actors
       ↓
Assets
       ↓
Business Rules
       ↓
State Machine
       ↓
Trust Boundaries
       ↓
Abuse Cases
       ↓
Security Tests

For example:

Pricing
   ↓
Customer
   ↓
Product / Money
   ↓
Price must be calculated server-side
   ↓
Basket → Checkout → Payment
   ↓
Browser / Server
   ↓
Price manipulation
   ↓
Modify price-related values

docs.title: Think in Rules Rather Than Payloads
docs.text:
Traditional vulnerability testing often starts with:

Input
 ↓
Payload
 ↓
Response

Business logic testing is different.

Think:

Rule
 ↓
Assumption
 ↓
Violation
 ↓
Business Impact

For example:

Rule:
A voucher may only be used once.

Assumption:
The application records voucher usage.

Violation:
Submit the voucher repeatedly.

Impact:
Repeated unauthorised discount.

This is the essence of business logic testing.

docs.title: Identify Business Rules
docs.text:
Business rules may come from:

Application behaviour
Requirements
Documentation
User stories
Terms and conditions
API documentation
Help pages
UI restrictions
Error messages
Developer interviews
Business owner interviews
Observed workflows

Examples:

A user may only redeem one voucher.

An order must be paid before shipment.

A refund cannot exceed the original payment.

A manager must approve transactions above €10,000.

A booking cannot contain a negative number of guests.

A free trial may only be activated once.

A user cannot approve their own request.

A customer cannot modify an order after shipment.

Each statement represents something worth testing.

docs.title: Convert Rules Into Tests
docs.text:
Take:

Rule:
A voucher can only be used once.

Turn it into:

Can the voucher be submitted twice?

Can it be submitted simultaneously?

Can it be applied to multiple baskets?

Can it be applied through the API after the UI rejects it?

Can case changes bypass the restriction?

Can the voucher be removed and re-added?

Can the same voucher be used from another session?

This technique is extremely effective.

docs.title: Example 1: Pricing Logic
docs.text:
Suppose the assessment scope includes an e-commerce application.

The relevant business process is:

Select Product
      ↓
Add to Basket
      ↓
Calculate Price
      ↓
Apply Discount
      ↓
Checkout
      ↓
Payment
      ↓
Order

The threat model should focus on:

Price integrity
Quantity integrity
Discount integrity
Currency
Shipping costs
Taxes
Payment amount
Order state

docs.title: Pricing Threat Model
docs.text:
Ask:

Where does the price originate?

Is the price calculated by the server?

Does the browser send the price?

Can the client control the currency?

Can the client control the discount?

Can the quantity become zero?

Can the quantity become negative?

Can the total become negative?

Can shipping costs be modified?

Can tax calculations be influenced?

Can an old price be reused?

Can the price change between basket and checkout?

Does the payment provider amount match the order amount?

docs.title: Inspect the Request
docs.text:
Suppose Burp shows:

POST /api/cart HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "productId": 1234,
    "quantity": 1,
    "price": 99.95
}

The immediately interesting property is:

"price": 99.95

Ask:

Why does the client need to tell the server the price?

The preferred design is:

Client
  ↓
productId = 1234
quantity = 1
  ↓
Server
  ↓
Lookup Product
  ↓
Price = €99.95
  ↓
Calculate Total

Not:

Client
  ↓
price = €99.95
  ↓
Server Trusts Price

docs.title: Price Manipulation
docs.text:
During an authorised test, controlled values might include:

99.95
99.94
1.00
0.00

The objective is not to obtain products fraudulently.

The objective is to determine:

Does the server independently determine the correct price?

Evidence should stop once the behaviour has been demonstrated.

docs.title: Quantity Manipulation
docs.text:
If the application accepts:

{
    "quantity": 1
}

consider business boundaries such as:

0
Negative values
Very large values
Decimal values
Values exceeding stock
Values exceeding account limits

The important question is:

What values make sense according to the business process?

For most physical products:

quantity > 0

should normally be enforced.

docs.title: Negative Quantity
docs.text:
Consider:

Product A
€100
Quantity: -1

If the application calculates:

€100 × -1 = -€100

the arithmetic may technically be correct.

The business logic is not.

Expected validation should resemble:

Quantity
   ↓
Integer?
   ↓
Greater Than Zero?
   ↓
Within Stock Limit?
   ↓
Calculate Price

docs.title: Discount Logic
docs.text:
Suppose:

WELCOME10

provides:

10% discount

The business rules may state:

One use per customer
Cannot combine with other vouchers
Only valid for selected products
Expires on a specific date
Minimum basket value applies

Convert each rule into a test.

Can WELCOME10 be reused?

Can WELCOME10 be applied twice?

Can multiple vouchers be stacked?

Can the voucher be applied after expiration?

Can the basket be changed after the voucher is validated?

Can the minimum basket requirement be bypassed?

Can a restricted product receive the discount?

docs.title: Discount Stacking
docs.text:
Expected:

€100
  ↓
WELCOME10
  ↓
€90

Potential logic issue:

€100
  ↓
WELCOME10
  ↓
€90
  ↓
WELCOME10
  ↓
€81
  ↓
WELCOME10
  ↓
€72.90

The vulnerability is not the mathematical calculation.

The vulnerability is that:

Single-use discount

became:

Repeatable discount

docs.title: Basket Manipulation
docs.text:
Test state transitions such as:

Add Product
     ↓
Apply Discount
     ↓
Modify Product
     ↓
Checkout

Ask whether security-relevant calculations are performed again after the basket changes.

For example:

Expensive Eligible Product
          ↓
Apply Voucher
          ↓
Replace Product
          ↓
Discount Remains

This may reveal a state validation problem.

docs.title: Currency Logic
docs.text:
Applications supporting multiple currencies introduce additional logic.

Example:

EUR
USD
GBP

Questions include:

Who chooses the currency?

Where is conversion performed?

Is the exchange rate trusted from the client?

Can currency change after the price is calculated?

Does the payment provider receive the same currency?

Can currency identifiers and numeric values become mismatched?

The threat model is:

Product
  ↓
Base Price
  ↓
Currency Conversion
  ↓
Displayed Price
  ↓
Payment Amount

Every transition should preserve value correctly.

docs.title: Pricing Logic Summary
docs.text:
PRICING
   ↓
Price
Quantity
Discount
Currency
Tax
Shipping
Payment Amount
   ↓
Can Any Client-Controlled Value Alter Financial Outcome?

docs.title: Example 2: Account Recovery Logic
docs.text:
Suppose the application provides:

Forgot Password
      ↓
Enter Email
      ↓
Recovery Token
      ↓
Verify Token
      ↓
Choose New Password

The threat model is completely different from pricing.

Assets:

User account
Credentials
Recovery token
Authenticated session

Primary threat:

Account takeover

docs.title: Recovery Threat Model
docs.text:
Ask:

Who may initiate recovery?

How is the user identified?

How is the recovery token generated?

How long is the token valid?

Can it be reused?

Is it tied to a specific account?

Is it invalidated after password change?

Does requesting another token invalidate the previous token?

Can recovery steps be skipped?

Can the target account change during the workflow?

Is MFA enforced after recovery where required?

docs.title: Recovery State Machine
docs.text:
Expected:

Unauthenticated
      ↓
Request Recovery
      ↓
Token Issued
      ↓
Token Verified
      ↓
Password Reset Authorised
      ↓
Password Changed
      ↓
Token Invalidated

Now identify forbidden transitions:

Unauthenticated
      ↓
Password Changed

or:

Token Issued
      ↓
Change Password

without:

Token Verified

Those forbidden transitions become security tests.

docs.title: Step Skipping
docs.text:
Suppose the workflow is:

Step 1: Enter email

Step 2: Enter verification code

Step 3: Set new password

Do not assume the UI represents server-side enforcement.

Test whether:

Step 1
  ↓
Step 3

is accepted directly.

This is a general business logic principle:

A multi-step user interface does not guarantee a multi-step server-side state machine.

docs.title: Token Reuse
docs.text:
Expected:

Recovery Token
      ↓
Password Changed
      ↓
Token Invalid

Potential vulnerability:

Recovery Token
      ↓
Password Changed
      ↓
Token Still Valid
      ↓
Password Changed Again

The security issue is a violation of the token lifecycle.

docs.title: Account Switching
docs.text:
Consider:

Request reset for Alice
        ↓
Verify Alice's token
        ↓
Change account identifier to Bob
        ↓
Submit new password

The server should bind the entire workflow to the same account.

Expected:

Recovery Token
      ↓
Specific User
      ↓
Specific Recovery Transaction

docs.title: Example 3: Approval Workflows
docs.text:
Consider a business application where transactions require approval.

Example:

Employee
   ↓
Creates Request
   ↓
Manager
   ↓
Approves Request
   ↓
Finance
   ↓
Processes Request

Business rules might include:

Creator cannot approve own request.

Requests above €10,000 require manager approval.

Requests above €50,000 require director approval.

Finance can only process approved requests.

Rejected requests cannot be processed.

These rules directly become tests.

docs.title: Approval Threat Model
docs.text:
Assets:

Money
Contracts
Purchases
Sensitive changes
Business records

Actors:

Requester
Manager
Director
Finance
Administrator

State machine:

Draft
  ↓
Submitted
  ↓
Pending Approval
  ↓
Approved
  ↓
Processed

Alternative:

Pending Approval
      ↓
Rejected

docs.title: Forbidden State Transitions
docs.text:
Potentially dangerous transitions include:

Draft → Approved

Submitted → Processed

Rejected → Processed

Pending Approval → Processed

Also ask:

Can the requester approve their own request?

Can approval level be changed?

Can the amount change after approval?

Can the beneficiary change after approval?

Can an approved request be replayed?

Can an old approval be reused?

docs.title: Modify After Approval
docs.text:
This is an important business logic pattern.

Expected:

Request €5,000
      ↓
Manager Reviews €5,000
      ↓
Approved
      ↓
€5,000 Processed

Potential issue:

Request €5,000
      ↓
Approved
      ↓
Change Amount to €50,000
      ↓
Process

The problem is:

Approval applies to one state

but:

Processing uses another state

Security-sensitive changes should invalidate previous approvals.

docs.title: Separation of Duties
docs.text:
Some business processes require:

Person A performs Action 1

Person B approves Action 1

This is separation of duties.

Test whether:

Person A
  ↓
Creates Request
  ↓
Changes Role / Request / Identifier
  ↓
Approves Own Request

is possible.

The relevant question is not merely:

Does endpoint /approve require authentication?

It is:

Is this authenticated user allowed to approve this particular transaction?

docs.title: Example 4: Booking and Reservation Logic
docs.text:
Consider:

Search
  ↓
Select Availability
  ↓
Reserve
  ↓
Pay
  ↓
Confirmation

Assets may include:

Seats
Rooms
Appointments
Tickets
Inventory
Time slots

Business rules may include:

A slot can only be booked once.

A reservation expires after 10 minutes.

Payment must occur before confirmation.

Users may only hold a limited number of reservations.

Past dates cannot be booked.

Capacity cannot be exceeded.

docs.title: Booking Threat Model
docs.text:
Ask:

Can unavailable inventory be booked?

Can a reservation be held indefinitely?

Can expired reservations be revived?

Can the date be changed after price calculation?

Can capacity be exceeded?

Can payment be skipped?

Can a reservation be duplicated?

Can the same resource be booked simultaneously?

Can a cheaper booking be changed into an expensive one after payment?

docs.title: Reservation State Machine
docs.text:
Expected:

Available
    ↓
Reserved
    ↓
Payment Pending
    ↓
Paid
    ↓
Confirmed

Timeout:

Reserved
    ↓
Expired
    ↓
Available

Forbidden transition:

Expired
   ↓
Confirmed

without a new valid reservation.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Booking systems are particularly interesting for race conditions.

Consider one remaining seat:

Available Seats = 1

Two simultaneous requests arrive:

Request A ─┐
           ├── Reserve Seat
Request B ─┘

The application must ensure:

Only One Request Succeeds

rather than:

Request A → Success
Request B → Success

Business logic testing therefore often overlaps with race condition testing.

docs.title: Example 5: Subscription and Entitlement Logic
docs.text:
Consider a SaaS platform:

Free
  ↓
Trial
  ↓
Professional
  ↓
Enterprise

Features may depend on subscription level.

Assets include:

Premium features
API usage
Storage
Licences
Credits
Seats
Data exports
Integrations

docs.title: Subscription Threat Model
docs.text:
Ask:

Can premium functionality be called directly?

Does the server enforce subscription level?

Can a free trial be activated repeatedly?

Can the subscription identifier be modified?

Can limits be bypassed through the API?

Can cancelled subscriptions continue using premium features?

Can downgrade and upgrade sequences create incorrect entitlements?

Can multiple accounts share a single entitlement unexpectedly?

Can usage counters be reset?

docs.title: Trial Abuse
docs.text:
Business rule:

One trial per eligible customer.

Possible abuse cases:

Create another trial

Cancel and restart trial

Change email address

Change organisation

Use another API endpoint

Replay activation request

Manipulate trial state

The exact tests depend on how the application defines:

Customer

That itself is an important business rule.

docs.title: Entitlement Enforcement
docs.text:
The UI might hide:

Export Report

for free users.

That does not prove the server enforces the restriction.

Test:

Free User
    ↓
Direct API Request
    ↓
/api/export

Expected:

Server Checks Subscription
        ↓
Denied

Not:

Button Hidden
     ↓
Assumed Secure

docs.title: From Scope to Threat Model
docs.text:
The general process should therefore be:

Assessment Scope
       ↓
Identify Business Functions
       ↓
Select Important Functions
       ↓
Create Logic Threat Model
       ↓
Identify Rules
       ↓
Identify State Machine
       ↓
Identify Abuse Cases
       ↓
Convert Abuse Cases Into Tests

docs.title: Example Scope Mapping
docs.text:
E-Commerce
    ↓
Pricing
Discounts
Basket
Checkout
Payments
Refunds
    ↓
Financial Logic Threat Model

Identity Platform
    ↓
Registration
Authentication
MFA
Password Reset
Account Recovery
    ↓
Identity Logic Threat Model

Business Workflow Platform
    ↓
Submission
Approval
Rejection
Processing
    ↓
Workflow Logic Threat Model

Booking Platform
    ↓
Availability
Reservation
Payment
Cancellation
    ↓
Resource Logic Threat Model

SaaS Platform
    ↓
Trials
Plans
Licences
Entitlements
Usage Limits
    ↓
Subscription Logic Threat Model

docs.title: Identify Actors
docs.text:
For every workflow, identify who participates.

Example:

Anonymous User
Customer
Employee
Manager
Administrator
Support
Finance
External Provider
Background Worker

Then ask:

What can each actor do?

What can each actor not do?

What actions require another actor?

Can one actor impersonate another workflow role?

Can one actor perform multiple supposedly separated roles?

docs.title: Identify Assets
docs.text:
Assets are what the business process is protecting.

Examples:

Money
Products
Accounts
Personal data
Documents
Approvals
Reservations
Credits
Discounts
Licences
Premium functionality
Inventory
Orders
Refunds

Knowing the asset makes the potential impact clearer.

docs.title: Identify Trust Boundaries
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities frequently appear when one component trusts another incorrectly.

Example:

Browser
   ↓
API
   ↓
Payment Service

Ask:

Does the API trust values from the browser?

Does the application trust payment status from the browser?

Does the payment callback independently identify the order?

Does the order service verify the payment amount?

Trust boundaries may exist between:

Browser ↔ API

API ↔ Database

Application ↔ Payment Provider

Application ↔ Identity Provider

Application ↔ Internal Service

User ↔ Administrator

Organisation A ↔ Organisation B

docs.title: Identify State
docs.text:
Business applications frequently operate as state machines.

Example:

Order
 ↓
CREATED
 ↓
PAYMENT_PENDING
 ↓
PAID
 ↓
SHIPPED
 ↓
DELIVERED

Alternative transitions:

PAYMENT_PENDING → CANCELLED

PAID → REFUNDED

Now ask:

Can CREATED become SHIPPED?

Can CANCELLED become DELIVERED?

Can REFUNDED become SHIPPED?

Can SHIPPED return to PAYMENT_PENDING?

Can the client directly choose the state?

docs.title: State Transition Testing
docs.text:
For every workflow:

List States
    ↓
List Allowed Transitions
    ↓
List Forbidden Transitions
    ↓
Test Forbidden Transitions

For example:

Current State Requested State Expected Draft Submitted Allowed Submitted Approved Role dependent Approved Processed Allowed Draft Processed Denied Rejected Processed Denied Cancelled Completed Denied

This simple exercise can reveal significant logic vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Sequence Testing
docs.text:
If the normal sequence is:

A
↓
B
↓
C
↓
D

test:

A → C

A → D

B → D

A → B → B → C

A → B → A → C

A → B → C → B

D → C

The objective is to determine whether the server enforces the workflow rather than relying on the user interface.

docs.title: Repeat Actions
docs.text:
Ask whether actions intended to occur once can occur multiple times.

Examples:

Redeem voucher
Claim reward
Use invitation
Activate trial
Receive refund
Apply credit
Accept bonus
Confirm email
Use recovery token
Approve transaction

Generic test:

Action
  ↓
Success
  ↓
Repeat Same Request
  ↓
What Happens?

docs.title: Replay Testing
docs.text:
Burp Repeater is particularly useful here.

Workflow:

Perform Valid Action
      ↓
Capture Request
      ↓
Send to Repeater
      ↓
Repeat Request
      ↓
Observe State

Look for:

Duplicate refund
Duplicate credit
Repeated discount
Repeated reward
Duplicate order
Repeated approval
Repeated state transition

docs.title: Client-Side Restrictions
docs.text:
Never assume a business rule is secure because the interface prevents the action.

Examples:

Disabled button
Hidden field
JavaScript validation
Dropdown restriction
Read-only field
Hidden menu
Client-side price calculation

The real question is:

Does the server enforce the rule?

docs.title: Hidden Parameters
docs.text:
Inspect requests for values such as:

price
amount
discount
role
status
approved
paid
currency
quantity
accountId
userId
organisationId
plan
subscription
credit
balance

These values are especially interesting when they represent business decisions.

docs.title: Server-Generated Values
docs.text:
Ask whether values that should be server controlled are being supplied by the client.

Examples:

Price
Tax
Discount percentage
Account balance
Payment status
Approval status
User role
Subscription level
Order state
Refund amount

Preferred architecture:

Client Provides Intent
        ↓
Server Determines Business Outcome

For example:

Client:
Buy product 123
Quantity 2

Server:

Product 123
      ↓
Lookup Price
      ↓
Check Stock
      ↓
Calculate Tax
      ↓
Calculate Total

docs.title: Trust the Intent, Not the Outcome
docs.text:
A useful design principle is:

Client Requests Action

rather than:

Client Declares Result

Good:

{
    "productId": 123,
    "quantity": 2
}

Suspicious:

{
    "productId": 123,
    "quantity": 2,
    "price": 1.00,
    "discount": 99,
    "paid": true,
    "status": "completed"
}

The latter exposes multiple business decisions to client control.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A practical business logic workflow is:

Use Application Normally
        ↓
Burp Proxy
        ↓
Map Complete Workflow
        ↓
Send Important Requests to Repeater
        ↓
Identify Business Parameters
        ↓
Create Baseline
        ↓
Modify One Assumption
        ↓
Replay
        ↓
Observe State
        ↓
Repeat With Another Rule

Business logic testing benefits greatly from understanding the normal workflow before modifying it.

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Use Repeater for:

Parameter modification
Request replay
Step skipping
Sequence changes
State manipulation
Role testing
Identifier changes
Boundary testing

A useful Repeater naming scheme is:

BL-PRICE-001
BL-DISCOUNT-001
BL-RECOVERY-001
BL-APPROVAL-001
BL-BOOKING-001

This keeps testing organised.

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer can help identify subtle differences between:

Normal Workflow
       vs
Modified Workflow

Compare:

Status codes
Response bodies
JSON properties
Headers
Cookies
Identifiers
State values

docs.title: Burp Sequencer
docs.text:
Sequencer may be relevant when business logic depends on security tokens such as:

Recovery tokens
Invitation tokens
Transaction identifiers
Coupon identifiers
One-time codes

Token predictability is a different vulnerability class, but it may affect the security of the overall business workflow.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Business logic rules sometimes work correctly when requests occur sequentially but fail when requests occur simultaneously.

Example:

Balance = €100

Two requests:

Withdraw €80
Withdraw €80

If both check:

Balance >= €80

before either updates the balance:

Request A → Approved
Request B → Approved

Result:

€160 withdrawn from €100 balance

This is a race condition affecting business logic.

docs.title: Race Condition Candidates
docs.text:
High-value operations include:

Payments
Withdrawals
Discount redemption
Voucher redemption
Reward claiming
Inventory
Bookings
Reservations
Account creation limits
Invitation usage
Password reset
MFA operations
Credit consumption
API quota enforcement

docs.title: Limit Testing
docs.text:
Whenever a business rule contains:

once
maximum
minimum
per day
per user
per account
per organisation
per transaction
only one
up to

there is a test opportunity.

Examples:

Maximum 5 tickets

One voucher per user

Maximum withdrawal €1,000

One free trial

10 API requests per minute

Maximum refund equal to original payment

Test boundaries:

limit - 1
limit
limit + 1

and where authorised:

Repeated
Concurrent
Alternative workflow
Different session
Different endpoint

docs.title: Refund Logic
docs.text:
Refund systems deserve their own mini threat model.

Expected:

Payment €100
     ↓
Maximum Refund €100

Ask:

Can refund exceed payment?

Can the same payment be refunded twice?

Can partial refunds exceed the original amount cumulatively?

Can cancelled payments be refunded?

Can another order identifier be supplied?

Can refund destination be modified?

Can the refund be repeated concurrently?

docs.title: Credit and Loyalty Logic
docs.text:
Applications may use:

Store credit
Points
Tokens
Rewards
Gift balances
Promotional balances

Threat model:

Earn
 ↓
Store
 ↓
Redeem
 ↓
Balance Updated

Ask:

Can credit be redeemed twice?

Can negative values increase balance?

Can points be transferred repeatedly?

Can expired credit be revived?

Can another user's balance identifier be supplied?

Can earn and redeem operations race?

docs.title: File and Document Workflows
docs.text:
Business logic also applies to non-financial applications.

Example:

Create Document
      ↓
Submit
      ↓
Review
      ↓
Approve
      ↓
Publish

Questions:

Can draft documents be published?

Can rejected documents be approved?

Can the document change after approval?

Can a user approve their own document?

Can review be skipped?

Can an old approval apply to a new document version?

This demonstrates that business logic testing is much broader than e-commerce.

docs.title: Logic Threat Modelling Template
docs.text:
For each important feature, create:

FEATURE:
Pricing

ASSET:
Financial integrity

ACTORS:
Customer
Application
Payment provider

EXPECTED WORKFLOW:
Product → Basket → Checkout → Payment → Order

BUSINESS RULES:
Server determines price
Quantity must be positive
Voucher can be used once
Payment amount must equal order amount

TRUST BOUNDARIES:
Browser → API
API → Payment provider

ABUSE CASES:
Price modification
Negative quantity
Voucher replay
Payment mismatch

TESTS:
Modify price
Test quantity boundaries
Replay voucher
Compare order amount with payment amount

docs.title: Another Logic Threat Model
docs.text:
FEATURE:
Password Recovery

ASSET:
User account

ACTORS:
Anonymous user
Account owner
Application

EXPECTED WORKFLOW:
Request → Token → Verify → Reset

BUSINESS RULES:
Token belongs to one user
Token expires
Token can only be used once
Verification must occur before reset

ABUSE CASES:
Skip verification
Reuse token
Switch account
Use expired token

TESTS:
Request final endpoint directly
Replay token
Change account identifier
Test token after expiration

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
[ ] Identify important business functions
[ ] Identify actors
[ ] Identify assets
[ ] Identify business rules
[ ] Identify trust boundaries
[ ] Identify workflow states
[ ] Identify allowed transitions
[ ] Identify forbidden transitions

docs.title: Client Control
docs.text:
[ ] Identify client-controlled prices
[ ] Identify client-controlled quantities
[ ] Identify client-controlled roles
[ ] Identify client-controlled status
[ ] Identify client-controlled account IDs
[ ] Identify client-controlled approval values
[ ] Identify client-controlled payment values

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
[ ] Skip steps
[ ] Repeat steps
[ ] Reverse steps
[ ] Perform steps out of order
[ ] Replay completed actions
[ ] Modify values between steps
[ ] Test stale workflow state

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
[ ] Test minimum
[ ] Test maximum
[ ] Test zero
[ ] Test negative values
[ ] Test limit + 1
[ ] Test repeated actions
[ ] Consider concurrency

docs.title: State
docs.text:
[ ] Map states
[ ] Test forbidden transitions
[ ] Modify object after approval
[ ] Modify object after payment
[ ] Test cancelled state
[ ] Test expired state
[ ] Test completed state

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Business logic findings require clear evidence because the requests themselves may appear completely legitimate.

Record:

Business function
Expected rule
Normal workflow
Modified workflow
Affected endpoint
Affected parameter
Original value
Modified value
Application response
Resulting application state
Business impact
Affected actor
Required privileges

docs.title: Example Evidence
docs.text:
Finding:
Product Price Manipulation

Business Rule:
Product prices must be determined by the server.

Normal Request:
productId=123
price=99.95

Modified Request:
productId=123
price=1.00

Observed Result:
Application accepted €1.00 as the order price.

Expected Result:
Server should ignore client-provided price and retrieve the current
price for product 123.

Impact:
A customer can manipulate the amount associated with an order.

In a real assessment, stop before completing a financially damaging transaction unless the agreed test procedure explicitly allows it.

docs.title: Reporting Business Logic Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
Avoid vague titles such as:

Business Logic Issue

Describe the violated rule.

Better titles include:

Product Price Can Be Manipulated During Checkout

Single-Use Discount Code Can Be Redeemed Multiple Times

Password Reset Verification Can Be Skipped

Requester Can Approve Their Own Transaction

Approved Transaction Amount Can Be Modified Before Processing

Expired Reservation Can Be Confirmed

Free Trial Can Be Activated Repeatedly

Refund Amount Can Exceed Original Payment

The title should immediately explain the business impact.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
A good description explains:

What the application is designed to do

What business rule should apply

How the workflow can be manipulated

Why server-side controls fail

What outcome becomes possible

Business context is especially important here.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Describe impact in terms of the affected business.

Examples:

Financial loss
Unauthorised discounts
Unauthorised refunds
Account takeover
Approval bypass
Subscription bypass
Inventory exhaustion
Reservation abuse
Unauthorised access to premium functionality
Violation of separation of duties
Workflow integrity failure

Avoid overstating impact.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities usually cannot be fixed with a generic security header or WAF rule.

The underlying business rule must be enforced.

docs.title: Enforce Rules Server-Side
docs.text:
All security-relevant business decisions should be validated server-side.

For example:

Client:
productId = 123
quantity = 2

Server:

Lookup Product
      ↓
Retrieve Price
      ↓
Validate Quantity
      ↓
Check Stock
      ↓
Apply Valid Discount
      ↓
Calculate Tax
      ↓
Calculate Total

docs.title: Validate Every State Transition
docs.text:
Do not only check whether the user is authenticated.

Check whether the requested transition is valid.

For example:

Current State = Pending Approval

Requested State = Processed

Server should ask:

Is Pending Approval → Processed allowed?

If not:

Reject

docs.title: Revalidate After Changes
docs.text:
If an important object changes after approval, validation should occur again.

Example:

Transaction
    ↓
Approved
    ↓
Amount Changes
    ↓
Approval Invalidated
    ↓
Reapproval Required

This applies to:

Amount
Beneficiary
Product
Quantity
Account
Document
Permissions
Scope

docs.title: Enforce Idempotency Where Required
docs.text:
Operations intended to happen once should not produce additional effects when replayed.

Examples:

Payment
Refund
Voucher redemption
Reward claim
Order creation
Approval

Where appropriate, use unique transaction identifiers and idempotency controls.

docs.title: Use Atomic Operations
docs.text:
For concurrency-sensitive business rules:

Check
  +
Update

should occur atomically where required.

This helps prevent:

Check Balance
      ↓
Concurrent Request
      ↓
Both Requests Succeed

docs.title: Business Logic Quick Reference
docs.text:
Understand Function
       ↓
What Is the Asset?
       ↓
Who Are the Actors?
       ↓
What Are the Rules?
       ↓
What Are the States?
       ↓
What Transitions Are Allowed?
       ↓
What Does the Client Control?
       ↓
What Does the Server Trust?
       ↓
What Happens If I:

Change a value?
Skip a step?
Repeat a step?
Reverse the sequence?
Replay a request?
Exceed a limit?
Use zero?
Use a negative value?
Change state after approval?
Send requests simultaneously?

docs.title: Five Useful Logic Threat Models
docs.text:
PRICING

Protect:
Money

Test:
Price
Quantity
Discount
Currency
Tax
Shipping
Payment amount

ACCOUNT RECOVERY

Protect:
Account

Test:
Token lifecycle
Step skipping
Account binding
Token reuse
State transitions

APPROVAL

Protect:
Business decision

Test:
Self-approval
Approval levels
Step skipping
Post-approval modification
Separation of duties

BOOKING

Protect:
Limited resource

Test:
Availability
Capacity
Reservation expiration
Payment
Concurrency
State transitions

SUBSCRIPTION

Protect:
Entitlements

Test:
Plan restrictions
Trials
Usage limits
Cancellation
Upgrade/downgrade
Feature access

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Business logic testing usually requires fewer specialised tools than injection testing.

Useful tools include:

Burp Suite
Burp Proxy
Burp Repeater
Burp Comparer
Burp Sequencer
Turbo Intruder
Browser Developer Tools
API documentation
Application documentation

The most important tool remains:

Understanding the business process

docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities:

https://portswigger.net/web-security/logic-flaws

PortSwigger provides practical examples covering flawed assumptions, excessive trust in client-side controls, inconsistent input handling, workflow bypasses and other application logic vulnerabilities.

docs.title: PortSwigger Race Conditions
docs.text:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/race-conditions

Useful when business rules fail because multiple operations can occur concurrently.

docs.title: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide
docs.text:
https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/

The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide contains testing guidance covering business logic and application workflows.

docs.title: OWASP Business Logic Testing
docs.text:
https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/10-Business_Logic_Testing/README

Useful reference for structured testing of application-specific business rules.

docs.title: Final Business Logic Workflow
docs.text:
Read Scope
    ↓
Understand Application
    ↓
Identify Business Functions
    ↓
Choose High-Value Functions
    ↓
For Each Function:
    ↓
Identify Actors
    ↓
Identify Assets
    ↓
Identify Business Rules
    ↓
Identify Trust Boundaries
    ↓
Map States
    ↓
Map Allowed Transitions
    ↓
Identify Forbidden Transitions
    ↓
Create Abuse Cases
    ↓
Convert Abuse Cases Into Tests
    ↓
Capture Normal Workflow in Burp
    ↓
Establish Baseline
    ↓
Change One Business Assumption
    ↓
Test Server-Side Enforcement
    ↓
Test Sequence
    ↓
Test Replay
    ↓
Test Boundaries
    ↓
Consider Concurrency
    ↓
Validate Business Impact
    ↓
Collect Minimum Necessary Evidence
    ↓
Report the Violated Business Rule

The key principle is:

Business logic testing should follow the business. If the application handles pricing, threat model pricing. If it handles account recovery, threat model recovery. If it handles approvals, threat model the approval process. If it manages bookings, threat model the lifecycle of the reserved resource. Understand the intended rules first, then systematically test whether those rules can be violated.

docs.title: Web Application Pentesting Checklist
docs.text:
This checklist provides a structured reference for web application security assessments.

It is designed to complement the Web Application Testing Methodology and can be used to track areas that have been reviewed during an authorised penetration test.

Authorised Security Testing

Use this checklist only for systems you own or have explicit permission to test.

docs.title: Domain and Infrastructure
docs.text:
• Identify the primary domain
  • Enumerate subdomains
  • Resolve discovered domains
  • Identify live HTTP and HTTPS services
  • Identify exposed ports and services
  • Identify IP addresses and hosting providers
  • Review DNS records
  • Check certificate transparency logs
  • Identify CDN usage
  • Identify reverse proxies
  • Identify WAF protection
  • Search for development and staging environments

docs.title: Historical Discovery
docs.text:
• Search historical URLs
  • Review archived application versions
  • Identify historical parameters
  • Identify deprecated endpoints
  • Search for old API endpoints
  • Look for exposed backup files
  • Review historical JavaScript files

docs.title: Technology Identification
docs.text:
• Identify web server
  • Identify application framework
  • Identify programming language
  • Identify CMS
  • Identify JavaScript frameworks
  • Identify API technologies
  • Identify authentication technologies
  • Identify third-party services
  • Identify exposed software versions
  • Check for outdated components
  • Review HTTP response headers
  • Review error messages for technology disclosure

docs.title: Attack Surface Mapping
docs.text:
• Map applications and sub-applications
  • Map authentication boundaries
  • Identify user roles
  • Identify administrative functionality
  • Identify API endpoints
  • Identify upload functionality
  • Identify download functionality
  • Identify import functionality
  • Identify export functionality
  • Identify search functionality
  • Identify integrations
  • Identify webhooks
  • Identify redirects
  • Identify URL processing functionality

docs.title: Content Discovery
docs.text:
• Enumerate directories
  • Enumerate files
  • Search for hidden endpoints
  • Search for administrative interfaces
  • Search for debug interfaces
  • Search for API documentation
  • Search for Swagger/OpenAPI documentation
  • Search for GraphQL endpoints
  • Search for source maps
  • Search for configuration files
  • Search for backup files
  • Search for temporary files
  • Search for log files
  • Review robots.txt
  • Review sitemap.xml
  • Review .well-known resources

docs.title: Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
• Identify GET parameters
  • Identify POST parameters
  • Identify JSON properties
  • Identify XML input
  • Identify path parameters
  • Identify HTTP header input
  • Identify cookie values
  • Identify multipart form fields
  • Identify file name input
  • Identify hidden form fields
  • Identify WebSocket messages
  • Extract parameters from JavaScript
  • Extract parameters from historical URLs

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
• Collect JavaScript files
  • Review application JavaScript
  • Review minified JavaScript where relevant
  • Search for hidden endpoints
  • Search for API routes
  • Search for parameter names
  • Search for internal URLs
  • Search for hard-coded credentials
  • Search for API keys and tokens
  • Search for sensitive comments
  • Review client-side authentication logic
  • Review client-side authorisation logic
  • Check for source maps
  • Review third-party JavaScript dependencies

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
• Test username enumeration
  • Test password enumeration behaviour
  • Review password policy
  • Test account lockout
  • Test rate limiting
  • Test brute-force protections
  • Test default credentials where applicable
  • Test authentication bypass conditions
  • Compare responses for valid and invalid accounts
  • Test alternative authentication endpoints

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text:
• Test username enumeration
  • Review reset token entropy
  • Test reset token expiration
  • Test reset token reuse
  • Test token invalidation
  • Test host header handling
  • Test password reset poisoning
  • Check whether old sessions remain valid
  • Test account recovery functionality

docs.title: Multi-Factor Authentication
docs.text:
• Verify MFA is enforced
  • Test MFA workflow bypass
  • Test direct access after primary authentication
  • Test code reuse
  • Test rate limiting
  • Test recovery mechanisms
  • Test trusted-device functionality
  • Test session state before MFA completion

docs.title: SSO and OAuth
docs.text:
• Identify supported identity providers
  • Review redirect URI validation
  • Review state handling
  • Review nonce handling
  • Test account linking
  • Test authentication flow manipulation
  • Review token exposure
  • Review logout behaviour

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
• Identify different user roles
  • Compare functionality between roles
  • Test horizontal privilege escalation
  • Test vertical privilege escalation
  • Test IDOR/BOLA
  • Modify object identifiers
  • Test forced browsing
  • Test administrative endpoints
  • Test hidden functionality
  • Test role parameter manipulation
  • Test HTTP method changes
  • Test API authorisation independently
  • Test access after account state changes
  • Verify server-side access controls

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
• Review session cookie attributes
  • Check Secure
  • Check HttpOnly
  • Check SameSite
  • Review session token entropy
  • Test session fixation
  • Test session expiration
  • Test idle timeout
  • Test logout invalidation
  • Test password-change invalidation
  • Test password-reset invalidation
  • Test concurrent sessions
  • Test session replay
  • Review remember-me tokens
  • Review JWT implementation where applicable

docs.title: Cross-Site Scripting
docs.text:
• Test reflected input
  • Test stored input
  • Test DOM-based input
  • Identify reflection contexts
  • Review HTML context
  • Review attribute context
  • Review JavaScript context
  • Review URL context
  • Review DOM sinks
  • Review sanitisation
  • Review encoding
  • Review Content Security Policy
  • Test file names and metadata where displayed
  • Test client-side rendering

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
• Identify database-backed parameters
  • Test query parameters
  • Test POST parameters
  • Test JSON input
  • Test cookies where relevant
  • Test headers where relevant
  • Check error behaviour
  • Test Boolean-based behaviour
  • Test time-based behaviour
  • Test UNION conditions where appropriate
  • Review second-order input
  • Determine database technology where possible

docs.title: Command Injection
docs.text:
• Identify functionality interacting with operating system commands
  • Test user-controlled command arguments
  • Test file-processing functionality
  • Test network utilities exposed through the application
  • Test asynchronous processing
  • Review command output handling
  • Review blind execution indicators
  • Review shell metacharacter handling
  • Review input sanitisation

docs.title: Server-Side Request Forgery
docs.text:
• Identify URL parameters
  • Identify webhook functionality
  • Identify URL preview functionality
  • Identify import-by-URL functionality
  • Identify image or document fetching
  • Test redirect handling
  • Test protocol restrictions
  • Test hostname validation
  • Test IP address validation
  • Review DNS resolution behaviour
  • Test internal resource access within authorised scope
  • Review blind SSRF indicators

docs.title: Server-Side Template Injection
docs.text:
• Identify dynamically rendered templates
  • Determine template engine where possible
  • Test whether expressions are evaluated
  • Review user-controlled template values
  • Review email/template functionality
  • Review document generation
  • Review error messages
  • Determine sandbox restrictions where applicable

docs.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery
docs.text:
• Identify state-changing requests
  • Review CSRF tokens
  • Test missing CSRF tokens
  • Test token validation
  • Test token reuse
  • Review SameSite cookie configuration
  • Review Origin validation
  • Review Referer validation
  • Test alternate content types where applicable
  • Review sensitive account actions

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
• Identify all upload functionality
  • Review allowed file extensions
  • Review MIME type validation
  • Review file signature validation
  • Review file size restrictions
  • Review file name handling
  • Test duplicate file names
  • Test special characters in file names
  • Review storage location
  • Determine whether uploaded files are publicly accessible
  • Review content transformation
  • Review image processing
  • Review document processing
  • Review archive extraction
  • Check for path traversal in file names
  • Verify uploaded content is served safely

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
• Identify file retrieval functionality
  • Identify download parameters
  • Identify template or resource parameters
  • Review path normalisation
  • Review encoded path handling
  • Review absolute and relative path handling
  • Review filename validation
  • Review archive extraction paths
  • Test traversal within the authorised environment

docs.title: XML External Entity Injection
docs.text:
• Identify XML endpoints
  • Identify SOAP services
  • Identify XML file uploads
  • Identify document parsers
  • Review external entity processing
  • Review DTD processing
  • Review parser configuration
  • Review error behaviour
  • Review out-of-band behaviour where authorised

docs.title: Deserialization
docs.text:
• Identify serialized data
  • Identify encoded object structures
  • Review cookies
  • Review hidden parameters
  • Review API payloads
  • Identify serialization technology
  • Review integrity protections
  • Review type handling
  • Review application libraries
  • Review unsafe deserialization patterns

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggling
docs.text:
• Identify reverse proxy architecture
  • Compare frontend and backend parsing
  • Review Content-Length handling
  • Review Transfer-Encoding handling
  • Test ambiguous requests only where explicitly authorised
  • Review HTTP/1.1 behaviour
  • Review HTTP/2 translation
  • Check for response desynchronisation indicators

docs.title: Business Logic
docs.text:
• Understand intended workflow
  • Test steps out of sequence
  • Test repeated actions
  • Test skipped steps
  • Test negative values
  • Test unusual quantities
  • Test boundary values
  • Test price calculations
  • Test discounts and coupons
  • Test account state transitions
  • Test approval workflows
  • Test race conditions
  • Test trust assumptions between components

docs.title: API Security
docs.text:
• Discover API endpoints
  • Identify API versions
  • Review API documentation
  • Review authentication
  • Test BOLA/IDOR
  • Test function-level authorisation
  • Review excessive data exposure
  • Review mass assignment
  • Review input validation
  • Review rate limiting
  • Review pagination
  • Review filtering
  • Review error handling
  • Test undocumented endpoints
  • Review deprecated API versions

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
• Identify GraphQL endpoint
  • Review introspection
  • Map available queries
  • Map mutations
  • Review object-level authorisation
  • Review field-level authorisation
  • Review excessive data exposure
  • Review batching
  • Review query depth controls
  • Review complexity limits

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
• Identify WebSocket endpoints
  • Review authentication
  • Review authorisation
  • Review Origin validation
  • Inspect messages
  • Modify messages
  • Test input validation
  • Review session handling
  • Test Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking conditions

docs.title: HTTP Security Headers
docs.text:
Review:

  • Content-Security-Policy
  • Strict-Transport-Security
  • X-Content-Type-Options
  • Referrer-Policy
  • Permissions-Policy
  • Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy
  • Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy
  • Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
  • Cache-Control where sensitive content is present

Also review obsolete or ineffective header configurations where encountered.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
• Review Access-Control-Allow-Origin
  • Test Origin reflection
  • Review credential support
  • Review trusted origins
  • Review null Origin behaviour
  • Review subdomain trust
  • Review preflight behaviour
  • Determine whether sensitive responses are accessible cross-origin

docs.title: Information Disclosure
docs.text:
• Review HTTP headers
  • Review verbose errors
  • Review stack traces
  • Review software versions
  • Review internal hostnames
  • Review internal IP addresses
  • Review source maps
  • Review comments
  • Review JavaScript
  • Review metadata
  • Review debug endpoints
  • Review API responses for excessive data
  • Review publicly accessible files
  • Review directory listings

docs.title: TLS and Transport Security
docs.text:
• Verify HTTPS enforcement
  • Review supported TLS versions
  • Review cipher suites
  • Review certificate validity
  • Review certificate hostname coverage
  • Review HSTS
  • Check for mixed content
  • Review insecure redirects
  • Review sensitive data transmitted over insecure channels

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• Trigger application errors safely
  • Review stack traces
  • Review database errors
  • Review framework errors
  • Review filesystem paths
  • Review internal hostnames
  • Review debugging information
  • Compare authenticated and unauthenticated errors

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
For each potential finding:

  • Reproduce the behaviour
  • Confirm the affected endpoint
  • Confirm affected parameters
  • Determine required privileges
  • Determine required user interaction
  • Determine affected users
  • Determine realistic impact
  • Check related endpoints
  • Check whether the issue can be chained
  • Capture sufficient evidence
  • Remove test artefacts where applicable

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
For each confirmed finding:

  • Write a clear title
  • Describe the vulnerability
  • Identify the affected component
  • Document prerequisites
  • Document reproduction steps
  • Include relevant HTTP evidence
  • Include screenshots where useful
  • Explain technical impact
  • Explain realistic business impact
  • Assign severity
  • Provide remediation guidance
  • Include relevant references

docs.title: Retesting
docs.text:
• Reproduce the original test
  • Verify the original vulnerability is resolved
  • Test related endpoints
  • Test alternative inputs
  • Verify server-side enforcement
  • Check for bypasses
  • Check for regression
  • Record retest evidence
  • Update finding status

docs.title: Assessment Completion
docs.text:
Before completing the assessment:

  • Review the original scope
  • Confirm all in-scope applications were assessed
  • Review notes for untested functionality
  • Review scanner results requiring manual validation
  • Review discovered endpoints
  • Review discovered parameters
  • Review all user roles
  • Review evidence
  • Remove testing artefacts
  • Verify findings are reproducible
  • Complete final report

docs.title: Clickjacking
docs.text:
Clickjacking is a client-side attack in which a user is tricked into interacting with an application element that is hidden, transparent or visually disguised beneath attacker-controlled content.

The victim believes they are clicking one element:

Visible Attacker-Controlled Page
             ↓
        "Click Here"

but their click is actually delivered to another application:

Visible Attacker-Controlled Page
             ↓
Transparent / Hidden iframe
             ↓
Target Application
             ↓
Sensitive Action

Clickjacking is sometimes referred to as:

UI redressing
User interface redressing
Frame-based UI manipulation

The vulnerability normally exists when a sensitive application can be embedded inside another website without sufficient framing protections.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform Clickjacking testing only against applications included in the authorised assessment scope. Use controlled accounts and harmless actions for proof-of-concept testing. Do not cause actions on behalf of real users.

docs.title: How Clickjacking Works
docs.text:
Consider an application containing:

<button>Delete Account</button>

The application may require the user to be authenticated before this button is available.

An attacker cannot necessarily submit the action directly because protections such as:

Authentication
Session cookies
CSRF tokens

may prevent direct request forgery.

However, if the application can be loaded inside an iframe, an attacker may attempt to place the legitimate interface underneath another element.

Conceptually:

Attacker Page
      ↓
Loads Target in iframe
      ↓
iframe Positioned Over Decoy Content
      ↓
Victim Clicks Decoy
      ↓
Click Reaches Target Application
      ↓
Authenticated Action Occurs

The browser performs the action using the victim's existing authenticated session where cookie and browser policies permit it.

docs.title: Basic Clickjacking Architecture
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Attacker-Controlled Page             │
│                                      │
│       Click to continue              │
│              ↓                       │
│ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ Transparent iframe              │ │
│ │                                  │ │
│ │ Target Application               │ │
│ │                                  │ │
│ │       Sensitive Button           │ │
│ └──────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘

The iframe may be:

Transparent
Nearly transparent
Positioned absolutely
Resized
Layered using z-index
Aligned with another element

The attacker attempts to make the user interact with the underlying application without understanding what they are actually clicking.

docs.title: Clickjacking Preconditions
docs.text:
Several conditions usually need to be present.

Target can be framed
        ↓
Victim can authenticate to target
        ↓
Sensitive UI exists
        ↓
UI can be positioned predictably
        ↓
Victim interaction performs action

Important questions include:

Can the target page be loaded in an iframe?

Does authentication remain available inside the iframe?

Does the browser send the required cookies?

Can a meaningful action be triggered with a click?

Does the application require additional confirmation?

Are framing protections present?

docs.title: Initial Testing
docs.text:
The first test is simple:

Can the page be framed?

Create a minimal local HTML page:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Clickjacking Test</title>
</head>
<body>

<h1>Clickjacking Test</h1>

<iframe
    src="https://target.example/"
    width="1200"
    height="800">
</iframe>

</body>
</html>

Open the page in a browser.

Possible results:

Target loads normally
Target refuses to load
Browser displays framing error
Target redirects elsewhere
Authentication disappears
Target loads but session is unavailable

docs.title: Minimal Proof of Concept
docs.text:
For an authorised assessment, begin with a visible iframe.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Clickjacking PoC</title>
</head>
<body>

<h1>Authorised Clickjacking Test</h1>

<iframe
    src="https://target.example/account"
    width="1200"
    height="800"
    style="border: 3px solid;">
</iframe>

</body>
</html>

Do not immediately make the iframe transparent.

First establish:

Can it be framed?
Does authentication work?
Does the target render correctly?

docs.title: Transparent iframe Test
docs.text:
Once framing has been confirmed, transparency can demonstrate the underlying Clickjacking condition.

Example:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Clickjacking PoC</title>

    <style>
        iframe {
            position: absolute;
            width: 1000px;
            height: 700px;
            opacity: 0.2;
            z-index: 2;
        }

        .decoy {
            position: absolute;
            top: 200px;
            left: 300px;
            z-index: 1;
        }
    </style>
</head>

<body>

<div class="decoy">
    <button>Click Here</button>
</div>

<iframe src="https://target.example/account"></iframe>

</body>
</html>

During development, keep the iframe partially visible:

opacity: 0.2;

This makes alignment easier to verify.

For a controlled proof of concept, the purpose is to demonstrate that an authenticated interface can be overlaid and interacted with.

docs.title: CSS Positioning
docs.text:
Typical Clickjacking demonstrations rely on CSS properties such as:

position
top
left
width
height
opacity
z-index

Example:

iframe {
    position: absolute;
    top: 0;
    left: 0;
    width: 1000px;
    height: 700px;
    opacity: 0.1;
    z-index: 2;
}

The important security issue is not the CSS itself.

The issue is:

Can an untrusted origin embed the sensitive application?

docs.title: Frameability Test
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Interesting Page
      ↓
Inspect Response Headers
      ↓
Check X-Frame-Options
      ↓
Check CSP frame-ancestors
      ↓
Attempt iframe
      ↓
Observe Browser Behaviour
      ↓
Test Authenticated State
      ↓
Identify Sensitive UI

docs.title: X-Frame-Options
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options is a response header designed to restrict framing.

Common values are:

X-Frame-Options: DENY

and:

X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

docs.title: DENY
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options: DENY

means the page should not be displayed in a frame.

Conceptually:

Any Parent Origin
       ↓
Attempt to Frame
       ↓
Browser Blocks

docs.title: SAMEORIGIN
docs.text:
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

allows framing only when the relevant origin requirements are satisfied.

Conceptually:

Same Origin
    ↓
Allowed

Different Origin
    ↓
Blocked

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Modern applications can control framing using CSP:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';

or:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

docs.title: frame-ancestors 'none'
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';

prevents the resource from being embedded in framing contexts.

This is conceptually similar to:

X-Frame-Options: DENY

docs.title: frame-ancestors 'self'
docs.text:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

restricts framing to the same origin.

docs.title: Allowing Specific Origins
docs.text:
Applications that legitimately require framing can define explicit trusted origins.

Conceptually:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted.example;

The policy should be as restrictive as the application's business requirements allow.

docs.title: CSP frame-src vs frame-ancestors
docs.text:
Do not confuse:

frame-src

with:

frame-ancestors

They solve different problems.

frame-src controls:

What this page may load inside frames

while frame-ancestors controls:

Which pages may embed this page

For Clickjacking protection, the relevant directive is:

frame-ancestors

docs.title: Checking Headers with Burp Suite
docs.text:
Browse to the target page through Burp Proxy.

Inspect the response.

Look for:

X-Frame-Options:

and:

Content-Security-Policy:

For CSP, specifically inspect:

frame-ancestors

Example:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

This indicates explicit framing protection.

docs.title: Missing Framing Headers
docs.text:
A response such as:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

with neither:

X-Frame-Options

nor:

CSP frame-ancestors

is worth investigating.

However:

Missing headers alone do not automatically demonstrate an exploitable Clickjacking vulnerability.

You should verify actual browser behaviour.

docs.title: curl Header Check
docs.text:
You can inspect headers using:

curl -I https://target.example/

or:

curl -s -D - -o /dev/null https://target.example/

Look for:

X-Frame-Options
Content-Security-Policy

docs.title: Testing Multiple Pages
docs.text:
Do not test only:

/

Framing policies may differ between endpoints.

Test security-sensitive pages such as:

/account
/profile
/settings
/preferences
/security
/admin
/dashboard
/payment
/checkout
/delete
/oauth

For example:

/                  → Protected
/account           → Protected
/profile/edit      → Missing protection
/settings/security → Missing protection

A single sensitive endpoint without framing protection may still be important.

docs.title: Authentication and Clickjacking
docs.text:
A Clickjacking vulnerability becomes more interesting when the target remains authenticated inside the iframe.

Test with a controlled account:

Login Normally
      ↓
Open Clickjacking PoC
      ↓
Target Loads in iframe
      ↓
Check Authentication State

Possible outcomes:

Authenticated
Unauthenticated
Redirected to login
Blocked by browser
Cookies unavailable

docs.title: SameSite Cookies
docs.text:
Modern cookie behaviour can influence Clickjacking.

A session cookie may use:

SameSite=Strict

SameSite=Lax

or:

SameSite=None; Secure

Whether the cookie is available in a cross-site iframe depends on browser cookie policies and the deployment context.

Therefore:

Do not determine Clickjacking exploitability solely from framing headers.

Test the real browser behaviour.

docs.title: Third-Party Cookie Restrictions
docs.text:
Modern browsers increasingly restrict third-party cookies.

This can affect traditional Clickjacking scenarios because the framed target may not receive the victim's authenticated session.

However:

Browser behaviour
Cookie attributes
Same-site relationships
Deployment architecture
Storage partitioning

can all influence the result.

Always test with the browsers relevant to the assessment.

docs.title: Clickjacking and CSRF
docs.text:
Clickjacking and Cross-Site Request Forgery are different vulnerabilities.

CSRF:

Attacker Causes Request
        ↓
Victim Browser Sends Request
        ↓
Application Processes Action

Clickjacking:

Attacker Frames Application
        ↓
Victim Physically Clicks
        ↓
Click Reaches Legitimate Interface
        ↓
Application Processes Action

A CSRF token may prevent traditional CSRF while Clickjacking remains possible.

Why?

Because the user is interacting with the legitimate application itself.

The legitimate page already contains the required token.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

docs.title: Clickjacking With CSRF Protection
docs.text:
Consider:

<form action="/account/delete" method="POST">

<input
    type="hidden"
    name="csrf"
    value="RANDOM-TOKEN">

<button>Delete Account</button>

</form>

An attacker may not know:

RANDOM-TOKEN

Therefore direct CSRF could fail.

But if the legitimate page can be framed:

Target Page
    ↓
Contains Valid CSRF Token
    ↓
Victim Clicks Legitimate Button
    ↓
Valid Request Submitted

This demonstrates why CSRF protection does not replace anti-framing controls.

docs.title: Sensitive Actions
docs.text:
Prioritise pages containing actions such as:

Change email
Change profile information
Modify privacy settings
Enable features
Disable features
Delete content
Create resources
Submit forms
Approve requests
Confirm operations
Modify subscriptions
Change notification settings

For proof-of-concept testing, use the least destructive action available.

docs.title: Clickjacking Testing by Business Logic
docs.text:
Do not test Clickjacking as simply:

Does iframe work?

Instead ask:

What business actions become possible if framing works?

Examples follow.

docs.title: Account Settings
docs.text:
Suppose the application allows:

Change display name
Change email
Modify profile visibility

If the settings page can be framed:

Attacker Page
      ↓
Victim Click
      ↓
Settings Button
      ↓
Account State Changes

Use a harmless profile modification with a controlled account to demonstrate the condition.

docs.title: Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
If an administrative interface can be framed, the impact may be greater.

Possible actions include:

Approve user
Disable user
Change configuration
Modify permissions
Publish content
Approve request

Do not perform destructive administrative actions.

Use a safe test action or stop once sufficient evidence exists.

docs.title: Financial Applications
docs.text:
Potential actions include:

Add beneficiary
Modify payment preference
Select subscription
Confirm purchase
Change billing setting

Financial actions can have real consequences.

Testing should use:

Test environments
Controlled accounts
Sandbox transactions
Explicitly authorised actions

docs.title: SaaS Applications
docs.text:
Interesting actions include:

Invite user
Create project
Change workspace settings
Enable integration
Generate API configuration
Modify notifications

Again, the objective is to demonstrate UI redressing, not to cause operational impact.

docs.title: Multi-Step Clickjacking
docs.text:
Some actions require multiple clicks.

Example:

Open Settings
      ↓
Click Security
      ↓
Click Disable
      ↓
Click Confirm

An attacker may theoretically attempt to guide a victim through multiple interactions.

This is known as:

Multi-step Clickjacking

For assessment purposes, demonstrate only as much interaction as is required to prove impact.

docs.title: Clickjacking With Form Input
docs.text:
Some actions require text input before submission.

A basic Clickjacking attack becomes more difficult when the victim must provide unpredictable data.

However, browser UI manipulation may sometimes combine:

Typing
Focus changes
Clicks
Keyboard navigation

Do not assume every form is exploitable simply because it can be framed.

Evaluate the complete interaction.

docs.title: Prepopulated Forms
docs.text:
Applications may prepopulate sensitive forms.

Example:

Email: user@example.com
Privacy: Public

If only a single click is required to submit a state change, Clickjacking may be more practical.

docs.title: Clickjacking and Confirmation Dialogues
docs.text:
A confirmation step can reduce exploitability.

Example:

Delete Account
      ↓
Are you sure?
      ↓
Confirm

But it does not necessarily eliminate Clickjacking if both interactions can be manipulated.

Evaluate:

Number of interactions
Predictability of UI
Placement
Timing
Additional authentication

docs.title: Reauthentication
docs.text:
Sensitive operations may require:

Password
MFA
Passkey
Security key
One-time code

Reauthentication significantly changes the practical impact of Clickjacking.

Document this clearly.

For example:

Page can be framed
but
sensitive action requires password re-entry

This should influence severity.

docs.title: Frame Busting
docs.text:
Some applications use JavaScript to attempt to prevent framing.

Historical examples include logic conceptually similar to:

if (top !== self) {
    top.location = self.location;
}

This is often called:

Frame busting

JavaScript-based frame busting should not be considered a strong replacement for browser-enforced policies such as:

CSP frame-ancestors
X-Frame-Options

docs.title: Why Frame-Busting JavaScript Is Weaker
docs.text:
Client-side scripts depend on:

JavaScript execution
Browser behaviour
Page loading order
Framing conditions
Implementation correctness

Browser-enforced response headers are more appropriate security controls.

docs.title: Nested Frames
docs.text:
Applications may use legitimate framing internally.

Example:

Parent Application
      ↓
Trusted iframe
      ↓
Embedded Component

Before recommending:

frame-ancestors 'none'

understand whether framing is part of the application's architecture.

The correct policy may instead allow explicitly trusted origins.

docs.title: Cross-Origin Framing
docs.text:
The central Clickjacking trust boundary is often:

Trusted Application
        ↓
Embedded by
        ↓
Untrusted Origin

For example:

target.example

should generally not be frameable by:

attacker.example

unless this is intentionally supported.

docs.title: Same-Origin Framing
docs.text:
Some applications intentionally frame their own content.

A policy such as:

X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

or:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

can permit this design while preventing arbitrary third-party framing.

docs.title: Subdomain Considerations
docs.text:
Suppose an organisation uses:

app.example.com
portal.example.com
support.example.com

Do not automatically assume all subdomains should be allowed to frame each other.

Different subdomains may have different trust levels.

Consider:

User-generated content
Third-party hosted subdomains
Legacy applications
Marketing systems
Support platforms

The framing policy should reflect actual trust boundaries.

docs.title: CSP Policy Review
docs.text:
When reviewing:

Content-Security-Policy:

identify:

frame-ancestors

Example:

Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    frame-ancestors 'self';

For Clickjacking, the important portion is:

frame-ancestors 'self'

docs.title: Multiple CSP Policies
docs.text:
Applications may return multiple CSP headers.

Do not inspect only one line and assume the effective policy.

Use browser Developer Tools and actual framing tests to confirm behaviour.

docs.title: Report-Only CSP
docs.text:
Be careful with:

Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only:

A report-only policy does not enforce the restriction.

For example:

Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: frame-ancestors 'none';

should not be treated as equivalent to:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none';

Verify the enforcing policy.

docs.title: X-Frame-Options and CSP Together
docs.text:
Applications may return both:

X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

and:

Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';

This can provide compatibility across different browser environments.

Modern browsers support CSP frame-ancestors, while X-Frame-Options remains common as an additional defence.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

Burp Proxy
     ↓
Browse Application
     ↓
HTTP History
     ↓
Identify Sensitive Pages
     ↓
Inspect Response Headers
     ↓
Check X-Frame-Options
     ↓
Check CSP frame-ancestors
     ↓
Build Visible iframe Test
     ↓
Open in Browser
     ↓
Test Authenticated Session
     ↓
Identify Safe Action
     ↓
Build Controlled PoC
     ↓
Document Result

docs.title: Burp Response Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose Burp shows:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Set-Cookie: session=...

but no:

X-Frame-Options:

and no:

frame-ancestors

This should trigger a framing test.

Do not report based solely on the headers.

docs.title: Browser Developer Tools
docs.text:
Developer Tools can help identify why a frame does not load.

Inspect:

Console
Network
Application
Elements

The Console may show browser messages relating to:

X-Frame-Options
CSP
frame-ancestors
Cookie restrictions
Cross-origin behaviour

docs.title: Console Example
docs.text:
When framing is blocked, the browser may report that the page refused to display because of:

X-Frame-Options

or:

Content Security Policy

The exact message varies by browser.

docs.title: Clickjacking PoC Development
docs.text:
A good development process is:

1. Start with visible iframe

2. Confirm target loads

3. Confirm authenticated state

4. Resize iframe

5. Identify target element coordinates

6. Position decoy content

7. Reduce opacity gradually

8. Verify alignment

9. Use harmless action

10. Capture evidence

This is much more reliable than immediately creating an invisible frame.

docs.title: Example Controlled PoC
docs.text:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">

<head>

<meta charset="UTF-8">

<title>Authorised Clickjacking Test</title>

<style>

body {
    font-family: sans-serif;
}

.target-frame {
    position: absolute;
    top: 100px;
    left: 100px;
    width: 1000px;
    height: 700px;
    opacity: 0.25;
    z-index: 2;
}

.decoy {
    position: absolute;
    top: 250px;
    left: 300px;
    z-index: 1;
}

</style>

</head>

<body>

<h1>Authorised Clickjacking Test</h1>

<div class="decoy">
    <button>Test Button</button>
</div>

<iframe
    class="target-frame"
    src="https://target.example/account">
</iframe>

</body>

</html>

During an authorised test, adjust:

top
left
width
height

to match the controlled target page.

docs.title: Serving the PoC Locally
docs.text:
You can save the proof of concept as:

clickjacking-poc.html

and open it directly in the browser.

If browser behaviour requires an HTTP origin, you can serve the directory locally:

python3 -m http.server 8000

Then browse to:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/clickjacking-poc.html

This is useful for controlled local testing.

docs.title: Testing Different Viewports
docs.text:
Clickjacking alignment can depend on:

Screen resolution
Browser window size
Zoom level
Responsive layout
Mobile layout
Application state

This affects practical exploitability.

A PoC that works only at one exact resolution may be less reliable than one targeting a stable interface element.

docs.title: Responsive Applications
docs.text:
Modern applications may reposition buttons based on:

Viewport width
Viewport height
Device type
Navigation state

Test whether the sensitive control has a predictable position.

docs.title: Scroll Position
docs.text:
The target element may not initially be visible.

Clickjacking scenarios can be affected by:

iframe scroll position
Page scrolling
Sticky navigation
Responsive components
Dynamic content

Document any interaction required before the sensitive control becomes reachable.

docs.title: Dynamic Interfaces
docs.text:
Single-page applications may load elements asynchronously.

Example:

iframe loads
    ↓
API request
    ↓
UI renders
    ↓
Button appears

Timing can affect alignment.

Do not assume a static HTML proof of concept accurately represents every interaction.

docs.title: Clickjacking and SPA Applications
docs.text:
Applications built using:

React
Angular
Vue
Next.js
Single-page application frameworks

are still subject to framing protections.

The framework itself does not prevent Clickjacking.

Check the HTTP response headers delivered by:

Application
Reverse proxy
CDN
Web server

docs.title: Clickjacking and APIs
docs.text:
Pure JSON APIs generally do not provide clickable user interfaces.

Therefore traditional Clickjacking is primarily relevant to browser-rendered pages.

However, an API-backed web interface may still be vulnerable through its frontend.

docs.title: Clickjacking and CORS
docs.text:
CORS and Clickjacking address different browser security mechanisms.

CORS controls whether scripts from another origin can read certain cross-origin responses.

Clickjacking concerns whether an application can be visually embedded and interacted with.

Therefore:

Strict CORS

does not automatically prevent:

Clickjacking

Refer to:

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

once that page is added.

docs.title: Clickjacking and SOP
docs.text:
The Same-Origin Policy can prevent an attacker from reading the contents of a cross-origin iframe.

However, Clickjacking does not necessarily require reading the frame.

Conceptually:

Cannot Read iframe
        ≠
Cannot Overlay iframe

This distinction is fundamental to understanding Clickjacking.

docs.title: Testing Administrative Actions Safely
docs.text:
If the application contains administrative functionality, avoid destructive tests.

Prefer actions such as:

Open tab
Change harmless preference
Toggle test setting
Select non-destructive option
Modify controlled test object

If simply demonstrating that the sensitive page is frameable is sufficient under the assessment methodology, stop there.

docs.title: Business Impact Analysis
docs.text:
The severity should be based on what an attacker can realistically cause.

Consider:

Is authentication required?

Does the session work inside the frame?

What action can be triggered?

How many clicks are required?

Is reauthentication required?

Is MFA required?

Does the action have material impact?

Is the UI predictable?

Does browser cookie policy interfere?

Can a realistic victim reach the vulnerable state?

docs.title: Weak Clickjacking Finding
docs.text:
Example:

Public informational page can be framed

with no sensitive actions.

This may have little or no security impact.

docs.title: Stronger Clickjacking Finding
docs.text:
Example:

Authenticated account settings page can be framed
        ↓
Session remains authenticated
        ↓
Sensitive state-changing control is predictable
        ↓
No reauthentication required
        ↓
Controlled action succeeds

This provides much stronger evidence.

docs.title: Do Not Report Headers Alone
docs.text:
Avoid findings such as:

Missing X-Frame-Options

without analysing impact.

A better approach is:

1. Identify missing anti-framing controls

2. Verify target can actually be framed

3. Determine whether authentication survives

4. Identify sensitive interaction

5. Demonstrate controlled impact

6. Report the resulting Clickjacking condition

docs.title: Testing Matrix
docs.text:
Create a matrix:

Endpoint X-Frame-Options frame-ancestors Frames? Authenticated? Sensitive Action / Missing Missing Yes N/A No /login Missing Missing Yes N/A No /account Missing Missing Yes Yes Yes /security SAMEORIGIN 'self' No N/A Yes /admin DENY 'none' No N/A Yes

This provides much better assessment coverage than checking only the home page.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
[ ] Identify sensitive pages
[ ] Identify sensitive buttons
[ ] Identify state-changing actions
[ ] Check authentication requirements
[ ] Check confirmation requirements
[ ] Check reauthentication requirements

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
[ ] Check X-Frame-Options
[ ] Check CSP
[ ] Check frame-ancestors
[ ] Check Report-Only CSP
[ ] Check policies on individual endpoints

docs.title: Browser Testing
docs.text:
[ ] Create visible iframe
