Reference documentation for the HTTP Host request header.

docs.title: Final Host Header Testing Model
docs.text:
HTTP REQUEST
                         ↓
                  HOST INFORMATION
                         ↓
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       ↓                 ↓                 ↓
      Host        X-Forwarded-Host      Forwarded
       ↓                 ↓                 ↓
       └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                         ↓
                 WHO TRUSTS THE VALUE?
                         ↓
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       ↓                 ↓                 ↓
   Application         Proxy              Cache
       ↓                 ↓                 ↓
       └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                         ↓
                  HOW IS IT USED?
                         ↓
    ┌──────────┬─────────┼─────────┬──────────┐
    ↓          ↓         ↓         ↓          ↓
 Password    Cache     Routing   Access     Tenant
 Reset                           Control    Selection
    ↓          ↓         ↓         ↓          ↓
 Token      Poison     SSRF      Bypass     Boundary
 Exposure
    ↓          ↓         ↓         ↓          ↓
    └──────────┴─────────┼─────────┴──────────┘
                         ↓
                SECURITY IMPACT?
                         ↓
                        YES
                         ↓
                  VERIFY SAFELY
                         ↓
                    DOCUMENT
                         ↓
                      REPORT

The key principle is:

The Host header and related forwarding headers are attacker-controlled input unless trusted infrastructure has explicitly normalised them. Host header testing should therefore focus on where that input crosses a security boundary, such as password reset URL generation, cache behaviour, backend routing, internal virtual hosts, access control or tenant selection.

docs.title: HTML Injection
docs.text:
HTML Injection occurs when attacker-controlled input is inserted into an HTML document without appropriate output encoding or sanitisation.

Unlike Cross-Site Scripting, HTML Injection does not necessarily require JavaScript execution.

A vulnerable application may allow an attacker to inject arbitrary HTML elements that alter:

Page content
Page structure
Links
Forms
Images
Headings
User interface elements
Displayed information

A simplified flow is:

User-Controlled Input
        ↓
Application
        ↓
Input Returned or Stored
        ↓
HTML Response
        ↓
Browser Parses Injected Markup
        ↓
Page Content Modified

HTML Injection can therefore be useful both as a vulnerability in its own right and as an indication that output handling should be investigated further for Cross-Site Scripting.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform HTML Injection testing only against applications included in the authorised assessment scope. Start with harmless visual markers and avoid deceptive forms, external content or actions that could affect real users.

docs.title: HTML Injection vs XSS
docs.text:
HTML Injection and Cross-Site Scripting are closely related, but they are not identical.

HTML Injection:

Attacker Input
      ↓
HTML Parsing
      ↓
Page Structure Changes

Cross-Site Scripting:

Attacker Input
      ↓
Browser Execution Context
      ↓
JavaScript Execution

For example:

<h1>HTML-INJECTION-TEST</h1>

may demonstrate HTML Injection.

It does not by itself demonstrate JavaScript execution.

The distinction is important when reporting findings.

Do not report:

Cross-Site Scripting

when the demonstrated behaviour is only:

HTML Injection

docs.title: Why HTML Injection Matters
docs.text:
Even without JavaScript execution, injected HTML may affect the security and integrity of an application.

Potential consequences include:

Page content manipulation
UI manipulation
Misleading information
Link injection
Form injection
Content spoofing
Brand impersonation
Phishing opportunities
User confusion
Security warning suppression
Modification of application presentation

The actual impact depends heavily on where the injection occurs and who can cause other users to view it.

docs.title: Types of HTML Injection
docs.text:
Useful categories include:

Reflected HTML Injection
Stored HTML Injection
DOM-Based HTML Injection
Attribute Injection

docs.title: Reflected HTML Injection
docs.text:
Reflected HTML Injection occurs when input from the request is immediately included in the response.

Example:

GET /search?q=AM-HTML-TEST HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

The response may contain:

<p>Search results for AM-HTML-TEST</p>

Start with a harmless marker:

AM-HTML-987654

Then determine whether HTML syntax is interpreted.

docs.title: Stored HTML Injection
docs.text:
Stored HTML Injection occurs when attacker-controlled HTML is saved and rendered later.

Possible storage locations include:

Profiles
Comments
Support tickets
Product reviews
User descriptions
Messages
Forum posts
Administrative notes
Company names
Address fields
Uploaded file metadata

Conceptually:

Input
 ↓
Database
 ↓
Another Page
 ↓
Browser
 ↓
HTML Parsed

Stored HTML Injection can have greater impact because multiple users may encounter the injected content.

docs.title: DOM-Based HTML Injection
docs.text:
DOM-based HTML Injection occurs when client-side JavaScript places attacker-controlled data into an HTML parsing sink.

Conceptually:

URL / Input
     ↓
JavaScript
     ↓
DOM Sink
     ↓
Browser Parses HTML

Potential sources include:

location.search
location.hash
location.href
document.URL
document.referrer
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage

Potential sinks include:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
document.writeln

Example pattern:

element.innerHTML = userInput;

The security question is:

Can attacker-controlled data reach the HTML sink without safe handling?

docs.title: Attribute Injection
docs.text:
User input may appear inside an existing HTML attribute.

Example:

<input value="USER_INPUT">

or:

<a href="USER_INPUT">Continue</a>

or:

<div title="USER_INPUT">

The relevant context is different from normal HTML body content.

Always determine exactly where the input appears.

docs.title: Context Matters
docs.text:
Before testing, identify the rendering context.

Possible contexts include:

HTML body
HTML attribute
URL attribute
HTML comment
Script block
Style block
DOM property
Template

Example body context:

<div>
USER_INPUT
</div>

Attribute context:

<input value="USER_INPUT">

URL context:

<a href="USER_INPUT">

Comment context:

<!-- USER_INPUT -->

Different contexts require different security controls.

docs.title: Start With a Marker
docs.text:
Always begin with a unique harmless marker.

Example:

AM-HTML-987654

Submit it to the application.

Then determine:

Is it reflected?

Is it stored?

Where is it rendered?

Is it encoded?

Is it inside an attribute?

Is it inserted through JavaScript?

Does another user see it?

docs.title: HTML Encoding
docs.text:
A secure application may transform:

<h1>TEST</h1>

into:

<h1>TEST</h1>

The browser displays:

<h1>TEST</h1>

rather than interpreting it as markup.

This is expected output encoding behaviour.

docs.title: Basic Harmless HTML Tests
docs.text:
Once reflection has been confirmed, simple formatting elements can establish whether HTML is interpreted.

Examples:

<b>AM-HTML-TEST</b>

<i>AM-HTML-TEST</i>

<h1>AM-HTML-TEST</h1>

<mark>AM-HTML-TEST</mark>

<small>AM-HTML-TEST</small>

These are preferable as initial tests because they visibly demonstrate HTML interpretation without JavaScript.

docs.title: Structural HTML Tests
docs.text:
You may also use simple structural elements:

<div>AM-HTML-DIV</div>

<p>AM-HTML-PARAGRAPH</p>

<ul>
<li>AM-HTML-ITEM</li>
</ul>

The objective is simply to establish:

Input
 ↓
HTML Parser
 ↓
Rendered Markup

docs.title: Link Injection
docs.text:
A useful controlled test is whether an anchor element can be inserted.

For example:

<a href="https://example.com">AM-HTML-LINK</a>

Using a harmless destination such as example.com avoids directing users to malicious infrastructure.

If rendered, determine:

Is the link clickable?

Can arbitrary destinations be supplied?

Is the link stored?

Can another user see it?

Does the application visually distinguish user content?

docs.title: Image Injection
docs.text:
A controlled image element may help determine whether markup is interpreted.

For example, when external requests are explicitly allowed within scope:

<img src="https://example.com/example.png" alt="AM-HTML-TEST">

However, external resources can generate outbound browser requests.

For many assessments, a simple formatting element is sufficient to demonstrate HTML Injection without introducing external network interaction.

docs.title: Form Injection
docs.text:
HTML Injection may permit forms to be inserted into trusted application pages.

Conceptually:

<form>
  <label>AM HTML Injection Test</label>
  <input type="text">
</form>

This can demonstrate that an attacker may create misleading interface elements.

Avoid creating deceptive login forms or collecting credentials.

The objective is to demonstrate UI manipulation, not to obtain user information.

docs.title: UI Manipulation
docs.text:
HTML Injection can sometimes alter the appearance of trusted content.

For example:

<h2>AM HTML Injection Test</h2>
<p>This text was inserted through user-controlled input.</p>

This demonstrates content injection without pretending to be an application security warning or requesting user action.

docs.title: HTML Injection in Search
docs.text:
Search functionality frequently reflects query values.

Example:

GET /search?q=AM-HTML-987654 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Response:

<h2>Search results for AM-HTML-987654</h2>

Workflow:

Search Parameter
      ↓
Response
      ↓
Locate Reflection
      ↓
Determine Context
      ↓
Test Encoding
      ↓
Test Harmless HTML

docs.title: HTML Injection in Error Messages
docs.text:
Applications may reflect values in errors.

Example:

Unknown account: USER_INPUT

or:

No results found for USER_INPUT

Error pages therefore deserve the same context analysis as normal application pages.

docs.title: HTML Injection in Profiles
docs.text:
Profile fields may include:

First name
Last name
Display name
Biography
Company
Job title
Address
Website

A useful workflow:

Account A
   ↓
Set Unique Marker
   ↓
View Own Profile
   ↓
View from Account B
   ↓
Determine Whether Stored
   ↓
Test Harmless HTML

Two controlled accounts help determine whether the injection affects other users.

docs.title: HTML Injection in Support Systems
docs.text:
Support functionality is particularly interesting because data may cross application boundaries.

Example:

Public Application
       ↓
Support Ticket
       ↓
Database
       ↓
Support Dashboard
       ↓
Support Agent Browser

Fields may include:

Subject
Name
Email
Company
Message
Ticket title
Attachment name

Start with markers rather than markup if an internal user may process the data.

docs.title: HTML Injection in File Names
docs.text:
Uploaded file names may later appear in:

Upload confirmation pages
File managers
Administrative interfaces
Download pages
Audit logs
Document management systems

Example workflow:

File Name
   ↓
Upload
   ↓
Metadata Stored
   ↓
Application Renders File Name

Begin with:

AM-HTML-FILENAME-987654.pdf

Then determine whether special characters are encoded correctly.

docs.title: HTML Injection in Email Templates
docs.text:
User-controlled content may be inserted into HTML email.

Conceptually:

User Input
    ↓
Application
    ↓
HTML Email Template
    ↓
Recipient Mail Client

Examples include:

Display name
Invitation message
Support message
Order information
Notification content

Testing email rendering can affect external recipients, so use only controlled mailboxes and authorised workflows.

docs.title: HTML Injection in PDFs and Generated Documents
docs.text:
Applications may convert user-controlled content into:

PDF
HTML report
Invoice
Receipt
Export
Printable page

The rendering engine may interpret HTML differently from the browser.

Test these workflows separately when they are in scope.

docs.title: HTML Injection in Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
A public input may later appear in an administrative interface.

Conceptually:

Public Input
    ↓
Stored
    ↓
Admin Interface
    ↓
Rendered

This overlaps with Blind XSS methodology.

Start with unique markers and determine where the value appears before attempting any callback-based testing.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A practical Burp workflow:

Proxy
  ↓
Browse Application
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Identify Input
  ↓
Send Request to Repeater
  ↓
Insert Unique Marker
  ↓
Locate Marker in Response
  ↓
Determine HTML Context
  ↓
Test Encoding
  ↓
Insert Harmless HTML
  ↓
Compare Response

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Suppose the baseline request is:

GET /search?q=hello HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Send it to Repeater.

Change:

hello

to:

AM-HTML-987654

Locate the marker in the response.

Then try:

<b>AM-HTML-TEST</b>

If the response contains:

<b>AM-HTML-TEST</b>

and the browser renders it as bold text, HTML interpretation has been demonstrated.

docs.title: Raw Response vs Browser Rendering
docs.text:
Do not rely solely on Burp's raw response.

For example:

<b>AM-HTML-TEST</b>

and:

<b>AM-HTML-TEST</b>

look similar when reading quickly but have completely different browser behaviour.

Always verify:

Raw response
+
Browser rendering

docs.title: Browser Developer Tools
docs.text:
Developer Tools can help determine whether injected markup appears in the DOM.

Inspect:

Elements
Network
Sources
Console

For DOM-based cases, identify whether JavaScript transforms:

Text

into:

HTML

after the original response loads.

docs.title: View Source vs DOM
docs.text:
There is an important distinction between:

View Source

and:

DOM shown in Developer Tools

DOM-based injection may not appear in the original HTTP response.

Conceptually:

Server Response
      ↓
JavaScript Executes
      ↓
DOM Modified

Therefore inspect both.

docs.title: JavaScript Source Review
docs.text:
Search JavaScript for HTML sinks such as:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
document.writeln

Example:

result.innerHTML = searchTerm;

Then trace where:

searchTerm

originates.

docs.title: Source-to-Sink Analysis
docs.text:
A useful model:

SOURCE
  ↓
User-Controlled Data
  ↓
TRANSFORMATIONS
  ↓
HTML SINK
  ↓
BROWSER PARSING

Example:

location.search
      ↓
URLSearchParams
      ↓
searchTerm
      ↓
innerHTML

This is more useful than simply collecting isolated payloads.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Applications may filter:

<
>
"
'
/
=

or particular element names.

Do not immediately conclude that the application is secure.

Determine:

What context is used?

Is output encoding present?

Is sanitisation used?

Is the filter applied consistently?

Does another rendering path exist?

docs.title: Sanitisation
docs.text:
Some applications intentionally allow limited HTML.

For example:

Blog comments
Rich-text editors
CMS content
Knowledge bases
Forums

The correct security control may therefore be:

HTML Sanitisation

rather than encoding all markup.

A sanitiser may allow:

<b>
<i>
<p>
<ul>
<li>

while removing dangerous constructs.

Allowed HTML is not automatically a vulnerability.

The security question is whether the sanitisation policy prevents unsafe content.

docs.title: Rich Text Editors
docs.text:
Rich-text functionality may intentionally support HTML.

Test:

Which elements are allowed?

Which attributes are allowed?

Are URL schemes restricted?

Is sanitisation performed server-side?

Does another renderer process the content differently?

Does the API enforce the same policy as the GUI?

Do not report expected formatting support as HTML Injection.

docs.title: Markdown Rendering
docs.text:
Applications may convert Markdown to HTML.

Example:

**hello**

becomes:

<strong>hello</strong>

The relevant question is:

Can raw or generated HTML escape the intended Markdown security policy?

The Markdown parser and HTML sanitiser may be separate components.

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
Content Security Policy can reduce the impact of certain browser-based attacks.

However:

CSP

does not fix unsafe HTML rendering.

HTML Injection may still allow:

Content manipulation
Links
Forms
Page structure changes

even when script execution is prevented.

docs.title: HTML Injection to XSS
docs.text:
When HTML Injection is confirmed, evaluate whether it can become Cross-Site Scripting.

Conceptually:

HTML Injection
      ↓
Can Browser Execution Be Reached?
      ↓
Yes
      ↓
XSS

If JavaScript execution is demonstrated, classify and report the more significant XSS condition appropriately.

Refer to:

Cross-Site Scripting

docs.title: HTML Injection and Open Redirect
docs.text:
Injected HTML may create links pointing to arbitrary destinations.

For example:

<a href="https://example.com">Continue</a>

This is different from an Open Redirect.

HTML Injection:

Attacker inserts a new link

Open Redirect:

Existing trusted application endpoint redirects browser to attacker-controlled destination

Keep the vulnerabilities conceptually separate.

docs.title: HTML Injection and Phishing
docs.text:
One possible impact of HTML Injection is UI spoofing.

For example, an attacker may be able to alter trusted application content.

However, testing should not involve collecting real credentials.

A safe proof of concept can demonstrate:

Injected heading
Injected explanatory text
Injected non-functional input
Injected harmless link

This is normally sufficient to demonstrate UI manipulation.

docs.title: Reflection Mapping
docs.text:
Create a simple table:

Input Reflected Context Encoded q Yes HTML body No name Yes Attribute Yes message No N/A N/A company Yes HTML body No

This helps prioritise testing.

docs.title: Stored Input Mapping
docs.text:
For stored values:

Input Storage Viewer HTML Parsed Display name Profile User No Biography Profile Other users Yes Ticket subject Support DB Support agent Unknown File name Upload DB Admin Unknown

This is particularly useful when testing applications with many workflows.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
[ ] Identify reflected parameters
[ ] Identify stored user-controlled fields
[ ] Identify DOM-controlled input
[ ] Identify administrative rendering paths
[ ] Identify file metadata
[ ] Identify generated documents
[ ] Identify email rendering

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
[ ] HTML body
[ ] HTML attribute
[ ] URL attribute
[ ] HTML comment
[ ] DOM sink
[ ] Rich-text context
[ ] Markdown context

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
[ ] Test <
[ ] Test >
[ ] Test "
[ ] Test '
[ ] Inspect entity encoding
[ ] Compare raw response and DOM

docs.title: HTML Interpretation
docs.text:
[ ] Test unique marker
[ ] Test harmless formatting
[ ] Test simple structural HTML
[ ] Test harmless link where appropriate
[ ] Determine whether injection is reflected or stored

docs.title: Stored Behaviour
docs.text:
[ ] View from same account
[ ] View from second controlled account
[ ] Check administrative workflow where authorised
[ ] Check persistence
[ ] Check editing
[ ] Check deletion

docs.title: DOM
docs.text:
[ ] Review JavaScript
[ ] Search innerHTML
[ ] Search outerHTML
[ ] Search insertAdjacentHTML
[ ] Search document.write
[ ] Trace source to sink

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
[ ] Can content be changed?
[ ] Can links be inserted?
[ ] Can forms be inserted?
[ ] Can trusted UI be imitated?
[ ] Does another user see the content?
[ ] Can it escalate to XSS?

docs.title: HTML Injection Decision Tree
docs.text:
User Input
    ↓
Reflected / Stored / DOM?
    ↓
Where Is It Rendered?
    ↓
HTML Body?
Attribute?
DOM?
    ↓
Is It Encoded?
    ↓
Yes → Likely Safe for That Context
    ↓
No
    ↓
Does Browser Parse Markup?
    ↓
No → Continue Context Analysis
    ↓
Yes
    ↓
HTML Injection Confirmed
    ↓
Stored?
    ↓
Other Users Affected?
    ↓
Can Script Execution Occur?
    ↓
Yes → Evaluate as XSS
    ↓
No
    ↓
Assess HTML Injection Impact

docs.title: HTML Injection Quick Reference
docs.text:
START

AM-HTML-987654

FORMATTING

<b>AM-HTML-TEST</b>
<i>AM-HTML-TEST</i>
<h1>AM-HTML-TEST</h1>
<mark>AM-HTML-TEST</mark>

STRUCTURE

<div>AM-HTML-DIV</div>
<p>AM-HTML-PARAGRAPH</p>

HARMLESS LINK

<a href="https://example.com">AM-HTML-LINK</a>

DOM SINKS

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
document.writeln

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a confirmed issue record:

Affected endpoint
Affected parameter
Injection type
Rendering context
Original request
Modified request
Raw response
Rendered result
Whether stored
Affected users
Required interaction
Security impact

Screenshots should clearly demonstrate the injected content without including unnecessary sensitive information.

docs.title: Example Finding
docs.text:
Finding:
Stored HTML Injection in User Biography

Affected Functionality:
User Profile

Affected Parameter:
biography

Expected:
User-controlled profile content should be safely encoded or sanitised before rendering.

Observed:
HTML supplied through the biography field was stored and subsequently interpreted as markup when another controlled user viewed the profile.

Proof of Concept:
<b>AM-HTML-TEST</b>

Impact:
An attacker can modify the appearance and structure of profile pages viewed by other users. Depending on the permitted HTML and browser context, this may facilitate misleading content or potentially form part of a broader browser-side attack.

docs.title: Reporting Titles
docs.text:
Prefer precise titles:

Reflected HTML Injection in Search Results

Stored HTML Injection in User Biography

HTML Injection Through Uploaded File Name

HTML Injection in Support Ticket Subject

DOM-Based HTML Injection Through URL Parameter

HTML Injection in Generated Email Content

Avoid reporting:

Cross-Site Scripting

unless browser script execution has actually been demonstrated.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
The correct remediation depends on whether HTML is intended.

If HTML is not required:

Context-aware output encoding

should normally be applied.

If HTML is intentionally supported:

Strict HTML sanitisation

should be used.

docs.title: Output Encoding
docs.text:
For HTML body content, characters such as:

&
<
>
"
'

should be handled according to the relevant output context.

Do not rely only on input filtering.

Security should be applied when data is rendered.

docs.title: Context-Aware Encoding
docs.text:
Different contexts require different encoding.

HTML body
HTML attribute
JavaScript
URL
CSS

A generic replace operation is not sufficient for every context.

Use framework-supported encoding functions.

docs.title: Sanitisation
docs.text:
If users are allowed to provide HTML:

Untrusted HTML
      ↓
Well-Maintained Sanitiser
      ↓
Allowed Elements / Attributes
      ↓
Safe HTML

Use established libraries rather than custom regular-expression filters.

docs.title: Server-Side Enforcement
docs.text:
Do not rely solely on client-side validation.

An attacker can bypass the browser UI and submit requests directly.

Controls should therefore be enforced where the data is processed and rendered.

docs.title: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

Useful guidance for context-aware output encoding and safe rendering.

docs.title: OWASP HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTML5_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html

Useful security guidance for modern HTML and browser functionality.

docs.title: PortSwigger Cross-Site Scripting
docs.text:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/cross-site-scripting

Useful for understanding the boundary between unsafe HTML handling and script execution.

docs.title: Final HTML Injection Testing Model
docs.text:
USER INPUT
                        ↓
                 UNIQUE MARKER
                        ↓
              WHERE DOES IT APPEAR?
                        ↓
       ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
       ↓                ↓                ↓
   Reflected          Stored            DOM
       ↓                ↓                ↓
       └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                        ↓
                RENDERING CONTEXT
                        ↓
       ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
       ↓                ↓                ↓
   HTML Body        Attribute        HTML Sink
       ↓                ↓                ↓
       └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                        ↓
                 OUTPUT ENCODING?
                        ↓
                 HTML INTERPRETED?
                        ↓
                       YES
                        ↓
                 HTML INJECTION
                        ↓
             WHO CAN VIEW THE DATA?
                        ↓
              WHAT CAN BE MODIFIED?
                        ↓
               CAN IT BECOME XSS?
                        ↓
                 ASSESS IMPACT
                        ↓
                      REPORT

The key principle is:

First determine where attacker-controlled data is rendered and whether the browser interprets it as HTML. Demonstrate HTML Injection with harmless markup before investigating whether the condition can escalate into Cross-Site Scripting or another browser-side vulnerability.

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggling
docs.text:
HTTP Request Smuggling, also known as HTTP desynchronisation or HTTP desync, occurs when multiple HTTP components disagree about where one request ends and the next request begins.

Modern web applications frequently sit behind multiple infrastructure components.

A request may travel through:

Client
  ↓
CDN
  ↓
Reverse Proxy
  ↓
Load Balancer
  ↓
WAF
  ↓
Web Server
  ↓
Application

If two components interpret the boundaries of an HTTP request differently, an attacker may be able to cause part of one request to be interpreted as the beginning of another.

Conceptually:

Attacker Request
      ↓
Front-End Server
      ↓
Interprets Request Boundary A
      ↓
Back-End Server
      ↓
Interprets Request Boundary B
      ↓
Connection Becomes Desynchronised

This can potentially affect subsequent requests using the same back-end connection.

Possible consequences include:

Access-control bypass
Front-end security bypass
Web cache poisoning
Web cache deception
Request routing manipulation
Session confusion
Response queue poisoning
Credential exposure
Cross-site scripting
Request interception
Access to internal endpoints
Other users receiving incorrect responses

HTTP request smuggling is highly architecture dependent.

Authorised Security Testing

HTTP request smuggling testing can affect other users because requests may share persistent back-end connections. Perform testing only against systems for which you have explicit authorisation. Prefer isolated test environments, PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs, staging systems and low-impact detection techniques. Stop testing once sufficient evidence has been collected.

docs.title: Understanding HTTP Request Boundaries
docs.text:
HTTP servers need to determine where the body of a request ends.

In HTTP/1.1, two important mechanisms are:

Content-Length
Transfer-Encoding

For example:

POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 11

hello=world

The server uses:

Content-Length: 11

to determine the size of the body.

Another mechanism is chunked transfer encoding:

Transfer-Encoding: chunked

Conceptually:

HTTP Request
     ↓
Determine Body Length
     ↓
Read Body
     ↓
Next Request Begins

Problems occur when different servers disagree about this process.

docs.title: Typical Architecture
docs.text:
Consider:

Internet
   ↓
Front-End Server
   ↓
Persistent Back-End Connection
   ↓
Application Server

The front end may process requests from multiple clients and forward them over persistent connections.

For example:

Client A ─┐
Client B ─┼── Front End ─── Back End
Client C ─┘

Normally:

Request A
Request B
Request C

remain correctly separated.

With desynchronisation:

Attacker Request
       ↓
Front End sees:

[ Request A ]

Back End sees:

[ Request A ][ Partial Request B ]

The leftover data can affect a subsequent request.

docs.title: Core Request Smuggling Concept
docs.text:
The basic issue is:

Front End
   ↓
Request Length = X

Back End
   ↓
Request Length = Y

where:

X ≠ Y

This causes the two systems to disagree about request boundaries.

docs.title: Classic HTTP Request Smuggling
docs.text:
Classic request smuggling generally involves disagreement between:

Content-Length

and:

Transfer-Encoding

The traditional categories are:

CL.TE
TE.CL
TE.TE

The notation indicates which mechanism each server uses.

docs.title: CL.TE
docs.text:
CL.TE means:

Front End
   ↓
Content-Length

Back End
   ↓
Transfer-Encoding

Conceptually:

             Front End
                 ↓
          Content-Length
                 ↓
          Entire Request
                 ↓
             Back End
                 ↓
        Transfer-Encoding
                 ↓
Different Request Boundary

A deliberately simplified structure looks like:

POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Length: ...
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

...

The exact body structure depends on the target and should be calculated carefully rather than copied blindly.

docs.title: TE.CL
docs.text:
TE.CL is the reverse.

Front End
   ↓
Transfer-Encoding

Back End
   ↓
Content-Length

Conceptually:

             Front End
                 ↓
        Transfer-Encoding
                 ↓
             Back End
                 ↓
          Content-Length
                 ↓
Different Request Boundary

Again, the important concept is not a specific payload.

It is the disagreement:

Front End Boundary
        ≠
Back End Boundary

docs.title: TE.TE
docs.text:
TE.TE occurs when both servers support Transfer-Encoding, but one server can be induced to ignore or interpret the header differently.

Conceptually:

Front End
   ↓
Recognises Transfer-Encoding

Back End
   ↓
Does Not Recognise Equivalent Header

or the reverse.

Historically, research has explored ambiguous variations of the header.

Modern infrastructure is generally stricter about malformed HTTP, so these techniques are increasingly dependent on implementation-specific parsing differences.

docs.title: Content-Length
docs.text:
Example:

Content-Length: 20

means the server expects 20 bytes of request body.

Conceptually:

Headers
   ↓
Content-Length = N
   ↓
Read N Bytes
   ↓
Next Request

docs.title: Transfer-Encoding
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 may use:

Transfer-Encoding: chunked

A chunked body consists conceptually of:

Chunk Size
Chunk Data

Chunk Size
Chunk Data

0

The terminating zero-sized chunk indicates the end of the body.

Request smuggling becomes possible when another component uses a different method for determining that boundary.

docs.title: Detecting HTTP Request Smuggling
docs.text:
A useful methodology is:

Identify Architecture
        ↓
Determine HTTP Version
        ↓
Inspect Proxy Behaviour
        ↓
Identify Front-End / Back-End Differences
        ↓
Test Request Framing
        ↓
Use Timing-Based Detection
        ↓
Use Differential Responses
        ↓
Confirm Carefully
        ↓
Determine Impact

Do not begin by attempting to interfere with another user's request.

Start with detection.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Burp Suite is particularly useful for HTTP request smuggling testing.

A practical workflow is:

Burp Proxy
     ↓
HTTP History
     ↓
Interesting Request
     ↓
Send to Repeater
     ↓
Inspect HTTP Version
     ↓
Modify Request Framing
     ↓
Send Controlled Test
     ↓
Observe Timing / Response

Burp Repeater allows requests to be manually modified and resent while comparing application behaviour.

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Send an interesting request to Repeater:

Proxy
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Right Click
  ↓
Send to Repeater

Then inspect:

HTTP version
Content-Length
Transfer-Encoding
Connection behaviour
Response timing
Response status
Connection reuse

Repeater is useful because request smuggling testing often requires precise control over HTTP messages.

docs.title: Disable Automatic Content-Length Updating
docs.text:
When manually testing HTTP/1 request framing, be aware that Burp may automatically update Content-Length.

Depending on the test, you may need precise control over this value.

Check the Repeater settings and Inspector when constructing controlled requests.

The important point is:

Automatic Request Normalisation
             ↓
May Change Test Request

Always verify the exact request being sent.

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggler
docs.text:
One of the most useful Burp extensions for request smuggling research is:

HTTP Request Smuggler

It was developed by PortSwigger researcher James Kettle and automates testing for numerous HTTP desynchronisation techniques.

The extension can assist with identifying:

CL.TE
TE.CL
TE.TE
HTTP/2 desync
H2.CL
H2.TE
CL.0
Other parser discrepancies

depending on the version and target architecture.

docs.title: Installing HTTP Request Smuggler
docs.text:
In Burp Suite:

Burp Suite
    ↓
Extensions
    ↓
BApp Store
    ↓
Search
    ↓
HTTP Request Smuggler
    ↓
Install

After installation, the extension becomes available within Burp.

The exact menus can change between Burp releases, but the extension can normally be accessed from relevant request context menus.

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggler Workflow
docs.text:
A typical authorised workflow is:

Browse Target
     ↓
Burp Proxy
     ↓
HTTP History
     ↓
Select Interesting Request
     ↓
Send / Launch Request Smuggling Test
     ↓
HTTP Request Smuggler
     ↓
Automated Desync Probes
     ↓
Review Findings
     ↓
Manually Confirm

The extension should be treated as:

Detection Assistant

rather than:

Automatic Proof of Vulnerability

Always manually investigate interesting results.

docs.title: Example HTTP Request Smuggler Usage
docs.text:
Suppose Burp contains:

POST /search HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 9

q=testing

A workflow might be:

1. Capture the request in Burp.

2. Confirm the host is explicitly authorised.

3. Send the request to Repeater.

4. Establish the normal baseline behaviour.

5. Right-click the request.

6. Launch the HTTP Request Smuggler extension.

7. Run the appropriate detection checks.

8. Review reported anomalies.

9. Send suspected cases to Repeater.

10. Manually verify the behaviour.

11. Stop once sufficient evidence exists.

Do not automatically assume every timeout means request smuggling.

Possible causes include:

Rate limiting
Network latency
WAF behaviour
Connection timeout
Application slowness
Proxy timeout
Server instability

Manual confirmation is important.

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggler Results
docs.text:
Interesting findings may indicate:

Possible CL.TE
Possible TE.CL
Possible CL.0
Possible HTTP/2 desync
Timeout anomaly
Differential response
Connection anomaly
Parser discrepancy

The next step should be:

Automated Detection
       ↓
Manual Reproduction
       ↓
Controlled Confirmation
       ↓
Impact Assessment

docs.title: Timing-Based Detection
docs.text:
Timing behaviour can help identify parser disagreements.

Conceptually:

Send Ambiguous Request
        ↓
One Server Waits for More Data
        ↓
Connection Delays
        ↓
Potential Desynchronisation Indicator

A suspicious delay may suggest that one server believes the request is incomplete while another believes it is complete.

However:

Timeout ≠ Vulnerability

Always repeat the test and compare against baseline behaviour.

docs.title: Differential Response Testing
docs.text:
Another useful technique is observing whether a carefully controlled request affects the interpretation of a subsequent request.

Conceptually:

Probe Request
     ↓
Potential Desync
     ↓
Follow-Up Request
     ↓
Unexpected Response

Examples of unexpected behaviour may include:

404 instead of 200
Different redirect
Different response body
Unexpected headers
Connection reset
Unexpected application route

Use endpoints you control where possible.

docs.title: Self-Contained Confirmation
docs.text:
The safest confirmation attempts to affect only your own subsequent request.

Conceptually:

Your Request A
      ↓
Potential Smuggled Prefix
      ↓
Your Request B
      ↓
Observable Difference

This is preferable to attempting to interfere with unrelated users.

docs.title: CL.0 Request Smuggling
docs.text:
CL.0 vulnerabilities represent another form of desynchronisation.

The general idea is:

Front End
   ↓
Uses Content-Length

Back End
   ↓
Effectively Treats Body Length as Zero

Conceptually:

POST Request
Content-Length: N

BODY

Front end:

BODY belongs to current request

Back end:

Current request has no body

BODY becomes next request data

This creates:

CL.0

desynchronisation.

docs.title: Why CL.0 Is Interesting
docs.text:
Traditional request smuggling testing focused heavily on:

CL.TE
TE.CL

CL.0 demonstrates that request smuggling does not necessarily require both:

Content-Length

and:

Transfer-Encoding

The vulnerability can arise simply because a back-end endpoint does not consume the body in the way expected by the front end.

docs.title: CL.0 Candidate Endpoints
docs.text:
Interesting endpoints may include those that:

Expect no request body
Return early
Redirect immediately
Serve static content
Produce server-level errors
Reject unsupported methods

Conceptually:

Front End
   ↓
Forwards Body

Back End
   ↓
Responds Before Consuming Body

Remaining Bytes
   ↓
Next Request

This is why early-response behaviour is important during modern desync testing.

docs.title: Client-Side Desync
docs.text:
Client-side desynchronisation extends desync concepts to the browser.

Conceptually:

Browser
   ↓
Front-End Server
   ↓
Connection Becomes Desynchronised
   ↓
Subsequent Browser Request
   ↓
Unexpected Interpretation

This differs from traditional request smuggling because the browser itself can participate in triggering the desynchronisation.

docs.title: Browser-Powered Request Smuggling
docs.text:
Modern request smuggling research has demonstrated that some desync vulnerabilities can be triggered using browser-compatible requests.

This creates potential attack flows such as:

Victim Browser
      ↓
Attacker-Controlled Page
      ↓
Request to Vulnerable Site
      ↓
Connection Desynchronised
      ↓
Subsequent Request Affected

These techniques are considerably more advanced than traditional CL.TE testing.

Use PortSwigger's dedicated Web Security Academy labs when learning them.

docs.title: HTTP/2
docs.text:
HTTP/2 handles message framing differently from HTTP/1.1.

HTTP/2 uses binary frames:

HTTP/2 Connection
       ↓
HEADERS Frame
       ↓
DATA Frame
       ↓
Built-In Frame Length

This largely removes the classic ambiguity around:

Content-Length
Transfer-Encoding

when HTTP/2 is used end to end.

However, problems can appear when HTTP/2 is downgraded.

docs.title: HTTP/2 Downgrading
docs.text:
A common architecture is:

Client
  ↓
HTTP/2
  ↓
Front End
  ↓
HTTP/1.1
  ↓
Back End

The front end must translate:

HTTP/2

into:

HTTP/1.1

This conversion may introduce request framing inconsistencies.

docs.title: H2.CL
docs.text:
H2.CL means:

Front End
   ↓
HTTP/2 Framing

Back End
   ↓
Content-Length

Conceptually:

HTTP/2 Request
      ↓
Front End
      ↓
Downgrade
      ↓
HTTP/1.1 + Content-Length
      ↓
Back End

If the generated Content-Length and actual request body are interpreted differently, desynchronisation may occur.

docs.title: H2.TE
docs.text:
H2.TE involves:

HTTP/2
   ↓
Front End
   ↓
Downgrade
   ↓
Transfer-Encoding
   ↓
Back End

Again, the security issue exists because:

Front-End Interpretation
          ≠
Back-End Interpretation

docs.title: Testing HTTP/2 in Burp
docs.text:
Burp Repeater allows requests to be sent using HTTP/1 or HTTP/2 where supported.

When testing a target, compare:

HTTP/1 Behaviour
        vs
HTTP/2 Behaviour

Interesting differences include:

Different status codes
Different headers
Different redirects
Different WAF behaviour
Different routing
Different request normalization

docs.title: Burp Inspector and HTTP/2
docs.text:
Burp's Inspector is useful for manipulating HTTP/2-specific request components.

HTTP/2 includes pseudo-headers such as:

:method
:path
:authority
:scheme

These are conceptually equivalent to important pieces of the HTTP/1 request.

Understanding them is important when investigating HTTP/2 request smuggling.

docs.title: HTTP/2 Pseudo-Headers
docs.text:
A simplified HTTP/2 request may contain:

:method = GET
:path = /
:authority = example.com
:scheme = https

Instead of:

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

HTTP/2 uses structured pseudo-header fields.

docs.title: Response Queue Poisoning
docs.text:
A particularly serious consequence of desynchronisation is response queue poisoning.

Normally:

Request A → Response A
Request B → Response B
Request C → Response C

After desynchronisation:

Request A → Response A
Request B → Response C
Request C → Response D

Responses become associated with the wrong requests.

This can potentially expose responses intended for other users.

Because of the potential impact on unrelated users, this should not be tested aggressively against production environments.

docs.title: Front-End Security Bypass
docs.text:
A front-end server may enforce security controls such as:

Authentication
IP restrictions
WAF rules
Path restrictions
Rate limiting
Access control

But the back end may trust requests received from the front end.

Conceptually:

Internet
   ↓
Security Controls
   ↓
Front End
   ↓
Back End

If a request can be smuggled through an already accepted front-end request, the back end may process something the front end never independently validated.

docs.title: Internal Header Discovery
docs.text:
Front-end servers frequently add internal headers.

For example:

X-Forwarded-For
X-Forwarded-Host
X-Real-IP
X-Original-URL
Internal routing headers
Authentication headers

Request smuggling research sometimes involves determining how the front end rewrites requests before forwarding them.

This can reveal important information about the internal architecture.

docs.title: Web Cache Poisoning
docs.text:
Request smuggling may sometimes be chained with caching behaviour.

Conceptually:

Request Smuggling
      ↓
Back-End Response Manipulation
      ↓
Cache Stores Response
      ↓
Other Users Receive Response

This can increase the persistence and impact of a desync vulnerability.

Related notes:

Web Cache Poisoning
Web Cache Deception
HTTP Host Header Attacks

should eventually have their own dedicated pages.

docs.title: Request Smuggling and XSS
docs.text:
A desynchronisation issue can sometimes be combined with reflected XSS.

Conceptually:

Smuggled Request
      ↓
Reflected Input
      ↓
Response
      ↓
Response Associated With Another Request

This demonstrates why the impact of request smuggling can extend beyond request routing.

docs.title: Request Smuggling and Authentication
docs.text:
Consider:

Front End
    ↓
Authentication Check
    ↓
Back End

If a smuggled request reaches the back end without passing through the expected front-end processing path, authentication assumptions may break.

Potentially interesting areas include:

/admin
/internal
/api/admin
/debug
/management

Only test endpoints explicitly included in the assessment scope.

docs.title: Request Smuggling and WAFs
docs.text:
Architecture:

Internet
   ↓
WAF
   ↓
Reverse Proxy
   ↓
Application

If:

WAF Parser
     ≠
Application Parser

the WAF may inspect a different request than the application ultimately processes.

This general class of problem is often called:

Parser Differential

Request smuggling is fundamentally a parser differential vulnerability.

docs.title: Identifying Infrastructure
docs.text:
Before testing, fingerprint the architecture.

Useful indicators include:

Server headers
Via
X-Cache
X-Served-By
X-Forwarded headers
CDN headers
Load-balancer cookies
TLS certificates
DNS records
HTTP/2 support
HTTP/3 support
Response behaviour

Tools include:

Burp Suite
curl
httpx
Nmap
testssl.sh
Browser DevTools

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
Check protocol support:

curl -I https://target.example/

Verbose output:

curl -vk https://target.example/

Test HTTP/1.1:

curl --http1.1 -vk https://target.example/

Test HTTP/2:

curl --http2 -vk https://target.example/

Compare behaviour.

docs.title: httpx
docs.text:
For authorised infrastructure discovery:

httpx -u https://target.example -title -status-code -tech-detect

This can help identify:

Status
Title
Technology
Server behaviour

It is not a request-smuggling detector by itself.

docs.title: Connection Reuse
docs.text:
Persistent connections are central to many request smuggling vulnerabilities.

Conceptually:

Front End
    ↓
Connection 1
    ↓
Request A
Request B
Request C

If the back end believes part of Request A belongs to Request B:

Request Boundary Corruption

occurs.

This is why simply replaying requests over separate TCP connections may fail to demonstrate certain desync behaviours.

docs.title: Burp Repeater Request Groups
docs.text:
Burp Repeater supports grouped requests.

This can be useful for carefully controlled sequences such as:

Probe Request
      ↓
Follow-Up Request

Testing on the same connection can be relevant for desynchronisation research.

Always verify whether the requests are actually using:

Same Connection

or:

Separate Connections

because the result can differ significantly.

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Before testing:

Send Normal Request
       ↓
Record Response
       ↓
Repeat Several Times
       ↓
Establish Stable Behaviour

Record:

Status code
Response length
Response time
Headers
Redirects
Cookies
Connection behaviour

Only then introduce request-framing changes.

docs.title: Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A structured approach is:

1. Confirm scope

2. Identify HTTP architecture

3. Determine HTTP versions

4. Establish normal baseline

5. Check for front-end infrastructure

6. Send request to Burp Repeater

7. Test low-impact framing discrepancies

8. Use HTTP Request Smuggler

9. Review timing anomalies

10. Review differential responses

11. Investigate CL.TE / TE.CL where appropriate

12. Investigate HTTP/2 downgrade behaviour

13. Investigate CL.0 behaviour

14. Confirm using your own requests

15. Determine security impact

16. Stop once sufficient evidence exists

17. Document the complete architecture and behaviour

docs.title: Request Smuggling Decision Tree
docs.text:
Target
  ↓
HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2?
  ↓
Is There a Front End?
  ↓
Are Connections Reused?
  ↓
Do Components Parse Requests Differently?
  ↓
CL.TE?
TE.CL?
TE.TE?
H2.CL?
H2.TE?
CL.0?
  ↓
Can Behaviour Be Reproduced?
  ↓
Can Own Follow-Up Request Be Affected?
  ↓
What Security Boundary Is Bypassed?

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Request smuggling testing can produce misleading behaviour.

Possible causes include:

Slow application
WAF rate limiting
CDN retries
Load balancer behaviour
Network latency
Connection pool exhaustion
Server errors
Application crashes
Request normalization
Proxy buffering

Therefore:

One Timeout
    ≠
Confirmed Request Smuggling

Look for reproducible behaviour.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each candidate, record:

Target
Endpoint
HTTP version
Front-end technology
Back-end technology if known
Request type
Desync classification
Original request
Modified request
Timing behaviour
Response behaviour
Connection behaviour
HTTP Request Smuggler output
Manual confirmation
Security impact
Timestamp

docs.title: Example Evidence Record
docs.text:
HRS-001

Endpoint:
POST /search

HTTP Version:
HTTP/1.1

Candidate:
CL.TE

Detection:
HTTP Request Smuggler

Observation:
Consistent timing anomaly

Manual Confirmation:
Controlled follow-up request affected

Affected User:
Tester only

Status:
Confirmed for further impact assessment

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
A request smuggling report should explain the infrastructure clearly.

For example:

Client
  ↓
Reverse Proxy
  ↓
Application Server

Then describe the parsing difference:

Reverse Proxy
     ↓
Uses Content-Length

Application Server
     ↓
Uses Transfer-Encoding

This causes:

Request Boundary Disagreement

docs.title: Example Finding Title
docs.text:
HTTP Request Smuggling Due to Front-End and Back-End Request Parsing Discrepancy

More specific:

CL.TE HTTP Request Smuggling

or:

HTTP/2 Downgrade Enables H2.CL Request Smuggling

or:

CL.0 HTTP Desynchronisation

Use the most accurate classification established during testing.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Potential impacts include:

Authentication bypass
Authorisation bypass
WAF bypass
Internal endpoint access
Cache poisoning
Cache deception
Cross-site scripting
Request interception
Response queue poisoning
Credential exposure
Session compromise
User-to-user response confusion

The actual report should describe only the impact demonstrated or strongly established.

Do not automatically report every request smuggling vulnerability as critical.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
The fundamental remediation is:

Ensure every component in the HTTP request chain agrees unambiguously on request boundaries.

docs.title: Prefer HTTP/2 End to End
docs.text:
Where possible:

Client
  ↓
HTTP/2
  ↓
Front End
  ↓
HTTP/2
  ↓
Back End

is preferable to:

Client
  ↓
HTTP/2
  ↓
Front End
  ↓
Downgrade
  ↓
HTTP/1.1
  ↓
Back End

Protocol translation introduces additional parsing complexity.

docs.title: Reject Ambiguous Requests
docs.text:
Infrastructure should reject requests containing ambiguous framing.

For example, requests containing conflicting framing information should not be forwarded.

Conceptually:

Ambiguous Request
      ↓
Front End
      ↓
Reject

rather than:

Ambiguous Request
      ↓
Normalize
      ↓
Forward

unless normalization is guaranteed to produce identical interpretation across every component.

docs.title: Avoid Front-End / Back-End Parser Differences
docs.text:
Ensure:

CDN
Reverse Proxy
Load Balancer
WAF
Web Server
Application Server

follow compatible request parsing rules.

Keep all infrastructure updated.

Request parsing vulnerabilities have historically appeared in many different HTTP implementations.

docs.title: Close Connections on Errors
docs.text:
Connection handling should prevent malformed or ambiguous requests from contaminating subsequent requests.

Conceptually:

Malformed Request
       ↓
Reject
       ↓
Close Connection

This can help prevent residual bytes from affecting another request.

docs.title: Do Not Rely Solely on a WAF
docs.text:
A WAF cannot reliably compensate for inconsistent request parsing between infrastructure components.

If:

WAF sees Request A

while:

Application sees Request B

security controls may be bypassed.

Fix the parser discrepancy itself.

docs.title: HTTP Request Smuggling Quick Reference
docs.text:
CL.TE

Front End  → Content-Length
Back End   → Transfer-Encoding

TE.CL

Front End  → Transfer-Encoding
Back End   → Content-Length

TE.TE

Both process Transfer-Encoding differently

H2.CL

Front End  → HTTP/2 framing
Back End   → Content-Length after downgrade

H2.TE

Front End  → HTTP/2 framing
Back End   → Transfer-Encoding after downgrade

CL.0

Front End  → Content-Length
Back End   → Effectively ignores body

docs.text:
Target Application
       ↓
Identify Architecture
       ↓
CDN / WAF / Proxy / Load Balancer?
       ↓
Determine HTTP Versions

Establish Baseline

Burp Proxy

       ↓

       ↓

       ↓

The key principle is:

HTTP request smuggling is fundamentally a disagreement between HTTP parsers. Understand how each component determines request boundaries, use automation such as HTTP Request Smuggler to identify candidates, and then manually confirm the behaviour using controlled requests before determining the real security impact.

docs.title: HTTP Security Headers
docs.text:
HTTP security headers allow a web application to instruct browsers how content should be handled and which browser security mechanisms should be enforced.

They provide an additional defensive layer against vulnerabilities such as:

Cross-Site Scripting
Clickjacking
MIME Sniffing
HTTPS Downgrade
Information Leakage
Cross-Origin Data Exposure
Uncontrolled Browser Features

Security headers do not replace secure application development.

Conceptually:

Secure Application
      +
Secure Browser Policy
      ↓
Defence in Depth

A typical response may contain:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()

The main security headers covered in this note are:

Content-Security-Policy
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only
Strict-Transport-Security
X-Content-Type-Options
Referrer-Policy
Permissions-Policy
X-Frame-Options
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy
Cache-Control
Clear-Site-Data

Related headers and controls include:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
Set-Cookie
Reporting-Endpoints

These require additional context and should not simply be evaluated as present or absent.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform security-header testing only against applications explicitly authorised for assessment. Header analysis is generally low impact, but active validation of CSP bypasses, CORS behaviour, framing, cross-origin isolation, cache behaviour, or related vulnerabilities should remain within the approved scope.

docs.title: Security Headers Testing Model
docs.text:
The basic workflow is:

HTTP Response
      ↓
Enumerate Headers
      ↓
Identify Missing Controls
      ↓
Analyse Existing Values
      ↓
Determine Application Context
      ↓
Test Browser Behaviour
      ↓
Identify Practical Security Impact
      ↓
Report Relevant Weaknesses

The most important principle is:

Missing Header
      ≠
Vulnerability Automatically

Instead:

Missing / Weak Header
        +
Relevant Attack Surface
        +
Demonstrable Security Impact
        ↓
Meaningful Finding

docs.title: Why Security Headers Matter
docs.text:
Browsers implement many security controls.

Applications can influence those controls through response headers.

For example:

Application
     ↓
Content-Security-Policy
     ↓
Browser
     ↓
Restrict Script Execution

Another example:

Application
     ↓
X-Frame-Options
     ↓
Browser
     ↓
Restrict Framing

Security headers therefore operate at the boundary between:

Application Security

and:

Browser Security

docs.title: Initial Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Start by retrieving the application response headers.

Using curl:

curl -I https://target.example/

For full headers:

curl -s -D - -o /dev/null https://target.example/

Follow redirects:

curl -s -L -D - -o /dev/null https://target.example/

docs.title: Important Limitation of HEAD Requests
docs.text:
curl -I sends:

HEAD

instead of:

GET

Some applications return different headers for HEAD requests.

Therefore verify interesting findings with:

curl -s -D - -o /dev/null https://target.example/

which performs a GET request.

docs.text:
Burp is particularly useful because security headers can vary by:

docs.title: Do Not Test Only the Homepage
docs.text:
Security headers may differ between:

/

and:

/login
/account
/admin
/api/
/upload/
/reset-password
/error

A reverse proxy may add headers globally while individual applications override them.

Alternatively:

Main Application
→ Strong Headers

Legacy Application
→ Weak Headers
