              └────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                               ↓
                     CONTROLLED RESET EMAIL
                               ↓

                         ↓             ↓
                        YES            NO
                         ↓             ↓
                      CONTINUE    RESET POISONING
                         ↓

                         ↓
              ┌──────────┼──────────────┐
              ↓          ↓              ↓
           REFERER     LOGGING      THIRD PARTY
              └──────────┼──────────────┘
                         ↓
                    WORKFLOW STATE
                         ↓
             ┌───────────┼────────────┐
             ↓           ↓            ↓
          OTP STEP    RESET STEP    CLIENT STATE
             ↓           ↓            ↓
         ENFORCED?    ENFORCED?    TRUSTED?
             └───────────┼────────────┘
                         ↓
                    SESSION STATE
                         ↓
             EXISTING SESSIONS / TOKENS
                         ↓
                    MFA INTERACTION
                         ↓
                  MFA STILL REQUIRED?
                    ↓             ↓
                   YES            NO
                    ↓             ↓
                 CONTINUE      INVESTIGATE
                    ↓
                    SSO
                    ↓
           SSO-ONLY ACCOUNT CAN
           CREATE LOCAL PASSWORD?
               ↓             ↓
              NO             YES
               ↓             ↓
            SECURE       INVESTIGATE
               ↓
             VERIFY
               ↓
       MINIMUM SAFE EVIDENCE
               ↓
             REPORT

The central principle is:

Password reset is an authentication mechanism, not merely a convenience feature. Reset tokens and recovery challenges must be unpredictable, short-lived, single-use, securely bound to the intended account and purpose, protected against brute force and leakage, and processed entirely through trusted server-side workflow state. A user should never receive weaker authentication guarantees simply because they entered the application through account recovery rather than normal login.

docs.title: Path Traversal
docs.text:
Path Traversal, also known as Directory Traversal, occurs when attacker-controlled input is used to construct a filesystem path without sufficiently restricting which files or directories can be accessed.

A vulnerable application may allow a user to escape the intended directory and access files elsewhere on the filesystem.

Typical traversal sequences include:

../
..\

The exact syntax depends on the operating system, application, framework and path normalisation behaviour.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform path traversal testing only against applications and systems for which you have explicit authorisation. Use minimally sensitive files for validation and stop once sufficient evidence has been obtained.

docs.title: Path Traversal Mental Model
docs.text:
Consider an application designed to retrieve files from:

/var/www/files/

The application receives:

filename=report.pdf

and constructs:

/var/www/files/report.pdf

If the application simply concatenates user input:

/var/www/files/ + USER_INPUT

an attacker may attempt:

../../../etc/hostname

resulting conceptually in:

/var/www/files/../../../etc/hostname

After filesystem path resolution:

/etc/hostname

A useful model is:

User-Controlled Input
        ↓
Application
        ↓
Path Construction
        ↓
Path Normalisation
        ↓
Filesystem API
        ↓
File / Directory

The central question is:

Can attacker-controlled input cause the final resolved path to escape the directory that the application intended to expose?

docs.title: Path Traversal Testing Workflow
docs.text:
A structured workflow can look like:

Map Application
      ↓
Identify File Functionality
      ↓
Identify Path-Like Parameters
      ↓
Establish Baseline
      ↓
Determine Operating System
      ↓
Test Basic Traversal
      ↓
Test Absolute Paths
      ↓
Understand Filtering
      ↓
Test Encoding / Normalisation
      ↓
Determine Accessible Files
      ↓
Confirm Minimal Impact
      ↓
Collect Evidence
      ↓
Report

Do not immediately send large traversal payload lists.

First understand how the application handles file paths.

docs.title: Where to Look for Path Traversal
docs.text:
Path traversal frequently appears in functionality involving files.

Interesting features include:

File download
Document download
Image retrieval
Profile pictures
Invoice download
Report download
Log viewer
Export functionality
Import functionality
Backup download
Template loading
Language selection
Theme loading
Static resources
Attachments
File preview
PDF retrieval
Configuration files
Archive extraction
Media retrieval

Pay particular attention to endpoints where the application accepts something resembling a file name or path.

docs.title: Interesting Parameter Names
docs.text:
Common parameter names include:

file
filename
filepath
path
document
doc
page
template
folder
directory
dir
image
img
download
attachment
resource
include
view
layout
theme
lang
language
locale
log
backup
export
report
name

Examples:

/download?file=report.pdf

/document?filename=invoice.pdf

/image?path=avatars/user.png

/view?page=help.html

/api/files?name=document.pdf

Parameter names are clues rather than proof of vulnerability.

docs.title: File Download Endpoints
docs.text:
File download functionality should receive particular attention.

Example:

GET /download?file=report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

The application may internally perform something conceptually similar to:

BASE_DIRECTORY + filename

For example:

/var/www/downloads/ + report.pdf

becomes:

/var/www/downloads/report.pdf

The security question becomes:

Can filename escape /var/www/downloads/?

docs.title: Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Always begin with a legitimate request.

Example:

GET /download?file=report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Record:

Status code
Content-Type
Content-Length
Response body
Content-Disposition
Response time
File contents

Then modify only the suspected path parameter.

docs.title: Determine the Operating System
docs.text:
Technology identification can help determine which filesystem syntax is relevant.

Linux and Unix-like systems commonly use:

/

Windows commonly uses:

\

although many Windows APIs also accept:

/

Potential clues include:

Error messages
Stack traces
Server headers
Framework
File paths
Source code
Default files
Application behaviour

Example Linux paths:

/etc/
/var/
/home/
/opt/
/tmp/
/proc/

Example Windows paths:

C:\Windows\
C:\Users\
C:\Program Files\
C:\ProgramData\

docs.title: Basic Linux Path Traversal
docs.text:
A basic Linux traversal test may look like:

../../../etc/hostname

Example request:

GET /download?file=../../../etc/hostname HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

If the application prepends:

/var/www/files/

the resulting path becomes:

/var/www/files/../../../etc/hostname

which may resolve to:

/etc/hostname

docs.title: Choosing a Linux Validation File
docs.text:
Prefer minimally sensitive files.

Useful candidates include:

/etc/hostname
/etc/os-release

Another commonly used proof is:

/etc/passwd

but /etc/hostname or /etc/os-release may provide sufficient evidence without exposing account information.

The objective is to demonstrate arbitrary filesystem access, not to collect sensitive data.

docs.title: Basic Windows Path Traversal
docs.text:
A Windows traversal test may look like:

..\..\..\Windows\win.ini

Example:

GET /download?file=..\..\..\Windows\win.ini HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

A useful minimally sensitive Windows validation target is:

C:\Windows\win.ini

docs.title: Forward Slashes on Windows
docs.text:
Do not assume Windows requires backslashes.

Many Windows APIs understand:

../../Windows/win.ini

as well as:

..\..\Windows\win.ini

Therefore, test path handling based on actual application behaviour rather than operating system assumptions alone.

docs.title: Absolute Paths
docs.text:
Sometimes traversal sequences are unnecessary because the application accepts absolute paths.

Linux example:

/etc/hostname

Windows example:

C:\Windows\win.ini

Conceptually:

file=/etc/hostname

or:

file=C:\Windows\win.ini

may be interpreted directly by an unsafe filesystem API.

docs.title: Relative vs Absolute Path Testing
docs.text:
A useful sequence is:

Normal File
    ↓
Relative Traversal
    ↓
Absolute Path
    ↓
Encoded Traversal
    ↓
Normalisation Analysis

For example:

report.pdf

then:

../report.pdf

then:

../../some-file

then an absolute path if relevant.

This helps identify how the application constructs paths.

docs.title: Determine Traversal Depth
docs.text:
If the application uses an unknown base directory, the number of traversal sequences required may not be obvious.

Conceptually:

../
../../
../../../
../../../../
../../../../../

Instead of guessing indefinitely, observe application responses.

Look for differences in:

Status
Length
Error message
Content-Type
Response body

docs.title: Excess Traversal Sequences
docs.text:
On many filesystems, additional traversal sequences beyond the root do not necessarily prevent the path from resolving.

For example:

../../../../../../etc/hostname

may still resolve to:

/etc/hostname

depending on the application and filesystem API.

This can make extra traversal depth useful when the base directory is unknown.

docs.title: Path Normalisation
docs.text:
Applications may normalise paths before accessing them.

For example:

/images/../config/file

may become:

/config/file

Different components may perform normalisation:

Reverse proxy
Web server
Framework
Application
Filesystem API
Operating system

The value visible in Burp may therefore not be identical to the path eventually processed by the filesystem.

docs.title: URL Encoding
docs.text:
Traversal sequences may be URL encoded.

For example:

../

can become:

%2e%2e%2f

or:

..%2f

A backslash may appear as:

%5c

Examples:

%2e%2e%2fetc%2fhostname

..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fhostname

The relevant question is:

At which layer is URL decoding performed?

docs.title: Double Encoding
docs.text:
Applications with multiple decoding layers may interpret double-encoded traversal sequences differently.

Conceptually:

../

becomes:

%2e%2e%2f

and the percent characters can themselves be encoded.

This produces values such as:

%252e%252e%252f

Processing might occur as:

%252e%252e%252f
        ↓
%2e%2e%2f
        ↓
../

This matters when one security layer validates the value before another layer performs additional decoding.

docs.title: Mixed Encoding
docs.text:
Different parts of the traversal sequence may be encoded independently.

Examples:

..%2f
%2e%2e/
.%2e/
%2e./

The purpose of testing these variations is to understand normalisation and decoding behaviour, not simply to generate a large payload list.

docs.title: Mixed Path Separators
docs.text:
Applications may process combinations such as:

../
..\

or mixed forms:

../..\

This is particularly relevant when:

Application framework

and:

Operating system

perform path handling differently.

docs.title: Nested Traversal Sequences
docs.text:
Some filters remove literal traversal sequences once.

For example, an application might perform:

replace("../", "")

A nested sequence may become meaningful after that replacement.

Conceptually:

....//

contains an overlapping traversal structure.

If the filter removes part of the value, the remaining string may become:

../

This is why security controls should normalise and validate paths rather than attempting simple string replacement.

docs.title: Path Traversal Filters
docs.text:
Common weak protections include:

Remove ../
Remove ..\
Block the word passwd
Block absolute paths
Require a file extension
Check string prefix
URL encode dangerous characters

These protections should be analysed individually.

The key question is:

What exact transformation occurs?

docs.title: Required Base Directory
docs.text:
Some applications require the path to begin with a particular directory.

For example:

/var/www/images/

A request might normally contain:

filename=/var/www/images/photo.jpg

Testing may reveal whether traversal is processed after the required prefix.

Conceptually:

/var/www/images/../../../etc/hostname

The important factor is the final resolved path.

docs.title: Required File Extension
docs.text:
Applications sometimes append a file extension automatically.

For example:

USER_INPUT + ".pdf"

A request for:

report

becomes:

report.pdf

This can influence path traversal testing.

Determine:

Is the extension appended?
Is it validated before or after decoding?
Does the filesystem API receive the appended value?

docs.title: Null Byte Considerations
docs.text:
Historically, some applications and native APIs were vulnerable to null byte termination.

A value conceptually containing:

%00

could cause one component to see:

../../../etc/passwd

while another expected:

../../../etc/passwd.pdf

Modern languages and frameworks generally handle this more safely.

Treat null byte behaviour as technology-specific rather than assuming it works universally.

docs.title: File Download APIs
docs.text:
Modern applications frequently expose download functionality through APIs.

Example:

GET /api/documents/download?filename=report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Authorization: Bearer ...

Interesting API properties include:

filename
path
document
resource
object
key
location

Send the request to Burp Repeater and determine how the backend interprets the value.

docs.title: JSON Path Traversal
docs.text:
Paths may also be supplied in JSON.

Example:

POST /api/download HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "filename": "report.pdf"
}

Testing then focuses on:

filename

rather than the URL.

Potential path-like JSON properties include:

file
filename
path
template
document
resource
directory

docs.title: POST Body Path Traversal
docs.text:
Do not restrict path traversal testing to GET parameters.

Example:

POST /download HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

file=report.pdf

The vulnerability depends on how the server uses the value, not where the parameter appears.

docs.title: Path Traversal in Cookies
docs.text:
Occasionally cookies control resources such as:

Language
Theme
Template
Layout

Example:

Cookie: language=en

If the server maps the value to a filesystem resource, it may become path traversal relevant.

docs.title: Language Parameters
docs.text:
Language functionality is historically interesting.

Examples:

?lang=en

?language=en_US

?locale=nl_NL

The application might internally load:

/languages/en.php

or:

/locales/en.json

Determine whether user input can escape the intended language directory.

docs.title: Template Parameters
docs.text:
Template selection can also expose filesystem paths.

Example:

?template=invoice

might cause:

/templates/invoice.html

to be loaded.

Potential issues include:

Path traversal
Local file inclusion
Template injection

depending on how the file is subsequently processed.

docs.title: File Names
docs.text:
User-controlled file names should also be considered.

Potential flow:

Upload File
    ↓
Store File Name
    ↓
Later Download
    ↓
Construct Filesystem Path

The vulnerability may therefore exist in the download functionality rather than the original upload endpoint.

docs.title: Upload and Download Workflows
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Upload File
    ↓
Observe Stored Name
    ↓
Retrieve File
    ↓
Capture Download Request
    ↓
Identify File Parameter
    ↓
Test Path Handling

Burp HTTP history is particularly useful here.

docs.title: File IDs vs File Names
docs.text:
Secure applications often expose an opaque identifier:

/download?id=8291

rather than:

/download?file=/var/www/files/report.pdf

However, IDs do not automatically make the application secure.

The server must still perform appropriate authorisation when mapping:

ID → File

This overlaps with IDOR and broken access control testing.

docs.title: Path Traversal vs IDOR
docs.text:
These are different vulnerability classes.

Path traversal:

Attacker Controls Path
       ↓
Escapes Intended Directory
       ↓
Reads Different Filesystem Resource

IDOR:

Attacker Controls Object Identifier
       ↓
Application Retrieves Another Object
       ↓
Missing Authorisation

Example:

/download?id=123

changing to:

/download?id=124

is more likely an authorisation test.

Changing:

file=report.pdf

to:

file=../../../etc/hostname

is path traversal testing.

docs.title: Path Traversal vs Local File Inclusion
docs.text:
Path Traversal and Local File Inclusion are related but not identical.

Path traversal usually means:

Attacker-Controlled Path
       ↓
Filesystem Access
       ↓
File Read / Write

LFI usually means:

Attacker-Controlled Path
       ↓
Application Includes File
       ↓
Interpreter / Template Engine Processes It

For example:

download?file=../../../etc/hostname

returning file bytes is primarily path traversal.

Whereas:

?page=../../../some-file

being included by an interpreter may represent LFI.

docs.title: Path Traversal vs Arbitrary File Read
docs.text:
A successful path traversal often results in:

Arbitrary File Read

but the terms describe different aspects.

Path Traversal

describes the technique or root cause.

Arbitrary File Read

describes the resulting capability.

A report title might therefore be:

Path Traversal Allows Arbitrary File Read

docs.title: Path Traversal vs Arbitrary File Write
docs.text:
Path traversal can also occur in write operations.

Conceptually:

User-Controlled File Name
        ↓
Application Constructs Path
        ↓
Traversal
        ↓
File Written Outside Intended Directory

Examples may involve:

Uploads
Exports
Backups
Archive extraction
Generated reports
Log files

Arbitrary file write can have substantially greater impact than file read.

Do not perform writes to sensitive locations unless explicitly authorised and necessary.

docs.title: Zip Slip
docs.text:
Archive extraction introduces a related vulnerability known as:

Zip Slip

An archive may contain entries such as:

../../some-file

If the extraction process fails to validate the final path:

Archive
   ↓
Extract
   ↓
Traversal Entry
   ↓
Write Outside Extraction Directory

This is path traversal during archive extraction.

docs.title: Archive Formats
docs.text:
Potentially relevant archive formats include:

ZIP
TAR
TAR.GZ
JAR
WAR
EAR

The exact behaviour depends on the archive library.

Archive extraction should ensure every extracted path remains inside the intended destination directory.

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Burp Suite provides an excellent manual path traversal workflow.

Proxy
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Find File Function
  ↓
Send to Repeater
  ↓
Establish Baseline
  ↓
Modify File Parameter
  ↓
Test Traversal
  ↓
Compare Response
  ↓
Confirm Minimal File Read

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Repeater should be the primary tool for manual validation.

Example workflow:

1. Capture legitimate file request

2. Send request to Repeater

3. Record baseline response

4. Modify suspected path parameter

5. Test one traversal sequence

6. Increase depth if required

7. Test absolute path if relevant

8. Analyse encoding if filtering occurs

9. Confirm with harmless target file

10. Save evidence

docs.title: Burp Intruder
docs.text:
Intruder can help test a controlled set of path variations.

Example request:

GET /download?file=§report.pdf§ HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

A focused payload list could contain variations relevant to the identified operating system and application behaviour.

Analyse:

Status
Length
Words
Lines
Content-Type

Interesting outliers should be investigated manually in Repeater.

docs.title: Example Linux Intruder Candidates
docs.text:
A small controlled list might contain:

../etc/hostname
../../etc/hostname
../../../etc/hostname
../../../../etc/hostname
../../../../../etc/hostname
/etc/hostname

If encoding appears relevant, investigate it separately rather than immediately multiplying every payload.

docs.title: Example Windows Intruder Candidates
docs.text:
For a Windows target:

..\Windows\win.ini
..\..\Windows\win.ini
..\..\..\Windows\win.ini
..\..\..\..\Windows\win.ini
C:\Windows\win.ini

Adjust testing to the actual target environment.

docs.title: ffuf
docs.text:
ffuf can help with targeted traversal testing when you already understand the vulnerable request structure.

Project:

https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf

For example, an authorised lab request might conceptually be tested with:

ffuf \
  -u 'https://target.example/download?file=FUZZ' \
  -w traversal.txt

Filter results based on the baseline.

Useful options include:

-fs
-fw
-fl
-fc

For example:

ffuf \
  -u 'https://target.example/download?file=FUZZ' \
  -w traversal.txt \
  -fc 404

Do not use enormous generic payload lists against production applications.

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
curl is useful for reproducing path traversal requests outside Burp.

Example:

curl -i \
  'https://target.example/download?file=../../../etc/hostname'

For authenticated applications:

curl -i \
  -H 'Cookie: session=YOUR_SESSION' \
  'https://target.example/download?file=../../../etc/hostname'

Avoid putting real session values in documentation or source repositories.

docs.title: DotDotPwn
docs.text:
DotDotPwn is a specialised directory traversal testing tool.

Project:

https://github.com/wireghoul/dotdotpwn

It can be useful for targeted testing after manual analysis has identified a likely path traversal location.

The preferred methodology remains:

Manual Discovery
      ↓
Understand Parameter
      ↓
Manual Traversal Testing
      ↓
Targeted Automation
      ↓
Manual Verification

Do not report findings solely from automated tool output.

docs.title: Payload Collections
docs.text:
Payload collections can help when a specific filtering or normalisation behaviour has been identified.

Useful references include:

PayloadsAllTheThings
HackTricks
PortSwigger Web Security Academy
OWASP WSTG

The correct sequence is:

Understand Application
       ↓
Understand Filter
       ↓
Select Relevant Payload

rather than:

Send Thousands of Payloads
       ↓
Hope Something Works

docs.title: Response Analysis
docs.text:
When testing traversal, compare:

Status
Content-Length
Content-Type
Response body
Content-Disposition
Response time
Application error

For example:

Normal file
200
application/pdf
124 KB

versus:

Traversal test
200
text/plain
18 bytes

Such differences deserve manual investigation.

docs.title: Error Messages
docs.text:
Errors can reveal useful path information.

Examples:

File not found
No such file or directory
Access denied
Permission denied
Invalid path
Path outside allowed directory
Cannot open file

Verbose errors may expose the application's base directory.

For example:

FileNotFoundException:
/opt/application/uploads/test.pdf

reveals:

/opt/application/uploads/

This can help determine traversal depth.

docs.title: Absolute Path Disclosure
docs.text:
Application errors may reveal absolute filesystem paths.

Examples:

/var/www/application/uploads/

/opt/app/data/

C:\inetpub\wwwroot\uploads\

Path disclosure alone may be a lower-severity issue, but it can significantly assist traversal testing.

docs.title: WAF Behaviour
docs.text:
A WAF may block common traversal sequences.

Indicators include:

403
406
Generic block page
Connection reset
Different server header
Request rejected before application

Separate:

WAF Behaviour

from:

Application Path Validation

A WAF blocking:

../

does not demonstrate that the underlying application handles paths securely.

docs.title: Reverse Proxy Normalisation
docs.text:
Reverse proxies and web servers may normalise paths before forwarding requests.

The request flow can be:

Browser
   ↓
CDN
   ↓
WAF
   ↓
Reverse Proxy
   ↓
Web Server
   ↓
Framework
   ↓
Application

Each layer may perform:

URL decoding
Path normalisation
Slash collapsing
Character filtering

This can explain differences between seemingly equivalent traversal tests.

docs.title: Path Traversal in REST APIs
docs.text:
REST-style paths can contain attacker-controlled segments.

Example:

/api/files/report.pdf

The route may internally map:

report.pdf

to a filesystem path.

Path traversal testing therefore should not focus only on query parameters.

Potential locations include:

/api/files/{filename}
/documents/{path}
/download/{resource}

docs.title: URL Path Traversal
docs.text:
A traversal sequence may appear directly in the URL path:

/files/../../../some-resource

However, browsers, proxies and servers may normalise these sequences automatically.

Burp Repeater is useful because it gives greater control over the exact request sent.

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
Client-side JavaScript can reveal hidden file functionality.

Search JavaScript for terms such as:

download
file
filename
path
document
attachment
export
report
template

For example:

fetch("/api/download?file=" + filename)

reveals a potentially interesting endpoint even if it is not obvious in the user interface.

docs.title: API Documentation
docs.text:
Review:

Swagger
OpenAPI
GraphQL schema
Developer documentation
JavaScript API clients
Mobile application APIs

for parameters such as:

file
path
filename
resource
template
document

These may expose functionality not reachable through normal navigation.

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text:
When source code is available, search for filesystem APIs.

The general flow is:

SOURCE
  ↓
Request Parameter
  ↓
Path Construction
  ↓
Normalisation
  ↓
Filesystem API
  ↓
FILE

The goal is to trace attacker-controlled data to filesystem operations.

docs.title: Python File Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Python functionality includes:

open()
pathlib.Path()
os.path.join()
os.path.abspath()
os.path.realpath()
send_file()
send_from_directory()

Example potentially unsafe pattern:

filename = request.args.get("file")

path = "/var/www/files/" + filename

return open(path, "rb").read()

docs.title: Python Path Joining
docs.text:
Do not assume:

os.path.join()

automatically prevents traversal.

For example:

os.path.join(BASE, user_input)

constructs a path but does not inherently prove that the resolved result remains inside BASE.

The application must validate the final resolved path.

docs.title: PHP File Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting PHP functions include:

file_get_contents()
readfile()
fopen()
include()
require()
include_once()
require_once()

Example:

$file = $_GET["file"];
readfile("/var/www/files/" . $file);

Functions such as:

include
require

may introduce LFI behaviour rather than simple file disclosure.

docs.title: Java File Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Java APIs include:

File
FileInputStream
Files.readAllBytes
Files.readString
Paths.get
Path.resolve
Resource
ClassPathResource
FileSystemResource

Example:

Path path = Paths.get(baseDir, filename);

Review whether the final canonical or normalised path is verified to remain within the expected directory.

docs.title: .NET File Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting .NET APIs include:

File.ReadAllText
File.ReadAllBytes
File.Open
FileStream
Path.Combine
Directory.GetFiles
PhysicalFile

Do not assume:

Path.Combine

alone prevents traversal.

Validate the final canonical path.

docs.title: Node.js File Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Node.js functionality includes:

fs.readFile()
fs.readFileSync()
fs.createReadStream()
path.join()
path.resolve()
res.sendFile()

Example:

const file = req.query.file;

fs.readFile("/app/files/" + file, callback);

Trace the request value into the filesystem operation.

docs.title: Go File Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Go functions include:

os.Open()
os.ReadFile()
filepath.Join()
filepath.Clean()
http.ServeFile()

Review whether cleaned and resolved paths remain inside the intended directory.

docs.title: Ruby File Sinks
docs.text:
Interesting Ruby functionality includes:

File.read
File.open
File.join
send_file
IO.read

Trace attacker-controlled path components to the filesystem operation.

docs.title: Search Source Code for File Sinks
docs.text:
A useful first pass with grep:

grep -RniE \
'open\(|readfile|file_get_contents|fopen|include\(|require\(|FileInputStream|Files\.read|Paths\.get|File\.Read|File\.Open|FileStream|fs\.readFile|fs\.createReadStream|sendFile|os\.Open|os\.ReadFile|filepath\.Join|File\.read|send_file' \
.

With ripgrep:

rg -n \
'open\(|readfile|file_get_contents|fopen|include\(|require\(|FileInputStream|Files\.read|Paths\.get|File\.Read|File\.Open|FileStream|fs\.readFile|fs\.createReadStream|sendFile|os\.Open|os\.ReadFile|filepath\.Join|File\.read|send_file'

Search results are potential sinks.

You still need to trace user input.

docs.title: Source to Sink Analysis
docs.text:
A useful model is:

SOURCE
  ↓
req.query.file
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Path Construction
  ↓
Path Normalisation
  ↓
Filesystem API
  ↓
FILE

Example:

req.query.filename
       ↓
downloadFile()
       ↓
path.join(uploadDir, filename)
       ↓
fs.createReadStream()

Then ask:

Is filename validated?

Is the final path normalised?

Is the canonical path checked?

Can it escape uploadDir?

docs.title: Secure Path Validation
docs.text:
A safer design is conceptually:

User Input
    ↓
Resolve Against Base Directory
    ↓
Canonicalise
    ↓
Verify Result Remains Inside Base
    ↓
Access File

For example:

BASE:
/var/www/files/

INPUT:
reports/report.pdf

RESOLVED:
/var/www/files/reports/report.pdf

The application should verify that the final path remains beneath:

/var/www/files/

docs.title: Prefix Validation
docs.text:
Be careful with naive string prefix checks.

Suppose the permitted directory is:

/var/www/files

A path such as:

/var/www/files-backup/

also begins with the string:

/var/www/files

Path validation should operate on properly resolved filesystem paths and directory boundaries.

docs.title: Prefer Indirect References
docs.text:
Where possible, avoid exposing filesystem paths to users.

Instead of:

/download?file=/var/www/reports/report.pdf

prefer something like:

/download?id=8f6c1e

The server then maps:

8f6c1e

to an approved file.

Authorisation must still be performed.

docs.title: File Allowlist
docs.text:
If only a small number of files can be downloaded, maintain an explicit mapping.

Conceptually:

report-2026
      ↓
Approved Mapping
      ↓
/srv/reports/report-2026.pdf

rather than allowing arbitrary user-controlled paths.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
Filesystem permissions provide important defence in depth.

The application process should not have unnecessary access to:

Operating system secrets
SSH keys
Application secrets
Other users' files
Backup files
Cloud credentials
Private configuration

Path traversal should still be fixed at the application layer, but least privilege reduces its impact.

docs.title: Path Traversal Validation
docs.text:
A strong finding should establish:

ATTACKER INPUT
      ↓
PATH CONSTRUCTION
      ↓
DIRECTORY ESCAPE
      ↓
UNINTENDED FILE
      ↓
FILE CONTENT RETURNED

For example:

filename
   ↓
/srv/downloads/ + filename
   ↓
../../../etc/hostname
   ↓
/etc/hostname
   ↓
Contents returned

docs.title: Avoid Excessive File Access
docs.text:
Once arbitrary file access has been demonstrated, avoid unnecessary enumeration.

You generally do not need to retrieve:

SSH private keys
Database passwords
Cloud credentials
Password hashes
Application secrets
User documents

to prove the vulnerability.

Use:

/etc/hostname

or:

C:\Windows\win.ini

where sufficient.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful evidence includes:

Affected endpoint
HTTP method
Affected parameter
Authentication requirement
Original request
Traversal request
Normal response
Traversal response
File retrieved
Operating system
Required traversal depth
Encoding required if applicable
Relevant screenshot

Avoid placing unnecessary sensitive file contents into reports.

docs.title: Path Traversal Reporting
docs.text:
A report should explain:

Which endpoint is affected
Which parameter controls the path
What directory should normally be accessible
How traversal escapes that directory
Which harmless file demonstrated the issue
What files the application account could potentially access
What security impact exists
How the issue should be remediated

docs.title: Example Finding Structure
docs.text:
Title
Path Traversal Allows Arbitrary File Read

Affected Endpoint
GET /api/documents/download

Affected Parameter
filename

Authentication Required
Yes

Description
The application uses the user-controlled filename parameter when
constructing a filesystem path without ensuring that the final
resolved path remains within the intended document directory.

By supplying directory traversal sequences, it was possible to
escape the document directory and retrieve a file elsewhere on
the server filesystem.

Validation
The vulnerability was demonstrated using a non-sensitive
operating system file.

Impact
An attacker with access to the affected functionality may be able
to read files accessible to the application service account.

Depending on filesystem permissions, this could expose application
configuration, source code or other sensitive information.

Recommendation
Resolve requested files against a fixed base directory and verify
that the canonical resulting path remains within that directory
before performing the filesystem operation.

Where possible, use indirect file identifiers rather than accepting
filesystem paths from users.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
A secure implementation should avoid directly trusting user-controlled filesystem paths.

Recommended controls include:

Use fixed base directories
Canonicalise paths
Validate final resolved path
Use indirect file identifiers
Use file allowlists where possible
Reject unexpected path separators
Apply least privilege
Avoid exposing absolute paths
Perform authorisation independently

docs.title: Do Not Rely on String Replacement
docs.text:
Avoid protections such as:

filename.replace("../", "")

or:

if "../" not in filename

These approaches can fail because of:

Encoding
Multiple decoding layers
Alternative separators
Nested sequences
Path normalisation
Operating system differences

Validate the final resolved filesystem path instead.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Prototype pollution is a JavaScript vulnerability in which an attacker modifies properties of an object's prototype.

Because JavaScript objects can inherit properties from prototypes, modifying a shared prototype can unexpectedly influence other objects throughout an application.

Prototype pollution can occur:

Client-side
Server-side

Depending on where the vulnerable JavaScript executes.

Potential impact includes:

DOM-based XSS
Authentication bypass
Authorisation bypass
Configuration manipulation
Application logic manipulation
Privilege escalation
Denial of service
Server-side code execution in specific circumstances

The vulnerability itself is usually a primitive.

The important question is:

What security-sensitive behaviour can be influenced after the prototype has been polluted?

A simplified attack chain is:

Attacker-Controlled Input
          ↓
Unsafe Object Operation
          ↓
Object Prototype Modified
          ↓
Another Object Inherits Property
          ↓
Application Uses Property
          ↓
Security-Sensitive Sink

Authorised Security Testing

Perform prototype pollution testing only against applications included in the authorised assessment scope. Begin with harmless canary properties and avoid changing properties that may destabilise a production application.

docs.title: JavaScript Prototypes
docs.text:
JavaScript uses prototype-based inheritance.

Consider:

const user = {
    username: "alice"
};

The object contains:

username

but it also inherits properties and methods from its prototype.

For example:

user.toString()

works even though toString was not explicitly defined on user.

Conceptually:

user
 ↓
Object.prototype
 ↓
Inherited Properties

docs.title: The Prototype Chain
docs.text:
JavaScript looks for properties through the prototype chain.

For example:

const user = {};

Accessing:

user.example

first checks:

user

If the property does not exist, JavaScript checks the prototype.

Conceptually:

user.example
     ↓
Property on user?
     ↓
     NO
     ↓
Object.prototype.example?
     ↓
Return inherited value

docs.title: Object.prototype
docs.text:
Many ordinary JavaScript objects ultimately inherit from:

Object.prototype

Example:

const a = {};
const b = {};

console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(a) === Object.prototype);
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(b) === Object.prototype);

Both objects normally share the same prototype.

This shared inheritance model is what makes prototype pollution security-relevant.

docs.title: Harmless Prototype Demonstration
docs.text:
In a local JavaScript environment:

const first = {};
const second = {};

Object.prototype.demo = "AM-PROTOTYPE-TEST";

console.log(first.demo);
console.log(second.demo);

Both objects can inherit:

AM-PROTOTYPE-TEST

even though the property was never explicitly assigned to either object.

Clean up afterwards:

delete Object.prototype.demo;

docs.title: Own vs Inherited Properties
docs.text:
Consider:

const user = {
    username: "alice"
};

Then:

user.hasOwnProperty("username")

returns:

true

But an inherited property may exist without being an own property.

For example:

Object.prototype.isAdmin = true;

const user = {};

console.log(user.isAdmin);
console.log(Object.hasOwn(user, "isAdmin"));

Conceptually:

user.isAdmin
      ↓
Own property?
      ↓
NO
      ↓
Prototype
      ↓
isAdmin = true

This distinction is extremely important when analysing prototype pollution.

docs.title: What Is Prototype Pollution?
docs.text:
Prototype pollution occurs when attacker-controlled input is able to modify properties associated with an object's prototype.

A simplified vulnerable operation may look like:

target[key] = value;

If the attacker controls:

key

or nested property paths, dangerous property names may reach prototype-related structures.

The resulting primitive can conceptually become:

Input
 ↓
Property Assignment
 ↓
Prototype Modified
 ↓
Other Objects Inherit Property

docs.title: Sources and Sinks
docs.text:
Prototype pollution analysis is easier when divided into:

SOURCE
 ↓
POLLUTION SOURCE / GADGET
 ↓
PROTOTYPE
 ↓
SINK

docs.title: Source
docs.text:
A source is attacker-controlled data.

Examples include:

URL query parameters
URL fragments
JSON
POST parameters
Cookies
WebSocket messages
Configuration objects
API request bodies
Object merge input

docs.title: Pollution Source
docs.text:
The vulnerable operation takes attacker-controlled properties and writes them into an object in an unsafe way.

Common patterns include:

Recursive object merge
Property assignment
Query-string parsing
Object cloning
Configuration merging
Deep-copy functions

docs.title: Prototype
docs.text:
The attacker-controlled property reaches a prototype.

Conceptually:

Attacker Input
     ↓
__proto__
     ↓
Object.prototype
     ↓
Injected Property

docs.title: Sink
docs.text:
A sink is where the polluted property produces security impact.

Examples may include:

DOM manipulation
HTML generation
Script creation
Configuration decisions
Authentication checks
Authorisation checks
Command construction
Template configuration
Network request options

Prototype pollution without an exploitable sink may have limited security impact.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Testing Model
docs.text:
A useful mental model is:

Can I Pollute?
      ↓
     YES
      ↓
What Property Can I Create?
      ↓
Where Is It Read?
      ↓
Does It Reach a Gadget?
      ↓
Does Gadget Reach Dangerous Sink?
      ↓
Can Security Impact Be Demonstrated?

docs.title: Client-Side Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Client-side prototype pollution occurs in JavaScript running in the browser.

A common attack surface is:

URL
 ↓
JavaScript Parser
 ↓
Object
 ↓
Prototype Pollution
 ↓
DOM Gadget
 ↓
DOM XSS

Potential sources include:

Query strings
URL fragments
postMessage
Cookies
Local storage
API responses

docs.title: Server-Side Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Server-side prototype pollution occurs in server-side JavaScript, most commonly Node.js applications.

A simplified flow is:

HTTP Request
      ↓
JSON / Parameters
      ↓
Object Merge
      ↓
Prototype Pollution
      ↓
Application Configuration
      ↓
Security-Sensitive Behaviour

Potential impact can be significantly different from browser-side pollution.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution vs DOM XSS
docs.text:
Prototype pollution and DOM XSS are not the same vulnerability.

Prototype pollution:

Attacker
 ↓
Prototype
 ↓
Property

DOM XSS:

Attacker
 ↓
DOM Source
 ↓
Dangerous Sink
 ↓
JavaScript Execution

However, prototype pollution may provide the source for a DOM XSS gadget.

Combined:

Prototype Pollution
       ↓
Polluted Property
       ↓
DOM Gadget
       ↓
Dangerous Sink
       ↓
DOM XSS

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Terminology
docs.text:
Important terms include:

Source
Prototype
Property
Pollution
Gadget
Sink
Prototype chain
Own property
Inherited property

Understanding these terms makes analysis considerably easier.

docs.title: proto
docs.text:
Historically, one of the most important prototype-related properties is:

__proto__

It can provide access to an object's prototype in many JavaScript environments.

For example:

const obj = {};

console.log(obj.__proto__ === Object.prototype);

During testing, determine whether attacker-controlled property paths containing:

__proto__

are accepted and processed.

docs.title: constructor.prototype
docs.text:
Filtering only:

__proto__

is not always sufficient.

Another important path is:

constructor.prototype

Conceptually:

object
  ↓
constructor
  ↓
Object
  ↓
prototype
  ↓
Object.prototype

Therefore, testing should consider whether application logic permits prototype access through alternate paths.

docs.title: Common Property Paths
docs.text:
Prototype pollution research commonly considers structures such as:

__proto__.property
constructor.prototype.property

The exact representation depends on how the application parses input.

For example:

Dot notation
Bracket notation
Nested JSON
Query-string parsing
Custom object paths

docs.title: Safe Canary Property
docs.text:
During authorised testing, start with a unique harmless property.

For example:

amPrototypeTest

with a value such as:

AM-PP-123456

Then determine whether a newly created object unexpectedly inherits it.

The goal is:

Canary
  ↓
Prototype
  ↓
Fresh Object
  ↓
Canary Inherited?

docs.title: Browser Console Verification
docs.text:
After sending a suspected pollution input, open the browser developer console.

Test:

({}).amPrototypeTest

If the result is:

AM-PP-123456

then prototype pollution may have occurred.

Another test:

Object.prototype.amPrototypeTest

Be careful when testing production applications.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
If your testing directly modifies a prototype in a controlled local environment, remove the test property afterwards:

delete Object.prototype.amPrototypeTest;

For web applications, refreshing the page may restore a clean JavaScript context for client-side pollution.

Do not assume that server-side pollution will be cleared by refreshing the browser.

docs.title: Query String Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
A common client-side source is query-string parsing.

Conceptually:

https://target.example/?parameter=value
                 ↓
           Query Parser
                 ↓
              Object

If the parser supports nested object notation and handles prototype-related keys unsafely:

URL
 ↓
Parser
 ↓
Prototype

may become possible.

docs.title: Example Testing Concept
docs.text:
Suppose an application parses nested parameters.

A controlled test may investigate whether a structure equivalent to:

__proto__
    ↓
amPrototypeTest
    ↓
AM-PP-123456

can reach the prototype.

After the request is processed, test:

({}).amPrototypeTest

The exact syntax required depends entirely on the application's parser.

docs.title: JSON Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
JSON-based APIs may expose another potential source.

Example application input:

{
  "profile": {
    "displayName": "Alice"
  }
}

If the server recursively merges arbitrary object properties, prototype-related properties deserve investigation.

A harmless testing structure can conceptually represent:

prototype path
      ↓
unique canary property
      ↓
unique canary value

Do not immediately attempt to modify application security properties.

First establish whether pollution itself is possible.

docs.title: Recursive Merge Functions
docs.text:
Custom recursive merge functions are a common place to look during source-code review.

Example:

function merge(target, source) {
    for (const key in source) {
        if (typeof source[key] === "object") {
            if (!target[key]) {
                target[key] = {};
            }

            merge(target[key], source[key]);
        } else {
            target[key] = source[key];
        }
    }

    return target;
}

The security question is:

Can attacker-controlled keys cause the recursion to traverse into prototype-related objects?

docs.title: Object Merge Operations
docs.text:
Search source code for operations involving:

merge
extend
clone
assign
defaults
deepMerge
set
copy

Pay particular attention when:

Attacker-controlled object

is recursively merged into:

Application object
Configuration object
Default object
Request object

docs.title: Object.assign
docs.text:
Object.assign() itself should not automatically be labelled vulnerable.

Example:

Object.assign(target, source);

The actual security behaviour depends on:

Source object
Target object
Runtime behaviour
Property definitions
Application logic

Analyse the complete data flow rather than flagging the function name alone.

docs.title: for...in
docs.text:
Loops such as:

for (const key in object) {
    target[key] = object[key];
}

deserve attention because for...in can enumerate inherited enumerable properties.

Safer code often needs to distinguish:

Own properties

from:

Inherited properties

docs.title: Object.keys
docs.text:
Using:

Object.keys(object)

returns the object's own enumerable property names.

This can reduce some prototype-related risks compared with blindly iterating inherited properties.

However, it does not automatically make arbitrary object merging secure.

docs.title: Object.hasOwn
docs.text:
Modern JavaScript provides:

Object.hasOwn(object, property)

Example:

if (Object.hasOwn(user, "isAdmin")) {
    // process explicitly defined property
}

This avoids trusting a property merely because it exists somewhere in the prototype chain.

docs.title: hasOwnProperty
docs.text:
Older code commonly uses:

object.hasOwnProperty("property")

However:

Object.hasOwn(object, "property")

is generally clearer and avoids relying on the target object's inherited hasOwnProperty method.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution Gadgets
docs.text:
Successfully polluting a prototype does not necessarily produce meaningful impact.

The next step is gadget discovery.

A gadget is application code that uses a potentially polluted property in a security-sensitive way.

Conceptually:

Polluted Property
       ↓
Application Reads Property
       ↓
Property Changes Behaviour
       ↓
Security Impact

docs.title: Client-Side Gadgets
docs.text:
Potential browser-side gadgets include code that constructs or modifies:

HTML
Scripts
iframes
URLs
DOM elements
Event handlers
Configuration objects

Interesting sinks may include:

innerHTML
outerHTML
document.write()
insertAdjacentHTML()
eval()
new Function()
setTimeout()
setInterval()

The presence of one of these functions does not automatically prove exploitability.

Trace attacker influence into the sink.

docs.title: Example Gadget Concept
docs.text:
Suppose application code behaves conceptually like:

const config = {};

if (config.transport_url) {
    const script = document.createElement("script");
    script.src = config.transport_url;
    document.body.appendChild(script);
}

If:

config.transport_url

does not exist as an own property, JavaScript may search the prototype chain.

Conceptually:

Object.prototype.transport_url
            ↓
config.transport_url
            ↓
script.src
            ↓
External Script

This creates a potentially interesting prototype pollution gadget.

docs.title: DOM XSS Gadget Discovery
docs.text:
A useful workflow is:

Confirm Pollution
      ↓
Search JavaScript
      ↓
Identify Reads of Missing Properties
      ↓
Trace Property
      ↓
Find DOM Sink
      ↓
Determine Context
      ↓
Validate Safely

docs.title: Search JavaScript
docs.text:
Use browser developer tools or downloaded JavaScript files.

Search for:

innerHTML
outerHTML
document.write
insertAdjacentHTML
createElement
script.src
iframe.src
eval
Function
setTimeout
setInterval

Also search for configuration-style properties:

url
src
href
html
template
callback
transport
script

These are leads, not confirmed vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Browser DevTools
docs.text:
Browser DevTools are extremely useful for prototype pollution analysis.

Useful areas include:

Console
Sources
Network
Debugger
DOM inspector
Search

The console can help verify whether a property has reached:

Object.prototype

while Sources can help identify gadgets.

docs.title: Breakpoints
docs.text:
JavaScript breakpoints can help determine:

Where property is read
What object contains it
Whether property is inherited
Where value flows next

This is particularly useful for complicated bundled JavaScript.

docs.title: Source Maps
docs.text:
If source maps are available:

.js.map

they can make gadget analysis substantially easier.

Source maps may reveal:

Original source files
Function names
Module structure
Configuration objects
Readable variable names

Refer to:

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: Server-Side Gadgets
docs.text:
Server-side prototype pollution may influence:

Application configuration
Authentication logic
Authorisation logic
HTTP request options
Template settings
Process options
File operations
Logging
Child process configuration

The exact impact is application-specific.

Do not assume that server-side prototype pollution automatically leads to remote code execution.

docs.title: Server-Side Detection Challenges
docs.text:
Client-side pollution can often be checked with:

({}).property

Server-side pollution is harder because you cannot directly inspect the server's JavaScript runtime.

Instead, you may need to observe changes in application behaviour.

For example:

Request
 ↓
Pollution Attempt
 ↓
Second Request
 ↓
Behaviour Changed?

docs.title: Non-Destructive Server-Side Detection
docs.text:
Prefer properties that cause harmless observable changes.

Potential categories include:

Response formatting
Status behaviour
JSON structure
Configuration defaults
Debug-style behaviour

Only use properties you understand.

Avoid guessing dangerous runtime properties on production systems.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Server-side pollution may persist:

For one request
Across requests
Until worker restart
Until process restart

depending on the vulnerable object and application architecture.

This makes server-side testing potentially disruptive.

docs.title: Worker Processes
docs.text:
Node.js applications may use:

Multiple workers
Clusters
Containers
Serverless functions

A polluted prototype may therefore affect only one execution context.

Testing may appear inconsistent:

Request 1 → affected worker
Request 2 → different worker
Request 3 → affected worker

Do not immediately conclude that inconsistent results are false positives.

docs.title: Denial of Service
docs.text:
Prototype pollution can sometimes destabilise an application.

For example, changing properties expected to contain:

Numbers
Strings
Booleans
Functions
Objects

may cause unexpected exceptions.

During authorised testing:

Avoid destructive properties
Use harmless canaries
Stop after sufficient evidence

docs.title: Authentication Logic
docs.text:
Consider insecure logic such as:

if (user.isAdmin) {
    showAdminPanel();
}

If:

isAdmin

is not explicitly defined on the object, inherited values may influence the check.

Secure logic should not depend on prototype inheritance for security-sensitive properties.

docs.title: Authorisation Logic
docs.text:
The same principle applies to:

role
permissions
isAdmin
isStaff
isOwner
canDelete
canApprove

A secure application should derive authorisation from trusted server-side state.

Prototype pollution should never be able to create an authorisation decision.

docs.title: Example Authorisation Pattern
docs.text:
Potentially dangerous conceptual pattern:

const user = {};

if (user.isAdmin) {
    allow();
}

If:

Object.prototype.isAdmin

can be influenced, the property lookup may produce an unexpected result.

Safer logic should use explicit trusted properties and robust authorisation checks.

docs.title: Configuration Objects
docs.text:
Configuration objects are particularly interesting.

Example:

const options = {};

performAction(options);

If downstream code checks:

options.someSetting

without ensuring it is an own property, an inherited value may influence behaviour.

docs.title: Default Values
docs.text:
Prototype pollution can interact with default-value logic.

Example:

if (!config.mode) {
    config.mode = "safe";
}

If:

config.mode

is inherited, the default may never be assigned.

This can alter application behaviour unexpectedly.

docs.title: Property Existence Checks
docs.text:
Be cautious with:

if (object.property) {

when the property controls security-sensitive behaviour.

This checks both:

Own properties
Inherited properties

Where appropriate, explicitly check ownership.

docs.title: The in Operator
docs.text:
Example:

"property" in object

returns true for both own and inherited properties.

Therefore:

"isAdmin" in user

does not establish that isAdmin was explicitly assigned to the user object.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution and JSON
docs.text:
An important nuance is that JSON parsing and prototype mutation are separate concepts.

A JSON document containing a property named:

__proto__

does not necessarily pollute the prototype simply by being parsed.

The danger often appears later when parsed data is:

Merged
Copied
Assigned
Traversed

into another object.

Think:

JSON Input
   ↓
JSON.parse()
   ↓
Ordinary Object
   ↓
Unsafe Merge
   ↓
Prototype Pollution

docs.title: Prototype Pollution and Query Parsers
docs.text:
Libraries that transform:

a[b][c]=value

into nested JavaScript objects deserve attention.

Conceptually:

Query String
     ↓
Parser
     ↓
Nested Object

The parser must safely handle prototype-related property names.

Modern versions of many libraries include protections, but outdated or custom implementations may behave differently.

docs.title: Dependency Review
docs.text:
During source-assisted testing, inspect JavaScript dependencies.

Look for:

Package name
Package version
Known prototype pollution history
Custom wrappers
Unsafe configuration

Do not report a vulnerability solely because a dependency version has historically been associated with prototype pollution.

Confirm whether the vulnerable functionality is actually reachable.

docs.title: package.json
docs.text:
For Node.js applications, review:

package.json
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml

These can help identify:

Libraries
Versions
Dependency chains
Parsing libraries
Merge libraries

docs.title: npm audit
docs.text:
In a controlled source-code environment:

npm audit

may identify known dependency vulnerabilities.

Treat results as leads.

You still need to determine:

Is vulnerable version present?
Is vulnerable functionality used?
Is attacker-controlled input reachable?
Is security impact possible?

docs.title: Static Source Search
docs.text:
Useful search terms include:

__proto__
prototype
constructor
merge
deepMerge
extend
clone
set
defaults
Object.assign
for...in

Example:

grep -RniE "__proto__|constructor|prototype|merge|extend|deepMerge" .

For JavaScript-heavy projects:

grep -RniE "innerHTML|outerHTML|document\.write|insertAdjacentHTML|eval|new Function" .

docs.title: DOM Invader Canary
docs.text:

Conceptually:

URL
 ↓
Prototype Pollution Source
 ↓
Canary

Object.prototype
 ↓

Once pollution is confirmed, investigate whether the property can reach a useful gadget.

docs.title: DOM Invader Gadget Detection
docs.text:
A gadget may take a polluted property and use it in a dangerous browser operation.

Conceptually:

Polluted Property
       ↓
JavaScript Gadget
       ↓
DOM Sink
       ↓
Potential XSS

DOM Invader can help identify these relationships.

Manual validation remains important.

docs.title: Burp Scanner
docs.text:
Depending on Burp Suite edition and application behaviour, automated scanning may identify prototype pollution-related issues.

Treat scanner findings as:

Potential vulnerability

until manually reproduced.

docs.text:
After a suspected client-side pollution attempt:

({}).amPrototypeTest

If undefined:

Pollution not confirmed

Then investigate:

Where did it come from?
Which input created it?
Which properties are useful?
Which gadget consumes them?

docs.title: Testing Different Sources
docs.text:
Potential client-side sources:

Query parameters
Fragments
postMessage
Cookies
Local storage
Session storage
JSON responses

Potential server-side sources:

JSON request bodies
Form parameters
Nested query parameters
Configuration APIs
Object update endpoints
WebSocket messages

docs.title: postMessage
docs.text:
Client-side applications may accept cross-window messages:

window.addEventListener("message", function(event) {
    // process event.data
});

If:

event.data

is merged into application objects, investigate whether prototype-related properties are handled safely.

Also verify origin validation independently.

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.text:
WebSocket applications frequently exchange JSON objects.

Example:

{
  "action": "update",
  "options": {
    "theme": "dark"
  }
}

If arbitrary nested objects are merged server-side or client-side, prototype pollution may become relevant.

Refer to:

docs/web/websockets.md

docs.title: API Testing
docs.text:
APIs commonly expose:

JSON
Nested structures
Patch operations
Configuration objects

Potentially interesting endpoints include:

/profile
/settings
/preferences
/config
/update
/import

Focus on endpoints that recursively process user-controlled objects.

Refer to:

API Security

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL mutations may accept nested input objects.

Example conceptually:

mutation {
    updateSettings(input: {
        theme: "dark"
    }) {
        success
    }
}

The GraphQL layer itself is not necessarily vulnerable.

Investigate what happens when nested input reaches JavaScript object-processing logic.

docs.title: Mass Assignment vs Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Mass assignment:

Attacker supplies legitimate object properties
        ↓
Application assigns properties it should not

Prototype pollution:

Attacker manipulates prototype-related properties
        ↓
Other objects inherit attacker-controlled values

These can appear in similar endpoints but are distinct vulnerability classes.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution vs Object Injection
docs.text:
Prototype pollution specifically involves:

Prototype chain manipulation

Generic object injection may involve attacker-controlled object properties without modifying shared prototypes.

Use precise terminology when reporting.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution vs Insecure Deserialization
docs.text:
Insecure deserialization involves unsafe processing of serialised objects or object graphs.

Prototype pollution involves unsafe manipulation of JavaScript prototype inheritance.

They may occur in related object-processing code, but they are separate issues.

Refer to:

Insecure Deserialization

docs.title: Prototype Pollution vs Parameter Pollution
docs.text:
HTTP parameter pollution involves duplicate or ambiguous HTTP parameters.

Prototype pollution involves JavaScript object prototypes.

Do not confuse:

Parameter Pollution

with:

Prototype Pollution

docs.title: Testing for Gadgets
docs.text:
After confirming pollution, create a list:

Pollutable Property
       ↓
Where Is It Read?
       ↓
What Type Is Expected?
       ↓
What Does It Control?
       ↓
Does It Reach a Sink?

For each candidate:

Property:
Expected type:
Read location:
Destination:
Security impact:

This makes analysis systematic.

docs.title: Property Types
docs.text:
A gadget may expect:

String
Boolean
Number
Object
Array
Function

The polluted value must normally match the application's expectations.

For example:

isAdmin → Boolean
url → String
timeout → Number
options → Object

Understanding expected types reduces unnecessary testing.

docs.title: Boolean Gadgets
docs.text:
A property may control whether functionality is enabled.

Conceptually:

if (options.enabled) {
    performAction();
}

If:

enabled

can be inherited from the prototype, pollution may alter application behaviour.

docs.title: String Gadgets
docs.text:
String properties commonly control:

URLs
HTML
File names
Template names
Commands
Paths

Example:

element.innerHTML = options.html;

If:

options.html

is inherited and attacker-controlled, investigate the resulting context.

docs.title: URL Gadgets
docs.text:
Potential properties include:

url
src
href
endpoint
callback
redirect
transport_url

Potential sinks include:

script.src
iframe.src
location
fetch()
XMLHttpRequest

The resulting vulnerability depends on context.

docs.title: DOM Sink Review
docs.text:
Important browser sinks include:

innerHTML
outerHTML
insertAdjacentHTML
document.write
eval
Function
script.src
iframe.src
location

Some sinks lead to:

HTML injection

others to:

JavaScript execution

and others to:

Navigation or network requests

Classify the actual behaviour.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution to DOM XSS
docs.text:
A typical chain is:

URL Parameter
     ↓
Prototype Pollution
     ↓
Polluted Property
     ↓
Application Configuration
     ↓
DOM Gadget
     ↓
Unsafe HTML / Script Sink
     ↓
DOM XSS

The finding should explain the complete chain.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution to Access Control
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Attacker Input
     ↓
Prototype
     ↓
isAdmin = true
     ↓
Application Checks user.isAdmin
     ↓
Inherited Value Accepted
     ↓
Authorisation Decision

This requires a real vulnerable application flow.

Do not claim privilege escalation simply because you can create an isAdmin property on a prototype.

docs.title: Prototype Pollution to Server-Side Code Execution
docs.text:
Server-side prototype pollution can, in specific application and runtime contexts, become part of a chain leading to code execution.

However:

Prototype Pollution
≠
Automatic RCE

A complete exploit requires a suitable server-side gadget.

During assessment:

Confirm pollution
Identify application/runtime gadget
Understand exact behaviour
Use minimum-impact validation

Do not attempt speculative destructive gadget chains on production systems.

docs.title: Detection Without Exploitation
docs.text:
A strong finding can sometimes be demonstrated with:

Controlled Input
      ↓
Prototype Pollution
      ↓
Harmless Property
      ↓
Observable Application Behaviour

You do not always need to demonstrate the worst theoretical impact.

Document:

Confirmed primitive
Reachable gadget
Realistic security impact

separately.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Do not report prototype pollution solely because:

__proto__ appears in source code
A dependency had a historical CVE
A scanner reports a possible issue
A query parameter is accepted
A property appears in an object

Confirm actual prototype modification.

docs.title: Verification Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

Can attacker-controlled input reach object processing?

Can prototype-related property names be supplied?

Does the prototype actually change?

Can a fresh object inherit the property?

Does the pollution persist?

Is there a useful gadget?

Can the gadget cross a security boundary?

docs.text:
Keep a table during testing:

ID Source Property Canary Result Gadget PP-001 Query amPrototypeTest AM-PP-001 Not inherited None PP-002 JSON amPrototypeTest AM-PP-002 Inherited Investigate PP-003 Fragment amPrototypeTest AM-PP-003 Not inherited None

This becomes particularly useful when an application has several JavaScript parsers.

docs.title: Example Finding: Client-Side Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Finding:
Client-Side Prototype Pollution via URL Query Parameters

Affected Endpoint:
/application

Observed:
The application processes nested query-string parameters using client-side JavaScript.

A controlled prototype pollution test introduced a unique harmless property into Object.prototype.

After processing the supplied input, a newly created JavaScript object inherited the controlled property even though it was not explicitly defined on that object.

Impact:
An attacker can influence properties inherited by JavaScript objects within the affected page. The security impact depends on whether polluted properties are consumed by security-sensitive application gadgets.

Recommendation:
Prevent prototype-related property names from being processed during object construction and use safe, maintained parsing and merge functionality.

docs.title: Example Finding: Prototype Pollution to DOM XSS
docs.text:
Finding:
Client-Side Prototype Pollution Leads to DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting

Observed:
Attacker-controlled URL input was able to introduce a property into Object.prototype.

Application JavaScript subsequently read the inherited property from a configuration object and passed the resulting value to a DOM sink without appropriate handling.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to execute JavaScript in the browser of a user who visits a crafted application URL.

Recommendation:
Prevent prototype pollution at the source and remove the unsafe gadget by ensuring untrusted values cannot reach executable DOM sinks.

docs.title: Example Finding: Server-Side Prototype Pollution
docs.text:
Finding:
Server-Side Prototype Pollution via JSON Object Merge

Affected Endpoint:
/api/settings

Observed:
The endpoint recursively merged attacker-controlled JSON properties into a server-side JavaScript object.

A controlled harmless property was introduced through a prototype-related property path and subsequently influenced newly created objects within the application.

Impact:
An attacker can manipulate inherited server-side object properties. Depending on available application gadgets, this may affect application configuration, security decisions or other server-side behaviour.

Recommendation:
Reject prototype-related property names, use safe object merge implementations and ensure security-sensitive configuration does not rely on inherited properties.

docs.title: Example Finding: Authorisation Impact
docs.text:
Finding:
Prototype Pollution Influences Server-Side Authorisation Logic

Observed:
A prototype pollution primitive allowed an inherited security-sensitive property to influence an application authorisation decision.

The affected logic trusted the inherited property without verifying that it was explicitly associated with the authenticated user.

Impact:
An attacker may be able to obtain functionality or permissions not assigned to their account.

Recommendation:
Prevent prototype pollution and derive authorisation decisions exclusively from trusted server-side identity and permission data. Security-sensitive properties should not be inherited from generic object prototypes.

docs.title: Reporting Titles
docs.text:
Prefer precise titles such as:

Client-Side Prototype Pollution via Query Parameter

Prototype Pollution Leads to DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting

Server-Side Prototype Pollution via Unsafe Recursive Object Merge

Prototype Pollution Influences Authorisation Logic

Prototype Pollution in Configuration Object Allows Application Behaviour Manipulation

Prototype Pollution via Unsafe Nested Parameter Parsing

Avoid vague titles such as:

JavaScript Issue

Prototype Issue

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Severity depends on the complete chain.

For example:

Prototype Pollution
      ↓
No Useful Gadget

may have limited demonstrated impact.

While:

Prototype Pollution
      ↓
DOM Gadget
      ↓
JavaScript Execution

may result in XSS.

Or:

Server-Side Prototype Pollution
      ↓
Security-Sensitive Gadget
      ↓
Authorisation Bypass

may have significantly greater impact.

Report the demonstrated security impact rather than assigning severity based solely on the pollution primitive.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Prototype pollution should be addressed at multiple layers.

A defence-in-depth model is:

Validate Input
     ↓
Reject Dangerous Keys
     ↓
Use Safe Object Operations
     ↓
Avoid Prototype Inheritance Where Unnecessary
     ↓
Use Own-Property Checks
     ↓
Update Dependencies
     ↓
Remove Dangerous Gadgets

docs.title: Reject Prototype-Related Keys
docs.text:
Applications that accept arbitrary object properties should reject dangerous property names where they are not required.

Examples include:

__proto__
prototype
constructor

Filtering must account for the complete object-processing logic.

Simply blocking one string is not necessarily sufficient.

docs.title: Schema Validation
docs.text:
Prefer explicit input schemas.

Instead of:

Accept arbitrary object

define:

Allowed property A
Allowed property B
Allowed property C

Conceptually:

Incoming JSON
     ↓
Schema Validation
     ↓
Known Property?
   ↓          ↓
 YES         NO
 ↓            ↓
Process      Reject

docs.title: Avoid Arbitrary Recursive Merging
docs.text:
Avoid recursively merging untrusted objects into application objects unless absolutely necessary.

Instead of:

User Object
    ↓
Recursive Merge
    ↓
Application Configuration

prefer explicitly copying required properties.

docs.title: Explicit Property Assignment
docs.text:
For example:

const settings = {
    theme: input.theme,
    language: input.language
};

This is generally easier to reason about than accepting an arbitrary nested object.

docs.title: Null-Prototype Objects
docs.text:
Where inheritance is unnecessary, objects can be created without a prototype:

const dictionary = Object.create(null);

Such objects do not inherit from:

Object.prototype

This can be useful for dictionary-style data structures.

It is not a universal replacement for normal objects.

docs.title: Object.freeze
docs.text:
In some environments, defensive use of:

Object.freeze()

may help protect specific objects from modification.

For example:

Object.freeze(Object.prototype);

can have significant compatibility implications and should not be introduced blindly.

Fix the vulnerable input processing rather than relying solely on runtime freezing.

docs.title: Own-Property Checks
docs.text:
Security-sensitive code should distinguish own properties from inherited properties.

Prefer:

Object.hasOwn(object, "property")

where appropriate.

For example:

if (
    Object.hasOwn(user, "isAdmin") &&
    user.isAdmin === true
) {
    // authorised behaviour
}

Authorisation should still rely on trusted server-side state.

docs.title: Dependency Updates
docs.text:
Keep JavaScript dependencies current.

Pay particular attention to packages performing:

Deep merging
Query parsing
Object cloning
Configuration processing
Property path assignment

Review:

package.json
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml

docs.title: Do Not Rely Only on Dependency Patching
docs.text:
Even when dependencies are current, custom application code may remain vulnerable.

Review:

Custom merge functions
Custom query parsers
Dynamic property assignment
Configuration merging

as well.

docs.title: Remove Gadgets
docs.text:
Defence should not stop at preventing prototype pollution.

Where possible, remove dangerous gadgets.

For example, avoid:

element.innerHTML = config.html;

when safe DOM APIs can be used.

This creates defence in depth:

Pollution Prevention
       +
Gadget Removal
       =
Reduced Exploitability

docs.title: Use Safe DOM APIs
docs.text:
Prefer:

textContent

when rendering text.

Example:

element.textContent = value;

rather than:

element.innerHTML = value;

when HTML interpretation is not required.

Refer to:

docs/web/xss.md

docs.title: Test After Remediation
docs.text:
After remediation, repeat:

Original source
 ↓
Prototype canary
 ↓
Prototype verification
 ↓
Gadget verification

Confirm that:

Dangerous keys rejected
Prototype unchanged
Fresh objects unaffected
Application functionality preserved
