The central principle is:

A SAML assertion should only create an authenticated session when its cryptographic integrity, trusted issuer, intended audience, recipient, destination, validity period, request relationship and identity mapping have all been validated. Testing therefore needs to go beyond decoding SAMLResponse: determine exactly which XML element is signed, which element the application consumes, which certificate establishes trust, and whether an assertion can be substituted, wrapped, replayed or mapped to an identity that the trusted IdP did not actually authenticate.

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
Session management controls how an application maintains a user's authenticated state across multiple HTTP requests.

Because HTTP is stateless, applications typically use session cookies, tokens, or other identifiers to associate requests with an authenticated user.

Weak session management can allow an attacker to hijack authenticated sessions, bypass authentication controls, maintain unauthorised access, or access another user's account.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform session management testing only against systems for which you have explicit authorisation. Use dedicated test accounts where possible and avoid accessing data belonging to real users.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
Session management testing should determine whether:

  • session identifiers are generated securely
  • session identifiers contain sufficient entropy
  • session cookies use appropriate security attributes
  • sessions are invalidated correctly
  • logout terminates the server-side session
  • password changes invalidate existing sessions where appropriate
  • authentication state is correctly enforced
  • sessions expire after an appropriate period
  • concurrent sessions are handled securely
  • session identifiers are not exposed unnecessarily
  • session fixation is prevented
  • tokens cannot be replayed after invalidation
  • sensitive operations require appropriate reauthentication

docs.title: Session Management Testing Methodology
docs.text:
A practical session management assessment can generally be approached as:

Identify Session Mechanism
        ↓
Inspect Cookies and Tokens
        ↓
Analyse Session Identifier
        ↓
Test Session Rotation
        ↓
Test Session Fixation
        ↓
Test Logout
        ↓
Test Session Expiration
        ↓
Test Password Change Behaviour
        ↓
Test Concurrent Sessions
        ↓
Test Session Replay
        ↓
Test Cross-Account Behaviour
        ↓
Test Sensitive Operations
        ↓
Document Findings

docs.title: Identify the Session Mechanism
docs.text:
Start by determining how the application maintains authentication state.

Common mechanisms include:

Cookies
JWTs
Bearer tokens
API tokens
Session IDs
OAuth tokens
Refresh tokens
Custom authentication headers

Use an intercepting proxy such as Burp Suite to compare requests before and after authentication.

Example:

GET /account HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Cookie: session=abc123

The authentication state may depend entirely on:

session=abc123

Alternatively:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

Determine which value actually controls the authenticated session.

docs.title: Identify Session Cookies
docs.text:
Review the Set-Cookie headers returned during authentication.

Example:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

Record:

Cookie name
Cookie value
Domain
Path
Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
Expiration

Multiple cookies may be present.

For example:

session
JSESSIONID
PHPSESSID
ASP.NET_SessionId
connect.sid
auth_token
remember_me

Do not assume every cookie is security sensitive. Determine which cookies affect authentication state.

docs.title: Cookie Security Attributes
docs.text: Important cookie attributes should be reviewed.

docs.title: Secure
docs.text:
The Secure attribute prevents the browser from transmitting the cookie over plaintext HTTP connections.

Expected:

Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure

A sensitive authentication cookie without Secure may potentially be exposed over an insecure connection.

docs.title: HttpOnly
docs.text:
The HttpOnly attribute prevents normal client-side JavaScript from directly reading the cookie.

Expected:

Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly

This provides additional protection against session theft through certain cross-site scripting scenarios.

It does not prevent XSS itself.

docs.title: SameSite
docs.text:
The SameSite attribute controls when browsers include cookies in cross-site requests.

Common values:

Strict
Lax
None

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=abc123; SameSite=Lax

If SameSite=None is used, modern browsers generally require:

Secure

Example:

Set-Cookie: session=abc123; SameSite=None; Secure

Do not treat SameSite as a complete replacement for CSRF protection.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
Review whether the cookie is unnecessarily available to subdomains.

Example:

Domain=.example.com

This could expose the cookie to:

app.example.com
api.example.com
legacy.example.com
dev.example.com

Where possible, sensitive cookies should have the narrowest appropriate scope.

docs.title: Path
docs.text:
Review the cookie path.

Example:

Path=/

A broader path makes the cookie available to more application routes.

Determine whether this is necessary for the application's design.

docs.title: Inspect Cookies in Burp Suite
docs.text:
In Burp Suite:

Proxy
    ↓
HTTP history
    ↓
Select authenticated request
    ↓
Inspect Cookie header

Example:

Cookie: session=abc123; preferences=dark

Remove cookies individually and resend the request.

For example:

Cookie: preferences=dark

If authentication disappears, the removed cookie is likely responsible for maintaining the authenticated session.

Burp Repeater is particularly useful for this.

docs.title: Session Identifier Analysis
docs.text:
Session identifiers should be unpredictable.

Potential warning signs include identifiers based on:

Username
Email address
Timestamp
Sequential number
User ID
Incrementing database ID
Predictable random values
Encoded user information

Example of a suspicious pattern:

10001
10002
10003
10004

Another example:

user123:1693400000

A secure session identifier should generally be generated using a cryptographically secure random mechanism.

docs.title: Collect Multiple Session Identifiers
docs.text:
Authenticate repeatedly and collect multiple session values.

Example:

Session 1: f62a76f6dfe349fdbe7d...
Session 2: 03f84ab71b7447d493f9...
Session 3: 9c739a8f6f5347a198e2...
Session 4: 38bc2c9e83f74cf29bb7...

Look for:

Repeated sections
Sequential values
Timestamp patterns
Constant prefixes
Constant suffixes
Encoded usernames
Predictable changes

Burp Sequencer can assist with statistical analysis of session tokens.

docs.title: Burp Sequencer
docs.text:
Burp Suite includes Sequencer for analysing token randomness.

Typical workflow:

Proxy
    ↓
Identify response containing session token
    ↓
Send to Sequencer
    ↓
Configure token location
    ↓
Start live capture

Sequencer can analyse characteristics such as:

Character distribution
Entropy
Bit-level randomness
Token correlation
Predictability indicators

Automated statistical analysis should support manual investigation rather than replace it.

docs.title: Session Rotation
docs.text:
Applications should generally issue a new session identifier when authentication state changes.

Capture the session before authentication:

session=AAA

Authenticate.

Then inspect the session again:

session=BBB

Ideally:

AAA != BBB

This is particularly important when transitioning from:

Unauthenticated
        ↓
Authenticated

It may also be appropriate when:

Privilege changes
MFA completes
Password changes
Account recovery completes
Security-sensitive authentication state changes

docs.title: Session Fixation
docs.text:
Session fixation occurs when an attacker can establish or predict a session identifier before authentication and the application continues using that same identifier after the victim authenticates.

Basic test:

1. Visit application while unauthenticated
2. Record session identifier
3. Authenticate
4. Record session identifier again
5. Compare both values

Example:

Before login:

session=ABC123

After login:

session=ABC123

This deserves further investigation.

Expected behaviour will commonly resemble:

Before login:

session=ABC123

After login:

session=F9D2A7E81...

The application should normally rotate the relevant session identifier when authentication occurs.

docs.title: Logout Testing
docs.text:
Logout should invalidate the authenticated session.

Basic procedure:

1. Authenticate
2. Capture authenticated request
3. Send request to Burp Repeater
4. Log out normally
5. Replay the captured request

Example captured request:

GET /account HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Cookie: session=abc123

After logout, replay it.

Expected result:

Redirect to login
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
Session invalid response

Potential vulnerability:

Authenticated content is still returned

This can indicate that logout only removed the browser cookie without invalidating the server-side session.

docs.title: Browser Cookie Deletion vs Server-Side Invalidation
docs.text:
A logout response might contain:

Set-Cookie: session=; Max-Age=0

This deletes the browser cookie.

However, this alone does not prove the session was invalidated on the server.

Always replay the original session identifier.

For example:

Cookie: session=OLD_SESSION_VALUE

If it remains authenticated, logout may not properly invalidate the session.

docs.title: Session Expiration
docs.text:
Sessions should not remain valid indefinitely.

Test both:

Idle timeout
Absolute timeout

docs.title: Idle Timeout
docs.text:
An idle timeout terminates a session after a period of inactivity.

Example:

Login
↓
Wait without sending requests
↓
Replay authenticated request

The appropriate timeout depends on the application's risk profile and business requirements.

docs.title: Absolute Timeout
docs.text:
An absolute timeout limits the total lifetime of a session regardless of activity.

Example:

Login
↓
Continue using application
↓
Session eventually expires
↓
Reauthentication required

Applications handling sensitive information may require stricter session lifetime controls.

docs.title: Password Change Testing
docs.text:
Determine what happens to existing sessions when the password changes.

Practical test:

Browser A
Login to account

Browser B
Login to same account

Browser A
Change password

Browser B
Refresh authenticated page

Determine whether Browser B remains authenticated.

Possible behaviours include:

All sessions invalidated
Only current session remains
Other sessions remain active
User chooses whether other sessions are terminated

The correct behaviour depends on the application's design and risk model.

However, applications should deliberately manage this behaviour rather than leaving stale sessions active unintentionally.

docs.title: Password Reset Testing
docs.text:
Password resets should also be tested against existing sessions.

Procedure:

1. Login in Browser A
2. Initiate password reset separately
3. Complete password reset
4. Return to Browser A
5. Attempt authenticated actions

Determine whether the old session remains valid.

This is especially important where password reset is intended to recover an account after suspected compromise.

docs.title: Concurrent Sessions
docs.text:
Determine whether the application allows multiple active sessions for the same account.

Example:

Chrome
Firefox
Mobile browser
API client

Authenticate using the same account.

Then determine:

Are all sessions active?
Can the user view active sessions?
Can individual sessions be revoked?
Does logout affect only one session?
Does "logout everywhere" exist?

Multiple concurrent sessions are not automatically a vulnerability.

The important question is whether session behaviour matches the security requirements of the application.

docs.title: Session Revocation
docs.text:
Applications may provide functionality such as:

Active Sessions
Connected Devices
Security Sessions
Login Activity
Sign Out Other Sessions
Sign Out Everywhere

Test whether revocation actually invalidates the selected session.

Procedure:

Browser A
        ↓
Login

Browser B
        ↓
Login

Browser A
        ↓
Revoke Browser B

Browser B
        ↓
Replay authenticated request

Browser B should no longer have access if revocation succeeded.

docs.title: Session Replay
docs.text:
Capture an authenticated request:

GET /profile HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Cookie: session=abc123

After an event expected to invalidate the session, replay the request.

Events worth testing include:

Logout
Password change
Password reset
Account lock
Session revocation
Account disablement
MFA reset
Role change

Determine whether the old session remains usable.

docs.title: Cross-Account Session Testing
docs.text:
Use two test accounts:

Account A
Account B

Capture the session for both.

Example:

Account A → session=AAA
Account B → session=BBB

Test application behaviour carefully when switching between authenticated contexts.

Look for:

Session confusion
Cached user data
Incorrect account association
Privilege leakage
Cross-user responses

Always use accounts specifically authorised for testing.

docs.title: Session Cookie Manipulation
docs.text:
Test whether modifying the session cookie affects identity or privileges.

Example:

Cookie: role=user

Change:

Cookie: role=admin

or:

Cookie: user_id=1001

to:

Cookie: user_id=1002

The application must not trust client-controlled values for security decisions without appropriate integrity protection and server-side authorisation.

docs.title: Encoded Session Values
docs.text:
Some session values may simply contain encoded data.

Example:

dXNlcj1hc2lmJnJvbGU9dXNlcg==

Base64 decoding may reveal:

user=asif&role=user

Linux:

echo 'dXNlcj1hc2lmJnJvbGU9dXNlcg==' | base64 -d

Encoding is not encryption.

Do not assume a value is securely protected merely because it is not immediately human readable.

docs.title: JWT-Based Sessions
docs.text:
Some applications use JSON Web Tokens for authentication.

Example:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...

A JWT normally consists of:

HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

Example structure:

xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz

Decode the header and payload to understand the claims.

Typical payload:

{
  "sub": "123",
  "username": "testuser",
  "role": "user",
  "iat": 1693400000,
  "exp": 1693403600
}

Review:

Algorithm
Expiration
Issuer
Audience
Subject
Roles
Permissions
Token lifetime
Refresh behaviour
Revocation behaviour

JWT testing should be considered part of both authentication and session management.

docs.title: Access Tokens and Refresh Tokens
docs.text:
Modern applications may use:

Access token
Refresh token

Typical model:

Login
  ↓
Access Token
  ↓
Expires
  ↓
Refresh Token
  ↓
New Access Token

Review:

Access token lifetime
Refresh token lifetime
Refresh token rotation
Token reuse
Logout invalidation
Password reset invalidation
Token storage
Revocation

Refresh tokens generally require stronger protection because they can be used to obtain new access tokens.

docs.title: Remember Me Functionality
docs.text:
Applications may provide:

Remember me
Keep me signed in
Stay signed in
Trust this device

Determine whether enabling the option creates an additional persistent token.

Compare authentication responses with and without the option.

Look for additional cookies such as:

remember_me
persistent_session
device_token
trusted_device

Test:

Expiration
Randomness
Rotation
Logout invalidation
Password reset invalidation
Revocation
Device binding where applicable

docs.title: Sensitive Operations
docs.text:
Some operations should require additional verification even when the user already has an authenticated session.

Examples:

Change password
Change email address
Disable MFA
Generate recovery codes
Add payment information
View highly sensitive information
Create API keys
Change security settings
Delete account

Test whether an old or unattended authenticated session can perform these operations without reauthentication.

Depending on the application's risk model, the application may require:

Current password
MFA
Recent authentication
Security confirmation

docs.title: Session Handling Across HTTP and HTTPS
docs.text:
Check whether session cookies can ever be transmitted over HTTP.

Attempt:

http://example.com

Determine whether the application:

Redirects immediately to HTTPS
Uses HSTS
Sets Secure cookies
Avoids sensitive content over HTTP

Sensitive session cookies should not be exposed over plaintext connections.

docs.title: Session Identifiers in URLs
docs.text:
Session identifiers should generally not appear in URLs.

Example:

https://example.com/account?session=abc123

or:

https://example.com/session/abc123/profile

URLs may be stored in:

Browser history
Proxy logs
Web server logs
Analytics systems
Monitoring systems
Screenshots
Referrer headers
Bookmarks

Prefer session identifiers in appropriately secured cookies or authentication headers.

docs.title: Session Identifiers in Responses
docs.text:
Search application responses for session identifiers or authentication tokens.

For example:

HTML
JavaScript
JSON
Debug information
Error messages
Redirect URLs

A session token should not be unnecessarily exposed in application content.

docs.title: Browser Storage
docs.text:
Modern applications may store authentication information in:

Cookies
localStorage
sessionStorage
IndexedDB

Use browser developer tools:

Developer Tools
    ↓
Application
    ↓
Storage

Review:

Cookies
Local Storage
Session Storage
IndexedDB

Sensitive tokens stored in JavaScript-accessible storage may have additional exposure if the application contains XSS.

docs.title: Cache Behaviour
docs.text:
Authenticated responses containing sensitive information should be reviewed for inappropriate caching.

Inspect headers such as:

Cache-Control:
Pragma:
Expires:

Depending on the application's requirements, sensitive responses may use controls such as:

Cache-Control: no-store

Test whether sensitive authenticated content remains accessible after logout through browser navigation or caching.

docs.title: Testing With Multiple Browsers
docs.text:
Using separate browsers or browser profiles is useful for session testing.

Example:

Chrome → Account A
Firefox → Account B
Private window → Account A
Burp Repeater → Captured session

This makes it easier to test:

Concurrent sessions
Session invalidation
Cross-account behaviour
Password changes
Logout behaviour
Role changes

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A practical Burp workflow:

Proxy
    ↓
Capture Login
    ↓
Identify Session Token
    ↓
Send Requests to Repeater
    ↓
Test Session Rotation
    ↓
Test Logout
    ↓
Test Expiration
    ↓
Test Password Change
    ↓
Test Replay
    ↓
Compare Responses

Useful Burp components include:

Proxy
Repeater
Comparer
Sequencer
Logger
Decoder

docs.title: Comparing Sessions
docs.text:
Burp Comparer can help identify differences between:

Unauthenticated request
Authenticated request
Logged-out request
Expired-session request
Account A request
Account B request

Pay attention to differences in:

Cookies
Headers
Response codes
Redirects
Response bodies
User identifiers
Role information
CSRF tokens

docs.title: Session Creation
docs.text:
• Identify session mechanism
  • Identify authentication cookies
  • Identify access tokens
  • Identify refresh tokens
  • Compare pre-authentication and post-authentication sessions
  • Verify session rotation after login
  • Check session identifier randomness
  • Check for predictable session values

docs.title: Cookie Security
docs.text:
• Check Secure
  • Check HttpOnly
  • Check SameSite
  • Review Domain
  • Review Path
  • Review cookie lifetime
  • Check for unnecessary persistent cookies

docs.title: Session Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Test logout invalidation
  • Replay session after logout
  • Test idle timeout
  • Test absolute timeout
  • Test password change behaviour
  • Test password reset behaviour
  • Test account disablement behaviour where authorised
  • Test session revocation
  • Test logout-all-sessions functionality

docs.title: Concurrent Sessions
docs.text:
• Test multiple simultaneous sessions
  • Determine whether active sessions are visible
  • Test individual session revocation
  • Test global session revocation
  • Test device/session management controls

docs.title: Token Handling
docs.text:
• Check tokens in URLs
  • Check tokens in responses
  • Check browser storage
  • Check token expiration
  • Check refresh token rotation
  • Check token reuse
  • Check token revocation

docs.title: Sensitive Operations
docs.text:
• Test password changes
  • Test email changes
  • Test MFA changes
  • Test API key generation
  • Test security setting changes
  • Check reauthentication requirements

docs.title: Common Findings
docs.text:
Common session management findings include:

Finding Description Missing Secure flag Authentication cookie may be transmitted over an insecure connection Missing HttpOnly flag Cookie is accessible to client-side JavaScript Weak SameSite configuration Cookie may be included in unintended cross-site requests Session fixation Session identifier is not rotated after authentication Logout does not invalidate session Old session remains usable after logout Excessive session lifetime Sessions remain active longer than necessary Weak session identifier Session value may be predictable Session token in URL Sensitive token may leak through logs or browser history Password reset does not revoke sessions Existing sessions remain active after account recovery Ineffective session revocation Revoked session continues to function Sensitive action without reauthentication Existing session is sufficient for high-risk account changes

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each potential finding, record:

Endpoint
HTTP method
Session mechanism
Cookie/token name
Relevant request
Relevant response
Expected behaviour
Observed behaviour
Reproduction steps
Security impact

Avoid including active authentication tokens in reports unnecessarily.

Redact sensitive values.

Example:

session=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...

can be documented as:

session=[REDACTED]

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Authenticated Session Remains Valid After Logout

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The application does not invalidate the authenticated session on the server when the user logs out. Although the browser removes the session cookie, the previously issued session identifier remains valid.

docs.title: Reproduction
docs.text:
1. Authenticate using a test account.
2. Capture an authenticated request.
3. Send the request to Burp Repeater.
4. Log out through the application.
5. Replay the original authenticated request.
6. Observe that authenticated functionality remains accessible.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text: An exposed or previously captured session token could remain usable after the legitimate user has logged out, increasing the window in which session hijacking could occur.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text: Invalidate the corresponding server-side session when the user logs out. Previously issued session identifiers should no longer provide authenticated access after logout.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
Session established
        ↓
Was identifier rotated after login?
        ↓
Are cookie attributes secure?
        ↓
Is identifier unpredictable?
        ↓
Does logout invalidate it?
        ↓
Does it expire?
        ↓
Does password reset revoke it?
        ↓
Can sessions be individually revoked?
        ↓
Are sensitive operations protected?

docs.title: Useful Tools
docs.text:
Common tools for session management testing include:

Burp Suite Proxy
Burp Repeater
Burp Sequencer
Burp Comparer
Burp Decoder
Browser Developer Tools
curl
JWT analysis tools

Example with curl:

curl -i https://example.com/login

Using a cookie:

curl -i \
  -H 'Cookie: session=SESSION_VALUE' \
  https://example.com/account

Store cookies:

curl -c cookies.txt \
  https://example.com/

Reuse cookies:

curl -b cookies.txt \
  https://example.com/account

docs.title: Key Principle
docs.text:
Session management testing is not simply checking whether a cookie contains Secure and HttpOnly.

The complete session lifecycle should be tested:

Creation
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Rotation
   ↓
Use
   ↓
Expiration
   ↓
Revocation
   ↓
Logout

A secure application should ensure that session identifiers are unpredictable, appropriately protected, rotated when authentication state changes, expired according to policy, and reliably invalidated when they should no longer provide access.

docs.title: SQL Injection
docs.text:
SQL Injection (SQLi) occurs when attacker-controlled input influences a database query in an unsafe manner.

SQL injection testing should not consist only of submitting common payloads. A structured approach first determines how an input affects application behaviour, whether the input is likely to interact with a database, what type of query may be involved, and how the application responds to controlled changes.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform SQL injection testing only against applications and systems for which you have explicit authorisation. These notes are intended for authorised penetration testing, lab environments, security research and responsible vulnerability disclosure.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
The primary objectives of SQL injection testing are to determine:

  • whether user-controlled input reaches a database query
  • whether input is safely parameterised
  • whether query structure can be influenced
  • whether database errors are exposed
  • whether responses change based on Boolean conditions
  • whether query execution time can be influenced
  • whether results from additional queries can be returned
  • whether injection exists in less obvious locations such as headers or JSON
  • which database technology is in use
  • what security impact can be demonstrated safely

A useful mental model is:

User Input
    ↓
Application
    ↓
Validation / Transformation
    ↓
Database Query
    ↓
Database
    ↓
Result
    ↓
Application Response

docs.title: SQL Injection Testing Workflow
docs.text:
A structured SQL injection assessment can generally follow:

Discover Input
      ↓
Establish Baseline
      ↓
Determine Input Type
      ↓
Introduce Controlled Changes
      ↓
Compare Responses
      ↓
Look for SQL Behaviour
      ↓
Identify Injection Technique
      ↓
Fingerprint Database if Necessary
      ↓
Determine Impact
      ↓
Manually Verify
      ↓
Document

The important principle is:

Understand how the parameter behaves before attempting complex SQL injection techniques.

docs.title: Common SQL Injection Locations
docs.text:
SQL injection may occur anywhere user-controlled data reaches a database query.

Common locations include:

GET parameters
POST parameters
JSON properties
Search fields
Filters
Sorting parameters
Object identifiers
Login forms
Registration forms
API parameters
GraphQL arguments
Cookies
HTTP headers
Stored application data

Example:

GET /products?id=123 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Potential backend logic:

SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = 123;

The security question is whether the application safely separates the parameter value from the SQL query structure.

docs.title: Types of SQL Injection
docs.text:
Common SQL injection categories include:

Error-Based SQL Injection
Boolean-Based Blind SQL Injection
Time-Based Blind SQL Injection
UNION-Based SQL Injection
Stacked Queries
Second-Order SQL Injection
Out-of-Band SQL Injection

Not every database or application architecture supports every technique.

docs.title: Start With a Baseline
docs.text:
Before modifying a parameter, send the original request.

Example:

GET /product?id=10 HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example

Record:

Status code
Response length
Response body
Response time
Error messages
Returned records
Redirect behaviour

Example:

Status: 200
Length: 4821
Response Time: 142 ms
Product: Test Product

This becomes the baseline.

docs.title: Input Type Identification
docs.text:
Determine the apparent data type.

Examples:

?id=123

likely represents a numeric value.

?username=alice

likely represents a string.

?date=2026-08-26

may be handled as a date.

?sort=name

may influence an SQL identifier or ORDER BY clause.

The apparent type can help you reason about the likely backend query.

docs.title: Controlled Character Testing
docs.text:
Start with small changes rather than complicated payloads.

Interesting characters can include:

'
"
`
\
;
(
)

For example:

?id=10'

Compare the result with:

?id=10

Look for:

Database errors
HTTP 500
Different content
Different response length
Different record count
Unexpected redirects
Different response time

A single quote causing an error is an indicator, not proof of SQL injection.

docs.title: Error-Based SQL Injection
docs.text:
Error-based SQL injection occurs when database errors reveal information about query processing.

Malformed input may result in messages containing references to:

SQL syntax
Database drivers
Table names
Column names
Query fragments
Database functions

Potential database indicators include:

MySQL
MariaDB
PostgreSQL
Microsoft SQL Server
Oracle
SQLite

docs.title: Error-Based Workflow
docs.text:
Baseline Request
      ↓
Modify Parameter
      ↓
Application Error?
      ↓
Database Error?
      ↓
Identify DBMS Clues
      ↓
Determine Whether Query Structure Is Influenced
      ↓
Manual Verification

Do not rely solely on verbose error messages.

Production applications often suppress database errors.

docs.title: Boolean-Based SQL Injection
docs.text:
Boolean-based SQL injection identifies situations where application behaviour changes depending on whether an injected condition evaluates to true or false.

The general concept is:

Original Query
     ↓
TRUE Condition
     ↓
Response A

Original Query
     ↓
FALSE Condition
     ↓
Response B

You are looking for a reliable difference between the two responses.

docs.title: Boolean Comparison
docs.text:
Compare:

Baseline
TRUE condition
FALSE condition

Observe:

Status
Length
Words
Lines
Returned objects
Page content
Redirects
JSON fields

A useful pattern is:

Baseline ≈ TRUE
FALSE ≠ Baseline

This may indicate that the condition is influencing database logic.

docs.title: Blind SQL Injection
docs.text:
Blind SQL injection occurs when the application does not directly display database errors or injected query output.

Information is instead inferred from application behaviour.

Common forms include:

Boolean-Based Blind SQL Injection
Time-Based Blind SQL Injection
Out-of-Band SQL Injection

The absence of database errors does not mean SQL injection is absent.

docs.title: Time-Based Blind SQL Injection
docs.text:
Time-based testing determines whether database processing can influence response time.

Conceptually:

Normal Request
     ↓
Normal Response Time

Controlled Database Delay
     ↓
Consistently Delayed Response

A single slow response is not sufficient evidence.

Network latency, application load, caching and backend processing can all affect timing.

docs.title: Time-Based Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Measure Baseline
      ↓
Repeat Baseline
      ↓
Determine Normal Variation
      ↓
Introduce Controlled Timing Test
      ↓
Repeat Test
      ↓
Compare Results
      ↓
Verify Correlation

Collect several measurements before reaching a conclusion.

docs.title: UNION-Based SQL Injection
docs.text:
UNION allows results from compatible SQL queries to be combined.

Conceptually:

SELECT name, price
FROM products

UNION

SELECT value1, value2;

For UNION injection to work, the queries generally need compatible:

Column counts
Data types
Query structure

A typical testing process therefore involves determining the structure of the original result set.

docs.title: Determining Column Count
docs.text:
Two common concepts used during authorised testing are:

ORDER BY behaviour
UNION column matching

The objective is to understand how many columns are present in the original query.

Conceptually:

Original Query
      ↓
Determine Column Count
      ↓
Determine Displayed Columns
      ↓
Determine Compatible Types
      ↓
Assess Accessible Data

Avoid extracting unnecessary sensitive data.

Proof should be limited to what is required to demonstrate the vulnerability.

docs.title: Displayed Columns
docs.text:
Even if a query contains several columns, not all values may be displayed in the HTTP response.

Conceptually:

Database Result
   ↓
Application Processing
   ↓
Selected Values
   ↓
HTML / JSON Response

Identify which output positions are actually observable.

docs.title: Stacked Queries
docs.text:
Some database technologies and drivers permit multiple statements within one database call.

Conceptually:

QUERY 1;
QUERY 2;

Support varies by:

DBMS
Driver
Application framework
Database API
Configuration

Because stacked queries may perform state-changing operations, avoid destructive validation.

docs.title: Second-Order SQL Injection
docs.text:
Second-order SQL injection occurs when malicious or unsafe input is stored safely at one point but later used unsafely in another database query.

Example:

User Input
    ↓
Stored in Database
    ↓
No Immediate Vulnerability
    ↓
Different Application Function
    ↓
Stored Value Used in SQL Query
    ↓
SQL Injection

This is conceptually similar to stored XSS because the vulnerable processing occurs later.

docs.title: Second-Order Testing Locations
docs.text:
Interesting areas include:

Usernames
Display names
Profile information
Organisation names
Address fields
Imported data
CSV data
Administrative notes
Stored search filters
Application configuration

The key question is:

Where is this value used later?

docs.title: SQL Injection in Authentication
docs.text:
Login functionality frequently interacts directly with database queries.

Example:

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=test&password=Password123

A secure application should use parameterised queries.

Unsafe conceptual logic might resemble:

SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE username = 'USER_INPUT'
AND password = 'PASSWORD_INPUT';

Testing should determine whether user input can alter the intended authentication query.

docs.title: Search Functionality
docs.text:
Search endpoints are common SQL injection candidates.

Example:

GET /search?q=laptop HTTP/1.1

Potential backend logic:

SELECT *
FROM products
WHERE name LIKE '%USER_INPUT%';

Search functionality may place input inside:

LIKE expressions
Full-text queries
Dynamic filters
Multiple database conditions

The surrounding query context may differ from a simple object identifier.

docs.title: Filter Parameters
docs.text:
Modern applications frequently expose filtering functionality:

category
status
type
price
date
country
role

Example:

/products?category=laptops&sort=price

Each parameter may influence a different part of the query.

Do not test only obvious identifiers.

docs.title: ORDER BY Injection
docs.text:
Sorting parameters deserve separate attention.

Example:

?sort=name

Potential backend logic:

SELECT *
FROM users
ORDER BY name;

Applications sometimes parameterise values correctly while dynamically concatenating:

Column names
Sort directions
Table names

These locations require careful review because SQL parameterisation works differently for identifiers than for normal values.

docs.title: JSON SQL Injection
docs.text:
Modern APIs frequently receive JSON.

Example:

POST /api/search HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "query": "laptop",
  "category": "electronics"
}

Test each property independently.

query
category
sort
filter
page
limit

Do not assume JSON input is inherently safe.

docs.title: Nested JSON
docs.text:
Input may be nested:

{
  "filter": {
    "username": "alice",
    "status": "active"
  }
}

Map each controllable value:

filter.username
filter.status

Automated tools sometimes require additional configuration to correctly test nested structures.

docs.title: SQL Injection in HTTP Headers
docs.text:
Applications may use HTTP headers in database operations.

Potential candidates include:

User-Agent
Referer
X-Forwarded-For
X-Real-IP
X-Forwarded-Host
Custom application headers
Tracking headers

Example:

HTTP Request
     ↓
User-Agent
     ↓
Application Logging
     ↓
Database INSERT

Start with harmless markers and controlled syntax changes.

docs.title: SQL Injection in Cookies
docs.text:
Cookies may also reach database queries.

Example:

Cookie: trackingId=12345

Potential uses include:

Tracking
Preferences
Session lookup
Analytics
Shopping carts
A/B testing

Do not restrict SQL injection testing to URL and body parameters.

docs.title: SQL Injection in APIs
docs.text:
API testing should include:

REST
GraphQL
JSON APIs
XML APIs
Mobile backends
Internal APIs

A practical API workflow:

Map Endpoint
      ↓
Identify Parameters
      ↓
Determine Types
      ↓
Baseline
      ↓
Controlled Input Changes
      ↓
Compare Responses
      ↓
Investigate Database Behaviour

docs.title: GraphQL and SQL Injection
docs.text:
GraphQL provides structured queries but backend resolvers may still construct unsafe database queries.

Example:

query {
  user(name: "alice") {
    id
    email
  }
}

The GraphQL layer itself does not automatically guarantee safe database access.

Trace:

GraphQL Argument
      ↓
Resolver
      ↓
ORM / Database Query

docs.title: ORM Considerations
docs.text:
Applications frequently use Object Relational Mapping libraries.

Examples include:

Hibernate
Entity Framework
SQLAlchemy
Sequelize
Prisma
Django ORM
ActiveRecord
Doctrine

ORM usage reduces some SQL injection risks when used correctly, but unsafe raw queries can still introduce vulnerabilities.

Look for:

Raw SQL
String concatenation
Dynamic query construction
Unsafe filters
Dynamic ORDER BY
Custom database functions

docs.title: Source Code Review
docs.text:
When source code is available, identify where user-controlled input reaches database operations.

Conceptually:

Source
  ↓
Transformation
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Database Sink

Example:

request parameter
      ↓
controller
      ↓
service
      ↓
repository
      ↓
SQL query

docs.title: Search Source Code for SQL Operations
docs.text:
Useful search terms include:

SELECT
INSERT
UPDATE
DELETE
execute
query
rawQuery
createNativeQuery
Statement
PreparedStatement

Example:

grep -RniE \
'SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|execute\(|query\(|rawQuery|createNativeQuery|Statement|PreparedStatement' \
.

Then determine whether attacker-controlled data reaches those locations.

docs.title: Dangerous Pattern
docs.text:
Conceptual unsafe pattern:

query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + username + "'"

The problem is that user-controlled data becomes part of SQL syntax.

docs.title: Safer Pattern
docs.text:
Use parameterised queries.

Conceptually:

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?",
    (username,)
)

The exact syntax depends on the database library.

The important principle is:

SQL Structure
      +
Parameter Values

should remain separate.

docs.title: Burp Suite SQL Injection Workflow
docs.text:
A practical Burp workflow:

Proxy
  ↓
HTTP History
  ↓
Identify Interesting Request
  ↓
Send to Repeater
  ↓
Establish Baseline
  ↓
Modify One Parameter
  ↓
Compare Response
  ↓
Identify SQL Behaviour
  ↓
Manual Verification

docs.title: Burp Repeater
docs.text:
Repeater should generally be the primary manual testing tool.

For each parameter:

1. Send original request
2. Record baseline
3. Modify one value
4. Send again
5. Compare
6. Restore original
7. Test next hypothesis

Keep testing controlled.

docs.title: Burp Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer can help identify subtle response differences.

Compare:

Baseline vs modified input

TRUE condition vs FALSE condition

Normal request vs suspected SQL behaviour

Useful differences include:

Words
HTML
JSON
Headers
Returned records

docs.title: Burp Intruder
docs.text:
Intruder can help test multiple controlled values.

Repeater
   ↓
Understand Parameter
   ↓
Send to Intruder
   ↓
Select Payload Position
   ↓
Configure Small Payload Set
   ↓
Run
   ↓
Sort Responses
   ↓
Identify Outliers
   ↓
Repeater
   ↓
Manual Verification

Useful columns include:

Status
Length
Words
Lines
Time

docs.title: Response Analysis
docs.text:
Do not look only at HTTP status codes.

Compare:

Status
Content length
Word count
Line count
Response body
JSON properties
Record count
Error message
Redirect location
Response time
Application state

A SQL injection indicator may be extremely subtle.

docs.title: Database Fingerprinting
docs.text:
If SQL injection has been established, identifying the DBMS may help select appropriate validation techniques.

Potential technologies include:

MySQL
MariaDB
PostgreSQL
Microsoft SQL Server
Oracle
SQLite

Fingerprinting can use:

Error messages
Database-specific syntax
Application technology
HTTP headers
Source code
Dependency files
Known platform architecture

Avoid unnecessary fingerprinting if the vulnerability can already be demonstrated safely.

docs.title: SQLMap
docs.text:
sqlmap can automate SQL injection detection and validation during authorised testing.

Basic usage:

sqlmap -u "https://target.example/product?id=10"

Specify the parameter:

sqlmap -u "https://target.example/product?id=10" -p id

docs.title: SQLMap With a Burp Request
docs.text:
Save a complete HTTP request from Burp as:

request.txt

Then:

sqlmap -r request.txt

This preserves:

Method
Headers
Cookies
POST body
JSON
Authentication
Parameters

Specify a particular parameter:

sqlmap -r request.txt -p id

docs.title: SQLMap Workflow
docs.text:
Manual Discovery
      ↓
Burp Repeater
      ↓
Suspicious Parameter
      ↓
Save request.txt
      ↓
sqlmap
      ↓
Review Results
      ↓
Manual Verification
      ↓
Minimal Impact Demonstration

Do not automatically report a finding solely because sqlmap identifies a parameter as potentially injectable.

docs.title: Ghauri
docs.text:
Ghauri is an automated SQL injection detection and exploitation tool.

It can be useful as an alternative or complementary tool to sqlmap when investigating suspected SQL injection.

GitHub:

https://github.com/r0oth3x49/ghauri

docs.title: Install Ghauri
docs.text:
Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/r0oth3x49/ghauri.git
cd ghauri

Install:

python3 -m pip install -e .

Check:

ghauri -h

docs.title: Basic Ghauri Testing
docs.text:
Test an authorised target:

ghauri -u "https://target.example/product?id=10"

Specify the parameter:

ghauri -u "https://target.example/product?id=10" -p id

docs.title: Ghauri With a Burp Request
docs.text:
Save the request from Burp as:

request.txt

Then:

ghauri -r request.txt

Specify the interesting parameter:

ghauri -r request.txt -p id

This can be particularly useful for requests containing:

POST parameters
Cookies
Authentication
Custom headers
JSON
Complex request bodies

docs.title: Ghauri Workflow
docs.text:
Application
     ↓
Burp Proxy
     ↓
Identify Interesting Parameter
     ↓
Burp Repeater
     ↓
Manual SQLi Testing
     ↓
Save Request
     ↓
Ghauri
     ↓
Review Detection
     ↓
Manual Verification
     ↓
Document Finding

docs.title: HBSQLI
docs.text:
HBSQLI is another SQL injection testing project that can complement manual SQL injection testing and other automated tools.

GitHub:

https://github.com/SAPT01/HBSQLI

Because specialist SQL injection tools can differ in the techniques and request patterns they handle, HBSQLI can provide an additional testing option when manually observed behaviour deserves further investigation.

Always review the project's current documentation and supported options before using it because command-line interfaces and capabilities may change between versions.

docs.title: Install HBSQLI
docs.text:
Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/SAPT01/HBSQLI.git
cd HBSQLI

Review the project files:

ls -la

Read the current documentation:

cat README.md

Then follow the installation instructions provided by the project.

Do not assume installation or command-line options from unrelated SQL injection tools are compatible with HBSQLI.

docs.title: HBSQLI Workflow
docs.text:
A sensible workflow is:

Interesting Parameter
        ↓
Burp Repeater
        ↓
Manual SQLi Analysis
        ↓
Suspicious Behaviour
        ↓
HBSQLI
        ↓
Review Results
        ↓
Manual Verification
        ↓
Document Evidence

HBSQLI should complement rather than replace manual analysis.

docs.title: Using Multiple SQL Injection Tools
docs.text:
Different SQL injection tools may produce different results depending on:

Request format
Injection context
Database technology
Response behaviour
Authentication
Filtering
WAF behaviour
Timing
Tool detection logic

Therefore, a useful workflow is:

                    Burp Suite
                        ↓
                  Manual Testing
                        ↓
              Suspicious Parameter
                        ↓
              ┌─────────┼─────────┐
              │         │         │
              ▼         ▼         ▼
           sqlmap     Ghauri     HBSQLI
              │         │         │
              └─────────┼─────────┘
                        ↓
                 Compare Results
                        ↓
               Manual Verification
                        ↓
               Minimal Evidence
                        ↓
                     Report

Do not simply run every tool against every parameter.

Use automation after manual testing identifies something worth investigating.

docs.title: Recommended SQLi Tool Workflow
docs.text:
Burp Proxy
     ↓
Map Parameters
     ↓
Burp Repeater
     ↓
Baseline
     ↓
Manual SQLi Testing
     ↓
Suspicious Behaviour?
     ↓
Save request.txt
     ↓
┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
│          │          │          │
▼          ▼          ▼          │
sqlmap   Ghauri     HBSQLI       │
│          │          │          │
└──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘
               ↓
        Compare Findings
               ↓
        Manual Reproduction
               ↓
      Determine Actual Impact
               ↓
       Collect Minimal Evidence
               ↓
             Report

docs.title: Data Extraction
docs.text:
Once SQL injection is confirmed, it may technically be possible to retrieve database information.

During professional testing, apply data minimisation.

Prefer demonstrating:

Current database name
Database version
Current database user
Known test record

rather than retrieving:

Password databases
Personal information
Production customer data
Large tables
Sensitive business information

Stop once sufficient evidence has been collected.

docs.title: Out-of-Band SQL Injection
docs.text:
Some database systems can generate network interactions.

Conceptually:

SQL Injection
     ↓
Database
     ↓
Network Interaction
     ↓
Controlled Callback Service

This can sometimes help identify blind SQL injection when HTTP responses provide no useful signal.

Out-of-band techniques depend heavily on:

DBMS
Privileges
Network access
Configuration
Environment

Use controlled callback infrastructure during authorised testing.

docs.title: WAF Behaviour
docs.text:
A WAF may interfere with SQL injection testing.

Indicators include:

403 responses
Connection termination
Generic security pages
Parameter-specific blocking
Rate limiting
Different behaviour for SQL keywords

Separate:

WAF Behaviour

from:

Application Behaviour

A WAF blocking one test does not prove that the underlying query is safe.

docs.title: Encoding and Normalisation
docs.text:
Applications may perform:

URL decoding
Unicode normalisation
JSON decoding
HTML entity decoding
Framework-specific transformations
Database driver escaping

Think about the complete processing chain:

HTTP Request
      ↓
Reverse Proxy
      ↓
Web Framework
      ↓
Validation
      ↓
Transformation
      ↓
ORM / Database Library
      ↓
Database

Different layers may interpret the same input differently.

docs.title: False Positives
docs.text:
Common causes of false SQL injection indicators include:

Generic application errors
WAF blocking
Input validation
Template errors
Backend API failures
Caching
Network latency
Rate limiting
Search engine behaviour
Application-specific filtering

Always reproduce manually.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A high-quality SQL injection finding should establish:

Source
 ↓
Affected Parameter
 ↓
Database Interaction
 ↓
Controllable Query Behaviour
 ↓
Security Impact

Avoid relying solely on:

A quote caused HTTP 500

or:

An automated tool reported SQL injection

Demonstrate reliable database-dependent behaviour.

docs.title: Evidence Collection
docs.text:
Useful evidence includes:

Affected endpoint
HTTP method
Affected parameter
Authentication requirement
Baseline request
Modified request
Baseline response
Modified response
Database error if relevant
Boolean difference if relevant
Timing measurements if relevant
Identified DBMS
Tool output if used
Manual reproduction
Security impact

docs.title: Timing Evidence
docs.text:
For time-based findings, record multiple measurements.

Example:

Request Baseline Test 1 140 ms 5.1 s 2 153 ms 5.2 s 3 147 ms 5.1 s 4 161 ms 5.2 s

Repeated and predictable behaviour is considerably stronger evidence than a single slow request.

docs.title: SQL Injection Reporting
docs.text:
A report should explain:

Where input originates
Which parameter is affected
How the input reaches the database
Which SQL injection technique was confirmed
How the behaviour was validated
Which DBMS is involved if known
What an attacker could achieve
What evidence was collected
How the vulnerability should be remediated

docs.title: Example Finding Structure
docs.text:
Title
SQL Injection in Product Identifier

Affected Endpoint
GET /product

Affected Parameter
id

Authentication Required
No

Technique
Boolean-Based SQL Injection

Description
The product identifier is incorporated into a database query without
sufficient separation between user-controlled input and SQL syntax.

Testing demonstrated repeatable differences between logically true and
false database conditions.

Impact
An attacker may be able to influence database queries and access
information outside the intended application functionality.

Recommendation
Replace dynamically constructed SQL queries with parameterised queries
or prepared statements and ensure database permissions follow the
principle of least privilege.

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
The primary defence against SQL injection is:

Parameterised Queries
Prepared Statements

Additional controls include:

Safe ORM usage
Input validation
Least-privileged database accounts
Avoiding dynamic SQL
Safe handling of ORDER BY and identifiers
Secure error handling
Database segmentation
Monitoring
WAF as defence in depth

docs.title: Dynamic SQL Identifiers
docs.text:
Prepared statements generally protect values, but developers sometimes need dynamic:

Column names
Table names
Sort directions

Do not concatenate arbitrary user input.

Use an allowlist:

User requests sort=name
      ↓
Application checks allowlist
      ↓
name → approved database column

Example allowlist:

name
price
created_at

Anything else should be rejected.

docs.title: Least Privilege
docs.text:
The application database account should have only the permissions required by the application.

Avoid unnecessary:

Administrative database privileges
Filesystem access
Operating-system integration
Cross-database access
Schema modification
User creation

SQL injection impact can be significantly reduced by appropriate database permissions.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Avoid exposing verbose database errors to users.

Instead of:

SQL syntax error near ...

return a generic application error while recording technical details securely in server-side logs.

Error suppression does not fix SQL injection, but it reduces unnecessary information disclosure.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• Identify GET parameters
  • Identify POST parameters
  • Identify JSON properties
  • Identify GraphQL arguments
  • Identify cookies
  • Identify interesting HTTP headers
  • Identify search functionality
  • Identify filters
  • Identify sorting
  • Identify login functionality
  • Identify stored input
  • Identify API endpoints

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text:
• Record status
  • Record response length
  • Record response body
  • Record response time
  • Record returned objects
  • Record normal errors

docs.title: Initial Testing
docs.text:
• Determine input type
  • Test controlled syntax changes
  • Test single quote handling
  • Test double quote handling where relevant
  • Compare response differences
  • Look for database errors
  • Look for application errors

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text:
• Error-based behaviour
  • Boolean-based behaviour
  • Time-based behaviour
  • UNION behaviour where relevant
  • Second-order behaviour
  • Out-of-band behaviour where appropriate

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
• Query parameters
  • POST body
  • JSON
  • Cookies
  • HTTP headers
  • Search
  • Filters
  • Sorting
  • APIs
  • GraphQL
  • Stored values

docs.title: Automation
docs.text:
• Confirm parameter manually
  • Save Burp request
  • Test with sqlmap where appropriate
  • Test with Ghauri where appropriate
  • Consider HBSQLI where appropriate
  • Start conservatively
  • Review automated output
  • Compare tool results
  • Manually reproduce findings

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Confirm repeatability
  • Exclude WAF behaviour
  • Exclude network timing variation
  • Confirm database-dependent behaviour
  • Minimise extracted data
  • Determine actual impact
  • Capture evidence

docs.title: Useful Tools
docs.text: Tool Purpose Burp Suite Request interception and SQL injection testing Burp Repeater Manual SQL injection validation Burp Intruder Controlled parameter testing Burp Comparer Response comparison Burp Scanner Automated testing where available sqlmap Automated SQL injection detection and validation Ghauri Automated SQL injection detection and exploitation HBSQLI Additional SQL injection testing and research Browser DevTools Frontend and API analysis curl Manual HTTP requests grep / ripgrep Source code and SQL sink discovery

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
A quote causing an error does not prove SQL injection.

An HTTP 500 response does not prove SQL injection.

A slow request does not prove time-based SQL injection.

Automated tool output should be manually verified.

A WAF blocking SQL syntax does not prove the application is secure.

ORM usage does not automatically eliminate SQL injection.

JSON APIs can still contain SQL injection.

GraphQL can still contain SQL injection.

Always establish:

INPUT → APPLICATION → QUERY → DATABASE BEHAVIOUR → IMPACT
