docs.title: Burp Suite Extensions
docs.text:
Burp Suite extensions can significantly improve the efficiency of web application security testing by automating repetitive tasks, highlighting suspicious behaviour and providing specialised testing capabilities.

This page contains a practical collection of Burp Suite extensions that are useful during authorised web application penetration testing and vulnerability research.

Authorised Security Testing

Use these extensions only against systems for which you have explicit permission to perform security testing.

docs.title: Extension Overview
docs.text:
Extension Primary Use Autorize Authorisation and access control testing AuthMatrix Role and permission testing JWT Editor JSON Web Token testing Param Miner Hidden parameter and header discovery Logger++ Advanced HTTP logging HTTP Request Smuggler HTTP request smuggling testing Backslash Powered Scanner Unusual server-side behaviour discovery Turbo Intruder High-performance request automation Collaborator Everywhere Out-of-band interaction discovery Active Scan++ Additional active scanning checks Error Message Checks Information disclosure detection

Extensions should complement manual testing rather than replace it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Autorize assists with identifying access-control vulnerabilities by automatically replaying requests using the credentials of another user.

It is particularly useful when testing applications containing multiple users, roles or privilege levels.

Typical examples include:

  • administrator and normal user
  • manager and employee
  • customer A and customer B
  • authenticated and unauthenticated users
  • privileged and low-privileged accounts

docs.title: Useful For
docs.text:
Autorize can assist with identifying:

  • Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR)
  • horizontal privilege escalation
  • vertical privilege escalation
  • missing authorisation controls
  • broken role-based access control
  • administrative functionality exposed to normal users
  • authenticated functionality accessible without authentication

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
Create Low-Privilege Account
        ↓
Authenticate as Low-Privilege User
        ↓
Capture Session Cookie
        ↓
Configure Autorize
        ↓
Authenticate as Higher-Privilege User
        ↓
Browse Application
        ↓
Autorize Replays Requests
        ↓
Compare Responses
        ↓
Investigate Potential Access-Control Issues

docs.title: Example Scenario
docs.text:
Assume the application contains two accounts:

administrator
normal-user

The administrator accesses:

GET /admin/users

with:

Cookie: session=ADMIN_SESSION

Autorize can replay the request using:

Cookie: session=NORMAL_USER_SESSION

If the application returns the administrative functionality to the normal user, this may indicate a vertical privilege escalation vulnerability.

docs.title: Horizontal Authorisation Testing
docs.text:
Autorize is also useful when testing users with the same privilege level.

Example:

User A
User B

User A accesses:

GET /api/account/1001

Autorize can help determine whether the request remains accessible when replayed using User B's session.

This may reveal horizontal access-control weaknesses.

docs.title: Manual Verification
docs.text:
Autorize findings should always be manually verified.

Send the interesting request to Repeater and compare:

Original User
      ↓
Original Request
      ↓
Baseline Response

against:

Different User
      ↓
Same Request
      ↓
Modified Session
      ↓
Response

Check more than the HTTP status code.

Compare:

  • response body
  • response length
  • returned objects
  • sensitive information
  • application behaviour
  • side effects
  • redirects
  • error messages

Tip

A 200 OK response does not automatically prove an authorisation vulnerability. The response may contain an access-denied message while still returning HTTP 200.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
AuthMatrix provides a structured method for testing access controls across multiple users and roles.

It is especially useful when an application has a complex permission model.

Example:

Administrator
Manager
Employee
Customer
Unauthenticated

Instead of manually testing every endpoint with every account, AuthMatrix allows requests and roles to be organised into an access-control matrix.

docs.title: Example Matrix
docs.text:
Function Admin Manager User Anonymous View profile ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ Edit own profile ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ View another user ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ Delete user ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ Admin panel ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗

The expected access model can then be compared against the application's actual behaviour.

docs.title: Useful For
docs.text:
AuthMatrix is particularly useful for:

  • role-based access control
  • multi-role applications
  • horizontal privilege escalation
  • vertical privilege escalation
  • administrative interfaces
  • API permission testing
  • complex authorisation models

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
A useful approach is:

Identify Roles
      ↓
Create Test Accounts
      ↓
Map Sensitive Functions
      ↓
Define Expected Access
      ↓
Capture Requests
      ↓
Test Requests Across Roles
      ↓
Identify Differences
      ↓
Verify Manually

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
JWT Editor assists with analysing and testing JSON Web Tokens.

JWTs are commonly used for:

  • authentication
  • API access
  • session management
  • identity information
  • role information
  • authorisation claims

docs.title: JWT Structure
docs.text:
A typical JWT consists of:

HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

For example:

eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9
.
eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwicm9sZSI6InVzZXIifQ
.
SIGNATURE

Decoded conceptually:

{
  "alg": "RS256"
}

{
  "sub": "1234567890",
  "role": "user"
}

docs.title: Useful Testing Areas
docs.text:
JWT Editor can assist when investigating:

  • token signatures
  • JWT claims
  • signing algorithms
  • key handling
  • token validation
  • expiration
  • issuer validation
  • audience validation
  • role claims
  • key confusion issues

docs.title: Claims to Review
docs.text:
Common claims include:

sub
iss
aud
exp
nbf
iat
jti

Applications may also introduce custom claims:

role
admin
permissions
user_id
tenant
scope

Pay particular attention to claims that appear to influence authorisation.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Capture JWT
    ↓
Decode Token
    ↓
Inspect Header
    ↓
Inspect Claims
    ↓
Identify Security-Relevant Fields
    ↓
Understand Signature Configuration
    ↓
Test Validation Behaviour
    ↓
Verify Server-Side Enforcement

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Param Miner helps discover parameters, headers and other inputs that may not be visible during normal application usage.

These hidden inputs can expose additional attack surface.

docs.title: Useful For
docs.text:
Param Miner can assist with discovering:

  • hidden GET parameters
  • hidden POST parameters
  • HTTP headers
  • cookies
  • undocumented application behaviour
  • cache-related behaviour
  • proxy behaviour

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A request may initially contain:

GET /account HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test

The application might also recognise an undocumented parameter:

?debug=true

or header:

X-Original-URL: /admin

Discovering hidden inputs can expose application functionality that was not visible through the normal interface.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Interesting Request
       ↓
Param Miner
       ↓
Guess Parameters / Headers
       ↓
Observe Response Differences
       ↓
Investigate Interesting Inputs
       ↓
Send to Repeater
       ↓
Manual Verification

docs.title: Particularly Useful During
docs.text:
Param Miner is valuable when investigating:

  • cache poisoning
  • routing behaviour
  • reverse proxies
  • hidden functionality
  • undocumented APIs
  • unusual authentication behaviour
  • header-based application logic

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Logger++ provides enhanced logging and filtering capabilities for HTTP traffic passing through Burp Suite.

Large applications can generate thousands of requests, making HTTP history difficult to analyse efficiently.

Logger++ can help organise this traffic.

docs.title: Useful For
docs.text:
Logger++ is useful for:

  • recording requests and responses
  • searching historical traffic
  • filtering requests
  • analysing large applications
  • identifying unusual responses
  • finding interesting parameters
  • reviewing previous test activity

docs.title: Useful Search Targets
docs.text:
During an assessment, search captured traffic for terms such as:

admin
debug
token
password
secret
apikey
api_key
authorization
bearer
session
internal
redirect
callback
upload
download
file

These searches can quickly identify interesting application functionality.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
HTTP Request Smuggler assists with testing applications for HTTP request smuggling vulnerabilities.

These vulnerabilities can occur when front-end and back-end systems interpret HTTP request boundaries differently.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
A common architecture might look like:

Client
  ↓
CDN / Reverse Proxy
  ↓
Load Balancer
  ↓
Web Server
  ↓
Application

Different components may parse requests differently.

That difference can introduce request desynchronisation behaviour.

docs.title: Useful For
docs.text:
The extension assists with investigating:

  • request parsing inconsistencies
  • proxy behaviour
  • front-end/back-end disagreement
  • request desynchronisation
  • HTTP request smuggling conditions

docs.title: Testing Approach
docs.text:
Identify Proxy Architecture
        ↓
Capture Request
        ↓
Analyse Request Handling
        ↓
Run Appropriate Checks
        ↓
Observe Timing / Response Behaviour
        ↓
Investigate Anomalies
        ↓
Manually Verify

Warning

Request smuggling testing can affect shared connections and other application users. Testing should be performed carefully within the agreed scope and rules of engagement.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Turbo Intruder provides a high-performance HTTP request engine for situations where a large number of requests or precise request timing is required.

It should generally be used when standard Burp Intruder is not suitable for the testing scenario.

docs.title: Useful For
docs.text:
Turbo Intruder can assist with:

  • race-condition testing
  • high-volume request testing
  • timing-sensitive application behaviour
  • large input sets
  • custom request workflows

docs.title: Typical Workflow
docs.text:
Interesting Request
       ↓
Send to Turbo Intruder
       ↓
Define Request Strategy
       ↓
Execute Controlled Requests
       ↓
Analyse Responses
       ↓
Identify Anomalies
       ↓
Verify Manually

Warning

High-volume testing can affect application availability. Configure request volume according to the agreed testing scope and rate limits.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Collaborator Everywhere helps identify functionality that may cause the target application to interact with external systems.

It works with Burp Collaborator to identify out-of-band interactions.

docs.title: Useful For
docs.text:
It can help discover potential:

  • server-side request behaviour
  • backend HTTP requests
  • DNS interactions
  • email interactions
  • asynchronous processing
  • blind vulnerabilities
  • external service integrations

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
Some vulnerabilities do not immediately appear in the HTTP response.

Instead:

Request
   ↓
Application
   ↓
Backend Processing
   ↓
External Interaction
   ↓
Burp Collaborator

The external interaction may provide evidence that user-controlled data reached a backend component.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Enable Collaborator Everywhere
          ↓
Browse Application
          ↓
Extension Adds Collaborator Payloads
          ↓
Application Processes Requests
          ↓
Monitor Collaborator
          ↓
Investigate Interactions
          ↓
Manual Verification

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Active Scan++ extends Burp Scanner with additional checks for web application vulnerabilities and unusual application behaviour.

It can complement Burp's built-in scanner during authorised assessments.

docs.title: Useful For
docs.text:
The extension may assist with identifying:

  • input validation weaknesses
  • unusual response behaviour
  • additional server-side issues
  • application-specific weaknesses

Automated findings should always be manually verified.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Backslash Powered Scanner uses unusual input transformations and response differences to identify potentially interesting server-side behaviour.

It can help identify inputs that warrant deeper manual investigation.

docs.title: Testing Philosophy
docs.text:
The extension is particularly useful for identifying behaviour such as:

Input
  ↓
Unexpected Server Processing
  ↓
Response Difference
  ↓
Potential Injection Point
  ↓
Manual Investigation

The extension should be considered a discovery tool rather than proof of vulnerability.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Error Message Checks assists with identifying verbose application error messages.

Verbose errors can disclose useful technical information about the application.

docs.title: Information That May Be Exposed
docs.text:
Examples include:

  • stack traces
  • framework versions
  • database errors
  • filesystem paths
  • SQL queries
  • internal hostnames
  • package names
  • source code references
  • debugging information

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Instead of:

Invalid request.

an application might return:

SQLException
Database connection failed
/var/www/application/controllers/UserController.php

This information can assist with technology identification and further vulnerability research.

docs.title: Built-In Burp Features
docs.text: Extensions are useful, but many important tests can be performed using Burp's built-in functionality.

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
Use Proxy for:

  • intercepting requests
  • modifying requests
  • viewing application traffic
  • understanding application behaviour
  • identifying interesting endpoints

A common workflow is:

Browser
   ↓
Burp Proxy
   ↓
Application

docs.title: HTTP History
docs.text:
HTTP history is one of the most valuable sources of information during an assessment.

Review it for:

  • API endpoints
  • authentication requests
  • administrative functions
  • object identifiers
  • file operations
  • redirects
  • interesting parameters
  • hidden functionality

Useful filters include:

MIME type
HTTP method
Status code
Search term
In-scope only

docs.title: Repeater
docs.text:
Repeater is one of the most important tools for manual web application testing.

Use it to repeatedly modify and resend requests.

Typical workflow:

Proxy
  ↓
Interesting Request
  ↓
Send to Repeater
  ↓
Establish Baseline
  ↓
Modify One Element
  ↓
Send
  ↓
Compare Response
  ↓
Repeat

Repeater is particularly useful for:

  • authentication testing
  • authorisation testing
  • input validation
  • API testing
  • injection testing
  • session testing
  • business logic testing

docs.title: Intruder
docs.text:
Intruder automates repeated requests using configurable payload positions.

It is useful when the same test must be performed against multiple values.

Examples include:

  • parameter enumeration
  • identifier testing
  • input fuzzing
  • endpoint testing
  • header testing
  • controlled wordlist-based testing

docs.title: Comparer
docs.text:
Comparer allows two pieces of data to be compared.

This is particularly useful for authorisation testing.

Example:

Administrator Response
          ↓
       Comparer
          ↑
Normal User Response

Differences may reveal whether sensitive information or functionality remains accessible.

docs.title: Decoder
docs.text:
Decoder can transform encoded data.

Common formats encountered during testing include:

URL encoding
Base64
Hex
HTML encoding

Decoder is useful when analysing:

  • cookies
  • parameters
  • tokens
  • API data
  • application-generated identifiers

docs.title: Sequencer
docs.text:
Sequencer analyses the randomness of tokens.

It can be useful when investigating:

  • session identifiers
  • CSRF tokens
  • password-reset tokens
  • application-generated security tokens

A typical workflow is:

Identify Token
     ↓
Capture Multiple Samples
     ↓
Sequencer
     ↓
Analyse Randomness
     ↓
Investigate Predictability

docs.title: Recommended Extension Workflow
docs.text:
Do not install extensions simply because they are available.

Select extensions according to the functionality being tested.

Application Mapping
        ↓
Identify Testing Area
        ↓
Select Relevant Extension
        ↓
Automated Assistance
        ↓
Review Interesting Results
        ↓
Repeater
        ↓
Manual Verification
        ↓
Evidence Collection
        ↓
Reporting

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Useful tools:

Proxy
Repeater
Intruder
Sequencer
Logger++

docs.title: Authorisation
docs.text:
Useful tools:

Autorize
AuthMatrix
Repeater
Comparer
Logger++

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
Useful tools:

Proxy
Repeater
Sequencer
Decoder
Logger++

docs.title: JWT
docs.text:
Useful tools:

JWT Editor
Repeater
Decoder
Logger++

docs.title: Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Useful tools:

Param Miner
Logger++
HTTP History
Target Sitemap

docs.title: HTTP Behaviour
docs.text:
Useful tools:

Param Miner
HTTP Request Smuggler
Repeater
Comparer

docs.title: Out-of-Band Testing
docs.text:
Useful tools:

Burp Collaborator
Collaborator Everywhere
Repeater

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
Useful tools:

Repeater
Turbo Intruder

docs.title: Suggested Core Extension Set
docs.text:
For a general web application penetration test, a useful starting collection is:

Autorize
AuthMatrix
JWT Editor
Param Miner
Logger++
HTTP Request Smuggler
Collaborator Everywhere
Turbo Intruder
Active Scan++
Backslash Powered Scanner
Error Message Checks

You do not necessarily need every extension for every assessment.

Choose extensions based on the application and attack surface.

docs.title: Manual Verification
docs.text:
Burp extensions should primarily be treated as assistants.

A useful principle is:

Extension Finding
       ↓
Understand Why It Was Flagged
       ↓
Send Request to Repeater
       ↓
Establish Baseline
       ↓
Reproduce Behaviour
       ↓
Determine Security Impact
       ↓
Capture Evidence
       ↓
Report

Tip

Do not report a vulnerability solely because a Burp extension marked a request as interesting or vulnerable. Reproduce the behaviour manually and determine the actual security impact.

docs.title: Practical Burp Toolkit
docs.text:
A useful way to think about Burp Suite during an assessment is:

                    BURP SUITE
                        │
        ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
        │               │               │
    DISCOVERY        TESTING         ANALYSIS
        │               │               │
     Proxy           Repeater         Logger++
 HTTP History        Intruder         Comparer
 Param Miner      Turbo Intruder      Decoder
        │               │             Sequencer
        └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                        │
                   SPECIALISED
                        │
             Autorize / AuthMatrix
                   JWT Editor
             HTTP Request Smuggler
            Collaborator Everywhere

The objective is not to automate the entire assessment.

The objective is to combine:

Application Understanding
          +
Manual Testing
          +
Burp Automation
          +
Specialised Extensions
          =
Effective Web Application Testing

docs.title: Related Notes
docs.text:
• Web Application Testing Methodology
  • Web Application Pentesting Checklist
  • Authentication Testing
  • Authorisation Testing
  • Session Management Testing
  • Burp Suite Testing Workflows

docs.title: Burp Suite Testing Workflows
docs.text:
Burp Suite is most effective when used as part of a structured testing methodology rather than simply intercepting requests and trying random payloads.

This page provides practical Burp Suite workflows for common web application security testing activities.

The objective is to move systematically from:

Application Mapping
        ↓
Request Identification
        ↓
Manual Analysis
        ↓
Controlled Manipulation
        ↓
Response Comparison
        ↓
Vulnerability Validation
        ↓
Evidence Collection

Authorised Security Testing

Perform these techniques only against applications and systems for which you have explicit authorisation. Use dedicated test accounts and test data where possible.

docs.title: 1. General Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
A useful general workflow for a web application assessment is:

Configure Target Scope
        ↓
Browse Application
        ↓
Proxy / HTTP History
        ↓
Build Application Map
        ↓
Identify Interesting Requests
        ↓
Send to Repeater
        ↓
Establish Baseline
        ↓
Modify One Element
        ↓
Compare Response
        ↓
Investigate Interesting Behaviour
        ↓
Use Specialised Tools / Extensions
        ↓
Manually Verify
        ↓
Capture Evidence
        ↓
Report

The most important principle is:

Understand the normal request before modifying it.

Without a baseline, it becomes difficult to determine whether a modification actually changed application behaviour.

docs.title: 2. Initial Burp Setup
docs.text:
Before testing, configure the target scope.

Navigate to:

Target
    ↓
Scope

Add the authorised target.

For example:

https://app.example.test

Where appropriate, include authorised subdomains:

*.example.test

Do not automatically assume every related domain is within scope.

docs.title: 3. Use Scope Aggressively
docs.text:
Once the target has been configured, use:

Show only in-scope items

where appropriate.

This makes large assessments considerably easier to manage.

Instead of seeing:

Google Analytics
CDNs
Fonts
Advertising
Third-party APIs
Target Application

you primarily see:

Target Application

docs.title: 4. Browser Mapping Workflow
docs.text:
Start by using the application normally.

Visit:

Home
Login
Registration
Profile
Account
Search
Upload
Download
Settings
API functionality
Administrative functionality

Use every feature available to your authorised account.

While doing this, Burp builds an HTTP history.

Browser
   ↓
Burp Proxy
   ↓
HTTP History
   ↓
Application Map

Do not immediately start injecting payloads.

First understand the application.

docs.title: 5. HTTP History Review
docs.text:
After browsing the application, review:

Proxy
    ↓
HTTP history

Look for interesting requests containing:

id
user
account
role
admin
file
filename
path
url
uri
redirect
return
callback
search
query
token
session
password
email
upload
download
export
import
template
debug
api

Also pay attention to:

POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

These often represent state-changing functionality.

docs.title: 6. Request Triage
docs.text:
A useful approach is to classify interesting requests.

Authentication
Authorisation
Session
Input
File
URL
API
Administrative
Business Logic

Example:

GET /api/users/123 HTTP/1.1

Classification:

API
Object Identifier
Authorisation
Potential IDOR / BOLA

Another example:

POST /api/fetch HTTP/1.1

url=https://example.test

Classification:

URL Input
Server-Side Processing
Potential SSRF

This helps determine the appropriate testing workflow.

docs.title: 7. Repeater First
docs.text:
For manual testing, Repeater should normally be the first destination for an interesting request.

HTTP History
      ↓
Right Click
      ↓
Send to Repeater

Shortcut:

Ctrl + R

Then:

Repeater
   ↓
Send Original Request
   ↓
Record Baseline
   ↓
Modify One Variable
   ↓
Send Again
   ↓
Compare

docs.title: 8. Establish a Baseline
docs.text:
Before changing anything, send the original request.

Record:

Status code
Response length
Response body
Headers
Redirects
Response time
Application state

Example:

200 OK
Length: 4281

Then modify one element.

This makes response differences easier to understand.

docs.title: 9. Modify One Thing at a Time
docs.text:
Avoid changing:

Cookie
Parameter
HTTP method
Header
Object ID
Payload

all at once.

Instead:

Baseline
   ↓
Change Parameter
   ↓
Observe
   ↓
Restore
   ↓
Change Header
   ↓
Observe

This makes it much easier to determine which modification caused the behaviour.

docs.title: 10. Authentication Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Start by capturing the login request.

Browser
   ↓
Login
   ↓
Proxy
   ↓
Capture Request
   ↓
Send to Repeater

Example:

POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: example.test
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=testuser&password=Password123!

docs.title: Authentication Workflow
docs.text:
Capture Login
     ↓
Identify Credentials
     ↓
Identify Additional Parameters
     ↓
Send to Repeater
     ↓
Establish Valid Login Baseline
     ↓
Test Invalid Credentials
     ↓
Observe Error Behaviour
     ↓
Test Authentication Logic
     ↓
Inspect Session Creation
     ↓
Test MFA if Present
     ↓
Test Password Reset
     ↓
Test Account Recovery

docs.title: 11. Authentication Response Comparison
docs.text:
Compare:

Valid Username + Valid Password
Invalid Username + Valid Password
Valid Username + Invalid Password
Invalid Username + Invalid Password

Look for differences in:

Response message
Status
Response length
Redirect
Response time
Headers
Cookies

Potential username enumeration may appear as:

Unknown username

versus:

Incorrect password

or through more subtle response differences.

docs.title: 12. Authentication Cookies
docs.text:
After successful authentication, inspect:

Set-Cookie:

Record:

Session cookie
Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
Domain
Path
Expiration

Then compare the session before and after authentication.

Unauthenticated Session
        ↓
Login
        ↓
Authenticated Session

Determine whether the relevant session identifier changes.

docs.title: 13. MFA Workflow
docs.text:
If MFA exists:

Username + Password
        ↓
MFA Challenge
        ↓
Authenticated Session

Capture requests around the transition.

Look for:

Session changes
MFA state parameters
Verification endpoints
Recovery functionality
Remember-device functionality
Alternative authentication paths

The key question is:

Does the server independently verify that MFA was completed before granting access to protected functionality?

docs.title: 14. Password Reset Workflow
docs.text:
Map the complete password reset process:

Request Reset
     ↓
Reset Token Generated
     ↓
Token Delivered
     ↓
Token Validated
     ↓
New Password
     ↓
Existing Session Behaviour

Capture each request.

Review:

Token location
Token lifetime
Token reuse
Session invalidation
Account identification
Host handling
Redirect behaviour

docs.title: 15. Authorisation Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Authorisation testing works particularly well with two test accounts.

Use:

User A
User B

Preferably also:

Administrator

docs.title: Horizontal Authorisation
docs.text:
Create or identify an object belonging to User A.

Example:

User A document ID:

1001

Capture:

GET /api/documents/1001 HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=USER_A

Send to Repeater.

Now replace only:

USER_A

with:

USER_B

Keep:

/document/1001

unchanged.

docs.title: Horizontal Workflow
docs.text:
User A
   ↓
Access User A Object
   ↓
Capture Request
   ↓
Repeater
   ↓
Replace Session with User B
   ↓
Keep User A Object ID
   ↓
Send
   ↓
Compare

Expected:

Access denied

If User B receives User A's object, investigate for IDOR / BOLA.

docs.title: 16. Autorize Workflow
docs.text:
Autorize can automate much of this comparison.

Low-Privilege User
       ↓
Capture Session
       ↓
Configure Autorize
       ↓
Browse as Privileged User
       ↓
Autorize Replays Requests
       ↓
Compare Responses
       ↓
Potential Findings
       ↓
Repeater
       ↓
Manual Verification

A practical example:

Administrator
     ↓
GET /admin/users
     ↓
Autorize
     ↓
Replay with USER session

If the normal user's response appears equivalent, investigate manually.

Tip

Never report an Autorize result solely because it is highlighted. Send the request to Repeater and verify the actual access and resulting application state.

docs.title: 17. Vertical Privilege Escalation Workflow
docs.text:
Use an administrator account to perform an administrative operation.

Example:

DELETE /api/admin/users/123 HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=ADMIN

Capture the request.

Replace:

ADMIN

with:

NORMAL_USER

Then replay.

Administrator
      ↓
Perform Admin Function
      ↓
Capture Request
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Replace Admin Session
      ↓
Normal User Session
      ↓
Replay
      ↓
Verify Result

This is generally more reliable than simply guessing /admin endpoints.

docs.title: 18. AuthMatrix Workflow
docs.text:
For applications with multiple roles:

Admin
Manager
Employee
Customer
Anonymous

build an access matrix.

Example:

Function Admin Manager User Anonymous Profile ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ Reports ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ User Management ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ Configuration ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗

Then test requests across the different identities.

Capture Requests
       ↓
Define Roles
       ↓
Define Expected Permissions
       ↓
Run Matrix
       ↓
Review Differences
       ↓
Manual Verification

docs.title: 19. IDOR / BOLA Workflow
docs.text:
Look for identifiers in:

URL paths
Query parameters
JSON
POST bodies
GraphQL variables
Headers
Cookies
WebSocket messages

Example:

GET /api/orders/7312 HTTP/1.1

Ask:

Who owns order 7312?

Then test with another authorised test identity.

docs.title: Practical IDOR Flow
docs.text:
Find Object ID
      ↓
Determine Owner
      ↓
Capture Valid Request
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Switch Identity
      ↓
Keep Object ID
      ↓
Replay
      ↓
Test READ
      ↓
Test UPDATE
      ↓
Test DELETE
      ↓
Verify

Do not stop after testing GET.

An application might prevent:

GET

while incorrectly allowing:

PATCH
DELETE

docs.title: 20. Session Management Workflow
docs.text:
Capture an authenticated request.

Example:

GET /account HTTP/1.1
Cookie: session=ABC123

Send it to Repeater.

docs.title: Session Workflow
docs.text:
Login
  ↓
Capture Session
  ↓
Inspect Cookie
  ↓
Record Session Value
  ↓
Test Rotation
  ↓
Test Logout
  ↓
Replay Old Session
  ↓
Test Password Change
  ↓
Replay Old Session
  ↓
Test Expiration
  ↓
Test Revocation

docs.title: 21. Logout Testing
docs.text:
Procedure:

1. Login
2. Capture authenticated request
3. Send to Repeater
4. Confirm request works
5. Logout normally
6. Return to Repeater
7. Replay original request

Expected:

Session rejected

Potential issue:

Old session remains authenticated

Do not rely only on the browser cookie disappearing.

Verify server-side invalidation.

docs.title: 22. Session Fixation Workflow
docs.text:
Record the session before login:

session=AAA

Authenticate.

Record it again:

session=BBB

Compare:

AAA
vs
BBB

Workflow:

Unauthenticated Session
        ↓
Record Token
        ↓
Authenticate
        ↓
Record Token
        ↓
Compare

A relevant session identifier should normally rotate when authentication state changes.

docs.title: 23. Sequencer Workflow
docs.text:
For tokens that should be unpredictable:

Identify Token
     ↓
Send Response to Sequencer
     ↓
Configure Token Location
     ↓
Capture Multiple Tokens
     ↓
Analyse Randomness
     ↓
Investigate Patterns

Useful targets include:

Session identifiers
CSRF tokens
Password reset tokens
Other security-sensitive random values

docs.title: 24. Parameter Testing Workflow
docs.text:
When you identify a parameter:

?id=123

do not immediately throw every payload at it.

First determine its purpose.

Parameter
    ↓
Change Value
    ↓
Observe Response
    ↓
Determine Data Type
    ↓
Determine Processing Context
    ↓
Choose Relevant Tests

docs.title: 25. Parameter Classification
docs.text:
A useful mental model:

id=
   ↓
Object Reference
   ↓
IDOR / BOLA

url=
   ↓
URL Processing
   ↓
SSRF / Redirect

file=
   ↓
Filesystem
   ↓
Path Traversal / File Handling

search=
   ↓
Application Input
   ↓
XSS / Injection

template=
   ↓
Template Processing
   ↓
SSTI

redirect=
   ↓
Navigation
   ↓
Open Redirect

Context should determine the test.

docs.title: 26. Hidden Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Param Miner can assist with discovering hidden inputs.

Workflow:

Interesting Request
       ↓
Param Miner
       ↓
Guess Parameters
       ↓
Guess Headers
       ↓
Observe Response Changes
       ↓
Interesting Candidate
       ↓
Repeater
       ↓
Manual Investigation

Useful areas include:

Hidden parameters
Debug functionality
Cache behaviour
Proxy headers
Routing headers
Undocumented features

docs.title: 27. XSS Testing Workflow
docs.text:
For XSS testing, first identify where input appears in the response.

Input
  ↓
Submit Unique Marker
  ↓
Find Marker in Response
  ↓
Determine Context
  ↓
Test Context Escape
  ↓
Determine Encoding
  ↓
Validate Execution Safely

Use a unique marker first:

XSSMARKER123

Then search the response.

docs.title: XSS Context Identification
docs.text:
Determine whether the marker appears in:

<div>XSSMARKER123</div>

or:

<input value="XSSMARKER123">

or:

<script>
var search = "XSSMARKER123";
</script>

or:

const data = {
    value: "XSSMARKER123"
};

The context determines the appropriate testing strategy.

docs.title: 28. XSS Burp Workflow
docs.text:
Proxy
  ↓
Identify User Input
  ↓
Repeater
  ↓
Submit Unique Marker
  ↓
Locate Reflection
  ↓
Determine Context
  ↓
Test Encoding
  ↓
Test Context-Specific Input
  ↓
Browser Validation
  ↓
Capture Evidence

Useful Burp components include:

Proxy
Repeater
Intruder
DOM Invader
Scanner

The dedicated XSS notes should contain the detailed testing methodology.

docs.title: 29. SQL Injection Workflow
docs.text:
Start with an input that appears to influence server-side data processing.

Parameter
   ↓
Baseline Request
   ↓
Controlled Input Changes
   ↓
Observe Errors / Behaviour
   ↓
Compare Responses
   ↓
Investigate Database Interaction

Useful indicators can include:

Database errors
Boolean response differences
Unexpected query behaviour
Timing differences

docs.title: SQL Injection Burp Flow
docs.text:
Proxy
  ↓
Interesting Parameter
  ↓
Repeater
  ↓
Baseline
  ↓
Controlled Test Input
  ↓
Compare Response
  ↓
Investigate Behaviour
  ↓
Scanner where authorised
  ↓
Manual Verification

Detailed SQL injection techniques belong in the dedicated SQL Injection page.

docs.title: 30. Command Injection Workflow
docs.text:
Identify parameters that may be passed to operating-system commands.

Common candidates include functionality involving:

Ping
DNS lookup
Network diagnostics
File conversion
Image processing
Backup
Archive handling
System utilities

Workflow:

Identify Function
      ↓
Understand Expected Input
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Establish Baseline
      ↓
Controlled Input Modification
      ↓
Observe Behaviour
      ↓
Investigate Server-Side Processing
      ↓
Validate Safely

Use non-destructive validation methods during authorised testing.

docs.title: 31. SSRF Workflow
docs.text:
Look for parameters that accept URLs or network locations.

Examples:

url
uri
endpoint
callback
webhook
image
avatar
feed
proxy
destination
redirect

Example:

POST /api/fetch HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "url": "https://example.test"
}

docs.title: SSRF Flow
docs.text:
Identify URL Input
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Baseline External URL
      ↓
Determine Server-Side Fetching
      ↓
Test Controlled Destination
      ↓
Observe Response
      ↓
Use Collaborator if Appropriate
      ↓
Investigate Restrictions
      ↓
Manual Verification

docs.title: 32. Burp Collaborator Workflow
docs.text:
For functionality that may perform server-side network interactions:

Generate Collaborator Address
        ↓
Insert into Controlled Input
        ↓
Send Request
        ↓
Poll Collaborator
        ↓
DNS Interaction?
        ↓
HTTP Interaction?
        ↓
Investigate

Possible applications include:

SSRF
Blind XXE
Blind injection
Webhook processing
Backend URL validation
Asynchronous processing

An interaction proves that some component reached the Collaborator infrastructure, but you should still determine which input and application component caused it.

docs.title: 33. Collaborator Everywhere Workflow
docs.text:
Enable Extension
       ↓
Browse Application
       ↓
Extension Injects Collaborator References
       ↓
Application Processes Traffic
       ↓
Monitor Collaborator
       ↓
Identify Interactions
       ↓
Trace Back to Request
       ↓
Repeater
       ↓
Manual Verification

This can help discover server-side behaviour that was not obvious from application responses.

docs.title: 34. File Upload Workflow
docs.text:
File upload functionality requires multiple layers of testing.

First determine:

Allowed extensions
MIME validation
Content validation
Filename handling
Storage location
File retrieval
Processing behaviour
Access control

docs.title: Burp File Upload Flow
docs.text:
Upload Normal File
       ↓
Capture Request
       ↓
Repeater
       ↓
Understand Multipart Structure
       ↓
Modify Filename
       ↓
Modify Content-Type
       ↓
Modify File Content
       ↓
Observe Validation
       ↓
Determine Storage / Processing
       ↓
Retrieve File
       ↓
Test Access Control

Example multipart structure:

Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="test.pdf"
Content-Type: application/pdf

Do not assume validation is based solely on:

filename

or:

Content-Type

Determine what the server actually validates.

docs.title: 35. File Download Workflow
docs.text:
Download endpoints frequently expose:

IDOR
Path traversal
Information disclosure
Missing authorisation

Example:

GET /download?id=123 HTTP/1.1

Workflow:

Capture Download
      ↓
Identify File Reference
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Test Ownership
      ↓
Test Identifier Changes
      ↓
Test Path Handling if Relevant
      ↓
Verify Access Controls

docs.title: 36. Path Traversal Workflow
docs.text:
Look for parameters that appear to reference files or paths.

Examples:

file
filename
path
document
template
page
download

Workflow:

Identify File Parameter
       ↓
Baseline Valid File
       ↓
Repeater
       ↓
Modify Path
       ↓
Observe Normalisation
       ↓
Observe Errors
       ↓
Determine Filesystem Interaction
       ↓
Validate Safely

Detailed traversal techniques belong in the dedicated Path Traversal page.

docs.title: 37. XXE Workflow
docs.text:
Identify functionality processing XML.

Look for:

Content-Type: application/xml

or:

Content-Type: text/xml

or XML-based file formats and integrations.

Workflow:

Identify XML Processing
      ↓
Capture Valid XML
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Understand Parser Behaviour
      ↓
Controlled XML Modification
      ↓
Observe Response
      ↓
Collaborator if Appropriate
      ↓
Manual Verification

docs.title: 38. SSTI Workflow
docs.text:
Template injection testing begins by identifying input rendered by a server-side template engine.

Input
  ↓
Rendered Output
  ↓
Determine Transformation
  ↓
Identify Possible Template Context
  ↓
Controlled Expression Testing
  ↓
Fingerprint Engine
  ↓
Assess Impact

Burp workflow:

Proxy
  ↓
Find Reflected Input
  ↓
Repeater
  ↓
Baseline
  ↓
Controlled Template Expression
  ↓
Compare Output
  ↓
Investigate

docs.title: 39. Open Redirect Workflow
docs.text:
Look for parameters such as:

redirect
redirect_uri
return
returnUrl
next
continue
url
destination
callback

Example:

/login?returnUrl=/dashboard

Workflow:

Identify Redirect Parameter
       ↓
Baseline Internal Redirect
       ↓
Repeater
       ↓
Controlled External Destination
       ↓
Observe Location Header
       ↓
Browser Validation
       ↓
Determine Security Impact

docs.title: 40. API Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Modern applications frequently expose significant functionality through APIs.

Start by mapping:

Endpoints
Methods
Authentication
Object identifiers
Content types
Roles
Versions

docs.title: API Flow
docs.text:
Browse Application
      ↓
HTTP History
      ↓
Filter API Requests
      ↓
Map Endpoints
      ↓
Identify Objects
      ↓
Identify Methods
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Test Authentication
      ↓
Test Authorisation
      ↓
Test Input Validation
      ↓
Test Business Logic

docs.title: 41. API Endpoint Classification
docs.text:
Classify endpoints:

/api/users
    ↓
User Management

/api/orders
    ↓
Business Objects

/api/admin
    ↓
Administrative

/api/files
    ↓
File Handling

/api/search
    ↓
Input Processing

/api/export
    ↓
Data Export

This makes testing more systematic.

docs.title: 42. API Method Testing
docs.text:
For relevant endpoints, determine supported methods:

GET
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

Do not assume security controls are identical across methods.

Example:

GET /api/user/123

may be protected while:

PATCH /api/user/123

uses different authorisation logic.

docs.title: 43. API Version Testing
docs.text:
Look for:

/api/v1/
/api/v2/
/api/v3/

Compare equivalent functionality across versions.

Current API
    ↓
Strong Controls

Legacy API
    ↓
Different Controls?

JavaScript and historical endpoints may reveal older versions.

docs.title: 44. GraphQL Workflow
docs.text:
Identify the GraphQL endpoint.

Common examples:

/graphql
/api/graphql
/graphql/api

Map:

Queries
Mutations
Objects
Arguments
Authentication
Authorisation

docs.title: GraphQL Flow
docs.text:
Identify GraphQL Endpoint
       ↓
Capture Valid Query
       ↓
Repeater
       ↓
Understand Query Structure
       ↓
Identify Object IDs
       ↓
Test Authorisation
       ↓
Test Mutations
       ↓
Test Nested Objects
       ↓
Validate Results

docs.title: 45. WebSocket Workflow
docs.text:
Burp can capture WebSocket traffic.

Review:

Proxy
    ↓
WebSockets history

Look for messages containing:

userId
messageId
channel
room
organisation
role
action

docs.title: WebSocket Flow
docs.text:
Establish Connection
       ↓
Capture Messages
       ↓
Understand Message Format
       ↓
Identify Object IDs
       ↓
Identify Actions
       ↓
Modify Controlled Fields
       ↓
Test Authorisation
       ↓
Observe Responses

docs.title: 46. Business Logic Workflow
docs.text:
Business logic vulnerabilities often require understanding the application's intended workflow.

Start with:

What is supposed to happen?

Then:

Can the workflow be performed differently?

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Normal:

Create Order
    ↓
Payment
    ↓
Confirmation
    ↓
Delivery

Testing questions:

Can steps be skipped?
Can steps be repeated?
Can steps be performed out of order?
Can values change between steps?
Can another user perform a step?
Can an expired step still be used?

docs.title: 47. Business Logic Burp Flow
docs.text:
Perform Normal Workflow
       ↓
Capture Every Request
       ↓
Send Important Requests to Repeater
       ↓
Understand State Transitions
       ↓
Replay Requests
       ↓
Change Order
       ↓
Change Values
       ↓
Skip Steps
       ↓
Repeat Steps
       ↓
Observe Server-Side Enforcement

This is an area where manual testing is particularly important.

docs.title: 48. Race Condition Workflow
docs.text:
Identify functionality where multiple requests occurring close together could create inconsistent state.

Examples include:

Coupon redemption
Invitation acceptance
Balance operations
One-time actions
Limit enforcement
Account creation
Resource allocation

Start with Burp Repeater's parallel request functionality where appropriate.

Conceptually:

Single Request
      ↓
Expected State Change
      ↓
Send Multiple Controlled Requests
      ↓
Observe Whether Constraint Holds

Turbo Intruder can be useful for more specialised testing.

Warning

Race-condition testing can create multiple transactions or state changes. Use dedicated test data and stay within agreed rate and impact limits.

docs.title: 49. HTTP Request Smuggling Workflow
docs.text:
Request smuggling testing should begin by understanding the architecture.

Client
  ↓
CDN
  ↓
Reverse Proxy
  ↓
Load Balancer
  ↓
Application

Potential parsing differences between systems can create request desynchronisation.

Workflow:

Identify Suitable Endpoint
       ↓
HTTP Request Smuggler
       ↓
Run Controlled Checks
       ↓
Observe Timing / Response Behaviour
       ↓
Investigate Anomalies
       ↓
Manual Verification

Warning

Request smuggling testing can interfere with shared backend connections. Use conservative testing and follow the agreed rules of engagement.

docs.title: 50. Cache Testing Workflow
docs.text:
Start by identifying cacheable responses.

Inspect:

Cache-Control
Age
Vary
ETag
CDN headers
X-Cache

Workflow:

Baseline Request
      ↓
Determine Cache Behaviour
      ↓
Identify Unkeyed Input Candidates
      ↓
Param Miner
      ↓
Controlled Modification
      ↓
Repeat Request
      ↓
Observe Cache Behaviour
      ↓
Verify Carefully

Avoid poisoning shared production caches with harmful or persistent content.

docs.title: 51. JavaScript Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
Burp HTTP history can help identify JavaScript files.

Filter for:

JS

Then search downloaded JavaScript for:

/api/
/admin/
/internal/
token
secret
apikey
password
debug
upload
download
graphql
websocket

Workflow:

Browse Application
      ↓
Capture JavaScript
      ↓
Identify Interesting Files
      ↓
Search for Routes
      ↓
Search for Parameters
      ↓
Search for Secrets / Config
      ↓
Add Endpoints to Testing Map
      ↓
Test Through Repeater

docs.title: 52. Response Comparison Workflow
docs.text:
Many vulnerabilities become visible only through subtle response differences.

Compare:

Valid vs Invalid
User A vs User B
Admin vs User
Authenticated vs Anonymous
Normal Input vs Modified Input
Existing Object vs Missing Object

Use:

Comparer

or manually compare:

Status
Length
Headers
Body
Timing
Side effects

docs.title: 53. Intruder Workflow
docs.text:
Intruder is useful when one controlled request needs to be repeated with multiple input values.

Repeater
   ↓
Request Understood
   ↓
Send to Intruder
   ↓
Select Payload Position
   ↓
Configure Payloads
   ↓
Run Controlled Test
   ↓
Sort Responses
   ↓
Identify Outliers
   ↓
Repeater
   ↓
Manual Verification

The important step is:

Intruder result
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Manual verification

docs.title: 54. Intruder Response Analysis
docs.text:
Useful columns include:

Status
Length
Words
Lines
Time

Look for outliers.

Example:

Payload Status Length test1 403 421 test2 403 421 test3 200 4832 test4 403 421

The interesting result is:

test3

Send it to Repeater and determine why it differs.

docs.title: 55. Decoder Workflow
docs.text:
Use Decoder when values appear encoded.

Examples:

Base64
URL encoding
Hex
HTML entities

Workflow:

Interesting Value
      ↓
Decoder
      ↓
Decode
      ↓
Understand Structure
      ↓
Modify if Relevant
      ↓
Encode
      ↓
Repeater
      ↓
Test

Encoding is not encryption.

docs.title: 56. Logger++ Workflow
docs.text:
For large assessments:

Proxy Traffic
      ↓
Logger++
      ↓
Filter
      ↓
Search
      ↓
Interesting Request
      ↓
Repeater

Useful search terms:

admin
token
password
secret
debug
internal
upload
download
redirect
callback
api
graphql
role
permission

docs.title: 57. Scanner Workflow
docs.text:
Where Burp Scanner is available and authorised:

Map Application
      ↓
Understand Functionality
      ↓
Select Appropriate Targets
      ↓
Run Scanner
      ↓
Review Findings
      ↓
Send Request to Repeater
      ↓
Manual Verification
      ↓
Determine Impact

Do not treat scanner output as automatically confirmed.

docs.title: 58. Evidence Collection Workflow
docs.text:
Once a vulnerability has been confirmed:

Clean Reproduction
       ↓
Baseline Request
       ↓
Modified Request
       ↓
Relevant Response
       ↓
Verify Impact
       ↓
Capture Evidence
       ↓
Record Steps

Keep evidence minimal and clear.

docs.title: 59. Repeater Tabs
docs.text:
Use descriptive Repeater tab names.

Instead of:

Tab 1
Tab 2
Tab 3
Tab 4

use:

AUTH Login
AUTH Reset
IDOR Documents
ADMIN Users
UPLOAD PDF
SSRF Webhook
API Orders

This becomes extremely useful during larger assessments.

docs.title: 60. Request Naming Strategy
docs.text:
A practical naming convention:

[CATEGORY] Function

Examples:

[AUTH] Login
[AUTH] Password Reset
[AUTHZ] User Profile
[IDOR] Download Invoice
[API] Update Account
[UPLOAD] Document
[SSRF] Webhook
[XSS] Search
[SQLI] Product ID

docs.title: 61. Burp Notes Strategy
docs.text:
For each interesting request, record:

What does this request do?
Which account was used?
Which object does it affect?
Which parameters are interesting?
What tests have already been performed?
What remains to be tested?

This prevents duplicated work.

docs.title: 62. Practical Testing Decision Tree
docs.text:
When you encounter an input:

                    INPUT
                      │
          ┌───────────┼───────────┐
          │           │           │
       Object        URL        File/Path
          │           │           │
      IDOR/BOLA     SSRF       Traversal
          │        Redirect      Upload
          │
          ├───────────────┐
          │               │
        Text            Template
          │               │
     XSS / SQLi          SSTI
          │
          └───────────────┐
                          │
                         XML
                          │
                         XXE

The parameter name alone is not proof of the backend processing context.

Use application behaviour to determine the appropriate test.

docs.title: 63. Practical Endpoint Decision Tree
docs.text:
When you discover an endpoint:

Endpoint
   ↓
Does it require authentication?
   ↓
Should this user access it?
   ↓
Does it reference an object?
   ↓
Who owns the object?
   ↓
Does it accept input?
   ↓
Where does the input go?
   ↓
Does it change application state?
   ↓
Can the workflow be manipulated?

This single process identifies a large amount of potential attack surface.

docs.title: 64. Recommended Workflow by Vulnerability
docs.text: Testing Area Burp Components Authentication Proxy, Repeater, Intruder, Comparer Authorisation Repeater, Comparer, Autorize, AuthMatrix Session Management Repeater, Sequencer, Decoder IDOR / BOLA Repeater, Autorize, Comparer XSS Repeater, DOM Invader, Intruder SQL Injection Repeater, Scanner, Intruder SSRF Repeater, Collaborator File Upload Proxy, Repeater Path Traversal Repeater, Intruder XXE Repeater, Collaborator SSTI Repeater Open Redirect Repeater API Security Proxy, Repeater, Autorize GraphQL Proxy, Repeater WebSockets WebSockets History Race Conditions Repeater, Turbo Intruder Request Smuggling HTTP Request Smuggler Cache Testing Repeater, Param Miner JWT Repeater, JWT Editor Hidden Parameters Param Miner Response Analysis Comparer, Logger++

docs.title: 65. Recommended Assessment Workflow
docs.text:
A complete practical assessment might look like:

                    TARGET
                      ↓
                 Configure Scope
                      ↓
               Browse Application
                      ↓
                  Proxy History
                      ↓
                Application Map
                      ↓
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        │             │             │
 Authentication  Authorisation    Inputs
        │             │             │
        ↓             ↓             ↓
   Sessions       IDOR/BOLA      Injection
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      ↓
                     API
                      ↓
                Business Logic
                      ↓
                Special Cases
                      ↓
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       │              │              │
   WebSockets      Caching        HTTP
       │              │              │
       └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                      ↓
               Manual Verification
                      ↓
                    Evidence
                      ↓
                    Report

docs.title: 66. Daily Burp Workflow
docs.text:
For a practical assessment, a simple repeatable process is:

1. Browse
2. Capture
3. Understand
4. Classify
5. Repeater
6. Establish baseline
7. Modify
8. Compare
9. Automate where useful
10. Verify manually
11. Record evidence
12. Continue mapping

Do not separate reconnaissance and vulnerability testing too rigidly.

During testing you will continuously discover:

New endpoints
New parameters
New roles
New APIs
New objects
New workflows

Add them back into the application map.

docs.title: 67. Testing Loop
docs.text:
A useful mental model is:

DISCOVER
   ↓
UNDERSTAND
   ↓
TEST
   ↓
COMPARE
   ↓
VERIFY
   ↓
DOCUMENT
   ↓
DISCOVER MORE
   ↺

Web application penetration testing is iterative.

A new API endpoint discovered during authorisation testing may expose another parameter, which may lead to another vulnerability class.

docs.title: 68. What Not to Do
docs.text:
Avoid approaching Burp as:

Intercept Request
      ↓
Insert Random Payload
      ↓
Nothing Happens
      ↓
Move On

Instead:

Understand Request
      ↓
Understand Input
      ↓
Understand Trust Boundary
      ↓
Choose Relevant Test
      ↓
Modify Carefully
      ↓
Compare Behaviour
      ↓
Verify

docs.title: 69. Automation vs Manual Testing
docs.text:
Automation is useful for:

Repetition
Discovery
Large input sets
Response comparison
Known vulnerability patterns

Manual testing is particularly important for:

Business logic
Authorisation
Authentication
Workflow manipulation
Complex application state
Chained vulnerabilities
Impact validation

The strongest methodology combines both.

Manual Understanding
        +
Targeted Automation
        +
Manual Verification
        =
Effective Testing

docs.title: 70. Final Burp Methodology
docs.text:
A mature Burp Suite workflow should therefore resemble:

Scope
  ↓
Proxy
  ↓
Map
  ↓
Understand
  ↓
Classify
  ↓
Repeater
  ↓
Baseline
  ↓
Controlled Modification
  ↓
Compare
  ↓
Extension / Intruder / Scanner
  ↓
Manual Verification
  ↓
Impact Analysis
  ↓
Evidence
  ↓
Reporting

The objective is not to use every Burp feature or extension.

The objective is to understand the application well enough to select the correct tool and test for each trust boundary.

docs.title: Interesting Request
docs.text:
HTTP History

Send to Repeater

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
Account A
    ↓
Capture Request
    ↓
Account B Session
    ↓
Replay

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
Capture Session
    ↓
Logout
    ↓
Replay
    ↓
Password Change
    ↓
Replay

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Unique Marker
    ↓
Find Reflection / Processing
    ↓
Determine Context
    ↓
Select Relevant Test

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Endpoint
    ↓
Method
    ↓
Authentication
    ↓
Authorisation
    ↓
Objects

Input
    ↓

docs.title: Finding
docs.text:
Potential Issue

docs.title: Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Reconnaissance is the process of discovering and mapping the externally accessible attack surface of a target.

During a web application penetration test, reconnaissance helps identify domains, subdomains, applications, technologies, endpoints and other assets that may require further investigation.

The objective is not simply to collect information. The collected information should be transformed into an organised view of the attack surface that guides the rest of the assessment.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform reconnaissance only against systems that are within the authorised scope of the security assessment.

docs.title: Reconnaissance Workflow
docs.text:
A practical reconnaissance workflow can be organised as:

Target Domain
      ↓
Passive Reconnaissance
      ↓
Subdomain Enumeration
      ↓
DNS Resolution
      ↓
HTTP Probing
      ↓
Technology Identification
      ↓
Content Discovery
      ↓
Crawling
      ↓
Historical URL Discovery
      ↓
Parameter Discovery
      ↓
JavaScript Analysis
      ↓
Attack Surface

The workflow is iterative. New domains, endpoints and technologies discovered during testing should be fed back into the reconnaissance process.

docs.title: Passive Reconnaissance
docs.text:
Passive reconnaissance gathers information without directly interacting with the target application where possible.

Useful sources may include:

  • Search engines
  • Certificate Transparency logs
  • DNS information
  • Public code repositories
  • Internet archives
  • Public documentation
  • Search engine caches
  • Publicly indexed files
  • Historical URLs
  • Internet-wide scanning databases

Passive reconnaissance can reveal assets that are difficult to discover through direct enumeration.

docs.title: Subdomain Enumeration
docs.text:
Subdomain enumeration expands the known attack surface beyond the primary domain.

For example:

example.com
│
├── www.example.com
├── api.example.com
├── portal.example.com
├── login.example.com
├── dev.example.com
├── staging.example.com
└── admin.example.com

Subdomains may expose:

  • Additional applications
  • APIs
  • Administrative interfaces
  • Development environments
  • Staging environments
  • Legacy systems
  • Third-party services

Multiple enumeration sources should normally be combined because individual tools and data sources may return different results.

Subdomain Enumeration

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Discovered hostnames should be validated through DNS resolution.

This separates potential hostnames from domains that currently resolve.

Useful information includes:

  • A records
  • AAAA records
  • CNAME records
  • MX records
  • TXT records
  • NS records

CNAME records are particularly useful for identifying externally hosted services and third-party infrastructure.

docs.title: HTTP Probing
docs.text:
A resolving hostname does not necessarily expose a web application.

HTTP probing can determine:

  • Whether HTTP or HTTPS responds
  • HTTP status code
  • Page title
  • Web server
  • Redirect location
  • Content type
  • Technology information
  • IP address

A reconnaissance pipeline may therefore follow:

Enumerated Subdomains
        ↓
DNS Resolution
        ↓
HTTP Probing
        ↓
Live Web Applications

This creates a more useful list for subsequent web application testing.

docs.title: Technology Identification
docs.text:
Identifying the technologies used by an application helps determine which testing techniques may be relevant.

Look for:

  • Web servers
  • Programming languages
  • Application frameworks
  • Content management systems
  • JavaScript frameworks
  • Reverse proxies
  • CDNs
  • WAFs
  • Authentication technologies
  • API technologies
  • Third-party libraries

Version information can also help identify outdated or unsupported components that require further investigation.

Technology Identification

docs.title: Content Discovery
docs.text:
Content discovery attempts to identify resources that may not be visible through normal application navigation.

Examples include:

/admin/
/api/
/backup/
/debug/
/internal/
/old/
/uploads/
/swagger/
/robots.txt
/sitemap.xml

Interesting resources may include:

  • Administrative interfaces
  • APIs
  • Backup files
  • Configuration files
  • Debug endpoints
  • Development interfaces
  • Documentation
  • Source maps
  • Temporary files
  • Legacy functionality

Content Discovery

docs.title: Crawling
docs.text:
Crawling follows links and application references to build a more complete picture of the accessible application.

Crawlers may discover:

  • URLs
  • Parameters
  • Forms
  • JavaScript files
  • API endpoints
  • Static resources
  • Hidden application routes

Crawling should complement content discovery rather than replace it.

docs.title: Historical URL Discovery
docs.text:
Historical data can reveal endpoints that are no longer linked from the current application.

Potential discoveries include:

  • Legacy endpoints
  • Old API versions
  • Historical parameters
  • Removed functionality
  • Backup resources
  • JavaScript files
  • Previously exposed directories

Historical URLs should be validated before being treated as part of the current attack surface.

docs.title: Parameter Discovery
docs.text:
Parameters are particularly important because they represent locations where user-controlled data enters an application.

Sources include:

GET parameters
POST parameters
JSON properties
XML elements
HTTP headers
Cookies
Path parameters
Multipart fields
WebSocket messages

Parameter names can also be discovered through:

  • Crawling
  • JavaScript
  • Historical URLs
  • API documentation
  • HTML forms
  • Automated parameter discovery

Parameter Discovery

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
Modern applications frequently expose significant information through JavaScript.

JavaScript files can reveal:

  • API endpoints
  • Hidden routes
  • Parameter names
  • Internal URLs
  • Feature flags
  • Authentication logic
  • Client-side access controls
  • Third-party services
  • Source maps
  • Potential secrets

JavaScript analysis should therefore be part of the standard reconnaissance workflow.

JavaScript Analysis

docs.title: Building the Attack Surface
docs.text:
Reconnaissance results become more useful when they are organised into a structured attack surface.

For example:

Target
│
├── Domains
│   ├── Main
│   ├── API
│   ├── Authentication
│   └── Development
│
├── Technologies
│   ├── Web Server
│   ├── Framework
│   ├── JavaScript
│   └── Infrastructure
│
├── Endpoints
│   ├── Public
│   ├── Authenticated
│   ├── Administrative
│   └── API
│
├── Input
│   ├── Parameters
│   ├── Headers
│   ├── Cookies
│   ├── Files
│   └── JSON / XML
│
└── Security Boundaries
    ├── Authentication
    ├── Authorisation
    ├── Roles
    └── Trust Relationships

This provides a foundation for the vulnerability testing phases that follow.

docs.title: Common Reconnaissance Tools
docs.text:
Purpose Tools Subdomain enumeration Subfinder, Amass, Assetfinder DNS resolution dnsx HTTP probing httpx Crawling Katana Content discovery ffuf, feroxbuster, dirsearch Historical URLs waybackurls, gau Parameter discovery ParamSpider, Arjun Technology identification Wappalyzer, WhatWeb Vulnerability discovery Nuclei JavaScript analysis LinkFinder, manual review

No single tool provides complete coverage. Combining different data sources generally produces better results.

docs.title: Reconnaissance Output
docs.text:
At the end of reconnaissance, useful outputs may include:

subdomains.txt
resolved-subdomains.txt
alive-hosts.txt
urls.txt
historical-urls.txt
parameters.txt
javascript-files.txt
technologies.txt
endpoints.txt

Keeping reconnaissance data organised makes it easier to reproduce the assessment and feed results into subsequent testing.
