docs.title: Content Discovery
docs.text:
Content discovery is the process of identifying hidden or unlinked resources within a web application.

Applications frequently expose endpoints that are not accessible through normal navigation. These may include administrative interfaces, API endpoints, backup files, configuration files, development resources, old application versions and forgotten functionality.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform content discovery only against systems for which you have explicit authorisation.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
Content discovery attempts to identify resources such as:

Directories
Files
API endpoints
Administrative interfaces
Backup files
Configuration files
Development environments
Documentation
Debug endpoints
Legacy applications
Source files
Temporary files
Exposed repositories

A typical workflow is:

Application
    ↓
Manual Exploration
    ↓
robots.txt / sitemap.xml
    ↓
Historical URL Collection
    ↓
Directory Discovery
    ↓
File Discovery
    ↓
Extension Discovery
    ↓
Response Analysis
    ↓
Manual Verification

The objective is not simply to generate thousands of requests.

The objective is to identify interesting application functionality that expands the attack surface.

docs.title: Start Manually
docs.text:
Before running automated discovery tools, browse the application manually.

Review:

Navigation
Links
Forms
JavaScript
API requests
Redirects
Static resources
Authentication flows
Error messages

Burp Suite's HTTP history and site map are particularly useful here.

A manually observed application might initially appear as:

/
├── /login
├── /register
├── /account
└── /contact

Content discovery might later reveal:

/
├── /login
├── /register
├── /account
├── /contact
├── /admin
├── /api
├── /swagger
├── /backup
├── /debug
└── /internal

The second view provides a much more complete picture of the application's attack surface.

docs.title: robots.txt
docs.text:
Always check:

/robots.txt

Example:

curl https://target.example/robots.txt

A response might contain:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /internal/
Disallow: /backup/

Although robots.txt is intended for web crawlers, it can provide useful reconnaissance information.

Note

A Disallow entry is not an access control mechanism.

docs.title: sitemap.xml
docs.text:
Check:

/sitemap.xml

Example:

curl https://target.example/sitemap.xml

Sitemaps may reveal:

Application pages
Legacy endpoints
Product pages
Documentation
API routes
Unlinked content

Also consider:

/sitemap_index.xml
/sitemap-index.xml
/sitemap1.xml

docs.title: security.txt
docs.text:
Check for:

/.well-known/security.txt
/security.txt

Example:

curl https://target.example/.well-known/security.txt

This file may provide:

Security contact
Responsible disclosure policy
Scope information
Acknowledgement pages
Security policy links

It is particularly useful during legitimate vulnerability research.

docs.title: Common Files
docs.text:
Some files are worth checking early because they may provide additional information about the application.

Examples:

/robots.txt
/sitemap.xml
/.well-known/security.txt
/favicon.ico
/manifest.json
/asset-manifest.json
/README.md

Framework-specific resources can also be valuable.

For example:

/_next/
/static/
/assets/
/swagger/
/api/

docs.title: Directory Discovery
docs.text:
Directory discovery attempts to identify resources that are not directly linked from the application.

Common tools include:

ffuf
feroxbuster
dirsearch
gobuster
Burp Suite

Do not immediately use extremely large wordlists.

Start with a sensible list and expand only when necessary.

docs.title: FFUF
docs.text:
FFUF is a fast and flexible web fuzzer.

Basic directory discovery:

ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt

The keyword:

FUZZ

is replaced with entries from the wordlist.

Potential output:

admin                   [Status: 302]
api                     [Status: 200]
backup                  [Status: 403]
internal                [Status: 403]
uploads                 [Status: 301]

These responses should then be manually investigated.

docs.title: FFUF Status Filtering
docs.text:
You can restrict interesting status codes:

ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt \
  -mc 200,204,301,302,307,401,403

Do not automatically discard:

401
403

A 403 Forbidden response can be extremely useful.

It confirms that something may exist at that location.

docs.title: Response Size Filtering
docs.text:
Applications frequently return custom error pages with HTTP 200 responses.

For example:

/nonexistent123

might return:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 4242

If every nonexistent resource returns the same size, filter it:

ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w wordlist.txt \
  -fs 4242

Useful FFUF filters include:

-fs    Filter response size
-fw    Filter number of words
-fl    Filter number of lines
-fc    Filter status codes

This is often more reliable than filtering only by HTTP status.

docs.title: FFUF Auto Calibration
docs.text:
FFUF can automatically attempt to identify baseline responses:

ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w wordlist.txt \
  -ac

Auto calibration can help reduce false positives caused by wildcard responses.

However, always verify important results manually.

docs.title: Feroxbuster
docs.text:
Feroxbuster is particularly useful for recursive content discovery.

Basic usage:

feroxbuster \
  -u https://target.example

Specify a wordlist:

feroxbuster \
  -u https://target.example \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt

Feroxbuster can recursively discover directories.

For example:

/admin
/admin/users
/admin/config
/admin/logs

This can reveal application structure that a single directory scan might miss.

docs.title: Feroxbuster Extensions
docs.text:
Search for specific file extensions:

feroxbuster \
  -u https://target.example \
  -x php,txt,json,xml,bak

Possible findings:

config.php
users.json
backup.bak
settings.xml
debug.txt

docs.title: Dirsearch
docs.text:
Dirsearch is another useful content discovery tool.

Basic usage:

dirsearch \
  -u https://target.example

Specify extensions:

dirsearch \
  -u https://target.example \
  -e php,asp,aspx,jsp,json,txt,bak

Useful options include:

-r    Recursive discovery
-x    Exclude status codes
-i    Include status codes

docs.title: Gobuster
docs.text:
Gobuster can also perform directory discovery:

gobuster dir \
  -u https://target.example \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt

With extensions:

gobuster dir \
  -u https://target.example \
  -w wordlist.txt \
  -x php,txt,bak,json

docs.title: Wordlists
docs.text:
SecLists provides a large collection of useful discovery wordlists.

Common location on Kali Linux:

/usr/share/seclists/

Useful directories include:

Discovery/Web-Content/
Discovery/DNS/
Fuzzing/
Passwords/
Usernames/

For content discovery:

/usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/

Useful starting lists include:

common.txt
raft-small-directories.txt
raft-medium-directories.txt
raft-small-files.txt
raft-medium-files.txt
directory-list-2.3-small.txt
directory-list-2.3-medium.txt

A practical approach is:

Small list
   ↓
Review Results
   ↓
Medium list
   ↓
Technology-Specific Lists
   ↓
Target-Specific Discovery

Avoid blindly starting with the largest available wordlist.

docs.title: Technology-Specific Discovery
docs.text:
Technology identification should influence content discovery.

For example, if the application uses PHP:

ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w wordlist.txt \
  -e .php

For ASP.NET:

ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w wordlist.txt \
  -e .aspx,.ashx,.asmx

For Java:

.jsp
.action
.do

For configuration-heavy applications:

.json
.xml
.yml
.yaml
.conf
.config

Technology-aware discovery produces more relevant results.

docs.title: File Extension Discovery
docs.text:
Do not assume that all resources are extensionless.

Useful extensions include:

.php
.asp
.aspx
.jsp
.do
.action
.json
.xml
.txt
.conf
.config
.yml
.yaml
.log
.bak
.old
.zip
.tar
.gz

Example:

ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w wordlist.txt \
  -e .php,.txt,.json,.xml,.bak,.old

docs.title: Backup Files
docs.text:
Backup files are particularly interesting because developers and administrators may accidentally leave them accessible.

Common patterns include:

index.php.bak
index.php.old
index.php~
config.php.bak
web.config.old
application.zip
backup.zip
site.tar.gz
www.zip

Potentially interesting extensions:

.bak
.backup
.old
.orig
.save
.tmp
~
.zip
.tar
.gz

If a legitimate application file is known:

config.php

consider whether authorised testing permits checking common backup variants:

config.php.bak
config.php.old
config.php~

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Potential configuration resources include:

.env
web.config
application.properties
application.yml
application.yaml
config.json
config.xml
settings.json

Configuration files can potentially expose:

Application settings
Internal hostnames
API endpoints
Database configuration
Debug settings
Environment information

Any discovered sensitive information should be handled according to the assessment's rules of engagement.

docs.title: Git Repository Exposure
docs.text:
Check whether repository metadata has accidentally been published:

/.git/

A simple request:

curl -I https://target.example/.git/HEAD

An exposed .git directory can potentially reveal application source code and repository history.

Also consider other version control artefacts:

/.svn/
/.hg/

Do not download or reconstruct repositories unless this is permitted by the assessment scope.

docs.title: API Discovery
docs.text:
Look for common API paths:

/api
/api/v1
/api/v2
/rest
/graphql
/swagger
/swagger-ui
/openapi.json
/api-docs
/v1
/v2

Example:

ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w api-wordlist.txt

API documentation can significantly expand the visible attack surface.

docs.title: Swagger and OpenAPI
docs.text:
Common locations include:

/swagger
/swagger-ui
/swagger-ui.html
/swagger.json
/openapi.json
/api-docs
/v2/api-docs
/v3/api-docs

If documentation is exposed, review:

Endpoints
HTTP methods
Parameters
Request schemas
Authentication requirements
Administrative functionality

Documentation should be treated as an attack surface map.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
Common GraphQL locations include:

/graphql
/graphiql
/api/graphql

Content discovery may identify GraphQL even when it is not linked from the main application.

Look for requests containing:

query
mutation
__typename

JavaScript files may also disclose GraphQL endpoints.

docs.title: Administrative Interfaces
docs.text:
Look for administrative and management functionality.

Common patterns include:

/admin
/administrator
/management
/manage
/console
/dashboard
/backend
/control
/panel
/internal

A 401, 403 or redirect can still be a meaningful result.

For example:

/admin       → 403
/management  → 401
/dashboard   → 302 /login

All three indicate potentially valid application functionality.

docs.title: Development and Debug Resources
docs.text:
Look for:

/debug
/dev
/test
/testing
/staging
/internal
/console
/actuator
/metrics
/health
/status

Development functionality can expose significantly more information than production interfaces.

docs.title: Spring Boot Actuator
docs.text:
If Spring Boot is identified, common Actuator endpoints may include:

/actuator
/actuator/health
/actuator/info
/actuator/env
/actuator/configprops
/actuator/mappings
/actuator/metrics

The exact exposed endpoints depend on application configuration and Spring Boot version.

Do not assume an endpoint is sensitive solely because it exists. Review the actual information exposed.

docs.title: Historical URLs
docs.text:
Current application navigation does not necessarily show everything that has existed historically.

Historical URL sources can reveal:

Old endpoints
Deprecated APIs
Backup resources
Legacy applications
Old parameters
JavaScript files
Previous directories

Tools commonly used for this include:

waybackurls
gau
urlfinder

docs.title: Waybackurls
docs.text:
Example:

echo target.example | waybackurls

Save results:

echo target.example | waybackurls > wayback.txt

Remove duplicates:

sort -u wayback.txt -o wayback.txt

Historical URLs can then be checked to determine whether they still exist.

docs.title: GAU
docs.text:
GetAllUrls can gather URLs from multiple public sources.

Example:

gau target.example

Save the results:

gau target.example > gau.txt

Then deduplicate:

sort -u gau.txt -o gau.txt

docs.title: URLFinder
docs.text:
URLFinder can also help discover URLs associated with a target.

Example:

urlfinder -d target.example

Save output:

urlfinder -d target.example -o urls.txt

Historical URL collection is particularly useful before parameter discovery.

docs.title: Combine URL Sources
docs.text:
Results from multiple sources can be combined:

cat wayback.txt gau.txt urlfinder.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > all-urls.txt

You can then inspect the discovered paths:

cat all-urls.txt

A large URL collection can reveal application functionality that normal crawling missed.

docs.title: Extract Unique Paths
docs.text:
If many URLs have been collected, extracting unique paths can make analysis easier.

For example:

https://target.example/admin/users
https://target.example/api/v1/users
https://target.example/account/settings

can be reduced conceptually to:

/admin/users
/api/v1/users
/account/settings

These paths can then inform further targeted discovery.

docs.title: JavaScript-Based Discovery
docs.text:
JavaScript often contains endpoints that directory brute forcing will never discover.

Look for:

/api/users
/api/admin
/internal/status
/auth/refresh
/graphql
/upload
/download

Search downloaded JavaScript:

grep -RniE \
  '(/api/|/admin|/internal|/graphql|/upload|/download)' \
  javascript/

JavaScript analysis should therefore complement traditional directory discovery.

docs.title: Crawling
docs.text:
Crawlers discover linked content rather than guessing filenames.

Useful tools include:

Katana
Burp Suite
Hakrawler
gospider

For example:

katana -u https://target.example

With greater depth:

katana \
  -u https://target.example \
  -d 3

Save results:

katana \
  -u https://target.example \
  -o katana.txt

Crawling and brute force discovery solve different problems:

Crawler
   ↓
Discover linked resources

Wordlist Discovery
   ↓
Discover unlinked resources

Use both.

docs.title: Response Code Interpretation
docs.text:
HTTP status codes provide useful clues.

Status Interpretation 200 Resource likely accessible 204 Resource exists with no body 301 Permanent redirect 302 Temporary redirect 307 Redirect preserving method 401 Authentication required 403 Resource may exist but access denied 404 Resource likely unavailable 405 Endpoint may exist but method is incorrect 500 Application processed something unexpectedly

Do not judge results solely by status code.

Compare:

Status
Response size
Word count
Headers
Redirect destination
Response body
Timing

docs.title: 403 Responses
docs.text:
Do not automatically ignore 403 Forbidden.

For example:

/admin        403
/internal     403
/backup       403

These responses indicate potentially valid resources.

A useful workflow is:

403 discovered
      ↓
Record endpoint
      ↓
Compare response fingerprint
      ↓
Determine expected access control
      ↓
Review application behaviour
      ↓
Continue testing within scope

The important finding may simply be that previously unknown functionality exists.

docs.title: 404 Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Not all 404 responses are identical.

Different application components may produce different error pages.

For example:

/does-not-exist

might return an nginx 404 while:

/api/does-not-exist

returns a JSON framework error.

This can indicate different backend components.

The 0xdf 404 cheatsheet is useful for recognising technology-specific error pages:

https://0xdf.gitlab.io/cheatsheets/404

This can complement technology identification during content discovery.

docs.title: Baseline Responses
docs.text:
Before running large discovery scans, establish a baseline.

Request random nonexistent paths:

curl -i https://target.example/randomdoesnotexist12345

Then another:

curl -i https://target.example/randomdoesnotexist67890

Compare:

Status
Content-Length
Body
Headers
Redirect

If both responses are identical, that response fingerprint can be filtered during discovery.

docs.title: Virtual Hosts
docs.text:
Sometimes content is separated by virtual host rather than path.

For example:

www.target.example
admin.target.example
api.target.example
dev.target.example

Subdomain enumeration therefore complements directory discovery.

The complete attack surface is usually:

Domains
   +
Subdomains
   +
Virtual Hosts
   +
Directories
   +
Files
   +
Parameters
   +
JavaScript Endpoints
   +
APIs

docs.title: Burp Suite Workflow
docs.text:
Burp Suite provides an excellent central location for reviewing discovered content.

Use:

Proxy
→ HTTP history

and:

Target
→ Site map

After automated discovery, send interesting endpoints through Burp for manual analysis.

Example:

/admin
/api/v1/users
/swagger
/internal
/upload

Then investigate:

Authentication
Authorisation
Parameters
Methods
Headers
Cookies
Input handling
Response behaviour

docs.title: Organising Discovery Results
docs.text:
Raw tool output quickly becomes difficult to manage.

Organise findings into categories:

Application
├── Authentication
├── Administration
├── API
├── Upload
├── Download
├── Internal
├── Debug
├── Documentation
└── Static Resources

For example:

Authentication
/login
/logout
/password-reset

Administration
/admin
/admin/users

API
/api/v1
/api/v1/users

Documentation
/swagger
/openapi.json

This turns content discovery into an actual application map.

docs.title: Prioritising Results
docs.text:
Not every discovered path deserves equal attention.

A useful priority order is:

Administrative functionality
        ↓
Authentication endpoints
        ↓
API endpoints
        ↓
File upload/download
        ↓
Debug functionality
        ↓
Internal functionality
        ↓
Backup/configuration files
        ↓
Legacy functionality
        ↓
Static resources

Prioritisation should also consider the application's purpose and assessment scope.

docs.title: Practical Workflow
docs.text: A practical content discovery workflow could be:

docs.title: 1. Manual browsing
docs.text:
Use:

Browser
Burp Suite
Developer Tools

docs.title: 2. Check standard resources
docs.text:
robots.txt
sitemap.xml
security.txt

docs.title: 3. Crawl
docs.text:
katana \
  -u https://target.example \
  -d 3 \
  -o katana.txt

docs.title: 4. Historical URLs
docs.text:
echo target.example | waybackurls > wayback.txt

gau target.example > gau.txt

docs.title: 5. Combine
docs.text:
cat katana.txt wayback.txt gau.txt \
  | sort -u \
  > discovered-urls.txt

docs.title: 6. Directory discovery
docs.text:
ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt \
  -ac

docs.title: 7. File discovery
docs.text:
ffuf \
  -u https://target.example/FUZZ \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-files.txt \
  -e .php,.json,.xml,.txt,.bak,.old \
  -ac

docs.title: 8. Review JavaScript
docs.text: Look for additional endpoints and API routes.

docs.title: 9. Manual verification
docs.text: Send interesting findings through Burp Suite.

docs.title: Recording Results
docs.text:
Keep a structured record of discovered resources.

For example:

Endpoint Status Type Priority Notes /admin 302 Administration High Redirects to login /api/v1 200 API High API root /swagger 200 Documentation High API documentation /internal 403 Internal High Resource exists /assets 301 Static Low Static files /health 200 Monitoring Medium Health endpoint

This provides a useful attack surface inventory for later testing.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
[ ] Browse application manually
[ ] Review Burp site map
[ ] Check robots.txt
[ ] Check sitemap.xml
[ ] Check security.txt
[ ] Establish baseline 404 response
[ ] Crawl application
[ ] Perform directory discovery
[ ] Perform file discovery
[ ] Test relevant extensions
[ ] Review 401 responses
[ ] Review 403 responses
[ ] Review unusual redirects
[ ] Search historical URLs
[ ] Review JavaScript endpoints
[ ] Look for APIs
[ ] Look for Swagger/OpenAPI
[ ] Look for GraphQL
[ ] Look for admin interfaces
[ ] Look for debug interfaces
[ ] Look for backup files
[ ] Look for configuration files
[ ] Check repository metadata
[ ] Record interesting endpoints
[ ] Manually verify findings

docs.title: Key Principle
docs.text:
Content discovery should not be treated as:

Run directory scanner
        ↓
Save output
        ↓
Done

A better methodology is:

Discover
   ↓
Classify
   ↓
Correlate
   ↓
Prioritise
   ↓
Verify
   ↓
Expand

Every interesting endpoint should answer a question:

What does this resource tell me about the application, and what should I test next?

The end result of content discovery should therefore be an increasingly accurate map of the application's attack surface, not simply a large collection of URLs.

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
JavaScript analysis is an important part of modern web application reconnaissance.

Client-side JavaScript frequently contains information about application functionality that may not be immediately visible through normal browsing. Reviewing JavaScript files can reveal API endpoints, parameters, hidden routes, authentication flows, third-party services, application architecture and functionality that should be investigated further.

This page provides a practical methodology for analysing JavaScript during authorised web application security assessments.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform these techniques only against systems for which you have explicit authorisation. JavaScript analysis should remain within the agreed scope of the assessment.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
JavaScript analysis can help identify:

  • API endpoints
  • Hidden application routes
  • Administrative functionality
  • Internal paths
  • API versions
  • Request parameters
  • GraphQL endpoints
  • WebSocket endpoints
  • Authentication functionality
  • Authorisation logic
  • File upload functionality
  • Debug functionality
  • Development endpoints
  • Feature flags
  • Third-party integrations
  • Cloud storage references
  • Source maps
  • Interesting comments
  • Hardcoded configuration
  • Accidentally exposed secrets
  • Client-side security controls
  • Potential vulnerability sinks

The objective is not simply to download JavaScript files.

The objective is to turn JavaScript into an attack surface map.

docs.title: JavaScript Analysis Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow can be represented as:

Target
  ↓
Crawl Application
  ↓
Collect JavaScript Files
  ↓
Normalise and Deduplicate URLs
  ↓
Download JavaScript
  ↓
Search for Endpoints
  ↓
Search for Parameters
  ↓
Search for Interesting Keywords
  ↓
Search for Secrets
  ↓
Inspect Source Maps
  ↓
Identify Sources and Sinks
  ↓
Map Application Functionality
  ↓
Validate Findings

Each stage should feed information into the next stage.

docs.title: 1. Collect JavaScript Files
docs.text:
Start by collecting JavaScript files referenced by the application.

There are several useful sources.

docs.title: Browser Developer Tools
docs.text:
Open the application in a browser and use:

Developer Tools
→ Network
→ JS

Reload the application.

This shows JavaScript resources loaded by the current page.

Also inspect:

Developer Tools
→ Sources

This is particularly useful for modern single-page applications.

docs.title: 2. Inspect the HTML
docs.text:
JavaScript files may be referenced directly in HTML.

Example:

<script src="/assets/app.js"></script>
<script src="/static/main.js"></script>
<script src="/js/application.js"></script>

Search downloaded HTML:

grep -Eo 'src="[^"]+\.js[^"]*"' index.html

Another simple approach:

grep -oE 'https?://[^"]+\.js' index.html

docs.title: 3. Crawl for JavaScript
docs.text:
Crawlers are usually more effective than inspecting pages manually.

Useful tools include:

  • Katana
  • gau
  • waybackurls
  • urlfinder
  • hakrawler

docs.title: Katana
docs.text:
Basic crawl:

katana -u https://example.com

Save results:

katana -u https://example.com -o katana.txt

Extract JavaScript:

grep -Ei '\.js($|\?)' katana.txt > javascript.txt

Sort and deduplicate:

sort -u javascript.txt -o javascript.txt

docs.title: Katana JavaScript Crawling
docs.text:
Katana can perform deeper JavaScript analysis.

katana -u https://example.com -jc

Useful combination:

katana \
  -u https://example.com \
  -jc \
  -kf all \
  -d 5 \
  -o katana.txt

Then extract JavaScript:

grep -Ei '\.js($|\?)' katana.txt | sort -u > javascript.txt

docs.title: 4. Historical JavaScript Files
docs.text:
Historical URLs can reveal JavaScript files that are no longer directly linked.

This can be useful because older application versions sometimes expose functionality or endpoints that remain accessible.

docs.title: gau
docs.text:
gau example.com

Extract JavaScript:

gau example.com |
grep -Ei '\.js($|\?)' |
sort -u > gau-javascript.txt

docs.title: waybackurls
docs.text:
echo example.com | waybackurls

Extract JavaScript:

echo example.com |
waybackurls |
grep -Ei '\.js($|\?)' |
sort -u > wayback-javascript.txt

docs.title: 5. Combine JavaScript Sources
docs.text:
Combine results from multiple tools.

cat \
javascript.txt \
gau-javascript.txt \
wayback-javascript.txt \
2>/dev/null |
sort -u > all-javascript.txt

Count discovered JavaScript URLs:

wc -l all-javascript.txt

docs.title: 6. Verify JavaScript Files
docs.text:
Historical sources often contain dead URLs.

Verify which resources still respond.

Using httpx:

cat all-javascript.txt |
httpx -silent > live-javascript.txt

Include status codes:

cat all-javascript.txt |
httpx -silent -status-code

Filter successful responses:

cat all-javascript.txt |
httpx -silent -mc 200 > live-javascript.txt

docs.title: 7. Download JavaScript
docs.text:
JavaScript can then be downloaded for local analysis.

Create a directory:

mkdir -p javascript

Simple loop:

while read -r url; do
    wget -q "$url" -P javascript/
done < live-javascript.txt

Be aware that different URLs can contain identical filenames.

For larger assessments, preserve the URL-to-file mapping rather than relying only on the basename.

docs.title: 8. Beautify Minified JavaScript
docs.text:
Production JavaScript is frequently minified.

Example:

function a(b){return fetch("/api/user?id="+b).then(c=>c.json())}

Beautification makes analysis significantly easier.

One option is js-beautify.

Install:

npm install -g js-beautify

Beautify:

js-beautify app.js > app-beautified.js

Process multiple files:

find javascript -type f -name "*.js" -exec js-beautify {} -o {}.beautified \;

docs.title: 9. Search for API Endpoints
docs.text:
One of the highest-value activities is identifying endpoints.

Search for common API strings:

grep -RniE '/api/|/v1/|/v2/|/v3/' javascript/

Examples might reveal:

/api/users
/api/profile
/api/admin
/api/upload
/api/export
/api/download
/api/search
/api/auth/login
/api/auth/reset
/api/internal/status

Create an endpoint candidate file:

grep -RhoE '["'\''][/][A-Za-z0-9_?&=./:%-]+["'\'']' javascript/ |
tr -d "\"'" |
sort -u > endpoint-candidates.txt

Manual validation is still necessary because JavaScript contains many strings that are not endpoints.

docs.title: 10. Search for Interesting Paths
docs.text:
Search for functionality commonly worth investigating.

grep -RniE \
'admin|internal|debug|upload|download|export|import|backup|restore|config|settings|profile|account|user|reset|password|token' \
javascript/

Interesting examples include:

/admin
/internal
/debug
/api/admin
/api/internal
/upload
/download
/export
/import
/backup
/config
/settings

docs.title: 11. Search for Parameters
docs.text:
JavaScript can reveal parameters that are difficult to discover through crawling alone.

Search for common parameter patterns:

grep -RniE \
'id|user|username|email|account|role|admin|file|filename|path|url|uri|redirect|callback|return|next|target|host|domain|query|search' \
javascript/

Examples:

userId
accountId
documentId
redirectUrl
callbackUrl
downloadUrl
filePath
returnUrl
target

These can then be added to the parameter discovery workflow.

docs.title: 12. Search for HTTP Requests
docs.text:
JavaScript reveals how the frontend communicates with the backend.

Search for:

grep -RniE \
'fetch\(|axios|XMLHttpRequest|\.ajax\(|\$\.get|\$\.post' \
javascript/

Examples:

fetch("/api/profile")

axios.post("/api/login", data)

$.ajax({
    url: "/api/admin/users"
})

These are particularly useful because they often reveal:

  • endpoint
  • HTTP method
  • request body
  • headers
  • expected response
  • authentication mechanism

docs.title: 13. Search for HTTP Methods
docs.text:
Search for explicit request methods:

grep -RniE \
'GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE|OPTIONS' \
javascript/

A JavaScript call such as:

fetch("/api/users/" + id, {
    method: "DELETE"
})

reveals both an endpoint and an operation.

docs.title: 14. Authentication Analysis
docs.text:
Search for authentication-related functionality.

grep -RniE \
'login|logout|signin|signout|authenticate|authentication|authorization|password|reset|forgot|mfa|2fa|otp|token|jwt|bearer|session' \
javascript/

Look for:

/login
/logout
/register
/reset-password
/forgot-password
/mfa
/verify
/token
/refresh

Also inspect how tokens are stored.

Search:

grep -RniE \
'localStorage|sessionStorage|document\.cookie|setItem|getItem' \
javascript/

Examples:

localStorage.setItem("token", token)

or:

sessionStorage.getItem("access_token")

These observations help map the application's authentication architecture.

docs.title: 15. JWT Usage
docs.text:
Search for JWT-related strings:

grep -RniE \
'jwt|access_token|refresh_token|bearer|authorization' \
javascript/

Look for code such as:

Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`

or:

localStorage.getItem("access_token")

Document:

Token acquisition
      ↓
Token storage
      ↓
Token transmission
      ↓
Token refresh
      ↓
Token invalidation

docs.title: 16. Client-Side Authorisation
docs.text:
JavaScript sometimes contains client-side checks controlling which functionality is displayed.

Search for:

grep -RniE \
'role|permission|isAdmin|admin|authoriz|privilege|access' \
javascript/

Examples:

if (user.role === "admin") {
    showAdminPanel();
}

or:

if (permissions.includes("DELETE_USER")) {
    enableDeleteButton();
}

Note

Client-side checks are not necessarily vulnerabilities. The important question is whether equivalent authorisation is enforced by the server.

Such findings identify functionality that should be tested directly against the backend.

docs.title: 17. Search for Administrative Functionality
docs.text:
grep -RniE \
'admin|administrator|superuser|manage|management|dashboard|console' \
javascript/

Potential discoveries:

/admin
/admin/users
/admin/settings
/management
/internal/admin
/api/admin

Do not assume an endpoint is protected simply because the normal interface hides it.

docs.title: 18. File Upload Functionality
docs.text:
Search for:

grep -RniE \
'upload|multipart|FormData|filename|fileName|content-type' \
javascript/

Example:

const data = new FormData();
data.append("file", selectedFile);

fetch("/api/upload", {
    method: "POST",
    body: data
});

This reveals:

Endpoint
HTTP method
Parameter name
Request format

which can then be investigated through the file upload testing methodology.

docs.title: 19. File Download Functionality
docs.text:
Search:

grep -RniE \
'download|filename|filepath|filePath|attachment|blob' \
javascript/

Example:

fetch("/api/download?file=" + filename)

This may identify functionality worth testing for:

  • path traversal
  • insecure direct object references
  • access control issues
  • arbitrary file retrieval

docs.title: 20. URL Processing
docs.text:
Search for functionality accepting URLs.

grep -RniE \
'url|uri|callback|webhook|redirect|returnUrl|next|target|endpoint|host' \
javascript/

Interesting examples:

callbackUrl
redirectUrl
webhookUrl
imageUrl
avatarUrl
feedUrl
targetUrl

These can indicate functionality requiring further validation for issues such as:

  • SSRF
  • open redirects
  • callback manipulation
  • webhook abuse

docs.title: 21. GraphQL
docs.text:
Search for GraphQL references:

grep -RniE \
'graphql|query{|mutation{|apollo' \
javascript/

Possible endpoint:

/graphql

or:

/api/graphql

Look for operation names:

query GetUser
mutation UpdateProfile
mutation DeleteAccount

These can reveal significant application functionality.

docs.title: 22. WebSockets
docs.text:
Search:

grep -RniE \
'WebSocket|wss://|ws://' \
javascript/

Example:

new WebSocket("wss://example.com/socket")

WebSocket functionality may expose:

  • chat
  • notifications
  • administrative events
  • real-time application state
  • internal APIs

docs.title: 23. Search for Source Maps
docs.text:
Source maps are particularly valuable during JavaScript analysis.

They commonly use:

.js.map

Example:

app.js
app.js.map

Test whether a corresponding source map exists:

curl -I https://example.com/assets/app.js.map

Search JavaScript files for:

grep -Rni 'sourceMappingURL' javascript/

Example:

//# sourceMappingURL=app.js.map

docs.title: Why Source Maps Matter
docs.text:
A minified bundle might look like:

function a(b){return fetch("/api/u/"+b)}

A source map may reconstruct original files such as:

src/
├── api/
│   ├── auth.js
│   ├── users.js
│   └── admin.js
├── components/
├── config/
└── routes/

This can significantly improve understanding of the application.

docs.title: 24. Search for Development Artifacts
docs.text:
Look for references to:

grep -RniE \
'localhost|127\.0\.0\.1|dev\.|development|staging|test\.|internal|debug' \
javascript/

Potential discoveries:

http://localhost:3000
https://dev.example.com
https://staging.example.com
https://api-internal.example.com

These may reveal additional architecture or environments.

They are not automatically in scope. Validate the authorised scope before interacting with newly discovered hosts.

docs.title: 25. Search for Hardcoded Secrets
docs.text:
JavaScript is publicly accessible to users, so secrets should generally not be embedded in frontend bundles.

Nevertheless, accidental exposures occur.

Search for common patterns:

grep -RniE \
'api[_-]?key|secret|password|passwd|token|access[_-]?key|private[_-]?key|client[_-]?secret' \
javascript/

Potential findings:

API_KEY
SECRET_KEY
ACCESS_TOKEN
CLIENT_SECRET
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID

However, keyword searches produce many false positives.

Every result should be validated manually.

docs.title: 26. Automated Secret Discovery
docs.text:
Tools such as TruffleHog and Gitleaks can assist with identifying secret-like values.

For downloaded JavaScript:

gitleaks detect --source javascript/

Results should be treated as candidates until validated.

Avoid unnecessary use of discovered credentials.

The security issue can often be demonstrated by confirming exposure and understanding the associated service without performing intrusive actions.

docs.title: 27. Cloud References
docs.text:
Search for cloud-related infrastructure.

grep -RniE \
'amazonaws\.com|s3\.|blob\.core\.windows\.net|storage\.googleapis\.com|firebaseio\.com' \
javascript/

Potential findings include:

S3 buckets
Azure Blob Storage
Google Cloud Storage
Firebase
CDN endpoints

Again, discovery does not automatically mean those resources are authorised targets.

docs.title: 28. Third-Party Services
docs.text:
Search for references to external services.

Examples include:

analytics
payment providers
authentication providers
CDNs
monitoring platforms
support platforms
error reporting

Useful searches:

grep -RniE \
'stripe|paypal|sentry|segment|firebase|auth0|okta|cloudflare|googleapis' \
javascript/

This helps map application dependencies.

docs.title: 29. Comments and Developer Notes
docs.text:
Comments can contain surprisingly useful information.

Search:

grep -RniE \
'TODO|FIXME|HACK|DEBUG|TEMP|REMOVE|DEPRECATED' \
javascript/

Examples:

// TODO remove old admin endpoint

// FIXME authentication bypass for testing

// deprecated API

Comments should be interpreted in context rather than assumed to represent exploitable behaviour.

docs.title: 30. Identify Client-Side Sources
docs.text:
For vulnerability research, it is useful to understand where attacker-controlled data enters JavaScript.

Common sources include:

location
location.href
location.search
location.hash
document.URL
document.documentURI
document.referrer
window.name
postMessage
localStorage
sessionStorage

Search:

grep -RniE \
'location\.href|location\.search|location\.hash|document\.URL|document\.documentURI|document\.referrer|window\.name|postMessage|localStorage|sessionStorage' \
javascript/

docs.title: 31. Identify Potential Client-Side Sinks
docs.text:
Potentially interesting sinks include:

innerHTML
outerHTML
document.write
document.writeln
insertAdjacentHTML
eval
Function
setTimeout
setInterval
location
location.href

Search:

grep -RniE \
'innerHTML|outerHTML|document\.write|document\.writeln|insertAdjacentHTML|eval\(|Function\(|setTimeout\(|setInterval\(' \
javascript/

A sink alone is not a vulnerability.

The important question is whether attacker-controlled input can reach the sink without appropriate validation or encoding.

Conceptually:

Source
  ↓
Transformations
  ↓
Validation / Encoding
  ↓
Sink

docs.title: 32. DOM XSS Investigation
docs.text:
For DOM-based XSS, identify flows such as:

location.search
      ↓
application processing
      ↓
innerHTML

Example:

const value = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("name");

document.getElementById("result").innerHTML = value;

The relevant task is tracing data flow from the source to the sink.

docs.title: 33. Redirect Logic
docs.text:
Search:

grep -RniE \
'location\.href|location\.assign|location\.replace|window\.open|redirect|returnUrl|next' \
javascript/

Example:

window.location.href = params.get("next");

This identifies redirect behaviour that may require further validation.

docs.title: 34. postMessage
docs.text:
Search:

grep -RniE \
'postMessage|addEventListener.*message|onmessage' \
javascript/

Review:

  • origin validation
  • message data handling
  • dangerous sinks
  • sensitive actions triggered by messages

Example:

window.addEventListener("message", function(event) {
    ...
});

Pay particular attention to whether event.origin is validated appropriately.

docs.title: 35. Framework Identification
docs.text:
JavaScript can reveal the frontend framework.

Common indicators include:

React
Angular
Vue
Next.js
Nuxt
Svelte
jQuery
Webpack
Vite

Search:

grep -RniE \
'react|angular|vue|next|nuxt|svelte|jquery|webpack|vite' \
javascript/

Framework identification can guide further testing.

docs.title: 36. Next.js
docs.text:
Next.js applications frequently expose:

/_next/static/

Look for:

/_next/static/chunks/
/_next/static/build/
/_next/data/

JavaScript bundles can contain:

  • routes
  • API paths
  • build information
  • feature names
  • internal application structure

Inspect:

/_next/static/

and JavaScript chunk references discovered through the application.

docs.title: 37. Angular
docs.text:
Angular applications commonly contain files such as:

main.js
runtime.js
polyfills.js
vendor.js

Search bundles for:

grep -RniE \
'api|endpoint|environment|production|baseUrl|apiUrl' \
javascript/

Pay particular attention to configuration embedded in environment objects.

docs.title: 38. React
docs.text:
React applications may expose:

static/js/main.*.js
static/js/*.chunk.js

Search for:

API URLs
routes
feature names
environment variables
authentication logic

Common environment variable prefix:

REACT_APP_

Search:

grep -Rni 'REACT_APP_' javascript/

docs.title: 39. Vue
docs.text:
Vue applications may contain configuration such as:

VUE_APP_API_URL
VUE_APP_BASE_URL

Search:

grep -Rni 'VUE_APP_' javascript/

docs.title: 40. JavaScript Endpoint Extraction Tools
docs.text:
Manual analysis should be complemented by automated extraction.

Useful tools include:

LinkFinder
JSFinder
SecretFinder
xnLinkFinder
Katana

Different tools use different extraction logic, so combining results can improve coverage.

docs.title: 41. LinkFinder
docs.text:
LinkFinder extracts endpoints from JavaScript.

Repository:

https://github.com/GerbenJavado/LinkFinder

Example:

python3 linkfinder.py \
-i https://example.com/assets/app.js \
-o cli

Recursive or downloaded JavaScript analysis can help identify endpoints that basic crawling misses.

docs.title: 42. SecretFinder
docs.text:
SecretFinder searches JavaScript for secret-like information.

Repository:

https://github.com/m4ll0k/SecretFinder

Example:

python3 SecretFinder.py \
-i https://example.com/assets/app.js \
-o cli

Treat results as candidates requiring manual validation.

docs.title: 43. xnLinkFinder
docs.text:
xnLinkFinder can discover endpoints and parameters from various input sources.

Example concept:

python3 xnLinkFinder.py \
-i https://example.com \
-o endpoints.txt

It can complement crawler-based discovery.

docs.title: 44. Burp Suite
docs.text:
Burp Suite is particularly useful for JavaScript analysis because it combines passive collection with manual testing.

Useful locations include:

Proxy
Target
Site map
HTTP history
Search

As the application is browsed, JavaScript files appear in the site map.

Search the site map for:

.js

Then inspect responses for:

/api/
admin
token
password
upload
download
redirect
debug
internal

docs.title: 45. Burp Search
docs.text:
Useful search strings include:

/api/
Authorization
Bearer
token
admin
password
secret
upload
download
redirect
callback
localhost
internal
debug

This is often faster than opening every JavaScript file manually.

docs.title: 46. Browser Pretty Print
docs.text:
Browser Developer Tools can beautify minified JavaScript.

Open:

Developer Tools
→ Sources
→ JavaScript file

Then select the pretty-print {} option.

This can make minified bundles significantly easier to inspect.

docs.title: 47. Application Route Discovery
docs.text:
Single-page applications frequently define routes client-side.

Search:

grep -RniE \
'route|router|path:' \
javascript/

Potential discoveries:

/dashboard
/profile
/settings
/admin
/admin/users
/reports
/internal
/debug

Routes hidden from normal navigation may still reveal useful functionality.

docs.title: 48. Feature Flags
docs.text:
Search:

grep -RniE \
'featureFlag|feature_flag|featureEnabled|enableFeature|experimental|beta' \
javascript/

Feature flags can reveal:

unfinished functionality
beta endpoints
administrative functionality
disabled application features

The backend should still enforce appropriate access controls regardless of whether a frontend feature is enabled.

docs.title: 49. Environment Configuration
docs.text:
Search:

grep -RniE \
'production|development|staging|environment|baseURL|baseUrl|apiURL|apiUrl' \
javascript/

Example:

const config = {
    apiUrl: "https://api.example.com",
    environment: "production"
};

This is useful for understanding application architecture.

docs.title: 50. Build an Endpoint Inventory
docs.text:
Do not leave discoveries scattered across terminal output.

Create an inventory.

Example:

Endpoint Method Source Parameters Authentication Notes /api/login POST auth.js username, password No Authentication /api/profile GET user.js id Bearer User profile /api/upload POST files.js file Bearer File upload /api/admin/users GET admin.js page Bearer Admin functionality /api/export POST reports.js format Bearer Export functionality

This becomes extremely valuable during later testing.

docs.title: 51. Build a Parameter Inventory
docs.text:
Similarly, record parameters.

Example:

Parameter Endpoint Source Potential Testing id /api/user user.js Access control file /api/download files.js Path handling url /api/import import.js Server-side URL processing redirect /login auth.js Redirect handling query /api/search search.js Input validation

This connects JavaScript analysis directly to later vulnerability testing.

docs.title: 52. Prioritisation
docs.text:
Not every JavaScript discovery deserves equal attention.

A practical prioritisation model is:

Authentication
      ↓
Authorisation
      ↓
Administrative Functionality
      ↓
File Operations
      ↓
Server-Side URL Processing
      ↓
User-Controlled Input
      ↓
Internal / Debug Functionality
      ↓
Client-Side Sources and Sinks
      ↓
General Application Routes

High-value keywords include:

admin
internal
debug
token
password
upload
download
import
export
callback
redirect
webhook
file
path
role
permission

docs.title: 53. Practical Recon Pipeline
docs.text:
A simple JavaScript reconnaissance pipeline might be:

katana \
-u https://example.com \
-jc \
-kf all \
-d 5 \
-o katana.txt

Extract JavaScript:

grep -Ei '\.js($|\?)' katana.txt |
sort -u > javascript.txt

Add historical sources:

gau example.com |
grep -Ei '\.js($|\?)' >> javascript.txt

echo example.com |
waybackurls |
grep -Ei '\.js($|\?)' >> javascript.txt

Deduplicate:

sort -u javascript.txt -o javascript.txt

Check live resources:

cat javascript.txt |
httpx -silent -mc 200 > live-javascript.txt

The result becomes the input for deeper JavaScript analysis.

docs.title: 54. Practical Keyword Search
docs.text:
After downloading JavaScript:

grep -RniE \
'api|admin|internal|debug|upload|download|export|import|token|password|secret|redirect|callback|webhook|graphql|socket|role|permission' \
javascript/

Then search client-side sources and sinks:

grep -RniE \
'location\.href|location\.search|location\.hash|document\.URL|document\.referrer|postMessage|innerHTML|outerHTML|document\.write|insertAdjacentHTML|eval\(' \
javascript/

This gives a useful first-pass view of the client-side attack surface.

docs.title: 55. What to Record
docs.text:
During JavaScript analysis, record at minimum:

JavaScript URL
Application route
API endpoint
HTTP method
Parameters
Authentication requirement
Interesting functionality
Potential source
Potential sink
Source map availability
Interesting configuration
Third-party dependency
Potential secret
Validation status

Good documentation prevents rediscovery later.

docs.title: Only inspecting main.js
docs.text:
Modern applications often split functionality across many chunks.

Analyse all relevant bundles.

docs.title: Ignoring historical JavaScript
docs.text:
Old JavaScript can reveal forgotten endpoints and functionality.

Include historical URL sources where appropriate.

docs.title: Treating Every Secret Pattern as a Secret
docs.text:
Strings containing words such as:

token
key
secret

are often harmless variable names.

Validate findings manually.

docs.title: Treating Every Sink as XSS
docs.text:
Finding:

innerHTML

does not prove XSS.

You must establish whether attacker-controlled data can reach the sink unsafely.

docs.title: Ignoring Source Maps
docs.text:
Source maps can transform a difficult minified bundle into understandable source code.

Always check for them.

docs.title: Ignoring API Calls
docs.text:
API requests made by JavaScript often provide more value than the visible frontend itself.

Map them carefully.

docs.title: 57. Recommended Output Structure
docs.text:
Store reconnaissance results consistently.

For example:

recon/
├── javascript/
│   ├── javascript.txt
│   ├── live-javascript.txt
│   ├── endpoint-candidates.txt
│   ├── parameters.txt
│   ├── interesting-strings.txt
│   ├── source-maps.txt
│   ├── secret-candidates.txt
│   └── downloaded/

This makes later analysis significantly easier.

docs.title: Collection
docs.text:
• Crawl application
  • Collect JavaScript URLs
  • Check historical sources
  • Deduplicate URLs
  • Verify live JavaScript files
  • Download relevant bundles

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
• Beautify minified JavaScript
  • Extract endpoints
  • Extract parameters
  • Identify HTTP methods
  • Identify authentication logic
  • Identify authorisation logic
  • Search administrative functionality
  • Search file operations
  • Search URL-processing functionality
  • Search GraphQL references
  • Search WebSocket references
  • Search source maps
  • Search development references
  • Search secret candidates
  • Search cloud references
  • Search third-party integrations
  • Search developer comments
  • Identify sources
  • Identify sinks
  • Identify client-side routes
  • Identify feature flags

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Validate endpoints
  • Validate parameters
  • Validate authentication requirements
  • Validate authorisation server-side
  • Validate source-to-sink flows
  • Validate potential secrets
  • Confirm newly discovered hosts are in scope

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Create endpoint inventory
  • Create parameter inventory
  • Record source maps
  • Record interesting JavaScript files
  • Record testing opportunities
  • Feed discoveries into later testing

docs.title: 59. JavaScript Analysis Mindset
docs.text:
The most useful way to approach JavaScript analysis is not:

Find JavaScript
      ↓
grep for secrets
      ↓
Done

Instead:

Collect JavaScript
      ↓
Understand Application Structure
      ↓
Extract Routes
      ↓
Extract APIs
      ↓
Extract Parameters
      ↓
Understand Authentication
      ↓
Understand Authorisation
      ↓
Identify Interesting Functionality
      ↓
Trace User-Controlled Data
      ↓
Identify Testing Opportunities
      ↓
Validate Manually

JavaScript should be treated as a source of information about how the application works.

docs.title: 60. Relationship With Other Testing
docs.text:
JavaScript analysis should feed directly into other sections of the assessment.

JavaScript Analysis
        │
        ├── API endpoints
        │       ↓
        │   API Security
        │
        ├── Parameters
        │       ↓
        │   Input Validation
        │
        ├── Authentication
        │       ↓
        │   Authentication Testing
        │
        ├── Roles / Permissions
        │       ↓
        │   Authorisation Testing
        │
        ├── Upload / Download
        │       ↓
        │   File Testing
        │
        ├── URL Parameters
        │       ↓
        │   SSRF / Redirect Testing
        │
        ├── Sources / Sinks
        │       ↓
        │   DOM XSS
        │
        └── GraphQL / WebSockets
                ↓
            Protocol-Specific Testing

This is why JavaScript analysis belongs early in the reconnaissance process.

docs.title: Crawl JavaScript
docs.text: katana -u https://example.com -jc -kf all -d 5

docs.title: Historical JavaScript
docs.text:
gau example.com |
