docs.title: Technology Identification
docs.text:
Technology identification is the process of determining the technologies, frameworks, libraries and infrastructure components used by a web application.

Accurate technology identification helps guide the rest of a web application security assessment. Knowing that an application uses technologies such as Next.js, Spring Boot, ASP.NET, WordPress or nginx can significantly influence which endpoints, configuration weaknesses and vulnerability classes should be investigated.

The objective is not simply to produce a list of technology names. The objective is to understand the application's technology stack and architecture well enough to make informed testing decisions.

Authorised Security Testing

Perform technology identification and subsequent security testing only against systems that are within the authorised scope of the assessment.

docs.title: Technology Identification Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow can be organised as:

Live Web Target
      |
      v
HTTP Response
      |
      +---- Headers
      |
      +---- Cookies
      |
      +---- HTML
      |
      +---- Error Pages
      |
      +---- JavaScript
      |
      +---- Static Assets
      |
      v
Automated Fingerprinting
      |
      +---- WhatWeb
      |
      +---- Wappalyzer
      |
      +---- httpx
      |
      +---- Nuclei
      |
      v
Manual Validation
      |
      v
Version Identification
      |
      v
Technology Inventory
      |
      v
Security Research
      |
      v
Controlled Validation

Multiple identification techniques should be combined because no single fingerprinting tool is completely reliable.

A useful principle is:

Technology Detected
        !=
Vulnerability Confirmed

Technology identification tells us what to investigate next. It does not prove that a vulnerability exists.

docs.title: 1. Start with the HTTP Response
docs.text:
Before running specialised tools, inspect the application's HTTP response.

A simple request can already reveal useful information:

curl -I https://example.com

Alternatively:

curl -skI https://example.com

Example:

HTTP/2 200
server: nginx/1.24.0
content-type: text/html
x-powered-by: Express
strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000

Potential technology indicators include:

Server
X-Powered-By
Via
X-AspNet-Version
X-AspNetMvc-Version
X-Generator
X-Drupal-Cache
X-Varnish
X-Cache
CF-Ray

Headers can reveal:

  • Web servers
  • Frameworks
  • Reverse proxies
  • CDNs
  • Caching infrastructure
  • Programming languages
  • Application platforms

However, headers can be removed, modified or deliberately misleading.

Treat them as evidence rather than proof.

docs.title: 2. Inspect the Full Response
docs.text:
Retrieve the complete response:

curl -ski https://example.com/

Save it if required:

curl -ski https://example.com/ > response.txt

Search interesting headers:

grep -Ei \
'server:|x-powered-by:|via:|x-aspnet|x-generator:|x-cache:|cf-ray:' \
response.txt

This provides a useful first-pass technology profile.

docs.title: 3. Cookies
docs.text:
Cookies frequently reveal application technologies.

Examples include:

PHPSESSID
JSESSIONID
ASP.NET_SessionId
connect.sid
laravel_session
csrftoken
wordpress_*

Some common associations are:

Cookie Possible Technology PHPSESSID PHP JSESSIONID Java ASP.NET_SessionId ASP.NET connect.sid Express / Node.js laravel_session Laravel csrftoken Commonly Django wordpress_* WordPress

Inspect cookies:

curl -skI https://example.com/ | grep -i set-cookie

Cookie names can be customised, so combine this information with other fingerprints.

docs.title: 4. HTML Source
docs.text:
HTML source can reveal significant information about the technology stack.

Download the page:

curl -sk https://example.com/ -o index.html

Inspect it:

less index.html

Search common indicators:

grep -Ei \
'generator|wordpress|drupal|joomla|next|react|angular|vue|webpack|vite' \
index.html

Interesting elements include:

  • Generator metadata
  • Framework-specific HTML attributes
  • JavaScript bundle names
  • CSS paths
  • Static asset paths
  • Comments
  • API URLs
  • Build identifiers
  • Framework-generated elements

docs.title: 5. Generator Metadata
docs.text:
Some applications expose technology information through HTML metadata.

For example:

<meta name="generator" content="WordPress">

or:

<meta name="generator" content="Drupal">

Search for it:

curl -sk https://example.com/ \
  | grep -i 'name="generator"'

Administrators may remove generator information, so its absence proves nothing.

docs.title: 6. Static Asset Paths
docs.text:
Static asset paths can reveal frameworks and content management systems.

Examples:

/wp-content/
/wp-includes/
/sites/default/files/
/_next/static/
/static/js/
/media/system/js/

Possible relationships include:

/wp-content/
      |
      v
   WordPress

/_next/static/
      |
      v
    Next.js

/sites/default/
      |
      v
     Drupal

Asset paths can sometimes be stronger indicators than response headers because they are required by the application's frontend.

docs.title: 7. JavaScript Analysis
docs.text:
JavaScript is one of the most valuable technology identification sources in modern applications.

Extract script references:

curl -sk https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Eo '<script[^>]+src="[^"]+"'

JavaScript can reveal:

  • Framework names
  • Build systems
  • API endpoints
  • Package names
  • Application versions
  • Internal URLs
  • Third-party integrations
  • Source maps
  • Environment information

Typical bundle names include:

main.js
app.js
runtime.js
vendor.js
webpack.js
chunk.js

Modern frameworks may generate hashed bundles such as:

main.8a2f1d.js
vendor.a991fe.js

JavaScript analysis gets its own dedicated reconnaissance note later because it can reveal much more than technology information alone.

docs.title: 8. Source Maps
docs.text:
Source maps can sometimes reveal original application source structures.

Look for:

.js.map

or references such as:

//# sourceMappingURL=app.js.map

Search downloaded JavaScript:

grep -R "sourceMappingURL" .

Source maps may expose:

  • Original filenames
  • Source directories
  • Framework structure
  • Internal comments
  • API calls
  • Application logic

Their presence does not automatically constitute a vulnerability, but they can significantly improve understanding of the application.

docs.title: 9. WhatWeb
docs.text:
WhatWeb is a useful command-line technology fingerprinting tool.

Basic usage:

whatweb https://example.com

More verbose output:

whatweb -v https://example.com

Multiple targets:

whatweb -i alive-hosts.txt

WhatWeb uses information such as:

  • HTTP headers
  • HTML patterns
  • Cookies
  • Scripts
  • Metadata
  • Known application signatures

Example output may resemble:

https://example.com
HTTPServer[nginx]
HTML5
Script
Title[Example]
X-Powered-By[Next.js]

docs.title: 10. Wappalyzer
docs.text:
Wappalyzer identifies technologies based on known fingerprints.

It can identify categories such as:

  • CMS
  • JavaScript frameworks
  • Web servers
  • Programming languages
  • Analytics
  • CDNs
  • Tag managers
  • E-commerce platforms
  • UI frameworks
  • Reverse proxies

Wappalyzer is particularly useful as a second opinion after manual inspection.

A useful workflow is:

Manual Inspection
      |
      v
WhatWeb
      |
      v
Wappalyzer
      |
      v
Compare Results
      |
      v
Manual Validation

Do not assume every detected technology is correct.

docs.title: 11. WappalyzerGo
docs.text:
WappalyzerGo provides technology detection functionality for Go applications and custom security tooling.

This can be useful when building reconnaissance pipelines where technology detection needs to be performed programmatically.

Conceptually:

HTTP Response
      |
      v
Headers + HTML
      |
      v
WappalyzerGo
      |
      v
Technology Fingerprints
      |
      v
Reconnaissance Pipeline

This is particularly useful when fingerprinting is integrated into custom asset discovery tooling.

docs.title: 12. httpx Technology Detection
docs.text:
ProjectDiscovery httpx can perform technology detection while probing live applications.

Single target:

httpx -u https://example.com -tech-detect

Multiple targets:

httpx -l alive-hosts.txt \
  -silent \
  -tech-detect

Collect more information:

httpx -l alive-hosts.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect \
  -server \
  -ip \
  -cname

Example:

https://portal.example.com [200] [Portal] [nginx,React]
https://api.example.com [403] [nginx]
https://shop.example.com [200] [Shop] [Cloudflare,WordPress]

This is particularly useful when hundreds of discovered web assets require initial classification.

docs.title: 13. Nuclei Technology Detection
docs.text:
Nuclei can complement other fingerprinting tools through technology detection templates.

For example:

nuclei -u https://example.com -tags tech

Against multiple targets:

nuclei -l alive-hosts.txt -tags tech

The results can help determine which technologies deserve further investigation.

Detection is not confirmation

A technology fingerprint is not evidence that a vulnerability exists. Any security issue must be validated independently.

docs.title: 14. Web Server Identification
docs.text:
Common web servers include:

nginx
Apache HTTP Server
Microsoft IIS
Caddy
LiteSpeed
Tomcat
Jetty

Potential indicators include:

Server: nginx
Server: Apache
Server: Microsoft-IIS/10.0

Check:

curl -skI https://example.com/ | grep -i '^server:'

Or:

httpx -u https://example.com -server

Be aware that:

Server: nginx

may identify only a reverse proxy.

The architecture could actually be:

Internet
   |
   v
nginx
   |
   +---- Node.js
   |
   +---- Java
   |
   +---- ASP.NET

Understanding the layers is important.

docs.title: 15. Reverse Proxy Identification
docs.text:
Many applications sit behind reverse proxies.

Common technologies include:

  • nginx
  • HAProxy
  • Envoy
  • Traefik
  • Apache
  • IIS
  • Cloudflare

Indicators can appear in:

Server
Via
X-Forwarded-*
X-Cache
CF-*

Architecture may resemble:

Internet
   |
   v
Cloudflare
   |
   v
nginx
   |
   v
Application

Fingerprinting only the outermost layer may therefore provide an incomplete picture.

docs.title: 16. CDN Identification
docs.text:
Content Delivery Networks can influence application behaviour and obscure underlying infrastructure.

Common providers include:

  • Cloudflare
  • Akamai
  • Fastly
  • Amazon CloudFront
  • Azure Front Door

Indicators may include:

CF-Ray
CF-Cache-Status
X-Amz-Cf-Id
X-Cache
Via
Server

DNS can also provide useful evidence:

dig example.com

or:

dnsx -d example.com -cname

docs.title: 17. WAF Identification
docs.text:
A Web Application Firewall may affect testing behaviour.

Possible indicators include:

  • Block pages
  • Specific response headers
  • Response code changes
  • Request-specific filtering
  • CDN infrastructure
  • JavaScript challenges

WAF detection can help explain why certain requests behave differently from normal application traffic.

However:

Request Blocked
      !=
Application Secure

A WAF is an additional security control and does not replace secure application design.

docs.title: 18. Error Page Fingerprinting
docs.text:
Error pages are an often overlooked technology fingerprint.

Request a resource that is unlikely to exist:

curl -ski https://example.com/this-page-should-not-exist-12345

Then inspect:

  • HTTP status code
  • Response headers
  • Response body
  • HTML structure
  • Error message wording
  • Content type
  • Response length
  • Server signatures
  • Framework-specific formatting

Conceptually:

https://example.com/does-not-exist
                 |
                 v
               404
                 |
        +--------+--------+
        |                 |
     Headers           Response
        |                 |
        v                 v
   Web Server       Error Template
                          |
                          v
                    Framework Clues

Default error pages can sometimes distinguish between technologies that otherwise expose very little information.

docs.title: Why 404 Pages Are Useful
docs.text:
Applications frequently customise their normal pages while leaving default error handling unchanged.

A request to:

/random-page-that-does-not-exist

may therefore reveal information that is not visible on:

/

Potential fingerprints include:

nginx
Apache
IIS
Flask
Django
FastAPI
aiohttp
Fiber
Gin
PHP-FPM
Laravel
Symfony
Express
Next.js
Tomcat
Spring Boot
Jetty
Ruby on Rails
Sinatra

0xdf maintains a particularly useful visual reference showing default 404 responses for these technologies:

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

It can be useful when comparing an unknown application's error response against known default pages.

docs.title: Test Multiple Random Paths
docs.text:
Do not rely on a single nonexistent URL.

Try several harmless random paths:

curl -ski https://example.com/does-not-exist-12345

curl -ski https://example.com/random-test-page-98765

curl -ski https://example.com/nonexistent/test/path

Different routing layers may handle errors differently.

For example:

/random
   |
   v
Reverse Proxy 404

while:

/api/random
   |
   v
Application Framework 404

This can reveal multiple layers of the application architecture.

docs.title: Compare Application Areas
docs.text:
Compare error handling across different application areas:

curl -ski https://example.com/random-404

curl -ski https://example.com/api/random-404

curl -ski https://example.com/admin/random-404

curl -ski https://example.com/static/random-404

You might discover:

Main Site
   |
   +---- nginx 404

API
   |
   +---- JSON framework error

Admin
   |
   +---- Application-specific error

That is useful evidence that different paths are handled by different components.

docs.title: Compare File Extensions
docs.text:
Extensions can sometimes cause requests to be processed by different backend components.

For example:

curl -ski https://example.com/does-not-exist

curl -ski https://example.com/does-not-exist.php

curl -ski https://example.com/does-not-exist.aspx

Compare:

Status Code
Headers
Response Length
Content-Type
Error Message
HTML Structure

For example, a web server may process a normal nonexistent path itself but forward a .php request to PHP-FPM.

This difference can provide additional architectural information.

docs.title: JSON Error Responses
docs.text:
APIs frequently return JSON instead of HTML.

For example:

{
  "detail": "Not Found"
}

or:

{
  "error": "Not Found",
  "status": 404
}

Inspect an API error:

curl -ski https://example.com/api/does-not-exist

Look at:

Content-Type
Response Structure
Header Behaviour
Error Wording

These characteristics may provide clues about the API framework.

docs.title: 404 Fingerprinting Workflow
docs.text:
A practical workflow is:

Request Random Path
        |
        v
Receive 404
        |
        +---- Response Headers
        |
        +---- HTML / JSON
        |
        +---- Error Text
        |
        +---- Response Length
        |
        v
Compare Known Fingerprints
        |
        v
Candidate Technology
        |
        v
Validate Using Other Evidence

Never identify a framework solely from the appearance of an error page.

Combine it with:

Headers
Cookies
HTML
JavaScript
Static Assets
WhatWeb
Wappalyzer
httpx
DNS
Framework Behaviour

docs.title: Architecture Matters
docs.text:
A default-looking 404 does not prove that the entire application uses that technology.

For example:

Internet
   |
   v
Cloudflare
   |
   v
nginx
   |
   +------------------+
   |                  |
   v                  v
Next.js             API
Frontend          Spring Boot

Different paths can therefore produce completely different error fingerprints.

Error-page fingerprinting should be treated as one component of a broader technology identification methodology.

docs.title: 19. WordPress Identification
docs.text:
Common WordPress indicators include:

/wp-admin/
/wp-login.php
/wp-content/
/wp-includes/
/wp-json/
xmlrpc.php

HTML may contain:

/wp-content/themes/
/wp-content/plugins/

Check:

curl -sk https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei 'wp-content|wp-includes|wordpress'

Technology identification can then be followed by version, theme and plugin analysis where this is relevant to the assessment.

docs.title: 20. Drupal Identification
docs.text:
Potential Drupal indicators include:

/sites/default/
/sites/all/
Drupal.settings
X-Drupal-Cache

Search:

curl -sk https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei 'drupal|sites/default|sites/all'

Headers may provide additional Drupal-specific information depending on the configuration.

docs.title: 21. Joomla Identification
docs.text:
Potential Joomla indicators include:

/administrator/
/media/system/js/
/components/
/modules/

Generator metadata may also identify Joomla.

Use multiple indicators before concluding that a technology is present.

docs.title: 22. PHP Identification
docs.text:
Potential PHP indicators include:

PHPSESSID
.php
X-Powered-By: PHP

For example:

X-Powered-By: PHP/8.x

Check:

curl -skI https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei 'php|phpsessid'

The absence of .php extensions does not mean PHP is not being used.

Modern routing frequently hides implementation details.

docs.title: 23. Laravel Identification
docs.text:
Potential Laravel indicators include:

laravel_session
XSRF-TOKEN

Other clues may appear in:

  • Error pages
  • HTML
  • JavaScript
  • Framework-specific paths
  • Response behaviour

Check cookies:

curl -skI https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei 'laravel|xsrf'

The default Laravel error page may also provide a useful fingerprint when it has not been customised.

docs.title: 24. ASP.NET Identification
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

ASP.NET_SessionId
__VIEWSTATE
__EVENTVALIDATION
X-AspNet-Version
X-AspNetMvc-Version

Search:

curl -sk https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei '__VIEWSTATE|__EVENTVALIDATION|ASP.NET'

Headers may expose:

X-Powered-By: ASP.NET

Classic ASP.NET applications can often be distinguished from newer ASP.NET Core applications through framework artefacts and application behaviour.

docs.title: 25. Java Application Identification
docs.text:
Potential Java indicators include:

JSESSIONID

Common Java application technologies include:

Tomcat
Jetty
Spring
Spring Boot
JBoss
WildFly
WebLogic
WebSphere

Check cookies:

curl -skI https://example.com/ \
  | grep -i jsessionid

Server headers, error pages and application behaviour may provide additional evidence.

docs.title: 26. Spring Boot Identification
docs.text:
Spring Boot applications may expose distinctive behaviour.

Potential indicators include:

Spring
Spring Boot
Whitelabel Error Page
JSESSIONID

Some deployments expose management functionality under paths such as:

/actuator
/actuator/health
/actuator/info

Whether those endpoints exist or are accessible depends on the application's configuration.

Technology detection should therefore lead to investigation rather than assumptions.

docs.title: 27. Node.js Identification
docs.text:
Potential indicators include:

X-Powered-By: Express
connect.sid

Check:

curl -skI https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei 'express|connect.sid'

Node.js itself may not be directly exposed through headers.

Application behaviour, JavaScript and framework fingerprints can provide additional evidence.

docs.title: 28. Express Identification
docs.text:
Express applications may expose:

X-Powered-By: Express

Check:

curl -skI https://example.com/ \
  | grep -i 'x-powered-by'

A default Express 404 can also provide a useful fingerprint.

For example, an uncustomised Express application commonly includes a short error response indicating that the requested method and path were not found.

Compare suspected error responses against the 0xdf 404 reference when useful.

docs.title: 29. Next.js Identification
docs.text:
Next.js applications have several useful fingerprints.

Potential indicators include:

/_next/static/
/_next/image
__NEXT_DATA__
Next.js
x-nextjs-cache
x-powered-by: Next.js

Search the HTML:

curl -sk https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei '_next|__NEXT_DATA__|nextjs'

Check headers:

curl -skI https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei 'next|powered'

Static resources may contain paths such as:

/_next/static/chunks/
/_next/static/css/
/_next/static/media/

A Next.js deployment may conceptually look like:

Browser
   |
   v
CDN / Reverse Proxy
   |
   v
Next.js
   |
   +---- React Frontend
   |
   +---- Server Components
   |
   +---- API Routes
   |
   +---- Middleware

Identifying Next.js should lead to further questions:

Next.js Detected
       |
       v
Can the Version Be Identified?
       |
       v
Which Features Are Used?
       |
       v
Middleware?
API Routes?
Server Components?
Image Optimisation?
       |
       v
Relevant Security Research

docs.title: 30. React Identification
docs.text:
Potential React indicators include:

  • React-specific JavaScript bundles
  • React Developer Tools artefacts
  • Build metadata
  • Framework-specific DOM behaviour
  • Next.js or other React-based frameworks

Static files may include:

static/js/main.*
static/js/runtime.*

React identification alone says little about the backend technology.

Architecture may be:

React
  |
  v
REST API
  |
  v
Java / .NET / Node.js / PHP

The frontend and backend should therefore be fingerprinted independently.

docs.title: 31. Angular Identification
docs.text:
Potential Angular indicators include:

ng-version
_nghost
_ngcontent
main.js
polyfills.js
runtime.js

Search:

curl -sk https://example.com/ \
  | grep -Ei 'ng-version|_nghost|_ngcontent'

JavaScript bundle structures can provide additional clues.

Where an Angular version is exposed, record it for later dependency and security research.

docs.title: 32. Vue Identification
docs.text:
Potential Vue indicators may appear in:

  • JavaScript bundles
  • Framework-specific DOM behaviour
  • Build artefacts
  • Vue development metadata

Automated tools such as Wappalyzer and WhatWeb can provide an initial indication, but manual validation is still useful.

docs.title: 33. API Technology Identification
docs.text:
APIs should be fingerprinted separately from the primary frontend.

Inspect:

curl -ski https://example.com/api/

Look at:

  • Content-Type
  • Error structure
  • Authentication headers
  • Server headers
  • CORS headers
  • JSON field names
  • Framework-specific errors

For example:

Frontend
   |
   +---- Next.js

API
   |
   +---- Spring Boot

or:

Frontend
   |
   +---- Angular

API
   |
   +---- ASP.NET Core

This distinction can significantly affect subsequent testing.

docs.title: 34. REST Identification
docs.text:
REST APIs commonly expose:

application/json

and resource-oriented paths such as:

/api/users
/api/orders
/api/v1/accounts

Look for:

  • API versioning
  • Authentication mechanisms
  • Documentation
  • Error structures
  • Framework-specific headers

docs.title: 35. GraphQL Identification
docs.text:
Potential GraphQL endpoints include:

/graphql
/api/graphql
/graphql/v1

GraphQL responses and error structures can provide additional framework information.

Technology identification may lead to investigation of:

  • GraphQL server implementation
  • Introspection configuration
  • Schema exposure
  • Authentication
  • Authorisation

Detailed testing belongs in the API Security notes.

docs.title: 36. SOAP Identification
docs.text:
SOAP services commonly expose XML and may provide WSDL documents.

Potential paths include:

/service
/services
?wsdl
/service?wsdl

Indicators include:

Content-Type: text/xml
SOAPAction
Envelope
WSDL

The underlying platform may be Java, .NET or another enterprise application stack.

docs.title: 37. TLS and Certificate Information
docs.text:
Certificates can also reveal infrastructure information.

Inspect:

openssl s_client \
  -connect example.com:443 \
  -servername example.com

Certificate information may reveal:

  • Subject Alternative Names
  • Related hostnames
  • Certificate authority
  • Organisation information
  • Infrastructure relationships

Certificate Transparency data can further expand this information during reconnaissance.

docs.title: 38. DNS as a Technology Source
docs.text:
DNS can reveal hosting and infrastructure technologies.

Check:

dig example.com

and:

dig CNAME example.com

Interesting CNAME values may reveal services such as:

CloudFront
Azure
Cloudflare
GitHub Pages
Netlify
Vercel
Heroku

For example:

app.example.com
      |
      v
project.vercel.app

This provides useful deployment context even if the application itself does not expose obvious technology information.

docs.title: 39. Version Identification
docs.text:
Technology names become significantly more useful when a reliable version can also be identified.

Potential version sources include:

HTTP headers
HTML
JavaScript
Static assets
Generator metadata
Error pages
Package files
API responses
Documentation
Public repositories

For example:

Technology: nginx
Version: 1.x

is more useful than:

Technology: nginx

However, version information must be validated carefully because banners can be stale or intentionally modified.

docs.title: 40. Avoid False Positives
docs.text:
Automated technology detection produces false positives.

For example:

Wappalyzer
    |
    +---- React
    +---- Next.js
    +---- nginx

should lead to:

Automated Detection
        |
        v
Manual Validation
        |
        +---- Headers
        +---- HTML
        +---- JavaScript
        +---- Cookies
        +---- Error Pages
        +---- Static Assets
        |
        v
Confirmed Technology Inventory

The stronger the conclusion, the more independent evidence should support it.

docs.title: 41. Technology Does Not Equal Vulnerability
docs.text:
One of the most important principles is:

Technology Detected
        !=
Vulnerability Confirmed

For example:

Next.js Detected
       |
       v
Determine Version
       |
       v
Research Security Advisories
       |
       v
Understand Preconditions
       |
       v
Check Application Configuration
       |
       v
Controlled Validation
       |
       v
Confirmed / Not Confirmed

Do not report a vulnerability simply because a technology appears in a vulnerability database.

docs.title: 42. Map Technologies to Security Research
docs.text:
Once a technology has been identified, research can begin.

Useful sources include:

  • Vendor security advisories
  • NVD
  • CVE records
  • GitHub Security Advisories
  • Release notes
  • Framework documentation
  • Security research publications
  • Exploit databases
  • Source code repositories

The objective is to answer:

What technology is this?
        |
        v
What version is it?
        |
        v
Is the version affected?
        |
        v
Are the vulnerable features enabled?
        |
        v
Are the attack prerequisites present?
        |
        v
Can the behaviour be safely validated?

docs.title: 43. Prioritise Technologies
docs.text:
Not every detected technology deserves the same level of investigation.

Prioritise components based on factors such as:

  • Internet exposure
  • Version
  • Authentication requirements
  • Known vulnerability history
  • Application role
  • Privilege level
  • Input processing
  • File processing
  • Network access
  • Administrative functionality

For example:

Technology Inventory
        |
        +---- Static CSS framework
        |
        +---- Analytics library
        |
        +---- Internet-facing CMS
        |
        +---- Authentication platform
        |
        +---- Server-side framework

The server-side framework and authentication platform may deserve more attention than a purely visual library.

docs.title: 44. Technology Inventory
docs.text:
Maintain an organised inventory.

For example:

Host Layer Technology Version Evidence www.example.com CDN Cloudflare Unknown Headers www.example.com Proxy nginx Unknown Server header www.example.com Frontend Next.js Unknown /_next/ api.example.com Backend Spring Boot Unknown Error response shop.example.com CMS WordPress Unknown /wp-content/

An additional column can track investigation status:

Technology Version Research Validation Next.js Unknown Pending Pending nginx Unknown Reviewed N/A WordPress Identified Pending Pending

This prevents useful fingerprinting information from being lost during a large assessment.

docs.title: 45. Practical Fingerprinting Pipeline
docs.text:
A practical workflow for multiple live hosts could start with:

httpx -l alive-hosts.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect \
  -server \
  -ip \
  -cname \
  > technology-scan.txt

Run WhatWeb:

whatweb -i alive-hosts.txt > whatweb.txt

Then manually investigate interesting targets.

The process becomes:

alive-hosts.txt
      |
      +---- httpx
      |
      +---- WhatWeb
      |
      +---- Wappalyzer
      |
      v
Candidate Technologies
      |
      v
Manual Inspection
      |
      +---- Headers
      +---- Cookies
      +---- HTML
      +---- JavaScript
      +---- Error Pages
      +---- DNS
      |
      v
Technology Inventory

docs.title: Headers
docs.text: curl -skI https://example.com/

docs.title: Full Response
docs.text: curl -ski https://example.com/

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
curl -skI https://example.com/ \
  | grep -i set-cookie

docs.title: HTML
docs.text: curl -sk https://example.com/ -o index.html

docs.title: Search HTML
docs.text:
grep -Ei \
'wordpress|drupal|joomla|next|react|angular|vue|generator' \
index.html

docs.title: WhatWeb
docs.text: whatweb https://example.com

docs.title: WhatWeb Verbose
docs.text: whatweb -v https://example.com

docs.title: httpx
docs.text:
httpx -u https://example.com \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect \
  -server

docs.title: Multiple Hosts
docs.text:
httpx -l alive-hosts.txt \
  -silent \
  -status-code \
  -title \
  -tech-detect \
  -server \
  -ip \
  -cname

docs.title: Nuclei Technology Detection
docs.text: nuclei -u https://example.com -tags tech

docs.title: Random 404
docs.text:
curl -ski \
  https://example.com/this-page-should-not-exist-12345

docs.title: API 404
docs.text:
curl -ski \
  https://example.com/api/this-page-should-not-exist-12345

docs.title: DNS
docs.text: dig example.com

docs.title: CNAME
docs.text: dig CNAME example.com

docs.title: 47. Final Workflow
docs.text:
The complete technology identification process can be summarised as:

                       Live Web Target
                              |
              +---------------+---------------+
              |               |               |
           Headers          HTML           Cookies
              |               |               |
              +---------------+---------------+
                              |
                 +------------+------------+
                 |                         |
             JavaScript                Error Pages
                 |                         |
                 +------------+------------+
                              |
                              v
                    Automated Detection
                              |
              +---------------+---------------+
              |               |               |
           WhatWeb        Wappalyzer        httpx
              |               |               |
              +---------------+---------------+
                              |
                            Nuclei
                              |
                              v
                     Manual Validation
                              |
              +---------------+---------------+
              |               |               |
          Frontend          Backend       Infrastructure
              |               |               |
              +---------------+---------------+
                              |
                              v
                     Version Identification
                              |
                              v
                      Security Research
                              |
                              v
                   Preconditions Present?
                              |
                     +--------+--------+
                     |                 |
                    No                Yes
                     |                 |
                     v                 v
                   Stop        Controlled Validation
                                       |
                                       v
                                Confirmed Finding?

Technology identification should ultimately answer more than:

What software is this application using?

The more useful questions are:

What is it?
What version is it?
Where in the architecture is it used?
How confident am I in the fingerprint?
Which functionality does it expose?
Does that technology change my testing methodology?
Are relevant security advisories applicable?
Can any suspected issue be independently validated?

That transforms technology fingerprinting from simple reconnaissance into actionable security assessment information.

docs.title: Default 404 Fingerprints
docs.text:
The following reference is particularly useful when manually comparing error responses:

0xdf - Default 404 Pages

It contains examples for technologies including nginx, Apache, IIS, Flask, Django, FastAPI, aiohttp, Fiber, Gin, PHP-FPM, Laravel, Symfony, Express, Next.js, Tomcat, Spring Boot, Jetty, Ruby on Rails and Sinatra.

docs.title: General Technology Research
docs.text:
Useful sources when researching identified technologies include:

  • Official vendor documentation
  • Vendor security advisories
  • NVD
  • CVE records
  • GitHub Security Advisories
  • Release notes
  • Project source repositories

Prefer primary vendor information when determining whether a particular version is affected by a security issue.

docs.title: Related Notes
docs.text:
• Reconnaissance Overview
  • Subdomain Enumeration
  • Content Discovery
  • Parameter Discovery
  • JavaScript Analysis
  • Web Application Testing Methodology
  • Web Application Pentesting Checklist

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Windows systems are a major part of enterprise environments and are frequently encountered during authorised penetration tests, red team assessments, security reviews, and Active Directory engagements.

This section provides a structured reference for assessing Windows hosts from the perspective of an authorised security tester.

The objective is not simply to collect commands. The objective is to understand the system, identify meaningful attack paths, evaluate security controls, validate observations, and document evidence in a repeatable way.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The Windows section focuses primarily on host-level assessment.

It covers:

  • Windows system enumeration
  • Local users and groups
  • Network configuration
  • Processes and services
  • Installed software
  • File and directory permissions
  • Registry configuration
  • Scheduled tasks
  • Windows privileges
  • PowerShell
  • Credential exposure
  • Local privilege escalation
  • Windows security controls
  • Application control
  • Logging and defensive controls

Active Directory-specific techniques are documented separately in the Active Directory section.

docs.title: Windows Assessment Flow
docs.text:
A Windows assessment should follow a structured process.

Initial Access / User Context
        |
        v
Identify Current Context
        |
        v
System Enumeration
        |
        +---- OS / architecture
        +---- hostname / domain
        +---- users / groups
        +---- privileges
        +---- network configuration
        |
        v
Security Control Enumeration
        |
        +---- Microsoft Defender
        +---- AppLocker
        +---- WDAC
        +---- PowerShell Language Mode
        +---- AMSI
        +---- ASR rules
        +---- Windows Firewall
        |
        v
Process / Service Enumeration
        |
        +---- running processes
        +---- services
        +---- service accounts
        +---- permissions
        |
        v
Application / Software Enumeration
        |
        +---- installed software
        +---- versions
        +---- development tools
        +---- management agents
        |
        v
Filesystem / Registry Review
        |
        +---- writable directories
        +---- configuration files
        +---- registry permissions
        +---- sensitive files
        |
        v
Credential Exposure Review
        |
        +---- configuration files
        +---- PowerShell history
        +---- Credential Manager
        +---- registry
        +---- application secrets
        |
        v
Privilege Escalation Analysis
        |
        +---- services
        +---- scheduled tasks
        +---- permissions
        +---- privileges
        +---- software
        +---- credential material
        |
        v
Validate Findings
        |
        v
Collect Evidence
        |
        v
Report and Remediate

docs.title: 1. Establish the Current Context
docs.text:
Before testing anything, determine the security context in which commands are executing.

Questions to answer include:

  • Which user am I?
  • Is the account local or domain-based?
  • Which groups does the user belong to?
  • Is the process elevated?
  • Which Windows privileges are assigned?
  • Is the host domain joined?
  • What integrity level is being used?

Basic commands:

whoami
whoami /user
whoami /groups
whoami /priv
hostname

PowerShell:

whoami
$env:USERNAME
$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:COMPUTERNAME

Check group membership:

whoami /groups

Look for membership in groups such as:

BUILTIN\Administrators

Do not assume that membership automatically means the current process is elevated. User Account Control can result in different access tokens being used.

docs.title: 2. Identify the Operating System
docs.text:
Determine the Windows version, architecture, build number, and patch level.

systeminfo

PowerShell:

Get-ComputerInfo

Useful properties:

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber, OsArchitecture

Alternative:

ver

Architecture:

echo %PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE%

PowerShell:

[Environment]::Is64BitOperatingSystem

The operating system version matters because security features, configuration options, and potential weaknesses vary between Windows releases and builds.

Do not report a vulnerability solely from an operating system or software version. Confirm that the relevant condition actually applies.

docs.title: 3. Determine Domain Membership
docs.text:
Determine whether the system is standalone, workgroup joined, or joined to Active Directory.

systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"Domain"

PowerShell:

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain

Environment variables can provide additional context:

$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:LOGONSERVER

Current computer:

$env:COMPUTERNAME

If the machine is domain joined, continue domain-specific investigation using the Active Directory section.

docs.title: 4. Enumerate Users
docs.text:
Local users:

net user

PowerShell:

Get-LocalUser

Inspect a particular account:

Get-LocalUser -Name "username"

Useful properties include:

Enabled
LastLogon
PasswordExpires
PasswordRequired
UserMayChangePassword

Current user:

whoami

Detailed identity information:

whoami /all

Testing should focus on identifying accounts that materially affect the security posture rather than simply producing a list of usernames.

docs.title: 5. Enumerate Local Groups
docs.text:
List local groups:

net localgroup

Administrators:

net localgroup Administrators

PowerShell:

Get-LocalGroup

Members of the local Administrators group:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators"

Pay attention to:

  • Local administrator accounts
  • Domain groups
  • Service accounts
  • Support accounts
  • Deployment accounts
  • Unexpected users
  • Nested administrative membership

Group membership should always be interpreted together with the current access token and integrity level.

docs.title: 6. Enumerate Windows Privileges
docs.text:
Windows privileges can significantly affect the security impact of an account.

whoami /priv

Examples worth reviewing include:

SeBackupPrivilege
SeRestorePrivilege
SeDebugPrivilege
SeImpersonatePrivilege
SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege
SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege
SeLoadDriverPrivilege
SeManageVolumePrivilege

The presence of a privilege does not automatically prove that privilege escalation is possible.

Record:

Privilege
State
Current integrity level
Execution context
Relevant system configuration

The practical impact should be validated separately.

docs.title: 7. Network Enumeration
docs.text:
Display network configuration:

ipconfig /all

PowerShell:

Get-NetIPConfiguration

Interfaces:

Get-NetAdapter

IP addresses:

Get-NetIPAddress

Routes:

route print

PowerShell:

Get-NetRoute

ARP cache:

arp -a

DNS cache:

ipconfig /displaydns

PowerShell:

Get-DnsClientCache

Listening ports and network connections:

netstat -ano

PowerShell:

Get-NetTCPConnection

Map a PID to a process:

Get-Process -Id 1234

Network enumeration can reveal:

  • Internal networks
  • Management networks
  • Listening services
  • Locally bound services
  • Remote connections
  • DNS infrastructure
  • Domain infrastructure
  • Proxy configuration
  • Potential pivoting opportunities

Network findings should be correlated with processes and services.

docs.title: 8. Process Enumeration
docs.text:
List running processes:

tasklist

PowerShell:

Get-Process

Detailed process information can help identify:

  • Security software
  • Management agents
  • Backup software
  • Monitoring agents
  • Database software
  • Web servers
  • Development tools
  • Administrative utilities
  • User applications

Process enumeration should be correlated with:

Services
Installed applications
Network listeners
Filesystem permissions
Execution context
Security products

A process name alone should not be treated as evidence of a vulnerability.

docs.title: 9. Service Enumeration
docs.text:
Services are one of the most important Windows assessment areas.

Basic enumeration:

sc query

PowerShell:

Get-Service

Detailed service information:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName

Important properties include:

Name
Display name
State
Start mode
Service account
Executable path
Arguments
Permissions

Potentially important relationships include:

Low-privileged user
        |
        v
Writable service resource
        |
        v
Privileged service
        |
        v
Potential privilege boundary

A service running as LocalSystem is not itself a vulnerability.

The security question is whether a lower-privileged user can influence the service configuration, executable, DLLs, configuration files, or another resource consumed by that service.

Continue with Windows Services.

docs.title: 10. Installed Software
docs.text:
Enumerate installed applications using the registry.

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher

Check 32-bit applications on 64-bit systems:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher

Review software for:

  • Unsupported versions
  • Privileged applications
  • Management agents
  • Backup clients
  • Development environments
  • Database clients
  • Remote management software
  • Security products
  • Deployment software
  • Custom enterprise applications

Do not conclude that software is vulnerable based only on a version string.

Confirm applicability before reporting a vulnerability.

docs.title: 11. Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
List scheduled tasks:

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

Useful properties include:

Task name
Principal
Trigger
Action
Executable
Arguments
Run level

When assessing scheduled tasks, review both configuration and filesystem permissions.

A task running with elevated privileges is not itself a vulnerability.

The security issue arises when an untrusted user can influence something the privileged task executes or consumes.

Assessment logic:

Scheduled Task
      |
      v
Execution Context
      |
      v
Action / Executable
      |
      v
File Permissions
      |
      v
Directory Permissions
      |
      v
Can Lower-Privileged User Influence It?

docs.title: 12. Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Windows filesystem permissions are critical during privilege escalation analysis.

Inspect permissions:

Get-Acl "C:\Path"

Example:

Get-Acl "C:\ProgramData" | Format-List

Using icacls:

icacls C:\Path

Look for inappropriate permissions granted to groups such as:

Everyone
Users
Authenticated Users
BUILTIN\Users

Permissions of interest include:

Write
Modify
FullControl

However, a writable directory alone is not necessarily a vulnerability.

The important question is:

Can a lower-privileged user modify content that will later be consumed or executed by a more privileged security context?

This distinction is important when reporting findings.

docs.title: 13. Writable Locations
docs.text:
A writable location can become security relevant when privileged software relies on files stored there.

Example permission inspection:

Get-Acl "C:\ProgramData\Example"

Using icacls:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Example"

Assessment logic:

Can the user write?
        |
        v
What can be modified?
        |
        v
Does another process consume it?
        |
        v
Which account runs that process?
        |
        v
Can execution or configuration be influenced?
        |
        v
Validate practical security impact

This prevents reporting writable folders without demonstrating why they matter.

docs.title: 14. Registry Enumeration
docs.text:
The Windows Registry contains extensive system and application configuration.

PowerShell provides registry drives:

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider Registry

Common locations include:

HKLM:\SOFTWARE
HKLM:\SYSTEM
HKCU:\Software

Registry analysis can reveal:

  • Application configuration
  • Service configuration
  • Startup entries
  • Security settings
  • Stored paths
  • User-specific configuration
  • Potential credential material

Example:

Get-ChildItem HKLM:\SOFTWARE

Registry findings should always be evaluated in context.

A writable registry key only becomes security relevant when it can influence a security-sensitive or privileged operation.

docs.title: 15. PowerShell
docs.text:
PowerShell is both an administrative platform and an important Windows security assessment interface.

Determine the PowerShell version:

$PSVersionTable

Check Language Mode:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible values include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

Language Mode should be considered together with the broader application-control architecture.

FullLanguage by itself is not automatically a vulnerability.

PowerShell can also be used for:

  • System enumeration
  • Registry inspection
  • File permission analysis
  • Network enumeration
  • Service inspection
  • Event log inspection
  • Security-control assessment
  • Evidence collection

Continue with PowerShell.

docs.title: 16. Microsoft Defender
docs.text:
Where permitted, inspect Microsoft Defender configuration.

Get-MpComputerStatus

Selected information:

Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AntivirusEnabled, AntispywareEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, BehaviorMonitorEnabled, IoavProtectionEnabled

Preferences:

Get-MpPreference

Potential assessment areas include:

Antivirus status
Real-time protection
Behaviour monitoring
Signature state
Exclusions
Cloud protection
Attack Surface Reduction
Tamper protection

During an assessment, security controls should primarily be documented and evaluated rather than disabled.

docs.title: 17. Attack Surface Reduction
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender Attack Surface Reduction rules can restrict commonly abused behaviours.

Where available:

Get-MpPreference | Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids, AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

When analysing ASR configuration, determine whether relevant rules are:

Disabled
Block
Audit
Warn

The exact representation can vary depending on Windows version and management configuration.

ASR configuration should be assessed together with:

Microsoft Defender
Application control
PowerShell restrictions
Office security controls
Endpoint management

docs.title: 18. Windows Firewall
docs.text:
Basic status:

netsh advfirewall show allprofiles

PowerShell:

Get-NetFirewallProfile

Review enabled rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True

Firewall analysis should consider:

Profile
Direction
Action
Protocol
Local port
Remote address
Application
Service

The existence of an allow rule does not automatically represent a weakness.

Consider:

Who can reach the service?
What service is listening?
Which account runs it?
Is authentication required?
Is the exposure necessary?

docs.title: 19. AppLocker
docs.text:
AppLocker can restrict executable, script, installer, packaged application, and DLL execution depending on policy configuration.

Inspect the effective policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Rule collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections

Test a specific file against the effective policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective | Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\test.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Possible policy decisions can include:

Allowed
Denied
DeniedByDefault

The effective policy matters more than simply determining that AppLocker components exist.

Review the relationship between:

Rule collection
        |
        v
Enforcement mode
        |
        v
Path / publisher / hash rules
        |
        v
User or group scope
        |
        v
Effective execution decision

docs.title: 20. Windows Defender Application Control
docs.text:
Windows Defender Application Control, or WDAC, provides application-control capabilities based on Windows Code Integrity.

Assessment should determine:

Is application control deployed?
Which policies are active?
Which files are trusted?
Which users or contexts are affected?
Is audit or enforcement mode being used?

Application-control assessment should focus on the effective security boundary rather than testing isolated executables without context.

WDAC and AppLocker are related areas of Windows application control, but they should not automatically be treated as equivalent controls.

docs.title: 21. AMSI
docs.text:
The Antimalware Scan Interface, commonly referred to as AMSI, provides an interface through which applications and services can integrate with antimalware products.

During an assessment, AMSI should be considered as part of the broader Windows security-control architecture.

Relevant context includes:

PowerShell
Script execution
Microsoft Defender
Third-party endpoint protection
Application control
Logging
Execution policy
Language Mode

The presence of AMSI does not guarantee that every script or execution path will be blocked.

Likewise, the ability to execute PowerShell does not demonstrate that AMSI is ineffective.

Security controls should be evaluated based on observed behaviour and effective policy.

docs.title: 22. Credential Exposure
docs.text:
Potential credential material may exist in:

Configuration files
Application settings
PowerShell history
Scripts
Scheduled tasks
Service configuration
Deployment files
Backup files
Registry entries
Credential Manager
User profiles

Credential searches should be targeted and authorised.

Sensitive material discovered during an assessment should be handled carefully and should not be unnecessarily copied into reports, screenshots, shell history, or shared storage.

Continue with Windows Credentials.

docs.title: 23. PowerShell History
docs.text:
PowerShell command history can sometimes expose operational information or sensitive values.

Common PSReadLine history location:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Display the history file where accessible:

Get-Content (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Potentially interesting content includes:

Administrative commands
Network locations
Application configuration
Authentication commands
Deployment operations
Hard-coded secrets

Treat any discovered credentials, tokens, or secrets as sensitive assessment evidence.

docs.title: 24. Environment Variables
docs.text:
List environment variables:

set

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Interesting variables can include:

USERNAME
USERDOMAIN
COMPUTERNAME
USERPROFILE
APPDATA
LOCALAPPDATA
TEMP
TMP
PATH
PSModulePath

Application-specific environment variables can also expose useful configuration.

Do not assume that an interesting value is sensitive simply because it appears in an environment variable. Determine what the value represents and whether it provides meaningful access.

docs.title: 25. PATH Analysis
docs.text:
Inspect the executable search path:

$env:PATH -split ";"

Check permissions on relevant directories rather than assuming a PATH entry is dangerous.

The important relationship is:

Search order
        +
Writable directory
        +
Privileged execution
        =
Potential security impact

All conditions must be investigated.

docs.title: 26. Interesting Directories
docs.text:
Common locations worth understanding include:

C:\Users
C:\ProgramData
C:\Program Files
C:\Program Files (x86)
C:\Windows
C:\Windows\Temp
C:\Temp

User-specific locations include:

%USERPROFILE%
%APPDATA%
%LOCALAPPDATA%
%TEMP%

These locations can contain:

  • Application configuration
  • User configuration
  • Logs
  • Temporary files
  • Scripts
  • Deployment artifacts
  • Service resources
  • Cached information

Do not recursively search an entire filesystem without considering scope, performance, privacy, and operational impact.

docs.title: 27. Startup and Persistence Locations
docs.text:
Windows contains several mechanisms that can cause software to execute automatically.

Assessment areas can include:

Services
Scheduled tasks
Startup folders
Registry Run keys
Logon scripts
Application-specific startup mechanisms

Examples of common Run key locations include:

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

These locations are not inherently vulnerable.

The important questions are:

What executes?
Who configured it?
Which account executes it?
Who can modify the referenced resource?
Is the behaviour expected?

docs.title: 28. Security Tooling
docs.text: Several tools can assist with authorised Windows security assessment.

docs.title: Sysinternals
docs.text:
Microsoft Sysinternals contains utilities for Windows troubleshooting, administration, and security analysis.

Useful tools include:

Autoruns
Process Explorer
Process Monitor
AccessChk
TCPView
Sigcheck
Strings
PsExec

Microsoft Sysinternals

docs.title: Seatbelt
docs.text:
Seatbelt performs Windows host security enumeration.

Typical areas include:

System information
Security products
Processes
Services
Users
Interesting files
Windows configuration

Seatbelt

Use automated enumeration as a supplement to manual validation rather than treating every result as a finding.

docs.title: SharpUp
docs.text:
SharpUp assists with identifying potential Windows privilege escalation conditions.

SharpUp

Findings should still be manually verified.

docs.title: PrivescCheck
docs.text:
PrivescCheck is a PowerShell-based Windows privilege escalation enumeration project.

PrivescCheck

docs.title: WinPEAS
docs.text:
WinPEAS provides extensive Windows privilege escalation enumeration.

PEASS-ng

Large automated enumeration tools can generate substantial output.

Use targeted execution where possible and manually validate significant findings.

docs.title: 29. Manual and Automated Enumeration
docs.text:
A strong assessment combines both approaches.

Manual Enumeration
        |
        +---- Understand environment
        +---- Establish security context
        +---- Form hypotheses
        |
        v
Automated Enumeration
        |
        +---- Increase coverage
        +---- Identify overlooked configuration
        +---- Prioritise candidates
        |
        v
Manual Validation
        |
        +---- Confirm permissions
        +---- Confirm execution context
        +---- Confirm relationships
        +---- Confirm practical impact
        |
        v
Evidence
        |
        v
Reporting

Automated tool output should not be copied directly into a penetration test report without validation.

docs.title: 30. Privilege Escalation Mindset
docs.text:
Privilege escalation should be treated as relationship analysis.

For example:

Low-privileged user
        |
        v
Writable resource
        |
        v
Privileged process uses resource
        |
        v
User can influence behaviour
        |
        v
Privilege boundary crossed

The existence of only one component does not necessarily create a vulnerability.

A better assessment asks:

What can I control?
        |
        v
Who consumes it?
        |
        v
Under which security context?
        |
        v
Can my control influence privileged behaviour?
        |
        v
Can the condition be safely validated?

Continue with Windows Privilege Escalation.

docs.title: 31. Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For each potentially significant finding, record:

Host
User
Integrity level
Relevant groups
Relevant privileges
Object or resource
Permissions
Security control state
Command used
Observed result
Security impact

Prefer reproducible evidence.

Example:

Observation:
A standard user has Modify permission on a directory.

Context:
The directory contains an executable used by a privileged Windows service.

Validation:
The service account and executable path were independently confirmed.

Impact:
The writable resource may allow the lower-privileged user to influence
execution performed by a higher-privileged service.

Recommendation:
Restrict write permissions and ensure privileged service resources can only
be modified by trusted administrative principals.

docs.title: 32. Reporting
docs.text:
A useful Windows finding should explain the relationship between configuration and security impact.

Avoid reporting only:

C:\Example is writable.

Prefer:

A standard user has Modify permission on C:\Example. The directory contains
a binary executed by a service running under a privileged account. This
creates a trust-boundary issue because an unprivileged user can influence a
resource consumed by a higher-privileged process.

The second statement explains why the configuration matters.

A good finding generally contains:

Observation
        |
        v
Affected Resource
        |
        v
Security Context
        |
        v
Attack Preconditions
        |
        v
Validated Impact
        |
        v
Recommendation

docs.title: 33. Remediation Principles
docs.text:
Common Windows hardening principles include:

  • Apply least privilege.
  • Restrict administrative membership.
  • Protect privileged service resources.
  • Harden filesystem ACLs.
  • Harden registry ACLs.
  • Protect credential material.
  • Remove unnecessary software.
  • Patch supported software.
  • Restrict unnecessary services.
  • Configure host firewall rules.
  • Deploy endpoint protection.
  • Apply application control where appropriate.
  • Enable appropriate PowerShell logging.
  • Monitor privileged execution.
  • Review scheduled tasks.
  • Protect administrative interfaces.
  • Centralise security telemetry.

Remediation should be proportional to the demonstrated risk.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• Identify current user
  • Identify user SID
  • Identify groups
  • Identify privileges
  • Determine integrity level
  • Determine domain membership

docs.title: System
docs.text:
• Identify Windows version
  • Identify architecture
  • Identify build
  • Review patch state
  • Identify installed software

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
• Enumerate interfaces
  • Enumerate IP addresses
  • Enumerate routes
  • Review DNS configuration
  • Review ARP cache where relevant
  • Enumerate listeners
  • Review active connections
  • Review firewall configuration

docs.title: Users and Groups
docs.text:
• Enumerate local users
  • Enumerate local groups
  • Review Administrators membership
  • Identify service accounts
  • Identify unexpected privileged accounts

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
• Enumerate processes
  • Identify privileged processes
  • Identify security products
  • Identify management software
  • Correlate processes with network listeners

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• Enumerate services
  • Review service accounts
  • Review executable paths
  • Review service permissions
  • Review associated filesystem permissions
  • Identify privileged service relationships

docs.title: Filesystem
docs.text:
• Identify interesting directories
  • Review writable locations
  • Review sensitive files
  • Review application configuration
  • Validate ACL findings

docs.title: Registry
docs.text:
• Review relevant application keys
  • Review startup configuration
  • Review service configuration
  • Review permissions where relevant
  • Identify sensitive configuration

docs.title: Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
• Enumerate scheduled tasks
  • Review principals
  • Review actions
  • Review referenced files
  • Review permissions
  • Determine execution context

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
• Review configuration files
  • Review PowerShell history
  • Review Credential Manager where authorised
  • Review application configuration
  • Review scripts
  • Review deployment artifacts
  • Protect collected evidence

docs.title: Security Controls
docs.text:
• Review Microsoft Defender
  • Review ASR configuration
  • Review Windows Firewall
  • Review AppLocker
  • Review WDAC where deployed
  • Review PowerShell Language Mode
  • Consider AMSI context
  • Review relevant logging controls

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Manually verify automated findings
  • Determine affected security boundary
  • Confirm practical impact
  • Collect reproducible evidence
  • Avoid unnecessary system modification
  • Document remediation

docs.title: 35. Windows Documentation Flow
docs.text:
Use the Windows pages in approximately this order during an assessment:

Windows Overview
        |
        v
Windows Enumeration
        |
        +-----------------------+
        |                       |
        v                       v
   PowerShell                Services
        |                       |
        +-----------+-----------+
                    |
                    v
               Credentials
                    |
                    v
          Privilege Escalation
                    |
                    v
             Validate Findings
                    |
                    v
                Reporting

The pages are intentionally connected.

Enumeration establishes what exists and the current security context.

PowerShell provides an important administrative and assessment interface.

Services focuses on privileged service relationships, permissions, executable paths, and service accounts.

Credentials focuses on sensitive authentication material and secret exposure.

Privilege Escalation brings evidence from the other areas together to determine whether a security boundary can actually be crossed.

docs.title: Recommended Reading Order
docs.text:
1. Windows Enumeration
  2. PowerShell
  3. Windows Services
  4. Windows Credentials
  5. Windows Privilege Escalation

For domain-joined systems, also use:

  • Active Directory
  • Active Directory Enumeration

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Microsoft Windows documentation
  • Microsoft Windows security documentation
  • Microsoft Sysinternals
  • Microsoft Defender for Endpoint documentation
  • AppLocker documentation
  • Windows application control documentation
  • MITRE ATT&CK
  • Seatbelt
  • SharpUp
  • PrivescCheck
