docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
PowerShell is one of the most important administrative, automation, investigation, and security assessment interfaces available on Windows.

During an authorised security assessment, PowerShell can be used to inspect:

  • System information
  • Users and groups
  • Processes
  • Services
  • Network configuration
  • Filesystem permissions
  • Registry configuration
  • Scheduled tasks
  • Event logs
  • Microsoft Defender
  • Attack Surface Reduction rules
  • AppLocker
  • PowerShell security controls
  • Credential exposure
  • Active Directory environments

PowerShell should not be viewed only as an execution mechanism. It is also an extremely capable native interface for understanding Windows security configuration.

docs.title: 1. PowerShell Assessment Flow
docs.text:
A useful PowerShell assessment workflow is:

PowerShell
    |
    v
Version / Edition
    |
    v
Current Security Context
    |
    +---- User
    +---- Groups
    +---- Privileges
    +---- Integrity
    |
    v
PowerShell Security Context
    |
    +---- Language Mode
    +---- Execution Policy
    +---- Logging
    +---- AMSI context
    |
    v
Windows Security Controls
    |
    +---- Defender
    +---- ASR
    +---- AppLocker
    +---- WDAC
    |
    v
Host Enumeration
    |
    +---- System
    +---- Network
    +---- Processes
    +---- Services
    +---- Registry
    +---- Filesystem
    |
    v
Validate Findings
    |
    v
Evidence
    |
    v
Reporting

The objective is to determine the effective security configuration rather than drawing conclusions from individual settings.

docs.title: 2. PowerShell Version
docs.text:
Display PowerShell information:

$PSVersionTable

Important properties can include:

PSVersion
PSEdition
GitCommitId
OS
Platform
PSCompatibleVersions
WSManStackVersion
SerializationVersion

Focused output:

$PSVersionTable.PSVersion

Edition:

$PSVersionTable.PSEdition

PowerShell environments may include:

Windows PowerShell 5.1
PowerShell 7+

PowerShell 7 is a separate modern product based on .NET, while Windows PowerShell 5.1 remains integrated into many supported Windows environments.

Do not assume that the presence of one version means another version is unavailable.

docs.title: 3. PowerShell Executables
docs.text:
Windows PowerShell is commonly located at:

C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe

The v1.0 directory name is historical and does not mean the installed PowerShell version is version 1.

PowerShell 7 commonly uses:

C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe

Locate PowerShell:

Get-Command powershell.exe

PowerShell 7:

Get-Command pwsh.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Executable path of the current process:

(Get-Process -Id $PID).Path

docs.title: 4. Current User
docs.text:
Determine the current identity:

whoami

Environment variables:

$env:USERNAME
$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:COMPUTERNAME

Windows identity:

[System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()

Name only:

[System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Name

SID:

[System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().User.Value

docs.title: 5. Groups
docs.text:
Command-line enumeration:

whoami /groups

Windows identity:

[System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Groups

Local groups:

Get-LocalGroup

Administrators:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators"

Group membership should be interpreted together with the current token and integrity level.

docs.title: 6. Determine Whether the Process Is Administrative
docs.text:
$identity = [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
$principal = New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal($identity)
$principal.IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)

Possible results:

True
False

This is useful for distinguishing an administrative process from a standard-user process.

Local Administrators group membership alone does not necessarily mean the current process is elevated because User Account Control can provide filtered tokens.

docs.title: 7. Windows Privileges
docs.text:
whoami /priv

Privileges worth understanding include:

SeBackupPrivilege
SeRestorePrivilege
SeDebugPrivilege
SeImpersonatePrivilege
SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege
SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege
SeLoadDriverPrivilege
SeManageVolumePrivilege

A privilege being present does not automatically mean it can be used to cross a security boundary.

See Windows Privilege Escalation.

docs.title: 8. Environment Variables
docs.text:
Enumerate all environment variables:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Useful individual variables:

$env:USERNAME
$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:COMPUTERNAME
$env:USERPROFILE
$env:APPDATA
$env:LOCALAPPDATA
$env:TEMP
$env:TMP
$env:PATH
$env:PSModulePath

PATH entries:

$env:PATH -split ';'

Environment variables can reveal:

  • Application paths
  • Proxy configuration
  • Development environments
  • Temporary directories
  • Management tooling
  • Custom enterprise configuration

Treat secrets discovered in environment variables as sensitive evidence.

docs.title: 9. PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
Determine the current Language Mode:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible values include:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

docs.title: FullLanguage
docs.text:
FullLanguage provides access to the complete PowerShell language subject to the permissions of the current process and other security controls.

Example:

FullLanguage

This is normal on many Windows systems.

It should not automatically be reported as a vulnerability.

docs.title: ConstrainedLanguage
docs.text:
ConstrainedLanguage restricts various PowerShell language capabilities.

Example:

ConstrainedLanguage

Constrained Language Mode is particularly relevant when it is applied as part of a broader application-control architecture.

The assessment question should therefore be:

What PowerShell restrictions are expected?
        |
        v
What application-control policy exists?
        |
        v
What Language Mode is effective?
        |
        v
Does observed behaviour match the security design?

docs.title: 10. Language Mode and Application Control
docs.text:
Language Mode should not be evaluated in isolation.

Consider:

PowerShell Language Mode
        |
        +---- AppLocker
        |
        +---- WDAC
        |
        +---- Endpoint security
        |
        +---- User privileges
        |
        +---- Script policy
        |
        +---- Logging

For hardened endpoints, organisations may use application control to restrict scripting environments and executable content.

A finding should explain the intended control objective and the demonstrated security impact.

docs.title: 11. Execution Policy
docs.text:
Display the effective execution policy:

Get-ExecutionPolicy

All scopes:

Get-ExecutionPolicy -List

Possible policies include:

Restricted
AllSigned
RemoteSigned
Unrestricted
Bypass
Undefined

Execution Policy is primarily intended to help control PowerShell script execution behaviour.

It should not be treated as a strong standalone security boundary.

For example:

ExecutionPolicy = RemoteSigned

does not by itself establish a vulnerability.

docs.title: 12. PowerShell Profiles
docs.text:
PowerShell profiles can execute commands when PowerShell sessions start.

Display profile information:

$PROFILE

All profile paths:

$PROFILE | Format-List *

Common profile scopes include:

CurrentUserCurrentHost
CurrentUserAllHosts
AllUsersCurrentHost
AllUsersAllHosts

Check whether the current profile exists:

Test-Path $PROFILE

Display it:

Get-Content $PROFILE -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Profile security depends heavily on permissions and execution context.

The important relationship is:

Profile executes automatically
        +
Higher-privileged user/process uses profile
        +
Lower-privileged user can modify profile
        =
Potential security issue

Do not treat the existence of a profile as a vulnerability.

docs.title: 13. PowerShell Modules
docs.text:
List available modules:

Get-Module -ListAvailable

Currently imported modules:

Get-Module

Module paths:

$env:PSModulePath -split ';'

Module information:

Get-Module -ListAvailable |
    Select-Object Name, Version, ModuleBase

Modules can provide information about:

  • Administrative tooling
  • Cloud tooling
  • Security software
  • Enterprise management
  • Active Directory management
  • Custom applications

docs.title: 14. Commands
docs.text:
List commands:

Get-Command

Search by name:

Get-Command *Firewall*

Search for AppLocker commands:

Get-Command *AppLocker*

Defender commands:

Get-Command *Mp*

Determine where a command originates:

Get-Command Get-MpComputerStatus | Format-List *

docs.title: 15. Command History
docs.text:
Session history:

Get-History

Aliases:

h

PSReadLine persistent history location:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Read persistent history:

Get-Content (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Common location:

%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt

History may reveal:

Administrative operations
Application configuration
Network shares
Remote systems
Deployment commands
Authentication operations

Any discovered credentials or tokens should be treated as sensitive evidence.

docs.title: 16. Clear Distinction Between History Types
docs.text:
PowerShell has different history concepts.

Get-History normally displays history associated with the current session:

Get-History

PSReadLine can persist command history to disk:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Therefore:

Get-History

and:

ConsoleHost_history.txt

should not be assumed to contain identical data.

docs.title: 17. System Information
docs.text:
PowerShell provides several ways to obtain system information.

Get-ComputerInfo

Focused:

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber, OsArchitecture

CIM:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem

Computer information:

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem

Useful focused output:

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem |
    Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain, Manufacturer, Model

docs.title: 18. Domain Membership
docs.text:
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem |
    Select-Object Name, Domain, PartOfDomain

Additional context:

$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:LOGONSERVER

If the host is domain joined, continue with Active Directory Enumeration.

docs.title: 19. Local Users
docs.text:
Get-LocalUser

Focused:

Get-LocalUser |
    Select-Object Name, Enabled, LastLogon, PasswordRequired

Specific account:

Get-LocalUser -Name "Administrator"

docs.title: 20. Local Groups
docs.text:
Get-LocalGroup

Administrators:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators"

Remote Desktop users:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Remote Desktop Users" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Remote Management users:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Remote Management Users" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: 21. Processes
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-Process

Focused:

Get-Process |
    Select-Object Id, ProcessName, Path

A process path may not be accessible from every security context.

CIM command-line information:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
    Select-Object ProcessId, Name, ExecutablePath, CommandLine

Search:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
    Where-Object Name -Like "*java*" |
    Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CommandLine

Process command lines can expose sensitive information. Handle output carefully.

docs.title: 22. Services
docs.text:
Get-Service

CIM provides additional information:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service

Useful output:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName

Running services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object State -eq "Running" |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

LocalSystem services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object StartName -eq "LocalSystem" |
    Select-Object Name, State, PathName

Continue with Windows Services.

docs.title: 23. Service Path Correlation
docs.text:
Suppose a writable directory is identified:

C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder

Determine whether services reference it:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object PathName -Match ([regex]::Escape($folder)) |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, State, PathName

This helps establish whether a writable location has a privileged consumer.

docs.title: 24. Network Configuration
docs.text:
Get-NetIPConfiguration

Adapters:

Get-NetAdapter

Addresses:

Get-NetIPAddress

IPv4:

Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4

Routes:

Get-NetRoute

IPv4 routes:

Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4

DNS:

Get-DnsClientServerAddress

DNS cache:

Get-DnsClientCache

docs.title: 25. TCP Connections
docs.text:
All TCP connections:

Get-NetTCPConnection

Listening:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

Established:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Established

Useful fields:

Get-NetTCPConnection |
    Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, State, OwningProcess

Map listeners to processes:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        LocalAddress = $_.LocalAddress
        LocalPort = $_.LocalPort
        PID = $_.OwningProcess
        Process = (Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).ProcessName
    }
}

docs.title: 26. Test Network Connectivity
docs.text:
PowerShell provides Test-NetConnection for connectivity diagnostics.

Test a host:

Test-NetConnection example.com

Test a TCP port:

Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443

Focused result:

Test-NetConnection example.com -Port 443 |
    Select-Object ComputerName, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, TcpTestSucceeded

This is useful for validating whether a particular TCP destination is reachable.

docs.title: 27. DNS Resolution
docs.text:
Resolve-DnsName example.com

Specific type:

Resolve-DnsName example.com -Type A

Nameserver records:

Resolve-DnsName example.com -Type NS

Use only domains and infrastructure within the authorised assessment scope.

docs.title: 28. Web Requests
docs.text:
PowerShell can make HTTP and HTTPS requests.

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://example.com"

Store the response:

$response = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://example.com"
$response.StatusCode

Headers:

$response.Headers

PowerShell 7 also provides modern web-request behaviour through the same cmdlet family.

Web requests should only target systems permitted by the assessment scope.

docs.title: 29. Files
docs.text:
List files:

Get-ChildItem

Recursive:

Get-ChildItem -Recurse

Files only:

Get-ChildItem -File

Directories only:

Get-ChildItem -Directory

Hidden items:

Get-ChildItem -Force

Avoid unnecessarily recursive enumeration of entire drives.

Target directories relevant to the assessment.

docs.title: 30. File Content
docs.text:
Read:

Get-Content "C:\Path\file.txt"

First ten lines:

Get-Content "C:\Path\file.txt" -TotalCount 10

Search:

Select-String -Path "C:\Path\file.txt" -Pattern "example"

Recursive targeted search:

Get-ChildItem "C:\Application" -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern "example" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Be careful when searching potentially sensitive data.

docs.title: 31. File Metadata
docs.text:
Get-Item "C:\Path\file.exe"

Useful properties:

Get-Item "C:\Path\file.exe" |
    Select-Object Name, FullName, Length, CreationTime, LastWriteTime

File version:

(Get-Item "C:\Path\file.exe").VersionInfo

Focused:

(Get-Item "C:\Path\file.exe").VersionInfo |
    Select-Object FileVersion, ProductVersion, CompanyName, ProductName

docs.title: 32. File Hashes
docs.text:
Calculate a SHA-256 hash:

Get-FileHash "C:\Path\file.exe" -Algorithm SHA256

Other supported algorithms can be specified where required.

Hashes are useful for:

  • Evidence
  • File comparison
  • Integrity verification
  • Malware triage
  • Application-control analysis

docs.title: 33. Digital Signatures
docs.text:
PowerShell can inspect Authenticode signatures:

Get-AuthenticodeSignature "C:\Path\file.exe"

Focused:

Get-AuthenticodeSignature "C:\Path\file.exe" |
    Select-Object Status, StatusMessage, SignerCertificate

Signature status can help during application and binary assessment.

A valid signature does not automatically mean software is safe.

docs.title: 34. Filesystem Permissions
docs.text:
Get-Acl "C:\Path"

Useful output:

Get-Acl "C:\Path" |
    Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Detailed ACL:

(Get-Acl "C:\Path").Access |
    Format-Table IdentityReference, FileSystemRights, AccessControlType, IsInherited

Potentially important broad principals include:

Everyone
BUILTIN\Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Users

Potentially important rights include:

Write
Modify
FullControl

A permission must be correlated with the resource's security relevance.

docs.title: 35. Controlled Write Test
docs.text:
A non-destructive temporary-file test can confirm whether the current user can write to a candidate directory.

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID-$(Get-Random).tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Host "[+] Write access confirmed: $file"
}
catch {
    Write-Host "[-] Write access denied: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}
finally {
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

This validates only write access.

It does not establish privilege escalation.

docs.title: 36. Registry
docs.text:
PowerShell exposes the Registry through providers.

Registry drives:

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider Registry

Common locations:

HKLM:\SOFTWARE
HKLM:\SYSTEM
HKCU:\Software

List:

Get-ChildItem HKLM:\SOFTWARE

Read values:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion"

Specific value:

Get-ItemPropertyValue "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion" -Name "ProgramFilesDir"

docs.title: 37. Registry Permissions
docs.text:
Get-Acl "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Vendor"

Access:

(Get-Acl "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Vendor").Access

Registry permissions become especially important when a key controls:

Service configuration
Startup behaviour
Privileged application settings
Executable paths
Security configuration

docs.title: 38. Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-ScheduledTask

Basic:

Get-ScheduledTask |
    Select-Object TaskPath, TaskName, State

Useful security-oriented summary:

Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        TaskName = $_.TaskName
        TaskPath = $_.TaskPath
        User = $_.Principal.UserId
        RunLevel = $_.Principal.RunLevel
        Actions = ($_.Actions | ForEach-Object {
            "$($_.Execute) $($_.Arguments)"
        }) -join "; "
    }
}

Investigate privileged tasks that reference user-modifiable resources.

docs.title: 39. Startup Configuration
docs.text:
CIM:

Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand |
    Select-Object Name, Command, Location, User

Current-user Run key:

Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Machine Run key:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Automatic execution is not inherently vulnerable.

Determine who controls the referenced resources and under which context they execute.

docs.title: 40. Installed Software
docs.text:
64-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

32-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

Current user:

Get-ItemProperty HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

Avoid using Win32_Product as a routine software-enumeration method because querying it can have undesirable Windows Installer side effects on some systems.

docs.title: 41. Hotfixes
docs.text:
Get-HotFix

Alternative:

Get-CimInstance Win32_QuickFixEngineering

Patch analysis should consider cumulative updates and supersedence.

Do not treat a missing KB identifier as definitive evidence of vulnerability without verifying the actual Windows build and applicable security update.

docs.title: 42. Microsoft Defender Status
docs.text:
Where Defender cmdlets are available:

Get-MpComputerStatus

Focused:

Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AntivirusEnabled, AntispywareEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, BehaviorMonitorEnabled, IoavProtectionEnabled

Additional information:

Get-MpComputerStatus |
    Select-Object AMServiceEnabled, AMProductVersion, AMEngineVersion, AntivirusSignatureVersion, AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated

Defender status should be documented rather than altered during normal enumeration.

docs.title: 43. Defender Preferences
docs.text:
Get-MpPreference

Potentially relevant areas include:

Exclusions
Cloud protection
Attack Surface Reduction
Controlled Folder Access
Network protection
Scan configuration

The exact settings available depend on Windows version and Defender configuration.

docs.title: 44. Defender Exclusions
docs.text:
Where permissions allow:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object ExclusionPath, ExclusionProcess, ExclusionExtension

Exclusions may be legitimate.

Potential security significance depends on:

Scope of exclusion
        |
        v
Who can write there?
        |
        v
What executes there?
        |
        v
What protection is removed?

Do not modify exclusions during routine assessment.

docs.title: 45. Attack Surface Reduction Rules
docs.text:
Retrieve ASR configuration:

Get-MpPreference |
    Select-Object AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids, AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions

Display pairs:

$p = Get-MpPreference

for ($i = 0; $i -lt $p.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids.Count; $i++) {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        RuleId = $p.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids[$i]
        Action = $p.AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions[$i]
    }
}

Interpret action values according to Microsoft documentation and the management configuration used by the organisation.

ASR should be evaluated as part of the complete endpoint-security architecture.

docs.title: 46. Windows Firewall
docs.text:
Profiles:

Get-NetFirewallProfile

Enabled rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True

Allow rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True -Action Allow

Block rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True -Action Block

Useful summary:

Get-NetFirewallProfile |
    Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction, DefaultOutboundAction

Firewall configuration should be correlated with actual listeners and network reachability.

docs.title: 47. AppLocker
docs.text:
Retrieve effective AppLocker policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Rule collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections

Summary:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType, EnforcementMode

Potential collections include:

Exe
Msi
Script
Dll
Appx

Not every environment configures every collection.

docs.title: 48. Inspect AppLocker Rules
docs.text:
(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    ForEach-Object {
        $_.Rules
    }

Rules can be based on:

Path
Publisher
Hash

The existence of an allow rule does not automatically mean it creates a weakness.

For path rules, determine whether the current user can write into an allowed path.

docs.title: 49. Test AppLocker Policy
docs.text:
Test a particular file:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\test.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Detailed output:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\test.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME" |
    Format-List FilePath, PolicyDecision, MatchingRule

Testing should use the exact:

User
Path
File type
Effective policy

that applies to the assessment scenario.

docs.title: 50. AppLocker and Writable Paths
docs.text:
A useful assessment relationship is:

AppLocker Allow Rule
        |
        v
Allowed Directory
        |
        v
Can Standard User Write?
        |
        +--> No
        |     |
        |     v
        |  Likely expected protection
        |
        +--> Yes
              |
              v
       What content is allowed?
              |
              v
       Can security boundary be crossed?

A broad allow rule should not automatically be labelled a bypass.

Validate the effective permissions and execution behaviour.

docs.title: 51. WDAC
docs.text:
Windows Defender Application Control uses Code Integrity policies to control trusted code.

Assessment questions include:

Are policies deployed?
Are they enforced or audited?
Which trust mechanisms are used?
Which binaries or scripts are permitted?
Are supplemental policies present?
What do Code Integrity events show?

Do not conclude that WDAC is absent merely because one PowerShell query or WMI/CIM class is unavailable.

Different Windows versions and deployment methods can expose configuration differently.

docs.title: 52. Code Integrity Logs
docs.text:
List relevant logs:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *CodeIntegrity* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Common operational log:

Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational

Recent events:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational" -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Focused:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational" -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, LevelDisplayName, Message

These events can provide evidence of application-control enforcement.

docs.title: 53. AppLocker Logs
docs.text:
List AppLocker logs:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *AppLocker* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Relevant channels may include:

Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/Packaged app-Deployment
Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/Packaged app-Execution

Example:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL" -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: 54. AMSI
docs.text:
The Antimalware Scan Interface provides an integration point between applications and antimalware products.

AMSI is used by multiple Windows scripting and application environments.

For security assessment purposes, AMSI should be considered alongside:

Microsoft Defender
Third-party endpoint protection
PowerShell
Script hosts
Application control
Logging

Avoid reducing AMSI assessment to:

Command executed = AMSI disabled

or:

Command blocked = AMSI enabled

Observed execution can be affected by several different controls.

docs.title: 55. PowerShell Logging
docs.text:
PowerShell can provide multiple logging mechanisms.

Important examples include:

Script Block Logging
Module Logging
Transcription
PowerShell Operational logging

Relevant policy path:

HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell

Inspect:

Get-ChildItem "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Current-user policy:

Get-ChildItem "HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.title: 56. Script Block Logging
docs.text:
A commonly relevant policy path is:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging

Inspect:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Relevant configuration can include:

EnableScriptBlockLogging

Logging behaviour should be verified through effective configuration and event telemetry rather than relying only on a registry value.

docs.title: 57. Module Logging
docs.text:
Relevant policy path:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging

Inspect:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Module Logging can provide visibility into PowerShell module and command activity depending on configuration.

docs.title: 58. PowerShell Transcription
docs.text:
Relevant policy path:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription

Inspect:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Potential configuration can include:

EnableTranscripting
EnableInvocationHeader
OutputDirectory

Transcripts may contain sensitive administrative information and should themselves be protected.

docs.title: 59. PowerShell Operational Event Log
docs.text:
Inspect recent PowerShell events:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Focused:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, LevelDisplayName, Message

The amount of information available depends on logging configuration.

docs.title: 60. Event Log Discovery
docs.text:
List logs:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *

Search:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *PowerShell*

AppLocker:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *AppLocker*

Code Integrity:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *CodeIntegrity*

Defender:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *Defender*

docs.title: 61. Microsoft Defender Event Log
docs.text:
A commonly relevant channel is:

Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational

Inspect:

Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational" -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

This can provide useful context about:

Detections
Configuration
Protection events
Operational changes

Access depends on the current security context.

docs.title: 62. Security Event Log
docs.text:
Recent events:

Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -MaxEvents 20

Specific event ID:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName = 'Security'
    Id = 4624
} -MaxEvents 20

Security log access may require elevated privileges depending on the environment.

Event logs can be useful for validating detection coverage during authorised purple team or security-control assessments.

docs.title: 63. System Event Log
docs.text:
Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 50

Filter:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName = 'System'
    Id = 7045
} -MaxEvents 20 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Event interpretation should consider Windows version, provider, and environment.

docs.title: 64. Exporting Structured Results
docs.text:
PowerShell objects can be exported to CSV:

Get-Process |
    Select-Object Id, ProcessName |
    Export-Csv "processes.csv" -NoTypeInformation

JSON:

Get-Process |
    Select-Object Id, ProcessName |
    ConvertTo-Json

Save JSON:

Get-Process |
    Select-Object Id, ProcessName |
    ConvertTo-Json |
    Set-Content "processes.json"

Structured output is useful for evidence collection and later analysis.

Do not export sensitive data to insecure locations.

docs.title: 65. Formatting Output
docs.text:
Table:

Get-Service | Format-Table

List:

Get-Service | Format-List

Select fields:

Get-Service |
    Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

Sort:

Get-Process |
    Sort-Object CPU -Descending

Filter:

Get-Service |
    Where-Object Status -eq "Running"

Good filtering makes assessment output easier to interpret and report.

docs.title: 66. Searching Objects
docs.text:
Use Where-Object:

Get-Service |
    Where-Object Name -Like "*Defender*"

Processes:

Get-Process |
    Where-Object ProcessName -Like "*sql*"

Services using a particular path:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object PathName -Like "*ProgramData*"

docs.title: 67. Select-String
docs.text:
Search a file:

Select-String -Path "C:\Path\file.txt" -Pattern "example"

Multiple patterns:

Select-String -Path "C:\Path\file.txt" -Pattern "user","server","database"

Recursive targeted search:

Get-ChildItem "C:\Application" -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-String -Pattern "password|secret|token" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Use sensitive searches only where authorised and necessary.

docs.title: 68. CIM
docs.text:
CIM provides structured access to Windows management information.

Operating system:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem

Computer:

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem

Processes:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process

Services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service

Logical disks:

Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk

Network adapters:

Get-CimInstance Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration |
    Where-Object IPEnabled

CIM is generally preferable to older WMI cmdlets for modern PowerShell administration.

docs.title: 69. SMB
docs.text:
Server configuration:

Get-SmbServerConfiguration

Client configuration:

Get-SmbClientConfiguration

Shares:

Get-SmbShare

Share permissions:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name "ShareName"

SMB configuration can be relevant to both local Windows security and Active Directory assessments.

See SMB.

docs.title: 70. WinRM
docs.text:
Service:

Get-Service WinRM

WSMan configuration:

Get-ChildItem WSMan:\localhost

Listeners:

Get-ChildItem WSMan:\localhost\Listener -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

WinRM is a legitimate administrative interface.

The security assessment should consider:

Network exposure
Authentication
Authorised users
Firewall configuration
Transport configuration
Endpoint configuration

See WinRM.

docs.title: 71. Remote Desktop
docs.text:
RDP service:

Get-Service TermService

Check for a listener:

Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 3389 -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Remote Desktop users:

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Remote Desktop Users" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

RDP exposure should be evaluated together with authentication, firewall, network reachability, and access controls.

docs.title: 72. PowerShell Remoting
docs.text:
PowerShell remoting commonly uses WinRM.

Inspect WSMan:

Get-ChildItem WSMan:\localhost

Session configurations:

Get-PSSessionConfiguration -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Remote management capabilities should be evaluated as administrative functionality rather than automatically classified as weaknesses.

docs.title: 73. Constrained Endpoints
docs.text:
PowerShell can expose restricted remoting endpoints.

List session configurations:

Get-PSSessionConfiguration

Restricted endpoints can be used to limit available commands and capabilities.

During assessment, review:

Who can connect?
What commands are available?
What security context is used?
What language capabilities are available?
What resources can be accessed?

docs.title: 74. Active Directory PowerShell Module
docs.text:
Where the Active Directory module is installed:

Get-Module -ListAvailable ActiveDirectory

Import:

Import-Module ActiveDirectory

The module provides commands such as:

Get-ADUser
Get-ADGroup
Get-ADComputer
Get-ADDomain
Get-ADForest

Detailed Active Directory enumeration belongs in the Active Directory section.

docs.title: 75. PowerShell and Credential Exposure
docs.text:
PowerShell itself does not automatically expose credentials, but administrative usage can leave sensitive information in:

History
Scripts
Configuration
Environment variables
Transcripts
Command lines
Logs

Review only locations permitted by the assessment.

See Windows Credentials.

docs.title: 76. Script Inspection
docs.text:
Display a script:

Get-Content "C:\Path\script.ps1"

Search for potentially sensitive configuration:

Select-String -Path "C:\Path\script.ps1" -Pattern "password|secret|token|credential"

Inspect metadata:

Get-Item "C:\Path\script.ps1"

Permissions:

Get-Acl "C:\Path\script.ps1" |
    Format-List Owner, AccessToString

A script used by a privileged process becomes particularly important when lower-privileged users can modify it.

docs.title: 77. Script Signatures
docs.text:
Check Authenticode signature:

Get-AuthenticodeSignature "C:\Path\script.ps1"

Possible status values can include:

Valid
NotSigned
HashMismatch
NotTrusted
UnknownError

Signature status should be interpreted together with the actual execution and application-control policy.

docs.title: 78. Execution Controls
docs.text:
PowerShell execution can be influenced by several independent controls.

PowerShell
    |
    +---- User permissions
    |
    +---- Execution Policy
    |
    +---- Language Mode
    |
    +---- AppLocker
    |
    +---- WDAC
    |
    +---- Defender / EDR
    |
    +---- ASR
    |
    +---- AMSI
    |
    +---- Logging / monitoring

No single setting should automatically be treated as representing the complete PowerShell security posture.

docs.title: 79. What Not to Report Automatically
docs.text:
Avoid automatically reporting:

PowerShell is installed
PowerShell can execute commands
LanguageMode is FullLanguage
ExecutionPolicy is RemoteSigned
rundll32.exe is allowed
wscript.exe exists
PowerShell history exists
AppLocker contains a broad rule
Defender has an exclusion

These may warrant investigation, but the security impact depends on context.

For example:

FullLanguage
      |
      v
Expected on workstation?
      |
      +--> Yes --> likely normal
      |
      +--> No
            |
            v
      Hardened endpoint design?
            |
            v
      Application control expected?
            |
            v
      Demonstrated security impact?

docs.title: 80. Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For PowerShell-related observations, record:

Host
Current user
PowerShell version
PowerShell edition
Language Mode
Execution Policy
AppLocker state
WDAC evidence
Defender state
ASR state
Relevant logging
Command
Output
Practical impact

Example:

Host:
WS01

User:
CORP\standarduser

PowerShell:
Windows PowerShell 5.1

Language Mode:
FullLanguage

AppLocker:
Enabled for executable and script collections

Observation:
PowerShell operates in FullLanguage mode for the assessed standard user.

Assessment:
The result should be evaluated against the organisation's intended
application-control architecture. FullLanguage mode alone does not
demonstrate a security vulnerability.

docs.title: 81. Application-Control Validation Model
docs.text:
Use:

Policy Exists
     |
     v
Effective Policy
     |
     v
Relevant Rule Collection
     |
     v
Current User
     |
     v
Exact File / Path
     |
     v
Policy Decision
     |
     v
Observed Execution
     |
     v
Security Impact

This is preferable to:

Tool exists
     |
     v
Tool allowed
     |
     v
Vulnerability

docs.title: 83. Quick PowerShell Enumeration
docs.text:
A compact first pass:

$PSVersionTable
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode
Get-ExecutionPolicy -List
whoami /all
Get-ComputerInfo
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem
Get-LocalUser
Get-LocalGroup
Get-NetIPConfiguration
Get-NetRoute
Get-NetTCPConnection
Get-Process

Get-ScheduledTask
Get-SmbShare
Get-NetFirewallProfile

Application-control checks:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

PowerShell logging:

Get-ChildItem "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Relevant event logs:

Get-WinEvent -ListLog *PowerShell* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-WinEvent -ListLog *AppLocker* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-WinEvent -ListLog *CodeIntegrity* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

docs.text:
Start PowerShell
      |
      v
Version / Edition
      |
      v
Current User
      |
      +---- Groups
      +---- Privileges
      +---- Integrity
      |
      v
Language Mode

Execution Policy

Application Control

Logging

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
PowerShell is available to the assessed standard user and operates in
FullLanguage mode.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
FullLanguage mode is the normal PowerShell language mode in many Windows
environments and should not be treated as a vulnerability by itself.

If the endpoint is intended to enforce a restrictive application-control
model, the effective PowerShell language mode should be evaluated together
with AppLocker or WDAC policy, script restrictions, endpoint protection,
and logging controls.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Where a restrictive endpoint-hardening model is required:

Consider enforcing appropriate application-control policies using WDAC or
AppLocker and validate whether PowerShell Constrained Language Mode forms
part of the intended design.

PowerShell logging, endpoint monitoring, least privilege, and Attack Surface
Reduction controls should be considered as complementary protections.

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
PowerShell Script Block Logging was not observed in the assessed policy
configuration.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Before reporting, determine whether equivalent visibility is provided by:

Endpoint Detection and Response
PowerShell Operational logging
Module Logging
Transcription
Centralised event collection
Other endpoint telemetry

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Where PowerShell activity represents a meaningful threat scenario, enable
appropriate PowerShell logging and forward relevant telemetry to a
centralised monitoring platform.

Ensure logs are protected from unauthorised modification and that monitoring
rules are capable of identifying suspicious PowerShell activity.

docs.title: 87. Defensive Monitoring
docs.text:
PowerShell monitoring can combine:

PowerShell Operational Events
        |
        +
Script Block Logging
        |
        +
Module Logging
        |
        +
Transcription
        |
        +
Process Creation
        |
        +
AMSI / Endpoint Telemetry
        |
        +
AppLocker / Code Integrity
        |
        v
Central Detection

No single telemetry source provides complete visibility.

Defenders should correlate PowerShell activity with:

  • Parent processes
  • User context
  • Network activity
  • File creation
  • Registry changes
  • Authentication activity
  • Application-control events
  • Endpoint detections

docs.title: 88. PowerShell in Purple Team Exercises
docs.text:
PowerShell is particularly useful during authorised purple team exercises because both execution and detection can be evaluated.

A simple validation model is:

Authorised Test Action
        |
        v
PowerShell Execution
        |
        v
Host Telemetry
        |
        +---- Process events
        +---- PowerShell events
        +---- AMSI / EDR
        +---- Network events
        |
        v
SIEM / EDR
        |
        v
Detection
        |
        v
Analyst Investigation
        |
        v
Feedback

Record:

Technique tested
Command or behaviour
Expected telemetry
Observed telemetry
Detection generated
Analyst response
Visibility gaps
Recommended improvement

docs.title: 89. Hardening Principles
docs.text:
PowerShell hardening should be layered.

Common principles include:

  • Apply least privilege.
  • Restrict unnecessary administrative access.
  • Use application control where appropriate.
  • Consider Constrained Language Mode as part of a managed application-control design.
  • Configure PowerShell logging appropriate to the threat model.
  • Centralise important telemetry.
  • Protect PowerShell transcripts and logs.
  • Monitor suspicious parent-child process relationships.
  • Use endpoint protection.
  • Configure ASR rules where appropriate.
  • Protect privileged scripts.
  • Protect module directories.
  • Avoid hard-coded credentials.
  • Protect administrative profiles.
  • Keep PowerShell and Windows supported and maintained.

PowerShell itself should not automatically be disabled simply because it can be used by attackers. It is an important Windows administrative and defensive platform.

docs.title: 90. Final Testing Model
docs.text:
Use the following model when evaluating PowerShell security:

PowerShell Available
        |
        v
Who Can Use It?
        |
        v
Which Security Context?
        |
        v
Which Language Mode?
        |
        v
Which Application-Control Policy?
        |
        v
Which Endpoint Controls?
        |
        v
Which Logging Exists?
        |
        v
What Behaviour Is Actually Allowed?
        |
        v
Can a Security Boundary Be Crossed?
        |
        v
Can Defenders Observe It?
        |
        v
Validated Finding

This avoids treating PowerShell capabilities as vulnerabilities without understanding the surrounding Windows security architecture.

docs.title: Windows Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Windows privilege escalation is the process of identifying security weaknesses that allow a lower-privileged user or process to gain additional permissions on a Windows system.

During an authorised assessment, the objective is not simply to obtain administrative privileges. The objective is to identify the underlying trust or permission relationship that makes the escalation possible, validate the security impact safely, and provide evidence that allows the weakness to be remediated.

Typical escalation paths involve:

  • Windows services
  • Weak filesystem permissions
  • Weak registry permissions
  • Scheduled tasks
  • Service configuration permissions
  • Unquoted service paths
  • DLL search behaviour
  • Stored credentials
  • User privileges
  • Application configuration
  • Installer policies
  • AutoRun locations
  • Vulnerable software
  • Credential reuse
  • Security-control misconfiguration

The central question is:

Can the current user influence something
that executes or operates with greater privileges?

docs.title: 1. Privilege Escalation Model
docs.text:
A useful model is:

Low-Privileged User
        |
        v
Enumeration
        |
        v
Identify Privileged Resource
        |
        v
Identify Controllable Component
        |
        v
Validate Permissions
        |
        v
Determine Execution Context
        |
        v
Confirm Security Boundary
        |
        v
Controlled Validation
        |
        v
Evidence
        |
        v
Remediation

Most meaningful privilege escalation findings contain three components:

Privileged Context
        +
Attacker-Controlled Resource
        +
Execution / Consumption Relationship
        =
Potential Privilege Escalation

For example:

SYSTEM Service
      +
User-Writable Executable
      =
Potential SYSTEM Execution

docs.title: 2. Initial Enumeration
docs.text:
Start by understanding the current security context.

whoami
whoami /user
whoami /groups
whoami /priv

Complete information:

whoami /all

PowerShell:

$env:USERNAME
$env:USERDOMAIN
$env:COMPUTERNAME

Check integrity level:

whoami /groups

Look for:

Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level
Mandatory Label\High Mandatory Level
Mandatory Label\System Mandatory Level

For broader host enumeration, see Windows Enumeration.

docs.title: 3. Determine Administrative Context
docs.text:
PowerShell:

$identity = [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
$principal = New-Object Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal($identity)
$principal.IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)

Possible output:

True

or:

False

Remember that local Administrators group membership does not necessarily mean the current process is elevated because User Account Control can provide a filtered token.

docs.title: 4. User Privileges
docs.text:
Enumerate privileges:

whoami /priv

Privileges worth investigating include:

Privilege Security Relevance SeBackupPrivilege Can permit reading protected files through backup semantics SeRestorePrivilege Can permit restoring or replacing protected resources SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege Can permit taking ownership of securable objects SeDebugPrivilege Provides powerful access to processes SeImpersonatePrivilege Allows impersonation in appropriate authentication contexts SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege Allows assignment of primary tokens in specific circumstances SeLoadDriverPrivilege Allows loading kernel drivers under applicable conditions SeManageVolumePrivilege Provides powerful volume-management capabilities SeTcbPrivilege Highly privileged operating-system capability

A listed privilege is not automatically exploitable.

Determine:

Privilege Present?
      |
      v
Enabled?
      |
      v
Relevant Resource Available?
      |
      v
Current Integrity Context?
      |
      v
Security Boundary Crossed?

docs.title: 5. Local Groups
docs.text:
Enumerate groups:

net localgroup

Administrators:

net localgroup Administrators

PowerShell:

Get-LocalGroup

Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators"

Other potentially important groups include:

Backup Operators
Remote Desktop Users
Remote Management Users
Hyper-V Administrators
Event Log Readers
Performance Log Users

Membership should be interpreted according to the capabilities granted on the particular host.

docs.title: 6. Operating System Information
docs.text:
systeminfo

PowerShell:

Get-ComputerInfo

Focused:

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, WindowsVersion, OsBuildNumber, OsArchitecture

CIM:

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

Version information helps determine whether known vulnerabilities or configuration behaviours may be relevant.

Do not infer vulnerability solely from an operating-system build number.

docs.title: 7. Services
docs.text:
Windows services are one of the most important privilege escalation areas.

Enumerate services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service

Useful fields:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName

Running services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object State -eq "Running" |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

Services running as LocalSystem:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object StartName -eq "LocalSystem" |
    Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, PathName

Other privileged identities may include:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
LocalSystem
NetworkService
LocalService
Privileged domain service accounts

A service running as SYSTEM is normal.

The important question is whether a lower-privileged user can influence something used by that service.

See Windows Services.

docs.title: 8. Service Executable Permissions
docs.text:
Suppose a service uses:

C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service\service.exe

Inspect the executable:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service\service.exe"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service\service.exe" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Inspect the parent directory:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Potentially dangerous permissions for broad principals include:

Write
Modify
FullControl

Potentially broad principals include:

Everyone
BUILTIN\Users
Authenticated Users
Domain Users

The combination matters:

Service runs as SYSTEM
        +
Standard user can modify service executable
        =
Potential privilege escalation

docs.title: 9. Writable Service Directories
docs.text:
Sometimes the executable itself is protected while its parent directory is writable.

Check:

icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service"

or:

(Get-Acl "C:\Program Files\Vendor\Service").Access

A controlled write test can validate permissions:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID.tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Host "[+] Write succeeded: $file"
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}
catch {
    Write-Host "[-] Write failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}

This proves only that the user can write to the directory.

It does not prove privilege escalation.

docs.title: 10. Correlating Writable Directories with Services
docs.text:
If a writable directory is identified, determine whether a service references it.

Example:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object PathName -Match ([regex]::Escape($folder)) |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, State, PathName

This is significantly stronger than simply reporting a writable folder.

Assessment logic:

Writable Folder
      |
      v
Used by Service?
      |
      +--> No --> Record only if otherwise relevant
      |
      +--> Yes
             |
             v
       Service Privileged?
             |
             +--> No --> Lower priority
             |
             +--> Yes
                    |
                    v
             Controllable Resource?
                    |
                    v
               Validate Impact

docs.title: 11. Service Configuration
docs.text:
Inspect a service:

sc qc ServiceName

Example:

sc qc Spooler

PowerShell:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='Spooler'"

Important properties include:

BINARY_PATH_NAME
SERVICE_START_NAME
START_TYPE
DEPENDENCIES

CIM equivalents:

PathName
StartName
StartMode

docs.title: 12. Service Security Descriptors
docs.text:
Query the service security descriptor:

sc sdshow ServiceName

Example:

sc sdshow Spooler

The output uses Security Descriptor Definition Language.

Security-sensitive service rights can include the ability to:

Change service configuration
Start service
Stop service
Delete service
Modify service permissions

A lower-privileged user with service configuration rights may be able to alter how a privileged service operates.

Validate the exact access granted before reporting.

docs.title: 13. AccessChk for Services
docs.text:
Microsoft Sysinternals AccessChk can simplify permission analysis.

AccessChk

AccessChk can inspect:

Services
Files
Directories
Registry keys
Processes
Named pipes

Always interpret AccessChk output in the context of the current user and the actual resource.

docs.title: 14. Unquoted Service Paths
docs.text:
A service path containing spaces may require further review if the executable path is not quoted.

Example:

C:\Program Files\Vendor Application\Service.exe

The important conditions are not simply:

Path contains spaces

A meaningful issue generally requires:

Unquoted service path
        +
Path parsing ambiguity
        +
Attacker-writable candidate location
        +
Privileged service
        =
Potential privilege escalation

Enumerate service paths:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object {
        $_.PathName -and
        $_.PathName -notmatch '^"' -and
        $_.PathName -match '\s'
    } |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

This is a candidate-generation technique only.

Each result requires manual validation.

docs.title: 15. Scheduled Tasks
docs.text:
Enumerate scheduled tasks:

schtasks /query /fo LIST /v

PowerShell:

Get-ScheduledTask

Useful summary:

Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        TaskName = $_.TaskName
        TaskPath = $_.TaskPath
        User = $_.Principal.UserId
        RunLevel = $_.Principal.RunLevel
        Actions = ($_.Actions | ForEach-Object {
            "$($_.Execute) $($_.Arguments)"
        }) -join "; "
    }
}

Look for tasks that:

Run as SYSTEM / Administrator
        +
Execute modifiable file
        =
Potential privilege escalation

docs.title: 16. Scheduled Task File Permissions
docs.text:
Suppose a task executes:

C:\ProgramData\Vendor\maintenance.ps1

Inspect:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\maintenance.ps1"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\ProgramData\Vendor\maintenance.ps1" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Also inspect the directory:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

Do not modify production scripts simply to demonstrate the issue.

Permission evidence combined with task configuration may already provide sufficient proof.

docs.title: 17. Startup Applications
docs.text:
Enumerate startup commands:

Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand |
    Select-Object Name, Command, Location, User

Registry locations include:

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce

PowerShell:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

A startup entry becomes security-relevant when a lower-privileged user can influence content that executes in a higher-privileged context.

docs.title: 18. Registry Permissions
docs.text:
Inspect a registry key:

Get-Acl "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Vendor"

Access entries:

(Get-Acl "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Vendor").Access

Look for broad write access such as:

SetValue
CreateSubKey
WriteKey
FullControl

Again, the permission alone is not enough.

Determine whether the registry value influences:

Privileged service
Privileged application
Startup mechanism
Security configuration
Executable path
DLL path

docs.title: 19. Autoruns
docs.text:
Microsoft Sysinternals Autoruns provides broad visibility into automatic execution locations.

Autoruns

It can enumerate areas such as:

Logon entries
Services
Drivers
Scheduled tasks
Explorer extensions
AppInit entries
Winlogon entries
Known DLLs
Boot execution

During privilege escalation analysis, investigate whether privileged automatic execution references lower-privileged writable resources.

docs.title: 20. Installed Applications
docs.text:
Enumerate installed applications through the registry.

64-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

32-bit applications:

Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallLocation

Investigate:

Unsupported applications
Old management software
Backup agents
Deployment clients
Custom enterprise applications
Privileged helper services

Do not associate a version with a CVE without verifying the affected version range and applicable configuration.

docs.title: 21. Application Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Custom software is often installed outside the standard protected directories.

Common locations include:

C:\ProgramData
C:\Vendor
C:\Apps
C:\Tools
C:\Company

Inspect:

icacls "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\ProgramData\Vendor" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

If writable, determine what uses the directory.

Search services:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\Vendor"

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object PathName -Match ([regex]::Escape($folder)) |
    Select-Object Name, StartName, PathName

Search scheduled tasks manually or through their actions.

The directory's consumers determine the actual impact.

docs.title: 22. DLL Search Behaviour
docs.text:
Applications may load DLLs from multiple locations.

Privilege escalation risk can arise when:

Privileged Process
       |
       v
Attempts DLL Load
       |
       v
Searches Attacker-Writable Location
       |
       v
Attacker Controls DLL Resolution

Do not assume that the absence of a DLL automatically means a hijack is possible.

Validate:

  • Actual DLL load attempt
  • Search order
  • Writable location
  • Process privilege
  • Architecture
  • Application behaviour
  • Existing mitigations

Process Monitor is useful for analysing runtime file and DLL activity.

Process Monitor

docs.title: 23. PATH Environment Variable
docs.text:
Inspect PATH:

echo %PATH%

PowerShell:

$env:PATH

Split entries:

$env:PATH -split ';'

Potential security concerns arise when:

Privileged application
        +
Searches PATH for executable or library
        +
PATH contains user-writable directory
        =
Potential execution-control issue

A writable PATH entry alone does not prove privilege escalation.

docs.title: 24. Environment Variables
docs.text:
Enumerate:

set

PowerShell:

Get-ChildItem Env:

Environment variables may reveal:

Custom application paths
Temporary directories
Development tools
Deployment configuration
Proxy configuration
Runtime paths

These can provide clues to applications and resources worth investigating.

docs.title: 25. Stored Credentials
docs.text:
List Windows Credential Manager entries:

cmdkey /list

This can reveal credential targets.

The presence of a credential entry does not necessarily mean the underlying credential can be extracted or reused.

Assess:

Target
Type
Current user
Associated service/application
Potential reuse context

See Windows Credentials.

docs.title: 26. PowerShell History
docs.text:
History location:

(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Read:

Get-Content (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

History may reveal:

Administrative commands
Network shares
Deployment commands
Application configuration
Operational paths
Authentication-related commands

Handle any discovered secrets as sensitive assessment evidence.

docs.title: 27. Configuration Files
docs.text:
Applications may store sensitive configuration in:

*.config
*.ini
*.xml
*.json
*.yml
*.yaml
*.conf

Search should be scoped to relevant application directories.

Example:

Get-ChildItem "C:\ProgramData\Vendor" -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object Extension -Match '\.(config|ini|xml|json|yml|yaml|conf)$'

Inspect configuration for:

Service accounts
Connection strings
API endpoints
Database configuration
Network shares
Credential references
Certificate locations

Avoid unnecessarily collecting sensitive content.

docs.title: 28. User Profiles
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-ChildItem C:\Users

Profiles:

Get-CimInstance Win32_UserProfile |
    Select-Object LocalPath, Loaded, Special

Interesting areas may include:

Documents
Desktop
Downloads
AppData
PowerShell history
SSH configuration
Cloud CLI configuration
Development configuration
Application configuration

Only access data permitted by the assessment scope and current account permissions.

docs.title: 29. AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
Windows Installer policies should be reviewed carefully.

Relevant registry values are traditionally associated with:

HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer
HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer

Inspect:

Get-ItemProperty "HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Focused query:

Get-ItemPropertyValue "HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Get-ItemPropertyValue "HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer" -Name AlwaysInstallElevated -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

A meaningful AlwaysInstallElevated condition historically requires the relevant policy to be enabled in both user and machine context.

Do not change the policy during routine testing.

docs.title: 30. UAC
docs.text:
User Account Control influences administrative token behaviour.

Basic information about the current token can be gathered through:

whoami /groups

and:

whoami /priv

Relevant registry configuration exists under:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System

Inspect:

Get-ItemProperty "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Important values can include:

EnableLUA
ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin
ConsentPromptBehaviorUser
PromptOnSecureDesktop
FilterAdministratorToken

UAC configuration should be interpreted in the context of administrative membership and endpoint security requirements.

docs.title: 31. Application Control
docs.text:
Application control can significantly affect privilege escalation opportunities.

Relevant technologies include:

AppLocker
Windows Defender Application Control
Microsoft Defender
Attack Surface Reduction
PowerShell Constrained Language Mode

AppLocker effective policy:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective

Collections:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections |
    Select-Object CollectionType, EnforcementMode

PowerShell Language Mode:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Defender:

Get-MpComputerStatus -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Application-control testing should focus on effective policy rather than the mere existence of individual Windows utilities.

docs.title: 32. AppLocker Allowed Paths
docs.text:
Path-based rules require particular attention.

Retrieve effective rules:

(Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective).RuleCollections | ForEach-Object {
    $_.Rules
}

The important relationship is:

AppLocker Allows Directory
          +
Standard User Can Write There
          =
Potential Application-Control Weakness

For example, an allowed %WINDIR%\* path does not automatically create a weakness because standard users normally cannot modify most protected Windows directories.

The correct next question is:

Can the assessed user write to any location covered by the allow rule?

docs.title: 33. Test Effective AppLocker Decisions
docs.text:
Test a file:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\file.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME"

Detailed output:

Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective |
    Test-AppLockerPolicy -Path "C:\Path\file.exe" -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME" |
    Format-List FilePath, PolicyDecision, MatchingRule

This is preferable to assuming that a file is allowed because its parent directory appears in a rule.

docs.title: 34. PowerShell Language Mode
docs.text:
Check:

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Possible modes:

FullLanguage
ConstrainedLanguage
RestrictedLanguage
NoLanguage

FullLanguage is normal on many Windows systems.

It should not be reported as a vulnerability by itself.

In hardened environments, determine whether the expected design requires Constrained Language Mode through application control.

docs.title: 35. Security Products
docs.text:
Microsoft Defender:

Get-MpComputerStatus -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Preferences:

Get-MpPreference -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Running services:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object State -eq "Running" |
    Select-Object Name, DisplayName, StartName

Do not disable or tamper with endpoint security during ordinary privilege escalation enumeration.

The goal is to understand the defensive environment.

docs.title: 36. Network Services
docs.text:
Listening ports:

netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING

PowerShell:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen

Map to processes:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | ForEach-Object {
    [PSCustomObject]@{
        Address = $_.LocalAddress
        Port = $_.LocalPort
        PID = $_.OwningProcess
        Process = (Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).ProcessName
    }
}

Local-only administrative applications may expose functionality that becomes security-relevant when accessible from a lower-privileged context.

docs.title: 37. Named Pipes
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-ChildItem \\.\pipe\

Named pipes can expose inter-process communication used by:

Services
Databases
Browsers
Management software
Security software
Custom applications

A named pipe is not inherently vulnerable.

Further analysis requires understanding its permissions and protocol behaviour.

docs.title: 38. Network Shares
docs.text:
net share

PowerShell:

Get-SmbShare

Permissions:

Get-SmbShareAccess -Name "ShareName"

Local shares may expose:

Scripts
Backups
Deployment packages
Configuration files
Application data

Evaluate both share permissions and NTFS permissions.

docs.title: 39. Process Enumeration
docs.text:
tasklist /v

PowerShell:

Get-Process

Command lines:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Process |
    Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CommandLine

Processes may reveal:

Privileged applications
Management agents
Backup software
Database services
Deployment agents
Custom applications

Correlate interesting processes with:

Executable path
Service
User context
Filesystem permissions
Network listeners
Configuration

docs.title: 40. Process Ownership
docs.text:
CIM can help correlate processes and services, but access to owner information may depend on permissions.

For service-backed processes, start with:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service |
    Where-Object State -eq "Running" |
    Select-Object Name, ProcessId, StartName, PathName

This provides:

Service
PID
Service account
Executable path

which can then be correlated with filesystem permissions.

docs.title: 41. Hotfix and Patch Analysis
docs.text:
Enumerate:

Get-HotFix

or:

Get-CimInstance Win32_QuickFixEngineering

Patch analysis should not rely solely on the absence of a particular KB.

Modern Windows servicing uses cumulative updates, supersedence, and servicing-stack behaviour that can make simple KB checks misleading.

Validate:

Windows version
Build
Revision
Installed updates
Affected product
Vulnerability prerequisites

before reporting a missing patch.

docs.title: 42. Automated Privilege Escalation Enumeration
docs.text:
Automated enumeration can improve coverage.

Useful tools include:

WinPEAS
PrivescCheck
SharpUp
Seatbelt
AccessChk
Autoruns
Process Monitor

Automated results are candidate findings, not final findings.

Every meaningful result should be manually validated.

docs.title: 43. WinPEAS
docs.text:
PEASS-ng

WinPEAS can identify:

System information
Users
Privileges
Services
Scheduled tasks
Applications
Credentials
Interesting files
Registry settings
Permissions
Security controls

Its output can be extensive.

Use it to identify areas for manual validation rather than treating every highlighted result as a vulnerability.

docs.title: 44. PrivescCheck
docs.text:
PrivescCheck

PrivescCheck provides PowerShell-based checks for common Windows privilege escalation conditions.

Potential areas include:

Services
Scheduled tasks
Registry
Credentials
Applications
Permissions
Security configuration

Manual verification remains necessary.

docs.title: 45. SharpUp
docs.text:
SharpUp

SharpUp focuses on identifying Windows privilege escalation opportunities.

Use tool findings as leads for deeper inspection.

docs.title: 46. Seatbelt
docs.text:
Seatbelt

Seatbelt performs broad Windows host reconnaissance and can help identify:

Security controls
Users
Processes
Services
Interesting configuration
Credentials
System information

It is particularly useful when privilege escalation analysis requires broader environmental context.

docs.title: 47. AccessChk
docs.text:
AccessChk

AccessChk is useful for identifying permissions on:

Files
Directories
Services
Registry keys
Processes
Named pipes

Permission output should always be correlated with resource usage.

docs.title: 48. Process Monitor
docs.text:
Process Monitor

Process Monitor can help investigate:

Filesystem access
Registry access
Process activity
DLL loading
Configuration access
Missing files

It is particularly useful when determining what resources a privileged application actually consumes.

docs.title: 49. Autoruns
docs.text:
Autoruns

Autoruns can help identify privileged automatic execution paths that reference modifiable resources.

This is often more useful than manually checking a small number of startup registry keys.

docs.title: 50. Manual Validation
docs.text:
Automated tools may report:

Writable directory
Unquoted service path
Interesting privilege
Weak registry ACL
Scheduled task
Stored credential

The next step should always be manual validation.

Example:

Tool reports writable service directory
             |
             v
Identify service
             |
             v
Determine service account
             |
             v
Inspect exact ACL
             |
             v
Confirm current user has write access
             |
             v
Determine what service consumes
             |
             v
Establish practical impact

docs.title: 51. Safe Validation
docs.text:
Privilege escalation testing can alter privileged resources.

Where possible, demonstrate the condition without modifying production executables or configurations.

Preferred evidence can include:

ACL showing write permission
        +
Service configuration showing privileged execution
        +
Current user identity
        +
Controlled write test using temporary file
        =
Strong evidence

A destructive or persistent payload is usually unnecessary.

docs.title: 52. Controlled Write Test
docs.text:
For a candidate directory:

$folder = "C:\ProgramData\CandidateFolder"
$file = Join-Path $folder "write-test-$PID-$(Get-Random).tmp"

try {
    New-Item -ItemType File -Path $file -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null
    Write-Host "[+] Write access confirmed: $file"
}
catch {
    Write-Host "[-] Write access denied: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}
finally {
    Remove-Item $file -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}

This demonstrates write capability without replacing an application file.

docs.title: 53. Permission Analysis
docs.text:
When a candidate resource is discovered, document:

Owner
ACL
Inherited permissions
Current user's effective group membership
Resource type
Privileged consumer

PowerShell:

Get-Acl "C:\Path" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Detailed:

(Get-Acl "C:\Path").Access |
    Format-Table IdentityReference, FileSystemRights, AccessControlType, IsInherited

Command Prompt:

icacls "C:\Path"

docs.title: 54. Important Permission Relationships
docs.text:
Common relationships worth investigating include:

Privileged Resource Controllable Component SYSTEM service Executable SYSTEM service Executable directory SYSTEM service Configuration file SYSTEM service Registry key Elevated scheduled task Script Elevated scheduled task Executable Privileged application DLL search directory Startup mechanism Referenced executable Deployment agent Package or script directory

The presence of the relationship is more important than either component individually.

docs.title: Writable directory without privileged consumer
docs.text:
User can write to:
C:\ProgramData\Example

but nothing privileged uses the directory.

Result:

Not sufficient for privilege escalation.

docs.title: SYSTEM service with protected executable
docs.text:
Service runs as SYSTEM.

but:

Executable protected
Directory protected
Configuration protected
Service configuration protected

Result:

Normal privileged service configuration.

docs.title: Unquoted service path without writable location
docs.text:
C:\Program Files\Vendor App\Service.exe

but the current user cannot write to any relevant candidate location.

Result:

No demonstrated privilege escalation path.

docs.title: FullLanguage PowerShell
docs.text:
LanguageMode = FullLanguage

Result:

Not inherently a vulnerability.

Evaluate against the intended hardening model.

docs.title: Allowed Windows utility
docs.text:
rundll32.exe = Allowed

Result:

Not inherently a vulnerability.

The practical security impact depends on what content can be executed, application-control objectives, writable paths, and other controls.

docs.title: 56. Evidence Collection
docs.text:
For a privilege escalation finding, capture:

Host
Current user
SID
Groups
Privileges
Integrity level
Affected resource
Resource owner
Resource permissions
Privileged consumer
Consumer identity
Configuration
Controlled validation
Security impact

Example:

Host:
WS01

Current user:
CORP\standarduser

Integrity:
Medium

Affected directory:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Service

Permission:
BUILTIN\Users - Modify

Service:
VendorService

Service account:
LocalSystem

Service executable:
C:\ProgramData\Vendor\Service\service.exe

Validation:
The current standard user successfully created and removed a temporary
file in the service directory.

Impact:
A lower-privileged user can modify resources within the directory used by
a LocalSystem service. The exact executable and service behaviour should
be validated to determine whether privileged code execution is possible.

docs.title: 57. Severity Assessment
docs.text:
Severity depends on practical impact.

A useful model:

Exploitability
     +
Privileges Gained
     +
User Interaction
     +
Reliability
     +
Scope
     =
Severity

Examples:

Condition Typical Importance Writable unused directory Informational / no finding Writable privileged application config Potentially significant Writable SYSTEM service executable High impact Weak task file permissions with SYSTEM execution High impact Stored privileged credential Potentially critical depending on reuse Broad AppLocker rule without writable allowed location Usually not sufficient alone

Use the organisation's agreed severity methodology for final ratings.

docs.title: 58. Remediation Principles
docs.text:
Privilege escalation remediation usually focuses on removing the trust relationship.

Common approaches include:

Restrict filesystem permissions
Restrict registry permissions
Protect service configuration
Protect scheduled task resources
Remove unnecessary local privileges
Remove unnecessary local administrators
Secure application directories
Quote service paths
Protect secrets
Patch vulnerable software
Harden application control
Monitor privileged execution

Remediation should target the root cause rather than only the demonstrated technique.

docs.title: 59. Service Remediation
docs.text:
For vulnerable services:

Protect executable
Protect executable directory
Protect configuration
Restrict service permissions
Use least-privileged service account where practical
Quote executable paths
Remove unnecessary user write access

A typical secure relationship is:

SYSTEM Service
      |
      v
Executable
      |
      v
Administrators / SYSTEM Modify
      |
      v
Standard Users Read and Execute Only

docs.title: 60. Scheduled Task Remediation
docs.text:
For privileged tasks:

Protect task definition
Protect executable
Protect script
Protect parent directory
Review task principal
Use least privilege
Remove obsolete tasks

Privileged scheduled tasks should not execute content writable by ordinary users.

docs.title: 61. Credential Remediation
docs.text:
If credentials are exposed:

Remove plaintext secrets
Rotate affected credentials
Use managed identities where possible
Use Windows Credential Manager appropriately
Use gMSA for applicable domain services
Restrict configuration-file permissions
Avoid credentials in command lines
Review credential reuse

For Active Directory service accounts, see gMSA.

docs.title: 62. Application Control Remediation
docs.text:
Where application control is part of the security design:

Review AppLocker / WDAC policy
Review broad path rules
Identify user-writable allowed locations
Restrict script execution where appropriate
Apply PowerShell controls
Enable relevant logging
Review ASR configuration

Application control should be designed as a complete policy rather than as isolated executable blocks.

docs.title: 64. Quick Manual Workflow
docs.text:
whoami /all
systeminfo
net localgroup Administrators
tasklist /v
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v
cmdkey /list
netstat -ano
net share

PowerShell:

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName
Get-ScheduledTask
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Select-Object Name, Command, Location, User
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators"

$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode

Then focus on the relationships identified by the initial enumeration.

docs.title: 65. Privilege Escalation Decision Tree
docs.text:
Current User
     |
     v
Privileged Already?
     |
     +--> Yes --> Confirm actual integrity/elevation
     |
     +--> No

           |
